Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.

p.seg: My brother-in-law's grandfather,
named Sòng Tāo,
was a stipendiary scholar in the county.
One day,
while lying ill,
he saw an official holding a summons
and leading a white-faced horse,
saying:
"Please come for the examination."
Mr. Sòng said:
"The examiner has not yet arrived,
how can the examination be held so soon?"
The official did not reply,
but urged him insistently.
Mr. Sòng, despite his illness, mounted the horse and followed him.
The road was very unfamiliar.
They arrived at a city,
like a royal capital.
After a while, they entered a government office,
with magnificent buildings.
More than ten officials were seated above,
none of whom he recognized,
except for Guān Zhuàngmóu.
Under the eaves were set two desks and two stools;
a scholar was already seated at the end,
and Mr. Sòng sat beside him.
On each desk were writing brushes and paper.
Soon, examination papers flew down; looking at them,
the topic consisted of eight characters:
"One person, two persons,
with intent, without intent."
When both men finished their essays,
they presented them in the hall.
In Mr. Sòng's essay, it was written:
"Doing good with intent,
though good, should not be rewarded;
doing evil without intent,
though evil, should not be punished."
The various deities praised it repeatedly.
Summoning Mr. Sòng forward,
they instructed him:
"Hénán lacks a city god,
and you are suited for the position."
Mr. Sòng then realized
and kowtowed, weeping:
"Though honored by this appointment,
how dare I decline?
But my mother is seventy years old,
with no one to care for her.
I beg to be allowed to see out her natural lifespan,
and only then will I accept the appointment."
One of the officials, who had the appearance of an emperor,
immediately ordered an examination of his mother's life register.
A long-bearded official,
holding a ledger, flipped through it once
and reported:
"She has nine years of life remaining."
As they were all pondering,
Guān Dì said:
"It would be fine to let Mr. Zhāng act in the post for nine years,
and then have him replaced."
Then he said to Mr. Sòng:
"You should assume the post immediately;
but in consideration of your filial heart,
you are granted a nine-year leave.
When the time comes, you will be summoned again."
He also encouraged the scholar with a few words.
Both men kowtowed and descended together.
The scholar shook hands with him
and saw him off to the outskirts,
introducing himself as a certain Mr. Zhāng from Chángshān.
He presented a poem as a farewell gift,
but the words are all forgotten,
except for the lines:
"With flowers and wine, spring lasts forever;
without candles or lamps, the night is bright of itself."
Mr. Sòng mounted his horse
and they parted.
When he reached home,
he awoke as if from a dream.
He had already been dead for three days.
His mother heard groaning from the coffin,
helped him out,
and only after half a day could he speak.
Inquiring in Chángshān,
there indeed was a Mr. Zhāng
who had died that very day.
Nine years later,
his mother indeed passed away.
After the funeral arrangements were completed,
he washed up, entered his room, and died.
His father-in-law's home was inside the west gate of the city.
Suddenly, they saw Mr. Sòng with engraved trappings and red tassels,
accompanied by many carriages and horses.
He ascended the hall,
bowed once, and left.
They were all surprised and puzzled,
not knowing he had become a deity.
Rushing to inquire in the village,
they learned he had already passed away.
Mr. Sòng had written a brief autobiography himself,
but unfortunately, it was lost after the chaos,
and this is merely a summary.
According to the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì."
Tán Jìnxuán
was a scholar in the county.
He firmly believed in the techniques of guiding and inducing qi,
practicing without pause through winter and summer.
After several months of practice,
he felt as if he had achieved something.
One day,
while sitting cross-legged,
he heard a faint whisper in his ear like a fly,
saying:
"You can see now."
When he opened his eyes, he no longer heard it;
but when he closed his eyes and calmed his breath,
he heard it again as before.
Thinking his elixir was about to be completed,
he secretly rejoiced.
From then on, he heard it every time he sat.
So he waited for it to speak again,
intending to respond to observe it.
One day,
it spoke again.
He then softly responded:
"You can see now."
Suddenly, he felt a rustling in his ear,
as if something was coming out.
Glancing slightly,
he saw a小人 about three inches tall,
with a fierce and ugly appearance like a yāchā,
spinning on the ground.
He was secretly astonished
and calmly focused to observe its changes.
Suddenly, a neighbor came to borrow something,
knocking on the door and calling out.
The小人 heard it,
seemed flustered,
and ran around the room
like a mouse that has lost its hole.
Tán felt as if his spirit and soul were lost,
and he no longer knew where the小人 had gone.
He then developed a mental disorder,
shouting and screaming incessantly.
After half a year of medical treatment,
he gradually recovered.
According to the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì."
In Yángxìn County, there was an old man
from Càidiàn Village.
The village was five or six li from the town.
The father and son ran a roadside inn
where traveling merchants stayed.
Several cart drivers
who came and went carrying goods
often lodged at their home.
One day at dusk,
four men arrived together,
seeking shelter at the door,
but the old man’s guest rooms were full.
The four men, having no other plan,
insistently begged to be taken in.
The old man pondered and thought of a place,
though he feared it might not suit the guests.
The guests said:
"We only ask for a space under the eaves,
and dare not be choosy."
At that time, the old man’s daughter-in-law had recently died,
and her corpse was laid in a room,
while her husband had gone out to buy coffin wood and had not yet returned.
Thinking the mourning chamber was quiet,
the old man led the guests through an alley to it.
Entering the room,
they saw a dim lamp on the table;
behind the table hung a curtain of mourning clothes,
with a paper shroud covering the deceased.
Looking at the sleeping area,
they saw a connected bed in an inner room.
The four guests, weary from their journey,
had just laid their heads down
when their breathing gradually grew heavy.
Only one guest was still half-awake.
Suddenly, he heard a rustling sound from the funeral bed.
He quickly opened his eyes,
and by the lamplight before the spirit tablet,
he could see quite clearly: the female corpse had thrown off the shroud
and risen;
soon she descended
and gradually entered the bedroom.
Her face was a pale golden color,
with a raw silk band tied around her forehead.
She bent close to the bed
and blew three times on each of the sleeping guests.
The guest was terrified,
fearing she would come to him,
so he stealthily pulled the covers over his head,
holding his breath and swallowing hard as he listened.
Before long,
the woman indeed came to him
and blew on him just as she had on the others.
He felt her leave the room,
and immediately heard the sound of the paper shroud.
Peeking out slightly,
he saw the corpse lying stiffly as before.
The guest was extremely frightened,
not daring to make a sound,
and secretly nudged the other guests with his foot;
but none of them moved at all.
Seeing no other option,
he thought it better to get dressed and flee.
Just as he rose to put on his clothes,
the rustling sound began again.
Terrified,
he lay back down,
pulling his head under the covers.
He felt the woman come again,
blowing on him repeatedly before leaving.
After a short while,
he heard a noise from the funeral bed,
knowing she had lain down again.
He then slowly reached out from under the covers for his trousers,
quickly put them on,
and ran out barefoot.
The corpse also rose,
as if to chase the guest.
By the time she left the curtain,
the guest had already unbolted the door and fled.
The corpse raced after him.
The guest ran and screamed,
but no one in the village was alerted.
He wanted to knock on the host’s door,
but feared he would be caught if he delayed.
So he headed toward the town road,
running with all his might.
Reaching the eastern outskirts,
he glimpsed a temple,
hearing the sound of a wooden fish,
and hurriedly pounded on the monastery gate.
The Daoist priest was surprised by the unusual disturbance
and did not immediately let him in.
In an instant,
the corpse arrived,
only a foot away from him.
The guest was in even greater distress.
Outside the gate stood a white poplar tree,
about four or five spans around,
so he used the tree as a shield;
when she went right, he went left,
when she went left, he went right.
The corpse grew even angrier.
But both were gradually tiring.
The corpse suddenly stood still.
The guest, sweating and panting,
took shelter behind the tree.
The corpse suddenly lunged,
stretching its arms around the tree to grab him.
The guest was so startled he fell.
The corpse, unable to catch him,
embraced the tree and stiffened.
The Daoist priest listened stealthily for a long time,
hearing no sound,
and gradually came out,
finding the guest lying on the ground.
Holding a candle to him, he saw he appeared dead,
but there was still a faint pulse in his chest.
Carrying him inside,
it took all night for him to revive.
After giving him some warm water to drink, the priest asked him what happened,
and the guest recounted everything.
By then, the morning bell had finished tolling,
and the dawn light was hazy.
The priest went to look at the tree
and indeed saw the stiffened woman.
Greatly alarmed,
he reported it to the county magistrate.
The magistrate personally went to investigate.
He ordered people to pull the woman’s hands away,
but they were stuck fast and would not open.
Upon closer inspection,
he saw that the four fingers of each hand
were curled like hooks,
sunk into the wood, with the nails buried deep.
Several men pulled with great effort
before they could free her.
The finger holes in the tree looked as if they had been drilled.
The magistrate sent officers to the old man’s home,
where they found everyone in an uproar over the missing corpse and the dead guest.
Chaos and clamor filled the place.
The officers explained the situation.
The old man then went with them
to carry the corpse back.
The guest tearfully told the magistrate:
"We four came out together,
but now only I return.
How can I make the villagers believe this story?"
The magistrate gave him an official document,
and he was escorted back home.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
When Mr. Sòng Yùshū from Láiyáng served as a ministry official,
the residence he rented
was quite desolate.
One night,
two maids were attending the elderly madam as she slept in the main hall
when they heard a *pupu* sound in the courtyard,
like a tailor spraying water.
The madam urged the maids to get up,
and they peeked through a hole in the window,
seeing an old woman,
short and hunchbacked,
with hair as white as a broom,
wearing a topknot
about two chi long.
She was circling the courtyard,
walking hurriedly with crane-like steps,
and as she walked, she sprayed water endlessly.
The water seemed inexhaustible.
The maids, stunned, went back to report.
The madam also got up in alarm,
and the two maids helped her to the window to watch together.
Suddenly, the old woman rushed to the window
and sprayed directly through the lattice;
the window paper tore,
and all three fell down,
but the other family members knew nothing of it.
When the morning sun rose,
the family gathered,
and knocking on the door brought no response,
they grew alarmed.
Prying the door open,
they found the mistress and two maids
lying dead together in the room.
One maid’s chest was still warm.
They lifted her and poured water into her mouth,
and after a while, she revived,
recounting what she had seen.
When Mr. Sòng arrived,
he was grief-stricken and furious, wishing to die.
Carefully investigating the spot where the old woman had disappeared,
they dug about three chi deep
and gradually uncovered white hair;
digging further,
they found a corpse
that matched the description,
with a face swollen and lifelike.
They ordered it to be struck,
and the flesh and bones were all rotten,
with only clear water inside the skin.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
In Cháng'ān there lived a scholar named Fāng Dòng,
who was quite famous for his talent,
but frivolous and lacking in decorum.
Whenever he saw a woman out walking on the road,
he would flirtatiously follow her.
One day before the Qingmíng Festival,
he happened to be strolling in the outskirts of the city,
when he saw a small carriage,
adorned with red silk and embroidered curtains;
several maidservants,
riding on slow horses, followed behind.
Among them was one maid,
riding a small steed,
whose beauty was absolutely stunning.
He gradually drew closer to take a look,
and saw that the carriage curtain was wide open,
inside sat a young maiden of about sixteen,
dressed in bright red and exceptionally beautiful,
more so than anyone he had ever seen in his life.
His eyes dazzled and his spirit was captivated,
he gazed with longing and could not bear to leave,
sometimes ahead, sometimes behind,
he followed the carriage for several miles.
Suddenly, he heard the young lady call the maid to the side of the carriage,
saying:
"Lower the curtain for me.
Where did this wild young man come from,
peeking and staring so frequently!"
The maid then lowered the curtain,
and angrily glared at the scholar, saying:
"This is the bride of the seventh young master of the Hibiscus City returning to her parents' home,
not some country girl,
to let a scholar gawk at freely!"
Having said this,
she scooped up some dirt from the wheel tracks and threw it at the scholar.
The scholar's eyes were stung and he could not open them.
As soon as he wiped them to see,
the carriage and horses had already vanished.
He returned home in shock and confusion.
He felt his eyes were never comfortable again.
He asked someone to lift his eyelids and examine them,
and found that a small film had grown over his pupils;
after a night, it worsened,
tears streaming down uncontrollably;
the film gradually grew larger,
and after a few days, it was as thick as a coin;
his right eye developed a spiral pattern,
and no medicine was effective.
Filled with regret and despair,
he began to think of repenting.
He heard that the "Sūtra of Light" could relieve misfortune.
He obtained a copy,
and asked someone to teach him to recite it.
At first, he was still restless and irritable,
but gradually, over time, he found peace.
Morning and evening, with nothing to do,
he would only sit cross-legged, fingering his prayer beads.
He persisted for a year,
and all worldly attachments were purified.
Suddenly, he heard a faint voice like a fly in his left eye,
saying:
"It's pitch black in here,
so unbearably stifling!"
His right eye responded:
"Let's go out for a stroll together,
to vent this stifling feeling."
Gradually, he felt a wriggling itch in both nostrils,
as if something was coming out,
leaving through the nostrils.
After a long while, they returned,
re-entering his eye sockets from his nose.
They spoke again:
"We haven't peeked into the garden for so long,
the pearl orchids have withered and died!"
The scholar had always loved fragrant orchids,
and had planted many in his garden,
watering them daily himself;
since losing his sight,
he had long neglected them.
Suddenly hearing this,
he urgently asked his wife:
"Why have the orchids withered and died?"
His wife asked how he knew,
so he told her the reason.
His wife hurried to check,
and indeed, the flowers and plants had dried up.
She was greatly astonished.
She quietly hid in the room to wait,
and saw tiny figures emerge from the scholar's nostrils,
no larger than beans,
buzzing about until they finally went out the door.
They gradually went farther away,
and were soon lost from sight.
After a while,
they returned arm in arm,
flew up to his face,
like bees or ants returning to their nest.
This went on for two or three days.
Then he heard the left one say:
"The tunnel is winding,
going back and forth is very inconvenient,
we should open our own door."
The right one responded:
"My wall is thick,
it won't be easy."
The left one said:
"Let me try to break through,
and then you can join me."
Then he felt a faint tearing sensation in his left eye socket.
After a moment,
he opened his eyes to look,
and could clearly see objects on the table.
He joyfully told his wife.
His wife examined it closely,
and saw that a small hole had broken through the membrane,
the black pupil shining brightly,
like a split pepper.
After one night,
the film completely disappeared.
Looking closely,
he actually had double pupils,
but the spiral in his right eye remained as before,
so he realized that two pupils now shared one eye socket.
Although the scholar had one impaired eye,
compared to those with two normal eyes,
he could see even more clearly.
From then on, he became even more disciplined,
and was praised in his village for his great virtue.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"In the countryside, there was a scholar,
traveling with two friends on the road,
when they saw from afar a young woman riding a donkey ahead of them,
he playfully recited: 'There is a beautiful lady!'
Then he turned to his two friends and said: 'Let's catch up to her!'
They laughed together and galloped forward.
Soon, they caught up,
and it turned out to be his daughter-in-law.
Embarrassed and deflated,
he fell silent.
His friends pretended not to know,
and made rather lewd comments.
The scholar, feeling awkward,
stammered and said: 'This is my eldest son's wife.'
Each of them hid their laughter and let the matter drop.
Those who act frivolously often bring shame upon themselves,
which is truly laughable.
As for having one's eyes stung and going blind,
that is a severe retribution from the spirits.
The lord of Hibiscus City,
I do not know what deity he is,
could he be an incarnation of a Bodhisattva?
Yet the young gentleman opened a door in his eye,
even though spirits may be malevolent,
they do not necessarily forbid people from reforming themselves."
Mèng Lóngtán from Jiāngxī
was staying in the capital with Provincial Graduate Zhū.
By chance, they entered a Buddhist monastery
where the halls and monks’ cells
were not particularly spacious.
Only one old monk was lodging there.
Seeing the visitors enter,
he straightened his robe and came out to greet them,
leading them on a tour.
In the main hall was a statue of the monk Zhìgōng.
The murals on the two walls were exquisitely painted,
with figures as lifelike as real people.
On the east wall was a painting of flower-scattering celestial maidens.
Among them was one with hair hanging loose,
holding a flower and smiling,
her cherry lips seeming about to move,
her eyes about to sparkle.
Zhū gazed at her for a long time,
unconsciously becoming captivated,
lost in reverie.
Suddenly, his body felt as if floating,
as if riding on clouds and mist,
and he was already on the wall.
He saw halls and pavilions layered one upon another,
no longer the human world.
An old monk was preaching from a dais,
with many listeners gathered around.
Zhū also stood among them.
After a while,
it seemed someone was secretly tugging his sleeve.
Turning to look,
he saw the girl with the loose hair,
who smiled and walked away.
He immediately followed her.
Passing through winding railings,
they entered a small room.
Zhū hesitated and dared not go forward.
The girl turned her head,
raised the flower in her hand,
and beckoned from afar.
Then he hurried toward her.
Inside the room, it was quiet and empty;
he abruptly embraced her,
and she did not resist much,
so they became intimate.
Afterward, she closed the door and left,
instructing him not to cough.
At night, she returned,
and this continued for two days.
Her companions discovered them together
and found the young man.
They teased the girl, saying:
"The little gentleman in your belly is already so big,
yet you still wear your hair loose like a maiden?"
Together, they brought hairpins and earrings,
urging her to put up her hair.
The girl blushed and said nothing.
One of them said:
"Sisters,
let's not stay long,
lest someone become unhappy."
They all laughed and left.
Zhū looked at the girl:
her hair was piled high like clouds,
her locks hung low like a breeze,
even more stunning than when her hair was loose.
Seeing no one around,
they gradually became intimate again,
the fragrance of orchids and musk intoxicating his heart,
their pleasure at its peak.
Suddenly, they heard the loud clatter of leather boots
and the clanking of chains;
then came the clamor of noisy arguments.
The girl started in alarm
and peeked out with Zhū.
They saw a messenger in golden armor,
his face as black as lacquer,
holding chains and a hammer,
surrounded by the girls.
The messenger asked:
"All here?"
They replied:
"All here."
The messenger said:
"If anyone is hiding a mortal from the lower world,
confess now,
lest you bring trouble upon yourselves."
Again, they answered in unison:
"None."
The messenger turned and scanned like a hawk,
as if about to search for hidden persons.
The girl was terrified,
her face ashen.
In panic, she said to Zhū:
"Quick, hide under the bed."
Then she opened a small door in the wall
and fled abruptly.
Zhū crouched down,
not daring to breathe.
Soon, he heard boots enter the room
and then leave.
Not long after,
the noise gradually faded away,
and his heart settled somewhat.
But outside, there were still voices coming and going.
Crouching for so long,
he felt a ringing in his ears,
fire in his eyes,
and could hardly bear the situation.
He only listened quietly, waiting for the girl to return,
completely forgetting how he had gotten there.
Meanwhile, Mèng Lóngtán in the hall
suddenly noticed Zhū was missing
and asked the monk in suspicion.
The monk smiled and said:
"He went to listen to a sermon."
Mèng asked:
"Where?"
The monk replied:
"Not far."
After a while,
he tapped the wall with his finger and called out:
"Why has Benefactor Zhū lingered so long on his journey without returning?"
Then they saw Zhū's image appear in the mural,
standing still and listening intently,
as if hearing something.
The monk called again:
"Your traveling companion has been waiting a long time."
Suddenly, Zhū drifted down from the wall,
dazed and wooden,
eyes wide, legs weak.
Mèng was greatly startled
and calmly asked him what happened.
It turned out he had been hiding under the bed
when he heard knocking like thunder,
so he came out to look and listen.
Together, they looked at the flower-holding girl in the painting:
her hair was now coiled high like a snail shell,
no longer hanging loose.
Zhū bowed to the old monk in astonishment
and asked for an explanation.
The monk smiled and said:
"Illusions arise from the human mind;
how could a humble monk like me explain it?"
Zhū was choked with emotion and unable to speak,
while Mèng was astounded and at a loss.
They then rose
and descended the steps to leave.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Illusions are created by people themselves;
these words sound like those of someone enlightened.
When a person has lustful thoughts,
scenes of licentiousness arise;
when a person has impure thoughts,
scenes of terror arise.
The Bodhisattva enlightens the ignorant,
creating a thousand illusions.
All arise from the movements of the human mind.
With such earnest compassion,
it is a pity they did not achieve great enlightenment upon hearing these words
and retreat with disheveled hair into the mountains."
Based on the manuscript version of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Sūn Tàibái once said: his great-grandfather studied at the Liǔgōu Temple in the southern mountains.
During the wheat harvest season, he returned home,
and after ten days, he went back.
Opening the door to his study,
he saw dust covering the desk,
and cobwebs filling the windows.
He ordered a servant to clean up,
and by evening, it finally felt tidy enough to sit in.
So he dusted off the bed and laid out the bedding,
bolted the door, and went to bed,
by which time moonlight was already flooding the window.
He tossed and turned for a while,
as all sounds fell silent.
Suddenly, he heard a rumbling wind,
and the temple gate creaked open with a loud noise.
He secretly thought the temple monks had forgotten to bolt it.
While he was pondering this,
the sound of the wind gradually approached his dwelling,
and soon the door to his room swung open.
He was greatly puzzled.
Before he could gather his thoughts,
the sound had already entered the room;
then came the clanking sound of boots,
gradually nearing the bedroom door.
He began to feel terrified.
Soon, the bedroom door swung open.
He looked urgently,
and saw a huge ghost bending over and squeezing in,
suddenly standing before the bed,
nearly as tall as the beam.
Its face was the color of old melon skin;
its eyes gleamed and flickered,
looking all around the room;
it opened its huge mouth like a basin,
with sparse teeth about three inches long;
its tongue moved and its throat rumbled,
making a roaring sound,
echoing throughout the four walls.
The gentleman was terrified to the extreme;
but then he thought that in such close quarters,
there was no way to escape,
so it would be better to stab it.
So he secretly drew the dagger from under his pillow,
suddenly pulled it out and hacked at the ghost,
striking its abdomen,
which made a sound like hitting a stone jar.
The ghost was furious,
and stretched out its huge claws to grab the gentleman.
The gentleman shrank back slightly.
The ghost grabbed the quilt,
shook it violently,
and left angrily,
while the gentleman fell with the quilt,
crouching on the ground and crying out.
His family members rushed over with torches,
but the door was still closed as before,
so they pushed open the window and entered,
saw the situation,
and were greatly shocked.
They helped him onto the bed,
and only then did he explain what had happened.
They all examined it together,
and found the quilt stuck in the crack of the bedroom door.
Opening the door and inspecting with a light,
they saw claw marks as big as a winnowing basket,
and where the five fingers had pressed, they had pierced through.
When day broke,
he dared not stay any longer,
and carrying his books, he returned home.
Later, he asked the monks,
but there were no further strange occurrences.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Shěn Línshēng said: his friend, an old man,
was taking a nap on a summer day,
and in his drowsiness,
he saw a woman lift the curtain and enter,
with a white cloth wrapped around her head,
wearing mourning clothes and a hemp skirt,
heading toward the inner room.
He suspected it was a neighbor woman visiting his wife;
but then he thought again,
why would she enter someone's house in mourning clothes so abruptly?
Just as he was feeling perplexed,
the woman came out.
Looking closely at her,
she appeared to be in her thirties,
with a sallow, swollen face,
her brows and eyes tightly knit,
and an expression that was fearsome.
She then hesitated and did not leave,
gradually approaching the bed.
So he pretended to be asleep,
to see what would happen.
Before long,
the woman lifted her clothes and climbed onto the bed,
pressing down on his abdomen,
and he felt as if a hundred pounds were weighing on him.
Though his mind was clear,
when he tried to raise his hand,
his hand felt bound;
when he tried to raise his foot,
his foot felt paralyzed.
He urgently wanted to cry for help,
but he could not make a sound.
The woman sniffed the old man's face with her beak,
covering his cheekbones, nose, brows, and forehead.
He felt her beak was cold as ice,
and her breath chilled him to the bone.
In his distress,
the old man thought of a plan: when she sniffed to his chin and cheeks,
he would bite her.
Not long after,
she indeed reached his chin.
The old man seized the opportunity and bit her cheek hard,
his teeth sinking into the flesh.
The woman, in pain, pulled away from his body,
struggling and crying.
The old man bit even harder.
He only felt blood flowing down his chin,
soaking the pillow beside him.
As they were locked in this struggle,
he suddenly heard his wife's voice outside the courtyard,
and urgently called out that there was a ghost,
but as soon as he relaxed his bite, the woman vanished in a flash.
His wife rushed in,
but saw nothing,
and laughed, saying he was having a nightmare.
The old man recounted the strange event,
and said there was evidence of blood.
They examined it together,
and found something like water from a leaky roof,
flowing over the pillow and soaking the mat.
Bending down to sniff it,
it had an unusually foul, fishy smell.
The old man then vomited violently.
Several days later,
there was still a lingering foul smell in his mouth.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Old Man Sūn
was the uncle of Qīngfú, a relative of mine by marriage.
He had always been courageous.
One day,
while lying down for a nap,
he felt as if something had climbed onto the bed,
and then felt his body swaying as if riding on clouds and mist.
He secretly wondered if it might be a fox spirit pressing on him?
Peeking slightly,
he saw a creature as big as a cat,
with yellow fur and a greenish beak,
coming from near his feet.
It crawled along slowly,
as if afraid the old man would wake.
It hesitantly attached itself to his body: wherever it touched his feet, his feet went numb;
wherever it touched his thighs, his thighs went weak.
Just as it reached his abdomen,
the old man suddenly sat up,
pressed down and grabbed it,
gripping its neck,
and the creature cried out urgently, unable to break free.
The old man urgently called his wife,
and used a belt to tie around its waist.
Then, holding both ends of the belt,
he said with a laugh:
"I've heard you're good at transforming,
now I'm watching you closely,
let's see how you transform."
As he spoke,
the creature suddenly shrank its abdomen,
becoming as thin as a pipe,
and nearly slipped away.
The old man was greatly startled,
and quickly tightened the belt,
but then it puffed up its abdomen again,
thicker than a bowl,
and too hard to tighten;
as soon as he relaxed his grip slightly,
it shrank again.
The old man, afraid it would escape,
told his wife to quickly kill it.
His wife looked around in a panic,
not knowing where the knife was.
The old man glanced to the left to show her where it was.
By the time he turned back,
the belt was in his hand like a loop,
and the creature had already vanished.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In Chángshān there was an old man named Ān,
who loved to work in the fields.
In autumn, when the buckwheat ripened,
he cut it and piled it up by the ridge.
At that time, there were thieves in the nearby village who stole crops,
so he ordered his tenant farmers
to transport the harvest to the threshing ground by moonlight;
after they had loaded up and returned,
he stayed behind to keep watch.
Thus he lay down in the open, using his spear as a pillow.
As his eyes began to close,
he suddenly heard someone stepping on the buckwheat roots,
making a crunching sound.
His heart suspected a robber.
Quickly raising his head,
he saw a huge ghost,
over ten feet tall,
with red hair and bristling beard,
already close to him.
Terrified,
he had no time for other plans,
leapt up suddenly,
and fiercely stabbed it.
The ghost roared like thunder and vanished.
Fearing it would return,
he shouldered his spear and went home.
Meeting the tenant farmers on the road,
he told them what he had seen,
and warned them not to go.
The crowd did not fully believe him.
The next day,
while sunning wheat on the threshing ground,
they suddenly heard a sound from the sky.
The old man cried in alarm:
"The ghost creature is coming!"
Then he fled,
and the others fled too.
After a while, they gathered again,
and the old man ordered them to set up many bows and crossbows to wait for it.
The following day,
it indeed came again.
Several arrows were shot together,
and the creature, frightened, fled.
For two or three days, it did not come again.
After the wheat was stored in the granary,
the stalks were scattered about,
so the old man ordered them to gather and stack them into a pile,
and personally climbed up to trample them solid,
until it was several feet high.
Suddenly, looking into the distance, he cried in alarm:
"The ghost creature has arrived!"
The crowd hurriedly searched for bows and arrows,
but the creature had already rushed toward the old man.
The old man fell,
and it bit his forehead and left.
Everyone climbed up to look,
and saw that a piece of his forehead bone, as big as a palm, was gone.
He was unconscious and unaware of people.
They carried him home,
and he soon died.
After that, it was never seen again.
No one knows what kind of monster it was.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In Chángshān, there was a certain Mr. Lǐ,
the nephew of the Minister of Justice.
His residence was haunted by many strange phenomena.
Once he saw a bench in the hall,
flesh-pink in color,
very smooth and sleek.
Since Mr. Lǐ originally had no such object,
he approached and stroked it,
and it bent with his touch,
almost as soft as flesh.
Startled, he retreated.
Turning back to look,
he saw its four legs moving,
gradually entering the wall.
Another time, he saw a white club leaning against the wall,
clean, glossy, and long.
Approaching to support it,
it fell greasily,
wriggled into the wall,
and after a while, disappeared completely.
In the seventeenth year of the Kāngxī reign,
a scholar named Wáng Jùnshēng set up a school in his house.
At dusk,
as the lamps were first lit,
the scholar, wearing shoes, lay on the couch.
Suddenly he saw a little man,
about three inches tall,
enter from outside,
circled briefly,
and then left again.
After a short while,
it carried two small stools in,
placed them in the hall,
exactly like those made by children from sorghum stalks.
Another moment later,
two little men carried in a coffin,
about four inches long,
and placed it on the stools.
Before the burial was completed,
a woman led several maidservants in,
all as tiny as before.
The woman wore mourning clothes,
with a hemp rope tied around her waist,
and a cloth wrapped around her head;
she covered her mouth with her sleeve,
sobbing and crying,
her voice like that of a large fly.
The scholar watched sidelong for a long time,
his hair standing on end,
as if frost had covered his body.
Thus he let out a great cry,
fled in haste,
tumbled under the bed,
and trembled, unable to get up.
Everyone in the schoolhouse heard the noise and gathered,
but the figures in the hall had vanished without a trace.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
There was a man surnamed Xǔ,
whose home was in the northern outskirts of Zībó,
and who made his living by fishing.
Every night,
he would bring wine to the riverbank,
drinking while fishing.
When he drank, he would pour a libation on the ground,
praying:
"May the drowned ghosts in the river drink."
This became his regular practice.
When others fished,
they often caught nothing,
but Xǔ alone would fill his basket.
One evening,
as he was drinking alone,
a young man came,
lingering by his side.
Xǔ invited him to drink,
and the young man gladly shared the drink with him.
After that, he did not catch a single fish all night,
and felt quite disappointed.
The young man stood up and said:
"Allow me to drive the fish for you downstream."
Then he drifted away.
After a short while,
he returned and said:
"A large school of fish has arrived."
Indeed, they heard the sound of fish nibbling.
Xǔ cast his net and caught several,
all over a foot long.
Overjoyed,
he expressed his thanks.
When about to leave,
he offered the young man some fish,
but the young man declined, saying:
"I have repeatedly enjoyed your fine wine;
such a small matter is hardly worth mentioning as repayment.
If you do not mind,
I would like to make this a long-term arrangement."
Xǔ said:
"We have only spent one evening together;
how can you say 'repeatedly'?
If you are willing to visit often,
it would truly be my great wish;
I am only ashamed that I have nothing to offer in return."
He asked for the young man's name,
and the young man said:
"My surname is Wáng,
and I have no courtesy name.
When we meet, you may call me Wáng Liùláng."
Then they parted.
The next day,
Xǔ sold his fish
and bought more wine.
In the evening, when he reached the riverbank,
the young man was already there waiting,
and they drank merrily together.
After a few cups,
the young man would drive fish for Xǔ.
Thus half a year passed.
Suddenly he told Xǔ:
"Since I had the honor of making your acquaintance,
our affection has surpassed that of flesh and blood.
Yet the day of our parting is near."
His words were filled with sorrow.
Xǔ, startled, asked him why.
Twice he seemed about to speak but stopped,
then said:
"As close as we two are,
perhaps you will not be shocked by what I say?
Now that we must part,
I might as well tell you plainly: I am actually a ghost.
I was always fond of wine,
and once, dead drunk, I drowned.
Several years have passed since then.
The reason you previously caught more fish than others
was entirely due to my secretly driving them toward you,
in repayment for your libations.
Tomorrow my term of expiation will be fulfilled,
and there should be a substitute.
I shall go to be reborn.
We have only this evening left together,
so I cannot help feeling moved."
At first Xǔ was greatly alarmed;
but having been intimate with him so long,
he felt no terror.
Instead, he sighed sorrowfully
and, pouring a cup, said:
"Liùláng, drink this,
and do not grieve.
That we must part so soon after meeting
is truly saddening.
But your term completed and your ordeal over,
this is precisely cause for congratulation.
Grief is out of place here."
Thereupon they drank heartily.
Xǔ then asked:
"Who is to be your substitute?"
He replied:
"Elder brother, watch by the river tomorrow.
Around noon,
a woman crossing the river will drown—
that is the one."
When they heard the village roosters crow,
they shed tears and parted.
The next day,
Xǔ waited respectfully by the river,
to observe the strange event.
Sure enough, a woman came carrying an infant,
and upon reaching the river, she fell in.
The child was thrown onto the bank,
waving its arms and legs and crying.
The woman sank and surfaced several times;
then suddenly, dripping wet, she clutched the bank and climbed out.
After resting briefly on the ground,
she picked up the child and went straight away.
While the woman was drowning,
Xǔ could not bear it in his heart
and thought of rushing to save her;
but then he reflected that she was to be Liùláng's substitute,
so he stopped himself and did not rescue her.
When the woman got out by herself,
he suspected Liùláng's words had not come true.
At dusk,
he was fishing at his old spot
when the young man came again
and said:
"Now we are reunited,
and let us not speak of parting again."
Xǔ asked the reason.
He said:
"The woman had already come to substitute for me;
but I pitied the child in her arms.
To replace one person
and thereby take two lives
was too much, so I let her go.
Who knows when the next substitute will come?
Perhaps the bond between us two is not yet exhausted?"
Xǔ said with deep feeling:
"Such a benevolent heart
can surely reach the Lord of Heaven."
From then on they stayed together as before.
A few days later,
he came again to bid farewell.
Xǔ suspected there was another substitute.
He said:
"No, it is not that.
My previous thought of compassion
truly reached the Heavenly Emperor.
Now I have been appointed as the local earth god of Wūzhèn in Zhāoyuǎn County,
and I shall take up my post tomorrow.
If you do not forget our old friendship,
do come to visit sometime—
do not fear the long, difficult journey."
Xǔ congratulated him:
"Your integrity has made you a god;
this greatly comforts people's hearts.
But the paths of humans and gods are separate;
even if I do not fear the long, difficult journey,
what can I do?"
The young man said:
"Just come,
and do not worry."
After repeated earnest injunctions, he departed.
Xǔ returned home,
and immediately began preparing for a journey east.
His wife laughed and said:
"That place is several hundred li away.
Even if the place exists,
I'm afraid a clay idol cannot hold a conversation."
Xǔ did not listen,
and eventually arrived in Zhāoyuǎn.
He asked the local residents,
and sure enough, there was a Wūzhèn.
He found his way to the place,
rested at an inn,
and asked where the temple was.
The innkeeper said in surprise:
"Could it be that your surname is Xǔ?"
Xǔ said:
"Yes.
How did you know?"
The innkeeper asked again:
"Could it be that you are from Zīchuān?"
Xǔ said:
"Yes.
How did you know?"
The innkeeper did not answer,
but hurried out.
Soon, men carrying children,
women peeking through doors,
came in a bustling crowd,
forming a circle like a wall.
Xǔ was even more astonished.
The crowd then told him:
"Several nights ago,
we dreamed that the god said: 'My friend Xǔ from Zīchuān will soon arrive,
you should assist him with travel funds.'
We have been waiting for you for a long time."
Xǔ also found this strange,
so he went to offer sacrifices at the temple and prayed:
"Since parting from you,
I have thought of you constantly, awake or asleep,
and have come from afar to fulfill our old promise.
I am also grateful that you informed the residents in a dream,
your kindness is deeply engraved in my heart.
I am ashamed that I have no generous gifts,
only a cup of wine;
if you do not disdain it,
let us drink as we did by the river."
After the prayer,
he burned paper money.
Suddenly, he saw a wind rise behind the altar,
whirling for a while,
before dispersing.
That night, he dreamed that the young man came,
dressed elegantly,
very different from his usual appearance.
He thanked him, saying:
"You have troubled yourself to come from afar to visit me,
my joy and tears mingle.
But as I hold a minor post,
it is inconvenient for us to meet;
though we are close, it feels like mountains and rivers separate us,
which saddens me deeply.
The residents have given you a modest gift,
as a small token of our old friendship.
When the time comes for you to return,
I will surely come to see you off."
After staying for several days,
Xǔ wanted to return home.
The crowd earnestly urged him to stay,
inviting him morning and evening,
with different hosts each day.
Xǔ firmly declined and insisted on leaving.
The crowd then wrote notes and brought bundles,
competing to present farewell gifts,
and before the morning was over,
his bags were filled with presents.
Old men and young children all gathered,
to see him off out of the village.
Suddenly, a whirlwind rose,
and followed him for over ten li.
Xǔ bowed again and said:
"Liùláng, take care!
Do not trouble yourself to escort me further.
With your benevolent heart,
you will surely bring blessings to this land;
there is no need for an old friend's reminder."
The wind whirled for a long time,
before finally departing.
The villagers also sighed in amazement and returned.
Xǔ returned home,
and his family became somewhat better off,
so he no longer fished.
Later, when he met someone from Zhāoyuǎn and asked about it,
it was said that the god's responses were as swift as an echo.
Some say: it is Shíkēng Zhuāng in Zhāngqiū.
It is not known which is correct.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"To rise to high position,
yet not forget one's humble origins,
this is what makes him divine.
As for the noble lords in carriages today,
would they still recognize the man in the bamboo hat?
In my hometown, there was a retired gentleman,
whose family was extremely poor.
He had a childhood friend
who held a lucrative official post.
He reckoned that if he sought him out, he would surely receive help.
He exhausted his efforts to prepare for the journey,
traveled a thousand li,
only to be greatly disappointed;
he had to empty his purse and sell his horse,
before he could return home.
His younger clansman was quite witty,
and composed a 'Monthly Ordinance' to mock him, saying: 'In this month,
elder brother arrives,
the sable hat is removed,
the umbrella is not opened,
the horse turns into a donkey,
and the boots finally fall silent.'
Thinking of this, one cannot help but laugh."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In my childhood, I went to the prefectural seat for the examinations,
which coincided with the Spring Festival.
According to old custom,
the day before,
various merchants and traders,
with colorful towers and music, would go to the Provincial Administration Commission,
in a ceremony called
"Performing Spring."
I followed my friends to watch the spectacle.
On that day, the crowd of spectators was like a wall.
In the hall sat four officials,
all dressed in red,
facing each other east and west.
I was young at the time,
and did not understand what officials they were.
I only heard the clamor of voices,
and the blaring of music.
Suddenly, a man,
leading a boy with disheveled hair,
carrying a pole on his shoulder, came forward,
as if to announce something;
amid the uproar of ten thousand voices,
I could not hear what he said.
I only saw the officials in the hall laughing.
Then a servant in black loudly ordered a performance.
The man, having received the order, was about to begin,
and asked:
"What performance shall I give?"
The officials on the hall exchanged a few words.
A clerk came down to ask what his specialty was.
He replied:
"I can reverse the seasons of living things."
The clerk reported this to the officials.
After a short while, he came down again,
and ordered him to fetch peaches.
The magician assented,
took off his coat and covered the basket with it,
then deliberately put on a look of resentment and
said:
"Your Honor is being quite unreasonable!
The ice hasn't thawed yet.
Where am I supposed to get a peach?
If I don't get one,
I'm afraid I'll incur the wrath of the man who sits facing south.
What am I to do?"
His son said:
"Since Father has already given his word,
how can he back out?"
The magician was disconsolate for a long time
before saying:
"I've thought it through from every angle.
At the beginning of spring, when snow is piled everywhere,
where in the human world can one be found?
Only in the garden of the Queen Mother of the West
are the four seasons free of withering and shedding.
There might be one there.
I'll have to steal it from Heaven
to make this work."
His son said:
"Hah!
Can you climb a stairway to Heaven?"
The magician said:
"I have a method."
He opened the basket
and took out a coil of rope
about ten zhang long.
He found the end of the rope
and threw it into the air;
the rope immediately stood upright in the air
as if it were hanging from something.
Before long
it went higher and higher with each throw
until it disappeared into the clouds;
the rope in his hand was also used up.
Then he called to his son:
"Come here, son!
I'm old and worn out.
My body is heavy and clumsy,
so I can't make the climb.
You'll have to go."
He handed the rope to his son
and said:
"Hold onto this and you can climb up."
The son took the rope
with a look of reluctance
and complained:
"Father is so muddleheaded!
He expects me to cling
to this flimsy thread of a rope
and climb to the heavens thousands of ren high.
If it breaks halfway,
what will become of my bones?"
His father cajoled and patted him
saying:
"I've already misspoken.
There's no use regretting it now.
I'll trouble you to make the trip.
Don't be upset, son.
If you manage to steal a peach,
you'll surely get a reward of a hundred taels of silver.
I'll get you a beautiful wife."
The son then took hold of the rope
and spiraled upward.
Hand over hand and foot over foot he went
like a spider running along its thread.
Gradually he entered the clouds
and could no longer be seen.
After a long time
a peach fell,
as big as a bowl.
The magician was overjoyed.
He took it and presented it in the courtroom.
The officials passed it around and looked at it for a long time,
but they could not tell whether it was real or fake.
Suddenly the rope fell to the ground.
The magician cried out in alarm:
"This is terrible!
Someone up there cut my rope.
What will my son hold onto?"
After a while
an object fell.
Looking at it,
they saw it was his son's head.
The magician picked it up and wept, saying:
"He must have been caught stealing the peach
by the guards.
My son is done for!"
After another while
a foot fell;
not long after,
limbs fell one after another.
Nothing remained intact.
The magician was grief-stricken.
He picked up the pieces one by one, put them in the basket and closed it.
Then he said:
"This old man had only this one son.
He followed me north and south every day.
Today he obeyed a strict command
and, unexpectedly, met with this bizarre and tragic end!
I'll have to carry him away and bury him."
He went up to the courtroom and knelt,
saying:
"For the sake of a peach,
my son has been killed!
If you take pity on this humble man and help with the burial,
I will repay you from beyond the grave."
The seated officials were shocked and amazed.
Each of them gave him money.
The magician took it and tied it around his waist.
Then he rapped on the basket and called out:
"Bābā'ér,
if you don't come out and thank them for the reward,
what are you waiting for?"
Suddenly a tousle-haired boy pushed the basket lid open with his head and came out.
He kowtowed toward the north
—it was his son.
Because his magic was so marvelous,
I remember it to this day.
Later I heard that the White Lotus Sect could perform this sort of magic.
I wonder if this man was a descendant of theirs.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
There was a villager selling pears in the marketplace.
They were quite sweet and fragrant,
and the price was high.
A Daoist priest in a tattered headcloth and padded robe
begged for one in front of the cart.
The villager berated him,
but he would not leave;
the villager grew angry
and began to curse him.
The priest said:
"There are several hundred pears on this cart.
This old monk only begs for one of them.
It won't be a great loss to you, sir.
Why get angry?"
The onlookers urged the villager to give him a poor-quality pear and send him away,
but the villager stubbornly refused.
A waiter from a shop,
seeing the incessant bickering,
took out money and bought a pear,
which he gave to the priest.
The priest bowed in thanks
and said to the crowd:
"Those who have left the family do not understand stinginess.
I have some fine pears.
I'll bring them out to serve all of you."
Someone said:
"If you have them,
why don't you eat them yourself?"
He replied:
"I especially need the pits for seeds."
Thereupon he took the pear and ate it with great relish.
When he had finished,
he held the pit in his hand,
took a spade from his shoulder,
dug a hole several inches deep in the ground,
put the pit in and covered it with soil.
Then he asked the people in the marketplace for hot water to pour on it.
A busybody got some boiling water from a shop by the road,
and the priest poured it into the hole.
Ten thousand eyes were fixed on the spot
as they saw a tiny sprout emerge
and gradually grow larger.
In no time it became a tree
with luxuriant branches and leaves.
Suddenly it blossomed;
suddenly it bore fruit:
large, fragrant pears
hung in clusters all over the tree.
The priest picked them from the tree and gave them to the onlookers.
In a moment they were all gone.
Then
he cut down the tree with his spade.
It took quite a while of *ding-ding* chopping
before it finally broke: he shouldered the leafy tree
and walked away at a leisurely pace.
At first,
when the Daoist priest performed his magic,
the villager also stood among the crowd,
craning his neck and staring intently,
completely forgetting about his own business.
After the Daoist priest had left,
he finally looked into his cart,
only to find that the pears were all gone.
He then realized that the pears that had just been distributed
were all his own.
Upon closer inspection, he also noticed that one of the cart’s shafts was missing,
and it had been freshly chopped off.
He was filled with great anger and resentment.
He hurriedly followed the trail,
turned around the corner of a wall,
and saw the broken shaft discarded beneath the wall.
Only then did he realize that the pear tree that had been chopped down
was actually his own cart shaft.
The Daoist priest was nowhere to be found.
The entire market burst into laughter.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"The villager was muddle-headed,
his foolish appearance almost tangible.
That he was laughed at by the people in the market
was not without reason.
Often, when I see those in the village who are called well-off,
if a good friend asks for rice,
they become displeased,
and calculate, saying:
'That is enough for several days’ provisions.'
Or if someone urges them to help someone in dire straits,
or to feed a lonely and destitute person,
they become indignant again,
and calculate once more, saying:
'This is enough to feed ten or five people.'
Even between fathers and sons, brothers,
they haggle over every trifle.
But when it comes to indulging in debauchery or gambling, which cloud their minds,
they do not hesitate to empty their purses;
when the knife or saw is at their necks,
they rush to buy their lives without delay.
Such cases as these
are too numerous to mention;
so what is there to wonder at in the foolishness of this villager?"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In the county, there was a scholar named Wáng,
the seventh in his family,
a descendant of an old and established family.
In his youth, he admired the Dao,
and hearing that Láo Mountain had many immortals,
he packed his books and went there to seek them.
He climbed to one of its peaks,
where there was a temple,
very secluded.
A Daoist priest sat on a rush cushion,
his white hair hanging down to his collar,
yet his spirit radiated vigor and vitality.
Wáng bowed and spoke with him,
and found his reasoning profoundly mysterious.
He asked to become his disciple.
The Daoist priest said:
"I fear you are too pampered and lazy to endure hardship."
Wáng replied:
"I can endure it."
The priest had many disciples,
and by dusk, they had all gathered.
Wáng bowed to each of them,
and thus stayed at the temple.
Early in the morning,
the Daoist priest called Wáng to him,
gave him an axe,
and made him follow the others to gather firewood.
Wáng respectfully accepted the instruction.
After more than a month,
his hands and feet were covered with thick calluses,
and he could no longer bear the hardship, secretly harboring thoughts of returning home.
One evening upon returning,
he saw two men drinking with the master.
The sun had already set,
yet there were still no lamps or candles.
The master then cut paper into the shape of a mirror
and pasted it on the wall.
In a moment,
the moonlight illuminated the room,
bright enough to see the finest hairs.
All the disciples gathered around to listen and bustle about.
One guest said:
"Such a fine evening and splendid enjoyment
should be shared by all."
He then took a pot of wine from the table
and distributed it among the disciples,
urging them to drink to their fill.
Wáng thought to himself: with seven or eight people,
how could one pot of wine suffice for all?
So they each fetched bowls and cups,
competing to drink first and pour libations,
fearing only that the wine would run out;
yet as they poured back and forth,
it never seemed to diminish.
He found this strange.
Soon another guest said:
"We have been graced with the moon's bright light,
yet we drink in such silence.
Why not summon Cháng'é to join us?"
He then threw a chopstick into the moon.
They saw a beautiful woman
emerge from the light.
At first she was not even a foot tall,
but upon reaching the ground, she grew to human size.
With a slender waist and elegant neck,
she gracefully performed
the "Rainbow Skirt Dance."
Afterward, she sang:
"Immortal, oh immortal,
shall I return,
or remain secluded in the vast cold palace!"
Her voice was clear and piercing,
resonant like the sound of flutes.
When the song ended,
she twirled and rose,
leapt onto the table,
and in the moment of their startled gaze,
she had turned back into a chopstick.
The three men laughed heartily.
Another guest said:
"Tonight has been most joyful,
but I can no longer hold my liquor.
Could you see me off to the Moon Palace?"
The three men moved their seats
and gradually entered the moon.
The disciples watched as the three,
sitting in the moon drinking,
their beards and eyebrows clearly visible,
like shadows in a mirror.
After a while,
the moon gradually dimmed;
when the disciples lit candles and came,
only the Dàoshi remained sitting, and the guests had vanished.
The food and leftovers on the table remained as before.
The moon on the wall
was merely a round piece of paper like a mirror.
The Dàoshi asked the disciples:
"Have you drunk enough?"
They replied:
"We have."
"If you have had enough, you should retire early,
and not neglect gathering firewood."
The disciples assented and withdrew.
Wáng secretly admired and longed for this,
and his thoughts of returning home subsided.
Another month passed,
and the hardship became unbearable,
yet the Dàoshi had not taught him a single skill.
Unable to wait any longer,
he took his leave, saying:
"I, your disciple, have traveled hundreds of lǐ to study under an immortal master.
Even if I cannot obtain the art of immortality,
if you could impart even a minor skill,
it would console my heart for seeking instruction;
now, after two or three months here,
all I do is gather firewood early and return at dusk.
When I was at home,
I never knew such hardship."
The Dàoshi laughed and said:
"I always said you couldn't endure hardship,
and now it's proven true.
Tomorrow morning, I shall send you on your way."
Wáng said:
"I have labored for many days,
if you could impart even a minor skill,
this journey would not have been in vain."
The Dàoshi asked:
"What skill do you seek?"
Wáng said:
"Every time I see you walk,
walls cannot block your path.
If I could just learn this method, it would suffice."
The Dàoshi laughed and agreed.
He then taught him the incantation,
and after having him recite it himself,
shouted:
"Go through!"
Wáng faced the wall
but dared not enter.
The Dàoshi said again:
"Try entering."
Wáng indeed walked calmly toward it,
but was blocked upon reaching the wall.
The Dàoshi said:
"Lower your head and rush in,
do not hesitate!"
Wáng indeed stepped back several paces from the wall,
ran and charged in;
upon reaching the wall,
it felt empty as if nothing were there;
turning to look back,
he was indeed outside the wall.
Overjoyed,
he went in to thank him.
The Dàoshi said:
"When you return, you must maintain purity and integrity,
otherwise it will not work."
He then provided travel funds
and sent him home.
Upon arriving home,
he boasted of meeting an immortal,
claiming that even solid walls could not block him.
His wife did not believe him.
Wáng imitated his earlier actions,
stepped back several feet from the wall,
ran and charged in,
but his head struck the hard wall,
and he fell over abruptly.
His wife helped him up to look,
and a bump had risen on his forehead,
like a large egg.
His wife mocked him.
Wáng, ashamed and angry,
could only curse the old Dàoshi for his lack of virtue.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Hearing this story,
there is no one who does not laugh heartily;
yet they do not realize that in this world, there are many like Wáng Shēng.
Indeed, there are quite a few.
Nowadays, there are vulgar men
who delight in flattery and fear honest criticism,
so there are those who lick ulcers and suck boils,
offering methods to display authority and exert cruelty,
to cater to their wishes,
deceiving them by saying: 'If you employ this method henceforth,
you can act without hindrance.'
At first trial, it may seem somewhat effective,
so they claim that in all the world,
everything can be done this way,
and they will not stop until they hit a hard wall and stumble headlong."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
The Monk of Chángqīng
was of high virtue and purity.
Over seventy years old, he was still healthy.
One day,
he collapsed and could not rise.
The temple monks rushed to help,
but he had already passed away.
The monk himself did not know he was dead;
his soul drifted away
and reached the region of Hénán.
In Hénán, there was the son of a former official,
leading a dozen or so riders,
hawking and hunting rabbits.
His horse bolted,
and he fell to his death.
Their souls happened to meet,
merged seamlessly,
and he gradually revived.
The servants came and asked him.
Opening his eyes, he said:
"How did I get here!"
They helped him back.
Entering the gate,
he saw women with powdered faces and painted eyebrows
gathering around to inquire.
Greatly alarmed, he said:
"I am a monk,
how did I get here!"
His family thought he was delirious,
and together they tried to make him see reason.
The monk did not try to explain himself,
but merely closed his eyes and spoke no more.
When offered plain rice, he ate;
wine and meat he refused.
At night, he slept alone,
not accepting the attentions of wives or concubines.
Several days later,
he suddenly thought of taking a short stroll.
Everyone was delighted.
Once he had gone out,
after he had settled down a bit,
the various servants came in a flurry,
with account books for money and grain,
all mixed together, requesting to settle accounts.
The young master excused himself on grounds of illness and fatigue,
and refused them all.
He only asked:
"Do you know of Chángqīng County in Shāndōng?"
They all replied:
"We know of it."
He said:
"I am depressed and bored,
I wish to go there for a visit,
you should prepare for the journey immediately."
They said he had just recovered,
and should not travel far.
He did not listen,
and set off the next day.
Upon reaching Chángqīng,
he saw the scenery was just as before.
Without needing to ask for directions,
he went straight to the temple.
Several disciples saw the noble guest arrive,
and prostrated themselves in greeting with great respect.
He then asked:
"Where has the old monk gone?"
They replied:
"Our teacher has long since passed away."
He asked for the location of the grave.
The group led him there,
and there was a solitary grave three feet high,
the wild grasses not yet grown over it.
The monks did not know his intention.
Soon after, he prepared his horse to return,
and instructed them:
"Your teacher was a monk of disciplined conduct,
the writings he left behind,
you should reverently preserve,
do not let them be damaged."
The monks all assented.
He then left.
After returning home,
he sat dispirited and wooden,
completely not attending to household affairs.
After residing there for several months,
he went out the door and fled by himself,
going directly to the old temple,
and said to the disciples:
"I am your teacher."
They suspected he was mistaken,
and looked at each other and laughed.
He then recounted the reason for his soul's return,
and also spoke of the deeds of his lifetime,
all of which matched.
They then believed,
let him stay in his old bed,
and served him as in the past.
Later, the young master's family repeatedly sent carriages and horses,
pleading sorrowfully with him,
but he paid them no heed at all.
Another year or so later,
his wife sent a steward,
bringing many gifts.
Gold and silk were all refused,
he only accepted one set of cloth robes.
Sometimes friends would come to his village,
and respectfully visit him.
They saw the man was silent, sincere, and earnest;
his age was only around thirty,
yet he would often speak of events from over eighty years ago.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"When a person dies, the soul disperses;
that which does not disperse over a thousand li,
is due to the nature being settled.
As for the monk,
I do not find strange his rebirth,
but find strange that in a place of dazzling luxury and splendor,
he was able to cut himself off from people and escape the world.
If one's eyes flash for a moment,
and orchids and musk perfume the heart,
there are those who seek death but cannot obtain it,
let alone a monk!"
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
The Snake Charmer A certain man from Dōngjùn
made his living by handling snakes.
He once kept two tame snakes,
both green in color: the larger one he called Dà Qīng,
the smaller one Èr Qīng.
Èr Qīng had a red dot on its forehead,
and was especially clever and tame,
coiling and circling, all as desired.
The snake charmer loved it,
differently from the other snakes.
After a year,
Dà Qīng died,
he thought to fill the vacancy,
but had not yet had the leisure.
One night,
he lodged at a mountain temple.
When it was light,
he opened the bamboo box,
and Èr Qīng was also gone.
The snake charmer was despondent and regretful, almost to death.
He searched darkly and called urgently,
but ultimately there was no trace or sign.
However, whenever he came upon lush woods and thick grass,
he would always release it to go,
letting it be at ease,
and it would soon return: because of this,
he hoped it would come of its own accord.
He sat waiting for it,
the sun already high,
and he had already given up hope,
disgruntled, he then set off.
A few paces out the door,
he heard from within the thicket of firewood and brambles,
a rustling sound.
He stopped his steps and looked back in surprise,
and it was Èr Qīng coming.
Overjoyed,
as if obtaining a precious jade disc.
He rested his load at the roadside,
and the snake also stopped.
Looking behind it,
a small snake was following.
Stroking it, he said:
"I thought you had gone forever.
Is this little companion recommended by you?"
He took out bait to feed it,
and also fed the small snake.
The small snake, though it did not leave,
shrank back timidly and did not dare eat.
Èr Qīng held food in its mouth for it,
just like a host urging a guest.
The snake charmer fed it again,
and then it ate,
after eating,
it followed Èr Qīng into the bamboo box.
Carrying it away, he taught it,
and soon its twists and turns all met the rules,
no different from Èr Qīng in the slightest,
so he named it Xiǎo Qīng.
Performing skills in all directions,
he gained immeasurable profit.
Generally, snake charmers keep their snakes to a length of about two chi;
if they grow too large and heavy,
they are promptly replaced.
—Because Èrqīng was tame,
he was not hastily discarded.
After two or three more years,
he grew to over three chi long,
and when he lay in the basket, it was filled to capacity.
Thus, the snake charmer decided to release him.
One day,
he reached the eastern mountains of Zīyì,
fed Èrqīng a fine morsel,
prayed, and set him free.
After Èrqīng left,
he returned shortly,
wriggling outside the basket.
The snake charmer waved him away, saying:
"Go!
In this world, no feast lasts a hundred years without dispersing.
From now on, hide yourself in the great valleys;
you will surely become a divine dragon.
How can you linger long in a basket?"
The snake then left.
The snake charmer watched him go.
After a while, Èrqīng returned again;
waving him away did not work,
and he bumped his head against the basket.
Xiǎoqīng inside also trembled and stirred.
The snake charmer understood and said:
"Could it be that you wish to bid farewell to Xiǎoqīng?"
He then opened the basket.
Xiǎoqīng came straight out,
and they touched heads and flicked tongues,
as if conversing.
After a while, they wriggled away together.
Just as the snake charmer thought Xiǎoqīng would not return,
soon he came back alone,
creeping desolately,
and finally entered the basket to lie down.
From then on, the snake charmer searched everywhere,
but never found a good one.
Meanwhile, Xiǎoqīng also gradually grew larger
and could no longer be handled.
Later, he obtained another snake,
which was also quite tame,
but it was never as good as Xiǎoqīng.
By then, Xiǎoqīng was already as thick as a child's arm.
Earlier, when Èrqīng was in the mountains,
he was often seen by woodcutters.
After several more years,
he grew several chi long
and as thick around as a bowl;
he gradually began to chase people,
so travelers warned each other
and dared not take that route.
One day,
the snake charmer passed through that area,
and the snake suddenly rushed out like the wind.
The snake charmer was terrified and fled.
The snake pursued him even more urgently,
and looking back, he saw it was about to catch up.
But when he looked at its head,
he saw the distinct red mark
and realized it was Èrqīng.
He put down his load and called out:
"Èrqīng, Èrqīng!"
The snake immediately stopped.
It raised its head for a long time,
then leaped and coiled around the snake charmer,
just as it used to do during performances.
Feeling that its intentions were not malicious,
but its body was huge and heavy,
he could not bear the coiling;
falling to the ground, he cried out and prayed,
and it released him.
It then bumped its head against the basket.
The snake charmer understood its meaning,
opened the basket, and let Xiǎoqīng out.
When the two snakes met,
they intertwined like maltose candy,
and only after a long time did they separate.
The snake charmer then prayed to Xiǎoqīng:
"I have long wanted to part with you;
now you have a companion."
To Èrqīng, he said:
"You originally brought him here;
you may now lead him away.
I have one more word of advice: the deep mountains are not lacking in food and drink;
do not disturb travelers,
lest you incur Heaven's punishment."
The two snakes bowed their heads,
as if accepting the advice.
Suddenly, they rose,
the larger one in front,
the smaller one behind,
and wherever they passed, the trees in the forest parted for them.
The snake charmer stood still and watched them
until they disappeared from sight, then left.
From then on, travelers passed through as usual,
not knowing where they had gone.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"The snake is a dull creature,
yet it clings with the sentiment of an old friend.
Moreover, it accepts advice as easily as turning a circle.
It is only strange that those who appear human,
with friendships forged over ten years of close companionship
or masters who have shown kindness for generations,
often think of pushing them down a well and then throwing stones.
If not,
when offered sincere advice,
they stubbornly disregard it,
even growing angry and hostile.
Such people should be ashamed before these snakes."
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
In Hútián Village, there was a man surnamed Hú
whose brothers went gathering firewood,
venturing deep into a secluded valley.
They encountered a giant python;
the elder brother, walking ahead,
was swallowed by it.
The younger brother was initially terrified and wanted to flee,
but seeing his brother being devoured,
he angrily took out his firewood axe
and struck the python's head.
Though injured, the python did not stop swallowing.
Although the head had already disappeared,
fortunately, the shoulders could not go down.
In his desperation, the younger brother had no other plan;
he grabbed his brother's feet with both hands
and struggled fiercely with the python,
eventually pulling his brother out.
The python, also in pain, slithered away.
Looking at his brother,
he saw that his nose and ears had melted away,
and he was on the verge of death.
Carrying his brother on his back,
he rested over ten times on the way
before finally reaching home.
After half a year of medical treatment and care,
he recovered, but to this day, his face is covered in scars,
with only holes remaining for his nose and ears.
Alas!
Among farmers,
there is indeed such a younger brother!
Some say:
"The python did not harm him
because it was moved by his virtue and righteousness."
Truly so!
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
A merchant named Jiǎ from Qīngzhōu
traveled abroad
and often did not return home for years.
His household kept a white dog,
and his wife led it to mate with her;
the dog became accustomed to it.
One day,
when the husband arrived
and slept with his wife,
the dog suddenly burst in,
leapt onto the bed,
and bit the merchant to death.
Later, the neighbors gradually heard of this
and felt it was unjust;
they brought the case to the authorities.
The official interrogated the woman,
but she refused to confess,
so she was detained.
He ordered the dog to be bound and brought in,
and only then was the woman taken out.
When the dog suddenly saw the woman,
it rushed forward, tore her clothes,
and acted as if to mate.
Only then did the woman have nothing to say.
The official ordered two bailiffs to escort them to the ministry,
one escorting the woman and the other the dog.
Some who wanted to see them mate
pooled money to bribe the bailiffs,
who then brought them together and made them mate.
Wherever they stopped,
the spectators often numbered in the hundreds,
and the bailiffs profited from this.
Later, both the woman and the dog were executed by dismemberment.
Alas!
How vast Heaven and Earth are,
truly nothing is impossible!
Yet, among those with human faces who mate with beasts,
is this woman the only one?
The Historian of the Strange passed judgment, saying:
"To meet by the Pú River,
was censured even in ancient times;
to rendezvous in the mulberry groves,
is something people scorn even now.
Yet this person,
unable to endure the hardship of chaste widowhood,
recklessly longed for the pleasure of illicit union.
A yaksha lay upon the bed,
turned out to be the female beast of the household;
a swift lover entered the hole,
and thus became the paramour beneath the quilt.
Before the terrace of clouds and rain,
she wildly shook her marten-like tail;
within the land of tenderness,
she repeatedly swayed her elephantine waist.
A sharp awl placed within a leather sack,
with one thrust of the thigh it bursts forth;
affection knotted upon the arrow's neck,
as soon as the feather drinks deep, it takes root.
To suddenly conceive of intercourse with a different species,
truly belongs to unthinkable, perverse imaginings.
The dragon-dog barked at adultery, yet became adulterous itself;
jealous, cruel, and murderous,
the laws of Xiāo Hé and Cáo Cān could hardly punish it.
Not a beast in form, yet a beast in truth;
adulterous, filthy, lewd, and rank,
even wolves and tigers would not eat its flesh.
Alas!
For a human committing adultery and murder,
the penalty for a woman is dismemberment;
as for a dog committing adultery and murder,
the world of the living has no punishment for it.
If a human is wicked,
they are punished by being reborn as a dog;
but when a dog is wicked,
the courts of the underworld should be at a loss for law.
It is fitting to dismember it to pursue its soul,
I request it be escorted for interrogation by Yánluó."
According to the manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Lord Wáng Jūncāng,
upon taking up his post in Chǔ,
intended to ascend Lónghǔ Mountain to visit the Celestial Master.
Reaching the lake,
he had just boarded the boat,
when a man arrived in a small skiff,
asking those on the boat to announce him.
The lord saw him,
his appearance tall and imposing.
He produced a name card from his bosom for the Celestial Master,
saying:
"Hearing your entourage was about to arrive,
I was sent ahead to bear the bow."
The lord was surprised he knew in advance,
and revered him all the more,
proceeding with sincere intent.
The Celestial Master prepared a feast to host him.
Those serving him,
in their dress, caps, beards, and whiskers,
mostly did not resemble ordinary people.
The earlier messenger also attended at his side.
After a short while,
he whispered to the Celestial Master.
The Celestial Master said to the lord:
"This gentleman is from your hometown,
do you not recognize him?"
The lord inquired who it was.
He said:
"This is the Hail God Lǐ Zuǒchē, as transmitted in the world."
The lord, startled, changed his expression.
The Celestial Master said:
"He just mentioned receiving an imperial decree to send down hail,
hence he is taking his leave."
The lord asked,
"Where to?"
He said:
"Zhāngqiū."
As it bordered his own district, the lord was concerned,
and rising from his seat, begged for exemption.
The Celestial Master said:
"This is the Jade Emperor's decree,
the hail has a prescribed amount,
how can I show favoritism?"
The lord pleaded incessantly.
The Celestial Master pondered for a long while,
then looked at the god and instructed:
"Let much of it fall in the valleys and mountains,
just do not harm the crops, that will do."
He further instructed:
"A noble guest is present,
go civilly, not martially."
The god went out,
reached the courtyard,
when suddenly smoke arose beneath his feet,
mist swirling all around the ground.
After a moment's delay,
with great effort he soared up,
only as high as the courtyard trees;
he rose again,
higher than the towers and pavilions.
With a clap of thunder,
he flew northwards,
the buildings shook,
the feast vessels rattled and swayed.
The lord exclaimed in astonishment:
"His departure creates thunderclaps!"
The Celestial Master said:
"I admonished him just now,
that's why he delayed;
otherwise,
with a single peal from level ground,
he would have been gone."
The lord bid farewell and returned,
noted the date,
and sent someone to inquire in Zhāngqiū.
That day, there truly was a great hailstorm,
the ditches and channels were all full,
yet in the fields there were only a few pellets.
According to the manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Yīn Tiāngōng of Lìchéng,
was poor in his youth,
but had courage and resourcefulness.
In the county, there was an old mansion,
covering several dozen *mǔ*,
with interconnected buildings and structures.
Strange phenomena were often seen there,
and for this reason it was abandoned, with no one living there;
after a long time,
weeds gradually overran it,
and even in broad daylight, none dared enter.
Once, Yīn was drinking with some scholars,
and someone joked:
"If anyone can spend a night there,
we'll all chip in for a feast."
Yīn sprang up and said:
"What's so difficult about that!"
He took a mat and went.
The others saw him to the gate,
joking:
"We'll wait here a while,
if you see anything,
shout for help immediately."
Yīn laughed and said:
"If there are ghosts or foxes,
I'll catch them as evidence."
He then entered,
seeing tall sedge grass obscuring the paths,
mugwort and wormwood thick as hemp.
It was the time of the first quarter moon,
fortunately the moonlight was dim and yellowish,
allowing the doors and windows to be discerned.
Groping his way through several courtyards,
he finally reached the rear building.
Ascending the moon-viewing terrace,
he found it clean and lovely,
and so settled there.
Looking west, the moon was bright,
only a sliver remained above the mountain line.
He sat for a long time,
with not the slightest unusual occurrence,
and secretly laughed at the falseness of the rumors.
Spreading his mat on the ground, using a stone as a pillow,
he lay watching the Herdboy and Weaving Maid stars.
