As the first watch drew to a close,
he grew drowsy and was about to doze off
when he heard footsteps downstairs
coming up in a noisy shuffle.
Pretending to sleep, he peeked out of the corner of his eye
and saw a servant in black clothes
holding a lotus-shaped lantern.
Suddenly catching sight of Yīn,
he started and drew back.
He said to those behind him:
"There's a living person here."
Someone below asked:
"Who is it?"
He answered:
"I don't know."
Soon an old man came up,
looked closely at Yīn,
and said:
"This is Minister Yīn.
He is already fast asleep.
Just attend to our business.
The minister is broad-minded;
he may not scold or blame us."
Then they all entered the building together,
and all the doors were opened wide.
After a while,
more and more people came and went.
The lights in the building were as bright as day.
Yīn shifted slightly
and gave a sneeze and a cough.
Hearing that Yīn was awake,
the old man came out,
knelt down, and said:
"I have a humble daughter
who is getting married tonight.
I did not expect to disturb a noble guest.
I hope you will not take deep offense."
Yīn got up,
helped him to his feet, and said:
"I did not know that tonight was such a joyous occasion.
I am ashamed that I have nothing to offer as a congratulatory gift."
The old man said:
"For a noble guest to grace us with your presence
is enough to ward off evil spirits.
That is already a great fortune.
If you would trouble yourself to join us and sit with us,
it would bring us even greater honor."
Yīn was pleased
and agreed.
He entered and looked around the building;
the furnishings were fragrant and beautiful.
Then a woman came out and bowed.
She appeared to be over forty years old.
The old man said:
"This is my humble wife."
Yīn bowed to her.
Soon he heard the clamor of reed pipes and music,
and someone came running up,
saying:
"They're here!"
The old man hurried to welcome them,
and Yīn also stood waiting.
After a short while,
a cluster of lanterns veiled in gauze
led the bridegroom in.
He appeared to be seventeen or eighteen years old,
handsome and youthful.
The old man told him to first pay respects to the honored guest.
The young man looked at Yīn.
Yīn acted as the groomsman,
performing the half-host ritual.
Next, the father-in-law and son-in-law exchanged bows.
After that,
they took their seats.
A short while later,
beautiful women came in like clouds,
and wine and meat were served in abundance like mist,
with jade bowls and golden cups
glittering on the tables.
After several rounds of wine,
the old man called a maid to ask the young lady to come out.
The maid assented and went in,
but did not come out for a long time.
The old man got up himself,
lifted the curtain, and urged her.
Soon several maids and elderly women escorted the bride out,
with the tinkling of jade pendants
and the fragrance of musk and orchids wafting about.
The old man told her to bow upward.
After rising,
she sat beside her mother.
Yīn glanced at her slightly:
with emerald hairpins and bright earrings,
her beauty was unparalleled in the world.
Then they poured wine into a golden goblet,
which could hold several dou.
Yīn thought that this object could be taken as proof to show his companions,
so he secretly tucked it into his sleeve.
Pretending to be drunk, he leaned on the table,
slumped over, and fell asleep.
Everyone said:
"The minister is drunk."
Not long after,
the bridegroom announced his departure.
Reed pipes and music suddenly burst forth,
and they all went downstairs and left in a flurry.
Afterward, the host gathered the wine vessels,
but found one goblet missing.
They searched everywhere but could not find it.
Someone quietly suggested that the sleeping guest might have taken it. The old man hastily warned them not to speak,
fearing that Yīn might hear.
After a while,
both inside and outside grew quiet,
and Yīn finally got up.
It was dark, with no lights,
only the scent of rouge and the smell of wine
filling the four walls.
Seeing that the east was already bright,
he leisurely went out.
Feeling in his sleeve,
he found the golden goblet still there.
When he reached the gate,
the other scholars were already waiting there,
suspecting that he had gone out at night and returned early.
Yīn took out the goblet and showed it to them.
They were astonished and asked about it,
and Yīn told them what had happened.
They all thought that such an object was not something a poor scholar would possess,
so they believed him.
Later, Yīn passed the jìnshì examination
and was appointed to an official post in Féiqiū.
A wealthy family named Zhū held a banquet for him
and ordered a large wine cup to be brought,
but it did not come for a long time.
A young servant covered his mouth and whispered to the host,
and the host showed an angry expression.
Soon, a golden goblet was presented to urge the guest to drink.
Looking closely at it,
its style and carved patterns
were no different from the fox's object.
Greatly puzzled,
he asked where it was made.
The host replied:
"There are eight such goblets in total.
When my father was a high official in the capital,
he sought skilled craftsmen to supervise their making.
These are heirlooms,
carefully stored away for a long time.
Because you, the esteemed prefect, have graced us with your presence,
we just took them from the chest.
Only seven remained;
we suspected that a servant had stolen one.
But the dust that had accumulated over ten years was undisturbed,
which is truly inexplicable."
Yīn laughed and said:
"The golden cup has taken flight like a feathered immortal.
However, a family heirloom should not be lost.
I happen to have one,
quite similar to it,
which I shall present to you as a gift."
After the banquet ended, he returned to his office,
selected the goblet, and sent it over by fast horse.
The host examined it carefully
and was utterly astonished.
He personally went to thank Yīn
and asked where it came from.
Yīn then recounted the whole story from beginning to end.
Only then did they realize that something from a thousand miles away
could be taken by a fox,
but it dared not keep it forever.
Based on the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Scholar Kǒng Xuělì
was a descendant of Confucius.
He was refined and cultured,
skilled in poetry.
A close friend of his was appointed magistrate of Tiāntāi,
and he sent a letter inviting him.
Kǒng went,
but the magistrate had just died.
Stranded and unable to return,
he stayed at Pǔtuó Temple,
working as a copyist for the temple monks.
About a hundred paces west of the temple,
there was the residence of a Mr. Shàn.
Mr. Shàn was originally from a wealthy family,
but due to a major lawsuit, his fortunes declined.
With few family members left,
he moved to the countryside,
and the house was left empty.
One day,
a heavy snow was swirling down,
and there were no travelers on the road.
By chance, he passed by the gate of the house,
and a young man came out,
whose demeanor was exceptionally elegant.
Seeing the scholar,
he hurried over to greet him,
offered a few words of consolation,
and immediately invited him inside.
The scholar was delighted with him,
and readily followed him in.
The rooms were not particularly spacious,
but everywhere was hung with brocade curtains,
and the walls were adorned with many ancient paintings and calligraphy.
On the desk was a book,
with a label that read:
"Lánghuán Suǒjì."
Flipping through it,
he found it contained things he had never seen before.
Since the scholar lived in the Shàn family's residence,
he assumed the young man was the master of the house,
and thus did not inquire about his official background.
The young man carefully asked about his circumstances,
felt pity for him,
and advised him to set up a school and take on students.
The scholar sighed and said:
"A traveler like me,
who would act as my patron?"
The young man said:
"If you do not reject me as a dull and clumsy student,
I would like to become your disciple."
The scholar was pleased,
but did not dare accept the role of teacher,
and instead asked to be friends.
He then asked:
"Why has this house been closed for so long?"
The reply was:
"This is the Shàn family's residence.
Previously, because the young master lived in the countryside,
it has long been unoccupied.
I am of the Huángfǔ family,
and my ancestors lived in Shǎn.
Because our family home was burned in a wildfire,
we are temporarily borrowing this place to settle."
Only then did the scholar realize he was not from the Shàn family.
That evening,
they talked and laughed very happily,
and he was invited to share the same bed.
At daybreak,
a servant boy lit a charcoal fire in the room.
The young man got up first and went inside,
while the scholar was still sitting wrapped in the quilt.
The servant entered,
and announced:
"The old master has come."
The scholar rose in surprise.
An old man entered,
his hair and temples white,
and earnestly thanked the scholar, saying:
"Sir, you did not disdain my stubborn son,
and were willing to instruct him.
The boy is just beginning to learn, scribbling like a crow,
so please do not, on account of your friendship,
treat him as your equal."
Then he presented a set of brocade clothes,
and a sable hat, socks, and shoes, each as a gift.
After watching the scholar wash and comb,
he called for wine and served food.
The tables, couches, robes, and clothes—
he did not know their names—
shone with dazzling brilliance.
After several rounds of wine,
the old man rose to take his leave,
and leaning on his cane, departed.
After the meal,
the young master presented his lessons,
which were all classical prose and poetry,
with none of the contemporary examination essays.
When asked about this,
he smiled and said:
"I do not seek official advancement."
As evening approached,
they drank again, and he said:
"Tonight we shall enjoy ourselves to the fullest,
but tomorrow it will not be allowed."
He called to the servant:
"Go see if the old master has retired;
if he has,
quietly summon Xiāngnú here."
The servant left,
and first brought a pipa in an embroidered bag.
After a short while,
a maid entered,
her red attire stunningly beautiful.
The young master ordered her to play "Xiāngfēi."
The maid plucked the strings with an ivory plectrum,
producing stirring, mournful, and intense melodies,
with rhythms unlike any he had heard before.
He then ordered large goblets for drinking,
and they did not finish until the third watch.
The next day,
they rose early to study together.
The young master was extremely bright,
able to recite after a single reading,
and after two or three months,
his writing became remarkably sharp and outstanding.
They agreed to drink together every five days,
and each time they drank, Xiāngnú was always summoned.
One evening,
drunk and flushed with excitement,
he fixed his gaze on her.
The young master already understood his thoughts,
and said:
"This maid is raised by my father.
You, brother, are alone and without a family,
and I have been thinking about this day and night for a long time.
I will soon find a good match for you."
The scholar said:
"If you truly wish to do me this kindness,
it must be someone like Xiāngnú."
The young master laughed and said:
"You are truly one who 'has seen little and marvels at much.'
If you consider this as the ideal,
then your wishes are easily satisfied."
After half a year,
the scholar wanted to go for a stroll in the outskirts.
When he reached the gate,
he found it locked from the outside.
He asked about it.
Gōngzǐ said:
"My father is afraid that socializing might distract your thoughts,
so he has declined visitors."
The scholar accepted this calmly.
At the time, it was the height of summer, hot and humid,
so he moved his study to the garden pavilion.
A swelling the size of a peach appeared on the scholar's chest,
and in one night it grew as large as a bowl,
causing him great pain and making him groan.
Gōngzǐ attended to him day and night,
neglecting both sleep and food.
After several more days,
the sore worsened,
and he stopped eating and drinking altogether.
Tàigōng also came,
and they faced each other with heavy sighs.
Gōngzǐ said:
"The other night, I was thinking about your illness, sir,
and remembered that my younger sister Jiāonuó can cure it.
I sent someone to our maternal grandfather's place to summon her back.
Why has she not arrived yet?"
Soon a servant boy entered and said:
"Miss Nuó has arrived,
and our aunt and cousin Sōnggū have come with her."
Father and son hurried inside.
After a short while,
they led the younger sister to see the scholar.
She was about thirteen or fourteen years old,
with charming, intelligent eyes,
and a slender, graceful figure like a willow.
When the scholar saw her beauty,
his groans ceased instantly,
and his spirits were greatly refreshed.
Gōngzǐ then said:
"This elder brother is a good friend,
no less than a sibling.
Sister, please treat him well."
The girl then composed her shy expression,
rolled up her long sleeves,
and approached the bed to examine him.
While holding his wrist,
he felt a fragrance more delightful than orchids.
The girl smiled and said:
"No wonder you have this illness—
your heart pulse is agitated.
Though the condition is critical,
it can be cured;
but the hardened lump of flesh has already solidified,
so cutting away the skin and flesh is necessary."
She then removed a gold bracelet from her arm and placed it over the affected area,
slowly pressing it down.
The sore protruded about an inch,
rising above the bracelet,
while the remaining swelling around the base
was all contained within it,
no longer as wide as a bowl as before.
Then, with one hand, she opened her silk garment,
took out a small knife,
whose blade was thinner than paper.
Holding the bracelet and the knife,
she gently cut along the base.
Purple blood flowed freely,
staining the bed mat,
but the scholar, captivated by her beauty,
not only felt no pain,
but even feared that the cutting would finish too quickly,
ending their close proximity.
Soon,
she cut away the rotten flesh,
which came off in a round lump like a gall cut from a tree.
She then called for water
to wash the cut area.
She spat out a red pill from her mouth,
the size of a bullet,
placed it on the flesh,
and pressed it to make it rotate: after just one revolution,
he felt a steaming heat;
after a second revolution,
a tingling itch;
after the third revolution,
a cool sensation spread throughout his body,
penetrating to the marrow.
The girl retrieved the pill and swallowed it,
saying:
"You are cured!"
She hurried out.
The scholar leaped up to thank her,
as if his severe illness had vanished.
But he could not stop thinking about her radiant beauty,
tormented by longing.
From then on, he abandoned his books and sat in a daze,
feeling utterly listless.
Gōngzǐ had already noticed this,
and said:
"I have found a good match for you, elder brother."
The scholar asked:
"Who is it?"
Gōngzǐ replied:
"She is also a relative of mine."
The scholar pondered for a long time,
then merely said:
"There is no need."
Facing the wall, he recited:
"Having seen the ocean, other waters seem unworthy;
having seen the clouds over Wūshān, no other clouds are clouds."
Gōngzǐ understood his meaning,
and said:
"My father admires your great talent
and has long wished to form a marriage alliance.
But he has only one younger sister,
who is too young.
There is my aunt's daughter, Ā Sōng,
who is eighteen years old
and quite refined.
If you do not believe me,
Sister Sōng often strolls in the garden pavilion.
If you wait in the front wing,
you can see her."
The scholar followed his advice
and indeed saw Jiāonuó coming with a beautiful lady.
Her painted eyebrows were like curved moth antennae,
her tiny feet like lotus hooks treading on phoenixes,
and she was nearly a match for Jiāonuó.
The scholar was overjoyed
and asked Gōngzǐ to act as matchmaker.
The next day, Gōngzǐ came out from the inner quarters
and congratulated him:
"It is settled."
They then prepared another courtyard
for the scholar's wedding ceremony.
That evening,
drums and pipes filled the air,
and dust swirled like flying mist.
To have the fairy he had admired
suddenly sharing his bed and curtains
made him doubt whether the Moon Palace
was truly up in the clouds.
After the wedding ceremony,
he was deeply satisfied.
One evening,
Gōngzǐ said to the scholar:
"The benefit of our mutual encouragement
can never be forgotten.
Recently, Shàn Gōngzǐ has resolved his lawsuit and returned,
demanding this residence urgently.
We intend to abandon this place and move west.
It seems unlikely we will meet again,
so feelings of parting weigh heavily on my heart."
The scholar expressed his wish to follow them.
Gōngzǐ advised him to return to his hometown,
but the scholar found it difficult.
Gōngzǐ said:
"Do not worry,
I can send you off immediately."
Soon after,
Tàigōng led Sōngniáng over
and presented the scholar with a hundred taels of gold.
Gōngzǐ then took the hands of the scholar and his wife with both of his own,
instructing them to close their eyes and not look.
They felt themselves floating through the air,
hearing only the sound of wind in their ears.
After a long time, Gōngzǐ said:
"We have arrived."
They opened their eyes
and indeed saw their old hometown.
Only then did they realize that Gōngzǐ was not human.
Joyfully, they knocked on their door.
His mother came out, astonished beyond expectation,
and upon seeing the beautiful bride,
they shared their happiness and relief.
But when they looked back,
Gōngzǐ had already vanished.
Sōngniáng served her mother-in-law with filial piety;
her beauty and virtuous reputation
became known far and wide.
Later, the young man passed the imperial examination and
was appointed as a judicial officer in Yán'ān,
taking his family along to assume his post.
His mother did not go due to the long journey.
Sōngniáng gave birth to a son,
named Xiǎoguān.
The young man offended an imperial inspector,
was dismissed from office,
and was entangled in difficulties, unable to return home.
While hunting in the wilderness one day,
he encountered a handsome youth,
riding a black steed,
who kept looking back at him.
Upon closer inspection,
it turned out to be Young Master Huángfǔ.
They reined in their horses and stopped,
overwhelmed with both sorrow and joy.
The young master invited him to his home,
and they arrived at a village
where the trees were dense and dark,
shading the sky and sun.
Entering the house,
he saw golden studs on the door,
resembling a noble family's residence.
He asked about his younger sister,
and was told she had married;
his mother-in-law,
had already passed away,
which deeply saddened him.
After staying overnight, he bid farewell and left,
returning with his wife.
Jiāonuó also came,
picked up the child and played with him, saying:
"Sister has muddled our lineage."
The young man bowed in gratitude for her past kindness.
She laughed and said:
"Brother-in-law is now noble.
The wound has healed,
but have you forgotten the pain?"
Her husband, Wú Láng,
also came to pay his respects.
They stayed for two nights before leaving.
One day,
the young master looked worried,
and said to the young man:
"A calamity has descended from heaven.
Can you save us?"
The young man did not know what the matter was,
but bravely took on the responsibility.
The young master hurried out,
summoned the entire family inside,
and they all knelt and bowed in the hall.
The young man was greatly alarmed,
and urgently asked for an explanation.
The young master said:
"I am not human,
but a fox.
Now we face a thunderbolt calamity.
If you are willing to risk your life to help us,
our whole family may survive;
otherwise,
please take your son and leave,
so as not to be implicated."
The young man swore to share life and death with them.
He was then instructed to stand guard at the door with a sword,
and was told:
"When the thunderbolts strike,
do not move!"
The young man followed the instructions.
Indeed, he saw dark clouds shrouding the daytime,
turning everything pitch black.
Looking back at the former residence,
there was no longer any gate or house,
only a towering grave mound,
with a bottomless pit.
Just as he was bewildered,
a thunderclap roared,
shaking the mountains;
torrential rain and fierce winds
uprooted old trees.
The young man was dazzled and deafened,
but stood firm without moving.
Suddenly, amidst the dense smoke and black haze,
he saw a demonic creature,
with sharp beak and long claws,
snatching a person from the pit,
and ascending with the smoke.
Catching a glimpse of the clothing and shoes,
he thought it resembled Jiāonuó.
He leaped into the air,
struck it with his sword,
and it fell to the ground.
Suddenly, a thunderbolt exploded violently,
and the young man collapsed,
dying on the spot.
After a while,
the sky cleared,
and Jiāonuó was able to revive herself.
Seeing the young man dead beside her,
she wailed:
"Master Kǒng died for me,
how can I live on!"
Sōngniáng also came out,
and together they carried the young man back.
Jiāonuó had Sōngniáng hold his head;
her brother used a golden hairpin to pry open his teeth;
she herself held his chin,
and with her tongue passed a red pill into his mouth,
then kissed him and breathed into him.
The red pill entered his throat with the breath,
making a rattling sound.
After a while,
he woke up as if from a dream.
Seeing his family gathered before him,
he felt as if awakening from a dream.
Thus, the whole family was reunited,
and after the shock subsided, they rejoiced.
The young man thought the dark tomb was no place to live long,
and proposed returning to his hometown together.
Everyone in the hall agreed,
only Jiāonuó was unhappy.
The young man invited Wú Láng to come along,
but worried that the old couple would not leave their young son,
so they discussed all day without reaching a conclusion.
Suddenly, a young servant from the Wú family,
sweating and panting, arrived.
Startled, they questioned him closely,
and learned that Wú Láng's family had also suffered the calamity on the same day,
and the entire household had perished.
Jiāonuó stamped her feet in grief,
weeping uncontrollably.
Everyone comforted and consoled her.
Thus, the plan to return together was decided.
The young man went into the city,
settled some matters over several days,
and then hurriedly packed overnight.
After returning home,
he housed the young master in a secluded garden,
often keeping the gate locked;
only when he and Sōngniáng came
would the gate be opened.
The young man, the young master, and his sister
played chess, drank, and conversed,
as if they were one family.
Xiǎoguān grew up,
handsome and elegant,
with a fox-like air.
When he went out to the city,
everyone knew he was the fox's son.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Regarding Master Kǒng,
I do not envy him for gaining a beautiful wife,
but rather for gaining an intimate friend.
Gazing upon her appearance can make one forget hunger,
listening to her voice can bring a smile to one's face.
To have such a good friend,
to converse and feast with from time to time,
is to experience 'souls mingling through mutual attraction,'
which is even better than 'disordered garments.'"
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
A man named Zhāng died suddenly,
and was taken away by ghostly messengers,
to see the King of the Underworld.
The King checked the register,
and angrily scolded the ghostly messengers for mistakenly capturing him,
ordering them to send him back.
As Zhāng descended,
he privately begged the ghostly messengers,
asking to see the hells of the underworld.
The ghost led him through the nine netherworlds,
pointing out each one: the Mountain of Knives, the Forest of Swords.
Finally, they arrived at a place
where a monk had a rope threaded through his thigh and was hung upside down,
screaming in agony as if about to die.
Looking closer,
it turned out to be his elder brother.
Zhāng was shocked and grieved to see him,
and asked:
"What crime brought you to this?"
The ghost said:
"He was a monk
who extensively collected money,
using it all for debauchery and gambling,
so he is punished thus.
To escape this torment,
he must repent on his own."
After Zhāng revived,
he suspected his brother had already died.
At that time, his brother resided at Xìngfú Temple,
so he went to visit him.
Upon entering the gate,
he immediately heard his brother's cries of pain.
Entering the room,
he saw sores on his thighs,
with pus and blood bursting forth,
and his feet hung on the wall,
exactly like the upside-down hanging in the underworld.
Astonished, he asked the reason.
The brother said:
"Hanging it up gives slight relief;
otherwise, the pain pierces my heart and innards."
Zhāng then told him what he had seen.
The monk was greatly terrified,
and thereafter abstained from meat and wine,
devoutly reciting sutras and incantations.
Within half a month, he gradually recovered.
Thus, he became an ascetic monk.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"The hells of ghosts are vague and distant,
and evildoers often use this to excuse themselves;
yet they do not know that the calamities in the bright world
are precisely the punishments of the dark realm.
How can one not fear them!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
There was a man named Yú,
who in his youth was chivalrous,
fond of martial arts,
and strong enough to wield a heavy kettle,
whirling it like a whirlwind dance.
During the Chóngzhēn era,
he went to the capital for the palace examination,
but his servant fell ill and could not rise,
which troubled him.
It happened that there was a skilled fortune-teller in the market
who could determine life and death,
so Yú decided to consult him on behalf of his servant.
Upon arriving,
he had not yet spoken
when the fortune-teller said:
"Do you wish to inquire about your servant's illness?"
Yú, astonished, affirmed it.
The fortune-teller said:
"The sick one is not in danger,
but you, sir, are in peril."
Yú then asked to have his own fortune told.
The fortune-teller cast the hexagram,
and said in astonishment:
"You will die in three days!"
Yú was shocked and bewildered for a long while.
The fortune-teller calmly said:
"I have a small technique;
if you repay me with ten taels of gold,
I can perform a ritual to avert it for you."
Yú thought to himself
that life and death are predetermined;
how could any technique alter it?
He gave no answer, stood up,
and prepared to leave.
The fortune-teller said:
"Regret this small expense,
and do not repent, do not repent!"
Those who cared for Yú were all afraid for him,
urging him to empty his purse to plead with the fortune-teller.
Yú did not listen.
Suddenly, the third day arrived.
Yú sat upright in the inn,
calmly observing,
and the whole day passed without incident.
When night fell,
he closed the door, lit the lamp,
and sat vigil with his sword at the ready.
As the first watch was nearly ending,
there was still no sign of death.
Just as he thought to retire to bed,
he suddenly heard a sound from the window crack.
Looking quickly,
he saw a small man carrying a spear entering;
upon reaching the ground,
he grew to human height.
Yú seized his sword and rose,
striking swiftly,
but the figure dodged and was not hit.
It then swiftly shrank,
seeking the window crack again,
intending to escape.
Yú struck swiftly at it,
and it fell at his touch.
Holding the candle to it,
he saw it was a paper man,
already cut in half at the waist.
Yú dared not lie down,
and sat waiting again.
After a while,
a creature came through the window,
grotesque and fierce like a ghost.
As soon as it touched the ground,
Yú struck swiftly,
cutting it into two pieces,
both of which wriggled.
Fearing it might rise again,
he struck repeatedly,
each blow hitting its mark,
but the sound was not soft.
Upon closer inspection,
it was a clay figurine,
already shattered into pieces.
Thereupon, he moved to sit by the window,
fixing his gaze on the crack.
After a long time,
he heard outside the window a sound like an ox panting,
and something pushed against the window lattice,
shaking the walls of the room,
threatening to collapse them.
Fearing being crushed,
Yú reckoned it better to go out and fight it,
so he suddenly unbolted the door
and rushed out.
He saw a giant ghost,
as tall as the eaves;
in the dim moonlight,
he saw its face was black as coal,
its eyes gleaming with a yellow light;
it wore no clothes above,
no shoes below,
holding a bow in hand and arrows at its waist.
Just as Yú was astonished,
the ghost drew its bow.
Yú used his sword to deflect the arrow,
which fell to the ground;
he tried to strike,
but the ghost drew again.
Yú quickly leaped aside to avoid it,
the arrow piercing the wall
with a clattering sound.
The ghost grew even angrier,
drew its saber,
and swung it like the wind,
aiming to cleave Yú with all its might.
Yú darted forward like a monkey,
the saber striking the courtyard stone,
which broke instantly.
Yú slipped between its legs,
slashing at the ghost's ankle,
producing a clanging sound.
The ghost roared like thunder in fury,
turned, and chopped again.
Yú ducked low once more;
the saber fell,
cutting his robe.
Yú had already reached under its ribs,
and hacked fiercely,
again producing a clanging sound,
and the ghost fell stiff.
Yú struck it wildly,
the sound hard like knocking on wood.
Holding the candle to it,
he saw it was a wooden puppet,
as tall as a man.
The bow and arrows were still wrapped around its waist,
carved with a ferocious expression;
where the sword had struck,
blood flowed.
Yú then held the candle until dawn,
and realized that these ghostly creatures were all sent by the fortune-teller,
intending to cause his death
to prove the efficacy of his technique.
The next day,
he informed all his friends,
and together they went to the diviner's place.
From afar, the diviner saw the gentleman,
and in a flash he was nowhere to be seen.
Someone said:
"This is the art of invisibility.
Dog blood can break it."
The gentleman followed this advice,
and prepared accordingly before going.
The diviner hid again as before.
Quickly, they splashed dog blood on the spot where he stood,
and only then did they see the diviner's head and face,
all smeared with dog blood,
his eyes glaring like a ghost standing there.
So they seized him and handed him over to the authorities, who executed him.
The Chronicler of the Tales remarks:
"I have always said that consulting diviners is a folly.
In this world, how many who practice this art can avoid error in matters of life and death?
If the divination is wrong,
it is as good as not having divined at all.
Moreover, even if they clearly tell me the arrival of my death,
what then can I do?
Especially since there are those who borrow human lives to make their arts seem divine—
isn't that even more terrifying!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
During the rebellion of Yú Qī,
people were slaughtered like hemp.
A villager named Lǐ Huàlóng
fled back from the mountains.
Encountering troops marching by night,
he feared he would suffer the calamity of being caught in the crossfire,
and having no place to hide in his panic,
he lay stiff among a pile of dead bodies,
pretending to be a corpse.
After the troops had all passed,
he still did not dare to come out immediately.
Suddenly, he saw headless and armless corpses
rising up like a forest.
Among them was a corpse with its severed head still attached to its shoulder,
and from its mouth came words:
"The wild dog is coming,
what shall we do?"
The group of corpses responded in uneven voices:
"What shall we do!"
In a moment,
they all toppled over with a thud,
and then there was silence.
Just as Lǐ, trembling with fear, was about to get up,
a creature came,
with the head of a beast and the body of a man,
crouching to bite people's heads,
sucking out their brains one by one.
Terrified,
Lǐ hid his head beneath a corpse.
The creature came and pushed Lǐ's shoulder,
trying to get at his head.
Lǐ pressed down with all his strength,
so it could not succeed.
The creature then pushed aside the covering corpse and moved it,
exposing Lǐ's head.
In great fear,
Lǐ groped around his waist,
and found a stone as big as a bowl,
which he gripped.
The creature bent down to bite.
Lǐ suddenly sprang up,
shouting loudly,
and struck its head,
hitting its mouth.
The creature howled like an owl,
covered its mouth, and ran away in pain,
spitting blood on the road.
Going to look,
he found two teeth in the blood,
curved in the middle and sharp at the ends,
over four inches long.
He took them back to show people,
but no one knew what kind of creature it was.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Liú Xiàolián
could remember events from his previous lives.
He was a fellow graduate with my late elder brother Wén Bēn,
and often recounted them in detail.
In one life, he was a gentleman-official,
but his conduct was often flawed.
He died at the age of sixty-two.
When he first saw the King of the Underworld,
he was treated with the courtesy due a village elder,
offered a seat,
and served tea.
Glancing at the King's cup,
he saw the tea was clear and pure;
in his own cup,
it was murky like muddy wine.
Secretly, he wondered if this might be the Soul-Confusing Soup?
Taking advantage of the King looking away,
he poured the contents of his cup under the corner of the table,
pretending to have drunk it all.
the King checked the record of his past evils;
enraged,
he ordered the ghosts to drag him down,
and punished him by making him a horse.
Immediately, a fierce ghost led him away.
Arriving at a house,
the threshold was very high,
and he could not cross it.
Just as he was hesitating,
the ghost struck him hard,
and the pain was so intense that he fell.
Looking at himself,
he found his body already under a manger.
Then he heard someone say:
"The black mare has given birth to a foal,
a male."
His mind was very clear,
but he could not speak.
Feeling very hungry,
he had no choice
but to seek milk from the mare.
After four or five years,
he grew tall and strong.
He greatly feared beatings,
and would flee in fear at the sight of a whip.
When his master rode him,
he would always use a saddlecloth,
holding the reins loosely and going slowly,
so it was still bearable;
but when the servants or grooms
rode without saddle or gear,
their ankles clamping and striking,
the pain pierced his heart.
Thus, in great anger,
he refused to eat for three days,
and died.
Arriving in the underworld,
the King of the Underworld found that his punishment period was not yet complete,
rebuked him for evading it,
stripped off his hide,
and punished him by making him a dog.
Disheartened and resentful,
he refused to go.
The ghosts beat him wildly,
and in extreme pain, he fled into the wilderness.
Thinking it better to die,
in anger he threw himself off a cliff,
but fell and could not get up.
Looking at himself,
he found his body lying in a den,
with a female dog licking and nurturing him—
then he knew he had been reborn into the human world again.
As he grew a little,
he knew that excrement was filthy;
yet he smelled it and found it fragrant,
but he resolved not to eat it.
After being a dog for a year,
he often wished to die in anger,
but feared being punished again for evasion.
Moreover, his master kept and fed him,
unwilling to kill him.
So he deliberately bit his master,
tearing off a piece of flesh from his thigh.
Enraged,
the master beat him to death with a stick.
The King of the Underworld examined the case,
angered by his madness,
whipped him hundreds of times,
and made him a snake.
Imprisoned in a dark room,
he could not see the sky.
Feeling very stifled,
he climbed up the wall,
and burrowed out through the roof.
Looking at himself,
he found his body lying in thick grass—
he was indeed a snake.
So he vowed not to harm living creatures,
and when hungry, he swallowed fruits.
After more than a year,
he often thought of suicide but could not bring himself to do it,
nor could he bear to harm others to bring about his own death;
he wanted to find a good way to die but had not yet found one.
One day,
lying in the grass,
he heard a carriage passing,
and suddenly darted out onto the road;
the carriage ran over him,
cutting him in two.
The King of the Underworld was surprised at his speedy arrival.
He then prostrated himself and explained his situation.
The King of the Underworld saw that he had been killed without guilt,
pardoned him,
and allowed him to return as a human after his term was fulfilled.
This was Liú Gōng.
From birth, Liú Gōng could speak,
and when it came to literature, books, and history,
he could recite them after just one reading.
In the year Xīnyǒu, he passed the provincial examination.
He often advised people: When riding a horse, one must use thick saddle flaps;
the punishment of being squeezed between the thighs
is worse than being whipped.
The Chronicler of the Tales remarks:
"Among creatures with fur and horns,
there are indeed princes, dukes, and great men;
the reason for this
is that among princes, dukes, and great men,
there are originally those who are no different from creatures with fur and horns.
Thus, when the lowly do good,
it is like planting a tree to seek flowers;
when the noble do good,
it is like nurturing the roots after the flowers have already bloomed: planting can lead to greatness,
nurturing can lead to longevity.
Otherwise,
they will end up pulling salt carts,
enduring bridles and reins,
becoming horses;
otherwise,
they will end up eating waste and fluids,
enduring slaughter and carving,
becoming dogs;
or otherwise,
they will end up covered in scales and shells,
buried in the bellies of cranes and storks,
becoming snakes."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
The wife of the Shí family in Wàn Village
was haunted by a fox,
troubled by it,
but unable to drive it away.
Behind the door was a vase,
and whenever she heard her father-in-law coming,
the fox would hide inside it.
The wife observed this closely,
secretly forming a plan without saying a word.
One day,
the fox slipped inside.
The wife quickly stuffed its mouth with cotton,
placed it in a pot,
and boiled it with scalding water.
As the vase heated up,
the fox cried out:
"It's too hot!
Don't play such a wicked trick."
The wife remained silent.
The fox screamed even more urgently,
but after a while, there was no sound.
She pulled out the cotton and checked,
finding only a pile of fur
and a few drops of blood.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
During the rebellion of Xiè Qiān,
the mansions of officials all became dens of bandits.
The residence of Education Commissioner Wáng Qīxiāng
was especially crowded with thieves.
When the city fell and soldiers entered,
they swept away the mob of villains,
filling the courtyard with corpses,
and blood flowed up to the gate.
When Wáng Gōng entered the city,
he cleared the corpses, washed away the blood, and lived there.
Often, ghosts were seen during the day;
at night, phosphorescent lights flew beneath the beds,
and ghosts wailed in the corners.
One day,
a scholar named Wáng Hàodí stayed overnight at Wáng Gōng's home.
He heard a faint voice from under the bed repeatedly calling:
"Hàodí!
Hàodí!"
Soon, the voice grew louder,
saying:
"I died in agony!"
Then it wept,
and the entire courtyard filled with weeping.
Wáng Gōng heard this,
took up his sword, and entered,
declaring loudly:
"Do you not recognize me, Education Commissioner Wáng?"
Only a hundred scornful chuckles were heard,
mocking him through their noses.
Wáng Gōng then held a grand Buddhist and Taoist ceremony,
commanding monks and priests to perform rites for the dead.
At night, when ghost food was scattered,
phosphorescent fires were seen flickering,
emerging from everywhere on the ground.
Earlier,
a gatekeeper named Wáng had fallen gravely ill,
remaining unconscious for several days.
That evening,
he suddenly stretched and seemed to wake.
His wife brought him food.
Wáng said:
"Just now, I don't know what the master was doing,
scattering food in the courtyard.
I also followed the crowd to eat.
Only after eating did I return,
so I didn't realize."
From then on, the hauntings ceased.
Could it be that the cymbals, bells, and drums,
the Buddhist rites and yoga,
truly had an effect?
The Chronicler of the Tales remarks:
"For evil and monstrous things,
only virtue can subdue them.
At the time the city fell,
Wáng Gōng's power was at its peak,
and those who heard his voice trembled with fear;
yet even ghosts mocked him.
Perhaps the ghosts foresaw that his end was near?
I hereby inform all great men and gentlemen of the world: even a human face cannot frighten ghosts,
so I hope you will not put on a ghostly face to frighten people!"
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In the Zhēndìng region,
there was an orphaned girl,
only six or seven years old,
who was taken in by her future husband's family.
After living with them for a year or two,
the husband seduced her and she became pregnant.
Her belly swelled, and she thought she was ill,
so she told her mother-in-law.
Her mother-in-law asked:
"Does it move?"
She replied:
"It moves."
This made her even more astonished.
However, because the girl was too young,
she dared not make a judgment.
Not long after,
she gave birth to a boy. Her mother-in-law sighed and said:
"Who would have thought that such a tiny mother
could give birth to such a sharp-pointed son!"
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
The household of Imperial Reader Dǒng Mò'ān
was being harassed by a fox.
Tiles, bricks and stones
suddenly fell like hail.
The family members ran to hide one after another.
They waited for the intervals
before daring to come out and work.
The gentleman was troubled by this,
so he borrowed the mansion of Minister of War Tíngsūn to move into and avoid the fox.
But the fox's harassment continued as before.
One day,
while waiting for the morning court session at the palace,
he happened to mention this strange occurrence.
A high-ranking official said: "There is a Taoist priest from east of the pass named Jiāo Míng,
who lives in the inner city.
He is skilled in exorcism and controlling spells,
and is quite effective."
The gentleman went to his residence and requested his help.
The Taoist priest drew a charm in red ink
and told him to take it back and paste it on the wall.
The fox was not afraid at all,
and threw things even more fiercely.
The gentleman reported back to the Taoist priest.
The Taoist priest became angry,
and personally went to the gentleman's home,
where he built an altar and performed rituals.
Soon, a huge fox was seen
lying beneath the altar.
The family members had suffered from its abuse for a long time,
and harbored deep hatred.
A maidservant approached and struck it.
The maidservant suddenly fell to the ground and stopped breathing.
The Taoist priest said:
"This creature is fierce and unruly.
Even I cannot subdue it immediately.
How dare you, a woman, lightly provoke it like this?"
After a moment, he said:
"I can borrow this to interrogate the fox,
which will also work."
He pointed his finger like a halberd and chanted for a while.
The maidservant suddenly stood up
and knelt respectfully.
The Taoist priest asked where the fox lived.
The maidservant spoke in the fox's voice:
"I am from the Western Regions.
There are eighteen of us who have come to the capital."
The Taoist priest said:
"Under the imperial carriage,
how can your kind be allowed to reside for long?
Leave quickly!"
The fox did not reply.
The Taoist priest struck the table angrily and said:
"Do you intend to disobey my order?
If you delay any further,
the spell will not spare you!"
The fox then showed a frightened expression
and expressed willingness to respectfully obey the command.
The Taoist priest urged it again.
The maidservant fell unconscious once more,
and it took a long time before she revived.
Soon, four or five white masses were seen,
rolling like balls,
moving along the eaves,
chasing one after another,
and in an instant, they were all gone.
From then on, peace was restored.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In Huáiyáng, there was a scholar named Yè,
whose given name is lost.
In essays, poetry, and prose,
he was unsurpassed in his time;
yet wherever he went, he met with misfortune,
and was trapped in the examination halls.
It happened that Liǎo Chénghè from east of the pass came to serve as magistrate of this county.
Upon reading his writings,
he found them extraordinary;
he summoned him for a conversation,
and was greatly pleased.
He had him stay at the government office,
providing him with study expenses;
and from time to time, he gave money and grain to support his family.
When the provincial examination came,
the magistrate praised him highly to the educational commissioner,
and he thus took first place.
The magistrate had high hopes for him.
After the examination,
he asked for his exam essay to read,
and applauded it with admiration.
Unexpectedly, fate limits people,
and fine writing is often at odds with fortune.
When the results were posted,
he once again failed.
Yè returned home dejected,
ashamed of having let down his patron,
emaciated to skin and bones,
and dull as a wooden puppet.
When the magistrate heard of this,
he summoned him to offer comfort.
Yè wept incessantly.
The magistrate pitied him
and promised that when his term of office was completed and he returned to the capital,
he would take him along to the north.
Yè was deeply grateful.
He bid farewell and returned home,
shutting his door and not going out.
Not long after,
he fell ill in bed.
The magistrate sent constant inquiries;
but though he took hundreds of doses of medicine,
there was no effect at all.
The magistrate happened to offend his superior and was dismissed,
and was about to leave his post.
He sent a letter to Yè,
which roughly said:
"I will be returning east soon;
the reason for my delay
is that I am waiting for you.
If you arrive in the morning,
I will depart in the evening."
The letter was delivered to his sickbed.
Yè held the letter and wept.
He told the messenger:
"My illness is critical and difficult to recover from quickly.
Please set out first."
When the messenger returned and reported this,
the magistrate could not bear to leave,
and waited slowly.
After several days,
the gatekeeper suddenly announced that Yè had arrived.
The magistrate was delighted
and went out to greet him and ask about his condition.
Yè said:
"Because of my lowly illness,
I have troubled you, my teacher, to wait so long,
causing you endless worry.
Now, fortunately, I can follow in your footsteps."
The magistrate then packed his belongings and prepared to depart at dawn.
Upon reaching his hometown,
he ordered his son to study under Yè as his teacher,
and they were together day and night.
The magistrate's son was named Zàichāng,
and was sixteen years old at the time,
still unable to write essays.
However, he was extremely intelligent.
For any literary piece, after going through it two or three times,
he would remember it without fail.
After staying with him for a year,
he was able to write essays as soon as he put pen to paper.
With the magistrate's influence added,
he entered the county school.
Yè took all the examination essays he had prepared in his lifetime
and copied them out for him to study.
In the provincial examination, all seven topics
were covered without omission,
and he placed second.
One day, the magistrate said to Yè:
"With the leftover threads of your talent,
you have made this young man famous.
But how sad that a great talent like you remains long abandoned!"
Yè said:
"This is probably fate.
By borrowing your good fortune to give vent to my literary talent,
and letting the world know that my half-life of obscurity
was not due to my own fault,
my wish is already fulfilled.
Moreover, if a scholar gains one true understanding friend,
he can have no regrets.
Why must one cast off plain clothing
to be considered successful?"
The magistrate, thinking he had been away from home for a long time,
feared he would miss the annual examination,
and urged him to return home for a visit.
Yè looked sorrowful and unhappy.
The magistrate could not bear to force him,
so he instructed his son, when he went to the capital,
to purchase an official position for him.
The son also passed the metropolitan examination,
and was appointed as a secretary in a ministry.
He took Yè along to the Imperial Academy,
and they spent their days and nights together.
After a year,
Yè took the provincial examination in the capital
and actually passed as a provincial graduate.
It happened that the son was assigned to duties on the southern river,
so he said to Yè:
"From here, it is not far from your honorable hometown.
Now that you have soared to the clouds,
it will be a joy to return in glory."
Yè was also pleased,
and chose an auspicious day to set out.
When they reached the border of Huáiyáng,
he ordered a servant and horse to escort Yè home.
Returning home, he found the household desolate,
and his heart was filled with sorrow.
Hesitantly, he entered the courtyard,
where his wife came out carrying a winnowing basket.
Upon seeing him,
she threw down the basket and fled in terror.
With deep sadness, he said,
"I have now achieved honor.
Though we have not seen each other for three or four years,
how is it that you no longer recognize me?"
From a distance, his wife replied,
"You have been dead for a long time.
How can you speak of honor?
The reason your coffin remains unburied
is because the family is poor and the child is young.
Now, our eldest son has already grown up,
and we are planning to choose a burial site.
Do not haunt us and frighten the living."
Upon hearing this,
he was overwhelmed with grief and melancholy.
Slowly, he entered the house,
and there he saw his own coffin, solemn and imposing.
He fell to the ground and vanished.
His wife, startled, looked at the spot,
and saw his clothes, hat, and shoes lying as if shed from his body.
Overcome with sorrow,
she embraced the garments and wept bitterly.
When their son returned from school,
he saw a carriage with four horses at the door.
After inquiring about its origin,
he rushed in fear to his mother.
His mother, wiping away tears, told him what had happened.
He then questioned the attendants in detail,
and finally learned the whole story.
When the attendants returned,
the young master heard of it,
and tears streamed down his chest.
He immediately ordered a carriage to go and mourn at the house: he took out funds to arrange the funeral,
burying him with the rites of a Xiàolián.
He also generously provided for his son,
hiring a tutor to teach him.
He spoke to the education commissioner,
and the following year, the son entered the county school.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Can a soul, following a true friend,
truly forget death?
Those who hear this may doubt it,
but I deeply believe it.
A devoted woman, sharing the same heart,
can even leave her soul upon the pillow;
a true friend from a thousand miles away,
can still recognize the path in a dream.
How much more so for those who, like silkworms spinning silk or flies leaving traces,
vomit out the heart and liver of a scholar;
or for those whose friendship, like flowing water and high mountains,
connects with the very life of our kind!
Alas!
Meeting one's match is hard to expect,
and encounters are often ill-fated.
Wandering alone,
facing one's shadow in endless sorrow;
with a proud and unyielding spirit,
scratching one's head in self-love.
Lamenting the bitterness of one's appearance,
inviting the mockery of ghosts and spirits.
Frequently dwelling among the failed candidates,
every strand of beard and hair seems ugly;
once falling outside the list of successful examinees,
every line of writing appears flawed.
Among those who weep in anguish throughout history,
only Biàn Hé is like you;
among those who are overlooked despite outstanding talent,
who is the Bólè?
Holding a visiting card in one's bosom,
for three years the writing fades;
turning to gaze,
there is no home in all the world.
In this life,
one need only close one's eyes and stride forward,
leaving everything to the will of fate.
In this world, how many are there like Yè Shēng,
noble yet fallen into obscurity?
But how can we expect Lìng Wēi to return,
so that we may follow him in life and death?
Alas!"
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Xīnchéng, the Grand Marshal Wáng
had a steward in charge of accounts,
whose family was considered wealthy without official rank.
Suddenly, he dreamed of a man rushing in,
who said,
"You owe forty thousand cash,
and now it is time to repay."
When asked,
he gave no answer,
but went straight inside.
After waking,
his wife gave birth to a son.
Knowing it was a karmic debt from a past life,
he set aside forty thousand cash in a separate room,
and all the child's expenses for clothing, food, medicine, and illness
were drawn from it.
After three or four years,
he checked the money in the room,
and found only seven hundred cash remaining.
Just then, the wet nurse brought the child over,
and was playfully teasing him nearby.
He then called out to the child,
"The forty thousand is almost gone,
it is time for you to leave."
As soon as he finished speaking,
the child's face suddenly changed, contorted in distress,
his neck twisted and eyes wide open.
When he touched him again,
the child had already stopped breathing.
He then used the remaining funds to prepare for the burial and interred him.
This can serve as a warning to those who owe debts.
In the past, there was an old man without children,
who asked a venerable monk about it.
The monk said,
"If you owe no one,
and no one owes you,
how can you have a child?"
For a good child is born
to repay a karmic connection;
a troublesome child is born
to collect a debt.
Let not the living rejoice,
nor the dead grieve.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Wéndēng, there was a young scholar named Zhōu,
who had shared brushes and inkstones with Chéng since childhood,
and thus they pledged a bond of friendship as steadfast as mortar and pestle.
Chéng was poor,
so he often relied on Zhōu throughout the year.
Since Zhōu was older in age,
Chéng addressed Zhōu’s wife as sister-in-law.
During festivals, he would visit their home,
and they were like one family.
Zhōu’s wife gave birth to a son,
but she died suddenly after childbirth.
Zhōu later married a woman from the Wáng family,
and because Chéng was younger,
he had never requested to meet her.
One day,
the younger brother of Madam Wáng came to visit his sister,
and a banquet was held in the inner chamber.
Chéng happened to arrive.
The servants announced his arrival,
and Zhōu, sitting inside, ordered him to be invited in.
Chéng did not enter,
but instead took his leave.
Zhōu moved the feast to the outer quarters,
chased after him, and brought him back.
As soon as they sat down,
someone reported that a servant from their country estate
had been severely flogged by the county magistrate.
Earlier,
a herdsman from the household of the Ministry Official Huáng
had let his cattle trample Zhōu’s fields,
leading to a quarrel.
The herdsman ran to inform his master,
who had Zhōu’s servant seized and sent to the authorities,
resulting in the servant being flogged and punished.
Upon learning the reason,
Zhōu flew into a rage and said:
“How dare a mere cowherd from the Huáng family act like this!
Who does he think he is?
His ancestors served my grandfather;
now that he has gained some power,
does he think there is no one left to stand up to him?”
Filled with anger,
he rose in fury,
intending to confront Huáng.
Chéng held him back and stopped him,
saying:
“In this world of brute force,
there is often no distinction between right and wrong.
Besides, aren’t half of today’s officials nothing more than bandits who don’t even carry spears and bows?”
Zhōu would not listen.
Chéng repeatedly tried to dissuade him,
even to the point of shedding tears,
and only then did Zhōu relent.
However, his anger remained unresolved,
and he tossed and turned until dawn.
He said to his family:
“The Huáng family has wronged me—they are my enemy,
but I will let that go for now.
The county magistrate is an official of the court,
not a servant of the powerful.
Even if there is a dispute,
both parties should be heard.
Why should he act like a dog obeying its master’s command?
I will also file a complaint against his herdsman
and see how he handles it.”
His family all urged him on,
and so he made up his mind.
He prepared a petition and submitted it to the magistrate,
but the magistrate tore it up and threw it away.
Enraged,
Zhōu spoke insultingly to the magistrate.
The magistrate, ashamed and furious,
had him arrested and imprisoned.
After the morning hours,
Chéng went to visit Zhōu,
only to learn that he had gone to the city to file a lawsuit.
He hurried to stop him,
but by then Zhōu was already in prison.
Stamping his feet in frustration, Chéng was at a loss for what to do.
At that time, three pirates had been captured,
and the magistrate, bribed by Huáng,
instructed them to falsely accuse Zhōu of being an accomplice.
Based on their testimony, Zhōu was stripped of his scholar’s cap and gown,
and subjected to brutal torture.
Chéng entered the prison,
and they looked at each other in sorrow and despair.
Chéng proposed appealing to the emperor.
Zhōu said:
“I am confined in a heavy prison,
like a bird in a cage.
Though I have a younger brother,
he can only provide me with prison meals.”
Chéng resolutely took on the responsibility himself,
saying:
“This is my duty.
If I do not act urgently in times of trouble,
what use is friendship?”
And so he set off.
When Zhōu’s brother went to see him off with gifts,
Chéng had already left long ago.
Arriving in the capital,
he found no way to submit his appeal.
Hearing that the emperor was about to go hunting,
Chéng hid in advance among the trees by the roadside.
Soon, the imperial procession passed by,
and he knelt, kowtowed, and cried out in sorrow.
His appeal was thus accepted.
He was sent back by post relay,
and the case was handed over to the Board of Justice for review and reporting.
By then, more than ten months had passed,
and Zhōu had already been forced to confess and was sentenced to death.
When the Board received the imperial decree,
they were greatly alarmed,
and ordered a retrial.
Huáng was also terrified
and plotted to kill Zhōu.
He bribed the jailers
to deprive Zhōu of food and drink.
When Zhōu’s brother came to deliver food and visit,
he was harshly refused.
Chéng again went to the Board to plead for justice,
and Zhōu was finally brought out for questioning,
but by then he was too weak from starvation to stand.
The presiding official was furious
and had the jailer beaten to death.
Huáng was terrified
and offered several thousand taels of silver,
bribing officials to secure an acquittal.
As a result, the case was vaguely resolved and Zhōu was exempted from punishment.
The magistrate was sentenced to exile according to the law.
Zhōu was released and returned home,
and he held Chéng in even higher regard, treating him as a true brother.
Chéng, having attempted suicide after being imprisoned due to a lawsuit,
had grown utterly disillusioned with worldly affairs,
and invited Zhōu to retire from the world with him.
Zhōu, however, was infatuated with his young wife,
and merely laughed off Chéng’s suggestion.
Though Chéng said nothing more,
his resolve was firm.
After they parted,
several days passed without Chéng’s return.
Zhōu sent someone to inquire at his home,
only to find that Chéng’s family suspected he was at Zhōu’s place;
since he was found at neither location,
they began to grow suspicious.
Sensing something unusual,
Zhōu dispatched people to trace his whereabouts,
searching temples, monasteries, ravines, and valleys,
leaving almost no place unexamined.
Meanwhile, he regularly sent money and goods to support Chéng’s son.
Eight or nine years later,
Chéng suddenly appeared on his own,
wearing a yellow headscarf and a feathered robe,
with the dignified bearing of a Daoist master.
Delighted,
Zhōu grasped his arm and said:
“Where have you been,
making me search for you everywhere?”
Chéng laughed and replied:
“Like a lone cloud or a wild crane,
I perch in no fixed abode.
Fortunately, since we parted, I have remained hale and hearty.”
Zhōu ordered wine to be served,
and after briefly catching up on the long separation,
he urged Chéng to change out of his Daoist attire.
Chéng only smiled without answering.
Zhōu said:
“How foolish!
Why abandon your wife and children as if they were worn-out shoes?”
Chéng replied with a laugh:
“Not so.
Others are the ones who will abandon me—
how could I be the one to abandon others?”
When asked where he resided,
he answered: at the Shàngqīng Temple on Láo Mountain.
Later, as they lay down to sleep foot to foot,
Zhōu dreamed that Chéng was lying naked on his chest,
making it hard for him to breathe.
Startled, he asked what Chéng was doing,
but received no reply.
Suddenly, he awoke in alarm,
and called out to Chéng, but there was no answer;
sitting up, he groped around—
Chéng had vanished without a trace.
After calming himself for a while,
he realized he was lying on Chéng’s bed.
Astonished, he exclaimed:
“I wasn’t drunk last night—
how could I have become so confused?”
He then called for his family.
When they brought a light,
it clearly revealed Chéng’s face.
Zhōu originally had a thick beard,
but when he felt it with his hand,
only a few strands remained.
Taking up a mirror to look at himself,
he cried out in shock:
“If Chéng is here,
then where have I gone?”
Suddenly, he understood—
realizing that Chéng had used magic to summon him into seclusion.
He intended to go back inside,
but his younger brother, alarmed by his changed appearance,
barred him from entering.
Zhōu had no way to prove his identity.
He immediately ordered a servant and a horse to go search for Chéng.
After several days,
they entered Láo Mountain.
The horse moved swiftly,
and the servant could not keep up.
Zhōu stopped to rest under a tree,
where he saw many Daoist priests coming and going.
One among them looked at Zhōu,
who then asked him about Chéng.
The Daoist smiled and said:
“I have heard his name—
I believe he is at Shàngqīng.”
Having said this,
he went straight on his way.
Zhōu watched him leave,
and saw that within a short distance,
the Daoist spoke with another person,
exchanging only a few words before departing.
The person he had spoken to gradually approached—
it turned out to be an old acquaintance from the same literary society.
Seeing Zhōu,
he exclaimed in surprise:
“It has been years since we last met—
people said you had gone to a famous mountain to study the Dao;
are you still wandering in the mortal world?”
Zhōu recounted his strange experience.
The man said in astonishment:
“I just met him,
and thought it was you.
He left not long ago—
he probably isn’t far.”
Greatly perplexed,
Zhōu said:
“How strange!
Why did I fail to recognize my own face when it was right before me?”
His servant soon caught up,
and they hurried onward,
but found no trace of Chéng.
Gazing at the vast, empty landscape,
Zhōu felt uncertain whether to advance or retreat.
Reflecting that he had no home to return to,
he resolved to pursue Chéng relentlessly.
However, the path grew too rugged and dangerous for riding,
so he sent the horse back with the servant
and continued alone on foot.
In the distance, he saw a young attendant sitting alone,
hurried over to ask for directions,
and explained his situation.
The attendant said he was Chéng’s disciple,
then shouldered Zhōu’s baggage and provisions,
guiding him along the way.
They ate under the stars and slept in the open,
traveling an extremely long distance—
after three days, they finally arrived,
though it was not the Shàngqīng known to the world.
It was then the tenth month,
yet mountain flowers bloomed along the path,
unlike early winter.
The attendant went in to announce the guest,
and Chéng immediately came out—
only then did Zhōu recognize his own form.
Taking Zhōu by the hand, Chéng led him inside,
where wine was served and they conversed.
Zhōu saw birds of extraordinary colors,
so tame they showed no fear of people,
singing with voices like reed pipes,
occasionally alighting on the seats to chirp.
He found this utterly marvelous.
Yet, his worldly attachments were strong,
and he had no desire to linger.
On the floor were two rush cushions;
Chéng pulled one over and they sat side by side.
After the second watch of the night,
when all thoughts had quieted,
Zhōu suddenly felt as if he had dozed off for a moment—
and then sensed that his body had exchanged places with Chéng’s.
Doubting this,
he stroked his own chin,
and found his thick beard had returned.
At daybreak,
he felt an overwhelming desire to go back.
Chéng firmly urged him to stay.
After three more days,
Chéng finally said:
“Please rest a little,
and I will see you off early.”
As soon as Zhōu closed his eyes,
he heard Chéng call out:
“Your travel gear is ready.”
So he rose and followed him.
The path he traveled was not the old route.
It seemed like no time at all had passed
before his hometown came into view.
Chéng sat waiting by the roadside,
telling Zhōu to go home by himself.
Zhōu insisted he come along, but to no avail,
so he trudged alone to his own gate.
He knocked, but no one answered.
Thinking to climb over the wall,
he felt his body light as a leaf,
and with one leap he was over.
He passed over several walls in this way
before reaching the bedroom.
Inside, lamplight flickered;
his wife was not yet asleep,
and she was murmuring as she spoke with someone.
He licked the window to peek inside
and saw his wife drinking from the same cup with a servant,
their manner very intimate and indecent.
At this, his anger blazed like fire.
He planned to catch them by surprise,
but feared his own strength would be insufficient.
So he slipped out, unbarred the gate,
ran to tell Chéng,
and begged for his help.
Chéng readily agreed
and went straight to the inner bedroom.
Zhōu raised a stone and pounded on the door;
inside, there was great panic.
The more urgently he pounded,
the more firmly they barred the door.
Chéng pried it open with his sword,
and with a crack, it suddenly gave way.
Zhōu rushed in;
the servant charged through the door and fled.
Chéng, standing outside,
struck him with his sword,
severing his shoulder and arm.
Zhōu seized his wife and interrogated her under torture;
only then did he learn that she had been carrying on with the servant since the time he was taken away.
Zhōu borrowed the sword and beheaded her,
then hung her entrails from a tree in the courtyard.
He then followed Chéng out
and found his way back.
Suddenly he awoke
to find himself lying on his bed.
Startled, he said:
"What a strange and disjointed dream—it terrified me!"
Chéng laughed and said:
"Brother, you take dreams for reality
and reality for dreams."
Zhōu stared in astonishment and asked what he meant.
Chéng took out his sword and showed it to him;
bloodstains were still upon it.
Zhōu, horrified and nearly fainting,
secretly suspected Chéng of using illusions to deceive him.
Chéng, knowing his thoughts,
hurriedly packed and escorted him home.
In what seemed like no time, they reached the village gate,
where Chéng said:
"Was it not right here, the other night,
that I leaned on my sword and waited for you?
I loathe the sight of foulness and corruption;
I will wait for you here.
If you do not return by late afternoon,
I shall go on my way."
Zhōu arrived home
to find the house desolate and silent,
as if no one lived there.
He went to his younger brother's house instead.
When the brother saw his elder brother,
tears immediately streamed down his face, and he said:
"After you left,
bandits came at night and murdered your wife,
gutting her and taking her entrails away.
It was a cruel and tragic death, lamentable indeed.
To this day, the authorities have not caught the culprits."
Zhōu awoke as if from a dream,
and so told his brother the truth,
warning him not to pursue the matter.
The brother stood dumbfounded for a long while.
Zhōu asked after his son,
and the brother had an old nurse bring the child.
Zhōu said:
"This child in swaddling clothes
is the one who carries on our family line.
Brother, take good care of him.
I wish to leave this human world."
With that, he rose
and walked straight out.
His brother, weeping, ran after him and tried to hold him back,
but Zhōu walked on, smiling, without looking back.
Reaching the wilderness,
he saw Chéng
and went off with him.
Looking back from afar, he called:
"Forbearance brings the greatest happiness."
His brother wanted to say something,
but Chéng gave a sweep of his wide sleeve,
and they vanished from sight.
The brother stood there disconsolately for a long time,
then returned home weeping bitterly.
Zhōu's younger brother was simple and honest,
not skilled at managing the household or making a living.
After a few years,
the family grew even poorer.
As Zhōu's son gradually grew up,
they could not afford to hire a tutor,
so the brother taught him to read himself.
One day,
he arrived early at the study
and saw a letter on the desk,
tightly sealed,
with the address label reading:
"For Second Brother to Open."
Examining it,
he recognized his elder brother's handwriting.
Opening it to look,
he found nothing inside—
only a fingernail,
about two fingers long.
He thought it strange.
Placing the nail on the inkstone,
he went out to ask the family where it had come from,
but no one knew.
When he looked back,
he saw the inkstone gleaming brightly—
it had turned to gold.
Greatly astonished,
he tried it on copper and iron,
and it worked the same way.
From then on, they became very wealthy.
He gave a thousand taels of gold to Chéng's son,
and so it came to be rumored that both families possessed the art of turning things to gold.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Jiāngnán Provincial Graduate Méi Ǒucháng
told of a fellow townsman of his, a certain Magistrate Sūn,
who, while serving as magistrate of Dézhōu,
tried a most unusual case.
It began when a villager
was marrying a wife for his son.
When the bride entered the household,
relatives and neighbors all came to offer congratulations.
They drank until past the first watch,
when the groom went out
and saw the bride, in dazzling attire,
hurrying around to the back of the house.
Suspicious, he followed her.
Behind the house was a long stream,
with a small bridge across it.
He saw the bride cross the bridge and go straight on,
which increased his suspicions.
He called to her, but she did not answer.
From afar, she beckoned to her husband with her hand.
The husband hurried after her,
but though they were never more than a foot apart,
he could never quite catch up.
After walking several *li*,
they entered a village.
The woman stopped
and said to her husband:
"Your home is too lonely;
I am not used to living there.
Please, let us stay at my home for a few days,
and then we will return together to visit your family."
Having said this,
she pulled out a hairpin and knocked on the gate.
With a creak, a young maid came to answer the door.
The woman entered first.
Having no choice,
he followed her.
Once inside,
he saw that both her parents were in the main hall.
They said to their son-in-law:
"Our daughter has been rather spoiled since childhood
and has never been away from our side for a moment.
Now that she has left her old home,
her heart is filled with sorrow.
Today she has come with you,
which greatly comforts our longing.
Stay a few days,
and then we will send you both back."
They then prepared a room for them,
with bed and bedding all provided,
and so they stayed there.
The guests at home, seeing that the groom had not returned for a long time,
all went to search for him.
Only the bride was in the room,
and no one knew where the groom had gone.
From then on, inquiries were made far and wide,
but there was no news at all.
The old couple shed tears,
believing he must be dead.
After nearly half a year,
the bride’s family, grieving that their daughter had no husband,
approached the groom’s father,
wishing to remarry their daughter.
The groom’s father was even more sorrowful,
saying:
"There are no remains or clothes to verify his death,
how can we know my son has become a ghost!
Even if he has indeed died,
it would not be too late to remarry her after a full year.
Why such haste!"
The bride’s father resented this even more,
and brought a lawsuit to court.
Magistrate Sūn found it strange and suspicious,
but had no way to resolve it,
so he ruled to wait for three years,
filed the case, and dismissed them.
The groom stayed at his wife’s home,
and the family treated him very kindly.
Whenever he discussed returning home with his wife,
she would agree,
but kept delaying and did not go immediately.
After more than half a year had passed,
he felt restless in his heart,
and was filled with anxiety.
He wanted to return alone,
but his wife firmly kept him.
One day,
the whole family became flustered and hurried,
as if facing an urgent crisis.
Hastily, they said to the son-in-law:
"We originally planned to send you and your wife back together in two or three days.
Unexpectedly, the dowry is not yet prepared,
and suddenly a misfortune has occurred;
we have no choice
but to send you back first."
Then they escorted him out the door,
turned back hurriedly,
their words and actions in dealing with him
were quite rushed.
Just as he was about to find his way,
he looked back and saw the courtyard buildings were gone,
only seeing tall graves.
Greatly shocked,
he hurriedly searched for the way home.
Arriving home,
he recounted the whole story in detail,
and together they went to the authorities to lodge a complaint.
Magistrate Sūn summoned the bride’s father and instructed him,
sending the daughter to be married,
and only then did they complete the wedding ceremony.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A certain Dàoshi at Cháotiān Guàn
was fond of breathing techniques.
An old man was lodging at the temple,
and happened to share the same interest,
so they became mystical friends.
After living there for several years,
every time the suburban sacrifices approached,
he would leave ten days in advance,
and return after the sacrifices.
The Dàoshi grew suspicious and asked him about it.
The old man said:
"We two are close friends,
so I can tell you the truth: I am a fox.
When the suburban sacrifice period arrives,
the various deities cleanse impurities,
and I have nowhere to hide,
so I go into hiding."
Another year,
he left at the usual time,
but did not return for a long time.
The Dàoshi wondered about it.
One day, he suddenly arrived.
So he asked the reason.
He replied:
"I almost never saw you again!
Previously, I wanted to hide far away,
but felt rather lazy,
and seeing the sewer was very hidden,
I secretly hid under a drain tile.
Unexpectedly, the Divine Official came to sweep here,
caught a glimpse of me,
and angrily wanted to whip me.
I was afraid and fled.
The Divine Official chased me very urgently.
When I reached the Huáng Hé,
he was almost upon me.
In great distress and with no plan,
I dashed and hid in a dry toilet.
The deity detested its filth,
and finally turned back and left.
After I came out,
the foul smell had contaminated me,
and I could no longer wander in the human world.
So I threw myself into water to wash,
then hid in a cave for nearly a hundred days,
before the grime and filth were finally clean.
Now I come to bid farewell,
and also to give a warning: you too should hide and go elsewhere,
a great calamity is coming,
this is no place of fortune."
Having said this,
he took his leave and departed.
The Dàoshi followed his advice and moved elsewhere.
Not long after, the Jiǎshēn Rebellion occurred.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Wáng Lán of Lìjīn died suddenly from illness.
The King of Hell reviewed the case,
and found it was a mistake by a ghost underling who had wrongly summoned him.
Ordered to send him back to life,
but his corpse had already decayed.
The ghost, fearing punishment,
said to Wáng:
"Being a human turned ghost is bitter,
but being a ghost turned immortal is joyful.
If it is joyful,
why must one live?"
Wáng thought this reasonable.
The ghost said:
"There is a fox here,
who has refined a golden elixir.
Steal its elixir and swallow it,
then your soul will not disperse,
and you can exist forever.
Whatever you wish to do,
nothing will fail to go as you desire.
Are you willing?"
Wáng agreed.
The ghost led him away,
entered a grand mansion,
saw pavilions and towers standing tall,
but it was quiet with no one in sight.
There was a fox under the moonlight,
raising its head to gaze at the sky.
With one exhalation,
a pill came out of its mouth,
flying straight up into the moon;
with one inhalation,
it fell back again,
caught in its mouth,
then it exhaled again: repeating like this endlessly.
The ghost secretly waited beside it,
and when it spat out the pill,
quickly snatched it in hand,
and gave it to Wáng to swallow.
The fox was startled,
and confronted them with fierce anger.
Seeing there were two of them,
it feared it could not match them,
and left in resentment.
Wáng bid farewell to the ghost,
and went to his home.
When his wife and children saw him,
they were all afraid and retreated.
Wáng explained the reason,
and they gradually gathered around.
From then on, he lived at home as usual.
His friend, a man named Zhāng,
heard about this and went to visit him.
When they met, they exchanged pleasantries.
Wáng then said to Zhāng:
"You and I have both been poor since long ago.
Now I have a method
that can make us rich.
Will you follow me on this journey?"
Zhāng assented.
Wáng continued:
"I can heal without medicine,
and divine without divination.
I wish to manifest myself,
but fear that those who recognize me will be alarmed by the strangeness.
If I attach myself to you and travel,
will that be acceptable?"
Zhāng again assented.
So that very day they packed their bags with haste
and arrived at the border of Shānxī.
A wealthy family had a daughter
who had fallen suddenly ill,
dizzy and unconscious.
Having exhausted all remedies and prayers,
Zhāng went to their residence
and boasted of his skills.
The rich man had only this daughter
and always cherished her dearly.
He said that whoever could heal her
would be rewarded with a thousand taels of gold.
Zhāng requested to examine her.
Following the old man into the inner chamber,
he saw the girl lying unconscious;
he lifted her quilt,
and touched her body—
the girl remained senseless.
Wáng privately told Zhāng:
"Her soul has wandered away.
We must go find it."
Zhāng then informed the old man:
"Though the illness is critical,
it can be cured."
The old man asked:
"What medicine is needed?"
Zhāng said none was required,
"The young lady's soul has strayed elsewhere.
I have already dispatched a spirit to search for it."
After about an hour,
Wáng suddenly returned,
announcing he had found it.
Zhāng then asked the old man to enter the room again,
and once more touched the girl.
After a short while,
the girl yawned and stretched,
and her eyes suddenly opened.
The old man was overjoyed
and comforted her with questions.
The girl said:
"Earlier, while playing in the garden,
I saw a young gentleman
shooting sparrows with a pellet bow;
several men leading fine horses
followed behind him.
I hurried to run and hide,
but was abruptly blocked and stopped.
The young man handed me his bow
and taught me to shoot.
Just as I was feeling ashamed and scolding him,
he took me onto his horse,
and we rode together.
He laughed and said:
'I enjoy playing with you; don't be shy.'
After several lǐ into the mountains,
I cried and cursed from the horse;
the young man grew angry,
pushed me off by the roadside,
and I had no way to return.
Then a man arrived,
grabbed my arm,
