and moved as swiftly as galloping—
in an instant I was home,
as if suddenly waking from a dream."
The old man thought him divine
and indeed gave him the thousand taels.
That night, Wáng discussed with Zhāng,
keeping two hundred taels for travel expenses,
and took the rest away.
He knocked on the door and gave it to his son;
he also instructed that three hundred be given to Zhāng's family,
and then returned.
The next day,
they bid farewell to the old man.
Not seeing where the gold was hidden,
he found it even more marvelous
and sent them off with generous gifts.
A few days later,
Zhāng met a fellow townsman named Hè Cái in the suburbs.
Cái was given to drinking and gambling and did not engage in productive work,
strangely poor as a beggar.
Hearing that Zhāng had acquired extraordinary skills
and obtained untold amounts of gold,
he rushed to seek him out.
Wáng advised giving him a small gift and sending him back.
Cái did not mend his ways,
squandering everything within ten days,
and intended to seek out Zhāng again.
Wáng already knew of this
and said:
"Cái is wild and unruly;
he cannot be associated with.
We should only bribe him to leave,
for even if disaster comes, it will still be minor."
The next day,
Cái indeed arrived,
insisting on going with them.
Zhāng said:
"I knew you would come again.
Daily given to drunkenness and gambling,
how can a thousand taels fill a bottomless pit?
If you truly reform your ways,
I will give you a hundred taels."
Cái agreed.
Zhāng poured out his purse and gave it to him.
After Cái left,
with a hundred taels in his pocket,
he gambled even more recklessly;
adding visits to brothels,
he spent money like dirt.
The local constables grew suspicious and arrested him.
Brought before the magistrate,
he was tortured cruelly.
Cái truthfully told where the gold came from.
So the magistrate dispatched officers to escort Cái to apprehend Zhāng.
After several days,
his wounds grew severe,
and he died on the road.
His soul, not forgetting Zhāng,
went again to cling to him,
thus meeting Wáng.
One day,
while drinking together at a beacon mound,
Cái, heavily drunk, shouted wildly.
Wáng tried to stop him but he wouldn't listen.
It happened that an imperial inspector was passing by;
hearing the shouts, he searched the area
and captured Zhāng.
Zhāng, afraid,
told the truth.
The inspector was angry,
flogged him, and submitted a report to the gods.
That night, he dreamed of a golden-armored deity who told him:
"Upon investigation, Wáng Lán died without guilt
and is now a ghost immortal.
Healing is also an act of benevolence;
he cannot be judged as a demon.
Now, by imperial decree,
he is appointed as a Clear Path Envoy.
Hè Cái was depraved and dissolute;
he has been punished and banished to Iron Enclosure Mountain.
Zhāng is without crime
and should be pardoned."
The inspector awoke, marveling at this,
and released Zhāng.
Zhāng packed his belongings and returned to his hometown.
He still had several hundred taels in his purse,
and respectfully gave half to the Wáng family.
The descendants of the Wáng family
thereby became wealthy.
Based on the manuscript version of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
The Prefectural City's Temple of the Eastern Peak,
is located in the southern outer city.
On either side of the main gate,
stand deities over ten feet tall,
commonly known as
"The Eagle and Tiger Deities,"
their fierce and terrifying appearance.
A Daoist priest surnamed Rèn resided in the temple,
who, every time the rooster crowed,
would rise to burn incense and chant scriptures.
A thief had hidden himself in advance within the corridor,
waiting for the priest to rise,
then stealthily entered the sleeping quarters,
to search and plunder valuables.
However, the room contained no possessions of worth,
only beneath the sleeping mat were three hundred coins found,
which he tucked into his waistband,
unlatched the door and left,
intending to ascend Qiānfó Shān.
He fled southward for quite some time,
before finally reaching the foot of the mountain.
There he saw a giant of a man,
descending from the mountain,
a gray eagle on his left arm,
and they happened to meet.
Looking closely at him,
his face was the color of verdigris,
vaguely resembling the familiar figure seen at the temple gate.
Greatly terrified,
he crouched down, trembling.
The deity exclaimed in surprise:
"Thief of money, where are you going?"
The thief became even more frightened,
kowtowing incessantly.
The deity seized him and ordered him back,
entered the temple,
made him pour out all the stolen coins,
and kneel guarding them.
The priest finished his recitations,
turned and saw them, shocked and alarmed.
The thief recounted everything in detail.
The priest collected the money and sent him away.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wáng Chéng,
was the son of an old, established family in Píngyuán,
and by nature extremely lazy.
His livelihood declined daily,
until only a few dilapidated rooms remained,
and he and his wife slept under ragged quilts,
their mutual reproaches unbearable.
It was then the height of summer, swelteringly hot,
and outside the village there was an old garden of the Zhōu family,
its walls and buildings all collapsed,
only a single pavilion remained;
many villagers lodged there temporarily,
and Wáng was among them.
When dawn broke,
all the sleepers had left;
the sun was already three poles high,
when Wáng finally arose,
lingering hesitantly, about to return home.
He saw a golden hairpin lying in the grass,
picked it up and looked at it,
finely engraved with the words:
"Made by the Residence of the Yíbīn."
Wáng's grandfather had been a yíbīn for the Héng princely estate,
and among the old family possessions,
many were of this style,
so he held the hairpin, lost in thought.
An old woman came searching for the hairpin.
Although Wáng was indeed poor,
he was principled by nature,
and promptly produced it and gave it to her.
The old woman was delighted,
praising his great virtue profusely,
saying:
"What is the hairpin's worth?
It is a keepsake from my late husband."
He asked:
"Who was your husband?"
She replied:
"The late yíbīn, Wáng Jiǎnzhī."
Wáng exclaimed in surprise:
"He was my grandfather.
How is it we meet?"
The old woman also cried out in surprise:
"You are the grandson of Wáng Jiǎnzhī?
I am a fox immortal.
A hundred years ago,
I was deeply attached to your grandfather.
After your grandfather passed,
I, this old body, went into seclusion.
Passing by, I lost this hairpin,
which恰好 fell into your hands—
is this not the will of Heaven!"
Wáng had also heard his grandfather had a fox wife,
believed her words,
and invited her to visit his home.
The old woman agreed.
Wáng called his wife out to meet her,
clad in tattered wadding,
her face sallow and dull from poor diet.
The old woman sighed:
"Alas!
The grandson of Wáng Jiǎnzhī,
has fallen into such poverty!"
She also noticed the broken stove held no smoke,
and said:
"With a household situation like this,
how do you manage to live?"
The wife then detailed their impoverished state,
sobbing and weeping quietly.
The old woman gave the hairpin to the wife,
telling her to temporarily pawn it for money to buy rice,
and to meet again three days later.
Wáng tried to detain her.
The old woman said:
"You cannot even support one wife yourselves;
if I stayed,
merely looking up at the rafters in idleness,
what benefit would that be?"
And so she departed directly.
Wáng explained the reason to his wife,
who was greatly afraid.
Wáng spoke of her righteous intent,
urging his wife to serve her as a mother-in-law,
and the wife agreed.
After three days,
she indeed returned.
She produced several taels of silver,
to buy a shí each of millet and wheat.
At night she shared a short bed with the wife.
The wife was initially afraid of her;
but observing her intentions were truly sincere and earnest,
she ceased to doubt her.
The next day,
she said to Wáng,
"Grandson, do not be idle.
You should take up a small trade;
how can you live long by sitting and eating?"
Wáng told her he had no capital.
She said:
"When your grandfather was alive,
gold and silk were taken as needed.
I, being of the world beyond,
had no need for such things,
so I never took much.
I saved forty taels from my rouge and powder money,
which remains to this day.
It has been stored for a long time and is of no use;
you may take it all to buy pongee,
set a date to go to the capital,
and you can earn a small profit."
Wáng followed her advice,
purchased over fifty bolts and returned.
The old woman urged him to pack quickly,
estimating it would take six or seven days to reach Yāndū.
She instructed him:
"Be diligent, not lazy;
be urgent, not slow: delay by a single day,
and regret will be too late!"
Wáng respectfully agreed,
packed his goods and set off.
On the way, he encountered rain,
soaking his clothes and shoes.
Wáng had never experienced hardship in his life,
and was utterly exhausted,
so he rested temporarily at an inn.
Unexpectedly, the rain pattered on until dusk,
and the eaves dripped like ropes.
After a night,
the mud became even worse.
Seeing travelers coming and going,
treading through mire up to their shins,
he felt fearful and distressed.
He waited until noon,
when the ground gradually dried,
but dark clouds gathered again,
and heavy rain poured once more.
He stayed another night before traveling.
As he neared the capital,
he heard that pongee prices had soared,
and secretly rejoiced.
Entering the capital,
he unpacked at an inn.
The innkeeper deeply regretted his lateness.
Earlier,
when the southern route had just opened,
pongee arrived in extremely small quantities.
The Bèilè's mansion urgently sought to purchase it,
causing prices to suddenly rise,
about three times higher than usual.
The day before, they had just bought enough,
and later arrivals were all disappointed.
The innkeeper told Wáng the reason.
Wáng was deeply disheartened.
The next day,
more pongee arrived,
and prices fell further.
Wáng, seeing no profit, refused to sell.
After delaying over ten days,
considering the mounting expenses for food,
he grew even more worried and depressed.
The innkeeper advised him to sell cheaply,
and change to another plan.
He agreed.
Losing over ten taels,
he sold it all off.
Getting up early,
he prepared to return home.
Opening his bag to look,
he found the money gone.
Shocked, he told the innkeeper.
The innkeeper had no plan.
Someone advised reporting to the authorities,
to hold the innkeeper responsible for compensation.
Wáng sighed and said:
"This is my fate;
what fault is it of the innkeeper?"
The innkeeper heard this and felt grateful to him,
giving him five taels of silver,
comforting him and urging him to return.
Wáng thought to himself that he had no face to see his grandmother,
pacing back and forth inside and out,
caught in a dilemma.
Just then, he saw people fighting gamecocks,
where a single bet amounted to several thousand;
each time a gamecock was bought,
it often cost over a hundred coins.
An idea suddenly struck him.
Calculating the funds in his bag,
it was just enough to trade in gamecocks.
He discussed it with the innkeeper.
The innkeeper eagerly encouraged him,
and moreover agreed to provide lodging and meals,
without charging him.
Wáng was delighted,
and set off.
He bought a full load of gamecocks,
and re-entered the capital.
The innkeeper was pleased,
congratulating him on a quick sale.
That night,
heavy rain lasted until dawn.
At daybreak,
the streets were like rivers,
and the drizzling rain still had not stopped.
He stayed waiting for clear weather.
For several days in a row,
there was no end to it.
Getting up to look in the cages,
he saw the gamecocks gradually dying.
Wáng was greatly alarmed,
not knowing what plan to devise.
The next day,
even more died;
only a few remained,
which he kept together in one cage to feed.
After a night, he went to check,
and found only one gamecock left.
He told the innkeeper,
unable to hold back his tears.
The innkeeper also felt regret for him.
Wáng reckoned his money was gone with no way to return,
and only wanted to seek death.
The innkeeper consoled and comforted him.
Together they went to see the gamecock.
After examining it carefully, the innkeeper said:
"This seems to be a fine creature.
The deaths of the other gamecocks
may well have been from fighting with this one.
Since you have leisure and nothing to do,
please train it;
if it is good,
gambling on fights can also be a way to make a living."
Wáng followed his advice.
Once it was tamed,
the innkeeper told him to take it to the street,
to gamble for wine and food.
The gamecock was very strong,
and always won.
The innkeeper was pleased,
and gave Wáng money,
telling him to gamble again with the young men;
he fought three times and won three times.
After about half a year,
he had saved twenty taels.
His heart was even more comforted,
and he regarded the gamecock as his life.
Earlier,
the Great Prince was fond of gamecocks,
and every year on the Lantern Festival,
he would allow commoners who trained gamecocks to enter his mansion to compete.
The innkeeper said to Wáng:
"Now great wealth can be instantly obtained;
the only uncertainty
lies in your fate."
He then explained the reason,
and guided him to go together.
He instructed him:
"If you lose,
then leave dejected.
But if by any chance,
your gamecock wins the fight,
the Prince will certainly want to buy it.
Do not agree;
if he insists strongly,
only look to me for a signal,
and agree only after I nod."
Wáng said:
"Agreed."
Arriving at the mansion,
he saw gamecock handlers crowding shoulder to shoulder in the courtyard below.
After a while,
the Prince came out and ascended the hall.
His attendants announced:
"Whoever wishes to fight, step forward."
Immediately, a man came forward holding a gamecock.
He strode forward.
The prince ordered his rooster released,
and the challenger did the same.
After a brief flurry of leaps,
the challenger's rooster was defeated.
The prince laughed heartily.
In a short while,
several more challengers ascended the platform and were defeated.
The host said:
"It's time."
They went up to the platform together.
The prince examined the rooster and
said:
"Its eyes show angry veins;
this is a formidable bird,
not to be taken lightly."
He ordered his iron-beaked rooster to face it.
After a couple of leaps and clashes,
the prince's rooster was defeated.
He selected a better one,
but it too was defeated, and again with another.
In desperation, the prince ordered his jade rooster from the palace to be brought.
Moments later, it was carried out—
its pure white feathers like an egret's,
majestic and extraordinary.
Wáng Chéng felt disheartened,
knelt, and begged to withdraw,
saying:
"Your Highness's rooster is
a divine creature;
I fear it will injure my bird
and ruin my livelihood."
The prince laughed and said:
"Release it.
If it dies in the fight,
I will compensate you handsomely."
So Chéng released his rooster.
The jade rooster charged straight at it.
As the jade rooster approached,
Chéng's bird crouched like an angry hen, waiting;
when the jade rooster pecked fiercely,
it rose like a soaring crane to strike back.
Advancing and retreating, locked in struggle,
they fought for about the time it takes to finish a meal.
The jade rooster gradually weakened,
while Chéng's bird grew fiercer,
attacking more urgently.
Before long,
snowy feathers were torn loose,
and the jade rooster fled with drooping wings.
A crowd of a thousand spectators
all sighed in admiration.
The prince then asked for the bird and held it himself,
examining it from beak to claws,
scrutinizing every part,
and asked Chéng:
"Is this rooster for sale?"
Chéng replied:
"I have no permanent property;
it is my companion for life.
I do not wish to sell it."
The prince said:
"I will grant you a generous price—
enough to secure a middling fortune.
Are you willing?"
Chéng bowed his head and thought for a good while.
He said:
"I am not inclined to part with it;
but since Your Highness favors it,
if it can provide me with clothing and food,
what more could I ask?"
The prince asked the price,
and Chéng replied, "A thousand taels of gold."
The prince laughed:
"Foolish man!
What treasure is this,
to be worth a thousand gold?"
Chéng said:
"If Your Highness does not consider it a treasure,
to me it is worth more than the Héshì Bì."
The prince asked:
"How so?"
Chéng replied:
"When I take it to the market,
I earn several taels daily,
exchanging them for bushels of grain.
My family of over ten mouths
has no fear of cold or hunger.
What treasure compares to this?"
The prince said:
"I will not shortchange you—
I will give you two hundred taels."
Chéng shook his head.
The prince added another hundred.
Chéng glanced at his host,
whose expression remained unchanged.
So he said:
"In deference to Your Highness,
I will reduce the price by a hundred."
The prince said:
"Enough!
Who would pay nine hundred for a rooster!"
Chéng put the bird in his bag and prepared to leave.
The prince called out:
"Rooster man, come back!
Rooster man, come back!
I will truly give six hundred.
If you agree, sell it;
otherwise, forget it."
Chéng again looked at his host,
who remained composed.
Chéng's heart swelled with desire,
fearing to miss the opportunity,
and said:
"Selling at this price,
I am truly dissatisfied;
but if the deal falls through,
the offense would be greater.
I have no choice—
let it be as Your Highness commands."
The prince was pleased
and immediately weighed out the gold.
Chéng pocketed the money,
bowed in thanks, and left.
His host complained:
"What did I tell you?
Why were you in such a hurry to sell?
If you had held out a little longer,
eight hundred taels would have been in your hand."
Chéng returned home,
tossed the gold on the table,
and asked his host to take his share,
but the host refused.
After repeated insistence,
the host calculated the cost of meals and accepted that amount.
Chéng packed his belongings and returned home.
Arriving home,
he recounted all that had happened
and brought out the gold to celebrate.
The old woman ordered three hundred mǔ of good land to be purchased,
houses built, and tools made—
they became a prosperous family.
The old woman rose early,
making Chéng supervise the farming
and his wife oversee the weaving.
If they showed any laziness,
she would scold them.
Husband and wife lived in harmony,
not daring to complain.
After three years,
the family grew even wealthier.
The old woman announced her intention to leave.
The couple tried to detain her,
even to the point of tears.
So she stayed.
But at dawn the next day, when they went to greet her,
she had vanished without a trace.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Wealth is usually gained through diligence;
here it was gained through laziness—
truly an unheard-of story.
Yet, though reduced to utter poverty,
his fundamental nature remained unchanged.
This is why Heaven at first abandoned him but later took pity on him.
Can laziness indeed lead to wealth and honor?"
From the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
The Gěng family of Tàiyuán
was once a prominent household,
with a vast and sprawling mansion.
Later, as their fortunes declined,
the interconnected towers and halls
were left half abandoned and dilapidated.
Consequently, strange phenomena occurred:
the main hall doors would open and close by themselves,
and the family members were often startled awake by clamor in the middle of the night.
Troubled by this, Gěng
moved to a separate villa,
leaving only an old caretaker to watch the gate.
From then on, the place became even more desolate.
Sometimes, the sounds of laughter, conversation, singing, and music could be heard.
Gěng had a nephew named Gěng Qùbìng,
who was wild, unrestrained, and uninhibited.
He instructed the old caretaker that if he heard or saw anything,
he should rush to inform him.
One night,
seeing lights flickering on and off in the upstairs rooms,
the caretaker ran to report it to the young master.
Gěng Qùbìng wished to enter and investigate the strangeness.
The old man tried to stop him,
but he wouldn't listen.
Being thoroughly familiar with the layout of the doors and rooms,
he pushed through the overgrown weeds and brambles
and made his way inside along winding paths.
He went upstairs,
but found nothing unusual at all.
Passing through the building,
he heard the murmur of people talking.
Peeping stealthily,
he saw two large candles burning,
their light bright as day.
An old man wearing a scholar's cap sat facing south,
with an old woman sitting opposite him,
both appearing to be in their forties.
Facing east was a young man,
perhaps around twenty;
to the right was a young lady,
barely of hair-pinning age.
Wine and meat dishes covered the table,
and they sat in a circle, laughing and chatting.
Gěng Qùbìng burst in abruptly,
laughing and calling out:
"An uninvited guest has arrived!"
The group, startled, fled and hid.
Only the old man came out,
and demanded angrily:
"Who are you, barging into people's private chambers?"
Gěng replied:
"These are *my* family's private chambers.
You have taken possession of them.
Enjoying fine wine all by yourselves,
without inviting the host even once—
isn't that rather too stingy?"
The old man scrutinized him carefully
and said:
"You are not the master of the house."
Gěng said:
"I am the wild Gěng Qùbìng,
the nephew of the master."
The old man paid his respects, saying:
"I have long looked up to you as to a great mountain or the Dipper!"
He then bowed Gěng in
and called for his family to change the dishes.
Gěng stopped him.
The old man then poured wine for his guest.
Gěng said:
"Our families are like old friends.
The guests present need not avoid me;
I beg you to still invite them to drink."
The old man called out:
"Xiào'ér!"
In a moment, the young man came in from outside.
The old man said:
"This is my foolish son."
He bowed and sat down,
and Gěng briefly inquired about their family background.
The old man said of himself:
"My name is Hú Yìjūn."
Gěng Qùbìng was by nature forthright and bold;
his conversation was spirited and lively.
Xiào'ér was also unrestrained and elegant;
as they poured out their thoughts,
they greatly admired and delighted in each other.
Gěng was twenty-one,
two years older than Xiào'ér,
so he addressed him as younger brother.
The old man said:
"I have heard your grandfather compiled 'The Unofficial Biography of Túshān.' Do you know of it?"
Gěng answered:
"Yes, I do."
The old man said:
"I am a descendant of the Túshān clan.
From the Táng dynasty onward,
I can still recall our genealogical records;
but from the Five Dynasties and earlier, there is no transmission.
I would be fortunate if you, young master, could impart some knowledge."
Gěng gave a brief account of the achievements of the Túshān woman in assisting Yǔ,
embellishing it with many words,
his wonderful ideas gushing forth like a spring.
The old man was greatly pleased
and said to his son:
"Today we are fortunate to hear what we have never heard before.
This young master is also not an outsider.
You may invite your mother and Qīngfèng to come
and listen together,
so they may also learn of the virtue of our ancestors."
Xiào'ér went behind the curtain.
After a short while,
the old woman came out with the young lady.
Gěng looked her over carefully:
her delicate manner was captivatingly lovely,
her autumn-wave eyes sparkled with intelligence—
no beauty in the human world could match her.
The old man pointed to the woman and said:
"This is my old wife."
Then pointing to the young lady:
"This is Qīngfèng,
my humble niece.
She is quite intelligent;
whatever she hears or sees, she remembers and does not forget,
so I called her to listen."
Gěng finished his account and drank,
his gaze turning to the young lady,
his eyes fixed and unmoving.
The girl noticed it
and immediately lowered her head.
Gěng secretly stepped on her tiny foot under the table;
she quickly drew her foot back,
but showed no anger.
Gěng's spirit soared,
he could no longer control himself.
Slapping the table, he exclaimed:
"To obtain a wife like this,
I wouldn't trade places with a king facing south!"
Seeing Gěng growing drunk
and even more unrestrained,
the old woman rose with the girl
and hastily lifted the curtain to leave.
Disappointed, Gěng
then took his leave of the old man and went out.
But his heart was entangled;
he could not forget his feelings for Qīngfèng.
When night fell,
he went again,
and the fragrance of orchids and musk still lingered.
He waited all night,
but there was not a sound.
Returning home, he discussed with his wife
the idea of moving the family there to live,
hoping to have an encounter.
His wife refused,
so Shēng went alone
and studied downstairs.
One night, as he was leaning on his desk,
a ghost with disheveled hair entered,
its face as black as lacquer,
staring wide-eyed at Shēng.
Shēng laughed,
dipped his finger in ink and smeared it on his own face,
glaring back at it intently.
The ghost, ashamed, left.
The next night,
when it was very late,
he extinguished the candle and was about to sleep
when he heard the sound of a lock being opened behind the building,
followed by the creak of a door swinging open.
He quickly got up to peek
and saw the door half-open.
Soon, he heard the soft patter of footsteps,
and candlelight emerged from the room.
Looking closely,
it was Qīngfèng.
Suddenly seeing Shēng,
she was startled and stepped back,
quickly closing both doors.
Shēng knelt down and pleaded:
"I have braved danger and hardship,
all for your sake.
Fortunately, there is no one else here.
If I could just hold your hand and share a smile,
I would die without regret."
The girl spoke from a distance:
"How could I not know
the depth of your affection?
But my uncle's household rules are strict,
and I dare not comply."
Shēng persisted in his entreaties,
saying:
"I dare not hope for physical intimacy,
but just seeing your face would be enough."
The girl seemed to consent,
opened the door and came out,
taking his arm and pulling him along.
Shēng was overjoyed,
and together they went downstairs,
where he embraced her and sat her on his lap.
The girl said:
"Fortunately, we are fated to be together;
but after this one night,
even longing will be useless."
He asked:
"Why?"
She replied:
"My uncle feared your boldness,
so he transformed into a fierce ghost to frighten you,
but you were unmoved.
Now he has chosen another place to live,
and the whole family is moving belongings to the new home.
I was left behind to watch over things,
but we depart tomorrow."
With these words,
she wanted to leave,
saying:
"I fear my uncle will return."
Shēng forcibly stopped her,
wanting to be intimate with her.
As they were arguing,
the old man suddenly entered.
The girl, ashamed and frightened, had nowhere to hide,
bowed her head and leaned against the bed,
twisting her sash in silence.
The old man angrily said:
"You disgraceful creature, shaming our family!
If you do not leave quickly,
the whip will follow!"
The girl lowered her head and hurried away,
and the old man also left.
Shēng followed and listened,
hearing endless scolding and abuse.
He heard Qīngfèng sobbing softly,
and his heart felt as if cut by a knife.
He shouted loudly:
"The fault is mine,
what does it have to do with Qīngfèng?
If you spare Fèng,
whether it be the knife, saw, axe, or halberd,
I am willing to bear it myself!"
For a long time, there was silence,
and Shēng returned to sleep.
From then on, the mansion was completely silent.
Shēng's uncle heard of this and found it strange,
willing to sell the house to him,
without haggling over the price.
Shēng was delighted,
and moved his family there.
After living there for over a year,
he was very comfortable,
but he never forgot Fèng for a moment.
On the way back from visiting the ancestral graves during the Qingming Festival,
he saw two small foxes
being chased and cornered by dogs.
One of them fled into the wilderness,
while the other ran anxiously along the road.
Seeing Gěng Qùbìng,
it clung to him, whimpering pitifully,
its ears flattened and head lowered,
as if begging for his help.
Moved by pity,
Gěng opened his robe,
picked it up, and carried it home.
Closing the door,
he placed it on the bed,
and it turned out to be Qīng Fèng.
Overjoyed,
he comforted and inquired after her.
The girl said:
"I was just playing with my maid
when we encountered this great peril.
Had it not been for you, sir,
I would surely have ended up in a dog's belly.
I hope you will not despise me for not being human."
Gěng said:
"Day and night, my thoughts have been fixed on you,
haunting my very dreams.
To see you is like obtaining a rare treasure;
how could I speak of disdain!"
The girl said:
"This is fate.
If not for this calamity,
how could I have come to be with you?
Yet it is fortunate,
for my maid will surely think I am dead,
and thus I can pledge myself to you forever."
Gěng was delighted
and arranged separate quarters for her.
More than two years later,
as Gěng was reading at night,
Xiào'ér suddenly entered.
Gěng stopped reading
and asked in surprise where he had come from.
Xiào'ér prostrated himself on the ground
and said sorrowfully:
"My father faces a sudden disaster,
and no one but you can save him.
He intended to come and plead in person,
but feared you would not receive him,
so he sent me instead."
Gěng asked:
"What is the matter?"
Xiào'ér said:
"Do you know a certain Mò Sānláng, sir?"
Gěng replied:
"He is the son of a family friend from my father's generation."
Xiào'ér said:
"He will be passing by tomorrow.
If he happens to have a hunted fox with him,
I beg you to keep it."
Gěng said:
"The humiliation I suffered downstairs that day
still weighs on my mind.
I dare not involve myself in other matters.
If you truly wish for my humble assistance,
then Qīng Fèng herself must come!"
Xiào'ér said with tears streaming down:
"My sister Fèng died in the wild three years ago!"
Gěng flicked his sleeves and said:
"In that case,
my resentment only deepens!"
He then picked up his book and began reciting aloud,
paying Xiào'ér no further attention.
Xiào'ér rose,
wept aloud,
and left covering his face.
Gěng went to Qīng Fèng
and told her what had happened.
Her face paled as she asked:
"Will you really save him?"
Gěng said:
"I will save him;
but my refusal just now
was merely to repay his former harshness."
Qīng Fèng then said happily:
"I was orphaned young
and was raised by my uncle.
Although he offended you in the past,
it was merely the discipline of our household."
Gěng said:
"Indeed,
but one cannot help feeling slighted.
If you had truly died,
I certainly would not have helped."
Qīng Fèng said with a laugh:
"How cruel!"
The next day,
Mò Sānláng indeed arrived,
with ornamented bridles and tiger-skin quivers,
and a retinue of great splendor.
Gěng went to the gate to welcome him.
Seeing that many game animals had been taken,
among them a black fox,
its fur matted with dark blood;
upon touching it,
he found its body still warm.
He then pretended his fur coat was worn
and asked if he could have the fox to mend it.
Mò generously took it off and gave it to him.
Gěng immediately handed it to Qīng Fèng
and then drank with his guest.
After the guest had left,
Qīng Fèng held the fox in her arms,
and after three days it revived,
twisting and turning until it transformed back into the old man.
Opening his eyes and seeing Fèng,
he doubted he was still in the world of men.
Qīng Fèng recounted the whole story in detail.
The old man then bowed to Gěng,
shamefully apologizing for his past offense.
Happily, he looked at Qīng Fèng and said:
"I always said you were not dead,
and now it is indeed so."
Qīng Fèng said to Gěng:
"If you care for me,
I beg you to lend us the house with the tower,
so that I may fulfill my desire to repay my uncle's care."
Gěng agreed.
The old man, blushing with shame, thanked him and left.
That night,
the whole family indeed moved in.
From then on, they lived together like one family, father and son,
with no more suspicion or jealousy.
Gěng lived in his study,
and Xiào'ér often came to chat and drink with him.
Gěng's eldest son by his principal wife gradually grew up,
so he had Xiào'ér tutor him;
for Xiào'ér taught with great patience and skill,
truly possessing the qualities of a teacher.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wáng Shēng of Tàiyuán,
while walking early one morning,
encountered a young woman
carrying a bundle
and walking with great difficulty.
Hurrying to catch up,
he saw she was a beautiful girl of about sixteen.
Feeling affection and delight,
he asked,
"Why are you walking alone so early in the morning?"
The girl said,
"A passerby like yourself
cannot dispel my sorrows;
why trouble yourself to ask?"
Wáng said:
"What sorrows do you have?
Perhaps I can be of service;
I would not refuse."
The girl said gloomily:
"My parents were greedy for bribes
and sold me into a wealthy household.
The principal wife was extremely jealous,
abusing me in the morning and beating me in the evening.
Unable to bear it any longer,
I have fled far away."
He asked:
"Where are you going?"
She said:
"A fugitive
has no fixed destination."
Wáng said:
"My humble dwelling is not far;
you are welcome to visit."
The girl, pleased,
followed him.
Wáng carried her bundle for her
and led her home together.
The girl, seeing no one in the room,
asked:
"Why do you have no family?"
He replied:
"This is my study."
The girl said:
"This place is quite good.
If you pity me and wish to save my life,
you must keep it secret and not tell anyone."
Wáng agreed.
Then they slept together.
He hid her in a secret room,
and for several days no one knew.
Wáng secretly told his wife.
His wife, Chén,
suspected she was a concubine from a wealthy family,
and urged him to send her away.
Shēng did not listen.
Once, he happened to go to the market,
where he met a Daoist priest.
The priest looked at Shēng and was startled,
asking:
"What have you encountered?"
Shēng replied:
"Nothing."
The priest said:
"Your body is surrounded by evil energy;
how can you say nothing?"
Shēng again strenuously denied it.
The priest then left,
saying:
"How deluded!
Truly, there are people in this world who are about to die and yet remain unaware."
Shēng, finding his words strange,
became somewhat suspicious of the woman;
but then he thought, such a clearly beautiful person,
how could she possibly be a monster?
He decided the priest was probably using exorcism and charms to make a living.
Not long after,
he arrived at his study door,
but the door was barred from inside,
and he could not enter.
Suspicious of what she was doing,
he climbed over the wall.
The inner room door was also closed.
Treading softly, he peeked through the window
and saw a ferocious demon,
its face a bluish-green,
its teeth like a saw.
It had spread a human skin on the bed,
and was painting it with a colored brush;
then it threw down the brush,
lifted the skin,
shook it out like a garment,
draped it over its body,
and transformed into the woman.
Witnessing this,
he was terrified,
and crawled out like an animal.
He hurried to find the priest,
but did not know where he had gone.
Searching everywhere,
he met him in the wilderness,
and knelt down pleading for rescue.
The priest said:
"I shall help you drive it away.
This creature has also suffered greatly;
it has only just found someone to take its place,
and I cannot bear to harm its life either."
He then gave Shēng a fly-whisk,
telling him to hang it on his bedroom door.
As they parted,
he arranged to meet at the Qīngdì Temple.
Shēng returned home,
did not dare enter his study,
but went to his inner chamber to sleep,
and hung the whisk there.
Around the first watch,
he heard a rustling sound outside the door.
He dared not look himself,
so he had his wife look.
She only saw the woman approach,
look at the whisk and not dare enter;
she stood there gnashing her teeth,
and after a long while, left.
A little later she returned,
cursing:
"The priest is trying to scare me.
Does he really think I'll spit out what's already in my mouth?!"
She took the whisk and smashed it,
broke through the bedroom door and entered.
She went straight to Shēng's bed,
ripped open his abdomen,
grabbed his heart, and left.
His wife wailed.
A maid entered with a candle,
and saw Shēng was already dead,
his chest cavity a bloody mess.
Chén was horrified, weeping, but dared not make a sound.
The next day,
she sent his younger brother Èrláng to run and tell the priest.
The priest angrily said:
"I originally pitied it,
but this demon actually dares to act like this!"
He immediately came with Shēng's brother.
The woman was already gone.
Then, looking up and scanning the surroundings,
he said:
"Fortunately, it hasn't fled far!"
He asked:
"Whose family lives in the southern compound?"
Èrláng said:
"That is my lodging."
The priest said:
"It is there now."
Èrláng was astonished,
thinking it impossible.
The priest asked:
"Has an unfamiliar person come?"
He replied:
"I left early for the Qīngdì Temple,
and truly don't know.
I should go back and ask."
He left and returned after a short while,
saying:
"Indeed there is.
This morning an old woman came,
wanting to hire herself as a servant to do chores,
my wife detained her,
and she is still there."
The priest said:
"That is the creature."
So they went together.
Holding a wooden sword,
he stood in the center of the courtyard,
and shouted:
"Evil demon!
Repay me my whisk!"
The old woman inside the room
turned pale with panic,
and rushed out the door trying to flee.
The priest pursued and struck her.
The old woman fell,
and the human skin split open and peeled off,
transforming into a fierce ghost,
lying on the ground howling like a pig.
The priest swung his wooden sword and beheaded it;
its body turned into thick smoke,
swirling on the ground into a heap.
The priest took out a gourd,
pulled out its stopper and placed it in the smoke.
It hissed as if sucking in air,
and in an instant the smoke was gone.
The priest stoppered it and put it in his bag.
They all looked at the human skin:
eyebrows, eyes, hands, and feet,
were all complete.
The priest rolled it up,
making a sound like rolling a scroll painting,
and also put it in his bag.
Then he bid farewell and prepared to leave.
Chén knelt to greet him at the door,
weeping and begging for a method to restore life.
The priest declined, saying he could not.
Chén grew even more grief-stricken,
prostrate on the ground and refusing to rise.
The priest pondered and said:
"My arts are shallow,
I truly cannot raise the dead.
I will point you to someone
who might be able to;
go and plead with him, it should certainly be effective."
She asked:
"Who is it?"
He said:
"There is a madman in the market,
who often lies in filth.
Try knocking and pleading with him pitifully.
If he wildly insults you, madam,
do not be angry."
Èrláng also knew of him by reputation.
So they parted from the priest,
and he went with his sister-in-law.
She saw a beggar singing wildly on the road,
with snot hanging three feet long,
so filthy that no one dared approach.
Chén crawled forward on her knees.
The beggar laughed and said:
"Does the beauty love me?"
Chén told him the reason.
He laughed even louder and said:
"Any man can be a husband,
why keep him alive?"
Chén pleaded with him earnestly.
Then he said:
"How strange!
Someone is dead, yet begs me to revive him.
Am I Yánmó?"
Angrily, he struck Chén with his staff.
Chén endured the pain and bore it.
Market-goers gradually gathered like a wall.
The beggar coughed up a handful of phlegm and spit,
held it toward Chén's mouth and said:
"Eat it!"
Chén flushed red in the face,
looking troubled: but then she remembered the Daoist priest's instruction,
and forced herself to swallow it.
She felt it enter her throat,
hard like a clump of cotton,
grating as it went down,
and stuck in her chest.
The beggar laughed loudly and said:
"The beauty truly loves me!"
Then he stood up,
and walked away without looking back.
She followed him,
into a temple.
Chasing after him to beg,
she could not find him anywhere;
she searched everywhere,
but found no trace at all,
and returned ashamed and resentful.
Grieving over the tragic death of her husband,
and ashamed of having swallowed the spit,
she wept in sorrow,
wishing only to die immediately.
Just as she was about to clean the blood and prepare the corpse,
the family stood watching from a distance,
none daring to come near.
Chén held the corpse and gathered the intestines,
arranging them while weeping.
Crying until her voice grew hoarse,
she suddenly felt like vomiting.
She felt the lump in her chest
rush out abruptly,
before she could turn her head,
it had already fallen into the chest cavity.
Startled, she looked:
it was a human heart.
In the cavity it throbbed and leaped,
steam rising from it like smoke.
Greatly astonished,
she quickly pressed the cavity closed with both hands,
squeezing with all her might.
When she relaxed slightly,
warm air seeped out from the缝隙.
So she tore silk cloth and hastily bound it.
Stroking the corpse with her hand,
it gradually grew warm.
She covered it with a quilt.
In the middle of the night, she lifted the cover to look:
there was breath from the nose.
By daybreak,
he had actually revived.
He said:
"It was like a vague dream,
I only feel a slight pain in my abdomen."
Looking at the wound,
a scab had formed like a coin,
and he soon recovered.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"How foolish are people in this world!
Clearly a demon,
yet they see it as beauty.
How deluded are the foolish!
Clearly loyalty,
yet they see it as falsehood.
However, if one covets another's beauty and preys upon it,
then one's own wife will also swallow another's spit and find it sweet.
Heaven's way favors retribution,
but the foolish and deluded do not realize it.
How lamentable indeed!"
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
A certain old man from Chǔ,
traded abroad.
His wife lived alone,
dreaming of intercourse with a man;
waking and touching him,
it was a little man.
Observing his nature,
different from a human,
she knew it was a fox.
Not long after,
he got off the bed and left,
the door not yet opened but he had already vanished.
When evening came,
she invited an old cook woman to keep her company.
She had a ten-year-old son,
who usually slept on a separate bed,
and she also called him to stay together.
Late in the night,
the old woman and the child both fell asleep,
and the fox came again.
The wife murmured as if talking in a dream.
The old woman woke,
called out to her,
and the fox then left.
From then on,
she felt dazed as if something were missing.
At night,
she dared not extinguish the candle,
warning her son not to sleep soundly.
Late at night,
the child and the old woman leaned against the wall and dozed off.
When they woke,
the wife was missing,
thinking she had gone out to relieve herself;
waiting long without her return,
they began to suspect.
The old woman was afraid,
not daring to go look for her.
The child took a light and searched everywhere with it,
reaching another room,
where his mother lay naked;
approaching to help her up,
she showed no shame or shrinking.
From then on she went mad,
singing, crying, shouting, and cursing,
in countless ways every day.
At night she disliked being with people,
making her son sleep on a separate bed,
and sending the old woman away.
Whenever the child heard his mother laughing and talking,
he would immediately light a fire to see.
His mother instead angrily scolded him,
but the child paid no mind,
so everyone admired the child's courage.
However, she played without restraint,
daily imitating masonry,
piling bricks and stones on the windows,
and would not stop when told.
If someone removed one stone,
she would roll on the ground crying like a spoiled child,
and no one dared provoke her.
After several days,
both windows were completely blocked,
with no light at all.
Then she mixed mud to plaster the holes in the walls,
busily working all day,
not weary of the labor.
After plastering,
having nothing else to do,
she took a kitchen knife and began sharpening it vigorously.
Those who saw her despised her obstinacy,
and did not regard her as human.
The child hid a knife in his bosom at midnight,
and covered the lamp with a gourd.
He waited until his mother began to talk in her sleep,
then quickly uncovered the lamp,
blocked the door, and shouted.
After a long while there was no unusual sound,
so he left the door and spoke loudly,
pretending to search.
Suddenly, a creature,
like a wildcat,
dashed toward the crack in the door.
He struck at it quickly,
but only cut off its tail,
about two inches long,
with blood still dripping.
Earlier,
when he lifted the lamp cover,
his mother began to curse him,
but the child acted as if he did not hear.
Failing to hit the creature,
he went to bed in frustration.
He thought to himself that although he had not killed it immediately,
he could at least hope it would not return.
At dawn,
he saw the bloodstains leading over the wall.
Following the trail,
he found it led into the Hé family's garden.
That night, it indeed did not come,
and the child secretly rejoiced.
But his mother lay in a stupor as if dead.
Not long after,
the merchant returned,
and went to the bed to inquire.
The wife cursed him,
looking at him as if he were an enemy.
The child told him what had happened.
The old man was shocked,
and called a doctor to treat her.
The wife poured out the medicine and cursed.
He secretly mixed the medicine into soup and had her drink it,
and after several days she gradually recovered.
Both father and son were delighted.
One night, they woke up
to find the wife missing;
father and son searched and found her in another room.
From then on, she became deranged again,
and did not want to stay in the same room with her husband.
Toward evening,
she would run to another room.
When they tried to pull her back,
she cursed even more fiercely.
The old man had no solution,
so he locked all the other doors.
But when the wife ran toward them,
the doors would open by themselves.
The old man was troubled by this,
and tried every possible exorcism,
but none had the slightest effect.
The child slipped into the Hé family's garden at dusk,
hiding in the undergrowth,
intending to find out where the fox was.
When the moon first rose,
he suddenly heard people talking.
Quietly parting the weeds,
he saw two people coming to drink,
with a long-bearded servant holding a pot,
wearing old brown clothes.
Their speech was soft and indistinct,
not very clear.
After a while,
he heard one of them say:
"Tomorrow, bring a jug of white wine."
A moment later,
they all left,
only the long-bearded one remained,
taking off his clothes and lying on a stone in the courtyard.
Looking closely,
his limbs were all like a human's,
but a tail hung from his back.
The child wanted to return,
but feared the fox would notice,
so he stayed hidden all night.
Before dawn,
he heard the two people returning one after another,
murmuring as they entered the bamboo grove.
Then the child went home.
The old man asked where he had been,
and he replied:
"Staying at uncle's house."
Once, when he went to the market with his father,
he saw a fox tail hanging in a hat shop,
and begged his father to buy it.
The old man ignored him.
The child tugged at his father's clothes,
whining and pestering him.
The old man could not bear to refuse him completely,
so he bought it.
While his father was trading in the market,
the child played nearby,
and when his father looked away,
he stole some money,
bought white wine,
and left it in the shop's corridor.
He had an uncle who lived in the city,
and made his living as a hunter.
The child ran to his house.
His uncle was out.
His aunt asked about his mother's illness,
and he replied:
"She has been slightly better these past few days.
But then a rat gnawed her clothes,
and she was so angry she couldn't stop crying,
so she sent me to ask for hunting poison."
His aunt opened a cabinet,
took out about a qian's worth,
wrapped it, and gave it to him.
The child thought it was too little.
His aunt wanted to make noodles to feed him.
The child saw that there was no one in the room,
opened the packet himself,
secretly took a handful, and hid it in his bosom.
Then he hurried to tell his aunt
not to light the fire,
"Father is waiting in the market,
and I have no time to eat."
Then he went straight out,
and secretly put the poison into the wine.
He wandered around the market,
and did not return until evening.
His father asked where he had been,
and he said he was at his uncle's.
From then on, the child roamed the market every day.
One day, he saw the long-bearded man among the crowd.
The child looked at him carefully,
and secretly followed him.
Gradually, he spoke to him,
asking where he lived.
The man replied:
"In the northern village."
He also asked the child,
and the child lied:
"In a cave."
The long-bearded man was surprised that he lived in a cave.
The child laughed and said:
"My family has lived in a cave for generations,
surely you don't?"
The man was even more surprised,
and asked his surname.
The child said:
"I am a son of the Hú family.
I once saw you somewhere,
following two gentlemen,
have you forgotten?"
The man looked at him carefully,
half believing, half doubting.
The child slightly lifted the hem of his clothes,
revealing a little of his fake tail,
and said:
"We mix among humans,
but this thing still remains,
which is truly hateful."
The man asked:
"What are you doing in the market?"
The child said:
"My father sent me to buy wine."
The man also said he was there to buy wine.
The child asked:
"Have you bought it yet?"
The man said:
"Most of us are poor,
so we often steal instead."
The child said:
"This task is also quite hard,
full of fear and worry."
The man said:
"I am sent by my master,
so I have no choice."
Then the child asked:
"Who is your master?"
The man said:
"They are the two gentlemen you saw before.
One is having an affair with Wáng's wife in the northern suburb,
and the other stays at an old man's house in the eastern village.
The old man's son is very fierce,
and cut off his tail,
it took ten days to heal,
and now he has gone back again."
Having finished speaking,
he was about to take his leave,
saying:
"Do not delay my business."
The boy said:
"Stealing is difficult;
it is not as easy as buying.
I will first buy some wine and leave it under the corridor,
respectfully offering it to you.
I still have some money left in my pouch,
so I am not worried about buying wine."
The man felt ashamed, having nothing with which to repay him.
The boy said:
"We are of the same kind;
why begrudge such a trifle?
When you have leisure,
I should still drink heartily with you."
Then he went with him,
fetched the wine and gave it to him,
and then returned.
When night came,
his mother actually slept peacefully,
and did not run away again.
Knowing something was amiss,
he told his father and together they went to investigate.
They found two foxes dead on the pavilion,
and one fox dead in the grass,
its beak still dripping with fresh blood.
The wine bottle was still there;
picking it up and shaking it,
they found it was not yet empty.
His father asked in surprise:
"Why didn't you tell me earlier?"
He replied:
"These creatures are most clever;
if I had revealed it,
they would have known."
The old man said joyfully:
"My son,
you are the Chén Píng of fox-hunting."
Thereupon, father and son carried the foxes home.
They saw that one fox had a bald tail,
with clear knife marks.
From then on, peace was restored.
But the woman was extremely emaciated;
her mind gradually became clear,
though her coughing worsened,
and she would vomit several sheng of phlegm,
but she soon recovered.
The wife of Wáng of the northern suburb,
had previously been haunted by a fox;
when they inquired about her now,
the fox was gone and her illness was also cured.
The old man, from then on, considered his son extraordinary,
and taught him riding and archery.
Later, he rose to high rank, becoming a Zǒngróng.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Lǚ Fèngníng, a servant of Wáng Pújīn from my hometown,
had a peculiar fondness for snakes.
Whenever he caught a small snake,
he would swallow it whole,
as if eating a scallion.
For larger ones,
he would cut them into inch-long pieces with a knife,
and then scoop them up to eat.
He chewed them with a crunching sound,
blood and water staining his cheeks.
Moreover, he was adept at smelling them;
once, he smelled the scent of a snake from beyond a wall,
hurriedly ran outside the wall,
and indeed found a snake over a foot long.
At the time, he had no knife on him,
so he first bit off its head,
while its tail still wriggled at the corner of his mouth.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Jīn Shìchéng
was a man of Chángshān.
He was usually unrestrained.
Suddenly, he left home to become a mendicant monk.
He seemed mad,
considering filth delicious to eat.
When dogs or sheep left excrement before him,
he would crouch down and eat it.
He called himself a Buddha.
Ignorant men and women, amazed by his behavior,
numbered in the thousands and tens of thousands who followed him as disciples.
Jīn would order them to eat excrement,
and none dared disobey.
He built halls and pavilions,
the expenses being immense,
yet people were all willing to contribute.
The county magistrate, Nán, detested his strangeness,
arrested him and had him flogged,
ordering him to repair the Confucian temple.
His disciples eagerly spread the word:
"The Buddha is in trouble!"
They vied to raise funds to rescue him.
The palace was completed within a month,
and the collection of money
was even swifter than the harsh demands of cruel officials.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"I have heard of Dàorén Jīn;
people all address him by his name,
calling him 'Jīn Shìchéng Fó'.
To stoop to eating filth
is the extreme.
Flogging him was not enough to disgrace him,
but punishing him happened to serve a purpose;
how excellent Magistrate Nán's handling of the law was!
Yet that the school temple fell into disrepair and had to rely on a demonic dàorén
is also a shame for the scholar-officials."
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Dǒng Shēng,
courtesy name Xiásī,
was a man from the western borderlands of Qīngzhōu.
One winter evening,
he spread his quilt on the bed and lit the charcoal brazier.
Just as he was about to light the lamp,
a friend happened to invite him for a drink,
so he locked the door and left.
Arriving at his friend's place,
among the guests was a physician
skilled in pulse diagnosis according to the Tàisù method,
and he examined all the guests.
Finally, he looked at Wáng Shēng Jiǔsī and Dǒng, saying:
"I have examined many people,
but none have pulses as strange as you two gentlemen: noble pulses yet with indications of baseness,
long-life pulses yet with signs of brevity.
This is beyond what I dare to determine.
However, it is particularly severe for you, Dǒng."
Everyone asked in alarm.
He said:
"At this point, I too am at a loss in my art,
and dare not make a rash judgment.
I urge you both to take care."
The two were initially very frightened,
but then considered it ambiguous talk,
and paid it no mind.
In the middle of the night,
Dǒng returned,
and seeing the study door slightly ajar,
he grew very suspicious.
In his drunken state, he recalled to himself,
that it must have been due to his hurried departure,
that he had forgotten to lock it.
Entering the room,
before he could light a lamp,
he first reached his hand under the covers,
to feel whether they were warm.
As soon as he reached in,
he felt the smoothness of someone lying there.
Greatly startled,
he withdrew his hand.
Hastily lighting a lamp,
he discovered it was actually a beautiful woman,
with a youthful face and tender age,
no different from a celestial being.
He was ecstatic.
Playfully, he reached to feel her lower body,
and felt a long, furry tail.
Terrified,
he wanted to flee.
The woman had already awakened,
reaching out to grab Dǒng's arm,
asking:
"Where are you going?"
Dǒng became even more frightened,
trembling and pleading:
"I beg the immortal to have mercy and forgive me!"
The woman laughed and said:
"What did you see that makes you fear me?"
Dǒng said:
"I do not fear the head, but I fear the tail."
The woman laughed again and said:
"You are mistaken.
What tail is there?"
Taking Dǒng's hand,
she forced him to feel again,
and her thigh flesh was like smooth fat,
the coccyx bone bare and smooth.
She laughed and said:
"How about that?
You were in a drunken, dazed state,
and didn't know what you were seeing,
thus wronging me like this."
Dǒng had always been delighted by her beauty,
and now he was even more bewildered,
instead blaming himself for the sudden mistake.
Yet he wondered how she had come without reason.
The woman said:
"Do you not remember the yellow-haired girl from the east neighbor?
Counting on my fingers since we moved away,
it has already been ten years.
At that time, I had not yet come of age,
and you were still a young boy."
Dǒng suddenly realized and said:
"Are you Ā Suǒ of the Zhōu family?"
The woman said:
"That's right."
Dǒng said:
"Now that you mention it,
I vaguely remember.
Ten years without seeing you,
and you've become so slender and graceful!
But how did you manage to come so suddenly?"
The woman said:
"I was married to a foolish husband for four or five years,
my parents-in-law passed away one after another,
and unfortunately, I became a widow like Zhūo Wénjūn,
leaving me all alone,
isolated with no one to rely on.
Remembering that from childhood, you were the only one I knew,
so I came to see you and seek refuge.
When I entered the gate, it was already dusk,
and someone inviting you for a drink happened to arrive,
so I hid and waited for your return.
Waiting for so long,
my feet grew cold and my skin prickled,
so I borrowed the quilt to warm myself,
I hope you do not suspect me."
Dǒng was overjoyed,
undressed and slept with her,
feeling extremely pleased with himself.
After more than a month,
he gradually became emaciated,
his family found it strange and asked,
but he always said he didn't know why.
After a long time,
his face and appearance grew increasingly haggard,
and then he became afraid,
going again to consult a skilled physician to take his pulse.
The doctor said:
"This is a demonic pulse.
The signs of impending death from before are now confirmed,
the illness cannot be treated."
Dǒng wept bitterly,
and refused to leave.
The doctor had no choice,
performed acupuncture on his hands and moxibustion on his navel,
and gave him medicine,
instructing him:
"If you encounter anything,
you must resolutely cut it off."
Dǒng also felt himself in danger.
After returning home,
the woman laughingly tried to detain him.
He angrily said:
"Do not entangle with me anymore,
I am about to die!"
He walked away without looking back.
The woman was greatly shamed,
and also angrily said:
"Do you still wish to live!"
That night,
Dǒng took the medicine and slept alone.
As soon as he closed his eyes,
he dreamed of coupling with the woman,
and upon waking, he had already had a nocturnal emission.
Even more terrified,
he moved to sleep inside,
with his wife and children keeping watch by lamplight.
The dream was the same as before.
Peeking, he found the woman had already disappeared.
After several days,
Dǒng vomited over a dou of blood and died.
Wáng Jiǔsī was in his study when
he saw a woman enter.
Enchanted by her beauty, he had an affair with her.
When he asked where she came from,
she said,
"I am a neighbor of Xiásī.
He used to be fond of me,
but unexpectedly, he was bewitched by a fox and died.
These creatures carry a malevolent aura,
and scholars should be careful to guard against them."
Wáng admired her even more,
and they continued their intimate relationship.
After a few days,
he became confused and fell ill, growing emaciated.
Suddenly, he dreamed that Dǒng said,
"The one who is intimate with you is a fox.
She killed me,
and now she wants to kill my friend.
I have already filed a complaint in the underworld,
to vent this hidden grievance.
On the seventh night,
you must light incense outside your room—
do not forget!"
Waking up, he found this strange.
He said to the woman,
"I am very ill,
and I fear I may soon perish.
Some have advised me to abstain from intimacy."
The woman said,
"If fate decrees a long life,
intimacy will not harm it;
if fate does not grant longevity,
abstaining from intimacy will not prevent death."
She sat with him, teasing and laughing.
Wáng could not control his heart,
and they were intimate again.
Afterward, he regretted it
but could not break it off.
When evening came,
he stuck incense on the door.
When the woman arrived,
she pulled it out and discarded it.
That night, he dreamed again that Dǒng came,
reproaching him for disobeying his instructions.
The next night,
he secretly instructed his family
to light the incense after he had gone to bed.
The woman, lying on the bed,
suddenly exclaimed in alarm,
"Have you placed incense again?"
Wáng said he did not know.
The woman hurriedly got up, found the incense,
and broke it, extinguishing it.
She came in and said,
"Who told you to do this?"
Wáng said,
"Perhaps my wife, worried about my illness,
believed a shaman and performed an exorcism."
The woman paced uneasily, displeased.
The family secretly saw that the incense had been extinguished
and lit it again.
The woman suddenly sighed and said,
"Your blessings are truly profound.
I mistakenly harmed Xiásī and then came to you,
which was truly my fault.
I will go with him to face judgment in the underworld.
If you do not forget our past affection,
do not damage my physical form."
She hesitated, got off the bed,
and fell to the ground, dead.
When they shone a light on her,
she was a fox.
Fearing she might revive,
Wáng immediately called his family,
who skinned her and hung the hide.
Wáng became gravely ill,
and saw the fox come to him, saying,
"I appealed to the court of law.
The court said that Dǒng, moved by lust,
deserved his death;
but it blamed me for bewitching people,
confiscated my golden elixir,
and ordered me to return to life.
Where is my physical form?"
Wáng said,
"My family did not know,
and they have already removed it."
The fox said sorrowfully,
"I have killed many people,
and my death is already overdue;
but how cruel you are!"
She left resentfully.
Wáng's illness nearly took his life,
and it took half a year for him to recover.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In the household of the elderly gentleman Wáng Qīnwén of Xīnchéng,
there was a stableman surnamed Wáng
who entered Láo Mountain in his youth to study the Dao.
After a long time,
he ceased eating cooked food,
consuming only pine nuts and white stones,
and hair grew all over his body.
After several years,
he thought of his elderly mother and returned home,
gradually resuming cooked food,
though he still ate stones as before.
Holding a stone up to the sun,
he could tell whether it was sweet, bitter, sour, or salty,
as if eating taro.
When his mother died,
he returned to the mountain,
and now another seventeen or eighteen years have passed.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Among the scholars of Xīnchéng was one Wáng Qǐhòu,
the great-grandson of Provincial Governor Wáng Xiàngkūn, styled Zhōngzì.
He saw a woman enter his room,
plump, dark, and unattractive.
She smiled and approached his bed,
her manner very indecent.
Wáng resisted her,
but she would not leave.
From then on, he saw her whether sitting or lying down.
But his resolve was firm,
and he never wavered.
The woman grew angry,
slapped his face,
which made a sound,
though it did not hurt much.
The woman hung a belt from the beam,
intending to hang herself together with him.
Unconsciously, Wáng threw himself under the beam,
stretching his neck as if to hang.
Others saw that his feet did not touch the ground,
and he stood rigidly in mid-air,
yet he could not die.
From then on, he became mad.
Suddenly, he would say,
"She is going to throw herself into the river with me."
He would race madly toward the river,
and had to be dragged back to stop.
In a hundred such ways,
this happened several times a day,
and neither spells nor medicine had any effect.
One day,
he suddenly saw a warrior enter with chains,
who angrily shouted,
"How dare you disturb an honest man!"
He immediately seized the woman by the neck,
pulling her out from within.
Just as they reached outside the window,
the woman no longer had human form:
her eyes flashed like lightning,
and her mouth was as red as a basin of blood.
He recalled that among the four clay demons at the entrance of the City God Temple,
one looked exactly like her.
Thereafter, his illness vanished.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Língyáng there lived a man named Zhū Ěrdàn,
whose courtesy name was Xiǎomíng.
He was bold and unrestrained by nature,
but had always been rather dull-witted.
Although he studied diligently,
he had not yet gained any fame.
One day,
the members of his literary society were drinking together.
Someone teased him, saying:
"You have a reputation for boldness.
If you can go to the Temple of the Ten Kings late at night,
carry back the Judge from the left corridor,
we'll all chip in to host a feast for you."
Now, in Língyáng there was a Temple of the Ten Kings,
where the gods and ghosts were all carved from wood,
adorned to look as if alive.
In the eastern corridor stood a Judge,
with a green face and a red beard,
his appearance especially fierce and hideous.
Sometimes at night, the sounds of interrogation and torture could be heard from the two corridors.
Those who entered
found their hair standing on end.
So the others used this to challenge Zhū.
Zhū laughed, stood up,
and went straight there.
Not long after,
they heard a loud shout from outside the gate:
"I have invited the bearded Master here!"
Everyone stood up.
In a moment, he carried the Judge in,
placed him on the table,
raised a cup,
and poured a libation three times.
When the others saw this,
they shrank back, uneasy in their seats,
and urged him to carry it back.
Zhū again poured wine on the ground,
and prayed, saying:
"Your disciple is wild and rash, lacking refinement.
I trust the great Master will not take offense.
My humble dwelling is not far.
You should come by when in the mood to seek a drink,
and I hope you will not stand on ceremony."
Then he carried it back.
The next day,
the others indeed invited him to drink.
Arriving at dusk,
he returned half-drunk,
his spirits still high,
and lit a lamp to drink alone.
Suddenly, someone lifted the curtain and entered.
Looking at him,
it was the Judge.
Zhū stood up and said:
"I suppose I am about to die!
The other night I offended you,
have you come now to punish me?"
The Judge parted his thick beard,
smiled and said:
"No.
Last night, moved by your noble gesture, you invited me.
Tonight I happened to be free,
and have respectfully come to fulfill the promise made by a man of understanding."
Zhū was greatly pleased.
He tugged at his sleeve, urging him to sit,
and himself got up to wash the utensils and heat the wine.
The Judge said:
"The weather is warm,
we can drink it cold."
Zhū complied,
placed the jar on the table,
and ran to tell his family to prepare dishes and fruit.
His wife heard this,
was greatly alarmed,
and warned him not to go out.
Zhū did not listen,
but stood waiting for the food to be prepared and brought out.
They exchanged cups and drank to each other,
and only then did Zhū ask his surname.
He said:
"My surname is Lù,
I have no given name."
When Zhū discussed ancient classics with him,
his responses came swift as echoes.
Zhū asked:
"Do you know the eight-legged essay?"
He said:
"I can also distinguish the good from the bad.
In the underworld, the reading and reciting
is somewhat similar to that in the world of the living."
Lù drank boldly,
downing ten cups at once.
As Zhū had been drinking all day,
he soon felt like a jade mountain toppling over,
and lay slumped over the table, drunkenly asleep.
When he awoke,
the remaining candle was dim and yellow,
and his ghostly guest had already left.
From then on, he came every two or three days,
their friendship growing ever closer,
and they often slept foot to foot.
Zhū presented his draft writings,
and Lù would always mark them in red,
saying they were all not good.
One night,
Zhū was drunk
and went to bed first,
while Lù continued drinking alone.
Suddenly, in a drunken dream,
Zhū felt a slight pain in his chest and belly;
waking and looking,
he saw Lù sitting solemnly by his bed,
having opened his chest and taken out his intestines and stomach,
arranging them strand by strand.
Startled, Zhū said:
"We have never had any enmity,
why do you kill me?"
Lù laughed and said:
"Don't be afraid.
I am changing your heart for a wiser one."
Calmly, he put the intestines back in,
closed the opening again,
and finally bound Zhū's waist with a strip of foot-binding cloth.
When the operation was finished,
he looked at the bed and there was no trace of blood.
Zhū felt a slight numbness around his belly.
He saw Lù place a lump of flesh on the table.
Asked about it,
he said:
"This is your heart.
Your essays do not flow smoothly,
because I know the pores of your heart are blocked.
Just now, in the underworld,
from among thousands of hearts,
I picked out a good one
and changed it for you.
I leave this one here to make up the number."
Then he got up,
closed the door, and left.
At daybreak, Zhū untied the cloth to look,
and found the wound had already healed,
leaving only a red mark like a thread.
From then on, his literary thinking greatly improved,
and he could remember everything at a glance.
A few days later,
he showed his essay to Lù again.
Lù said:
"It's acceptable now.
But your fortune is thin,
you cannot achieve great nobility,
only up to the provincial and metropolitan examinations."
Zhū asked:
"When?"
He said:
"This year you will certainly come out top."
Not long after,
Zhū came first in the preliminary examination,
and in the autumn provincial examination, he indeed passed as Jīngyuán.
His fellow society members had always mocked him;
but when they saw his examination essay,
they looked at each other in astonishment,
and only after careful inquiry did they learn of the strange affair.
Together they begged Zhū to introduce them first,
wishing to befriend Lù.
Lù agreed.
They prepared a grand feast to await him.
At the first watch,
Lù arrived,
his red beard lively,
eyes shining like lightning.
The others turned pale with fright,
their teeth chattering;
and gradually they slipped away.
Zhū then took Lù back to drink,
and when they were thoroughly drunk,
Zhū said:
"You have cleansed my intestines and purged my stomach,
and I have already received much favor.
There is still one more matter I would like to trouble you with,
I wonder if it is possible?"
Lù then asked what it was.
Zhū said:
"If the heart and intestines can be exchanged,
I imagine the face can also be changed.
My wife,
the one I married in my youth,
has a lower body that is not at all unpleasing,
but her head and face are not very beautiful.
I would still like to trouble you with your knife and axe,
what do you think?"
Lù laughed and said:
"Agreed,
allow me to plan it slowly."
After several days,
he came knocking at the door in the middle of the night.
Zhū hurriedly got up and invited him in.
Holding a candle to look,
he saw something wrapped in his lapel.
When questioned,
he said:
"What you entrusted me with before,
I had difficulty finding.
Just now I obtained the head of a beautiful woman,
and I respectfully report to fulfill your command."
Zhū opened it to look,
and the blood on the neck was still wet.
Lù immediately urged him to go in quickly,
so as not to alarm the fowl and dogs.
Zhū worried that the doors were locked at night.
When Lù arrived,
with one hand he pushed the door,
and it opened by itself.
He led him to the bedroom,
where they saw the wife sleeping on her side.
Lù handed the head to Zhū to hold;
he himself took out from his boot a white blade like a dagger,
pressed it against the wife's neck,
and applied force as if cutting through rotten material,
meeting the blade and splitting apart,
the head fell beside the pillow;
he quickly took the beautiful woman's head from Zhū's bosom,
placed it on the neck,
carefully adjusted it to be straight and proper,
and then pressed it down.
Afterward, he moved the pillow to fill the space by the shoulder,
ordered Zhū to bury the head in a quiet place,
and then left.
When Zhū's wife woke up,
she felt a slight numbness around her neck,
and her cheeks were rough like scales;
rubbing them,
she got flakes of blood,
and was greatly alarmed.
She called a maid to fetch water for washing;
the maid saw the face covered in blood,
and was shocked to death.
When she washed,
the basin water turned completely red.
Raising her head, she saw that her face was completely changed,
and was again extremely frightened.
The wife took a mirror to look at herself,
bewildered and unable to understand.
Zhū entered and told her;
then repeatedly examined her closely,
and saw long eyebrows covering the temples,
dimples appearing on the cheekbones when she smiled,
she was like a person from a painting.
Unfastening the collar to examine,
there was a red line all around,
the flesh color above and below,
was clearly different.
Previously,
Imperial Censor Wú had a daughter who was very beautiful,
but before she could marry, she lost two husbands,
so at nineteen she was still unmarried.
During the Lantern Festival, she visited the Temple of the Ten Kings,
at that time the crowd was very mixed,
and among them was a rogue thief who saw her and coveted her beauty,
so he secretly inquired about her residence,
took advantage of the night to climb in with a ladder,
broke through the bedroom door,
killed a maid under the bed,
and forced the girl to have intercourse;
the girl resisted with all her strength and shouted,
the thief became angry,
and killed her too.
Madame Wú faintly heard the noise,
called a maid to go see,
who saw the corpse and was shocked to death.
The whole household got up,
placed the corpse in the hall,
and put the head beside the neck,
the whole family wailed and cried,
in turmoil all night.
At dawn when they lifted the quilt,
the body was there but the head was missing.
They beat all the maidservants,
saying they had not guarded properly,
causing it to be buried in a dog's belly.
The Imperial Censor reported to the commandery.
The commandery set strict deadlines to capture the thief,
but after three months the criminal was not caught.
Gradually, there were those who told Sir Wú about the strange affair of the head exchange at the Zhū household.
Wú was suspicious,
and sent an old woman to investigate their home;
entering and seeing the wife,
she fled in alarm to report to Sir Wú.
Sir Wú saw that his daughter's corpse was still preserved,
and was shocked and puzzled, unable to decide for himself.
He suspected that Zhū had killed his daughter using unorthodox methods,
and went to question Zhū.
Zhū said:
"My wife dreamed that her head was exchanged,
I truly do not understand the reason;
to say that I killed her,
is an injustice."
Wú did not believe,
and brought a lawsuit.
The family members were arrested and interrogated,
and it was just as Zhū said.
The commandery governor could not decide.
Zhū returned,
and sought a plan from Lù.
Lù said:
"It is not difficult,
I should make his daughter speak for herself."
That night Wú dreamed that his daughter said:
"Your daughter was killed by Yáng Dànián of Sūxī,
and it has nothing to do with Provincial Graduate Zhū.
He was not satisfied with his wife's beauty,
and Judge Lù took your daughter's head and exchanged it with hers,
so that your daughter's body is dead but her head lives on.
I hope you will not hold a grudge."
Waking up, he told his wife,
and their dreams were the same.
Then they reported it to the officials.
When questioned,
there indeed was a Yáng Dànián;
he was arrested and put in shackles,
and then confessed his crime.
Wú then went to Zhū,
requested to see the wife,
and from then on they became father-in-law and son-in-law.
Then they joined Zhū's wife's original head with the girl's corpse and buried them.
Zhū entered the examination hall three times,
but each time was expelled for violating examination rules.
Thus he became disheartened about pursuing an official career,
and this went on for thirty years.
One evening,
Lù told him:
"Your lifespan is not long."
Asked when,
he replied in five days.
"Can you save me?"
He said:
"It is up to Heaven's decree,
how can man act selfishly?
Moreover, from the perspective of a wise man,
life and death are one and the same,
why must one find joy in life,
and sorrow in death?"
Zhū thought it reasonable.
He immediately prepared burial clothes, quilts, coffin, and outer coffin;
once completed,
he dressed in full ceremonial attire and passed away.
The next day,
as his wife was leaning against the coffin weeping,
Zhū suddenly appeared, drifting in from outside.
His wife was frightened.
Zhū said:
"I am indeed a ghost,
no different from when I was alive.
I am concerned about you, a widowed mother with an orphaned child,
and feel deeply attached."
His wife wept bitterly,
tears streaming down her chest;
Zhū lingered affectionately, comforting and consoling her.
His wife said:
"In ancient times, there were tales of souls returning to the body.
Since you have a spirit,
why not come back to life?"
Zhū said:
"Heaven's decree cannot be defied."
She asked,
"What duties do you perform in the underworld?"
He said:
"Lù Pàn recommended me to oversee case affairs,
granting me an official rank,
and it is not particularly difficult."
His wife wanted to speak further,
but Zhū said:
"Lord Lù has come with me,
you should prepare wine and food."
He hurried out.
His wife followed his instructions and made preparations.
They could only hear laughter and drinking in the room,
with bright voices and loud talk,
just as when he was alive.
At midnight, when she peeked in,
they had already vanished without a trace.
From then on, he would come once every few days,
sometimes staying overnight in tender affection,
managing household matters as needed.
His son Wěi was just five years old,
and whenever Zhū came, he would pick him up and hold him;
by the time he was seven or eight,
Zhū would teach him to read by lamplight.
The boy was also intelligent,
able to write essays by age nine,
and at fifteen, he entered the county school,
never realizing he had no father.
From then on, his visits gradually became less frequent,
only occurring once a month or so.
One evening, he came again,
and said to his wife:
"Now I bid you farewell forever."
She asked:
"Where are you going?"
He said:
"I have received the Emperor's command to become the Minister of Tàihuà,
and will soon depart for a distant place.
The duties are numerous and the journey far,
so I will not be able to come again."
Mother and son clung to him, weeping.
He said:
"Do not be like this!
Our son has already grown up,
and the family's livelihood can still be sustained.
How can there be mandarin ducks that never part for a hundred years!"
Turning to his son, he said:
"Strive to be a good person,
do not let your father's legacy fall.
We will meet again in ten years."
He went straight out the door and left,
and from then on, he never returned.
Later, when Wěi was twenty-five, he passed the imperial examination and became a jìnshì,
serving as an official messenger.
Ordered to offer sacrifices at the Western Peak,
while passing through Huàyīn,
he suddenly encountered a carriage with feather canopies and attendants,
rushing through his procession.
He was astonished.
Looking closely at the person in the carriage,
it was his father.
He dismounted and knelt weeping by the roadside.
His father stopped the carriage and said:
"Your official reputation is good,
