I can close my eyes in peace."
Wěi remained kneeling, unwilling to rise;
Zhū urged the carriage forward,
speeding away without looking back.
After a few steps,
he turned back to look,
untied a dagger from his waist, and sent someone to present it as a gift.
From afar, he called out:
"Wearing this will bring you honor."
Wěi wanted to chase after him,
but saw the carriage, horses, and attendants
vanish like the wind,
disappearing in an instant.
He grieved for a long time;
drawing the dagger to look at it,
its craftsmanship was extremely fine,
with a line of engraved characters,
saying:
"Be bold in ambition but cautious in heart,
wise in thought but upright in conduct."
Wěi later rose to the rank of Sīmǎ.
He had five sons,
named Chén,
Qián,
Wěi,
Hún,
and Shēn.
One night,
he dreamed of his father saying:
"The dagger should be given to Hún."
He followed this advice.
Hún served as Zǒngxiàn,
earning a reputation for good governance.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"To shorten a crane and lengthen a duck is the folly of forced alteration;
grafting flowers onto a tree
is the ingenuity of the creator;
how much more so is carving into the liver and intestines,
applying knife and awl to the neck and throat!
As for Lord Lù,
one could say he has beauty hidden within his bones.
From the late Míng dynasty to the present,
not many years have passed—
does Lord Lù of Língyáng still exist?
Does his spirit still linger?
To hold his whip
would be my delight and admiration."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Wáng Zǐfú
was a native of Luódiàn in Jǔ.
He lost his father early.
Exceptionally intelligent,
he entered the county school at fourteen.
His mother loved him dearly
and seldom allowed him to wander in the countryside.
He was betrothed to a woman from the Xiāo family,
but she died before the marriage,
so his search for a phoenix mate remained unfulfilled.
During the Lantern Festival,
his maternal cousin, Wú Shēng,
invited him to go sightseeing.
Just as they reached the outskirts of the village,
a servant from his uncle's family arrived,
summoning Wú away.
Wáng saw crowds of young women out enjoying the festival,
and, feeling inspired, wandered alone.
He noticed a young lady accompanied by a maid,
holding a sprig of plum blossoms,
her beauty peerless,
her smile radiant.
Wáng stared fixedly, unable to look away,
completely forgetting all restraint.
After the young lady had passed a few paces,
she turned to her maid and said:
"That young man's eyes are blazing like a thief's!"
She dropped the flower on the ground
and walked away, laughing and chatting.
Picking up the flower, the young man was filled with melancholy,
his spirit seemed lost,
and he returned home dejectedly.
Upon reaching home,
he hid the flower under his pillow,
lay down with his head lowered,
neither speaking nor eating.
His mother grew worried.
Rituals and exorcisms only worsened his condition,
and he grew rapidly thinner.
When a physician examined him,
prescribed medicine to induce sweating,
he became dazed and confused.
His mother stroked him and asked the cause,
but he remained silent and did not answer.
Just then, Wú Shēng arrived,
and she secretly urged him to inquire.
Wú approached the bedside,
and at the sight of him, the young man shed tears.
Wú sat by the bed to comfort him,
gradually pressing for details.
The young man poured out the whole truth,
and begged for advice.
Wú laughed and said:
"Your wish is truly foolish!
What difficulty is there in fulfilling it?
I shall seek her out for you.
Walking in the wilds,
she surely is not from a noble family.
If she is not yet betrothed,
the matter can certainly be settled: if not,
we can offer a generous bribe,
and I am sure it will be agreed to.
Once you recover,
I will handle the matter."
Hearing this,
the young man could not help but smile.
Wú went out and told his mother,
then sought the girl's village,
but after an exhaustive search,
found no trace.
His mother grew deeply worried,
not knowing what to do.
However, after Wú left,
the young man's expression brightened,
and he began to eat a little.
A few days later,
Wú returned.
The young man asked about his efforts.
Wú deceived him, saying:
"I have found her.
Who do you think she is?
She is the daughter of my paternal aunt,
your cousin,
and is still awaiting betrothal.
Although marriage between close relatives is frowned upon,
if we explain the situation,
there should be no problem."
Joy spread across the young man's face,
and he asked:
"Where does she live?"
Wú lied, saying:
"In the mountains to the southwest,
about thirty lǐ from here."
The young man repeatedly urged him,
and Wú confidently took on the task and left.
From then on, the young man gradually ate more,
and day by day recovered.
He looked under his pillow,
and though the flower had withered,
it had not yet fallen apart.
Gazing at it and playing with it in thought,
it was as if he saw her.
Wondering why Wú did not return,
he sent a letter inviting him.
Wú made excuses and refused to come.
The young man grew angry,
and became sullen and unhappy.
Fearing he would fall ill again,
his mother hastily arranged a marriage;
but whenever she mentioned it,
he would shake his head in refusal,
only hoping for Wú's return day after day.
As Wú still brought no news,
his resentment grew.
Then it occurred to him that thirty lǐ was not far,
why rely on others?
Tucking the plum blossom into his sleeve,
he set off in a fit of pique,
without his family's knowledge.
Walking alone,
with no one to ask for directions,
he simply headed toward the southern mountains.
After about thirty lǐ,
he found himself among overlapping wild peaks,
the clear green air refreshing his skin,
with no sign of human presence,
only paths for birds.
Gazing into the valley below,
amid a profusion of flowers and trees,
he faintly saw a small village.
Descending into the village,
he saw not many houses,
all thatched cottages,
yet with an air of elegance and refinement.
One house facing north
had silky willows before its gate,
and within the walls, peach and apricot trees were especially abundant,
interspersed with tall bamboos;
wild birds chirped among them.
Thinking it might be a garden pavilion,
he dared not enter abruptly.
Looking back at the house opposite,
there was a large, smooth, clean rock,
so he sat on it to rest awhile.
Suddenly, from within the wall, he heard a girl's voice,
calling out long
"Xiǎo Róng!"
in a delicate, soft tone.
As he stood listening,
a young maiden came from east to west,
holding an apricot blossom,
lowering her head to pin it in her hair.
Raising her head and seeing him,
she did not pin the flower,
but smiling, twirled it and went inside.
Looking closely,
she was the girl he had met on the road during the Lantern Festival.
His heart leaped with joy.
But he thought of no way to approach;
he wanted to call out to his aunt,
yet considering they had never visited,
he feared making a mistake.
There was no one inside the gate to ask.
He sat, lay down, paced back and forth,
from morning until the sun began to set,
gazing intently until his eyes grew weary,
forgetting both hunger and thirst.
From time to time, he saw the girl peeking out with half her face,
as if surprised he had not left.
Suddenly, an old woman leaning on a cane came out,
looked at him and said:
"Where are you from, young sir?
I hear you have been here since morning,
and are still here now.
What do you intend?
Are you perhaps hungry?"
The young man quickly rose and bowed to her,
replying:
"I have come to visit relatives."
The old woman was hard of hearing and did not hear.
He repeated it loudly.
Then she asked:
"What is the surname of your noble relative?"
The young man could not answer.
The old woman laughed and said:
"How strange!
You don't even know the name,
what relative are you visiting?
I see you, young sir,
are also a book-addled fool.
Better come with me,
have some coarse food,
we have a short couch where you can rest.
Wait until tomorrow to return,
find out the surname,
and come again to visit,
it won't be too late."
The young man was indeed hungry and wanted to eat,
and this would also bring him closer to the beauty,
so he was overjoyed.
Following the old woman inside,
he saw a white stone-paved path within the gate,
with red flowers lining both sides,
petals falling piece by piece on the steps;
winding westward,
they passed through another gate,
and bean trellises and flower frames filled the courtyard.
Ushering the guest into the house,
the whitewashed walls shone bright as mirrors;
outside the window, branches of crabapple blossoms reached into the room,
and the tables and couches
were all spotlessly clean.
As soon as he sat down,
someone seemed to be peeking furtively from outside the window.
The old woman called out:
"Xiǎo Róng!
Quickly prepare a meal."
A maidservant's voice answered from outside.
While seated,
they discussed their family backgrounds.
The old woman said:
"Your maternal grandfather,
was his surname Wú?"
He said:
“Indeed.”
The old woman exclaimed in surprise:
“He is my nephew!
Your esteemed mother,
is my younger sister.
Over the years, due to our family’s poverty,
and having no sons,
we gradually lost contact.
My nephew has grown so tall,
yet I did not recognize him.”
The young man said:
“I came here precisely to visit my aunt,
but in my haste, I forgot your surname.”
The old woman said:
“My surname is Qín,
but I have no children of my own;
I only have one frail daughter,
who is also from a concubine.
Her mother remarried,
leaving her to my care.
She is not unintelligent,
but lacks discipline,
and is playful, knowing no sorrow.
In a moment,
I will have her come to greet you.”
Before long,
the maid prepared a meal,
with plump young chickens.
After the old woman urged him to eat,
the maid came to clear the table.
The old woman said:
“Call Nínggū here.”
The maid assented and left.
After a long while,
faint laughter was heard outside the door.
The old woman called again:
“Yīngníng,
your cousin is here.”
Outside the door, giggling continued without end.
The maid pushed her inside,
but she still covered her mouth,
unable to contain her laughter.
The old woman glared and said:
“We have a guest here,
what is all this giggling and chattering?
What kind of behavior is this?”
The girl stifled her laughter and stood still,
and the young man bowed to her.
The old woman said:
“This is Master Wáng,
your aunt’s son.
Even family members do not recognize each other,
how laughable.”
The young man asked:
“How old is my cousin?”
The old woman did not understand.
The young man repeated himself.
The girl laughed again,
unable to look up.
The old woman said to the young man:
“I said she lacks discipline,
and this proves it.
She is already sixteen,
yet as naïve as an infant.”
The young man said:
“She is one year younger than I.”
She said:
“My nephew is already seventeen,
could it be that you were born in the year of the horse, Gēngwǔ?”
The young man nodded in agreement.
She asked again:
“Who is your wife?”
He replied:
“I have none.”
She said:
“With your talent and appearance,
how is it that at seventeen you are still not betrothed?
Yīngníng also has no husband’s family,
and you would be a perfect match;
it is a pity there is the obstacle of being close relatives.”
The young man said nothing,
his gaze fixed on Yīngníng,
not sparing a glance elsewhere.
The maid whispered to the girl:
“His eyes are blazing,
his thievish look unchanged!”
The girl burst into laughter again,
turning to the maid and saying:
“Go see if the peach blossoms have bloomed?”
She quickly rose,
covering her mouth with her sleeve,
and walked out with small, hurried steps.
Once outside the door,
her laughter finally erupted freely.
The old woman also rose,
called the maid to prepare bedding,
and arranged accommodations for the young man.
She said:
“It is not easy for my nephew to come,
you should stay for three to five days,
and I will send you back later.
If you find it too quiet and lonely,
behind the house there is a small garden,
where you can pass the time;
there are also books to read.”
The next day,
he went behind the house,
and indeed there was a half-acre garden,
with fine grass like a carpet,
and willow catkins sprinkled along the path;
there was a thatched cottage with three rooms,
surrounded by flowers and trees.
Strolling among the flowers,
he heard a rustling sound from the treetops,
and looking up,
saw Yīngníng above.
Seeing him approach,
she laughed wildly, nearly falling.
The young man said:
“Stop,
you will fall!”
The girl descended while laughing,
unable to control herself.
Just as she was about to reach the ground,
she lost her grip and fell,
and her laughter ceased.
The young man helped her up,
secretly squeezing her wrist.
The girl burst into laughter again,
leaning against the tree, unable to walk,
and only after a long while did she stop.
The young man waited for her laughter to subside,
then took a flower from his sleeve to show her.
The girl took it,
and said:
“It is withered.
Why keep it?”
He said:
“This was left by you during the Lantern Festival,
so I kept it.”
She asked:
“Why keep it?”
He said:
“To show that I love you and have not forgotten.
Since meeting you during the Lantern Festival,
I have been pining away, falling ill,
and thought I would become a ghost;
never expecting to see your face again,
I beg for your pity.”
The girl said:
“This is such a trivial matter.
Among close relatives, what is there to begrudge?
When you leave,
from the garden flowers,
I will call the old servant,
to break off a large bundle and carry it for you.”
The young man said:
“Are you foolish, cousin?”
The girl said:
“Why call me foolish?”
The young man said:
“It is not the flower I love,
but the person who held the flower.”
The girl said:
“The affection between distant relatives,
goes without saying.”
The young man said:
“The love I speak of,
is not the love between distant relatives,
but the love between husband and wife.”
The girl said:
"Is there any difference?"
She replied:
"Only that we share the same pillow and mat at night."
The girl bowed her head and thought for a long time,
then said:
"I am not accustomed to sleeping with a stranger."
Before she finished speaking,
the maid secretly arrived,
and the young man, frightened and flustered, fled.
A short while later,
they met at the mother's place.
The mother asked:
"Where have you been?"
The girl replied that they had been talking together in the garden.
The old woman said:
"The meal has been ready for a long time.
What lengthy conversation
could be so drawn out like this?"
The girl said:
"Big brother wanted me to sleep with him."
Before she finished speaking,
the young man was greatly embarrassed,
and urgently glared at her with his eyes.
The girl smiled slightly and stopped.
Fortunately, the old woman did not hear,
and still chattered on, questioning them closely.
The young man hastily covered it up with other words,
and then softly scolded the girl.
The girl said:
"Just now, was that something I shouldn't have said?"
The young man said:
"That is talk to be said behind others' backs."
The girl said:
"We can talk behind others' backs,
but how can we talk behind our old mother's back?
Besides, sleeping together is a common matter;
why avoid mentioning it?"
The young man hated her foolishness,
but had no way to make her understand.
Just as they finished eating,
people from his home arrived leading two donkeys to search for the young man.
Earlier,
his mother had waited a long time for the young man to return,
and began to suspect something;
they had searched the village several times,
but found no trace or sign of him.
So they went to inquire with Wú.
Wú recalled what had been said before,
and thus told his son to go search in the southwestern mountain villages.
They passed through several villages in all,
before finally arriving here.
As the young man went out the door,
he happened to meet them,
so he went in to tell the old woman,
and requested to take the girl back with him together.
The old woman said happily:
"This has been my wish,
not just for a morning or an evening.
But with this frail body, I cannot travel far.
If my nephew can take my younger sister's daughter away,
to get to know her aunt,
that would be excellent!"
She called for Yīngníng.
Níng came, laughing.
The old woman said:
"What is so joyful
that you laugh without ceasing?
If you didn't laugh,
you would be a perfect person."
Then she glared at her angrily.
And said:
"Big brother wants to take you with him;
you can get ready now."
She also provided wine and food for the family members,
then saw them off, saying:
"Your aunt's family has abundant fields and property,
and can support extra people.
Once you get there, don't come back for now;
learn a little poetry and etiquette,
and it will also be good for serving your future parents-in-law.
I will trouble your aunt
to choose a good match for you."
The two then set off.
When they reached the mountain col,
looking back,
they could still faintly see the old woman leaning against the gate, gazing northward.
Upon arriving home,
his mother saw the beautiful girl and
asked in surprise who she was.
Shēng replied that she was his aunt’s daughter.
His mother said,
"What Wú Láng told you earlier
was false.
I have no elder sister,
so how could I have a niece?"
She asked the girl,
and the girl said,
"I am not my mother’s biological child.
My father’s surname was Qín.
When he passed away,
I was still in swaddling clothes,
so I cannot remember."
His mother said,
"I did have an elder sister who married into the Qín family,
that is true;
but she has been dead for a long time,
how could she still be alive?"
She then carefully inquired about the girl’s facial features and distinctive marks,
and everything matched.
Yet she remained doubtful and said,
"It is indeed her.
But she has been dead for many years,
how could she still exist?"
While she was still puzzled,
Wú Shēng arrived,
and the girl retreated into the inner room.
Wú inquired about the situation,
and was lost in thought for a long time.
Suddenly he said,
"Is this girl named Yīngníng?"
Shēng confirmed it.
Wú repeatedly exclaimed that it was strange.
When asked how he knew,
Wú said,
"After my aunt from the Qín family passed away,
my uncle lived as a widower,
and was haunted by a fox spirit,
falling ill and dying of emaciation.
The fox gave birth to a daughter named Yīngníng,
who was wrapped in swaddling clothes and placed on the bed,
and everyone in the family saw her.
After my uncle died,
the fox still came from time to time;
later, they sought a celestial master’s talisman and pasted it on the wall,
and the fox then took the girl away.
Could this be her?"
They were all suspicious and uncertain.
But then they heard giggling from the inner room—it was Yīngníng’s laughter.
His mother said,
"This girl is too silly and naive."
Wú requested to see her.
His mother went into the inner room,
but the girl was still laughing heartily and paid no attention.
His mother urged her to come out,
and only then did she try hard to suppress her laughter.
She faced the wall for a while,
before finally coming out.
As soon as she bowed in greeting,
she suddenly turned and rushed back inside,
bursting into loud laughter.
All the women in the room
could not help but laugh along.
Wú offered to go and investigate the strange matter,
and also to act as a matchmaker.
He searched for the village,
but found no houses at all,
only scattered mountain flowers.
Wú recalled that his aunt’s burial place
seemed not far away;
but the grave mound had been obliterated,
and he could not identify it,
so he returned in astonishment and sighed.
His mother suspected that the girl was a ghost.
When they told her what Wú had said,
the girl showed no sign of fear;
when they expressed sympathy for her having no family,
she also showed no sadness,
only continuing to laugh foolishly.
No one could understand her.
His mother had her share a room with the young maid.
At dawn, she would come to pay her respects,
and her needlework was exquisitely skillful and unparalleled.
But she loved to laugh,
and even when told to stop, she could not help it;
however, her laughter was charming,
wild yet not detracting from her beauty,
and everyone enjoyed it.
The neighboring girls and young women
all vied to welcome her.
His mother chose an auspicious day to hold the wedding ceremony,
but still feared she might be a ghost.
She secretly observed her in the sunlight,
and her form and shadow showed no abnormality.
On the wedding day,
they had her dress in finery and perform the bride’s rituals;
but she laughed so hard she could not bow properly,
so the ceremony was abandoned.
Shēng, thinking her silly and naive,
feared she might reveal private matters from the bedroom;
but the girl was extremely discreet,
never uttering a word about it.
Whenever his mother was worried or angry,
as soon as the girl arrived,
a single laugh would resolve the situation.
If a servant girl made a small mistake
and feared being whipped,
she would ask to go to his mother to talk;
when the guilty maid went to see her,
she was often spared punishment.
The girl had a passion for flowers,
and sought them everywhere among relatives and friends;
she even secretly pawned her gold hairpins
to buy fine varieties.
Within a few months,
the steps, railings, fences, and even the latrine
were all covered with flowers.
In the backyard, there was a trellis of mùxiāng flowers,
which bordered the neighbor’s house to the west.
The girl often climbed onto it
to pick flowers for her hair or to admire.
Whenever his mother saw this,
she would scold her.
But the girl never changed.
One day,
the son of the western neighbor saw her
and stared, utterly captivated.
The girl did not avoid him but laughed.
The western neighbor’s son thought she was interested in him,
and his heart grew even more restless.
The girl pointed to the base of the wall, laughed, and climbed down.
The western neighbor’s son thought she was indicating a meeting place,
and was overjoyed.
At dusk, he went there,
and the girl was indeed there.
He approached and tried to have his way with her,
but felt a sharp pain as if pierced by an awl,
which penetrated to his heart.
He cried out loudly and collapsed.
Looking closely, he saw it was not the girl,
but a dry log lying by the wall,
and what he had touched was a water-soaked hole.
The neighbor’s father heard the noise,
rushed over to investigate,
but the son only groaned and would not speak.
When his wife came,
he finally told the truth.
They lit a torch to examine the hole,
and saw a huge scorpion inside,
as big as a small crab.
The old man smashed the log, caught it, and killed it.
He carried his son home,
but by midnight, the son died.
The neighbor sued Shēng,
accusing Yīngníng of being a demon.
The county magistrate had long admired Shēng’s talent,
and knew well that he was an honest and virtuous scholar.
He declared the neighbor’s accusation false,
and was about to have him beaten as punishment.
Shēng pleaded for leniency,
and the neighbor was released.
His mother said to the girl,
"Your silliness and wildness are like this—
I knew early on that excessive joy would bring hidden worries.
Fortunately, the county magistrate is wise,
and we were not implicated;
if it had been a muddle-headed official,
he would surely have arrested the women to testify in court.
How could my son face his relatives and neighbors then?"
The girl became serious
and vowed never to laugh again.
His mother said,
"Everyone laughs,
but it must be at the right time."
From then on, the girl never laughed again,
even when deliberately teased,
she still would not laugh;
yet she never showed a sad expression all day long.
One evening,
she faced Shēng in tears.
He found this strange.
The girl sobbed and said:
"Before, because the time I had followed you was short,
I feared telling you would cause alarm and suspicion.
Today, observing my mother-in-law and you, sir,
you both love me exceedingly and have no different intentions,
so perhaps telling you directly is harmless?
I was originally born of a fox.
When my mother was about to leave,
she entrusted me to my ghost mother.
We depended on each other for over ten years,
only then did I come to this day.
I also have no brothers,
the one I rely on is only you.
My old mother lies lonely on the mountain slope,
with no one to pity her and bury her together (with her husband),
in the underworld she is always grieving and regretful.
If you, sir, do not begrudge the trouble and expense,
and can let the one underground dispel this resentment and sorrow,
then perhaps those who raise daughters will not be so heartless as to drown or abandon them."
Shēng promised her,
but worried the grave mound would be lost amidst the wild grass.
The girl just said not to worry.
On the appointed day,
husband and wife went by carriage with a coffin.
The girl, amidst the desolate mist and tangled undergrowth,
pointed out the location of the grave.
Sure enough, they found the old woman's body,
her skin and flesh still intact.
The girl caressed it, weeping mournfully.
They carried it back,
then sought out the Qín family tomb and buried them together.
That night,
Shēng dreamed the old woman came to thank him,
and upon waking, he recounted it.
The girl said:
"I saw her last night,
she told me not to startle you, sir."
Shēng regretted not inviting her to stay.
The girl said:
"She is a ghost.
Living people are many,
their yang energy is strong,
how could she dwell here long?"
Shēng asked about Xiǎo Róng.
She said:
"She is also a fox,
most cunning.
My fox mother left her to watch over me.
She often fetched food to feed me,
so I am grateful to her and she is always on my mind.
Yesterday I asked my mother,
she said she has already married her off."
From then on, every year at the Cold Food Festival,
husband and wife would ascend to the Qín family tomb,
paying respects and sweeping it without fail.
The girl, after another year,
gave birth to a son.
While in his mother's arms,
he was not afraid of strangers,
and upon seeing people would always laugh,
also greatly possessing his mother's manner, it is said.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Observing her diligent, simple laughter,
she seems utterly heartless;
yet her mischievous prank under the wall,
whose cunning could be greater?
As for her mournful attachment to her ghost mother,
turning laughter to weeping,
my Yīng Níng is perhaps one who hides behind laughter.
I have privately heard that in the mountains there is a grass,
named 'Laugh-Then-Stop'.
Smelling it,
one laughs uncontrollably.
If one planted this variety in their chamber,
then the 'Joint Happiness' and 'Forget Sorrow' flowers,
would both be without color.
As for the 'Flower that Understands Speech',
one would precisely dislike its affectations."
Based on the manuscript version of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Níng Cǎichén,
was from Zhèjiāng.
His nature was forthright and unrestrained,
upright and self-respecting.
He often said to others:
"In my life, I have been faithful to one."
He happened to be going to Jīnhuá,
arriving at the northern outer wall,
he unpacked his luggage at a temple.
The monastery's halls and pagoda were grand and beautiful;
yet mugwort and weeds grew higher than a man,
seeming utterly devoid of human traces.
The monks' quarters to the east and west,
their double doors were ajar;
only a small building to the south,
had a lock and bolt as if new.
where tall bamboos grew thick as one's grasp;
below the steps was a large pond,
wild lotuses already in bloom.
He felt very pleased with its secluded quiet.
It happened the Examiner's circuit was arriving,
lodgings in the city were expensive,
so he thought it convenient to stay here,
and thus strolled about waiting for the monk's return.
At dusk,
a scholar came,
opening the southern door.
Níng hurried over to greet him,
and also told him his intention.
The scholar said:
"There is no landlord here,
I am also a temporary resident.
If you can endure the desolation,
and favor me with your instruction morning and evening,
it would be most fortunate."
Níng was pleased.
He spread straw to serve as a bed,
propped up a plank to make a table,
planning for a long stay.
That night,
the moon was bright, lofty, and pure,
its clear light like water.
The two sat knee-to-knee in the corridor of the hall,
each stating their name.
The scholar said of himself:
"My surname is Yān,
courtesy name Chìxiá."
Níng suspected he was a candidate for the examinations,
but listening to his accent,
it was nothing like that of Zhèjiāng.
Questioning him,
he said himself:
"I am from Qín."
His speech was very simple and sincere.
After a while, facing each other, words were exhausted,
so they bowed in farewell and returned to sleep.
Nìng Yǐxīn, in his new lodgings,
could not fall asleep for a long time.
He heard murmuring voices north of the house,
as if from a family.
He got up and went to the stone window in the north wall,
peeking out slightly.
He saw a small courtyard beyond a low wall,
where a woman of about forty;
and an old woman dressed in crimson,
wearing a coarse hairpin,
with a hunched back like a turtle's,
were chatting under the moonlight.
The woman said:
"Why hasn't Xiǎoqiàn come for so long?"
The old woman said:
"She should be here soon."
The woman said:
"Could it be that she has complaints toward you, Granny?"
She replied:
"I haven't heard any,
but she seems rather troubled."
The woman said:
"That little maid shouldn't be treated too kindly."
Before she finished speaking,
a girl of seventeen or eighteen arrived,
appearing exceptionally beautiful.
The old woman laughed and said:
"We shouldn't speak of others behind their backs.
Just as we two were talking,
this little enchantress came silently without a trace.
Fortunately, we weren't criticizing her faults."
She added:
"This young lady is truly like a painting,
even if I were a man,
I'd be captivated."
The girl said:
"If you, Granny, don't praise me,
who else will speak well of me?"
The woman and the girl then spoke further, but their words were unclear.
Nìng thought they were neighbors' family members,
and went back to bed without listening further.
After some time,
it finally fell silent.
Just as he was about to fall asleep,
he felt someone enter his sleeping quarters.
He quickly rose to look carefully,
and it was the girl from the north courtyard.
Startled, he asked her.
The girl smiled and said:
"On this moonlit night, unable to sleep,
I wish to cultivate intimacy."
Nìng sternly replied:
"You should guard against gossip,
and I fear people's talk;
with one misstep,
the path of integrity is lost."
The girl said:
"No one will know at night."
Nìng rebuked her again.
The girl hesitated as if wanting to say more.
Nìng shouted:
"Leave quickly!
Otherwise,
I'll call the scholar in the south house to know."
The girl, afraid,
then retreated.
Reaching the door, she turned back,
placing a gold ingot on the bedding.
Nìng picked it up and threw it into the courtyard,
saying:
"Unrighteous wealth
defiles my belongings!"
The girl, ashamed,
went out,
picked up the gold, and muttered to herself:
"This man must be made of iron and stone."
The next morning,
a scholar from Lánxī arrived with a servant to await the examination,
lodging in the east wing.
That night, he died suddenly.
There was a small hole in the sole of his foot,
as if pierced by an awl,
with a trickle of blood.
No one knew the cause.
After one night,
the servant also died,
with the same symptoms.
Toward evening,
Yàn Shēng returned.
Nìng questioned him about it,
and Yàn thought it was a demon.
Nìng, being upright and fearless,
paid little heed.
At midnight,
the girl came again,
and said to Nìng:
"I have seen many men,
but none as firm-hearted as you.
You are truly a sage,
I dare not deceive you.
I am Xiǎoqiàn,
surnamed Niè,
who died at eighteen,
buried beside the temple.
I am constantly threatened by a demon,
forced to perform lowly tasks;
facing people like this
is truly not my wish.
Now there is no one left in the temple to kill,
I fear a yaksha will be sent."
Nìng, alarmed, asked for a plan.
The girl said:
"Sharing a room with Yàn Shēng can spare you."
He asked:
"Why don't you bewitch Yàn Shēng?"
She replied:
"He is an extraordinary man,
I dare not approach."
He asked:
"How do you bewitch people?"
She said:
"Those who become intimate with me,
I secretly pierce their feet with an awl,
and they become dazed and confused,
then I draw their blood for the demon to drink;
or sometimes with gold,
which is not real gold,
but a rakshasa's bone,
keeping it can cut out a person's heart and liver: these two methods
are merely to suit people's preferences."
Nìng thanked her.
He asked when to be on guard,
and she replied the next night.
Parting in tears, she said:
"I have fallen into a dark sea,
unable to find shore.
Your righteousness reaches the clouds,
and you can surely save me from suffering.
If you would take my decaying bones,
and return them to a peaceful burial,
it would be no less than a rebirth."
Nìng resolutely promised.
He then asked the burial place,
and she said:
"Just remember, atop the white poplar tree,
where there is a crow's nest."
With these words, she went out the door
and vanished into mist.
The next day,
fearing Yàn might go out,
Nìng went early to invite him.
After morning, he prepared wine and food,
observing Yàn carefully.
Having agreed to share lodging,
Yàn declined, citing his solitary nature.
Nìng insisted,
forcefully bringing his bedding over.
Yàn had no choice,
moving his bed to join him,
and instructed:
"I know you are a true man,
and I greatly admire you.
But I have a secret,
hard to reveal suddenly.
Please do not peek into my box,
or it will harm us both."
Nìng respectfully accepted the advice.
Then each went to bed.
Yàn placed a small chest on the windowsill,
and shortly after lying down,
began snoring like thunder.
Nìng could not sleep.
Around the first watch,
a faint human shadow appeared outside the window.
Soon it approached the window to peek,
its eyes gleaming.
Nìng, frightened,
was about to call Yàn,
when suddenly something burst from the chest,
shining like a bolt of silk,
struck and broke the stone window lattice,
flashed out like an arrow,
then swiftly retracted,
vanishing like lightning.
Yàn awoke and rose,
while Nìng pretended to sleep to watch.
Yàn picked up the chest to examine it,
took out an object,
and sniffed and looked at it under the moonlight.
It gleamed white and crystalline,
about two inches long,
and as wide as a leek leaf.
Then he wrapped it in several layers,
and placed it back in the broken chest.
Muttering to himself:
"What kind of old monster is this,
to be so bold,
as to ruin my box."
Then he lay back down.
Níng found this extremely strange,
so he got up and asked him about it,
and also told him what he had seen.
Yàn said:
"Since we know and care for each other,
how dare I hide it deeply.
I,
am a swordsman.
If it weren't for the stone,
the demon would have been killed instantly;
even so,
it was still injured."
Níng asked:
"What is sealed inside?"
He said:
"A sword.
Just now, smelling it,
there was a demonic aura."
Níng wanted to see it.
Yàn generously took it out to show him,
it was a small sword gleaming faintly.
From then on, Níng respected Yàn even more.
The next day,
looking outside the window,
there were traces of blood.
So he went north of the temple,
and saw mounds of desolate graves,
indeed there was a white poplar,
with a crow's nest atop it.
Once his affairs were settled,
he packed his bags intending to return home.
Yàn Shēng set up a farewell feast,
his feelings and kindness were profound.
He gave Níng a worn leather bag,
saying:
"This is a sword pouch.
Treasuring it can ward off evil spirits from afar."
Níng wished to learn his arts from him.
He said:
"Someone like you, trustworthy, righteous, firm, and upright,
could undertake this.
However, you are still a man destined for wealth and honor,
not one of those in this path."
Níng then claimed he had a sister buried there,
excavated the girl's bones,
wrapped them in clothing,
hired a boat and returned.
Níng's study faced the wilderness,
so he built a grave and buried them outside the study.
He offered sacrifices and prayed, saying:
"Pitying your lonely soul,
I bury you near my humble dwelling,
so that songs and cries may be heard between us,
hoping you won't be bullied by fierce ghosts.
A bowl of plain water to drink,
is hardly clear or fine,
I hope you do not disdain it!"
After the prayer, he turned back.
Then someone called out:
"Wait slowly, let's go together!"
Looking back,
it was Xiǎoqiàn,
who joyfully thanked him, saying:
"Your trustworthiness and righteousness,
even dying ten times would not be enough to repay.
Please allow me to follow you home,
to pay respects and meet your parents,
serving as a concubine or maid, I would have no regrets."
Looking at her carefully,
her skin glowed like flowing rosy clouds,
her feet were delicate like slender bamboo shoots,
seen clearly in daylight,
her beauty was especially peerless.
So he went with her to his study.
He instructed her to sit and wait a while,
and first went in to tell his mother.
His mother was astonished.
At that time, Níng's wife had been ill for a long time,
so his mother warned him not to speak,
fearing it would startle her.
While they were talking,
the girl had already gracefully entered,
bowing and prostrating herself on the ground.
Níng said:
"This is Xiǎoqiàn."
His mother looked at her in shock, too flustered to react.
The girl said to his mother:
"Your child drifts alone,
far from parents and brothers.
Thanks to the young master's sheltering grace,
his kindness covers even my hair and skin,
I wish to take up broom and dustpan,
to repay his great righteousness."
His mother saw she was graceful and lovely,
and finally dared to speak with her,
saying:
"Young lady, you favor my son,
this old woman is overjoyed.
But I have only this son in my life,
to continue the ancestral line,
I dare not let him have a ghostly partner."
The girl said:
"Your child truly has no other intentions.
Being one from the underworld,
since I am not trusted by you, mother,
I ask to serve him as an elder brother,
rely on your esteemed presence,
and serve you morning and evening,
how would that be?"
His mother pitied her sincerity,
and agreed.
She immediately wanted to bow to her as sister-in-law.
His mother declined due to illness,
so she stopped.
The girl then went into the kitchen,
taking over the cooking duties for his mother.
Entering rooms and crossing beds,
she seemed like a long-time resident.
As dusk fell,
his mother grew afraid of her,
dismissed her and told her to retire to sleep,
without setting up a bed or mat for her.
The girl, sensing his mother's intent,
immediately left.
Passing by the study, she wanted to enter,
but retreated,
pacing outside the door,
as if afraid of something.
Níng called to her.
The girl said:
"The room has sword energy that frightens people.
The reason I did not appear to you on the road earlier,
was truly because of this."
Níng realized it was the leather bag,
took it and hung it in another room.
The girl then entered,
and sat by the candlelight.
After a while,
she didn't speak a word.
After a long time,
she asked:
"Do you read at night?
I recited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* when young,
but now most of it is forgotten.
I beg to borrow a volume,
in my spare time at night,
to have you, elder brother, correct it."
Níng agreed.
She sat again,
silently,
as the second watch was nearly ending,
she didn't speak of leaving.
Níng urged her.
She said sorrowfully:
"A lonely soul from a strange land,
is especially timid of desolate graves."
Níng said:
"There is no other bed in the study,
and as brother and sister, we should also avoid suspicion."
The girl rose,
her brows furrowed as if about to cry,
her feet hesitant and unwilling to step,
she slowly went out the door,
descended the steps and vanished.
Níng secretly pitied her,
wanting to let her stay on another couch,
but feared his mother's anger.
The girl attended his mother in the morning,
holding water for washing,
going about household chores,
fulfilling his mother's wishes in every detail.
At dusk, she would take her leave,
always passing by the study,
reading scriptures by candlelight.
Sensing Níng was about to sleep,
she would then sadly depart.
Previously,
Níng’s wife was bedridden with illness,
and his mother was exhausted beyond endurance;
ever since she got this girl,
she was greatly relieved,
and felt grateful to her.
As days passed and familiarity grew,
she loved her as her own child,
and eventually forgot she was a ghost;
unwilling to let her leave in the evening,
she kept her to sleep and rise together.
When the girl first came, she did not eat or drink,
but after half a year, she gradually began to sip thin gruel.
Both mother and son doted on her,
avoiding mention of her being a ghost,
and others could not tell either.
Not long after,
Níng’s wife passed away.
His mother secretly intended to take the girl as a wife for her son,
but feared it might bring harm to him.
The girl subtly perceived this,
and seized an opportunity to tell the mother:
"Having lived here for over a year,
you should know my innermost heart.
Not wishing to bring disaster to others,
I followed your son here.
My humble self has no other intentions,
only because the young master is open and upright,
admired and watched over by heaven and men alike,
I truly wish to rely on and assist him for a few years,
to borrow the chance to earn an imperial title,
and bring glory to the underworld."
The mother also knew she meant no harm,
but only feared she could not continue the family line.
The girl said:
"Children are bestowed only by heaven.
The young master is recorded in the register of blessings,
with three sons who will glorify the clan,
and this will not be taken away because of a ghost wife."
The mother believed her,
and discussed it with her son.
Níng was delighted,
and thus arranged a banquet to inform relatives and friends.
Some requested to see the new bride,
and the girl readily appeared in splendid attire,
leaving the whole hall staring in amazement,
not suspecting she was a ghost,
but suspecting she was an immortal.
From then on, all the female relatives from the five degrees of kinship,
came with gifts to congratulate,
vying to bow and meet her.
The girl was skilled at painting orchids and plums,
and would often reciprocate with small paintings,
which the recipients treasured and kept wrapped,
considering it an honor.
One day,
bending her neck by the window,
she appeared melancholy and lost.
Suddenly she asked:
"Where is the leather bag?"
He said:
"Because you feared it,
I sealed it and placed it elsewhere."
She said:
"I have absorbed living energy for a long time now,
and should no longer fear it,
it would be best to fetch it and hang it by the bed."
Níng asked her meaning,
she said:
"For three days now,
my heart has been palpitating without cease,
thinking the demon creature from Jīnhuá,
resenting my distant escape,
may seek me out morning or night."
Níng indeed brought the leather bag.
The girl examined it repeatedly,
and said:
"This is what sword immortals use to hold human heads.
Worn and tattered to this state,
who knows how many people it has killed!
Even today, looking at it,
my flesh still prickles."
Then she hung it up.
The next day,
she again ordered it moved and hung above the door.
At night, she sat facing the candle,
asking Níng not to sleep.
There was a creature,
like a flying bird falling.
The girl, alarmed, hid between the curtains.
Níng looked at it,
the creature resembled a yaksha in form,
with lightning eyes and a bloody tongue,
flashing and grabbing forward.
Reaching the door, it stepped back;
hesitating for a long time,
it gradually approached the leather bag,
using its claws to pluck at it,
as if about to tear it apart.
Suddenly the bag made a cracking sound,
growing as large as a basket;
dimly, a ghostly creature seemed to appear,
thrusting out half its body,
seized the yaksha and pulled it in,
then the sounds fell silent,
and the bag instantly shrank back as before.
Níng was astonished.
The girl also came out,
greatly pleased, saying:
"All is safe now!"
Together they looked inside the bag,
finding only several pecks of clear water.
Several years later,
Níng indeed passed the imperial examination and became a jìnshì.
The girl bore a son.
After taking a concubine,
each bore another son,
all who entered official service and gained repute.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Yáng Tiānyī said: he saw two mice come out,
one was swallowed by a snake;
the other stared with eyes like peppercorns,
seeming full of hatred and anger,
yet gazing from afar, not daring to approach.
The snake, its belly full,
wriggled into its hole: just as half its body had entered,
the mouse rushed over,
and fiercely bit its tail.
The snake, enraged,
withdrew its body back out.
The mouse, naturally agile,
fled away.
The snake pursued but could not catch it and returned.
When it was about to enter the hole again,
the mouse came again,
biting as before.
When the snake went in, it came;
when the snake came out, it went,
this went on for a long time.
The snake came out,
spat the dead mouse onto the ground.
The mouse came and sniffed it,
chirping as if mourning and sighing,
then carried it away in its mouth.
My friend Zhāng Lìyǒu composed "The Ballad of the Righteous Mouse" about this.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
On the seventeenth day of the sixth month in the seventh year of the Kāngxī reign, during the xū hour,
a great earthquake occurred.
I happened to be a guest in Jìxià,
just drinking by candlelight with my cousin Lǐ Dǔzhī.
Suddenly we heard a sound like thunder,
coming from the southeast,
heading toward the northwest.
Everyone was shocked and puzzled,
not understanding the reason.
Soon tables and chairs shook and swayed,
wine cups overturned;
house beams, rafters, and pillars,
made cracking and breaking sounds.
We looked at each other, faces pale.
After a long while,
we realized it was an earthquake,
and each hurriedly rushed out.
We saw towers, pavilions, houses, and buildings,
falling and rising again;
the sounds of collapsing walls and houses,
mixed with children’s cries and women’s wails,
clamorous like a boiling cauldron.
People, dizzy and unable to stand,
sat on the ground,
rolling and turning with the ground’s movement.
River water surged over ten feet high,
ducks quacked and dogs barked throughout the city.
After over an hour,
it gradually began to calm slightly.
Looking at the streets,
men and women gathered naked,
eagerly telling each other,
all forgetting they were not dressed.
Later we heard that at a certain place, a well tilted,
making it impossible to draw water;
at a certain house, a tower’s orientation shifted from north-south;
Qīxiá Mountain split;
the Yíshuǐ River sank into a cavern,
several acres wide.
This was truly an extraordinary and strange catastrophe.
There was a woman from the town who,
getting up at night to relieve herself,
returned to find a wolf carrying off her child in its mouth.
The woman frantically struggled with the wolf.
The wolf momentarily relaxed its grip,
and the woman snatched her child out,
holding him in her arms.
The wolf crouched and refused to leave.
The woman screamed loudly.
Neighbors came running and gathered around,
and only then did the wolf leave.
Once the fright had passed, the woman became overjoyed,
gesturing wildly to heaven and earth,
describing how the wolf had carried off her child,
and how she had snatched him back.
After a long while,
she suddenly realized she was not wearing a single stitch of clothing,
and ran off.
This is the same situation as when, during an earthquake, men and women both forgot themselves.
It is the same state of affairs.
How laughable it is
how people, in their panic and desperation, lose all sense of planning!
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
On the ancient island of Dōnghǎi,
there were five-colored winter jasmine flowers
that bloomed all year round without fading.
In ancient times, no one lived on the island,
and people rarely visited it.
A scholar named Zhāng from Dēngzhōu,
who was curious by nature
and fond of traveling and hunting,
heard of its beauty and excellence,
prepared wine and food,
and rowed a small boat there by himself.
When he arrived, the flowers were in full bloom,
their fragrance wafting for miles;
some of the trees were so large they measured over ten arm-spans around.
He lingered there, going back and forth,
thoroughly satisfied with what he loved.
He opened his wine jar and poured himself a drink,
regretting that he had no companion to share the journey with.
Suddenly, a beautiful woman emerged from among the flowers,
her red dress dazzling to the eyes,
with almost no equal.
Seeing Zhāng,
she smiled and said:
"I thought my enthusiasm was extraordinary,
but I never expected someone else shared the same taste."
Zhāng asked in surprise:
"Who are you?"
She replied:
"I am a courtesan from Jiāo.
I just came here with Hǎi Gōngzǐ.
He is off exploring the scenic spots and soaring about,
but I found it difficult to keep up on foot,
so I stayed here."
Zhāng, who had been suffering from loneliness,
was overjoyed to meet this beauty,
greatly pleased,
and invited her to sit and drink with him.
The woman's words were gentle and graceful,
captivating his spirit.
Zhāng grew fond of her.
Fearing that Hǎi Gōngzǐ might come,
preventing them from fully enjoying themselves,
he pulled her close and made advances.
The woman willingly complied.
While they were still intimate,
suddenly they heard a rustling wind,
and the sound of grass and trees bending and breaking.
The woman hurriedly pushed Zhāng away,
saying:
"Hǎi Gōngzǐ has arrived."
Zhāng hastily dressed and looked around in alarm,
but the woman had already disappeared.
Soon he saw a huge snake,
emerging from the thicket,
thicker than a large barrel.
Zhāng was terrified,
hiding behind a large tree,
hoping the snake would not see him.
The snake approached,
coiling its body around both him and the tree,
winding several times;
his arms were pinned straight against his sides,
unable to bend even slightly.
The snake raised its head
and flicked its tongue at Zhāng's nose.
Blood poured from his nose,
flowing onto the ground and forming a puddle,
which the snake then lowered its head to drink.
Zhāng thought he was surely going to die,
when he suddenly remembered the pouch hanging at his waist,
which contained poison for foxes.
Using two fingers, he pulled it out,
tore the wrapping, and poured the powder into his palm;
then he tilted his head to let his blood drip onto the powder,
allowing the blood to mix with the poison,
and in moments, his palm was full.
The snake indeed came to drink from his palm.
Before it could finish drinking,
it suddenly stretched its body,
thrashing its tail with a sound like thunder,
striking a tree,
causing half of the tree to collapse,
and the snake fell to the ground like a beam and died.
Zhāng was also dizzy and unable to get up,
and it was some time before he regained consciousness.
He loaded the snake onto his boat and returned.
He was seriously ill for over a month.
He suspected the woman was also a snake spirit.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Dīng Qiánxī
was from Zhūchéng.
He was wealthy in money and grain.
He was chivalrous and fond of righteousness,
admiring Guō Xiè's character.
When the imperial censor's office came to investigate him,
Dīng fled.
Arriving in Ānqiū,
he encountered rain,
and took shelter at an inn.
The rain did not stop by noon.
A young man came,
providing generous lodging and meals.
As dusk fell,
he stayed overnight at the young man's house;
beans were fed to the livestock,
and he was served attentively.
When asked his name,
the young man said:
"The master of the house is surnamed Yáng,
and I am his nephew.
The master enjoys making friends,
but he happens to be away,
and only the mistress is at home.
We are poor and cannot provide lavish hospitality,
but I hope you will understand."
When asked what the master did for a living,
it turned out the family had no assets,
and they only set up a gambling table daily
to earn a meager living.
The next day,
the rain still did not stop,
but the provisions were not neglected.
By evening,
fodder was cut;
the bundles of fodder were wet,
and quite uneven.
Dīng found this strange.
The young man said:
"To be honest with you, sir: our family is too poor to feed the livestock,
and the mistress just stripped thatch from the roof."
Dīng was even more surprised,
thinking their intention was to get payment.
At daybreak,
he offered them money,
but they refused;
when he insisted,
the young man took it inside.
Soon he came out,
still returning it to the guest,
saying:
"The mistress says: I am not in this business to hunt for profit.
When the master is away,
he often goes for days without bringing back a single coin;
when a guest comes to our home,
how could we demand payment?"
Dīng sighed in admiration and bid farewell.
He instructed them:
"I am Dīng from Zhūchéng.
When the master returns,
please tell him.
I would be honored if he visited me when he has time."
Several years passed with no news.
Then came a year of great famine,
and Yáng was in dire straits,
with no plan of action.
His wife casually suggested visiting Dīng,
and he agreed.
Arriving in Zhū,
he gave his name to the gatekeeper.
Dīng was at a loss and could not recall;
after further explanation, he finally remembered.
He hurried out in his slippers,
and invited the guest in with a bow.
Seeing his clothes worn and his heels exposed,
Dīng placed him in a warm room,
set out a feast to entertain him,
and treated him with exceptional favor and courtesy.
The next day,
he had clothes and a hat made for him,
warm both inside and out.
Yáng was grateful;
yet inwardly he grew more anxious,
and his narrow heart could not help feeling a little disappointed.
After staying for several days,
Dīng still did not mention giving him a parting gift.
Yáng was very anxious,
and told Dīng:
"I dare not hide it: when I came,
there was not even a full shēng of rice at home.
Now, having received such excessive kindness and support,
I am certainly happy;
but what about my wife and children!"
Dīng said:
"There is no need to worry about that,
I have already taken care of it for you.
Please relax and stay a little longer,
I will help with travel expenses."
He went out to summon various gamblers,
had Yáng sit and take a cut from the winnings,
and by the end of the night, Yáng had obtained a hundred taels,
then Dīng sent him back.
Returning home, Yáng saw his wife,
her clothes and shoes fresh and neat,
with a young maidservant attending her.
He asked in surprise.
His wife said:
"Since you left,
the very next day, carts and followers came one after another, delivering cloth, silk, beans, and grain,
piling up to fill the house,
saying it was a gift from guest Dīng.
Also, this maidservant with ten fingers,
is here for me to command."
Yáng was moved beyond words.
From then on, they lived in modest comfort,
and he disdained his old profession.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Being poor yet fond of hosting guests,
is something that those who indulge in drinking and gambling and lead a dissolute life are good at;
but the most unusual thing
is his wife alone.
To receive another's charity and not repay it,
is that human?
However, not forgetting the kindness of a single meal,
Dīng indeed possessed that virtue."
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Originally, there were no mountains by the seashore.
One day,
suddenly steep ridges were seen overlapping,
stretching continuously for several lǐ,
and everyone was astonished and perplexed.
Another day,
the mountains suddenly moved elsewhere,
transformed into nothingness.
It is said that a huge fish in the sea,
on the Qīngmíng Festival,
would take its family to visit its grave,
hence it is often seen during the Hánshí period.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Old Gentleman Zhāng,
was from Shānxī.
He was about to marry off his daughter,
so he took his family to Jiāngnán,
personally to purchase dowry items.
When the boat reached Jīnshān,
Zhāng first crossed the river,
instructing his family on the boat
not to have any meat smells.
For in the river there was a monstrous soft-shelled turtle,
which, upon smelling fragrance, would emerge,
destroy boats and swallow travelers,
having been a scourge for a long time.
After Zhāng left,
his family forgot,
and roasted meat in the boat.
Suddenly a huge wave capsized the boat,
and his wife and daughter both perished.
Zhāng turned the boat back,
grieving and wishing to die.
He then ascended Jīnshān,
visited the temple monks,
inquired about the strange turtle,
intending to take revenge on it.
The monks heard this,
and said in alarm:
"We live close to it daily,
fearing it will bring disaster;
we only worship it as a deity,
praying it not to be angry;
from time to time we slaughter sacrificial animals,
throw half the body to it,
and it leaps up, swallows, and leaves.
Who can possibly take revenge on it!"
Zhāng heard this,
and suddenly thought of a plan.
He summoned ironworkers,
set up a furnace halfway up the mountain,
smelted red-hot iron,
weighing over a hundred jīn.
Having ascertained where it usually lurked,
he had two or three strong men
lift it with large tongs and throw it in.
The turtle leaped out,
swiftly swallowed it and went down.
After a short while,
waves surged like mountains.
Moments later the waves subsided,
and the turtle, already dead, floated on the water.
Travelers and temple monks were all pleased,
built a shrine for Old Gentleman Zhāng,
placed his portrait inside,
regarding him as the water deity,
and prayers to him were always answered.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Shuǐmǎng is a poisonous plant.
It creeps like kudzu;
its flowers are purple,
resembling hyacinth beans.
If eaten,
one dies immediately,
becoming a Shuǐmǎng ghost.
It is commonly said that such ghosts cannot reincarnate,
and must wait until another poisoned person dies
to replace them.
Therefore, in the Táohuā River area of Chǔ,
such ghosts are especially numerous.
People in Chǔ call those born in the same year "tóngnián,"
exchange cards and visit each other,
address each other as "Gēng elder brother" and "Gēng younger brother,"
while sons and nephews call them "Gēng uncle,"
such is the custom.
There was a student named Zhù who visited his tóngnián,
and on the way felt parched and thirsty, wanting a drink.
Suddenly he saw an old woman by the roadside,
who had set up a shed offering drinks,
and he hurried over.
The old woman welcomed him into the shed,
and served him very attentively.
Smelling an unusual odor,
unlike tea,
he set it aside without drinking,
got up and left.
The old woman hastily stopped the guest,
and called out:
"Sānniáng,
bring a cup of good tea."
Soon a young girl appeared,
carrying tea from behind the shed.
She was about fourteen or fifteen,
her appearance stunningly beautiful,
with a ring on her finger and bracelets on her arm,
sparkling and reflecting light.
The student took the cup, his spirit captivated;
he smelled the tea,
its fragrance intense beyond compare.
He finished it and asked for more.
Seeing the old woman leave,
he playfully grasped her slender wrist,
and slipped off a ring.
The girl blushed and smiled,
and the student became even more infatuated.
He briefly asked about her household,
and the girl said:
"If you come at dusk,
I will still be here."
The student asked for a pinch of tea leaves,
and hiding the ring, he left.
Arriving at his tóngnián's home,
he felt nausea in his heart,
suspecting the tea was the cause,
and told his friend the situation.
His friend exclaimed in alarm:
"You are done for!
That is a Shuǐmǎng ghost.
My late father died from this.
It is incurable,
what can be done?"
The student was terrified,
took out the tea leaves to examine them,
and indeed it was Shuǐmǎng grass.
He also took out the ring,
and described the girl's appearance.
His friend pondered and said:
"This must be Kòu Sānniáng."
Since the name matched exactly,
the student asked:
"How do you know?"
The reply was:
"She is the daughter of the wealthy Kòu family from the southern village,
long renowned for her beauty.
Several years ago,
she died from eating water-hemlock,
so this must be her ghost."
Some said that if a victim of a ghost
knew the ghost's surname,
they could seek out the ghost's old underpants,
boil and consume them to recover.
The man hurried to the Kòu residence,
truthfully explained the situation,
knelt and pleaded earnestly;
but the Kòus, thinking he would die in their daughter's place,
stubbornly refused to give them.
The man returned in anger,
and reported this to the student.
The student also gnashed his teeth in hatred, saying:
"When I die,
I will not let their daughter escape rebirth!"
The man carried him back,
but he died just before reaching his home.
His mother wept and buried him.
He left behind a son,
barely a year old.
His wife could not uphold her widow's chastity,
and remarried after half a year.
The mother kept the orphan to nurse herself,
toiling and suffering unbearably,
weeping day and night.
One day,
while holding the child and crying in the room,
the student quietly entered.
His mother was terrified,
wiping her tears to ask him.
He replied:
"Your son heard your cries from the underworld,
and it pained my heart greatly,
so I have come to serve you morning and evening.
Though I am dead,
I already have a wife,
and she has come with me to share your burdens.
Please do not grieve."
His mother asked:
"Who is your wife?"
He said:
"The Kòu family sat by and watched me die,
and I deeply resented them.
After death, I wanted to find Sānniáng,
but did not know where she was;
recently, I met a certain elder,
who finally pointed the way.
When I went,
Sānniáng had already been reborn into the family of Minister Rèn;
I rushed there
and forcibly brought her back.
Now she is my wife,
and we get along well,
with little hardship."
After a while,
a young woman entered from outside,
dressed in splendid attire and radiantly beautiful,
and knelt to bow to the mother.
The student said:
"This is Kòu Sānniáng."
Though not among the living,
seeing her,
the mother felt somewhat comforted.
The student then had Sānniáng do chores.
Sānniáng was not accustomed to such work,
but she obeyed dutifully and was quite endearing.
From then on, they lived in the old house
and stayed without leaving.
The woman asked the mother to inform her family.
The student thought it best not to,
but the mother, following the woman's wish,
eventually told them.
The old couple of the Kòu family,
hearing this, were greatly alarmed,
and hurried over by carriage.
Looking at her,
it was indeed Sānniáng.
They wept facing each other, unable to speak,
and the woman urged them to stop.
The old woman saw that the student's family was very poor,
and felt deeply distressed.
The woman said:
"I am already a ghost,
why should I despise poverty?
Moreover, my husband and his mother
are sincere and affectionate,
and I am truly content here."
Then she asked:
"Who is the old tea-seller woman?"
The reply was:
"Her surname is Ní.
Ashamed that she could not lure travelers herself,
she sought my help.
Now she has been reborn into a family of porridge sellers in the prefectural city."
Then, turning to the student, she said:
"Since you are my husband,
yet you do not bow to your parents-in-law,
how can I bear it?"
The student then knelt and bowed.
The woman went into the kitchen,
took over the cooking from the mother,
and served the old couple.
The old woman watched with a heavy heart.
After returning home,
she immediately sent two maidservants
to serve them;
along with a hundred catties of silver and several dozen bolts of cloth;
wine was sent from time to time,
making the student's mother quite well-off.
The Kòus also often invited their daughter back for visits.
After staying a few days,
she would say:
"There is no one at home,
you should send me back early."
If they deliberately delayed,
she would drift back on her own.
The old man then built a grand house for the student,
with all preparations made to perfection.
However, the student never once visited the old man's home.
One day,
a villager who had been poisoned by water-hemlock
died and then revived,
which was passed around as a marvel.
The student said:
"It was I who saved him.
He was harmed by Lǐ Jiǔ,
and I drove away the ghost for him."
His mother said:
"Why don't you find someone to take your place?"
He replied:
"I deeply despise such people,
and I intend to drive them all away.
How could I stoop to such a thing!
Moreover, serving you, Mother, brings me the greatest joy;
I have no desire to be reborn."
From then on, those who were poisoned
would often prepare lavish feasts
and pray in his courtyard,
and it was often effective.
After more than ten years,
his mother died.
The student and his wife also grieved deeply,
but they did not receive guests,
only instructing their son to wear mourning clothes and perform the rituals.
After burying his mother,
two more years passed,
and they married their son to a wife.
The wife was the granddaughter of Minister Rèn.
Earlier,
Minister Rèn's concubine had given birth to a daughter,
who died after a few months.
Later, hearing of the student's extraordinary story,
he ordered his carriage to their home
to establish a father-in-law and son-in-law relationship.
By this time,
he married his granddaughter to their son,
and they visited each other frequently.
One day,
the student said to his son:
"The Lord of Heaven, recognizing my merits to the human world,
has appointed me as the Dragon Lord of the Four Rivers.
Now I must go."
Soon, four horses appeared in the courtyard,
harnessed to a yellow-canopied carriage,
with scales covering the horses' legs.
The couple, dressed in splendid attire, came out
and boarded the carriage together.
Their son and daughter-in-law wept and bowed,
and in an instant, they vanished.
That day,
the Kòu family saw their daughter arrive,
bow to bid farewell to the old couple,
just as the student had said.
The old woman wept and tried to keep her,
but the woman said:
"My husband has already left."
She went out the door and was never seen again.
Their son was named È,
courtesy name Líchén.
He requested from Old Man Kòu
that Sānniáng's remains be buried together with the student's.
Based on the manuscript version of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
The arts of delusion and befuddlement
are practiced in various ways.
Sometimes an alluring bait is offered,
and when a person is tricked into eating it,
he becomes confused and dazed,
following the other person away.
This is commonly called
"beating the cotton,"
while in Jiāngnán it is known as
"pulling the cotton."
Young children, being ignorant,
often fall victim to it.
There is also the practice of transforming people into livestock,
called
"making livestock."
This art is still rare north of the river,
but south of the river it is more common.
At an inn in Yángzhōu,
a man arrived leading five donkeys
and tied them up briefly at the trough,
saying:
"I'll be back in a moment."
He also instructed:
"Don't let them eat or drink."
Then he left.
The donkeys were left under the scorching sun,
kicking and biting noisily.
The innkeeper led them to a cooler spot.
When the donkeys saw water,
they rushed toward it,
and he let them drink freely.
After rolling in the dust once,
they transformed into women.
Astonished,
he questioned them about what had happened,
but their tongues were stiff and they couldn't answer.
So he hid them in a room.
Soon, the owner of the donkeys returned,
driving five sheep into the courtyard,
and asked in alarm where his donkeys were.
The innkeeper pulled the guest to sit down,
served him food and drink,
and said:
"Please eat first, sir;
your donkeys will be here soon."
The innkeeper went out,
gave all five sheep water to drink,
and they transformed one after another into children.
He secretly reported it to the prefecture,
and officers were sent to arrest the man,
who was then executed by beheading.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A scholar from Fèngyáng
traveled far with his books on his back.
He said to his wife:
"I'll return in half a year."
But after more than ten months,
there was still no news from him.
His wife waited anxiously, longing for his return.
One night,
just as she lay down on her pillow,
with moonlight filtering through the gauze curtains and shadows swaying,
thoughts of separation filled her heart.
As she tossed and turned,
a beautiful woman appeared,
with pearl-adorned hair and a crimson cape,
lifted the curtain and entered,
asking with a smile:
"Sister,
do you wish to see your husband?"
The wife quickly rose to respond.
The beautiful woman invited her to go together.
The wife worried about the long and difficult journey,
but the beautiful woman urged her not to worry.
She then took the wife's hand and led her out,
and they walked together under the moonlight,
covering about the distance of an arrow's flight.
The wife noticed that the beautiful woman walked swiftly,
while her own steps were slow and labored.
She called out for the beautiful woman to wait a moment,
saying she would go back to put on sturdier shoes.
The beautiful woman led her to sit by the roadside,
then took hold of her feet herself,
removed her own shoes, and lent them to her.
The wife happily put them on,
and fortunately, they fit perfectly.
She stood up and continued walking,
now with strides as swift as flight.
After a while,
they saw the scholar approaching on a white mule.
Seeing his wife, he was greatly surprised,
quickly dismounted,
and asked:
"Where are you going?"
The wife replied:
"I was coming to see you."
He then turned to ask who the beautiful woman was.
Before the wife could answer,
the beautiful woman covered her mouth and laughed, saying:
"Don't ask questions now.
Your wife has had a difficult journey;
you, sir, have been galloping through the night,
and both man and beast must be exhausted.
My home is not far,
so please rest here for a while.
You can leave at dawn,
and it won't be too late."
Looking a few steps away,
they saw a village,
and so they went together.
Entering a courtyard,
the beautiful woman roused a sleeping maid to attend to the guests,
saying:
"Tonight the moonlight is bright and clear;
there's no need for candles.
We can sit on the small stone platform."
The scholar tied his mule to a pillar under the eaves,
and they sat down.
The beautiful woman said:
"The shoes are too big for you,
so they must have been quite cumbersome on the journey.
Since you have a mount to ride back on,
I'd like to ask for them back."
The wife thanked her and returned them.
After a short while,
wine and fruits were set out.
The beautiful woman poured a drink and said:
"The phoenixes have long been parted,
but tonight they reunite;
let us drain this cup of turbid wine,
to respectfully offer congratulations."
The scholar also raised his cup in return.
Host and guest laughed and talked,
their shoes and slippers intermingling.
The scholar gazed at the beautiful woman,
repeatedly teasing her with flirtatious words.
Though husband and wife had just reunited,
they did not exchange a single word of greeting.
The beautiful woman also cast amorous glances,
speaking seductive, enigmatic words.
The wife merely sat in silence,
pretending to be foolish.
After a long time, they grew gradually intoxicated,
and the two spoke even more intimately.
Then, with a large goblet, she urged the guest to drink.
The scholar declined, pleading drunkenness,
but she pressed him even more insistently.
The scholar laughed and said:
"If you sing a song for me,
I will drink it."
The beautiful woman did not refuse,
and immediately, plucking the strings with an ivory plectrum, she sang to the tune of the fiddle:
"At dusk, I remove my fading makeup,
outside the window, the west wind chills through the gauze, listening to banana leaves rustling,
as a steady drizzle falls.
With whom can I idly chat?
Gazing until my eyes grow weary,
still he does not return home,
tears streaming down like hemp fibers.
Missing him again,
resenting him again,
holding a red embroidered slipper to divine ghostly omens."
When the song ended,
she laughed and said:
"This is just a vulgar street ballad,
unworthy of sullying your ears.
But as it is favored by popular taste,
I merely imitate it crudely."
Her voice was seductive,
her manner flirtatious and indecent.
The scholar was swayed and confused,
as if unable to control himself.
After a short while,
the beautiful woman pretended to be drunk and left the banquet;
the scholar also rose
and followed her away.
A long time passed, and they did not return.
The maidservant, exhausted,
had fallen asleep in the corridor.
The wife sat alone,
solitary and without companion,
her heart filled with indignation and rage,
finding it hard to endure.
She thought of fleeing back home,
but the night was dim and hazy,
and she could not recall the way.
Tossing and turning, unable to decide,
she got up to spy on them.
Just as she approached their window,
the sounds of broken clouds and scattered rain
could faintly be heard.
Listening further,
she heard her husband describing in detail the intimate acts he usually performed with her,
pouring out everything.
At this point,
the wife's hands trembled and her heart shook,
almost unable to restrain herself.
She thought it better to go out and throw herself into a ditch or ravine to die.
Filled with fury, she was about to leave
when she suddenly saw her younger brother Sānláng arriving on horseback.
He quickly dismounted and asked,
and the wife told him everything.
Sānláng was furious.
He immediately went back with his sister,
straight into the house,
where the room door was bolted shut,
and pillow talk could still be heard murmuring.
Sānláng lifted a stone as big as a peck measure
and hurled it at the window lattice,
shattering it into three or five pieces.
From inside came a loud cry:
"The young master's head is broken!
What shall we do!"
Hearing this,
the wife was stunned,
and burst into loud weeping.
She said to her brother:
"I did not plot with you to kill my husband.
What shall we do now?"
Sānláng glared and said:
"You sobbed and urged me to come;
I was just able to vent the anger in my chest,
and now you protect your man and blame your brother.
I am not accustomed to being ordered around by a maidservant!"
He turned to leave,
but the wife grabbed his sleeve, saying:
"If you don't take me with you,
where will I go?"
Sānláng pushed his sister to the ground
and freed himself to leave.
The wife suddenly awoke with a start,
realizing it had all been a dream.
The next day,
the scholar indeed returned,
riding a white mule.
The wife found it strange but said nothing.
That night, the scholar also had a dream,
and what he saw and experienced
matched exactly what she described,
leaving them both astonished.
Later, Sānláng heard that his brother-in-law had returned from afar,
and also came to visit.
During their conversation,
he said to the scholar:
"Last night I dreamed of your return,
and today it truly happened.
How very strange."
The scholar laughed and said:
"Fortunately, I was not killed by the huge stone."
Sānláng asked in surprise why he said that,
and the scholar told him about the dream.
Sānláng found it extremely strange.
For that night,
Sānláng had also dreamed of meeting his sister, who tearfully told her story,
and in his anger he had thrown a stone.
The three dreams matched,
but they did not know who the beautiful woman was.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Gěng Shíbā of Xīnchéng,
critically ill,
knew he would not recover.
He said to his wife:
"Our eternal parting is near, within days or even tonight.
After I die,
whether you remarry or remain a widow is up to you.
Please tell me your intention."
The wife remained silent.
Gěng pressed her,
and added:
"Remaining a widow is certainly good,
but remarrying is also common.
Speak plainly—
what harm could it do?
I am about to bid you farewell.
If you remain a widow,
my heart will be comforted;
if you remarry,
my attachment will be severed."
The wife then said sorrowfully:
"The household lacks even a peck or a bushel of grain.
Even with you here, we barely manage—
how could I remain a widow?"
Hearing this,
Gěng suddenly gripped his wife's arm,
and said with a voice full of resentment:
"How cruel!"
With these words, he died.
His hand would not open.
The wife wailed.
When the family members arrived,
two people pried his fingers,
using all their strength to break his grip,
before they could open it.
Gěng did not know he was dead.
He went out the door
and saw over ten small carriages,
each carrying ten people,
with names written on square labels
pasted on the carriages.
The driver saw Gěng
and urged him to board.
Gěng saw that there were already nine people in the carriage,
making ten including himself.
Looking at the pasted list,
his own name was last.
The carriage moved with a creaking sound,
its noise shaking his ears,
and he did not know where he was going.
Soon they arrived at a place,
where he heard someone say:
"This is the place of homesickness."
Hearing its name,
he was suspicious.
Then he heard the driver muttering to himself:
"Today we executed three people."
Gěng was alarmed again.
Upon listening carefully to his words,
they were all about matters of the underworld,
and he realized:
"Could it be that I have become a ghost?"
Suddenly thinking of his home,
there was nothing left to worry about,
except that his elderly mother was advanced in years,
and after his wife remarried,
she would lack care;
thinking of this,
he could not help but shed tears.
After another while,
he saw a platform,
several ren high,
with many travelers;
those with heads covered and feet shackled,
sobbing as they went up and down,
and he heard people say it was
"Wàngxiāng Tái"
When the others reached this point,
they all stepped down from the carriage,
scrambling to climb up.
The driver either whipped them
or stopped them,
but when it came to Gěng,
he urged him to climb.
After climbing several dozen steps,
he finally reached the top.
Lifting his head to look,
he saw the gates, alleys, and courtyards,
as if before his eyes.
But the inner rooms were faintly visible,
as if shrouded in mist.
Overwhelmed with sorrow,
he turned around,
and saw a man in short clothes standing beside him,
who immediately asked Gěng his name.
Gěng told him everything.
The man also said he was a craftsman from Dōnghǎi.
Seeing Gěng in tears,
he asked:
"What troubles your heart?"
Gěng told him.
The craftsman suggested they escape by leaping off the platform.
Gěng feared pursuit from the underworld,
but the craftsman insisted it was safe.
Gěng also worried about falling from the high platform,
but the craftsman told him to follow him.
So he jumped first,
and Gěng indeed followed.
Upon landing,
they were unharmed.
Relieved that no one noticed,
they looked at the carriage they had ridden,
still below the platform.
The two hurriedly ran.
After a few steps,
Gěng suddenly remembered his name was attached to the carriage,
fearing he would be pursued by name;
so he turned back to the carriage,
dipped his finger in saliva,
wiped off his name,
then ran again,
panting heavily,
not daring to pause.
Shortly after,
they entered the village gate,
and the craftsman escorted him to his room.
Suddenly seeing his own corpse,
he awoke with a start.
Feeling exhausted, parched, and thirsty,
he urgently called for water.
His family was greatly alarmed,
and gave him water,
which he drank over a shí.
Then he suddenly stood up,
bowing and prostrating himself;
after that, he went outside to bow in thanks,
and only then returned,
but upon returning, he lay stiff and motionless.
His family found his behavior strange,
