suspecting he was not truly alive;
but as they gradually observed him,
there was nothing else unusual.
Slowly approaching to ask,
he recounted the whole story clearly.
They asked:
"Why did you go outside?"
He said:
"To bid farewell to the craftsman."
"Why did you drink so much water?"
He said:
"At first, I drank it,
but later the craftsman drank it."
They gave him broth,
and after a few days, he recovered.
From then on, he grew cold toward his wife,
no longer sharing a bed with her.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
A commoner of Chángzhōu, Lǐ Huà,
was wealthy with land and property.
Over fifty years old,
he had no sons.
He had a daughter named Xiǎohuì,
beautiful and graceful,
whom the couple cherished deeply.
At fourteen,
she suddenly fell ill and died,
leaving the household desolate,
with even less joy.
He then took a maid as a concubine,
and after over a year,
she bore a son,
whom he treasured like a precious jewel,
naming him Zhū'ér.
As the boy grew,
he was sturdy and lovable.
But he was extremely foolish,
even at five or six, unable to tell beans from wheat;
his speech was halting and unclear.
Lǐ still doted on him, unaware of his flaws.
There was a one-eyed monk,
who begged for alms in the market,
and could know people's private affairs,
so they were awed as if he were divine;
and he claimed
he could decide life, death, fortune, and misfortune for people.
Demanding tens, hundreds, or thousands,
he would call them by name to demand payment,
and no one dared refuse.
He came to Lǐ to ask for a hundred mín.
Lǐ found it difficult.
Offering ten taels of gold,
the monk refused;
it gradually increased to thirty taels.
The monk sternly said:
"It must be a hundred mín,
not a single coin less!"
Lǐ also grew angry,
took back the gold, and left abruptly.
The monk rose angrily and said:
"Don't regret it,
don't regret it!"
Not long after,
Zhū'ér suddenly felt severe heart pain,
writhing on the bed,
his face ashen.
Lǐ was terrified,
and took eighty taels to the monk to beg for help.
The monk laughed and said:
"A large sum of gold is not easily obtained!
But what can a humble monk do?"
Lǐ returned to find his son already dead.
Lǐ was deeply grieved,
and reported the matter to the county magistrate.
The magistrate arrested the monk for interrogation,
but the monk defended himself with clever words and no confession.
When he was flogged,
it sounded like striking a leather drum.
Ordered to search his person,
they found two wooden figures, a small coffin, and five small flags.
The magistrate was enraged,
and raised his hand to perform a spell.
The monk then became afraid,
and kowtowed repeatedly.
The magistrate paid no heed,
and had him beaten to death.
Lǐ kowtowed in thanks and returned home.
It was already dusk,
and I was sitting on the bed with my wife.
Suddenly a small child
entered the room
and said:
"Grandfather, why are you walking so fast?
I tried my hardest but couldn't catch up."
Looking at his appearance,
he seemed to be about seven or eight years old.
Lǐ was startled.
Just as he was about to question him,
he saw the child flickering in and out of sight,
vague and mist-like.
In the blink of an eye,
he had already climbed onto the bed and sat down.
Lǐ pushed him off,
and he fell to the ground without a sound.
He said:
"Grandfather, why are you doing this?"
In an instant, he climbed back up.
Lǐ became frightened
and fled with his wife.
The child called out "Father! Mother!"
babbling incessantly.
Lǐ entered his concubine's room
and hurriedly closed the door.
Looking back,
he saw the child was already at his knees.
Lǐ, alarmed,
asked what he wanted.
He replied:
"I am from Sūzhōu,
surnamed Zhān.
I lost both parents at age six
and was not tolerated by my elder brother and sister-in-law,
so I was sent to live with my maternal grandparents.
Once while playing outside the gate,
I was bewitched and killed by an evil monk under a mulberry tree.
He forced me to serve like a chāng ghost,
trapped in the underworld with my grievances,
unable to be reborn.
Fortunately, I relied on you, Grandfather, to clear my name,
and I wish to become your son."
Lǐ said:
"Humans and ghosts belong to different realms.
How can we depend on each other?"
The child said:
"Just clear out a small room
and set up a bed and bedding for me.
Pour a cup of cold congee for me daily,
and nothing else is needed."
Lǐ agreed.
The child was pleased
and thus slept alone in the room.
He came and went through the inner chambers in the morning,
as if he were born into the family.
Hearing the concubine crying for her son,
he asked:
"How many days has Zhū'ér been dead?"
He was told it had been seven days.
He said:
"The weather is severely cold,
so the corpse likely hasn't decayed.
Try opening the grave to take a look.
If it's undamaged,
the child can be revived."
Lǐ was overjoyed.
He went with the child
and opened the grave to examine it.
The body was intact.
Just as he was grieving,
he looked back
and found the child gone.
Astonished,
he carried the corpse home.
Just as he placed it on the bed,
its eyes began to flicker.
Soon it called for broth,
drank it and began to sweat,
and after sweating, it got up.
Everyone was delighted that Zhū'ér had come back to life,
and he was even more clever and agile than before,
completely different from the past.
However, at night he lay stiff,
with no breath at all.
When everyone turned him over,
he remained unconscious as if dead.
Greatly alarmed,
they thought he had died again.
As dawn approached,
he finally awoke as if from a dream.
Everyone gathered to ask him.
He replied:
"When I followed the evil monk before,
there were two of us children.
One was named Gēzi.
Yesterday I couldn't catch up with Father,
so I stayed behind to bid farewell to Gēzi.
Now in the underworld,
I am the adopted son of Clerk Jiāng,
and I live quite comfortably.
At midnight,
he always invites me to play.
Just now, he sent me back on a white-nosed horse."
His mother then asked:
"Did you see Zhū'ér in the underworld?"
He said:
"Zhū'ér has already been reborn.
He had no father-son bond with Grandfather.
He was merely Yán Zǐfāng from Jīnlíng,
coming to collect a debt of a hundred thousand cash."
Earlier,
Lǐ had traded in Jīnlíng
and owed Yán for goods he hadn't paid for.
Yán had died,
and no one knew about this matter.
When Lǐ heard this,
he was greatly shocked.
His mother asked:
"Did you see your sister Huì?"
The child said:
"I don't know.
Next time I go, I'll look for her."
After two or three more days,
he said to his mother:
"Sister Huì is doing very well in the underworld.
She married the young lord of Prince Chǔjiāng,
with pearls and jade adorning her hair.
Whenever she goes out,
hundreds of attendants shout to clear the way."
His mother said:
"Why doesn't she come back for a visit?"
He said:
"Once a person dies,
they no longer feel connected to their flesh and blood.
Only if someone recounts their past life in detail
will they suddenly feel moved.
Yesterday, through Clerk Jiāng's connections,
I managed to see my sister.
Sister called me to sit on her coral bed.
I told her how our parents missed her,
but she seemed as if asleep.
I said: 'When you were alive,
you loved embroidering twin flowers.
Once you pricked your finger with scissors,
and blood stained the silk.
You embroidered it into a red cloud.
Mother still hangs it on the wall by the bed,
thinking of it constantly.
Have you forgotten?'
Only then did Sister feel sorrow and emotion.
She said: 'I must tell my husband
and return to visit Mother.'"
His mother asked when,
and he replied he didn't know.
One day, he told his mother:
"Sister is coming soon.
Her entourage is large,
so we should prepare plenty of wine and congee."
A moment later,
he ran into the room and said:
"Sister is here!"
He moved a couch to the central hall
and said:
"Sister, please sit for a while.
Don't cry too much."
No one else could see anything.
The child led people outside to burn paper money and pour libations.
Returning, he said:
"The attendants have been sent away for now.
Sister says: 'The green brocade quilt I used to cover with,
which once got a bean-sized burn from a candlewick—
is it still there?'"
His mother said:
"It is."
She immediately opened a chest and took it out.
The child said:
"Sister told me to arrange it in her old room.
She is tired
and will rest for a while,
and tomorrow she'll talk with Mother again."
The daughter of the Zhào family, their eastern neighbor,
had been close friends with Huì.
That night,
she suddenly dreamed of Huì visiting with a scarf and purple cape,
laughing and talking as in life.
Huì said:
"I am now a different being.
Facing my parents
is like facing mountains and rivers.
I'll borrow your body to speak with my family,
so don't be frightened."
At daybreak,
just as she was about to tell her mother,
she suddenly collapsed, unconscious.
After a while, she awoke
and said to her mother:
"It has been several years since Xiǎohuì parted from her aunt,
and suddenly white hairs have grown!"
The mother exclaimed in shock:
"Child, have you gone mad?"
The girl bowed in farewell and immediately left.
The mother knew something was strange,
and followed her.
She went straight to Lǐ's place,
embraced her mother, and wept sorrowfully.
The mother was startled and did not understand what was happening.
The girl said:
"Yesterday when I returned,
I was quite exhausted,
and had no time to say a word.
I am unfilial,
abandoning my parents midway,
causing my parents grief and longing,
how can such a sin be redeemed!"
The mother suddenly understood,
and began to cry.
After a while, she asked:
"I heard that you are now noble,
which greatly comforts my heart.
But you reside in the Wáng family,
how could you come here?"
The girl said:
"My husband and I are extremely affectionate,
my parents-in-law also treat me with love and care,
and they do not consider me jealous or ugly."
When Huì was alive,
she liked to rest her chin on her hand;
as the girl spoke,
she repeatedly assumed this familiar posture,
her expression and manner exactly alike.
Not long after,
Zhū'ér rushed in and said:
"The people to fetch elder sister have arrived."
The girl then stood up,
bowed in farewell with tears falling,
and said:
"I am leaving now."
After speaking,
she fell down again,
and after a while, she revived.
Several months later,
Lǐ fell critically ill,
and medicine had no effect.
The child said:
"I fear she may not survive the day or night!
Two ghosts are sitting by the bedside,
one holding an iron staff,
the other holding a ramie rope,
about four or five feet long,
and no matter how I plead day and night, they will not leave."
The mother cried,
and prepared burial clothes and quilts.
When evening came,
the child hurried in and said:
"Miscellaneous people and women,
please step aside for now,
elder sister's husband has come to see father."
In a moment,
he clapped his hands and laughed.
The mother asked him,
and he said:
"I am laughing at the two ghosts,
when they heard elder sister's husband coming,
they both hid under the bed like turtles."
A little later,
he looked into the air and exchanged greetings,
asking about elder sister's well-being.
Then he clapped his hands and said:
"The two ghost slaves, no matter how I pleaded, they wouldn't leave,
now this is most satisfying!"
Then he went out to the door,
turned back,
and said:
"Elder sister's husband has left.
The two ghosts are locked on the horse's yoke.
Father should be fine now.
Elder sister's husband said: upon returning, he will report to the great king,
to beg for a hundred years of life for father and mother."
The whole family was overjoyed.
By night,
the illness had indeed subsided,
and within a few days, she fully recovered.
They hired a teacher to teach the child to read.
The child was very intelligent,
at eighteen he entered the county school,
and could still speak of matters from the underworld.
When he saw sick people in the village,
he would point out where the ghostly hauntings were,
and by burning there,
they often recovered.
Later, he fell suddenly ill,
his skin turned blue and purple,
and he said himself that the ghosts and spirits were punishing him for revealing secrets,
and from then on, he spoke no more of it.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain Grand Historian,
I have forgotten his surname.
He was lying in his study during the day,
when suddenly a small procession,
emerged from the corner of the hall.
The horses were as big as frogs,
the people finer than fingers.
There were several dozen teams of small ceremonial guards;
one official wore a black gauze hat,
dressed in embroidered robes,
riding in a sedan chair,
they went out the door in a flurry.
The Grand Historian found it strange,
secretly suspecting it was an illusion of sleep.
Suddenly he saw a small person,
return into the room,
carrying a felt bundle,
as big as a fist,
and actually came to the foot of the bed.
He announced:
"My master has a humble gift,
respectfully presented to the Grand Historian."
After speaking,
he stood facing him,
but did not present the item.
After a short while,
he laughed to himself and said:
"Such a trivial thing,
I suppose the Grand Historian has no use for it,
it would be better to give it to me."
The Grand Historian nodded.
Delighted, he took it and left.
He was not seen again afterwards.
It is a pity that the Grand Historian was too timid,
and did not inquire where they came from.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Shàng Shēng,
from Tàishān.
He lived alone in a quiet study.
It happened to be an autumn night,
the Milky Way shone brightly,
the bright moon hung in the sky,
he wandered among the flower shadows,
lost in distant thoughts.
Suddenly a woman climbed over the wall and came,
smiling, she said:
"Scholar, what are you thinking so deeply about?"
Shēng looked closely,
her beauty was like that of an immortal.
Overjoyed, he embraced her and brought her in,
and they were extremely intimate.
She said herself:
"My surname is Hú,
named Sānjiě."
When asked about her residence,
she only smiled without answering.
Shēng also did not press further,
only hoping they would be together forever.
From then on,
she came every night without fail.
One night,
sitting close with Shēng by the lamp curtain,
Shēng adored her,
gazing without turning away.
The woman laughed and said:
"Why are you staring at me so intently?"
He said:
"I look at you as if you were red peonies and green peaches,
even if I gaze all night,
I would not grow tired."
Sānjiě said:
"I am of plain appearance,"
"yet I have received such favor from you;
if you were to see my fourth sister,
I do not know how captivated you would be."
The scholar became even more enthralled,
wishing desperately to see her beauty,
and knelt down pleading earnestly.
The next evening,
she indeed brought Fourth Sister along.
She was just of marriageable age,
like lotus powder adorned with dew,
apricot blossoms misted with moisture,
smiling sweetly,
charming and beautiful beyond compare.
The scholar was overjoyed,
and invited her to sit.
Third Sister chatted and laughed with the scholar;
Fourth Sister only played with her embroidered sash,
keeping her head bowed.
Before long,
Third Sister rose to leave,
and her sister wished to follow.
The scholar grabbed her and would not let go,
turning to Third Sister and saying:
"Please, my dear, help me convey my feelings."
Third Sister then laughed and said:
"The passionate scholar is impatient!
Little sister, stay a while for him."
Fourth Sister said nothing,
and her elder sister left.
The two of them enjoyed each other fully,
then resting arms as pillows,
they poured out their life stories,
holding nothing back.
Fourth Sister confessed she was a fox.
The scholar, enamored with her beauty,
did not find it strange.
Fourth Sister then said:
"My elder sister is vicious,
having already killed three men.
Those bewitched by her
invariably meet their end.
Fortunately, I have received your deep affection,
and cannot bear to see you destroyed,
so you must break with her early."
The scholar grew fearful,
and asked how to handle it.
Fourth Sister said:
"Though I am a fox,
I have learned the proper methods of immortals.
I shall write a talisman to paste on your bedroom door,
which can repel her."
So she wrote it.
At dawn,
Third Sister came,
saw the talisman and retreated,
saying:
"That ungrateful girl,
so devoted to her new groom,
forgets the matchmaker who brought them together.
You two are fated to be together,
I bear no grudge,
but why must it be like this?"
Then she left directly.
A few days later,
Fourth Sister went elsewhere,
promising to return the following night.
That day,
the scholar happened to go out to gaze into the distance.
Below the mountain there was an old grove,
and from within the dense greenery,
emerged a young woman,
also quite charming.
Approaching the scholar, she said:
"Scholar, why must you daily cling so fondly to the Hú sisters?
They cannot even give you a single coin."
She then handed him a string of cash,
saying:
"Take this home first,
buy some fine wine;
I will bring some small dishes,
and we shall enjoy ourselves together."
The scholar pocketed the money and returned,
doing exactly as instructed.
After a short while,
the woman indeed arrived,
placing on the table a roasted chicken
and a salted pig's leg each,
then drew a knife to slice them into pieces;
pouring wine and exchanging flirtatious banter,
their merriment was exceptional.
Then they extinguished the candle and went to bed,
their intimacy exceedingly wanton.
Only at dawn did they rise.
As she sat on the edge of the bed,
holding her foot to change shoes,
suddenly they heard voices;
listening closely,
someone had already entered the bed curtains—
it was the Hú sisters.
At the sudden sight,
the woman fled in panic,
leaving a shoe on the bed.
The two sisters then scolded:
"Lecherous fox!
How dare you share a bed with a man!"
They chased after her,
returning after some time.
Fourth Sister reproached the scholar:
"You are incorrigible,
consorting with a lecherous fox,
I cannot stay near you anymore!"
And she angrily prepared to leave.
The scholar, terrified, threw himself at her feet,
pleading with earnest, sorrowful words.
and Fourth Sister's anger gradually subsided,
from then on they were as close as before.
One day,
a man from Shǎnxi arrived on a donkey at the gate, saying:
"I have been searching for these demonic creatures,
not just for a day or two,
and now I have finally found them."
The scholar's father, finding his words strange,
inquired where he came from.
He said:
"I roam the misty waves daily,
traveling the four directions,
for over ten months each year,
often eight or nine away from my hometown,
because a demonic creature bewitched and killed my younger brother.
Returning in deep grief and resentment,
I vowed to seek it out and exterminate it.
Having traveled thousands of miles,
I found no trace at all.
Now it is in your household.
If not eliminated,
there will be others who die after my brother."
At that time, the scholar and the girl were intimate,
and his parents had vaguely noticed,
hearing the guest's words,
they became greatly afraid,
invited him in,
and asked him to perform his arts.
He produced two bottles,
placed them on the ground,
and chanted spells for a long time.
Four wisps of black mist
separately entered the bottles.
The guest said joyfully:
"The whole family is here."
Then he sealed the bottle mouths with pig bladders,
wrapping them tightly.
The scholar's father was also pleased,
and insisted on the guest staying for a meal.
The scholar felt pity in his heart,
approached the bottles and peeked,
hearing Fourth Sister inside say:
"To sit and watch without helping,
how can you be so heartless?"
The scholar was even more moved.
He hurriedly tried to open the seal,
but the knot could not be undone.
Fourth Sister said again:
"No need for that,
just knock over the flag on the altar,
pierce the bladder with a needle to make a hole,
and I will come out."
The scholar did as requested.
Indeed, a thin strand of white vapor
emerged from the hole,
and soared into the sky, disappearing.
The guest came out,
saw the flag lying on the ground,
and exclaimed in shock:
"She escaped!
This must be the young master's doing."
Shaking the bottle and listening closely,
he said:
"Fortunately, only one is missing.
This creature is fated not to die,
so she may be pardoned."
Then he took the bottles and departed.
Later, while in the fields,
overseeing hired hands cutting wheat,
the scholar saw Fourth Sister from afar sitting under a tree.
He approached her,
took her hand and asked how she was.
And she said:
"Ten years have passed since we parted,
and my great elixir is now complete.
Yet my longing for you has not faded,
so I have come once more to pay my respects."
The scholar wished to take her back with him.
The woman said:
"I am not what I once was;
I cannot be tainted by worldly affections.
We shall meet again in the future."
Having spoken,
she vanished without a trace.
More than twenty years later,
the scholar happened to be living alone
when Sìjiě appeared from outside.
Delighted, the scholar spoke with her.
She said:
"My name is now listed among the immortals;
I should not tread the mortal world again.
But moved by your devotion,
I respectfully come to inform you of the time of your passing.
You should settle your affairs early;
do not grieve or worry.
I shall guide you to become a ghost immortal—
there will be no suffering."
Then she bid farewell and left.
When the day arrived,
the scholar indeed passed away.
Shàng Shēng was a close friend of the author's acquaintance Lǐ Wényù,
who personally witnessed this.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In Zhù Village, Jìyáng, there was an old man named Zhù,
over fifty years old,
who fell ill and died.
As his family was preparing for the burial,
they suddenly heard the old man calling urgently.
Everyone rushed to the mourning chamber,
and saw that the old man had revived.
They were overjoyed and comforted him.
The old man only said to his wife:
"I had just left,
determined not to return.
But after walking several *li*,
it occurred to me that leaving you, this old bag of bones, in the hands of our children,
dependent on them for warmth and care,
would bring you no joy in life.
It would be better for you to come with me.
So I returned
to take you along."
Everyone thought his words were the ravings of someone newly revived,
and did not take them seriously.
The old man repeated himself.
His wife said:
"That might indeed be good.
But I have just come back to life—
how can I die again so soon?"
The old man waved her off, saying:
"That is not difficult.
Hurry and put our household affairs in order."
His wife laughed and did not move.
The old man urged her again.
She then went outside,
lingered for a while, and returned,
deceiving him by saying:
"Everything is settled."
The old man told her to dress quickly.
His wife still did not go,
and the old man grew even more impatient.
Not wishing to disappoint him,
she put on her skirt and came out.
Her daughters-in-law and granddaughters stifled their laughter.
The old man moved his head on the pillow
and patted the bed, telling her to lie down.
His wife said:
"All the children are here—
what kind of sight would it be for the two of us to lie stiffly side by side?"
The old man pounded the bed, saying:
"What is so funny about dying together?"
Seeing the old man's agitation,
the children all urged the old woman to humor him.
Following their advice,
she lay stiffly beside him on the pillow.
The family again laughed at them.
After a moment, they noticed
the old woman's smile suddenly fade,
and gradually her eyes closed.
After a long while, there was no sound—
she seemed to have fallen asleep.
Everyone drew closer to look
and found her skin already cold and her breath gone.
Testing the old man, they found the same,
and only then were they shocked and dismayed.
In the twenty-first year of the Kāngxī reign,
the old man's sister-in-law was employed in the household of Provincial Governor Bì,
and she recounted this story in detail.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Did the old man have some extraordinary conduct in a past life?
The road to the underworld is vast and obscure—
to come and go as he pleased is truly strange!
Moreover, wishing for his white-haired wife to depart,
he simply called for her to go—
how remarkably at ease he was!
At the moment of death,
what one is most reluctant to part with
is the intimate companion by one's bedside.
If his method could be widely applied,
then the distribution of slippers and parting with incense
would become unnecessary."
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
The pig-dragon
is found in the Xī Jiāng.
It resembles a dragon but is shorter
and can fly sideways.
It often emerges along the riverbanks to prey on geese and ducks.
If someone catches one,
they sell its meat to the Chén and Kē families.
These two surnames are descendants of Chén Yǒuliàng,
and for generations they have eaten pig-dragon meat,
while other clans dare not consume it.
A traveler from Jiāngyòu
once obtained one
and tied it up in his boat.
One day,
while moored at Qiántáng,
the bonds loosened slightly,
and it suddenly leaped into the river.
In an instant,
great waves arose,
and the merchant boat capsized and sank.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
A certain gentleman from Shǎnyòu,
a Jìnshì of the Xīnchǒu year,
could remember his previous life.
He once said that in his past life he was a scholar
who died in middle age.
After death, he saw King Yama judging cases,
with cauldrons, tripods, oil pans, and woks
just as legends describe.
In the eastern corner of the hall,
several racks were set up,
draped with the skins of pigs, sheep, dogs, and horses.
The clerk called names from the register,
and some were sentenced to become horses,
others to become pigs.
All were stripped naked
and had skins taken from the racks to cover them.
When it was the gentleman's turn,
he heard King Yama say:
"This one should become a sheep."
A demon fetched a white sheepskin
and pressed it over the gentleman's body.
The clerk reported:
"He once saved a person from death."
King Yama checked the records and reviewed them,
then declared:
"Spare him.
Though his evils are many,
this good deed can redeem him."
The demons then stripped off the woolen hide.
The hide had already adhered to his body
and could not be moved.
Two demons grabbed his arms and pressed his chest,
pulling with all their might to remove it.
The pain was indescribable;
the skin broke into pieces
and could not be completely removed.
After it was torn off,
a patch of sheepskin the size of a palm remained stuck near his shoulder.
After the gentleman was reborn,
a clump of sheep's wool grew on his back,
and even when cut, it grew back.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In the late Míng dynasty,
the Jì region had many bandits.
Each county stationed soldiers,
who would kill any bandits they captured.
Zhāngqiū had especially many bandits.
One soldier carried an exceptionally sharp sword
that always cut cleanly through the joints.
One day,
he captured more than ten bandits
and escorted them to the execution ground.
One of the bandits recognized the soldier
and hesitantly pleaded:
"I have heard your sword is the swiftest,
never requiring a second cut to behead.
I beg you to kill me!"
The soldier said:
"Agreed.
Stay close to me
and do not stray."
The bandit followed him to the execution site.
The soldier drew his sword and swung—
with a clean slash, the head fell.
Several steps away,
the head was still rolling
and loudly praised: "What a swift sword!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Mr. Gù,
a native of Jīnlíng,
was talented in many arts,
but his family was extremely poor.
Moreover, because his mother was old,
he could not bear to leave her side,
so he only made a living daily by
accepting payment for his calligraphy and paintings.
He was twenty-five years old,
yet still without a wife.
Across the way was an old, empty house,
where an old woman and a young girl rented and lived.
Since there were no men in their household,
he had never inquired who they were.
One day,
returning home from outside by chance,
he saw the young lady coming out of his mother's room.
She was about eighteen or nineteen,
graceful, beautiful, and elegant,
rarely matched in the world.
Seeing Mr. Gù, she quickly avoided him,
her demeanor cold and stern.
Mr. Gù went in and asked his mother.
His mother said:
"That is the young lady from across the way.
She came to borrow scissors and a ruler.
She mentioned that her family also consists only of a mother.
This girl doesn't seem like the product of a poor family.
When I asked why she wasn't betrothed,
she used her mother's old age as an excuse.
Tomorrow I should go visit her mother,
and subtly hint at our intentions;
if their expectations aren't too high,
you could support her mother for her."
The next day, she visited their home.
Their mother was merely a deaf old woman.
Looking at their room,
there wasn't even food for the next day.
When asked about their livelihood,
they relied on the girl's ten fingers.
Slowly, she tested the idea of sharing meals with them.
The old woman seemed receptive,
but then consulted her daughter;
the girl remained silent,
appearing very unhappy.
The mother then returned home.
Pondering the situation, she said suspiciously:
"Could it be that the girl dislikes our poverty?
She doesn't speak or smile,
beautiful as peach and plum blossoms,
yet cold as frost and snow—
what a strange person!"
Mother and son speculated and sighed, then let it be.
One day,
while Mr. Gù was sitting in his study,
a young man came seeking a painting.
His appearance was very handsome,
but his manner rather frivolous.
Asked where he was from,
he
"neighboring village"
as his reply.
After that, he came every two or three days.
Gradually becoming familiar,
he began with teasing and banter;
Mr. Gù embraced him intimately,
and he didn't refuse much,
so they became intimate.
From then on, their往来 became very close.
Once, when the young lady passed by,
the young man followed her with his eyes
and asked who she was.
Mr. Gù replied
"neighbor's daughter."
The young man said:
"So stunningly beautiful,
yet her expression is so intimidating?"
A little later,
Mr. Gù went inside.
His mother said:
"Just now, that girl came to beg for rice,
saying they hadn't lit a stove for a whole day.
This girl is extremely filial,
their poverty is truly pitiable.
We should offer them some relief."
Following his mother's words,
Mr. Gù carried a peck of rice to their door,
conveying his mother's intentions.
The girl accepted it
but did not express thanks.
She often came to Mr. Gù's home,
and seeing his mother making clothes and shoes,
would help with the sewing;
moving about the hall,
she worked like a daughter-in-law.
Mr. Gù felt even more grateful to her.
Whenever he received food gifts,
he would always share some with her mother,
yet the girl never mentioned it with a single word.
Once, Mr. Gù's mother developed a boil in a private place,
crying out day and night.
The girl often came to the bedside to check on her,
washing the wound and applying medicine for her,
three or four times a day.
Mr. Gù's mother felt very uneasy about this,
but the girl was not disgusted by the filth.
The mother said:
"Ah!
If only I had a daughter-in-law like you,
to care for me in my old age until death!"
Having said this,
she choked with sorrow.
The girl comforted her, saying:
"Your son is greatly filial,
far surpassing us, a widowed mother and orphaned daughter, by ten or a hundred times."
The mother said:
"Those chores by the bedside,
how can a filial son manage them?
Moreover, I am already nearing my end,
my days are numbered,
and I deeply worry about continuing the family line."
While speaking,
Mr. Gù entered.
His mother said tearfully:
"We have troubled the young lady greatly,
you must not forget to repay her kindness."
Mr. Gù bowed deeply to her.
The girl said:
"You respect my mother,
I do not thank you;
why should you thank me?"
From then on, he respected and loved her even more.
However, her behavior remained stiff and aloof,
and not the slightest intimacy could be forced.
One day,
the woman went out,
and Shēng gazed at her intently.
Suddenly, she turned her head,
and smiled sweetly.
Shēng was overjoyed beyond expectation,
and hurriedly followed her to her home.
He made advances,
and she did not refuse,
so they happily made love.
Afterward,
she warned Shēng, saying:
"This can happen once, but not again!"
Shēng did not respond and returned home.
The next day,
he tried to arrange another meeting.
The woman turned stern and, ignoring him, left.
He came frequently,
and sometimes they met,
but she never gave him any words or looks of affection.
If he teased her a little,
her cold words would chill him to the bone.
Suddenly, in a secluded spot, she asked Shēng:
"Who is that young man who has been coming lately?"
Shēng told her.
The woman said:
"His manner and behavior
have been disrespectful toward me many times.
Because of your intimacy with me,
I have let it pass.
Please relay a message for me: if he does it again,
he does not wish to live anymore!"
That evening,
Shēng told the young man,
and said:
"You must be careful,
she is not to be offended!"
The young man said:
"If she cannot be offended,
why did you privately offend her?"
Shēng protested that he had not.
The young man said:
"If you did not,
then how did those indecent words
reach your ears?"
Shēng could not answer.
The young man said:
"I also trouble you to relay a message: tell her not to pretend to be coy;
otherwise,
I will spread the word everywhere."
Shēng was very angry with him,
and his feelings showed on his face,
so the young man left.
One evening,
Shēng was sitting alone
when the woman suddenly arrived,
smiling and saying:
"My bond of affection with you is not yet broken—
is this not fate?"
Shēng was ecstatic and embraced her.
Hearing the sound of hurried footsteps,
the two started up in alarm,
and the young man pushed the door open and entered.
Shēng asked in surprise:
"What are you doing here?"
The young man laughed and said:
"I came to see the chaste and pure one."
Turning to the woman, he said:
"Aren't you blaming others today?"
The woman's eyebrows shot up and her cheeks flushed red,
but she remained silent.
Suddenly, she flipped open her upper garment,
revealing a leather pouch,
and from it she drew out
a gleaming dagger about a foot long.
When the young man saw it,
he was terrified and backed away.
She chased him out the door,
but looking around, he was nowhere to be seen.
The woman threw the dagger into the air,
and it made a sharp sound,
gleaming like a long rainbow.
In a moment, something fell to the ground with a thud.
Shēng quickly lit a candle to look,
and saw a white fox,
its head and body separated.
He was greatly shocked.
The woman said:
"This was your catamite.
I had already forgiven him,
but what could I do when he insisted on not wanting to live!"
She put the dagger back into its pouch.
Shēng pulled her, urging her to come inside.
She said:
"Just now, that monster ruined the mood.
Let's meet tomorrow night."
She went out the door and left directly.
The next night,
the woman indeed came,
and they were intimate together. When Shēng asked about her skills,
she said:
"This is not for you to know.
You should keep it secret;
if it is revealed, I fear it will bring you no good fortune."
He also brought up marriage,
but she said:
"We share the same pillow and mat,
and I fetch water for you—
if this is not being a wife, what is it?
Since we are already husband and wife,
why speak of marriage again?"
Shēng said:
"Is it because you despise my poverty?"
She replied:
"You are indeed poor,
but am I rich?
Tonight's meeting
is precisely because I pity your poverty."
As she was leaving, she instructed him:
"Improper conduct
should not be repeated.
When I should come,
I will come on my own;
when I should not come,
forcing it will be of no use."
Afterward, whenever they met,
Shēng often tried to draw her aside for private conversation,
but she would always avoid him.
However, she mended his clothes and cooked his meals,
managing everything for him,
no less than a wife would.
After several months,
her mother died,
and Shēng exhausted his efforts to bury her.
From then on, the woman lived alone.
Shēng thought that, since she was living alone, he could take advantage of the situation.
He climbed over the wall and entered,
calling to her repeatedly outside her window,
but she never responded.
Looking at her door,
he found the room empty and locked.
He secretly suspected that she had an appointment with someone else.
That night he went again,
and it was the same.
So he left a jade pendant in the window and left.
The next day,
they met at his mother's place.
After they came out,
she followed behind him and said:
"Do you suspect me, sir?
Each person has their own heart,
and cannot tell others.
Now if I want to make you have no doubts,
how can it be done?
But there is one urgent matter I need you to plan for."
He asked what it was,
and she said:
"I am already eight months pregnant,
and I fear I will give birth any day now.
'My status is not clear,'
I can bear it for you,
but I cannot raise it for you.
You can secretly tell your mother,
to find a wet nurse,
pretending to be adopting a child,
and not mention me."
Shēng agreed,
and told his mother.
His mother laughed and said:
"How strange this girl is!
She wouldn't accept a formal proposal,
yet she privately favors my son."
She happily followed the plan and waited.
After more than a month,
the girl did not come for several days.
His mother grew suspicious,
went to knock at her door,
it was desolate and quiet.
After knocking for a long time,
the girl finally came out with disheveled hair and a dirty face.
She opened the door to let her in,
then closed it again.
Entering her room,
there was a crying baby on the bed.
His mother asked in surprise:
"When was it born?"
She replied:
"Three days ago."
She lifted the swaddling cloth to look at it,
it was a boy,
and with full cheeks and a broad forehead.
She said happily:
"You have already borne a grandson for this old woman,
but you are all alone,
where will you entrust yourself?"
The girl said:
"My small hidden feelings,
I dare not fully reveal to you, old mother.
Wait until night when no one is around,
you can take the child away."
His mother returned and told her son,
and they secretly found it strange together.
At night they went and brought the child back.
After several nights,
close to midnight,
the girl suddenly knocked and entered,
carrying a leather bag in her hand,
and said with a smile:
"My great task is finished,
I bid farewell from now on."
He urgently asked the reason,
and she said:
"The kindness of raising my mother,
I never forget for a moment.
Previously I said 'it can be once but not twice,'
because repaying you was not in the bedchamber.
Because you were poor and could not marry,
I wanted to continue your family line.
I originally hoped to get it with one try,
but unexpectedly my menses came again,
so I broke the rule and did it a second time.
Now your kindness is repaid,
my wish is also fulfilled,
I have no regrets."
He asked:
"What is in the bag?"
She said:
"The head of my enemy."
He checked and looked inside,
beard and hair tangled and blood blurred.
He was terrified,
and asked again for details.
She said:
"The reason I didn't tell you before,
was because secret matters must not be leaked,
I feared there would be exposure.
Now the matter is done,
it's no harm to tell you: I am from Zhèjiāng.
My father was an official, a Sīmǎ,
who was framed by an enemy,
and they confiscated our family property.
I carried my old mother out,
hid my name,
and kept my head down,
for three years already.
The reason I didn't take revenge immediately,
was only because my mother was alive;
after my mother passed,
there was another piece of flesh burdening my belly,
so it was delayed for a long time.
Those nights I went out for no other reason,
the roads and doors were not familiar,
I feared there might be mistakes."
After speaking,
she went out the door.
She also instructed:
"The child I bore,
take good care of him.
You have thin fortune and no longevity,
this child can bring glory to the family.
It's late at night, I must not disturb the old mother,
I am leaving!"
Just as he was sadly about to ask where she was going,
the girl flashed like lightning,
in a glance she was gone.
Shēng sighed regretfully and stood woodenly,
as if he had lost his soul.
The next day he told his mother,
and they sighed in wonder together.
Three years later,
Shēng indeed died.
His son at eighteen passed the Jìnshì examination,
and supported his grandmother until her old age.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"One must have a chaste and righteous woman at home,
before one can keep a catamite.
Otherwise,
you love his youth,
and he loves your sow!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
There was a man named Chē Shēng,
whose family was not well-off,
but he was addicted to drinking,
at night he could not sleep without three cups of wine,
so the wine jar by his bed was often not empty.
One night he woke from sleep,
turning over,
it seemed like someone was sleeping with him,
he thought it was just the quilt falling.
Feeling it,
there was something furry,
like a cat but bigger;
lighting a candle to look,
it was a fox,
drunk and sleeping like a dog.
Looking at his wine bottle,
it was empty.
So he laughed and said:
"This is my drinking buddy."
Not wanting to startle it,
he covered it with his clothes and put his arm around it,
and slept with it.
He left the candle to see what would happen,
at midnight,
the fox stretched and yawned.
Shēng laughed and said:
"What a beautiful sleep!"
Lifting the cover to look,
it was a handsome man in scholar's attire.
He got up and bowed before the bed,
thanking him for not killing him.
Shēng said:
"I am addicted to wine,
and people think I'm foolish;
you, sir,
are my Bào Shū.
If you do not doubt me,
we should be good friends in the wine hills."
He pulled him onto the bed,
and they slept again.
And he said:
"You can come often,
do not be suspicious."
The fox agreed.
When Shēng woke up,
the fox had already left.
So he prepared a jar of fine wine,
specially waiting for the fox.
By evening,
she indeed arrived,
and they sat close together, drinking merrily.
The fox had a great capacity for liquor
and was skilled at witty banter,
so they regretted having met so late.
The fox said:
"I have repeatedly enjoyed your fine wine;
how can I repay your kindness?"
Shēng replied:
"The pleasure of sharing a cup of wine—
why even mention it!"
The fox said:
"Even so,
you are a poor scholar,
and money for wine is not easily come by.
I should help you secure a little wine money."
The next evening,
she came and told him:
"Seven li southeast from here,
by the roadside, there is some lost gold;
you can go fetch it early."
At dawn he went,
and indeed found two pieces of gold.
He then bought fine delicacies
to accompany their evening drinking.
The fox again told him:
"Behind the courtyard there is a hidden stash;
you should dig it up."
Following her words,
he indeed found over a hundred thousand cash.
Delighted, he said:
"Now my purse is full;
I need not worry about buying wine anymore."
The fox said:
"Not so.
How can water from a rut be scooped for long?
We must plan further."
Another day,
she said to Shēng:
"The price of buckwheat in the market is low;
this rare commodity can be hoarded."
He followed her advice,
purchasing over forty dàn of buckwheat.
Everyone ridiculed him for it.
Not long after,
a great drought occurred,
and all the grain and beans withered,
only buckwheat could be planted;
he sold the seeds,
making a tenfold profit.
From then on, he grew even richer,
acquiring two hundred mǔ of fertile land.
Whenever he consulted the fox,
if he planted more wheat, the wheat harvest was good;
if he planted more millet, the millet harvest was good;
all matters regarding the timing of planting
were decided by the fox.
As their days grew more intimate,
she called Shēng's wife "sister-in-law"
and regarded his children as her own.
Later, when Shēng passed away,
the fox never came again.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Shēng Sāng,
given name Xiǎo,
courtesy name Zǐmíng,
was from Yízhōu.
Orphaned young,
he lived as a tutor in Hónghuābù.
Sāng was a quiet, composed man who kept to himself,
going out only twice a day
to eat at the eastern neighbor's,
spending the rest of the time sitting steadfastly alone.
The eastern neighbor lad once came by
and teased him:
"Aren't you afraid of ghosts and foxes, living alone like this?"
He laughed and replied:
"Why should a man fear ghosts and foxes?
If a male comes, I have a sharp sword;
if a female comes, I might even open the door and welcome her in."
The neighbor lad returned,
conspired with a friend,
and had a courtesan climb over the wall using a ladder,
then tapped on the door.
Peering out, Shēng asked who it was,
and the courtesan claimed to be a ghost.
Shēng was terrified,
his teeth chattering audibly.
The courtesan hesitated and then left.
The neighbor lad came early to Shēng's study the next morning,
and Shēng recounted what he had seen,
saying he planned to return home.
The neighbor lad clapped his hands and said:
"Why didn't you open the door and welcome her in?"
Shēng suddenly realized it was a trick,
and so he settled back in as before.
After half a year had passed,
a woman came knocking at his study one night.
Thinking his friend was playing another trick,
Shēng opened the door and invited her in;
she was a beauty capable of toppling cities.
Startled, he asked where she came from.
She said:
"I am Liánxiāng,
a courtesan from the western household."
As there were indeed many brothels in the port,
he believed her.
They extinguished the candle and went to bed,
becoming deeply intimate.
From then on, she would come once every three to five nights.
One evening,
he sat alone in deep thought
when a girl came flitting in.
Thinking it was Liánxiāng,
he rose to greet her and speak.
But when he saw her face, she was not Liánxiāng at all. She was only fifteen or sixteen,
with sleeves hanging loosely
and an elegant, graceful beauty.
As she walked
she seemed to hesitate between coming and going.
He was greatly startled
and suspected she was a fox.
The girl said:
"I am
a girl from a respectable family
named Lǐ.
I admire your refined elegance
and hope you will not spurn me."
The scholar was pleased.
He took her hand.
It was cold as ice.
He asked:
"Why are you so cold?"
She said:
"My young body is frail and thin.
At night it is exposed to frost and dew.
How could it be otherwise?"
Later, when her silk garments were loosened,
she proved to be a virgin.
The girl said:
"I have given myself for love.
My delicate body
has lost its innocence in a single day.
If you do not find me too lowly,
I wish to serve you always at your pillow.
Is there no one else in your room?"
The scholar said:
"No one else,
only a neighbor girl,
but she does not come often."
The girl said:
"I must carefully avoid her.
I am not like the girls from the pleasure quarters.
Keep it secret and do not tell.
When she comes, I will go;
when she goes, I will come. That will do."
When the cock crowed, she prepared to leave.
She gave him an embroidered slipper,
saying:
"This is something I wore on my foot.
Playing with it can convey longing and admiration.
But if there is someone else, be careful not to play with it!"
He accepted it and looked at it.
It curved up like the tip of an awl.
He was very fond of it.
The next evening, when no one was around,
he took it out to examine and admire.
The girl suddenly appeared, flitting in,
and they became intimate.
From then on, whenever he took out the slipper,
the girl would surely come in response to his thoughts.
He found it strange and questioned her.
She laughed and said:
"It just happens to be the right time."
One night Liánxiāng came
and exclaimed in surprise:
"Why do you look so listless and weak?"
The scholar said:
"I don't feel it myself."
Liánxiāng then bade farewell,
arranging to meet again in ten days.
After she left,
Lǐ came every night without fail.
She asked:
"Why hasn't your lover come for so long?"
So he told her about the arrangement.
Lǐ laughed and said:
"How do you think I compare with Liánxiāng in beauty?"
He said:
"You could be called two unmatched beauties.
But Liánxiāng's skin is warm and soft."
Lǐ's expression changed and she said:
"You say we are both beautiful,
but you say that to me.
She must be a fairy from the moon palace—
of course I am not her equal."
Then she became unhappy.
She counted on her fingers
and found that the ten-day period was up.
She told him not to let on
and said she would secretly watch.
The next night,
Liánxiāng indeed came.
Their conversation was very congenial.
When they went to bed,
Liánxiāng was greatly alarmed and said:
"It's serious!
I haven't seen you for ten days.
How have you become so exhausted and weak?
Are you sure you haven't had another encounter?"
The scholar asked her why.
She said:
"I judged by your spirit and energy—
I examined it.
Your pulse is scattered like tangled threads—
it's a ghostly ailment."
The next night,
when Lǐ came,
the scholar asked:
"What did you think of Liánxiāng when you watched her?"
She said:
"Beautiful.
I always said there was no such beauty in the world.
She is indeed a fox.
When she left,
I followed her—
she lives in a cave in the southern hills."
The scholar suspected she was jealous
and answered casually.
The next evening,
he teased Liánxiāng, saying:
"I certainly don't believe it,
but someone said you are a fox."
Liánxiāng urgently asked:
"Who said that?"
He laughed and said:
"I was just teasing you."
Liánxiāng said:
"How is a fox different from a human?"
He said:
"Those bewitched by them become ill,
and in severe cases die.
That is what is frightening."
Liánxiāng said:
"Not so.
At your age,
three days after intimacy,
your vital energy can recover.
Even if it were a fox, what harm?
But if you indulge every day and exhaust yourself,
there are humans who are worse than foxes.
All those in the world who become emaciated corpses or consumptive ghosts—
do you think they all died from fox bewitchment?
Even so,
someone must have been talking about me."
The scholar strenuously denied there was anyone,
but Liánxiāng pressed him harder.
The scholar had no choice
and revealed it.
Liánxiāng said:
"I did wonder why you were so exhausted.
But how could it have come to this so quickly?
Could it be that she is not human?
Don't say anything.
Tomorrow night,
I will watch her as she watched me."
That night when Lǐ came,
after only a few words,
they heard a cough outside the window.
She hurriedly fled.
Liánxiāng came in and said:
"You are in danger!
She is truly a ghost!
If you cling to her beauty and do not break off quickly,
the road to the underworld is near!"
The scholar thought she was jealous
and remained silent.
Liánxiāng said:
"I know you cannot forget your feelings,
but I cannot bear to watch you die.
Tomorrow,
I will bring medicine
to cure you of the yin poison.
Fortunately, the root of the illness is still shallow.
In ten days you should be well.
Let me share your bed to watch your recovery."
The next night,
she indeed brought out a dose of medicine and made him take it.
In a moment,
he had three or two bouts of diarrhea.
He felt his internal organs cleared and empty,
and his spirit suddenly refreshed.
Though in his heart he was grateful to her,
he still did not believe Lǐ was a ghost.
Liánxiāng shared the bed with Shēng every night;
when Shēng wished to unite with her,
she always stopped him.
After several days,
his flesh and skin became full and healthy.
When she was about to leave,
she earnestly urged him to break off with Lǐ.
Shēng deceitfully agreed.
After closing the door and trimming the lamp,
he would hold the shoe and think longingly.
Lǐ suddenly arrived.
Having been separated for several days,
she wore a rather resentful expression.
Shēng said:
"She has been acting as a witch doctor for me night after night,
please do not resent her;
my affection lies with you."
Lǐ became slightly appeased.
Shēng whispered intimately on the pillow:
"I love you dearly,
yet there are those who say you are a ghost."
Lǐ was speechless for a long while,
then cursed:
"It must be that seductive fox who has confused your hearing! If you do not cut her off,
I will not come again!"
She then sobbed and wept.
Shēng comforted and placated her with a hundred words,
and she finally stopped.
The next night,
Liánxiāng arrived,
and upon learning that Lǐ had come again,
she angrily said:
"Do you truly wish to die!"
Shēng laughed and said:
"Why are you so deeply jealous?"
Lián grew even angrier:
"You have planted the seed of death;
I am trying to remove it for you.
If I were not jealous, what then?"
Shēng made an excuse and teased:
"She said the illness from before
was caused by a fox's haunting."
Lián then sighed:
"If what you say is true,
and you remain deluded and unawakened,
if by any chance something untoward happens,
how could I, with a hundred mouths, explain myself?
I beg to take my leave from now on.
After a hundred days,
I shall see you lying on your sickbed."
He tried to keep her, but she would not stay;
she left angrily and directly.
From then on, he was with Lǐ day and night.
After about two months or more,
he felt greatly exhausted.
At first he still tried to comfort himself;
day by day he grew thinner and weaker,
able only to drink a bowl of porridge.
He wished to return home to receive care,
but still felt attached and could not bear to leave abruptly.
Procrastinating for several days,
he became gravely ill and could no longer rise.
A neighboring scholar, seeing his severe illness,
daily sent a servant from the school to bring him food and drink.
Shēng, by this point, began to doubt Lǐ,
and thus said to her:
"I regret not having listened to Liánxiāng's words,
which led to this!"
Having spoken, he closed his eyes.
After a while he revived,
opened his eyes and looked around;
Lǐ had already left,
and from then on she ceased to come.
Shēng, emaciated, lay in the empty study,
longing for Liánxiāng as one yearns for the year's end.
One day,
just as he was lost in thought,
suddenly someone lifted the curtain and entered—
it was Liánxiāng.
Approaching the bed, she smiled and said:
"You country bumpkin,
was I not right!"
Shēng choked with sobs for a long time,
admitting he knew his fault,
and only begged for salvation.
Lián said:
"The illness has entered the vitals;
truly there is no cure.
I have come merely to bid a final farewell,
to prove I am not jealous."
Shēng, greatly sorrowful, said:
"There is an object beneath the pillow;
I trouble you to break it for me."
Lián searched and found the shoe,
held it near the lamp,
and turned it over and over, examining it.
The girl Lǐ entered,
and suddenly seeing Liánxiāng,
turned to flee.
Lián blocked the door with her body;
Lǐ, in distress and urgency, did not know how to get out.
Shēng reproached and enumerated her faults;
Lǐ could not reply.
Lián said with a laugh:
"Now I can finally confront you face to face, sister.
You once said the gentleman's former illness
might not have been caused by me;
what do you say now?"
Lǐ bowed her head and admitted her fault.
Lián said:
"Such a beauty as you,
yet you turn love into enmity?"
Lǐ immediately threw herself to the ground, weeping,
begging for pity and rescue.
Lián then helped her up,
and inquired in detail about her life.
She said:
"I
am the daughter of Assistant Prefect Lǐ;
I died young,
and was buried outside the wall.
Like a spring silkworm that has died,
its silk thread is not yet exhausted.
To be together with the gentleman in love
is my wish;
to cause his death
was truly not my original intention."
Lián said:
"I have heard that ghosts benefit from people's deaths,
because after death they can be together constantly;
is this so or not?"
She replied:
"It is not so.
When two ghosts meet,
there is no joy in it;
if there were joy,
are there few young gentlemen in the underworld?"
Lián said:
"How foolish!
Doing it night after night,
even a human could not bear it,
let alone a ghost!"
Lǐ asked:
"Foxes can kill people;
by what art do you alone not?"
Lián said:
"Those are of the kind that absorb vitality;
I am not of that sort.
Therefore, in the world there are foxes that do not harm people,
but there are certainly no ghosts that do not harm people,
because their yin energy is too strong."
Hearing their words,
Shēng finally knew that both fox and ghost were real;
fortunately, being accustomed and familiar with them,
he was not much frightened.
But thinking of his remaining breath being as thin as a thread,
he could not help crying out in great pain.
Lián turned and asked:
"How are you going to deal with the young master?"
Lǐ blushed and humbly apologized.
Lián said with a smile:
"I'm afraid the young master is too strong and healthy,
the jealous lady wants to eat waxberries."
Lǐ adjusted her sleeves and said:
"If there is a physician skilled enough to heal the nation,
who can make me not fail the young master,
I would be willing to bury my head underground,
how would I dare to show my face in the human world again!"
Lián took out medicine from her pouch,
and said:
"I knew this day would come long ago,
after parting, I gathered herbs on the three mountains,
it took three months in total,
before all the ingredients were prepared.
Even if one is dying from consumption or poison,
administering this will revive them without fail.
However, the cause of the illness must be matched with the corresponding catalyst,
so I must ask for your assistance."
She asked:
"What is needed?"
Lián said:
"Just a drop of fragrant saliva from your cherry lips.
When I feed him a pill,
I'll trouble you to pass it with a kiss and a spit."
Lǐ's cheeks flushed crimson,
she lowered her head and turned to look at her shoes.
Lián teased:
"The only thing my sister is proud of is her shoes!"
Lǐ felt even more ashamed,
bowing and looking around as if she had nowhere to hide.
Lián said:
"This is a skill you're usually familiar with,
why be stingy now?"
So she placed the pill into the young man's mouth,
and urged her on.
Lǐ had no choice,
and spat.
Lián said:
"Again!"
She spat once more.
After three or four spits in total,
the pill had been swallowed.
After a short while,
his stomach rumbled like thunder.
She fed him another pill,
and herself pressed her lips to his to pass her breath.
The young man felt a fiery heat in his dāntián,
and his spirits revived.
Lián said:
"He's cured!"
Lǐ heard the rooster crow,
and reluctantly took her leave.
Since the young man had just recovered,
he still needed recuperation,
and it was unwise for him to go out for meals;
so she bolted the door from the outside,
pretending the young man had returned home,
to cut off social interactions,
and guarded him day and night.
Lǐ also came every evening without fail,
serving diligently,
treating Lián like an elder sister.
Lián also deeply cherished and loved her.
After three months,
the young man was as healthy as before.
Lǐ then stopped coming for several nights;
when she did come occasionally,
she would leave after just one glance.
When they were face to face,
she also seemed unhappy and sorrowful.
Lián often asked her to stay and sleep together,
but she always refused.
The young man chased after her,
carried her back in his arms,
her body as light as a straw effigy.
The girl could not escape,
so she lay down dressed,
her body not even two chǐ tall.
Lián pitied her even more,
and secretly had the young man hold her intimately,
but even shaking her could not wake her.
The young man fell asleep;
when he woke and searched for her,
she had already vanished.
More than ten days later,
she never came again.
The young man missed her deeply,
often taking out her shoes to fondle.
Lián said:
"So graceful and delicate,
even I feel pity for her,
let alone a man."
The young man said:
"In the past, whenever I played with the shoes, she would come,
so I had my suspicions,
but I never expected she was a ghost.
Now, facing the shoes and thinking of her appearance,
truly fills me with sorrow."
And he began to weep.
Previously,
a wealthy family named Zhāng had a daughter named Yàn’ér,
who at the age of fifteen
died without sweating.
After a full night, she revived,
rose and looked around, wanting to flee.
Zhāng locked the door,
preventing her from leaving.
The girl said herself:
"I am the soul of the magistrate's daughter.
Moved by Master Sāng's affection,
the shoe I left behind is still at his place.
I am truly a ghost;
what good does imprisoning me do?"
Since her words had a basis,
they questioned her about how she came to be here.
The girl hesitated and looked back,
utterly confused herself.
Someone mentioned that Sāng had fallen ill and returned home,
but the girl insisted this was false.
Her family grew very suspicious.
The scholar from the eastern neighbor heard of this,
climbed over the wall to spy,
and saw Sāng speaking with a beautiful woman;
he rushed in to confront them,
but in the confusion, she had already vanished.
The neighbor, shocked, questioned him.
Sāng laughed and said:
"I told you before,
if it's a female, I'll take her in."
The neighbor recounted Yàn’ér's words.
Sāng then opened the door,
intending to go investigate,
but had no means to do so.
When Madame Zhāng heard that Sāng had indeed not returned,
she found it even stranger.
So she sent an old maidservant to ask for the shoe,
and Sāng took it out and gave it to her.
Yàn’ér was delighted to receive it.
She tried it on,
but the shoe was a full inch smaller than her foot,
and she was greatly alarmed.
Looking at herself in the mirror,
she suddenly realized with clarity that she had been reborn by borrowing another's body,
and thus explained the whole story.
Only then did her mother believe her.
The girl looked in the mirror and wailed:
"In my former appearance,
I was quite confident,
but whenever I saw Sister Lián,
I still felt ashamed.
Now it's the opposite;
as a human, I am not as good as I was as a ghost!"
Clutching the shoe, she wept,
and no amount of consoling could ease her.
She covered herself with the quilt and lay stiffly.
When food was offered,
she refused to eat,
and her body became swollen all over;
for seven days she ate nothing,
yet she did not die,
and the swelling gradually subsided;
feeling unbearably hungry,
she finally ate again.
After a few days,
her whole body itched,
and her skin peeled off completely.
One morning upon waking,
her sleeping slipper fell off,
and when she searched for it to put on,
it was immensely large.
So she tried on the previous shoe,
and it fit perfectly in width and length,
which pleased her.
Looking in the mirror again,
her eyebrows, eyes, cheeks, and chin
vividly resembled her former self,
delighting her even more.
After washing and combing, she went to see her mother,
and all who saw her were astonished.
When Liánxiāng heard of this marvel,
she urged Sāng to propose marriage;
but due to the vast disparity in wealth,
he dared not proceed hastily.
It happened to be the old lady's birthday,
so he went with her sons and sons-in-law
to offer congratulations.
Seeing Sāng's name, the old lady
purposely had Yàn’ér peek through the curtain to identify the guest.
Sāng arrived last,
and the girl suddenly rushed out,
grabbed his sleeve,
and wanted to go home with him.
Her mother scolded her severely,
and only then, ashamed, did she go inside.
Sāng looked closely and saw it was truly her,
unable to hold back his tears,
he knelt and bowed, refusing to rise.
The old lady helped him up,
not taking offense.
After Sāng left,
he asked the girl's uncle to act as matchmaker.
The old lady agreed to choose an auspicious day for Sāng to marry into their family.
Sāng returned and told Liánxiāng,
discussing how to handle the situation.
Lián was melancholy for a long while,
then said she wished to leave.
Sāng was greatly alarmed and wept.
Lián said:
"You will hold a wedding at another's home;
what face would I have if I followed you there?"
Sāng proposed returning to his hometown first
and then fetching Yàn,
to which Lián agreed.
Sāng explained the situation to the Zhāng family.
When they heard he already had a wife,
they angrily reproached him.
Yàn’ér strenuously defended him,
and they finally agreed to his request.
On the appointed day,
Sāng went to fetch his bride.
The preparations at his home were rather hasty;
but upon returning,
from the gate to the hall,
the ground was covered with rugs,
and hundreds of lanterns and candles
shone brilliantly like brocade.
Liánxiāng helped the bride into the bridal chamber,
and when the veil was lifted,
their joy was as if they had known each other in a past life.
Lián joined in the wedding toast,
and asked in detail about the marvel of the resurrection.
Yàn said:
"That day, depressed and bored,
merely feeling myself a strange creature,
I was conscious of my own ugliness.
After parting, in my resentment I did not return to the grave,
but drifted with the wind.
Whenever I saw living people, I envied them.
By day I relied on plants and trees,
by night I wandered aimlessly.
By chance I came to the Zhāng house,
saw a young girl lying on the bed,
approached and attached myself to her,
not knowing I would thus come back to life."
Hearing this, Lián
fell silent as if deep in thought.
After two months,
Lián gave birth to a son,
but after the delivery she fell gravely ill,
growing weaker by the day.
Grasping Yàn’s arm, she said:
"I dare to burden you with this ill-fated child;
my son is as your son."
Yàn wept,
and tried to comfort her.
They called for shamans and doctors,
but she refused them all.
As her condition worsened and she lingered near death,
her breath was as thin as a thread.
Both Sāng and Yàn wept.
Suddenly she opened her eyes and said:
"Do not!
You delight in life,
I delight in death.
If fate allows,
we may meet again in ten years."
With these words, she passed away.
When they opened the quilt to prepare the body,
the corpse had transformed into a fox.
Sāng could not bear to treat it as different,
and buried it with full honors.
The son was named Hú’ér,
and Yàn raised him as her own.
Every Qingming Festival,
she would carry the child to her grave and weep.
Later, the young man passed the provincial examination,
and the family gradually became prosperous.
But Yàn was distressed by her inability to bear children.
The fox child was quite intelligent,
yet frail and often ill.
Yàn often considered taking a concubine for her husband.
One day,
a maid suddenly reported:
"There is an old woman outside the gate,
with a daughter for sale."
Yàn called them in.
Upon seeing her,
she was greatly startled and said:
"Is this Lián elder sister reborn?"
The young man looked at her,
and indeed she resembled Lián,
he too was astonished.
He asked:
"How old are you?"
She replied:
"Fourteen."
"What is the bride price?"
She said:
"This old body has only this one piece of flesh,
if only she can find a good place,
and I too can have a place to eat,
so that in the future my old bones won't be discarded in a ditch,
that is enough."
The young man paid a generous price and kept her.
Yàn took the girl's hand,
entered a private room,
lifted her chin and smiled, saying:
"Do you recognize me?"
She replied:
"I do not."
Asked about her surname,
she said:
"My surname is Wéi.
My father was a seller of fermented rice drink in Xúchéng,
he died three years ago."
Yàn counted on her fingers and pondered,
Lián had died exactly fourteen years.
She looked closely at the girl again,
her appearance and demeanor,
were all uncannily similar.
Then she patted her head and called out:
"Lián elder sister,
Lián elder sister!
The promise to meet again in ten years,
surely you did not deceive me!"
The girl suddenly seemed to wake from a dream,
enlightened, she said:
"Ah!"
She stared intently at Yàn.
The young man laughed and said:
"This is 'the swallow returns, seemingly familiar.'"
The girl said with tears:
"It is so.
I heard my mother say,
when I was born I could speak,
they thought it inauspicious,
and made me drink dog's blood,
thus I forgot my past causes.
Only today do I wake as from a dream.
Madam, are you not ashamed to be the ghostly Lǐ sister?"
They spoke of their past lives together,
mingling sorrow and joy.
One day,
during the Cold Food Festival,
Yàn said:
"This is the day each year that I and my husband weep for elder sister."
So they went together to visit her grave,
the wild grass was lush,
the trees had already grown thick.
The girl also sighed deeply.
Yàn said to the young man:
"I and Lián elder sister,
have been close for two lifetimes,
I cannot bear to be separated from her,
we should let our white bones share the same grave."
The young man followed her words,
opened Lǐ's grave to retrieve her bones,
carried them back and buried them together.
Relatives and friends heard of this marvel,
and came in festive attire to the gravesite,
unexpectedly gathering several hundred people.
I, in the year Gēngxū, traveled south to Yí,
was delayed by rain,
and rested at an inn.
There was a scholar named Liú Zǐjìng,
a relative of his,
brought out a biography of Scholar Sāng written by Wáng Zǐzhāng of the same literary society,
about ten thousand words long,
which I was able to finish reading.
This is just a brief outline of it.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"Alas!
The dead seek to live again,
the living seek death,
is not the human body what is hardest to obtain in the world?
Why do those who possess this body
often neglect it,
so that in life they are not as good as a fox,
and in obscure death, not as good as a ghost."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Sūn Zǐchǔ from Yuèxī,
was a famous scholar.
He was born with an extra finger.
His nature was slow and reticent,
if people deceived him,
he would believe it to be true.
If there happened to be singing girls among the guests,
he would surely look from afar and retreat.
Some who knew this about him,
would lure him over,
and have the girls flirt with and press him,
then his face would turn red down to his neck,
and sweat would drip down in beads.
Thus they all laughed at him.
They then depicted his foolish appearance,
spreading ugly words through correspondence,
and gave him the name
"Sūn the Idiot."
A certain wealthy old merchant in the county,
was as rich as princes and marquises.
His relatives and in-laws were all nobles.
He had a daughter named Ābǎo,
of peerless beauty.
Daily he sought a good match for her,
sons of great families vied to send betrothal gifts,
but none satisfied the old man.
Sūn was then widowed,
some who teased him,
urged him to send a matchmaker.
Sūn, without much self-reflection,
indeed followed their advice.
The old man had long heard of his name,
but considered him poor.
As the matchmaking old woman was about to leave,
she happened to meet Bǎo,
who asked about it,
and she told her.
The girl joked, saying:
"If he removes his extra finger,
I will marry him."
The old woman told Sūn.
Sūn said:
"That is not difficult."
After the matchmaker left,
Sūn took an axe and cut off his own finger,
the pain pierced his heart,
blood poured out profusely,
and he nearly died.
After several days,
he was finally able to get up,
went to see the matchmaker and showed her.
The old woman was shocked.
She ran to tell the girl.
The girl also found it strange,
and jokingly asked him to also rid himself of his foolishness.
Sūn heard this and argued loudly,
claiming he was not foolish;
yet he had no way to see her and explain himself.
Then it occurred to him that Ābǎo might not be as beautiful as a heavenly being,
why should she hold herself in such high regard?
Thus his former thoughts suddenly cooled.
It happened to be the Qingming Festival,
when according to custom,
women would go out for an outing.
Frivolous young men
would also form groups to follow them,
freely passing judgment.
Several members of the same literary society
insistently invited Shēng to join them.
Someone teased him, saying:
"Don't you want to see if there are any beauties?"
Shēng knew they were making fun of him;
however, because he had been mocked by the girl,
he also wanted to see what kind of person she was,
and so he happily went along with the crowd to look for her.
From afar, they saw a girl resting under a tree,
surrounded by a wall-like ring of rowdy youths.
The crowd said:
"This must be Ā Bǎo."
They hurried over,
and it was indeed Bǎo.
Looking at her carefully,
she was exquisitely beautiful, without equal.
After a short while,
the crowd grew even denser.
The girl stood up
and quickly left.
The crowd was utterly captivated,
commenting on her head and feet,
in a frenzy of excitement.
Only Shēng remained silent.
When the crowd went elsewhere,
they looked back
and saw Shēng still standing dazedly in the same spot,
unresponsive when called.
The group pulled at him, saying:
"Has your soul followed Ā Bǎo away?"
He still did not answer.
Since he was usually reticent,
they did not find it strange,
and some pushed him, others pulled him back home.
Upon reaching home,
he went straight to bed,
lying there all day without getting up,
as if in a trance or drunk,
unresponsive when called.
His family suspected he had lost his soul,
and performed summoning rituals in the wilderness,
but to no effect.
When they pressed him with questions,
he answered vaguely:
"I am at Ā Bǎo's house."
But when questioned in detail,
he fell silent again.
His family was bewildered and could not understand.
Earlier,
when Shēng saw the girl leave,
he could not bear to part from her,
and felt his body following her as she walked.
Gradually, he drew close to her garments,
and no one scolded him.
Thus, he followed the girl home,
staying close to her whether she sat or lay down,
and at night he would be intimate with her,
getting along very well;
however, he felt extremely hungry in his stomach,
and thought of returning home once,
but was lost and did not know the way.
The girl often dreamed of being with a man,
and when she asked his name,
he said:
"I am Sūn Zǐchǔ."
She found this strange,
but could not tell anyone.
Shēng lay in bed for three days,
his breath faint as if about to fade away.
His family was greatly alarmed,
and sent someone to tactfully inform the old man,
wishing to perform a soul-summoning at his house.
The old man laughed and said:
"We have never had any dealings before,
how could his soul be left at my house?"
The family pleaded earnestly,
and only then did the old man agree.
The shaman took old clothes and a straw mat and went there.
The girl learned the reason
and was extremely shocked.
She did not let him go elsewhere,
but led him straight into her room,
letting him perform the summoning before leaving.
When the shaman returned to the door,
Shēng on the bed was already groaning.
After waking up,
he described in detail the cosmetics and various items in the girl's room—
their colors and names—
without a single error.
When the girl heard this,
she was even more astonished,
and secretly moved by the depth of his affection.
Once he had left the bed and gotten up,
he sat or stood in deep thought,
as if he had forgotten something.
He watched for Ābǎo every chance he got,
hoping to meet her once more.
On the day of the Buddha Bathing Festival,
he heard that she would be going to the Incense and Moon Temple to burn incense,
so he went early in the morning and waited by the roadside,
his eyes straining until they ached.
When the sun was past noon,
the girl finally arrived.
Peeking from the carriage and seeing the student,
she lifted the curtain with her slender hand
and gazed at him without turning away.
The student was even more stirred,
and followed behind her.
Suddenly, the girl ordered her maid to come and ask his name.
The student eagerly introduced himself,
and his soul was further shaken.
Only after the carriage had left
did he return home.
Back home, he fell ill again,
lying unconscious and refusing to eat,
calling out Bǎo’s name in his dreams.
He often regretted that his soul was no longer agile.
His family had long kept a parrot,
which suddenly died.
A child was playing with it on the bed.
The student thought to himself: If only I could become a parrot,
I could flap my wings and reach the girl’s room.
Just as his mind was fixed on this thought,
his body had already fluttered into a parrot,
and he flew away at once,
straight to Ābǎo’s place.
The girl was delighted and caught him,
fastened a chain to his leg,
and fed him hemp seeds.
He cried out loudly:
"Sister, don’t chain me!
I am Sūn Zǐchǔ!"
The girl was greatly alarmed,
unfastened the chain,
but he still did not leave.
The girl prayed:
"Your deep affection is already engraved in my heart.
But now you are a bird and I am human—different species.
How can our marriage be restored?"
The bird said:
"To be close to your fragrant presence
is already enough to fulfill my wish."
When others fed him,
he would not eat;
when the girl fed him herself,
he ate.
When the girl sat,
he would perch on her knee;
when she lay down,
he would stay by her bed.
This went on for three days.
The girl pitied him greatly,
and secretly sent someone to inquire.
It turned out the student was lying stiffly,
having stopped breathing for three days,
only his heart was not yet cold.
The girl prayed again:
"If you can become human again,
I vow to follow you unto death."
The bird said:
"You’re deceiving me!"
The girl then swore an oath.
The bird tilted its head as if pondering something.
After a short while,
the girl untied her bound feet,
took off her shoes under the bed,
and the parrot suddenly swooped down,
grabbed a shoe in its beak, and flew away.
The girl cried out urgently,
but it had already flown far.
The girl sent an old woman to check,
and found that the student had already awakened.
His family saw the parrot bring an embroidered shoe,
drop it to the ground, and die,
and they were all astonished.
Once the student revived,
he immediately asked for the shoe.
No one knew why.
Just then, the old woman arrived,
went in to see the student,
and asked where the shoe was.
The student said:
"This is Ābǎo’s pledge.
Please convey my words: I have not forgotten her golden promise."
The old woman returned with the message.
The girl found it even more extraordinary,
so she deliberately had her maid reveal the situation to her mother.
The mother investigated and found it to be true,
then said:
"This young man’s talent and reputation are not bad,
but he is as poor as Sīmǎ Xiàngrú.
After choosing a son-in-law for several years, to end up with someone like this
might make us a laughingstock among the prominent families."
Because of the shoe,
the girl vowed not to marry anyone else.
Her parents complied.
They sent word to the student.
The student was overjoyed,
and his illness suddenly healed.
The father proposed having the student marry into their family.
The girl said:
"A son-in-law should not stay long at his wife’s family home.
Besides, my husband is poor;
staying longer will only make others look down on him.
Since I have promised him,
I am content to live in a thatched hut and eat coarse food—
I will not complain."
The student then went in person to welcome her, and the wedding was held.
Their reunion felt like a joy from another lifetime.
From then on, with the girl’s dowry,
the family became somewhat prosperous,
and their possessions increased considerably.
But the student was obsessed with books,
and knew nothing about managing the household or making a living;
the girl was skilled at accumulating wealth,
and did not burden him with other matters.
