After three years of marriage,
the family grew even wealthier.
The student suddenly fell ill with diabetes,
and died.
The girl mourned him bitterly,
her eyes never dry from tears,
to the point where she stopped sleeping and eating.
When others tried to persuade her, she would not listen,
and one night she tried to hang herself.
Her maid discovered her,
saved her in time, and she revived,
but still refused to eat.
Three days later,
relatives gathered
to prepare for the student’s burial.
They heard moaning and breathing from inside the coffin,
opened it,
and found he had revived.
He said:
"I saw the King of the Underworld,
who, because of my lifelong honesty and sincerity,
appointed me as a ministry official.
Suddenly, someone reported: ‘The wife of Official Sūn is about to arrive.’
The King checked the register of ghosts,
and said: ‘She is not supposed to die yet.’
The report continued: ‘She has not eaten for three days.’
The King then said: ‘I am moved by your wife’s integrity and loyalty,
so I will grant you rebirth.’
He then had a groom control a horse and send me back."
From then on, his health gradually recovered.
During the year of the provincial examinations,
before entering the examination hall,
some young men played a trick on him.
Together, they came up with seven obscure and rarely seen essay topics,
led him to a secluded place to talk,
and said:
"These are the key topics from a certain family’s connections.
We respectfully pass them on to you in secret."
The student believed them,
and day and night he pondered and practiced,
writing seven essays.
The others secretly laughed at him.
At that time, the chief examiner, concerned that familiar topics might lead to plagiarism,
deliberately went against convention.
When the examination papers were handed out,
all seven topics matched exactly.
As a result, the student came out first in the selection.
The following year,
he passed the imperial examination and became a jìnshì,
and was appointed to the Hànlín Academy.
The emperor heard of this unusual story,
summoned him, and asked about it.
The student reported everything in detail.
The emperor was greatly pleased.
Later, he summoned Ābǎo for an audience;
and rewarded them generously.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"When one is obsessed, their will becomes focused.
Thus, those obsessed with books will excel in writing,
and those obsessed with arts will master their skills.
Those in the world who drift aimlessly and achieve nothing
all claim they are not obsessed.
Moreover, squandering wealth on women and pleasure,
losing fortunes over gambling—
are these the deeds of obsessed people?
From this, we know that excessive cleverness and cunning
are the true obsession.
How can Sūn Zǐchǔ be considered obsessed!"
A collection of ten types of obsession:
"Hoarding money yet living in poverty.
Boasting of one’s child’s cleverness in front of guests.
Loving one’s child too much to make them study.
Hiding an illness for fear others will know.
Spending money to lure others into visiting brothels.
Sneaking off to banquets to lure others into gambling.
Asking someone else to write essays to deceive one’s father and brothers."
Father and son keeping accounts too clear.
Using machinery in the household.
Delighting in disciples who are skilled at gambling.”
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
The appended note is supplemented based on manuscript copy No. 703 held by the Shāndōng Museum
There was a man surnamed Lǐ from Cáozhōu,
a scholar in the county.
His family had always been wealthy.
However, his residence was not particularly spacious;
behind the house was a garden of several acres,
left abandoned.
One day,
an old man came to rent a house,
offering a hundred taels of silver.
Lǐ declined on the grounds that he had no house available.
The old man said:
“Please accept the payment,
and do not trouble yourself with worries.”
Lǐ did not understand his meaning,
but he accepted the money anyway,
to observe what strange events might follow.
The next day,
villagers saw carriages, horses, and family members entering Lǐ’s house,
a bustling and numerous crowd,
and they all wondered how Lǐ’s residence could accommodate them,
so they asked him about it.
Lǐ himself had no idea;
he returned home to investigate,
but found no trace or sound of them.
After a few days,
the old man suddenly came to visit.
He said:
“We have been sheltered under your roof for several days now.
Everything has been hastily arranged,
setting up stoves and making fires,
and we have not yet had the leisure to extend the courtesy due to a guest.
Now, I have sent my daughters to prepare a meal,
and I hope you will honor us with a visit.”
Lǐ agreed.
He then entered the garden,
and suddenly saw splendid buildings,
brand new and gleaming.
Entering the rooms,
he found them elegantly furnished.
Wine cauldrons were boiling in the corridor,
and the steam of tea wafted from the kitchen.
Soon, wine was served and dishes were presented,
all exceptionally delicious.
From time to time, he saw young people in the courtyard,
coming and going in great numbers.
He also heard the murmuring of children,
and laughter and conversation from behind the curtains.
Family members, maids, and servants
seemed to number in the dozens or even hundreds.
Lǐ knew in his heart that they were foxes.
After the banquet ended and he returned home,
he secretly harbored murderous intentions.
Every time he went to the market,
he purchased saltpeter and sulfur,
accumulating several hundred catties,
and secretly spread them almost completely across the garden.
He then suddenly set them on fire,
and the flames soared to the sky,
like a black lingzhī mushroom,
with a scorching stench and blinding smoke that made it impossible to approach;
only the sounds of crying, wailing, and commotion could be heard,
a cacophony grating on the ears.
Once the fire had died down, he went in to look,
and found the ground covered with dead foxes,
those with scorched heads and mangled faces
were too numerous to count.
As he was inspecting the scene,
the old man came in from outside,
his face filled with grief and anguish,
and he rebuked Lǐ, saying:
“We had no prior grievances;
I paid you a hundred taels for the use of this abandoned garden for a year,
which was not a small sum;
how could you bear to exterminate my entire clan like this?
This is a terrible and tragic enmity,
and it will surely be avenged!”
He then left in anger.
Lǐ suspected that the old man would throw stones to cause calamity,
but for over a year, nothing strange occurred.
At that time, in the early years of the Shùnzhì reign,
bands of bandits arose in the mountains,
gathering in numbers exceeding ten thousand,
and the authorities were unable to capture them.
Lǐ, because his family was large,
worried daily about the chaos and displacement.
It so happened that a fortune-teller came to the village,
calling himself
“Old Man of the Southern Mountains,”
who spoke of people’s fortunes and misfortunes
as clearly as if he had seen them with his own eyes,
and his fame spread widely.
Lǐ summoned him to his home,
asking him to divine his fate.
The old man rose in astonishment and respect,
saying:
“This is the true sovereign!”
Lǐ was greatly alarmed upon hearing this,
thinking it absurd.
The old man, with a solemn expression, insisted on his words.
Lǐ was half-convinced and half-doubting,
so he said:
“How can someone with empty hands receive the Mandate and become emperor?”
The old man replied:
“Not so.
Since ancient times, emperors and kings
mostly arose from among commoners;
who was born an emperor?”
Lǐ was swayed by his words,
and he moved his mat forward to ask for advice.
The old man resolutely took upon himself the role of
“the Sleeping Dragon.”
He asked first to prepare several thousand sets of armor and helmets, and several thousand bows and crossbows.
Lǐ worried that no one would follow him.
The old man said:
“I beg to forge alliances with the various mountain bands for Your Majesty,
forming deep bonds.
Let those who spread rumors say that Your Majesty is the true Son of Heaven,
and the soldiers in the mountains
will surely respond.”
Lǐ was pleased,
and sent the old man on his way.
He took out his stored silver,
to manufacture armor and helmets.
The old man returned after several days,
saying:
“By borrowing Your Majesty’s prestige and fortune,
and adding my three-inch tongue,
none of the mountain bands are unwilling to take up the whip and bridle,
to follow under your banner.”
Within ten days,
indeed, several thousand people pledged their allegiance.
Thereupon, Lǐ appointed the old man as his military advisor;
he raised a grand banner,
and set up colorful flags like a forest;
he established a stockade in the mountains,
and his influence shook the region.
The county magistrate led troops to suppress them,
but the old man directed the bandits,
and dealt them a major defeat.
The magistrate, terrified,
reported the emergency to Yǎn.
Troops from Yǎn came from afar,
and the old man again ambushed and attacked them with his bandits,
resulting in a great rout,
with many officers and soldiers killed or wounded.
Their momentum grew even more formidable,
and their followers numbered in the tens of thousands,
so Lǐ proclaimed himself
“the King of the Nine Mountains.”
The old man was concerned about the lack of horses,
and it happened that horses were being transported from the capital to Jiāngnán,
so he dispatched a troop to intercept them on the main road and seize them.
From then on,
the name of “the King of the Nine Mountains”
became widely known.
He further honored the old man as
“Great General Who Protects the State.”
Lǐ reclined in his mountain stronghold,
openly full of himself,
believing that the yellow robe of emperorship
would be bestowed upon him in no time.
The Governor of the Eastern Region, because of the seizure of the horses,
was just about to launch a campaign to suppress them;
and having also received the report from Yǎn,
he dispatched several thousand elite troops,
joining forces from six directions to surround and advance.
Military banners and flags
filled the mountain valleys.
“The King of the Nine Mountains”
was greatly frightened,
and summoned the old man to discuss the situation,
but the old man was nowhere to be found.
“The King of the Nine Mountains,”
in desperate straits and without a plan,
climbed a mountain and gazed out, saying:
“Now I understand how formidable the power of the imperial court is!”
The mountain was breached,
he was captured,
and his wife and children were executed.
Only then did he realize that the old man was the aged fox,
who had taken revenge on Lǐ for the extermination of his clan.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"A man who embraces his wife and children,
shutting his door and going bareheaded,
where could he get the chance to kill?
Even if he did kill,
how could it lead to the extermination of his clan?
The fox's scheme was indeed cunning.
But if the soil lacks the seed,
even watering will not make it grow;
that man's cruelty in killing the foxes
already contained the root of thievery in his heart,
so the fox could nurture its sprout and exact revenge.
Now, try stopping a passerby and telling him:
'You shall be emperor!'
There is none who would not flee in terror.
Clearly guiding him towards acts that would exterminate his clan,
yet he still listens gladly;
that his wife and children were slaughtered
is hardly worth mentioning.
However, when a man listens to treacherous words,
at first he hears them and becomes angry,
then he becomes doubtful,
and finally he believes;
by the time his body and reputation are both ruined,
he finally realizes his error.
Most cases are like this."
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Lord Qiū from Zhūchéng was the circuit intendant of Zūnhuà.
The yamen had long been plagued by many foxes.
The last building,
was densely inhabited by a clan of them,
who considered it their home.
They often came out to harm people,
and efforts to drive them away only made them more rampant.
Officials serving here would only set out sacrificial animals and pray to them,
not daring to relocate.
When Lord Qiū took up his post,
he heard of this and was enraged.
The foxes, fearing his stern and fierce nature,
transformed into an old woman who told his family:
"I beg you to inform His Excellency: do not make an enemy of us.
Allow us three days,
and we will take our young and leave."
Upon hearing this, Lord Qiū
remained silent and said nothing.
The next day,
after reviewing the troops,
he ordered them not to disperse,
but to have them carry all the large cannons from the camps and suddenly enter,
surrounding the building and firing a thousand shots simultaneously;
the several-zhàng tall building
was instantly leveled to the ground,
with fur, flesh, and blood
raining down from the sky.
All that could be seen in the thick dust and poisonous fog
was a wisp of white vapor,
rising through the smoke and soaring into the sky.
The crowd watched and said:
"One fox escaped."
And from then on, the yamen was peaceful.
Two years later,
Lord Qiū sent a trusted servant to deliver a sum of silver to the capital,
intending to seek promotion.
Before the matter was settled,
he temporarily stored it in the home of a yamen runner.
Suddenly, an old man went to the capital to lodge a complaint,
saying his wife and children had been unjustly slaughtered;
he also accused Lord Qiū of embezzling army provisions
and currying favor with those in power,
claiming the silver was currently stored in a certain house
and could be verified.
By imperial decree, officials were sent to investigate.
Arriving at the runner's house,
they searched thoroughly but found nothing.
The old man merely tapped the ground with one foot, making them realize his meaning.
Digging it up,
they indeed found the silver;
engraved on it were the characters
"Consignment from such-and-such commandery."
When they later looked for the old man,
he was nowhere to be found.
They tried to find him based on his village and name,
but ultimately, no such person existed.
Lord Qiū was thus implicated and met with disaster.
Only then did they realize the old man was the escaped fox.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Foxes that haunt and harm people
certainly deserve execution.
However, if they submit and are spared,
it also preserves our benevolence.
Lord Qiū could be said to be
'too severe in his hatred.'
Moreover, if Lord Yáng from Guānxī had done this,
how could a hundred foxes have escaped him!"
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
There was a man named Zhāng from Yù,
whose ancestors were from Qí.
In the late Míng dynasty, when Qí was in great turmoil,
his wife was captured by northern troops.
Zhāng often traveled in Yù,
and eventually settled there.
He married a woman from Yù,
who bore him a son named Nè.
Not long after,
his wife passed away.
He married a second wife,
who bore him a son named Chéng.
The second wife, Niú shì, was fierce
and often envied Nè,
treating him like a slave
and feeding him coarse, unpalatable food.
She made him gather firewood,
demanding a shoulder-load each day;
if he failed, she would beat, curse, and revile him,
making it unbearable.
Secretly, she stored sweet and delicate treats for Chéng
and sent him to study with a tutor.
As Chéng grew older,
his nature became filial and fraternal.
Unable to bear seeing his elder brother toil,
he privately urged his mother.
His mother would not listen.
One day,
Nè went into the mountains to gather firewood.
Before he finished,
a great storm arose.
He took shelter under a cliff,
and by the time the rain stopped, the sun had already set.
His stomach was terribly empty,
so he carried the firewood home.
His stepmother checked and found it too little,
angrily refusing to give him food.
Hunger burned in his heart,
and he went into his room and lay down stiffly.
Chéng returned from school
and saw his brother looking dejected.
He asked:
"Are you ill?"
Nè replied:
"Just hungry."
Chéng asked the reason,
and Nè told him the situation.
Chéng looked distressed and left.
After a while,
he returned with a cake hidden in his clothes to feed his brother.
His brother asked where it came from.
Chéng said:
"I secretly took some flour and asked a neighbor woman to make it.
Just eat it, and don't say anything."
Nè ate it.
He admonished his brother:
"Don't do this again.
If the matter is exposed, it will implicate you.
Besides, one meal a day
should keep me from starving to death."
Chéng said:
"Brother, you are naturally weak.
How can you gather much firewood!"
The next day,
after eating,
Chéng secretly went to the mountains
and arrived at the place where his brother was gathering firewood.
His brother saw him
and asked in surprise:
"What are you going to do?"
He replied:
"I'm going to help you gather firewood."
Nè asked:
"Who sent you?"
Chéng said:
"I came on my own."
His brother said:
"Never mind that you can't gather firewood;
even if you could,
it still wouldn't be right."
So he urged him to return home.
Chéng would not listen.
Using his hands and feet, he broke branches to help his brother.
Moreover, he said:
"Tomorrow I'll bring an axe."
His brother stepped closer to stop him.
Seeing that his fingers were already cut
and his shoes worn through,
Nè said sorrowfully:
"If you don't return home quickly,
I will cut my own throat with the axe and die!"
Only then did Chéng return.
His brother accompanied him halfway
before turning back.
After finishing his firewood gathering and returning home,
Nè went to the school
and said to the teacher:
"My younger brother is still young.
You should keep him confined.
There are many tigers and wolves in the mountains."
The teacher said:
"I don't know where he went before noon.
I have already caned him for it."
Returning home, Nè said to Chéng:
"If you don't listen to me,
you'll get a whipping and a scolding."
Chéng laughed and said:
"That won't happen."
The next day,
he hid an axe and went again.
His elder brother exclaimed in alarm:
"I told you not to come,
why are you doing this again?"
Chéng did not answer,
but cut firewood with great urgency,
sweat streaming down his cheeks without a moment's rest.
When he had roughly gathered one bundle,
he left without a word of farewell.
The teacher scolded him again,
so he told him the truth.
The teacher sighed at his virtue,
and thereafter did not forbid him.
His elder brother repeatedly tried to stop him,
but he would not listen.
One day,
while gathering firewood in the mountains with others,
suddenly a tiger arrived.
Everyone was terrified and crouched down.
The tiger actually seized Chéng and carried him off.
The tiger, burdened with a person, moved slowly,
allowing Nè to catch up.
Nè struck it forcefully with his axe,
hitting its haunch.
The tiger, in pain, fled wildly,
and could not be found or pursued.
Nè returned weeping bitterly.
The others tried to comfort and console him,
but his weeping grew even more sorrowful.
He said:
"My brother
is not like other people's brothers;
moreover, he died for me,
how can I live on!"
Thereupon, he used the axe to cut his own throat.
The others rushed to save him,
but the blade had already sunk in over an inch,
blood gushed forth like a fountain,
and he grew dizzy, vision blurred, and fell unconscious.
The others were horrified,
tore strips from their clothes to bind the wound,
and supported him as they returned together.
His mother wept and cursed him:
"You killed my son,
and now you want to cut your throat to shirk responsibility!"
Nè groaned and said:
"Mother, do not distress yourself.
If my brother is dead,
I certainly will not live!"
They laid him on the bed,
but the wound pained him so he could not sleep,
only sitting leaning against the wall day and night, weeping.
His father, fearing he too would die,
occasionally went to his bedside to feed him a little,
but Niú would immediately scold and berate him.
Nè then refused to eat,
and died after three days.
In the village was a shaman who could travel to the underworld,
Nè met him on the road,
and recounted in detail his past sufferings.
He then inquired about his brother's whereabouts,
but the shaman said he had not heard of him.
He then turned and guided Nè onward.
They reached a large city,
and saw a man in black clothing
coming out from within the city.
The shaman stopped him and asked on Nè's behalf.
The man in black took out a register from his pouch and examined it carefully;
there were over a hundred men and women listed,
but none named Zhāng.
The shaman suspected his name was on another register.
The man in black said:
"This road is under my jurisdiction,
how could there be a mistake?"
Nè did not believe him,
and insisted the shaman enter the inner city with him.
Inside the city, new ghosts and old ghosts bustled to and fro,
and there were also some old acquaintances.
Nè approached and asked them,
but in the end, no one knew.
Suddenly, everyone began clamoring:
"The Bodhisattva has arrived!"
Looking up into the clouds,
they saw a majestic figure,
whose radiant light illuminated all above and below,
instantly making the whole world bright and clear.
The shaman congratulated him:
"Eldest Young Master, you are blessed! The Bodhisattva enters the underworld only once every few decades,
to deliver beings from suffering,
and today you happen to encounter him."
He then pulled Nè down to kneel.
The multitude of ghost prisoners became a noisy, jostling crowd,
joining their palms and reciting in unison pleas for the Bodhisattva's compassion to save them from suffering,
their clamor rising tumultuously and shaking the earth.
The Bodhisattva sprinkled sweet dew everywhere with a willow branch,
fine as dust.
Soon, the mist cleared and the light withdrew,
and he was gone.
Nè felt dew moisten his neck,
and the axe wound no longer pained him.
The shaman still guided him and they returned together.
When they saw the village gate,
he bid farewell and left.
Nè had been dead for two days,
when suddenly he revived,
and recounted all he had experienced,
saying Chéng was not dead.
His mother thought it was fabricated falsehood,
and instead berated and cursed him.
Nè, bearing this injustice with no way to vindicate himself,
felt the scar—it was indeed well healed.
Summoning his strength, he rose,
bowed to his father and said:
"I shall go now, piercing the clouds and entering the seas to search for my brother.
If I cannot find him,
do not expect me to return in this lifetime.
I beg you, Father, to consider your son as dead."
The old man led him to a secluded spot and wept with him,
not daring to keep him.
Nè then left.
He often searched for news of his brother at busy crossroads,
but his travel funds ran out along the way,
so he begged for food as he journeyed.
After more than a year,
he reached Jīnlíng.
His clothes were ragged and patched,
and he walked hunched over on the road.
Once, he saw over ten riders passing by,
so he hurried to the side of the road to avoid them.
Among them was one who seemed like an official,
around forty years old,
with robust soldiers and spirited horses,
galloping back and forth.
A young man riding a small steed
kept looking at Nè.
Nè, thinking he was a noble young master,
did not dare to look up.
The young man stopped his horse and paused briefly,
then suddenly dismounted
and called out:
"Isn't that my elder brother?"
Nè raised his head and looked closely—
it was indeed Chéng.
They grasped hands and wept bitterly,
unable to hold back their sobs.
Chéng also cried and said:
"Brother, how did you become so destitute?"
Nè explained the situation,
and Chéng grew even more sorrowful.
The riders all dismounted to ask what had happened,
and Chéng reported it to the official.
The official ordered a horse to be provided for Nè,
and they rode side by side back to his home,
where they began to inquire in detail.
Initially,
when the tiger carried Chéng away,
it was unclear when it dropped him by the roadside,
but he lay there on the road overnight.
It happened that Biéjià Zhāng was coming from the capital
and passed by.
Seeing Chéng's refined appearance,
he took pity on him and comforted him,
and Chéng gradually revived.
When asked about his hometown,
it turned out to be very far away.
So Biéjià took him along on his return journey.
He also applied medicine to Chéng's wounds,
and after a few days, Chéng fully recovered.
As Biéjià had no sons of his own,
he adopted Chéng as his son.
This was why Chéng happened to be out sightseeing with him.
Chéng told his elder brother everything.
While they were talking,
Biéjià entered,
and Nè bowed repeatedly in gratitude.
Chéng went inside
and brought out fine silk clothes
to present to his brother.
Then they set out wine for a feast and conversation.
Biéjià asked:
"How many adult males are there in your esteemed clan in Yù?"
Nè replied:
"None.
My father was originally from Qí
but settled in Yù as a migrant."
Biéjià said:
"I am also from Qí.
Which district does your esteemed hometown belong to?"
Nè answered:
"I once heard my father say
it was under the jurisdiction of Dōngchāng."
Startled, Biéjià exclaimed:
"We are fellow townsmen!
Why did you move to Yù?"
Nè said:
"During the late Míng, Qing troops entered the area,
and they abducted my father's first wife.
My father suffered from the ravages of war,
losing his home and family.
He first engaged in trade along the western routes,
traveling back and forth frequently and becoming familiar with the area,
so he settled there."
Even more astonished, Biéjià asked:
"What is your father's name?"
Nè told him.
Biéjià stared wide-eyed,
lowered his head as if puzzled,
and hurried inside.
Not long after,
the elderly lady came out.
They all bowed together,
and then
she asked Nè:
"Are you the grandson of Zhāng Bǐngzhī?"
Nè said:
"Yes."
The elderly lady wept bitterly
and said to Biéjià:
"This is your younger brother."
Nè and his brother were utterly confused.
The elderly lady explained:
"I was married to your father for three years
before being separated and taken north.
For half a year, I belonged to Hēi Gùshān,
and gave birth to your elder brother.
Another half year later,
Gùshān died,
and your elder brother inherited his position under the banner and was appointed to this official post.
He has now retired from his position.
He constantly longed for his hometown,
so he withdrew from the banner registry
and restored his original lineage name.
He repeatedly sent people to Qí to search,
but found no trace.
Who would have thought your father had moved west!"
Then she said to Biéjià:
"You took your younger brother as your son—
this is a great misfortune!"
Biéjià said:
"When I asked Chéng before,
he never mentioned being from Qí.
I suppose he was too young to remember."
Then they arranged themselves by age:
Biéjià was forty-one,
the eldest;
Chéng was sixteen,
the youngest;
Nè was twenty-two,
so he became the second eldest.
Biéjià was overjoyed to have gained two brothers
and shared living quarters with them,
learning all the details of their separation.
They began planning their return home.
The elderly lady feared they might not be accepted.
Biéjià said:
"If they accept us, we'll live together;
if not, we'll separate.
Is there any place under heaven where a fatherless person belongs?"
So they sold their house to prepare for the journey
and set a date to depart westward.
Upon reaching their hometown,
Nè and Chéng rushed ahead to inform their father.
After Nè had left,
his father's wife had also soon passed away.
Left utterly alone, an old widower,
he mourned his solitary shadow.
Suddenly seeing Nè enter,
he was overjoyed,
stunned and startled.
Then seeing Chéng,
he was ecstatic,
unable to speak,
tears streaming down.
When told that Biéjià and his mother had arrived,
the old man stopped crying, stunned,
unable to feel either joy or sorrow,
standing there in a daze.
Soon after,
Biéjià entered
and paid his respects.
The elderly lady embraced the old man, and they wept facing each other.
Seeing the maids, servants, and attendants,
filling the house inside and out,
he sat and stood, not knowing what to do.
Chéng, not seeing his mother,
asked about her
and only then learned she had died.
He wailed until he lost his breath
and revived only after the time it takes to eat a meal.
Biéjià provided funds
to build towers and pavilions
and hired a tutor to teach his two younger brothers.
Horses neighed in the stables,
and the house bustled with people—
it had truly become a great household.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"As I listened to this story to the end,
I shed tears several times.
A boy of just over ten years,
chopping firewood to help his brother,
inspired me to exclaim with admiration:
'Is this not a reappearance of Wáng Lǎn?'
At this, I shed my first tears.
When the tiger carried Chéng away,
I couldn't help but cry out:
'Is the Way of Heaven so confused?'
At this, I shed more tears.
When the brothers suddenly met,
I shed tears of joy.
Gaining an elder brother
added another cause for sorrow,
so I shed tears for Biéjià.
The whole family reunited,
with shocks beyond expectation,
and joys beyond expectation,
leaving me with no reason for tears,
so I shed them for the old man.
I wonder if in later generations
there will be anyone as prone to weeping as I am?"
In Fénzhōu, there was a Judge Zhū,
whose official residence was infested with foxes.
One night, as he sat alone,
a woman appeared, moving back and forth under the lamplight.
At first, he thought she was a servant from his household,
and did not bother to look closely;
but when he raised his eyes,
he realized he did not recognize her,
and her beauty was utterly dazzling.
Sensing she was a fox,
yet captivated by her,
he abruptly called her over.
The woman paused and said with a smile:
"Speaking to someone so harshly—
am I your maid or servant?"
Zhū laughed and stood up,
pulling her to sit beside him and apologizing.
From then on, they became intimate,
and over time grew as close as husband and wife.
One day, she suddenly said to him:
"Your official rank is due for promotion,
but the day of parting is near."
He asked:
"When?"
She replied:
"Very soon.
But while those bringing congratulations are at your gate,
mourners will already be in your lane—
you will not be able to take up the post."
Three days later,
the news of his promotion indeed arrived.
The next day,
he received the obituary of his mother.
Zhū resigned from his post
and wished to take her back with him.
The fox refused.
He saw her off to the riverbank.
Urging her to board the boat,
she said:
"You do not understand—
foxes cannot cross rivers."
Unwilling to part,
Zhū lingered sorrowfully by the river.
Suddenly, the woman reappeared,
saying she would visit an old acquaintance.
After a while, she returned,
and soon a guest came to pay a return visit.
She spoke with him in a separate room.
After the guest left, she came back and said:
"Please board the boat now,
I will accompany you across."
Zhū asked:
"Earlier you said you could not cross—
why do you say so now?"
She replied:
"The one I visited was none other
than the River God.
For your sake,
I specially requested his permission.
He limited me to ten days for the round trip,
so I can accompany you temporarily."
Thus they crossed together.
When the ten days were up,
she indeed bid farewell and left.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Guǎngdōng, there was a gentleman named Fù,
over sixty years old.
He had a son,
named Lián,
who was very intelligent,
but born a eunuch—
by seventeen,
his genitals were no larger than a silkworm.
Far and wide, people knew of this,
and no one would give him a daughter in marriage.
Fearing his lineage would end,
he worried day and night,
but could do nothing about it.
Lián studied under a tutor.
Once, when the tutor was away,
a monkey show happened to pass by outside the gate.
Lián watched it
and neglected his studies.
Fearing the tutor’s return,
he ran away from home.
A few miles from home,
he saw a young woman in plain white clothes,
walking ahead with a little maid.
When she turned her head,
her enchanting beauty was beyond compare.
Her steps were delicate and slow,
so Lián quickened his pace to overtake her.
The woman looked back at her maid and said:
"Ask the young man
if he happens to be going to Qióng."
The maid indeed called out to ask.
Lián inquired why she asked.
The woman said:
"If you are going to Qióng,
I have a letter
I would trouble you to deliver to my home along the way.
My elderly mother is there
and can serve as your host."
Lián had no fixed destination to begin with,
and thought crossing the sea would be fine,
so he agreed.
The woman took out the letter and handed it to the maid,
who passed it to the young man.
When asked her name and residence,
she said:
"My surname is Huá,
and I live in Qínnǚ Village,
about three or four miles north of the outer wall."
Lián boarded a boat and set off.
Arriving at the northern outskirts of Qióngzhōu,
the sun had already set and dusk had fallen.
I inquired about Qín Nǚ Village,
but no one knew of it.
Heading north for four or five lǐ,
the stars and moon were already shining brightly,
fragrant grasses blurred the view,
and the vast wilderness offered no inn,
leaving me in great distress.
Seeing a tomb by the roadside,
I thought of resting beside the grave,
but I was terribly afraid of tigers and wolves.
So I climbed a tree like a monkey,
crouching atop it.
Listening to the rustling of pine trees,
and the mournful chirping of nocturnal insects,
my heart was uneasy,
filled with burning regret for having come.
Suddenly, I heard voices below,
and looking down,
I saw a courtyard as if it were real;
a beautiful woman sat on a stone,
with two maids holding painted candles,
standing in attendance on either side.
The beautiful woman glanced to the left and said:
"Tonight the moon is bright and the stars sparse,
the tuán tea gifted by Huá Gū,
we can brew a cup,
and enjoy this fine night."
I suspected they were ghosts or demons,
my hair standing on end,
not daring to make the slightest sound.
Suddenly, a maid looked up and said:
"There's someone in the tree!"
The woman rose in alarm and said:
"Where did this bold fellow come from,
secretly spying on people!"
I was terrified,
with nowhere to hide or escape,
so I climbed down,
prostrating myself on the ground to beg for mercy.
The woman approached and took a glance,
her anger turning to delight,
and she pulled me to sit beside her.
Looking at her,
she appeared to be about seventeen or eighteen,
with an exceptionally beautiful appearance.
Listening to her speak,
her accent was not local.
She asked:
"Where are you heading, sir?"
I replied:
"I am delivering a letter for someone."
The woman said:
"The wilderness is full of bandits,
it is dangerous to sleep in the open.
If you do not mind my humble abode,
I hope you will stay and rest."
She invited me inside.
The room had only one bed,
and she ordered the maid to lay out two quilts on it.
Feeling ashamed of my unworthy appearance,
I offered to sleep on the floor.
The woman laughed and said:
"When a fine guest is met,
how dare I, a woman, lie high and aloof?"
I had no choice,
so I shared the bed with her,
trembling with fear and not daring to relax.
Before long,
the woman stealthily slipped her delicate hand under the covers,
lightly pinching my legs.
I pretended to be asleep,
as if unaware.
After another moment,
she lifted the quilt and slipped in,
shaking me,
but I remained motionless.
She then reached down to explore my private parts.
She stopped her hand, disappointed,
and quietly slipped out from under the quilt.
Soon, I heard weeping.
I was filled with shame and had no way to face her,
only resenting Heaven for its imperfections.
The woman called the maid to light the lantern.
The maid saw her tear-stained face,
and asked in surprise what was wrong.
The woman shook her head and said:
"I am lamenting my own fate."
The maid stood before the bed,
gazing intently at her expression.
The woman said:
"Wake the gentleman,
and send him on his way."
Hearing this,
I felt even more ashamed;
and fearing the late hour,
with nowhere to go in the vast darkness.
As I was pondering,
a woman pushed the door open and entered.
The maid announced:
"Huá Gū has arrived."
Peeking at her,
she appeared to be over fifty years old,
yet still graceful.
Seeing the woman still awake,
she immediately began questioning.
The woman did not answer.
Noticing someone lying on the bed,
she asked:
"Who is sharing the bed?"
The maid answered for her:
"A young gentleman stayed here for the night."
The woman laughed and said:
"I didn't know Qiǎoniáng had celebrated her wedding night."
Seeing the woman's tears not yet dry,
she exclaimed in surprise:
"On the night of the wedding,
such sorrowful weeping is improper;
could it be that the gentleman was rough?"
The woman remained silent,
growing even more sorrowful.
The woman wanted to lift the covers to look at me,
but as she shook the clothes,
the letter fell onto the bed.
The woman picked it up to look,
and cried out in shock:
"This is my daughter's handwriting!"
She opened and read it, sighing in astonishment.
The woman asked about it.
The woman said:
"This is a letter from home from Sānjiě,
saying that Wú Láng has died,
leaving her alone with no one to rely on,
what is to be done?"
The woman said:
"He did say he was delivering a letter for someone,
fortunately we haven't sent him away."
The woman called me to rise,
and questioned me thoroughly about where the letter came from.
I recounted everything in detail.
The woman said:
"Troubling you to deliver a letter from afar,
how can we repay you?"
Then she looked closely at me,
and asked with a smile:
"What offense did you commit against Qiǎoniáng?"
I said:
"I am unaware of any wrongdoing."
She then questioned the woman.
The woman sighed and said:
"I lament that in life I was wed to a eunuch,
and in death I fled to a castrated man,
that is why I grieve."
The woman looked at me and said:
"Clever lad,
are you truly male but like a female?
You are my guest,
you cannot long disturb others."
Then she led me to the eastern wing,
reaching into my trousers to examine me.
She laughed and said:
"No wonder Qiǎoniáng sheds tears.
But fortunately there is a root,
and something can still be done."
She lit a lamp and searched through the trunks,
found a black pill,
gave it to the young man,
telling him to swallow it immediately,
secretly instructing him not to make a sound,
and then left.
The young man lay alone, pondering,
not knowing what illness the medicine was meant to cure.
As the fifth watch approached,
he first awoke,
feeling a strand of heat beneath his navel,
rushing straight to his private parts;
there was a wriggling sensation as if something hung between his thighs;
he reached down to explore,
and found his body had become that of a virile man.
His heart was startled and delighted,
as if he had just received the nine imperial gifts.
As dawn began to break,
the woman entered,
bringing steamed buns into the young man's room,
urging him to sit patiently,
and locked the door from the outside.
She went out and said to Qiǎoniáng:
"The young man has the trouble of delivering a letter,
so I will keep him here and invite Sānniáng to come,
to establish a sisterly bond.
And I will keep him confined again,
to avoid annoying others."
Then she went out the door.
The young man paced around, bored,
often approaching the crack in the door,
like a bird peering from a cage.
Whenever he saw Qiǎoniáng,
he wanted to call out and present himself,
but shame and hesitation stopped him.
When night fell,
the woman finally brought the girl back.
Opening the door, she said:
"The young gentleman must be bored to death!
Sānniáng, come and pay your respects."
The person on the road hesitantly entered,
and bowed to the young man.
The woman told them to address each other as brother and sister.
Qiǎoniáng laughed and said:
"Sisters would be fine too."
They all went out to the hall,
sat in a circle and had drinks.
While drinking,
Qiǎoniáng playfully asked:
"Do eunuchs also feel moved by beauty?"
The young man said:
"The lame do not forget walking,
the blind do not forget seeing."
They all laughed together.
Qiǎoniáng, seeing that Sānniáng was tired,
urged her to rest now.
The woman looked at Sānniáng,
telling her to go with the young man.
Sānniáng blushed with shame and would not go.
The woman said:
"This is a man in woman's clothing,
why fear him?"
She urged them to go together.
Privately, she instructed the young man:
"In secret, be my son-in-law,
openly, be my son,
that will do."
The young man was delighted,
took her arm and went to bed,
like a newly sharpened blade put to the test,
the pleasure can be imagined.
Then, on the pillow, he asked the girl:
"Who is Qiǎoniáng?"
She said:
"A ghost.
Unmatched in talent and beauty,
but her fate is unfortunate.
She was married to the young son of the Máo family,
who was ill and castrated,
eighteen years old but unable to perform as a man,
so she was depressed and unhappy,
harboring resentment as if in the dark."
The young man was startled,
suspecting Sānniáng was also a ghost.
The girl said:
"To tell you the truth,
I am not a ghost,
but a fox.
Qiǎoniáng lives alone without a partner,
my mother and I have no home,
so we borrow this place to stay."
The young man was greatly astonished.
The girl said:
"Do not fear,
although we are ghosts and foxes,
we do not bring harm."
From then on, they talked and feasted together daily.
Although he knew Qiǎoniáng was not human,
his heart loved her beauty,
only regretting that he had no opportunity to offer himself.
The young man was refined,
skilled at flattery and jesting,
and won Qiǎoniáng's affection.
One day,
when Huà and her daughter were going elsewhere,
they locked the young man in the room again.
The young man, feeling stifled,
paced around the room and called Qiǎoniáng through the door.
Qiǎoniáng had the maidservant try several keys,
and finally opened it.
The young man whispered in her ear, asking for privacy.
Qiǎoniáng sent the maidservant away.
The young man pulled her to the bed,
and embraced her.
The girl playfully cupped below his navel,
and said:
"Pity that such a lovely person lacks something here."
Before she finished speaking,
her hand touched a full grasp.
Startled, she said:
"Why was it so tiny before,
and now suddenly so substantial!"
The young man laughed and said:
"Before, I was shy to meet guests,
so it shrank;
now, because your mockery is hard to bear,
I have made it swell like an angry frog."
Then they became intimate.
Afterwards, she said angrily:
"Now I know why the door was locked.
In the past, mother and daughter wandered with no place to stay,
and borrowed this house to live in.
Sānniáng learned embroidery from me,
and I never kept any secrets from her.
Yet she is so jealous!"
The young man comforted her,
and told her the truth.
Qiǎoniáng still harbored resentment.
The young man said:
"Keep it secret,
Huàgū instructed me strictly."
Before he finished speaking,
Huàgū slipped in.
The two hurriedly got up.
Huàgū glared angrily,
and asked:
"Who opened the door?"
Qiǎoniáng laughed and stepped forward to admit it.
Huà grew even angrier,
and chattered incessantly.
Qiǎoniáng deliberately sneered and said:
"Old lady, you are also quite laughable!
This is a man in woman's clothing,
what can he do?"
Sānniáng, seeing her mother and Qiǎoniáng bitterly opposing each other,
felt uneasy,
and tried to mediate between the two,
until each turned anger into joy.
Although Qiǎoniáng's words were fierce,
from then on she humbly served Sānniáng.
But Huàgū kept watch day and night,
so the two could not express their feelings freely,
only exchanging meaningful glances.
One day,
Huàgū said to the young man:
"My daughters have both served you.
I think staying here is not a long-term plan,
you should return and tell your parents,
and arrange a permanent union soon."
She then packed his luggage and urged him to leave.
The two girls faced each other,
their expressions sad and distressed;
and Qiǎoniáng was especially unbearable,
tears rolling down like broken strings of pearls,
with no end in sight.
Huàgū pushed her to stop,
and pulled the young man out.
Outside the door,
there was no courtyard or house,
only a desolate grave.
Huàgū escorted him to the boat,
and said:
"After you leave,
I will take my two daughters and rent a house in your hometown.
If you do not forget our past affection,
in the abandoned garden of the Lǐ family,
you can come to fetch your bride."
The young man then returned home.
At that time, Fù's father was unable to find his son and
was deeply anxious.
Seeing his son return,
he was overjoyed beyond expectation.
The young man briefly recounted the events,
and also mentioned his engagement to Huà.
His father said:
"How can such demonic words be believed?
The only reason you were able to return alive
was because you were castrated;
otherwise,
you would have died!"
The young man said:
"Although she is a different kind of being,
her feelings are still human;
moreover, she is intelligent and beautiful—
marrying her would not bring ridicule from our relatives."
His father did not speak,
but merely scoffed.
The young man then retreated, his skills itching,
unable to remain content with his lot.
He began secretly consorting with maidservants;
gradually, he engaged in open debauchery even during the day,
intending to shock his parents into hearing about it.
One day,
he was spied upon by a young maidservant,
who ran to inform his mother.
His mother did not believe it,
but went to observe discreetly,
and only then was she shocked.
She called the maidservant for a thorough inquiry,
and learned the full extent of the situation.
Overjoyed,
she told everyone she met,
to show that her son was not castrated,
and planned to arrange a marriage with a prominent family.
The young man privately told his mother:
"I will marry no one but Huà."
His mother said:
"The world is not lacking in beautiful women;
why must it be a ghostly creature?"
The young man said:
"If not for Huà Gū,
I would never have known the ways of man;
to betray her would be inauspicious."
Fù's father agreed,
and sent a servant and an old woman to investigate.
They went four or five li east of the outer city,
searching for Lǐ's garden.
Among the broken walls, bamboo, and trees,
they saw wisps of cooking smoke.
The old woman dismounted from her carriage,
went straight to their door,
and found mother and daughter wiping tables and washing utensils,
as if waiting for something.
The old woman bowed and conveyed her master's message.
Upon seeing Sānniáng,
she exclaimed in surprise:
"Is this our young mistress?
Even I feel affection for her—
no wonder the young gentleman's soul longs for her and dreams of her."
She then asked about the elder sister.
Huà Gū sighed and said:
"She was my adopted daughter.
Three days ago,
she suddenly passed away."
She then offered food and drink to the old woman and the servant.
When the old woman returned,
she described Sānniáng's appearance and demeanor in detail,
and both parents were pleased.
Lastly, she reported the news of Qiǎoniáng's death,
and the young man felt deeply sorrowful, on the verge of tears.
On the night of the wedding procession,
he saw Huà Gū and personally asked her.
She replied:
"She has already been reborn in the northern lands."
The young man sighed for a long time.
He welcomed Sānniáng home,
but could never forget his feelings for Qiǎoniáng.
Whenever someone came from Qióng,
he would summon them to ask.
Some said that at night, ghostly weeping could be heard from Qín Nǚ's tomb.
The young man was astonished by this strangeness
and went to tell Sānniáng.
Sānniáng pondered for a long while,
then said with tears:
"I have wronged my sister!"
When questioned,
she replied:
"When my mother and I came,
we truly did not let her know.
This resentful weeping now—
could it be her?
I wanted to tell you earlier,
but feared exposing my mother's fault."
Hearing this,
the young man felt sorrow, then joy.
He immediately ordered a carriage,
traveling day and night without rest,
and hastened to her tomb.
Knocking on the tomb's wood, he called out:
"Qiǎoniáng,
Qiǎoniáng!
I am here."
Soon, he saw the young lady holding an infant,
emerging from the grave,
raising her head with a heartbroken cry,
full of endless resentment.
The young man also shed tears.
Reaching into his bosom, he asked whose child it was.
Qiǎoniáng said:
"This is your留下的孽种,
born three months ago."
The young man sighed and said:
"I mistakenly believed Huà Gū's words,
causing mother and child to bury their sorrow underground—
how can I escape blame!"
He then took them in the same carriage,
and returned by sea.
Holding the child, he informed his mother.
His mother looked at it,
and seeing its robust and majestic physique,
unlike a ghostly creature,
she was even more pleased.
The two women lived in harmony,
and served their mother-in-law with filial piety.
Later, Fù's father fell ill,
and a doctor was summoned.
Qiǎoniáng said:
"The illness cannot be cured;
his soul has already left its dwelling."
She oversaw the preparation of funeral items,
and when they were ready, he passed away.
The child grew up,
extremely resembling his father;
he was especially intelligent,
and at fourteen, he entered the county school.
An old man named Wēng Zǐxiá from Gāoyóu,
while traveling in Guǎng, heard of this.
The location's name was omitted,
and the ultimate outcome is also unknown.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A certain magistrate of Wú,
his name and courtesy name forgotten,
was known for his integrity and strong principles.
The custom in Wú placed the greatest importance on the City God,
carved from wood,
clothed in brocade,
and animated with mechanisms as if alive.
On the god's birthday,
the residents would pool funds for a festival,
parading the statue through the main streets on a carriage;
banners and flags were erected,
mixed with ceremonial guards,
forming solemn rows,
with music playing as they marched,
creating a continuous, bustling noise,
filling the entire road.
This had become a custom,
and no one dared neglect it year after year.
The magistrate, going out,
happened to encounter it,
stopped and asked about it.
The residents explained.
He also inquired and learned the expenses were quite extravagant.
The magistrate became angry,
pointed at the god and reprimanded him:
"The City God is supposed to govern this entire city.
If you are foolish and without spiritual power,
then you are a licentious and ignorant ghost,
unworthy of worship;
if you do have spiritual power,
then resources should be cherished.
How can you allow such wasteful expenses
to drain the people's hard-earned wealth?"
After speaking,
he dragged the god to the ground
and gave him twenty strokes with a cane.
From then on, the custom was abruptly reformed.
The magistrate was upright and selfless,
but as a young man, he enjoyed mischief.
After more than a year in office,
he once climbed a ladder in his office to catch sparrows under the eaves,
lost his footing and fell,
broke his thigh,
and soon died.
People heard from the City God temple
the magistrate loudly arguing in anger,
as if disputing with the god,
and this continued for several days without ceasing.
The people of Wú, not forgetting his virtues,
gathered to pray and mediate,
and built another temple to honor him,
after which the noise ceased.
This temple was also named City God Temple,
and he was sacrificed to in spring and autumn,
even more prominently than the former god.
To this day, Wú has two City Gods.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A woman came to the village,
about twenty-four or twenty-five years old.
She carried a medicine bag,
selling her medical services.
When someone asked about an illness,
she could not prescribe a remedy herself,
but would wait until nightfall to consult the gods.
In the evening, she would clean a small room,
close herself inside it.
The crowd would gather around the doors and windows,
listening intently in silence,
only whispering softly,
not daring to cough.
Inside and out, all movement and sound ceased.
Around midnight,
suddenly the sound of the curtain was heard.
The woman inside said:
"Has Ninth Aunt arrived?"
A woman's voice answered:
"I've come."
She said again:
"Did Làméi come with Ninth Aunt?"
What seemed like a maidservant replied:
"Not yet."
The three chatted intermittently,
chattering incessantly.
Soon the curtain hook moved again,
and the woman said:
"Sixth Aunt has arrived."
She said in a flurry:
"Did Chūnméi also bring the little boy?"
A woman said:
"That stubborn boy!
No matter how I coaxed him, he wouldn't sleep,
insisting on coming with his mother.
He's as heavy as a hundred jun,
such a burden!"
Then came the sound of the woman's warm greetings,
Ninth Aunt's inquiries,
Sixth Aunt's small talk,
the two maidservants' words of comfort,
the little boy's joyful laughter,
and the sound of a kitten,
all mingling in a noisy clamor.
Then the woman laughed and said:
"The little gentleman is quite playful too,
bringing his kitten from so far away."
After a while, the sounds gradually subsided,
the curtain rustled again,
and the whole room erupted in chatter,
saying:
"Why is Fourth Aunt so late?"
A young girl's delicate voice replied:
"The road was over a thousand li long,
and walking with Auntie took this long to arrive.
Auntie walks rather slowly."
Then each exchanged greetings,
along with the sounds of moving seats,
calling for extra seats,
all rising and falling together,
filling the room with noise and bustle,
which took about the time of a meal to settle.
Then the woman began inquiring about the illness,
Ninth Aunt thought ginseng was suitable,
Sixth Aunt thought astragalus was suitable,
Fourth Aunt thought atractylodes was suitable.
After deliberating for a while,
Ninth Aunt was heard calling for brush and inkstone.
Before long,
came the rustling sound of folding paper,
the clinking of pulling the brush from its cap,
the rumbling of grinding ink;
then the brush was set down, hitting the table,
the inkstone tapped, making a sound,
and then the rustling of gathering and wrapping the medicine was heard.
Shortly after,
the woman pushed aside the curtain,
called the patient and handed over the medicine and prescription.
She turned back into the room,
and immediately the three aunts were heard bidding farewell,
the three maidservants bidding farewell,
the little boy babbling,
the kitten meowing,
all rising at once again.
Ninth Aunt's voice was clear and high-pitched,
Sixth Aunt's voice was slow and aged,
Fourth Aunt's voice was delicate and gentle,
and as for the three maidservants' voices,
each had its own tone and timbre,
all distinctly audible and distinguishable.
The crowd marveled, believing them to be real gods.
But when they tried her prescription,
it was not very effective.
This was what is called vocal mimicry,
merely used to sell her craft.
Yet it was still remarkable!
Wáng Xīnyì once said: While in the capital, he happened to pass by the market,
and heard the sound of string music and singing,
with onlookers packed like a wall.
Peering closer,
he saw a young man singing a tune in a melodious voice.
He had no musical instruments,
only using one finger to press against his cheek,
pressing and singing simultaneously;
listening, it sounded clanging and resonant,
no different from stringed instruments.
This too is a descendant of vocal mimicry.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì"
Jiāo Shēng,
was the younger brother of Zhāngqiū Shíhóng Xiānshēng.
He studied in a garden.
Late at night,
two beautiful women came,
both of peerless beauty.
One appeared about seventeen or eighteen,
the other around fourteen or fifteen,
leaning on the table and smiling.
Jiāo knew they were foxes,
and sternly rejected them.
The elder said:
"Your beard is like halberds,
why do you lack a man's spirit?"
Jiāo said:
"In my life, I have never dared to be unfaithful."
The woman laughed and said:
"How pedantic!
Are you still clinging to those stale rules?
In the realm of ghosts and spirits,
everything turns black into white,
let alone trivial matters of the bedchamber?"
Jiāo again rebuked them.
The woman knew he could not be moved,
and then said:
"You are a renowned scholar,
I have a couplet,
please compose a matching line,
if you can match it, I will leave on my own: 'Wù' and 'xū' share the same form,
only lacking a dot in the belly."
Jiāo pondered deeply but could not complete it.
The woman laughed and said:
"Is this how a renowned scholar is?
I can match it for you: 'Jǐ' and 'sì' follow the same trace,
why not lift both feet?"
With a laugh, she left.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì"
The Li family of Wéiyì County had a separate residence.
Suddenly, an old man came to rent it,
offering fifty taels of gold per year.
They agreed.
After he left, there was no news,
so Li instructed his family to rent it to someone else.
The next day,
the old man arrived
and said:
"I have already negotiated renting this house,
why do you want to lease it to someone else?"
Li explained his doubts.
The old man said:
"I intend to live here long-term;
the reason for my delay
is that the auspicious day falls ten days from now."
He then paid a year's rent in advance,
saying:
"Even if it remains empty all year,
do not ask about it."
Li saw him out,
asked for the date,
and the old man told him.
Several days after the date had passed,
there was still no sign of him.
When Li went to check,
he found the double doors closed from the inside,
with cooking smoke rising and the sound of people talking.
Surprised,
he sent in his card to request a visit.
The old man hurried out,
welcomed him inside,
and was amiable and cheerful.
After returning home,
Li sent gifts to the old man's household;
the old man reciprocated with lavish rewards.
A few days later,
Li hosted a banquet to invite the old man,
and they enjoyed a very cordial gathering.
When asked about his hometown,
he replied it was in Qínzhōng.
Li expressed surprise at the distance.
The old man said:
"Your honorable hometown is a blessed land.
Qínzhōng is not a place to live,
as a great calamity is about to occur."
At that time, peace prevailed,
so Li did not inquire further.
The next day,
the old man sent a formal invitation to return the hospitality,
with furnishings, food, and drink
extremely luxurious and splendid.
Li grew even more astonished,
suspecting he was a high official.
The old man, due to their friendship,
then confessed that he was a fox spirit.
Li was utterly shocked
and told everyone he met.
The local gentry, hearing of this marvel,
daily came in carriages to his door,
wishing to befriend the old man,
who always received them with humble courtesy.
Gradually, even county officials occasionally visited.
Only the county magistrate sought an audience,
but was always declined for some reason.
The magistrate then asked the host, Li, to make an introduction,
but the old man refused.
Li asked him why.
The old man left his seat, approached his guest, and whispered:
"You do not know,
but in his previous life, he was a donkey.
Now, though he appears dignified above the people,
he is one who gets drunk even on dregs.
I, though of a different kind,
am ashamed to associate with him."
Li then made an excuse to tell the magistrate,
saying the fox feared his divine wisdom,
and thus dared not meet him.
The magistrate believed it and stopped.
This happened in the eleventh year of the Kāngxī reign.
Not long after,
Qínzhōng suffered the ravages of war.
The fox could foreknow the future,
truly.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"The donkey as a creature
is bulky and large.
When angered, it brays and neighs,
its eyes bigger than bowls,
its breath coarser than an ox's;
not only is its voice hard to bear,
its appearance is also unpleasant.
If one holds a bundle of hay to lure it,
it will lower its ears and bow its head,
gladly accepting the halter.
For such a one to be placed above the people,
it is fitting that he gets drunk even on dregs.
I hope those who govern the people
take the donkey as a warning,
and seek to be counted among foxes,
then virtue will daily advance."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Guǎngpíng, there was an old man named Féng who had a son,
named Xiàngrú.
Both father and son were scholars.
The old man was nearly sixty,
upright and stubborn by nature,
and the family was often impoverished.
Over several years,
his wife and daughter-in-law died one after another,
so he had to manage household chores himself.
One night,
as Xiàngrú sat under the moonlight,
he suddenly saw a girl from the eastern neighbor peeping over the wall.
Looking at her,
she was beautiful.
Approaching her,
she smiled.
He beckoned her with his hand,
but she neither came nor left.
He insisted,
so she climbed over using a ladder,
and they slept together.
He asked her name,
and she said:
"I am your neighbor, Hóngyù."
The young man was greatly delighted,
and pledged eternal love with her.
The girl agreed.
They met nightly,
for about half a year.
One night, the old man got up
and heard laughter and talking from his son's room.
Peeping in,
he saw the girl.
Angered,
he called his son out,
scolding:
"Beast! What are you doing!
In such desolate circumstances,
instead of studying hard,
you learn to be frivolous?
If others find out,
you lose your virtue;
if they don't,
it shortens your life!"
The son knelt and confessed,
weeping that he knew his mistake.
The old man rebuked the girl:
"A girl who does not keep to women's quarters,
not only defiling herself
but also defiling others.
If this matter comes to light,
it will not only bring shame to our humble home!"
After scolding,
he angrily returned to bed.
The girl wept and said:
"The reproach from your father
is truly shameful and humiliating!
Our缘分 is over!"
The young man said:
"With my father alive, I cannot decide for myself.
If you have feelings for me,
please endure the disgrace and stay with me."
The girl firmly refused,
and the young man shed tears.
The girl stopped him, saying:
"We have no matchmaker's words,
no parents' approval,
climbing walls and peeping through cracks—
how can we grow old together?
There is a good match here
you can marry."
He told her of his poverty.
The girl said:
"Wait for me tomorrow night,
I will help you plan it."
The next night,
the girl indeed came,
giving the young man forty taels of silver.
She said:
"Sixty lǐ from here,
in Wúcūn, there is a Wèi family girl,
eighteen years old,
priced high,
so she remains unmarried.
If you offer a generous betrothal gift,
it will surely be agreed."
Having said this,
she left.
Shēng took the opportunity to speak to his father,
wishing to go and see her.
But he dared not mention the hidden gold.
The old man, considering himself without funds,
for this reason,
stopped him.
Shēng then spoke gently:
"Let me just try, and if it works out, then it's done."
The old man nodded.
Shēng then borrowed a servant and horse,
and went to the Wèi family.
Wèi was originally a country farmer.
Shēng called him out,
and led him aside to speak privately.
Wèi knew Shēng came from a distinguished family,
and seeing his dignified and open demeanor,
was inwardly pleased,
but worried he might be stingy with money.
Shēng, hearing his hesitant and ambiguous words,
understood his meaning,
and emptied his purse, placing it all on the table.
Wèi was then delighted,
asked a neighboring scholar to act as go-between,
and wrote the marriage contract on red paper.
Shēng entered to pay respects to the old woman.
She lived in a side room,
the girl hiding behind her mother.
He stole a glance at her;
though dressed in plain cotton clothes,
her expression was radiantly beautiful,
and he secretly rejoiced.
Wèi borrowed a house to entertain his son-in-law,
and said:
"You need not come personally to fetch the bride.
Wait until we prepare some clothes and makeup,
and we will send her over in a sedan chair."
Shēng set a date and returned home.
He deceitfully told his father,
saying Wèi valued their respectable family background,
and did not demand a dowry.
The old man was also pleased.
On the appointed day,
Wèi indeed sent the girl over.
The girl was diligent and frugal,
virtuous and obedient,
and the couple was deeply harmonious.
After two years,
she bore a son,
named Fú'ér.
During the Qingmíng Festival, carrying her son to visit the graves,
she encountered a local gentry named Sòng.
Sòng had been a Censor,
but was dismissed for accepting bribes,
and lived in retirement,
wielding great power and cruelty.
That day he was also returning from visiting graves,
saw the girl and was struck by her beauty.
He asked the villagers,
and learned she was Shēng's wife.
Guessing Féng was a poor scholar,
he tried to tempt him with a heavy bribe,
hoping he could be swayed,
and sent a servant to hint at it.
Shēng, hearing this suddenly,
showed anger on his face;
but then, considering he was no match for Sòng's power,
suppressed his anger and forced a smile,
and went home to tell his father.
The old man was furious,
rushed out,
faced the servant,
gesturing wildly,
and cursed him extensively.
The servant scurried away like a rat.
Sòng was also angry,
and actually sent several men into Shēng's home,
beating the old man and his son,
causing a great uproar.
The girl, hearing this,
threw the child on the bed,
rushed out with disheveled hair, crying for help.
The crowd seized her and carried her off,
noisily departing.
Father and son, injured and maimed,
lay groaning on the ground,
the child wailing in the room.
The neighbors, pitying them,
helped them onto their beds.
After a day,
Shēng, leaning on a stick, could rise.
The old man, in rage, refused to eat,
vomited blood and soon died.
Shēng wept bitterly,
carried his son and filed a lawsuit,
appealing up to the Governor,
but though he sued everywhere,
ultimately obtained no justice.
Later, hearing his wife had died resisting,
his grief increased.
Injustice choked his heart and throat,
with no way to seek redress.
He often thought of waylaying and assassinating Sòng,
but worried about his many attendants,
and also had no one to entrust his child to.
Day and night he grieved and brooded,
his eyelids never meeting in sleep.
Suddenly a man came to offer condolences at his home,
with a curly beard and broad jaw,
whom he had never met before.
Shēng pulled him to sit,
wanting to ask his name and origin.
The guest abruptly said:
"You have the hatred of a murdered father,
the enmity of a stolen wife,
yet you forget to seek revenge?"
Shēng suspected he was a spy from the Sòng family,
and so pretended to agree.
The guest's eyes blazed with anger,
and he abruptly stood to leave, saying:
"I thought you were a man,
but now you seem no better than a worthless wretch!"
Shēng, sensing something unusual,
knelt and held him back,
saying:
"I truly feared you were from the Sòngs.
Now I speak from the heart: I have been enduring hardships, biding my time,
for a long while indeed.
But I pity this thing in swaddling clothes,
fearing the ancestral line may be cut off.
You are a righteous man,
can you be my Chéng Yīng?"
The guest said:
"That is a matter for women and children,
not something I can do.
What you wish to entrust to others,
please undertake yourself;
what you wish to undertake yourself,
I am willing to do in your stead."
Hearing this,
Shēng kowtowed, knocking his head on the ground.
The guest left without looking back.
Shēng chased after him to ask his name,
but he said:
"If I fail,
I will not accept your resentment;
if I succeed,
I will not accept your gratitude either."
And so he left.
Shēng, fearing disaster would strike,
took his child and fled.
That night,
the entire Sòng household was asleep,
when someone scaled the high walls and entered,
killing the Censor, his three sons,
and a daughter-in-law and a maidservant.
The Sòng family submitted a plaint to the authorities.
The officials were greatly alarmed.
The Sòngs insisted it was Xiàngrú,
so officers were dispatched to arrest Shēng,
but Shēng had fled, his whereabouts unknown,
making the accusation seem even more true.
Sòng's servants, together with the officers, searched everywhere.
At night they reached the southern hills,
heard a child crying,
tracked it down,
and bound Shēng, leading him away.
The child cried even more fiercely,
and the crowd snatched it away and abandoned it.
Shēng, filled with冤屈 and fury, wished only for death.
Brought before the county magistrate,
he was asked:
"Why did you kill?"
Shēng said:
"How unjust!
He died at night,
while I went out during the day,
and I was holding a crying infant—
how could I have climbed over the wall to kill someone?"
The magistrate said:
"If you didn’t kill anyone,
why did you run away?"
Féng shēng was at a loss for words
and could not defend himself.
So he was taken to prison.
Féng shēng wept and said:
"My death is of little consequence,
but what crime has the orphan committed?"
The magistrate said:
"You have killed many people’s sons;
if your son is killed,
why complain?"
Féng shēng was stripped of his scholar’s status,
repeatedly tortured cruelly,
and in the end had nothing to say.
That night, as the magistrate was lying down,
he heard something strike the bed,
with a loud, rumbling sound.
Terrified, he cried out.
The whole household was startled awake,
gathered around, and lit a candle to look:
it was a short knife,
sharp as frost,
embedded over an inch deep into the wooden bed,
firmly stuck and impossible to pull out.
When the magistrate saw it,
he lost his soul in fear.
Armed men searched everywhere,
but found no trace.
Secretly, his courage failed.
Moreover, since Sòng shì was already dead,
there was nothing more to fear,
so he reported in detail to his superiors,
pleading on Féng shēng’s behalf for clemency,
and eventually released Féng shēng.
Féng shēng returned home,
his jars empty of even a peck or a pint,
a solitary shadow facing the bare walls.
Fortunately, neighbors took pity and brought him food and drink,
allowing him to barely get by.
When he thought of the great revenge already taken,
he would break into a smile of joy;
when he recalled the cruel disaster
that nearly wiped out his family,
tears would stream down his face;
and when he considered his lifelong poverty, down to the bone,
and the lack of an heir to continue the family line,
he would weep aloud in deserted places,
unable to restrain himself.
This went on for half a year,
when the search and restrictions gradually relaxed.
He then pleaded with the county magistrate,
asking for a judgment to have Wèi shì’s remains returned.
After the burial, returning home,
grief-stricken and wishing for death,
he tossed and turned on his empty bed,
seeing no way to go on living.
Suddenly, there was a knock at the door.
Holding his breath and listening quietly,
he heard someone outside the door
murmuring to a child.
Féng shēng hurriedly got up to peek,
and it seemed to be a woman.
As soon as the door opened,
she asked:
"Your great injustice has been redressed—
I’m glad to see you safe and sound!"
Her voice was familiar,
but in his haste he could not recall who it was.
Holding a candle to see,
it was Hóng Yù.
She was holding a little boy,
who was laughing and playing at her feet.
Féng shēng had no time to ask questions;
he embraced the woman and wept.
She too was deeply saddened.
Then she pushed the child forward and said:
"Have you forgotten your father?"
The child tugged at her clothes,
his bright eyes fixed on Féng shēng.
Looking closely,
it was Fú’er.
Greatly astonished,
he asked through tears:
"How did my son get here?"
She said:
"To tell you the truth: when I said before that I was a neighbor’s daughter,
that was untrue.
I am actually a fox spirit.
One night while out walking,
I saw a child crying at the valley entrance,
so I took him to raise in Qín.
Hearing that your great troubles were over,
I brought him here to reunite with you."
Féng shēng wiped his tears and bowed in gratitude.
The child in her arms,
as if clinging to his own mother,
no longer recognized his father.
Before dawn,
Hóng Yù got up hurriedly.
When asked,
she replied:
"I wish to leave."
Féng shēng knelt naked by the bedside,
weeping so hard he could not lift his head.
She laughed and said:
"I was teasing you.
Now that the household is newly established,
we must rise early and retire late."
Then she cut weeds and cleared brush,
working like a man.
Féng shēng worried about their poverty,
fearing they could not support themselves.
She said:
"Just focus on studying behind the curtain,
don’t worry about plenty or lack—
perhaps we won’t starve to death."
Then she took out money to buy weaving tools;
rented several dozen mu of land,
and hired laborers to farm.
She shouldered the hoe to clear weeds,
mended the roof with vines,
working like this every day.
The villagers, hearing of the wife’s virtue,
were even more willing to help them.
In about half a year,
the household flourished,
like a well-off family.
Féng shēng said:
"From the ashes,
you have rebuilt everything with bare hands.
But one matter remains unsettled—
what shall we do?"
When she asked what it was,
he replied:
"The examination date is approaching,
but my scholar’s status has not yet been restored."
She laughed and said:
"Some time ago, I sent four taels of silver to the education official,
and your name has already been reinstated on the register.
If I had waited for you to mention it,
it would have been too late long ago."
Féng shēng admired her even more.
That year, he passed the provincial examination.
He was then thirty-six years old,
with fertile fields stretching far,
and grand houses standing tall.
Hóng Yù was slender and graceful, as if about to float away with the wind,
yet she worked harder than a farmwife;
even in harsh winters, toiling herself,
her face and hands remained smooth as grease.
She said she was twenty-eight,
but to others,
she often looked around twenty.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"The son was worthy,
the father virtuous,
thus the retribution was chivalrous.
Not only are humans chivalrous—
foxes are too.
Such an encounter is indeed extraordinary!
Yet the officials were negligent and indifferent,
making one’s hair stand on end.
The knife, with a rumbling sound, embedded in the wood—
why could it not have shifted half a foot toward the bed?
Had Sū Zǐměi read this,
he would surely raise his cup and say: ‘What a pity it didn’t hit the mark!’"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In the Běizhí region, a falling dragon entered a village.
Its movements were heavy and clumsy,
and it went into a certain gentry’s house.
The doorway was only large enough for its body,
so it squeezed through.
The family all fled.
They climbed the tower, shouting noisily,
firing guns and cannons with a roar.
The dragon then went out.
Outside the gate, stagnant water was stored,
shallow, not even a foot deep.
The dragon entered it,
turned and twisted in the water,
its body covered in mud;
it tried with all its might to leap up,
but fell back after rising only a little over a foot.
It wallowed in the mud for three days,
with flies gathering on its scales.
Suddenly, there was heavy rain,
and with a clap of thunder, it soared into the sky and flew away.
Student Fáng and his friend ascended Niú Mountain,
entering a temple to stroll and gaze.
Suddenly, from among the rafters, a small yellow snake coiled upon a brick,
as slender as an earthworm.
Suddenly it coiled once around,
becoming thick as a finger;
another coil,
and it was already like a belt.
All were startled,
knowing it was a dragon,
and hurriedly descended.
Just as they reached halfway down the mountain,
they heard a thunderclap from the temple,
shaking the mountain valley.
In the sky, black clouds gathered like a lid,
a huge dragon writhed sinuously within them,
and after a while, it vanished.
In Xiǎoxiànggōng Village, Zhāngqiū,
there was a commoner woman who went to the fields,
encountered a great wind,
and dust and sand blew against her face.
She felt something in one eye,
as if containing a wheat awn,
rubbing and blowing it,
but it never healed.
Lifting her eyelid to examine it closely,
the eyeball itself was unharmed,
but there was a red line winding through the flesh.
Someone said:
"This is a dormant dragon."
The woman worried and feared, awaiting death.
After more than three months had accumulated,
the sky poured with heavy rain,
suddenly a great thunderclap sounded,
and it cracked her eyelid and left.
The woman suffered no harm.
Yuán Xuānsì said:
"In Sūzhōu,
during overcast gloom,
thunderclaps erupted greatly.
The crowd saw a dragon hanging at the edge of the clouds,
its scales moving,
in its claws clutching a human head,
the beard clearly visible at the back;
after a while,
it entered the clouds and vanished.
Nor was it heard that anyone had lost their head."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Dàoyǐn Chén Bǎoyào of Qīngzhōu,
was from Mǐn.
Sitting alone at night,
a woman lifted the curtain and entered.
Looking at her,
he did not recognize her;
yet she was stunningly beautiful,
wearing palace attire with long sleeves.
She said with a smile:
"Sitting solitary on a clear night,
must you not be lonely?"
The Dàoyǐn asked in surprise:
"Who are you?"
She said:
"My home is not far,
nearby to the west."
The Dàoyǐn thought she was a ghost,
yet his heart was fond of her.
Grasping her sleeve, he pulled her to sit,
her speech was elegant and refined,
greatly pleasing him.
Embracing her,
she did not resist much.
Looking around, she said:
"Is there no one else here?"
The Dàoyǐn hurriedly closed the door,
saying:
"No."
Urging her to loosen her garments,
she appeared very shy and timid.
The Dàoyǐn attentively helped her.
The woman said:
"I am twenty years old,
still a maiden,
such wildness will be unbearable."
After the intimacy concluded,
red stains soaked the mat.
Then, whispering by the pillow,
she herself said
she was "Lín Sìniáng".
The Dàoyǐn questioned her in detail.
She said:
"A lifetime of steadfast chastity,
has now been nearly utterly轻薄 by you.
If you have a heart that loves me,
only seek eternal affection, that is all,
why chatter on?"
Before long,
the rooster crowed,
and she rose and left.
From then on, she came every night without fail.
Often they would close the door and drink elegantly.
When discussing music and tones,
she could always analyze and understand the notes in detail.
The Dàoyǐn thus thought she was skilled at composing songs.
She said:
"Something practiced since childhood."
The Dàoyǐn requested a performance of an elegant tune.
The woman said:
"It has been long since I entrusted myself to music,
half or more of the rhythms are forgotten,
I fear being laughed at by those who know."
Pressed again,
she then bowed her head, beat time,
and sang a tune of Yīliáng,
her voice mournful and plaintive.
After singing,
tears fell.
The Dàoyǐn also felt sorrowful,
embracing and comforting her, saying:
"Please do not sing such music of a fallen state,
it makes one melancholy."
The woman said:
"Sound expresses intent,
one who is sorrowful cannot be made joyful,
just as one who is joyful cannot be made sorrowful."
The two were intimate and affectionate,
surpassing even the harmony of lutes.
After a long time,
the family secretly listened,
and those who heard her singing
could not help but shed tears.
The wife glimpsed her appearance,
doubting that such bewitching beauty existed in the human world,
if not a ghost, she must be a fox;
fearing she was a bewitching calamity,
she urged the Dàoyǐn to break it off.
The Dàoyǐn would not listen,
but firmly questioned her instead.
The woman said with a changed expression:
was a palace maid of the Héng princely estate.
I met with disaster and died,
seventeen years ago.
Because of your noble righteousness,
