I entrusted myself as your companion,
yet I truly dare not bring calamity upon you.
If you are suspicious and fearful,
I shall take my leave from now on."
The Dàoyǐn said:
"I do not find you objectionable;
but with such intimacy as this,
one cannot not know the truth of it."
Then he asked about affairs in the palace.
The woman recounted in detail,
vividly and delightfully listenable.
When speaking of the time of decline,
she then choked and could not finish her words.
The woman slept very little,
every night she would rise and recite the Zhǔntí, Jīngāng, and other sūtras and mantras.
The Dàoyǐn asked:
"Can one repent for oneself in the underworld?"
She said:
"It is the same.
I think of my lifetime of downfall,
wishing to seek salvation in the next life."
She also often discussed and critiqued poetry and lyrics with the Dàoyǐn,
finding fault with flaws;
when encountering good lines,
she would drawl them out in a delicate chant.
Her mood and demeanor were charming and graceful,
making one forget weariness.
The Dàoyǐn asked:
"Are you skilled at poetry?"
She said:
"In life, I also occasionally composed."
The Dàoyǐn requested a gift from her.
She said with a laugh:
"Such words of love and affection are unworthy of a noble man's hearing."
They lived together for three years.
One evening,
she suddenly sorrowfully announced her departure.
The gentleman was startled and asked her why.
She replied:
"The King of the Underworld, because I committed no sins in my former life,
and even after death did not forget the sutras and incantations,
has decreed that I be reborn into a royal family.
Our parting is tonight,
and we shall never meet again."
Having spoken,
she was deeply grieved.
The gentleman also shed tears.
Then he set out wine and they drank deeply together.
The girl sang with fervent emotion,
her voice mournful and lingering,
each word turning a hundred times;
whenever she reached a sorrowful passage,
she would choke with sobs.
She stopped and started several times before finishing the song,
and they could not drink with ease.
Then she rose,
hesitating as if to leave.
The gentleman firmly detained her,
and she sat a while longer.
Suddenly a rooster crowed,
and she said:
"I truly cannot stay any longer.
However, you have often wondered why I refused to display my clumsiness;
now that we are parting forever,
I shall hastily compose a verse."
She asked for a brush and composed it,
saying:
"My heart is sad and my thoughts disordered,
I cannot refine the words;
the sounds are discordant and the rhythm flawed,
please be careful not to show it to others."
Covering her face with her sleeve, she left.
The gentleman saw her out the door,
where she vanished without a trace.
The gentleman grieved and mourned for a long time.
Looking at her poem,
the characters were elegantly formed,
and he treasured it, storing it away.
The poem said:
"In tranquil seclusion deep within the palace for seventeen years,
Who will ask of my homeland beneath the azure sky?
Idly watching the palace halls sealed by towering trees,
Weeping, I gaze as my sovereign transforms into a cuckoo.
The sea kingdom's waves slant beneath the setting sun's glow,
The Hàn house's pipes and drums fall silent, beacon fires extinguished.
A beauty's strength is weak, unable to become a vengeful spirit,
A gentle soul, heart sorrowful, only turns to meditation.
Daily reciting the Bodhi mantra a thousand hundred times,
Idly reading two or three leaves of the palm-leaf scriptures.
Loudly singing in the Pear Garden, using song to replace weeping,
I beg you, listen alone, and you too will shed tears."
The poem contained repetitions and disjointed passages,
suggesting there might be errors.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Wáng Shèngyú traveled south,
and moored his boat in the middle of the river.
After retiring to bed,
seeing the moonlight bright as silk,
he could not sleep,
and had his servant boy massage him.
Suddenly he heard on the boat's roof what sounded like a child walking,
the sound of footsteps on the reed matting,
coming from the far end of the boat,
gradually approaching the cabin window.
Fearing it was a thief,
he quickly got up and asked the boy.
The boy had also heard it.
While they were talking,
they saw a person crouched on the boat's roof,
hanging his head to peer into the cabin.
Greatly alarmed,
he gripped his sword and called to the servants;
everyone on the boat awoke.
He told them what he had seen.
Some suspected it was a mistake.
Soon the sound occurred again.
Everyone rose and looked all around,
but there was no one in sight,
only the bright stars and moon,
and the vast, rolling river waves.
Everyone sat in the boat,
and soon saw a blue flame like a lantern,
suddenly emerge from the water's surface,
floating along with the current;
as it gradually neared the boat,
the flame suddenly went out.
Immediately a black figure abruptly rose,
standing erect on the water,
and using its hands to clutch the boat, moved along with it.
The crowd cried out:
"It must be this thing!"
They wanted to shoot it.
Just as they drew their bows,
it suddenly submerged into the water,
and could not be seen.
They asked the boatman.
The boatman said:
"This is an ancient battlefield,
ghosts often appear and disappear here,
it is nothing to be surprised about."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Zhāoyuǎn's Zhāng Yúdàn,
was by nature unrestrained and unconventional.
He studied at a desolate temple.
At that time, the county magistrate, Lǔ Gōng,
was from Sānhán.
He had a daughter who loved hunting.
Zhāng happened to meet her in the wilderness,
and saw her graceful and beautiful appearance,
dressed in a brocade sable coat,
riding a small black colt,
elegant as if from a painting.
Returning home, he recalled her lovely countenance,
and thought of her with utmost admiration.
Later, he heard the girl had died suddenly,
and he mourned and sighed, heartbroken.
Because Lǔ's home was far away,
he placed her coffin temporarily in the temple,
which was precisely where Zhāng studied.
Zhāng paid respects to her as to a deity,
each morning he would burn incense,
and at meals he would make offerings.
Each time he poured a libation, he would pray:
"Having glimpsed your face but once,
I am forever bound in dreams and soul;
never imagining such a jade-like person
would suddenly pass from this world.
Now you are near, within a foot,
yet distant as mountains and rivers—
how I hate this separation!
Yet in life there were constraints,
in death there are no taboos;
if your spirit in the netherworld has awareness,
you should come with tinkling jade,
to comfort my ardent admiration."
He prayed day and night like this
for almost half a month.
One evening,
trimming the lamp to read at night,
he suddenly looked up
to see the girl standing smiling beneath the lamp.
Startled, Zhāng rose and greeted her.
The girl said:
"Moved by your feelings,
I could not restrain myself,
and so did not avoid the suspicion of an illicit elopement."
Zhāng was overjoyed,
and they shared joyful intimacy.
From then on, not a night passed without her visit.
She said to Zhāng:
"In life, I loved bow and horse,
taking pleasure in shooting deer and killing roe deer;
my sins are deep and heavy,
and in death I have no place to return.
If you sincerely love me,
I trouble you to recite for me the full number of the Diamond Sutra,
and I will never forget it through life after life."
Zhāng reverently accepted her instruction;
every night he would rise
and before the coffin, fingering his prayer beads, chant the sutra.
Once, during a festival,
he wanted to take her home with him.
The girl worried her feet were too weak
to walk the distance.
Zhāng offered to carry her as they went,
and the girl laughingly agreed.
It was like carrying an infant,
not heavy or burdensome at all.
Thereafter it became their custom.
When he went for examinations, he also took her along.
However, they always traveled by night.
When Zhāng was about to go for the autumn provincial examinations,
the girl said:
"Your fortune is thin,
it would be a futile exertion."
So he heeded her words and did not go.
After four or five years had passed,
Lǔ was dismissed from office,
and being poor, could not transport the coffin,
and was about to bury it there,
but struggled to find burial ground.
Zhāng then stated on his own behalf:
"I have a small plot of land near the temple,
and wish to bury the young lady there."
Lǔ Gōng was pleased.
Zhāng also strenuously arranged the burial.
Lǔ was grateful to him,
but could not understand the reason.
After Lǔ left,
the two were as affectionate as in the past.
One night,
she leaned against his bosom,
tears falling like beans,
and said:
"Our five years of affection
end today!
The kindness and devotion I have received from you
could not be repaid in several lifetimes!"
The scholar asked in surprise.
She said:
"Thanks to your grace reaching the dead,
the sutras and incantations have filled the storehouse,
and now I am to be reborn into the family of the Lú Ministry of Revenue official in Héběi.
If you do not forget today,
fifteen years from now,
on the sixteenth day of the eighth month,
I beg you to come for a meeting."
The scholar wept and said:
"I am already over thirty;
in another fifteen years,
I will be near the coffin—
what use would a meeting be?"
She also wept and said:
"I wish to serve as your slave to repay you."
After a while, she said:
"Please escort me for six or seven lǐ.
The road ahead is full of thorns,
and my long robe makes it difficult to pass."
So she embraced his neck.
The scholar escorted her to the main road,
where he saw a cluster of carriages and horses by the roadside.
On the horses, some had one person,
some two;
in the carriages, some had three, four, or even over ten people;
only one ornate carriage,
with embroidered tassels and vermilion decorations,
had just an old woman inside.
Seeing the girl arrive,
she called out:
"Are you coming?"
The girl replied:
"I am coming."
Then she turned back to the scholar and said:
"This is as far as you go;
please leave now;
do not forget what was said."
The scholar promised.
The girl approached the carriage,
and the old woman reached out her hand to help her up.
The wheels immediately started rolling,
and the carriages and horses rumbled away.
The scholar returned disheartened
and noted the date on the wall.
Thinking of the efficacy of the sutras and incantations,
he recited them even more devoutly.
He dreamed that a divine being told him:
"Your resolve is truly commendable.
But you must go to the South Sea."
He asked:
"How far is the South Sea?"
The being said:
"It is close, right in the square inch of your heart."
Upon waking, he understood the meaning,
and with a fervent aspiration for Bodhi,
he cultivated his conduct with redoubled purity.
Three years later,
his second son, Míng, and his eldest son, Zhèng,
successively achieved high honors in the examinations.
Though the scholar suddenly became eminent,
he did not cease his virtuous deeds.
One night, he dreamed of a servant in black inviting him away.
He saw a person seated in a palace hall,
resembling a Bodhisattva,
who greeted him, saying:
"It is praiseworthy that you do good.
It is a pity you lack longevity,
but fortunately, I have pleaded on your behalf to the Heavenly Emperor."
The scholar prostrated and kowtowed.
He was raised up
and offered a seat;
tea was served to him,
its fragrance like orchids.
Then a youth was ordered to lead him away
to bathe in a pool.
The pool water was clear and pure,
with fish visible as they swam;
entering it, he found it warm,
and scooping it up, it carried the scent of lotus leaves.
After a while,
he gradually went into deeper water,
lost his footing and sank,
submerging over his head.
He awoke with a start,
finding it strange.
From then on, his body grew healthier,
and his eyesight clearer.
Stroking his beard,
he found the white hairs all falling out rustlingly;
after some more time,
the black ones also fell out increasingly.
The wrinkles on his face gradually smoothed.
After several months,
his chin was bald and his face childlike,
just as when he was fifteen or sixteen.
He even took to playful activities,
still like a child.
He became overly concerned with his appearance;
his sons would then admonish and correct him.
Not long after,
his wife died of old age and illness.
His sons wanted to seek a new wife for him from a noble family.
The scholar said:
"Wait until I go to Héběi,
and after I return, then I will marry."
Counting on his fingers, he realized the appointed time had arrived,
so he ordered his servant and horse to head north of the river.
He inquired about the place,
and indeed there was a Minister of Revenue named Lú.
Previously,
Mr. Lú had a daughter,
who could speak from birth,
and as she grew older, she became even more intelligent and beautiful.
Her parents cherished her dearly.
When noble families sent betrothal gifts,
the girl always refused.
Puzzled, they asked her why,
and she recounted in detail the promise from her previous life.
They calculated the years together,
and laughed heartily, saying:
"Silly girl!
Your Zhāng láng must be over fifty by now.
With the changes of human affairs,
his bones are likely already decayed.
Even if he is still alive,
he would be bald and toothless!"
The girl paid no heed.
Seeing her determination unwavering,
her mother discussed with Mr. Lú,
instructing the gatekeeper not to admit any guests,
hoping to sever her hopes once the appointed time passed.
Not long after,
the young man arrived,
but the gatekeeper turned him away.
He retreated to an inn,
filled with sorrow and regret, unsure of what to do.
He wandered idly through the outskirts of the city,
gradually making discreet inquiries.
The girl, thinking the young man had broken his promise,
wept and refused to eat.
Her mother said:
"If he hasn’t come,
he must already be dead.
Even if not,
the fault of breaking the vow
does not lie with you."
The girl remained silent,
lying in bed all day.
Worried, Mr. Lú
also wished to see what kind of person the young man was,
so he pretended to go on an outing
and encountered him in the countryside.
Looking at him,
he saw a young man,
and was astonished.
Sitting on the grass, they chatted briefly,
and he found him quite dashing and unrestrained.
Delighted, Mr. Lú
invited him to his home.
Just as he was about to inquire further,
Mr. Lú suddenly stood up,
asked the guest to wait alone for a moment,
and hurried inside to inform his daughter.
The girl was overjoyed,
and struggled to get up by herself.
Peeking at him, she saw his appearance did not match,
and returned in tears,
resenting her father for deceiving her.
Mr. Lú insisted it was indeed him.
The girl said nothing,
only weeping incessantly.
Mr. Lú went out,
his mood dejected and frustrated,
and treated the guest with little courtesy.
The young man asked,
"Is there anyone in your esteemed family who served as Minister of Revenue?"
Mr. Lú replied absentmindedly.
He looked away,
as if paying no attention to the guest.
The young man sensed his rudeness,
and took his leave.
The girl wept for several days and then died.
That night, the young man dreamed the girl came to him,
saying:
"Was the one who came indeed you?
Your age and appearance were so different,
that when we met, we missed each other.
I have already died of sorrow and indignation.
Please hurry to the local earth god temple to summon my soul,
so I may live again.
If delayed, it will be too late."
Upon waking,
he hurried to the Lú residence,
and indeed, there was a daughter
who had died two days earlier.
The young man was overcome with grief,
and entered to mourn in her chamber.
He then told Mr. Lú about his dream.
Mr. Lú followed his advice,
summoned her soul back,
uncovered her quilt,
stroked her body,
and called out to her with prayers.
Soon, a gurgling sound was heard in her throat.
Suddenly, her cherry-red lips parted,
and a lump of phlegm, cold as ice, fell out.
They helped her move to the bed,
and gradually she began to moan softly.
Mr. Lú was overjoyed,
respectfully escorted the guest out,
and prepared a feast.
He inquired in detail about his family background,
and learning he came from a prominent family,
he was even more pleased.
An auspicious day was chosen for the wedding.
After living there for half a month,
he took his bride and returned home.
Mr. Lú accompanied them to their home,
and stayed for half a year before leaving.
The couple lived together,
as harmonious as a young pair,
and many who didn’t know them mistook the daughter-in-law for the mother-in-law.
Mr. Lú passed away the following year.
His son was still very young,
and was slandered by local bullies,
nearly losing the entire family fortune.
The young man took him in to support him,
and they settled there together.
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Mr. Hán came from a family of officials for generations.
He enjoyed hosting guests.
A man named Xú from the same village
often drank at his home.
During one gathering,
a Taoist priest appeared at the gate with his alms bowl.
The servants offered him money and grain,
but he accepted neither;
nor did he leave.
Angered, the servants
ignored him and went back inside.
Hearing the persistent knocking,
Mr. Hán inquired about it,
and the servants explained the situation.
Before they finished speaking,
the priest walked right in.
Mr. Hán invited him to sit.
The priest raised his hand in greeting to both host and guests,
then took a seat.
After some questioning,
they learned he had recently taken up residence in the dilapidated temple east of the village.
Mr. Hán said:
"When did you, noble crane, perch at the eastern temple?
I hadn’t heard,
and have thus failed in my duty as host."
The priest replied:
"I, a rustic newcomer,
have no acquaintances here.
Hearing of your generosity,
I deeply wished to share a drink with you."
Mr. Hán ordered wine to be served.
The priest could drink heartily.
Xú, seeing his dirty and shabby clothes,
treated him rather disdainfully
and showed little respect.
Mr. Hán, however, treated him as he would a seasoned traveler.
The priest downed over twenty cups in a row,
then took his leave and departed.
From then on, every time there was a banquet,
the Daoist priest would come.
If there was food, he would eat;
if there was drink, he would drink.
Hán gradually grew tired of his frequent visits.
During a drinking session,
Xú mocked him, saying:
"Reverend, you are a guest every day—
wouldn’t you like to play host for once?"
The Daoist priest smiled and said:
"A man of the Dao and a lay devotee are alike—
both rely on a pair of shoulders to carry a single mouth."
Xú was ashamed and could not reply.
The Daoist priest said:
"Nevertheless,
this humble Daoist has long been sincere in his heart.
I should do my utmost to offer a modest token of gratitude."
After drinking,
he instructed them:
"I would be honored by your esteemed presence tomorrow at noon."
The next day,
they went together as invited,
doubting that he would have anything prepared.
As they walked along,
the Daoist priest was already waiting on the road.
Chatting as they walked,
they soon arrived at the temple gate.
Entering the gate,
they saw the courtyard was completely renewed,
with interconnected pavilions stretching like clouds.
Greatly astonished,
they said:
"It has been a long time since we last came here—
when was all this built?"
The Daoist priest replied:
"The construction was completed not long ago."
When they entered his chambers,
the furnishings were splendid and luxurious,
surpassing even those of noble families.
The two men were filled with awe and respect.
As soon as they sat down,
wine was served and food brought out,
all by clever youths of sixteen,
dressed in brocade robes and red shoes.
The wine and dishes were fragrant and delicious,
extremely abundant and lavish.
After the meal,
there was another small course.
There were many rare fruits whose names they did not know,
stored in vessels of crystal and jade,
their light illuminating the tables and couches.
They drank from glass cups,
about a foot in circumference.
The Daoist priest said:
"Summon the Shí sisters."
The youth left for a short while,
and two beautiful women entered.
One was slender and tall,
like a delicate willow;
the other was short in stature,
and the youngest in age;
both were enchantingly graceful and peerless.
The Daoist priest immediately had them sing to accompany the drinking.
The younger one clapped castanets and sang,
while the elder harmonized with a vertical flute,
their voices clear and delicate.
When the song ended,
the Daoist priest raised his cup and urged them to drink,
then ordered wine to be poured all around.
Turning to the beauties, he asked:
"It has been a long time since you danced—
can you still do it?"
Immediately, servants spread a woolen carpet beneath the banquet,
and the two women danced facing each other.
Their long sleeves fluttered wildly,
scented dust scattering in all directions.
When the dance ended,
they leaned gracefully against a painted screen.
The two men felt their hearts uplifted and spirits soaring,
unconsciously growing intoxicated.
The Daoist priest paid no heed to his guests;
he drained his cup,
stood up, and said to them:
"Please help yourselves to more wine for now.
I will rest briefly
and return shortly."
With that, he left.
Against the wall of the southern room,
there was an inlaid mother-of-pearl bed.
The women laid out brocade covers
and helped the Daoist priest lie down.
He then pulled the elder woman to sleep with him
and ordered the younger one to stand by the bed and scratch his back.
Seeing this, the two men
felt quite indignant.
Xú then shouted loudly:
"Daoist priest, do not be so improper!"
He went over to disrupt them.
The Daoist priest hurriedly got up and fled.
Seeing the young woman still standing by the bed,
Xú, in his drunkenness, pulled her toward the northern couch
and openly embraced her to sleep.
Looking at the beauty on the bed,
who was still sleeping on the embroidered couch,
he said to Hán:
"Why are you so rigid?"
Hán then went straight to the southern couch;
he wanted to be intimate with her,
but the beauty was fast asleep
and would not turn over no matter how he nudged her.
So he held her and slept together.
When dawn broke,
both wine and dreams had faded.
He felt something cold in his embrace chilling him;
looking at it,
he found himself holding a long stone, lying on the green steps below.
He quickly looked for Xú,
who was still not awake;
he saw him using a dung-stained stone as a pillow,
sleeping soundly in a dilapidated latrine.
Hán kicked him awake,
and they stared at each other in shock.
Looking around,
they saw only a courtyard of wild grass
and two rundown rooms.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Zhílì, there was a wealthy family
who wanted to hire a tutor.
Suddenly, a scholar
came to their door to recommend himself.
The host invited him in.
His words were open and clear,
and they soon became fond of each other.
The scholar said his surname was Hú,
so they accepted his gifts and hired him as a tutor.
Hú was very diligent in his teaching,
and his knowledge was profound, far surpassing that of ordinary scholars.
However, he often went out,
returning only late at night;
the doors would be firmly locked,
yet without hearing any knocking, he would already be inside the room.
So they began to suspect he was a fox.
But observing Hú’s intentions, they found nothing malicious,
so they treated him with respect and courtesy,
not letting his peculiarities affect their manners.
Hú learned that the host had a daughter
and sought to marry her,
hinting at it repeatedly,
but the host pretended not to understand.
One day,
Hú took leave and departed.
The next day,
a guest came to visit,
leading a black donkey at the gate.
The host welcomed him inside.
The guest was over fifty years old,
his clothes and shoes fresh and clean,
and his demeanor serene and elegant.
After sitting down,
he introduced himself,
and they learned he was acting as a matchmaker for the Hú family.
The host fell silent,
and after a long while said:
"I and Mr. Hú
are already close friends—
why must we become relatives by marriage?
Moreover, my daughter is already betrothed.
Please convey my apologies to Mr. Hú."
The guest said:
"I know for certain that your daughter is still awaiting a match—
why do you refuse so firmly?"
He repeated his request several times,
but the host would not agree.
The guest looked embarrassed,
and said:
"The Hú family is also of a distinguished lineage—
why should they be considered inferior to you?"
The host told him frankly:
"There is no other reason—
I simply dislike that they are not of our kind."
Hearing this, the guest grew angry;
the host also became angry,
and their confrontation escalated.
The guest stood up
and grabbed the host.
The host ordered his servants to beat him and drive him out,
and the guest fled.
He left his donkey behind.
Looking at it,
its fur was black,
with drooping ears and a long tail—
a large creature.
When they tried to lead it, it would not move;
when they drove it, it collapsed at the slightest touch,
but it was merely a straw insect.
The host, seeing his words were angry,
knew there would be enmity,
and prepared defenses.
The next day,
indeed a great host of foxes arrived: some on horseback, some on foot,
some with spears, some with crossbows,
horses neighing, men clamoring,
their momentum fierce and overwhelming.
The host did not dare go out.
The foxes threatened to burn the house,
and the host grew even more fearful.
A strong man
led the family members out with shouts,
hurling stones and shooting arrows,
both sides clashing,
each suffering casualties.
The foxes gradually weakened,
and withdrew in disarray.
They left knives on the ground,
gleaming like frost and snow;
but when picked up close,
they were sorghum leaves.
Everyone laughed and said:
"Their tricks are only this much."
Yet fearing they would return,
they prepared even more.
The next day,
as everyone was gathered talking,
suddenly a giant descended from the sky: over ten feet tall,
several feet wide;
wielding a door-like broadsword,
he chased and killed people.
The group grabbed arrows and stones and struck him wildly,
and he toppled over dead—
it was a straw effigy.
Everyone grew even more contemptuous.
For three days the foxes did not return,
and everyone relaxed somewhat.
The host happened to go to the outhouse,
and soon saw fox soldiers,
arriving with drawn bows and arrows,
shooting wildly at him;
arrows stuck in his buttocks.
Greatly frightened,
he hurriedly shouted for everyone to rush and fight,
and the foxes then left.
Pulling out the arrows to look,
they were all mugwort stems.
This went on for over a month,
their comings and goings irregular,
though not very harmful,
yet requiring daily vigilance,
and the host was troubled and distressed by it.
One day,
Hú Shēng led a group to the house.
The host went out in person,
and Hú, seeing him,
hid among the crowd.
The host called to him,
and with no alternative,
he came out.
The host said:
"I consider myself to have shown no disrespect to you, sir;
why then raise arms?"
The group of foxes wanted to shoot,
but Hú stopped them.
The host stepped forward, took his hand,
and invited him into the old study,
setting out wine to entertain him.
Calmly he said:
"You, sir, are an enlightened man,
surely you will understand.
Given our friendship,
would I not gladly join in marriage?
But your carriages, horses, and palaces
are mostly unlike those of humans;
for my frail daughter to follow you,
even you, sir, must know it is not possible.
Moreover, as the saying goes:
'Fruits plucked unripe are unpleasant to taste.'
What gain is there for you, sir, in this?"
Hú was greatly ashamed.
The host said:
"No harm done,
our old friendship remains.
If you do not reject us for our dusty impurity,
my young son at home,
fifteen years old,
wishes to become your son-in-law.
I wonder if you have a suitable match?"
Hú happily said:
"I have a younger sister,
one year younger than your young master,
not at all ugly or inferior.
To serve with broom and dustpan,
how would that be?"
The host rose and bowed,
and Hú returned the bow.
Then they drank to each other very merrily,
forgetting all past grievances.
He ordered wine and food set out,
rewarding all the attendants,
and everyone was joyful and pleased.
Then he inquired in detail about their residence,
intending to send betrothal gifts.
Hú declined.
As dusk fell, candles were lit,
and they drank until tipsy before parting.
From then on, peace prevailed.
Over a year later,
Hú had not come.
Some suspected his promise was false,
but the host steadfastly waited.
Another half year passed,
when Hú suddenly arrived.
After exchanging pleasantries,
he said:
"My younger sister has grown up.
Please choose an auspicious date,
so she may be sent to serve her parents-in-law."
The host was delighted,
and together they set a date before Hú left.
That night,
indeed a carriage and horses delivered the bride.
Her dowry was lavish and abundant,
filling the room almost completely.
The bride met her parents-in-law,
gentle and beautiful beyond ordinary.
The host was overjoyed.
Hú Shēng and a younger brother came to escort the girl,
their conversation refined and elegant,
and they were also good drinkers.
They left at dawn.
Moreover, the bride could foretell whether the year would bring abundance or scarcity,
so plans for livelihood
all followed her guidance.
Hú Shēng and his brothers, as well as an elderly woman of the Hú family,
occasionally came to visit the girl,
and everyone saw them.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
There was a performer of the barrel trick;
the barrel could hold a shēng measure;
it had no bottom,
was hollow inside,
just like common tricks.
The performer laid two mats on the street,
took a shēng measure and put it into the barrel;
spinning it out,
immediately the shēng was full of white rice,
which he poured onto the mat;
fetching more and pouring again,
in a moment both mats were full.
Then he measured it all back in,
finished and lifted the barrel,
and it was still empty.
The wonder lay in the quantity.
Lìjīn's Lǐ Jiàntián,
while leisurely visiting the pottery kilns at Yánzhèn,
wanted to buy a large urn,
haggled over the price with the potter,
failed to agree, and left.
That night,
over sixty urns remained unfired in the kiln,
but upon opening, they were all empty.
The potter was greatly alarmed,
suspected Lǐ,
and went to his door to seek them.
Lǐ apologized, saying he did not know.
The potter pleaded earnestly,
and then he said:
"I took them out of the kiln for you,
not a single urn damaged;
aren't they at the foot of Kuíxīng Lóu?"
Going to look as told,
indeed every one was there.
The tower was on the southern hill of the town,
over three lǐ from the kiln.
Hired laborers moved them,
taking three days to finish.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
In Jǐ'nán, there was a monk,
unknown from where.
Barefoot, wearing a patchwork robe,
daily at places like Fúróng Guǎn and Mínghú Guǎn,
he chanted scriptures and sought alms.
Offered wine, food, money, or grain,
he would not accept;
asked what he needed,
he gave no answer.
Throughout the day, no one ever saw him eat a meal.
Someone advised him, saying:
"Since you, Master, do not consume meat or wine,
you should seek alms in remote mountain villages and secluded alleys.
Why do you come and go daily in these bustling, foul-smelling markets?"
The monk closed his eyes and chanted scriptures,
his eyelashes as long as a finger,
as if he did not hear.
After a short while,
the person spoke to him again.
The monk abruptly opened his eyes and said sternly:
"I must beg for alms this way!"
And he resumed his chanting without cease.
After a long time,
he got up and left on his own.
Someone followed behind him,
persistently questioning why he absolutely had to act this way,
but he walked on without responding.
After being pressed several times,
he again said sternly:
"This is not for you to know!
This old monk must beg for alms this way!"
After several days had passed,
he suddenly went out of the southern city gate,
lay down by the roadside as if dead,
and did not move for three days.
The local residents, fearing he would starve to death
and become a burden to the outskirts of the city,
gathered to persuade him to move elsewhere,
offering to give him food if he wanted food,
and money if he wanted money.
The monk lay with closed eyes, unmoving.
The crowd shook him and spoke to him.
The monk became enraged,
drew a short knife from his robe,
and slit open his own abdomen;
reaching his hand inside,
he pulled out his intestines onto the road,
and then his breath ceased.
The horrified crowd reported it to the commandery authorities,
who buried him in a rough coffin.
Some days later, dogs dug into the grave,
exposing the matting.
When stepped on, it seemed hollow;
upon opening it to look,
the matting was sealed as before,
but it was empty like a silkworm cocoon.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
A certain Grand Historian
was bewitched by a fox,
and fell ill, becoming emaciated.
After exhausting all methods of charms and exorcisms,
he requested leave to return home,
hoping he could escape.
The Grand Historian departed,
but the fox followed him.
Greatly terrified,
he could think of no plan.
One day,
he stopped at Zhuō.
Outside the gate was an itinerant doctor with a bell,
who claimed he could subdue foxes.
The Grand Historian invited him in.
The doctor administered medicine to him,
which turned out to be an aphrodisiac.
Urged to take it immediately,
once he engaged with the fox,
he became fiercely unstoppable.
The fox retreated in fear,
pleading pitifully to stop;
he would not listen,
and pressed on even more vigorously.
The fox struggled and tried to escape,
but found it impossible to get away.
After a while, there was no sound;
looking at it,
the fox had revealed its true form and died.
In the past, there was a certain scholar in my hometown,
who had a reputation for being exceptionally virile,
and said he had never once experienced true satisfaction in his life.
One night, he lodged in a solitary inn,
with no neighbors on any side.
Suddenly, a woman came rushing in;
the door had not been opened, yet she was already inside.
Knowing in his heart she was a fox,
he was nonetheless delighted and happily engaged in intimate relations with her.
Just as her garments were loosened,
he penetrated straight through like an arrow piercing leather.
The fox cried out in shock and pain,
its shrieks sharp and shrill;
like a hawk escaping its bonds,
it fled through the window and was gone.
The scholar still gazed out the window, making coaxing, intimate sounds,
calling to it mournfully,
hoping it would return,
but all was already silent.
This man was truly a fierce general in the campaign against foxes!
He should post a sign on his gate
reading "Fox Exorcist,"
and make it his profession.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Lord Qū, the Silver Terrace official of Wūlíng,
was reading in his upstairs study.
During an overcast, gloomy, rainy spell,
he saw a tiny creature,
glowing like a firefly,
crawling along.
Where it passed,
it left a trail black as a slug's track.
Gradually, it coiled its way up the scroll,
and the scroll became scorched.
Realizing it might be a dragon,
he respectfully picked up the scroll to escort it out.
Reaching the doorway,
he stood holding it for a long time,
but it remained curled up, not moving in the slightest.
The lord said:
"Could it be you think I am not respectful enough?"
He took the scroll back,
placed it again on the desk,
and, donning his official cap and belt, made a deep bow to see it off.
Just as he reached the eaves,
he saw it raise its head and suddenly stretch out,
leaving the scroll and flying off horizontally,
with a hissing sound,
a streak of light like a thread;
a few paces away,
it turned its head back toward the lord,
and its head was now larger than a jar,
its body dozens of arm-spans around;
with another twist and turn,
a thunderclap shook the heavens,
and it soared into the clouds and was gone.
Looking back at the path it had taken,
he saw it had indeed come winding out from within the scroll case.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
When Gāo Míngtú served as prefect of Chēnzhōu,
there was a commoner's daughter, Sū-shì,
who was washing clothes in the river.
In the river was a large rock,
and the girl was perched upon it.
There was a strand of moss,
green and slippery, lovely to behold,
floating and undulating on the water,
that circled the rock three times.
The girl looked at it,
and her heart was stirred.
After returning home, she became pregnant,
and her belly gradually grew large.
Her mother questioned her privately,
and the girl told her the truth.
Her mother could not understand it.
After several months,
she actually gave birth to a son.
She considered abandoning him in a narrow alley,
but the girl could not bear it,
so she hid him in a chest and raised him.
She then vowed not to marry,
to demonstrate her unwavering fidelity.
However, becoming pregnant without a husband
was ultimately a source of shame for her.
By the time the child was seven years old,
he had never been brought out to be seen by others.
The child suddenly said to his mother:
"I am gradually growing up.
How can this confinement last long?
I will leave,
so as not to be a burden to you, Mother."
She asked where he would go.
He said:
"I am not of human stock.
I am about to soar among the clouds and look down over valleys."
The girl tearfully asked when he would return.
He replied:
"Wait until you, Mother, are on the verge of death,
then I will come.
After I leave,
if you should ever have any needs,
you can open the chest where I was hidden and seek within,
and you will certainly get your wish."
Having said this,
he bowed to his mother and then departed.
She went out to watch him,
but he had already vanished without a trace.
The girl told her mother,
and her mother found it exceedingly strange.
The girl held firmly to her old resolve,
and lived with her mother,
but the family grew increasingly impoverished.
One morning, they had no food for breakfast,
and gazing at the roof, she had no plan.
Suddenly she remembered her son's words,
went to open the chest,
and indeed found rice,
relying on it to light the fire.
From then on, whatever she asked for, it was granted.
After three years,
her mother fell ill and died;
all the burial necessities,
were taken from the chest.
After the burial,
the girl lived alone for thirty years,
never once looking out the door.
One day,
a neighbor woman came to borrow fire,
saw her sitting motionless in the empty room,
and after talking for a while, finally left.
Not long after,
suddenly colorful clouds were seen encircling the girl's house,
rising gracefully like a canopy,
and within them stood a person in splendid attire.
Looking closely,
it was Sū Nǚ.
She hovered for a long time,
gradually rising higher until she disappeared.
The neighbors all wondered about it.
Peeking into her room,
they saw the girl sitting still in beautiful attire,
but her breath had already ceased.
Since she had no one to rely on,
they discussed arranging her funeral.
Suddenly a young man entered,
handsome and majestic in appearance,
and thanked the crowd.
The neighbors had previously heard in secret that the girl had a son,
so they did not doubt him.
The young man used money to bury his mother,
planted two peach trees by the grave,
then bid farewell and left.
After a few steps,
clouds formed beneath his feet,
and he could no longer be seen.
Later, the peach trees bore sweet and fragrant fruit,
and the local people called them
"Sūxiān Táo,"
the trees flourishing year after year,
never withering.
Officials stationed there
often took the fruit to give as gifts to relatives and friends.
According to the "Liáozhāi Zhìyì" Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy
Lǐ Shēng Bóyán,
was from Yíshuǐ.
He was upright and courageous.
Suddenly he fell seriously ill,
and his family offered him medicine,
but he refused, saying:
"My illness cannot be cured by medicine;
the position of Yánluó in the underworld is vacant,
and they want me to temporarily take up his duties.
Do not bury me when I die,
but wait."
That day, he indeed died.
Attendants guided him away,
and he entered a palace,
where he was presented with ceremonial robes;
clerks and officials waited respectfully in solemn order.
On the desk were piles of documents.
One case,
involved a certain man from Jiāngnán,
who was found to have privately seduced eighty-two women from good families in his lifetime.
When interrogated,
the evidence was undeniable.
According to underworld law,
he deserved the punishment of burning on a bronze pillar.
Below the hall stood a bronze pillar,
eight or nine feet high,
about an arm's span in circumference;
it was hollow inside and filled with burning charcoal,
glowing red hot inside and out.
A group of demons drove him with iron-spiked whips to climb it,
and he moved his hands and coiled his feet to ascend.
Just as he reached the top,
smoke and flames billowed,
and with a loud crack like a firecracker,
he fell;
curled up for a while,
he then revived.
They whipped him again,
and he exploded and fell as before.
After the third fall,
he scattered on the ground like smoke,
and could no longer take form.
Another case involved
a fellow townsman named Wáng,
who was sued by a maidservant's father for unlawfully possessing his daughter.
Wáng was a relative by marriage of the living.
Previously,
someone had sold a maidservant.
Wáng knew her origin was improper,
but tempted by the low price,
he purchased her.
Then Wáng suddenly died.
The next day,
his friend Zhōu met him on the road,
realized he was a ghost,
and fled into his study to hide.
Wáng followed him inside.
Terrified, Zhōu prayed and
asked what he wanted.
Wáng said:
"I just need you to bear witness for me in the underworld court."
Zhōu asked in alarm:
"What matter?"
Wáng replied:
"I bought that maidservant at a fair price,
but now I'm wrongly accused.
You witnessed this yourself;
I only ask you to speak truthfully,
nothing more."
Zhōu firmly refused.
Wáng left, saying:
"I'm afraid it won't be up to you."
Not long after,
Zhōu indeed died,
and they went together to face trial before Yánluó.
When Lǐ saw Wáng,
he secretly felt inclined to favor him.
Suddenly, fire erupted in the hall,
flames licking the beams and pillars.
Lǐ was greatly alarmed
and stood aside nervously.
A clerk hurried forward and said:
"The underworld is not like the human world;
a single selfish thought cannot be tolerated.
Quickly dismiss that thought,
and the fire will extinguish itself."
Lǐ collected his spirit and calmed his mind,
and the fire immediately went out.
Then the trial proceeded;
Wáng and the maidservant's father argued back and forth bitterly.
When Zhōu was questioned,
he told the truth.
Wáng was sentenced to caning for intentional offense.
After the caning,
they were both sent back to life.
Both Zhōu and Wáng revived after three days.
After Lǐ finished his duties,
he returned by carriage.
On the way, he saw hundreds of ghosts with severed heads and broken legs,
kneeling on the ground wailing pitifully.
He stopped his carriage to inquire,
and learned they were ghosts from other regions
who longed to return to their native lands,
but feared barriers and checkpoints would block them,
so they begged for travel passes.
Lǐ said:
"I acted as substitute for only three days
and have already stepped down;
how can I help?"
The crowd said:
"Hú Shēng of South Village
is about to hold a religious ceremony;
if you convey our request, it can be done."
Lǐ agreed.
Arriving home,
his attendants all left,
and Lǐ then revived.
Hú Shēng, styled Shuǐxīn,
was on good terms with Lǐ.
Hearing Lǐ had returned to life,
he went to visit him.
Lǐ abruptly asked:
"When is the purification ceremony?"
Hú exclaimed in surprise:
"After the ravages of war,
my wife and children barely survived.
I once made this vow with my wife,
but haven't told a soul.
How did you know?"
Lǐ told him everything.
Hú sighed:
"A single word spoken in the inner chamber
was broadcast in the underworld—
how frightening!"
He then respectfully agreed and left.
The next day,
Lǐ went to Wáng's place;
Wáng was still lying down exhausted.
Seeing Lǐ,
he rose respectfully
and expressed gratitude for his protection.
Lǐ said:
"The law cannot show leniency.
Are you fortunately unharmed now?"
Wáng said:
"There are no other symptoms,
only the caning wounds are festering with pus."
After more than twenty days he finally recovered;
the flesh on his buttocks had rotted away,
leaving scars as if from caning.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Punishments in the underworld
are more cruel than in the mortal world;
their judgments are also harsher.
However, since influence-peddling doesn't work there,
those who suffer cruelty bear no resentment.
Who says the grave lacks the light of justice?
It's just a pity there's no fire to burn down the halls of those who oppress the people!"
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Hé Shīcān,
styled Zǐxiāo,
lived in a studio east of the Tiáoxī River,
facing open wilderness.
One evening he went out and
saw a woman riding a donkey approach,
followed by a youth.
The woman appeared about fifty,
with an elegant and refined demeanor.
Turning to look at the youth,
he seemed about fifteen or sixteen,
with beauty surpassing that of a lovely girl.
Hé had always had a fondness for male beauty.
Seeing him,
he was utterly captivated;
he stood on tiptoe watching until
their shadows vanished before returning.
The next day,
he waited early.
As dusk fell,
the youth finally passed by.
Hé eagerly greeted him,
smiling and asking where he came from.
He replied
"from my maternal grandfather's house."
Hé invited him to rest awhile in his studio;
he declined, saying he had no time.
Hé insistently pulled him,
and he entered.
After sitting briefly, he rose to leave,
firmly refusing to stay.
Hé held his hand seeing him off,
earnestly urging him to visit when passing by.
The youth assented and left.
From then on, Hé yearned for him intensely,
gazing back and forth,
unable to stand still.
One day,
as the sun was setting halfway below the horizon,
the young man arrived.
Overjoyed,
Shēng invited him in,
and ordered his study attendant to serve wine.
He asked the young man’s name,
to which he replied:
"My surname is Huáng,
and I am the ninth son.
As a youth, I have no courtesy name."
Shēng asked:
"Why do you pass by here so frequently?"
He replied:
"My mother is staying at my maternal grandfather’s house,
and she is often ill,
so I visit her frequently."
After several rounds of wine,
he wished to take his leave.
Shēng grabbed his arm to detain him,
and locked the door.
Jiǔláng had no choice,
and reluctantly sat down again.
By lamplight, they chatted together;
his demeanor was as gentle as a maiden’s;
but when the conversation turned to playful matters,
he would become bashful,
turning his face toward the wall.
Before long,
Shēng invited him to share the same quilt.
Jiǔláng refused,
firmly excusing himself on the grounds of having poor sleeping habits.
After repeated urging,
he finally removed his outer garments,
and lay on the bed wearing only his trousers.
Shēng extinguished the lamp;
after a short while,
he moved to share the same pillow,
curving his elbow over Jiǔláng’s thigh and embracing him intimately,
earnestly seeking intimacy.
Jiǔláng angrily said:
"I thought you were a refined gentleman,
which is why I lingered with you;
but to act like this—
is to treat me like a beast and love me like an animal!"
Before long,
as the morning stars twinkled faintly,
Jiǔláng left directly.
Shēng feared he would cut off contact for good,
so he watched for him again,
pacing anxiously and gazing intently,
his eyes piercing the Northern Dipper.
After several days,
Jiǔláng finally arrived.
Shēng joyfully welcomed him and apologized for his offense;
he pulled him forcefully into the study,
urged him to sit and chatted with him merrily,
secretly relieved that Jiǔláng did not hold a grudge.
Not long after,
removing his shoes and climbing onto the bed,
he again pleaded pitifully.
Jiǔláng said:
"Your affectionate feelings
have already been engraved in my heart;
but why must affection be expressed in this way?"
Shēng sweet-talked and persisted,
only asking to touch his jade-like skin once.
Jiǔláng consented.
Shēng waited until he was asleep,
then stealthily approached to take liberties.
Jiǔláng awoke,
grabbed his clothes and rose abruptly,
fleeing under cover of night.
Shēng was despondent as if he had lost something,
forgetting to eat and neglecting sleep,
growing increasingly haggard day by day.
He only sent his study attendant out daily to patrol and watch for him.
One day,
Jiǔláng passed by the door,
and was about to go straight past.
The attendant pulled him by the sleeve and brought him in.
Seeing Shēng’s emaciated appearance,
he was greatly shocked,
and inquired with concern.
Shēng truthfully told him the situation,
tears streaming down with his words.
Jiǔláng said softly:
"My humble intention
was truly that such affection would bring no benefit to me,
but would harm you,
which is why I did not agree.
Since you find pleasure in it,
why should I begrudge it?"
Shēng was overjoyed.
After Jiǔláng left,
his illness suddenly diminished,
and within a few days he recovered.
Jiǔláng indeed came,
and they became deeply attached.
He said:
"Now I reluctantly comply with your wishes,
but I hope you will not make this a regular occurrence."
After a while, he said:
"I have a request to make;
would you be willing to help?"
Shēng asked what it was,
and he replied:
"My mother suffers from heart pain,
and only Imperial Physician Qí Yěwáng’s Xiāntiān Dān can cure it.
You are on good terms with him,
so you should be able to obtain it."
Shēng promised.
Before leaving, Jiǔláng reminded him again.
Shēng went into the city to seek the medicine,
and by evening he gave it to him.
Jiǔláng was pleased,
and raised his hands in gratitude.
Shēng again insisted on intimacy.
Jiǔláng said:
"Do not persist in this.
I will carefully find a beautiful woman for you,
far superior to me."
Shēng asked who.
Jiǔláng said:
"I have a cousin,
unparalleled in beauty.
If you can show interest,
I will act as matchmaker."
Shēng smiled faintly and did not reply.
Jiǔláng took the medicine and left.
Three days later, he returned,
again asking for medicine.
Shēng resented his delay,
and his words were full of reproach.
Jiǔláng said:
"Originally, I could not bear to bring misfortune upon you,
so I kept my distance;
since you do not understand,
please do not regret it later."
From then on, they met every evening without fail.
Every three days, Jiǔláng would ask for medicine once.
Qí Yěwáng found this frequency strange,
and said:
"No one has ever taken this medicine more than three doses;
why has the illness not healed after so long?"
He then wrapped three doses together and gave them to him.
He also looked at Shēng and said:
"Your complexion is dark and gloomy;
are you ill?"
Shēng said:
"No."
Taking his pulse,
Qí was startled and said:
"You have a ghostly pulse,
the illness lies in the Shàoyīn meridian;
if you do not take care, it will be dangerous!"
Shēng told Jiǔláng about this upon returning.
Jiǔláng sighed and said:
"He is an excellent physician!
I am actually a fox,
and prolonged contact with me may not bring you good fortune."
Shēng suspected he was deceiving him,
so he hid some of the medicine,
not giving it all to him,
fearing he would not return.
Not long after,
Shēng indeed fell ill.
He summoned Qí for diagnosis,
who said:
"Previously you did not tell the truth;
now your soul has already wandered to the wilderness;
what can even Qín Huǎn do?"
Jiǔláng came daily to visit and attend to him,
saying:
"You did not listen to my words,
and now it has come to this!"
Shēng soon died.
Jiǔláng wept bitterly and left.
Previously,
in the county there was a certain Grand Historian,
who in his youth had shared brush and inkstone with Hé Zǐxiāo;
at seventeen, he was selected for the Hànlín Academy.
At that time, the Prince of Qín was greedy and cruel,
and bribed court officials,
with none daring to speak out.
The Grand Historian submitted a memorial denouncing his wickedness,
but was dismissed for overstepping his authority.
The Prince was promoted to Provincial Censor of that province,
and daily watched for an opportunity against the Grand Historian.
The Grand Historian had enjoyed a reputation for brilliance since youth,
and had once attracted the favor of a rebellious prince;
the Prince of Qín thus purchased old letters of correspondence between them,
and used them to threaten the Grand Historian.
Fearing for his life,
he hanged himself.
His wife also took her own life by hanging.
A day later, the Grand Historian suddenly awoke,
saying:
"I am Hé Zǐxiāo."
When questioned,
everything he said pertained to Hé family affairs,
and they realized his soul had returned in another's body.
They could not keep him,
so he fled to his old residence.
The local magistrate suspected deceit,
and was determined to frame him,
sending someone to demand a thousand taels of silver from him.
Hé Zǐxiāo pretended to agree,
but was overwhelmed with worry and despair.
Suddenly, Jiǔláng arrived,
and Hé Zǐxiāo joyfully conversed with him,
their emotions mingling sorrow and happiness.
He then wished to resume their intimate relations.
Jiǔláng said:
"Do you have three lives to spare?"
Hé Zǐxiāo replied:
"I regret that life is toilsome;
death would be more restful."
He then poured out his grievances and suffering.
Jiǔláng pondered deeply with concern.
After a while, he said:
"Fortunately, we are reunited in life.
You are alone without a partner;
I mentioned my cousin before—
she is intelligent, beautiful, and resourceful,
and will surely share your burdens."
Hé Zǐxiāo wished to see her face.
Jiǔláng said:
"That is not difficult.
Tomorrow she will come to accompany my elderly mother,
and will pass this way.
Pretend to be my sworn brother,
and I will pretend to be thirsty and ask for a drink.
You say, 'The donkey has run away,'
and I will agree."
Having settled the plan, they parted.
At noon the next day,
Jiǔláng indeed passed by the gate with the young lady.
Hé Zǐxiāo clasped his hands and chatted incessantly with him.
Glancing briefly at the young lady,
he saw her brows were delicate and graceful,
truly a fairy maiden.
Jiǔláng asked for tea,
and Hé Zǐxiāo invited them in to drink.
Jiǔláng said:
"Third Sister, do not be alarmed;
this is my sworn brother,
it is fine to rest here briefly."
Helping her down,
he tethered the donkey at the gate and entered.
Hé Zǐxiāo personally rose to brew tea.
Then, looking at Jiǔláng, he said:
"Your previous words did not do her justice.
Now I have found the place to die!"
The young lady seemed to understand his words referred to her,
rose from the couch,
and said in a soft voice:
"Let us leave!"
Hé Zǐxiāo looked outside and said:
"The donkey has run away!"
Jiǔláng rushed out in haste.
Hé Zǐxiāo embraced the young lady and sought union.
Her face flushed crimson,
and she was as distressed as a trapped prisoner,
calling loudly for Ninth Brother,
but there was no response.
She said:
"You already have a wife;
why destroy my modesty and honor?"
Hé Zǐxiāo declared he had no wife.
The young lady said:
"If you can swear by the mountains and rivers
not to cast me aside like an autumn fan,
then I will obey your wishes."
Hé Zǐxiāo then swore by the sun.
The young lady offered no further resistance.
After the affair,
Jiǔláng arrived.
The young lady, flushed with anger, reproached him.
Jiǔláng said:
"This is Hé Zǐxiāo,
formerly a renowned scholar,
now a Grand Historian.
He and I are closest friends,
and he is someone you can rely on.
Even if my aunt hears of it,
she surely will not blame us."
As evening approached,
Hé Zǐxiāo urged them to stay and would not let them leave.
The young lady feared her aunt would be shocked and suspicious.
Jiǔláng boldly took responsibility,
mounted the donkey, and rode straight off.
After several days,
a woman passed by with a maidservant,
around forty years of age,
her demeanor and bearing
very much resembling Sānniáng.
Hé Zǐxiāo called the young lady to come and look,
and indeed it was her mother.
Catching sight of her daughter,
the mother asked in surprise:
"How did you come to be here?"
The young lady was too ashamed to answer.
Hé Zǐxiāo invited the mother in,
bowed, and explained the situation.
The mother smiled and said:
"Jiǔláng is so childish—
why did he not consult me again?"
The young lady went into the kitchen,
prepared food for her mother,
and after the meal, her mother departed.
The gentleman obtained a beautiful companion,
which greatly pleased his heart's desires;
yet a sense of foreboding lingered in his heart,
and he constantly wore a worried, frowning expression.
The woman asked him about it,
and the gentleman recounted the whole story from beginning to end.
The woman laughed and said:
"This is something only Ninth Brother can resolve,
why are you worried?"
The gentleman inquired about the reason.
The woman said:
"I have heard that Governor Fǔ indulges in music and song and is fond of handsome youths,
these are precisely Ninth Brother's strengths.
Present him with what he fancies,
and your resentment can be dissolved,
your grievance can also be avenged."
The gentleman worried that Ninth Brother would be unwilling.
The woman said:
"Just plead with him earnestly."
The next day,
the gentleman saw Ninth Brother coming,
and went out to meet him.
Ninth Brother said in surprise:
"We are friends across two lifetimes,
I would only seek to serve you,
not sparing even my head or heels.
Why do you suddenly adopt such a manner towards me?"
The gentleman fully informed him of the plan.
Ninth Brother showed a troubled expression.
The woman said:
"I gave myself to you,
who was truly responsible for that?
If you were to perish midway,
where would that leave me?"
Ninth Brother had no choice,
and agreed.
The gentleman then plotted with him,
sending a swift letter to the well-regarded Grand Historian Wáng,
and presented Ninth Brother to him.
Wáng understood their intent,
prepared a grand feast,
and invited Governor Fǔ to drink.
He had Ninth Brother dress as a maiden,
performing the Tiānmó dance,
looking exactly like a beautiful woman.
Governor Fǔ was captivated,
and urgently entreated Wáng,
wishing to purchase Ninth Brother with a heavy sum of gold,
fearing only that it might not be acceptable.
Wáng deliberately pondered deeply to make it difficult for him.
After a long delay,
he finally presented him on the gentleman's behalf.
Governor Fǔ was delighted,
and his previous grievances vanished entirely.
From the moment he obtained Ninth Brother,
they were inseparable in every movement and rest;
his more than ten concubines
he regarded as mere dust.
Ninth Brother's food, drink, and provisions were like those of a king;
he was bestowed with gold amounting to tens of thousands.
After half a year,
Governor Fǔ fell ill.
Ninth Brother knew he was nearing the road to the underworld,
so he transported the gold and silks by carriage,
and returned them to the gentleman's home under pretext.
Soon after, Governor Fǔ passed away.
Ninth Brother used his funds,
built houses and acquired utensils,
kept maids and servants,
and settled the mother, son, and aunt together there.
When Ninth Brother went out,
his carriages and horses were exceedingly splendid,
and people did not know he was a fox.
I have a
"Laughing Judgment"
and record it here as well: Man and woman dwelling together,
is the great principle of husband and wife;
dry and moist interchanging,
is the proper aperture of yīn and yáng.
Facing the wind and awaiting the moon,
still invites criticism of transgressing bounds;
cutting sleeves and sharing peaches,
hardly avoids the shame of covering one's nose.
One must be a man of strength,
to dare open the bird's path;
if the cave is not Táoyuán,
how can the fisherman's pole mistakenly enter?
Now a certain one follows the lower current and forgets to return,
abandons the right path and does not follow it.
Clouds and rain have not risen,
yet already he moves his hands up and down;
yīn and yáng are turned back to back,
actually conspiring inside and out.
Placing the flowery pool in a useless land,
falsely claims the old monk enters meditation;
the barbarian cave is a barren place,
thus making the one-eyed commander raise his spear.
Tethering the red hare before the camp gate,
as if about to shoot the halberd;
reaching for the great bow in the state treasury,
directly desires to break through the pass.
Perhaps it is the yellow within the prison,
visiting an old friend last night;
clearly the vermilion plum of the Wáng family,
seeking recompense for drilling in the next life.
That black pine forest, where armed horses suddenly come,
indeed finds mutual peace;
suppose the yellow dragon mansion, where the tide suddenly arrives,
how can one withstand it?
Should sever the root of his drilling and stabbing,
and also block the path of sending and welcoming.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A resident of Yíshuǐ, Zhào Mǒu,
returning from the city for some reason,
saw a woman in white weeping by the roadside,
very sorrowful.
Glancing at her,
she was beautiful.
He was pleased by her,
and stared fixedly without leaving.
The woman said tearfully:
"You, sir,
do not go on your way but gaze at me!"
Zhào said:
"I, seeing the wilderness empty of people,
and you weeping so bitterly,
truly felt sorrow in my heart."
The woman said:
"My husband is dead and I have no road to take,
hence my sorrow."
Zhào urged her to choose another good match.
She said:
"Alone in this vast world,
how can I choose?
If I find someone to rely on,
being a concubine would suffice."
Zhào gladly offered himself,
and the woman consented.
Zhào, because his home was far,
wanted to find a means of transport.
The woman said:
"No need."
Then she went ahead,
floating like an immortal running.
Upon reaching home,
she diligently performed household chores.
After more than two years had passed,
she said to Zhào:
"Moved by your lingering affection,
I rashly followed you,
and suddenly three years have passed.
Now I should leave."
Zhào said:
"Earlier you said you had no family,
where will you go now?"
She said:
"At that time I casually said such words,
how could I have no family?
My father sells medicine in Jīnlíng.
If you wish to meet again,
you can bring medicine there,
and I can help with travel expenses."
Zhào made arrangements,
and hired a carriage and horse.
The woman declined them,
went out the door and left directly;
he could not catch up to her,
and in an instant she vanished.
After a long time had passed,
he began to feel quite nostalgic,
so he bought some medicine and went to Jīnlíng.
He stored his goods at an inn,
and went searching through the streets and markets.
Suddenly, an old man at a medicine shop saw him and exclaimed,
My son-in-law has arrived!”
He invited him inside.
His daughter was washing clothes in the courtyard,
and when she saw him, she neither spoke nor smiled,
continuing to wash without pause.
Zhào, bearing resentment, abruptly left.
The old man pulled him back in.
The woman paid him no mind, just as before.
The old man ordered a meal to be prepared.
He planned to give him a generous gift,
but his daughter stopped him, saying,
His fortune is meager,
and too much will be more than he can bear.
It would be better to slightly ease his hardships,
and then select a dozen or so medical prescriptions to give him,
so he will have more than enough to live on.”
The old man asked about the medicine he had brought.
The woman said,
It has already been sold,
and the money is right here.”
The old man then gave him the prescriptions and the money,
and sent Zhào on his way.
When he tried the prescriptions,
they proved remarkably effective.
In Yíshuǐ, there are still those who know these prescriptions.
One of them involves catching rainwater from the thatched eaves with a garlic mortar,
and using it to wash warts and growths—
it is one of the prescriptions,
and works very well.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
Lord Tāng, named Pìn,
was a Jìnshì of the Xīnchǒu year.
He fell ill and was on the brink of death.
Suddenly, he felt a surge of heat rising from his lower body upward:
when it reached his thighs,
his feet died;
when it reached his abdomen,
his thighs died in turn;
when it reached his heart,
the death of the heart was the most difficult.
All the events from his childhood,
down to the trivial matters long forgotten,
came flooding back with the surge of blood in his heart,
each one washing over him.
If it was a good deed,
his heart felt clear, pure, and tranquil;
if it was an evil deed,
he felt remorseful, agitated, and restless,
as if oil were boiling in a cauldron.
The unbearable state of it
could not be fully described with words.
He still remembered when he was seven or eight years old,
he had once taken a baby bird from its nest and killed it—
this single event alone
caused the hot blood in his heart to surge violently,
and it took the time of a meal for it to pass.
He had to wait until all the deeds of his lifetime
had washed over him one by one,
before he felt threads of heat
pierce through his throat into his brain,
and emerge from the crown of his head,
rising upward like steam from cooking.
After several dozen moments,
his soul finally left its shell,
forgetting its physical body.
But it drifted aimlessly with nowhere to return,
wandering along the paths of the outskirts.
A giant came,
nearly ten feet tall,
picked him up,
and placed him into his sleeve.
Inside the sleeve,
he was squeezed shoulder to shoulder and thigh to thigh,
with many others packed together.
The stifling heat and lack of air
were almost unbearable.
Lord Tāng suddenly thought that only Buddha could relieve his distress,
so he chanted the name of Buddha.
After only three or four recitations,
he drifted and fell out of the sleeve.
The giant put him back in.
Three times he was put in, and three times he fell out,
so the giant finally left him.
Lord Tāng stood alone, bewildered,
unsure of where to go.
Remembering that Buddha was in the Western Land,
he headed west.
Before long,
he saw a monk sitting cross-legged by the roadside.
He hurried over, bowed, and asked for directions.
The monk said,
The records of life and death for scholars
are managed by Wénchāng and Confucius.
You must have your name removed from both places
before you can go elsewhere.”
Lord Tāng asked where they resided,
and the monk showed him the way.
He hurried there.
Before long,
he arrived at the Temple of the Sage,
and saw Confucius sitting facing south.
He bowed and prayed as before.
Confucius said,
The removal of your name from the register
must still be done by the Emperor of the Eastern Peak.”
He then pointed the way.
Lord Tāng hurried there.
He saw a palace hall
like the residence of a king.
He bent down and entered,
and indeed, there was a deity
resembling the image of the Emperor of the Eastern Peak as commonly depicted.
He prostrated himself and prayed.
The Emperor of the Eastern Peak checked the register and said,
Your heart is sincere and upright,
so you should be restored to life.
But your physical body has decayed,
and only Bodhisattva can help.”
He then pointed the way and urged him to go quickly.
Lord Tāng followed his instructions.
Soon, he saw lush forests and tall bamboo,
with magnificent halls and pavilions.
He entered
and saw the dignified figure with a spiral-shaped topknot,
a golden countenance like the full moon;
a vase held willow branches,
their emerald green hanging like mist.
Lord Tāng bowed solemnly
and recounted what the Emperor of the Eastern Peak had said.
Bodhisattva found it difficult.
Lord Tāng pleaded and prayed without cease.
A venerable one beside him spoke up, saying,
If Bodhisattva employs his great power,
he can gather earth to make flesh
and break willow branches to make bones.”
Bodhisattva then granted the request,
breaking a willow branch with his hand,
pouring water from the vase,
and mixing it with pure earth to make mud,
which he patted onto Lord Tāng’s body.
He then had a young attendant lead him back to where his spirit resided
and pushed him to merge with it.
Moans and movements came from the coffin,
and suddenly, the illness was cured.
His family, astonished, gathered around,
helped him out,
and calculated that he had been dead for seven weeks.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
Lǐ Zhōngzhī, a Xiùcai from Láiwú,
was by nature straightforward, honest, and unyielding.
Every few days,
he would die,
lying stiff as a corpse,
and wake up three or four days later.
When asked what he had seen,
he kept it secret and did not reveal it.
At that time, there was a man named Zhāng in the county
who also died every few days.
He told people,
Lǐ Zhōngzhī is Yánluó.
When I go to the underworld,
I am also one of his subordinates.”
He could even recite
the couplets on the gates and halls of his residence.
Someone asked,
What did Lǐ do in the underworld yesterday?”
Zhāng said,
I cannot describe it in detail.
I only know he interrogated Cáo Cāo
and sentenced him to twenty lashes.”
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
The case of Ā Mán
must have passed through dozens of Yánluós by now.
The paths of beasts, the mountain of swords—
Yáng Yúwèi
moved to live by the Sìshuǐ River.
His study faced a vast wilderness,
and beyond the wall were many ancient graves.
At night, he would hear the white poplars rustling,
their sound like surging waves.
Late at night, holding a candle,
he would feel even more desolate and heartbroken.
Suddenly, from beyond the wall, someone chanted:
"In the dark night, a mournful wind blows backward,
fireflies brush the grass and cling to the curtains."
The chant was repeated over and over,
its sound sorrowful and bitter.
Listening closely,
it was delicate and gentle, like a woman's voice.
He was suspicious.
The next day,
he looked beyond the wall,
but there was no trace of anyone.
Only a purple sash
was left among the brambles;
he picked it up,
and placed it on the windowsill.
That night, around the second watch,
the chanting resumed as before.
Yáng moved a stool to look over the wall,
and the chanting abruptly stopped.
Realizing it was a ghost,
he nonetheless felt drawn and admiring.
The following night,
he lay in wait atop the wall.
As the first watch was nearing its end,
a woman emerged gracefully from the grass,
leaning on a small tree,
bowing her head and chanting mournfully.
Yáng gave a slight cough,
and the woman suddenly vanished into the wild grass.
From then on, Yáng waited beneath the wall,
and after hearing her finish her chant,
he continued from the other side of the wall:
"Who sees the hidden sorrow and bitter thoughts?
When emerald sleeves feel the chill as the moon rises."
For a long time,
there was silence.
Yáng then went inside.
Just as he sat down,
he suddenly saw a beautiful woman enter from outside,
who straightened her sleeves and said:
"You, sir, are truly a man of refinement,
yet I have been too fearful and evasive."
Yáng was delighted,
and pulled her to sit.
She was slender, timid, and seemed to hold a chill,
as if her clothes were too heavy for her.
He asked:
"Where is your home?
How long have you been lingering here?"
She replied:
"I am from Lǒngxī,
and drifted here with my father.
I died suddenly of a violent illness at seventeen,
and now it has been over twenty years.
In the netherworld's wilds,
I am as lonely and isolated as a wild duck.
The chants
are my own compositions,
to convey my hidden sorrows.
My thoughts had long been disconnected;
thanks to you continuing them for me,
joy has sprung even in the grave."
Yáng wished to be intimate with her.
Frowning, she said:
"A decaying bone from the dark realm
cannot compare to a living person.
If we were to share hidden pleasures,
it would shorten your lifespan.
I could not bear to bring misfortune upon you, sir."
Yáng then desisted.
Playfully, he reached to touch her chest,
and found the flesh like chicken heads,
still that of a maiden.
He then wanted to look at the tiny feet beneath her skirt.
The woman lowered her head and laughed:
"What a reckless scholar, too meddlesome!"
Yáng held and examined them,
and saw brocade stockings the color of moonlight,
tied with a strand of colored thread.
Looking at the other,
he saw it was fastened with a purple sash.
He asked:
"Why not wear both with sashes?"
She said:
"Last night, fearing you, I fled,
and do not know where I dropped it."
Yáng said:
"Let me replace it for you."
He then took the one from the windowsill and gave it to her.
Startled, she asked where it came from,
and he told her the truth.
The woman then removed the thread and tied on the sash.
Turning over the books on the table,
she suddenly saw "The Ballad of Liánchāng Palace,"
and said with emotion:
"When alive, I loved reading this most.
Now looking at it,
it is almost like a dream!"
Discussing poetry and literature with her,
she was clever and lovely.
Trimming the candle by the west window,
it was like gaining a good friend.
From then on, every night he would only hear soft chanting,
and shortly she would arrive.
She always urged him:
"Keep this secret, do not reveal it.
I am somewhat timid,
and fear malicious intruders might come to harm me."
Yáng agreed.
The two were as happy as fish in water,
though they did not cross into impropriety,
yet within the boudoir,
there were certainly things more intimate than painting eyebrows.
The woman often wrote out texts for Yáng by lamplight,
her handwriting elegant and charming.
She also selected a hundred palace poems herself,
copying and reciting them.
She had Yáng prepare a Go board,
and bought a pipa.
Every night she taught Yáng to play Go,
or else she would pluck the strings.
Playing
"Raindrops on Banana Leaves"
its melancholy pierced the heart;
Yáng could not bear to listen to the end,
so she played
"Orioles Singing at Dawn in the Garden"
and immediately he felt his heart lighten and comforted.
By lamplight, they engaged in playful games,
so happy they would forget the dawn.
Seeing the first light at the window,
she would hastily flee.
One day,
Xuē Shēng came to visit
and found Yáng asleep during the day.
Looking around the room,
he saw a pipa and a chessboard lying about,
and knew these were not Yáng's usual interests.
He then flipped through a book and found some palace-style poems,
and seeing the neat, elegant handwriting,
he grew even more suspicious.
When Yáng awoke,
Xuē asked him:
"Where did these playthings come from?"
Yáng replied:
"I wanted to learn them."
Xuē then asked about the poetry scroll,
and Yáng excused himself, saying he had borrowed it from a friend.
Xuē examined it repeatedly,
and on the last page, he saw a line written in small characters:
"Written on such-and-such a day by Lián Suǒ."
He laughed and said:
"This is a young lady's informal name—
why are you deceiving me so thoroughly?"
Yáng was greatly embarrassed
and could not find words to reply.
Xuē pressed him even more insistently,
but Yáng would not tell him.
Xuē rolled up the scroll and took it,
and Yáng, even more flustered,
finally told him the truth.
Xuē asked to see her once.
Yáng then recounted her instructions.
Xuē admired her eagerly;
Yáng had no choice
and agreed.
At midnight,
the girl arrived,
and Yáng conveyed Xuē's intentions to her.
The girl angrily said:
"What have you been saying?
You've already been chattering away to others!"
Yáng explained the actual situation.
The girl said:
"My bond with you is finished!"
Yáng tried to console and explain with a hundred words,
but she remained unhappy.
She rose to leave,
saying:
"I shall avoid this for now."
The next day,
Xuē came,
and Yáng conveyed on her behalf that it was not possible.
Xuē suspected it was an excuse.
In the evening, he came with two fellow students,
lingered and would not leave,
deliberately causing a disturbance: they made noise all night long,
greatly earning Yáng's disdainful looks,
but there was nothing he could do.
After several nights with no sign of her,
they gradually felt like leaving,
and the clamor slowly subsided.
Suddenly, they heard the sound of chanting poetry.
They all listened:
it was mournful and poignant to the extreme.
Just as Xuē was leaning in, utterly absorbed,
one among them, a military student named Wáng,
picked up a large rock and threw it,
shouting loudly:
"Putting on airs and not seeing guests—
how can that produce good lines?
All this whimpering and sorrow
makes one feel stifled!"
The chanting abruptly stopped.
The others were very annoyed with him.
Yáng's anger and resentment showed in his words and expression.
The next day,
they finally all left together.
Yáng stayed alone in the empty studio,
hoping the girl would return,
but there was not a trace of her.
After two days,
the girl suddenly came,
weeping and saying:
"You brought those awful guests—
they nearly scared me to death!"
Yáng hurriedly apologized.
The girl rushed out,
saying:
"I already said our bond was finished.
From now on, farewell."
By the time he tried to hold her back, she had vanished.
For over a month after that,
she did not come again.
Yáng missed her
until he grew gaunt and emaciated,
with no way to retrieve her.
One night,
he was drinking alone
when suddenly the girl lifted the curtain and entered.
Yáng was overjoyed
and said:
"Have you forgiven me?"
Tears streamed down the girl's chest,
and she remained silent.
Yáng urgently asked her,
and she seemed about to speak but held back,
finally saying:
"I left in a fit of pique,
and now, in urgency, I come seeking help—
it's hard to avoid feeling ashamed."
After Yáng pressed her repeatedly,
she said:
"I don't know where a filthy yamen runner came from,
forcing me to be his concubine.
Considering I am of pure descent,
how could I stoop to become the ghost of a lowly servant?
But with my frail, delicate frame,
how could I resist?
If you still count me among your intimate partners,
you surely will not let me manage this on my own."
Yáng was furious,
burning with the desire to fight to the death;
but he worried that humans and ghosts were of different realms,
and he might be powerless to help.
The girl said:
"Tomorrow night, go to sleep early,
and I will invite you into a dream."
So they conversed intimately again,
sitting together until dawn.
As the girl was leaving,
she instructed him not to sleep during the day,
but to stay awake and wait for their nighttime appointment.
Yáng agreed.
Therefore, in the afternoon he drank a little,
and while slightly intoxicated, he climbed into bed,
pulled the covers over himself and lay down.
Suddenly he saw the girl come,
hand him a dagger,
and lead him away by the hand.
They arrived at a courtyard house,
and just as they were closing the gate and talking,
they heard someone pounding on the gate with a stone.
The girl cried out in alarm:
"The enemy is here!"
Yáng opened the door and rushed out.
He saw a man in a red hat and black clothes,
with bristly hair around his mouth.
Yáng angrily shouted at him.
The runner glared back with hostility,
his words fierce and abusive.
Yáng, enraged,
charged at him.
The runner grabbed stones and hurled them,
swift as a sudden rainstorm;
one hit Yáng's wrist,
and he could no longer hold the dagger.
Just at this critical moment,
he saw someone in the distance,
with arrows at his waist, out hunting.
Looking closely,
it was Wáng Shēng.
Yáng shouted loudly for help.
