Wáng Shēng quickly drew his bow and arrived,
shooting the runner in the thigh;
he shot again,
and the runner fell dead.
Yáng joyfully thanked him.
Wáng asked what had happened,
and Yáng told him everything.
Wáng was pleased that his previous offense could now be redeemed,
and so he went with Yáng into the girl's room.
The girl trembled fearfully and shrank back shyly,
standing at a distance without saying a word.
On the table was a small knife,
only about a foot long,
but adorned with gold and jade. Taking it from its sheath,
its gleam was bright enough to reflect one's image.
Wáng admired it, unable to put it down.
After speaking briefly with Yáng
and seeing the girl's ashamed, fearful, pitiable state,
he then left,
and they parted ways.
Yáng also headed back alone.
As he climbed over a wall, he fell,
and with that, he awoke with a start,
hearing the village roosters already crowing chaotically.
He felt a sharp pain in his wrist: looking at it in the morning,
he saw the skin and flesh were red and swollen.
When they stopped,
Wáng Shēng came over
and spoke of the strange dream he had that night.
Yáng said,
"Did you dream of shooting an arrow?"
Wáng was amazed that he knew in advance.
Yáng showed him his hand
and told him the reason.
Recalling the girl's appearance in the dream,
Wáng regretted not seeing her in person;
glad that he had done the girl a favor,
he asked Yáng to introduce him first.
At night,
the girl came to express her thanks.
Yáng credited Wáng Shēng for the merit,
and conveyed his sincere request.
The girl said,
"The help of a strong friend,
I dare not forget in righteousness.
However, he is so valiant and fierce,
I am truly afraid of him."
After a while, she said,
"He admired my dagger.
The dagger was actually bought by my father when he was on a mission to Yuèzhōng,
for a hundred taels of gold.
I loved it and kept it,
wrapped it with golden threads,
and adorned it with bright pearls.
My father pitied my early death,
and used it to bury with me.
Now I am willing to part with it and give it to him,
seeing the dagger is like seeing me."
The next day,
Yáng conveyed this intention.
Wáng was overjoyed.
When night came,
the girl indeed brought the dagger,
saying,
"Tell him to treasure it,
this is not an object from Zhōnghuá."
From then on, they interacted as before.
After several months,
she suddenly smiled at Yáng under the lamp,
as if wanting to say something,
her face flushed three times but she stopped.
Yáng held her and asked.
She replied,
"For a long time, I have received your affection,
I have absorbed the vitality of a living person,
daily consuming the smoke and fire of the human world,
my white bones suddenly have signs of life.
But I need the essence and blood of a living person,
to revive."
Yáng laughed and said,
"It's you who were unwilling,
how could I deliberately begrudge it?"
The girl said,
"After the union,
you will certainly have over twenty days of serious illness,
but medicine can cure it."
Thus they made love.
Afterward, she dressed and got up,
and said again,
"I still need a drop of fresh blood,
can you endure the pain for love?"
Yáng took a sharp blade and pierced his arm to draw blood;
the girl lay on the bed,
and let it drip into her navel.
Then she got up and said,
"I will not come again.
Remember the hundred-day deadline,
look at my grave,
when there are blue birds singing on the treetop,
immediately open the tomb."
Yáng carefully received the instruction.
As she went out the door, she again instructed,
"Remember carefully, do not forget,
neither too late nor too early is acceptable!"
Then she left.
After more than ten days,
Yáng indeed fell ill,
his abdomen swollen as if about to die.
The doctor administered medicine,
and he excreted foul matter like mud,
recovering after twelve days.
Counting to the hundredth day,
he had his family carry shovels and wait.
As evening fell,
they indeed saw a pair of blue birds singing.
Yáng joyfully said,
"It's time."
Then they cleared the thorns and opened the tomb.
They saw the coffin had already decayed,
but the girl's appearance was as if alive.
Touching her, she was slightly warm.
They covered her with clothes and carried her back,
placed her in a warm spot,
her breath was faint,
finer than a thread.
Gradually they fed her broth,
and by midnight she revived.
She often said to Yáng,
"Over twenty years,
it was like a dream."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Hán Gōngzǐ,
was from a prominent family in the county.
There was a Dān Dàoshi,
skilled in magical performances,
the young master loved his arts,
and considered him a guest of honor.
Dān, when walking or sitting with others,
would suddenly disappear.
The young master wanted to learn his method,
but Dān refused.
The young master insisted earnestly.
Dān said,
"It is not that I am stingy with my art,
but I fear it would ruin my path.
If passed on to a gentleman, it would be fine;
otherwise,
there might be those who use it to commit theft.
Although you certainly need not worry about this,
but if you happen to see a beauty and take a fancy,
and invisibly enter someone's inner chambers,
that would be aiding evil and promoting licentiousness.
I dare not comply."
The young master could not force him,
but was angry in his heart,
secretly plotting with his servants to beat and humiliate him.
Fearing he might escape and hide,
they spread fine ash on the threshing floor: thinking that practitioners of unorthodox arts can become invisible,
but their footsteps would leave prints,
so they could strike quickly following the prints.
Thus they lured Dān there,
and had people stand ready with ox whips to beat him.
Dān suddenly disappeared,
and indeed there were footprints on the ash,
they struck wildly left and right,
but in a moment they were confused.
When the young master returned home,
Dān was also there.
He said to the servants,
"I can no longer stay here!
I have troubled you with your service before,
now we part,
I should have something to repay."
From his sleeve, he took out a vessel of fine wine,
then retrieved a dish of delicacies,
and placed them together on the table.
After setting them out,
he retrieved more;
after about ten more retrievals,
the table was already full.
Then he invited everyone to drink,
and all got drunk;
he then put everything back into his sleeve one by one.
Hán, hearing of this marvel,
asked him to perform again.
Dān drew a city on the wall,
pushed and knocked with his hand,
and the city gate suddenly opened.
Then he took his bag, clothes, and boxed belongings,
and threw them all inside the gate,
then bowed in farewell, saying,
"I am leaving!"
He leaped into the city,
the city gate then closed,
and the Dàoshi suddenly vanished.
Later it was heard that in the market of Qīngzhōu City,
he taught children to draw ink circles on their palms,
and playfully threw them at people,
wherever they were thrown,
whether on face or clothes,
the circle would come off,
leaving a printed mark there.
It was also heard that he was skilled in bedroom arts,
able to make his lower part suck up heated wine,
emptying a whole vessel.
The young master once tested this personally.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Wú Qīng'ān,
Yún,
was renowned from a young age.
Historiographer Gé, upon reading his writings,
often praised and admired them.
He entrusted a mutual acquaintance to invite Wú to his home,
to observe his speech and demeanor.
He said:
"How could someone as talented as Wú remain in poverty and low status forever?"
Thus, he had a neighbor convey this message:
"If Qīng'ān strives to soar among the clouds,
I shall offer my daughter to serve as his wife."
At that time, the Historiographer had an exceptionally beautiful daughter.
Upon hearing this, Wú was overjoyed,
firmly confident in himself.
Later, when he failed the provincial examination,
he sent someone to tell the Historiographer:
"Wealth and honor are destined for me;
only the timing is uncertain.
Please wait for me for three years.
If I do not succeed by then, you may marry her off."
Thereafter, he applied himself to his studies with even greater diligence.
One night,
under the bright moonlight,
a scholar came to visit him.
He had fair skin, a short beard,
a slender waist, and long fingernails.
When asked where he came from,
he said:
"My surname is Bái,
styled Yùyù."
After a brief conversation,
Wú found his words enlightening and refreshing.
Pleased with him,
Wú invited him to stay overnight.
At dawn, as Bái prepared to leave,
Wú urged him to visit often when passing by.
Touched by Wú's sincerity,
Bái agreed to lodge there temporarily,
and they parted after setting a date.
On the appointed day,
an elderly servant first arrived with cooking utensils.
Shortly after,
Bái arrived,
riding a magnificent horse like a dragon.
Wú prepared a separate room for him.
Bái ordered his servant to take the horse away.
Thus, they spent their days and nights together,
delighting in each other's company.
Wú noticed that the books Bái read
were not commonly seen or heard of,
and contained none of the contemporary examination essays.
Surprised, he asked about it.
Bái smiled and said:
"Scholars each have their own aspirations;
I am not a man of fame and fortune."
At night, Bái often invited Wú to drink,
and once presented him with a volume
on breathing and meditation techniques,
most of which Wú did not understand.
Thus, he set it aside as impractical.
Another day, Bái said to Wú:
"What I gave you earlier
is the essential path of the 'Huángtíng'
and the ladder to immortality."
Wú laughed and said:
"My urgent concerns lie elsewhere.
Moreover, those who seek immortality must sever all emotional ties
and still all worldly thoughts—
I fear I am incapable of that."
Bái asked:
"Why is that?"
Wú expressed his worry about continuing the family line.
Bái said:
"Why have you not married for so long?"
Wú replied with a smile:
"'I have a fault: I am fond of beauty.'"
Bái also laughed and said:
"'May the King not be fond of petty beauty.'
What kind of beauty do you admire?"
Wú told him the whole story.
Bái doubted whether the girl was truly beautiful.
Wú said:
"This is known far and wide,
not merely my own humble judgment."
Bái gave a slight smile and let the matter drop.
The next day,
he suddenly packed his belongings and announced his departure.
Wú spoke to him sorrowfully,
chattering on without end.
Bái then ordered his page to carry the luggage ahead.
The two lingered, reluctant to part.
Suddenly, a green cicada alighted chirping on the table.
Bái bid farewell, saying:
"The carriage is ready;
let us part here.
If you miss me,
sweep my bed and sleep on it."
As Wú was about to ask more,
in an instant,
Bái shrank to the size of a finger,
lightly mounted the cicada's back,
and with a chirping sound,
flew away, vanishing into the clouds.
Only then did Wú realize that Bái was no ordinary man.
Stunned for a long while,
he felt lost and despondent.
After several days,
a fine rain suddenly gathered,
and he thought of Bái Yùlián with intense longing.
Looking at the bed where he had slept,
he saw the scattered traces of mice;
however, after sweeping and cleaning,
he laid out a mat and prepared to sleep.
Not long after,
he saw a young servant from Bái's household come to summon him,
and he joyfully followed.
Soon, a tóngfèng (a mythical bird) soared and alighted,
and the servant caught it, saying to the scholar:
"The dark path is difficult to travel;
you can ride this as a substitute for walking."
The scholar worried that it was too small to bear his weight.
The servant said:
"Try riding it."
The scholar did as requested,
and found it surprisingly spacious with plenty of room;
the servant also attached himself to its tail.
With a sudden cry,
they soared into the sky.
Before long,
they saw a vermilion gate.
The servant descended first,
and helped the scholar down as well.
The scholar asked:
"What place is this?"
The servant replied:
"This is the Gate of Heaven."
Beside the gate, a giant tiger crouched and lay in wait.
The scholar was terrified,
but the servant shielded him with his body.
He saw that the scenery everywhere
was vastly different from the mortal world.
The servant led him into the Guanghán Palace,
where the steps inside were made of crystal,
and people walking seemed to be inside a mirror.
There were two cassia trees,
towering into the sky, their trunks so large they could be embraced;
the fragrance of their flowers, carried by the wind,
was unceasingly sweet.
The pavilions and halls all had red windows,
and from time to time, beautiful women came and went,
with enchanting faces and elegant bones,
unmatched in all the world.
The servant said:
"The beauties in the Queen Mother's palace are even more exquisite."
However, fearing that his master had been waiting too long,
he had no time to linger,
and led the scholar to hurry out.
After a while,
they saw Bái Yùlián waiting at the gate.
He took the scholar's hand and led him inside,
where outside the eaves, clear water and white sand
flowed and overflowed gently;
with jade steps and carved railings,
it almost seemed like the Cassia Palace.
As soon as they sat down,
two charming sixteen-year-old maids
came to offer fragrant tea.
After a short while,
he ordered wine to be served.
Four beautiful women
adjusted their sleeves and chimed in,
attending to them on both sides.
As soon as he felt a slight itch on his back,
one of the beauties would use her slender fingers and long nails
to reach inside his clothes and scratch for him.
The scholar felt his heart and spirit swaying,
unable to find any peace.
Soon, slightly intoxicated,
he gradually lost self-control,
smiled at the beauties,
and tried to engage them in flirtatious conversation.
The beauties would laugh and avoid him.
Bái ordered them to sing songs to accompany the drinking.
One dressed in crimson silk
raised a cup to the guest,
and then right before the feast,
began to sing a clear, melodious song.
The other beauties played flutes and pipes vigorously,
humming and harmonizing in a cacophony.
When she finished,
one dressed in emerald robes
also drank and sang.
There was still one in purple,
and another in soft white silk,
giggling softly in the shadows,
each deferring to the other, unwilling to step forward.
Bái ordered them to drink and sing in turn.
The one in purple then came to hold the cup.
The scholar pretended to take the cup,
playfully brushing against her slender wrist.
The girl laughed and lost her grip,
and the wine cup fell.
Bái scolded her.
The girl picked up the cup, smiling,
bowed her head, and whispered:
"Cold as a ghost's hand,
forcing itself to grab someone's arm."
Bái laughed heartily,
and punished her by making her sing and dance.
After she finished dancing,
the one in light white robes flew another goblet over.
The scholar declined, saying he couldn't drink anymore,
and the girl holding the wine looked ashamed,
so he forced himself to drink it.
Looking closely at the four women,
their graceful charm was captivating,
and each was a peerless beauty.
He abruptly said to his host:
"In the mortal world, even one exceptional beauty
is hard for me to find;
yet you have gathered a cluster of blossoms here.
Can you truly make me lose my soul?"
Bái laughed and said:
"Your heart already holds a beauty of its own;
how could these be worthy of your discerning gaze?"
The scholar said:
"Now I realize how limited my experience has been."
Bái then summoned all the women,
allowing him to choose for himself.
The scholar was so overwhelmed he couldn't decide.
Since Bái noticed the scholar had taken a liking to the one in purple,
he had her attend to the guest.
Later, in the intimacy of bed and pillow,
they were deeply affectionate.
The scholar asked for a keepsake,
and the girl took off a gold bracelet from her wrist and gave it to him.
Suddenly, the servant entered and said:
"The paths of immortals and mortals are different;
you should leave now."
The girl hurriedly got up
and fled.
The scholar asked about his host,
and the servant said:
"He went early to attend the morning court;
when he left, he instructed me to see you off."
The scholar reluctantly followed him,
retracing the old path.
As they neared the gate,
he looked back at the servant,
only to find he had disappeared at some point.
A tiger suddenly roared,
and the scholar fled in panic.
Looking down, he saw a bottomless abyss,
and his feet stumbled and fell.
With a start, he awoke,
to find the morning sun already red.
As he was about to shake out his clothes,
something smooth and heavy fell onto the bedding.
Looking at it,
it was the bracelet.
His heart grew even more astonished.
From then on, his former ambitions turned to ashes,
and he often wished to seek out the immortal Chìsōngzǐ,
but he was still worried about continuing his family line.
After more than ten months,
while he was sleeping soundly during the day,
he dreamed that the lady in purple came from outside,
holding a swaddled infant in her arms, saying:
"This is your flesh and blood.
It is difficult to keep such a thing in heaven,
so I respectfully bring it to you."
She then laid it on the bed,
pulled the clothes over it,
and hurriedly prepared to leave.
The scholar tried to force her to stay and be intimate.
She said:
"The first time was for our wedding;
this time is for our eternal farewell.
A hundred years of marriage
ends here.
If you have the will,
we may meet again."
The scholar awoke,
and saw an infant lying on the bedding.
He wrapped it up and told his mother.
His mother was overjoyed,
hired a wet nurse to feed it,
and named it Mèngxiān.
The scholar then sent someone to inform the Grand Historian,
saying that he himself intended to become a recluse,
and asked him to choose another good match.
The Grand Historian refused.
The scholar firmly insisted.
The Grand Historian told his daughter,
and the girl said:
"Everyone near and far knows that I am promised to Wú Láng.
To change that now
would be to serve two heavens."
She then conveyed this meaning to the scholar.
The scholar said:
"I not only have no ambition for fame and fortune,
but I have also severed all feelings for romantic love.
The only reason I haven't entered the mountains yet
is because my elderly mother is still alive."
The Grand Historian again consulted his daughter.
The girl said:
"When Wú Láng was poor,
I was content with his humble fare;
when Wú Láng left,
I served his mother: I am determined not to marry another."
Messengers were sent three or four times,
but no agreement was reached.
So a day was chosen, carriages, horses, and dowry were prepared,
and she was married into the scholar's family.
The scholar, moved by her virtue,
respected and loved her deeply.
The wife served her mother-in-law with filial piety,
striving to please her in every way,
surpassing even girls from poor families.
After more than two years,
the mother died.
The wife pawned her dowry to provide for the funeral,
leaving no rite unfulfilled.
The scholar said:
"With a wife like you,
what worries do I have!
But I recall the saying: 'When one attains the Dao,
his whole household ascends to heaven.'
I am going far away,
and leave everything to you."
The wife was calm,
and did not try to detain him at all.
The scholar then departed.
The wife managed the household affairs externally,
and taught the orphaned child internally,
all in an orderly and methodical manner.
Mèngxiān gradually grew up,
exceptionally intelligent and talented.
At fourteen,
as a child prodigy, he passed the provincial examination,
and at fifteen entered the Hànlín Academy.
Whenever honors were conferred,
as his mother's surname was unknown,
only his grandmother, Madame Gé, was enfeoffed.
On occasions of frost and dew (ancestral remembrance days),
he would ask about his father's whereabouts,
and his mother told him everything.
He then wished to resign his post and go search for him.
His mother said:
"Your father left to become a monk,
it has been over ten years now,
he has likely attained immortality;
where could you search?"
Later, he was ordered to offer sacrifices at Nányuè,
and on the way encountered bandits.
In his dire straits,
a Daoist priest, sword in hand, entered,
the bandits were all routed,
and the siege was lifted.
Grateful to him,
he offered him gold,
but he would not accept it.
He took out a letter
and entrusted it, saying:
"I have an old friend,
from the same village as Your Excellency,
I trouble you to convey my greetings."
He asked:
"What is his name?"
He replied:
"Wáng Lín."
He then recalled there was no such name in the village.
The Daoist priest said:
"A humble villager of low status,
a high official naturally would not know him."
As he was leaving,
he took out a gold bracelet and said:
"This is a woman's ornament.
A Daoist picking this up
has no use for it,
so I offer it in return."
Looking at it,
it was inlaid and carved with exquisite craftsmanship.
He carried it back and gave it to his wife.
His wife loved it,
and ordered a skilled artisan to make a matching one based on its style,
but it never matched its fineness.
He asked all around the village,
but there was no one named Wáng Lín.
He privately opened the letter,
which said:
"Three years as husband and wife,
parted to different corners of the sky;
burying my mother and teaching my son,
all relied on your virtue.
Having no way to repay your kindness,
I offer one pill of medicine;
split it and eat it,
and you can become an immortal."
Signed at the end:
"To Madame, in her dressing chamber, Línniáng"
After reading it,
he did not understand who it was for,
and took it to tell his mother.
His mother took the letter and wept,
saying:
"This is a letter from your father.
Lín
is my childhood name."
Only then did he suddenly realize
"Wáng Lín"
was a riddle formed by splitting characters.
He regretted it endlessly.
He also showed the bracelet to his mother.
His mother said:
"This is your mother's keepsake.
When your father was at home,
he once showed it to me."
Looking at the pill again,
it was as big as a bean.
He said joyfully:
"My father is an immortal;
eating this will surely grant longevity."
His mother did not swallow it immediately,
but received it and stored it away.
When Grand Historian Gé came to see his nephew,
the wife recited Wú the scholar's letter,
and then offered the elixir as a longevity gift.
The Grand Historian split it and they shared it.
In an instant,
their spirits were refreshed.
The Grand Historian was then over seventy,
quite decrepit;
suddenly he felt strength surging through his skin and flesh,
so he abandoned his carriage and walked,
his stride vigorous and swift,
his family members had to pant to keep up.
The following year,
a great fire broke out in the capital,
the flames burned all day without ceasing.
At night, they dared not sleep,
all gathered in the courtyard.
Seeing the fire raging chaotically,
encroaching on the neighboring houses.
The whole family was anxious,
not knowing what to do.
Suddenly, the gold bracelet on the wife's arm
made a clanging sound,
flew off her arm and away.
Looking at it,
it appeared several acres in size;
it circled and covered the house,
shaped like a moon halo;
its opening faced the southeast corner,
clearly visible.
Everyone was greatly astonished.
After a moment,
the fire came from the west,
nearing the halo, it veered diagonally eastward.
When the fire had moved far away,
they secretly thought the bracelet was lost and could not be recovered;
suddenly they saw a red light suddenly contract,
and the bracelet clanged as it fell at their feet.
In the capital, tens of thousands of civilian houses were burned down,
left, right, front, and back,
all reduced to ashes,
only the Wú residence was unharmed,
except for a small pavilion in the southeast,
which vanished without a trace,
precisely where the bracelet's opening had left a gap in its coverage.
Madame Gé was over fifty,
some who saw her
said she still looked like a woman in her twenties.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Jiaozhou there was a man named Xú,
who sailed the seas as a merchant.
Suddenly, a great wind blew him away.
When he opened his eyes, he had arrived at a place
of deep, vast, and verdant mountains.
Hoping there might be inhabitants,
he moored his boat and went ashore,
carrying dried provisions and cured meat with him.
Just as he entered,
he saw that both cliffs were full of cave openings,
dense as a honeycomb;
from within came faint human-like sounds.
He went to the outside of a cave,
stopped, and peeked in.
Inside were two yakshas,
their teeth like a dense forest of halberds,
their eyes flashing like twin lanterns,
tearing apart a live deer with their claws and eating it.
Terrified out of his wits,
he urgently wanted to flee back down,
but the yakshas had already spotted him.
They stopped eating and seized him, dragging him inside.
The two creatures spoke to each other,
sounding like the cries of birds or beasts.
They fought to tear Xú's clothes,
as if intending to...
Xú was greatly frightened.
He took the dried provisions from his bag,
along with some beef jerky, and offered them.
The yakshas shared and ate them, finding them very tasty.
They then rummaged through Xú's bag again.
Xú shook his hands to show there was nothing left.
The yakshas grew angry
and seized him once more.
Xú pleaded with them, saying:
"Release me.
In my boat, I have a pot and a steamer,
and I can cook."
The yakshas did not understand his words
and remained angry.
Xú again used hand gestures,
and the yakshas seemed to vaguely understand.
They followed him to the boat,
fetched the utensils, and brought them into the cave.
He gathered firewood, lit a fire,
cooked the leftover deer meat,
and when it was done, presented it to them.
The two creatures were delighted.
At night, they blocked the entrance with a huge rock,
as if afraid Xú would escape.
Xú curled up and slept far inside,
deeply fearing he would not be spared.
At daybreak,
the two creatures went out
and blocked the entrance again.
After a short while,
they brought a deer and gave it to Xú.
Xú skinned it,
and at a deep part of the cave where water flowed,
he drew water and cooked several pots full.
Soon, several more yakshas arrived.
They gathered and devoured everything,
then pointed at the pot,
as if finding it too small.
After three or four days,
one yaksha brought a large pot on his back,
like those commonly used by humans.
From then on, the group of yakshas each brought wolves and deer.
Once the meat was cooked,
they called Xú to eat with them.
After living there for several days,
the yakshas gradually became familiar with Xú.
When they went out, they no longer confined him,
and they lived together like a family.
Xú gradually learned to discern their meaning from their sounds
and began imitating their speech,
speaking the yaksha language.
The yakshas were even more pleased.
They brought a female yaksha to be Xú's wife.
At first, Xú was afraid
and dared not move;
the female herself opened her thighs and approached Xú,
so Xú then had intercourse with her.
The female was greatly delighted.
She often saved meat to feed Xú,
and they were as harmonious as lute and zither.
One day,
the yakshas got up early,
each wearing a string of bright pearls around their necks.
They took turns going out the door,
as if awaiting an honored guest.
They ordered Xú to cook a lot of meat.
Xú asked the female about it,
and she said:
"Today is the Celestial Longevity Festival."
The female went out
and said to the other yakshas:
"Husband Xú has no gǔtūzi."
Each of them took off five pearls,
and gave them to the female.
The female also took off ten from her own,
making a total of fifty.
Using wild ramie as a cord,
she strung them and hung them around Xú's neck.
Xú looked at them:
a single pearl was worth over a hundred taels of gold.
Soon, they all went out.
After Xú finished cooking the meat,
the female came to invite him, saying:
"To receive the Heavenly King."
They arrived at a large cave,
several acres in expanse.
In the center was a stone,
smooth and level like a table;
the top seat was covered with a leopard skin,
the rest with deer skins.
Twenty or thirty yakshas
sat in rows filling the space.
After a short while,
a great wind raised dust,
and they all hurried out in excitement.
They saw a huge creature approaching,
also resembling a yaksha.
It rushed straight into the cave
and sat arrogantly, looking around like a hawk.
The group followed it in,
standing in rows to the east and west,
all lifting their heads,
crossing their arms in an 'X' shape.
The great yaksha counted them by looking at each head,
and asked:
"Are all the people of Wòméi Shān
gathered here?"
The crowd roared in affirmation.
It looked at Xú and said:
"Where did this one come from?"
The female answered
"son-in-law."
The crowd also praised his cooking.
Immediately, two or three yakshas
ran to fetch the cooked meat and set it on the table.
The great yaksha scooped it up and ate its fill,
praising it highly as excellent and delicious,
and ordered that it be regularly supplied.
It then looked at Xú and said:
"Why is his gǔtūzi so short?"
The crowd said:
"He is newly arrived and not yet equipped."
The creature took the pearl string from its own neck,
removed ten pearls, and gave them to him.
They were all as large as fingertip beads,
round like pellets.
The female hurriedly took them
and strung them for Xú.
Xú also crossed his arms and thanked it in the yaksha language.
The creature then left,
treading on the wind as it went,
swift as flight.
Only then did the crowd enjoy the leftover food and disperse.
After residing there for over four years,
the female suddenly gave birth,
delivering two males and one female in a single litter,
all in human form,
unlike their mother.
All the yakshas were delighted with her offspring,
and would often fondle and play with them.
One day,
they all went out to hunt for food,
leaving Xú alone sitting inside.
Suddenly, a female from another cave came,
wishing to have an affair with Xú,
but Xú refused.
The yaksha grew angry,
pounced on Xú, and pinned him to the ground.
Xú’s wife returned from outside,
flew into a violent rage and fought with her,
biting off her ear.
A short while later,
the other two also returned,
From then on, the female always guarded Xú,
never leaving his side whether he was active or at rest.
After another three years,
the children were all able to walk.
Xú then taught them human speech,
and gradually they could speak;
in their chirping voices,
there was a human quality.
Although they were children,
they ran over the mountains as if treading on level ground;
and they were affectionately attached, showing the sentiments of father and children.
One day,
the female went out with one son and one daughter,
and did not return for half a day.
Meanwhile, a strong north wind arose.
Xú felt sorrowful and thought of his hometown;
he took his son to the seashore,
and saw that his old boat was still there.
He planned to return home together with him.
The son wanted to inform his mother,
but Xú stopped him.
Father and son boarded the boat,
and after a day and a night reached Jiāozhǐ.
Arriving home,
he found his wife had already remarried.
He took out two pearls,
sold them for a fortune in gold,
and his household became quite wealthy.
He named his son Biāo.
By the age of fourteen or fifteen,
he could lift immense weights,
and was rough, reckless, and fond of fighting.
The commander of Jiāozhǐ saw him and considered him extraordinary,
appointing him as a qiānzǒng.
At that time, there was unrest on the border,
and wherever he went, he achieved merit;
by eighteen, he was promoted to fùjiàng.
At that time, a merchant was sailing the sea,
and was also blown by the wind to Wòméi.
Just as he came ashore,
he saw a youth,
and upon looking at him, was startled.
Knowing he was from Zhōngguó,
he asked where he lived.
The merchant told him.
The youth pulled him into a secluded valley, into a small stone cave;
outside the cave were thickets of brambles;
and he instructed him not to go out.
After a while,
he brought venison to feed Shāng.
He said of himself:
"My father was also a man of Jiāo."
Shāng asked about him,
and learned it was Xú,
whom Shāng had once known while traveling.
So he said:
"He is my old friend.
Now his son is a deputy general."
The youth did not understand what that title meant.
Shāng said:
"This is an official title in China."
He asked further:
"What does it mean to be an official?"
Shāng replied:
"When going out, one rides in carriages or on horses;
when entering, one resides in lofty halls;
one call from above and a hundred responses from below;
those who see him look askance,
and stand with their feet turned aside: this is called being an official."
The youth was very much stirred and envious.
Shāng said:
"Since your esteemed father is in Jiāo,
why have you lingered here so long?"
The youth told him the situation.
Shāng urged him to return south.
He said:
"I have often thought of this.
But my mother is not Chinese,
her speech and appearance are very different;
moreover, if others of her kind find out,
they will surely harm us: that is why I have been hesitating."
Then he went out and said:
"Wait until the north wind rises,
I will come to see you off.
Please, at my father and brother's place,
send a message of inquiry."
Shāng hid in the cave for almost half a year.
From time to time he peered out through the thorns,
and saw that there were often yèchāi coming and going in the mountains;
he was greatly afraid,
and dared not move at all.
One day,
the north wind rustled,
the youth suddenly arrived,
led him and hurriedly fled.
He instructed:
"Do not forget what was said."
Shāng agreed.
He also placed meat on the table,
and Shāng then returned.
Respectfully arriving in Jiāo,
he reached the deputy commander's residence,
and recounted in detail what he had seen.
Biāo heard it and was grieved,
wishing to go and search for him.
His father feared the sea waves were a den of monsters,
perilous and difficult to brave,
and strenuously stopped him.
Biāo beat his chest and wept bitterly,
his father could not stop him.
So he informed the commander of Jiāo,
and took two soldiers to the sea.
Adverse winds hindered the boat,
which tossed on the sea for half a month.
Looking all around, there was no shore in sight,
within a foot, all was bewildering and oppressive,
with no way to distinguish north from south.
Suddenly, surging waves reached the Milky Way,
and the boat capsized.
Biāo fell into the sea,
floating and sinking with the waves.
After a long time,
he was dragged away by a creature;
arriving at a place,
there were actually houses.
Biāo looked at it,
the creature resembled a yèchāi.
Biāo then spoke in the yèchāi language.
The yèchāi was startled and questioned him,
Biāo then told him where he was going.
The yèchāi said happily:
"Wòméi,
that is my hometown.
How rude of me, I deserve blame!
You have strayed eight thousand lǐ from the original route.
From here it leads to the Poison Dragon Kingdom,
the way to Wòméi is not this direction."
Then he found a boat to send Biāo off.
The yèchāi pushed the boat in the water like an arrow,
covering a thousand lǐ in an instant,
after one night,
they had already reached the northern shore.
He saw a youth,
gazing out by the stream.
Biāo knew there were no humans in the mountains,
and suspected it was his brother;
approaching him,
it was indeed his brother.
So he took his hand and wept.
Afterward he asked about his mother and sister,
and was told both were healthy and safe.
Biāo wanted to go with him,
but his brother stopped him,
and hurriedly left.
Turning back to thank the yèchāi,
he had already gone.
Not long after,
his mother and sister both arrived,
seeing Biāo, they all wept.
Biāo told them his intention.
His mother said:
"I fear if we go, we will be bullied by others."
Biāo said:
"Your son is very honored and noble in China,
people dare not bully us."
The decision to return was settled,
but they were troubled by the adverse wind, difficult to cross.
While mother and son were anxiously hesitating,
suddenly they saw a cloth sail moving southward,
its sound rustling.
Biāo said joyfully:
"Heaven is helping us!"
They boarded the boat one after another,
the waves surged like arrows;
in three days they reached shore.
Those who saw them all fled.
Biāo took off some of his robe and trousers for the three.
Arriving home,
the mother yèchāi saw the old man and angrily scolded him,
resenting that he had not consulted her.
Xú apologized incessantly.
The family servants paid respects to the mistress of the house,
none were not trembling with fear.
Biāo urged his mother to learn to speak Chinese,
wear brocade clothes,
and enjoy fine grain and meat,
then she was greatly pleased.
Mother and daughter both wore men's clothing,
similar to Mǎn style.
After several months, they could somewhat distinguish the language,
the younger brother and sister also gradually became fair-skinned.
The younger brother was named Bào,
the younger sister was named Yè'ér,
both were exceptionally strong.
Biāo was ashamed of not knowing books,
so he taught his younger brother to read.
Bào was the most intelligent,
once going through the classics and histories, he understood them completely.
But he did not wish to pursue the scholarly profession;
still he was made to draw strong bows,
and gallop fierce horses.
He passed the military imperial examination.
He was betrothed to the daughter of Adjutant Ā.
Yè'ér, being of a different kind,
had no one to marry her.
It happened that Battalion Commander Yuán under Biāo's command had lost his spouse,
so he forced him to marry her.
Yè'ér could draw a hundred-dàn bow,
and shoot small birds from over a hundred paces away,
never missing.
Whenever Yuán went on campaigns,
he always took his wife with him.
He successively held the posts of Assistant Prefect and General,
half of his extraordinary achievements came from within the women's quarters.
Bào at thirty-four received the seal of command.
His mother once followed him on a southern campaign,
whenever facing a formidable enemy,
she would don armor and grasp weapons,
to support her son,
those who saw her could not help but retreat in fear.
An imperial edict conferred upon her the title of baron.
Bào submitted a memorial on behalf of his mother declining it,
and she was instead granted the title of Lady.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"A yèchāi wife,
is also rarely heard of,
yet upon careful thought, it is not rare: in every household, at the head of the bed, there is a yèchāi present."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A certain resident of Chángshān,
while at leisure at home,
would often have a short-statured visitor come,
and over time they conversed at length.
He had never known the visitor’s background,
and felt quite suspicious.
The visitor said:
"In a few days I will move house,
and become your neighbor."
After four or five days,
he said again:
"Now we are in the same neighborhood,
I can receive your guidance morning and night."
The resident asked:
"Where have you moved to?"
He did not give a clear answer,
but merely pointed north with his hand.
From then on,
he came once every day.
He often borrowed utensils from people;
if someone was unwilling to lend,
the item would disappear on its own.
Everyone suspected he was a fox.
North of the village was an ancient tomb,
sunken and unfathomable,
and they thought he must live there.
Together they took weapons and went.
They lay in wait and listened,
but for a long time there was no unusual sound.
As the first watch was about to end,
they heard rustling noises from the hole,
as if dozens or hundreds of people were whispering.
The crowd stayed silent and motionless.
Soon, foot-tall little people,
emerged in succession,
until they were too many to count.
The crowd shouted and rose,
attacking them together.
Every strike of their staffs produced fire,
and in an instant they scattered in all directions.
Only a small hair bun was left behind,
like a walnut shell,
adorned with gauze and golden thread.
Smelling it,
it was indescribably foul.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Two monks came from the Western Regions,
one heading for Wǔtái,
the other taking up residence at Tàishān.
Their clothing, appearance, and speech
were all different from those in China.
They said of themselves:
"We passed through the Flaming Mountain,
with its many layers of peaks,
where the air steamed and billowed like a furnace.
Travel had to be done after rain,
with focused mind and fixed gaze,
treading lightly with careful steps;
if one mistakenly kicked a mountain stone,
flames would instantly flare up and scorch.
We also crossed the Quicksand River,
in which stood a crystal mountain,
with sheer cliffs piercing the sky,
transparent and clear on all sides,
as if there were no barriers.
There was also a narrow pass,
wide enough for only a single cart;
two dragons, horns interlocked and mouths facing each other, guarded it.
Those wishing to pass must first bow to the dragons;
if the dragons permitted passage,
their mouths and horns would open of their own accord.
The dragons were white,
their scales and manes all like crystal."
The monks said:
"We have spent eighteen years on the journey.
Twelve left the Western Lands,
but only two of us reached China.
In the Western Lands, four famous mountains of China are spoken of:
one is Tàishān,
one is Huàshān,
one is Wǔtái,
and one is Luòjiā.
It is said that these mountains are covered with gold everywhere,
and that Guānyīn
and Wénshū are still alive there.
If one can reach that place,
then one’s body itself becomes a Buddha,
attaining immortality."
Hearing their descriptions,
it is just like the people of this world yearning for the Western Lands.
If a traveler to the West
and one crossing eastward were to meet midway,
each telling what they know,
they would surely look at each other and laugh,
sparing both the arduous journey.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Xíng Dé,
a man of Zézhōu,
was an outstanding figure among the greenwood.
He could draw a strong crossbow
and shoot linked arrows,
a skill hailed as unparalleled in his time.
Yet throughout his life he was down on his luck,
unsuccessful in business ventures,
and would lose his capital whenever he traveled.
Major merchants from the two capitals
often liked to have Xíng accompany them,
relying on him for safety on the road.
Once, in early winter,
two or three merchants
lent him a small sum
and invited him to join in trading;
Xíng also emptied his own purse,
intending to pool resources for goods.
He had a friend skilled in divination,
so he went to consult him.
The friend divined and said:
"This hexagram signifies 'regret,'
the business you undertake
will not only fail to yield profit but will even incur loss."
Xíng was displeased
and wanted to withdraw,
but the merchants insisted and urged him to go.
Upon reaching the capital,
things turned out exactly as predicted.
As the year was nearing its end,
he rode alone out of the capital gate.
Thinking of having no funds for the new year,
he felt doubly depressed and vexed.
At dawn, when the mist was still thick,
Xíng Délìn temporarily headed to a roadside inn
to unpack and seek a drink.
He saw a white-haired old man
with two youths,
drinking beneath the north window.
A young servant attended them,
his yellow hair tousled and wild.
Xíng took a seat to the south,
facing the old man, and rested.
As the servant was serving wine,
he accidentally overturned the tray,
soiling the old man's clothes.
One of the youths grew angry,
immediately pinching the servant's ear.
He then took a towel
and wiped the old man's clothes for him.
Xíng noticed that the servant had iron rings on both thumbs,
each half an inch thick;
each one
weighed about two taels or more.
After they finished eating,
the old man ordered the youths
to take out silver ingots from a leather bag,
piling them on the table.
They weighed and calculated for a while;
by the time they had drunk several cups of wine,
they finally wrapped everything up securely.
One of the youths led a black lame mule from the stable,
helped the old man mount it;
the servant also straddled a lean horse and followed,
and they left through the gate.
The two youths each carried bows and arrows at their waists,
took their horses, and went out together.
Xíng, seeing the large amount of silver,
stared intently, glancing sideways,
his greedy desire burning like fire.
He stopped drinking,
and hurriedly followed them.
Seeing the old man and the servant still moving slowly ahead,
he left the main road and galloped diagonally to get in front of the old man.
He then drew his bow tight,
and glared angrily at him.
The old man bent down, took off his left boot,
and said with a smile:
"Don't you recognize Old Tāo?"
Xíng shot an arrow at him with full force.
The old man lay back on the saddle,
stretched out his foot,
and opened two toes like pincers,
catching the arrow.
He laughed and said:
"Is this all the skill you have?
Why bother making your old man use his hands to deal with you?"
Xíng grew furious,
and unleashed his ultimate skill:
as soon as one arrow was released,
the next followed immediately.
The old man caught one with his hand,
seemingly unprepared for the rapid succession;
the second arrow shot straight into his mouth,
and he toppled and fell,
lying stiffly with the arrow in his mouth.
The servant also dismounted.
Xíng was delighted,
thinking the old man was dead,
and approached him.
Suddenly, the old man spat out the arrow and leaped up,
clapping his hands and saying:
"This is our first meeting,
why play such a nasty trick?"
Xíng was greatly shocked,
and his horse bolted in fright.
Realizing the old man was extraordinary,
he dared not return.
After traveling thirty or forty li,
he encountered an official's steward,
carrying goods to the capital;
he robbed him,
obtaining nearly a thousand taels of silver,
and his spirits finally lifted.
Just as he was galloping swiftly,
he heard hoofbeats behind him;
turning his head,
he saw the servant riding the lame mule,
speeding along like flight.
The servant shouted:
"Stop right there, man!
The loot you seized
should be shared a little."
Xíng said:
"Do you know 'Xíng, the master of rapid-fire arrows'?"
The servant replied:
"I've just had a lesson from you."
Xíng, seeing the servant's unimpressive appearance
and that he carried no bow or arrows,
underestimated him.
He shot three arrows in quick succession,
one after another without pause,
like a flock of falcons soaring.
The servant remained utterly calm,
catching two with his hands
and catching one in his mouth.
He laughed and said:
"With skills like these,
you're utterly embarrassing!
Your old man was in a hurry earlier,
and didn't have time to fetch his bow;
these things are useless anyway,
so I'll just throw them back to you."
He then took off an iron ring from his finger,
threaded the arrows through it,
and threw them with force from his hand,
creating a whistling sound like the wind.
Xíng hurriedly blocked with his bow;
the bowstring happened to strike the iron ring,
snapping with a clang,
and the bow itself split open.
Xíng was utterly stunned.
Before he could dodge or evade,
the arrow shot through his ear,
and he fell from his horse without realizing it.
The servant dismounted
and proceeded to search him.
Xíng, lying on the ground, struck at him with his bow.
The servant snatched the bow away,
bent it and broke it in two;
then broke it into four pieces,
and tossed them aside.
After that,
he gripped Xíng's arms with one hand,
and pressed down on his legs with one foot;
Xíng's arms felt bound,
his legs crushed,
unable to move even with all his strength.
The belt around his waist was doubled over,
about three fingers thick;
the servant pinched it with one hand,
and it broke apart like ashes.
After taking the silver,
he leaped onto his mount,
raised a hand in farewell,
and said
"My apologies for the rudeness,"
before
swiftly riding away.
Xíng returned home
and eventually became an upright man.
He often recounted his past experiences without concealment.
This story is quite similar to that of Liú Dōngshān.
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Qiáoshēng was a native of Jìnníng.
In his youth, he was renowned for his talent.
Though over twenty years old,
he remained obscure and unsuccessful.
He was a man of courage and loyalty.
He was good friends with Gùshēng;
when Gù died,
Qiáoshēng regularly provided for his widow and children.
The county magistrate, impressed by his literary talent, held him in high regard.
When the magistrate died in office,
his family, stranded and unable to return home,
was aided by Qiáoshēng, who bankrupted himself to escort the coffin back,
traveling over two thousand li there and back.
Because of this, the scholarly community esteemed him even more,
but his family fortunes declined further as a result.
Historian Xiàolián had a daughter,
named Liánchéng,
skilled in embroidery
and well-read.
Her father doted on her.
He displayed an embroidery she had made,
the "Weary Embroidery" picture,
and invited young men to compose poems on it,
intending to choose a son-in-law.
Qiáoshēng presented a poem:
"Her languid chignon, high and coiled, dark locks cascading,
Early by the orchid window she embroiders green lotus;
Stitching mandarin ducks, her soul near breaking,
Secretly she halts the needle, knitting her moth-eyebrows."
He also praised the skill of her embroidery:
"The embroidered threads seem to sketch from life,
Flowers and birds in the piece formed by nature's hand;
In years past, weaving brocade was no great art—
Fortunate that her palindrome moved the sage emperor."
The girl was delighted upon receiving the poem
and praised it to her father.
Her father, however, considered Qiáoshēng poor.
The girl praised it to everyone she met;
moreover, she sent an old woman, pretending her father's order,
to give Qiáoshēng money to aid his studies.
Qiáoshēng sighed and said:
"Liánchéng is my true friend!"
He poured out his heart and cherished the thought,
yearning like hunger.
Not long after,
the girl was betrothed to Wáng Huàchéng, son of a salt merchant,
and Qiáoshēng despaired;
yet in his dreams, he still cherished her.
Soon after,
the girl fell ill with consumption,
bedridden with a grave illness.
A Western monk
claimed he could cure her,
but required a piece of flesh, one qian in weight, from a man's chest,
to be pounded and mixed with medicinal powder.
Historian sent someone to inform his son-in-law, the Wang family.
The son-in-law laughed and said:
"The foolish old man wants me to cut the flesh from my heart!"
The messenger returned.
Historian then announced to people:
"Whoever can cut the flesh shall marry her."
Upon hearing this, Qiáoshēng went
and, drawing his own blade,
cut flesh from his chest and gave it to the monk.
Blood soaked his robe and trousers;
the monk applied medicine to stop it.
He compounded three pills.
In three days, she finished them,
and the illness vanished.
Historian intended to fulfill his promise,
first informing Wang.
Wang was furious
and threatened to sue.
Historian then set a feast and invited Qiáoshēng,
placing a thousand taels of gold on the table,
saying:
"I have deeply wronged your great virtue;
please accept this as repayment."
He then explained the reason for breaking the pledge.
Qiáoshēng angrily said:
"The reason I did not begrudge the flesh from my chest
was merely to repay a true friend—
do you think I sell flesh?"
He flicked his sleeves and left.
When the girl heard of it,
she felt deeply pained
and sent the old woman to comfort and explain to him.
Moreover, she said:
"With his talent,
he should not remain long in obscurity.
Why worry that the world lacks fair maidens?
I have had ominous dreams;
within three years, I will surely die—
no need to contend with others for this underworld creature."
Qiáoshēng told the old woman:
"'A scholar dies for one who knows him'—
not for beauty.
I only fear Liánchéng may not truly know me;
if we are not united, what harm is there?"
The old woman conveyed the girl's sincere oath and heartfelt explanation.
Qiáoshēng said:
"If so,
when we meet,
if she will smile for me,
I shall die without regret!"
After the old woman left,
a few days later,
Qiáoshēng happened to go out
and met the girl returning from her uncle's house.
He glanced at her.
The girl turned her autumn-wave eyes
and parted her lips in a radiant smile.
Overjoyed, Qiáoshēng said:
"Liánchéng truly knows me!"
Just then, the Wang family came to discuss an auspicious wedding date,
and the girl's former illness recurred,
dying within a few months.
Qiáoshēng went to mourn at her bier
and, overcome with grief, died.
Historian had his body carried back to his home.
Shēng, knowing he had died,
felt no sorrow either.
He left the village,
still hoping to see Liánchéng one more time.
Looking into the distance, he saw a road stretching north and south,
crowded with travelers like ants,
so he mingled among them.
After a short while,
he entered an official bureau,
where he encountered Gù Shēng,
who asked in surprise:
"How did you get here?"
He immediately took Shēng by the hand to send him back.
Shēng sighed deeply,
saying:
"My heart's matter is far from settled."
Gù said:
"I am in charge of documents here,
and hold some authority.
If I can be of service,
I will spare no effort."
Shēng asked about Liánchéng.
Gù then led Shēng through many twists and turns,
where they saw Liánchéng with a young woman in white,
her tearful lashes and sorrowful brows
as she sat leaning in a corner of the corridor.
Seeing Shēng arrive,
she suddenly rose as if overjoyed,
briefly asking how he had come.
Shēng said:
"Since you died,
how dare I live!"
Liánchéng wept and said:
"Such an ungrateful man,
and yet you still do not reject him—
what use is it for me to die for him?
But I can no longer promise you life in this world;
I vow to be with you in the next life."
Shēng told Gù:
"You may attend to your duties;
I would rather die happily than live.
I only trouble you to find out where Liánchéng will be reborn,
so I may go with her."
Gù agreed and left.
The young woman in white asked who Shēng was,
and Liánchéng recounted everything in detail.
Upon hearing this,
the young woman seemed overwhelmed with grief.
Liánchéng told Shēng:
"This is my namesake,
her childhood name is Bīnniáng,
daughter of Shǐ, the prefect of Chángshā.
We have traveled together,
and have grown fond of each other."
Shēng looked at her,
finding her demeanor pitiable.
Just as he was about to inquire further,
Gù returned,
congratulating Shēng:
"I have settled the matter for you—
I will have the young lady return to life with you,
is that acceptable?"
Both were overjoyed.
As they were about to bid farewell,
Bīnniáng wailed loudly:
"Elder sister leaves,
where shall I go?
I beg for your pity and rescue;
I am willing to serve as your maid."
Liánchéng was heartbroken,
at a loss for what to do,
and turned to Shēng for advice.
Shēng again pleaded with Gù.
Gù found it difficult,
firmly stating it was impossible.
Shēng insisted forcefully.
Then Gù said:
"Let me try recklessly."
He left for the time of a meal and returned,
waving his hand:
"What did I say!
It truly is utterly impossible to manage!"
Hearing this,
Bīnniáng sobbed pitifully,
clinging only to Liánchéng's sleeve,
fearing she would leave immediately.
In deep distress with no solution,
they faced each other in silence;
yet seeing her sorrowful face and mournful expression,
made one's heart ache with tenderness.
Gù Shēng said indignantly:
"Please take Bīnniáng with you.
If there are any repercussions,
I will bear them myself!"
Bīnniáng then rejoiced,
and followed Shēng out.
Shēng worried about the long journey without companions.
Bīnniáng said:
"I will go with you,
I do not wish to return."
Shēng said:
"You are too foolish.
If you do not return,
how can you come back to life?
If I come to Húnán someday,
do not run away and hide—
that would be my great fortune."
It happened that two old women were taking documents to Chángshā,
so Shēng entrusted Bīnniáng to them,
and she parted in tears.
On the road,
Liánchéng walked slowly and with difficulty,
resting every li or so;
after more than ten such rests,
they finally saw the village gate.
Liánchéng said:
"After being reborn,
I fear there may be reversals.
Please fetch my remains,
and if I come to your home as your wife,
there should be no regrets."
Shēng agreed.
They went together to Shēng's home.
The woman trembled as if unable to walk,
and Shēng waited for her.
She said:
"Since arriving here,
my limbs have been shaking,
as if not under my control.
I fear my wish may not be fulfilled;
we should still plan carefully;
otherwise,
how can we be free after returning to life?"
They went together into a side room.
After sitting quietly for a while,
Liánchéng smiled and said:
"Do you detest me?"
Shēng asked in surprise why.
Blushing, she said:
"I fear things may not work out,
and I would fail you again.
Let me repay you first as a ghost."
Shēng was delighted,
and they shared utmost joy and affection.
Thus, they lingered and dared not return to life hastily,
staying in the side room for three days.
Liánchéng said:
"As the proverb says:
'The ugly daughter-in-law must eventually meet her in-laws.'
Hiding anxiously here
is no long-term plan."
She urged Shēng to enter.
As soon as they reached the mourning chamber,
he suddenly revived.
His family was astonished,
and brought him broth.
Shēng then sent someone to invite Shǐ over,
requesting Liánchéng's corpse,
claiming he could revive her.
Shǐ was pleased
and complied.
Just as they carried her into the room,
they saw she had awakened.
She told her father:
"I have already given myself to young master Qiáo;
there is no reason for me to return.
If anything changes,
I will simply die again!"
Shǐ returned home
and sent maids to serve her.
When Wáng heard of this,
he filed a formal complaint.
The official accepted bribes
and ruled in Wáng's favor.
Shēng was filled with indignation and wished to die,
but there was nothing he could do.
When Liánchéng went to the Wáng household,
she refused to eat or drink in anger,
only begging to die quickly.
When no one was in the room,
she hung herself from a beam.
The next day,
she grew weaker,
nearly on the verge of death.
Wáng grew fearful
and sent her back to Shǐ.
Shǐ again carried her to Shēng.
When Wáng learned of this,
he could do nothing,
and so peace was restored.
After Liánchéng recovered,
she often thought of Bīnniáng
and wanted to send a messenger to inquire about her,
but the road was long and travel difficult.
One day,
a servant announced:
"There are carriages and horses at the gate."
The couple went out to look
and saw Bīnniáng already in the courtyard.
They met with mixed sorrow and joy.
Shēng Yán was invited inside.
The prefect said:
"My young daughter, thanks to you, has returned to life,
and she vows not to marry anyone else.
Now I follow her wish."
Shēng bowed in gratitude according to ritual.
The Xiàolián also arrived,
and they discussed their shared clan ties.
Shēng's given name was Nián,
his courtesy name was Dànián.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"For the understanding found in a single smile,
she pledged her person to him.
Some in the world might criticize her as foolish;
but were those five hundred men of Tián Héng
all fools?
This is the value of rare understanding,
the reason why the worthy and heroic are moved and bound, unable to restrain themselves.
Yet, looking across the vast land,
it has come to this: that a man of brocade talent
can only pour out his heart for the smile of a lovely woman.
Truly, it is lamentable!"
Main text based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
"The Historian of the Strange remarks" added based on the twenty-four volume manuscript copy.
Huò Shēng of Wéndēng
and Yán Shēng were intimate in youth
and teased each other as they grew.
In their witty banter and exchanges,
they only feared not being skillful enough.
Huò had an old woman neighbor
who had once assisted Yán's wife during childbirth.
By chance, speaking with Huò's wife,
she mentioned that Yán's wife had a wart on her private parts.
The wife told Huò.
Huò conspired with his companions,
and when they saw Yán was about to arrive,
he deliberately whispered:
"So-and-so's wife is most intimate with me."
The others did not believe him.
Huò then fabricated details,
and said:
"If you don't believe me,
she has a pair of warts on the side of her privates."
Yán stopped outside the window,
heard everything clearly,
and left without entering.
Upon reaching home,
he savagely beat his wife;
she did not admit to it,
so he tortured her even more cruelly.
Unable to endure the abuse,
she hanged herself.
Only then did Huò feel great remorse,
yet he dared not confess the falsehood to Yán.
After Yán's wife died,
her ghost cried at night,
and the whole household could not find peace.
Not long after,
Yán died suddenly,
and the ghost then stopped crying.
Huò's wife dreamed of a woman with disheveled hair who shouted:
"My death was so bitter,
how can you and your husband be happy and joyful!"
She awoke and fell ill,
and died a few days later.
Huò also dreamed of a woman pointing, counting, and cursing him,
then slapping his mouth with her palm.
He awoke with a start,
felt a vague pain on his lips,
which swelled up high,
and in three days formed a pair of warts,
which became a chronic ailment.
He dared not laugh or speak loudly;
if he opened his mouth too suddenly,
the pain was unbearable.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"That the dead can become a fierce ghost
is due to the energy of their grievance.
But to inflict a private ailment upon the lips,
though spiritual, borders on the playful."
A certain Wáng of the district,
was intimate with a fellow student.
When that man's wife was returning to her parents' home,
Wáng, knowing her donkey was easily startled,
first hid in a thicket,
waited for the woman to arrive,
and suddenly leapt out;
the donkey bolted and the woman fell.
Only one servant boy accompanied her,
unable to help the woman remount.
Wáng then very attentively helped her up and held the reins,
and the woman did not recognize who he was.
Wáng swaggered about, quite pleased with himself over this,
and told the servant boy to chase the donkey away,
then took the opportunity to have his way with the woman in the thicket,
describing her trousers and shoes in great detail.
When the husband heard this,
he was greatly ashamed and left.
A little while later,
Wáng saw through a crack in the window the man holding a knife in one hand
and dragging his wife with the other,
looking extremely furious and vicious.
Terrified,
Wáng vaulted over the wall and fled.
The man pursued him,
chased for two or three li but could not catch up,
and finally returned.
Wáng ran with all his might,
his lungs straining open,
and from this contracted a wheezing illness,
which did not heal for several years.
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Wāng Shìxiù
was a man of Lúzhōu.
He was strong, brave, and powerful,
able to lift a stone mortar.
Both father and son were skilled at cùjū (ancient football).
When his father was over forty,
he drowned crossing the Qiántáng River.
Eight or nine years later,
Wāng happened to travel to Húnán,
and moored his boat on Dòngtíng Lake at night.
At the time, the moon was rising in the east.
The clear river was like a silk ribbon.
Just as he was gazing out,
suddenly five men emerged from the lake,
carrying a large mat,
which they spread flat on the water's surface,
roughly half an acre in size.
They laid out wine and food in abundance;
the vessels clinked as they touched,
yet the sound was warm and mellow,
unlike pottery or earthenware.
Soon, three of them stepped onto the mat and sat,
while two attended and poured wine.
Of those seated, one wore yellow,
two wore white;
the headscarves they wore were all black,
towering high and extending down to their shoulders and backs,
of an extremely ancient and unusual style.
But the moonlight was faint,
making it hard to see clearly.
The attendants both wore brown clothes;
one seemed like a youth,
the other like a clerk.
Then they heard the man in yellow say:
"Tonight the moonlight is splendid,
perfect for a hearty drink."
One of the men in white said:
"The scenery this evening
greatly resembles when Guǎnglì Wáng feasted on Líhuā Island."
The three urged each other to drink,
raising their cups and draining them in one go.
But their speech grew somewhat softer,
and soon became inaudible.
The boatman hid, lying low,
not daring to move or breathe.
Wāng Xì examined the attendant closely,
and the old man looked exactly like his father;
but listening to his speech,
it was not his father's voice.
As the second watch was about to end,
suddenly someone said:
"Let's take advantage of this bright moon
and have some fun with a kick."
Immediately, they saw the servant boy dive into the water,
and bring out a round object,
large enough to fill one's arms,
filled inside like quicksilver,
transparent from the inside out.
All those seated stood up.
The man in yellow called the old man to kick it together.
Kicked up over ten feet high,
its light shimmered and dazzled the eyes.
Suddenly, it soared high into the distance,
flying and falling into the boat.
Wāng, itching to show his skill,
kicked it with all his might,
feeling it unusually light.
Kicking too fiercely, it seemed to burst,
soaring up about ten feet;
light leaked from within,
shooting down like a rainbow;
then it swiftly fell,
like a comet streaking across the sky,
plunging straight into the water,
making a bubbling sound as it vanished.
Everyone at the gathering angrily said:
"What kind of living creature is this,
ruining our pure enjoyment!"
The old man laughed and said:
"Not bad, not bad,
this is my family's 'Meteor Kick'."
The man in white was annoyed by his playful words,
and angrily said:
"We are all annoyed and troubled,
how can this old slave be so cheerful?
Go together with Little Wūpí and catch that madman;
otherwise,
your legs will taste the club!"
Wāng saw no way to escape,
but he was not afraid either,
grabbing his knife and standing in the boat.
Suddenly, he saw the servant boy and the old man coming with weapons.
Wāng stared intently,
it was truly his father,
and he urgently called out:
"Father!
Your son is here."
The old man was greatly shocked,
looking at each other in sorrow and despair.
The servant boy immediately turned and left.
The old man said:
"Son, quickly hide.
Otherwise,
we will all die!"
Before he finished speaking,
the three men suddenly boarded the boat.
Their faces were all pitch black,
their eyes larger than pomegranates,
and they seized the old man out.
Wāng struggled to snatch him back,
rocking the boat and breaking the rope.
Wāng cut off one of their arms with his knife,
and the man in yellow fled.
A man in white rushed at Wāng;
Wāng chopped off his head,
which fell into the water with a sound;
with a loud commotion, they all vanished.
Just as they were planning to cross the lake at night,
suddenly a huge beak emerged from the water,
deep as a well.
Water from all sides rushed into it,
making a booming sound.
Suddenly, it spurted out,
and the waves reached the stars,
rocking thousands of boats.
The people on the lake were terrified.
On the boat were two stone drums,
each weighing a hundred catties.
Wāng lifted one and threw it,
stirring the water like thunder,
and the waves gradually subsided;
he threw the other,
and the wind and waves all calmed.
Wāng suspected his father was a ghost.
The old man said:
"I actually never died.
Of the nineteen people who drowned in the river,
all were eaten by demonic creatures;
I survived because I could kick the ball.
The creature offended Qiántáng Jūn,
so it moved to avoid him and came to Dòngtíng.
Those three were fish spirits,
and what we kicked was a fish bladder."
Father and son reunited joyfully,
and in the middle of the night, they rowed away.
At dawn,
they saw a shark fin in the boat,
about four or five feet in diameter,
and realized it was the arm cut off that night.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In the city of Zhūgě,
there was a scholar named Shāng Shìyǔ,
a man of letters.
Once, in a drunken state, he offended a local tycoon with his jesting.
The tycoon incited his servants to beat him savagely.
He was carried home and died.
Shìyǔ had two sons,
the elder named Chén,
the younger named Lǐ,
and a daughter named Sānguān.
Sānguān was sixteen years old,
and her wedding date had been set,
but it was not carried out due to her father’s death.
Her two brothers went to court to file a lawsuit,
but after a year, no resolution was reached.
The fiancé’s family sent someone to consult the mother,
asking to proceed with the wedding under the circumstances.
The mother was about to agree.
But the daughter stepped forward and said:
"How can we hold a joyous ceremony while my father’s body is still cold?
Do they have no parents of their own?"
When the fiancé’s family heard this,
they felt ashamed and stopped pressing the matter.
Not long after,
the two brothers lost their lawsuit,
and returned home aggrieved and wronged.
The whole family was filled with grief and indignation.
The brothers planned to keep their father’s body unburied,
as grounds for filing another lawsuit.
Sānguān said:
"When a person is killed and justice is not served,
the state of affairs is clear.
Do you think Heaven will specially create a Judge Bāo for you two?
To leave our father’s bones exposed—
how can we bear it in our hearts?"
The two brothers heeded her words,
and buried their father.
After the burial,
Sānguān fled one night,
and no one knew where she went.
Her mother, ashamed and anxious,
fearing the fiancé’s family would find out,
did not dare inform the clan,
but only instructed her two sons to secretly investigate.
After nearly half a year,
there was still no trace of her.
It happened that the tycoon was celebrating his birthday,
and hired actors to perform.
An actor named Sūn Chún,
brought two disciples to serve.
One was named Wáng Chéng,
whose appearance was ordinary,
but whose voice was clear and resonant,
earning praise from the crowd.
The other was named Lǐ Yù,
whose face was as lovely and delicate as a beautiful girl’s.
When asked to sing,
he declined, saying he was not familiar with songs;
pressed further,
the tunes he sang were half mixed with children’s folk ditties,
and the whole audience applauded him.
Sūn Chún was greatly embarrassed,
and explained to the host:
"This boy has not been learning long,
he only knows how to serve wine.
I beg you not to blame him."
He was then ordered to serve wine.
Yù went back and forth serving,
skillfully gauging the host’s intentions.
The tycoon took a liking to him.
When the wine ended and the guests dispersed,
he kept Yù to sleep with him.
Yù prepared the bed and removed the tycoon’s shoes for him,
attending to him with utmost care.
When the tycoon, drunk, made advances,
Yù only smiled in response.
The tycoon became even more infatuated,
and sent all the other servants away,
keeping only Yù.
Yù waited until the servants had left,
then closed the door and bolted it.
The servants went to another room to drink.
After a while,
they heard a clattering sound from the main hall.
One servant went to check,
but saw the room dark and silent,
with no sound at all.
As he was about to turn back,
suddenly there was a loud noise,
like a heavy object being hung and its rope snapping.
He urgently called out,
but there was no response.
He called the others, and they forced the door open to enter,
only to find their master’s body and head severed;
Yù had hanged himself,
the rope had broken and he fell to the ground,
with a remnant of rope still hanging from the beam and around his neck.
Everyone was horrified,
and the news was relayed to the inner quarters,
but no one could understand what had happened.
They moved Yù’s body to the courtyard,
and noticed that his socks and shoes seemed empty, as if he had no feet;
when they removed them,
they saw white shoes curved like hooks—
it was a woman.
They were even more shocked.
They called Sūn Chún to question him.
Chún was terrified,
and did not know how to respond.
He only said:
"Yù came to me as a disciple a month ago,
wishing to serve the master on his birthday—
I truly do not know where he came from."
Because she was dressed in mourning clothes,
they suspected she was an assassin sent by the Shāng family.
They temporarily assigned two men to guard the body.
The woman’s face looked as if she were alive; when touched,
her body was still warm.
The two men secretly plotted to violate her.
One of them turned the body over,
and was just about to loosen her garments,
when suddenly, as if struck on the head,
he vomited blood violently from his mouth,
and died in an instant.
The other was terrified,
and reported to the others.
Everyone then revered her as a deity.
They reported the matter to the prefectural authorities.
The prefectural officials questioned Chén and Lǐ,
and both said:
"We do not know.
But our sister disappeared
half a year ago."
They were ordered to go and identify the body,
and it was indeed Sānguān.
The officials marveled at this,
and ruled that the two brothers should take her body for burial,
ordering the tycoon’s family not to seek revenge.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"To have a female Yù Ràng in the family and not know it—
then one can imagine what kind of men her brothers were.
Yet as for Sānguān’s character,
even the rushing waters of the Yì River
would feel ashamed to flow before her;
how much more so the mediocre who drift with the world!
I wish that all women in the world
would buy silk to embroider her image—
the merit of doing so would be no less than worshipping Lord Guān."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Among the villagers was Yú Jiāng,
whose father, while sleeping in the fields,
was eaten by a wolf.
Jiāng was sixteen at the time,
and when he found his father’s remaining shoe,
he was grief-stricken and wished to die.
At night, after his mother had fallen asleep,
he secretly took an iron hammer and left,
sleeping where his father had been,
hoping to avenge his father.
After a while,
a wolf came,
cautiously sniffing around.
Jiāng remained still.
Not long after,
it wagged its tail, brushing his forehead,
then gradually lowered its head to lick his leg.
Jiāng still did not move.
Then it leaped forward joyfully,
to seize him by the collar.
Jiāng quickly struck the wolf’s head with his hammer,
killing it instantly.
He got up and placed it in the grass.
After a while,
another wolf came,
behaving as before.
He killed it as well.
Until midnight,
no more came.
He dozed off briefly,
and dreamed of his father saying:
"Killing these two creatures
is enough to vent my hatred.
But the one that first killed me
had a white nose—
these two are not it."
Jiāng woke up,
and lay still, waiting.
When dawn came,
he had caught nothing more.
He wanted to drag the wolves home,
but feared alarming his mother,
so he threw them into a dry well and returned.
That night he went again,
but still no wolves came.
This went on for three or four nights.
Suddenly, a wolf came,
bit his foot,
and dragged him along.
After a few steps,
thorns pierced his flesh,
and stones scraped his skin.
Jiāng felt as if he were dying.
The wolf then set him down on the ground,
intending to eat his belly.
Jiāng suddenly rose and hammered it,
knocking it down;
he hammered it repeatedly,
and it died.
Upon closer inspection,
it was indeed White Nose.
Overjoyed,
he carried it back,
and only then told his mother.
His mother, weeping, followed him,
searched the dry well,
and found two wolves there.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"Among the farming folk,
could there be such a heroic figure?
His righteous valor sprang from heartfelt sincerity,
not mere bravery alone,
but his wisdom was also extraordinary."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Téng County, Zhào Wàng,
husband and wife, revered the Buddha,
abstaining from meat and blood,
and in the village, they had
the reputation of
"good people."
Their family was considered moderately well-off.
They had a daughter, Xiǎo'èr,
exceptionally intelligent and beautiful,
whom Zhào cherished dearly.
At the age of six,
she was sent to study with her elder brother Chángchūn,
both learning from a teacher,
and within five years, she had mastered the Five Classics.
A fellow student, Dīng,
styled Zǐmò,
three years older than the girl,
was talented and refined,
and they greatly admired each other.
He privately expressed his feelings to his mother,
seeking marriage with the Zhào family.
Zhào hoped to marry his daughter into a prominent family,
so he did not consent.
Not long after,
Zhào became deluded by the White Lotus Sect;
after Xú Hóngrú rebelled,
the entire family fell into becoming rebels.
Xiǎo'èr, being literate and quick-witted,
mastered all techniques of paper soldiers and bean horses
at first sight.
Among the six female disciples who studied under Xú,
only Xiǎo'èr was considered the best,
and thus she learned all his arts.
Because of his daughter, Zhào
gained significant responsibilities.
At that time, Dīng was eighteen,
studying at the Téng County school,
yet he refused to discuss marriage,
his heart still set on Xiǎo'èr.
He secretly fled,
joining Xú's ranks.
The girl was delighted to see him,
treating him with exceptional courtesy.
As Xú's top disciple,
she oversaw military affairs;
coming and going day and night,
even her parents could not control her.
Dīng often visited her at night,
and she would dismiss all attendants,
staying until the third watch.
Dīng privately told her,
"My coming here,
do you know my humble intentions?"
The girl said:
"I do not know."
Dīng said:
"I do not recklessly aspire to climb the dragon's gate,
the reason for my actions
is truly for you.
Heretical paths lead nowhere,
only to destruction.
You are wise,
do you not consider this?
If you can flee with me,
then my sincere heart will not be betrayed."
The girl was lost in thought for a moment,
then suddenly awakened as if from a dream,
saying:
"To leave my parents and go,
is unfilial;
let me tell them."
The two went to explain the pros and cons,
but Zhào remained unenlightened,
saying:
"Our master is a divine being,
how could there be any mistake?"
Knowing persuasion was futile,
the girl changed her hairstyle from a child's to a married woman's bun.
She took out two paper kites,
and she and Dīng each mounted one;
the kites rustled as they spread their wings,
like a pair of lovebirds,
flying side by side.
At dawn,
they reached the border of Láiwú.
The girl pinched the kites' necks with her fingers,
and they suddenly folded and descended.
They then stored the kites.
Switching to two donkeys,
they galloped to Shānyīn Village,
pretending to be refugees,
and rented a house to live in.
The two of them left in haste,
poorly equipped,
with no provisions for firewood or supplies.
Dīng was deeply worried.
He tried to borrow grain from neighbors,
but none would lend him even a peck or a bushel.
The woman showed no sign of distress;
she merely pawned her hairpins and earrings.
They shut the door and quietly faced each other,
guessing lantern riddles,
recalling lost books,
and using these to compete for superiority;
the loser
would have two fingers pressed together to tap their wrist or arm.
An old man surnamed Wēng lived to the west,
a hero of the greenwood.
One day,
he returned from hunting.
The woman said:
" 'Wealth comes from one's neighbors,'
so why should I worry?
Let's borrow a thousand taels of silver for a while—
he'll give it to us!"
Dīng thought it would be difficult.
The woman said:
"I will make him happily hand it over."
