Then she cut paper into the shape of a judge,
placed it on the ground,
and covered it with a chicken coop.
After that, she took Dīng by the hand and climbed onto the bed,
heated some stored wine,
and took out the *Rites of Zhōu* to set drinking rules: each would name a certain volume,
a certain page,
and then they would flip through it together.
Whoever found a character with the radical for "food," "water," or "wine" would drink,
and whoever found a character from the "wine" radical section would drink double.
Soon after, the woman happened to get
"wine steward,"
so Dīng filled a large goblet and urged her to drink.
The woman then prayed:
"If we manage to borrow the gold,
you should get a character from the 'wine' radical section."
Dīng flipped through the pages
and got
"turtle steward."
The woman laughed heartily and said:
"The matter is settled!"
She poured wine drop by drop and handed him the cup.
Dīng protested.
The woman said:
"You are of the aquatic kind,
so you should drink like a turtle."
Just as they were arguing noisily,
they heard a clattering sound from the coop.
The woman stood up and said:
"It's here."
She opened the coop to check,
and there was a cloth bag filled with a large amount of gold,
overflowing.
Dīng was overwhelmed with astonishment and joy.
Later, an old woman from the Wēng family came over carrying a child to play,
and she whispered:
"When my master first returned,
he sat by a lantern at night.
Suddenly, the ground split open violently,
so deep that the bottom could not be seen.
A judge emerged from within.
He said: 'I am an officer from the underworld.
The Emperor of Tàishān is convening all the underworld officials,
and because of the evil deeds of violent bandits,
a thousand silver lantern stands are needed,
each weighing ten taels;
if you donate a hundred stands,
your sins will be absolved.'
My master was terrified,
burned incense and kowtowed in prayer,
and offered a thousand taels of gold.
The judge gradually retreated inside,
and the ground closed up again."
The husband and wife listened to her words,
and intentionally clicked their tongues in feigned astonishment.
From then on, they gradually bought oxen and horses,
kept servants and maids,
and built a mansion for themselves.
A local ruffian, seeing their wealth,
gathered a group of troublemakers,
scaled the wall, and robbed Dīng.
Dīng and his wife were just waking from their dreams
when torches illuminated the room,
and bandits filled the house.
Two of them seized Dīng;
another reached his hand into the woman's bosom.
The woman threw off the covers and stood up,
pointing with her finger and shouting:
"Stop,
stop!"
The thirteen bandits
all stuck out their tongues and stood dumbfounded,
as still as wooden puppets.
The woman then put on her trousers and got off the bed,
called the servants together,
tied each of their arms behind their backs one by one,
and forced them to confess everything clearly.
Then she rebuked them:
"We came from afar to bury ourselves in this remote valley,
hoping to support each other;
how could you be so unkind!
Everyone faces times of urgency;
if you were in dire straits, you could have told us openly—
am I the kind to hoard wealth for myself?
Such wolfish behavior
deserves to be utterly exterminated;
but I cannot bear to do it,
so I'll let you go for now,
but if you offend again, there will be no pardon!"
The bandits kowtowed in thanks and left.
Not long after,
Hóngrú was captured,
and Zhào and his wife and children were all executed.
Dīng took money to redeem Chángchūn's young son and brought him back.
The child was three years old at the time;
they raised him as their own,
gave him the surname Dīng,
and named him Chéngtiāo.
From then on, the villagers gradually learned that they were relatives of the White Lotus Sect.
Just then, a locust plague damaged the crops;
the woman released hundreds of paper kites in the fields,
and the locusts stayed far away,
not entering their land,
so they remained unharmed.
The villagers all grew jealous of them,
and together they reported to the authorities,
claiming they were remnants of Hóngrú's faction.
The officials, eyeing their wealth,
regarded them as prey,
and arrested Dīng.
Dīng bribed the magistrate heavily,
and only then was he spared.
The woman said:
"The wealth we gained came unexpectedly,
so it is only natural that it should scatter and vanish.
Moreover, a place full of snakes and scorpions
is no place to stay long."
So they sold their property at a low price and left,
settling in the western outskirts of Yìdū.
The woman was clever and dexterous,
skilled at managing and accumulating wealth,
and her business acumen surpassed that of men.
She often operated a glassware workshop,
hiring workers and instructing them,
producing all kinds of chess pieces and lanterns.
Their unique designs and fantastical colors
were unmatched by other shops,
so they fetched high prices and sold quickly.
After several years,
her wealth grew even more prominent.
Yet she supervised the maids and servants strictly,
with hundreds of dependents and no idle mouths.
In her leisure, she would brew tea and play chess with Dīng,
or enjoy reading books and histories.
Financial matters,
as well as the duties of the servants,
were reviewed every five days;
the woman would hold the counting rods herself,
while Dīng checked the registers and called out names and numbers.
The diligent were rewarded accordingly,
while the lazy were whipped or punished by kneeling.
On that day,
they were given leave and did not work at night;
the couple would set out food and wine,
calling the maids to sing rustic songs for amusement.
The woman was as discerning as a deity,
and no one dared deceive her.
Moreover, her rewards often exceeded the labor,
so tasks were easily accomplished.
In the village of over two hundred households,
she provided capital to the poor according to their needs,
and thus the village had no idlers.
During a severe drought,
she had the villagers set up an altar in the wild,
rode out in a carriage,
performed Yu steps and worked magic,
and sweet rain poured down,
ensuring ample harvests within five li.
People revered her even more as divine.
The woman never veiled her face when going out,
and all the villagers saw her.
Sometimes young men gathered
and privately discussed her beauty;
but when they encountered her face to face,
they all became solemn and dared not look up.
Every autumn,
she gave money to village children unable to work in the fields,
instructing them
to gather thistles and artemisia,
and after nearly twenty years,
they filled an entire storeroom.
People secretly mocked her.
Then, when a great famine struck Shāndōng,
and people resorted to cannibalism;
the woman brought out the vegetables,
mixing them with millet to feed the starving,
so the nearby villages survived intact,
with no one fleeing.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Her actions
were likely heaven-sent,
not merely human effort.
Yet without that one word of enlightenment,
she would have long perished alongside him.
From this we see that
in the world, those endowed with extraordinary talents
who stray into wickedness and perish
must also be many.
How can we know that among the six classmates,
there was no such person?
It makes one lament that they did not encounter a Dīng Shēng."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Jīn Dàyòng
was from an old family in Zhōngzhōu.
He was betrothed to the daughter of Prefect Yóu,
named Gēngniáng,
who was beautiful and virtuous.
Their marital affection was deep.
Due to the chaos of roving bandits,
the family scattered.
Jīn fled south with his household.
On the road, they met a young man,
also fleeing with his wife,
who called himself Wáng Shíbā of Guǎnglíng,
and offered to lead the way.
Jīn was pleased,
and they traveled together.
Upon reaching the river,
Gēngniáng secretly told Jīn:
"Do not board the same boat as that young man.
He has repeatedly glanced at me,
his eyes shifting and expression changing—
his intentions are unfathomable."
Jīn agreed.
But Wáng eagerly sought a large boat,
helped Jīn with his luggage,
and toiled diligently.
Jīn could not bear to refuse.
Moreover, considering Wáng had a young wife with him,
he thought there should be no harm.
The wife stayed with Gēngniáng,
and her demeanor seemed gentle and amiable.
Wáng sat at the bow of the boat,
chatting intimately with the boatman,
as if they were old acquaintances or relatives.
Before long,
the sun set,
and the waterway stretched far,
vast and indistinguishable north from south.
Jīn looked around at the dark, perilous surroundings
and grew suspicious.
Soon after,
the bright moon rose,
revealing endless reeds as far as the eye could see.
Once moored,
Wáng invited Jīn and his father outside for some air,
then seized the chance to push Jīn into the water.
Jīn's elderly father,
seeing this, tried to cry out.
The boatman struck him with a pole,
and he drowned as well.
Jīn's mother heard the noise and came out to look,
and was also struck and drowned.
Only then did Wáng shout for help.
When the mother came out,
Gēngniáng was behind her
and had glimpsed it slightly.
Upon hearing the whole family had drowned,
she showed no alarm,
but wept, saying:
"My parents-in-law are both gone,
where shall I go now!"
Wáng urged her:
"Do not worry, madam,
please come with me to Jīnlíng.
My family has fields and houses,
enough to provide for you,
and you will be safe."
The woman wiped her tears and said:
"If it can be so,
my wishes are satisfied."
Wáng was overjoyed,
and attended to her with great殷勤.
When night fell,
he pulled her, seeking intimacy.
The woman pleaded her condition,
so Wáng went to sleep with his wife.
After the first watch had passed,
the couple began arguing loudly,
though the cause was unknown.
Only the wife was heard saying:
"For what you have done,
thunder will surely shatter your skull!"
Wáng then beat her.
The wife cried out:
"Let me die then!
I truly refuse to be the wife of a murderous thief!"
Wáng roared in anger,
and the wife went out.
Then came a thudding sound,
followed by cries that the wife had drowned.
Not long after,
they arrived at Jīnlíng.
He led Gēngniáng to his home,
and upon entering the hall, they met the old woman.
The old woman was surprised that this was not her former daughter-in-law.
Wáng said:
"My wife fell into the water and died;
this is my new bride."
Returning to the room,
he again tried to force himself upon her.
Gēngniáng laughed and said:
"A man of about thirty,
and you haven't yet experienced the ways of men and women?
Even street urchins, when first married,
must share a cup of weak wine;
your family is wealthy,
surely this isn't difficult.
To face each other sober,
what kind of behavior is that?"
Wáng was pleased,
and prepared wine to drink together.
Gēngniáng held the cup,
urging him to drink with earnest hospitality.
Wáng gradually became drunk,
and declined to drink more.
Gēngniáng took a large bowl,
and with forced charm, urged him on.
Wáng could not bear to refuse,
and drank it.
Thereupon, thoroughly drunk,
he stripped naked and urged her to bed.
Gēngniáng cleared away the utensils and candles,
excusing herself to relieve herself;
she left the room,
entered with a knife,
and in the dark, felt for Wáng's neck with her hand.
Wáng, still holding her arm, made intimate sounds.
Gēngniáng exerted all her strength and cut him,
but he did not die;
he cried out and rose up;
she struck again,
and only then did he perish.
The old woman seemed to have heard something,
and hurried towards them.
The woman killed her as well.
Wáng's younger brother, Shíjiǔ, became aware of it.
Gēngniáng knew she could not escape,
and quickly tried to cut her own throat;
the knife was blunt and the metal would not penetrate,
so she opened the door and fled.
Shíjiǔ pursued her,
but she had already thrown herself into the pond;
he called out and informed the neighbors,
but by the time they rescued her, she was already dead,
her beauty as in life.
Together they examined Wáng's corpse,
and saw a letter on the window.
Opening it to read,
they found the woman had detailed her grievances.
The crowd considered her chaste and heroic,
and planned to pool funds for her burial.
At daybreak,
thousands gathered to look;
seeing her countenance,
they all bowed to her in reverence.
Throughout the day,
they collected a hundred taels of gold,
and so buried her in the southern outskirts.
Those fond of good deeds provided her with a pearl crown and burial robes,
and she was interred with rich offerings.
Earlier,
when Jīnshēng had fallen into the water,
he floated on a plank,
and did not die.
As dawn approached,
he reached the Huái River,
and was rescued by a small boat.
The boat belonged to a wealthy old man, Yīn Wēng, who had specifically set it up to save the drowning.
After Jīn revived,
he went to thank Yīn Wēng.
Yīn Wēng treated him generously,
and asked him to stay and teach his son.
Jīn, not knowing the fate of his parents,
wished to go and inquire,
so he was undecided.
Suddenly, it was reported:
"We have fished out an old man and an old woman, dead."
Jīn suspected they were his parents,
and rushing to verify, it was indeed so.
Yīn Wēng arranged for coffins on his behalf.
Jīn was just mourning bitterly,
when it was reported again:
"We have rescued a drowning woman,
who says Jīnshēng is her husband."
Jīn, wiping his tears, rushed out in surprise,
and the woman had already arrived,
but it was not Gēngniáng at all,
but rather the woman Shíbā.
She wept bitterly to Jīn,
begging him not to abandon her.
Jīn said:
"My heart is in turmoil;
how can I find time to plan for others?"
The woman grew even more sorrowful.
Yīn, understanding the situation,
was pleased, considering it heaven's retribution,
and urged Jīn to take the woman as his wife.
Jīn declined on grounds of mourning,
saying, "Moreover, I intend to seek revenge,
and fear that a delicate woman would be a burden."
The woman said:
"If what you say is so,
supposing Gēngniáng were still alive,
would you abandon her for revenge and mourning?"
Yīn Wēng, considering her words reasonable,
asked to temporarily take her in to raise,
and Jīn then agreed.
When the burial of the old couple was divined,
the woman wept,
as if mourning her own parents-in-law.
After the burial,
Jīn, carrying a blade and begging bowl,
set out for Guǎnglíng.
The woman stopped him, saying:
"I, your servant, am of the Táng family;
my ancestral home is in Jīnlíng.
That brute is from the same hometown;
his earlier claim of being from Guǎnglíng
was a lie.
Moreover, half the river pirates
are his accomplices;
you will not achieve revenge,
but only bring disaster upon yourself."
Jīn paced back and forth, not knowing what to plan.
Suddenly, news spread of a woman avenging a wrong,
filling the rivers and canals,
with her name clearly known.
Jīn heard this and felt a moment of relief,
but then grew even more sorrowful.
He bid farewell to the woman, saying:
"Fortunately, I have not dishonored you.
Having such a chaste and heroic wife at home,
how could I bear to be unfaithful and marry again?"
The woman, as the matter was already settled,
refused to part midway,
and wished to serve as a concubine.
It happened that Deputy General Yuán,
who was an old acquaintance of Yīn's,
was about to depart westward,
and visited Yīn;
seeing Jīn,
he took a great liking to him,
and asked him to serve as his secretary.
Not long after,
rebel bandits rose in rebellion,
and Yuán achieved great merit;
Jīn, having participated in planning military affairs,
was recognized for his service,
and was appointed a Yóujī officer before returning.
Only then did the couple perform the wedding ceremony.
After a few days,
he took his wife to Jīnlíng,
intending to visit Gēngniáng's grave.
Passing by Zhènjiāng temporarily,
they wished to ascend Jīnshān.
As their boat drifted in midstream,
another boat passed by,
in which there was an old woman and a young woman.
He was struck by how much the young woman resembled Gēngniáng.
The boat passed swiftly,
and the woman peered at Jīn from the window,
her expression even more alike.
Startled and doubtful, he dared not pursue and ask,
but urgently called out:
"Look, a flock of ducklings flying up to the sky!"
The young woman heard this,
and also called out:
"Greedy child, wanting to eat the fishy cat!"
For these were private jokes from their past boudoir days.
Jīn was greatly astonished,
turned the boat to approach,
and it was truly Gēngniáng.
A maid in blue helped her over to their boat,
and they embraced, weeping sorrowfully,
moving the travelers with their grief.
Mrs. Táng paid respects to Gēngniáng with the etiquette due a principal wife.
Gēngniáng asked in surprise,
and only then did Jīn fully recount the circumstances.
Gēngniáng took her hand and said:
"That conversation we had on the same boat,
I have never forgotten.
I never thought we would become one family despite being from different places.
You buried my parents-in-law on my behalf;
for that I should first thank you.
Why do you offer me such formalities?"
Then, by order of age,
Táng was one year younger than Gēngniáng,
and so became her younger sister.
Earlier,
after Gēngniáng was buried,
she herself did not know how many years had passed.
Suddenly, someone called out:
"Gēngniáng,
your husband is not dead,
you should still be reunited."
Then, as if waking from a dream,
she looked around
and saw walls on all sides,
only then realizing she had died and been buried.
She only felt stifled,
but suffered no other pain.
Some wicked youths, seeing her burial goods were rich and fine,
dug up the grave and broke open the coffin.
Just as they were about to plunder,
they saw Gēngniáng was still alive,
and they were all terrified.
Fearing they would harm her, Gēngniáng
pleaded with them, saying:
"Fortunately, you all came,
allowing me to see the light of day again.
The hairpins and earrings on my head,
take them all.
I wish to be sold to become a nun,
which could fetch you a bit more money.
I will also not reveal anything."
The robbers kowtowed and said:
"Madam, your chastity and fortitude
are revered by both gods and men.
We lowly ones are merely poor and desperate,
driven to commit this unrighteous act.
If you do not expose us,
that would be fortunate enough;
how dare we sell you to become a nun!"
Gēngniáng said:
"This is what I myself desire."
Another robber said:
"In Zhènjiāng, there is a Lady Gěng,
a widow without children.
If she sees you,
she will surely be delighted."
Gēngniáng thanked them.
She herself removed her pearl ornaments,
and gave them all to the robbers.
The robbers dared not accept them;
she insisted on giving them,
so they finally bowed and accepted.
They then carried her away,
arriving at Lady Gěng's home,
pretending they were lost due to boat winds.
Lady Gěng,
from a wealthy family,
was a widow living alone.
Seeing Gēngniáng, she was overjoyed,
and treated her as her own daughter.
It happened that mother and son were returning from Jīnshān.
Gēngniáng recounted the whole story in detail.
Jīn then boarded the boat to pay respects to the mother,
and the mother treated him like a son-in-law.
She invited them to her home,
where they stayed for several days before returning.
Afterwards, their visits back and forth never ceased.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"When a great calamity arises,
the licentious survive,
while the chaste perish.
The survivors provoke people's rage,
while the dead move people to tears.
As for one who remains calm and smiling, unalarmed,
and personally slays a formidable enemy,
even among the heroic men throughout the ages,
how many can match her?
Who says that women
cannot compare to Yànyún?"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Liǔ Fānghuá,
was from Bǎodìng.
His wealth dominated the entire region,
and he was generous and hospitable,
often having a hundred guests at his table.
He urgently helped those in urgent need,
not begrudging even a thousand in gold.
Guests and friends borrowing money often did not repay.
Only one guest, Gōng Mèngbì,
from Shǎnxi,
never made any requests in his life.
Whenever he came,
he would stay for a year.
His speech was refined and elegant,
and Liǔ spent the most time with him, sharing his quarters.
Liǔ's son was named Hé,
then still a young boy wearing his hair in tufts,
and he called Gōng uncle.
Gōng also enjoyed playing with Hé.
Whenever Hé returned from school,
Gōng would often lift the floor tiles with him,
burying stones,
pretending to bury gold for fun.
The house had five bays,
and they had almost dug up the entire place.
Everyone laughed at his childish behavior,
but Hé alone delighted in and loved him,
being even closer to him than to the other guests.
More than ten years later,
the family gradually declined,
unable to meet the demands of many guests,
so the guests gradually grew ashamed and became scarce;
however, a dozen or so people talking all night
was still common.
As the years grew late,
the family's fortunes daily declined further,
yet they still sold land for money,
to prepare chicken and millet for guests.
Hé also spent lavishly,
emulating his father by making young friends,
and Liǔ did not stop him.
Before long,
Liǔ fell ill and died,
to the point there was no money for funeral arrangements.
Gōng then took money from his own purse,
to manage Liǔ's affairs.
Hé felt even more grateful to him.
Matters great and small,
were all entrusted to Uncle Gōng.
Gōng, whenever he came in from outside,
would always have tiles and rubble in his sleeves,
and upon entering the room, would toss them into dark corners,
leaving people even more puzzled about his intention.
Hé often expressed his worries about poverty to Gōng.
Gōng said:
"You do not know the hardship of toil.
Never mind having no gold;
even if I gave you a thousand in gold,
you could squander it instantly.
A man should worry about not standing on his own,
why worry about poverty?"
One day,
he bid farewell, wishing to return home.
Hé tearfully urged him to come back quickly,
Gōng promised,
and then left.
Hé, poor and unable to support himself,
gradually pawned everything away.
Daily he hoped Gōng would come,
thinking he would manage things,
but Gōng vanished without a trace,
gone like the yellow crane.
Earlier,
while Liǔ was alive,
he had arranged a marriage for Hé with the Huáng family of Wújí,
a family of long-standing wealth.
Later, hearing the Liǔ family was poor,
they secretly regretted it.
When Liǔ died,
they were notified of the obituary,
but did not even come to offer condolences;
they still excused themselves citing the long distance.
After Hé completed the mourning period,
his mother sent him to his prospective father-in-law's place himself,
to set the wedding date,
hoping Huáng would take pity and show consideration.
Upon arrival,
Huáng, hearing his clothes and shoes were worn and shabby,
ordered the gatekeeper not to admit him.
He sent a message saying:
"Go back and secure a hundred in gold,
then you may come again;
otherwise,
let us end it here."
Hearing this, Hé wept bitterly.
An old woman named Liǔ across the street,
took pity on him and gave him food,
presenting him with three hundred coins,
comforted him and urged him to return home.
His mother also grieved and despaired, with no plan.
Thinking that eight or nine out of ten old guests owed them debts,
she had him go seek help from the wealthy ones.
Hé said:
"Those who befriended me in the past
did so for my wealth.
If I had a carriage with four horses,
borrowing a thousand in gold
would also not be difficult.
In our current state,
who would still remember past kindness or old friendships?
Moreover, when father gave people money and resources,
there were never contracts or guarantees,
so demanding repayment would also be hard to enforce."
His mother insisted strongly.
Hé obeyed her instruction,
but for over twenty days,
he could not obtain a single coin;
only an actor named Lǐ Sì,
who had received kindness and aid in the past,
hearing of the situation,
righteously gifted one tael of gold.
Mother and son wept bitterly,
and from then on, they gave up hope.
Huáng Nǚ was already of marriageable age.
Upon hearing that her father had broken off the engagement with Hé,
she secretly disapproved of his actions.
Huáng wanted his daughter to marry someone else.
The girl wept and said:
"Liǔ Láng was not born into poverty.
Had he become twice as wealthy as before,
how could those who resent us have taken him away?
Now that he is poor, to abandon him
is unkind!"
Huáng was displeased,
and tried every means to persuade her.
But the girl remained unwavering.
Both her father and mother grew angry,
cursing and spitting at her day and night.
Yet the girl remained calm.
Not long after,
bandits raided their home at night,
and Huáng and his wife were tortured nearly to death,
their household completely looted.
Three years passed by,
and the family grew even more destitute.
A merchant from the west, hearing of the girl's beauty,
offered fifty taels of silver as betrothal gifts.
Huáng, tempted by the money, agreed,
intending to force his daughter into the marriage.
The girl discovered their plan,
ruined her appearance and smeared her face,
and fled under cover of night.
She begged for food along the way,
and after two months,
finally reached Bǎodìng.
She inquired about Hé's residence
and went straight to his home.
Hé's mother, thinking she was a beggar's wife,
shouted at her to leave.
The girl sobbed and explained herself.
The mother took her hand and wept, saying:
"Child, how have you been reduced to such a state!"
The girl then tearfully recounted what had happened.
Mother and son both cried.
They then helped her wash and groom herself,
and her complexion regained its radiance,
her eyes and brows shining brightly.
Both mother and son were overjoyed.
However, the family of three
could only afford one meal a day.
The mother wept and said:
"It is only right that we mother and son endure this;
what pains me is
that we have wronged such a virtuous wife!"
The girl smiled and comforted her, saying:
"Having lived among beggars,
I am well acquainted with hardship.
Looking at our situation now,
it feels like the difference between heaven and hell."
The mother was cheered by her words.
One day, the girl entered an unused room,
where she saw clumps of withered grass
covering every inch of the ground.
She gradually made her way to the inner chamber,
where dust had accumulated in piles.
In a dark corner, something was heaped up.
Kicking it, she felt resistance underfoot,
and picking it up, she saw it was all silver.
Startled, she ran to tell Hé.
Hé went with her to investigate,
and found that the tiles and rubble he had discarded in his childhood
had all turned into silver.
He then recalled that as a child, he often buried stones in the room—
could they all have turned into gold?
But their old house had already been mortgaged to the neighbor to the east.
He hurried to redeem it.
Broken tiles and残缺 bricks lay scattered about,
and the stones he had hidden were clearly exposed.
He felt somewhat disappointed,
but when he lifted the other bricks,
he found gleaming silver ingots underneath.
In an instant,
he had acquired tens of thousands of taels.
From then on, he redeemed his family's land and property,
bought servants,
and his household became even more splendid than before.
He resolved to himself:
"If I do not strive to establish myself,
I will have failed my uncle Gōng!"
He devoted himself to his studies,
and within three years, he passed the provincial examination.
He then personally took silver
to repay Old Woman Liú.
Dressed in bright clothes that dazzled the eyes,
with more than ten attendants
all riding spirited horses like dragons,
he arrived at the old woman's humble cottage.
Hé sat on her bed,
while the commotion of people and horses
filled the entire neighborhood.
Since his daughter's disappearance, Old Man Huáng
had been pressured by the western merchant to return the betrothal gifts,
and had already spent nearly half of it.
He had to sell his house
to repay the debt.
Thus, he became as impoverished as Hé had once been.
Hearing of his former son-in-law's newfound glory,
he could only shut his door and lament.
Old Woman Liú prepared wine and food to entertain Hé,
and spoke of Huáng Nǚ's virtues,
regretting that she had run away.
She asked Hé:
"Have you married?"
Hé replied:
"Yes, I have."
After the meal,
he insisted that the old woman come see his new wife,
and took her back with him in the carriage.
Upon arriving home,
Huáng Nǚ came out in splendid attire,
surrounded by maidservants like an immortal.
The old woman was astonished to see her,
and they reminisced about the past.
Huáng Nǚ earnestly inquired after her parents' well-being.
After staying for several days,
she was treated with great warmth and generosity.
Fine clothes were made for her,
renewing her entire wardrobe,
before she was sent back home.
The old woman went to Huáng's place,
reported the news of their daughter,
and also conveyed her regards.
The couple was greatly astonished.
The old woman urged them to go seek refuge with their daughter,
but Huáng showed a reluctant expression.
Later, as the cold and hunger became unbearable,
they had no choice but to go to Bǎodìng.
Upon arriving at the gate,
they saw it was imposing and splendid,
and the gatekeeper glared angrily;
they waited all day without gaining entry.
A woman came out,
and Huáng, with a gentle expression and humble words,
told her his name,
asking her to secretly inform his daughter.
After a short while,
the woman came out
and led them into a side room,
saying:
"The young lady is extremely eager to see you;
but she fears her husband might find out,
so she must wait for an opportunity.
When did you arrive here, sir?
Are you perhaps hungry?"
Huáng then poured out his hardships.
The woman brought out a jug of wine and two dishes of food,
placing them before Huáng.
She also gave him five taels of silver,
saying:
"The young master is feasting in his chamber,
so the young lady likely cannot come.
Tomorrow morning,
you should leave early,
and do not let the young master hear of it."
Huáng agreed.
He rose early to pack his things,
but the gate was still locked,
so he waited inside the gate,
sitting on his bundle.
Suddenly, there was a commotion as the master came out.
Huáng tried to hide,
but Hé had already spotted him,
and asked in surprise who he was,
but none of the servants could answer.
Hé angrily said:
"This must be a villain;
seize him and take him to the authorities."
The servants responded,
brought out a short rope,
and tied him to a tree.
Huáng, ashamed and frightened, could not find words to say.
Not long after,
the woman from the previous evening came out,
knelt down, and said:
"This is my maternal uncle.
Because he arrived late last night,
I did not have time to inform the master."
Hé ordered him untied.
The woman saw him out the gate,
saying:
"I forgot to instruct the gatekeeper,
which led to this misunderstanding.
The young lady says: when you miss her,
you can have the old lady pretend to be a flower seller,
and come with Old Woman Liú."
Huáng agreed,
and upon returning, told his wife.
The old woman missed her daughter desperately,
so she told Old Woman Liú,
who indeed went with her to Hé's house.
They passed through more than ten gates
before reaching the daughter's quarters.
The daughter wore a cape and her hair in a topknot,
adorned with pearls, jade, and fine silks,
her fragrance wafting around her;
with a soft call,
maids and old women,
large and small, rushed in and filled the room.
A golden armchair was moved over,
and a pair of footrests placed.
A clever maid served tea;
they exchanged greetings in veiled language,
gazing at each other with tears glistening.
When evening came,
a room was prepared for the two old women;
the bedding was warm,
finer than anything they had experienced even in their wealthiest days.
After staying for three to five days,
the daughter treated them with deep affection.
The old woman would often lead her to a secluded spot,
weeping and confessing her past wrongs.
The daughter said:
"How could I, as your child, hold any grudge against my mother?
But my husband's anger has not subsided,
and I fear he might find out."
Whenever Hé arrived,
she would quickly hide.
One day,
as they were sitting close together,
Hé suddenly entered,
saw them,
and angrily scolded:
"What kind of country bumpkin is this old woman,
daring to sit so close to my wife!
She ought to have all her hair plucked out!"
Old Woman Liú hurriedly stepped forward and said:
"This is a relative of mine,
Sister Wáng, a flower seller.
Please do not blame her."
Hé then clasped his hands and apologized.
He sat down and said:
"You have been here for several days, Grandma,
but I have been very busy,
and have not had time to chat with you.
Is that old beast of the Huáng family still alive?"
She replied with a smile:
"They are both well.
Only they are so poor they can hardly get by.
Since you, sir, are so wealthy and noble,
why not think of the bond between father-in-law and son-in-law?"
Hé slammed the table and said:
"If it hadn't been for your compassion years ago, Grandma,
giving me a bowl of porridge,
how could I have ever returned to my hometown!
Now I wish I could skin him alive and sleep on his hide—
what bond is there to think of!"
As he spoke in his fury,
he stamped his feet and rose to curse.
The daughter, angered, said:
"Even if they were unkind,
they are still my parents.
I came from far away,
my hands chapped and frostbitten,
the soles of my feet worn through,
and I thought I had done nothing to let you down.
How can you curse my father in front of his child,
making it so hard for me to bear?"
Hé finally restrained his anger
and got up to leave.
Old Woman Huáng, ashamed and crestfallen, turned pale,
and asked to leave.
The daughter secretly gave her twenty taels of silver.
After returning home,
there was no news for a long time,
and the daughter worried deeply.
Hé then sent someone to invite them.
The couple arrived,
ashamed and unable to face anyone.
Hé apologized, saying:
"Last year when you honored us with your visit,
I was not clearly informed,
and thus offended you greatly."
Huáng could only murmur in agreement.
Hé had them change their clothes and shoes.
They stayed for over a month,
but Huáng still felt uneasy at heart,
and repeatedly asked to return home.
Hé gave him a hundred taels of silver,
saying:
"The Western merchant offered fifty taels,
but I am doubling it."
Huáng accepted it, sweating with shame.
Hé sent them back in a carriage with horses,
and in their later years, they lived in modest comfort.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
After the tears at Yōngmén,
the pearl-adorned guests vanished without a trace,
making one so indignant as to shut the door,
unwilling to befriend another guest.
Yet when a good friend buries one's bones,
and turns stone into gold,
it cannot be said that this is not the reward for being generous and hospitable.
The lady of the chamber sits and enjoys high status,
dignified as an imperial consort,
and if not for one as chaste and exceptional as Lady Huáng,
who could bear this without shame?
Thus it is clear that the Creator does not bestow blessings recklessly.
In the village there was a wealthy man,
who hoarded goods to amass profits,
and squeezed others to the bone.
He had stored away several hundred strings of cash in a cellar,
and fearing others might know,
he wore tattered clothes and ate chaff and husks to feign poverty.
When relatives or friends occasionally visited,
he never once prepared a chicken and millet meal for them.
If someone said his family was not poor,
he would glare in anger,
treating the person as a sworn enemy.
In his later years,
he daily ate a liter of elm bark powder,
the skin on his arms hung in folds an inch long,
yet he still refused to dig up the money he had stored.
Later, he gradually grew emaciated.
Nearing death,
his two sons gathered around asking him,
but he still would not tell them promptly;
only when he realized the situation was truly critical,
and wanted to tell his sons,
by the time they arrived,
his tongue was already stiff and he could not speak,
he only clawed at his chest,
uttering incoherent sounds.
After his death,
his sons and grandsons could not afford a coffin,
so they buried him wrapped in straw.
Alas!
If hoarding gold can be considered wealth,
then the treasury’s tens of millions,
why not point to them and say they are mine?
How foolish!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Wáng Fénbīn said: In his hometown, there was a man who kept a myna,
taught it to speak,
and became very intimate with it,
whenever he went out traveling, he always took it with him,
and they had been together for several years.
One day,
as he was about to pass through Jiàngzhōu,
his travel funds were exhausted,
and the man was distressed with no plan.
The bird said:
"Why not sell me?
Send me to the prince’s residence,
you should get a good price,
and won’t have to worry about lacking funds for the return journey."
The man said:
"How could I bear to?"
The bird said:
"It’s no matter.
Once you get the price, leave quickly,
and wait for me under the big tree twenty li west of the city."
The man agreed.
He took it to the city,
they conversed back and forth,
and gradually a crowd gathered to watch.
A palace eunuch saw it,
and reported it to the prince.
The prince summoned him in,
wanting to buy it.
The man said:
"This humble one depends on it for life,
and does not wish to sell."
The prince asked the bird:
"Are you willing to stay?"
It said:
"I am willing to stay."
The prince was pleased.
The bird then said:
"Give a price of ten taels of gold,
no more."
The prince was even more pleased,
and immediately gave ten taels.
The man pretended to look regretful and left.
The prince spoke with the bird,
and it responded quickly and cleverly.
He called for meat to feed it.
After eating,
the bird said:
"Your subject wishes to bathe."
The prince ordered a golden basin filled with water,
opened the cage and let it bathe.
After bathing,
it flew to the eaves,
preened its feathers and shook them out,
still chattering incessantly with the prince.
After a while,
its feathers dried,
it fluttered up gracefully,
and speaking in a Shānxī accent said:
"Your subject is leaving now!"
In the blink of an eye, it was gone.
The prince and the palace attendants,
looked up and sighed.
They hurriedly searched for the man,
but he had already vanished.
Later, someone going to Qínzhōng,
saw the man with the bird at the market in Xī'ān.
Recorded by Mr. Bì Zǎijī.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Liú Hǎishí,
a man from Pútái,
took refuge from turmoil in Bīnzhōu.
At the time he was fourteen years old,
and shared a teacher with Bīnzhōu native Liú Cāngkè,
thus they became close,
and pledged to be sworn brothers.
Not long after,
Hǎishí lost his parents,
and returned home to attend the funerals,
after which news was cut off.
Cāngkè’s family was quite well-off.
At forty years old,
he had two sons: the eldest, Jí,
seventeen years old,
was a renowned scholar in the county;
the second son was also clever.
Cāngkè also took as a concubine a woman from the county named Ní,
and doted on her greatly.
Half a year later,
the eldest son fell ill with a brain ailment and died,
husband and wife were deeply grieved.
Not long after,
his wife also fell ill and died;
a few months later,
the eldest daughter-in-law also died;
and the deaths of maids and servants
followed one after another: Cāngkè mourned,
almost unable to bear it.
One day,
as he sat brooding,
suddenly the gatekeeper announced Hǎishí had arrived.
Cāngkè was overjoyed,
hurried out to welcome him in.
Just as he was about to exchange greetings,
Hǎishí suddenly exclaimed in alarm:
"Brother, you have a calamity that will wipe out your family,
don’t you know?"
Cāngkè was stunned,
not understanding why.
Hǎishí said:
"Having long lost contact,
I secretly suspected your recent circumstances might not be good."
Cāngkè shed tears,
and thus told him the situation.
Hǎishí sighed.
Then he smiled and said:
"The disaster is not yet over,
at first I came to mourn for you.
But fortunately you met me,
allow me to congratulate you."
Cāngkè said:
"Long time no see,
have you recently mastered the 'art of Yuèrén'
Hǎishí said:
"That is not my forte.
But for the fēngshuǐ of dwellings and physiognomy,
I am quite practiced."
Cāngkè was pleased,
and asked him to examine his house.
Hǎi Shí entered the residence,
and looked all around inside and out.
Then he requested to see all the family members;
Cāng Kè followed his instruction,
having his sons, daughters-in-law, maidservants, and concubines
all appear in the hall.
Cāng Kè pointed them out one by one.
When it came to Ní,
Hǎi Shí looked up at the sky,
and laughed heartily without stopping.
Everyone was just becoming alarmed and suspicious,
when they saw the Ní girl trembling and turning pale,
her body suddenly shrinking,
until she was only a little over two feet tall.
Hǎi Shí struck her head with a ruler,
which made a sound like a stone jar.
Hǎi Shí grabbed her hair,
examined the back of her head,
and saw several strands of white hair,
which he intended to pull out.
The girl drew in her neck, knelt down, and cried,
saying she would leave immediately,
but begged him not to pull them out.
Hǎi Shí angrily said:
"Has your murderous heart not yet died?"
And he pulled them out from the back of her neck.
The girl changed form as soon as he did,
turning black like a wildcat.
Everyone was greatly terrified.
Hǎi Shí picked her up and put her in his sleeve,
then turned to the daughter-in-law and said:
"You have been deeply poisoned,
there must be something unusual on your back,
please let me examine it."
The woman was ashamed,
and unwilling to bare it for inspection.
Liú Zǐgù forced her,
and they saw white hairs on her back,
about four fingers long.
Hǎi Shí picked them out with a needle,
and said:
"These hairs have already aged,
in seven days it would have been incurable."
He then looked at Liú Zǐ,
who also had hairs,
only two fingers long.
He said:
"With this, you could have lived for just over a month."
For Cāng Kè and the maids and servants,
he pricked them all.
He said:
"If I had not come just now,
not a single soul in this household would have survived."
They asked:
"What is this creature?"
He replied:
"Also a type of fox.
It absorbs people's vital energy to gain power,
and is most deadly to humans."
Cāng Kè said:
"It has been a long time since I last saw you,
how have you become so divinely extraordinary!
Are you perhaps an immortal?"
He laughed and said:
"I have merely learned a small skill from my master,
how can you suddenly call me an immortal."
They asked about his master,
and he replied:
"Dàoshān Shídào Rén.
As for this creature,
I cannot kill it,
I will take it back to present as a captive to my master."
Having said this,
he bid farewell.
But then he felt his sleeve was empty,
and exclaimed in alarm:
"I forgot!
There was a large hair at the end of its tail that I didn't remove,
now it has escaped."
Everyone was horrified.
Hǎi Shí said:
"The hairs on its neck are all gone,
it cannot transform into a human,
it can only turn into an animal,
so it cannot have escaped far."
So he went into the rooms to look at their cats,
went out the door to check their dogs,
and said none of them were it.
Opening the pigpen, he laughed and said:
"It's here."
Cāng Kè looked,
and there was an extra pig.
Hearing Hǎi Shí laugh,
it immediately lay down,
not daring to move at all.
Hǎi Shí grabbed it by the ear and pulled it out,
and saw a single white hair on its tail,
hard as a needle.
Just as he was about to examine and pull it out,
the pig twisted and turned, crying pitifully,
unwilling to let him pull it.
Hǎi Shí said:
"You have committed so many evils,
and you still won't let me pull out a single hair?"
He held it firmly and pulled it out,
and it immediately transformed back into a wildcat.
He put it in his sleeve and prepared to leave.
Cāng Kè earnestly urged him to stay,
so he stayed for a meal.
Asked when they would meet again,
he said:
"That is hard to predict.
My master has made a great vow,
often sending us into the world,
to rescue all living beings,
so it is not impossible that we may meet again."
After they parted,
Cāng Kè pondered his name carefully,
and finally realized:
"Hǎi Shí is probably an immortal!
'Shān Shí'
combined makes the character 'Yán'
which is the taboo name of Immortal Lǚ."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
When Shàngshū Shí Màohuá of Qīngzhōu was still a student,
outside the city gate there was a large deep pool,
which never dried up even when it didn't rain.
Several dozen major bandits captured in the county
were executed beside the pool.
Their ghosts gathered and caused hauntings,
and passersby were often dragged in.
One day,
a certain Mr. Jiǎ was in just such a predicament,
when he suddenly heard the ghosts panic and flee, saying:
"Shàngshū Shí is coming!"
Not long after,
the lord arrived,
and Jiǎ reported the situation to him.
The lord wrote an announcement on the wall with whitewash, stating:
"Shí so-and-so issues this prohibition: It is observed that due to your wicked thoughts,
you incurred the wrath of thunder;
because your schemes were treacherous,
you suffered execution by axe.
You should only turn back your ghostly hearts,
and strive to repent;
so you may wash the blood from your skulls,
and escape this submerged misery.
Yet though you were severely punished in life,
in death you still gather to do evil.
Leaping and bounding forth,
with disheveled hair in crowds;
hesitating and lingering ahead,
beating your chests to become fiends.
Plugging your ears with yellow mud,
you recklessly display the ferocity of devils;
working sorcery in broad daylight,
you nearly cut off the road for travelers!
Beyond those three-foot mounds,
jurisdiction belongs to men;
how can it be that within the two great realms of heaven and earth,
you villains act as you please?
After this proclamation, each of you should hide your traces,
and not persist in your wickedness.
The bones by the Wúdìng River,
quietly await reincarnation;
the souls in golden chamber dreams,
may yet return to their native soil.
If you repeat your former transgressions,
you will surely regret it later!"
From then on, the ghostly troubles ceased,
and the pool soon dried up.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In my hometown, Táng Tàishǐ Jìwǔ,
when he was several years old,
a certain cousin of his
took him along to play in a temple.
Tàishǐ, even as a child, was open and forthright,
and exceptionally bold.
Seeing a clay ghost in the corridor,
with glazed eyes open wide,
very bright and large;
he took a liking to them,
and secretly gouged them out with his finger,
then carried them home in his lapel.
Upon arriving home,
his cousin suddenly fell ill,
and remained speechless for a while.
Then he suddenly got up,
and said in a fierce voice:
"Why did you dig out my eyes!"
He kept shouting and screaming.
No one knew what was happening,
until Tàishǐ told them what he had done.
The family then prayed, saying:
"The child is ignorant,
he injured your esteemed eyes in play,
we will return them immediately."
Then the ghost said loudly:
"If that is so,
I shall go now."
Having spoken,
he fell to the ground and expired.
After a long while,
when asked what he had said,
he was utterly unaware.
So they sent the eyeball back, still safely placed in the ghost's socket.
The Chronicler of the Tales remarks:
"To enter the hall and demand an eye—
how spiritual was that clay idol!
But why did the Hanlin Academician, upon gouging out his own eye,
then vent his anger on his fellow traveler?
It must be because of the noble status of a member of the Hanlin Academy,
and moreover his unyielding, staunch nature.
Observe him submitting a memorial to the northern palace gates,
then flicking his sleeves and retiring to the southern mountains.
Even spirits would stand in awe of him,
let alone ghosts!"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
The grandfather of Mr. Wáng Chūnjì,
was on the closest terms with my late uncle, Gōng Yùtián.
One night,
he dreamed that Gōng arrived at his home,
and they conversed in low, somber tones.
He asked:
"What brings you here?"
Gōng replied:
"I am about to depart on a long journey,
and so have come to bid you farewell."
He asked:
"Where are you going?"
Gōng said:
"Far away."
With that, he went out.
Accompanying him to a valley,
he saw a fissure in a stone cliff.
Gōng then clasped his hands in farewell,
turned his back to the fissure,
and hesitantly backed into it.
He called out, but received no answer,
and thus awoke with a start.
At daybreak,
he told Tàigōng Jìngyī,
and had him prepare the funeral items,
saying:
"Gōng Yùtián has passed away!"
Tàigōng suggested first sending someone to inquire,
and if it were true,
then proceed.
He would not listen,
and went directly in mourning clothes.
Upon reaching the gate,
he found the funeral streamers already hung.
Alas!
The ancients in their friendships
had such mutual trust concerning life and death.
The funeral carriage awaited Jù Qīng before proceeding—
was that mere legend!
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
A servant of Hán Guānglù Dàqiān
was sleeping one night in a lodge,
when he saw a light upstairs,
bright as a star.
Before long,
it glimmered and drifted down,
turning into a dog upon reaching the ground.
Watching it,
he saw it go around to the back of the building.
He quickly got up
and stealthily followed it.
Entering a garden,
it transformed into a woman.
Knowing in his heart she was a fox,
he returned and lay down in his original spot.
Soon after,
the woman came from behind.
The servant pretended to be asleep to observe her actions.
The woman bent over and shook him.
The servant feigned waking up
and asked who she was.
The woman did not answer.
The servant said:
"The light upstairs—
wasn't that you?"
The woman said:
"Since you know,
why ask?"
Thereupon they stayed together.
Parting by day and meeting by night
became their routine.
His master found out
and had two men sleep on either side of the servant.
When the two men awoke,
they found themselves lying beneath the bed,
not knowing when they had fallen.
The master grew even angrier
and said to the servant:
"When she comes next,
you must seize her and bring her to me;
otherwise,
you will face the whip!"
The servant dared not speak,
but assented and withdrew.
He pondered: seizing her would be difficult;
not seizing her,
he feared punishment.
He tossed and turned, without a plan.
Suddenly he recalled the woman's little red jacket,
which she wore tightly against her body,
never taking it off even briefly.
It must be vital to her,
and by grasping it he could coerce her.
At midnight,
the woman arrived
and asked:
"Did your master order you to seize me?"
He said:
"Indeed he did.
But given the affection between us two,
how could I do such a thing?"
When they went to bed,
he secretly grabbed her jacket.
The woman cried out urgently,
struggled free, and fled.
From then on, she ceased to come.
Later, when the servant was returning from elsewhere,
he saw from afar the woman sitting by the roadside.
As he approached,
she raised her sleeve to cover her face.
The servant dismounted
and called out:
"Why act this way?"
The woman then stood up,
took his hand, and said:
"I thought you had forgotten our former affection.
Since you still cling to the feelings of an old friend,
your sentiment can be forgiven.
What happened before was due to your master's command;
I do not blame you for it.
But our destined bond is now exhausted.
Today I have prepared a small feast;
please come in so we may part properly."
It was early autumn,
and the sorghum was lush.
The woman led him in with her,
and there appeared a large mansion.
He tethered his horse and entered;
in the hall, wine and dishes were already laid out.
They had just sat down
when a group of maidservants began serving the food.
As dusk approached,
the servant, having business,
wished to report back to his master,
and so took his leave.
Once outside,
it was merely fields and ridges again.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Monk Tǐkōng relates:
"In Qīngzhōu,
I saw two foreign monks,
their appearance strangely ancient.
Their ears were adorned with double rings;
they wore yellow cloth,
and their hair and beards were curly.
They said they came from the Western Regions.
Hearing that the prefect revered Buddhism,
they went to pay their respects.
The prefect dispatched two clerks
to escort them to a monastery.
The abbot, Líng Cān,
did not treat them with much courtesy.
The monastery's steward, seeing they were unusual men,
privately received them hospitably
and let them stay.
Someone asked: 'The Western Regions have many extraordinary people.
Do you arhats possess miraculous arts?'
One of them chuckled
and produced from his sleeve a hand,
in whose palm rested a small pagoda,
just over a foot tall,
exquisite and lovely.
On the highest part of the wall
was a small niche.
The monk tossed the pagoda into it,
where it stood upright and straight,
not leaning in the slightest.
Looking, they saw *śarīra* emitting light from the pagoda,
illuminating the entire room.
After a short while,
he beckoned with his hand,
and it fell back into his palm.
The other monk then bared his arm,
extending his left forearm,
which grew to some six or seven feet long,
while his right forearm shrank to nothing.
Then he extended his right forearm,
and it became just like the left."
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Liú Dòngjiǔ from Láiwú
served as an official in Fénzhōu.
Sitting alone in his office,
he heard laughter and chatter approaching from outside the pavilion.
Entering the room,
were four women: one about forty,
one around thirty,
one around twenty-four or twenty-five,
and the last one with her hair still hanging loose, a young girl.
They stood side by side in front of the table,
looking at each other and smiling.
Liú knew that government offices often harbored foxes,
so he paid them no attention.
After a short while,
the young girl took out a red scarf
and playfully tossed it onto his face.
Liú picked it up and threw it toward the window,
still ignoring them.
The four women laughed and left.
One day,
the eldest woman came
and said to Liú:
"My younger sister is destined to be with you;
I hope you will not reject her despite her humble origins."
Liú casually agreed.
The woman then left.
Soon, she returned with a maid,
bringing the young girl with her,
and made her sit shoulder to shoulder with Liú.
She said:
"A fine pair of phoenix companions,
tonight you shall celebrate your wedding.
Serve Liú láng well,
I am leaving."
Liú looked closely at her—
her beauty was unmatched—
and so he became intimate with her.
When he asked about her origins,
she said:
"I am not human,
yet I am human.
I am
the daughter of a former official.
Bewitched by a fox,
I died suddenly
and was buried in the garden.
The foxes used their magic to revive me,
and so I became ethereal, like a fox."
Liú then reached to feel her lower back.
The girl noticed this
and laughed, saying:
"Are you perhaps thinking that foxes have tails?"
She turned around and said:
"Please, try feeling it."
From then on,
she stayed and did not leave.
Whenever she walked or sat,
she was accompanied by a young maid.
The household all respected her with the etiquette due to a mistress.
When maids and elderly women came to pay their respects,
she rewarded them generously.
On Liú's birthday,
there were many guests,
requiring over thirty banquet tables,
and a large number of cooks was needed.
Orders had been sent out in advance to summon them,
but only one or two arrived.
Liú was extremely angry.
The girl learned of this
and said:
"Do not worry.
Since there are not enough cooks,
it would be better to dismiss even those who have come.
Though I am not particularly talented,
preparing thirty tables is not difficult for me."
Liú was pleased
and ordered that fish, meat, ginger, and cinnamon
all be moved to the inner office.
Those in the household only heard the sounds of chopping and pounding,
incessant and rapid.
Inside the door, a table was set,
and the servers placed dishes on it.
When they turned to look,
the table was already filled with platters of food.
As soon as they were taken away, more appeared,
with over ten people shuttling back and forth along the path,
taking dishes without end.
Finally,
the servers came to ask for soup noodles.
A voice from inside said:
"The master did not give prior instructions;
how can we prepare them in an instant?"
After a moment, it said:
"Well then,
we shall borrow some."
Shortly after,
they called for the soup noodles to be taken.
Looking at them,
there were over thirty bowls,
steaming on the table.
After the guests had left,
she said to Liú:
"You must take some money
to repay a certain family for the soup noodles."
Liú sent someone with the payment.
It turned out that family had lost their soup noodles
and were just marveling at the strange occurrence.
When the messenger arrived,
their suspicions were resolved.
One evening,
while drinking at night,
Liú happened to think of the bitter liquor from Shāndōng.
The girl offered to fetch it.
She then went out the door
and returned after a while, saying:
"There is one jar outside
that can supply several days of drinking."
Liú went to look
and indeed found liquor,
the very same "Spring at the Jar's Mouth" from his home.
A few days later,
his wife sent two servants to Fénzhōu.
On the way, one servant said:
"I heard that the fox lady rewards generously;
with the reward from this trip,
I can buy a fur coat."
The girl in the office already knew of this
and said to Liú:
"People from home are about to arrive.
How hateful that rude servant is;
I must teach him a lesson."
The next day,
as soon as the servant entered the city,
his head began to ache terribly.
When he reached the office,
he held his head and wailed.
Everyone suggested giving him medicine.
Liú laughed and said:
"No need for treatment;
when the time comes, he will recover on his own."
The crowd suspected he had offended the mistress.
The servant thought to himself: I just arrived and haven't even unpacked;
how could I have committed any offense?
With no one to appeal to,
he randomly knelt and crawled, pleading for mercy.
A voice from behind the curtain said:
"If you call me 'Madam,'
that would be fine,
but why say 'fox'?"
The servant then understood
and kowtowed repeatedly.
The voice added:
"Since you wanted a fur coat,
how could you be so rude?"
After a moment, it said:
"You are healed."
As soon as the words were spoken,
the servant's illness vanished as if it had never existed.
The servant bowed and was about to leave
when suddenly a bundle was thrown out from behind the curtain.
The voice said:
"This is a lambskin coat;
you may take it."
The servant opened it to look
and found five taels of silver.
When Liú asked for news from home,
the servant said: everything was fine,
except that one night, a jar of stored liquor went missing.
Checking the date,
it was the night the liquor was fetched.
Everyone was in awe of her supernatural abilities
and called her
"Holy Immortal."
Liú had a small portrait painted of her.
At that time, Zhāng Dàoyī was the education commissioner.
Hearing of her extraordinary nature,
he visited Liú on account of their shared hometown ties,
wishing to request an audience with her.
The woman refused him.
Liú showed him her portrait,
which Zhāng forcibly took and left with.
Returning home, he hung it by his seat,
and morning and evening he prayed to it, saying:
"With your exquisite beauty,
what match would be unsuitable?
Yet you entrust yourself to that old man!
This humble official is certainly no worse than Dòng Jiǔ;
why not bestow a single visit upon me?"
The woman, in the yamen,
suddenly said to Liú:
"Commissioner Zhāng has been disrespectful;
he should receive a small punishment."
One day,
as Zhāng was praying,
it seemed as if someone struck his forehead with a ruler,
with a sharp crack, causing great pain.
Greatly frightened,
he returned the portrait.
Liú questioned him,
making him conceal the real reason and give a false reply.
Liú laughed and said:
"Might the master's forehead be in pain?"
Unable to deceive him,
he told the truth.
Not long after,
her son-in-law, Qí Shēng, came,
requesting an audience with her.
The woman firmly declined.
Qí insisted strongly.
Liú said:
"A son-in-law is not an outsider;
why refuse him so adamantly?"
The woman said:
"If I meet the son-in-law,
I must certainly have a gift for him.
His expectations of me are extravagant;
I judge myself unable to satisfy his desires,
which is precisely why I did not wish to see him.
Since he insists so firmly,
I will consent to see him in ten days."
When the day arrived,
Qí entered,
bowed to her from behind the curtain,
and exchanged a few words of greeting.
Her appearance was vaguely discernible,
but he dared not look closely;
after withdrawing,
a few steps away,
he turned his head to gaze back intently.
Then he heard the woman say:
"Son-in-law is looking back!"
Having said this,
she laughed heartily,
a piercing sound like the cry of an owl.
Hearing it, Qí
felt his legs go weak,
swaying unsteadily as if his soul had departed.
Once outside,
he sat for a long while
before gradually regaining his composure.
Then he said:
"Just now, hearing that laughter
was like hearing a thunderclap;
I truly felt I no longer possessed my own body."
A moment later,
a maid, on the woman's orders,
presented him with twenty taels of silver.
Qí accepted it
and said to the maid:
"The Holy Immortal lives daily with my father-in-law;
surely she knows I am by nature extravagant
and unaccustomed to handling small sums?"
The woman, hearing this, said:
"I knew it would be so.
My purse happens to be empty just now;
recently I journeyed with companions to Biànliáng,
but the city was occupied by the River Earl,
and the treasury stores were all submerged in water.
Diving in, each of us retrieved only a little;
how could that satisfy insatiable demands?
Moreover, even if I could give generously,
his meager fortune could not bear it."
The woman could foresee all matters;
whenever difficulties or doubts arose,
discussing them with her
invariably led to clear resolution.
One day,
as they sat together,
she suddenly looked up at the sky in great alarm and said:
"A great calamity approaches;
what is to be done?"
Startled, Liú asked about his family,
and she said:
"The rest are all safe,
only the second young master is a cause for concern.
This place will soon become a battlefield;
you should seek an official assignment far away,
so as to avoid the disaster."
Liú followed her advice,
petitioned his superior,
and obtained a mission to transport military provisions between Yúnnán and Guìzhōu.
The journey was long and distant;
those who heard of it pitied him,
but the woman alone congratulated him.
Not long after,
Jiǎng Xiáng rebelled,
and Fénzhōu fell, becoming a bandit stronghold.
Liú's second son, coming from Shāndōng,
happened to encounter the upheaval
and was killed.
When the city fell,
officials all suffered the calamity,
only Liú, being away on official business, escaped harm.
After the bandits were pacified,
Liú returned.
Soon after, he was implicated in a major case and dismissed from office,
reduced to such poverty that he could not provide daily meals;
moreover, the local authorities made many demands,
so that in his distress he nearly wished for death.
The woman said:
"Do not worry.
Under the bed are three thousand taels of silver,
which can support your expenses."
Liú was overjoyed
and asked:
"From where were they stolen?"
She said:
"In this world, ownerless things
are inexhaustible to take;
what need is there for theft?"
Liú, relying on her counsel, managed to extricate himself and return home,
and the woman accompanied him.
Several years later, she suddenly departed,
leaving behind a paper parcel containing several items as gifts.
Among them was a small funeral banner for hanging at a bereaved household's gate,
about two inches long.
Everyone considered it inauspicious.
Liú died not long after.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Lè Yúnhè and Xià Píngzǐ
were childhood neighbors,
studied together in their youth,
and were the closest of friends.
Xià was exceptionally intelligent from a young age
and was renowned by the age of ten.
Lè humbly learned from him,
and Xià also tirelessly guided him,
so that Lè's literary skill improved daily,
and their fame grew together.
Yet they repeatedly failed the imperial examinations,
defeated each time they sat for them.
Not long after,
Xià contracted an epidemic and died,
his family too poor to bury him.
Lè stepped forward and took responsibility himself.
Xià left behind an infant son and a widow;
Lè regularly provided relief to their household.
Whenever he obtained even a peck or a pint of grain,
he would invariably divide it into two shares,
so that Xià's wife and child relied on him to survive.
Thus, the gentry and officials esteemed Lè even more.
Lè's own permanent assets were not plentiful,
and bearing the burden of Xià's family's needs,
his household finances grew increasingly strained.
He sighed and said:
"Even one as talented as Píngzǐ
ended up obscure and passed away;
how much more so someone like me!
If a man is to attain wealth and honor, he must seize the moment;
toiling in anxiety year after year,
I fear I will die and fill a ditch before the dogs and horses,
betraying this life of mine.
It would be better to plan for myself early."
So he abandoned his studies and turned to trade.
After half a year in business,
his family's resources became somewhat comfortable.
One day,
while staying in Jīnlíng,
he rested at an inn.
He saw a man tall and lanky,
with sinews and bones protruding,
pacing restlessly beside him,
his expression gloomy,
bearing a sorrowful look.
Lè asked:
"Do you want something to eat?"
The man did not reply.
Lè pushed food toward him to eat;
he then scooped it up with his hands,
and in an instant, it was all gone.
Lè added more food, enough for two people.
He ate it all again.
So Lè ordered the innkeeper to cut a pork shoulder,
piling it with steamed buns;
he finished the meal meant for several people,
and only then, with his belly full, did he thank him, saying:
"For three years now,
I have never eaten so heartily."
Lè said:
"You are clearly a strong man,
why are you wandering like this?"
He replied:
"I have incurred Heaven's punishment for my sins,
it cannot be spoken of."
Asked where he lived,
he said:
"On land, I have no house;
on water, I have no boat,
drifting from village in the morning to town by evening."
Lè packed his belongings and prepared to leave,
the man followed him,
clinging and unwilling to part.
Lè tried to dismiss him.
He said:
"You are about to face great danger,
I cannot bear to forget the kindness of a single meal."
Lè found this strange,
so he traveled together with him.
On the journey, Lè urged him to eat with him.
He declined, saying:
"I eat only a few meals a year."
Lè found this even more extraordinary.
The next day,
while crossing the river,
a violent storm arose,
merchant boats all capsized,
Lè and the man were both submerged in the river.
Soon the wind calmed,
the man carried Lè on his back, treading on the waves to emerge,
boarded a passenger boat,
then broke through the waves again;
a short while later,
he pulled a boat over,
helped Lè in,
instructed Lè to lie down and stay put,
then leaped back into the river,
using both arms to carry out goods,
tossing them into the boat;
he went in again: several times he went in and out,
lining the boat full of goods.
Lè thanked him, saying:
"You have saved my life, that is more than enough,
how dare I hope for the return of my pearls!"
Checking the goods and valuables,
nothing was lost.
Even more delighted,
he was astonished, considering him a divine being.
They set sail to continue;
the man announced his departure,
Lè earnestly urged him to stay,
so they crossed the river together.
Lè said with a laugh:
"This calamity,
only cost me a single golden hairpin."
The man wanted to go retrieve it.
As Lè tried to dissuade him,
he had already plunged into the water and disappeared.
Lè was stunned for a long while.
Suddenly, he saw him emerge with a smile,
handing the hairpin to Lè, saying:
"Fortunately, I did not fail the mission."
Everyone on the river was astonished.
Lè returned with him,
sharing the same quarters.
He would eat only once every ten days or so,
and when he ate, he consumed an immeasurable amount.
One day,
he spoke of parting again,
Lè firmly urged him to stay.
Just then, the day darkened as if about to rain,
and thunder was heard.
Lè said:
"I wonder what it's like among the clouds?
And what exactly is thunder?
If only I could go up to the sky and see for myself,
then this doubt could be resolved."
The man laughed and said:
"Do you wish to take a journey among the clouds?"
A short while later,
Lè grew very tired,
and lay down on the couch for a nap.
Upon waking,
he felt his body swaying,
unlike being on a couch;
opening his eyes,
he was amidst clouds and mist,
his whole body feeling like cotton.
Startled, he stood up,
dizzy as if on a boat.
Stepping down,
there was no ground beneath.
Looking up at the stars,
they seemed right before his eyes.
He began to suspect it was a dream.
Looking closely, the stars embedded in the sky,
were like old lotus seeds in a pod,
the largest like jars,
the next like pots,
the smallest like bowls.
Trying to shake them with his hand,
the larger ones were firm and immovable;
the smaller stars swayed,
as if they could be plucked and brought down.
So he plucked one,
and hid it in his sleeve.
Parting the clouds to look down,
he saw a vast silvery sea,
with towns as small as beans.
Astonished, he thought to himself: if he were to slip,
what would become of his body?
Suddenly, he saw two dragons coiling gracefully,
pulling a plain carriage.
With a flick of their tails,
it sounded like a cowherd's whip.
On the carriage were vessels,
each several zhang in circumference,
filled with water.
Dozens of people
used the vessels to scoop water,
sprinkling it all over the clouds.
Suddenly noticing Lè,
they all found it strange.
Lè recognized the strong man he had befriended among them,
who said to the crowd:
"This is my friend."
He then took a vessel,
handed it to Lè, and told him to sprinkle.
At that time, there was a severe drought,
Lè took the vessel, parted the clouds,
roughly aiming toward his hometown,
and poured out the water with all his heart.
Not long after,
the man said to Lè:
"I am originally a Thunder Officer.
Previously, I mistakenly performed rain duties,
and was punished with three years of exile;
now my heavenly sentence is fulfilled,
I must bid you farewell."
He then threw forward a ten-thousand-foot rope from the carriage,
telling Lè to hold the end and lower himself down.
Lè felt it was dangerous.
The man said with a laugh:
"No harm."
Lè did as he was told,
and in an instant, reached the ground.
Looking around,
he found himself standing outside a village;
the rope gradually retracted into the clouds,
and was no longer visible.
At that time, there had been a long drought,
ten lǐ away,
the rain was only a finger's depth,
but only in Lè's village were the ditches and streams all full.
Returning home, he felt in his sleeve,
the plucked star was still there.
Taking it out and placing it on the table,
it was dark and dull like a stone:
at night,
it shone brilliantly,
illuminating the four walls.
He treasured it even more,
wrapping it in multiple layers for safekeeping.
Whenever he had esteemed guests,
he would bring it out to light their drinking.
Looking directly at it,
rays of light shot into the eyes.
One night,
his wife sat opposite him, holding her hair,
when suddenly she saw the starlight gradually shrink to the size of a firefly,
floating and flying sideways.
Just as she was exclaiming in surprise,
it had already entered her mouth,
she tried to cough it out but couldn't,
and it was swallowed.
Astonished, she ran to tell Lè,
who also found it strange.
Mèng Xià Píngzǐ came in a dream,
saying:
"I am the Shǎowēi star.
Your kindness and friendship
I have not forgotten in my heart.
Moreover, I am indebted to you for bringing me back from the heavens,
which can be said to be predestined.
Now I shall become your heir
to repay your great virtue."
Lè, who was thirty years old and childless,
was overjoyed upon having this dream.
From then on,
his wife indeed became pregnant;
and when she was about to give birth,
a brilliant light filled the room,
just like when the star was on the table.
Therefore, they named him
"Xīng'ér."
He was exceptionally clever and alert.
At sixteen years old,
he passed the highest imperial examination.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Lè's literary fame was renowned for a generation,
yet he suddenly realized that the heavens had not placed him there for that purpose,
so he abandoned his writing brush as if discarding worn-out shoes.
How is this any different from
Bān Chāo casting aside his brush upon being told he had the jaw of a marquis?
As for Léi Cáo being moved by the kindness of a single meal,
and Shǎowēi repaying the understanding of a good friend,
are these merely private acts of gratitude by gods and men?
Rather, they are the impartial recompense of the Creator for the virtuous and outstanding."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Dàoshi Hán
resided in the Tiānqí Temple within the county town.
He possessed many magical arts,
and people commonly called him
"Immortal."
My late father was on the best terms with him,
and whenever he went to the city,
he would always visit him.
One day,
while going to the county town with my late uncle,
they planned to visit Hán.
They happened to meet him on the road.
Hán handed them a key, saying:
"Please go ahead and open the door to sit inside;
I will arrive shortly."
They did as he said.
Upon reaching the temple and unlocking the door,
Hán was already sitting inside the room.
There were many such instances.
Previously,
there was a poor clansman of ours who was addicted to gambling.
Through my father, he also became acquainted with Hán.
It happened that a monk came to the Dàfó Temple
who specialized in gambling
and wagered very heavily.
Our clansman saw him and was delighted,
staking all his funds to gamble,
but suffered great losses.
His heart grew even more fervent;
he mortgaged his fields and property to gamble again,
losing everything overnight.
Depressed and discontented,
he dropped by to see Hán on the way,
his spirit despondent
and his speech incoherent.
Hán asked him about it,
and he told the whole truth.
Hán said with a laugh:
"In constant gambling, there is no principle of not losing.
If you can swear off gambling,
I will recover your losses for you."
The clansman said:
"If I can regain my lost pearls,
I will smash the dice with an iron pestle!"
Hán then wrote a talisman on paper
and gave it to him to wear inside his clothing belt.
He instructed him:
"Just recover what was originally yours and stop there;
do not covet Shu after gaining Lǒng."
He also gave him a thousand coins,
agreeing to be repaid if he won.
The clansman went off joyfully.
The monk checked his funds,
looked down on him,
and disdained to gamble with him.
The clansman insisted,
asking to gamble just one throw.
The monk laughed and agreed.
So he staked all thousand coins as a single wager.
The monk threw the dice without winning or losing decisively.
The clansman took the dice
and with one throw achieved a winning combination.
The monk then wagered two thousand coins,
and lost again.
Gradually increasing to over ten thousand,
even when the dice clearly showed a losing combination,
with a shout from him,
they all turned into winning combinations.
Calculating his previous losses,
they were all recovered in an instant.
Secretly thinking that winning several thousand more would be even better,
he gambled again,
but the dice gradually turned unfavorable.
Puzzled in his heart,
he got up to check his belt,
only to find the talisman already gone.
Greatly startled, he stopped.
Carrying the money back to the temple,
after deducting what he owed Hán,
and calculating the remainder,
including the losses from the final round,
it exactly matched the original amount.
Then he shamefully apologized for losing the talisman.
Hán said with a laugh:
"It is already here.
I specifically warned you not to be greedy,
but you did not listen, so I took it back."
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"In all the world, nothing ruins a family
faster than gambling;
in all the world, nothing corrupts virtue
more than gambling.
Those who enter into it
are like sinking into a sea of delusion,
not knowing where the bottom lies.
As for merchants and farmers,
they each have their proper occupations;
scholars of poetry and books
especially treasure every moment.
Carrying plows and holding classics
is indeed the proper path to establishing a family;
refined conversation and modest drinking
are still a life of cultivated interests.
Yet they become intimate with dissolute companions,
lingering through the long night.
Emptying their bags and overturning their trunks,
they hang their gold on the unpredictable heavens;
shouting for winning combinations,
they beg for luck from bewitched bones.
Spinning the five dice,
like chasing round pearls;
holding many ivory markers,
like grasping round fans.
Glancing left at others and right at oneself,
they strain their ghostly eyes;
outwardly showing weakness while secretly using strength,
they exhaust the tricks of demons.
Guests wait at the door,
yet they linger obsessively at the gambling table;
smoke rises from the kitchen stove,
still they stare intently at the dice bowl.
Forgetting food and neglecting sleep,
they become deeply addicted over time;
tongues weary and lips parched,
they look at each other like ghosts.
"By the time their entire fortune is lost,
their eager eyes gaze vacantly.
Looking at the gaming table, they hear loud shouts,
itching with the hero's urge to try their skill;
checking their purse, the strings of cash are empty,
chilling the heart of the brave.
Craning their necks, pacing back and forth,
they realize their empty hands are of no help;
hanging their heads in desolation,
only then do they return home in the dead of night.
Fortunately, the scolding wife is asleep,
fearing to startle the dogs;
suffering from long-empty stomachs,
they dare not complain about leftover soup.
Then they sell their children and mortgage their fields,
hoping to recover their pearls from Hé Pǔ:
unexpectedly, the fire burns until the fur is gone,
and they end up fishing for the moon in the vast river.
Only after suffering defeat do they reflect,
already having become lowly creatures;
if asked who is best at gambling,
all point to the man without pants.
Even worse, with empty stomachs unbearable,
they take shelter with bandits;
scratching their heads with no way out,
they resort to depending on their wives' dowries. Alas!
Corrupted virtue, ruined conduct,
lost property, perished selves—
is it not all caused by the path of gambling?"
Jǐng Xīng of Wéndēng
had a fine reputation from a young age.
He lived next door to a certain Mr. Chén,
their studies separated only by a low wall.
One day,
Chén was passing by a desolate, abandoned place in the evening,
when he heard a woman weeping amidst some pine and cypress trees.
Approaching to look,
he saw a sash hanging from a horizontal branch of a tree,
as if she intended to hang herself.
Chén questioned her,
and she replied through her tears:
"My mother has gone far away,
