and entrusted me to my maternal cousin.
I never imagined he had the heart of a wolf,
and would not care for me to the end.
Being so utterly alone,
it's better to die!"
Having said this,
she wept again.
Chén untied the sash
and urged her to marry someone.
The woman worried there was no one she could entrust herself to.
Chén invited her to stay temporarily at his home,
and she agreed.
Once they returned,
he lit a lamp and examined her closely;
her beauty and grace were exceptionally stunning.
Greatly delighted,
he tried to force himself upon her.
The woman resisted fiercely and loudly,
the sounds of their struggle
reached the neighboring house.
Jǐng came over the wall to see what was happening,
and only then did Chén release the woman.
When the woman saw Jǐng,
she fixed her gaze on him, staring intently,
and after a long moment, she ran away.
Both men chased after her,
but had no idea where she went.
Jǐng returned home,
closed his door and was about to sleep,
when the woman gracefully emerged from his room.
Startled, he asked her,
and she replied:
"His virtue is shallow, his fortune meager;
he is not someone to entrust myself to for life."
Jǐng was overjoyed,
and asked her name.
She said:
"My ancestral home is in Qí.
My surname is Qí,
and my childhood name is Āxiá."
He flirted with her with playful words,
and she smiled without strongly refusing,
so they slept together.
As many friends came and went in his study,
the woman always hid herself in the inner rooms.
After several days,
she said:
"I shall leave for now.
This place is too noisy and chaotic,
it's quite exhausting.
From now on,
let us meet by night."
He asked:
"Where is your home?"
She said:
"Just not far away."
So she left early.
That night she indeed returned,
and their love and intimacy grew deep and strong.
After several more days,
she said to Jǐng:
"Though our affection is wonderful,
it remains an illicit union.
My father holds an official post in the western frontier,
tomorrow I will follow my mother there,
allow me to find an opportunity to inform them,
so I may follow you for life."
He asked:
"How many days until we part?"
She promised to return within ten days.
After she left,
Jǐng thought staying in his study wasn't a permanent solution;
moving her into the main house,
he feared his wife's jealousy.
He decided it would be best to divorce his wife.
Once his mind was made up,
whenever his wife came near, he would curse and berate her.
Unable to bear the humiliation,
his wife wept and wished to die.
Jǐng said:
"If you die, I fear it will implicate me;
please return to your family early."
So he hastened his wife's departure.
His wife cried, saying:
"I have served you for ten years,
never having failed in my virtue.
Why are you so utterly heartless!"
Jǐng paid no heed,
and pressed her even more urgently.
His wife then left through the gate.
From then on, he whitewashed the walls and swept the dust clean,
stretching his neck in eager anticipation;
unexpectedly, no message arrived from the blue bird,
it was like a stone sinking into the sea.
After his wife was sent back to her family,
she repeatedly entreated mutual friends
to plead with Jǐng for reconciliation,
but Jǐng would not accept her;
she then married a man named Xiàhóu.
Xiàhóu's village residence bordered Jǐng's land,
and because of a boundary dispute over fields,
their families had been enemies for generations.
When Jǐng heard this,
his anger and resentment grew even greater.
Yet he still hoped Āxiá would return,
which somewhat consoled him.
After more than a year passed,
there was still no trace or news of her.
It happened that there was a celebration for the Sea God's birthday,
and men and women from inside and outside the temple gathered like clouds;
Jǐng was also there.
From afar, he saw a woman
who looked very much like Āxiá.
Jǐng approached her,
but she disappeared into the crowd;
he followed her,
and she went out the gate;
he followed again,
but she drifted away as if floating.
Jǐng could not catch up,
and returned full of regret and resentment.
Half a year later,
he happened to be traveling on the road,
when he saw a young lady
dressed in vermilion robes,
followed by an old servant,
riding a black donkey towards him.
Looking at her,
it was Xiá.
He then asked her attendant:
"Who is this lady?"
The reply was:
"She is the second wife of Master Zhèng of Náncūn Village."
He asked again:
"How long ago did he marry her?"
The answer was:
"Just half a month."
Jǐng thought,
could this be a mistake?
The young lady heard the conversation,
turned her head and glanced back,
Jǐng looked,
it was truly Xiá.
Seeing she had married another,
rage filled his breast,
and he shouted loudly:
"Lady Xiá!
Why have you forgotten our old promise?"
Hearing him address their mistress so familiarly,
the attendants wanted to use their old fists.
The woman quickly stopped them.
Lifting her veil, she said to Jǐng:
"What face does a faithless man have to see me?"
Jǐng said:
"You are the one who betrayed me;
how have I ever betrayed you?"
The woman said:
"Betraying your wife is worse than betraying me!
If you treat your lawful wife like that,
what can be expected regarding others?
Previously, because your ancestral virtue was substantial,
and your name was listed among those destined for official rank,
I gave myself to you;
but now, because you abandoned your wife,
the underworld has stripped away your official salary and rank.
The second-place graduate in this year's examinations, Wáng Chāng,
is the one who replaced your name.
I have already married Master Zhèng;
there is no need for you to think of me anymore."
Jǐng hung his head submissively,
unable to utter a single word in reply.
Watching the woman
urge her donkey forward as if flying away,
he could only brood in regret and resentment.
In that examination,
Jǐng failed,
and the second-place winner was indeed Wáng Chāngmíng.
Zhèng also passed.
Because of this, Jǐng gained a reputation for being shallow.
At forty, he remained unmarried,
and his family grew increasingly impoverished,
often relying on relatives and friends for meals.
Once, he visited Zhèng,
who treated him kindly,
and let him stay overnight.
The woman peeked at the guest,
saw him and took pity on him.
She asked Zhèng:
"The guest in the hall,
isn't that Jǐng Qìngyún?"
When asked how she knew him,
she said:
"Before I married you,
I once took refuge in his home,
and received much care from him.
Though his conduct is lowly,
his ancestral virtue is not yet severed;
moreover, since he is your old friend,
you should show him the kindness of a silk robe."
Zhèng agreed,
changed his tattered clothes,
and kept him for several days.
At midnight, as he was about to sleep,
a maid brought over twenty taels of silver for Jǐng.
The woman spoke from outside the window:
"This is my private savings,
a small repayment for past kindness.
Take it,
and find yourself a good wife.
Fortunately, your ancestral virtue is deep,
enough to extend to your descendants.
Do not repeat your old ways,
lest you shorten your remaining years."
Jǐng thanked her.
After returning home,
he used over ten taels to buy a maid from an official family,
who was very ugly and fierce.
She bore him a son,
who later passed both the provincial and metropolitan examinations.
Zhèng rose to the position of Vice Minister of Personnel.
After his death,
the woman accompanied the funeral procession back,
but when the carriage was opened, it was empty—no one was inside.
Only then did they realize she was not human.
Alas!
When a person lacks virtue,
abandoning the old and seeking the new,
in the end, the eggs are broken and the bird flies away.
Heaven's retribution is indeed severe!
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Lǐ Sījiàn
was a provincial graduate from Yǒngnián.
On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month in the fourth year of the Kangxi reign,
he beat his wife, Lǐ shì, to death.
The local authorities reported to Guǎngpíng,
and an investigation was ordered in Yǒngnián.
Sījiàn, in front of the prefectural office,
suddenly snatched a butcher's knife from under a meat rack,
rushed into the City God Temple,
climbed onto the opera stage,
and knelt before the deity.
He said:
"The deity rebukes me for listening to wicked people,
confusing right and wrong in the village,
and orders me to cut off my ear."
He then cut off his left ear
and threw it off the stage.
He also said:
"The deity rebukes me for swindling people's money,
and orders me to chop off my finger."
He then chopped off his left finger.
He also said:
"The deity rebukes me for committing adultery with women,
and makes me cut off my kidney."
He then castrated himself,
and fell unconscious, stiff and prostrate.
At that time, Governor Zhū Yúnmén submitted a memorial recommending his dismissal and punishment,
and imperial approval had already been received,
but Sījiàn had already suffered divine punishment.
From the official gazette.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Chàng Tǐyuán from Héjīn,
courtesy name Rǔyù.
When he was a scholar,
he dreamed someone called him
"Wǔ Gǔ Dàfū"
and he was pleased, thinking it a good omen.
Later, when he encountered the chaos of the rebel bandits,
they stripped him of all his clothes,
and locked him in an empty room at night.
It was winter,
and extremely cold.
Groping in the dark,
he found several sheepskins to cover himself,
barely avoiding death.
At dawn,
he looked at them,
and the number exactly matched five.
He laughed silently, realizing the deity was playing a trick on him.
Later, he became a Mingjing scholar and was appointed magistrate of Luònán.
Recorded by Mr. Bì Zǎijī.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Mǎ Tiānróng, a farmer's son,
was in his twenties.
He had lost his wife,
and was too poor to remarry.
Once, while weeding in the fields,
he saw a young woman in splendid attire,
stepping over the crops and crossing the paths.
Her face was ruddy,
and her demeanor was charming.
Mǎ suspected she was lost.
Seeing no one around in the wilderness,
he playfully flirted with her.
The woman also subtly accepted.
He wanted to have a tryst with her.
She laughed and said:
"Under the bright sky and broad daylight,
how can we do such a thing?
You go back,
close the door and wait.
At dusk, I will come."
Mǎ did not believe her,
so she swore an oath.
Mǎ then told her the location and direction of his house,
and the woman left.
At midnight,
she indeed arrived,
and they delighted in each other's company.
He felt her skin was extremely tender;
when he lit a light to look,
her skin was ruddy and thin like a baby's,
with fine hair all over her body.
He found it strange.
He also doubted her origins were unfathomable,
and wondered to himself if she might be a fox.
So he playfully questioned her.
The woman also admitted it without concealment.
Mǎ said:
"Since you are an immortal,
surely there is nothing you cannot obtain.
Since you have bestowed your affection upon me,
couldn't you give me some silver to relieve my poverty?"
The woman agreed.
The next night when she came,
Mǎ asked for the silver.
The woman pretended to be surprised and said:
"I forgot it just now."
As she was about to leave,
Mǎ reminded her again.
That night,
he asked:
"Perhaps you haven't forgotten what I asked for?"
The woman laughed,
and asked to postpone it to another day.
After several days,
Mǎ asked again.
The woman smiled and took out two ingots of silver from her sleeve,
weighing about five or six taels,
with raised edges and fine patterns,
elegant and delightful to behold.
Mǎ was overjoyed,
and hid them deeply in a box.
After half a year,
he happened to need silver,
so he took them out to show someone.
The person said:
"This is tin."
When he bit them,
they broke with a snap.
Mǎ was greatly alarmed,
collected them, and returned home.
That night,
when the woman came,
he angrily reproached her.
The woman laughed and said:
"Your fate is too thin,
you cannot bear real gold."
With a laugh, the matter ended.
Mǎ said:
"I've heard that fox immortals are all beauties of the land,
but it seems that is not necessarily the case."
The woman said:
"We all manifest according to the person we are with.
You don't even have the fortune to possess a single tael of gold,
so how could you possibly enjoy
a beauty who could make wild geese fall and fish sink?
With my clumsy and plain appearance,
I am certainly not fit to serve a man of high status;
but compared to those with big feet and hunchbacks,
I am indeed a beauty of the land."
After several months,
she suddenly gave Mǎ three taels of gold,
saying:
"You have repeatedly asked for money,
but I knew your fate did not include hoarding gold.
Now that the time for matchmaking and marriage is near,
I offer you the funds for a wife as a gift,
and also as a farewell present."
Mǎ protested that he had no plans to marry.
The woman said:
"In a day or two, a matchmaker will surely come."
Mǎ asked:
"What is the appearance of the woman you mentioned?"
She replied:
"Since you desire a beauty of the land,
she naturally will be one."
Mǎ said:
"That is something I dare not hope for.
But how can three taels of gold buy a wife?"
The woman said:
"This is decreed by the Old Man Under the Moon,
not something human effort can change."
Mǎ asked:
"Why do you speak of parting so suddenly?"
She replied:
"Roaming under the moon and stars,
is ultimately not a permanent solution.
'You, sir, already have a wife,'
why keep evading?"
At dawn, she departed,
handing him a small spoonful of yellow powder,
saying:
"After we part, you may fall ill;
take this to cure it."
The next day,
a matchmaker indeed came.
Mǎ first inquired about the woman's appearance,
and the matchmaker replied:
"Somewhere between pretty and plain."
"How much is the bride price?"
"About four or five taels."
Mǎ did not find the price difficult,
but insisted on seeing the person himself.
The matchmaker feared that a respectable family's daughter would not show herself.
Eventually, she arranged to go with him,
waiting for an opportune moment.
When they reached the village,
the matchmaker went ahead first,
leaving Mǎ to wait outside the village.
After a long while,
she returned and said:
"It's settled.
My cousin lives in the same courtyard.
I went over just now,
and saw the girl sitting in the room.
Please pretend to visit my cousin and pass by;
you can catch a glimpse from just a few steps away."
Mǎ followed her suggestion.
He indeed saw a woman sitting in the hall,
leaning over the bed,
asking someone to scratch her back.
Mǎ hurried past,
glancing at her with his eyes,
and her appearance was exactly as the matchmaker had described.
When discussing the bride price,
they did not haggle over the amount,
but only asked for one or two taels of gold,
to dress the girl for marriage.
Mǎ found this even more reasonable,
so he paid the gold;
including fees for the matchmaker and the scribe for the marriage contract,
he spent exactly three taels in total,
not a single coin more.
He chose an auspicious day to welcome the bride home.
Upon entering the door,
he saw that her chest and back were both hunched,
her neck shrunk like a turtle's,
and looking down at her skirt,
her feet were like boats a foot long.
Only then did he realize the meaning behind the fox's words.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Manifesting according to the person,
may be the fox maiden's way of consoling herself; yet her words about fortune and blessings
are truly worthy of deep belief.
I often say: without several generations of virtuous conduct by one's ancestors,
one cannot attain high office;
without several lifetimes of virtuous conduct by oneself,
one cannot obtain a beautiful woman.
Those who believe in cause and effect
will surely not consider my words to be empty talk."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Luó Zǐfú,
a person.
Both his parents died early.
At eight or nine years old,
he relied on his uncle, Luó Dàyè.
Dàyè served as an official in the Imperial Academy,
wealthy in gold and silk but without a son,
and loved Zǐfú as his own.
At fourteen,
he was led astray by unscrupulous people into visiting brothels.
There happened to be a courtesan from Jīnlíng,
residing temporarily in the commandery,
and the young man was delighted and infatuated with her.
When the courtesan returned to Jīnlíng,
he secretly followed and fled with her.
He lived at the madam's house for half a year,
until his money ran out,
and was greatly scorned by the courtesan sisters.
Yet she did not immediately cut him off.
Not long after,
he developed severe sores that festered and stank,
contaminating the bed and mat,
and was driven out.
He begged in the market,
and people would avoid him from afar upon seeing him.
Fearing he would die in a strange land,
he begged for food while traveling westward;
covering thirty or forty lǐ a day,
he gradually reached the border of his hometown.
He also thought of his tattered clothes and foul sores,
too ashamed to enter the village gate,
and still hesitated near the town.
As dusk had fallen,
he wanted to hurry to a mountain temple to spend the night.
He encountered a woman,
whose appearance was like that of an immortal.
Approaching, she asked:
"Where are you going?"
The scholar told her the truth.
The woman said:
"I am a renunciant,
and dwell in a mountain cave,
where you can lodge,
and need not fear tigers or wolves."
The scholar was delighted,
and followed her.
Entering deep into the mountains,
he saw a cave dwelling.
Upon entering, a stream crossed the doorway,
with a stone bridge spanning it.
After a few more paces,
there were two stone chambers,
brightly illuminated,
with no need for lamps or candles.
She told the scholar to remove his tattered clothes,
and bathe in the stream.
She said:
"Wash yourself,
and your wounds will heal."
Then she opened the bed-curtain, smoothed the bedding, and urged him to sleep,
saying:
"Please sleep now,
I will make trousers for you, sir."
She then took large leaves resembling plantain,
cut and sewed them into clothing.
The scholar lay watching her.
It did not take long to make,
and she folded them at the head of the bed,
saying:
"Put them on in the morning."
Then she slept on the bed opposite.
After bathing,
the scholar felt no pain from his sores.
When he awoke,
he felt them,
and found they had formed thick scabs.
At dawn,
as he was about to rise,
he doubted that plantain leaves could be worn.
Taking them for a closer look,
he found they were smooth, exquisite green brocade.
After a short while,
a meal was prepared.
The woman took mountain leaves, called them cakes,
and when eaten,
they were indeed cakes;
she also cut them into shapes of chicken and fish and cooked them,
all as if they were real.
In a corner of the chamber was a jar,
storing fine wine,
which she repeatedly fetched to drink;
when it decreased slightly,
she would replenish it with stream water.
After several days,
the scabs had all fallen off,
and he approached the woman seeking to share her bed.
The woman said:
"You frivolous fellow: barely settled comfortably,
and already giving rise to wild fancies!"
The scholar said:
"Merely to repay your kindness."
So they shared the bed,
and greatly delighted in each other.
One day,
a young woman entered laughing,
saying:
"You little imp Piānpiān, happy to death!
When did Sister Xuē's sweet dream
come true?"
Piānpiān welcomed her with a laugh, saying:
"Madam Huāchéng,
your noble steps have not trodden here for long,
today the southwest wind is strong,
it blew you here!
Have you given birth to a little boy yet?"
She said:
"Another little girl."
Piānpiān laughed and said:
"Madam Huā is a tile kiln indeed!
Why didn't you bring her?"
She said:
"Just now she was crying,
but has fallen asleep."
So they sat and drank cordially.
Then, looking at the scholar, she said,
"This young gentleman burns fine incense indeed."
The scholar looked at her:
she was twenty-three or twenty-four,
graceful and exceedingly lovely.
He felt attracted to her.
While peeling a fruit, he accidentally dropped it under the table,
and bending down as if to pick it up,
secretly pinched her delicate phoenix-toed shoe.
Huāchéng looked away and smiled,
as if unaware.
Just as the scholar was utterly captivated,
he suddenly felt his robe and trousers grow cold;
looking at what he wore,
it had all turned into autumn leaves.
He was nearly terrified to death.
Sitting stiffly for a while,
they gradually changed back as before.
He secretly庆幸 that the two women had not seen.
After a short while,
during the toasting,
he again used his fingers to scratch her slender palm;
Huāchéng remained composed, laughing and joking,
completely unaware.
In the midst of his pounding heart,
his clothes had already turned into leaves,
and only after a while did they change back.
From then on, he felt ashamed, ceased his thoughts,
and dared not entertain wild fancies.
Huāchéng laughed and said:
"Your little husband here,
is most improper!
If not for the vinegar-gourd lady,
I fear he would have leapt to the clouds."
Piānpiān also teased:
"You frivolous fellow,
you truly deserve to freeze to death!"
They clapped their hands together,
and Huāchéng rose from her seat, saying:
"My little maid is waking,
I fear her crying will break her heart."
Piānpiān also stood up, saying:
"So greedy to lure another's man,
you've forgotten your little Jiāngchéng must be crying her heart out."
After Huāchéng had left,
he feared he would incur ridicule and责备;
but Piānpiān eventually treated him as usual.
Not long after,
as autumn deepened and winds grew cold,
frost fell and trees shed their leaves,
the girl gathered the fallen leaves
to store provisions for the winter.
Seeing Shēng shivering,
she picked up the white clouds at the cave entrance, using them as wadding for a padded garment.
When he wore it, it was as warm as a lined robe,
and always as light and soft as new cotton.
After a year,
they had a son,
extremely intelligent and beautiful.
They spent their days in the cave, delighting in playing with the child.
Yet Shēng often thought of his old home
and begged her to return with him.
The girl said:
"I cannot follow you;
if not,
you may go alone."
Thus they lingered for two or three years.
As the child gradually grew,
they arranged a marriage alliance with Huāchéng.
Shēng often worried about his aging uncle.
The girl said:
"Your uncle's years are indeed advanced,
but fortunately he remains strong and healthy.
There is no need for anxious concern.
After Bǎo'er's wedding,
whether to stay or go will be up to you."
In the cave,
the girl would take leaves and write characters to teach the boy to read.
He understood everything at a glance.
The girl said:
"This child has the appearance of fortune.
If sent into the mortal world,
he would have no trouble reaching high office."
Before long,
the boy turned fourteen.
Huāchéng personally came to escort her daughter.
The girl arrived in splendid attire,
her radiant beauty illuminating all around.
Husband and wife were overjoyed,
and the whole family gathered.
Piānpiān tapped her hairpin and sang:
"I have a fine son,
I envy not the noble palaces.
I have a fine daughter-in-law,
I envy not silks and satins.
Tonight we gather together,
all should be joyful.
I pour wine for you,
I urge you to eat heartily."
Soon after, Huāchéng departed.
They lived opposite the young couple's chamber.
The new bride was filial,
clinging affectionately to their knees,
as if she were their own child.
Shēng again spoke of returning.
The girl said:
"You have a mortal bone,
ultimately not of immortal quality.
Our son is also destined for wealth and honor.
You may take him with you,
I will not hinder his life's course."
The new bride longed to bid farewell to her mother,
and Huāchéng had already arrived.
The children were reluctant to part,
tears filling their eyes.
The two mothers comforted them, saying:
"Go for now,
you may return again."
Piānpiān then cut leaves into donkeys,
and had the three of them ride them back.
Dàyè, now old and retired to the countryside,
had thought his nephew dead.
Suddenly seeing him return with a fine grandson and beautiful wife,
he was as delighted as finding a treasure.
Upon entering the house,
they looked at each other's clothes—
all were banana leaves;
when torn,
the wadding steamed and floated away.
So they all changed their garments.
Later, Shēng missed Piānpiān,
and went with his son to seek her.
But yellow leaves covered the path,
the cave entrance lost and the way confused.
They returned with streaming tears.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"Piānpiān and Huāchéng,
are they perhaps immortals?
Feasting on leaves and clothing themselves in clouds,
how strange indeed!
Yet behind bed-curtains, with playful banter,
intimacy and bearing children—
how does this differ from the human world?
Fifteen years in the mountains,
though without the change of 'people and city walls'
as in the old tale;
yet clouds obscure the cave mouth,
no trace to be found.
Witnessing this scene,
it truly resembles the time when Liú Chén and Ruǎn Zhào turned their boat back."
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
I heard from the venerable Lǐ Jìngyī:
"A certain gentleman in Shěnyáng,
was feasting atop a mountain.
Looking down at the foot of the mountain,
he saw a tiger-like creature approach.
It used its claws to dig a hole in the ground,
buried something, and left.
Someone was sent to probe the burial spot,
and found a dead deer.
They took the deer and loosely covered the hole.
After a short while,
the tiger led a black beast there,
with fur several inches long.
The tiger walked ahead,
as if inviting an honored guest.
Upon reaching the hole,
the beast crouched, glaring and waiting.
The tiger probed the hole, found the deer missing,
and trembled, prostrating itself, not daring to move.
The beast, angered by the deception,
struck the tiger's forehead with its claw,
and the tiger instantly died.
The beast then went straight away."
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"The beast's name is unknown.
Yet from its described form,
it was not much larger than a tiger.
Why then did the tiger stretch out its neck to receive death,
fearing it to such an extreme degree?
All creatures have their respective masters,
a principle hard to fathom.
For instance, monkeys most fear the yǔ;
from afar seeing it,
they gather in groups of tens or hundreds,
kneeling in a circle,
none daring to flee.
With fixed gaze and held breath,
they wait for the yǔ to arrive,
which uses its claws to feel each for fat or thin;
marking the fat ones with a stone chip on their heads.
Bearing the stone, they crouch,
terrified as wooden chickens,
fearing only that it might fall.
After the yǔ has felt and marked them,
it then takes them in order according to the stones and eats them,
the rest then scattering noisily.
I have said that greedy officials resemble this.
They too feel the people for fat or thin and mark them,
then tear and devour them;
and the people, resigned to being eaten,
dare not even breathe heavily.
The simple, ignorant state of the people
is also just like this.
How lamentable!"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Yǐn Túnán of Wǔchāng
had a separate residence,
which he once rented to a xiùcai.
For half a year,
he had not made any inquiries.
One day,
he met him at the gate.
The man was very young,
yet his demeanor, furs, and horse
were exceedingly elegant and handsome.
Yǐn hurried to speak with him,
and found him refined and likable.
He thought this strange.
Returning home, he told his wife.
His wife sent a maid under pretext of delivering something to spy on his rooms.
There was a beautiful woman inside,
more lovely than a fairy;
all the flowers, rocks, clothing, and curios
were unlike anything ever seen or heard of.
Yǐn could not guess who they were.
He went to their gate to pay a visit,
but happened to find them away.
The next day,
they came to return the call.
Reading their name card,
he learned the surname was Yú, name Dé.
During conversation,
he carefully inquired about official background,
but the answers were vague and evasive.
When pressed firmly,
the man said:
"If you wish for our acquaintance to continue,
I dare not cut it off myself.
You should know we are not fugitives from banditry or theft;
why must you press to know our origins?"
Yǐn apologized.
He ordered wine for a feast,
and they talked and laughed very merrily.
As evening approached,
a dark-skinned servant arrived holding a horse and lantern,
to escort and guide him away.
The next day,
I sent a note to the host.
Yǐn arrived at his house,
and saw that the walls were all pasted with glossy paper,
clean as a mirror.
A golden lion-shaped censer emitted exotic fragrance.
A green jade vase
held two phoenix-tail and two peacock feathers each,
each over two chǐ long.
A crystal vase
held a branch of pink flowers,
whose name I did not know,
also about two chǐ tall,
with drooping branches covering the table;
its leaves were sparse, its flowers dense,
still in bud, not yet blooming;
the flowers looked like damp butterflies folding their wings;
the calyxes were like whiskers.
The banquet had no more than eight dishes,
yet they were exceptionally sumptuous and delicious.
Afterward,
he ordered a boy to beat a drum to urge the flowers as a drinking game.
Once the drumming began,
the flowers in the vase trembled as if about to burst open;
soon the butterfly wings gradually spread;
then the drumming stopped,
and with a deep sound,
the calyx and whiskers suddenly fell off,
turning into a butterfly,
which flew and landed on Yǐn's clothes.
I laughed and stood up,
and was made to drink a huge goblet;
just as I finished the wine,
the butterfly also flew away.
After a moment,
the drum sounded again,
and two butterflies flew to gather on my hat.
I laughed and said:
"I've brought this on myself."
I also drank two goblets.
After the third drumming ended,
flowers fell in disorder,
fluttering down,
brushing sleeves and staining lapels.
The drumming boy came laughing and counted the tallies: Yǐn got nine tallies,
I got four.
Yǐn was already slightly drunk,
and could not finish his tallies,
so he forced himself to drink three cups,
then left the seat and fled.
From then on, I found him even more extraordinary.
However, he was unsociable,
often staying behind closed doors,
and did not participate in condolences or celebrations with others.
Yǐn would spread the word about him to everyone he met;
those who heard of his marvels
competed to befriend me,
and carriages and caps were often seen outside my gate.
I grew rather impatient,
and suddenly bid farewell to the host and left.
After I left,
Yǐn went to his house,
and found the empty courtyard swept clean without a speck of dust;
candle drippings were piled beneath the green steps;
scattered cloth and broken threads were by the window,
with fingerprints still visible.
Only behind the house was left a small white stone vat,
which could hold about a dàn.
Yǐn took it back,
filled it with water, and raised red fish in it.
After a year,
the water remained as clear as when first stored.
Later, a servant moved the stone,
and accidentally broke it.
The stored water did not spill out.
Looking at it,
the vat seemed to be there,
but touching it felt empty.
When a hand was put into it,
the water flowed out with the hand;
when the hand was withdrawn,
it closed again.
In winter, it did not freeze either.
One night,
it suddenly crystallized,
but the fish swam as before.
Yǐn, afraid others would find out,
often kept it in a secret room,
and would not show it except to his sons-in-law.
Over time, word gradually spread,
and those seeking to view it crowded the door.
On a winter night,
it suddenly melted into water,
soaking the ground,
and the fish also vanished.
The remnants of the old vat and stones still remained.
Suddenly, a Dàoshi came to the door seeking it.
Yǐn brought it out to show him.
The Dàoshi said:
"This is a water storage vessel from the Dragon Palace."
Yǐn described how it broke but did not leak.
The Dàoshi said:
"This is the soul of the vat."
He earnestly begged for a small piece.
Asked what it was for,
he said:
"Grinding it into powder for medicine
can grant longevity."
Yǐn gave him a piece,
and he joyfully thanked him and left.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
When Bì, the Minister of Revenue, was appointed from home to prepare troops for Táomín,
a Qiānzǒng named Yáng Huàlín came to welcome him.
While traveling with his entourage,
he happened to see a man relieving himself by the roadside,
and Yáng drew his bow to shoot him,
but Bì urgently stopped him.
Yáng said:
"This slave is rude,
he deserves a little scare."
Then he shouted from afar:
"You who are defecating!
I present you with a Huìjī rattan hairpin to tie your hair!"
He immediately shot an arrow,
which hit the man's hair bun.
The man hurriedly ran,
and his waste soiled the ground.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In the sixth month of the twenty-sixth year,
in a villager's garden west of the county,
a cucumber vine grew again,
bearing one watermelon,
as large as a bowl.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Chéng, a scholar from Báixià,
was open and straightforward by nature,
not bound by conventions.
One day,
returning from outside,
he loosened his belt,
and felt the end of the belt heavy,
as if something had fallen.
Looking,
he saw nothing.
As he turned,
a woman emerged from behind his clothes,
brushed her hair and smiled,
extremely beautiful.
Chéng suspected she was a ghost,
but the woman said:
"I am not a ghost,
but a fox."
Chéng said:
"If I can have a beauty,
I wouldn't fear even a ghost,
let alone a fox."
Thus he became intimate with her.
After two years,
they had a daughter,
nicknamed Qīngméi,
and she often told Chéng:
"Do not marry,
I will bear you a son."
Chéng believed her,
and did not marry.
Relatives and friends all ridiculed him.
Chéng's resolve wavered,
and he became engaged to Wáng of Húdōng.
The fox, hearing this, was angry,
nursed the girl,
and left her with Chéng, saying:
"This is your family's money-losing goods,
whether she lives or dies,
is up to you.
Why should I act as a wet nurse for others!"
She went out the door and left directly.
Qīngméi grew up intelligent;
her appearance was lovely and delicate,
very much resembling her mother.
Later, Chéng fell ill and died,
and Wáng remarried and left.
Qīngméi went to live with her paternal uncle;
the uncle was dissolute and immoral,
and wanted to sell her for his own gain.
It happened that a Jìnshì named Wáng,
was at home awaiting an official appointment,
and hearing of her intelligence,
bought her for a high price,
making her serve his daughter Ā Xǐ.
Xǐ was fourteen years old,
with peerless beauty.
Seeing Méi, she was delighted,
and shared a room with her.
Méi was also good at anticipating needs,
able to listen with her eyes,
and speak with her eyebrows,
so the whole family came to cherish and love her.
In the town there was a scholar named Zhāng,
style Jièshòu.
His family was poor and destitute,
with no permanent property,
and he rented a house in the Wáng estate.
He was pure and filial by nature,
his conduct was strict and not careless,
and he was also devoted to his studies.
Qīngméi happened to visit his home,
and saw Zhāng sitting on a stone eating porridge made from chaff;
entering the room, she chatted with his mother,
and saw on the table a prepared pig’s trotter.
At that time, the old man was lying ill,
Zhāng entered,
embraced his father and attended to his needs.
Urine and excrement soiled his clothes,
the old man noticed it and was filled with self-reproach;
Zhāng concealed the traces,
hurried out to wash himself,
fearing his father would know.
Méi was greatly astonished by this.
Returning, she described what she had seen,
and said to the young lady:
“Our tenant,
is no ordinary man.
If you, young lady, do not wish to obtain a good match, then so be it;
but if you wish to obtain a good match,
Scholar Zhāng is the man.”
The young lady feared her father would dislike his poverty.
Méi said:
“Not so,
it lies with you, young lady.
If you consider it acceptable,
I will secretly inform him,
and have him seek a matchmaker.
The mistress will certainly summon you to discuss it: just answer ‘Yes’
and it will be settled.”
The young lady feared that remaining poor would make them a laughingstock to the world.
Méi said:
“I consider myself able to judge men of the world,
and I will certainly not be mistaken.”
The next day,
she went to tell Madame Zhāng.
The old lady was greatly startled,
saying her words were inauspicious.
Méi said:
“The young lady has heard of the young master and considers him worthy,
so I have observed her intentions to speak thus.
When the matchmaker goes,
the two of us will support it,
and the plan should succeed.
Even if it does not,
what shame is there for the young master?”
The old lady said:
“Yes.”
Then she entrusted the matter to a flower seller named Hóu to go.
The mistress heard it and laughed,
and told Wáng.
Wáng also laughed heartily.
He summoned his daughter,
and related Hóu’s proposal.
Before the daughter could answer,
Qīngméi urgently praised his worthiness,
and insisted he would certainly become noble.
The mistress asked again:
“This is a matter for your whole life.
If you can eat chaff,
then I will consent for you.”
The young lady bowed her head for a long time,
then facing the wall answered:
“Wealth and poverty are matters of fate.
If fate is generous,
then poverty will not last long: and the time without poverty will be endless.
If fate is meager,
even those princely grandsons in brocade and embroidery,
are there few among them who have not even a place to stand an awl?
It lies with my parents.”
At first,
when Wáng consulted his daughter;
it was to provoke laughter;
but upon hearing her words,
he was displeased and said:
“Do you wish to marry into the Zhāng family?”
The daughter did not answer;
asked again,
again she did not answer.
Angrily he said:
“Base bones,
utterly without ambition!
You wish to carry a basket and become a beggar’s wife,
wouldn’t you rather die of shame!”
The young lady flushed crimson and choked with anger,
holding back tears she withdrew.
The matchmaker also fled.
Qīngméi, seeing it would not succeed,
thought to arrange for herself.
After several days,
at night she visited Zhāng.
Zhāng was reading,
and startled, asked where she had come from;
her words were hesitant and evasive.
Zhāng sternly refused her.
Méi wept and said:
“I am from a respectable family,
not one who elopes for lust;
only because you are worthy,
do I wish to entrust myself to you.”
Zhāng said:
“You love me,
and say I am worthy.
Actions in the dark of night,
are not done by those who value themselves,
and can one who is worthy do them?
To begin with disorder and end with union,
even a gentleman says it cannot be;
moreover, if union cannot be achieved,
how would we each place ourselves?”
Méi said:
“If by any chance it can succeed,
would you deign to pick me up?”
Zhāng said:
“To obtain someone like you,
what more could I ask?
But there are three things that cannot be helped,
therefore I dare not lightly promise.”
She said:
“What are they?”
He said:
“If you cannot decide for yourself,
then it cannot be helped;
even if you can decide for yourself,
if my parents are not pleased,
then it cannot be helped;
even if they are pleased,
your bride-price will certainly be high,
and I am poor and cannot manage it,
then especially it cannot be helped.
You must leave quickly,
the suspicion of melons and plums is to be feared!”
As Méi was about to leave,
she again urged:
“If you have any intention,
I beg you to plan it together.”
Zhāng agreed.
Méi returned,
the young lady questioned where she had been,
so she knelt and confessed.
The young lady was angry at her elopement,
and was about to beat and punish her.
Méi wept and declared there was nothing else,
and thus truthfully told her.
The young lady sighed and said:
“Not to unite carelessly,
is propriety;
to certainly inform parents,
is filial piety;
not to promise lightly,
is trustworthiness: possessing these three virtues,
Heaven will certainly aid him,
and he need not worry about poverty.”
Then she said:
“What will you do?”
She said:
“Marry him.”
The young lady laughed and said:
“Silly maid, can you decide for yourself?”
She said:
"If I cannot succeed,
then I will follow it with death."
The young lady said:
"I will certainly fulfill my wish."
Méi kowtowed and bowed to her.
After several more days,
she said to the young lady:
"Were those words spoken earlier in jest,
or do you truly wish to be compassionate?
If it is indeed so,
I still have a small request,
and I beg for your pity as well."
The young lady asked her about it,
and she replied:
"Master Zhāng cannot afford the betrothal gifts,
and I, as a maid, have no means to redeem myself.
If you must demand the full price,
then marrying me off would be no different from not marrying me off."
The young lady pondered and said:
"This is beyond my ability to help.
If I say I will marry you off,
I fear it may not be appropriate;
but to say you must not demand any payment,
that is something my father would certainly not allow,
and something I dare not speak of either."
Qīngméi heard this,
tears streaming down her face,
and only begged for pity and rescue.
The young lady thought for a long time,
then said:
"If there is no other way,
I have some private savings of a few taels of silver,
and I will empty my purse to help you."
Méi bowed in gratitude,
and secretly informed Zhāng.
Zhāng's mother was overjoyed,
and through various means begged for loans,
managing to gather a certain sum,
waiting in anticipation for good news.
It happened that Wáng was appointed magistrate of Qūwò,
and the young lady, seizing the opportunity, told her mother:
"Qīngméi is already grown up,
and now that we are about to take up our post,
it would be better to send her away."
The lady had always considered Qīngméi too cunning,
fearing she might lead her daughter astray,
and had often wanted to marry her off,
but worried her daughter would be unhappy.
Hearing her daughter's words, she was very pleased.
After two days,
a servant woman conveyed the Zhāng family's intentions.
Wáng laughed and said:
"He is only fit to be paired with a maid.
How presumptuous he was before!
However, if we sell her as a concubine to a wealthy family,
the price should be double what it was before."
The young lady urgently interjected:
"Qīngméi has served me for a long time.
Selling her as a concubine
is truly unbearable."
Wáng then relayed the message to the Zhāng family,
still using the original sum to draw up the contract,
and married Qīngméi off to the young man.
Upon entering the household,
she served her parents-in-law with filial piety,
attending to every detail with obedience,
even surpassing her husband;
and she worked even more diligently,
not minding the hardship of eating chaff and husks.
From then on, everyone in the household loved and respected Qīngméi.
Méi also took up embroidery as her work,
selling it quickly,
with merchants waiting at the door to buy,
fearing they might miss out.
The income she earned somewhat alleviated their poverty.
Moreover, she urged her husband not to let domestic concerns interfere with his studies,
taking full responsibility for managing the household.
When her master was about to take up his post,
she went to bid farewell to Āxǐ.
Xǐ saw her,
wept, and said:
"You have found your place,
but I am certainly not as fortunate."
Méi said:
"Whose gift is this,
that I would dare forget it?
But if you think you are not as fortunate as a maid,
I fear it may shorten this maid's life."
They then parted in tears.
Wáng went to Jìn,
and after half a year,
his wife passed away,
and her coffin was placed in a temple.
Two years later,
Wáng was dismissed from his post for accepting bribes,
fined tens of thousands in reparations,
and gradually became so poor he could not support himself,
with his followers scattering.
At this time,
a great epidemic broke out,
and Wáng fell ill and also died.
Only an old maidservant remained with the young lady.
Not long after,
the maidservant also died.
The young lady was left alone and in even greater hardship.
A neighboring old woman advised her to remarry,
but the young lady said:
"Whoever can bury my parents for me,
I will follow them."
The old woman pitied her,
gave her a peck of rice, and left.
Half a month later, she returned,
and said:
"I have tried my best for you, young lady,
but it is difficult to arrange: the poor cannot afford the burial,
and the wealthy dislike you for being the descendant of a fallen family.
What can be done?
There is still one plan,
but I fear you may not agree to it."
The young lady said:
"What is it?"
She said:
"There is a Master Lǐ here
who is seeking a concubine.
If he sees your beauty,
he will surely arrange a lavish burial,
and will not hesitate to spend."
The young lady wept bitterly and said:
"Am I, a descendant of an official family, to become someone's concubine!"
The old woman said nothing,
and left.
She ate only one meal a day,
clinging to life while waiting for a suitable offer.
After half a year,
she could no longer endure.
One day,
the old woman came.
The young lady tearfully told her:
"In such dire straits,
I often think of ending my life;
but what keeps me clinging to this wretched existence
is solely because of the two coffins.
If I were to die in a ditch,
who would gather my parents' bones?
So I think it would be better to follow your words."
The old woman then brought Lǐ over,
and when he caught a glimpse of the young lady,
he was greatly pleased.
He immediately provided money for the burial,
and both coffins were properly interred.
Afterward,
he took the young lady away,
and she went to pay respects to the principal wife.
The principal wife was notoriously fierce and jealous,
and Lǐ had not dared to mention taking a concubine at first,
only claiming he had bought a maid.
But when she saw the young lady,
she flew into a rage,
beat her and drove her out,
refusing to let her enter the house.
The young lady, with disheveled hair and streaming tears,
had nowhere to go.
An old nun passed by,
and invited her to live together,
which she gladly accepted.
Upon arriving at the nunnery,
she bowed and begged to have her hair shaved off.
The nun refused,
saying:
"I see that you, young lady,
are not one destined to lie in the dust of the world for long.
In this nunnery, we have earthenware and coarse grains,
just enough to sustain ourselves.
Stay here for a while and wait.
When the time comes,
you will leave on your own."
Not long after she settled in,
some ruffians in the market caught sight of her beauty,
and would often bang on the door and shout lewd remarks as a joke,
which the nun could not stop.
The girl wept and wanted to end her life.
The nun went to seek help from a certain official in the Ministry of Personnel, who issued a strict prohibition,
and the troublemakers began to restrain themselves.
Later, someone tried to break through the temple wall at night,
but fled when the nun shouted an alarm.
She reported it again to the Ministry of Personnel official,
and the ringleader was caught,
sent to the prefecture for flogging and punishment,
after which things gradually calmed down.
Another year or so passed,
and a noble young master visited the nunnery,
saw the girl, and was utterly captivated.
He pressured the nun to convey his affections,
and also offered her a generous bribe.
The nun gently told him:
"She is from an official family,
and would not be content as a concubine.
Please return for now, young master,
and in due time, I will have an answer for you."
After he left,
the girl wanted to take poison and die.
That night, she dreamed of her father coming to her,
and saying with deep regret:
"I did not follow your wishes,
leading you to this state.
It is too late for regrets now,
but if you hold on a little longer and do not die,
your long-held wish may yet be fulfilled."
The girl found this strange.
At daybreak,
after washing up,
the nun looked at her and exclaimed in surprise:
"Looking at your face now,
all the murky energy has dissipated,
and adversity need no longer be feared.
Good fortune is about to arrive,
do not forget this old woman."
Before she finished speaking,
there came a knocking at the door.
The girl turned pale,
thinking it must be the servants of the noble family.
The nun opened the door,
and indeed it was.
They urgently asked about the matter.
The nun responded with sweet words,
only asking for a delay of three days.
The servants relayed their master's words:
if the matter was not accomplished,
the nun herself would have to report back.
The nun respectfully agreed,
thanked them and sent them away.
The girl was deeply sorrowful,
and again wanted to end her life.
The nun stopped her.
The girl worried that in three days they would return,
and she would have no words to respond.
The nun said:
"As long as this old woman is here,
I will take the blame and punishment myself."
The next day,
around mid-afternoon,
a torrential downpour poured like overturned basins,
when suddenly they heard several people banging on the door and making a great clamor.
The girl thought trouble had come,
and was frightened and at a loss.
The nun braved the rain to open the gate,
and saw a sedan chair stopped there;
several maidservants
were escorting a beautiful lady out;
the attendants were imposing,
and their attire and carriage were very elegant.
Startled, she asked who they were,
and they said:
"This is the family of the Judicial Commissioner,
seeking temporary shelter from the storm."
She led them into the main hall,
moved a couch and respectfully invited them to sit.
The family women all hurried to the meditation rooms,
each seeking a place to rest.
Entering the room and seeing the girl,
they were struck by her beauty,
and ran to tell the lady.
Before long,
the rain stopped,
and the lady rose,
asking to see the meditation room.
The nun led her in,
and upon seeing the girl's stunning beauty,
she gazed fixedly without blinking.
The girl also looked back at her for a long while.
The lady was none other
than Qīngméi.
Each cried out in surprise,
and then recounted their journeys.
It turned out that old man Zhāng had fallen ill and died,
and after the young master's mourning period ended and he resumed office,
he passed successive exams and was appointed Judicial Commissioner.
He first took his mother to his post,
and later moved the rest of the family.
The girl sighed and said:
"Seeing each other today,
how different our situations are, as far apart as heaven and earth!"
Méi smiled and said:
"Fortunately, you, young lady, have suffered setbacks and remained unmarried;
heaven must have intended for the two of us to be reunited.
If not for the rainstorm,
how could we have met like this?
There are surely spirits and gods behind this,
not merely human effort."
Then she took out a pearl headdress and brocade garments,
and urged the girl to change her attire.
The girl hesitated.
The nun joined in encouraging her.
The girl worried that living together would not be proper in name.
Méi said:
"In the past, our positions were already settled;
how would your servant dare forget your great virtue!
Think of young master Zhāng—
is he one to betray righteousness?"
She insisted on dressing her up.
They bid farewell to the nun and left.
Upon arriving at the post,
both mother and son were overjoyed.
The girl bowed and said:
"Now I have no face to see you, mother."
The mother smiled and comforted her.
They then discussed choosing an auspicious date for the wedding.
The girl said:
"If there had been even a thread of a livelihood in the nunnery,
I would not have followed the lady here.
If you remember our old friendship,
and I can be given a small hut,
just enough to hold a meditation cushion, that will suffice."
Méi smiled without saying a word.
When the day arrived,
she came carrying splendid wedding attire.
The girl was flustered and did not know what to do.
Suddenly, music and drums began to play loudly,
and the girl could no longer control herself.
Méi led the maids and elderly women to forcibly dress her,
and supported her as they led her out.
Seeing the young master bowing in his court robes,
she unconsciously found herself gracefully bowing in return.
Méi pulled her into the bridal chamber,
saying:
"I have kept this place empty, waiting for you for a long time."
Then she turned to the young master and said:
"Tonight you can repay her kindness,
do well by her."
She turned to leave.
The girl grabbed her sleeve,
and Méi smiled and said:
"Don't keep me here,
this is something I cannot do for you."
She freed her hand and left.
Qīngméi served the girl respectfully,
never daring to claim the night for herself.
But the girl remained ashamed and uneasy.
So the mother ordered them to address each other as "Madam."
Méi, however, always observed the etiquette of a servant-concubine,
never daring to slacken.
After three years,
Zhāng was summoned to the capital for an appointment,
and passing by the nunnery,
he offered five hundred taels of silver to the nun as a gift.
The nun would not accept it.
After he insisted,
she finally accepted two hundred taels,
and used it to build a Guānyīn shrine,
and erect a stele for Lady Wáng.
Later, Zhāng rose to the position of Vice Minister.
Madam Chéng bore two sons and a daughter,
and Madam Wáng bore four sons and a daughter.
Zhāng submitted a memorial stating the circumstances,
and both were granted the title of Madam.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Heaven creates beauties
precisely to reward men of worth and virtue;
yet the worldly princes and lords
keep them to bestow upon the dissolute and profligate.
This is a matter over which the Creator must contend.
And so, through strange and wondrous twists,
those who bring about unions engage in endless machinations,
showing that the workings of nature are indeed arduous.
Only Lady Qīng was able to recognize a hero amidst the dust and grime,
vowing to marry him,
resolved even unto death;
how is it that those who appear dignified in official caps and robes,
instead cast aside virtue and conduct to seek rich food and fine clothing—
why is their wisdom inferior even to that of a maidservant!"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Mǎ Jì,
style name Lóng Méi,
was the son of a merchant.
He was handsome in appearance.
In his youth, he was free-spirited and unconventional,
fond of singing and dancing.
He often joined theatrical troupes,
wrapping his head with a brocade kerchief,
looking as beautiful as a lovely maiden,
and thus earned
the nickname
"the Handsome One."
At fourteen,
he entered the prefectural school,
and soon became well-known.
His father grew old and frail,
gave up trade, and retired.
He said to his son:
"A few volumes of books
cannot be boiled to stave off hunger,
nor worn to ward off cold.
My son, you should continue your father's trade."
Mǎ thus gradually began to deal in goods for profit.
He followed others on a sea voyage,
was blown off course by a typhoon,
and after several days and nights reached a great city.
Its people were all extremely ugly;
seeing Mǎ arrive,
they thought him a monster,
and fled in a clamorous crowd.
When Mǎ first saw their appearance,
he was greatly frightened;
but upon realizing that the people of the country were terrified of him,
he then used this to his advantage to intimidate the locals.
When he encountered people eating or drinking,
he would rush towards them;
they would flee in alarm,
and he would then consume what they left behind.
After a long while,
he entered a mountain village.
Among them were some whose shapes and features somewhat resembled humans,
but they were ragged like beggars.
Mǎ rested beneath a tree,
and the villagers dared not approach,
only watching him from afar.
After a long time,
sensing that Mǎ was not a man-eater,
they gradually began to draw near.
Mǎ smiled and spoke with them.
Although their speech was strange,
he could understand about half of it.
Mǎ then explained where he came from.
The villagers were pleased,
and informed all the neighbors,
that the guest was not capable of seizing and devouring people.
However, the extremely ugly ones would take one look and leave,
never daring to come forward;
those who did approach
had facial features—mouths and noses—
that were still similar to those of people from Zhōngguó.
Together they brought out wine and food to offer Mǎ.
Mǎ asked the reason for their fear,
and they replied:
"We have heard from our grandfathers: twenty-six thousand *li* to the west,
there is a Zhōngguó,
whose people's appearances are generally bizarre and abnormal.
We only knew this by hearsay,
but now we believe it."
Mǎ asked why they were so poor.
They said:
"What our country values
is not literary talent,
but physical appearance.
Those of the utmost beauty
become high ministers;
the next serve in local government;
those of the lower ranks
still manage to gain the favor of the noble and powerful,
and thus obtain rich provisions to support their wives and children.
As for people like us, at birth,
our parents all consider us inauspicious,
and often abandon us;
those who cannot bear to abandon us
do so only for the sake of continuing the family line."
Mǎ asked:
"What is the name of this country?"
They replied:
"Dà Luóchà Guó.
The capital is thirty *li* to the north."
Mǎ requested a guide to go and see it.
So they rose at cockcrow,
and led him there together.
At daybreak,
they reached the capital.
The city walls were made of black stone,
as dark as ink,
with towers and pavilions nearly a hundred feet high.
However, they had few tiles,
being roofed with red stone;
picking up a broken piece and rubbing it on a fingernail,
it was no different from cinnabar.
It happened to be the time when court had adjourned,
and officials wearing caps and canopies were emerging from the court,
the villager pointed and said:
"This is the Prime Minister."
Looking at him,
both ears grew backwards,
he had three nostrils,
and his eyelashes covered his eyes like curtains.
Several more riders came out,
saying:
"This is a high official."
They pointed out each one's official positions in turn,
all of them strange and bizarre;
however, as the ranks gradually became lower,
the ugliness also gradually diminished.
Before long,
Mǎ returned,
and when the people on the streets saw him,
they clamored, ran, stumbled, and fell,
as if encountering a monster.
The villagers explained with a hundred mouths,
and only then did the townspeople dare to stand at a distance.
After returning,
the whole country came to know that the village had a strange man,
so the gentry and officials,
vying to broaden their knowledge,
ordered the villagers to invite Mǎ.
However, each time he arrived at a house,
the gatekeepers would immediately close the doors,
and men and women would whisper and peek through the cracks in the doors;
by the end of the day,
no one dared to invite him in.
A villager said:
"Here there is a retired court official,
who once served as an envoy to foreign countries for the former king,
having seen many people,
perhaps he will not be afraid of you."
They went to the official's gate.
The official was indeed pleased,
and greeted him as an honored guest.
Looking at his appearance,
he seemed like a man of eighty or ninety years old.
His eyes bulged out,
and his beard was curled like a hedgehog's.
He said:
"I, in my youth, received the king's orders,
and went on the most diplomatic missions;
only I have never been to Zhōnghuá.
Now over one hundred and twenty years old,
I have the chance to see a person from the superior country,
this must be reported to the Son of Heaven.
However, I have been living in retirement in the woods,
and have not stepped onto the court steps for over ten years.
Tomorrow morning,
I will go for you."
Then he prepared food and drink,
and observed the etiquette of host and guest.
After several rounds of wine,
he brought out over ten female musicians,
who took turns singing and dancing.
Their appearances resembled yakshas,
all with white brocade wrapped around their heads,
and trailing red garments reaching the ground.
Their performance and singing were of unknown lyrics,
and the tunes and rhythms were bizarre.
The host looked on with delight,
and asked:
"Does Zhōngguó also have such music?"
Mǎ replied:
"Yes."
The host asked him to imitate the sound,
so he tapped the table to perform a tune.
The host happily said:
"How strange!
The sound is like the cry of a phoenix or the roar of a dragon,
I have never heard such a thing before."
The next day,
he hurried to court,
and recommended Mǎ to the king.
The king gladly issued an edict,
but two or three high officials,
mentioning his strange appearance,
feared it would startle the royal body.
The king then stopped.
The official came out and told Mǎ,
deeply regretting it.
After staying for a long time,
he drank with the host and became drunk,
took up a sword and danced,
and painted his face with soot to resemble Zhāng Fēi.
The host thought it beautiful,
and said:
"Please let the Prime Minister see you as Zhāng Fēi,
the Prime Minister will surely be pleased to employ you,
and a high salary will not be hard to obtain."
Mǎ said:
"Ha!
Playing around is fine,
but how can I change my face to seek honor and glory?"
The host insisted strongly,
and Mǎ then agreed.
The host set up a banquet,
inviting influential people to drink,
and had Mǎ paint his face and wait.
Before long,
the guests arrived,
and he called Mǎ out to meet them.
The guests exclaimed in surprise:
"How strange!
Why was he ugly before and handsome now!"
Then they drank together,
very happily.
Mǎ danced gracefully and sang
the "Yìyáng Melody"
and the entire gathering was utterly captivated.
The next day,
they submitted memorials recommending Mǎ.
The king was pleased,
and summoned him with a ceremonial banner.
After the audience,
he asked about the principles of governance and peace in Zhōngguó,
and Mǎ explained in detail,
receiving great praise and admiration,
and was granted a banquet at the detached palace.
When the wine was in full swing,
the king said:
"I hear you are skilled in elegant music,
can you let me hear it?"
Mǎ immediately danced,
also imitating the white brocade head wrapping,
and performed decadent music.
The king was greatly delighted,
and that day appointed him as a junior high official.
He often attended private banquets,
receiving exceptional favor and宠爱.
Over time, the officials and various functionaries gradually became aware that his face was fake;
wherever he went,
he would see people whispering,
and they did not treat him very cordially.
Mǎ became isolated,
and felt uneasy.
So he submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
but it was not granted;
he then asked for leave,
and was given a three-month vacation.
Then he took a carriage loaded with gold and treasures,
and returned to the mountain village.
The villagers welcomed him on their knees.
Mǎ distributed the gold and funds among his old friends,
and cheers thundered.
The villagers said:
"We humble folk have received the gentleman's kindness,
and tomorrow we are going to the Sea Market,
where we shall seek rare treasures
to repay the gentleman."
He asked,
"Where is the Sea Market?"
They replied,
"It is a market in the sea,
where the jiāorén from the four seas
gather to trade pearls and jewels;
the twelve kingdoms from all directions
all come to trade.
Many divine beings roam there for amusement.
Clouds and rosy mists veil the sky,
and waves surge intermittently.
Noble people value their safety,
and dare not brave the dangers,
so they entrust us with gold and silk,
to purchase exotic treasures on their behalf.
Now the time for it is not far off."
He asked how they knew,
and they said:
"Whenever we see red birds flying back and forth over the sea,
after seven days,
the market is held."
Mǎ asked about the departure date,
wishing to accompany them and see it,
but the villagers urged him to value himself.
Mǎ said,
"I am but a traveler on the vast sea,
why should I fear wind and waves?"
Before long,
indeed someone came to the door to entrust funds,
so he packed his belongings and boarded the boat.
The boat could hold several dozen people,
with a flat bottom and high railings.
Ten men rowed the oars,
churning the water like arrows.
After three days,
they saw from afar, amidst the shimmering water and clouds,
towers and pavilions layered upon layers;
trading vessels
gathered like ants.
After a short while,
they reached the city wall.
Looking at the bricks on the wall,
each was as long as a person.
The watchtowers soared high into the clouds.
They moored the boat and entered,
and saw the goods displayed in the market,
rare treasures and exotic jewels,
whose brilliance dazzled the eyes,
many of which were not found in the human world.
A young man came riding a fine horse,
and the market people all fled to avoid him,
saying he was
"the Third Prince of the Eastern Ocean"
As the prince passed by,
he looked at the scholar and said:
"Is this not a man from a foreign land?"
Immediately, a horseman in front came to inquire about his hometown.
The scholar bowed by the roadside,
and fully explained his lineage and country.
The prince said happily,
"Since you have honored us with your presence,
our bond is not shallow!"
Then he gave the scholar a horse,
and invited him to ride side by side.
They then went out of the western city.
Just as they reached the island shore,
the horse they rode neighed and leaped into the water.
The scholar cried out in great alarm,
then saw the seawater part,
standing like a wall.
Soon he beheld a palace,
with beams of tortoiseshell,
and tiles of fish scales;
the four walls were crystal clear,
reflecting light that dazzled the eyes.
They dismounted and entered with a bow.
Looking up, he saw the Dragon King seated above,
and the prince reported:
"While I was wandering in the market,
I found a worthy scholar from Zhōnghuá,
and have brought him to meet Your Majesty."
The scholar stepped forward and performed a ceremonial bow.
The Dragon King then said:
"Sir, as a man of letters,
you must be able to surpass Qū Yuán and Sòng Yù.
I would like to trouble you to wield your great brush and compose a rhapsody on the 'Sea Market,'
and hope you will not begrudge us your pearls and jades."
The scholar kowtowed and accepted the command.
He was given a crystal inkstone,
a brush made of dragon's mane,
paper as smooth as snow,
and ink with a fragrance like orchids.
The scholar immediately composed over a thousand words,
and presented it in the hall.
The Dragon King clapped in admiration and said:
"Sir, with your great talent,
you bring glory to the Water Kingdom!"
Then he gathered all the dragon clans,
and held a banquet in the Cǎixiá Palace.
After several rounds of wine and food,
the Dragon King raised his cup and addressed the guest:
"I have a beloved daughter,
who has not yet found a suitable match,
and I wish to burden you with her.
Do you have any intention, sir?"
The scholar rose from his seat, feeling both ashamed and grateful,
and merely murmured his assent.
The Dragon King turned and spoke to his attendants.
Before long,
several palace maids
escorted a young lady out.
The sound of her jade pendants tinkled,
and music suddenly burst forth.
After the bows were completed,
he glanced at her,
and indeed she was a fairy maiden.
The lady bowed and then left.
Soon the banquet ended,
and two maids with double buns carried painted lanterns,
leading the scholar into a side palace.
The lady sat waiting in heavy makeup.
The coral bed
was adorned with eight treasures;
outside the bed curtain, tassels
were hung with pearls as large as pecks;
the quilts and mattresses were all fragrant and soft.
As dawn broke,
young maids and charming attendants
rushed in and filled the room.
The scholar rose,
hurried out to offer morning thanks.
He was appointed Imperial Son-in-Law Commandant.
His rhapsody was swiftly circulated throughout the seas.
The Dragon Kings of all seas,
all sent delegates to offer congratulations;
they vied to send invitations for the imperial son-in-law to drink.
The scholar, dressed in embroidered robes,
rode a green qiú dragon,
with attendants clearing the way ahead and following behind.
Dozens of mounted warriors,
carrying carved bows on their backs,
and shouldering white staffs,
shone brilliantly as they crowded around.
On horseback, they played the zhēng,
and in the carriage, jade instruments were played.
Within three days,
he traveled through all the seas.
From then on,
the name "Lóng Méi"
became famous throughout the four seas.
In the palace, there was a jade tree,
whose trunk could be encircled by two arms;
its trunk was translucent,
like white glass,
with a core inside,
pale yellow in color,
slightly thinner than an arm;
its leaves resembled green jade,
about the thickness of a coin,
finely textured with dense shade.
He often chanted poems with the lady beneath it.
When the tree bloomed, it was covered with flowers,
resembling zhīfú.
Each time a petal fell,
it made a clinking sound.
Picking it up to look,
it was like carved red agate,
bright and lovely.
Occasionally, exotic birds came to sing,
with feathers of gold and jade green,
tails longer than their bodies,
their voices like mournful jade,
piercing to the heart.
Whenever the scholar heard them,
he would think of his homeland.
So he said to the lady:
"It has been three years since I left home,
separated from my parents' kindness,
and whenever I think of it,
tears soak my chest and sweat drenches my back.
Can you follow me back home?"
The lady said:
"The paths of immortality and the mortal world are separate,
we cannot depend on each other.
Nor can I bear to let the love between fish and water
take away the joy of being close to one's parents.
Let me think of a way slowly."
Hearing this,
the scholar could not hold back his tears.
The lady also sighed and said:
"This is a situation where both cannot be fully satisfied!"
The next day,
the scholar returned from outside.
The Dragon Lord said:
"I hear the Commandant longs for his native land.
If you prepare to depart at dawn,
would that be acceptable?"
The scholar expressed his gratitude:
"A solitary traveler and humble subject,
I have received excessive favor and affection.
My sincerity in repaying this
is engraved in my heart and liver.
Allow me to return home briefly to visit my family,
and I shall plan to reunite with you again."
As evening fell,
the maiden prepared wine for their farewell conversation.
The scholar arranged for a future meeting.
The maiden said:
"Our romantic bond has reached its end."
The scholar was greatly sorrowful.
The maiden said:
"Returning to care for both parents
shows your filial piety.
The gatherings and separations of human life—
even a hundred years is but like morning and evening.
Why act like children weeping in sorrow?
Hereafter, I shall remain chaste for you,
and you shall remain faithful to me.
Though in two separate places, we share one heart—
that itself is a marital union.
Why must we stay together day and night
to call it growing old together?
If we violate this vow,
our marriage will be inauspicious.
If you worry about lacking someone to manage the household,
you may take a maidservant as concubine.
There is one more matter I entrust to you:
since attending to your garments,
it seems there is a favorable sign.
I trouble you to give a name."The scholar said:
"If it is a girl,
she may be named Lónggōng;
if a boy,
he may be named Fúhǎi."
The maiden requested an object as a token of faith.
The scholar brought out a pair of red jade lotuses
he had obtained in the Luóchà Kingdom and gave them to the maiden.
The maiden said:
"Three years from now, on the eighth day of the fourth month,
you should sail to the southern island,
and I will return your flesh and blood to you."
The maiden made a pouch from fish leather,
filled it with pearls and jewels,
and gave it to the scholar, saying:
"Treasure this well.
For several generations, you will have ample food and clothing."
As the sky grew faintly bright,
the king set up a farewell feast,
bestowing generous gifts.
The scholar bowed in farewell and left the palace.
The maiden rode in a white goat carriage,
escorting him to the seashore.
The scholar disembarked and dismounted from his horse.
The maiden bid him take good care of himself,
turned her carriage around, and departed.
In a short while, she was far away.
The sea surged forth and closed again,
and she could no longer be seen.
Shēng then returned home.
He had gone away by sea,
and everyone thought he had died;
when he reached home,
his family was astonished without exception.
Fortunately, his parents were well,
but his wife alone had remarried.
Only then did he realize that the Dragon Princess’s
“keeping faith”
words
had already been foreknowledge.
His father wanted to arrange another marriage for Shēng;
Shēng refused,
but took a maidservant as concubine.
Mindful of the three-year deadline,
he sailed to the island.
He saw two children sitting afloat on the water,
slapping the waves and laughing playfully,
neither moving nor sinking.
Drawing near to pull them in,
the children, giggling, grabbed Shēng’s arms,
and leaped into his embrace.
One of them cried loudly,
as if angry that Shēng had not helped him.
Shēng pulled him up as well.
Upon close inspection,
one was a boy, the other a girl,
both with gentle and lovely features.
On their foreheads, floral crowns were adorned with jade,
and there lay the red lotus.
On their backs were brocade pouches;
opening them to look,
he found a letter that said:
“I trust Father and Mother are both well.
Swiftly three years have passed;
the mortal world is forever cut off;
the vast expanse of water,
makes even the blue bird hard to reach.
Longing turns to dreams,
craning my neck has wearied me;
the boundless blue sky,
how can I bear this regret!
Yet thinking of Cháng’é who fled to the moon,
still dwells alone in the Cassia Palace;
and the Weaving Maid who threw her shuttle,
still laments the Silver River.
What kind of person am I,
that I could enjoy eternal love?
Whenever this thought arises,
I then break into smiles through tears.
Two months after parting,
I unexpectedly gave birth to twins.
Now they already babble in my arms,
and quite understand speech and laughter;
seeking dates and grabbing pears,
they can live without their mother.
I respectfully return them to you.
The red jade lotus you gave me
adorns their crowns as a token.
When you hold the children on your knees,
it is as if I am by your side.
Hearing that you have kept your former vow,
my heart finds comfort.
In this life I will not be unfaithful,
until death I will not change.
In my dressing case, precious things
no longer hold orchid-scented ointments;
in the mirror, my new attire
long ago abandoned powder and mascara.
You are like a traveler afar,
I act the part of a faithful wife;
even if set aside and not attended to,
how can it be said we are not like lute and zither?
Only I reckon that Father and Mother now have grandchildren,
yet have never once seen their new daughter-in-law;
considering reason and sentiment,
this too is a deficiency.
After the year when Mother is laid to rest,
I shall come to the grave,
to fulfill a wife’s duty.
Beyond that time,
then ‘Dragon Palace’
remains well,
there will be no lack of chances to meet;
‘Fúhǎi’
lives long,
there may be a path for coming and going.
I humbly beg you to take care,
more than words can express.”
Shēng read the letter over and over, wiping away tears.
The two children clung to his neck and said:
“Let’s go home!”
Shēng wept even more bitterly,
stroking them and saying:
“Children, do you know where home is?”
The children cried,
babbling that they wanted to go home.
Shēng gazed at the vast, boundless sea;
reaching the horizon, there was no end;
the mist-haired lady was gone,
the misty waves blocked the way.
Holding the children, he turned the boat back,
and sorrowfully returned home.
Shēng knew his mother’s life would not be long,
so he prepared all funeral items in advance,
and planted over a hundred pines at the gravesite.
A year later,
the old lady indeed passed away.
When the funeral carriage reached the burial ground,
a woman appeared by the grave.
Just as everyone was staring in shock,
suddenly wind raged and thunder roared,
followed by a downpour,
and in an instant she was gone.
The newly planted pines and cypresses had mostly withered,
but from then on, they all revived.
When Fúhǎi grew a bit older,
he often missed his mother,
and once suddenly threw himself into the sea,
returning only after several days.
As a girl, Lónggōng could not go,
and often shut her door to weep.
One day,
in broad daylight it turned dark,
and the Dragon Princess suddenly entered,
stopping her and saying:
“Child, you will have your own family someday,
why are you crying?”
Then she bestowed an eight-foot coral tree,
a packet of borneol incense,
a hundred luminous pearls,
and a pair of gold-inlaid eight-treasure boxes,
as a dowry.
Hearing this, Shēng rushed in,
grasped her hands and sobbed.
In a moment,
a sudden thunderbolt shattered the roof,
and the woman was gone.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
“Fawning with painted faces,
worldly feelings are like ghosts.
The taste for scabs,
is the same everywhere under heaven.
‘A little shame brings a little praise,
great shame brings great praise.’
If one were to openly parade with a beard and eyebrows through the marketplace,
those who would not flee in terror are indeed few.
That foolish man of Língyáng,
where will he go to weep, holding his priceless jade?
Alas!
Glory, splendor, wealth, and honor
should be sought in the mirage towers and sea markets!”
Based on the manuscript edition of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Wǔ Chéngxiū
was a man of Liáoyáng.
He delighted in making friends,
and all his associates were men of note.
One night he dreamed that someone told him,
"Your friendships extend throughout the land,
but they are all indiscriminate associations.
There is only one man who can share your hardships with you.
Why, on the contrary, do you not know him?"
He asked,
"Who is this man?"
The reply came,
"Isn't it Tián Qīláng?"
He awoke and thought it strange.
The next morning,
whenever he saw his friends,
he would ask about Qīláng.
One guest recognized him as a hunter from the eastern village.
Wǔ respectfully called at his home,
knocking on the door with his horsewhip.
Before long,
a man came out,
over twenty years old,
with sharp eyes and a slender waist,
wearing a greasy cap
and a black apron,
patched with many white stitches.
He cupped his hands to his forehead and asked where he was from.
Wǔ gave his name;
and, claiming he was unwell from the journey,
asked to borrow his hut to rest.
He asked for Qīláng.
The reply was,
"I am he."
Thereupon he invited the guest inside.
Wǔ saw several rafters of a dilapidated house,
propped up with forked wooden poles against the walls.
Entering a small room,
he saw tiger skins and wolf pelts
hanging between the pillars,
with no chairs or couches to sit on.
Qīláng spread a tiger skin on the ground.
Wǔ spoke with him;
his words were simple and sincere,
and Wǔ was greatly pleased.
He hastily offered him money for his livelihood,
but Qīláng would not accept it.
When Wǔ insisted on giving it,
Qīláng took it to tell his mother.
A moment later he returned,
firmly declining and refusing to accept.
Wǔ forced it upon him repeatedly.
His mother, aged and tottering, came out
and said sternly,
"This old woman has only this son;
I do not wish him to serve noble guests!"
Wǔ withdrew in shame,
and on the way home he pondered,
unable to understand her meaning.
It happened that his attendant overheard the mother's words behind the house,
and thus informed Wǔ.
Earlier,
when Qīláng took the money to tell his mother,
she had said,
"I just saw the young master;
