he has ominous lines on his face,
and is sure to meet with a strange calamity.
I have heard it said: He who receives another's recognition shares that person's worries;
he who receives another's kindness rushes to that person's aid in times of difficulty.
The rich repay others with wealth;
the poor repay others with righteousness.
To receive a heavy gift without cause
is inauspicious,
for I fear he will require you with his death."
When Wǔ heard this,
he deeply admired the mother's wisdom;
yet he admired Qīláng even more.
The next day,
he prepared a feast and invited him,
but Qīláng declined and did not come.
Wǔ went to his hall,
sat down, and asked for a drink.
Qīláng personally served the wine,
and presented dried venison, showing utmost courtesy.
Another day passed,
and Wǔ invited him in return,
whereupon he came.
They conversed cordially and were very happy.
Wǔ offered him money,
but he would not accept it.
Wǔ then asked him to buy a tiger skin,
and only then did he accept.
Returning home, he looked at his stored pelts,
and reckoned they were insufficient to repay the debt,
so he thought to hunt again and then present them.
He went into the mountains for three days,
but caught nothing.
Then his wife fell ill,
and he tended to her medicine,
with no leisure to pursue his work.
After ten days,
his wife suddenly died.
To arrange the funeral and burial,
he gradually used up the money he had received.
Wǔ personally came to offer condolences and see her off,
with generous rituals and gifts.
After the burial,
he shouldered his crossbow into the mountains,
thinking even more of how to repay Wǔ,
but still he gained nothing.
When Wǔ learned the reason,
he urged him not to hurry.
He earnestly hoped Qīláng would just come for a visit;
but Qīláng always regretted his debt,
and would not come.
Wǔ therefore first asked for his old stored pelts,
to hasten his coming.
When Qīláng examined the old hides,
he found them moth-eaten and ruined,
with all the fur fallen off,
and he became even more distressed.
When Wǔ learned of this,
he hurried to his courtyard,
and did his utmost to console him.
Looking at the ruined hides, he said,
"These are also quite good.
What I wanted
was not originally for the fur."
Thereupon he rolled them up and took them away,
and also invited Qīláng to come along.
Qīláng would not agree,
so Wǔ returned alone.
Qīláng thought that he still had not repaid Wǔ sufficiently,
so he packed provisions and went into the mountains.
After several nights,
he caught a tiger,
and presented it whole.
Wǔ was delighted,
prepared a feast,
and asked him to stay for three days.
Qīláng firmly declined.
Wǔ locked the courtyard gate,
so that he could not leave.
The guests, seeing Qīláng's simple and rustic appearance,
secretly said the young master was making friends recklessly,
but Wǔ attended to Qīláng
very differently from the other guests.
He tried to change him into new clothes,
but Qīláng refused to accept them;
so Wǔ took advantage of his sleep to secretly change them,
and Qīláng had no choice but to accept.
After he left,
his son, following the old woman's orders,
returned the new clothes
and asked for his old garments.
Wǔ laughed and said,
"Go back and tell the old lady
that the old clothes have already been torn up to make shoe linings."
From then on,
Qīláng daily sent him rabbits and deer,
but when summoned, he would no longer come.
One day Wǔ went to visit Qīláng,
and found he was out hunting and had not returned.
The old woman came out
and spoke at the gate:
"Do not lead my son on again;
you mean no good!"
Wǔ treated her with respect,
but withdrew in shame.
About half a year later,
a servant suddenly reported:
"Qīláng has killed a man in a fight
over a leopard he hunted,
and has been taken to the authorities."
Wǔ was greatly alarmed,
and hurried to see him,
only to find that Qīláng had already been shackled and imprisoned.
When Qīláng saw Wǔ, he said nothing,
only remarking:
"From now on, I must trouble you to look after my mother."
Wǔ left in deep sorrow,
and immediately bribed the county magistrate with a large sum of money;
he also gave a hundred taels to the family of the deceased.
After more than a month without further incident,
Qīláng was released and returned home.
His mother said with emotion:
"My son's life was saved by Master Wǔ,
so it is no longer mine to cherish.
I only pray that the young master may live a hundred years free from calamity—
that would be my son's fortune."
Qīláng wished to go and thank Wǔ,
but his mother said:
"Go if you must,
but do not thank the young master when you see him.
Small favors may be thanked,
but great kindness cannot be repaid with thanks."
Qīláng went to see Wǔ;
Wǔ spoke to him kindly and comfortingly,
and Qīláng merely assented.
The servants all thought him cold and distant;
but Wǔ, delighted by his sincerity and steadfastness,
treated him even more generously.
From then on, Qīláng often stayed at Wǔ's home for several days at a time.
He accepted whatever gifts were given,
without declining,
nor did he speak of repaying them.
On one occasion, it was Wǔ's birthday,
and there were many guests and attendants,
so that the rooms were filled to capacity at night.
Wǔ shared a small room with Qīláng,
while three servants slept on straw mats on the floor.
As the second watch was nearing its end,
all the servants had fallen asleep,
but the two of them were still chatting away.
Qīláng's sword, which hung on the wall,
suddenly leaped several inches out of its scabbard of its own accord,
emitting a clanging sound,
its light flashing like lightning.
Wǔ started up in alarm,
and Qīláng also rose,
asking:
"Who is lying under the bed?"
Wǔ replied:
"They are all servants."
Qīláng said:
"Among them there must be an evil man."
Wǔ asked why,
Qīláng said:
"This sword was purchased from a foreign land,
it has killed people without ever being stained.
To this day, it has been worn for three generations.
The heads it has severed number in the thousands,
yet it remains as sharp as if freshly ground.
When it sees an evil man, it hums and leaps,
indicating that killing is not far off.
You, young master, should draw close to gentlemen
and keep away from petty men,
then perhaps you may avoid disaster."
Wǔ nodded in agreement.
Qīláng remained unhappy,
tossing and turning on the bed.
Wǔ said:
"Fortune and misfortune are matters of fate,
why worry so deeply?"
Qīláng said:
"I myself have no fears,
it is only because I have an old mother."
Wǔ said:
"Why speak so gravely?"
Qīláng said:
"If nothing happens, that would be best."
Now, the three men under the bed: one was Lín'ér,
an old favorite,
who knew how to please his master;
one was a young servant,
twelve or thirteen years old,
whom Wǔ often employed;
one was Lǐ Yìng,
the most stubborn and clumsy,
who often argued fiercely with the young master over trivial matters,
and Wǔ was always angry with him.
That night, Wǔ pondered silently,
suspecting it must be this man.
The next morning,
he called him over,
and with kind words, dismissed him for good.
Wǔ's eldest son, Shēn,
married a woman from the Wáng family.
One day,
Wǔ was away,
and left Lín'ér to guard the house.
The chrysanthemums in the study were just in full bloom.
Thinking that since her father-in-law was out,
the study courtyard would be quiet,
the young bride went to pick chrysanthemums.
Lín'ér suddenly emerged and flirted with her.
The woman tried to flee,
but Lín'ér forcibly dragged her into the room.
She cried and resisted,
her face changing color and her voice growing hoarse.
Shēn rushed in,
and only then did Lín'ér release her and escape.
When Wǔ returned and heard of this,
he angrily searched for Lín'ér,
but he had already disappeared without a trace.
After two or three days,
he learned that Lín'ér had taken refuge in the household of a certain Censor.
This official was stationed in the capital,
and all household affairs were entrusted to his younger brother.
Appealing to their shared official background,
Wǔ sent a letter demanding Lín'ér's return,
but the younger brother simply ignored it.
Wǔ grew even more furious,
and filed a complaint with the county magistrate.
Although a warrant was issued,
the constables did not arrest him: the magistrate also took no action.
Just as Wǔ was seething with anger,
Qīláng arrived.
Wǔ said:
"Your words have come true."
And told him what had happened.
Qīláng's face turned grim,
but he said not a word,
and left directly.
Wǔ instructed his trusted servants to patrol and watch for Lín'ér.
Lín'ér returned at night,
was caught by the patrol,
and brought before Wǔ.
Wǔ had him beaten.
Lín'ér insulted Wǔ.
Wǔ's uncle, Héng,
an elderly gentleman,
fearing his nephew's violent rage would lead to disaster,
advised him to hand the matter over to the authorities.
Wǔ agreed,
bound Lín'ér, and took him to court.
But just then, a letter from the Censor's household arrived by post;
the magistrate released Lín'ér,
and handed him over to the Censor's steward.
Lín'ér became even more brazen,
openly spreading rumors among the crowd, falsely accusing the master's wife of having an affair with him.
Wǔ could do nothing,
choked with rage, he felt he would die of anger.
He galloped to the Censor's gate,
and shouted insults up and down.
Relatives and neighbors comforted and persuaded him to return home.
The next night,
suddenly a servant reported:
"Lín'ér has been cut to pieces,
his body thrown in the wilderness."
Wǔ was both shocked and pleased,
feeling some relief.
Soon he heard that the Censor's household had accused him and his uncle,
so he went with his uncle to answer the charges.
The magistrate refused to hear their defense,
and wanted to flog Héng.
Wǔ protested loudly:
"The murder charge is baseless!
As for insulting a gentleman,
I am indeed responsible for that,
it has nothing to do with my uncle."
The magistrate paid no heed.
Wǔ, eyes wide with rage, tried to rush forward,
but the attendants restrained him.
The constables wielding the rods were all lackeys of the gentry,
and Héng was old and frail,
before half the strokes were administered,
he suddenly died.
Seeing Wǔ's uncle near death,
the magistrate pursued the matter no further.
Wǔ wailed and cursed,
but the magistrate acted as if he heard nothing.
So he carried his uncle's body home,
grieving and furious, with no plan of action.
He then thought of seeking Qīláng's advice.
But Qīláng did not come to offer condolences or inquire.
Wǔ thought to himself: I treated Qīláng well,
why does he now act like a stranger?
He also suspected that Qīláng must have killed Lín'ér.
But then he thought again: if so,
why didn't he consult me?
So he sent someone to investigate Qīláng's home,
but when they arrived, the door was locked and all was quiet,
and the neighbors knew nothing of his whereabouts.
One day,
the Censor's younger brother was in the inner office,
discussing matters with the magistrate.
Just as firewood and water were being delivered in the morning,
suddenly a woodcutter appeared before them,
set down his load, drew a sharp blade,
and charged straight at him.
The man panicked,
tried to block the blade with his hand,
but the blade fell and severed his wrist;
with another slash,
his head was finally cut off.
The magistrate was terrified,
and fled.
The woodcutter still looked around wildly.
The clerks quickly closed the yamen gates,
and shouted while wielding their rods.
The woodcutter then slit his own throat and died.
People gathered in confusion to look,
and those who recognized him knew it was Tián Qīláng.
When the magistrate had calmed down,
he came out to examine the scene.
He saw Qīláng lying stiff in a pool of blood,
still gripping the blade in his hand.
Just as he stopped to look closely,
the corpse suddenly leapt up,
and cut off the magistrate's head,
then fell down again.
The yamen officers went to arrest his mother and son,
but they had already fled several days earlier.
When Wǔ heard of Qīláng's death,
he rushed to mourn him with deep sorrow.
Everyone said he had instigated Qīláng.
Wǔ exhausted his wealth to curry favor with those in power,
and only then was he spared.
Qīláng's corpse was left in the wilderness for over thirty days,
with birds and dogs circling and guarding it.
Wǔ retrieved it and gave him a lavish burial.
Qīláng's son wandered to Dēng,
and changed his surname to Tóng.
He enlisted in the army,
and through merit rose to the rank of Tóngzhī General.
When he returned to Liáo,
Wǔ was already over eighty,
and showed him his father's grave.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Not lightly accepting a single coin,
is precisely the one who dares not forget a single meal.
How virtuous was the mother!
As for Qīláng,
his wrath not fully avenged,
even in death he sought redress,
how divine was that?
If Jīng Kē had been like this,
then for a thousand years there would be no lingering regret.
If such men exist,
they can mend the gaps in Heaven's net."
The ways of the world are vast and obscure,
regretting that Qīláng died young.
Alas! "
According to the manuscript of "Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio"
During the Rénxū period,
in Yì County's Xíng Village, there was a woman of the Lǐ family.
Her husband died,
and she was left pregnant.
Suddenly, her belly swelled like a jar,
and then suddenly constricted to the size of a fist.
When she went into labor,
she could not give birth for a full day and night.
Looking at her,
they saw a dragon's head,
which would retract as soon as it was seen.
The family was terrified,
and no one dared approach.
There was an old woman named Wáng,
who burned incense and performed ritual steps,
pressing and chanting incantations.
Before long,
the placenta fell,
and the dragon was no longer seen;
only a few scales remained,
each as large as a cup.
Afterward, a girl was delivered,
her flesh translucent like crystal,
with her internal organs clearly visible.
According to the manuscript of "Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio"
Before Wú Fān rebelled,
he once instructed his generals and soldiers: anyone who could single-handedly capture a tiger
would be generously rewarded with provisions and salary,
and given the title
"Tiger-Catcher General."
Among the soldiers,
one named Bǎozhù
was as agile as a monkey.
In the mansion, a tall tower was being built,
and the beams had just been set.
Bǎozhù climbed along the corner of the tower,
reaching the top in an instant;
he stood on the ridge beam,
walked swiftly back and forth,
three or four times in total;
after finishing,
he leaped down,
landing upright and steady.
The king had a beloved concubine,
who excelled at playing the pipa.
The pipa she played
had tuning pegs made of warm jade,
and when held, it warmed the entire room.
The concubine treasured it,
and unless the king personally ordered,
she would not show it to anyone.
One evening during a banquet,
a guest requested to see this marvel.
The king happened to be feeling lazy,
and promised to show it the next day.
At that time, Bǎozhù was by his side,
and said:
"Without Your Majesty's command,
I can retrieve it."
The king sent someone to rush to the mansion and inform them,
ensuring internal and external precautions were in place,
before dispatching him.
Bǎozhù scaled over a dozen walls,
finally reaching the concubine's courtyard.
He saw the room illuminated by lamplight,
but the door was tightly locked,
and he could not enter.
Under the corridor, a parrot was resting on its perch.
Bǎozhù then imitated the cry of a kitten;
afterward, he mimicked the parrot's call,
shouting urgently:
"A cat is coming!"
The sounds of flapping and struggling grew increasingly frantic.
He heard the concubine say:
"Lǜnú, quickly go check,
the parrot is being killed!"
Bǎozhù hid himself in the shadows.
Soon, a maid came out with a lantern,
and as soon as she left the door,
Bǎozhù slipped inside.
He saw the concubine guarding the pipa on the table,
grabbed it directly, and hurried out.
The concubine cried out in shock,
"Thieves are here!"
and all the guards sprang into action.
Seeing Bǎozhù running with the pipa,
they pursued him but could not catch up,
showering him with arrows like rain.
Bǎozhù leaped onto a tree.
Below the wall, there were originally over thirty large locust trees,
and Bǎozhù moved through the treetops,
like a bird hopping between branches;
when the trees ended, he climbed onto roofs,
and when the roofs ended, he ascended towers;
he dashed across halls and pavilions,
as if he had wings,
and in the blink of an eye, he was nowhere to be found.
The guests were still drinking,
when Bǎozhù, holding the pipa, flew down and landed before the banquet table,
the doors still locked as before,
with no sound from chickens or dogs.
According to the manuscript of "Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio"
In the case of Yú Qī's rebellion,
those implicated and executed
were most numerous in Qīxiá and Láiyáng counties.
One day,
hundreds of captives
were all slaughtered in the military training ground.
Green blood covered the ground,
and white bones reached toward the sky.
The officials, out of compassion,
donated coffins,
and the workshops in Jì City
were emptied of lumber.
Thus, the executed souls of the east
were mostly buried in the southern suburbs.
During the Jiǎyín period,
a scholar from Láiyáng arrived in Jìxià,
and two or three of his relatives and friends were also among those executed,
so he purchased paper offerings
and poured libations in the overgrown ruins.
He then rented lodging from the monks in the lower temple.
The next day,
he went into the city to attend to some matters,
and by dusk, he had not returned.
Suddenly, a young man
came to his room for a visit.
Seeing that the scholar was not there,
he took off his hat, climbed onto the bed,
and lay on his back with his shoes on.
The servant asked who he was,
but he closed his eyes and did not reply.
Soon, the scholar returned,
and in the dim twilight,
he could not see clearly.
He approached the bed and asked.
The young man glared and said:
"I am waiting for your master,
yet you keep pestering me with questions.
Am I some kind of bandit?!"
The scholar laughed and said:
"The master is right here."
The young man immediately got up, put on his hat,
bowed, and sat down,
exchanging polite greetings.
Listening to his voice,
the scholar felt he had heard it before.
He urgently called for a lamp,
and saw it was Zhū Shēng from the same county,
who had also died in the Yú Qī calamity.
Terrified, the scholar backed away.
Zhū pulled him and said:
"You and I were literary friends.
Why are you so cold?
Though I am a ghost,
my thoughts of old friends
remain steadfast in my heart.
Now I have a request to make,
and I hope you will not treat me differently because I am a supernatural being."
The scholar then sat down
and asked what he wanted.
Zhū said:
"Your niece is now widowed and alone.
I wish to take her as my wife.
I have repeatedly sent matchmakers,
but she always refuses, citing the lack of an elder's permission.
I hope you will not begrudge your kind words on my behalf."
Earlier,
the scholar had a niece
who lost her mother early
and was raised by the scholar.
At fifteen, she returned to her own family.
When captured and brought to Jǐnán,
she heard that her father had been executed,
and died of shock and grief.
The scholar said:
"She has her own father.
Why come to me?"
Zhū said:
"His father has taken the coffin away for burial as a nephew,
and is not here now."
He asked:
"Whom has your niece been relying on?"
She replied:
"She has been living with an old neighbor woman."
Shēng was concerned that a living person could not act as a ghostly matchmaker.
Zhū said:
"If you would be so kind as to give your golden promise,
I must trouble your jade steps to come with me."
Then he stood up and grasped Shēng's hand.
Shēng firmly declined,
asking:
"Where are we going?"
Zhū said:
"Just come along!"
Reluctantly, Shēng followed him.
After walking north for about a li,
they came upon a large village,
with roughly several hundred households.
They arrived at a mansion,
where Zhū knocked on the gate.
An old woman immediately came out.
She opened both doors wide,
and asked Zhū:
"What is it?"
He said:
"Please inform the young lady that her maternal uncle has arrived."
The old woman turned back inside,
and after a moment came out again,
inviting Shēng to enter.
Looking at Zhū, she said:
"Our two-room thatched cottage is too cramped,
so I must trouble you, young master, to wait outside the gate for a little while."
Shēng followed her inside.
He saw a half-acre of desolate courtyard,
with two small rooms arranged in a row.
His niece met him at the door, sobbing,
and Shēng also wept.
The lamplight in the room was faintly flickering.
The girl's appearance was as elegant and pure as when she was alive.
Gazing intently, her eyes brimming with tears,
she asked all about her maternal aunt and paternal aunt.
Shēng said:
"They are all well,
but my wife has passed away."
The girl sobbed again and said:
"Since childhood, I received the care and upbringing from my uncle and aunt,
yet I have not repaid them even an inch of kindness.
I never thought I would be buried in a ditch first,
which is truly a source of deep regret.
Last year,
the eldest brother from Uncle's family moved Father away,
leaving me here without a single thought;
hundreds of li away,
I am as lonely and helpless as an autumn swallow.
Uncle did not consider this sunken soul as something to be discarded,
and moreover, you bestowed gold and silk upon me,
which I have already received."
Shēng then told her what Zhū had said.
The girl lowered her head and remained silent.
The old woman said:
"Young Master Zhū previously entrusted Old Woman Yáng to come three or five times.
I thought it was an excellent match;
but the young lady was unwilling to be hasty about it herself.
Now that her uncle is here to decide the matter,
she will finally be content with this arrangement."
While they were speaking,
a young lady of about seventeen or eighteen,
followed by a maidservant,
suddenly slipped in;
catching sight of Shēng,
she turned around to flee.
The niece tugged at her sleeve and said:
"There's no need for that!
This is my maternal uncle,
not an outsider."
Shēng bowed to her.
The young lady also performed a curtsy.
The niece said:
"Jiǔniáng,
is a Gōngsūn from Qīxiá.
Her father was from an old family,
but now he's also a 'poor Persian,'
disheartened and discontent.
She often visits with me."
The scholar glanced at her,
her smile curved like the autumn moon,
her shy blush like morning clouds,
truly a celestial being.
He said:
"No wonder she's from a great house;
how could a humble cottage dweller be so graceful and lovely?"
The niece laughed and said:
"Moreover, she is a learned lady,
highly skilled in poetry and lyrics.
I received some instruction from her yesterday."
Jiǔniáng smiled slightly and said:
"This little maid senselessly ruins people,
making her uncle look down on me."
The niece laughed again and said:
"Uncle's broken string has not been restrung;
what about this young lady,
would she bring you much joy?"
Jiǔniáng laughed and ran out,
saying:
"This maid is acting crazy!"
And so she left.
Though the words were nearly jest,
the scholar was deeply fond of her.
The niece seemed to notice slightly,
and said:
"Jiǔniáng's talent and beauty are unmatched;
if uncle does not suspect her due to humble origins,
I shall ask her mother."
The scholar was greatly pleased.
Yet he worried that human and ghost could hardly match.
The woman said:
"No harm,
she and you have a predestined bond."
The scholar then went out.
The woman saw him off,
saying:
"In five days,
when the moon is bright and people are quiet,
I shall send someone to fetch you."
The scholar reached outside the door,
but did not see Zhū.
Lifting his head to gaze west,
the moon chariot showed half its rim,
in the dusk he could still recognize the old path.
He saw a mansion to the south,
with Zhū sitting on the stone by the gate.
He rose to greet him, saying:
"I have been waiting long;
please honor my humble home with a visit."
Then hand in hand they entered,
and Zhū earnestly expressed his thanks.
He brought out a golden goblet and a hundred pearls,
saying:
"I have nothing else of value,
let these serve in place of a betrothal gift."
Then he said:
"We have coarse wine at home,
but things from the dark chamber
are insufficient to entertain a distinguished guest,
what can be done!"
The scholar declined and withdrew.
Zhū accompanied him halfway,
then they parted.
The scholar returned,
and the monk and servants gathered to ask.
He concealed the truth, saying:
"Those who speak of ghosts
are mistaken.
I merely went to drink with a friend."
Five days later,
indeed he saw Zhū come,
straightening his shoes and swinging his fan,
looking very pleased and comfortable.
As soon as he reached the courtyard,
he bowed upon seeing the dust.
After a moment,
he said with a smile:
"Your fine wedding is now arranged,
the celebration is tonight,
please trouble yourself to come."
The scholar said:
"As there was no reply,
I have not yet sent betrothal gifts;
how can the ceremony be so sudden?"
Zhū said:
"I have already delivered them on your behalf."
The scholar felt deeply grateful,
and followed him away.
They went straight to the bedroom,
where the niece greeted him with a smile, dressed in splendid attire.
The scholar asked:
"When did you marry?"
The woman said:
"Three days ago."
The scholar then took out the pearls he had received,
to assist the niece with her trousseau.
The woman declined three times before accepting,
and said to the scholar:
"I conveyed your intentions to Madame Gōngsūn,
and she was greatly delighted.
But she said that being old and with no other kin,
she did not wish Jiǔniáng to marry far away,
hoping that you would go to her home tonight to be the live-in son-in-law.
Her family has no men,
so you may go with the young man."
Zhū then led him away.
As they neared the end of the village,
a mansion gate opened,
and the two ascended to the hall.
Soon it was announced:
"The old madame has arrived."
Two maids
supported the old woman up the steps.
The scholar wished to bow in greeting,
but the madame said:
"I am old and decrepit,
unable to perform formalities;
let us dispense with ceremony."
Then she directed the maids,
to serve wine for a grand feast.
Zhū then called for his family,
to bring out separate dishes,
arranged before the scholar;
also setting out another pot,
to toast the guest.
The dishes served at the banquet
were no different from those in the human world.
However, the host raised his own cup,
but did not urge others to drink.
After the feast ended,
Zhū returned home.
The maids led the scholar away,
into a chamber,
where Jiǔniáng awaited by the bright candles.
Meeting with shared affection,
they enjoyed utmost intimacy and joy.
Earlier,
Jiǔniáng and her mother
had been escorted to the capital.
Upon reaching the commandery,
the mother could not endure the hardship and died,
and Jiǔniáng also took her own life.
On the pillow, recalling past events,
she sobbed and could not sleep.
Then she improvised two quatrains:
"Gone to dust are the silken robes of yesteryear,
Vainly blaming past lives for this karmic fruit.
Ten years of dew-cold maple woods beneath the moon,
Tonight first meeting spring in this painted chamber."
"Wind and rain around the lone grave where white poplars grow,
Who would think clouds still form at the sunny terrace?
Suddenly opening the inlaid golden box to look,
Bloodstains still dye the old silk skirt."
As dawn approached,
she urged him:
"You should leave now,
do not startle the servants."
From then on, he came by day and left by night,
deeply infatuated and enchanted.
One evening,
he asked Jiǔniáng:
"What is the name of this village?"
She said:
"Láixiá Lǐ.
Most here are new ghosts from two places,
hence the name."
Hearing this, the scholar sighed.
The woman said sorrowfully:
"A tender soul a thousand miles away,
drifting rootlessly like duckweed;
mother and child lonely and scattered,
speaking of it brings grief.
I beg you, remember one night's kindness,
gather my bones and bury them by my mother's grave,
so I may have a place to rest for a hundred years,
and I shall not perish even in death."
The scholar promised.
The woman said:
"The paths of human and ghost are different;
you should not linger long."
Then she gave the scholar a pair of silk stockings,
and urged him to leave with tearful waves.
The scholar left sorrowfully,
anguished as if bereaved,
his heart aching, unwilling to return.
So he went and knocked on the Zhū family's door.
Zhū came out barefoot to greet him;
the niece also rose,
her cloud-like hair disheveled,
startled, she came to inquire.
The scholar remained despondent for a while,
then recounted Jiǔniáng's words.
The woman said:
"Even if my aunt does not speak of it,
I have also been thinking of it day and night.
This is not the world of the living,
it is truly not suitable to stay here long."
Thus they faced each other with tears,
and Shēng also parted with tears in his eyes.
He knocked on the door of his lodging and returned to sleep,
tossing and turning until dawn.
He wanted to find Jiǔniáng's grave,
but had forgotten to ask for a marker.
When night fell he went again,
but there were thousands of graves piled upon each other,
and he lost his way among the village paths,
returning with sighs of regret.
Unfolding the silk stockings to look at them,
they broke into pieces in the wind,
rotted like ashes,
so he packed his belongings and headed east to return home.
For half a year he could not free himself from this,
and again went to Jìmén,
hoping to encounter something.
When he reached the southern outskirts,
the sun was already setting,
so he rested his carriage under a tree in the courtyard,
and hurried to the burial grounds.
But all he saw were graves stretching endlessly,
his eyes bewildered by overgrown brambles;
will-o'-the-wisps and foxes crying,
terrifying to the heart and eyes.
Shocked and grieving, he returned to his lodging.
Disheartened, he wandered about,
then turned his carriage eastward.
After traveling about a li,
he saw from afar a young woman walking alone among the graves,
her demeanor and expression
strangely resembled Jiǔniáng.
He whipped his horse to approach and look,
and it was indeed Jiǔniáng.
Dismounting to speak to her,
the woman actually walked away,
as if she did not recognize him;
when he approached her again,
her expression turned angry,
and she raised her sleeve to shield herself.
Suddenly he called out
"Jiǔniáng",
and she vanished like smoke.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"The fragrant grass sank with Qu Yuan, his blood filling his breast;
the jade pendants of Shēn Bǎo, tears soaking the sand and mud:
in ancient times there were filial sons and loyal ministers
who, even unto death, were not understood by their rulers or fathers.
Could it be that Gōngsūn Jiǔniáng, because the entrustment of her bones was not fulfilled,
harbored unrelenting resentment in her heart?
What is within the breast
cannot be scooped out to show others—
how unjust!"
Based on the manuscript version of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
During the Xuāndé reign,
the palace was fond of cricket-fighting games,
and levied them annually from the common people.
This creature was originally not a product of the western regions;
there was a magistrate of Huàyīn who wanted to curry favor with his superior,
and presented one cricket,
which was tested in fighting and proved talented,
so he was ordered to regularly supply them.
The magistrate ordered the village heads to provide them.
Idle youths in the market
would get good ones and raise them in cages,
driving up their price,
hoarding them as rare goods.
Cunning local clerks
used this to impose levies on the people,
and each time a cricket was demanded,
it would bankrupt several families.
In the county there was a man named Chéng,
who studied for the imperial examinations
but had long not succeeded.
Being pedantic and slow of speech,
he was reported by a cunning clerk to serve as village head,
and despite all attempts he could not escape the duty.
Within a year,
his meager assets were exhausted.
It happened that crickets were being levied,
and Chéng did not dare collect from households,
nor had anything to compensate with,
so he worried himself to death.
His wife said:
"What good is dying?
Better to search for them yourself,
in hopes of a one-in-ten-thousand chance of finding one."
Chéng agreed.
He went out early and returned late,
carrying bamboo tubes and copper-wire cages,
probing among broken walls and thick grass, turning over stones and digging holes,
no method left untried,
but to no avail;
even if he caught two or three,
they were too weak and did not meet the standards.
The magistrate set strict deadlines and imposed punishments;
after more than ten days,
Chéng had received a hundred strokes,
pus and blood flowing between his legs,
and he could not even go to catch crickets anymore.
Tossing and turning by his bedside,
he only thought of ending his own life.
At that time, a hunchbacked shamaness came to the village,
who could divine through spirits.
Chéng’s wife gathered money and went to ask her.
She saw young girls and old women,
filling the doorway.
Entering the shamaness’s dwelling,
there was a secluded room with a hanging curtain,
and outside the curtain an incense table was set up.
Those seeking answers would light incense in the tripod,
and bow twice.
The shamaness, standing to the side, gazed into the air and prayed on their behalf,
her lips opening and closing,
though no one knew what words she spoke.
Everyone stood respectfully listening.
After a short while,
a piece of paper was tossed out from behind the curtain,
immediately stating what was on the person’s mind,
without the slightest error.
Chéng’s wife placed money on the table,
lit incense and bowed as the previous person had done.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
the curtain moved,
and a slip of paper was thrown down.
Picking it up to look,
it was not writing but a drawing: in the center was painted a hall and pavilion,
resembling a temple;
behind a small hill,
strange rocks lay scattered,
with thorny bushes growing thickly,
and a Qīngmátóu cricket crouching there;
beside it was a toad,
as if about to leap and dance.
Unfolding and examining it, she could not understand it.
But seeing the cricket,
it secretly matched her thoughts.
She folded it and kept it,
returning home to show Chéng.
Chéng turned it over in his mind,
thinking, “Could this be showing me where to hunt for crickets?”
Looking closely at the scene,
it truly resembled the great Buddha Pavilion east of the village.
So he forced himself up, leaning on a cane,
and holding the picture, went to the back of the temple.
There was an ancient tomb mound rising lushly;
following the mound, he walked on,
and saw crouching rocks layered like scales,
exactly like the painting.
Then among the weeds and brambles,
he listened carefully and walked slowly,
as if searching for a needle or a mustard seed;
but his eyes, mind, and hearing were all exhausted,
with absolutely no trace or sound.
While he was still searching intently,
a scabby-headed toad suddenly leaped away.
Chéng was even more startled,
and hurriedly chased after it.
The toad went into the grass.
Following its trail and parting the grass to search,
he saw a cricket crouching at the root of a thorn bush;
he quickly pounced on it,
but it went into a stone hole.
Prodding with a sharp blade of grass,
it did not come out;
pouring water into the hole with a tube,
it finally emerged.
Its appearance was extremely handsome and robust,
and he chased and caught it.
Examining it closely,
it had a large body and long tail,
a green neck and golden wings.
Overjoyed, he caged it and returned home,
the whole family celebrating,
as if it were a priceless jade worth many cities.
He put soil in a pot and raised it,
feeding it crab meat and chestnut kernels,
taking the utmost care and affection,
keeping it until the deadline,
to fulfill the official demand.
Chéng had a son, nine years old,
who peeked when his father was not there,
secretly opened the pot,
and the cricket leaped straight out,
too quick to catch;
by the time he caught it in his hand,
its leg was broken and its belly split,
and it soon died.
The boy was frightened,
and cried as he told his mother.
When the mother heard this,
her face turned ashen,
and she scolded loudly:
“You little troublemaker!
Your time of death has come!
When your father returns,
he’ll settle accounts with you!”
The boy went out weeping.
Not long after, Chéng returned,
and hearing his wife’s words,
felt as if doused with ice and snow.
Angrily searching for his son,
he found the boy had vanished without a trace.
Later, finding his body in a well,
he turned his anger into grief,
beating his chest and wailing, nearly dying of grief.
Husband and wife faced the corner,
the thatched hut without smoke from cooking,
sitting silently opposite each other,
with nothing left to live for.
As dusk approached,
they took the boy for a rough burial.
Approaching to touch him,
they felt faint breath.
Joyfully, they placed him on the bed,
and by midnight he revived.
The couple’s hearts were slightly comforted.
But the cricket cage was empty,
and looking at it made them choke with despair,
nor did they dare to pursue the matter with their son further.
From dusk until dawn,
their eyes did not close.
As the sun rose in the east,
they lay stiffly, filled with long sorrow.
Suddenly, they heard a cricket chirping outside the door,
startled, they got up to look,
and the cricket seemed to still be there.
Joyfully, they tried to catch it,
but with one chirp it leaped away,
moving quickly.
Covering it with a hand,
it felt as if there were nothing there;
as soon as the hand was lifted,
it leaped away swiftly again.
They hurriedly chased it.
Turning past a corner of the wall,
they lost track of where it went.
Pacing back and forth, looking all around,
they saw a cricket crouching on the wall.
Examining it carefully,
it was short and small,
blackish-red in color,
clearly not the previous one.
Chéng, considering it small,
thought it inferior.
Only wandering and looking around,
searching for the one they had chased.
The small insect on the wall
suddenly leaped down onto his lapel and sleeve;
looking at it,
its shape was like a mole cricket,
with plum-blossom patterned wings,
a square head and long legs,
seeming of good quality.
Joyfully, he kept it.
Intending to present it at the official hall,
he was anxious, fearing it might not meet expectations,
and thought to test it in a fight to see.
In the village, there was a young man fond of stirring things up,
who had tamed and raised a cricket,
personally naming it
“Crab-Shell Green,”
and daily pitted it against others’ crickets,
never losing.
He wanted to keep it for profit,
and set a high price for it,
but there were no buyers.
He went straight to Chéng’s home to visit him.
Seeing what Chéng had kept,
he covered his mouth and chuckled.
Then he brought out his own cricket,
placing it in the comparison cage.
Chéng looked at it,
large and imposing,
and felt even more ashamed,
not daring to match them.
The young man insisted strongly.
But thinking that keeping an inferior creature was ultimately useless,
it would be better to risk it for a laugh.
So together they placed them in the fighting pot.
The small cricket crouched motionless,
stupid as a wooden chicken.
The young man laughed again.
Trying with a pig’s bristle,
to tease the cricket’s antennae,
it still did not move.
The young man laughed once more.
After repeated teasing,
the cricket suddenly became enraged,
charging straight ahead,
and they began leaping and attacking each other,
stirring vigorously, making sounds.
Soon, they saw the small cricket leap up,
spreading its tail and extending its antennae,
and bite straight at the other’s neck.
The young man was greatly alarmed,
and separated them to stop the fight.
The cricket raised itself proudly, chirking triumphantly,
as if reporting to its owner.
Chéng was overjoyed,
and as they were admiring it together,
a chicken glanced over and came,
It darted forward to peck.
Chéng stood dumbfounded and cried out in alarm.
Fortunately, the peck missed its mark,
and the cricket leaped away a foot or more.
The rooster charged ahead,
chasing it closely,
and the cricket was already under its claws.
Chéng, in his panic, did not know how to save it,
stamping his feet and turning pale.
Suddenly he saw the rooster stretching its neck and flapping about;
looking closer,
he saw the cricket perched on the rooster’s comb,
biting down hard and not letting go.
Chéng was even more astonished and delighted.
He picked it up and placed it in the cage.
The next day he presented it to the magistrate.
When the magistrate saw how small it was,
he angrily scolded Chéng.
Chéng recounted its extraordinary abilities,
but the magistrate did not believe him.
He tried pitting it against other crickets,
and all were defeated;
he then tried it with a rooster,
and indeed it was as Chéng had said.
Thereupon he rewarded Chéng.
He presented it to the provincial governor.
The governor was greatly pleased,
and sent it to the emperor in a golden cage,
with a detailed report of its abilities.
Once it entered the palace,
all the tributes from across the land—butterflies, mantises, oily lìtà, green-threaded foreheads…
every kind of unusual specimen—
were tested against it,
and none could surpass it.
Whenever it heard the sound of zithers and lutes,
it would dance in time with the rhythm.
This made it even more remarkable.
The emperor was greatly delighted,
and issued an edict bestowing fine horses and silk robes upon the governor.
The governor did not forget the source of this favor;
not long after,
the magistrate was
“Outstanding”
in his report.
The magistrate was pleased,
and exempted Chéng from his duties.
He also instructed the education commissioner
to admit Chéng into the county school.
From then on, Chéng became famous for his skill in raising crickets,
and repeatedly received special favor from the governor.
Within a few years,
he owned a hundred qǐng of farmland,
buildings with tens of thousands of rafters,
and hundreds of cattle and sheep.
Whenever he went out,
his furs and horses surpassed those of noble families.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
“When the Son of Heaven occasionally uses an object,
he may well forget about it afterward;
yet those who carry out his orders treat it as a fixed rule.
Add to this the greed of officials and the cruelty of clerks,
and the people daily pawn their wives and sell their children,
with no end in sight.
Thus every single step of the Son of Heaven
is tied to the lives of the people,
and cannot be neglected.
Only this son of the Chéng family became poor because of the cricket,
and rich because of the cricket,
flaunting his furs and horses.
When he was a village head and suffered beatings and reprimands,
could he have imagined reaching this point?
Heaven wished to reward the honest and kind,
and thus made the governor and magistrate
also receive the cricket’s beneficent shade.
I have heard: when one person attains immortality,
even his chickens and dogs ascend to heaven.
How true it is!”
Based on the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In the late Míng dynasty,
locusts appeared between Qīngzhōu and Yǎnzhōu,
gradually gathering in Yíxiàn.
The magistrate of Yí was worried about this.
Retiring to rest in his office,
he dreamed a scholar came to visit him,
wearing a tall hat and green robes,
with a tall and imposing appearance.
He claimed to have a strategy to deal with the locusts.
When questioned,
he replied:
“Tomorrow on the road to the southwest,
there will be a woman riding a large-bellied female donkey—
she is the Locust Goddess.
Beg her for mercy,
and you may be spared.”
The magistrate found this strange,
prepared offerings, and went south of the city.
Waiting for a long time,
indeed there was a woman with a high chignon and a brown cloak,
alone leading an old gray donkey,
slowly trudging northward.
He immediately lit incense,
held up a cup of wine,
and bowed to greet her by the roadside,
grabbing the donkey to prevent it from leaving.
The woman asked:
“What does the official intend to do?”
The magistrate then pleaded earnestly:
“This humble district
hopes for your compassion to escape the locusts’ mouths.”
The woman said:
“Hateful Scholar Willow for his loose tongue,
revealing my secret plan!
He shall bear the consequences himself,
and I will not harm the crops.”
She then drank three cups,
and vanished in an instant.
Later, when the locusts came,
they flew so thickly they blotted out the sun,
yet they did not land on the grain fields,
but gathered only on willow trees,
stripping them bare wherever they passed.
Only then did he realize the scholar was the Willow Spirit.
Some say:
“This was due to the magistrate’s concern for the people moving the gods.”
Truly so!
Based on the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In the twenty-first year of the Kāngxī reign,
there was a severe drought,
lasting from spring to summer,
leaving the land barren without a blade of green grass.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month, a light rain fell,
and only then did some begin planting millet.
On the eighteenth day, a heavy rain thoroughly soaked the ground,
and they planted beans.
One day,
in Shímén Village, an old man
saw two oxen fighting on a mountain in the evening,
and said to the villagers:
“A great flood is coming!”
He then took his family and moved away.
The villagers all laughed at him.
Not long after,
rain poured down violently,
continuing unabated through the night,
until the flatlands were several feet deep in water,
and all the houses were submerged.
One farmer abandoned his two children,
and with his wife helped his elderly mother flee to high ground.
Looking down at the village,
it had already become a vast lake,
and he no longer thought of his children.
When the water receded and he returned home,
he saw the entire village had turned into ruins and graves.
Entering his own gate to look,
only one house remained,
with his two children sitting together on the bed,
playing and laughing, unharmed.
All said this was the reward for the couple’s filial piety.
This happened on the twenty-second day of the sixth month.
In the thirty-fourth year of the Kāngxī reign,
there was an earthquake in Píngyáng,
killing seventy or eighty percent of the people.
The city walls and buildings were completely reduced to ruins;
only one house remained,
which belonged to a certain filial son.
In the vast and boundless calamity,
only the filial descendants were unharmed.
Who says Heaven has no sense of right and wrong?
Based on the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A certain Mister Jiǎ, a student of my teacher Mr. Sūn Jǐngxià, told this story: In his hometown, there was a certain Mister Jiǎ.
During the chaos of the roving bandits,
he was killed,
his head falling onto his chest.
After the bandits retreated,
his family found the corpse
and were about to carry it away for burial.
Then they heard a faint, thread-like breath;
upon closer inspection,
they saw that a strip of flesh, as thick as a finger, still connected his throat.
So they supported his head
and carried him home.
After a full day and night, he began to moan.
They fed him small amounts of food and drink with a spoon and chopsticks,
and after half a year, he actually recovered.
More than ten years later,
he was chatting with two or three others.
Someone told a joke that made everyone laugh,
and the whole group roared with laughter.
Jiǎ also clapped his hands.
But as he bent forward and leaned back,
the old knife wound suddenly split open,
his head fell off, and blood flowed.
Everyone looked at him;
he had already stopped breathing.
His father sued those who had laughed.
The group pooled money to bribe him,
and also buried Jiǎ,
before the matter was resolved.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"To laugh so hard that one's head falls off—
this is the greatest laugh of all time.
His neck was connected by a mere thread, yet he did not die,
only to become a 'laughing lawsuit' ten years later.
Could it be that those two or three neighbors owed him a debt from a past life?"
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Lord Zhāng Huádōng of Zōupíng
was ordered by imperial decree to offer sacrifices at the Southern Peak.
His journey took him through the region between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
and he planned to stay at a relay station for the night.
His advance guard reported:
"There are strange occurrences at the station;
staying there will surely lead to trouble."
Zhāng did not listen.
At midnight,
he sat wearing his official cap and holding his sword.
Suddenly, he heard footsteps entering,
and saw an old man with graying hair,
wearing a black gauze cap and a black belt.
Finding this strange, Zhāng questioned him.
The old man bowed and said:
"I am the treasury official.
I have been in charge of the treasury for Your Excellency for some time.
Fortunately, your ceremonial axe has arrived from afar,
and I, your humble official, can now be relieved of this heavy burden."
Zhāng asked:
"How much is stored in the treasury?"
The old man replied,
"Twenty-three thousand five hundred taels of gold."
Lord Zhāng, concerned that carrying so much gold would be cumbersome,
arranged to check the inventory upon his return.
The old man assented and withdrew.
When Zhāng reached the southern regions,
he received quite generous gifts.
Upon his return,
he again stayed at the relay station,
and the old man came out to greet him once more.
When asked about the treasury goods,
he said:
"They have already been allocated as military provisions for Liáodōng."
Zhāng was deeply surprised by the contradiction between the earlier and later statements.
The old man said:
"In the human world, one's official salary and destiny
are all predetermined in amount;
not a single coin can be added or subtracted.
Your Excellency, on this journey,
you have already received the amount you were destined to receive.
What more do you seek?"
Having said this,
he departed.
Zhāng then calculated what he had gained,
and it exactly matched the amount the old man had stated for the treasury.
Only then did he sigh, realizing that one's gains and sustenance are predetermined,
and cannot be recklessly sought.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Outside Dū County, there was a cave
so deep it was unfathomable,
traditionally said to be the office of Yánluó, the King of the Underworld.
All the instruments of punishment inside
were borrowed from the human world.
When shackles and fetters rotted and decayed,
they were thrown out at the cave entrance.
The county magistrate would then replace them with new ones,
which would disappear by the next day.
The expenses for supplying these items
were recorded in the official budget.
During the Ming Dynasty, there was a Censor Huà Gōng
who was on an inspection tour and arrived at Dū.
Hearing this story,
he did not believe it
and wanted to enter the cave to resolve his doubts.
People all said it was not possible.
Lord Huà did not listen.
Carrying a candle, he entered,
followed by two attendants.
After going deep inside for about a *li*,
the candle suddenly went out.
Looking around,
he saw steps and pathways, broad and bright,
with over ten large halls,
where dignified officials sat in rows,
their robes and tablets imposing; only the seat at the eastern end was empty.
The dignified officials, seeing Lord Huà arrive,
descended the steps to welcome him,
and asked with a smile:
"Have you arrived?
Have you been well since we parted?"
Lord Huà asked:
"What place is this?"
The dignified official said:
"This is the underworld."
Lord Huà, startled, asked to leave.
The dignified official pointed to the empty seat and said:
"This is your seat.
How can you return now?"
Lord Huà grew even more frightened
and earnestly begged for leniency.
The dignified official said,
"How can one escape what is predestined!"
He then checked a volume and showed it to Lord Huà.
It was annotated as follows:
"On such-and-such month and day,
so-and-so will return to the underworld in his physical body."
After reading it,
Lord Huà trembled as if drenched in ice water.
Thinking of his elderly mother and young children,
he shed tears of sorrow.
Suddenly, a golden-armored deity
arrived holding a yellow silk document.
After the group bowed, danced, and finished reading it,
they congratulated Lord Huà, saying:
"You have a chance to return to the world of the living."
Lord Huà happily asked for details.
They said:
"We have just received an imperial decree
granting a great amnesty to the underworld.
We can make an exception for you,
based on the original precedent."
They then showed Lord Huà the way out.
After walking a few paces,
it became pitch black like lacquer,
and he could not see the path.
Lord Huà was in great distress.
Suddenly, a divine general
strode in majestically.
He had a red face and a long beard,
and his radiance shone for several feet.
Lord Huà approached, bowed, and pleaded with him.
The divine general said:
"Reciting Buddhist scriptures can get you out."
Having said this, he left.
Lord Huà thought to himself that he could not remember many sutras or mantras,
but he had studied the *Diamond Sutra* quite a bit.
So he clasped his hands and began to recite it.
Immediately, he felt a thread of light
illuminating the path ahead.
If he happened to forget a line,
the area before him would instantly turn dark.
After concentrating for a while,
he would recite again, and the light would return.
Thus, he was finally able to get out.
As for his two attendants,
there was no news of them.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
In Yíshuǐ, during heavy rain,
a dragon suddenly fell from the sky.
Both of its eyes were missing,
and it was barely breathing.
The county magistrate used eighty mats to cover it,
but they could not cover its entire body.
He also arranged a野外祭 for it.
It still thrashed about, striking the ground with its tail,
making a *bāng* sound.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Wàn Fú,
courtesy name Zǐxiáng,
was from Bóxīng.
In his youth, he studied Confucian classics.
His family was moderately well-off but his fortune was exceptionally poor;
by the time he was over twenty years old,
he still had not even passed the lowest level of the imperial examinations.
In his hometown, there was a corrupt custom
where wealthy households were often conscripted for corvée labor,
and even the most honest and generous families could be ruined by it.
Wàn happened to be conscripted for such service,
and in fear, he fled
to Jǐnán,
where he rented a room at an inn.
One night, a woman rushed into his room;
her appearance was quite beautiful.
Wàn was delighted and had an intimate relationship with her,
then asked for her name.
The woman said:
"I am actually a fox,
but I will not bring any harm upon you."
Wàn was pleased and did not doubt her.
The woman instructed him not to share her with guests,
and from then on, she came daily,
sleeping with him.
All daily necessities
were provided by the fox.
Not long after,
two or three acquaintances
came to visit,
often staying for two nights without leaving.
Wàn was annoyed by this
but could not bear to refuse them;
having no other choice,
he told the guests the truth.
The guests wished to catch a glimpse of the immortal's appearance.
Wàn relayed this to the fox.
The fox said to the guests:
"Why do you want to see me?
I am just like any human."
They could hear her voice,
clear and melodious, as if she were right before them,
but when they looked around, she was nowhere to be seen.
Among the guests was one named Sūn Déyán,
who was skilled at jesting and banter.
He insisted on seeing her,
saying:
"Having heard your lovely voice,
my soul is already captivated;
why be so stingy with your beauty,
leaving us to pine for you only through your voice?"
The fox laughed and said:
"How virtuous you are, Master Sūn!
Do you wish to paint a portrait of your great-great-grandmother for her pleasure?"
All the guests laughed.
The fox said:
"Since I am a fox,
allow me to tell you a fox tale.
Would you like to hear it?"
Everyone assented.
The fox said:
"Once, in a certain village inn,
there were many foxes,
and they often haunted the guests.
The guests learned of this
and warned each other not to stay there.
After half a year,
the inn became deserted.
The innkeeper was deeply worried
and avoided mentioning foxes altogether.
Suddenly, a traveler from afar arrived,
claiming to be from a foreign land,
and sought lodging at the inn.
The innkeeper was overjoyed.
Just as he invited the traveler inside,
a passerby secretly warned him:
'This house has foxes.'
The traveler was frightened
and told the innkeeper
he wanted to move elsewhere.
The innkeeper vehemently denied it as nonsense,
so the traveler stayed.
As soon as he lay down in his room,
he saw a swarm of mice scurrying out from under the bed.
The traveler was terrified,
dashed out,
and cried out urgently:
'There are foxes!'
The innkeeper asked in alarm.
The traveler complained:
'Foxes have made their nest here;
why did you deceive me by saying there were none?'
The innkeeper asked again:
'What did you see?'
The traveler said:
'What I saw just now,
tiny and insignificant,
if not fox cubs,
must certainly be fox grandchildren!'"
After finishing the tale,
the guests burst into laughter.
Sūn said:
"Since you refuse to grant us an audience,
we should stay overnight
and not leave,
blocking your romantic encounters."
The fox laughed and said:
"Staying overnight is fine;
but if there are any minor offenses,
I hope you won't hold grudges."
The guests, fearing she might play pranks,
all dispersed.
However, they would come every few days,
seeking the fox's laughter and banter.
The fox was extremely witty;
with every remark,
One day,
Wàn set out wine for a grand party.
Wàn sat in the host’s seat,
Sūn and two other guests sat to his left and right,
and a couch was placed above them for the fox.
The fox declined to drink,
so everyone asked her to sit and talk,
and she agreed.
After several rounds of wine,
the guests began to play a dice game called “the vine of melons.”
When one guest rolled the melon face,
he was supposed to drink,
but he playfully passed the cup to the upper seat, saying:
“Lady Fox is too clear-headed;
please lend me a cup.”
The fox smiled and said:
“I truly do not drink,
but I would like to tell a story
to help you gentlemen drink.”
Sūn covered his ears, unwilling to listen.
The guests all said:
“Anyone who insults others should be fined.”
The fox smiled and said:
“What if I insult a fox?”
Everyone said:
“That’s fine.”
So they all leaned in to listen.
The fox said:
“Once there was a high minister
who went as an envoy to the Red-Haired Country.
He wore a fox-fur hat
when he met the king.
The king saw it and was surprised,
asking:
‘What kind of fur is this, so warm and thick?’
The minister replied that it was fox.
The king said:
‘I have never heard of this creature before.
How is the character for “fox” written?’
The envoy wrote in the air and reported:
‘On the right is a big melon,
on the left is a small dog.’”
The host and guests burst into laughter again.
The two guests
were brothers of the Chén family,
one named Suǒjiàn,
the other named Suǒwén.
Seeing Sūn in great embarrassment,
they said:
“Where is the male fox,
letting the female run wild like this?”
The fox said:
“Just now, a story
was not yet finished
when it was interrupted by a pack of barks.
Let me finish it.
The king saw the envoy riding a mule
and was very surprised.
The envoy told him:
‘This is born from a horse.’
The king was even more astonished.
The envoy said:
‘In China, horses give birth to mules,
and mules give birth to colts.’
The king asked in detail how this happened.
The envoy said:
‘Horses giving birth to mules
is “what I have seen”;
mules giving birth to colts
is “what I have heard.”’”
Everyone at the table laughed again.
Knowing they were no match for her,
they agreed:
whoever started a joke from then on
would be fined to host the next gathering.
After a while,
when they were drunk,
Sūn playfully said to Wàn:
“I have a couplet for you to complete.”
Wàn said:
“What is it?”
Sūn said:
“A courtesan goes out to visit her lover,
coming with ‘ten thousand blessings,’
leaving with ‘ten thousand blessings.’”
Everyone at the table thought hard but could not come up with a matching line.
The fox smiled and said:
“I have it.”
Everyone listened.
She said:
“The Dragon King issues an edict seeking honest advice,
the turtle ‘gets to speak,’
the tortoise ‘gets to speak.’”
Everyone at the four tables roared with laughter.
Sūn was furious and said:
“We just made a pact—
why did you break it again?”
The fox smiled and said:
“The fault is indeed mine;
but without this,
the couplet would not be perfect.
Tomorrow I will host a feast
to redeem my offense.”
They laughed and ended the party.
The fox’s wit and humor
were too numerous to recount.
After a few months,
she returned with Wàn.
When they reached the border of Bóxīng,
she said to Wàn:
“I have a distant relative here,
and our contact has been cut off for a long time.
I must pay a visit.
It is getting dark;
let us stay here together tonight
and leave at dawn.”
Wàn asked where it was,
and she pointed, saying:
“Not far.”
Wàn suspected there had never been a village there before,
but he followed her anyway.
After about two lǐ,
they indeed saw a manor
he had never visited before.
The fox went to knock on the gate,
and an old servant came to answer.
Inside, there were layered gates and pavilions,
just like a noble family’s estate.
Soon the hosts appeared—
an old man and an old woman—
who bowed to Wàn and invited him to sit.
A lavish feast was laid out,
and they treated Wàn as a relative by marriage.
They stayed the night there.
The next morning, the fox said to Wàn:
“If I suddenly return with you,
it might shock people.
You should go first,
and I will follow later.”
Wàn followed her advice,
arriving first
and informing his family in advance.
Not long after,
the fox arrived.
She talked and laughed with Wàn,
and everyone could hear her,
but no one could see her.
A year later,
Wàn went again to Jì,
and the fox went with him.
Suddenly, several people arrived,
and the fox went to talk with them,
exchanging warm greetings.
Then she said to Wàn:
“I am originally from Shǎnzhōng,
and because of a past connection with you,
I have followed you for this long.
Now my brothers have come,
and I will go back with them.
I cannot stay to serve you.”
In Bīnzhōu, there was a scholar
studying in his studio.
Someone knocked at the door;
opening it to look,
he saw a white-haired old man,
whose appearance was very ancient.
He invited him in
and asked his name.
The old man said himself:
"Yǎngzhēn,
surnamed Hú,
actually a fox immortal.
I admire your noble elegance,
and wish to share mornings and evenings with you."
The scholar was by nature broad-minded,
and did not find it strange.
So they discussed and debated ancient and modern matters.
The old man was exceptionally erudite,
his speech carved and embroidered like flowers,
brilliant as ivory;
when he occasionally drew upon the meaning of the classics,
his principles were profound and deep,
especially making one feel they were beyond expectation.
The scholar was astonished and impressed,
and kept him for a long time.
One day,
he secretly entreated the old man, saying:
"You love me very deeply.
But I am so poor like this;
if you merely lift a hand,
money should be obtainable instantly.
Why not give me a little support?"
The old man fell silent,
as if not approving.
After a while,
he laughed and said:
"This is a very easy matter.
But I need a dozen or so coins as seed money."
The scholar complied with his request.
The old man then went with him into a secret room,
performed Yǔ steps and chanted incantations.
In a moment,
coins numbering in the hundreds of thousands
came clinking down from between the beams,
with the force of a sudden rain,
in an instant covering their knees;
pulling their feet out to stand,
it covered their ankles again.
In a room ten feet wide,
the coins were about three or four feet deep.
Then, turning to speak to the scholar:
"Does this rather satisfy your wish?"
He said:
"Enough."
The old man waved his hand,
and the coins immediately stopped as if cut off.
Then they opened the door and went out together.
The scholar secretly rejoiced,
thinking himself suddenly rich.
Shortly after,
entering the room to take and use them,
he found the room full of that stuff had all vanished,
only the dozen or so seed coins remained sparse and few.
The scholar, disappointed,
angrily confronted the old man,
rather resentful of his deception.
The old man angrily said:
"I originally befriended you for literary exchange,
not to conspire with you to become thieves!
If it's as the scholar wishes,
you should only seek friendship with 'Mr. Beam-top',
this old man cannot comply!"
Then he brushed his sleeves and left.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A certain wealthy family in the western outskirts of Yìdū,
possessed great wealth,
kept a concubine,
quite graceful and beautiful,
but the principal wife oppressed and humiliated her,
indiscriminately whipping and beating.
The concubine served her with utmost care.
The master pitied her,
often privately comforting and soothing her.
The concubine never uttered any complaint.
One night,
several dozen people climbed over the wall and entered,
banging against their door until it nearly broke.
The master and his wife were terrified and lost their spirits,
trembling and shaking, not knowing what to do.
The concubine rose,
silently without a sound,
groped in the dark in the room,
found a carrying pole for water,
unbolted the door and rushed out.
The band of thieves was in chaos like tangled hemp.
The concubine brandished the pole,
it whistled like a phoenix and clanged like a hook,
striking four or five men to the ground;
the thieves were all routed,
terrified, scrambling to flee over the wall,
but unable to climb up quickly,
tumbling and yelping,
losing their souls and lives.
The concubine propped the pole on the ground,
looked back and laughed, saying:
"Such creatures,
not even worth striking with my hand,
yet they try to be thieves!
I won't kill you,
killing would disgrace me."
She let them all escape.
The master was greatly astonished,
asked,
"How could you do this?"
It turned out her father was formerly a spear and staff master,
and she had fully learned his skills,
capable of facing perhaps a hundred men.
The wife was especially terrified,
regretting her past blindness in judging people.
From then on, she treated the concubine kindly.
The concubine never showed the slightest discourtesy.
Neighboring women sometimes said to the concubine:
"Sister-in-law, you beat the thieves like pigs and dogs,
yet why do you bow your head and endure whipping?"
The concubine said:
"That is my lot,
what else dare I say."
Those who heard esteemed her even more.
The Strange Historian says:
"Possessing extraordinary skills,
living for years without others knowing,
yet ultimately defending against calamity and warding off disaster,
transforming a hawk into a dove.
Alas!
When the pheasant is shot and captured,
the wife beams with smiles;
when victory is won at board games,
the noble princess shares the carriage.
That skills should not be neglected is indeed like this!"
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Chángshān's Xú Yuǎngōng,
was a scholar in the former Míng dynasty.
After the dynastic change,
he abandoned Confucianism to seek the Way,
gradually learning exorcism and restraint arts,
and his fame spread far and wide.
A certain high official from a county,
prepared gifts,
sent a sincere letter,
and invited him with a horse.
Xú asked:
"Why have you summoned me?"
The servant excused himself, saying,
"I do not know.
I was only instructed to insist that you honor us with your presence."
Xú then set off.
Upon arrival, a feast was laid out in the central courtyard,
and he was treated with great respect; yet the host never revealed the reason for inviting him.
Growing impatient,
Xú asked,
"What is it you truly wish?
I beg you to dispel my doubts."
The host merely said,
"It is nothing."
He only urged him to drink.
His words were evasive,
leaving Xú utterly perplexed.
As they conversed,
evening approached unnoticed.
The host invited Xú to drink in the garden.
The garden was exquisitely designed,
but bamboo and trees cast deep shadows,
creating a gloomy atmosphere.
Clusters of wild flowers
were half-buried among the weeds.
They reached a pavilion,
its ceiling boards hung with tangled spiderwebs,
large and small, high and low,
too numerous to count.
After several rounds of wine,
the sky grew dusky,
and candles were called for to continue drinking.
Xú declined, claiming he could drink no more,
so the host ended the wine and called for tea.
The servants hastily cleared away the dishes and utensils,
placing them all on a table in the left chamber of the pavilion.
Before half the tea was drunk,
the host made an excuse and abruptly left.
A servant then took a candle and led Xú to stay in the left chamber.
After placing the candle on the table,
he hurriedly turned and left,
in a rather rushed manner.
Xú thought perhaps the servant would return with bedding to keep him company,
but after a long while,
there was no sign of anyone.
So he got up, bolted the door, and went to bed.
Bright moonlight shone through the window,
flooding the room and his bed;
night birds and autumn insects
chirped and buzzed all at once.
Feeling uneasy at heart,
he could not fall asleep.
After a while,
there came a tapping sound from the ceiling boards,
like footsteps,
growing increasingly loud.
Soon it descended the stairs,
then approached the bedroom door.
Xú was terrified,
his hair standing on end.
He hastily pulled the quilt over his head,
but the door suddenly swung wide open.
Xú lifted a corner of the quilt to peek out.
He saw a creature
with the head of a beast and the body of a man;
covered in hair all over,
tall as a horse,
and deep black in color;
its teeth gleamed like rows of peaks,
and its eyes shone like twin torches.
Reaching the table,
it crouched to devour the leftover food from the dishes;
with a sweep of its tongue,
several dishes were instantly cleaned as if swept.
Then it approached the bed,
sniffing at Xú's quilt.
Xú suddenly sprang up,
flung the quilt over the monster's head,
and pressed down on it while shouting wildly.
Caught off guard,
the monster was startled and broke free,
opened the outer door, and fled.
Xú threw on his clothes and tried to escape,
but the garden gate was bolted from the outside,
and he could not get out.
He ran along the wall,
chose a low section to climb over,
and found himself in the host's stable.
The stableman was startled;
Xú explained what had happened,
and asked to stay there for the night.
As dawn approached,
the host sent someone to check on Xú,
but he was nowhere to be found.
Greatly alarmed,
they soon discovered him in the stable.
Xú emerged,
filled with resentment,
and angrily said:
"I am not accustomed to exorcising monsters: you sent for me,
yet kept it secret without a word;
I have a Rúyì hook in my bag,
yet you did not deliver it to my sleeping quarters: this would have been the death of me!"
The host apologized, saying:
"I intended to tell you,
but feared you would find it difficult.
I also did not know you had a hidden hook in your bag.
I beg your forgiveness ten times over!"
Xú remained displeased,
and asked for a horse to ride home.
From then on, the monster never appeared again.
Whenever the host entertained guests in the garden,
he would laugh and say to them:
"I have not forgotten Master Xú's功劳."
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
" 'Be it a yellow cat or a black cat,
he who catches the mouse is the hero.'
This is no empty saying.
Had he, after flipping the quilt and shouting wildly,
concealed his fear,
and openly claimed credit for the monster's flight as his own doing,
the world would surely have hailed Xú as a peerless divine man."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
The Grand Councillor Máo Gōng of Yèxiàn
came from a humble family.
His father often herded cattle for others.
At that time, a prominent family named Zhāng
had a new burial ground on the southern side of Dōngshān.
When someone passed by its side,
they heard a voice from the tomb shout:
"You there, leave quickly!
Do not linger and defile a nobleman's residence!"
Upon hearing this, Zhāng
did not entirely believe it.
Later, he repeatedly had dreams
warning him:
"Your family's burial ground
is originally the fine resting place of Máo Gōng.
How can you long occupy it?"
Thereafter, his household encountered frequent misfortunes.
A guest advised him to relocate the graves for good fortune,
and Zhāng heeded the advice,
moving them elsewhere.
One day,
the Grand Councillor's father was herding cattle
near the Zhāng family's former graves
when he was suddenly caught in rain.
He took shelter in an abandoned tomb pit.
Soon the rain poured down more heavily,
floodwaters rushed into the cavity,
causing it to collapse and fill with water,
and he drowned.
The Grand Councillor was still a child at the time.
His mother went to see Zhāng herself,
begging for a tiny plot of land
to bury her child's father.
When Zhāng learned their surname,
he was greatly astonished.
He went to inspect the drowning site
and found it precisely where a coffin should be placed,
which further alarmed him.
He then allowed the burial in the old tomb pit.
Moreover, he instructed her to bring the child along.
After the burial,
the mother and child went to Zhāng to express their thanks.
As soon as Zhāng saw the boy,
he took an immediate liking to him,
kept him at his home,
taught him to read,
and treated him as one of his own children.
He also proposed marrying his eldest daughter to the boy.
The mother dared not consent.
Zhāng's wife said:
"Since the words have been spoken,
how can we go back on them?"
They finally agreed to the marriage.
However, this girl held the Máo family in great contempt,
and her feelings of resentment and shame
were evident in her words and expression.
Whenever someone mentioned them,
she would cover her ears;
often saying to others:
"I would rather die than follow that cowherd boy!"
When the wedding day arrived,
the groom entered for the banquet,
the decorated sedan chair was at the gate,
yet the girl covered her face with her sleeve, turned toward the corner, and wept.
They urged her to dress up,
but she would not;
persuasion also failed to sway her.
Soon the groom announced his departure,
drums and music began to play loudly,
yet the girl still had tears falling like rain and her hair was disheveled as flying weeds.
Her father stopped the son-in-law,
went in himself to persuade his daughter,
but she wept as if she heard nothing.
Angered, he pressed her harder,
and she cried even more bitterly, losing her voice.
Her father was at a loss.
Then a servant came to report:
The groom wished to leave.
Her father hurried out,
saying:
"Her attire and makeup are not yet finished,
I beg you, sir, to wait a little longer."
He then rushed back in to check on his daughter.
He went back and forth,
without pausing in his steps.
After delaying for a short while,
the situation grew more urgent,
yet the girl showed no sign of relenting.
Her father, with no plan left,
was so anxious he felt like dying himself.
Her younger sister was at her side,
quite critical of her elder sister,
and earnestly urged and pressed her.
The elder sister angrily said:
"You little chit,
you also learn to chatter like others!
Why don't you go with him instead?"
The younger sister replied:
"Father originally did not betroth me to Master Máo;
if he had betrothed me to Master Máo,
why would I need my elder sister to urge the carriage?"
Her father, finding her words spirited and straightforward,
secretly discussed with her mother,
to substitute the younger for the elder.
The mother then said to the girl:
"This disobedient maid refuses to follow her parents' command;
now we intend to have you take your sister's place,
are you willing?"
The girl said resolutely:
"If my parents tell me to go,
even as a beggar I would not refuse;
moreover, how can we know that seeing Master Máo means lifelong starvation and death?"
Hearing her words,
her parents were overjoyed,
and immediately dressed the younger sister in the elder's wedding attire,
hurriedly sending her off in the carriage.
Entering the household,
husband and wife were harmonious and deeply affectionate.
However, the girl had long suffered from thinning hair,
which slightly bothered Master Máo.
Over time, he gradually learned of the marriage substitution,
and even more regarded her as a confidante, grateful to her.
Not long after,
Master Máo passed the county-level examination to become a xiùcai,
and went to take the provincial examination.
On the way, he passed by Wáng Shèrén's inn,
where the innkeeper had dreamed the night before of a deity saying:
"Soon there will come a Xièyuàn named Máo,
who will later deliver you from hardship."
Therefore, he rose early,
watching for guests coming from the east.
When he encountered Master Máo,
he was very pleased.
He provided exceptionally fine hospitality,
asking for no payment.
He especially entrusted himself deeply based on the dream's omen.
Master Máo also rather prided himself;
privately, because of his wife's hair,
he feared being laughed at by eminent people,
and thought to replace her after gaining wealth and honor.
Later, when the dawn announcement was posted,
he actually fell below the passing mark,
sighing as he trudged along,
filled with regret and losing heart.
Ashamed to face his former host,
he dared not pass by Wáng Shè again,
returning by another route.
Three years later,
he went again for the examination,
and the innkeeper welcomed and waited for him as before.
Master Máo said:
"Your words previously did not come true,
I am deeply ashamed of your devoted service."
The host said:
"Because you, xiùcai, secretly intended to change your wife,
you were demoted by the underworld officials;
how could a strange dream fail to be fulfilled?"
Startled, Master Máo asked the reason.
It turned out that after parting, the host had dreamed again and was told this.
Hearing this,
Master Máo was awed, repentant, and fearful,
standing woodenly like a puppet.
The host said:
"Xiùcai, you should take care of yourself,
you will eventually become the top candidate."
Not long after,
he indeed placed first in the provincial examination.
His wife's hair also soon grew long,
her cloud-like tresses hanging dark and lush,
making her even more charming.
The elder sister had married the son of a wealthy family in the village,
and was quite haughty in demeanor.
Her husband was dissolute and lazy,
the family gradually declined,
their empty house lacking even cooking smoke.
Hearing her younger sister was the wife of a provincial graduate,
she felt even more ashamed.
The sisters would avoid each other on the road.
Not long after,
her husband died,
and the family fell into ruin.
Soon after,
Master Máo was further promoted as a jìnshì.
The elder sister heard this,
bitterly hating herself to the bone,
and in anger, renounced the world to become a nun.
When Master Máo returned home as a chancellor,
she forcibly sent a nun disciple to his residence to pay respects,
hoping for some gifts.
When she arrived,
the lady of the house gave several bolts of fine silk and gauze,
placing gold inside them,
but the disciple did not know.
She brought them back to show her master.
The master, disappointed,
said angrily:
"If they gave me money,
I could still use it for firewood and rice expenses;
what need have I for such ceremonial items!"
