So she ordered them returned.
Master Máo and his wife were puzzled.
Opening them, they found the gold still inside,
and then understood the reason for the refusal.
Taking out the gold, they laughed and said:
"Your master cannot even accept a hundred-some taels of gold,
how could she have the fortune to follow my old minister?"
They then gave fifty taels of gold to the nun to take away,
saying:
"Take this for your master's expenses.
More might be hard for one with thin fortune to bear."
The disciple returned
and reported everything.
The master silently sighed to herself,
reflecting on her lifelong actions,
how they had always been contrary,
avoiding what was good and pursuing what was bad—
could this be determined by others?
Later, the innkeeper was arrested and imprisoned due to a manslaughter case,
and Master Máo exerted his influence to explain and clear his crime.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"The Zhāng family's old gravesite,
the Máo family's fine burial ground—
this is already strange.
I have heard contemporaries joke about
'the elder sister's husband becoming the younger sister's husband,
the former Xièyuàn becoming the later Xièyuàn'—
could this be something the clever and cunning can calculate?
Alas!
That vast heaven above,
long has it been beyond questioning;
why, when it comes to Master Máo,
does it respond like an echo?"
In Fújiàn, there was a Presented Scholar named Zēng,
who, after achieving high honors in the imperial examinations,
went for an excursion in the outskirts of the city with two or three other newly successful candidates.
They roamed the countryside.
By chance, they heard that at the Pílú Buddhist Monastery,
a fortune-teller was staying,
so they rode together to visit and have their fortunes told.
They entered, bowed, and sat down.
The fortune-teller, seeing their high spirits,
flattered them with smooth talk.
Zēng, shaking his fan and smiling,
then asked:
"Do I have the fate to wear the python robe and jade belt?"
The fortune-teller solemnly promised him twenty years as a peaceful prime minister.
Zēng was greatly delighted,
and his spirits soared even higher.
It happened to be drizzling,
so he and his companions took shelter from the rain in the monks' quarters.
In the room was an old monk,
with deep-set eyes and a high nose,
sitting on a rush cushion,
aloof and not returning their greetings.
The group merely raised their hands in acknowledgment,
then climbed onto the couch and began chatting among themselves,
all congratulating Zēng on becoming prime minister.
Zēng, feeling particularly proud,
pointed to his companions and said:
"When I become prime minister,
I will recommend Elder Zhāng to be the Southern Governor,
my cousin to be a Military Advisor,
and even my old servant can get a minor official post—
then my wishes will be fulfilled."
Everyone burst into laughter.
Soon, they heard the rain outside pouring down even harder,
and Zēng, feeling weary, lay down on the couch.
Suddenly, he saw two palace eunuchs arrive,
bearing an imperial edict from the Son of Heaven,
summoning Grand Academician Zēng to decide on state affairs.
Zēng, elated,
hurried to the court.
The Emperor leaned forward on his mat,
and spoke warmly with him for a long time.
He decreed that all officials of the third rank and below
were subject to Zēng's promotions and dismissals.
He also bestowed upon him a python robe, jade belt, and famous horses.
Zēng, dressed in his new robes, kowtowed and left.
Upon returning home,
he found it was no longer his old residence,
but a mansion with painted beams and carved rafters,
extremely magnificent and splendid.
He himself could not understand
how he had suddenly come to this.
However, when he stroked his beard and called out softly,
the responses thundered like echoes.
Soon, high officials came to present gifts from afar,
bowing and scraping with utmost deference,
crowding in and out of his gate.
When ministers of the six boards arrived,
he would rush out to welcome them, even putting his shoes on backwards;
for vice-ministers,
he would bow and speak with them;
for those of lower rank,
he would merely nod.
The Governor of Shānxī sent ten female musicians as a gift,
all of them beautiful women.
The most outstanding among them were
Niǎoniǎo and Xiānxiān,
and these two received special favor and attention.
He would often relax bareheaded during his days off,
spending his time enjoying music and songs.
One day,
he recalled how, in his humble days, he had received aid from the local gentry, Wáng Zǐliáng.
Now that he had risen high in the clouds,
while Wáng was still struggling in his official career,
why not give him a helping hand?
Early the next morning, he submitted a memorial,
recommending Wáng as a Remonstrance Official,
and immediately received imperial approval,
leading to Wáng's prompt promotion.
He also remembered that the Grand Coachman, Guō, had once given him a hostile look,
so he summoned the Supervising Secretary, Lǚ, and the Censor, Chén Chāng, among others,
and conveyed his intentions to them.
The next day,
memorials of impeachment arrived one after another,
and an imperial decree was issued to strip Guō of his position and dismiss him.
Having settled these old scores,
he felt quite satisfied.
Once, while traveling on a suburban road,
a drunkard happened to bump into his procession,
so he ordered his men to bind the offender and hand him over to the Capital Prefect,
who immediately had him beaten to death.
Those who owned vast estates adjoining his
all feared his power and offered him their fertile lands.
From then on,
his wealth rivaled that of the state.
Not long after, Niǎoniǎo and Xiānxiān
passed away one after the other,
and he missed them day and night.
Suddenly, he remembered seeing a girl from a neighboring family years ago who was exceptionally beautiful.
He had often thought of buying her to be his concubine,
but his limited means had prevented him from fulfilling this long-held wish.
Now, fortunately, he could satisfy his desire.
So he sent several capable servants
to forcibly deliver betrothal gifts to her family.
In no time,
a sedan chair carried her over,
and she was even more stunningly beautiful
than when he had glimpsed her in the past.
Reflecting on his life,
he felt all his wishes were now fulfilled.
Another year passed,
and court officials began to whisper among themselves,
as if harboring silent disapproval.
Yet each acted like a ceremonial horse—keeping silent—
while Zēng remained haughty and arrogant,
paying no heed to their sentiments.
A scholar from the Dragon Diagram Academy named Bāo submitted a memorial,
which read in summary:
"I humbly submit that Zēng Mǒu
was originally a drinker, gambler, and scoundrel,
a petty man from the marketplace.
Through a single agreeable remark,
he gained the emperor's favor,
with his father and sons draped in purple and crimson robes—
the pinnacle of imperial grace.
Instead of devoting himself body and soul
to repay even a ten-thousandth of this kindness,
he has indulged his whims,
arbitrarily wielding power and influence.
His capital crimes
are too numerous to count!
He treats official positions and honors of the court
as rare commodities,
assessing the profitability of vacancies
to set their prices.
Thus, ministers, generals, and officers
all rush to his gate,
calculating and currying favor
as if engaged in trade.
Those who gaze upon his dust and seek his breath
are beyond reckoning.
If there are outstanding scholars or virtuous ministers
who refuse to flatter and attach themselves to him,
they are lightly relegated to idle posts
or heavily stripped of rank and made commoners.
Even a single gesture of non-allegiance
offends his treacherous 'deer-called-horse' schemes;
a mere word of dissent
leads to exile to lands of jackals and wolves.
Court officials are chilled to the heart,
leaving the court isolated.
Moreover, the fertile lands of common people
are wantonly encroached upon;
daughters from good families
are forcibly taken in marriage.
Miasma of grievance and冤气
darkens the sky!
When his servants arrive,
prefects and magistrates cater to their whims;
when a letter is delivered,
ministries and courts bend the law.
Even the sons of his servants
or distant relatives by marriage
travel with official carriages,
swift as wind and thunder.
If local provisions are slightly delayed,
whips immediately fall from horseback.
They torment the people,
enslave the officials,
and wherever their entourage passes,
the fields are left barren.
Yet Zēng remains blazingly powerful,
clinging to favor without remorse.
He receives audiences at the palace gates,
while slanders are presented before the sovereign;
he retires leisurely from court duties,
only for music and song to rise in the rear gardens.
Indulging in sensual pleasures, dogs, and horses,
he wallows in debauchery day and night;
matters of state and people's livelihood
never cross his mind.
Has the world ever seen such a prime minister?
Inside and outside the court, there is shock and turmoil,
public sentiment seething.
If he is not swiftly executed,
he will surely bring about the disasters of a Cáo or a Wáng Mǎng.
I, your servant, am filled with fear day and night,
unable to rest in peace,
and dare to list these charges at the risk of death,
humbly presenting them to Your Majesty.
I beg that the head of this treacherous sycophant be severed,
his ill-gotten wealth confiscated,
to appease Heaven's wrath above
and satisfy public sentiment below.
If my words are false or mistaken,
let the blades, saws, cauldrons, and boilers
be applied to my person."
And so on.
When the memorial was submitted,
Zēng heard of it,
his spirit seized with terror,
as if he had drunk ice water.
Fortunately, the emperor was lenient
and kept the memorial in the palace without issuing a response.
But then censors, circuit inspectors, and the nine ministers
submitted successive memorials of impeachment;
even those who once bowed at his gate and called him foster father
now turned against him.
An edict was issued to confiscate his property
and exile him to the Yúnyǔ army.
His son, the prefect of Píngyáng,
was already being summoned for interrogation.
Zēng had just heard the edict in shock and despair
when several dozen warriors arrived,
bearing swords and spears,
marching straight into his inner chambers,
stripping him of his robes and cap,
and binding him together with his wife.
Soon he saw several men hauling his assets into the courtyard:
gold, silver, coins, and notes amounting to millions,
pearls, jadeites, agates, and jades by the hundreds of hu,
along with tents, curtains, beds, and the like,
numbering several thousand items,
down to children's swaddling clothes and women's shoes,
scattered across the courtyard steps.
Zēng looked at each one,
his heart aching and eyes stinging.
Then, a man dragged out his beautiful concubine,
her hair disheveled, weeping pitifully,
her jade-like face distraught.
Grief burned in his heart like fire,
but he swallowed his rage, not daring to speak.
Soon, his towers, pavilions, and storehouses
were all sealed and inventoried.
He was harshly ordered out.
The guards pulled and dragged him along.
Husband and wife swallowed their sobs and set out on the road,
begging for even a poor, worn-out cart
to serve as a modest conveyance,
but were denied.
After ten lǐ,
his wife's feet grew weak,
and she stumbled,
at which point Zēng used one hand to support her.
After another ten-plus lǐ,
he himself grew exhausted.
Seeing a high mountain
that pierced the heavens,
he worried they could not climb it,
and from time to time held his wife's hand as they wept together.
But the guards glared over, watching closely,
allowing no pause or rest.
Seeing also that the setting sun had dipped low,
with nowhere to seek shelter,
they had no choice
but to hobble along unevenly.
When they reached the mountainside,
his wife's strength gave out,
and she sat weeping by the roadside.
Zēng also rested,
ignoring the guards' curses.
Suddenly, a clamor of a hundred voices arose,
and a band of robbers, each wielding sharp blades,
leapt forward.
The guards were terrified
and fled.
Zēng knelt down
and said:
"I am a lone man exiled far away,
with nothing of value in my pack."
He begged for mercy.
The robbers glared and declared:
"We are all wronged people who have suffered harm.
We seek only the head of this treacherous villain—
we ask for nothing else."
Zēng shouted angrily:
"Though I am awaiting punishment,
I am still an official appointed by the court.
How dare you bandits act like this!"
The robbers grew furious
and swung a giant axe at Zēng's neck.
He felt his head fall to the ground with a thud,
his soul still reeling in shock and disbelief,
when two demons came,
bound his hands behind his back,
and drove him forward.
After walking for several hours,
they entered a large city.
Soon after,
he saw a palace;
on the hall sat a king of ugly appearance,
leaning on a table and deciding people's fates.
Zēng stepped forward
and prostrated himself to plead for mercy.
The king reviewed the records,
and after reading only a few lines,
he immediately thundered in anger:
"This is the crime of deceiving the sovereign and ruining the state,
he should be thrown into the oil cauldron!"
Ten thousand ghosts echoed in unison,
their voices like thunder.
Immediately, a giant ghost came to the steps below.
Zēng saw a cauldron about seven feet high,
with burning charcoal all around,
and its legs glowing red.
Zēng trembled and wailed pitifully,
but there was no way to escape.
The ghost grabbed his hair with its left hand,
and seized his ankle with its right,
then threw him into the cauldron.
He felt his whole body
rising and falling with the boiling oil;
his skin and flesh were scorched,
and the pain pierced his heart;
the boiling oil entered his mouth,
frying and cooking his innards.
He wished to die quickly,
but despite all his efforts, he could not die.
After about the time it takes to eat a meal,
the ghost finally used a giant fork to pull Zēng out,
and he prostrated himself again in the hall below.
The king then checked the records again,
and angrily said:
"For abusing power to oppress others,
he should suffer the Mountain of Knives punishment!"
The ghost dragged him away again.
He saw a mountain,
not very vast;
but steep and sheer like a wall,
covered with sharp blades crisscrossing,
dense as bamboo shoots.
Several people were already impaled through their bellies on it,
their cries and screams
were unbearably horrifying.
The ghost urged Zēng to climb,
but Zēng cried loudly and retreated.
The ghost stabbed his brain with a poisonous awl,
and Zēng, in pain, begged for mercy.
The ghost, enraged,
grabbed Zēng and lifted him,
then threw him forcefully into the air.
He felt himself flying high into the clouds,
then dizzyingly falling,
and the blades pierced his chest,
the pain was indescribable.
After another while,
his body felt heavy and cumbersome,
the knife wounds gradually widened;
suddenly, he fell off,
his limbs curled up like a caterpillar.
The ghost then drove him to see the king again.
The king ordered an accounting of all the money he had gained in his lifetime from selling official titles and reputations,
perverting the law to seize property.
Immediately, a bearded man holding counting rods and doing calculations
said:
"Three million two hundred and ten thousand."
The king said:
"Since he accumulated it,
let him drink it back!"
After a short while,
they brought the money and piled it on the steps,
like hills.
Gradually, they melted it in an iron cauldron,
using a fierce fire.
Several ghost attendants
took turns ladling it into his mouth,
when it flowed over his cheeks, his skin cracked and stank,
when it entered his throat, his organs boiled.
In life, he worried about having too little of this thing,
now he worried about having too much of it.
Half a day passed before it was finished.
The king ordered him to be taken to Gānzhōu to be reborn as a woman.
After walking a few steps,
he saw an iron frame,
several feet in circumference,
holding a wheel of fire,
its size immeasurable, hundreds of yóuxún,
flames of five colors,
its light reaching the clouds.
The ghost whipped him to climb onto the wheel.
Just as he closed his eyes and jumped on,
the wheel turned with his feet,
he felt as if he were falling,
his whole body turning cold.
Opening his eyes to look at himself,
he found he had become an infant,
and moreover, a girl.
Looking at his parents,
they were dressed in tattered rags.
In an earthen hut,
a gourd ladle and a stick remained.
He knew in his heart he was the child of beggars.
Every day, he followed the beggars begging with a bowl,
his stomach growling, often not getting a full meal.
Wearing ragged clothes,
the wind often pierced to the bone.
At fourteen,
he was sold to Scholar Gù as a concubine,
clothing and food were barely enough to sustain himself.
But the main wife was extremely fierce,
daily using the whip on her,
often branding her chest and breasts with red-hot iron.
Fortunately, her husband was quite loving,
which gave her some comfort.
An evil youth from the east neighbor
suddenly climbed over the wall to force himself on her.
She then thought of the evil deeds in her previous life,
already punished by the ghosts,
how could she do this again now.
So she cried out loudly.
Her husband and the main wife both got up,
and the evil youth fled.
Not long after,
the scholar stayed in her room,
on the pillow, chattering,
just as she was pouring out her grievances and sufferings.
Suddenly, there was a loud crash,
the room door was flung open,
two bandits with knives entered,
cut off the scholar's head,
and looted all the belongings.
She curled up under the quilt,
not daring to make another sound.
After the bandits left,
she ran crying to the main wife's room.
The main wife was greatly shocked,
and together they wept and examined the scene.
Then they suspected that the concubine had used a lover to kill her husband,
so they reported the case to the prefect.
The prefect interrogated strictly,
and under torture, she falsely confessed,
and according to the law, was sentenced to death by dismemberment.
Tied up and taken to the execution ground,
the injustice in her chest felt stifling,
she stomped and cried out her grievance,
feeling that even the deepest hells
were not as dark as this.
Just as she was wailing in sorrow,
she heard a fellow traveler call out:
"Brother, are you having a nightmare?"
Suddenly, she woke up,
and saw the old monk still sitting cross-legged on his seat.
Her companions said to each other:
"It's getting dark and our stomachs are empty,
why have you been sleeping so long?"
Zēng then got up, looking pale.
The monk smiled and said:
"Did the prediction about becoming prime minister come true?"
Zēng was even more astonished,
and bowed, asking for guidance.
The monk said:
"Cultivate virtue and practice benevolence,
even in the fire pit, a blue lotus can grow.
What does this mountain monk know?"
Zēng had come full of pride,
but now returned dejected.
His thoughts of becoming a high official
faded from then on.
He entered the mountains, and no one knew his end.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"Blessing the good and punishing the wicked,
is the constant way of Heaven.
Those who hear about becoming prime minister and feel joy in their hearts,
are certainly not happy about serving diligently and exhaustively, that much is clear.
At that time, in their minds,
mansions, wives, and concubines,
they had everything.
However, dreams are indeed illusory,
but thoughts are not real either.
They act with emptiness,
and the spirits respond with illusions.
When the millet is about to be cooked,
such dreams are inevitable,
and this should be added to the story of Hándān."
Based on the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
It is commonly said that dragons draw water from rivers and lakes to make rain,
but this is merely a speculative notion.
When Xú Dōngchī traveled south,
he moored his boat by the riverbank.
He saw a blue dragon descending from the clouds,
stirring the river water with its tail.
Waves surged up,
following the dragon's body as it rose.
From a distance, the shimmering water
appeared broader than three bolts of white silk.
After a while,
the dragon retracted its tail,
and the water immediately calmed.
Soon after, heavy rain poured down,
filling the ditches and channels to the brim.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
When Wèi Zhōngtáng of Shānxī was still a scholar,
he grew weary of the constant disturbances
and moved to a monk's quarters.
However, the room was infested with bedbugs, mosquitoes, and fleas,
making it impossible for him to sleep through the night.
After a meal,
he lay down to rest on his bed.
Suddenly, a tiny warrior appeared,
wearing pheasant feathers on his head,
standing about two inches tall,
and riding a horse the size of a grasshopper.
On his arm was a green falconer's sleeve,
with a falcon as small as a fly.
He entered from outside,
circling around the room,
moving swiftly.
As Wèi watched intently,
another person entered,
similarly dressed,
with a small bow and arrows at his waist,
leading a hunting dog as large as a giant ant.
Soon after,
foot soldiers and horsemen
arrived in droves, numbering in the hundreds,
with hundreds of falcons on their arms
and hundreds of hunting dogs.
Whenever a mosquito or fly took flight,
the falcons were released to attack,
killing them all.
The hunting dogs climbed onto the bed and along the walls,
searching for and biting lice and fleas.
No matter where they hid in the cracks,
the dogs sniffed them out.
In no time,
they were nearly all exterminated.
Wèi pretended to sleep and watched them.
Falcons perched and dogs scurried over his body.
Then, a man in yellow robes appeared,
wearing a flat-topped crown,
like a king.
He climbed onto another couch,
and tethered his carriage in the reed matting.
His attendants dismounted,
presenting captured birds and animals,
gathering around him in great numbers.
Wèi could not understand what they were saying.
Before long,
the king boarded a small carriage,
and his guards hastily
saddled their horses.
Thousands of hooves thundered as they galloped away,
scattering like beans,
amidst flying dust and mist.
In an instant, they had all vanished.
Wèi witnessed everything clearly,
astonished and bewildered by what had happened.
He slipped on his shoes and peered outside,
but there was no trace or sound of them.
Turning back, he looked around the room,
but found nothing.
Only a tiny dog remained on a brick in the wall.
Wèi quickly grabbed it,
and it was quite tame.
He placed it in an inkstone box,
admiring it repeatedly.
Its fur was extremely fine and soft,
with a small ring around its neck.
When he offered it grains of rice,
it sniffed and immediately rejected them.
It leaped onto the bed,
searched through the seams of his clothes,
and bit to death any lice or nits it found.
Then it returned to lie down.
The next day,
Wèi thought it might have left,
but when he looked,
it was curled up as before.
When Wèi lay down to sleep,
it climbed onto the bed mat,
and whenever it encountered bugs, it devoured them,
so that no mosquitoes or flies dared to land.
Wèi cherished it
more than a priceless jade.
One day,
while napping,
the dog hid beside him.
As Wèi turned in his sleep,
he accidentally crushed it under his waist.
Feeling something,
he suspected it was the dog.
He quickly got up to check,
and found it flattened and dead,
as if cut out of paper.
However, from then on, there were no more bugs on the walls.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Liáng Gōng, the General of Yángzhōu,
had retired to his hometown.
Every day, he carried chess and wine,
wandering among the woods and hills.
On the Double Ninth Festival, while climbing a height,
he was playing chess with a guest.
Suddenly, a man approached,
lingering by the chessboard,
engrossed in watching and unwilling to leave.
Looking at him,
his appearance was shabby,
wearing tattered clothing.
Yet his demeanor was gentle and refined,
with the air of a scholar.
Liáng Gōng greeted him courteously,
and he sat down.
He was also very humble.
Liáng Gōng pointed to the chessboard and said to him:
"You must be skilled at this, sir.
Why not play a game with my guest?"
The man politely declined for a while,
but eventually joined the game.
He lost the match,
and his expression grew agitated,
as if he could not control himself.
He played again and lost once more,
becoming even more ashamed and angry.
When offered wine,
he refused to drink,
insisting on playing another game with the guest.
From morning until sunset,
he did not even take a break to relieve himself.
As they argued over a single move,
quarreling loudly,
the scholar suddenly stood up from his seat, trembling,
his face pale and distressed.
A moment later,
he knelt before Liáng Gōng,
kowtowing and begging for help.
Liáng Gōng was shocked and puzzled.
He helped him up and said:
"This is just a game.
Why go to such lengths?"
The scholar replied:
"Please instruct your stableman
not to tie a rope around my neck."
Liáng Gōng found this even stranger.
He asked:
"Which stableman?"
The scholar said:
"Mǎ Chéng."
Earlier,
Liáng Gōng had a stableman named Mǎ Chéng,
who served as a messenger to the underworld.
Every ten days or so, he would enter the realm of the dead,
carrying documents to summon souls.
Liáng Gōng found the scholar's words odd,
so he sent someone to check on Mǎ Chéng.
They found him lying stiff, as if dead, for two days.
Liáng Gōng then scolded Mǎ Chéng, ordering him not to be disrespectful.
In an instant,
the scholar vanished into the ground.
Liáng Gōng sighed in amazement for a long time,
finally realizing he had been a ghost.
The next day,
Mǎ Chéng woke up,
and the Duke summoned him for questioning.
Chéng said:
"The scholar was from Húxiāng,
obsessed with playing chess,
and squandered all his family's wealth.
His father worried about him,
and locked him in his study.
Yet he would climb over the wall,
sneak away to secluded places,
and associate with chess players.
His father scolded and cursed him,
but ultimately could not stop him.
His father, filled with anger and resentment, eventually died.
Yánmó Wáng, considering the scholar immoral,
shortened his lifespan,
and sentenced him to the Hungry Ghost Prison,
where he has been for seven years now.
It happened that Dōngyuè's Phoenix Tower was completed,
and notices were sent to various prefectures,
seeking scholars to compose an inscription for the monument.
The King released him from prison,
and ordered him to answer the call to redeem himself.
Unexpectedly, he delayed along the way,
greatly exceeding the deadline.
The Emperor of the Eastern Peak sent an official to hold the King accountable.
The King was furious,
and ordered us minions to search for him everywhere.
Earlier, following my master's command,
I dared not bind him with ropes."
The Duke asked:
"What will become of him today?"
He replied:
"He will be handed back to the prison guards,
with no hope of ever being reborn."
The Duke sighed and said:
"Obsessions can mislead people,
to such an extent!"
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Upon seeing chess, he forgot about death;
and when he died,
upon seeing chess, he forgot about life.
Is it not that his desire for it surpassed even life itself?
Yet with such an obsession,
he still never achieved a single masterful move,
merely leaving behind in the underworld,
an undying chess-playing ghost.
How pitiful indeed!"
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Master Féng of Guǎngpíng,
was a man of the Zhèngdé era.
In his youth, he was frivolous and unrestrained,
indulging in drink.
At dawn, he happened to be out walking,
when he encountered a young maiden,
wearing a red cape,
whose appearance was lovely and charming.
Followed by a young servant girl,
they hurried through the dew,
their shoes and stockings soaked through.
Secretly, he was smitten with her.
At dusk, returning drunk,
by the roadside there was an old temple,
long fallen into ruin and overgrown,
when a woman emerged from within,
it was the beauty from earlier.
Suddenly seeing Féng approach,
she immediately turned and went back inside.
He thought to himself: How could such a beauty be in a Buddhist monastery?
Tethering his donkey at the gate,
he went in to spy on this oddity.
Entering, he saw broken walls in disarray,
and on the steps, fine grass like a carpet.
While hesitating,
an old man with grizzled hair came out,
his clothes and hat neat and tidy,
and asked:
"Where does our guest come from?"
Féng said:
"I happened to pass by this ancient temple,
and wished to pay a visit.
And you, sir, why are you here?"
The old man said:
"This old man has no fixed abode,
and is temporarily lodging his family here.
Since you have graced us with your presence,
I have some mountain tea that can serve as wine."
Then he respectfully invited the guest inside.
They saw behind the main hall a courtyard,
with a stone path clean and bright,
no longer overgrown with brambles.
Entering the room,
there were curtains, drapes, beds, and screens,
with fragrant mist spraying from them, captivating.
Sitting, they exchanged names,
and he said:
"This old man's surname is Xīn."
Féng, emboldened by drink, abruptly asked:
"I heard you have a daughter,
not yet betrothed to a good match.
Presumptuously, without considering my own worth,
I wish to offer myself as a suitor."
Old Man Xīn smiled and said:
"Allow me to discuss it with my wife."
Féng immediately asked for a brush and wrote a poem:
"A thousand in gold I seek the jade pestle,
Earnestly I shall bring it forth with my own hands.
If Yún Yīng is willing,
I will personally pound the elixir for her."
The host smiled and handed it to his attendants.
After a short while,
a maid whispered into Old Man Xīn's ear.
Xīn rose to soothe the guest, asking him to wait patiently,
and drew aside the curtain to go inside.
Faintly, a few words were heard,
then he hurried back out.
Féng thought there must be good news;
but Old Man Xīn merely sat and joked with him,
saying nothing more on the matter.
Féng could not bear it,
and asked:
"I do not yet know your intention,
I beg you to relieve my anxious heart."
Old Man Xīn said:
"You are an outstanding scholar,
I have long admired your style.
But there is a private matter,
which I dare not speak of."
Féng insisted on asking.
Old Man Xīn said:
"I have nineteen daughters,
twelve are already married.
The matter of marriage is left to my wife,
this old man does not intervene."
Féng said:
"I only desire the one who this morning led the young servant girl through the dew."
Old Man Xīn did not respond,
and they sat facing each other in silence.
Hearing soft, delicate speech from within the room,
Féng, emboldened by drink, lifted the curtain and said:
"Since a marital match cannot be obtained,
at least let me see her face,
to dispel my regret."
From inside came the sound of hooks moving,
and many stood up in surprise, looking around.
Indeed, there was a person in red,
shaking her sleeves and tilting her hair ornaments,
standing gracefully, fingering her sash.
Seeing Féng enter,
the whole room was thrown into panic.
Old Man Xīn was furious,
and ordered several men to drag Féng out.
The wine surged up even more,
and he collapsed amidst the brambles.
Tiles and stones fell like rain,
but fortunately none hit him.
Lying there for a while,
he heard his donkey still chewing grass by the roadside,
so he got up and mounted the donkey,
staggering along.
The night was dark and confusing,
and he mistakenly entered a ravine,
where wolves ran and owls cried,
making his hair stand on end and his heart turn cold.
Hesitating, he looked all around,
not knowing where he was at all.
In the distance, amidst a dark forest,
lights flickered on and off,
and suspecting it must be a village,
he hurriedly rode towards it.
Looking up, he saw a grand gate,
and with his whip, he knocked on the door.
Someone inside asked:
"What gentleman is this,
coming here in the middle of the night?"
Féng explained that he had lost his way,
and the person inside said:
"Wait while I inform the master."
Féng stood on tiptoe, craning his neck like a crane, waiting.
Suddenly, he heard the sound of a bolt being drawn and the gate opening,
and a sturdy servant came out,
taking the donkey from the guest.
Féng entered,
and saw the rooms were very splendid and fine,
with lanterns hung in the hall.
He sat for a short while.
A woman came out,
and asked the guest his name.
Féng told her.
After a while,
several maids supported an old woman out,
who said:
"The Jùnjūn has arrived."
Féng stood up,
and respectfully prepared to bow.
The old woman stopped him,
and sitting, said to Féng:
"Are you not the grandson of Féng Yúnzǐ?"
He said:
"Yes."
The old woman said:
"Then you must be my grandnephew.
I am like a bell and water-clock both run dry,
my remaining years are nearly spent,
and among my own flesh and blood,
I have been quite cut off."
Féng said:
"I lost my father young,
and of those who associated with my grandfather,
I do not recognize even one in ten.
I have never paid my respects before,
I beg you to instruct me."
The old woman said:
"You will know in time."
Féng did not dare ask further,
and sat facing her, lost in thought.
The old woman said:
"Nephew, why have you come here so late at night?"
Féng, priding himself on his courage,
then recounted everything he had encountered.
The old woman laughed and said:
"This is a very good thing.
Moreover, you are a renowned scholar,
it would certainly not disgrace the marriage alliance,
how can that wild fox spirit put on such airs?
Nephew, do not worry,
I can arrange it for you."
Féng thanked her, saying "Yes, yes."
The old woman looked at her attendants and said:
"I didn't know Old Man Xīn's daughter
was so proper and lovely."
A maid said:
"He has nineteen daughters,
all graceful and elegant, with style,
I wonder which one the gentleman is seeking to marry?"
Féng said:
"She is about fifteen years old or so."
The maid said:
"That is the fourteenth young lady.
In the third month,
she once came with her mother to wish the Jùnjūn a happy birthday,
how could you forget?"
The old woman laughed and said:
"Is she not the one who carved lotus petals into high clogs,
filled them with fragrant powder,
and walked with them veiled in gauze?"
The maid said:
"That's her."
The old woman said:
"This maid is truly adept at capturing one's fancy,
displaying such charming artifice.
Yet she is indeed graceful and lovely;
my nephew's discernment is not mistaken."
She then said to the maidservant:
"Send the little cat to summon her here."
The maidservant assented and left.
After a while,
she entered and announced:
"I have summoned the Xīn family's Fourteenth Niang."
Presently, a young woman in red was seen,
bowing deeply before the old lady.
The old lady pulled her up, saying:
"Henceforth, you shall be my nephew's wife;
you need not perform the formalities of a maid."
The young woman rose,
standing gracefully,
her red sleeves hanging low.
The old lady smoothed her hair,
pinched her earlobe,
and said:
"What have you been doing lately in your chamber, Fourteenth Niang?"
The girl replied softly:
"In my leisure time, I merely do embroidery."
Turning her head, she saw the scholar and
shrank back shyly, ill at ease.
The old lady said:
"This is my nephew.
He earnestly wishes to marry you.
Why then did you lead him astray,
making him wander through streams and valleys all night long?"
The girl hung her head in silence.
The old lady said:
"I summoned you for no other reason
than to act as matchmaker for my nephew."
The girl remained silent.
The old lady ordered the bed to be prepared and the bedding spread out,
intending to have them perform the wedding ceremony immediately.
The girl demurred, saying:
"I must still inform my parents."
The old lady said:
"Since I am acting as your go-between,
what fault could there be?"
The girl said:
"My parents would not dare disobey the command of the Jùnjūn.
However, to proceed in such a hasty manner—
even if I were to die,
I would not dare obey such an order!"
The old lady laughed and said:
"This young lady's will cannot be swayed;
she truly is a fitting wife for my nephew!"
She then plucked a golden flower from the girl's hair
and handed it to the scholar for safekeeping.
She instructed him to return home and consult the almanac
to select an auspicious date for the wedding.
Then she sent the maidservant to escort the girl back.
Hearing the distant rooster crow,
she had someone lead the donkey to send the scholar off.
After walking a few paces,
he looked back
and found the village house had vanished;
all he saw were dense, dark pines and oaks,
with clumps of weeds covering grave mounds.
After pondering for a while,
he realized the place was the tomb of Minister Xuē.
Minister Xuē had been the younger brother of the scholar's late paternal grandmother,
hence he had addressed the scholar as nephew.
The scholar knew he had encountered a ghost,
but he still did not know who Fourteenth Niang was.
Sighing, he returned home
and casually checked the almanac while waiting,
though in his heart he feared a ghost's promise might be unreliable.
He went again to the temple,
but found the halls desolate and deserted.
Asking the local residents,
he learned that foxes were often seen in the temple.
He thought to himself: If I can obtain such a beauty,
even a fox would be fine.
On the appointed day,
he cleaned the rooms and swept the path,
repeatedly sending servants to watch into the distance.
By midnight, all was still silent.
The scholar had given up hope.
Shortly after,
a commotion arose outside the gate.
Slipping on his shoes, he went to look
and saw a bridal sedan had stopped in the courtyard,
with two maids supporting the girl as she sat in the wedding tent.
Her trousseau contained no extravagant items,
only two long-bearded servants carrying a large money-box,
as big as a jar,
which they set down in a corner of the hall.
Delighted to have obtained such a beautiful wife,
the scholar did not suspect she was of a different kind.
He asked the girl:
"That dead ghost—
why does your family obey her so readily?"
The girl replied:
"Minister Xuē has been appointed as the Patrol Commissioner of the Five Capitals;
all the ghosts and foxes for hundreds of li serve in his retinue,
so he seldom returns to his tomb."
The scholar did not forget the matchmaker.
The next day,
he went to offer sacrifices at the tomb.
Upon returning, he saw two maidservants
bringing brocaded silk as a congratulatory gift;
they simply placed it on the table and left.
The scholar told the girl about it,
and she, looking at it, said:
"This is the Jùnjūn's gift."
In the county, there was the son of Vice-Minister Chǔ,
who had studied together with the scholar in their youth
and was on familiar terms with him.
Hearing that the scholar had married a fox wife,
he sent gifts to celebrate
and came to the hall to offer toasts.
A few days later,
he sent a note inviting the scholar for a drink.
Hearing this, the girl said to the scholar:
"When the young master came before,
I peeked at him through a hole in the wall.
That man has the eyes of an ape and the nose of a hawk;
you should not associate with him for long.
It would be best not to go."
The scholar agreed.
The next day,
the young master came to the door,
demanding an explanation for breaking the appointment
and presenting some new poems.
The scholar made mocking comments about them,
greatly shaming the young master,
who left displeased.
Returning home,
the scholar laughingly recounted this in their room.
The girl said sorrowfully:
"That young master is a wolf;
you must not be familiar with him!
If you do not heed my words,
disaster will befall you!"
The scholar laughed and dismissed her concerns.
Later, when he and the young master met, they often exchanged flatteries and jokes,
and the previous incident was gradually forgotten.
During the Provincial Examination,
the young master placed first,
the scholar second.
The young master, smugly pleased with himself,
came to invite the scholar for a drink.
The scholar declined,
but after repeated invitations, he went.
Upon arrival, he learned it was the young master's birthday;
the hall was full of guests,
and the banquet was sumptuously laid out.
The young master showed his examination paper to the scholar.
Relatives and friends crowded around, sighing in admiration.
After several rounds of wine,
music was played in the hall,
but the drums and pipes were crude and vulgar.
Host and guests were merry,
when suddenly the young master said to the scholar:
"As the proverb says: 'In the examination hall, do not discuss literary merit.'
Now I know this saying is wrong.
The reason I humbly rank above you
is that the opening lines of my essay
are slightly superior."
Having said this,
all present praised him.
The scholar, drunk and unable to contain himself,
laughed loudly and said:
"Do you still, to this day,
believe your essay reached such heights?"
As soon as the scholar spoke,
everyone present changed color.
The young master, ashamed and furious, was choked with anger.
The guests gradually departed,
and the scholar also slipped away.
Sobering up, he regretted his words
and told the girl about it.
Unhappy, the girl said:
"You truly are a frivolous fellow from the countryside!
Such a flippant attitude,
if directed at a gentleman,
would cost you your virtue;
if directed at a petty man,
it would cost you your life.
Your calamity is not far off!
I cannot bear to see you brought to ruin,
so I shall take my leave from now on."
Frightened, the scholar wept
and told her of his remorse.
The girl said:
"If you wish me to stay,
I have a condition: from now on, shut your doors and cease socializing,
and do not indulge in reckless drinking."
Shēng respectfully accepted her instruction.
Shísìniáng was diligent, frugal, and free-spirited,
spending her days weaving as her occupation.
Occasionally, she would return to her parents' home,
but never stayed overnight.
She also often used gold and silk to manage their livelihood.
Whenever there was a surplus,
she would toss it into a piggy bank.
She kept the doors closed daily,
and if visitors came, she would instruct the old servant to decline them.
One day,
Chǔ Gōngzǐ sent a letter by express messenger,
but Shísìniáng burned it without letting Shēng know.
The next day,
Shēng went out to offer condolences in the city,
and encountered Gōngzǐ at the home of the bereaved.
Gōngzǐ grabbed his arm and earnestly invited him.
Shēng declined with an excuse.
Gōngzǐ had his groom take hold of the reins,
and escorted him along.
Upon arriving at Gōngzǐ's home,
he immediately ordered a lavish feast.
Shēng tried to excuse himself and leave early.
Gōngzǐ persistently blocked his way,
and brought out his household musicians to play the zhēng for entertainment.
Shēng, by nature unrestrained,
having been confined to his courtyard recently,
felt quite stifled and bored;
suddenly encountering heavy drinking,
his spirits soared,
and he no longer harbored any lingering concerns.
Consequently, he became thoroughly drunk,
and collapsed asleep on the mat.
Gōngzǐ's wife, Madame Ruǎn,
was extremely fierce and jealous,
and the maids and concubines dared not apply makeup.
A few days prior,
a maid had entered the study,
and was caught by Madame Ruǎn,
who struck her head with a stick,
splitting her skull and killing her instantly.
Gōngzǐ, bearing a grudge against Shēng for his mockery and disrespect,
had been thinking daily of how to get revenge,
and thus plotted to get him drunk and frame him.
Taking advantage of Shēng's drunken slumber,
they carried the corpse and placed it beside the bed,
then closed the door and left directly.
When Shēng sobered up at the fifth watch,
he first realized he was lying on a table;
getting up to look for his pillow and bed,
he felt something slippery,
entangling his steps;
feeling it,
it was a person: he thought the host had sent a servant boy to sleep with him.
He nudged it, but it didn't move and was stiff.
Greatly alarmed,
he ran out the door shouting in astonishment.
All the servants rushed over,
saw it,
and upon seeing the corpse,
seized Shēng angrily and made a commotion.
Gōngzǐ came out to examine it,
accused Shēng of forcing himself on the maid and killing her,
and had him arrested and sent to Guǎngpíng.
The next day,
Shísìniáng finally learned of it,
and said tearfully:
"I knew this day would come!"
She then sent money daily for Shēng to meet with the prefect,
but there was no justice to be had,
and he was beaten morning and night,
until his skin and flesh were completely torn.
Shísìniáng went personally to inquire.
When Shēng saw her,
sorrow choked his heart,
and he could not speak.
Knowing the trap was deep,
she advised him to falsely confess,
to avoid further torture.
Shēng tearfully obeyed.
During her comings and goings,
people within a short distance could not catch a glimpse of her.
Returning home, sighing with regret,
she immediately sent her maid away.
After living alone for several days,
she again entrusted a matchmaker to purchase a girl from a good family,
named Lù'ér,
who had just reached marriageable age,
and was quite beautiful;
she lived and ate with her,
treating her with affection unlike the other servants.
Shēng, having confessed to accidental killing, was sentenced to hanging.
The old servant brought the news back,
weeping so bitterly he could not speak coherently.
When Shísìniáng heard,
she remained calm as if it didn't concern her.
Later, when the autumn executions were approaching,
she finally became anxious and restless,
going out by day and returning by night,
without stopping her steps.
Often in quiet places,
she would lament sorrowfully,
to the point of losing sleep and appetite.
One day,
at dusk,
the fox maid suddenly arrived.
Shísìniáng immediately rose,
and led her aside for a private talk.
When she emerged, her face was full of smiles,
and she managed the household as usual.
the old servant went to the prison,
and Shēng sent a message asking his wife to come once for a final farewell.
The old servant reported back.
Shísìniáng responded casually,
showing no grief or sorrow,
treating it with remarkable indifference.
The family privately discussed her heartlessness.
Suddenly, news spread like wildfire: Chǔ Yíntái had been stripped of his rank;
and the Píngyáng Surveillance Commissioner had received a special decree to handle Féng Shēng's case.
When the old servant heard,
he joyfully informed his mistress.
Shísìniáng was also pleased,
and immediately sent someone to the prefecture to check,
where they found Shēng had already been released from prison.
They met, both sorrowful and joyful.
Soon, Gōngzǐ was arrested and brought in,
and after one interrogation,
the whole truth was revealed.
Shēng was immediately released and returned home.
Returning to see his wife inside,
tears streamed down his face,
and Shísìniáng also faced him with sorrow,
their grief turning to joy.
Yet, they still did not know how the matter had reached the emperor's ears.
Shísìniáng smiled, pointing at the maid, and said:
"This is your benefactor."
Féng Shēng was startled and asked the reason.
Previously,
the girl had sent a maidservant to Yāndū,
hoping to reach the imperial palace,
to plead Féng's injustice.
When the maidservant arrived,
she found the palace guarded by spirits,
and she wandered around the imperial moat,
unable to enter for several months.
Fearing she would fail in her mission,
she was about to return and devise another plan
when she suddenly heard that the emperor was going to visit Dàtóng.
The maidservant went ahead,
pretending to be a wandering courtesan.
When the emperor arrived at the pleasure quarters,
she received great favor and affection.
Suspecting that she did not seem like a woman of the demimonde,
the maidservant shed tears.
The emperor asked:
"What grievance do you have?"
The maidservant replied:
"I am originally from Guǎngpíng,
the daughter of a scholar named Féng.
My father is about to die due to an unjust imprisonment,
so I was sold into the pleasure quarters."
The emperor was deeply moved,
and bestowed a hundred taels of gold upon her.
As she was about to leave,
he inquired in detail about the whole story,
writing down the names with pen and paper;
and said he wished to share wealth and honor with her.
The maidservant said:
"I only wish for father and daughter to be reunited,
I do not desire splendor."
The emperor nodded,
and she departed.
The maidservant relayed this situation to Féng Shēng.
Féng Shēng hastily bowed,
tears streaming down his face.
Not long after,
the girl suddenly said to Féng Shēng:
"If I were not bound by emotional ties,
where would I find such troubles?
When you were arrested,
I rushed about among relatives and connections,
and not a single person offered any help.
The bitterness in my heart at that time,
truly cannot be described.
Now, looking upon the mundane world, I find it increasingly detestable and wearisome.
I have already secured a good match for you,
we may part from now on."
Upon hearing this,
Féng Shēng wept and prostrated himself, refusing to rise.
The girl then relented.
At night, she sent Lù'er to attend to Féng Shēng in his bedchamber,
but Féng Shēng refused and did not accept her.
In the morning, looking at Shísìniáng,
her radiant appearance had suddenly diminished;
after another month or so,
she gradually aged;
half a year later,
she became dark and wrinkled like a village crone: Féng Shēng respected her,
and never wavered.
The girl suddenly spoke of parting again,
and said:
"You already have a fine companion,
why keep this hag around?"
Féng Shēng wept sorrowfully as before.
Another month passed,
and the girl suddenly fell seriously ill,
refusing all food and drink,
lying emaciated in her boudoir.
Féng Shēng attended to her with medicine and soup,
as if serving his own parents.
Shamans and doctors were of no avail,
and she eventually passed away.
Féng Shēng was grief-stricken, almost to the point of death.
He then used the gold bestowed by the maidservant
to arrange for Buddhist services and burial.
A few days later,
the maidservant also left,
and so he took Lù'er as his wife.
A year later,
they had a son.
However, the harvests were poor year after year,
and the family became increasingly destitute.
Husband and wife had no plan,
facing their shadows in long sorrow.
Suddenly, Féng Shēng remembered the clay savings jar in the corner of the hall,
into which he had often seen Shísìniáng drop coins,
and wondered if it was still there.
Approaching to look,
he saw that pots for fermented beans and salt jars
were arranged almost filling the spot.
Moving them aside one by one,
he tried to probe inside with chopsticks,
but it was solid and impenetrable;
he smashed it,
and gold coins spilled out.
From then on, they suddenly became very well-off.
Later, an old servant went to Tàihuà Shān,
and encountered Shísìniáng,
riding a black mule,
with a maidservant following on a donkey.
She asked:
"Is Féng Láng well?"
And said:
"Convey my regards to your master,
I have already been registered among the immortals."
Having said this,
she disappeared.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Frivolous and disparaging words,
often come from the scholar class,
which is something gentlemen lament and regret.
I have often risked the reputation of being inappropriate,
speaking of injustice may already be considered pedantic;
yet I have never failed to strive diligently and encourage myself,
in hopes of joining the ranks of gentlemen,
and theories of fortune and misfortune are not part of this.
As for someone like Féng Shēng,
a single slight remark,
nearly cost him his life.
If not for having an immortal in his household,
how could he have escaped imprisonment,
to be reborn in this world?
How frightening!"
According to the manuscript version of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
There was a certain follower of the White Lotus Sect,
from Shānxī,
whose name is forgotten,
probably a disciple of Xú Hóngrú.
Using heterodox teachings to delude the masses,
many who admired his arts took him as their teacher.
One day, he was about to go elsewhere,
and placed a basin in the hall,
with another basin covering it,
instructing his disciples to sit and guard it,
warning them not to open it to look.
After he left,
the disciples opened it,
and saw the basin contained clear water,
with a grass boat floating on the water,
complete with sails and masts.
and it tilted over immediately;
they hurriedly righted it as before,
and covered it again.
Soon the master returned,
angrily rebuking them:
"Why did you disobey my command?"
The disciples immediately protested their innocence.
The master said:
"Just now a boat capsized in the sea,
how can you deceive me?"
Another evening,
he lit a large candle in the hall,
instructing them to guard it diligently,
and not let the wind blow it out.
After the second watch,
the master had not returned.
Feeling weary,
they lay on the bed for a brief nap;
upon waking,
the candle had already gone out,
and they hurriedly relit it.
Soon the master entered,
and rebuked them again.
The disciples said:
"We certainly did not sleep,
how could the candle have gone out?"
The master angrily said:
"Just now you made me walk over ten miles in darkness,
and you still say such things?"
The disciples were greatly astonished.
Such strange deeds,
are too numerous to record.
Later, he had a beloved concubine who had an affair with one of his disciples.
When he discovered it,
he kept it hidden and said nothing.
He sent the disciple to feed the pigs;
the disciple entered the pen,
and immediately transformed into a pig.
He then called for a butcher to slaughter it,
and sold the meat.
No one knew about this.
The disciple’s father, wondering why his son had not returned,
came to inquire,
but he was told that the disciple had not been seen for a long time.
The disciple’s family searched everywhere,
but found no trace of him.
A fellow disciple,
who secretly knew about the matter,
revealed it to the disciple’s father.
The disciple’s father reported it to the county magistrate.
Fearing that he might flee,
the magistrate did not dare to arrest him;
instead, he reported it to his superior,
requesting a thousand armored soldiers,
who surrounded his residence,
and his wife and children were all captured.
They were confined in cages,
to be transported to the capital.
On the way, they passed through the Tàiháng Mountains,
where a giant emerged from the mountains,
as tall as a tree,
with eyes like basins,
a mouth like a pot,
and teeth over a foot long.
The soldiers stood frozen in fear, not daring to move.
He said:
"This is a monster,
my wife can repel it."
Following his words,
they untied his wife.
His wife took up a spear and went forward.
The giant grew angry,
sucked her in, and swallowed her.
The crowd grew even more terrified.
He said:
"Since he has killed my wife,
he must now take my son."
They then brought out his son,
who was also swallowed,
just as before.
Everyone looked at each other,
not knowing what to do.
He wept and said angrily:
"He has killed my wife,
and now my son;
how can I bear this!
But unless I go myself, it cannot be done."
They indeed took him out of the cage,
gave him a blade, and sent him off.
The giant met him with fierce anger.
They fought for a while,
then the giant grabbed him, put him in its mouth,
stretched its neck, and swallowed him,
then calmly walked away.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wèi Yùnwàng,
a native of Pénguán in Yìdū,
was from an old, prominent family.
Later, the family declined,
and he could no longer afford to study.
In his twenties,
he gave up his studies
and went to work for his father-in-law in the wine trade.
One evening,
Wèi was lying alone in the wine shop’s upstairs room,
when he suddenly heard footsteps downstairs.
Startled, he got up and listened intently.
The sound grew closer,
ascending the stairs,
each step echoing loudly.
Before long,
two maids appeared holding lanterns,
and stood by his bed.
Behind them was a young scholar,
leading a maiden,
who approached the bed and smiled.
Wèi was greatly astonished.
Realizing they were foxes,
he felt his hair stand on end,
and bowed his head, not daring to look.
The scholar said with a laugh:
"Do not be suspicious.
My younger sister has a predestined bond with you,
and is thus meant to serve you."
Wèi looked at the scholar,
whose brocade and sable dazzled the eye,
and felt ashamed of his own shabbiness,
too embarrassed to reply.
The scholar left with the maids, taking the lanterns.
Wèi examined the maiden closely;
she was delicate and lovely as a fairy,
and he was very pleased.
Yet, feeling ashamed, he could not bring himself to flirt.
The maiden looked back at him and laughed:
"You are not some wooden-headed scholar,
why act so stiff?"
She then approached the bed,
warming her hands in his embrace.
Only then did Wèi’s expression soften,
and they teased each other, loosening their clothes,
and became intimate.
Before the morning bell had sounded,
the two maids came to lead her away.
They arranged to meet again that night.
When evening came,
the maiden indeed arrived,
and said with a laugh:
"What fortune, foolish man,
without spending a single coin,
to gain such a fine wife,
who comes to you night after night on her own."
Delighted to be alone,
Wèi set out wine and drank with her,
playing finger-guessing games.
The maiden won nineteen out of twenty rounds.
She then laughed and said:
"Why not let me hide the token,
and you guess where it is?
If you guess right, you win,
if not, you lose.
If I were to guess,
you would never win."
They did as she said,
and enjoyed themselves all night.
When they were about to sleep,
she said:
"Last night the bedding was cold and rough,
quite unbearable."
She then called for the maids to bring bedding,
which they spread on the bed,
fragrant and elegant.
Soon after,
they loosened their garments and embraced,
her fragrant breath enveloping him—
truly a rival to the legendary "Land of Gentle Bliss."
From then on,
this became their routine.
Half a year later,
Wèi returned home.
One moonlit night, as he was talking with his wife by the window,
he suddenly saw the maiden, splendidly dressed, sitting on the wall,
beckoning to him with her hand.
Wèi approached her.
She helped him,
and they climbed over the wall,
where she took his hand and said:
"Now I must bid you farewell.
Please walk with me a few steps,
to mark the affection of these past six months."
Startled, Wèi asked the reason,
but she said:
"Marriage bonds are predetermined by fate;
what more is there to say?"
As they spoke,
they reached the outskirts of the village,
where the maids waited with two lanterns;
they then headed for the southern mountains,
climbed to a high place,
and there she bade Wèi farewell.
Wèi could not persuade her to stay,
and she departed.
Wèi stood there, bewildered,
watching the two lanterns flicker in the distance,
until they gradually vanished from sight,
and he returned, heavy-hearted.
That night, the lanterns on the mountain
were seen by all the villagers.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Lǐ Gōng Zhùmíng was the son of Magistrate Jīn Zhuó of Suīníng County.
He was a man of bold and forthright character, never cowed or timid.
He was the brother-in-law of Wáng Jìliáng of Xīnchéng.
Mr. Wang’s residence had many towers and pavilions,
and strange phenomena were often witnessed there.
Once, during the summer, Gōng came to stay as a guest.
He enjoyed the cool evening air in a tower,
and though someone tried to dissuade him from staying there because of the strange happenings,
Gōng laughed and paid no heed,
insisting that a bed be set up for him.
The host complied with his request
and instructed servants to sleep with him,
but Gōng declined, saying,
“I like to sleep alone and have never known fear in my life.”
The host then had incense lit in a burner,
inquired how he wished to arrange the bedding,
and finally extinguished the candle, closed the door, and left.
Gōng had just laid his head on the pillow when,
in the moonlight,
he saw a teacup on the table
tilt and spin around
without falling or stopping.
Gōng shouted at it,
and it clattered to a halt.
Then it seemed as if someone pulled out the incense stick
and waved it in the air,
trailing patterns of flowery strands.
Gōng rose and shouted,
“What kind of demon dares to act like this!”
He threw off the covers and got out of bed,
intending to seize it.
Feeling around under the bed with his foot,
he found only one shoe.
Not taking time to search carefully in the dark,
he struck at the place where the incense was being waved with his bare foot.
The incense stick was abruptly thrust back into the burner,
and all became quiet with no further sign.
Gōng bent down and felt around every dark corner.
Suddenly something flew up and struck him on the cheek;
it felt like a shoe.
He searched for it but could not find it.
He then opened the door and went downstairs,
calling for his attendants to bring a torch.
They found nothing,
so he went back to bed.
At daybreak,
he had several people search for the shoe.
They turned over the mat and the bed but could not find it.
The host gave Gōng another pair of shoes.
The next day,
Gōng happened to look up
and saw a shoe wedged between the rafters.
He poked it down with a pole—it was indeed his shoe.
Gōng was originally from Yìdū but was staying in the Sūn family residence in Zībó.
The estate was extremely spacious,
with many vacant areas;
Gōng occupied only half of it.
The southern courtyard faced a tall tower,
separated only by a wall.
From time to time, the tower door was seen opening and closing by itself,
but Gōng paid it no mind.
Once, while talking with his family in the courtyard,
he saw the tower door open
and suddenly a little man,
facing north and seated,
less than three feet tall,
wearing a green robe and white socks.
Everyone pointed and stared at him,
but he did not move.
Gōng said,
“This is a fox spirit.”
He quickly fetched a bow and arrows
and aimed at the open door, intending to shoot.
The little man saw this
and made a mocking, jeering sound,
then disappeared.
Gōng grabbed a knife and climbed the tower,
cursing and searching as he went,
but found nothing and returned.
After that, the strange occurrences ceased.
Gōng lived there for several years,
peaceful and unharmed.
Gōng’s eldest son, Yǒusān,
was related to me by marriage,
and he witnessed these events.
The Chronicler of the Tales remarks:
“I was born too late
to have had the honor of serving Gōng,
but from what I have heard from the elders,
he was by and large a generous, resolute, and stalwart man.
These two incidents give a glimpse of his character.
When one’s heart is filled with uprightness,
what have ghosts and foxes to do with him!”
From the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Lǐ Gōng Zhùmíng was generous and fond of helping others.
A certain villager
worked as a tenant in Gōng’s house.
This man had been idle and lazy since youth,
unable to manage farming,
and his family was extremely poor.
However, he had some minor skills
and often performed odd jobs,
for which Gōng always rewarded him generously.
Whenever he had no food for the morning meal,
he would go to Gōng and plead pitifully,
and Gōng would give him a measure of grain.
One day,
he said to Gōng,
“I receive your generous aid daily,
and my family of three or four is fortunate not to starve;
but how can this go on forever?
I beg you, master, to lend me a picul of beans as capital.”
Gōng gladly agreed and immediately ordered it given to him.
The man carried it away,
and after more than a year,
he had not repaid anything.
When asked about it,
he said the bean capital had already been exhausted.
Gōng took pity on his poverty
and did not press him for repayment.
Gōng was studying at a Buddhist temple.
More than three years later,
he suddenly dreamed that the man came to him and said,
“I owe you the value of the beans,
and now I have come to repay it.”
Gōng comforted him, saying,
“If I demanded repayment from you,
how could all the debts you have incurred over the years ever be counted?”
The man said sorrowfully,
“That is true.
If a man receives a thousand pieces of gold for something he has done,
he may not repay it.
But if he receives aid for no reason,
even a measure of grain should not be forgotten,
let alone a larger amount!”
Having said this, he left.
Gōng was even more puzzled.
Soon afterward, a servant reported to Gōng,
“Last night, the donkey gave birth to a foal,
and it is quite sturdy and tall.”
Gōng suddenly realized and said,
“Could it be that the foal is that man?”
A few days later, he returned home,
saw the foal,
and playfully called it by the man’s name.
The foal ran over to him
as if it understood.
From then on, that became its name.
Gōng rode it to Qīngzhōu,
where a eunuch from the Héng princely estate saw it and liked it,
wishing to buy it for a high price.
They had not yet settled on a sum
when Gōng had to return home due to urgent family matters.
Another year passed,
and the foal, kept in the same stable as a stallion,
broke a leg bone
and could not be cured.
An ox doctor came to Gōng’s house,
saw it,
and said to Gōng,
“I beg you to entrust the foal to me.
I will tend and nurse it day and night,
though it will take time.
If by chance it recovers,
the proceeds from its sale will be divided equally with you.”
Gōng agreed as requested.
Several months later,
the ox doctor sold the donkey
for 1,800 coins
and gave half to Gōng.
When Gōng received the money,
he suddenly realized
that the amount exactly matched the price of the beans.
Alas!
A debt incurred in the clear light of day
was repaid in the obscurity of the unseen realm.
This is enough to encourage people.
From the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
From the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Scholar Dù Jiǔwǎn’s
wife fell ill.
It happened to be the Double Ninth Festival,
and he was invited by a friend to a dogwood gathering.
He rose early,
washed up,
and told his wife where he was going.
Just as he was dressed and about to leave,
he suddenly saw his wife fall into a daze,
muttering as if speaking to someone.
Dù found this strange
and approached the bed to ask about it.
His wife then
called him
"son."
The family members sensed something was amiss.
At the time, Dù’s mother’s coffin had not yet been buried,
so he suspected her spirit might be possessing his wife.
Dù prayed, saying:
"Could it be my mother?"
His wife scolded:
"You beast! Why don’t you recognize your own father?"
Dù said:
"If you are my father,
why have you come home to haunt your daughter-in-law?"
His wife called him by his childhood name, saying:
"I came specifically for your wife.
Why do you resent me instead?
Your wife was supposed to die;
four people came to take her away,
led by Zhāng Huáiyù.
I pleaded with them endlessly,
and only then did they agree.
I promised them a small offering,
so you should give it to them promptly."
Dù did as told,
burning paper money outside the door.
His wife spoke again:
"The four have left.
They couldn’t bear to refuse my face,
so in three days,
we must prepare a feast to thank them.
Your mother is old,
frail and unable to manage the kitchen.
When the time comes,
we’ll still need your wife to go."
Dù said:
"The realms of the living and the dead are separate;
how can she take over the cooking?
I beg you, Father, to forgive us."
His wife said:
"Don’t be afraid, son.
She’ll go and return quickly.
This is her duty,
so she shouldn’t fear the toil."
With that,
she fell unconscious
and only revived after a long while.
Dù asked what she had said,
but she had no memory of it.
She only said:
"Just now, four people came
to seize me.
Fortunately, Father-in-law pleaded for me
and even took out money to bribe them,
so they left.
I saw that Father-in-law still had two ingots left in his money pouch,
and I wanted to steal one
to help with our livelihood.
But he caught sight of me
and scolded: ‘What are you trying to do?
This is not something you can use!’
So I withdrew my hand and dared not move."
Dù, seeing his wife critically ill,
was half-convinced and half-doubtful.
Three days later,
while they were chatting and laughing,
she suddenly stared wide-eyed for a long time
and said:
"Your wife is terribly greedy.
Earlier, when she saw my silver,
she coveted it.
But mainly it’s because of poverty,
so it’s not worth blaming.
I’ll take her with me
to help with the kitchen duties.
Don’t worry."
As soon as she finished speaking,
she suddenly died.
After about half a day,
she revived
and told Dù:
"Just now, Father-in-law called me over
and said: ‘You don’t need to do any work.
I have people to handle the cooking.
You just need to sit firmly and give instructions.’
In the underworld, we prefer abundance,
so all the dishes should overflow beyond the plates.
Be sure to remember this.’
I agreed.
When I went to the kitchen,
I saw two women working with knives and cutting boards,
both wearing dark blue cloaks with green trim.
They called me sister-in-law.
Every time they served a roasted dish in a guǐ,
they would ask me to inspect it.
The four from earlier were all at the banquet.
After the dishes were served,
and the wine vessels were arranged,
Father-in-law told me to return."
Dù was greatly astonished
and often spoke of this to his friends.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In Láiwú, there was a man named Zhāng Xūyī,
the second elder brother of Education Commissioner Zhāng Dàoyī.
He was by nature unrestrained and free-spirited.
Hearing that a certain house in the county
was inhabited by foxes,
he respectfully prepared a name card and went to visit,
hoping to meet them.
He presented his card.
After a while,
the door opened by itself.
His servant was greatly startled
and stepped back.
Zhāng straightened his clothes and entered respectfully.
He saw tables and couches in the hall, all in order,
but it was silent and empty.
He bowed and prayed:
"I, a humble scholar, have come after fasting and purification.
Since the immortal has not rejected me outside the gate,
why not grace me with your presence?"
Suddenly, a voice was heard from the empty room:
"Thank you for your visit.
It is truly a welcome sound of footsteps.
Please sit and grant me your teachings."
Immediately, two seats moved to face each other.
As soon as he sat down,
a carved lacquer tray
holding two teacups
appeared before him.
They each took one and drank,
sipping audibly,
but the other person remained unseen.
After tea,
wine was served.
When Zhāng inquired about his background,
he replied:
"My humble surname is Hú,
and I am the fourth among my siblings.
Call me Xiànggong,
as others do."
They then toasted and conversed,
finding their temperaments quite compatible.
Dishes of turtle and dried venison
were mixed with fragrant herbs.
Those serving wine and roasted meats
seemed to be many young attendants.
After drinking, Zhāng felt like having tea,
and as soon as the thought arose,
fragrant tea was already placed on the table.
Whatever he thought of,
it would appear as soon as he wished for it.
Zhāng was delighted
and only returned after getting thoroughly drunk.
From then on, he would visit Hú every few days,
and Hú would also visit Zhāng’s home from time to time,
both treating each other with the courtesy of host and guest.
One day,
Zhāng asked Hú,
"In the southern city, there is a witch
who daily uses the fox spirit to swindle money from sick families.
I don't know if the fox in her household
is known to you, sir?"
He replied,
"She is lying;
there is actually no fox."
A short while later,
Zhāng got up to relieve himself
and heard a small voice say,
"Regarding what was just said about the fox witch in the southern city,
I don't know what kind of person she is.
I wish to follow you, sir, to go and observe her,
and I trouble you to ask the master for permission."
Zhāng knew it was a little fox
and replied,
"Agreed."
He then returned to his seat and requested of the fox,
"I wish to have one or two of your attendants
to go and investigate the fox witch,
and I respectfully ask for your permission."
The fox insisted it was unnecessary.
Zhāng repeated his request several times,
and only then did he agree.
After Zhāng went out,
a horse came on its own,
as if someone were leading it.
Once he mounted and rode off,
the foxes spoke to each other along the way,
saying to Zhāng,
"When you, sir, are on the road later,
if you feel fine sand scattered on your clothes,
that will be us following you."
As they spoke, they entered the city
and arrived at the witch's house.
When the witch saw Zhāng arrive,
she greeted him with a smile, saying,
"Why has the noble one suddenly come to visit?"
Zhāng said,
"I heard that the fox in your household is very efficacious;
is that true?"
The witch put on a serious expression and said,
"Such frivolous words
should not come from a noble person!
How can you speak of 'fox' so casually?
I fear my Huā Jiě will be displeased!"
Before she finished speaking,
half a brick flew from the air,
hitting the witch's arm,
and she staggered, about to fall.
Shocked, she said to Zhāng,
"Why did you, sir, throw something and hit this old woman?"
Zhāng laughed and said,
"You old woman are blind!
When have you ever seen someone with a broken forehead
falsely accuse a bystander?"
The witch was bewildered and didn't know what was happening.
As she was still confused,
another stone fell,
hitting the witch,
and she stumbled and fell;
filthy mud rained down,
smearing her face like a ghost's.
She could only wail and beg for mercy.
Zhāng requested that she be spared,
and it stopped.
The witch hurriedly got up and ran,
fled into her room,
and closed the door, not daring to come out.
Zhāng called out to her and said,
"Is your fox like my fox?"
The witch could only apologize.
Zhāng looked up into the air
and warned not to harm the witch again,
and only then did the witch cautiously come out.
Zhāng laughed and admonished her,
then returned.
From then on, whenever he traveled alone on the road,
if he felt dust and sand rustling,
he would call out to the foxes to speak,
and they would always respond without fail.
Whether facing tigers, wolves, or violent bandits,
he relied on them and had no fear.
This went on for over a year,
and he became even closer with Hú.
Once he asked Hú his age,
but he couldn't remember at all,
only saying,
"I remember Huáng Cháo's rebellion
as if it were yesterday."
One evening as they were talking,
suddenly there was a rustling sound from the top of the wall,
and the noise was very loud.
Zhāng found it strange,
and Hú said,
"This must be my elder brother."
Zhāng said,
"Why not invite him to join us?"
Hú said,
"His cultivation is rather shallow;
he only knows how to snatch chickens to eat,
and that's enough for him."
Zhāng said to the fox,
"The friendship between us two
can be said to be without regret;
however,
I have never once seen your face,
which is truly a pity."
Hú said,
"As long as we have a good friendship, that is enough;
what is the point of meeting face-to-face?"
One day,
Hú prepared wine and invited Zhāng,
and also bid farewell.
Zhāng asked,
"Where are you going?"
Hú said,
"I was born in Shǎnzhōng,
and I am returning there.
You have often regretted not seeing my face,
so now I ask you to recognize a friend of several years,
so that in the future we may recognize each other."
Zhāng looked around but saw nothing.
Hú said,
"Please try opening the bedroom door,
and I will be there."
Zhāng pushed the door open and took a look,
and inside was a handsome young man,
who looked at him and smiled.
His clothes were elegant,
and his features were as if painted.
In the blink of an eye,
he was no longer visible.
Zhāng turned and walked away,
and immediately there was the sound of footsteps following behind him,
saying,
"Today I have relieved your regret."
Zhāng was reluctant to part.
The fox said,
"Partings and reunions are fated;
why be troubled by it?"
He then urged Zhāng to drink with a large cup.
They drank until midnight,
and then Hú escorted Zhāng back with a lantern.
When Zhāng went to visit the next morning,
the house was empty and desolate.
Later, Dào Yī Xiānshēng became the education commissioner of Sìchuān.
Zhāng was still as poor as before,
so he went to visit his brother,
with high hopes.
After over a month, he returned,
very disappointed with the outcome,
sighing on horseback,
dejected as if he had lost his soul.
Suddenly, a young man riding a black colt
caught up with him from behind.
Zhāng looked back
and saw that his furs and horse were very fine,
and his demeanor was refined,
so he spoke with him.
The young man noticed Zhāng was unhappy
and asked him why.
Zhāng sighed and told him the reason.
The young man also comforted him.
They traveled together for about a lǐ,
and when they reached a fork in the road,
the young man clasped his hands and bid farewell,
saying,
"Ahead on the road, there is someone
who will deliver something to you from an old friend;
please accept it with a smile."
Before Zhāng could ask further,
he galloped away on his horse.
Zhāng didn't understand what was happening.
After another two or three lǐ,
he saw an old servant
holding a small box,
who presented it before his horse, saying,
"Hú Sì Xiànggong respectfully sends this to you, sir."
Zhāng suddenly understood.
He accepted it and opened it to look,
and it was filled with silver.
When he turned to look at the old servant,
he had already disappeared.
Based on the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì."
The Historian of the Strange remarks: Human feelings are as treacherous as ghosts and demons,
found everywhere;
but on the main thoroughfares between north and south,
the harm is especially severe.
Those who, like strong bows and spirited horses,
rob people outside the city gates—
everyone knows about them.
Then there are those who carry hidden daggers in their bags,
snatching goods in the market;
a traveler turns his head,
and his wealth is already gone.
Are these not the most ghostly and demonic of all?
Yet there are also those who meet by chance like duckweed on water,
their sweet words like fine wine.
Their approach is gradual,
their penetration deep.
Mistaking them for friends met by chance,
one thus falls victim to the disaster of losing one's resources.
They set traps according to opportunity,
their methods varying;
common folk, because their words seep in gradually,
call them
"Niànyāng."
Now there are many of them on the northern routes,
and those who suffer from them are especially numerous.
In my hometown, there was a man named Wáng Zǐxùn,
a county scholar.
He had a clansman elder serving in the capital as a Grand Historiographer of the Bannermen registry,
and he planned to go visit him.
Preparing his luggage, he headed north,
left Jǐnán,
and traveled several li when
a man riding a black donkey
caught up and traveled alongside him.
From time to time, he engaged Wáng in casual conversation,
and Wáng responded quite readily.
The man said of himself:
"My surname is Zhāng,
I am a runner from Qīxiá,
dispatched by the magistrate on official business to the capital."
His manner of address was humble and obsequious,
attentive and eager to please.
He followed along for several tens of li,
proposing they lodge together.
When Wáng was ahead,
he whipped his donkey to catch up;
when behind,
he waited respectfully by the roadside.
Wáng's servant grew suspicious
and sternly refused him, driving him away,
not allowing him to follow.
Zhāng appeared quite ashamed,
flicked his whip, and left.
When dusk fell,
they rested at an inn.
Wáng happened to stroll to the courtyard gate
and saw Zhāng drinking in the outer quarters.
Just as he was startled and suspicious,
Zhāng spotted Wáng,
dropped his hands and stood respectfully with clasped hands,
humble as a servant,
