and exchanged a few words of greeting.
Wáng also thought it was merely a chance encounter,
and did not suspect anything,
but his servant remained on guard all night.
When the rooster crowed,
Zhāng came to call them to travel together.
The servant rebuked him and refused,
so he left.
The morning sun was already up
when Wáng finally set out.
After traveling about half a day,
ahead was a man riding a white donkey,
around forty years old,
neatly dressed;
his head drooped, nodding off,
drowsy and about to fall.
Sometimes he was ahead,
sometimes behind,
drifting along for over ten li.
Wáng, finding it strange, asked:
"What did you do last night,
to be so dazed and weary like this?"
The man, hearing this,
suddenly stretched and yawned,
saying:
"I am from Qīngyuàn,
surname Xǔ.
The magistrate of Línzī, Gāo Qíng, is my cousin.
My elder brother is a private tutor in the yamen,
I went to visit him,
and received a few gifts.
Last night at the inn,
I mistakenly lodged with a Niànyāng,
so alarmed and wary I dared not close my eyes,
hence I am drowsy and muddled in broad daylight."
Wáng deliberately asked:
"What does 'Niànyāng' mean?"
Xǔ said:
"You, sir, have little travel experience,
and are unaware of the dangers and deceptions.
Now there are villainous types
who use sweet words to lure travelers,
ingratiate themselves to lodge together,
and then seize the opportunity to cheat and swindle.
Yesterday, a distant relative of mine
lost his travel funds this way.
We all should be on guard."
Wáng nodded.
Earlier,
the magistrate of Línzī and Wáng were old acquaintances,
Wáng had once served in his retinue,
and knew there indeed was a tutor surnamed Xǔ among his staff,
so he no longer doubted.
They exchanged pleasantries about the weather,
and Wáng also inquired about his brother's situation.
Xǔ proposed they share lodging that evening,
and Wáng agreed.
The servant remained suspicious of his falseness,
secretly plotted with his master,
delayed and did not advance,
so they became separated,
and Xǔ vanished.
The next day,
at high noon,
they met another youth,
about sixteen or seventeen years old,
riding a sturdy mule,
his hat and clothes elegant and neat,
his appearance very handsome.
They traveled together for a long time
without exchanging a single word.
When the sun was in the west,
the youth suddenly said:
"The Qūlǜdiàn ahead is not far."
Wáng faintly acknowledged.
The youth then sighed and sobbed,
as if unable to bear it.
Wáng briefly questioned him.
The youth sighed and said:
"I am from Jiāngnán, surname Jīn.
Three years of burning the midnight oil,
hoping to pass the examinations,
never imagined I would actually fail!
My elder brother is a Director in one of the Ministries,
so I brought my family along,
hoping to find some distraction.
Unaccustomed to traveling all my life,
the dust and sand blowing in my face
make me utterly vexed."
He took out a red handkerchief to wipe his face,
sighing and lamenting incessantly.
Listening to his speech,
he had a southern accent,
soft and delicate like a woman's.
Wáng took a liking to him,
and offered some words of comfort.
The youth said:
"Just now I rode ahead,
my family has been waiting long without my return,
why haven't my servants arrived either?
The sun is about to set,
what shall I do!"
He lingered, looking ahead,
walking very slowly.
Wáng then went ahead,
and the distance between them gradually widened.
Late, they arrived at an inn.
Upon entering the room,
they saw a bed against the wall,
where another traveler had already unpacked his belongings.
Wáng asked the innkeeper.
Immediately, a man entered,
took the traveler by the hand, and led him out,
saying:
"Please make yourself comfortable;
I will move him elsewhere."
Wáng looked at the traveler—
it was Xǔ.
Wáng stopped him and insisted they share the room,
so Xǔ stayed.
They sat down to talk.
After a short while,
another traveler entered with his luggage.
Seeing Wáng and Xǔ in the room,
he turned and hurried out,
saying:
"There are already guests here."
Wáng looked closely—
it was the young man from the road.
Before Wáng could speak,
Xǔ quickly rose and pulled him back,
so the young man sat down.
Xǔ then inquired about his background,
and the young man repeated what he had told Xǔ on the road.
Soon after,
he opened his purse and took out money,
a considerable amount;
he weighed out over two taels,
handed it to the innkeeper,
and asked him to prepare food and wine
for an evening conversation.
The other two tried to dissuade him,
but he would not listen.
Before long, wine and roasted meat were served.
During the meal,
the young man discussed literature with great elegance.
Wáng asked about the examination topics in Jiāngnán,
and the young man told him everything.
He even recited his own opening arguments
and the lines from his essay he was most proud of.
After speaking,
he seemed deeply resentful.
They all shared his frustration.
The young man also mentioned that he had become separated from his family,
had no servants for the night,
and was worried about not knowing how to tend to the horses.
Wáng then ordered his servant to take care of the fodder.
The young man was very grateful.
Not long after,
he suddenly stomped his foot and said:
"My life has been full of setbacks,
and even traveling brings no good fortune.
Last night at the inn, I shared a room with a scoundrel
who threw dice and shouted,
making such a racket it disturbed my peace
and kept me awake."
In the southern dialect, dice are called "dōu,"
which Xǔ did not understand,
so he pressed for an explanation.
The young man gestured to mimic the shape.
Xǔ then laughed,
took a die from his bag,
and said:
"Is this it?"
The young man confirmed.
Xǔ then proposed using the die for a drinking game,
and they drank merrily.
When the wine was nearly finished,
Xǔ suggested they play dice,
with the loser treating everyone.
Wáng declined, saying he did not know how.
Xǔ then played dice with the young man, shouting bets.
He secretly told Wáng:
"Don't say a word.
This southern lad is quite well-off,
and he's young,
so he probably doesn't know the tricks of dice.
I'll win a bit from him,
and tomorrow I'll treat you."
The two then went into the adjoining room.
Soon, the clamor of gambling grew loud.
Wáng peeked in
and saw the clerk from Qīxiá among them.
Greatly suspicious,
he spread out his quilt and lay down to sleep.
After a while,
the others tried to pull Wáng into the game.
Wáng firmly refused, saying he did not know how.
Xǔ offered to play on his behalf,
but Wáng still refused.
So they forced him to let Xǔ play for him.
After a short while,
Xǔ came to the bed and told Wáng:
"You've won a few rounds."
Wáng answered half-asleep.
Suddenly, several men pushed the door open and entered,
speaking in a foreign tongue.
Their leader said his surname was Tóng
and that he was a banner officer sent to arrest gamblers.
Gambling was strictly forbidden at the time,
so everyone was terrified.
Tóng shouted threats at Wáng,
but Wáng countered by mentioning his status as a member of the Imperial Academy.
Tóng's anger subsided,
and he found common ground with Wáng as fellow countrymen.
He laughingly suggested they resume gambling for fun.
The others, still stunned, started gambling again,
and Tóng joined in.
Wáng said to Xǔ:
"I don't want to hear about wins or losses.
I just want to sleep,
so don't disturb me."
Xǔ ignored him
and kept coming over to report.
When the game ended,
they tallied the scores,
and Wáng owed a considerable amount.
Tóng then searched Wáng's luggage to collect the debt.
Wáng angrily protested.
The young man grabbed Wáng's arm
and whispered:
"These men are scoundrels,
and their intentions are unfathomable.
We are scholarly friends,
and we must look out for each other.
Just now in the game, I won a certain amount,
which can offset your debt.
This is what should be collected from Xǔ,
so let's switch it: have Xǔ pay Tóng,
and you pay me.
This is just to deceive the others for now;
after this, I'll return it to you.
After all,
how could a friend bound by duty and righteousness
actually take payment from you?"
Wáng, being honest and kind-hearted,
believed him.
The young man went out
and told Tóng about the plan to switch debts.
Then, in front of everyone, they opened Wáng's luggage
and estimated its value into their own bags.
Tóng then turned to demand payment from Xǔ and the clerk before leaving.
The young man was then brought in,
and shared a pillow with Wáng;
the quilts and bedding were all exquisite.
Wáng also invited the servant to sleep on the couch,
and each lay quietly resting on their pillows.
After a long while,
the young man deliberately turned over,
pressing his lower body against the servant.
The servant shifted away to avoid him;
the young man approached again,
his skin touching the servant's thigh,
smooth and greasy like fat.
The servant's heart stirred,
and he tried to engage in intimacy;
the young man was exceedingly eager,
and the quilts rustled with movement.
Wáng heard it quite clearly,
and though he was greatly shocked and puzzled,
he never suspected anything else.
At daybreak,
the young man got up immediately,
urging them to leave early.
He also said:
"You are weary and exhausted,
the things entrusted to me last night,
I will hand them over to you ahead on the road."
Wáng had not yet spoken,
when the young man had already packed and mounted his horse.
Wáng had no choice,
but to follow him.
The mule moved swiftly,
and they gradually went far away.
Wáng thought he would wait for them ahead,
and initially did not mind.
Then he asked the servant about what he had heard during the night,
and the servant told him the truth.
Only then did Wáng exclaim in alarm:
"Now we have been deceived by swindlers!
How could a scholar-official of a distinguished family
seek intimacy with a servant?"
But then he reconsidered that the young man's speech was elegant and refined,
which swindlers could not manage.
He hurriedly pursued for dozens of miles,
but there was no trace at all.
Only then did he realize that Zhāng, Xǔ, and Tóng were all part of the same gang,
if one scheme did not work,
they would switch to another,
determined to ensnare their target.
Repaying the debt and changing clothes
had already concealed a plan to cheat;
if the scheme of carrying the luggage did not work,
they would surely have seized it by force and fled.
For a few dozen taels of silver,
they trailed for hundreds of miles;
fearing the servant would expose their plot,
they used their bodies to win his favor,
their methods were indeed desperate.
Several years later,
there was the affair of Mr. Wú.
In the county, there was a Mr. Wú,
styled Ānrén.
At thirty, he lost his spouse,
and slept alone in an empty study.
A xiùcai came to chat with him,
and they became close friends.
He had a young servant,
named Guǐtóu,
who also got along well with Wú's servant, Bào'ér.
After a long time, they realized he was a fox spirit.
Whenever Wú traveled far,
he would always accompany him.
In the same room,
others could not see him.
When Wú was a guest in the capital,
about to return home,
he heard that Mr. Wáng had suffered from swindlers,
so he warned his servant to be on guard.
The fox laughed and said:
"No need,
this journey will be without misfortune."
When they reached Zhuō,
a man was sitting in a tobacco shop with his horse tied up,
wearing elegant fur clothing.
Seeing Wú pass by,
he also stood up,
mounted his horse and followed him.
Gradually, he spoke with Wú,
saying of himself:
"My surname is Huáng, from Shāndōng,
serving in the Ministry of Revenue.
I am returning east,
and am glad to have company on the road, so it won't be lonely."
Thus, whenever Wú stopped, he stopped too;
every time they ate together,
he would always pay for Wú.
Wú outwardly felt grateful but inwardly suspected him.
Privately, he asked the fox,
but the fox only said:
"It's fine."
Wú's mind was then put at ease.
By evening,
they looked for lodging together,
and a handsome young man was already sitting inside.
Huáng entered,
and exchanged greetings with him.
He happily asked the young man:
"When did you leave the capital?"
The reply was:
"Yesterday."
Huáng then pulled him to stay together.
Turning to Wú, he said:
"This is Shǐ Láng,
my cousin,
also a man of letters,
he can assist you in discussing poetry and elegance,
so our night conversations won't be dull."
Then he took out money,
and prepared a feast for them to drink together.
The young man was charming and refined,
and he and Wú greatly admired each other.
During the drinking,
he would wink at Wú to cheat in drinking games,
penalizing Huáng,
forcing him to drink,
and clapping and laughing.
Wú liked him even more.
Afterward, Shǐ and Huáng plotted to gamble,
and together they pulled Wú in,
so each took out money from their bags as stakes.
The fox instructed Bào'ér to secretly lock the wooden door,
and told Wú:
"If you hear people making noise,
just sleep and ignore it."
Wú agreed.
Whenever Wú threw the dice,
he would lose with small bets,
but win with large bets.
After the first watch,
he had won two hundred taels of silver.
Shǐ and Huáng's money bags were nearly empty,
so they discussed pawning their horses.
Suddenly, there was a fierce knocking at the door,
Wú hurriedly got up,
threw the dice into the fire,
and covered himself with the quilt, pretending to sleep.
After a long while,
he heard the innkeeper could not find the key,
so he broke the lock and opened the door,
and several people rushed in noisily,
searching for the gamblers.
Shǐ and Huáng both said there were none.
One of them actually pulled off Wú's quilt,
pointing at him as a gambler.
Wú shouted at him angrily.
Several people forcibly searched Wú's luggage.
Just as he could not resist them,
suddenly, the sound of carriages, horses, and attendants clearing the way was heard outside.
Wú hurried out and cried for help,
and the crowd became afraid,
pulling him inside,
only begging him not to make noise.
Wú then calmly handed over the bribe to the innkeeper.
After the procession had gone far,
the crowd left through the door.
Huáng and Shǐ both acted surprised and delighted,
and took turns looking for a place to sleep.
Huáng told Shǐ to share the bed with Wú.
Wú placed his money bag under the pillow,
and then told them to cover themselves and sleep.
Not long after,
Shǐ lifted Wú's quilt,
and slipped naked into his embrace,
whispering:
"I admire your straightforwardness, brother,
and wish to be intimate with you."
Wú knew it was a trick,
but thought it a good opportunity,
so they embraced each other.
Shǐ tried his best to serve him,
but did not expect Wú to be a well-endowed man,
and it was a terrible mismatch,
he moaned, almost unable to bear it,
and secretly begged to stop.
Wú insisted on finishing.
When he touched with his hand,
blood flowed like a flood.
Then he released him and let him go.
By dawn,
Shǐ was too exhausted to get up,
claiming a sudden illness,
he only asked Wú and Huáng to leave first.
Before parting,
Wú gave him money for medicine.
On the road, he spoke with the fox,
and learned that the procession last night
was all arranged by the fox.
Huáng Yútú,
increasingly flattered and served Wú.
In the evening, they again shared a room,
a cramped chamber, very narrow,
barely able to accommodate one bed;
it was rather warm and clean,
but Wú found it too cramped.
Huáng said:
"This place is cramped for two people to sleep,
but if you sleep alone, it's spacious enough,
so what's the harm?"
After eating,
he went straight away.
Wú was also pleased to sleep alone, as he could then receive his fox friend.
He sat for a long time,
but the fox did not come.
Suddenly, he heard from a small door in the wall
the sound of fingers tapping.
Wú pulled the bolt and peered out;
a young woman, gorgeously made up, hurriedly entered,
bolted the door herself,
and smiled at Wú,
as beautiful as an immortal.
Wú, delighted, inquired in detail,
and she turned out to be the daughter-in-law of the innkeeper.
Thus, they became intimate,
and greatly loved and delighted in each other.
Suddenly, the woman shed tears.
Wú, startled, asked her why,
and she said:
"I dare not hide it from you;
I am actually someone the innkeeper sent to entrap you.
In the past, when I entered a room,
I would be seized immediately;
I don't know why he hasn't come for so long tonight?"
Then, sobbing, she said:
"I am a girl from a good family,
and I am unwilling in my heart.
Now I have given my heart to you;
I beg you to rescue me!"
Wú, hearing this, was terrified and frightened,
unable to think of any plan,
and only urged her to leave quickly.
The woman merely bowed her head and wept.
Suddenly, they heard Huáng and the innkeeper making a great clamor outside.
They heard Huáng say:
"I have served you all along the way,
thinking you were a decent person;
how could you then seduce my brother's wife!"
Wú, frightened,
pressed the woman to leave.
They heard the sound of pounding and beating outside the wall door as well.
Wú, in a panic, sweated profusely,
and the woman also crouched weeping.
Then they heard someone trying to persuade the innkeeper to stop.
The innkeeper would not listen,
and pounded on the door even more urgently.
The persuader said:
"May I ask the innkeeper,
what do you intend to do?
If you want to kill them,
there are several of us guests here,
and we certainly will not sit idly by and watch such violence.
If one of the two escapes,
how can you avoid taking the blame?
If you want to take this to court,
with the impropriety of the inner chambers exposed,
you would only bring shame upon yourself.
Moreover, you run an inn for travelers,
and it is clear that you are setting a trap;
how can you guarantee that the woman won't say something different?"
The innkeeper stared wide-eyed, unable to speak.
Wú, hearing this,
secretly felt grateful and admiring,
but did not know who it was.
Earlier,
just as the shop door was about to close,
a xiùcai arrived with a servant,
and took a room in the outer quarters.
They had brought fine wine,
and poured drinks for everyone in the shared quarters,
especially urging Huáng and the innkeeper to drink.
The two tried to decline and get up,
but the xiùcai tugged at their sleeves,
insisting they not leave.
Later, seizing an opportunity, they escaped,
grabbed clubs, and rushed to Wú's room.
The xiùcai, hearing the commotion,
then came in to mediate.
Wú, crouching by the window to peek,
saw it was his fox friend,
and secretly rejoiced.
Seeing that the innkeeper's resolve was weakening,
he then spoke loudly to intimidate him.
He also said to the woman:
"Why are you silent and not saying a word?"
The woman wept and said:
"I regret that I am not as good as others,
driven and employed for such base tasks!"
The innkeeper, hearing this,
turned as pale as ashes.
The xiùcai scolded and cursed:
"The beastly nature of you people
is already fully exposed;
this is something all travelers would be indignant about!"
Huáng and the innkeeper both put down their knives and clubs,
and knelt down to plead.
Wú also opened the door and came out,
immediately cursing angrily.
The xiùcai again persuaded Wú to stop,
and the two sides finally reconciled.
The woman wept again,
preferring death to returning.
An old woman and a maidservant rushed out from inside,
grabbed the woman, and tried to make her go in.
The woman lay on the ground,
crying even more sorrowfully.
The xiùcai persuaded the innkeeper to sell the woman to Wú for a high price.
The innkeeper bowed his head and said:
"Having been a midwife for thirty years,
today I have swaddled the baby upside down;
what more is there to say?"
Thus, he followed the xiùcai's suggestion.
Wú firmly refused to pay a large sum;
the xiùcai mediated between host and guest,
and they settled on fifty taels of silver.
After the money and the person were exchanged,
the morning bell had already sounded,
so they hurriedly packed their belongings,
loaded the woman onto the carriage, and departed.
The woman had never ridden a horse before,
and the galloping was quite exhausting for her.
At noon,
they rested a bit.
When about to set off again,
they called for Bào'ér,
but did not know where he had gone.
The sun had already set in the west,
and there was still no trace or sound of him,
which made them quite suspicious and surprised,
so they asked the fox about it.
The fox said:
"Don't worry,
he will come on his own."
The stars and moon had already come out,
when Bào'ér finally arrived.
Wú questioned him,
and Bào'ér laughed and said:
"Young master used fifty taels to fatten that villainous fellow;
I secretly felt it was unfair.
Just now, I plotted with Guǐtóu,
and turned back to get it back."
Then he placed the silver on the table.
Wú, startled, asked how this came about.
It turned out that Guǐtóu knew the woman had only one elder brother,
who had been away for over ten years and had not returned,
so he transformed to look like her brother,
and had Bào'ér pretend to be the younger brother,
went to the inn to demand their sister.
The innkeeper, terrified,
falsely claimed she had died of illness.
The two servants threatened to take it to the authorities,
and the innkeeper became even more frightened,
bribing them with silver,
gradually increasing it to forty taels,
and only then did the two servants leave.
Bào'ér recounted the whole story.
Wú then rewarded him.
Wú returned home,
and the couple was extremely harmonious.
The family became even wealthier.
Upon detailed questioning of the woman,
it turned out that the handsome young man from before was her husband,
and it seems Shǐ was actually Jīn.
He wore a jacket of coarse silk,
saying he had obtained it from a certain Wáng in Shāndōng.
It seems their gang was very numerous,
and the innkeepers
were all of their kind.
Who would have thought that the person Wú encountered
was the very one for whom Wáng Zǐxùn cried out to heaven in bitterness—
isn't that delightful!
How true are the ancient words:
"He who rides often falls."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wáng Zǐxùn said:
"While in the capital,
I once saw a man performing tricks in the market.
He carried a wooden box with compartments,
altogether having twelve holes;
in each hole crouched a frog.
When he tapped their heads with a thin stick,
they would croak loudly.
If someone gave him money,
he would then randomly strike the frogs' heads,
like playing a yúnluó,
and the musical notes and melodies
could be clearly distinguished."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
It is also said:
"A man performed a mouse show in the marketplace of Cháng'ān.
He carried a bag on his back,
in which he kept over ten little mice.
Whenever he was among a dense crowd,
he would take out a small wooden frame,
place it on his shoulder,
making it look exactly like a theater stage.
Then he would beat a drum and clappers,
and sing ancient variety plays.
As soon as his singing began,
mice would emerge from the bag,
wearing masks,
dressed in miniature costumes,
climb up from his back onto the stage,
and stand upright to dance.
The sorrows and joys of men and women
all perfectly matched the plot of the play."
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
In Luócūn, there was a man named Chén Dài,
who was foolish and ugly from a young age.
He married a certain woman,
who was quite beautiful.
Feeling that her husband was inferior to others,
she was depressed and discontent.
However, she maintained her chastity and integrity,
and she and her mother-in-law lived peacefully together.
One night, while sleeping alone,
she suddenly heard the wind blow the door open,
and a scholar entered,
took off his clothes and headscarf,
and went to bed with the woman.
The woman was terrified,
and resisted bitterly;
but her muscles and bones went limp,
and she allowed him to fondle her before he left.
From then on, he came almost every night without fail.
After more than a month,
her appearance became haggard and emaciated.
Her mother found it strange and questioned her.
At first, she was ashamed and unwilling to speak;
but pressed insistently,
she finally told the truth.
Her mother exclaimed in horror:
"This is a demon!"
She tried every method to cast spells and exorcise it,
but ultimately could not stop it.
So she had Chén Dài hide in the room,
holding a stick to wait.
At midnight,
the scholar indeed returned,
placed his hat on the table;
and took off his robe,
hanging it on the rack.
Just as he was about to climb onto the bed,
he suddenly exclaimed in alarm:
"Tut-tut!
There's a living human's smell!"
He hurriedly put his clothes back on.
Chén Dài suddenly sprang up from the darkness,
striking his waist and ribs,
making a clattering sound.
Looking around the four walls,
the scholar had vanished.
They lit a bundle of firewood to see,
a piece of mud-stained clothing had fallen to the ground,
and a mud-stained headscarf still remained on the table.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
There was a man named Wáng Bǐng from Qiáowáng,
who went out of the village
and saw a beautiful woman emerging from the shrine of the local earth god.
She looked at him with great eagerness.
He flirted with her using indecent words,
and she happily accepted them.
With no place for intimacy,
they arranged to elope at night.
Wáng Bǐng then told her where he lived.
That night,
she indeed came,
and they were extremely fond of each other.
When he asked her name,
she firmly refused to tell him.
From then on, they came and went without cease.
Sometimes when Wáng Bǐng shared a bed with his wife,
the beautiful woman would also come to have relations with him,
and his wife remained completely unaware of anyone else's presence.
Wáng Bǐng was surprised and asked her about it.
The beautiful woman said:
"I am the wife of the local earth god."
Wáng Bǐng was greatly alarmed,
and urgently wanted to break it off,
but no matter what he tried, he could not stop her.
This dragged on for half a year,
until he fell ill and could not get up.
The beautiful woman came even more frequently,
and all the family members could see her.
Not long after,
Wáng Bǐng indeed died.
The beautiful woman still came once a day.
Wáng Bǐng's wife scolded her, saying:
"Shameless lustful ghost!
The man is already dead,
why do you still come?"
The beautiful woman then left,
and never returned.
Though the local earth god is minor,
he is still a deity.
How could he allow his wife to elope freely?
Even if muddle-headed, it should not come to this.
Who knows what kind of lewd and deluded creature it was,
causing people for ages to say that this village has a filthy, base, and careless deity.
What an injustice!
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
There was a Dàoist from Jǐnán,
no one knew where he was from,
nor his surname or given name.
In winter and summer, he wore a single unlined jacket,
tied with a yellow silk ribbon,
and no inner garment.
He often used half a comb to comb his hair,
then held it between his teeth at the top of his hair knot,
like a crown.
During the day, he walked barefoot in the marketplace;
at night, he slept on the street,
but several feet away from his body,
all ice and snow would melt.
When he first arrived,
he would perform magic tricks for people,
and the townsfolk competed to give him gifts.
There was a rogue from the neighborhood,
who offered him wine,
and begged to learn his magic,
but he refused.
Once, when the Dàoist was bathing in the river,
the rogue suddenly grabbed his clothes to threaten him.
The Dàoist bowed and said:
"Please return them to me,
and I will not be stingy with my magic."
The rogue feared he was being tricked,
and stubbornly refused to let go.
The Dàoist said:
"So you really won't give them back?"
The rogue said:
"That's right."
The Dàoist fell silent and did not speak;
soon, they saw the yellow silk ribbon turn into a snake,
several hand-spans thick,
coiling around the rogue's body six or seven times,
glaring with angry eyes and raising its head,
flicking its tongue toward him.
The rogue was greatly shocked,
fell to his knees,
his face pale and breath short,
only begging for his life.
The Dàoist then finally took back the ribbon.
The ribbon turned out not to be a snake;
there was another snake,
slithering into the city.
From then on, the Dàoist's fame grew even greater.
The gentry, hearing of his extraordinary abilities,
invited him to socialize,
and from then on he frequented the homes of the local gentry.
The provincial commissioner and circuit intendant had both heard of his name,
and whenever they held banquets,
they always had the Daoist accompany them.
One day,
the Daoist requested to host a banquet for the various officials at the Shuǐmiàn Pavilion.
When the day arrived,
the officials found on their desks an invitation from the Daoist urging them to attend,
though they did not know how it had arrived.
The guests went to the banquet location,
where the Daoist, hunched over, came out to greet them.
Once inside,
the hall was empty and silent,
with no tables or chairs set up,
leading some to suspect it was a hoax.
The Daoist looked at the officials and said:
"This poor Daoist has no servants,
so I must trouble you to lend me your attendants,
to help with the running about."
The officials all agreed.
The Daoist painted a double door on the wall,
and knocked on it with his hand.
Someone inside answered the door,
and with the turn of a latch, it opened.
Everyone rushed to look inside,
and saw bustling figures moving about within;
screens, curtains, beds, and tables
were all there as well.
Immediately, people began passing items out the door.
The Daoist instructed the clerks to receive and arrange them in the pavilion,
and warned them not to speak with those inside.
The two sides handed things over,
only glancing and smiling.
In a moment,
the pavilion was fully furnished,
extremely luxurious and splendid.
Soon, fragrant fine wine
and steaming hot roasted meats
were all passed out from within the wall.
The seated guests were all astonished.
The pavilion originally backed onto the lake,
and every June,
for dozens of acres,
lotus flowers stretched as far as the eye could see.
But the banquet was held in deep winter,
and outside the window was a vast expanse,
with only misty green water.
One official sighed and said:
"This gathering today is wonderful,
but it's a pity there are no lotus flowers to adorn it!"
The others all murmured in agreement.
After a short while,
a servant in black rushed in to report:
"The pond is full of lotus leaves!"
Everyone at the table was shocked.
Pushing open the window to look out,
they indeed saw a vast expanse of green,
dotted with lotus buds.
In an instant,
thousands of branches and blooms
all opened at once;
the north wind blew on their faces,
carrying the penetrating fragrance of lotus.
The group considered it miraculous.
They sent a servant to row a boat and pick lotus flowers.
From afar, they saw the servant enter the depths of the flowers;
after a while, he turned the boat back,
and came to see them empty-handed.
The official questioned him,
and the servant said:
"I rowed the boat out,
and saw the flowers in the distance;
as I gradually reached the north shore,
they turned out to be far away in the southern part of the lake."
The Daoist laughed and said:
"These are but illusory flowers of a dream."
Before long,
the wine was finished,
and the lotuses also withered;
a sudden north wind arose,
breaking the lotus leaves,
until none remained.
The Surveillance Commissioner of Jìdōng was very pleased with him,
and took him back to his office,
spending time with him daily in intimate amusement.
One day,
the commissioner was drinking with a guest.
The commissioner had a family heirloom of fine wine,
and he always limited it to one dou per occasion,
unwilling to let it be consumed recklessly.
That day,
the guest found the wine delicious after drinking it,
and persistently asked for more.
The commissioner firmly insisted it was all gone.
The Daoist smiled and said to the guest:
"If you must satisfy your gluttony,
you can ask this poor Daoist."
The guest requested it.
The Daoist put the pot into his sleeve,
and after a moment took it out,
pouring wine for everyone at the table;
it was no different
from the commissioner's stored wine.
They enjoyed themselves to the full before stopping.
The commissioner was suspicious,
and went to check the wine;
the seal was intact as before,
but the container was empty.
Secretly ashamed and angry,
he seized the Daoist, considering him a demon,
and had him beaten.
As soon as the cane struck,
the commissioner felt a sharp pain in his own thigh;
with another strike,
the flesh of his buttocks felt as if it would split.
Although the Daoist was crying out under the steps,
the commissioner was already bleeding on his seat.
So he stopped the beating,
and drove the Daoist away.
The Daoist then left Jì,
and no one knew where he went.
Later, someone met him in Jīnlíng,
dressed as before;
when asked,
he only smiled and did not answer.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Miào Yǒngdìng
was a senior licentiate selected from Jiāngxī.
He was habitually given to heavy drinking,
and most relatives and friends feared and avoided him.
Once, he happened to visit his clan uncle's home.
Miào was a witty and humorous person,
and a guest, conversing with him,
took a liking to him,
so they drank together heartily.
Miào became drunk,
and under the influence of alcohol, he cursed those at the table,
offending the guest.
The guest grew angry,
and the whole gathering was in an uproar.
The uncle tried to mediate left and right.
Miào thought he was siding with the guest,
and became even more enraged.
The uncle, at his wits' end,
ran to inform Miào's family.
His family came,
and helped him back home.
As soon as they laid him on the bed,
all four limbs went stiff;
feeling him,
he had already stopped breathing.
When Miào died,
a man in a black cap came and took him away.
After a while,
they arrived at a government office,
with pale green tiles on the roof,
more magnificent than anything in the mortal world.
Reaching the steps,
it seemed he was to wait to see the official.
He thought to himself: What crime have I committed?
It must be that guest suing over the fight.
Looking back at the man in the black cap,
whose eyes were glaring like an ox's,
he dared not ask.
However, he reckoned:
A senior licentiate quarreling with someone
probably isn't a major crime.
Suddenly, a clerk in the hall announced,
ordering those involved in lawsuits to wait early the next day.
Then the people below the hall scattered in confusion,
like birds and beasts dispersing.
Miào also followed the black-capped man out,
with nowhere to go,
so he hunched his head and stood under the eaves of a shop.
The black-capped man angrily said:
"Drunken good-for-nothing!
It's almost dusk,
everyone is going to find food and sleep, so where will you go?"
Miào trembled and said:
"I don't even know what this is about,
and I haven't told my family,
so I have no money at all;
how could I go back?"
The black-capped man said:
"Drunken thief!
If you bought it yourself,
you'd have spending money!
If you keep making excuses,
I'll smash your drunken skull with my fist!"
Miào hung his head and dared not make a sound.
Suddenly, a person emerged from inside the house.
Seeing Miào,
he exclaimed in surprise:
"How did you get here?"
Miào looked at him—
it was his maternal uncle.
His uncle, surnamed Jiǎ,
had been dead for several years.
Seeing him,
Miào suddenly realized that he himself was already dead.
His heart filled with even greater sorrow and fear.
Turning to his uncle with tears streaming down, he said:
"Uncle, save me!"
Jiǎ looked at the man in the black cap and said:
"Dōnglíng is no stranger;
please honor my humble abode with your presence."
The two then entered.
Jiǎ bowed deeply again to the man in the black cap,
and entreated him to show favor.
After a short while,
wine and food were brought out,
and they sat in a circle drinking together.
Jiǎ asked:
"What has my nephew done,
to trouble you to bring him here?"
The man in the black cap said:
"The Great King was on his way to visit Fúluó Jūn,
when he encountered your nephew cursing wildly,
which is why I was sent to fetch him."
Jiǎ asked:
"Has he seen the King yet?"
The man replied:
"Fúluó Jūn is holding a meeting on the Huāzi case,
and the King has not yet returned."
Jiǎ asked further:
"What punishment will my nephew receive?"
The man answered:
"It is not yet known.
However, the Great King is quite angry with such people."
Miào, standing to the side,
heard their conversation,
trembling and sweating profusely,
unable to lift his cup or chopsticks.
Before long,
the man in the black cap stood up,
and said gratefully:
"I have enjoyed your generous feast,
and am already thoroughly drunk.
I shall now entrust your nephew to you.
When the King returns,
I will come again to visit."
With that, he left.
Jiǎ said to Miào:
"You have no brothers,
and your parents loved you like a pearl in their palm,
often unable to bear even a single scolding.
When you were sixteen or seventeen,
after a few cups of wine,
you would mutter and seek out others' faults;
at the slightest disagreement,
you would pound on doors and curse naked.
We still thought you were young and immature.
I never expected that after more than ten years apart,
you would show no improvement at all.
What can be done now!"
Miào fell to the ground weeping,
saying only that it was too late for regrets.
Jiǎ pulled him up and said:
"Your uncle runs a wine business here,
and has some small reputation.
I will certainly do my utmost.
The man we just drank with is the Dōnglíng envoy.
I often treat him to wine,
and we are on quite good terms.
The Great King is busy with myriad affairs daily,
and may not necessarily remember this.
I will speak to him tactfully,
and beg him to release you as a personal favor.
Perhaps he will agree."
Then he thought again and said:
"This matter carries a heavy responsibility,
and cannot be settled without a hundred thousand."
Miào thanked him,
eagerly taking on the responsibility himself,
and agreed.
Miào then stayed overnight at his uncle's place.
The next day,
the man in the black cap came early to check.
Jiǎ asked for a private word,
and after speaking for a while,
he came back to tell Miào:
"It's settled.
He will return shortly.
I will first use all I have
as a deposit for the agreement;
the rest can be gathered gradually
after you return home."
Miào said happily:
"How much is needed in total?"
Jiǎ said:
"A hundred thousand."
Miào asked:
"Where can I get such a sum?"
Jiǎ said:
"Only a hundred bundles of gold and silver paper money
will suffice."
Miào said joyfully:
"That is easy to arrange."
They waited until nearly noon,
but the man in the black cap did not arrive.
Miào wanted to go out to the market,
to stroll and look around a bit.
Jiǎ warned him not to wander too far,
and Miào agreed before leaving.
He saw street vendors and traders,
just like in the human world.
He came to a place
with high, steep thorny walls,
which seemed like a prison.
Opposite the gate was a tavern,
bustling with many people coming and going.
Outside the tavern flowed a long stream,
with dark, swirling water,
deep and bottomless.
Just as he stopped to peer,
he heard someone inside the tavern call out:
"How did you get here, Mr. Miào?"
Miào quickly looked—
it was Wēng Shēng from the neighboring village,
an old literary friend from ten years ago.
He hurried over to shake hands,
as joyful as if they had just met.
They then went into the tavern for a drink,
and each recounted their experiences since parting.
In his relief,
Miào was delighted to meet an old friend again,
and poured out his heart.
Drunk and merry,
he momentarily forgot that he was dead,
and his old habits returned.
He began to nitpick and find fault with Wēng.
Wēng said:
"After so many years apart,
are you still like this?"
Miào had always disliked others criticizing his behavior when drunk,
and hearing Wēng's words,
he grew even angrier,
pounding the table and cursing.
Wēng glanced at him,
then flicked his sleeves and walked out.
Miào chased him to the edge of the stream,
and grabbed Wēng's hat.
Wēng said angrily:
"You truly are an unreasonable man!"
Then he pushed Miào, who tumbled into the stream.
The stream water was not very deep, but it was filled with sharp blades like hemp stalks,
piercing his ribs and legs,
making it hard to move,
and the pain penetrated to his bones and brain.
The black water was mixed with filth and urine,
and as he inhaled, it entered his throat,
making it even more unbearable.
People on the bank watched and laughed, forming a crowd,
but no one offered to help.
Just as he was in dire straits,
Jiǎ suddenly arrived.
Seeing him, Jiǎ was greatly alarmed,
pulled him out, and took him back, saying:
"You are hopeless!
Even in death, you have not learned your lesson,
and are not fit to be a human again!
I suggest you go back to Dōnglíng and accept the axe."
Miào was terrified,
and said through tears:
"I know my wrongdoing."
Jiǎ then said:
"Just now, Dōnglíng came,
waiting for you to sign the agreement,
but you were out drinking and wandering, and did not return.
He was in a hurry and could not wait.
I have already signed the agreement on your behalf,
and paid a thousand strings to send him away;
the rest is due within ten days.
When you return home,
you must urgently arrange it.
At night, in the open wilderness outside the village,
call out my name and burn the paper money.
Then this matter can be settled."
Miào agreed to everything.
Jiǎ then urged him to leave,
escorted him outside the city,
and warned him again:
"You must not break your word and bring trouble upon me."
Then he showed him the way home.
At that time, Miào had already been lying stiff for three days,
and his family thought he had died drunk.
Yet his faint breath was like a dangling thread.
That day he revived,
vomiting heavily,
and spewed out several dou of black fluid,
so foul-smelling it was unbearable.
After vomiting,
he sweated so much it soaked the mattress,
and only then did his body begin to cool.
He told his family about the strange occurrence.
Soon he felt pain and swelling at the pricked spot,
which overnight turned into a sore,
fortunately without festering badly.
After ten days, he could barely walk with a cane.
His family all begged him to repay the underworld debt.
Miào calculated the cost,
and realized it would require several taels of silver to settle,
so he grew rather stingy,
saying:
"That was probably just a drunken dream or illusion.
Even if it wasn't,
since he released me privately,
how dare I let the underworld lord know?"
His family urged him,
but he wouldn't listen.
Nevertheless, his heart remained fearful,
and he dared not indulge in drinking again.
The villagers all rejoiced at his moral improvement,
and gradually drank with him again.
After over a year,
he gradually forgot about the underworld retribution,
his will grew lax,
and his old habits slowly returned.
One day,
while drinking at a relative's house,
he again cursed his host at the table.
The host expelled him,
shut the door, and went straight away.
Miào clamored for a while,
until his son finally found out,
and went to support him home.
Upon entering the room,
he knelt facing the wall for a long time,
knocking his head countless times,
saying:
"I'll repay your debt now!
I'll repay your debt now!"
After speaking,
he collapsed to the ground.
Looking at him,
he had already stopped breathing.
According to the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì"
Yángwǔ Hóu Xuē Gōng Lù,
was from Jiāo's Xuējiā Dǎo.
His father, Xuē Gōng, was extremely poor,
and herded cattle for a local gentleman.
The gentleman had some wasteland,
and while Xuē Gōng herded there,
he often saw snakes and rabbits fighting in the grass,
which he found strange;
so he requested the owner to let him build a dwelling there,
and constructed a thatched hut to live in.
Several years later,
when the lady was about to give birth,
it happened to rain heavily;
just then, two commanders were ordered to inspect the coast,
and passed by that way,
taking shelter from the rain in the hut.
They saw crows and magpies flocking on the roof,
actually using their wings to cover the leaks,
and found it strange.
Soon the old man came out,
and the commanders asked:
"What just happened?"
He told them about the childbirth.
They asked what was born,
and he said:
"A boy."
The commanders were even more astonished,
saying:
"He must be extremely noble.
Otherwise,
why would we two commanders be guarding his door?"
They sighed and left.
When the Marquis grew up,
his face was dirty and his nose ran,
and he was far from clever.
The Xuē clan on the island
had originally been registered as military households.
That year, the old man's family was required to provide one man for garrison duty in Liáoyáng,
and the eldest son was deeply worried.
At that time, the Marquis was eighteen,
and people considered him too foolish,
so no one would marry him.
Suddenly he said to his elder brother:
"Big brother, you're sighing and fretting—
is it because we have no one to send for garrison duty?"
The brother said:
"Yes."
He laughed and said:
"If you're willing to give me a maid as wife,
I'll take on this duty."
The brother was delighted,
and immediately matched him with a maid.
The Marquis then took his wife to the garrison post.
They had only traveled a few dozen lǐ,
when a sudden heavy rain poured down.
By the roadside was a steep cliff,
and the couple rushed to take shelter beneath it.
After a short while,
the rain stopped,
and they set off again.
They had only gone a few steps,
when the cliff rocks collapsed and fell.
The locals saw from afar two tigers leap out,
and press close to the two people before disappearing.
From then on, the Marquis became exceptionally brave and strong,
and his demeanor suddenly changed.
Later, for his military achievements, he was enfeoffed as Yángwǔ Hóu with a hereditary title.
By the Qǐ and Zhēn eras,
when a certain Duke who had inherited the Marquisate died,
he had no sons,
only a posthumous child,
so a collateral branch temporarily took over.
In all hereditary noble families, when a consort became pregnant,
it was reported to the emperor,
and officials sent matrons to accompany and guard her,
until after childbirth.
Over a year later,
the lady gave birth to a daughter.
After delivery,
her belly still stirred,
and for fifteen years in total,
through several matrons,
she gave birth to a son.
He should have been granted the title as the legitimate heir.
The collateral branch clamored against it,
claiming he was not a Xuē offspring.
The officials detained the matrons,
and subjected them to all kinds of torture,
but none gave differing testimony.
Thus the title was confirmed.
According to the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì"
In Zhàochéng, there was an old woman
over seventy years old,
who had only one son.
One day, he went into the mountains
and was devoured by a tiger.
The old woman was grief-stricken,
almost wishing to die,
and wailed as she pleaded with the magistrate.
The magistrate laughed and said:
"How can a tiger be governed by official laws?"
The old woman wailed even more loudly,
and he could not stop her.
The magistrate scolded her,
but she showed no fear.
Feeling pity for her old age,
he could not bear to use his authority to anger her,
so he promised to capture the tiger.
The old woman knelt and refused to leave,
insisting on waiting until the arrest warrant was issued
before she would go.
The magistrate had no choice,
so he asked his attendants,
"Who is willing to go?"
One attendant named Lǐ Néng,
drunk from wine,
came before the magistrate
and said:
"I can do it."
He took the warrant,
and the old woman finally left.
When Lǐ Néng sobered up, he regretted it;
still thinking the magistrate's promise was just a pretense,
meant only to placate the old woman's disturbance,
he did not take it seriously.
He returned the warrant,
but the magistrate angrily said:
"You said you could do it,
how can you regret it now?"
Lǐ Néng was greatly embarrassed,
and requested a warrant to summon hunters.
The magistrate agreed.
Lǐ Néng gathered several hunters,
and they lay in ambush day and night in the mountains,
hoping to catch a tiger,
so they could fulfill their duty.
After over a month,
he had received hundreds of blows,
and his grievances could not be appealed.
So he went to the Yuè Temple in the eastern suburbs,
knelt and prayed,
crying until he lost his voice.
Not long after,
a tiger came from outside.
Lǐ Néng was startled,
afraid he would be bitten and devoured.
The tiger entered,
paying no attention to anything else,
and crouched in the middle of the doorway.
Lǐ Néng prayed:
"If you are the one who killed the old woman's son,
then bow your head and let me bind you."
He then took out a rope and tied it around the tiger's neck,
and the tiger lowered its ears and allowed itself to be bound.
He led it to the county office,
and the magistrate asked the tiger:
"Did you devour that woman's son?"
The tiger nodded.
The magistrate said:
"Those who kill must die,
according to ancient law.
Moreover, the old woman had only one son,
and you killed him.
Her remaining years are nearly spent—
how will she live?
If you can become like a son to her,
I will pardon you."
The tiger nodded again.
So he released it and let it go.
The old woman was still resentful that the magistrate had not killed the tiger to avenge her son,
but at dawn the next day,
when she opened her door,
she found a dead deer;
the old woman sold its meat and hide,
using the money to support herself.
From then on, this became a regular occurrence,
and the tiger often brought gold and silk, tossing them into her courtyard.
The old woman grew prosperous from this,
and the tiger's care surpassed that of her own son.
In her heart, she secretly felt grateful to the tiger.
When the tiger came,
it would often lie beneath the eaves,
staying all day without leaving.
Humans and beast lived in peace,
with no suspicion or fear between them.
Several years later,
the old woman died,
and the tiger came roaring into the hall.
The wealth the old woman had accumulated
was more than enough for a funeral,
and her relatives buried her together.
Just as the grave mound was completed,
the tiger suddenly came rushing,
and all the guests fled.
The tiger went straight to the grave,
howling like thunder,
and only after a long while did it leave.
The local people built
a "Righteous Tiger Shrine"
in the eastern suburbs,
which still exists today.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
There was a man named Zhāng,
who was walking through a mountain stream valley,
when he heard a fierce sound from the cliff above.
He found a path to climb and look,
and saw a huge snake, as thick as a bowl,
thrashing among the trees,
striking willow trees with its tail,
causing the willow branches to break and collapse.
It writhed and stumbled about,
as if something had seized it.
Yet upon careful inspection, he saw nothing,
which puzzled him greatly.
Gradually approaching to observe,
he saw a mantis perched on its head,
gripping the snake's head with its sickle-like forelegs,
and no matter how the snake thrashed, it could not shake it off.
After a long time,
the snake finally died.
Looking at the skin and flesh on its forehead,
it had already been torn apart.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Lǐ Chāo,
courtesy name Kuíwú,
was from the western outskirts of Zībó.
He was bold and straightforward,
and generous.
Once, a monk came begging for alms,
and Lǐ fed him until he was full.
The monk was very grateful,
and said:
"I come from Shàolín.
I have some modest skills,
and I would like to teach them to you."
Lǐ was delighted,
housed him in a guest room,
provided him with ample supplies,
and studied with him day and night.
After three months,
his skills had become quite refined,
and he felt very pleased with himself.
The monk asked:
"Have you improved?"
He replied:
"I have improved.
Everything my master can do,
I can now do as well."
The monk smiled,
and asked Lǐ to demonstrate his skills.
Lǐ then took off his outer garment, spat on his hands,
leaping like a monkey,
landing like a bird,
jumping and moving about for a while,
then stood proudly facing the monk.
The monk smiled again and said:
"That's good.
Since you have mastered all my skills,
let us have a match to see who is superior."
Lǐ happily agreed,
and they both assumed fighting stances.
They then grappled and resisted each other,
and Lǐ often tried to exploit the monk's weaknesses;
but the monk suddenly kicked out with one foot,
and Lǐ was thrown back over ten feet.
The monk clapped his hands and said:
"You have not yet mastered all my skills."
Lǐ pressed his palms to the ground,
ashamed and discouraged, and asked for further instruction.
A few days later,
the monk bid farewell and left.
From then on, Lǐ became famous for his martial arts,
traveling north and south,
with no one to match him.
Once he happened to be in Lìxià,
where he saw a young nun
performing skills in an arena,
surrounded by a packed crowd.
The nun announced to the onlookers:
"Performing all alone
is rather dull.
If any enthusiasts are present,
why not step into the arena for a friendly bout?"
She repeated this three times.
The crowd looked at each other,
but no one responded.
Lǐ, standing nearby,
could not resist the itch to show his skill,
and strode forward with eager confidence.
The nun smiled and joined her palms in greeting.
They had barely crossed hands
when the nun called a halt and said:
"This is the Shàolín school."
She then asked:
"Who is your esteemed master?"
At first, Lǐ did not answer.
Pressed insistently,
he finally named the monk.
The nun clasped her hands and said:
"Is Hān the monk your teacher?
If so,
there is no need for us to exchange blows—
I willingly acknowledge your superiority."
Lǐ repeatedly urged her to continue,
but she refused.
Encouraged by the crowd,
the nun then said:
"Since you are a disciple of Master Hān,
we are both insiders of the same path—
a friendly bout would be harmless.
But let us understand each other's intent."
Lǐ agreed.
However, because she seemed delicate and frail,
he underestimated her;
moreover, being young and eager to win,
he thought of defeating her
to gain fame for the day.
Just as they were locked in struggle,
the nun abruptly stopped.
Lǐ asked why,
but she only smiled without answering.
Lǐ thought she was timid,
and insisted on another round.
The nun then rose.
A moment later,
Lǐ launched a kick.
The nun brought five fingers together and slashed down at his thigh;
Lǐ felt as if struck below the knee by an axe,
and fell, unable to rise.
The nun smiled apologetically and said:
"I have been rash and offended you—
I hope you will not hold it against me!"
Lǐ was carried home,
and only recovered after more than a month.
Over a year later,
the monk visited again,
and Lǐ recounted the incident.
The monk exclaimed in alarm:
"You were far too reckless!
Why provoke her?
Fortunately, you mentioned my name first;
otherwise,
your leg would have been broken!"
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
During the Kāngxī reign,
a magician carried a small cabinet,
inside which was hidden a tiny person
about a foot tall.
When a coin was thrown,
he would open the cabinet and let the person out,
who would sing a song and then retreat.
Arriving in Yéxiàn,
the county magistrate had the cabinet brought into his office
and questioned the tiny person closely about his origins.
At first, he dared not speak.
Pressed insistently,
he finally told of his hometown and clan.
It turned out he was a schoolboy
returning from his studies
when the magician bewitched him,
then gave him a drug,
causing his limbs to shrink violently;
the magician then carried him around,
using him as a plaything.
The magistrate was enraged
and had the magician killed.
He kept the boy, hoping to cure him,
but had not yet found a method.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Láizhōu, a scholar named Qín
prepared medicinal wine,
but mistakenly added a poisonous ingredient.
Unwilling to discard it,
he sealed it and stored it away.
After more than a year,
he felt a craving for wine one night,
but had none available.
Suddenly remembering his stored brew,
he opened the seal and sniffed it—
its rich, potent aroma burst forth,
making his insides itch and his mouth water,
beyond all restraint.
He fetched a cup and was about to taste it
when his wife earnestly pleaded with him.
The scholar laughed and said:
"To die after a satisfying drink
is far better than dying of craving and thirst."
After draining one cup,
he tipped the bottle to pour another.
His wife knocked the bottle over,
spilling its contents across the floor.
The scholar crouched and lapped it up like an ox.
Soon after,
his belly ached and his jaw locked—
by midnight, he was dead.
His wife wailed,
prepared a coffin,
and proceeded with the burial rites.
The following night,
a beautiful woman suddenly entered,
less than three feet tall,
went straight to the bier,
and poured a bowl of liquid into his mouth,
whereupon he abruptly revived.
Questioned earnestly,
she said:
"I am a fox immortal.
My husband went to the Chén household,
stole wine, got drunk, and died;
I went to rescue him and bring him back.
Passing by your home,
he took pity on this gentleman for sharing his plight,
so he sent me with the leftover medicine to revive him."
Having spoken,
she vanished.
My friend, the Provincial Graduate Qiū Xíngsù,
was fond of drinking.
One night he craved wine,
but had no way to buy any,
and after tossing and turning, could bear it no longer,
so he thought of substituting vinegar.
He consulted his wife,
who scoffed at him.
Qiū insisted stubbornly,
so she warmed some vinegar and brought it to him.
After finishing the pot,
he finally undressed and slept contentedly.
The next day,
he scraped together the cost of a pot of wine
and sent a servant to buy it.
On the way, the servant met Qiū's younger cousin Xiāngchén,
who, learning the reason,
suspected his sister-in-law was unwilling to help her husband get wine.
The servant said:
"My mistress said: 'We don't have much vinegar stored at home—
last night half of it was already used up; if we have another pot,
the vinegar roots will be cut off.'"
Those who heard this all laughed.
They did not realize that when the craving for wine first grows strong,
even poison tastes sweet—
how much more so vinegar?
This, too, is worth passing on.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
The scholar Wáng Wén,
a native of Dōngchāng,
was honest and sincere from his youth.
He traveled to Chǔ,
passing through Liùhé,
and rested at an inn,
then went for a walk outside the gate.
He encountered a fellow villager, Zhào Dōnglóu,
a great merchant,
who often did not return home for years.
Seeing Wáng,
he grasped his hand warmly,
and invited him to his lodgings.
Arriving at his place,
Wáng saw a beautiful woman sitting in the room,
and startled, he stepped back.
Zhào pulled him in,
and called through the window for the girl to leave,
so Wáng entered.
Zhào prepared wine and food,
and they exchanged pleasantries.
Wáng asked:
"What place is this?"
Zhào replied:
"This is a small brothel.
As I have been away from home for a long time,
I have temporarily borrowed a bed here to sleep."
While they were talking,
the girl frequently came in and out.
Wáng felt uneasy and constrained,
and rose to take his leave.
Zhào forcibly held him and made him sit down.
Soon, he saw a young girl
pass by outside the door,
who, upon seeing Wáng,
cast frequent glances at him with her autumn-wave eyes,
her brows and eyes filled with affection,
her demeanor graceful and gentle—
truly a fairy maiden.
Wáng had always been upright and principled,
but at this moment, he felt lost and bewildered,
and asked:
"Who is that beauty?"
Zhào said:
"She is the second daughter of the madam,
her pet name is Yātóu,
and she is fourteen years old.
Those seeking her favors have repeatedly offered the madam large sums of money,
but the girl firmly refuses,
causing her mother to whip and beat her,
and she pleads for mercy on account of her youth.
She is still waiting to be betrothed."
Upon hearing this,
Wáng bowed his head and sat silently in a daze,
his responses all awry.
Zhào teased him:
"If you are interested,
I will act as the matchmaker."
Wáng sighed and said:
"This is a thought I dare not entertain."
However, as the day drew toward evening,
he made no mention of leaving.
Zhào teased him again and offered to arrange it.
Wáng said:
"I deeply appreciate your kind intention,
but my purse is empty—what can I do?"
Zhào knew the girl's temperament was strong-willed,
and she would certainly not consent,
so he promised to contribute ten taels of silver to help.
Wáng bowed in thanks and hurried out,
gathered all his funds,
and came up with five taels,
urging Zhào to present them to the madam.
The madam indeed considered it too little.
Yātóu said to her mother:
"Mother, you daily scold me for not being a money tree;
now I ask to fulfill your wish.
I am just beginning to learn how to be a person;
there will be a day when I repay you.
Do not let go of the God of Wealth over such a small amount."
The madam, knowing her daughter's stubborn nature,
was simply delighted to have her consent,
and was overjoyed.
Thus she agreed,
and sent a maid to invite Master Wáng.
Zhào found it difficult to go back on his word,
so he added more silver and gave it to the madam.
Wáng and the girl were deeply affectionate.
Afterward,
she said to Wáng:
"I am a lowly courtesan,
unworthy to be your match;
yet since you have shown me such tenderness,
our bond is now of utmost importance.
You have spent all your money for this one night of joy—
what will you do tomorrow?"
Wáng shed tears and sobbed sadly.
The girl said:
"Do not grieve.
I have been cast into the world of pleasure,
but it was never my wish.
However, I have never met anyone as sincere and reliable as you.
Let us flee together tonight."
Wáng was overjoyed,
and quickly rose;
the girl also rose.
They heard the watchtower drum had already struck three times.
The girl hastily changed into men's clothing,
and they hurriedly left together,
knocking on the innkeeper's door.
Wáng had originally come with two donkeys,
and using urgent business as a pretext,
he ordered the servant to set off immediately.
The girl attached talismans to the servant's thigh and the donkey's ears,
and they let the reins go and galloped at full speed,
their eyes unable to open,
hearing only the whistling of wind behind their ears;
at dawn, they reached the mouth of the Hàn River,
rented a house, and settled there.
Wáng was astonished by the strangeness of it all.
The girl said:
"If I tell you,
will you not be afraid?
I am not human—
I am a fox.
My mother is greedy and licentious,
and I suffered daily abuse,
my heart filled with resentment.
Now I am fortunate to have escaped that sea of bitterness.
Beyond a hundred li,
she will not know where we are,
so we can hope to be safe."
Wáng showed no doubt or hesitation,
and calmly said:
"Facing a beauty like a lotus flower in my chamber,
yet with a house bare of all but four walls,
I truly find it hard to console myself,
and fear you will eventually abandon me."
The girl said:
"Why worry about that?
Goods for the market can all be sold;
for a family of three or four,
a modest living can be sustained.
We can sell the donkey for capital."
Wáng followed her advice,
and set up a small shop in front of the house,
where he and the servant personally worked,
selling wine and beverages.
The girl made shawls
and embroidered lotus pouches,
earning a daily profit,
so their livelihood was quite comfortable.
After more than a year,
they gradually could afford to hire maidservants.
From then on, Wáng no longer wore work clothes,
but only supervised.
One day, the girl suddenly grew quiet and sad,
saying:
"Tonight, disaster is sure to strike—
what can we do?"
Wáng asked her about it,
and she said:
"My mother has already learned of my whereabouts,
and will surely come to oppress me.
If she sends my elder sister,
I have no worries;
but I fear my mother will come herself."
Late in the night,
she happily said:
"It's all right—
my elder sister has come."
Not long after,
the girl pushed the door open and entered.
Yātóu smiled and went to greet her.
The girl scolded her:
"You shameless maid,
sneaking off to hide with him!
My mistress ordered me to tie you up and take you back."
She immediately pulled out a rope to bind the girl's neck.
The girl angrily said:
"What crime is there in following one's husband?"
The maidservant grew even more furious,
grabbed the girl, and tore her collar.
All the maids and old women in the house gathered.
The maidservant became afraid
and ran out.
The girl said:
"Once my sister returns,
my mother will surely come herself.
Great disaster is not far off,
we must quickly make plans."
So she hurriedly packed her belongings,
preparing to move again.
Suddenly, the old woman burst in,
her face filled with anger,
saying:
"I knew this maid had no manners,
I had to come myself!"
The girl knelt to greet her, weeping pitifully.
The old woman said nothing,
grabbed her by the hair, and dragged her away.
Wáng paced back and forth, heartbroken and distressed,
unable to eat or sleep.
He hurried to Liùhé,
hoping to offer a bribe for her ransom.
When he arrived, the gate and courtyard were as before,
but the people were already gone.
He asked the residents,
but none knew where they had moved.
He returned in mourning and despair.
Thus, he dismissed his traveling companions,
packed his funds, and headed east for home.
Several years later,
he happened to enter Yāndū,
and passing by an orphanage,
he saw a child,
seven or eight years old.
His servant found it strange how much the child resembled his master,
and stared at him intently.
Wáng asked:
"What are you looking at?"
The servant replied with a laugh.
Wáng also laughed.
Looking closely at the child,
he saw he had a dignified and impressive bearing.
Thinking he lacked an heir,
and because the child resembled him,
he grew fond of him and ransomed him.
When asked his name,
he called himself Wáng Zī.
Wáng said:
"You were abandoned as an infant,
how do you know your surname?"
He replied:
"My teacher once said
that when I was found,
there were characters on my chest,
which read: 'Son of Shāndōng's Wáng Wén.'"
Wáng was greatly astonished and said:
"I am Wáng Wén,
how could I have a son?"
He thought it must be someone with the same name,
but secretly felt pleased,
and grew very fond of the child.
When they returned home,
those who saw him knew without asking that this was Wáng's son.
As Zī grew older,
he became exceptionally strong and powerful,
fond of hunting,
neglecting productive work,
and delighting in fighting and killing.
Wáng could not control him.
He also claimed he could see ghosts and foxes,
but no one believed him.
It happened that someone in the village was troubled by a fox,
and invited Zī to go and investigate.
When he arrived, he pointed to the fox's hiding place,
and ordered several men to strike where he pointed.
Immediately, the cry of a fox was heard,
and fur and blood fell together.
From then on, the place was peaceful.
Thus, people regarded him as even more extraordinary.
One day, while strolling through the marketplace,
Wáng suddenly encountered Zhào Dōnglóu,
whose cap and robe were disheveled,
and whose appearance was gaunt and sallow.
Startled, Wáng asked where he had come from.
Zhào, with a sorrowful expression, requested a private conversation.
Wáng then took him back home
and ordered wine.
Zhào said:
"After the old madam got Yātou,
she subjected her to brutal beatings.
After moving north,
she further tried to break her will.
But the girl vowed to remain faithful unto death,
so she was imprisoned.
She gave birth to a boy,
who was abandoned in a winding alley;
I heard he was in an orphanage,
and likely has grown up by now.
He is your flesh and blood."
Wáng shed tears and said:
"By heaven's grace, that unfortunate child has already returned."
He then recounted the whole story.
He asked:
"How did you fall into such destitution?"
Zhào sighed and said:
"Now I realize that pleasures in the brothels
should not be taken too seriously.
What more is there to say!"
Previously,
when the old madam moved north,
Zhào followed her as a traveling merchant.
Goods that were heavy and difficult to transport
were all sold off cheaply.
Travel expenses and daily provisions along the way
incurred enormous costs.
Consequently, he suffered great losses.
The girl Nīzi made especially extravagant demands.
Within a few years,
ten thousand in gold was completely exhausted.
Seeing the money at her bedside depleted,
the old madam began treating him with contempt day and night.
Nīzi gradually started staying overnight at wealthy households,
often not returning for several nights.
Zhào was furious and could hardly bear it,
yet there was nothing he could do.
Once, when the old madam was away,
Yātou called to Zhào from the window:
"In brothels, there is no true affection;
the intimacy you hear of
is all about money.
If you linger here, unwilling to leave,
you will bring upon yourself a strange disaster."
Zhào grew afraid
and awoke as if from a dream.
Before departing,
he secretly went to see the girl.
She gave him a letter to deliver to Wáng,
and Zhào then returned home.
It was this situation that he now recounted to Wáng.
He then produced Yātou's letter.
The letter said:
"I know that Zīr is already by your side.
As for my hardships and suffering,
Lord Dōnglóu can relate them in detail.
The sins of a past life—
what more can be said!
Confined in a dark room,
without a glimpse of sky or sun,
whip wounds split my skin,
the fire of hunger torments my heart;
each passing dawn and dusk
feels like years.
If you have not forgotten that snowy night on the Hàn River,
when we shared a single quilt and warmed each other in embrace,
then please discuss with our son,
and surely you can rescue me from this plight.
Though my mother and sister are cruel,
they are still my flesh and blood.
I only ask that you ensure they are not injured or maimed—
that is my wish."
After reading it,
Wáng wept uncontrollably,
and gave Zhào gold and silk before he left.
At that time, Zī was eighteen years old.
Wáng told him the whole story from beginning to end,
and showed him his mother's letter.
Zī was so enraged his eyes seemed about to burst;
he set off for the capital that very day.
Inquiring about Old Madam Wú's residence,
he found carriages and horses crowding the entrance.
Zī strode straight in.
Nīzi was drinking with a guest from Hú,
and upon seeing Zī,
she stood stunned, her face changing color.
Zī rushed forward and killed her.
The guests were terrified,
thinking bandits had attacked.
But when they looked at the woman's corpse,
it had already transformed into a fox.
Zī, gripping his blade, charged further inside.
He saw the old madam supervising maids making soup.
As Zī rushed toward the room's entrance,
the old madam suddenly vanished.
Zī looked around,
quickly drew an arrow,
and shot toward the roof beam;
a fox, pierced through the heart, fell down,
and he promptly cut off its head.
Soon finding where his mother was held,
he threw a stone to break the lock,
and mother and son both cried out, losing their voices.
His mother asked about the old madam.
He said:
"Already executed."
His mother reproached him:
"Son, why did you not heed my words!"
She ordered him to take the body and bury it in the wilderness.
Zī pretended to agree,
but skinned it and hid the pelt.
Searching through the old madam's trunks and boxes,
he took all the gold and valuables,
and escorted his mother home.
Husband and wife were reunited,
mingling sorrow and joy.
When she asked about Old Madam Wú,
Zī said:
"In my bag."
Startled, she questioned him,
and he took out two leather pelts to present.
His mother grew angry,
scolding him:
"You unfilial son!
How could you do such a thing!"
She wailed in grief, striking herself,
tossing and turning as if wishing to die.
Wáng did his utmost to comfort her,
and rebuked their son to bury the pelts.
Zī said resentfully:
"Now that you have a place of peace and comfort,
have you so quickly forgotten the whippings and beatings?"
His mother grew even angrier,
weeping incessantly.
Only after Zī buried the pelts and returned to report
did she gradually calm down.
After his wife's return,
Wáng's household grew even more prosperous.
Feeling grateful to Zhào,
he repaid him with a large sum of gold.
Zhào then realized that the old madam and her daughter were both foxes.
Zī served his parents with utmost filial piety;
however, if someone accidentally offended him,
he would roar with vicious curses.
His mother said to Wáng:
"Our son has a stubborn tendon;
if it is not cut out,
he will eventually commit murder and ruin the family fortune."
One night, waiting until Zī was asleep,
she secretly bound his hands and feet.
Zī woke and said:
"I have done no wrong."
His mother said:
"I am going to cure your cruelty;
do not suffer over it."
Zī shouted loudly,
struggling but unable to break free.
His mother took a large needle and pierced the side of his ankle bone,
about three or four fen deep,
then forcefully dug and severed it;
there was a snapping sound.
She did the same at his elbow and near his temple.
After finishing,
she released the bonds,
patting him to sleep peacefully.
At daybreak,
Zī rushed to attend his parents,
weeping and saying:
"Thinking back day and night on my past actions,
they were all inhuman!"
His parents were overjoyed.
From then on, he became as gentle as a maiden,
and was esteemed by the local community.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"All courtesans are foxes.
Yet one would not expect there to be foxes who are courtesans;
as for foxes who are madams,
they are beasts acting as fowl.
Destroying principle and injuring human relations—
what is there to be surprised about?
But to endure a hundred twists and a thousand grindings,
remaining steadfast unto death without changing—
this is difficult even for humans to achieve,
so how could it be found in a fox?
Táng Tàizōng said of Wèi Zhēng that he possessed even more charm;
I say the same of Yātou."
Based on the manuscript edition of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Chángshān lived a man named Liú,
who was corpulent and fond of drinking.
Whenever he drank alone,
he would finish an entire jar.
He owned three hundred mǔ of farmland near the city walls,
half of which he planted with millet;
and as his family was wealthy,
he did not consider drinking a burden.
A foreign monk saw him
and said he had a strange ailment.
Liú replied:
"No."
The monk said:
"Do you ever drink without getting drunk?"
He said:
"Yes."
The monk said:
"This is the wine worm."
Liú was startled
and asked for treatment.
The monk said:
"Easy."
Liú asked:
"What medicine is needed?"
The monk said none was required.
He only had Liú lie face down at noon,
bound hand and foot;
half a chǐ or so from his head,
a vessel of fine wine was placed.
After a while,
he grew parched and thirsty,
desiring drink to the extreme.
The aroma of wine entered his nostrils,
cravings flared up fiercely,
yet he suffered from being unable to drink.
Suddenly he felt a violent itch in his throat,
and something came out with a retch,
falling straight into the wine.
Untying the bonds to look,
it was a piece of red flesh about three cùn long,
writhing like a swimming fish,
with mouth and eyes fully formed.
Liú was amazed and thanked him.
He offered gold as reward,
but the monk would not accept,
only asking for the worm.
Liú asked,
"What will you use it for?"
The monk said:
"This is the essence of wine: store water in a jar,
put the worm in and stir it,
and it becomes fine brew."
Liú had him try it,
and indeed it was so.
From then on, Liú hated wine like an enemy.
His body gradually grew thin,
and his family also became poorer day by day,
until later he could not even afford food and drink.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"Drinking a dàn a day
did not diminish his wealth;
not drinking a single dǒu
only increased his poverty: could it be that drinking and eating are predetermined by fate?
Some say: 'The worm was Liú's blessing,
not Liú's ailment;
the monk deceived him to perfect his art.'
Is this true or not?"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
The merchant Bái Yǒugōng said:
"On the Luòkǒu River,
I saw a man carrying a bamboo basket,
leading two large dogs.
From the basket he took out a wooden carved beauty,
over a chǐ tall,
whose hands moved by themselves,
adorned as if alive.
He also placed a small brocade saddle on the dog's back,
then had her ride astride.
After arranging this,
he shouted for the dog to run swiftly.
The beauty stood up by herself,
learning to perform various equestrian tricks,
hanging from the stirrups and hiding under the belly,
bending at the waist and dangling from the tail,
kneeling, bowing, standing up,
agile and flawless.
He also performed Zhāojūn Leaving the Frontier: taking another wooden carved figure,
inserting pheasant tail feathers,
draping a sheepskin coat,
riding a dog to follow her.
Zhāojūn frequently looked back,
the sheepskin-clad figure whipped and chased,
truly as if alive."
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Fàn Shíyīniáng
was the daughter of the Chancellor of the Imperial Academy in Lùchéng.
From a young age she was strikingly beautiful,
especially graceful and refined.
Her parents doted on her,
and when suitors came seeking marriage, they let her choose for herself;
but the girl was seldom satisfied.
On the occasion of the Lantern Festival,
the nuns of Shuǐyuè Temple
held
the Ullambana Festival.
On that day,
visiting women were as numerous as clouds,
and the girl also went there.
While wandering and enjoying the sights,
a young woman followed closely behind her,
repeatedly gazing at her face,
as if wanting to say something.
Looking closely,
she was a peerless beauty of sixteen.
Fàn took a liking to her,
and turned to gaze intently.
The young woman smiled and said:
"Aren't you Elder Sister Fàn Shíyīniáng?"
She replied:
"Yes."
The young woman said:
"I have long heard of your fine reputation;
people's words are indeed not false."
Shíyīniáng also inquired about her residence.
The young woman said with a smile:
"I am of the Fēng family,
the third daughter,
living nearby in a neighboring village."
They held each other's arms and laughed joyfully,
her words gentle and graceful,
and so they greatly loved and delighted in each other,
reluctant to part.
Shíyīniáng asked:
"Why are you without companions?"
She said:
"My parents died early,
and at home there is only an old maidservant
keeping watch over the household,
so I could not come with others."
As Shíyīniáng was about to return,
Fēng gazed tearfully,
and Shíyīniáng also felt sorrowful,
so she invited her to visit.
Fēng said:
"Young lady, your home has vermilion gates and embroidered doors;
I have no close relatives,
and fear causing ridicule or suspicion."
Shíyīniáng insisted on inviting her.
She replied:
"Wait for another day."
Shíyīniáng then took off a gold hairpin and gave it to her,
and Fēng also took a green hairpin from her bun to give in return.
After Shíyīniáng returned home,
she thought of her intensely.
Taking out the gifted hairpin,
it was neither gold nor jade,
and none in the household recognized it,
finding it very strange.
Day after day she hoped for her to come,
and in melancholy she fell ill.
Her parents learned the reason,
and sent people to inquire in nearby villages,
but no one knew of her.
At the time it was the Double Ninth Festival,
and Shíyīniáng, weak and listless,
asked her maid to support her to glimpse the garden,
setting a mat under the eastern fence.
Suddenly a young woman climbed the wall to peek,
and looking closely,
it was Fēng.
She called out:
"Help me down with your strength."
The maid complied,
