and she suddenly descended.
Shíyīniáng was pleasantly surprised,
immediately rose,
pulled her to sit on the mat,
chided her for breaking her promise,
and asked where she had come from.
She replied:
"My home is still far from here;
I often come to my uncle's house to play.
When I previously said I lived in a nearby village,
it was because of my uncle's house.
After we parted, I missed you terribly;
however, when someone of humble status associates with a noble person,
before even setting foot at the door,
one first feels ashamed and uneasy,
fearing to be looked down upon by the servants,
and thus I never came.
Just now, passing by outside the wall,
I heard a woman's voice,
so I climbed up to look,
hoping it was you, young lady,
and now it has indeed turned out as I wished."
Shíyīniáng then recounted the cause of her illness.
Fèng wept tears like rain,
and said:
"My coming here must be kept secret.
Those who spread rumors and stir up trouble,
with their malicious gossip,
are something I cannot bear."
Shíyīniáng agreed.
They returned together and shared a bed,
happily pouring out their hearts.
Her illness soon recovered.
They pledged to be sisters,
and their clothes, shoes, and slippers
were often exchanged and worn.
When they saw someone coming,
they would hide behind the curtains.
After five or six months had passed,
the lord and his wife heard quite a bit about it.
One day,
while the two were playing chess,
the wife suddenly entered.
Looking closely,
she exclaimed in surprise:
"She truly is a friend for my daughter!"
Then she said to Shíyīniáng:
"To have a good friend in the women's quarters,
is a joy for both of us,
why didn't you tell us earlier?"
Shíyīniáng then conveyed Fèng's wishes.
The wife turned to Sānniáng and said:
"To accompany my daughter,
brings me great joy and comfort,
why keep it hidden?"
Fèng blushed with shyness,
silently fiddling with her sash.
After the wife left,
Fèng bid farewell.
Shíyīniáng pleaded with her to stay,
so she remained.
One evening,
Fèng rushed in from outside the door in a panic,
weeping and saying:
"I always said I shouldn't stay,
and now I have indeed suffered this great humiliation!"
Shocked, Shíyīniáng asked what happened.
She said:
"Just now, when I went out to change clothes,
a young man
came forward to harass me,
and I was fortunate to escape.
After this,
what face do I have left!"
Shíyīniáng asked in detail about his appearance,
and apologized, saying:
"Don't be upset,
that was my foolish elder brother.
I will inform my mother,
and have him punished with a cane."
Fèng firmly insisted on leaving.
Shíyīniáng asked her to wait until dawn.
Fèng said:
"My uncle's house is just a stone's throw away,
I only need a ladder to help me over the wall."
Shíyīniáng knew she could not be kept,
and sent two maids to climb over the wall and escort her.
After walking about half a li,
Fèng thanked them and went on alone.
When the maids returned,
Shíyīniáng lay on the bed, grieving and lamenting,
as if she had lost her spouse.
Several months later,
the maid happened to go to the eastern village,
and as she was returning in the evening,
she met Fēng Sānniáng coming along with an old woman.
The maid was delighted,
and bowed in greeting.
Fēng Sānniáng was also deeply moved,
and inquired after Fàn Shíyīniáng's well-being.
The maid grasped her sleeve and said:
"Third Miss, please come visit us.
My young mistress misses you to death!"
Fēng Sānniáng said:
"I miss her too,
but I don't want her family to know.
Go back and leave the garden gate open,
I will come myself."
The maid returned and told Fàn Shíyīniáng;
Fàn Shíyīniáng was overjoyed,
and followed her advice.
When she did, Fēng Sānniáng was already in the garden.
They met,
each telling the other of their long separation,
and talked endlessly, unable to sleep.
Seeing that the maid was sound asleep,
Fēng Sānniáng got up,
moved to share a pillow with Fàn Shíyīniáng,
and whispered to her:
"I knew all along that you, young lady, were not yet betrothed.
With your talent, beauty, and family standing,
why worry about not finding a noble husband?
But those sons of wealthy families,
are arrogant and not worth considering.
If you wish to find a good match,
please do not judge by wealth or poverty."
Fàn Shíyīniáng agreed.
Fēng Sānniáng said:
"At the place where we met last year,
a religious ceremony is being held again.
Tomorrow, trouble yourself to go there once more,
and I will show you a satisfactory young gentleman.
I read books on physiognomy when I was young,
and I am rarely mistaken."
At dawn,
Fēng Sānniáng left,
arranging to wait at the temple.
Fàn Shíyīniáng indeed went,
and Fēng Sānniáng was already there.
After looking around for a while,
Fàn Shíyīniáng invited her to share her carriage.
Hand in hand, they went out the gate,
and saw a scholar,
about seventeen or eighteen years old,
wearing plain cloth robes without adornment,
yet with a handsome and impressive appearance.
Fēng Sānniáng secretly pointed and said:
"This is a talent for the Imperial Academy."
Fàn Shíyīniáng glanced at him briefly.
Fēng Sānniáng bid farewell, saying:
"Young lady, you go back first,
I will follow shortly."
When evening fell,
she indeed arrived,
and said:
"I have just made very detailed inquiries,
that man is Mèng Ānrén from the same neighborhood."
Fàn Shíyīniáng knew he was poor,
and did not think he was suitable.
Fēng Sānniáng said:
"How could you, young lady, also sink into worldly prejudices!
If this man remains poor and lowly forever,
I will gouge out my own eyes,
and never again read the faces of the world's men."
Fàn Shíyīniáng said:
"Then what should we do?"
She replied:
"I wish to have an object from you,
to take and pledge a betrothal with him."
Fàn Shíyīniáng said:
"Sister, why are you so hasty?
My parents are alive;
what if it doesn't work out?"
Fēng Sānniáng said:
"My doing this
is precisely because I fear it won't work out.
If his will is firm,
how can life or death change it?"
Fàn Shíyīniáng absolutely refused.
Fēng Sānniáng said:
"Your marriage fate is already stirring,
but the demonic tribulation has not yet been dispelled.
The reason for my coming
is to repay our former friendship.
I must take my leave now.
I will take the golden phoenix hairpin you gave me,
and falsely claim it is your order to give it to him."
As Fàn Shíyīniáng was planning to discuss it further,
Fēng Sānniáng had already gone out the door and left.
At that time, Mèng Ānrén was poor but very talented.
He intended to choose a spouse,
so at eighteen he was still not betrothed.
That day,
he suddenly saw two beauties,
and upon returning, fell into deep reverie.
As the first watch was nearly ending,
Fēng Sānniáng gently knocked and entered.
Holding a candle to her,
he recognized her as the one he had seen during the day,
and joyfully questioned her.
She said:
"I am of the Fēng family,
a companion of Fàn Shíyīniáng."
The scholar was overjoyed,
without leisure to examine carefully,
he abruptly stepped forward to embrace her.
Fēng Sānniáng resisted, saying:
"I am not Máo Suì,
but rather Cáo Qiūshēng.
Fàn Shíyīniáng wishes to form a lasting union with you,
please allow me to act as matchmaker."
The scholar was startled and did not believe her.
Fēng Sānniáng then showed him the hairpin.
The scholar was beside himself with joy,
and swore:
"Since you show such concern for me,
if I do not obtain Fàn Shíyīniáng,
I would rather remain a bachelor forever."
Fēng Sānniáng then left.
The next morning,
the scholar entreated a neighboring old woman to visit Madame Fàn.
Madame considered him poor,
and without even consulting her daughter,
immediately sent her away.
When Fàn Shíyīniáng learned of this,
her heart was filled with disappointment,
and she deeply resented Fēng Sānniáng for misleading her;
but the golden hairpin was difficult to retrieve,
so she could only vow to die for it.
A few days later,
a certain gentry sought a marriage for his son,
fearing it might not succeed,
he entreated the county magistrate to act as go-between.
At that time, that gentry held a powerful position,
and Magistrate Fàn feared him in his heart.
He asked Fàn Shíyīniáng,
but she was not pleased.
Her mother questioned her,
she mumbled without speaking clearly,
only shedding tears.
She secretly had someone inform Madame,
that if it were not Mèng Ānrén,
she would rather die than marry.
When the Magistrate heard,
he grew even angrier,
and actually promised her to the gentry's family.
Moreover, he suspected Fàn Shíyīniáng had improper feelings for the scholar,
so he selected an auspicious date to hasten the wedding ceremony.
Fàn Shíyīniáng, indignant, refused to eat,
and spent her days lying listlessly in bed.
On the eve before the groom came to fetch the bride,
she suddenly got up,
took a mirror and applied her makeup.
Madame secretly rejoiced.
Soon a maidservant came running to report:
"The young lady has hanged herself!"
The entire household was shocked and wept,
agonizing with regret, but it was too late for anything.
After three days, she was buried.
Mèng Ānrén, upon hearing the old woman's report from next door,
was filled with such indignation and despair that he wished to die.
Yet, from afar, he continued to inquire,
vainly hoping to win her back.
When he learned that the beauty was already promised to another,
the fire of resentment burned within him,
and all his hopes were severed.
Not long after,
he heard that the jade was buried and the fragrance interred,
and he was overwhelmed with grief and sorrow,
wishing he could have died alongside the lovely one.
As evening approached, he went out,
intending to take advantage of the darkness to weep at Shíyīniáng's grave.
Suddenly, someone approached,
and as they drew near,
it turned out to be Fēng Sānniáng.
She said to Mèng,
"Congratulations, your marriage can now be fulfilled."
Mèng said tearfully,
"Don't you know that Shíyīniáng has died?"
Fēng replied,
"What I mean by 'fulfilled'
is precisely because she has died.
Quickly call your servants to open the grave,
for I have a miraculous medicine
that can revive her."
Mèng followed her instructions,
opened the grave and broke open the coffin,
then covered the burial site again.
Mèng carried the corpse on his back,
and together with Sānniáng, they returned home,
placing it on the bed;
after administering the medicine,
she revived after some time.
Looking around and seeing Sānniáng,
she asked,
"Where is this?"
Fēng pointed to Mèng and said,
"This is Mèng Ānrén."
Then she explained what had happened,
and only then did Shíyīniáng feel as if she had awoken from a dream.
Fearing that the secret might leak out,
they traveled together for fifty li,
hiding in a mountain village.
Fēng wanted to take her leave,
but Shíyīniáng tearfully begged her to stay as a companion,
so she was given a separate courtyard to live in.
They sold the burial ornaments,
using the proceeds for their livelihood,
and managed to live comfortably.
Whenever Fēng encountered Mèng coming,
she would always avoid him.
Shíyīniáng said calmly,
"We sisters are as close as flesh and blood,
but in the end, we cannot stay together for a hundred years.
It would be better to follow the example of Éhuáng and Nǚyīng."
Fēng said,
"Since I was young, I have obtained an extraordinary method,
through breathing exercises that can lead to longevity,
which is why I do not wish to marry."
Shíyīniáng laughed and said,
"The world is filled with countless books on the art of nurturing life,
enough to fill a house to the rafters,
but who has actually practiced them successfully?"
Fēng replied,
"What I have obtained is not something ordinary people know.
The methods passed down in the world are not the true techniques,
only Huà Tuó's Five Animal Frolics can be considered somewhat reliable.
All those who cultivate themselves
aim for nothing more than the smooth flow of blood and qi.
If one suffers from hiccups,
assuming the tiger posture will immediately stop it—
isn't that proof?"
Shíyīniáng secretly plotted with Mèng,
making it appear as though he had gone on a long journey.
That night,
she strongly urged Fēng to drink wine;
once she was drunk,
Mèng stealthily entered and violated her.
When Sānniáng woke up, she said,
"Little sister, you have harmed me!
If I had not broken the precept of lust,
upon achieving the Way, I would have ascended to the First Heaven.
Now, having fallen into your cunning plot,
it is fate!"
Then she got up to bid farewell.
Shíyīniáng expressed her sincere intentions and apologized sorrowfully.
Fēng said,
"To tell you the truth: I am a fox.
Because I caught sight of your beautiful appearance,
I suddenly felt love and admiration,
like a silkworm entangling itself in its own cocoon,
leading to today.
This is a tribulation of the demon of passion,
not something within human power to control.
If I stay any longer,
the demon will arise again,
with no end in sight.
Madam, your blessings and prosperity lie far ahead,
take care and cherish yourself."
Having said this, she vanished,
leaving the husband and wife astonished and sighing for a long time.
A year later,
Mèng indeed passed the provincial and metropolitan examinations with success,
and was appointed to the Hànlín Academy.
He sent his card to visit Mr. Fàn,
but Mr. Fàn, ashamed and regretful, refused to see him.
After Mèng insisted,
he finally agreed.
When Mèng entered,
he performed the rites of a son-in-law,
bowing respectfully.
Mr. Fàn felt both ashamed and angry,
suspecting Mèng of being frivolous and insincere.
Mèng requested a private conversation,
and recounted the entire story.
Mr. Fàn did not fully believe him,
but sent someone to investigate his household,
and only then was he greatly surprised and delighted.
He secretly warned them not to publicize it,
fearing there might be calamitous changes.
Two years later,
a certain gentleman was exposed for using connections improperly,
and he and his son were exiled to the Liáohǎi army.
Only then did Shíyīniáng return to her parents' home for a visit.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
My friend Bì Yí'ān,
was unconventional and outstanding,
proud of his unrestrained and free-spirited nature.
He had a plump and stout appearance,
with a thick beard.
He was well-known among scholars.
Once, for a reason, he went to the country estate of his uncle, the prefect,
and rested upstairs.
It was said that the building had long been inhabited by many foxes.
Whenever Bì read the story of Qīngfèng,
his heart yearned for such an encounter,
regretting that he had never met one.
So, while in the building,
he concentrated his thoughts and meditated deeply.
Later, he returned to his study,
as the day was already growing dark.
It was the hot summer month, sweltering,
so he slept by the door.
In his sleep, someone shook him.
Waking up and looking back,
he saw a woman,
over forty years old,
yet still elegant and refined.
Bì rose in surprise,
asking who she was.
She smiled and said,
"I am a fox.
Touched by your constant thoughts of me,
I secretly feel grateful and drawn to you."
Hearing this, Bì was delighted,
and began to banter and jest with her.
The woman laughed and said,
"My age is advancing,
even if others do not find me repulsive,
I feel ashamed and disheartened myself.
I have a daughter who has just come of age,
and she can serve you as your wife.
Tomorrow night,
make sure no one else is in the room,
and she will come."
Having said this, she left.
That night,
he burned incense and sat waiting.
The woman indeed brought her daughter.
Her demeanor was graceful and gentle,
unparalleled in the world.
The woman said to her daughter,
"Young Master Bì has a predestined bond with you,
so you should stay here now.
Return early tomorrow morning,
and do not sleep in."
Bì held her hand and entered the bed curtains,
where they were intimate in every way.
After the act,
she laughed and said,
"This plump young man is so heavy and clumsy,
it's almost unbearable."
Before dawn, she left.
In the evening she came of her own accord
and said,
"My sisters are going to congratulate me on my marriage.
I would like you to go with me tomorrow."
"Where is it?" he asked.
"Where is it?" he asked.
"My eldest sister is giving the feast.
"My eldest sister is giving the feast.
It's not far from here."
Bì waited for her as promised.
After a long wait she still had not come.
He gradually grew tired and drowsy.
He had just laid his head on the desk
when the girl suddenly walked in and said,
"I've kept you waiting a long time."
Then she took his hand and led him away.
Suddenly they arrived at a place
with a large courtyard.
They went straight to the central hall,
where they saw flickering candles
shining like stars.
In a moment the hostess arrived.
She was nearly twenty years old
and exquisitely beautiful in light makeup.
After she had curtsied and offered her congratulations,
they were about to take their seats
when a maid came in and announced,
"The second young lady is here."
They saw a girl walk in.
She was about eighteen or nineteen years old
and said laughingly to the girl:
"My little sister, you've been deflowered.
Is your bridegroom to your liking?"
The girl hit her on the back with a fan
and gave her a dirty look.
The second sister said:
"I remember when we were children wrestling for fun,
you were afraid someone would tickle your ribs.
I would wiggle my fingers at you from a distance
and you would laugh until you couldn't stand it.
Then you would get angry at me
and say I was going to marry the dwarf prince of the Jiāoyáo Kingdom.
I said that you would marry a man with a thick beard someday
and have your little lips pricked.
Now it's come true."
The eldest sister said with a laugh:
"No wonder Third Sister cursed you in anger!
The bridegroom is right here.
How can you be so silly and rambunctious?"
After a while
they sat close together around the wine vessel
and enjoyed themselves with laughter and conversation.
Suddenly a young girl
carrying a cat in her arms arrived.
She was about eleven or twelve years old.
Her hair was still downy like a baby bird's,
but she was bewitchingly beautiful to the core.
The eldest sister said:
"Does Fourth Sister want to see her brother-in-law too?
There's no place for you to sit."
So she lifted the girl onto her lap
and fed her tidbits and fruit.
After a while
she moved her to Second Sister's lap and said:
"She's making my legs sore!"
"She's making my legs sore!"
Second Sister said:
"This girl is so big
and heavy as a thousand catties.
I'm too frail to bear it.
Since you want to see your brother-in-law,
and your brother-in-law is so big and strong,
his fat knees can take the sitting."
So she picked the girl up and put her in Bì's lap.
In his arms she was fragrant and soft,
light as if no one were there.
Bì held her and drank from the same cup with her.
The eldest sister said:
"Little girl, don't drink too much.
If you get drunk and lose your manners,
your brother-in-law might laugh at you."
The young girl grinned broadly
and stroked the cat with her hand.
The cat let out a meow.
The eldest sister said:
"If you don't put it down,
you'll get fleas and lice all over you!"
Second Sister said:
"Let's use the cat to set a rule:
we'll pass chopsticks around,
and whoever it meows at has to drink."
Everyone did as she said.
Whenever it came to Bì, the cat meowed.
Bì was a prodigious drinker to begin with,
so he downed several goblets in a row.
Then he realized the little girl was purposely making the cat meow,
so everyone laughed uproariously.
Second Sister said:
"Little sister, go home now!
If you crush your brother-in-law to death,
Third Sister will blame us."
The little girl then carried the cat away.
Seeing that Bì was a good drinker,
the eldest sister took a hair ornament from her head to hold wine and urged him to drink.
It looked as if it could only hold a pint or so,
but when he drank from it,
he felt as if he had downed several pecks.
When he looked at it closely,
it was a lotus leaf.
Second Sister also wanted to toast him.
Bì declined, saying he could not drink any more.
Second Sister took out a rouge box
bigger than a pellet
and poured wine into it, saying:
"Since you can't drink any more,
let this serve as a token of my feelings."
Bì looked at it and thought
he could drain it in one gulp, but after a hundred sips
it still was not dry.
The girl at his side replaced the box with a small lotus-shaped cup, saying:
"Don't let that sly person make a fool of you."
"Don't let that sly person make a fool of you."
She put the box on the table,
and it became a huge bowl.
Second Sister said:
"What business is it of yours?
After only three days as husband and wife, you're this close already!"
Bì raised the cup to his mouth and drained it.
It felt greasy and soft in his hand.
Upon closer inspection,
it was not a cup
but one of a pair of silk stockings,
exquisitely embroidered.
Second Sister snatched it away and scolded:
"You sly girl!
When did you steal my shoe?
No wonder my feet felt cold!"
Then she got up
and went into the inner room to change her shoes.
The girl suggested that Bì take his leave.
She escorted him out of the village
and told him to go back by himself.
Suddenly he woke up
and realized it had all been a dream.
But his mouth and nose were reeking
with a strong smell of wine, which struck him as strange.
with a strong smell of wine, which struck him as strange.
At dusk
the girl came
and said,
"Didn't you drink yourself to death last night?"
Bì said,
"I was just thinking it was a dream."
The girl said,
"My sisters were afraid you would raise a ruckus,
so they passed it off as a dream,
but it wasn't a dream at all."
Whenever the girl played chess with Bì,
he always lost.
The girl said laughingly:
"You're so fond of this game every day,
I thought you must be a master.
But now that I see you play,
you're only average."
Bì asked her to teach him.
The girl said:
"When it comes to the art of chess,
you have to grasp it for yourself.
What can I do for you?
If you keep at it day and night,
you may improve."
After a few months
Bì felt he had made some progress.
The girl tested him
and said with a laugh:
"Not yet,
not yet."
Bì went out
and played with people he had played with before.
They noticed a difference in him
and were all amazed.
Bì was an open, straightforward person
who did not keep things to himself,
so he let slip a little.
The girl found out
and scolded him:
"No wonder people in our line don't associate with madcaps.
I've told you time and again to be careful and keep quiet.
Why are you still acting this way?"
Angrily she made as if to leave.
Bì apologized profusely,
and the girl relented a little.
But from then on she visited him less and less often.
After more than a year,
one evening she came,
sitting silently facing him.
When he invited her to play chess,
she declined;
when he asked her to stay the night,
she refused.
After a long, melancholy silence,
she said:
"How do you think I compare to Qīngfèng?"
He replied:
"You likely surpass her."
She said:
"I feel ashamed, for I am not her equal.
However, since Liáozhāi and you are literary friends,
I would trouble you to write a short biography of me.
Perhaps a thousand years from now, there may be someone who loves and remembers me as you do."
Bì said:
"I have long had this intention;
but previously I followed your old instruction,
so I kept it secret."
The woman said:
"I gave that instruction before,
but now we are about to part,
what is there to conceal anymore?"
He asked:
"Where are you going?"
She said:
"My fourth younger sister and I have been summoned by the Queen Mother of the West to serve as envoys of flowers and birds,
and will not be able to come again.
In the past, there was an elder sister among us
who, with your family's uncle-brother,
had already given birth to two daughters before parting,
and that debt remains unpaid to this day;
fortunately, you and I have no such burdens."
Bì asked for parting words.
She said:
"Temper your arrogance,
and faults will naturally lessen."
Then she rose,
took his hand and said:
"Please see me off."
After walking about a li,
they parted in tears.
She said:
"Since we both have our aspirations,
it is not impossible that we may meet again."
Then she left.
On the nineteenth day of the twelfth lunar month in the twenty-first year of the Kāngxī reign,
Master Bì and I shared a bed in the Chuòrán Hall,
and he recounted this strange tale in detail.
I said:
"If there are foxes like this,
then Liáozhāi's writings are truly honored."
Thus I recorded it.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain man from Chángqīng,
who made his living selling cloth,
was staying in Tài'ān.
Hearing there was a fortune-teller skilled in astrological fate calculation,
he went to inquire about his fortune.
The fortune-teller, after推算, said:
"Your fate is extremely bad,
you should return home quickly."
The man, frightened,
took his money and headed north.
On the road, he met a man in short clothes,
who seemed to be a yamen runner.
Gradually engaging him in conversation,
they became acquainted and friendly.
The cloth seller often bought food and drink,
inviting the other to share.
The short-clothed man felt very grateful to him.
The cloth seller asked what business he was on,
and he replied:
"I am going to Chángqīng
to apprehend some people."
Asked who they were,
the short-clothed man took out a warrant,
showing it for him to see for himself: the first name was his own.
Startled, he said:
"For what reason am I being apprehended?"
The short-clothed man said:
"I am not a living person,
but a runner under the command of the Eastern Fourth Judge of Hāolǐ Mountain.
I suppose your allotted lifespan has ended."
The man wept and begged for rescue.
The ghost said:
"I cannot.
However, there are many names on the warrant.
It will still take some time to gather them all.
You hurry home,
settle your affairs,
I will summon you last.
This is how I repay our friendship."
Not long after,
they reached a riverbank,
where the bridge was broken,
making it difficult for travelers to cross.
The ghost said:
"You are about to die,
and not a single coin can you take with you.
Why not build a bridge here immediately,
to benefit travelers;
though it may cost a fair amount,
it might not be without some small benefit for you."
The man agreed.
Upon returning home,
he told his wife and children to prepare burial necessities.
He set a date to gather workers and build the bridge.
A long time passed,
but the ghost never came.
He secretly grew suspicious.
One day,
the ghost suddenly appeared and said:
"I have already reported the bridge-building matter to the City God,
who forwarded it to the underworld authorities.
They said this act could extend your lifespan.
Now your name has been removed from the warrant,
and I respectfully come to report this."
The man was overjoyed and thanked him.
Later, when he went to Tàishān again,
not forgetting the ghost's kindness,
he respectfully prepared paper money and ingots,
called the ghost's name and made a libation offering.
After he left,
he saw the short-clothed man hurrying towards him, saying:
"You nearly brought disaster upon me!
Just now the Judge was presiding over affairs,
fortunately he did not hear.
Otherwise,
what could be done!"
He escorted him a few paces,
and said:
"Do not come again in the future.
If I have business northward,
I will naturally make a detour to visit you."
Then they parted and he left.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A farmer was hoeing at the foot of a mountain,
and his wife brought him food in an earthenware pot.
After eating,
he left the pot by the ridge.
Towards evening, when he looked,
the leftover porridge in the pot was completely empty.
This happened repeatedly.
Suspicious,
he watched stealthily to observe.
A fox came,
sticking its head into the pot.
The farmer, hoe on shoulder, crept up
and struck at it with force.
The fox fled in alarm.
The pot stuck on its head,
and it struggled painfully, unable to shake it off;
the fox stumbled and fell,
the pot hit something and shattered,
freeing its head.
Seeing the farmer,
it fled even more desperately,
and disappeared over the mountain.
Several years later,
a noble family's daughter south of the mountain
was tormented by a fox's haunting,
and exorcisms had no effect.
The fox said to the girl:
"Paper talismans and incantations,
what can they do to me!"
The girl tricked it, saying:
"Your magical arts are truly profound,
we can fortunately be together forever.
But I wonder, in your life, is there anything you fear?"
The fox said:
"There is nothing I fear.
But ten years ago, when I was on the northern mountain,
I once stole food from a field,
and was nearly killed by a man wearing a broad-brimmed hat,
holding a curved weapon.
I still tremble at the memory."
The girl told her father.
Her father thought of exploiting what it feared,
but did not know the man's name
or where he lived,
and had no way to inquire.
It so happened that I went to a mountain village on some business,
and when I mentioned this story casually to someone,
a man nearby exclaimed in surprise:
"This matches exactly what happened to me years ago.
Could it be that the fox I chased back then
has now learned to cause mischief?"
I found this strange,
and upon returning, I told my host about it.
My host was delighted
and immediately ordered me to fetch the farmer.
He respectfully explained his request.
The farmer laughed and said:
"It's true that I encountered such a thing back then,
but it's not certain that this is the same creature.
Moreover, if it can transform and cause mischief,
how could it fear a mere farmer?"
The wealthy family insisted,
so they had him dress and act as he did that day.
He entered the room, planted his hoe on the ground,
and shouted:
"I've been searching for you all day and couldn't find you,
but you've been hiding here!
Now that I've caught you,
I'll definitely kill you without mercy!"
As soon as he finished speaking,
the sound of a fox crying was heard in the room.
The farmer intensified his fierce display of anger.
The fox immediately pleaded for its life in a pitiful voice.
The farmer scolded it:
"Leave quickly,
and I'll spare you."
The young lady saw the fox flee with its head in its hands, scurrying away like a rat,
and from then on, peace was restored.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Qī Shēng from Wèihuī
was a young man of refined bearing,
courageous and responsible.
At the time, a wealthy family had a large mansion
where ghosts were seen during the day,
and deaths occurred one after another,
so they were willing to sell it cheaply.
Qī Shēng bargained for a low price
and purchased it to live in.
However, the mansion was vast and sparsely populated,
and in the eastern courtyard's pavilion,
weeds and mugwort had grown into a forest,
so it was left abandoned for the time being.
At night, the servants would often get frightened
and clamor about ghosts.
After more than two months,
a maidservant died.
Not long after,
Qī Shēng's wife went to the pavilion at dusk,
and upon returning, fell ill,
dying a few days later.
The family grew even more fearful
and urged Qī Shēng to move elsewhere.
He refused to listen.
Feeling solitary and without a partner,
he grieved in loneliness.
The servants often chattered about strange occurrences,
which angered Qī Shēng.
In a fit of rage, he took his bedding
and slept alone in the desolate pavilion,
leaving a candle lit to observe any anomalies.
After a long while with nothing unusual,
he eventually fell asleep.
Suddenly, someone reached under the covers,
groping around repeatedly.
Qī Shēng woke up and saw
an elderly maidservant,
with crooked ears and disheveled hair,
exceedingly bloated.
Knowing she was a ghost,
he grabbed her arm and pushed her away,
laughing as he said:
"Your esteemed appearance is hardly worth my attention!"
The maidservant, ashamed,
withdrew her hand and shuffled away.
A moment later,
a young woman emerged from the northwest corner,
graceful and lovely in demeanor.
She strode boldly to the lamp
and angrily scolded:
"Where did this reckless fellow come from,
daring to sleep so soundly here!"
Qī Shēng rose and said with a laugh:
"I am the master of this estate,
waiting here to collect rent from you."
He then got up
and, naked, tried to seize her.
The young woman quickly fled.
Qī Shēng hurried to the northwest corner first,
blocking her escape route.
With nowhere to go,
she sat down on the bed.
Drawing closer to her,
he saw by the candlelight that she was as beautiful as a fairy;
gradually, he embraced her.
The young woman laughed and said:
"Aren't you afraid of ghosts, reckless man?
You'll bring disaster upon yourself and die!"
Qī Shēng forcibly removed her skirt and jacket,
and she did not resist much.
Afterward, she confessed:
"I am of the Zhāng family,
and my childhood name is Ā Duān.
I was mistakenly married to a dissolute man
who was stubborn and cruel,
subjecting me to unjust abuse.
In anger and sorrow, I died young
and have been buried here for over twenty years.
This mansion is built atop graves."
He asked:
"Who is the old maidservant?"
She replied:
"She is also a ghost from the past,
who serves me.
When living people reside above,
ghosts cannot rest peacefully in their tombs at night,
so I sent her to drive you away."
He asked:
"Why was she groping around?"
She laughed and said:
"This maidservant hasn't known a man in thirty years,
which is pitiable;
but she was also too presumptuous.
In essence,
those who are timid and weak
are more likely to be bullied and teased by ghosts;
those with firm resolve
dare not be provoked."
Hearing the neighboring temple bell cease its ringing,
she dressed and got out of bed,
saying:
"If you do not doubt me,
I will return tonight."
As evening fell,
she indeed arrived,
and their intimacy grew even more joyful.
Shēng said:
"My wife unfortunately passed away,
and I cannot release my grief from my heart.
Can you bring her to me?"
Upon hearing this, the woman became even more sorrowful,
saying:
"I have been dead for twenty years,
and who has ever thought of me!
You are truly a man of deep feeling,
I shall do my utmost.
However, I have heard she is destined to be reborn into a noble family.
I do not know if she is still in the underworld."
The next evening,
she told Shēng:
"Your wife is to be reborn into a noble household.
Because in her previous life she lost an earring,
she beat a maidservant,
who then hanged herself.
This case remains unresolved,
hence her stay is delayed.
She is currently lodged under the Medicine King's corridor,
with guards watching over her.
I sent a maidservant to bribe them,
so she may come soon."
Shēng asked:
"Why are you so free and unoccupied?"
She replied:
"All ghosts who died unjustly do not present themselves voluntarily;
King Yánmó is unaware of them."
As the second watch was nearing its end,
an old maidservant indeed led Shēng's wife to him.
Shēng took her hand, overwhelmed with grief,
and his wife, tears in her eyes, could not speak.
The woman departed,
saying:
"You two can speak of your long separation,
and we shall meet again another night."
Shēng inquired about the maidservant's death.
His wife said:
"It is of no concern,
the matter is being settled."
They went to bed, embracing each other,
their affection as deep as in life.
From then on, this became a regular occurrence.
Five days later,
his wife suddenly wept, saying:
"Tomorrow I must go to Shāndōng,
the pain of separation will be long,
what can we do!"
Hearing this, Shēng
shed tears profusely,
overcome with sorrow.
The woman advised:
"I have a plan
that may allow a temporary reunion."
They both wiped their tears and asked her.
She requested ten bundles of spirit money,
to be burned under the apricot tree in the southern hall,
to bribe the officer in charge of rebirth,
so he would delay the time.
Shēng complied.
That evening,
his wife arrived,
saying:
"Thanks to Duānniáng,
we now have ten days together."
Shēng was overjoyed,
and insisted the woman not leave,
keeping her to share the bed,
from dusk till dawn,
fearing only that their joy would end.
After seven or eight days,
as the deadline approached,
husband and wife wept all night.
They sought advice from the woman,
who said:
"The situation makes it difficult to scheme again.
But let me try;
it will require no less than a million in underworld currency."
Shēng burned that amount.
The woman returned,
joyfully saying:
"I sent someone to negotiate with the rebirth officer;
at first it was very difficult;
but upon seeing the large sum of money,
his mind began to waver.
Now he has substituted another ghost in her place."
From then on,
she no longer left even during the day,
and had Shēng seal the windows and doors,
keeping lamps and candles burning constantly.
Thus over a year passed,
when the woman suddenly fell ill,
suffering dizziness and distress,
as if seeing ghosts in a trance.
His wife stroked her, saying:
"This is a ghostly illness."
Shēng said:
"Duānniáng is already a ghost;
what other ghost could make her ill?"
His wife replied:
"Not so.
When a person dies, they become a ghost;
when a ghost dies, they become a jiàn.
Ghosts fear jiàn
just as people fear ghosts."
Shēng wanted to hire a shaman healer.
She said:
"How can a ghost be treated by a human?
The old woman Wáng in the neighborhood
now practices her arts in the underworld;
you may summon her.
However, she lives over ten lǐ from here,
and my feet are too weak to walk;
I trouble you to burn a straw horse."
Shēng complied.
As soon as the horse was ignited,
he saw a maidservant leading a red-maned horse,
handing the reins in the courtyard,
and in an instant she vanished.
Shortly after,
she returned with an old woman riding double,
and tied the horse to a corridor pillar.
The old woman entered,
and began examining the woman's ten fingers.
After a while, he sat upright,
and began to nod his head.
He fell to the ground and lay there for some time,
then jumped up and said:
"I am the Great King of Hēishān.
Your wife's illness is very serious,
but fortunately you have encountered a minor deity like me,
so your blessings are not shallow!
This is a vengeful ghost causing trouble,
but it's no matter,
no matter!
However, once the illness is cured,
you must provide me with generous offerings:
one hundred ingots of gold, one hundred strings of cash,
and a grand feast,
none of which may be lacking."
His wife agreed to each demand.
The old woman then fell down again and revived,
scolding the sick woman,
and only then stopped.
After a while, she prepared to leave.
The wife escorted her outside the courtyard,
presented her with a horse,
and she left happily.
Returning to look at the young woman,
she seemed slightly more lucid.
The couple was overjoyed,
and comforted her with questions.
The young woman suddenly said:
"I fear I may not walk among the living again.
Whenever I close my eyes, I see vengeful ghosts—
such is fate!"
With that, she wept.
The next night,
her illness grew even more severe and critical,
her body trembling and contorted,
as if she were seeing illusions.
She pulled the scholar to lie with her,
burying her head in his chest,
as if afraid of being seized.
Whenever the scholar got up,
she would scream in terror and unrest.
This went on for six or seven days,
and the couple was at a loss for what to do.
Once, when the scholar was away,
he returned after half a day
to hear his wife crying.
Startled, he asked,
and learned that Duānniáng had already died on the bed,
her empty shell still remaining.
When they opened it,
only stark white bones were inside.
The scholar wept bitterly
and buried her with the rites of the living beside the ancestral graves.
One night,
his wife sobbed in her sleep.
He shook her awake and asked,
and she replied:
"Just now I dreamed Duānniáng came
and said her husband had become a jiàn ghost,
angry that she had changed her allegiance in the underworld,
and bore a grudge, demanding her life.
She begged me to hold a Buddhist service."
The scholar rose early
and prepared to follow her request.
His wife stopped him, saying:
"Exorcising ghosts is not something you can manage."
She then got up and left.
After a short while, she returned
and said:
"I have already sent someone to invite monks.
We should first burn paper money for expenses."
The scholar agreed.
As the sun set,
the monks all gathered,
with golden cymbals and ritual drums,
just as in the human world.
The wife often said the noise was deafening,
but the scholar heard nothing unusual.
After the service concluded,
his wife dreamed again of Duānniáng coming to thank her,
saying:
"The grievance has been resolved,
and I am to be reborn as the daughter of the City God.
Please convey this."
Three years passed,
and the family, initially fearful upon hearing this,
gradually grew accustomed.
When the scholar was not home,
they would report matters through the window.
One night,
she wept to the scholar, saying:
"The official who previously detained me
has now had his misconduct exposed,
and the investigation is urgent,
so I fear we cannot stay together much longer."
A few days later,
she indeed fell ill,
and said:
"Where love is deeply rooted,
one would rather die long ago
than live on.
Now we must part forever—
is this not fate?"
The scholar panicked and sought a solution.
She said:
"This cannot be helped."
He asked:
"Will you be punished?"
She replied:
"There will be a light penalty.
But the crime of stealing life is great,
while the crime of stealing death is small."
With these words,
she grew still.
Upon closer inspection,
her face, form, and substance
gradually faded away.
The scholar often slept alone in the pavilion,
hoping for another encounter,
but in the end, all remained silent,
and people's hearts grew calm.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Scholar Hán lived in a villa for half a year,
and only returned at the end of the year.
One night,
as his wife lay in bed,
she heard footsteps.
Looking around,
she saw the coal fire in the stove
burning brightly.
She saw an old woman,
perhaps eighty or ninety years old,
with wrinkled skin and a hunched back,
her sparse hair countable.
She said to the woman:
"Would you like some bótuō?"
The woman was frightened
and dared not reply.
The old woman then used iron chopsticks to stir the fire,
placing a pot on it;
then she poured in water.
Soon, the sound of boiling water was heard.
The old woman lifted her skirt and opened a pouch at her waist,
taking out dozens of bótuō,
which she dropped into the boiling water,
making distinct sounds.
She said to herself:
"I'll go find chopsticks."
With that, she went out the door.
Seizing the opportunity while the old woman was away,
the woman quickly got up, grabbed the pot, and poured its contents behind the bamboo mat,
then covered herself with the quilt and lay down.
A moment later,
the old woman returned
and pressed her about where the pot and boiling water had gone.
The woman cried out in terror.
The whole family woke up,
and the old woman finally left.
They lifted the bamboo mat to look,
and found dozens of ground beetles
piled up there.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Jīn Yǒngnián of Lìjīn
was eighty-two years old and childless.
His wife was also seventy-eight,
and they had given up hope.
Suddenly, he dreamed a deity told him:
"You were destined to have no descendants,
but considering your fair trade in business,
I grant you a son."
He woke and told his wife.
She said:
"This is truly wishful thinking.
Both of us are nearing the grave—
how could we bear a child?"
Not long after,
the wife's belly began to stir;
ten months later,
she indeed gave birth to a son.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Ān Yòuyú was a senior licentiate
from Shǎnxi.
He was by nature
open-handed and fond of righteous deeds,
and he took pleasure in setting living things free.
Whenever he saw hunters with captured birds,
he would not begrudge the expense
of buying them and releasing them.
Once, when his maternal uncle’s family was holding a funeral,
he went to help with the burial.
On his way back at dusk,
he passed by Mount Huà
and lost his way, straying into a mountain valley.
He was greatly frightened.
About an arrow-shot away,
he suddenly saw lamplight
and hurried toward it.
After a few paces,
he abruptly saw an old man,
bent over and leaning on a cane,
walking swiftly along a side path.
Ān halted his steps
and was about to ask a question
when the old man first demanded who he was.
Ān told him he had lost his way;
he also said that the place with lamplight must be a mountain village
and that he intended to seek lodging there.
The old man said:
“This is no land of ease and comfort.
Fortunately, I have come along;
you may follow me.
My thatched cottage can provide a place for you to stay.”
Ān was greatly pleased
and followed him for about a li,
where he saw a small village.
The old man knocked on a bramble gate,
and an old woman came out.
Opening the gate, she said,
“Has the young master come?”
The old man said:
“Yes.”
Once inside,
he saw the dwelling was low and cramped.
The old man trimmed the lamp and urged him to sit,
then ordered that food be prepared according to what was available.
He also said to the old woman:
“This is no stranger;
he is my benefactor.
Since you, old woman, cannot walk well,
call Huāgūzi to warm the wine.”
Soon a young woman came in with the food utensils
and stood beside the old man,
her autumn-wave eyes glancing sidelong.
Ān looked at her:
her fragrant countenance and youthful teeth
were almost like those of a heavenly fairy.
The old man turned and told her to warm the wine.
In the western corner of the room was a coal stove;
the girl went into the room to stir the fire.
Ān asked:
“Who is this gentleman?”
The old man replied:
“This old man’s surname is Zhāng.
In seventy years, I have only had this daughter.
Farming households have few servants;
since you, sir, are not an outsider,
I dared to let my wife and child appear.
I hope you will not laugh.”
Ān asked:
“Where is her husband’s family?”
He replied:
“Not yet.”
Ān praised her grace and beauty,
his praise flowing incessantly.
The old man was just modestly declining
when they suddenly heard the young woman cry out in alarm.
The old man rushed in;
the wine was boiling over and the fire was leaping up.
The old man then rescued the situation and stopped it,
scolding:
“You big old maid,
don’t you know that when it’s soaked, it becomes fierce?!”
Turning his head,
he saw by the stove a heart-shaped Shu embroidery with an unfinished image of the goddess Zǐgū,
and scolded again:
“With hair so disheveled,
you’re just like a baby!”
Holding it up to Ān, he said:
“Being greedy for this pastime
caused the wine to boil over.
To receive your praise, sir,
is this not shameful to death!”
Ān examined it carefully:
the eyebrows, eyes, robe, and clothing
were crafted with extreme skill.
He praised:
“Though it is close to child’s play,
it also shows a clever mind.”
After drinking for a while,
the girl frequently came to serve wine,
smiling sweetly
without any shyness.
Ān gazed at her, his feelings stirred.
Suddenly hearing the old woman call,
the old man left.
Ān, seeing no one else was around,
said to the girl:
“Seeing your immortal countenance
has made me lose my soul.
I wish to send a matchmaker,
but fear it may not succeed.
What should I do?”
The girl held the pot toward the fire,
silent as if she had not heard;
he asked several times, but she did not answer.
Ān gradually moved into the room.
The girl stood up,
with a stern expression said:
“Wild man entering the inner chamber,
what are you going to do?!”
Ān knelt down and pleaded with her.
The girl tried to rush out the door to leave.
Ān suddenly rose and blocked her way,
intimately kissing her cheek.
The girl trembled and cried out urgently;
the old man hurriedly came in and asked what was happening.
Ān released her and stepped back,
feeling extremely ashamed and afraid.
The girl calmly said to her father:
“The wine boiled over again;
if the young master hadn’t come,
the pot would have melted.”
Hearing the girl’s words,
Ān’s heart finally settled,
and he felt even more grateful to her.
His soul was in turmoil,
and he lost what he had intended.
So he pretended to be drunk and left the seat,
and the girl also left.
The old man laid out bedding,
closed the door, and then left.
Ān could not sleep;
before dawn,
he called to take his leave.
Upon reaching home,
he immediately asked a close friend to go to their cottage to propose marriage,
but the friend returned after a whole day,
having been unable to find their village.
Ān then ordered a servant and horse
and went to search for the way himself.
When he arrived, there were only sheer cliffs and rocks;
there was no village at all.
He inquired among nearby villages,
but the surname Zhāng was extremely rare.
He returned disappointed
and forgot both food and sleep.
From this, he fell into a dazed illness: if he forced himself to eat soup or porridge,
he would feel nauseous and about to vomit;
in his confused state,
he would often call out “Huāgūzi.”
His family did not understand
but kept watch around him all night,
as his condition was critical.
One night,
the watchers were exhausted and all fell asleep.
In his drowsy state,
Ān felt someone shaking and pulling him.
Slightly opening his eyes,
he saw Huāgūzi standing by his bed.
Unconsciously, his spirit cleared,
and he gazed intently at the young woman, tears silently falling.
The girl tilted her head and smiled, saying:
“Silly boy, how did you get to this state?”
Then she climbed onto the bed,
sat on Ān’s thighs,
and used both hands to press his temples.
Ān felt an extraordinary fragrance of brain and musk,
penetrating his nose and seeping into his bones.
After pressing for a while,
he suddenly felt sweat covering his forehead,
gradually reaching his limbs.
She whispered:
“There are many people in the room;
it is not convenient for me to stay.
I will come to see you again in three days.”
Then, from her embroidered sleeve, she took out several steamed buns and placed them by the bedside,
then quietly left.
By midnight,
Ān had sweated and began to think of food;
he felt for the buns and ate them.
He did not know what ingredients they contained,
but they were exceptionally sweet and delicious,
so he finished three of them.
He also covered the remaining buns with his clothes
and fell into a deep sleep.
At dawn, he awoke,
feeling as if a heavy burden had been lifted.
After three days,
when the buns were finished,
his spirits were doubly refreshed.
So he sent his family members away.
Worried that the girl might not find her way in,
he secretly went out to the courtyard
and removed all the locks and bolts.
Before long,
the girl indeed arrived.
She said with a smile:
"Silly fellow!
Aren't you going to thank the shaman?"
Ān was overjoyed.
He embraced her and they became intimate,
their love and affection reaching its peak.
Afterward, she said:
"I have risked danger and endured disgrace
for a reason—
to repay your great kindness.
But in truth, we cannot be together forever.
I hope you will make other plans soon."
Ān remained silent for a long while,
then asked:
"We have never met before.
Where did our families have a prior connection?
I truly cannot recall."
The girl did not answer,
only saying:
"Think on it yourself."
Ān insisted on a lasting union.
The girl said:
"Repeatedly sneaking out at night
is certainly not possible;
becoming permanent spouses
is also impossible."
Hearing this,
Ān felt sorrowful and dejected.
The girl said:
"If you truly wish to be together,
come to my home tomorrow night."
Ān then set aside his sorrow and became joyful.
He asked:
"The road is long and distant.
With your delicate steps,
how were you able to come here?"
She replied:
"I actually never returned home.
The deaf old woman in the east end is my aunt.
For your sake,
I have stayed there until now.
My family is probably suspicious and wondering about me."
Ān shared the bed with her.
He felt that her breath and skin
were fragrant everywhere.
He asked:
"What perfume do you use
that penetrates your flesh and bones?"
The girl said:
"I have been like this since birth,
not due to perfumes or adornments."
Ān found her even more extraordinary.
The girl rose early to bid farewell.
Ān worried about losing his way.
The girl agreed to wait for him on the road.
Ān hurried there at dusk.
The girl was indeed waiting,
and they went together to the old place.
The old man and woman welcomed them joyfully.
The wine and dishes were not exquisite,
consisting of mixed wild vegetables.
Afterward, they invited the guest to retire for the night.
The girl showed no particular attention,
which made Ān somewhat suspicious.
When the night grew deep,
the girl finally arrived,
saying:
"My parents kept chattering and wouldn't sleep,
making you wait so long."
They spent the entire night in intimate harmony.
She said to Ān:
"After this night's meeting,
it will be a separation of a hundred years."
Ān asked in alarm.
She replied:
"My father finds this small village too lonely and isolated,
so he plans to move far away.
Our happy union
ends with this night."
Ān could not bear to part,
overcome with grief and sorrow.
As they lingered in attachment,
the night gradually brightened into dawn.
Suddenly, the old man burst in,
cursing:
"You disgraceful girl, you have sullied our pure family name,
making me ashamed to death!"
The girl turned pale,
and hastily ran off.
The old man also left,
cursing as he went.
Ān was terrified and trembling with fear,
feeling he had no place to hide.
He secretly fled and returned home.
For several days he wandered restlessly,
his state of mind almost unbearable.
He thought of going again at night,
climbing over the wall to see if there was an opportunity.
The old man had spoken of kindness,
so even if the matter were discovered,
there should be no severe reprimand.
So he took advantage of the night to sneak there,
wandering through the mountains,
confused and not knowing where to go.
He became greatly afraid.
Just as he was searching for the way back,
he saw a house faintly visible in the valley.
Delighted, he went toward it.
The gate was tall and imposing,
resembling that of a noble family.
The heavy doors were not yet open.
Ān asked the gatekeeper about the Zhāng family's residence.
A servant in dark clothing came out,
asking:
"Who inquires about the Zhāng family in the dark of night?"
Ān said:
"They are my dear friends.
I have lost my way to their home."
The servant said:
"Sir, do not ask about the Zhāng family.
This is her aunt's home.
Huāgū is here right now.
Allow me to inform her."
He went in and, shortly after,
came out to invite Ān.
As soon as Ān stepped onto the corridor,
Huāgū hurried out to greet him,
saying to the servant:
"Ān-láng has traveled through the night.
He must be exhausted.
Prepare a bed for him to rest."
After a short while,
they went hand in hand into the bedchamber.
Ān asked:
"Why is there no one else in your aunt's house?"
The girl said:
"My aunt has gone out,
leaving me to watch the house.
Fortunately, I met you.
Is this not predestined?"
However, as they embraced,
Ān detected a strong, gamey odor,
and his heart grew suspicious.
The girl wrapped her arms around Ān's neck
and suddenly licked his nostrils with her tongue.
It pierced his brain like a thorn.
Ān was terrified.
He tried desperately to break free,
but his body felt bound by thick ropes.
Soon after,
he lost consciousness.
Ān did not return home,
and his family sent people out to search for him, but they found no trace.
Some said they had seen him at dusk on a mountain path.
His family went into the mountains,
and there they found him lying naked and dead at the foot of a steep cliff.
Shocked and bewildered, they could not determine the cause,
so they carried him home.
As everyone gathered to mourn and weep,
a young woman came to offer condolences,
wailing loudly as she entered through the gate.
She stroked the corpse and pressed his nose,
letting her tears and mucus fall into it,
crying out:
"Heavens,
heavens!
How could you be so foolish and blind as this!"
She wept bitterly until her voice grew hoarse,
and only after a long while did she stop.
She told the family:
"Leave him for seven days,
do not encoffin him."
No one knew who she was,
and as they were about to ask,
the woman, proud and without courtesy,
with tears in her eyes, went straight out,
ignoring their pleas to stay.
They followed her,
but in the blink of an eye, she had vanished.
Everyone suspected she was a deity,
and they carefully followed her instructions.
That night she came again,
weeping as before.
On the seventh night,
Ān suddenly revived,
turning over and groaning.
His family was utterly terrified.
The woman entered,
and they faced each other, sobbing.
Ān raised his hand,
waving for everyone to leave.
The woman took out a bundle of green herbs,
boiled them in about a liter of water,
and immediately fed it to him at the bedside.
In a moment, he could speak.
He sighed and said:
"It was you who killed me again,
and it was also you who brought me back to life!"
He then recounted what he had experienced.
The woman said:
"That was a snake spirit impersonating me.
When you lost your way earlier,
the lamplight you saw
was that creature."
Ān asked:
"How are you able to revive the dead and restore flesh to bones?
Are you perhaps an immortal?"
She replied:
"I have long wanted to tell you,
but feared it would cause shock and alarm.
Five years ago,
did you buy a hunted river deer on the path of Huàshān and release it?"
He said:
"Yes,
that did happen."
She said:
"That was my father.
Earlier I spoke of your great virtue,
and it was because of this.
You had already been reborn in the household of Wáng Zhǔzhèng in the western village.
My father and I pleaded your case before Yánmó Wáng,
but Yánmó Wáng was not favorable.
My father was willing to abandon his cultivation and die in your place,
and after grieving for seven days,
he finally succeeded.
Our meeting now
is fortunate indeed.
However, though you have revived,
you will surely suffer from paralysis and numbness;
only by drinking snake blood mixed with wine
can the illness be cured."
Ān gnashed his teeth in hatred,
but worried he had no means to capture it.
The woman said:
"It is not difficult.
But taking many lives
will hinder my ascension to immortality for a hundred years.
Its lair is in the old cliff.
At dusk, gather straw and burn it,
and prepare crossbows outside as a precaution.
The demon creature can then be captured."
Having said this,
she bid farewell:
"I cannot stay with you forever,
which truly saddens me.
But for your sake,
my accumulated virtue has already been reduced by seventy percent.
I hope you will pity and forgive me.
For the past month, I have felt slight movement in my abdomen—
I fear it is a karmic burden.
Whether it is a boy or a girl,
in a year I will send it to you."
She left in tears.
After a night,
Ān felt everything below his waist had died,
and scratching brought no pain or itch.
He then told his family what the woman had said.
His family went
and did as instructed,
setting a fierce fire in the cave.
A huge white snake rushed out through the flames.
Several crossbows fired at once,
killing it.
When the fire died down, they entered the cave
and found hundreds of snakes, large and small,
all charred and foul-smelling.
The family returned
and presented the snake blood.
Ān took it for three days,
and gradually his legs could turn and move.
After half a year, he could stand.
Later, while walking alone in the valley,
he met an old woman who handed him a baby wrapped in swaddling clothes, saying:
"My daughter sends her regards to you, sir."
Just as he was about to ask for details,
she vanished in an instant.
He opened the swaddling clothes to look—
it was a boy.
He carried him home
and never married again.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"What distinguishes humans from beasts is but a slim margin,
yet this is not a definitive judgment.
To receive kindness and form bonds,
remaining loyal unto death—
in this, humans may feel ashamed before beasts.
As for Huāgū,
at first, she concealed her wisdom in simplicity,
and in the end, she entrusted her feelings in detachment.
From this, we know that detachment is the height of wisdom,
and detachment is the utmost expression of affection.
An immortal indeed,
an immortal indeed!"
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Wǔ Xiàolián Shí Mǒu,
carrying funds to the capital,
intended to seek an official appointment.
Upon reaching Dézhōu,
he fell violently ill,
spitting blood and unable to rise,
lying long in the boat.
His servant stole the money and fled.
Shí was greatly enraged,
and his illness worsened,
with his provisions cut off.
The boatman planned to abandon him.
It happened that a woman traveling by boat
anchored nearby at night.
Hearing of this,
she volunteered to take Shí on her boat.
The boatman was pleased
and helped Shí board the woman's boat.
Shí looked at her—
a woman over forty,
dressed in splendid attire,
her demeanor still elegant.
He groaned in gratitude.
The woman examined him closely and said:
"You have long had the root of consumption,
and now your soul has already wandered to the grave."
Hearing this,
Shí wailed mournfully.
The woman said:
"I have a pill medicine
that can revive the dead.
If your illness is cured,
do not forget me."
Shí wept and swore an oath.
The woman then fed him the medicine.
After half a day,
he felt somewhat recovered.
The woman served him delicacies at his bedside,
attending to him more diligently than a wife.
Shí felt even more indebted to her.
After over a month,
his illness was largely cured.
Shí approached on his knees,
respecting her as a mother.
The woman said:
"I am alone and without support.
If you do not despise me for my fading beauty,
I wish to serve as your wife."
At the time, Shí was over thirty,
and had been widowed for a year.
Hearing this,
he was overjoyed beyond expectation,
and they became intimate.
The woman then took out her stored gold
and sent him to the capital to manage affairs,
agreeing to return together afterward.
Shí went to the capital to seek connections,
and was selected as the provincial military commander;
he used the remaining gold to buy horses and saddles,
making his carriage and attire resplendent.
Considering that his wife was already advanced in years,
and not a suitable match after all,
he spent a hundred gold to betroth a daughter of the Wáng family as his second wife.
In his heart, he was fearful and timid,
afraid that his wife would find out,
so he avoided the road to Dézhōu,
taking a roundabout route to assume his post.
Over a year passed,
with no news exchanged.
A cousin of Shí's,
happened to come to Dézhōu,
and became neighbors with the wife.
The wife learned of this,
and went to inquire about Shí's situation.
The cousin answered truthfully.
The wife cursed loudly,
and told him the whole story.
The cousin also felt indignant on her behalf,
comforting and explaining:
"Perhaps the official duties are too busy,
and he hasn't had the time yet.
Please write a letter,
and I will deliver it for you, sister-in-law."
The wife did as he said.
The cousin respectfully delivered it to Shí,
but Shí paid it no mind at all.
Another year or so later,
the wife went herself to return to Shí,
staying at an inn,
and asked the official gatekeeper to announce her name.
Shí ordered to refuse her.
One day,
while he was feasting and drinking,
he heard noisy cursing;
putting down his cup and listening intently,
he saw his wife had already lifted the curtain and entered.
Shí was greatly alarmed,
his face ashen.
The wife pointed and scolded:
"Heartless man!
Are you happy now?
Think about where your wealth and status came from!
My feelings for you were not shallow,
even if you wanted to take a concubine,
why not discuss it with me?"
Shí stood trembling, holding his breath,
unable to make a sound.
After a long while,
he knelt down and threw himself at her feet,
making excuses and begging for forgiveness.
The wife's anger gradually subsided.
Shí discussed with Wáng,
asking her to meet the wife with the courtesy due a younger sister.
Wáng was unwilling;
Shí pleaded with her persistently,
and she finally went.
Wáng bowed,
and the wife returned the bow.
She said:
"Sister, do not fear,
I am not a jealous shrew.
What happened before,
is truly unbearable for any person,
even you, sister, would not want such a husband."
Then she recounted the whole story to Wáng in detail.
Wáng also became indignant,
and together they cursed Shí.
Shí could find no way out,
and could only seek to redeem himself,
so they eventually settled peacefully.
Earlier,
before the wife entered,
Shí had warned the gatekeeper not to let her in.
At this point,
he was angry with the gatekeeper,
and secretly reprimanded him.
The gatekeeper insisted that the keys had not been used,
and no one had entered,
refusing to accept blame.
Shí was suspicious but dared not ask his wife,
and though they spoke and laughed together,
he was never truly fond of her.
Fortunately, the wife was gentle and graceful,
and did not compete for his nights.
After three meals,
she would close her door and sleep early,
never asking where her husband spent the night.
Wáng was initially still wary;
seeing her like this,
she respected her even more.
In the morning, she would go to pay respects,
as if serving her parents-in-law.
The wife managed the household with leniency and propriety,
and was as discerning as a deity.
One day,
Shí lost his official seal,
and the entire office was in an uproar,
with people scurrying back and forth,
unable to find a solution.
The wife said with a laugh:
"Do not worry,
drain the well and you will find it."
Shí followed her advice,
and indeed found it.
When asked how she knew,
she only smiled without answering.
Vaguely,
it seemed she knew the thief's name,
but she never revealed it.
After living with her for a year,
he observed many strange things about her behavior.
Shí suspected she was not human,
and often after she went to bed, he would send someone to eavesdrop,
but only heard the sound of clothes rustling on the bed all night,
without knowing what she was doing.
The wife and Wáng were very fond of each other.
One evening,
Shí had gone to the provincial judicial commissioner and had not returned,
the wife and Wáng were drinking,
and without realizing it, became too drunk,
lying down on the mat,
she transformed into a fox.
Wáng pitied her,
and covered her with a brocade quilt.
Not long after,
Shí returned,
and Wáng told him of the strange event.
Shí wanted to kill her.
Wáng said:
"Even if she is a fox,
what wrong has she done to you?"
Shí would not listen,
and hurriedly looked for his sword.
But the wife had already awakened,
and cursed:
"With the behavior of a viper,
and the heart of a wolf,
I can no longer stay here!
The medicine I gave you before,
I ask you to return it!"
She then spat in Shí's face.
Shí felt a chilling cold as if doused with ice water,
and his throat began to itch intensely;
he vomited,
and the pill came out as before.
The wife picked it up,
angrily strode out,
and when pursued, she had already vanished.
That night, Shí's old illness recurred,
with incessant coughing of blood,
and he died within half a year.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Shí, the Provincial Graduate,
was elegant like a scholar.
Some said he humbled himself and treated scholars with respect,
speaking to others as if afraid of hurting them.
He died young,
and the scholarly community mourned him.
But upon hearing of his betrayal of the fox wife,
how is he any different from Lǐ Shíláng?"
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Chén Shēng Bìjiào,
courtesy name Míngyǔn,
was from Yān.
His family was poor,
and he served as a secretary under Deputy General Jiǎ Suō,
anchoring their boat on Dòngtíng Lake.
It happened that a Chinese alligator surfaced,
and Jiǎ shot it in the back.
A fish held onto the alligator's tail and would not let go,
so both were captured.
They were tied up and placed by the mast,
barely alive;
the alligator's mouth opened and closed,
as if pleading for rescue.
Chén felt pity and compassion,
and asked Jiǎ to release them.
He had some wound medicine with him,
and playfully applied it to the injured spot,
then released them into the water,
where they floated and sank for a while before disappearing.
More than a year later,
the scholar traveled northward,
passing again by Dòngtíng Lake,
when a great storm capsized his boat.
Fortunately, he managed to cling to a bamboo raft,
drifting all night long,
until he caught hold of some wood and stopped.
As he climbed ashore,
a floating corpse followed close behind,
which turned out to be his servant.
He pulled him out with effort,
but the servant had already died.
Grief-stricken and at a loss,
he sat facing the body to rest.
He saw only small hills rising emerald-green,
slender willows swaying in fresh verdure,
with hardly any travelers about,
and no one to ask for directions.
From dawn until past the hour of Chén,
he wandered aimlessly, not knowing where to go.
Suddenly, the servant’s limbs twitched slightly,
and the scholar, overjoyed, felt him.
Before long,
the servant vomited several dou of water,
and awoke with a start, fully revived.
Together they spread their clothes on rocks to dry,
and by nearly noon they were dry enough to wear.
Yet their empty stomachs growled,
and their hunger became unbearable.
So they hurried over the mountains,
hoping to find a village.
Just as they reached halfway up the mountain,
they heard the sound of a gong.
While still wondering where it came from,
two young women came riding on fine horses,
galloping as if scattering beans.
Each wore a red silk band across her forehead,
with pheasant feathers stuck in her hair;
they were dressed in tight-sleeved purple garments,
their waists bound with green brocade;
one carried a slingshot,
the other had a blue falconer’s sleeve.
As they passed over the ridge,
several dozen riders were hunting in the thickets,
all of them beautiful maidens,
dressed identically.
The scholar dared not approach.
A man came running on foot,
seemingly an attendant,
so he went to ask him.
The man replied:
“This is the Princess of the West Lake hunting on Shǒu Mountain.”
The scholar explained where he had come from,
and told him of his hunger.
The attendant untied his provisions and gave them to him,
warning:
“You should leave immediately and keep far away,
for offending the royal procession means death!”
The scholar grew afraid.
He hurried down the mountain.
Amid the dense forest, he glimpsed halls and pavilions,
thinking it was a temple.
Drawing closer,
he saw whitewashed walls winding around,
with a stream flowing across;
a vermilion gate stood half-open,
and a stone bridge led inside.
Peering through the gate,
he saw terraces and pavilions encircled by clouds,
rivaling the imperial gardens,
and wondered if it might be a noble family’s estate.
Hesitantly, he entered,
where creeping vines blocked the path,
and fragrant flowers brushed against him.
Passing several winding railings,
he came to another courtyard,
with dozens of weeping willows,
their high branches brushing the vermilion eaves.
When a mountain bird sang once,
flower petals flew all around;
when a gentle breeze stirred the deep garden,
elm seeds fell of their own accord.
It delighted the eye and gladdened the heart,
as if not of this mortal world.
Passing through a small pavilion,
he saw a swing set,
reaching up to the clouds;
yet its ropes hung still and heavy,
with no trace of anyone around.
Suspecting it was near the women’s quarters,
he felt timid and dared not venture further.
Suddenly, he heard horses stamping at the gate,
and what seemed like women’s laughter and chatter.
The scholar and his servant hid among the thick flowers.
Before long,
the laughter drew nearer,
and he heard one woman say:
“Today’s hunt was not very successful,
we caught very few birds.”
Another woman said:
“If not for the princess shooting down a wild goose,
we would have toiled in vain with our horses and servants.”
Soon after,
several women in red attire
escorted a young lady to sit in the pavilion.
She wore a military-style outfit with narrow sleeves,
and appeared about fourteen or fifteen years old.
Her hair was gathered like mist,
her waist so slender it seemed startled by the wind,
more exquisite than jade stamens or jasper blossoms,
beyond compare.
The other women served tea and lit incense,
their splendor like piled brocade.
After a while,
the princess rose,
descended the steps.
One woman said:
“Princess, though weary from riding,
can you still swing on the swing?”
The princess smiled and agreed.
Then some supported her shoulders,
others held her arms,
lifted her skirt,
and carried her shoes,
helping her up onto the swing.
The princess stretched her fair wrists,
stepped onto the swing with sharp shoes,
light as a flying swallow,
kicking up into the clouds.
Soon she was helped down.
The group exclaimed:
“The princess is truly an immortal!”
They laughed and left.
The scholar watched for a long time,
his spirit soaring.
When the voices had faded into silence,
he went to the swing,
pacing and lost in thought.
He noticed a red scarf beneath the fence,
realizing it had been left by the beauties,
and happily tucked it into his sleeve.
Ascending to the pavilion,
he saw writing implements on the table,
and so inscribed on the scarf:
“What elegant game mimics the half-immortal?
Clearly, a jade maiden reveals her golden lotus.
Among the moon palace maids, jealousy may stir,
Do not believe she ascends the ninth heaven on rippling steps.”
Having written this,
he recited it and left.
Trying to retrace his path,
he found the gates locked tight.
Wandering helplessly,
he turned back, and the towers, pavilions, and terraces,
he had traversed nearly all.
A woman suddenly appeared,
asking in surprise:
“How did you get here?”
The scholar bowed and said:
“I am a lost traveler,
I beg for your mercy and help.”
The woman asked:
“Did you pick up a red scarf?”
The scholar said:
“Yes, I have it.
But it has been stained,
what should I do?”
And he produced it.
The woman was greatly alarmed and said:
“You are as good as dead!
This is something the princess often uses,
and you have scribbled on it like this,
what can be done?”
The scholar turned pale,
pleading for a way to escape punishment.
The woman said:
"To have secretly observed the palace rituals,
is a crime beyond pardon.
Considering that you are a scholar of refined bearing,
I wished to spare you out of personal sympathy;
but now you have brought this misfortune upon yourself,
what plan can be made for you?"
Then she hurriedly took the handkerchief and left.
The scholar's heart pounded and his flesh trembled,
wishing he had wings,
and could only crane his neck awaiting death.
After a long while,
the girl came again,
and quietly congratulated him:
"You have hope of living!
The princess looked at the handkerchief three or four times,
smiling without any angry expression;
perhaps she will release you.
You should endure and wait patiently,
do not try to climb trees or burrow through walls;
if discovered, you will not be spared."
The day had already turned to dusk,
and whether it was auspicious or ominous he could not be sure;
while the flames of hunger burned within him,
tormented with worry as if about to die.
Not long after,
the girl came with a lamp.
A maid carried a pot and hamper,
bringing out wine and food to feed the scholar.
The scholar urgently asked for news,
the girl said:
"Just now I seized an opportunity to say: 'The scholar in the garden,
if he can be forgiven then release him;
otherwise,
he will starve to death.'
The princess pondered and said: 'In the deep of night, where can we send him?'
So she ordered food to be given to you.
This is not bad news."
The scholar spent the night in anxious fear,
uneasy and insecure in his peril.
As the morning hour was nearly past,
the girl again brought him food.
The scholar begged her to intercede for him,
the girl said:
"The princess neither speaks of killing,
nor of releasing.
We servants,
how dare we pester her with repeated requests?"
Soon the setting sun turned westward,
and as he was eagerly gazing out,
the girl rushed in breathlessly,
saying:
"It's over!
Someone who talks too much has revealed the matter to the princess consort;
the consort unfolded the handkerchief and threw it to the ground,
cursing wildly at the rude fellow,
disaster is not far off!"
The scholar was greatly alarmed,
his face ashen as dirt,
and knelt long pleading for advice.
Suddenly he heard the clamor of many voices,
the girl waved her hand and slipped away.
Several people holding ropes
rushed fiercely into the room.
One maid among them looked closely and said:
"Who did I think it was,
it's Chén Láng, isn't it?"
Then she stopped those holding the ropes,
saying:
"Wait, wait,
let me report to the princess consort."
She turned and hurried away.
After a short while she returned,
saying:
"The princess consort requests Chén Láng to enter."
Trembling with fear, the scholar followed her.
Passing through dozens of doors,
they reached a palace hall,
with green curtains and silver hooks.
Immediately a beautiful maiden lifted the curtain,
announcing:
"Chén Láng has arrived."
Above sat a lovely lady, her robe dazzling and splendid.
The scholar prostrated on the ground, kowtowing, and said:
"A solitary subject from ten thousand miles away,
I beg for mercy on my life."
The consort quickly rose and personally helped him up,
saying:
"If not for you, sir,
I would not be alive today.
The maids were ignorant,
causing our honored guest to be detained,
how can this crime be redeemed!"
She then set a magnificent feast,
and poured wine into engraved cups.
The scholar was bewildered, not understanding the reason.
The consort said:
"The grace of saving my life,
I regret having no way to repay.
My daughter has received the affection of your inscribed handkerchief,
which must be heavenly fate;
tonight I shall send her to serve you."
This was beyond the scholar's expectations,
his spirit dazed and ungrounded.
As dusk fell,
a maid came forward and announced,
"The princess has finished dressing formally."
Then she led the scholar to the bridal chamber.
Suddenly pipes and flutes resounded loudly,
and the steps were all covered with floral carpets;
from the main hall to the side rooms and privies,
everywhere was lit with lanterns.
Dozens of enchanting maidens
supported the princess as they exchanged bows.
The scent of musk and orchids
filled the hall and courtyard.
Then they entered the bed curtains together,
mutually enamored.
The scholar said:
"I am but a traveler far from home,
who in my life has never known such service.
To have stained your fragrant handkerchief,
and yet escaped execution,
is fortune enough;
to be granted marriage instead,
is truly beyond my hopes."
The princess said:
"My mother,
is the consort of the Lord of the Lake,
and daughter of the King of Yángjiāng.
Last year when she returned to her parents' home,
she happened to be touring the lake,
and was struck by a stray arrow.
Thanks to you she escaped,
and you also gave her medicinal treatment,
our whole family is indebted to you,
and never ceases to remember.
Please do not doubt me because I am not human.
I have obtained the secret of longevity from the Dragon Lord,
and wish to share it with you."
Then the scholar realized she was a divine being,
and asked:
"How did the maid recognize me?"
She replied:
"That day on the boat at Dòngtíng Lake,
there was a little fish following behind,
that was this maid."
He asked further:
"Since you did not have me killed,
why did you delay in releasing me?"
She laughed and said:
"I truly admired your talent,
but could not decide myself.
I tossed and turned all night,
something others could not know."
The scholar sighed and said:
"You,
are my Bào Shū.
Who was the one who brought me food?"
She said:
"Ā Niàn,
