also my trusted confidante."
The scholar said:
"How can I repay her kindness?"
She laughed and said:
"There will be time to serve you,
we can slowly plan how to repay her later."
He asked:
"Where is the great king?"
She replied:
"He has followed Guān Shèng to battle and has not yet returned."
After living there several days,
the scholar worried that there was no news from home,
and his concern grew intense,
so he first sent a servant home with a letter of safety.
At home, they had heard that the boat at Dòngtíng Lake had capsized,
and his wife had been in mourning clothes for over a year.
When the servant returned,
they learned he was not dead;
but communication was blocked,
and they still feared he might drift and find it hard to return.
Another half year passed,
when the scholar suddenly arrived,
his furs and horses most elegant,
and his bags filled with precious gems.
From then on, his wealth amounted to millions,
his music, women, and luxury
surpassed even those of noble families.
In seven or eight years,
he had five sons.
Every day he feasted with guests,
the offerings of palace chambers, food and drink,
were extremely lavish and abundant.
When asked about his experiences,
he spoke of them without the slightest concealment.
There was a childhood friend of his named Liáng Zǐjùn,
who had been an official in the southern provinces for over ten years.
On his way back, he passed by Dòngtíng Lake,
where he saw a painted pleasure boat,
with carved railings and vermilion windows,
from which came the faint, delicate sound of pipes and singing,
as it drifted slowly through the misty waves.
At that moment, a beautiful woman leaned out of the window to gaze into the distance.
Liáng fixed his eyes on the boat
and saw a young man,
bareheaded and sitting cross-legged,
with a sixteen-year-old beauty beside him,
rubbing and caressing him.
Liáng thought he must be a high-ranking official from Chǔ,
but there were very few attendants.
He stared intently and scrutinized him carefully,
only to realize it was Chén Míngyǔn.
Without thinking, he leaned against the railing and shouted loudly.
Hearing the call, Chén stopped rowing
and came out to the bow of the boat,
inviting Liáng over.
Liáng saw the table covered with leftover dishes,
and the air still thick with the aroma of wine.
Chén immediately ordered them to be cleared away.
After a moment,
three or five beautiful maids
served wine and brewed tea,
bringing out rare delicacies from land and sea
that Liáng had never seen before.
Liáng exclaimed in surprise:
"It's been ten years since we last met—
how did you become so wealthy and noble?"
Chén laughed and said:
"Did you think a poor scholar like me could never rise to prominence?"
Liáng asked:
"Who was drinking with you just now?"
Chén replied:
"Just my wife."
Liáng found this even more strange.
He asked:
"Where are you taking your family?"
Chén answered:
"We're heading west across the lake."
Liáng wanted to ask more,
but Chén hastily ordered singing to accompany the wine.
As soon as he finished speaking,
a thunderous noise filled their ears,
with the clamor of voices and instruments,
making it impossible to hear any conversation or laughter.
Seeing so many beautiful women before him,
Liáng, emboldened by drink, boasted:
"Míngyǔn, my friend,
can you truly let me experience ecstasy?"
Chén laughed and said:
"You're drunk!
But I have the means to acquire a beautiful concubine
and can give her to an old friend."
He then ordered a maidservant to present a bright pearl,
saying:
"It's not hard to buy a Lǜzhū,
but I want to show I'm not stingy."
Then he hurriedly bid farewell, saying:
"I have some urgent matters to attend to,
so I can't linger with an old friend."
He escorted Liáng back to his boat,
untied the ropes, and sailed straight away.
When Liáng returned home,
he went to Chén's house to inquire,
only to find Chén drinking with guests.
This made him even more suspicious.
So he asked:
"Yesterday at Dòngtíng Lake,
how did you return so quickly?"
Chén replied:
"I wasn't there."
Liáng then recounted everything he had seen, astonishing everyone present.
Chén laughed and said:
"You must be mistaken.
How could I have the ability to be in two places at once?"
Everyone found it strange,
but in the end, no one could explain it.
Later, Chén lived to be eighty-one before passing away.
When it was time for his burial,
they were surprised at how light his coffin was.
Upon opening it,
they found it empty.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"The bamboo basket did not sink,
and the poem was inscribed on the red paper—
these things surely involved ghosts and spirits.
Yet all of it stemmed from a single compassionate thought.
But when it comes to mansions, wives, and concubines,
enjoying the luxuries of both worlds in one body—
that is truly inexplicable.
In the past, there were those who wished for beautiful wives and concubines,
noble sons and worthy grandsons,
along with immortality,
but they only achieved half of it.
Could it be that among immortals, there are also figures like Fényáng and Jìlún?"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
East of Xiāngshān in Qīngzhōu,
there was a man named Zhōu Shùntíng,
who served his mother with utmost filial piety.
His mother developed a large ulcer on her thigh,
causing unbearable pain,
and she groaned day and night.
Zhōu tended to her skin and administered medicine,
to the point of forgetting to eat or sleep.
After several months without improvement,
Zhōu was deeply worried and at a loss for what to do.
He dreamed that his father told him:
"Your mother's illness depends on your filial piety.
However, this sore cannot heal unless human fat is applied to it.
Your anxious efforts are in vain."
He woke up and found this strange.
So he got up,
took a sharp knife, and cut a piece of flesh from his side. The flesh came off,
and he felt little pain.
He quickly wrapped his waist with cloth,
and the bleeding stopped.
He then cooked the flesh to extract the fat
and applied it to his mother's sore.
Immediately, the pain ceased completely.
His mother joyfully asked:
"What medicine is so miraculously effective?"
Zhōu gave an evasive answer.
Soon, his mother's sore healed.
Zhōu always concealed the place where he had cut himself,
so even his wife and children did not know.
After he recovered,
there was a large scar the size of a palm.
His wife questioned him,
and only then did she learn the truth.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Cutting flesh from one's thigh is an act that harms life,
and a gentleman does not value it.
But how could ignorant men and women understand that harming one's life is an act of unfiliality?
They simply act according to what their hearts cannot restrain.
If there are such people, then the true essence of filial piety
still exists between heaven and earth.
Those in charge of moral education
have many important duties,
with no time to publicly commend them.
Thus, to illuminate the obscure and reveal the subtle,
we must rely on such humble accounts."
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
When Xiānluó presented a lion as tribute,
wherever it stopped,
crowds of onlookers gathered like walls.
Its appearance was vastly different from what was depicted in embroideries and paintings.
Its fur was black and yellow,
several inches long.
When a chicken was thrown to it,
it would first grasp it with its claws and blow on it.
With one blow,
all the feathers would fall off as if swept away—
a truly strange phenomenon.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Lǐ Jiǔcháng was a native of Línqú.
One day, while drinking in the countryside,
he saw a whirlwind swirling toward him.
He respectfully poured out a libation to it.
Later, when he was traveling elsewhere on business,
he saw a large mansion by the roadside,
with halls and pavilions that were grand and beautiful.
A servant in black came out from inside
and invited Lǐ in.
Lǐ firmly declined,
but the servant insisted urgently.
Lǐ said,
"I have never met you before.
Could this be a mistake?"
The servant replied,
"It is no mistake."
He then mentioned Lǐ's name.
Lǐ asked,
"Whose house is this?"
The servant answered,
"You will know once you enter."
Lǐ went in and passed through one gate,
where he saw a woman nailed by her hands and feet to a door.
Drawing closer,
he realized it was his sister-in-law.
He was greatly alarmed.
Lǐ had a sister-in-law who had been suffering from a malignant ulcer on her arm
and had been bedridden for over a year.
He wondered how she could have ended up here,
and began to suspect that he had been summoned for some malicious purpose.
Frightened, he hesitated to proceed.
The servant urged him on,
and he finally entered.
In the main hall,
a man sat above,
dressed like a king,
with an imposing and majestic presence.
Lǐ knelt and prostrated himself,
not daring to look up.
The king ordered him to rise
and comforted him, saying,
"Do not be afraid.
I disturbed your drinking in the past,
and I wished to meet you to express my gratitude.
There is no other reason."
Lǐ's heart finally calmed,
though he still did not understand the reason.
The king then said,
"Do you not recall pouring a libation in the countryside?"
Lǐ suddenly understood
and realized he was in the presence of a deity.
He kowtowed and said,
"Just now, I saw my sister-in-law
subjected to such severe punishment.
Out of familial affection,
I am deeply saddened.
I beg Your Majesty to show mercy and pardon her!"
The king replied,
"She is extremely vicious and jealous,
and deserves this punishment.
Three years ago,
when your brother's concubine gave birth and her intestines prolapsed,
your sister-in-law secretly pierced them with a needle,
causing her constant pain in her internal organs to this day.
How could anyone act so inhumanely?"
Lǐ pleaded earnestly for her.
The king then said,
"For your sake, I shall pardon her.
When you return, you must urge this vicious woman to reform her ways."
Lǐ thanked him and left.
When he looked back at the door,
the woman was no longer there.
Returning home, he saw his sister-in-law lying on her bed,
with blood from her wound staining the mat.
At that moment, she was cursing and scolding
because the concubine had displeased her.
Lǐ quickly advised her,
"Sister-in-law, do not continue like this!
The suffering you endure today
is the result of your usual jealousy and malice."
His sister-in-law angrily retorted,
"Young master, you are such a fine man!
And your wife is as virtuous as Mèng Gū,
allowing you to sleep east and west
without uttering a word.
You must have excellent authority in your own household,
but that doesn't mean you can come and subdue your elder brother's wife!"
Lǐ smiled faintly and said,
"Sister-in-law, do not be angry.
If I tell you the truth,
I fear you will have no time for tears."
She replied,
"I have never stolen a thread from the Queen Mother's basket,
nor have I ever winked at the Jade Emperor's incense table attendant.
My heart is clear and untroubled.
Why should I have any reason to cry?"
Lǐ whispered,
"What punishment is fitting for piercing someone's intestines with a needle?"
His sister-in-law's face suddenly changed color,
and she asked why he said that.
Lǐ told her what had happened.
She trembled uncontrollably,
wept bitterly, and wailed,
"I will not dare to do it again!"
Before her tears had dried,
she felt the pain suddenly cease.
Within ten days, she recovered.
From then on, she completely reformed her ways
and became known for her virtue and kindness.
Later, when the concubine gave birth again,
her intestines prolapsed once more,
and the needle was still embedded in them.
After it was removed,
the intestinal pain finally healed.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Some say there are many in the world as vicious and jealous as this woman,
and it is a pity that the net of the underworld lets so many escape.
I believe otherwise.
The punishments of the underworld
may be even more severe than being nailed to a door,
but there is no way to send word back to the living."
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
In Yíshuǐ County, there was a man surnamed Mǎ,
who married a woman from the Wáng family.
Their marital harmony was profound.
Mǎ died young,
and Wáng's parents wished to change her resolve (to remarry).
Wáng vowed she would not marry another.
Her mother-in-law, pitying her youth,
also urged her,
but Wáng would not listen.
Her mother said:
"Your resolve is truly admirable; however, you are too young,
and there is no child.
I have often seen those who force themselves at the beginning,
only to bring shame later.
It would certainly be better to remarry early;
this is the common sentiment."
Wáng straightened her appearance,
swearing to die rather than remarry.
Her mother then left her to her own will.
The woman commissioned a sculptor to make a likeness of her husband.
At each meal, she would pour a libation and offer it as if he were alive.
One evening,
as she was about to retire,
she suddenly saw the clay figure stretch and descend.
Startled and alarmed, she looked on,
and it had already grown violently to human size,
truly her husband.
The woman was terrified,
and called for her mother.
The ghost stopped her, saying:
"Do not.
I am moved by your deep affection;
in the dark underworld, it brings bitter sorrow.
That one household possesses such loyalty and chastity
brings honor to generations of ancestors.
My father in life committed deeds that harmed virtue,
and thus deserved to have no heir,
which led to cutting short my flourishing youth.
The underworld authorities, mindful of your bitter fidelity,
therefore ordered me to return,
to be with you and father a son to continue the ancestral line."
The woman's tears also soaked her lapels,
and they were intimate as in life.
At cockcrow,
he would descend from the bed and leave.
After more than a month like this,
she felt a slight movement in her belly.
The ghost then wept and said:
"The allotted time is full;
from now on, it is eternal farewell!"
And then he was gone.
The woman did not speak of it at first;
later, as her belly gradually grew large,
she could not conceal it,
and secretly told her mother.
Her mother suspected it was delusion;
yet observing her daughter showed no other issues,
she was greatly puzzled and could not understand.
After ten months,
she indeed gave birth to a boy.
When she told others,
those who heard it all secretly laughed;
the woman also had no way to vindicate herself.
There was a village headman who had an old grudge against Mǎ,
and reported it to the county magistrate.
The magistrate detained and questioned the neighbors,
but none gave any differing account.
The magistrate said:
"I have heard ghost children cast no shadow;
if it has a shadow, it is false."
He held the child in the sunlight,
and its shadow was faint, like wispy smoke.
He also pricked the child's finger and smeared the blood on the clay figure;
it immediately soaked in without a trace.
Taking another figure and smearing it,
it wiped right off.
By this, he believed it.
When the child grew several years older,
its mouth, nose, speech, and movements
were all exactly like Mǎ's.
Only then did the crowd's doubts dissolve.
According to the manuscript version of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Chén Huānlè
was a person from Chángzhì in Lù Prefecture.
He had a daughter, clever and beautiful.
A Daoist priest came begging,
glanced at her, and left.
From then on, he daily held his bowl near the marketplace.
It happened that a blind man came out from the Chén household,
and the Daoist priest caught up and walked with him,
asking where he came from.
The blind man said:
"I just passed by the Chén household to cast a horoscope."
The Daoist priest said:
"I heard they have a young lady;
a cousin of mine wishes to seek marriage,
but does not know her birth date and time."
The blind man recounted it for him,
and the Daoist priest then parted and left.
After several days,
the girl was embroidering in her room,
when she suddenly felt her feet go numb,
gradually reaching her thighs,
and then gradually to her waist and abdomen;
in a moment, she felt dizzy and collapsed.
After a fixed interval,
she began hazily able to stand,
and went to find and tell her mother.
Upon going out the door,
she saw only vast, dark waves,
with a path like a thread;
horrified, she retreated,
but the gate, house, and dwellings
were already submerged by black water.
Looking again at the road,
there were very few pedestrians,
only the Daoist priest walking slowly ahead.
So she distantly followed him,
hoping to see a fellow villager to speak with.
After walking several *lǐ*,
she suddenly saw village dwellings,
looked at them,
and it was her own family's gate.
Greatly startled, she said:
"I ran so far,
yet I am still in the village.
Why was I so bewildered just now?"
Joyfully, she entered the gate,
but her parents had not yet returned.
She went back again to her own room,
and the embroidered shoes she was working on
were still on the bed.
Feeling utterly exhausted from the running,
she sat on the bed to rest.
The Daoist priest suddenly entered,
and the girl, greatly alarmed, tried to flee.
The Daoist priest grabbed and pressed her down.
The girl wanted to scream,
but was mute and could not make a sound.
The Daoist priest swiftly used a sharp blade to cut out the girl's heart.
The girl felt her soul floating, leaving its shell, and standing there.
Looking around, the family home was completely changed,
only crumbling cliffs as if overturned.
She saw the Daoist priest use her heart's blood to daub a wooden figure,
then repeatedly point and chant curses;
the girl felt the wooden figure then merge with herself.
The Daoist priest instructed:
"From now on, you must obey my commands,
do not dare disobey or err!"
He then wore and carried it.
The Chén family had lost their daughter,
and the entire household was in a state of panic and confusion.
They searched all the way to the Ox Head Ridge,
where they finally heard villagers spreading rumors
that a woman had been found dead at the foot of the ridge, her heart cut out.
Mr. Chén rushed to verify,
and indeed, it was his daughter.
Weeping, he reported the matter to the magistrate.
The magistrate detained the residents living at the foot of the ridge,
subjecting nearly all of them to torture,
but to no avail in uncovering any clues.
He temporarily imprisoned the group of suspects,
awaiting further investigation.
A Daoist priest, having left several miles away,
sat under a willow tree by the roadside
and suddenly said to the girl:
"Now I assign you your first task:
go to spy on the trial proceedings in the county.
When you go, you must conceal yourself in the warm pavilion above.
If you see the magistrate using his official seal,
you must immediately flee and avoid it—
remember this well, do not forget!
I give you from the hour of Chén to go and the hour of Sì to return.
If you are late by one kè,
I will pierce your heart with one needle,
causing you acute pain; if by two kè,
I will pierce it with two needles;
and by three kè,
I will cause your soul to vanish completely."
Upon hearing this,
the girl trembled in fear throughout her body,
and she drifted away ethereally.
In an instant, she arrived at the government office
and, as instructed, hid in the pavilion above.
At that time, the people from the foot of the ridge were kneeling in rows in the hall below,
and the interrogation had not yet begun.
Just as the magistrate was about to stamp an official document with his seal,
the girl had no time to avoid it,
and the seal had already been taken out of its case.
The girl felt her body grow heavy and cumbersome,
as if the paper lattice could not bear her weight,
and it made a sudden cracking sound.
Everyone in the hall looked around in astonishment.
The magistrate ordered the seal to be raised again,
and the same sound occurred as before;
on the third raise,
the girl tumbled and fell to the ground.
All present heard it.
The magistrate stood up and prayed, saying:
"If you are a wronged ghost,
you should speak directly and truthfully,
so that I may clear your name."
The girl, sobbing, stepped forward
and recounted in detail how the Daoist priest had killed her and how he had sent her on this mission.
The magistrate dispatched officers to rush to the scene,
and when they reached the willow tree,
the Daoist priest was indeed there.
They captured him and brought him back,
and after a single interrogation, he confessed.
The other suspects were then released.
The magistrate asked the girl:
"Now that your wrong has been righted, where will you go?"
The girl replied:
"I will follow you, my lord."
The magistrate said:
"There is no place in my office to accommodate you;
it would be better for you to return to your home for now."
After a long silence, the girl said:
"The government office is my home,
and I will enter it now."
When the magistrate asked again,
her voice had already fallen silent.
Upon returning to his residence,
he found that his wife had just given birth to a daughter.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
A certain man from Lù'ān
had a father imprisoned and facing execution.
He gathered all his savings,
amounting to a hundred taels of silver,
and set out for the prefecture to lobby for his father's release.
As he rode out on his mule,
the black dog he kept followed him.
He shouted and drove it back;
but once he started moving,
it followed him again,
and even whipping it would not make it return.
It followed him for dozens of miles.
The man dismounted
and hurried to the side of the road to relieve himself.
Afterward,
he threw stones at the dog,
and only then did the dog run away.
As the man continued on his journey,
the dog suddenly reappeared,
biting at the mule's tail and legs.
Enraged, the man whipped it,
but the dog kept barking incessantly.
Suddenly, it leaped ahead,
angrily biting the mule's head,
as if trying to block its path.
The man considered this a bad omen
and grew even angrier.
He turned his mule around and chased after the dog.
Seeing that the dog had run far away,
he turned back and galloped swiftly,
arriving at the prefecture by dusk.
When he felt for the money pouch at his waist,
half of the silver was gone.
Sweat poured down his face,
and he was utterly distraught.
Tossing and turning all night,
he suddenly realized that the dog's barking must have had a reason.
He waited for the city gates to open
and carefully retraced his route.
He also thought to himself that since this was a major north-south thoroughfare,
with pedestrians swarming like ants,
there was little chance the lost silver would still be there.
Hesitantly, he arrived at the spot where he had dismounted,
and there he saw the dog lying dead in the grass,
its fur soaked with sweat as if washed.
Lifting it by the ears to take a look,
he found the sealed silver intact.
Touched by the dog's loyalty,
he bought a coffin and buried it,
and people regarded it as a righteous and loyal dog.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Zhái Zhànchí
was serving as a judicial officer in Ráozhōu
and was passing by Póyáng Lake.
On the lake, there was a temple dedicated to deities,
so he stopped his carriage to visit and look around.
Inside, statues of loyal ministers who had died for their principles were carved,
including one deity with the surname Zhái,
seated in the lowest position.
Zhái said:
"A member of my own clan—
how can he be seated below others!"
He then moved the statue to a higher seat.
Afterward, he boarded his boat,
but a strong wind tore the sail,
and the mast tilted dangerously,
causing his entire family to cry out in fear.
Suddenly, a small boat
came cutting through the waves;
as it drew near the official boat,
someone quickly helped Zhái onto the small boat,
and then his entire family boarded as well.
Upon closer inspection,
the person looked exactly like the deity with the surname Zhái.
Before long,
the waves calmed,
and when they searched for him, he had vanished without a trace.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Wáng Dǐng from Qínyóu,
courtesy name Xiānhú,
was a generous and strong man
with a wide circle of friends.
At the age of eighteen,
he was not yet married,
as his wife had passed away.
He often traveled far from home,
sometimes not returning for a whole year.
His elder brother, Wáng Nài,
a renowned scholar north of the Yangtze River,
was deeply affectionate toward his brother.
He advised his brother not to travel anymore,
promising to find him a spouse.
But Wáng Dǐng would not listen.
He took a boat to Zhènjiāng to visit a friend.
His friend was away,
so he rented a room in an inn upstairs.
The river water was clear and calm,
and the entire mountain was in view,
which pleased him greatly.
The next day,
his friend came
and invited him to move to his place,
but Wáng Dǐng declined and stayed where he was.
After residing there for over half a month,
he dreamed one night of a young maiden,
around fourteen or fifteen years old,
with a graceful and beautiful appearance.
She climbed onto the bed and joined with him,
and upon waking, he found he had had a nocturnal emission.
He found it quite strange,
but thought it was merely a coincidence.
That night,
he dreamed of her again.
This happened for three or four nights in a row.
Greatly perplexed,
he dared not extinguish the candle,
and though he lay down,
he remained vigilant and alert.
As soon as his eyelids met,
he dreamed the maiden came again;
just as they were being intimate,
he suddenly awoke with a start;
hurriedly opening his eyes,
he saw the young girl, ethereal as an immortal,
clearly still in his embrace.
Seeing Wáng awake,
she immediately felt ashamed and timid.
Though Wáng knew she was not human,
he was also quite pleased;
without time for questions,
he directly engaged with her passionately.
The girl seemed unable to bear it,
saying:
"So violent and rough,
no wonder people dare not tell you openly."
Only then did Wáng begin to question her,
and she replied:
"I am Wǔ Qiūyuè.
My late father was a renowned scholar,
profoundly versed in the numerology of the Yìjīng.
He always cherished me dearly;
but he said I would not live long,
so he did not allow me to be betrothed.
Later, at fifteen, I indeed died young,
and was buried hastily to the east of the pavilion,
level with the ground,
with no grave marker.
Only a stone slab was placed beside the coffin,
inscribed:
'Girl Qiūyuè,
buried without a mound,
in thirty years,
to marry Wáng Dǐng.'
Now thirty years have passed,
and you have just arrived.
Overjoyed,
I was eager to offer myself;
but feeling shy and timid,
I resorted to appearing in dreams."
Wáng was also delighted,
and asked to finish their intimacy.
She said:
"I need a little yang energy,
hoping to return to life,
but I truly cannot endure such stormy passion.
We will have endless joyful unions in the future,
why must it be tonight?"
Then she rose and left.
The next day,
she came again,
sitting opposite him, laughing and bantering,
happy as if in life.
Extinguishing the candle and getting into bed,
she was no different from a living person;
but once the girl arose,
there would be emissions flowing,
staining the mattress.
One evening,
the moonlight was bright and clear,
and they took a short stroll in the courtyard.
Wáng asked the girl:
"Are there cities and walls in the underworld too?"
She replied:
"Just the same.
The underworld's city and prefecture
are not here,
but about three or four lǐ away.
Only, they take night for day."
He asked:
"Can living people see it?"
She answered:
"They can."
Wáng requested to go see it,
and the girl agreed.
They went under the moonlight,
the girl fluttering like the wind,
Wáng striving hard to keep up.
Suddenly they reached a place,
and the girl said:
"Not far now."
But Wáng looked ahead and saw nothing at all.
The girl applied her saliva to his two eyes,
and when he opened them,
his sight was twice as clear as usual,
seeing the night no different from daytime.
Immediately he saw battlements amidst distant mist;
on the road, pedestrians
were hurrying as if to a market.
Soon, two yamen runners dragged three or four people past,
the last one strangely resembling his elder brother.
Hurrying closer to look,
it was indeed his brother.
Astonished, he asked:
"Brother, how did you get here?"
Seeing Wáng, his brother
shed tears sorrowfully,
saying:
"I don't know what for,
I was forcibly seized and imprisoned."
Wáng angrily said:
"My brother is a gentleman who upholds propriety,
how could he be bound like this!"
He then entreated the two runners,
hoping they would temporarily release him.
The runners refused,
acting extremely arrogant and contemptuous.
Enraged,
Wáng wanted to argue with them.
His brother stopped him, saying:
"This is an official order,
we should comply with the law.
But I lack funds,
and their demands for bribes are truly harsh.
Brother, return home
and make arrangements."
Wáng grasped his brother's arm,
weeping uncontrollably.
The runners grew angry,
violently yanking the rope around his neck,
causing his brother to stumble and fall.
Seeing this,
Wáng was filled with furious rage,
unable to restrain himself.
Immediately drawing his dagger,
he beheaded one runner on the spot.
The other runner shouted and screamed,
and Wáng beheaded him too.
The girl exclaimed in great alarm:
"Killing official messengers is an unpardonable crime!
Delay will bring disaster!
Please quickly find a boat and head north,
return home and do not remove the funeral streamer,
bar the doors and cease all comings and goings.
In seven days, you will surely be safe."
Wáng then took his brother and that night hired a small boat,
urgently crossing north.
Returning home, he saw mourners at the door,
and knew his brother had indeed died.
He closed the gate and locked it,
then entered.
Looking, his brother had already vanished;
entering the room,
he saw the deceased had revived,
and was calling out:
"I'm starving!
Quickly prepare some soup and noodles."
By then, he had been dead for two days,
and the whole family was astonished.
Wáng then explained everything in detail.
After seven days, they opened the gate,
removed the funeral streamer,
and people then learned he had revived.
Relatives and friends gathered to ask,
but they only gave false answers.
Thinking of Qiūyuè,
he was deeply troubled by longing.
So he went south again,
to the old pavilion,
and holding a candle, waited a long time,
but the girl never came.
Drowsy and about to sleep,
he saw a woman come,
who said:
"Lady Qiūyuè sends her regards to you, sir: previously, due to official duties, she was killed,
the murderer fled,
they seized the lady and took her away,
she is now imprisoned,
suffering harsh treatment.
She longs for you day and night,
you should plan to manage this."
Wáng was grief-stricken and furious,
and followed the woman.
They reached a city,
entered the western outer wall,
and she pointed to a gate, saying:
"The lady is temporarily held here."
Wáng entered,
saw many buildings,
with many prisoners detained,
but Qiūyuè was not among them.
He went further through a small door,
in a tiny room there was lamplight.
Wáng approached the window to peek,
and saw Qiūyuè sitting on a couch,
covering her face with her sleeve, sobbing.
Two guards were beside her,
pinching her chin and grabbing her shoes,
teasing and mocking her.
The girl cried even more desperately.
One guard pulled her by the neck, saying:
"Since you're a criminal,
still guarding your chastity?"
Wáng was enraged,
without time for words,
he took his knife and charged straight in,
one guard, one slash,
cutting them down like hemp,
then snatched the girl and left.
Fortunately, no one noticed.
Just as they reached the inn,
he suddenly woke up.
He was just wondering about the ominous dream,
when he saw Qiūyuè standing there, gazing at him.
The scholar, startled, rose and pulled her to sit,
telling her about the dream.
The girl said:
"It was real,
not a dream."
The scholar exclaimed in shock,
"What should we do now!"
The girl sighed and said:
"This is fate.
I was to wait until the end of the month,
before I could live again;
but now it's like this,
how can I wait urgently?
You should quickly go to my burial place,
carry me back with you,
call my name frequently every day,
and in three days I can revive.
But before the time is full,
my bones will be soft, my feet weak,
unable to manage household chores for you."
Having said this,
she hastily prepared to leave.
Turning back, she said:
"I almost forgot,
what if the underworld pursues?
When I was alive,
my father passed down talismanic writings to me,
saying that after thirty years,
they could be worn by a couple."
She then asked for a brush and quickly wrote two talismans,
saying:
"One you wear yourself,
one paste on my back."
He saw her off,
noted where she disappeared,
dug about a foot deep,
and saw the coffin,
already decayed.
Beside it was a small stele,
indeed as the girl had said.
Opening the coffin to look,
the girl's complexion was as if alive.
He carried her into the room,
her clothes turned to dust in the wind.
After pasting the talisman,
he wrapped her tightly in a quilt,
carried her to the riverbank;
hailed a boat to moor,
pretending his sister was critically ill,
and was taking her back home.
Fortunately, a strong south wind blew,
and by dawn they had reached his hometown gate.
Carrying the girl to settle her,
he then told his elder brother and sister-in-law.
The whole family looked on in shock,
but none dared openly question his delusion.
The scholar opened the quilt,
called Qiūyuè's name repeatedly,
and each night held the corpse to sleep.
Gradually it grew warm.
On the third day she revived,
by the seventh she could walk;
changing clothes, she bowed to her sister-in-law,
graceful and no different from an immortal.
But beyond ten steps,
she needed someone to walk with her;
otherwise she would sway with the wind,
often about to topple.
Those who saw her thought she had this ailment,
which only added to her charm.
She often advised the scholar, saying:
"Your sins are too deep,
you should accumulate virtue and recite sutras to repent.
Otherwise,
I fear your life may not be long."
The scholar had never been devout to Buddhism,
but from then on he converted with great piety.
Later, he remained unharmed.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"I wish to propose a law:
'For those who kill public servants,
their crime should be reduced by three degrees compared to ordinary people,'
for such people are all deserving of death.
Thus, those who can eliminate corrupt officials
are the truly good and law-abiding;
even if slightly harsh,
it cannot be called cruelty.
Moreover, in the underworld there are no fixed laws;
if there are evil people,
knives, saws, cauldrons, and woks
are not considered cruel.
What pleases human hearts
is what pleases the King of the Underworld.
How can one, guilty enough to be pursued by the underworld,
luckily escape?" Based on the manuscript version of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Dòu Xù from Jiāozhōu,
courtesy name Xiǎohuī,
was taking a nap one day when
he saw a man in brown clothes standing before his bed.
The man hesitated and looked around anxiously,
as if wanting to say something.
Dòu asked him,
and he replied:
"My lord requests your presence."
"Who is your lord?"
The man said:
"He lives nearby."
Dòu followed him out.
They turned past walls and houses,
and were led to a place
with layered pavilions and towering buildings,
thousands of rafters interconnected.
They walked through winding paths,
feeling as if there were countless doors and gates,
utterly unlike the human world.
They also saw palace ladies and female officials
coming and going in great numbers,
all asking the man in brown:
"Has Young Master Dòu arrived?"
The man in brown affirmed.
Soon,
a high-ranking official came out
and greeted Dòu with great respect.
Once they entered the hall,
Dòu inquired:
"Since we have never met before,
I have not paid my respects.
Yet you have shown me such kindness and welcome,
which fills me with doubt."
The high official said:
"My humble king, admiring your noble lineage and virtuous family,
has long yearned to meet you
and deeply wishes to converse with you."
Dòu grew even more astonished,
asking,
"Who is this king?"
The reply was:
"You will know shortly."
Before long,
two female officials arrived
and led Dòu forward with a pair of banners.
Passing through multiple gates,
he saw a king seated in the main hall.
Upon seeing Dòu,
the king descended the steps to greet him,
and they exchanged the rituals of host and guest.
After the formalities,
they took their seats,
and a lavish feast was laid out.
Looking up, Dòu saw a plaque on the hall
that read "Guìfǔ" (Cassia Palace).
Dòu felt constrained and unable to speak.
The king said:
"Being neighbors with your esteemed self,
our connection is profound.
Please relax and enjoy yourself,
and do not be suspicious or fearful."
Dòu assented meekly.
After several rounds of wine,
music and singing began below,
with no drums or gongs,
only soft, delicate melodies.
After a while,
the king suddenly looked around and said:
"I have a line,
and I ask you all to compose a matching couplet: 'A talented man ascends the Cassia Palace.'"
As everyone was pondering,
Dòu immediately responded:
"A gentleman loves the lotus flower."
The king was greatly pleased and said:
"How marvelous!
Lotus is the princess's childhood name.
How could it match so perfectly?
Is this not predestined?
Send word to the princess
that she must come out to meet this gentleman."
After a while,
the sound of jade pendants drew near,
and the fragrance of orchids and musk grew strong—
the princess had arrived.
She was sixteen or seventeen years old,
exquisitely beautiful beyond compare.
The king instructed her to bow to Dòu,
saying:
"This is my youngest daughter, Liánhuā (Lotus)."
After bowing, she left.
Dòu gazed at her,
his heart stirred,
sitting woodenly in deep thought.
The king raised his cup to urge him to drink,
but Dòu did not even notice.
The king seemed to sense his feelings and said:
"My daughter would be a suitable match for you,
but I fear she is not worthy.
What do you think?"
Dòu remained dazed as if entranced,
again hearing nothing.
Someone nearby nudged him and said:
"Did you not see the king bow to you?
Did you not hear the king's words?"
Dòu felt lost and bewildered,
ashamed of himself,
and rose from his seat, saying:
"I have been treated with such generosity,
and without realizing it, I have become overly intoxicated.
I have neglected proper etiquette,
and I beg your forgiveness.
Moreover, as the day grows late,
I must take my leave."
The king stood up and said:
"Having met you, sir,
my heart is truly delighted.
Why speak of departure so hastily?
Since you are unwilling to stay,
I dare not force you.
If you are troubled by lingering thoughts,
I shall invite you again."
He then ordered a eunuch to escort Dòu out.
On the way,
the eunuch said to Dòu:
"Earlier, the king said his daughter would be a suitable match,
as if intending to propose a marriage alliance.
Why did you remain silent?"
Dòu stamped his foot in regret,
lamenting with every step,
until he arrived home.
Suddenly, he awoke from his dream,
and the evening glow was fading.
Sitting quietly in meditation,
the events remained vivid in his mind.
That evening, after extinguishing the lamp,
he hoped to revisit the old dream,
but the road to Hándān was distant,
leaving him only with sighs of regret.
One night,
while sharing a bed with a friend,
he suddenly saw the previous eunuch arrive,
summoning him on the king's orders.
Delighted, Dòu followed him.
Upon seeing the king, he prostrated himself.
The king helped him up
and invited him to sit in a corner, saying:
"Since we parted, I knew you would long for us.
I presumptuously offer my daughter to serve you,
hoping you will not find her unworthy."
Dòu immediately bowed in gratitude.
The king ordered scholars and ministers
to accompany them at the banquet.
As the wine feast concluded,
a palace attendant announced:
"The princess has finished dressing."
Soon, dozens of palace maids
escorted the princess out.
Covered with a red brocade over her head,
she walked with light, graceful steps,
was led onto the woolen carpet,
and performed the wedding ceremony with Dòu.
Afterwards, they were escorted to the bridal chamber.
The wedding chamber was warm and fragrant,
exquisitely luxurious.
Dòu said:
"With you before my eyes,
I am so happy I could forget death.
But I fear today's encounter
is but a dream."
The princess covered her mouth and said:
"Clearly, it is you and I here.
How could it be a dream?"
The next morning, after rising,
Dòu playfully applied makeup for the princess;
then he measured her waist with a belt
and the size of her feet with his fingers.
The princess laughed and asked:
"Are you mad?"
Dòu replied:
"I have been deceived by dreams many times,
so I am carefully noting the details.
If this is a dream,
it will still be enough to cherish in memory."
As they were bantering,
a palace maid rushed in and said:
"A monster has entered the palace gates!
The king has taken refuge in a side hall,
and disaster is imminent!"
Dòu was greatly alarmed
and hurried to see the king.
The king clasped his hand and wept, saying:
"Just as we were united,
hoping for eternal happiness,
who could have expected calamity from heaven?
The kingdom is about to fall—
what can we do now!"
The student asked in surprise what he meant.
The king took a memorial from the table
and handed it to the student to open and read.
The memorial said:
"Your subject, Black Wing, Grand Secretary of the Hánxiāng Hall,
presents this report on an extraordinary and monstrous event,
beseeching that the capital be moved early
to preserve the nation's vitality: According to a report from the palace gatekeepers, since the sixth day of the fifth month,
a giant serpent a thousand zhang long has come,
coiled itself outside the palace,
and devoured over thirteen thousand eight hundred officials and commoners, both inside and outside the palace;
all the palaces it passed through have been reduced to ruins,
and so on.
Your subject bravely went forward to observe
and indeed saw the monstrous serpent:
its head like a mountain peak,
its eyes like rivers and seas;
raising its head, it swallows halls and pavilions whole;
stretching its body, it overturns towers and walls entirely.
Truly a ferocity unseen for a thousand years,
a calamity not encountered for ten thousand generations!
The altars of state and the ancestral temples
are in imminent peril!
I beg Your Majesty to lead the palace household early
and swiftly move to a land of joy."
And so on.
After reading it,
the student's face turned ashen.
Immediately, a palace attendant rushed in to report:
"The monster has arrived!"
The entire hall wailed in grief,
a tragedy that blotted out the sky and sun.
The king, flustered and at a loss what to do,
could only weep and look at him, saying:
"My daughter has already burdened you, sir."
The student, panting, hurried back.
The princess was just holding her head and wailing with her attendants.
Seeing the student enter,
she tugged at his sleeve and said:
"Husband, where will you place me?"
The student, heartbroken and on the verge of despair,
grasped her wrist and thought, then said:
"I am but a poor and humble scholar,
ashamed that I have no golden house.
I have a few thatched huts;
for now, shall we hide there together?"
The princess, tears in her eyes, said:
"In such urgency, how can one choose?
I beg you to take me there quickly."
The student then helped her out by the arm.
Before long,
they reached his home.
The princess said:
"This is a very safe dwelling,
far better than my former country.
But since I have come with you,
what will my parents rely on?
Please build another house,
and surely the whole country will follow."
The student found this difficult.
The princess wailed:
"If you cannot help others in their urgent need,
what use is a husband!"
The student tried to comfort and console her a little,
but she had already entered the room.
The princess lay prostrate on the bed, weeping bitterly,
and could not be persuaded to stop.
Tormented by worry and without any solution,
he suddenly awoke
and realized it was all a dream.
Yet the sound of weeping by his ear
still buzzed faintly, not yet ceased.
Listening carefully,
he found it was not a human sound at all,
but rather two or three bees
flying and buzzing on his pillow.
He cried out in astonishment at this strange event.
His friend asked him about it,
so he told him the dream.
His friend also marveled at the oddity.
Together they got up to look at the bees,
which clung affectionately to their sleeves and robes,
not leaving even when brushed away.
His friend advised him to build a hive for them.
The student did as suggested
and oversaw the workers constructing it.
Just as two walls were raised,
swarms of bees came from outside the wall,
streaming in like a rope.
Before the roof was even joined at the top,
they had gathered, filling a peck measure.
Tracing where they came from,
it turned out to be the old garden of the neighbor, an old man.
In the garden was a beehive
that had been there for over thirty years,
breeding quite prolifically.
Someone told the old man about the student's affair.
The old man went to inspect it
and found the beehive silent.
Opening its wall,
he discovered a snake occupying it,
over ten feet long.
He caught and killed it.
Then they realized the giant serpent was this creature.
The bees entered the student's house
and multiplied even more prosperously,
with no other unusual occurrences.
Based on the manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Yú Shēng, named Jǐng,
styled Xiǎosòng,
was from Yìdū.
He studied at the Lǐquán Temple.
One night, as he was reading aloud,
suddenly a woman outside the window praised him, saying:
"Young Master Yú, how diligently you study!"
He thought to himself: In this deep mountain, where could a woman come from?
Just as he was pondering in doubt,
the woman had already pushed the door open, entered with a laugh,
and said:
"How diligently you study!"
Yú stood up in surprise,
looked at her,
and saw she wore a green dress with a long skirt,
graceful and lovely beyond compare.
Yú knew she was not human,
so he firmly questioned her about her hometown.
The woman said:
"Sir, look at me—I am surely not one who bites or devours,
why trouble yourself with such thorough questioning?"
Yú was fond of her in his heart,
so he then slept with her.
Once her silk jacket was removed,
her waist was so slender it could barely be grasped.
When the night watch was just ending,
she flitted away.
From then on, she came every night without fail.
One evening, as they drank together,
in their conversation she displayed a wonderful understanding of music.
Yú said:
"Your voice is delicate and fine,
if you would sing a tune,
it would surely captivate the soul."
The woman laughed and said:
"I dare not sing a tune,
for fear of captivating your soul."
Yú insisted on his request.
She said:
"It is not that I am stingy or reluctant,
but I fear others might hear.
Since you insist on it,
allow me to make a fool of myself;
but let it be just a faint voice to convey the meaning."
Then, lightly tapping the footrest with her lotus-like shoe,
she sang:
"The blackbird in the tree,
tricked me into parting at midnight.
I do not resent my embroidered shoes getting wet,
only fear my lord has no companion."
Her voice was as fine as a fly's,
barely discernible.
Yet listening quietly,
it was melodious, smooth, and vibrant,
stirring the ears and shaking the heart.
After singing,
she opened the door to peek out and said:
"Beware of someone outside the window."
She circled the house to look around,
then came back in.
Yú said:
"Why are you so deeply suspicious and fearful?"
She smiled and said:
"As the proverb says: 'A thieving ghost is always afraid of people.'
That describes me."
Later, when they went to bed,
she became uneasy and unhappy,
saying:
"The bond of our lives,
does it end here?"
Yú urgently asked her,
and the woman said:
"My heart is stirred,
my allotted fortune is exhausted."
Yú comforted her, saying:
"Hearts stir and eyes blink,
that's quite normal,
why speak of it so urgently?"
The woman became slightly relieved,
and they again became intimate.
When the night watch had ended,
she put on her clothes and got out of bed.
Just as she was about to open the door,
she hesitated and turned back,
saying:
"I don't know why,
but I feel timid and fearful.
I beg you to see me out the door."
Yú indeed got up
and saw her out the door.
The woman said:
"Stand and watch me;
after I climb over the wall and leave,
you may return."
Yú said:
"Yes."
He watched as the woman turned past the corridor,
and then she vanished without a trace.
Just as he was about to return to bed,
he heard the woman crying for help very urgently.
Yú rushed over,
looked around but saw no trace,
the sound came from under the eaves.
Raising his head to look carefully,
he saw a spider as big as a pellet,
seizing something,
which was crying out hoarsely in distress.
Yú broke the web and picked it down,
removed the bindings,
and it was a green bee,
barely alive and about to die.
He took it back to his room,
placed it on the desk.
After resting and reviving for a while,
it was able to walk.
Slowly it climbed onto the inkstone pool,
dipped itself into the ink,
came out and lay on the table,
walking to form
the character "Xiè" (謝, thanks).
It repeatedly spread its wings,
then flew out through the window.
From then on, she never returned.
According to the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì".
Xiè Zhōngtiáo of Lóngmén
was frivolous and without virtue.
At thirty, he lost his wife,
leaving behind two sons and a daughter,
who cried and wailed morning and night,
causing him much distress and trouble.
He planned to marry a second wife,
but negotiations fell through due to disagreements.
He temporarily hired an old woman to care for the children.
One day,
as he was strolling along a mountain path,
suddenly a woman appeared behind him.
Waiting to get a look,
she was a beautiful woman,
around twenty years old.
He was pleased with her,
and teased, saying:
"Madam, walking alone,
are you not afraid?"
The woman walked on without answering.
He said again:
"Madam, with such delicate steps,
the mountain path is quite difficult."
The woman still paid no attention.
Xiè looked around and saw no one,
approached her side,
suddenly grabbed her wrist,
dragged her into a secluded valley,
intending to force himself on her.
The woman angrily cried out:
"Where did this ruffian come from,
to intrude upon me so rudely!"
Xiè dragged her along,
without stopping.
The woman stumbled in her steps,
and in her distress, having no other plan,
said:
"Is this what I sought in a gentle and pleasing match?
If you will ease up on me,
I will comply with you."
Xiè agreed.
Together they entered a secluded ravine,
and after their wild union was done,
they grew fond and loving toward each other.
The woman asked about his hometown and surname,
and Xiè told her truthfully.
He then also asked the woman,
who said:
"I am Lí shì.
Unfortunately, I was widowed early,
and my mother-in-law has also passed away,
leaving me utterly alone,
with no one to rely on,
so I often go to my maternal home."
Xiè said:
"I am also a widower.
Could you come with me?"
The woman asked:
"Do you have children or not?"
Xiè said:
"To be honest with you:
when it comes to matters of the pillow,
I have had quite a few intimate partners.
But the crying of children,
I cannot bear."
The woman hesitated and said:
"This is a very difficult matter!
Looking at the style of your clothes, socks, and shoes,
they are only ordinary,
and I think I can manage that.
But being a stepmother is hard,
and I fear I may not withstand the blame and reproach."
Xiè said:
"Please do not doubt or hesitate.
I myself will not say anything,
so how can others interfere?"
The woman slightly consented.
Then, turning worried, she said:
"My body has already been touched,
how could I not follow you?
But I have a fierce elder brother,
who always treats me as a rare commodity,
and I fear he will not agree to this match.
What then shall we do?"
Xiè also grew anxious and fearful,
and suggested they flee together.
The woman said:
"I have also thought this through thoroughly.
What worries me is that if my family finds out,
it will be inconvenient for both sides."
Xiè said:
"That is a minor matter.
In my home, there is only an old maid,
whom I can dismiss immediately."
The woman was pleased,
and so went home with him.
First, they hid in an outer room;
then Xiè went in and dismissed the old maid,
cleaned the bed, and welcomed the woman,
and they were extremely joyful and loving.
The woman then set to work,
mending clothes for the children as well,
toiling diligently and earnestly.
Xiè, having gained this woman,
doted on her exceptionally,
and day after day shut the door to be with her,
not receiving any guests.
After more than a month,
he happened to go out on official business,
and locked the door behind him when he left.
When he returned,
he found the main gate tightly shut,
and knocking brought no response.
He pushed the door open and entered,
but there was no trace of anyone.
Just as he reached the bedroom,
a huge wolf charged out through the door and leaped away,
nearly frightening him to death.
Going inside to look,
he found the children gone,
the ground soaked in fresh blood,
and only three heads remaining.
He turned to chase the wolf,
but it had already gone, no one knew where.
The Chronicler of the Tales remarks:
"A scholar without virtue
receives a tragic retribution indeed.
Those who remarry
are all leading a wolf into their home;
how much more so when seeking a virtuous wife from a wild union and flight!"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Zōng Xiāngruò of Húzhōu
was a scholar.
One autumn day, while inspecting the fields,
he saw a spot where the crops were thick and dense
shaking violently.
Suspicious,
he crossed the path to take a look,
and found a man and a woman engaged in a wild union.
With a laugh, he was about to turn back.
Then he saw the man, embarrassed, tying his belt,
and hastily making his way off.
The woman also stood up.
Looking at her closely,
she was exceedingly graceful and lovely.
His heart was drawn to her,
and he wished to join in intimate embrace,
but felt ashamed of such base desire.
So he approached slightly and brushed off her clothes, saying:
"Was your tryst in the mulberry grove enjoyable?"
The woman smiled without answering.
Zōng drew near and opened her clothing;
her skin was smooth as grease.
Thereupon he caressed her up and down several times,
and the woman laughed and said:
"You pedantic scholar!
If you want something,
just do it;
why grope so wildly?"
He asked her name.
She said:
"After one encounter like a spring breeze,
we part east and west;
why trouble to inquire in detail?
Do you intend to leave my name on a chastity arch?"
Zōng said:
"In wild fields among dew and grass—
that is what rustic pig-herders do;
I am not used to it.
With your beautiful quality,
even a secret rendezvous should be conducted with self-respect;
why stoop to such triviality?"
Hearing this, the woman
greatly appreciated and accepted his words.
Zōng said:
"My humble study is not far;
please come over for a while."
The woman said:
"I have been out too long,
and fear others may suspect;
midnight would be fine."
She asked in detail about the markers and features of Zōng's household,
then hurried along a slanting path,
and swiftly went away.
At the beginning of the first watch,
she indeed came to Zōng's study.
Their cloud-and-rain encounter
was extremely intimate and loving.
This went on for days and months,
with no one in the know.
It happened that a foreign monk took up residence at the village temple,
and upon seeing Zōng, exclaimed in surprise:
"You have an evil aura about you;
what have you encountered?"
Zōng replied:
“No.”
After several days,
he suddenly fell ill.
Each evening, the girl brought fine fruits to feed him,
tending to him with great care,
as intimate as husband and wife.
However, after lying down, she would always force Zōng to couple with her.
Zōng, being ill,
found this quite unbearable.
He began to suspect she was not human,
but had no way to make her leave, even temporarily.
So he said:
“Before, the monk said I was bewitched by a demon,
and now I am indeed ill.
His words have proven true.
Tomorrow I shall invite him here,
and ask for talismans and incantations.”
The girl’s expression changed to one of deep sorrow.
Zōng grew even more suspicious.
The next day,
he sent someone to tell the monk the situation.
The monk said:
“This is a fox.
Her powers are still shallow,
easy to subdue.”
He then wrote two talismans,
and instructed, saying:
“Return and place a clean jar before the bed,
then stick one talisman on the jar’s mouth.
Wait until the fox darts inside,
quickly cover it with a basin,
then stick the other talisman on the basin.
Place it in a cauldron of boiling water over a fierce fire to cook;
she will die in a short while.”
The family servant returned
and did exactly as the monk instructed.
Late at night,
the girl finally arrived.
Reaching into her sleeve for golden tangerines,
she was just about to approach the bed to inquire after him
when suddenly, with a *whoosh* from the jar’s mouth,
the girl was sucked inside.
The servant sprang up,
covered the mouth and affixed the talisman,
and was about to proceed with the boiling.
Zōng saw the golden tangerines scattered all over the floor,
and, recalling their past affection,
was moved with sudden pity.
He urgently ordered her release.
Removing the talisman and the cover,
the girl emerged from the jar,
in a sorry and nearly exhausted state.
She kowtowed and said:
“My great path was nearing completion,
and in a single moment, I was almost reduced to ashes!
You are a benevolent man.
I vow I will surely repay you.”
With that, she left.
Several days later,
Zōng’s condition worsened, lingering gravely,
as if on the verge of death.
A family servant hurried to the market
to purchase wood for his coffin.
On the road, he met a young woman,
who asked:
“Are you a servant of Zōng Xiāngruò?”
He replied:
“Yes.”
The woman said:
“Young Master Zōng is my cousin.
I heard his illness is critical,
and was about to visit him,
but something came up preventing me from going.
Here is a packet of miraculous medicine;
I trouble you to deliver it to him.”
The servant took it and returned home.
Zōng reflected that among his maternal and paternal relatives, he had no sisters,
and knew this was the fox’s repayment.
He took the medicine,
and indeed recovered greatly,
returning to normal health within ten days.
Grateful in his heart,
he prayed into the empty air,
wishing to see her once more.
One night,
he was drinking alone behind closed doors,
when suddenly he heard a tapping at the window.
Drawing the bolt and going out to look,
it was the fox maiden.
Overjoyed,
he took her hand, expressing thanks,
and invited her in to drink together.
The girl said:
“Since we parted, it has weighed on my mind;
I’ve thought of no way to repay your great kindness.
Now I have found a fine match for you.
Will this perhaps suffice to discharge my obligation?”
Zōng asked:
“Who is it?”
She said:
“It is not for you to know yet.
Tomorrow during the Chén hour (7-9 AM),
go early to the south of the lake.
If you see a girl picking water chestnuts,
wearing a pale silk cape,
you must quickly take a boat and pursue her.
If you lose sight of where she went,
then look by the embankment for a short-stemmed lotus flower hidden beneath a leaf,
pluck it and bring it home.
Light the stem with a candle flame,
and you will obtain a beautiful wife,
and also attain longevity.”
Zōng carefully received her instructions.
Then she prepared to leave,
and Zōng firmly tried to detain her.
The girl said:
“Since suffering that calamity,
I have suddenly comprehended the Great Path.
How could I, for the sake of the love of the bedchamber,
invite another’s hatred and resentment?”
With a stern expression, she took her leave.
Zong did as told,
went to South Lake,
and saw many beautiful lotus blossoms in the pond.
Among them was a maiden with flowing hair,
dressed in ice-silk gauze,
a beauty beyond compare.
He urged his boat closer,
but suddenly she vanished.
He parted the lotus leaves
and found a single red lotus,
its stem less than a foot tall.
He broke it off and returned home.
Entering his room, he placed it on the table,
carved a candle beside it,
intending to light it.
When he turned back,
it had transformed into a stunning beauty.
Zong, overjoyed, knelt and bowed.
The woman said:
"Foolish man!
I am a fox spirit,
and I will bring calamity upon you!"
Zong paid no heed.
The woman asked:
"Who taught you this?"
He replied:
"I recognized you on my own,
why would I need teaching?"
He grabbed her arm and pulled,
and as she came down,
she turned into a strange stone,
about a foot tall,
exquisitely carved on all sides.
He carried it to the altar,
burned incense, bowed again, and prayed.
At night,
he barred the doors and sealed the cracks,
fearing she might disappear.
At dawn, he looked again—
it was no longer stone
but a sheer silk robe,
from which a faint fragrance wafted;
unfolding the collar,
he found traces of her scent still lingering.
Zong covered it and held it close as he slept.
That evening, he rose to trim the lamp,
and when he returned,
the maiden with flowing hair was lying on his pillow.
Overjoyed,
but afraid she might transform again,
he pleaded with her before approaching.
The woman laughed and said:
"What a nuisance!
I wonder who gossiped,
making this madman pester me to death!"
Then she no longer refused.
But during their intimacy,
she seemed unable to endure,
repeatedly begging to stop.
Zong would not listen.
The woman said:
"If so,
I will transform and leave!"
Zong, frightened, ceased.
From then on, their affection grew harmonious.
Gold and silk often filled his chests,
though he knew not where they came from.
The woman was meek in company,
as if unable to speak;
Zong also avoided mentioning her strangeness.
After more than ten months of pregnancy,
the time for birth arrived.
Entering the room,
she told Zong to bar the door and refuse visitors,
then cut open her lower abdomen with a knife,
took out the child,
and had Zong tear cloth to bind it.
By the next day, she had healed.
Another six or seven years passed,
when she said to Zong:
"My karmic debt is repaid,
I must bid farewell."
Zong wept upon hearing this,
saying:
"When you came to me,
I was poor and could not stand on my own;
relying on you, I prospered slightly.
How can I bear to part so suddenly?
Moreover, you have no family or clan.
In the future, our child will not know his mother—
that too is a regret."
The woman also sighed sorrowfully:
"Gatherings must end in partings—
such is the way of the world.
Our son has a fortunate appearance,
and you will live to a great age.
What more is there to seek?
I was originally surnamed Hé.
If you remember me fondly,
hold my old belonging and call out:
'Héhuā Sānniángzǐ!'
Then you may see me."
With these words, she freed herself,
saying:
"I am leaving."
In his startled gaze, she soared higher than his head.
Zong leaped up,
grabbed hastily,
and caught a shoe.
The shoe fell to the ground
and turned into a stone swallow,
redder than cinnabar,
translucent inside and out,
like crystal.
He picked it up and kept it.
Checking his chest,
he found the ice-silk gown she wore when she first arrived.
Whenever he missed her,
he would hold it and call
"Sānniángzǐ,"
and the maiden would appear,
her joyful face and smiling brows
just as in life;
only she did not speak.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A resident of Báijiāzhuāng west of the county
stole a neighbor's duck and cooked it.
That night,
he felt an itch on his skin.
At dawn, he looked—
fine duck feathers had grown,
painful to the touch.
Terrified,
he found no cure.
That night, he dreamed of a man telling him:
"Your illness is heaven's punishment.
You must be cursed by the one you stole from,
then the feathers will fall."
But the old neighbor was always magnanimous;
when things went missing in the past,
he never showed anger in voice or expression.
The thief deceitfully told the old man:
"The duck was stolen by so-and-so.
He fears being cursed terribly;
cursing him might warn him for the future."
The old man laughed:
"Who has energy to curse a wicked man?"
And he never cursed.
The thief grew more desperate,
so he confessed truthfully to the old neighbor.
The old man then cursed him,
and his illness truly ceased.
The Strange Historian remarks:
"How severe
is the fear for thieves: one theft and duck feathers grow!
How severe
is the caution against cursing: one curse and the thief's crime lessens!
Yet there is an art to doing good—
that old neighbor
used cursing to practice kindness."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Liǔ Xīchuān of Jiāozhōu
was the chief accountant steward of Vice Minister Fǎ.
Over forty years old,
he had a son
whom he doted on excessively.
He indulged him in everything,
fearing to cross him.
When the son grew up,
he became wildly extravagant and unruly,
emptying his father's savings.
Not long after,
the son fell ill.
The old man had kept a fine mule.
The son said:
"That mule is fat enough to eat.
Kill it for me to eat,
and my illness may heal."
Liǔ planned to kill an inferior mule instead.
The son heard of this,
flew into a rage and cursed,
and his illness worsened.
Liǔ, afraid,
killed the fine mule and served it.
The son was pleased;
but after one taste,
he pushed it away.
The illness did not abate,
and soon he died.
Liǔ mourned and sighed, wishing he could die too.
Three or four years later,
villagers went on a pilgrimage to Mount Tài.
Halfway up the mountain,
they saw a man riding a mule swiftly toward them.
He looked like Liǔ’s son.
When he drew near,
it was indeed him.
He dismounted and bowed all around,
exchanging pleasantries with everyone.
The villagers were all astonished,
but dared not question him about his death.
They only asked,
"What are you doing here?"
He replied,
"Nothing much,
just running around east and west."
He then asked the innkeeper’s name,
and they told him.
Liǔ’s son cupped his hands and said,
"I have a small matter to attend to now,
no time to catch up.
I’ll visit tomorrow."
He mounted his mule and left.
After the villagers returned to their lodging,
they thought he might not come.
At dawn they waited,
and the son indeed arrived.
He tied his mule to a stable post,
and hurried in with smiles and conversation.
The villagers said,
"Your father misses you dearly every day.
Why not return home to see him?"
The son asked in surprise,
"Who are you talking about?"
They answered, "Liǔ."
The son’s expression changed completely.
After a long pause, he said,
"Since he misses me,
please go back and tell him: I’ll wait for him here on the seventh day of the fourth month."
With that,
he bid farewell and left.
The villagers returned
and relayed the message to the old man.
The old man wept bitterly,
and went as scheduled.
He told the innkeeper his reason for coming.
The innkeeper stopped him, saying,
"When I saw the young master before,
his demeanor was cold and detached.
It didn’t seem like he had good intentions.
Judging by this,
it’s probably best not to see him."
Liǔ wept and refused to believe it.
The innkeeper said,
"I’m not trying to stop you,
but spirits are unpredictable.
I fear you might come to harm.
If you insist on meeting him,
please hide in this cabinet.
Wait until he comes,
observe his words and expression.
If it seems safe, then come out."
Liǔ did as he was told.
Soon the son indeed arrived.
He asked,
"Has Liǔ come?"
The innkeeper replied,
"No."
The son angrily cursed,
"That old beast!
How dare he not come!"
The innkeeper exclaimed in shock,
"Why curse your own father?"
He answered,
"What father of mine?
At first, we were companions in business.
I never expected he would harbor evil intentions,
conceal my hard-earned money,
and stubbornly refuse to return it.
Now I wish I could get my hands on him and have my satisfaction.
What father is he to me!"
With that,
he went out the door, saying,
"He got off easy!"
Liǔ, inside the cabinet,
heard everything clearly.
Sweat poured down to his heels,
and he dared not make a sound.
The innkeeper called him,
and only then did he come out,
returning in utter disarray.
The Chronicler of the Tales remarks:
"How joyful it is to suddenly gain great wealth!
What is hard to bear is repayment.
Even after squandering it all,
one still cannot forget it in the grave.
How deep is the resentment and poison in the human heart!"
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In the third month of the Guǐhài year,
I went to Jìxià with Gāo Jìwén,
and we stayed together at an inn.
Jìwén suddenly fell ill.
It happened that Gāo Zhènměi also came to the commandery with Niàndōng Xiānshēng,
so we sought medical treatment together.
We heard from Yuán Língōng that the Liáng family in the southern suburbs had a fox immortal
skilled in
"the arts of Chángsāng."
So we went together to visit.
Liáng was a woman around forty,
with a seductive, fox-like demeanor.
Entering her house,
we saw a red curtain hanging in the inner room.
Peeking behind the curtain,
we saw a statue of Guānyīn hanging on the wall,
along with two or three scrolls depicting figures on horseback wielding spears,
with attendants bustling about.
Under the north wall was a table;
on it was a small seat,
no taller than a foot,
covered with a small brocade cushion.
It was said that when the immortal arrived,
he would sit here.
We all burned incense and bowed in a row.
The woman struck a chime three times,
muttering indistinct words under her breath.
After the prayer,
she respectfully invited the guests to sit on the outer couch.
The woman stood under the curtain,
tidying her hair and resting her chin on her hand as she spoke with the guests,
recounting the miraculous deeds of the immortal.
After a long while,
the sun began to set.
Fearing it would be difficult to return at night,
we asked her to pray again.
The woman struck the chime and prayed once more.
Turning around, she stood and said,
"The immortal most enjoys conversing at night.
Often at other times, one cannot meet him.
Last night, a scholar awaiting the examinations brought food and wine to drink with the immortal.
The immortal also brought out fine wine to toast the guests,
composing poems and laughing joyfully.
When they dispersed,
the night was almost over."
Before she finished speaking,
a faint, bustling sound came from the room,
like bats flying and chirping.
As we listened intently,
suddenly something like a large stone fell onto the table,
making a loud noise.
The woman turned and said,
"That almost scared me to death!"
Then we heard a sighing sound from the table,
like that of a robust old man.
The woman used a palm-leaf fan to shield the small seat.
A loud voice from the seat exclaimed,
"What a fortunate encounter!
What a fortunate encounter!"
It loudly offered seats,
and seemed to bow in greeting.
Then it asked the guests,
"What brings you here?"
Gāo Zhènměi, following Niàndōng Xiānshēng’s intention, asked,
"Have you seen Bodhisattva?"
It replied,
"The South Sea is a familiar path for me.
How could I not have seen her?"
He also asked,
"Does Yánluó also change?"
It said,
"Just like in the mortal world."
"What is Yánluó’s surname?"
It said,
"Surname Cáo."
Then we asked for medicine for Jìwén.
It said,
"Return and offer tea and water in a night sacrifice.
I will ask the Bodhisattva for medicine and present it to you.
What illness cannot be cured?"
Everyone had their own questions,
and it answered them all clearly.
Then we bid farewell and returned.
The next day,
Jìwén improved slightly.
I and Zhènměi packed and returned home,
so we had no time to visit again.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Senior Vice Minister Gāo Niàndōng said:
"During the Chóngzhēn reign,
there was a monkey immortal
named Jìngshān.
He possessed an old man from Héjiān,
discussed poetry and essays with people,
predicted fortunes and misfortunes,
and spoke tirelessly.
When food and fruit were placed on the table,
he would eat and drink messily,
but he could not be seen."
At that time, the minister's grandfather was bedridden with illness.
Someone sent a letter saying:
"Hóu Jìngshān
is a man of a hundred years,
you must meet him."
So they sent a servant and horses to summon the old man.
The old man arrived and spent a day,
but the immortal had not yet come.
They burned incense and prayed to him.
Suddenly, a loud voice from the roof sighed in admiration:
"What a fine household!"
Everyone looked around in surprise.
Soon, the voice spoke again from under the eaves.
The old man stood up and said:
"The great immortal has arrived."
The group followed the old man, adjusting their caps, and went out to welcome him.
They heard the sound of someone bowing in greeting.
After entering the room,
he laughed heartily and spoke freely.
At that time, the vice minister and his brother were still students,
having just returned from the imperial examinations.
The immortal said:
"Both of your examination papers are also good;
but you are not yet well-versed in the classics,
you must work harder,
and your path to success is not far off."
The two respectfully asked about their grandfather's illness,
and he said,
"Life and death are great matters,
their principles are difficult to understand."
From this, they all knew it was an ill omen.
Not long after,
their grandfather passed away.
There was once a monkey trainer
who performed with a monkey in the village.
The monkey broke its chain and escaped,
could not be caught,
and went into the mountains.
For decades,
people still saw it.
It moved swiftly,
and when it saw people, it would flee.
Later, it gradually entered the village,
stealing food and fruit,
but no one could see it.
One day,
it was spotted by a villager,
chased into the wild,
and shot to death.
But the monkey's ghost did not realize it was dead,
only feeling its body as light as a leaf,
traveling a hundred li in a single breath.
It then went to possess the old man from Héjiān.
It said:
"If you can serve me,
I will make you rich."
Thus, it called itself Jìngshān.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Liú Zōngyù from Yíshuǐ said: his servant Dù Hé,
while in the garden,
saw money flowing like water,
about two or three feet deep and wide.
Dù was overjoyed,
scooped up handfuls with both hands,
and then lay down on top of it.
When he got up to look,
the money had all disappeared;
only what he held in his hands remained.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Guō Shēng
was from Dōngshān in the county.
He loved reading from a young age,
but in the mountain village, there was no one to correct him,
so by his twenties,
his handwriting was full of errors.
Previously,
his household was plagued by a fox,
and food, utensils, and belongings
often went missing,
causing great distress.
One night while studying,
he left his book on the table,
and it was scribbled on by the fox;
in the worst parts,
it was so messy that the text was illegible.
He selected the slightly cleaner parts to read,
and only managed to get through sixty or seventy pieces.
He was furious but could do nothing.
He also accumulated over twenty practice essays,
waiting to show them to a renowned scholar.
One morning,
he found them scattered on the table,
almost entirely covered in thick ink stains.
He was deeply resentful.
It happened that a certain Wáng,
who had come to the mountains for a reason,
and who was on good terms with Guō,
visited him.
Seeing the defaced book,
he asked about it.
Guō told him all his troubles,
and showed Wáng the remaining essays.
Wáng examined them carefully,
and the parts the fox had left untouched
seemed to have merit;
looking again at the stained pages,
they appeared redundant and could be deleted.
He said in surprise:
"The fox seems intentional.
Not only should you not resent it,
you should take it as your teacher."
After a few months,
looking back at his old works,
he suddenly felt the fox's markings were quite accurate.
So he rewrote two topics,
placed them on the table,
to observe any changes.
By dawn,
they were marked again.
After more than a year,
the fox stopped marking;
instead, it splashed thick ink in large dots,
covering the pages.
Guō found this strange,
and took them to show Wáng.
Wáng read them and said:
"The fox is truly your teacher,
your excellent essays can now be submitted."
That year,
he indeed entered the county school.
Guō was grateful to the fox,
and often set out chicken and millet
for the fox to eat and drink.
Whenever he bought famous literary works,
he did not choose them himself,
but let the fox decide.
Thus, in two examinations, he ranked near the top,
and in the provincial exam, he placed as a deputy candidate.
At that time, the works of gentlemen like Yè and Miào,
elegant and ornate,
were recited in every household.
Guō had a copy,
which he treasured greatly.
Suddenly, a bowl of thick ink was poured over it,
staining it almost beyond recognition;
he also drafted topics and composed essays,
feeling quite pleased with himself,
but they were all scribbled over: so he gradually lost faith in the fox.
Not long after,
Mr. Yè was arrested for promoting improper literary styles,
and he began to somewhat acknowledge the fox's foresight.
However, every time he wrote an essay,
after painstaking effort,
it would be stained.
Since he had often ranked at the top,
he was rather proud,
and thus grew more suspicious of the fox's whims.
He then copied the essays with many ink dots to test it,
and the fox stained them all again.
He laughed and said:
"This is truly absurd!
Why was it right before but wrong now?"
So he stopped setting out food for the fox,
and locked his books in a chest.
In the morning, he saw the chest still sealed,
but upon opening it, the cover was marked with four strokes,
thick as a finger;
the first chapter had five strokes,
the second also five,
and after that, there were no more.
From then on, the fox fell silent.
Later, Guō placed fourth in one exam,
and fifth in two others,
and only then realized the omen was hidden in the strokes.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Pride invites loss,
humility brings gain,
such is the way of heaven.
With a little fame,
one becomes self-righteous,
clinging to the outdated habits of Yè and Miào,
stubborn and unwilling to change,
and will not stop until utterly defeated.
Such is the harm of pride!"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Jīn Shēngsè was a native of Jìnníng.
He married a woman surnamed Mù from the same village.
They had a son,
who was just one year old.
Jīn suddenly fell ill,
and believing he would certainly die,
he said to his wife:
"After I die,
you must remarry.
Do not remain a widow!"
Upon hearing this,
his wife sweetly pleaded and solemnly vowed
that she would certainly die rather than remarry.
Jīn waved his hand and called to his mother:
"After I die,
please take care of the child.
Do not let her remain a widow."
His mother tearfully agreed.
Soon after, Jīn indeed died.
Old Lady Mù came to offer condolences.
After weeping,
she said to Jīn's mother:
"Heaven has brought this calamity,
and my son-in-law met his fate so suddenly.
My daughter is still so young and frail—
what is she to do?"
In her grief,
Jīn's mother heard these words
and became extremely indignant.
Angrily, she replied:
"She must remain a widow!"
Old Lady Mù, ashamed, let the matter drop.
That night, she slept beside her daughter
and privately said to her:
"Any man can be a husband.
