With your fine looks,
why worry about not finding a good match?
If a young woman doesn't start a family early,
but instead stares blankly, guarding this swaddled infant,
isn't she just a fool?
If they insist on making you remain a widow,
you shouldn't show them a pleasant face."
Jīn's mother passed by
and overheard some of this talk,
which made her even angrier.
The next day,
she said to Old Lady Mù:
"The deceased left a will
that originally did not instruct his wife to remain a widow.
Now, since you are in such a hurry you cannot wait,
she must remain a widow!"
Old Lady Mù left in a rage.
That night, Jīn's mother dreamed that her son came to her,
weeping and urging her not to make his wife remain a widow.
She found this strange.
She sent someone to tell the Mù family
that after the funeral, the widow could go wherever she wished.
But when she consulted a diviner,
he said the burial orientation was unfavorable that year.
The widow, wanting to show herself off to find a new husband,
even while in mourning clothes,
did not forget to adorn herself.
At home, she still dressed plainly;
but whenever she returned to her parents' home,
she appeared strikingly new and glamorous.
Jīn's mother knew of this
and disapproved in her heart;
but since the widow was soon to become another man's wife,
she endured it in silence.
Thus, the widow became even more unrestrained.
In the village, there was a rogue named Dǒng Guì
who saw her and fancied her.
He bribed an old woman neighbor of the Jīn family with money,
asking her to convey his ardent attentions to the widow.
At midnight,
he climbed over the wall from the old woman's house to reach the widow's place
and thus joined her.
Their comings and goings continued for about ten days.
Scandalous rumors spread everywhere;
the only one unaware was Jīn's mother.
At night, the widow's room had only one young maidservant,
who was her confidante.
One night,
just as the two were in the midst of passion,
they heard the coffin shake with a noise
like firecrackers.
The maidservant, on the outer couch,
saw the deceased emerge from behind the curtain,
wearing a sword, and enter the bedroom.
Soon, she heard the two cry out in shock.
A moment later,
Dǒng ran out naked.
Not long after,
Jīn, dragging the widow by her hair, also came out.
The widow screamed loudly.
Jīn's mother woke in alarm
and saw the widow, naked, running away,
just about to open the gate.
She called to her, but got no reply.
Going out the door to look after her,
she heard no sound in the stillness
and completely lost track of where she had gone.
Entering the widow's room,
she saw the lamp still lit.
Spotting a man's shoes,
she called the maidservant.
The maidservant, trembling with fear, finally came out
and told of the strange events.
They could only stare at each other in shock and wonder.
Dǒng had fled to the neighbor's house
and crouched, curled up in a corner of the wall.
After a while,
he heard the voices gradually cease
and finally stood up.
Without a stitch of clothing on,
he shivered bitterly from the cold
and intended to borrow clothes from the old woman.
Seeing a room in the courtyard
with its double doors slightly ajar,
he slipped inside for the moment.
Groping in the dark onto the bed,
he touched a woman's feet
and realized it was the neighbor's wife.
Instantly, lustful thoughts arose in him.
Taking advantage of her sleep,
he stealthily approached and had his way with her.
The woman woke and asked:
"Is that you?"
He replied:
"Yes."
The woman, unsuspecting,
proceeded to be intimate with him in every way.
Earlier,
the neighbor had gone to the northern village on some business,
instructing his wife to leave the door unlatched for his return.
When he came back,
he heard sounds inside the room.
Suspicious, he listened carefully
and heard utterly lewd noises and movements.
Furious,
he seized a weapon and entered the room.
Dǒng, terrified,
scrambled under the bed.
The neighbor went over and killed him.
He then wanted to kill his wife;
but she wept and explained it was a mistake,
so he spared her.
However, he could not figure out who the man under the bed was.
He called his mother to get up,
and together they brought a light to look.
They could barely recognize him.
Looking closely,
they saw he still had a faint breath.
When questioned about where he came from,
he was still able to confess.
But with several knife wounds
and blood flowing incessantly,
he died shortly after.
The old woman, flustered and at a loss,
said to her son:
"You caught them in adultery but killed only the man—
what will you do now?"
The son, having no alternative,
then killed his wife as well.
That night,
Old Man Mù was just going to bed
when he heard a chaotic noise outside his door;
he went out to look
and saw flames blazing under the eaves,
while the arsonist was still lingering and had not yet left.
The old man shouted loudly,
and all the family members gathered.
Fortunately, the fire had just started,
so it was still easy to extinguish.
He ordered people to take bows and crossbows
and chase after the arsonist.
They saw a person as agile as an ape,
who actually leaped over the wall and escaped.
Outside the wall was the old man's peach orchard,
and the surrounding walls of the orchard were all steep and solid.
Several people climbed up ladders to look,
but the trail was completely lost;
only a lump at the base of the wall was moving slightly.
They called out, but there was no response;
they shot at it, and it felt soft.
They opened the gate and went to inspect,
and found a woman lying naked,
with an arrow piercing her chest and brain.
Upon closer inspection with a candle,
it turned out to be the old man's daughter and Jīn's wife.
They were horrified and informed the master.
The old man and his wife were shocked and grief-stricken, almost fainting,
unable to understand the reason.
The woman's eyes were closed,
her face ashen,
her breath as fine as a thread.
They had someone pull out the arrow from her brain,
but it wouldn't come out;
they stepped on her head and neck before it came out.
The woman let out a faint moan,
blood gushed out violently,
and her breath ceased.
The old man was terrified,
and had no plan of action.
When dawn came,
he truthfully told Jīn's mother,
kneeling and pleading sorrowfully.
But Jīn's mother showed no resentment or anger,
only explaining the reason,
and told him to arrange the burial himself.
Jīn had a cousin named Shēngguāng,
who angrily went to the old man's house,
scolding him for his past wrongs.
The old man was ashamed and discouraged,
and bribed him to leave.
But they never found out who the woman's secret lover was.
Soon, the neighbor's son confessed to having caught them in adultery,
and after a light reprimand, he was released;
but the woman's brother, Mǎ Biāo, who was always litigious,
filed a complaint about his sister's injustice.
The officials summoned the old woman;
the old woman was afraid,
and confessed everything from beginning to end.
They also called Jīn's mother;
she feigned illness,
and sent Shēngguāng to testify on her behalf,
who fully explained the inside story.
Thus, the previous matters were all brought to light,
and Old Man Mù and his wife were both implicated and brought out,
and all the facts were thoroughly investigated.
Mù was convicted of teaching his daughter to remarry,
and for condoning adultery,
he was flogged;
he was ordered to redeem himself,
and his family property was wiped out.
The neighbor's old woman, for leading others into adultery,
was beaten to death with a cane.
The case was thus concluded.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Jīn's son, how divine he was!
He earnestly instructed his remarried wife,
how wise he was indeed!
Without killing a single person,
he avenged all grievances,
can he not be called divine!
The neighbor's old woman seduced another's wife,
but ended up with her own wife being seduced: Old Woman Mù loved her daughter,
but ultimately caused her daughter's death.
Alas!
'If you want to know the cause of the future,
look at what you are doing now,'
retribution comes even faster than in the next life!"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In Láizhōu, there was a scholar named Péng Hàogǔ,
who studied at a separate estate,
quite far from home.
During the Mid-Autumn Festival, he had not returned,
and felt lonely without a companion.
Thinking that there was no one in the village worth talking to;
only Qiū Shēng was a famous scholar in the county,
but he had always had hidden vices,
so Péng often looked down on him.
When the moon rose,
he felt even more bored,
and had no choice
but to send an invitation to Qiū.
While drinking,
there was a knock at the door.
The study boy went to answer,
and it was a scholar,
who wanted to visit the master.
Péng left his seat,
and respectfully invited the guest in.
They bowed and sat in a circle,
and then inquired about each other's family and residence.
The guest said:
"I am from Guǎnglíng,
and share the same surname as you,
my courtesy name is Hǎiqiū.
On such a fine night,
the loneliness of the inn is doubly hard to bear.
Hearing of your elegance and refinement,
I took the liberty of visiting without an introduction."
Looking at the person,
he wore plain but neat clothes,
and his conversation and laughter were refined.
Péng was overjoyed and said:
"You are my clansman.
What a night this is,
to have such a fine guest!
He immediately ordered wine,
and treated him as if they were old friends.
Observing his manner,
he seemed to look down on Qiū;
Qiū tried to engage him in conversation,
but he was arrogant and did not respond politely.
Péng felt ashamed on his behalf,
so he interrupted the conversation,
and asked to first sing a folk song to accompany the drinking.
Then he looked up at the sky and cleared his throat twice,
and sang
"The Song of the Gallant Man from Fúfēng."
They laughed and enjoyed themselves together.
The guest said:
"I cannot match your elegance,
and cannot repay your refined song.
May I ask someone to sing on my behalf?"
Péng said:
"As you wish."
The guest asked:
"Are there any famous courtesans in Láichéng?"
Péng replied:
"No."
The guest fell silent for a long while,
then said to the page boy:
"I just summoned someone
who is outside the gate;
you may lead her in."
The page went out
and indeed saw a young woman hesitating outside the door.
He brought her in.
She was about sixteen years old,
as graceful as a fairy.
Péng was utterly astonished
and helped her to sit down.
She wore a willow-yellow cape,
and her fragrance filled the entire room.
The guest then comforted her, saying:
"You must have endured quite a journey over a thousand miles."
The girl smiled and nodded in agreement.
Péng found this strange
and pressed for an explanation.
The guest said:
"Your esteemed hometown sadly lacks beauties,
so I just summoned one from a boat on West Lake."
He said to the girl:
"The song 'Ballad of the Fickle Lover' you sang earlier on the boat
was excellent.
Please sing it once more."
The girl sang:
"Fickle lover,
leading his horse to wash in the spring pond.
Human voices fade away,
horse hooves grow faint;
the river and sky stretch high,
the mountain moon appears small.
He turns his head and leaves, never to return,
as dawn breaks white in the courtyard.
I do not resent our many partings,
but only sorrow that our joyful meetings are few.
Where shall I sleep?
Do not become willow catkins drifting with the wind.
Even if you never earn a noble title,
do not go to Línqióng!"
The guest took out a jade flute from his stocking
and accompanied her melody.
When the song ended, the flute stopped.
Péng sighed in amazement and said:
"From West Lake to here
is surely more than a thousand miles.
To summon someone in an instant—
are you not an immortal?"
The guest replied:
"How dare I claim to be an immortal?
I merely see ten thousand miles as no farther than my own courtyard gate.
Tonight, the breeze and moon over West Lake
are even more splendid than before.
We must not miss this sight.
Would you care to join me for a visit?"
Péng, eager to witness his marvels,
agreed, saying:
"It would be my great pleasure."
The guest asked:
"By boat or
by horseback?"
Péng thought traveling by boat would be more leisurely,
so he answered:
"I prefer a boat."
The guest said:
"Calling a boat here would take too long,
but there should be a ferry in the Milky Way."
Then, raising his hand toward the sky, he called out:
"Boat, come!
Boat, come!
We wish to go to West Lake
and will not begrudge the fare."
Before long,
a painted boat
descended from the sky,
wreathed in mist and clouds.
They all boarded.
They saw a man holding a short oar;
the end of the oar was densely lined with long feathers,
shaped like a feather fan.
With each wave of the feathers,
a cool breeze whispered.
The boat gradually ascended into the clouds,
heading southward,
swift as an arrow.
After a short while,
the boat landed on water.
They heard only the clamor of strings and pipes,
and the noisy sound of voices.
Stepping out of the boat to look around,
they saw the moon reflected on misty waves,
with pleasure boats crowding like a market.
The boatman stopped rowing,
letting the boat drift freely.
Looking closely,
it was indeed West Lake.
The guest fetched exotic delicacies and fine wine from the stern
and they drank merrily together.
After a while,
a large pleasure boat gradually approached
and sailed alongside them.
Peering through the window,
they saw two or three people inside,
playing chess and laughing boisterously.
The guest flew a goblet over to the girl and said:
"Drink this to send you off."
As the girl drank,
Péng lingered with longing,
fearing she would leave.
He nudged her with his foot.
The girl glanced at him sideways.
Péng grew even more stirred
and begged for a future rendezvous.
The girl said:
"If you truly love me,
just ask for the name Juānniáng—
everyone knows it."
The guest then handed Péng's silk handkerchief to the girl,
saying:
"I shall make a three-year appointment on your behalf."
He then stood up,
placed the girl on his palm,
and said:
"An immortal!
An immortal!"
Then, leaning toward the neighboring boat's window,
he pushed the girl inside.
The window opening was as large as a plate,
yet the girl slipped through like a snake,
without feeling cramped at all.
Soon, they heard from the neighboring boat:
"Juānniáng has awakened."
That boat then drifted away.
From afar, they saw it moor,
and the people on board scattered and departed.
Péng's mood for sightseeing vanished at once.
He then told the guest
that he wished to go ashore
to stroll and gaze around a bit.
They had just begun to discuss the matter when
the boat came to shore on its own.
They left the boat and walked on land,
covering over a li
before the guest caught up,
leading a horse.
He told Péng to hold it,
then left again,
saying:
"Wait while I borrow two more horses."
He did not return for a long time.
The passersby had grown sparse;
looking up, they saw the slanting moon turning westward,
and the sky beginning to brighten.
Qiū was nowhere to be found either.
Holding the horse, Péng was at a loss,
unsure whether to advance or retreat.
He tugged the reins and went back to where the boat had moored,
but both the people and the boat were gone.
Thinking of his empty money pouch at his waist,
he grew even more anxious and alarmed.
When it was fully light,
he noticed a small embroidered pouch on the horse;
reaching into it,
he found three or four taels of silver.
He bought food and waited intently,
unaware that it was already noon.
He decided it would be better to visit Juānniáng for the time being,
so he could slowly inquire about Qiū's whereabouts.
But when he asked around for Juānniáng's name,
no one knew of her,
and his spirits sank.
The next day, he set off.
The horse was well-trained,
fortunately not lame or inferior,
and he returned home after half a month.
Back when the three of them had taken the boat upstream,
the acolyte returned and reported:
"The master has become an immortal and left."
The whole family wept in sorrow,
believing he would not return.
When Péng returned,
he tied up the horse and went inside.
His family gathered around in surprise and joy, asking questions,
and Péng finally recounted the strange events in detail.
Thinking that he had returned alone to his hometown,
he feared the Qiū family would hear of it and come asking questions,
so he warned his family not to spread the news.
As they spoke,
he mentioned how he had gotten the horse.
Everyone, thinking it was left by an immortal,
went together to the stable to examine it.
When they arrived,
the horse suddenly vanished,
and there was only Qiū,
tied to the manger with a straw rope.
Astonished,
they called Péng out to see.
They saw Qiū hanging his head under the manger,
his face ashen as if dead.
When questioned, he did not speak,
only opening and closing his eyes.
Péng could not bear it,
so he untied him and helped him to a bed,
where he lay as if his soul had left him.
They fed him some broth,
and he was able to swallow a little.
In the middle of the night, he revived slightly
and urgently needed to use the toilet;
supported and helped there,
he passed several lumps of horse dung.
After drinking a little more,
he was finally able to speak.
Péng went to his bedside and pressed him for details.
Qiū said:
"After getting off the boat,
he led me aside for idle talk.
When we reached an empty spot,
he playfully patted my neck,
and I fell into a daze and collapsed.
After lying still for a moment,
I looked at myself and saw I had become a horse.
My mind was clear,
but I couldn't speak.
This is a great humiliation and shame,
and I truly cannot tell my wife and children.
I beg you not to reveal it!"
Péng agreed
and ordered a servant to take him home by horse-drawn carriage.
From then on, Péng could not forget Juānniáng.
Another three years passed,
and as his brother-in-law was serving as a judge in Yángzhōu,
he went to visit him.
In the prefecture, there was a young master Liáng,
who was a family friend of Péng's.
He hosted a banquet and invited Péng to drink.
At the banquet, several singing girls
came to pay their respects.
The young master asked about Juānniáng,
and his attendants reported that she was ill.
The young master angrily said:
"That maid thinks too highly of herself because of her reputation.
Take a rope and tie her up to bring her here!"
Hearing Juānniáng's name, Péng
asked in surprise who she was.
The young master said:
"She is the madam's daughter,
the top beauty in Guǎnglíng.
Because she has some fame,
she acts arrogantly and without manners."
Péng suspected it might be a coincidence of names;
but his heart pounded anxiously,
and he desperately wanted to see her.
Before long,
Juānniáng arrived,
and the young master angrily berated her.
Péng looked closely
and saw it was indeed the girl he had met on the Mid-Autumn Festival.
He said to the young master:
"She and I are old acquaintances.
I hope you will forgive her."
Juānniáng looked carefully at Péng,
seeming equally startled.
The young master did not have time to ask further
and immediately ordered the wine to be served.
Péng asked:
"Do you still remember
the song 'The Fickle Lover'?"
Juānniáng was even more astonished.
She gazed at him for a long time
before beginning to sing the old tune.
Listening to her voice,
it was exactly like that Mid-Autumn night years ago.
When the drinking ended,
the young master ordered her to attend to the guest for the night.
Péng took her hand and said:
"The three-year promise—
are we fulfilling it now?"
Juānniáng said:
"Back then, I was boating on West Lake with others,
and after drinking only a few cups,
I suddenly felt drunk.
In a daze,
I was taken away by someone
and placed in a village.
A youth led me inside;
among the three guests at the table,
you were one of them.
Later, we took a boat to West Lake,
and he sent me back through the window lattice,
holding my hand earnestly.
Whenever I thought of it,
I believed it was an illusion or a dream;
but the silk scarf was real,
and I still keep it carefully wrapped away."
Péng told her what had happened,
and they sighed together in amazement.
Juānniáng threw herself into his arms
and said tearfully:
"The immortal has already acted as a good matchmaker.
Please do not abandon me because I am from the world of pleasure,
and forsake someone suffering in this sea of bitterness."
Péng said:
"The promise made in the boat
has never left my mind for a single day.
If you are willing,
I would empty my purse and sell my horse
without hesitation."
The next morning,
he informed the young master;
he also borrowed money from the Deputy Prefect,
spent a thousand taels to remove her from the register,
and took her home with him.
When they occasionally visited the country estate,
she could still recognize the place where they had drunk that year.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"A horse that becomes a man—
he must have been a man who became a horse.
If he were made a horse,
one would regret he was not a man.
Lions, elephants, cranes, and rocs—
all are subject to the whip and spur.
How can we say this is not the benevolent love of divine beings?
Even the three-year promise
was a means to ferry her across the sea of bitterness."
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
In Yízhōu, the family of Assistant Minister of Rites Sòng Jūnchǔ
had always esteemed geomancy;
even the women of the household could read its books
and understand its principles.
After Lord Sòng passed away,
his two sons each established their own households,
and sought to select a burial site for their father.
Hearing of anyone skilled in the art of geomancy,
they spared no distance,
competing to enlist them.
Thus, the geomancers gathered by the two households
numbered nearly a hundred;
every day they rode out in groups across the countryside,
going east and west on separate paths,
like two armies.
After more than a month,
each had found an auspicious burial site—
one claimed it would bring nobility,
the other said it would produce a prime minister.
The brothers refused to yield to each other,
and in their stubbornness, they ceased to consult one another,
proceeding to prepare burial grounds separately.
With brocade canopies and colorful banners,
both sites were fully equipped.
When the funeral procession reached the fork in the road,
each brother led his followers to contend for their chosen path,
from morning until dusk,
unable to reach a decision.
The guests all departed.
The pallbearers, having changed shoulders ten times,
were exhausted and could no longer lift the coffin,
so they left it by the roadside.
Thus, the burial was halted,
and workers were gathered to build a hut
to shelter it from wind and rain.
The elder brother built a hut nearby,
leaving laborers to guard it;
the younger brother also built a hut like his brother’s;
the elder built another,
and the younger built yet another: in three years, it became a village.
After many years,
the brothers passed away one after the other;
their wives, the sisters-in-law, finally joined forces,
resolutely breaking the deadlock of their predecessors’ rivalry,
and went together into the fields
to inspect the two chosen sites.
Both declared them inauspicious,
so they pooled their resources to hire a geomancer
to select another site for them.
Each time a site was found,
a map was presented to the women’s quarters,
for them to judge its suitability.
Several maps were submitted daily,
all of which they found fault with.
After more than ten days,
they finally selected a burial ground.
The elder sister-in-law examined the map
and said happily:
"This will do."
She showed it to the younger sister-in-law.
The younger said:
"This site will first produce a military举人."
Three years after the burial,
the eldest grandson of Lord Sòng indeed became a military举人 through the provincial examination.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"The art of geomancy
may have its principles;
but to be obsessed with it and believe in it blindly
is foolish.
Moreover, to contend out of stubbornness,
leaving the coffin by the roadside,
shows no regard for the principles of filial piety and fraternal duty—
how can one hope to benefit descendants through geomancy!
As for the harmonious sisters-in-law,
they are truly refined and worthy of being remembered."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Nán Sānfù
was from an aristocratic family in Jìnyáng.
He owned a country estate,
about ten里 from his residence,
and he would ride there daily.
Once, encountering rain on the way,
he saw a small village along the road,
and at a farmer’s house,
the gateway appeared spacious,
so he sought shelter there.
The villagers nearby all held Nán in high esteem.
After a short while,
the host came out to invite him in,
behaving with great deference and respect.
Entering the house,
he found it cramped.
After the guest was seated,
the host began to take a broom,
and diligently swept the floor.
Then he brewed honey as tea.
Only when asked to sit did he dare to do so.
When asked his name,
he replied:
"Tíngzhāng,
surname Dòu."
Soon after,
he brought wine and cooked a chick,
attending to his guest with utmost care.
A young woman of marriageable age served the food,
lingering outside the door at times,
occasionally revealing half her figure—
she was fifteen or sixteen,
graceful and exceedingly beautiful.
Nán was captivated.
When the rain stopped and he returned home,
he thought of her incessantly.
The next day,
he brought grain and silk as gifts,
using this as a pretext to visit again.
From then on, he often visited the Dòu household,
sometimes bringing food and wine,
and they would linger together.
The girl gradually became familiar with him,
and no longer avoided him much,
often moving about in front of him.
When he glanced at her,
she would lower her head and smile.
Nán became even more infatuated,
visiting no less than every three days.
One day,
finding Dòu absent,
he sat for a long time,
and the girl came out to attend to the guest.
Nán grabbed her arm and embraced her.
The girl, ashamed and flustered,
sternly refused, saying:
"Though I am poor,
I intend to marry properly—
how can you, a nobleman, bully me like this!"
At that time, Nán had lost his wife,
so he bowed to her and said:
"If you would take pity on me and accept me,
I vow not to marry anyone else."
The girl demanded an oath;
Nán pointed to the sky and sun,
swearing to keep his promise forever,
and only then did she consent.
From then on,
whenever he saw Dòu go out,
he would go to her for intimate moments.
The girl urged him:
"A secret affair like this
cannot last long.
Under the shelter of my parents’ roof,
if you would deign to marry me,
my parents would surely be honored,
and there should be no obstacle.
You must make plans quickly!"
Nán agreed.
But then he thought, how could a farmer’s daughter be a suitable match?
So he merely gave empty promises to delay.
Meanwhile, a matchmaker came to propose a marriage with a wealthy family;
at first he hesitated,
but upon hearing of her beauty and wealth,
he made up his mind.
The girl, now pregnant,
pressed him even more urgently,
but Nán ceased visiting altogether.
Not long after,
the girl went into labor
and gave birth to a boy.
Her father angrily beat her.
The girl told him the truth,
saying:
"Nán promised to marry me."
Dòu then released his daughter
and sent someone to question Nán;
Nán flatly denied it.
Dòu then abandoned the infant
and beat his daughter even more severely.
The girl secretly begged a neighboring woman
to tell Nán of her suffering.
Nán ignored it.
One night, the girl fled,
and finding the abandoned child still alive,
she carried him and ran to Nán’s house.
Knocking on the gate, she said to the gatekeeper:
"If only I can have a word from my master,
I may not have to die.
Even if he does not care for me,
how can he not care for his son?"
The gatekeeper relayed her words to Nán,
but Nán ordered him not to let her in.
The girl leaned against the gate, weeping bitterly,
until the fifth watch, when her cries were heard no more.
At dawn, they looked—
the girl sat rigid, holding the child in her arms, dead.
Dòu was furious,
and brought a lawsuit against Nán before the higher authorities,
who all considered Nán’s actions unrighteous,
and wanted to punish him.
Nán was afraid,
and bribed his way out of trouble with a thousand taels of gold.
The wealthy family dreamed that the girl, with disheveled hair and holding a child, came to tell them:
“You must not agree to the heartless man’s proposal;
if you do,
I will surely kill him!”
The wealthy family, coveting Nán’s wealth,
still agreed to the marriage.
After the wedding ceremony,
the dowry was abundant,
and the bride was also beautiful.
However, she was prone to sadness,
and throughout the day, she was never seen with a joyful expression;
in bed,
she often shed tears.
When asked,
she did not speak.
After a few days,
the bride’s father came,
and as soon as he entered the door, he wept.
Before Nán could ask the reason,
they went together into the inner room.
Seeing the girl, he was shocked and said:
“Just now in the back garden,
I saw my daughter hanging dead on a peach tree;
who is this in the room?”
Upon hearing this,
the girl’s expression suddenly changed,
and she fell down dead.
Looking at her,
it was Dòu’s daughter.
They hurried to the back garden,
and indeed, the new bride had hanged herself.
Utterly terrified,
they went to report to Dòu.
Dòu opened his daughter’s grave,
and found the coffin open and the corpse gone.
His previous anger had not subsided,
and now it doubled in intensity,
so he brought another lawsuit before the authorities.
The officials considered the circumstances fantastical,
and were undecided on how to assign blame.
Nán again heavily bribed Dòu,
pleading with him to drop the case;
the officials also accepted Nán’s bribes and instructions,
and the matter was dropped.
However, from then on, Nán’s family gradually declined.
Moreover, the strange events were widely spread,
and for several years, no one dared to marry their daughter to him.
Nán had no choice,
and arranged to marry the daughter of Jìnshì Cáo from over a hundred li away.
Before the wedding could take place,
it happened that among the people, a rumor spread
that the imperial court was going to select daughters from good families to fill the imperial harem,
so those who had daughters
all sent them to their husbands’ homes.
One day,
an old woman led a sedan chair to Nán’s house,
claiming to be from the Cáo family, delivering the bride.
She helped the girl into the room,
and said to Nán:
“The selection of palace ladies is urgent,
and in haste, we cannot follow the proper rituals,
so we are sending the young lady here.”
Nán asked:
“Why are there no attendants?”
She replied:
“There is a modest dowry,
which is following behind.”
The old woman hastily left.
Nán saw that the girl was also charming,
so he joked and laughed with her.
The girl lowered her head and played with her sash,
her demeanor strikingly similar to Dòu’s daughter.
Nán felt disgusted in his heart,
but did not dare to speak.
The girl climbed onto the bed,
pulled the quilt over her head, and slept.
Nán thought this was normal for a new bride,
and did not pay it much mind.
As dusk fell,
the Cáo family had not arrived,
and he began to suspect.
He pulled back the quilt to ask the girl,
but she was already cold and lifeless.
Shocked and bewildered, not knowing the reason,
he sent a messenger to inform the Cáo family,
but the Cáo family had never sent their daughter.
People spread the story as something strange.
At that time, the daughter of Xiàolián Yáo had recently been buried,
and the next night, her grave was robbed,
the coffin broken and the corpse missing.
Hearing of this strange event,
Yáo went to Nán’s place to investigate,
and indeed, it was his daughter.
Lifting the quilt for a look,
her body was completely naked.
Yáo was furious,
and brought a formal complaint to the authorities.
The officials, because Nán had repeatedly behaved immorally,
despised him,
and convicted him of grave robbery and exposing a corpse,
sentencing him to death.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
“To first violate her and then marry her is not virtuous;
how much more so when vows were made at the beginning and broken later?
When she was beaten inside the house,
he allowed it;
when she cried at the door,
he still allowed it: how heartless he was!
And the retribution he received
was even more tragic than that of Lǐ Shíláng!”
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Liáng Yàn of Xúzhōu
suffered from a runny nose and sneezing,
which persisted for a long time without relief.
One day,
while lying down,
he felt an intense itch in his nose,
and quickly got up to sneeze violently.
Something shot out and fell to the ground,
shaped like a roof tile dog,
about the size of a fingertip.
He sneezed again,
and another one fell.
After four sneezes, four had fallen in total.
They moved sluggishly,
gathering together and sniffing each other.
Soon, the stronger ones bit the weaker ones to eat them;
after eating one,
their bodies suddenly grew.
In an instant, they devoured each other,
leaving only one,
larger than a flying squirrel.
It stretched out its tongue and licked all around,
cleaning its mouth.
Liáng was greatly alarmed,
and stepped on it,
but the creature climbed up his sock,
gradually reaching his thigh.
He grabbed his clothes and shook them,
but it clung tightly and would not come off.
Soon, it entered under his collar,
scratching and clawing at his waist and ribs.
Terrified,
he quickly took off his clothes and threw them to the ground.
Feeling around,
the creature had already attached itself to his waist.
Pushing it did not move it,
pinching it caused pain,
and it eventually became a wart;
its mouth and eyes had closed,
like a crouching mouse.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Grand Historian Jiāng Yùxuán said:
“Beneath Lóngduī,
if you dig several feet into the ground,
there is dragon meat filling it.
People may cut and take it freely,
but they must not say the word ‘dragon.’
If someone says, ‘This is dragon meat,’
then thunderclaps will rumble,
striking the person dead.”
The Grand Historian had once eaten the meat,
and it was indeed true.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Sòng Guóyīng
was a native of Dōngpíng.
Having served as an instructor, he was appointed magistrate of Lùchéng.
He was greedy, cruel, and unkind,
especially harsh in collecting taxes.
Those who died under the rod
lay scattered in the courtyard.
My fellow townsman Xú Báishān happened to be passing by
and witnessed his tyranny.
He admonished him, saying:
"As a parent to the people,
is it proper for your authority and power to reach such extremes?"
Sòng, looking smug and proud, replied with self-satisfied words:
"Oh!
I dare not claim such!
Though my office is small,
in the hundred days since I assumed my post,
I have executed fifty-eight people."
Half a year later,
while he was sitting at his desk attending to official duties,
he suddenly stared wide-eyed and stood up,
his hands and feet flailing wildly,
as if struggling with someone.
He cried out:
"I deserve death for my crimes,
I deserve death for my crimes!"
He was helped into his residence,
and shortly afterward, he died.
Alas!
Fortunately, the underworld also oversees the affairs of the living;
otherwise,
with the accumulation of ill-gotten gains,
then
"outstanding"
reputations would arise,
and how would the poison of such corruption ever end?
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"The region of Lùchéng is an ancient land,
and its people possess a resolute spirit,
hence they become heroic ghosts.
Nowadays, whenever an official holds authority above,
there are bound to be one or two base individuals
who flatter and fawn upon him.
When he is at the height of his power,
they exhaust the remaining wealth of the people,
presenting him with embroidered screens as gifts.
When he is about to fall,
they drive the people, whose limbs are not yet broken,
to beg for his retention.
Whether an official is greedy or honest,
each time he assumes a post,
these two things are certain to occur.
As long as the mighty one has not departed for a single day,
the simple folk dare not disobey.
This accumulated practice, passed down through tradition,
has become an established custom.
Surely, it must also be mocked by the ghosts of Lùchéng!"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Yáng Wànshí
was a scholar from Dàmíng.
Throughout his life, he suffered from
"the fear of Jìcháng."
His wife, Yǐn shì,
was exceptionally fierce and domineering.
If he slightly displeased her,
she would resort to whipping him.
Yáng's father was over sixty and widowed,
yet Yǐn treated him as no better than a slave.
Yáng and his younger brother, Wànzhōng, often secretly gave their father food,
not daring to let their wives know.
However, as he wore tattered clothes,
they feared he would become an object of ridicule,
so they did not allow him to meet guests.
Wànshí, at forty, had no son,
so he took a concubine named Wáng,
but he dared not exchange a single word with her day or night.
The brothers were in the prefectural city awaiting the examinations
when they met a young man
whose appearance and attire were both elegant.
They spoke with him
and took a liking to him.
They asked his name,
and he replied:
"Jièfǔ,
surname Mǎ."
From then on, their friendship grew closer daily,
and they burned incense to swear an oath of brotherhood.
After parting,
about half a year later,
Mǎ suddenly visited Yáng with his servant.
He happened upon Yáng's father outside the gate,
basking in the sun and picking lice.
Mistaking him for a hired servant,
he gave his name and asked him to inform the master.
The old man, wrapped in his ragged clothes, went inside.
Someone told Mǎ:
"That is his father."
Mǎ was just expressing his surprise
when the Yáng brothers came out to greet him, wearing their caps.
After bowing in the hall,
Mǎ requested to pay his respects to their father.
Wànshí excused himself, saying his father was unwell.
They sat together, chatting and laughing,
unaware that evening was approaching.
Wànshí repeatedly said that food would be served,
but it never arrived.
The brothers took turns going in and out,
and finally a thin servant brought a pot of wine.
It was quickly finished.
They sat waiting for a long time,
and Wànshí frequently rose to urge the servants,
sweat beading on his forehead and cheeks.
Soon, the thin servant brought out the dishes,
but the rice was coarse and poorly cooked,
far from delicious.
After the meal,
Wànshí hastily left.
Wànzhōng brought his bedding to keep the guest company for the night.
Mǎ reproached him, saying:
"Previously, I admired your noble character,
and thus we swore brotherhood.
Now, your father does not even have warmth or enough to eat,
a fact that would shame any passerby!"
Wànzhōng said with tears in his eyes:
"The feelings in my heart
are difficult to express fully.
Our household is unfortunate,
having encountered a fierce sister-in-law.
Our elders and the weak
are cruelly mistreated.
Were it not for our deep bond of brotherhood,
I would not dare to reveal this disgrace."
Mǎ was shocked and sighed for a while,
then said:
"I originally intended to leave early tomorrow morning,
but now that I have heard this extraordinary tale,
I must witness it for myself.
Please lend me an empty room,
and I will cook for myself."
Wànzhōng followed his advice,
clearing out a room for Mǎ to settle in.
Late at night, he secretly brought vegetables and rice,
fearing his wife would find out.
Mǎ understood his intention
and firmly declined.
He also requested that Yáng's father eat and sleep with him.
He went to the city market himself,
bought cloth and silk,
and had them made into robes and trousers for the old man.
Father and sons were all moved to tears.
Wànzhōng had a son named Xǐ'er,
just seven years old,
who slept with his grandfather at night.
Mǎ patted him and said:
"This child's fortune and longevity will surpass his father's,
but he will be orphaned and suffer hardship in his youth."
When the wife heard that the old man was comfortable and well-fed,
she flew into a rage,
cursing incessantly,
saying that Mǎ was meddling in other people's affairs.
At first, her harsh words were confined to the inner chambers,
but gradually she drew closer to Mǎ's residence,
intending to show her displeasure through her music.
The Yáng brothers were sweating and pacing anxiously,
unable to stop her;
yet Mǎ acted as if he heard nothing.
The concubine, Wáng,
was five months pregnant,
and when the wife found out,
she stripped her clothes and beat her cruelly.
Afterward,
she called Wànshí over and made him kneel to receive a woman's headscarf,
then chased him out with a whip.
As it happened, Mǎ was outside,
and Wànshí, ashamed and hesitant, dared not move forward.
Only when she pressed him further
did he finally go out.
The wife followed him out,
crossing her arms and stamping her feet,
while onlookers crowded around.
Mǎ pointed at the wife and shouted,
"Go away,
go away!"
The wife immediately turned and fled,
as if chased by a ghost.
Her pants and shoes fell off,
and her foot bindings tangled on the road;
she returned barefoot,
her face ashen.
After calming down a little,
a maid brought her socks and shoes.
Once dressed,
she wailed loudly.
No one in the household dared to ask what happened.
Mǎ pulled Wànshí aside to remove the headscarf.
Wànshí stood stiffly, holding his breath,
as if afraid it would fall off;
Mǎ forcibly removed it.
But Wànshí remained restless,
still fearing he would be punished for removing it without permission.
Only after he confirmed the wife had finished crying
did he dare enter,
hesitating as he approached.
The wife did not utter a single word,
but suddenly stood up,
entered her room, and went to bed.
Wànshí finally relaxed,
and he and his brother secretly marveled at this.
The entire household found it strange,
gathering to whisper about it.
The wife overheard some of this,
growing even more ashamed and angry,
and beat all the maids and servants.
She called for the concubine,
but the concubine was too injured to get up.
The wife thought she was faking,
went to her bed and beat her,
causing her to miscarry.
Wànshí, in a secluded spot,
wept sorrowfully to Mǎ.
Mǎ comforted and consoled him.
He called a servant to prepare a feast,
and as the night watch sounded twice,
he still did not let Wànshí return home.
The wife, in her chamber,
resented her husband for not returning,
and was seething with anger;
hearing the sound of the door being forced open,
she urgently called for a maid,
but the room door had already swung open.
A giant entered,
his shadow darkening the entire room,
his appearance fierce as a ghost.
Soon, several more men entered,
each holding a sharp blade.
The wife, terrified, was about to scream,
but the giant pressed a knife to her neck and said:
"Scream and I'll kill you!"
The wife hastily offered gold and silk to ransom her life.
The giant said:
"I am an envoy from the underworld,
I don't want money,
I only want the heart of this shrew!"
The wife grew even more frightened,
and knocked her head on the ground.
The giant then used his sharp blade to trace lines over her heart, counting as he went:
"For such-and-such a deed,
do you think you deserve death?"
And with each count, he made a mark.
Every act of cruelty and violence
was enumerated almost completely,
the blade tracing marks on her skin,
no fewer than several dozen.
Finally, he said,
"The concubine's child,
was also your family's descendant,
how could you bear to beat her until she miscarried?
This crime cannot be forgiven!"
He then ordered several men to bind her hands behind her back,
to cut open and examine the shrew's heart and intestines.
The wife kowtowed, begging for her life,
saying only that she knew she was wrong.
Suddenly, they heard the middle gate open and close,
and a voice said:
"Yáng Wànshí has arrived.
Since she has already repented,
we shall spare her life for now."
The figures scattered in confusion.
Not long after,
Wànshí entered,
and saw his wife naked and bound,
with knife marks crisscrossing her chest,
too many to count.
He untied her and asked what happened,
and upon learning the reason,
was greatly shocked,
secretly suspecting Mǎ.
The next day,
he told Mǎ about it.
Mǎ also acted surprised.
From then on, the wife's ferocity gradually subsided,
and for several months she did not utter a single harsh word.
Mǎ was overjoyed,
and said to Wànshí:
"To be honest with you,
please do not reveal this: I used a little trick to frighten her.
Now that you two are getting along well,
I shall take my leave for now."
And so he departed.
Every evening,
the wife would try to keep Wànshí by her side as a companion,
greeting him with laughter and warmth.
Wànshí had never experienced such joy in his life,
and now that he suddenly encountered it,
he felt restless and uneasy.
One night, the wife remembered the giant's appearance,
and trembled with fear.
Wànshí, wanting to please his wife,
subtly revealed that it was all a trick.
The wife immediately stood up,
relentlessly questioning him.
Wànshí realized he had misspoken,
but it was too late to take it back,
so he told her the truth.
The wife erupted in furious curses.
Wànshí, terrified,
knelt by the bed for a long time.
The wife ignored him,
and he pleaded until the third watch of the night.
The wife said:
"If you want my forgiveness,
you must let me trace knife marks on your chest as many times as I did,
only then will my anger subside."
She then got up and grabbed a kitchen knife.
Wànshí, terrified, fled,
with the wife chasing after him.
Dogs barked and chickens flapped,
and the entire household was awakened.
Wànzhōng did not know what was happening,
but he shielded his brother with his body.
The wife was still cursing wildly
when she suddenly saw the old man approaching.
Seeing his robe,
her anger flared even more fiercely;
she immediately tore the old man's clothes to shreds,
slapped his face, and pulled out his beard.
Wànzhōng, seeing this, grew furious,
picked up a stone, and struck the wife,
hitting her head,
and she fell dead.
Wànzhōng said:
"If my death can save my father and brother,
what regret do I have!"
He then threw himself into a well,
and by the time they rescued him, he was already dead.
After a while, the wife revived,
and upon hearing that Wànzhōng was dead,
her anger subsided.
After the funeral,
Wànzhōng's widow, attached to her child,
vowed not to remarry.
The wife cursed her and refused to give her food,
forcing her to remarry.
The orphaned child
was beaten morning and night.
Only after the rest of the family had finished eating
was he given cold leftovers.
After half a year,
the child grew emaciated,
barely clinging to life.
One day,
Mǎ suddenly arrived.
Wànshí instructed the family members,
"Don't tell my wife."
When Mǎ saw the old man still in tattered clothes as before,
he was greatly shocked;
hearing that Wànzhōng had died,
he stamped his feet in sorrow.
The son, hearing Mǎ had come,
came over to cling to him affectionately,
calling out "Uncle Mǎ" from afar.
Mǎ couldn't recognize him,
only after careful scrutiny did he realize who it was,
and exclaimed in surprise:
"Why has the child become so haggard!"
The old man then stammered out the whole story.
Mǎ angrily said to Wànshí:
"I said before that you were not a real man,
and indeed I wasn't wrong.
The two of you only have this one descendant,
if she kills him,
what will you do then?"
Wànshí said nothing,
only bowing his head submissively and weeping.
After sitting and talking for a while,
the wife already knew about it,
but didn't dare come out herself to drive the guest away,
instead she called Wànshí in,
and slapped him, ordering him to break off with Mǎ.
Wànshí came out with tears in his eyes,
the slap marks clearly visible.
Mǎ angrily said:
"If you can't assert your authority,
can't you at least divorce her?
She beats your father and killed your brother,
yet you endure it peacefully—
how can you call yourself a man!"
Wànshí stretched and yawned,
seeming somewhat moved.
Mǎ further provoked him:
"If she doesn't leave,
you must use force to compel her;
even if you kill her,
don't be afraid.
I have two or three close friends
who all hold important positions—
they will certainly do their utmost
to ensure there's no loss for you."
Wànshí agreed,
and strode off angrily,
rushing inside.
He happened to meet his wife,
who shouted at him:
"What are you doing?"
Wànshí turned pale with panic,
and kneeling on the ground said:
"Mr. Mǎ told me to divorce you."
The wife became even more furious,
looking around for a knife or stick.
Wànshí, frightened, retreated.
Mǎ spat at him:
"You really are beyond teaching!"
Then he opened his case,
took out a dose of medicine,
mixed it with water and gave it to Wànshí to drink,
saying:
"This is the 'Husband's Rebirth Powder.'
The reason I don't use it lightly
is because it can harm people.
But now there's no choice—
let's try it temporarily."
After drinking it,
a short while later,
Wànshí felt anger filling his chest,
as if a raging fire were burning inside him,
unbearable for even a moment.
He went straight to the inner chamber,
shouting like thunder.
Before his wife could question him,
Wànshí kicked her with his foot,
and she fell several feet away.
Then he clenched stones into fists
and pummeled her countless times,
until her body was almost covered with wounds,
yet she still cursed shrilly.
Wànshí drew a dagger from his waist,
and the wife cursed:
"Drawing a knife—
dare you kill me?"
Wànshí said nothing,
but cut a piece of flesh from her thigh,
as big as a palm,
and threw it on the ground.
Just as he was about to cut again,
the wife wailed pitifully, begging for mercy.
Wànshí ignored her
and cut another piece.
The family members, seeing Wànshí's ferocious madness,
gathered together
and with all their strength dragged him out.
Mǎ went to meet him,
grasping his arm to comfort him.
Wànshí's anger had not yet subsided,
and he repeatedly tried to rush back in,
but Mǎ stopped him.
After a while,
the medicine's effect gradually wore off,
and he became dejected as if having lost something.
Mǎ instructed him:
"Brother, don't lose heart.
The restoration of your masculine authority
depends on this one move.
The reason a wife becomes domineering
isn't something that happens overnight—
it develops gradually over time.
It's like dying yesterday and being reborn today;
you must wash away the old and renew yourself from now on.
If you lose heart again,
then nothing can be done."
He sent Wànshí in to check on her.
The wife trembled with fear in heart and limbs,
asking a maid to help her up,
intending to approach on her knees.
Wànshí stopped her,
and only then did she cease.
Coming out to tell Mr. Mǎ,
father and son congratulated each other.
Mǎ wanted to leave,
but father and son together urged him to stay.
Mǎ said:
"I happen to have a trip to the Eastern Sea,
so I'm just passing by.
When I return, we can meet again."
Over a month later,
the wife recovered,
and served her husband with the respect due a guest.
But after a long time, feeling she had exhausted her tricks like the donkey of Guìzhōu,
she gradually became familiar again,
then began to mock,
and gradually to curse;
not long after,
her old behavior fully returned.
The old man couldn't bear it,
and fled at night
to Hénán,
where he registered as a Taoist priest.
Wànshí also didn't dare to search for him.
Over a year later,
Mǎ came
and learned of the situation.
After angrily scolding them,
he immediately called the son over,
placed him on a donkey,
and drove it straight away.
From then on, all the villagers looked down on Wànshí.
When the education commissioner came on inspection,
he was expelled for misconduct.
Another four or five years later,
they suffered a fire,
and their house and belongings
were all reduced to ashes;
it spread to burn the neighbors' houses.
The villagers seized him and reported to the commandery,
where he was fined heavily.
Thus his family property gradually exhausted,
until he had no house left.
Nearby villages warned each other
not to give Wànshí lodging.
The Yǐn brothers,
angry at their sister's behavior,
also refused him completely.
Wànshí, now destitute,
pawned his concubine to a wealthy family
and traveled south with his wife.
When they reached the border of Hénán,
their travel funds were exhausted.
The wife refused to follow him further,
nagging her husband to let her remarry.
It happened there was a widowed butcher
who paid three hundred coins to take her.
Wànshí, alone,
begged for food in villages near and far from the city walls.
Once he came to a vermilion gate,
where the gatekeeper roughly refused to let him approach.
After a short while,
an official came out.
Wànshí knelt on the ground, sobbing.
The official looked at him carefully for a long time,
asked his name briefly,
then exclaimed in surprise:
"It's my uncle!
How have you become so poor?"
Wànshí examined him closely
and realized it was Xǐ'ér.
He couldn't help but weep loudly.
Following him inside,
he saw the hall gleaming with gold and jade.
In a short while,
the father came out supporting the boy,
and they faced each other, choking with grief.
Wàn Shí then recounted what had happened to him.
In the beginning,
Mǎ had brought Xǐ’ér here,
and after a few days,
he went out to find the old man Yáng,
so that grandfather and grandson could live together.
He also hired a teacher to instruct the boy.
At fifteen, the boy entered the county school,
and the following year he passed the provincial examination,
after which he was married.
Then Mǎ prepared to leave.
Grandfather and grandson wept and tried to keep him,
but Mǎ said,
"I am not human—
I am actually a fox immortal.
My companions on the path have been waiting for me for a long time."
With that, he departed.
When the Xiàolián told this story,
he could not help but feel sorrowful,
and remembering how he and his stepmother had both suffered cruel abuse in the past,
he was even more deeply moved.
So he used his carriage, horses, and funds to redeem Wáng Shì and bring her back.
Over a year later,
she gave birth to a son,
and he therefore regarded her as his principal wife.
Yǐn had been with the butcher for half a year,
and her wild, unruly temper was as before.
Her husband grew angry,
and with his butcher's knife he pierced her thigh,
threading it with a coarse rope,
and hung her from a beam,
then shouldered his meat and went out.
She screamed until her voice grew hoarse,
and only then did the neighbors find out.
They untied her and pulled out the rope;
with each tug, her cries of pain
shook the entire neighborhood.
From then on, whenever she saw the butcher coming,
her hair and bones would stand on end.
Later, though the wound on her leg healed,
broken bristles remained embedded in the flesh,
so she never walked properly again;
yet she still served day and night,
not daring to slack off in the slightest.
The butcher was violent and tyrannical,
and whenever he returned drunk,
he would beat and curse her without mercy.
Only then did she realize
that what she had inflicted on others in the past
was just like this.
One day,
when Madame Yáng and her stepmother went to burn incense at Pǔtuó Temple,
peasant women from nearby villages all came to pay their respects.
Yǐn stood among them, hesitant and not stepping forward.
Wáng Shì deliberately asked,
"Who is that?"
A servant came forward and replied,
"That is the butcher Zhāng's wife."
She then called her forward
to kowtow to the senior lady.
Wáng said with a smile,
"Since this woman is married to a butcher,
she should not lack for meat to eat—
why is she so thin and emaciated?"
Yǐn felt ashamed and resentful,
and upon returning home, she tried to hang herself,
but the rope was too weak and she did not die.
The butcher despised her even more.
Over a year later,
the butcher died.
On the road, she met Wàn Shí,
and from a distance,
she approached on her knees,
tears streaming down like ropes.
Wàn Shí was hindered by his servants,
and they did not exchange a single word.
He returned and told his nephew,
hoping to arrange for her return,
but his nephew firmly refused.
The woman was scorned and rejected by the villagers,
and for a long time she had nowhere to go,
so she joined a group of beggars for food.
Wàn Shí would still occasionally visit Yǐn in a deserted temple,
but his nephew considered this a disgrace
and secretly instructed the beggars to harass and humiliate her,
so he stopped going.
I do not know how this matter ultimately ended;
the last few lines
were written by Bì Gōngquán.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Fear of one's wife
is a common affliction throughout the world.
Yet who could have imagined that between heaven and earth
there would be a man like Yáng Láng? Is this not an anomaly?
I once composed a sequel to the 'Scripture of Wonderful Sounds,'
which I have appended here for a bit of amusement:
'I humbly submit that the Way of Heaven transforms and gives birth to all things,
heavily relying on the completion by the Earth.
A man's ambition lies in the four directions,
yet he especially requires assistance from within.
Sharing sweetness but enduring bitterness alone,
toiling through ten months of groaning;
moving from wet to dry,
suffering through three years of frowning and smiling.
This is why, contemplating the ancestral temple, one is moved to thought,
and thus a gentleman seeks a spouse;
gazing at the well and mortar, one cherishes memories,
and thus the ancients spoke of love like fish and water.
But now the banners of the feminine teaching are daily raised,
and the dignity of the masculine principle is utterly lost.
At first, the sound of disrespect
may be met with great retaliation and small repayment;
later, the respect due to a guest
ends up going forth without return.
Merely because of deep affection for children,
heroes are made to lose their spirit.
When a night demon sits upon the bed,
even a Vajra must lower his brows;
when poisonous smoke rises from the cauldron,
even an iron man cannot keep his neck stiff.
The companion of the autumn pounding block, so pitiable,
does not pound clothes on moonlit nights;
the claws of Má Gū, capable of scratching,
lightly try the lotus-like face.
Receiving a little and fleeing greatly,
truly like Mèng Mǔ throwing her shuttle;
the wife sings and the husband follows,
wishing instead to establish rites like Zhōu Pó.
Dancing and leaping in a frenzy,
stopping to watch the passersby filling the road;
chattering and screeching,
scattering a flock of delicate birds.
How dreadful!
Crying out to heaven and earth,
suddenly disheveling hair before the silver bed.
How ugly!
Rolling eyes and shaking head,
shamelessly wishing to hang oneself by a rope around the jade neck.
At such a time: underground, many gallbladders are already shattered,
beyond the heavens, souls are further startled.
Běi Gōng Yǒu would not necessarily not flee,
Mèng Shīshě—how could he be without fear?
The general's spirit, like thunder and lightning,
once entering the central courtyard,
immediately returns to the land of nothingness;
the great one's face, like ice and frost,
upon reaching the bedroom door,
creates a place not to be inquired about.
Is it truly the aura of powder and rouge,
imposing without force?
How then can a filthy body
tremble without cold?
Still understandable: a demon maiden with raised hair comes under the moon,
why not prostrate oneself and convert?
Most unjust: a Hārītī with disheveled head comes to the human world,
and still demands incense and flowers as offerings.
Hearing the roar of an angry lion,
both nostrils point to the sky;
hearing the crow of a hen,
the five limbs prostrate to the ground.
Dēngtúzǐ, licentious and forgetting ugliness,
the "Huíbō" lyrics, pitiful yet mocking.
If one were the son-in-law of Fényáng,
immediately attaining honor and glory,
flattering one's beloved would have good reason;
if one were attached to the family of Wàihuáng,
unavoidably enslaved,
what would one seek by bowing and scraping?
That poor ghost, feeling himself disgraced,
allows trees to be cut and flowers destroyed,
only seeking tolerance from the shrew;
if the God of Money could be said to have power,
yet even he offends the scales and violates rules,
unable to seek help from Brother Square.
Is it to bind the wanderer's heart
only by this bird's path?
Or to dissipate the hegemon's spirit
by relying on this vast chasm?
Yet to die in the same grave,
to live under the same quilt,
did it ever teach one to chant
"white head"?
And morning clouds,
evening rain,
always wishing to独占巫山.
How hateful
"the pond water is clear,"
vainly striking the red ivory and jade clappers;
pitying your concubine's fate is thin,
alone enduring the cold watches of the long night.
The cicada sheds its shell, the egret treads the shore,
rejoicing that the Black Dragon is just asleep;
the calf cart with a drooping tail,
regretting that the inferior horse does not run.
The person sharing the couch,
beaten away, only then known to be the uncle;
the guest long tied before the bed,
dragged away, already transformed into a sheep.
What is urgently needed lasts but a moment,
the flow of poison has no end.
Buying laughter and wrapping the head,
thus creating one's own calamity,
Tàijiǎ would surely say it is hard to avoid;
bowing head and pasting ears,
receiving unwarranted punishment,
Lǐ Yáng also said it is not permissible.
The sour wind, biting cold,
blows away the spring of the ornate chamber;
the sea of vinegar, vast and wide,
drowns the moon of the Blue Bridge.
Or again, a grand gathering suddenly encountered,
good friends immediately seated,
a jug of wine hidden and not set out,
and from the room comes a letter expelling guests;
old friends estranged and not included,
thus from myself broadens the discourse of severing ties.
Even more, wild geese shadows flying apart,
tears vainly staining the thorn tree;
phoenix glue sought again,
change then arises from the reed flowers.
In ancient times, drinking at Yángchéng,
in the whole hall there were only brothers;
blowing the yuè at Shāngzǐ,
past seventy years, still without wife and family.
The ancients in this
had hidden pain.
Alas!
A hundred-year mandarin duck pair,
ends up becoming an attached bone ulcer;
five liǎng of deer skin,
perhaps buys the pain of stripping the bed.
One with a beard like a halberd is like this,
who with a gallbladder like a peck?
Truly, one dares not cut off the source of calamity under the horse's manger,
and who can go to the silkworm chamber to sever the root of evil?
The娘子军running rampant in its violence,
bitterly, there is no cure for jealousy;
the胭脂虎devouring all living beings,
fortunately, there is a raft for crossing the delusion.
Heavenly incense at night's banquet,
fully clarifies the waves of the boiling cauldron;
flower rain flying in the morning,
entirely extinguishes the fire of the sword-wheel.
In the realm of ultimate joy,
colorful wings roost in pairs;
from the tip of the long tongue,
blue lotuses bloom in pairs.
Pulling out suffering from the land of Upāsikā,
establishing a place of enlightenment on the banks of the river of love.
Ah!
May these few chapters of palm-leaf scripture
be sprinkled as a drop of willow water!'"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Zhāng Jìzì of Yùnchéng,
lying down but not asleep,
suddenly saw brightness filling the room.
Startled, he looked:
a ghost holding a brush stood,
like the form of Kuíxīng.
He hurriedly rose and bowed in reverence.
The light also soon vanished.
From this, he became self-assured,
thinking it a portent of coming first in the examinations.
Later, he actually drifted without success;
his family also declined,
bone and flesh died one after another,
only he alone remained alive.
That Kuíxīng—
why did it bring not fortune but calamity?
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Shè Dàyǒu,
styled Jūnshí,
was a native of Yángxiàn in Hànzhōng.
As a military graduate, he served under Zǔ Shùshùn.
Zǔ treated him generously,
and he was repeatedly promoted,
rising to the rank of commander under the false Zhōu regime.
Later, realizing the general situation was lost,
he secretly led troops against Zǔ.
Zǔ resisted and injured his hand,
whereupon he was captured and bound.
Shè then surrendered to Governor Cài.
Upon reaching the capital,
he dreamed of going to the underworld,
where the King of Hell was angered by his lack of righteousness.
The king ordered a ghost to pour boiling water on his feet.
Upon waking,
his feet were unbearably painful.
Later they swelled and festered,
until all his toes fell off.
He was further afflicted with malaria.
He would often cry out:
"I have truly betrayed righteousness!"
And so he died.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Serving a false court naturally does not merit discussion of loyalty;
however, for a man of state or a commoner,
to know how to repay kindness,
is how the worthy and heroic should regard themselves.
This truly can serve as a warning to all subjects of the realm who harbor duplicity."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In the year Guǐhài,
I was residing in the Chuòrán Hall of Provincial Governor Bì.
His family's gardens and trees were most flourishing,
and in leisure moments I would follow the Governor, staff in hand,
able to indulge in leisurely strolls and appreciation.
One day,
having returned from gazing afar,
utterly weary and thinking of sleep,
I removed my shoes and ascended the bed.
I dreamed of two young ladies, dressed in dazzling finery,
who approached and requested:
"We have a matter to entrust to you,
and venture to trouble your esteemed presence."
Startled, I rose and asked:
"Who summons me to an audience?"
They replied:
"It is none other than Consort Jiàng."
Vaguely, not understanding what was meant,
I hastily followed them away.
Soon I beheld halls and pavilions,
towering to touch the Milky Way.
Below were stone steps,
ascending layer upon layer;
after climbing roughly over a hundred steps,
I finally reached the summit.
I saw vermilion gates standing wide open,
and two or three more beautiful women
hurried inside to announce the guest.
Shortly,
arriving outside a hall,
with golden hooks and azure blinds,
its brilliance dazzled the eyes.
A woman from within descended the steps to come out,
her jade pendants tinkling crisply,
her appearance like that of a noble consort.
Just as I was about to bow in greeting,
the Consort spoke first:
"Having respectfully troubled you, sir,
it is proper that I first express thanks."
She called her attendants to lay felt mats on the ground,
as if about to perform a formal salute.
I was so alarmed and uneasy I knew not where to stand,
and thus addressed her:
"A humble, lowly man from the wilds,
to have received the undeserved honor of your summons,
already brings me more glory than I deserve.
How much less dare I presume to meet you as an equal,
which would only increase my offense
and diminish my fortune!"
The Consort ordered the mats removed and a banquet set,
and we sat facing each other across the feast.
After several rounds of wine,
I declined, saying:
"Your servant becomes drunk after little wine,
and fears breaching etiquette.
What are your instructions?
I beg you to dispel my doubts."
The Consort did not speak,
but urged me to drink with a large cup.
I repeatedly requested her command.
Then she said:
"I, your handmaid,
am the goddess of flowers.
My whole family is delicate and frail,
dwelling here for shelter.
We have repeatedly suffered from that maid of the Feng family,
who wantonly destroys us.
Now we wish to stake everything on one final battle,
and trouble you, sir, to draft a proclamation of war for us."
I rose in trepidation and replied:
"Your servant's learning is shallow and his writing unrefined;
I fear I may fail this weighty commission.
But having received your gracious command,
how dare I not exhaust the utmost of my humble sincerity?"
The Consort was pleased,
and immediately bestowed brush and paper in the hall.
The several lovely ladies wiped the table and dusted the seat,
ground the ink and moistened the brush.
Another, a young maiden with hanging hair,
folded paper to serve as a pad,
and placed it beneath my wrist.
I had barely written a line or two,
when two or three of them crowded behind my back to peek.
I am normally slow-witted,
but at that moment felt my thoughts gushing forth like a spring.
After a short while,
the draft was completed.
They eagerly snatched it away
and presented it, opened, to Consort Jiàng.
The Consitor unrolled and read it through once,
and remarked that it was quite without flaw.
Then she escorted me back.
Waking, I remembered it;
the events were vivid and clear.
But more than half the wording of the proclamation was forgotten,
so I supplemented it to completion:
"According to the Feng family records: It is by nature wild and unrestrained,
with a heart full of jealousy and envy.
It uses its talents to aid evil,
envying others to the marrow;
it shoots at people from the shadows,
delighting in slander like the sand-spitting creature.
In ancient times, Emperor Yú was bewitched by its fox-like charms,
and even Yīng and Huáng were insufficient to dispel his worries;
instead, he relied on it to vent his frustrations.
King Chǔ was ensnared by its seductions,
and even the worthiest talents could not satisfy him;
only by obtaining it could he feel triumphant.
The hero of Pèi,
as clouds flew, longed for fierce warriors;
the Son of Heaven at Màolíng,
as autumn deepened, yearned for a beautiful woman.
From then on, it grew increasingly arrogant, relying on favor,
and thus became unrestrained and without restraint.
It howled through ten thousand crevices,
shattering jade-like sounds in the royal palace;
it surged at midnight,
stirring cold whispers among autumn trees.
Suddenly, in the depths of mountain forests,
it borrowed the tiger's might;
at times, amidst the Yànyù Duī,
it stirred the river's waves.
Moreover,
curtain hooks frequently trembled,
emitting clear melodies from lofty pavilions;
eaves' iron suddenly clanged,
shattering the secluded dreams of parted lovers.
Seeking beneath curtains and descending to couches,
it became an uninvited guest in the inner chambers;
pushing open doors and ascending halls,
it turned into a book-flipping visitor.
Without ever having met in life,
it boldly entered through open doors;
had it not been for the skirt left on the palm,
it would have nearly swept the consort away.
It spewed rainbow threads into the azure sky,
daring to form barriers with the moon;
it stirred willow waves in the green countryside,
falsely claiming to send messages for flowers.
Those who wrote of returning to the fields,
having just begun their journey home,
felt their robes of ivy flutter lightly;
those who ascended high towers,
at the peak of their joy,
had their cornelian hats gently blown off.
Duckweed and rushes rolled up and down,
as the autumn whirlwinds swept through the sky;
the sound of zithers rose to the clouds,
snapping the hundred-foot strings of mandarin ducks.
Without awaiting the Empress Dowager's summons,
it hastened the blooming of flowers;
before the guests' ties were undone,
it extinguished the lamps.
At its worst, it raised dust and scattered soil,
leveling Lǐ Hè's mountains;
it called for rain and summoned clouds,
tearing apart Dù Líng's house.
Féngyí rose to beat the drums,
and young maidens advanced to play their flutes;
as it surged forth,
even the grass bowed low;
as it roared and rushed,
tiles threatened to take flight.
Before unleashing its power to churn the waters,
river dolphins surfaced to pay homage;
suddenly displaying its sky-obscuring might,
geese could not form their lines in the written sky.
It aided the swift sails at Mǎdāng,
for which it had its purposes;
but why did it tug at the emerald curtains of the Jade Terrace?
As for the sea bird with its spirit,
it still sought refuge by the gates of Lǔ.
If only travelers could be kept safe,
we would call Yóuláng back.
In ancient times, there were wise and heroic men
who rode it to break through ten thousand miles;
in this age, how many are there among the lofty scholars
who can harness it for travel?
Riding the mad clouds of the artillery bull,
it grew arrogant as Yèláng;
relying on the rebellious spirit of the greedy wolf,
it presumptuously honored Hé Bó as supreme.
Sisters and maidens all suffered its devastation,
and entire clans were trampled under its feet.
Blushing red and startling green,
how endless was the concealment and withering?
Twisting willows and wailing branches,
how boundless was the desolation?
Rain fell upon the Golden Valley,
woven into mats for resting guests;
dew chilled the Huálín Garden,
turning into floss that clings to mud.
Burying fragrance and interring jade,
remnants of makeup flew away as they were removed;
vermilion pavilions and carved railings,
scattered ornaments fell in disarray.
Diminishing spring's radiance in a single day,
ten thousand points drifted in sorrow;
seeking fading reds east and west,
the fifth watch was not a time for misplaced regret.
The graceful maiden of Jiānghàn,
her bow-shaped shoes idly trod the spring garden;
the lonely lady of the king's tower,
her pearl-adorned bridle vainly neighed amid fragrant grass.
At this time: those grieving for spring harbored emotions hard to bear,
and seekers of beauty sang songs of helplessness.
Then, with head held high and spirits soaring,
it unleashed groundless vigor;
destroying the covered and shaking the fallen,
it stirred ceaseless, tottering motion.
Alas, though green trees remained,
the rustling leaves fell of their own accord around the walls;
long had the vermilion banners not been raised,
and who pitied the delicate ones shedding tears?
Falling into privies or clinging to fences,
their fragrant souls perished in a single day;
blooming in the morning and withering by evening,
in what year would they escape such cruelty?
Lamenting how easily silken robes opened,
empty curses were heard at midnight;
accusing the wild lord of rampant tyranny,
yet no memorial reached the heavenly court.
We proclaim to our fragrant neighbors:
let us learn to form battalions like the moth-eyebrowed ones;
all who share our breath,
rise together as soldiers of grass and trees.
Do not say the willow and the reed are powerless,
but let the fences and hedges have resolve.
Behold the orioles and swallows, companions in waves,
publicly avenging the theft of love;
join with butterfly friends and bee allies,
to swear oaths of shared heart.
With orchid oars and cassia sculls,
we can wage war at Kūnmíng;
under mulberry canopies and with willow pushes,
we shall review troops in the imperial garden.
The recluse of the eastern fence,
shall also emerge from his thatched hut;
the great tree general,
should harbor righteous indignation.
Quell its arrogance,
wash away the grievances of a thousand years of powdered faces;
annihilate its tyranny,
Héjiān was a scholar.
In his threshing ground, wheat sheaves were piled up like a hill.
His family took them daily for firewood,
and hollowed it out.
A fox lived inside,
often appearing to the master of the house,
an old man.
One day,
he invited the master for a drink,
ushering the scholar into the cave.
The scholar hesitated,
but after being urged, he entered.
Inside were splendid halls and rooms.
Once seated,
fragrant tea and wine were served.
But the daylight was dim,
making it impossible to distinguish noon from dusk.
After the feast, he emerged,
and the scenery had vanished completely.
The old man went out every night and returned early in the morning,
and no one could trace his whereabouts.
When asked,
he said friends had invited him for drinks.
The scholar asked to go along,
but the old man refused;
after persistent pleading,
the old man finally agreed.
He took the scholar’s arm,
and they sped like riding the wind.
In the time it takes to cook millet,
they reached a city.
Entering a tavern,
they saw many guests seated,
drinking noisily in groups.
The old man led the scholar upstairs.
Looking down at the drinkers,
their tables, trays, and meals
could be counted on one’s fingers.
The old man went downstairs,
freely taking wine and fruits from the tables,
and brought them to the scholar.
None of the feasting guests seemed to notice.
After a while,
the scholar saw a man in red robes with golden oranges placed before him,
and asked the old man to fetch them.
The old man said:
"This is an upright man,
we cannot approach him."
The scholar thought to himself: The fox befriends me,
thinking I am wicked.
From now on,
I must be upright!
As soon as this thought occurred,
he felt his body move involuntarily,
and he fell dizzyingly downstairs.
The drinkers were greatly alarmed,
shouting about a monster.
The scholar looked up,
and realized he was not upstairs,
but on a beam.
He told everyone the truth.
They examined the situation and found it true,
gave him gifts, and sent him off.
When asked where he was,
it was Yútái,
a thousand li away from Héjiān.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Liáng Yǒucái,
originally from Jìn,
drifted to Jì,
and made a living as a small peddler.
He had no wife, children, or land.
He followed villagers to climb Dài.
Dài,
in the fourth month,
was crowded with pilgrims.
There were also upāsikās and upāsakas,
leading groups of men numbering in the hundreds,
kneeling mixed before the deity’s altar,
measuring time by the burning of incense sticks,
called
"kneeling incense."
Cái saw among the crowd a young woman,
seventeen or eighteen years old and beautiful,
and took a liking to her.
Pretending to be a pilgrim,
he knelt near the young woman;
feigning exhaustion in his knees,
he deliberately rested his hand on her foot.
The woman turned her head as if annoyed,
and moved away on her knees.
Cái again moved closer on his knees;
after a short while,
he touched her again.
The woman noticed,
stood up abruptly,
stopped kneeling,
and left through the door.
Cái also stood up,
and followed her out,
tracking her footsteps,
but did not know where she went.
Feeling hopeless,
he walked dejectedly.
On the road, he saw the young woman with an old woman,
who seemed to be her mother.
Cái hurried over.
The old woman and the young woman walked while talking.
The old woman said:
"You were able to pay respects to the goddess,
that’s wonderful!
You have no younger siblings,
but with the goddess’s unseen protection,
you will find a good husband.
As long as he is filial and respectful,
he doesn’t have to be a noble son or a wealthy prince."
Cái secretly delighted,
and gradually engaged the old woman in conversation.
The old woman said her surname was Yún,
her daughter’s name was Cuìxiān,
and she was her child.
Their home was forty li west of the mountain.
Cái said:
"The mountain path is rough,
with mother so frail,
and sister so delicate,
how can you make it there?"
She replied:
"It’s already late,
we plan to stay at her uncle’s house for the night."
Cái said:
"You just mentioned finding a husband,
not minding poverty,
nor despising low status.
I am unmarried,
do I meet mother’s approval?"
The old woman asked her daughter,
but the girl did not respond.
The old woman asked several times,
and the girl said:
"He lacks fortune,
and is dissolute and immoral,
fickle and frivolous at heart,
easily changing his mind.
I cannot be the wife of such a frivolous man."
Cái heard this,
and earnestly professed his honesty,
swearing solemn oaths.
The old woman was pleased,
and agreed to it.
The girl was unhappy,
but could only fume.
Her mother insisted and soothed her.
Cái was attentive,
paid from his own pocket,
hired two mountain sedan chairs,
and carried the old woman and the girl.
