He followed on foot,
like a servant.
At narrow passes,
he warned the carriers not to jolt or shake them,
showing great care.
Soon they reached the village house,
and he was invited into the uncle’s home.
The uncle came out, an old man,
the aunt came out, an old woman.
They were called elder brother and sister-in-law by Yún.
They said:
"Cái is our son-in-law.
Today is auspicious,
no need to choose another day,
let it be tonight."
The uncle was also pleased,
and brought out wine and food to entertain Cái.
Afterwards,
Cuìxiān came out in fine attire,
and they prepared the bed for sleep.
The girl said:
"I knew you were not righteous,
but forced by my mother’s command,
I reluctantly followed along.
If you are a decent man,
we need not worry about living together."
Cái meekly listened and accepted.
The next morning, rising early,
the mother said to Cái:
"You should go ahead first,
I will bring my daughter later."
Cái had just returned home
and was sweeping the doorway
when the old woman indeed brought the girl to him.
Upon entering and looking around the room,
she found it completely empty
and said:
"How can you support yourself like this?
I'll go back quickly
and help you a little with your hardships."
She then left.
The next day,
several men and women
each carrying clothing, food, and utensils
filled the entire room with them.
Without eating, they all left,
leaving only one maidservant behind.
From then on, Cái lived in comfort and warmth,
but he spent his days inviting local ruffians to drink and gamble,
gradually stealing the girl's hairpins and earrings to fund his gambling.
The girl tried to persuade him,
but he wouldn't listen;
she grew quite impatient with him
and strictly guarded her boxes and cases,
as if defending against bandits.
One day,
gambling companions knocked on the door to visit Cái,
and upon catching sight of the girl,
they were utterly astonished.
They jokingly said to Cái:
"You are immensely wealthy;
why worry about poverty?"
Cái asked the reason,
and they replied:
"Earlier, we saw your wife;
she is truly a fairy maiden.
She is not at all suited to your family's circumstances.
If you sell her as a concubine,
you could get a hundred taels of gold;
if as a courtesan,
you could get a thousand.
With a thousand gold in the house,
how could you lack funds for drinking and gambling?"
Cái said nothing,
but in his heart, he agreed.
Upon returning home,
he often sighed to the girl,
constantly saying they were too poor to get by.
The girl paid no attention,
so Cái frequently banged the table,
threw down spoons and chopsticks,
cursed the maidservant,
and put on all sorts of acts.
One evening,
the girl bought wine and drank with him.
Suddenly, she said:
"Husband, because of poverty,
you worry day and night.
I cannot ward off poverty
or share your worries;
how can I not feel ashamed?
But I have no valuables;
only this maidservant remains.
If we sell her,
it could slightly aid our livelihood."
Cái shook his head and said:
"How much could she be worth!"
After drinking a little more,
the girl said:
"What have I not done for you, husband?
But my strength is exhausted.
Considering we are so poor,
even if I followed you to death,
it would only mean sharing a lifetime of hardship.
What chance is there for prosperity?
It would be better to sell me to a wealthy family,
benefiting both parties,
and the price might be higher than for a maidservant."
Cái pretended to be shocked and said:
"How could it come to this!"
The girl insisted,
her expression serious.
Cái happily said:
"Let me think it over."
He then contacted a powerful eunuch
to sell her into a music registry.
The eunuch personally visited Cái,
and upon seeing the girl, was greatly pleased.
Fearing he might not get her immediately,
he drew up a contract for eight hundred strings of cash,
and the matter was nearly settled.
The girl said:
"My mother often worried
about my husband's family being poor.
Now that our ties are severed,
I will briefly return to visit her;
and since you and I are parting,
how can we not inform my mother?"
Cái feared her mother would object.
The girl said:
"I am doing this willingly;
I guarantee there will be no mistakes."
Cái agreed.
Approaching midnight,
they finally arrived at her mother's home.
Knocking on the gate,
they saw splendid buildings and pavilions,
with maids and servants bustling about.
Though Cái had lived with the girl,
he had often asked to visit her mother,
but she always stopped him,
so in over a year as a son-in-law,
he had never once been to his wife's family home.
Now he was greatly astonished,
and because her family was so wealthy,
he feared they would not tolerate him selling her as a courtesan.
The girl led Cái upstairs.
Her mother asked in surprise:
"Why have you two come?"
The girl said resentfully:
"I always said he was unrighteous;
now it's proven true."
She then took two ingots of gold from under her clothes,
placed them on the table,
and said:
"Fortunately, the scoundrel didn't swindle them away;
now I return them to you, Mother."
Her mother asked in shock for the reason.
The girl said:
"He was going to sell me,
so hiding the gold was useless."
Pointing at Cái, she scolded:
"You wolf-rat!
In the past, carrying a shoulder pole,
your face was covered in dust like a ghost.
When you first approached me,
you reeked of sweat,
your skin grime seemed about to crumble,
and the calluses on your hands and feet were an inch thick,
making people disgusted all night.
Since I came to your home,
you sat comfortably and ate your fill,
and only then did your ghostly skin shed.
With Mother here,
am I lying?"
Cái hung his head,
not daring to utter a sound.
The girl continued:
"Though I lack stunning beauty
and am unworthy of serving nobles,
for a man like you,
I thought we were well-matched.
What wrong did I do
that you showed not a trace of marital affection?
Couldn't I have built mansions and bought fertile land?
But considering your fickle, shallow bones and beggarly appearance,
you were never a lifelong partner!"
As she spoke,
maids and old women linked arms,
slowly surrounding him.
Hearing the girl's accusations,
they all spat and cursed,
saying together:
"Better to kill him;
why say more?"
Cái was terrified;
he prostrated himself on the ground,
only saying he knew he was wrong.
The girl said angrily:
"Selling one's wife is already a great evil,
but that's not the worst of it;
how could you bear to swindle your own bedmate into becoming a prostitute!"
Before she finished speaking,
everyone's eyes blazed with anger,
and they all took sharp hairpins
and scissors to stab his ribs and thighs.
Cái wailed pitifully, begging for his life.
The girl stopped them,
saying:
"Release him for now.
Though he is heartless,
I cannot bear to see him trembling in fear."
She then led everyone downstairs.
He had just sat down to listen for a while when
the voices and sounds all fell silent,
and he thought of slipping away unnoticed.
Suddenly, looking up,
he saw the Milky Way;
the east was already bright,
and the wilderness stretched vast and gray.
The lamp also soon went out.
There was no house or building at all;
he was sitting on the face of a sheer cliff.
Looking down into a bottomless chasm,
he was terrified,
fearing he would fall.
As he shifted his body slightly,
with a crash,
the rock beneath him crumbled and fell.
Halfway down the cliff was a withered tree,
and he caught on it,
preventing his fall.
His belly rested on the withered trunk,
but his hands and feet found no hold.
Looking down into the boundless depths,
he had no idea how many fathoms deep it was.
Not daring to turn or move,
he screamed in terror until his voice grew hoarse,
his whole body swelling,
and his eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and strength all exhausted.
As the sun gradually rose higher,
woodcutters finally saw him from afar;
they soon brought ropes,
lowered themselves down,
and brought him up to the cliff top,
where he was nearly dead.
They carried him back to his home.
When he arrived, the door was wide open,
and the house was desolate like a ruined temple.
The bed, chests, and various utensils were all gone,
only a rope-bed and a broken table remained—
these were old items from his own home,
scattered but still there.
He lay down in despair.
When hungry,
he begged for food from the neighbors once a day.
Later, the swelling festered into sores.
The villagers despised his conduct,
and all spurned him.
Cái had no other plan,
so he sold the house and lived in a cave,
begging on the roads,
always carrying a knife with him.
Some advised him to trade the knife for food;
Cái refused,
saying:
"Living in the wild, I need it to guard against tigers and wolves,
for self-defense."
Later, on the road, he met the man who had previously urged him to sell his wife.
Approaching him with pitiful words,
he suddenly drew his knife and stabbed him to death,
and was thus arrested.
The officials learned the full circumstances,
and could not bear to treat him cruelly,
so they imprisoned him,
and he soon died emaciated.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"To obtain a beauty like distant mountains and lotus blossoms,
and share a humble home with her—
is that any easier than becoming a king facing south?
If one is oneself inhuman,
and then resents meeting wicked friends—
therefore, those who befriend others must know to be cautious.
Whenever a dissolute person lures another into debauchery and gambling,
leading them into all manner of unrighteous acts,
even if the affair does not come to light,
though the victim may not resent it, they will feel no gratitude either.
By the time one has no jacket for the body,
and the wife has no trousers,
pointed at by a thousand people,
even without illness, one will be near death.
Thoughts of poverty and ruin
constantly linger in the heart; hatred for poverty and ruin
constantly gnaws at the teeth.
In the quiet night, wrapped in coarse cloth,
one tosses and turns, unable to sleep.
Only then does one clearly recall the time before the fall,
clearly recall the time just before the fall,
and clearly recall the causes that led to the fall,
and thus also the person who initiated the events leading to the fall.
Reaching this point,
the weak rise,
wrapping themselves in quilts to sit and curse;
the strong endure the cold, strip naked,
light a torch to search for a knife,
and whet it with a swishing sound,
not waiting for the night to end.
Thus, to guide others with goodness
is like giving them olives;
to lure others with evil
is like offering them tainted dried meat.
The listener should certainly reflect,
but should the speaker not also fear!"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
In the custom of Jìzhōu: When someone among the people falls ill,
the womenfolk divine through spirit mediums.
They hire an old shamaness to strike an iron ring and a single-sided drum,
swaying and posturing,
called
"Jumping the Spirits."
And this custom is especially prevalent in the capital.
Young women from respectable families
often perform it themselves.
In the hall, meat is placed on the table,
wine in the basin,
arranged abundantly on the altar.
Huge candles are lit,
bright as day.
The woman ties on a short skirt,
bends one leg,
performing the
"Shāngyáng Dance."
Two people hold her arms,
supporting her left and right.
The woman chatters incessantly in a琐絮 manner,
seeming to sing,
and also seeming to pray;
the words vary in number and length,
without fixed rhythm but with a melodic tone.
Several drums in the room are beaten chaotically like thunder,
their booming pounding the ears.
The woman's lips open and close,
mixed with the drum sounds,
making it hard to distinguish clearly.
Then her head droops,
her eyes slant sideways: she stands entirely supported by others,
and would fall if not held.
Suddenly she stretches her neck and leaps mightily,
rising over a foot off the ground.
The various women in the room,
with solemn awe, look at each other in surprise and say:
"The ancestors have come to eat."
Then with one puff,
they blow out the lamp,
and inside and out is plunged into darkness.
People stand in the dark holding their breath,
not daring to exchange a single word;
even if they spoke, they could not be heard,
for the drumming is too chaotic.
After the time of a meal,
hearing the woman sharply call out the childhood names of the parents-in-law, husband, and sisters-in-law,
they finally relight the candles together,
and bowing, ask about fortunes and misfortunes.
Looking at the wine vessel, the basin, and the table,
they find them all empty again.
They observe the woman's expression,
watching for signs of anger or pleasure.
Reverently, they surround her with questions,
and she answers like an echo.
If among them someone harbors silent criticism,
the spirit already knows,
and will point out, "So-and-so is sneering at me,
showing great disrespect;
I will strip off your trousers."
The critic then finds herself,
already completely naked,
and her trousers are often found hanging on a tree outside the door.
Mǎnzhōu women
serve the spirits with even greater devotion.
At the slightest doubt,
they must seek a decision through this.
Dressed in solemn attire at the time,
riding a fake tiger or fake horse,
holding a long weapon,
they dance on the couch,
called
"Jumping the Tiger Spirit."
The horse and tiger postures are made fiercely angry,
and the possessed person's voice is rough and crude.
Some say it is Guān Yǔ, Zhāng Fēi, or Xuántán,
not under a single title.
Their imposing aura is stern and chilling,
especially able to terrify people.
If a man peeps through a hole in the window,
he is often pierced through the window by the long weapon, his hat knocked off,
and pulled inside.
All the women of the household, whether mothers-in-law, wives, sisters, or sisters-in-law,
stand solemnly and cautiously,
in a goose-file line,
with no divergent thoughts,
and no slack posture.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Shā Huízǐ had mastered the Iron Shirt and Great Strength techniques.
He could harden his fingers,
and with a forceful chop,
sever
an ox’s neck;
thrusting horizontally,
he could pierce through an ox’s belly.
Once, at the home of Young Master Péng Sān,
they suspended a wooden beam in the air,
had two strong servants push it away with all their might,
then suddenly reversed its direction;
Shā bared his abdomen to receive the beam,
and with a loud bang,
the beam was sent flying far away.
He also exposed his private parts on a stone,
and had someone strike them forcefully with a wooden club,
suffering not the slightest injury.
However, he feared blades.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Chá Yīkuí
was from Zhèjiāng.
While drinking at a country temple during the Qingmíng Festival,
he saw an ancient bell in front of the hall,
larger than two stone jars;
yet the traces of earth and handprints on its top and bottom
were smooth and fresh,
which puzzled him.
Peering underneath,
he saw a bamboo basket that could hold about eight shēng,
but did not know what was stored inside.
He had several men grasp the bell’s handles,
and they strained to lift it,
but it did not budge in the slightest.
He was even more astonished.
So he sat drinking, waiting for the person involved.
Not long after,
a beggar entered,
carrying the dried provisions he had obtained,
and piled them beneath the bell.
Then, with one hand he lifted the bell,
and with the other scooped the food into the basket: he went back and forth several times,
until it was all inside.
After finishing,
he closed the bell again,
and left.
After a while, he returned,
reached in to take food and eat.
After eating, he reached in again,
as lightly as opening a box.
Everyone present was utterly amazed.
Chá asked:
“Why does a man like you go begging?”
He replied:
“I eat too much,
and no one will hire me.”
Seeing his strength,
Chá urged him to join the army.
The beggar looked distressed, worried he had no means to do so.
Chá then took him home and fed him;
he calculated his food intake.
It was roughly five or six times that of an ordinary person.
He gave him new clothes and shoes,
and also presented him with fifty taels of gold for his journey.
More than ten years later,
Chá’s nephew was serving as a magistrate in Mǐn,
when a certain General Wú Liùyī
suddenly came to pay a visit.
During their cordial conversation,
he asked,
“What relation is Yīkuí to you?”
The nephew replied:
“He is my uncle.
Where did you become acquainted with the general?”
He said:
“He is my teacher.
After ten years apart,
I miss him greatly.
I would trouble you to convey my invitation for him to visit.”
The nephew casually agreed.
He thought to himself: My uncle is a renowned scholar; how could he have a military disciple?
When Yīkuí arrived,
he told him about it.
Yīkuí was utterly unable to recall.
But because the general’s inquiry was so earnest,
he immediately ordered a servant and horse,
and sent his card to the gate.
The general hurried out,
greeting him outside the main gate.
Looking at him,
Chá had no recollection of ever meeting him.
Secretly suspecting the general had made a mistake,
yet the general bowed even more humbly and respectfully.
Ushering the guest inside,
he opened three or four inner gates deeply,
when suddenly he saw women coming and going,
and realized this was the private residence.
He halted his steps and stood still.
The general bowed to him again,
and shortly after, they ascended the hall,
where those rolling up the curtains
and moving the seats
were all young maidens.
Once seated,
just as he was about to begin asking questions,
the general gave a slight nod of his chin,
and a maiden brought forth court robes.
The general immediately rose to change clothes.
Chá did not know what he was doing.
The maidens helped adjust his sleeves and straighten his attire,
then first ordered several people to press Chá into his seat to prevent him from moving,
after which the general performed a court bow,
as if paying homage to a sovereign or father.
Chá was greatly astonished,
unable to comprehend the reason.
After the bowing was done,
the general changed into informal clothes and sat in attendance.
He said with a smile:
“Does the gentleman not recall the beggar who lifted the bell?”
Only then did Chá understand.
Soon, a magnificent banquet was laid out,
with household musicians performing below.
When the wine was nearly finished,
the maidens stood in rows attending.
The general entered the inner chamber,
inquired about bedding arrangements,
and then left.
Chá, drunk, rose late,
and the general had already inquired three times outside his bedroom door.
Chá felt uneasy,
and wished to take his leave and return.
The general threw away the linchpin and locked the gate,
confining him inside.
Chá observed that the general did nothing else all day
except count his maidens, servants, and retainers,
as well as his mules, horses, clothing, and utensils,
supervising the recording of registers,
and cautioning against any loss or omission.
Chá, considering this the general’s household affairs,
did not inquire deeply.
One day,
holding the register, the general said to Chá:
“That I, an unworthy man, have attained my present position
is entirely due to your generous and profound kindness.
Not a single maid or object
dare I keep for myself;
I dare offer half to you, sir.”
Chá was stunned and refused to accept.
The general would not listen.
He brought out tens of thousands in stored silver,
and divided it equally between them.
Checking against the register,
antiques, beds, and tables
filled nearly the entire hall, inside and out.
Chá firmly tried to stop him,
but the general paid no heed.
After verifying the names of the maids and servants,
he immediately ordered the men to prepare luggage
and the women to pack the utensils,
instructing them to serve the gentleman respectfully.
A hundred voices responded in awe.
He personally watched as the maidens boarded the carriages,
and the stable hands led out the mules and horses.
Amidst the clamor, they all set off together,
and only then did he return to bid farewell to Chá.
Later, Chá was implicated in a case concerning the compilation of history,
arrested due to association,
but ultimately escaped punishment,
all thanks to the general’s efforts.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
“To bestow great kindness without asking the recipient’s name—truly a chivalrous and heroic man of ancient times!
And the general’s repayment,
so generous and forthright,
is especially rare throughout the ages.
With such breadth of mind,
he naturally should not have ended his days in obscurity.
From this we know that the meeting of these two worthies
was no accident.”
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
The leader of the White Lotus bandits, Xú Hóngrú,
obtained a book of heretical arts,
enabling him to command ghosts and spirits.
When he tested it on a small scale,
all who witnessed it were terrified,
and those flocking to his door were as numerous as wild ducks.
Thus, he secretly harbored rebellious intentions.
He then produced a mirror,
claiming it could reveal a person’s entire destiny.
Hanging it in the courtyard,
he had people look at themselves:
some appeared with turbans,
some with gauze caps,
embroidered robes and sable-tail ornaments—
the forms that manifested varied.
People grew even more astonished.
As a result, word spread along the roads,
and those coming to his door seeking a glimpse
crowded together, sweating profusely.
Xú then declared:
"All civil and military officials seen in the mirror
are destined by the Tathāgata Buddha to be among the attendees of the Dragon Flower Assembly.
Each should strive diligently,
and must not shrink back."
He then faced the mirror himself before the crowd,
and there appeared a crown with hanging beads and dragon robes—
the unmistakable image of a king.
The people looked at each other in shock,
and the entire assembly prostrated themselves.
Xú then raised his banner and grasped his battle-axe;
none failed to joyfully leap to follow him,
hoping to match what they had seen in the mirror.
Within a few months,
he had gathered a following numbering in the tens of thousands,
and the areas of Zōu and Fèng
submitted at the mere rumor of his approach.
Later, when the imperial troops advanced to suppress them,
there was a Commander Péng,
a man from Chángshān,
whose martial skill and courage were unparalleled.
The rebels sent out two girls to fight him.
Each girl wielded a pair of blades,
sharp as frost;
they rode large horses,
snorting fiercely with rage.
Darting about and circling,
from morning until dusk,
they could not harm Péng,
nor could Péng gain victory over them.
After three days like this,
Péng felt his strength completely exhausted,
and he gasped for breath until he died.
After Hóngrú was executed,
his followers were captured, interrogated, and put in shackles,
and only then was it learned that the blades were wooden knives,
and the horses were wooden benches.
For phantom soldiers and horses to kill a real general—
how strange indeed!
Based on the manuscript version of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
A certain scholar from Shùntiān,
his family was poor.
During a year of famine,
he followed his father to Luòyáng.
His nature was dull;
at seventeen,
he could not compose a complete essay.
Yet his appearance was handsome and elegant,
he could engage in refined banter,
and was skilled at writing letters.
Those who met him did not realize he lacked substance within.
Not long after,
his parents passed away one after the other,
leaving him alone,
and he became a tutor in the village of Luòruì.
At that time, in the village, there was an orphaned daughter of the Yán family,
a descendant of a renowned scholar.
She was intelligent from a young age.
While her father was alive,
he had taught her to read,
and she could remember anything after a single glance.
By the age of ten or so,
she learned to compose poetry like her father.
Her father said:
"Our family has a female academician;
it’s a pity she doesn’t wear a scholar’s cap."
He doted on her,
hoping to select a noble son-in-law.
After her father died,
her mother held to this wish,
but for three years it went unfulfilled,
and then her mother also passed away.
Some advised her to marry a worthy scholar,
and she agreed but had not yet done so.
Just then, a neighbor woman climbed over the wall to visit,
and came to chat with her.
the girl opened it to look,
and it was a letter from that scholar,
addressed to the neighbor’s son.
After reading it over and over, she grew fond of it.
The neighbor woman discerned her feelings,
and privately said to her:
"This is an elegant and handsome young man,
an orphan like yourself,
and around the same age.
If you are inclined,
I will ask him to arrange a match."
The girl remained silent, her feelings hidden.
The woman returned home,
and conveyed the idea to her husband.
The neighbor’s son had long been on good terms with the scholar,
so he told him,
and the scholar was overjoyed.
He had a gold hairpin left by his mother,
which he entrusted to the neighbor to deliver.
A wedding date was set,
and they were as harmonious as fish and water.
But when she saw the scholar’s essays,
she laughed and said:
"Your writing seems to belong to a different person from you.
If things remain like this,
when will you ever succeed?"
Morning and night she urged him to study diligently,
strict as a teacher or friend.
At dusk,
she would first light the lamp and sit at the desk reciting aloud,
setting an example for her husband,
and would not stop until the third watch.
After more than a year like this,
the scholar became quite proficient in the eight-legged essay;
yet he failed the examinations twice,
and his reputation declined,
with even daily meals becoming scarce.
Feeling disheartened and lonely,
he sobbed and wept bitterly.
His wife asked him:
"Aren’t you a man?
Failing to live up to that cap of yours!
If I were to change my hairpin for a cap,
high rank would be as easy as picking up a mustard seed!"
The scholar, already frustrated,
heard his wife’s words
and glared angrily, saying:
"A woman of the inner chambers,
who has never set foot in the examination hall,
thinks winning fame and wealth is as easy as you fetching water in the kitchen to cook plain rice porridge.
If a cap were placed on your head, I’m afraid you’d be just like anyone else!"
His wife laughed and said:
"Don’t be angry.
When the examination time comes,
let me change clothes and go in your place.
If I fail as miserably as you,
then I wouldn’t dare look down on the scholars of the world anymore."
The scholar also laughed:
"You don’t know the bitterness of the exam grind,
so it’s only right you try it yourself.
But I’m afraid you’ll be exposed
and laughed at by the neighbors."
His wife said:
"I was only joking.
But I’ve heard that in Yān there is a vacant house;
let me dress as a man and go back with you,
pretending to be your younger brother.
Since you left as an infant,
who would be able to tell it’s not true?"
The scholar agreed.
His wife went into the room,
came out in men’s clothing,
and said:
"Look, can I pass as a young man?"
The scholar looked at her:
truly, she was a handsome youth who would admire his own reflection.
Delighted,
he bid farewell to all in the village.
Close friends gave modest gifts,
and he bought a thin donkey,
riding with his wife back home.
The elder brother was still alive,
and seeing his two younger brothers as handsome as jade-adorned youths,
he was very pleased,
caring for them morning and night.
He also saw them studying diligently day and night,
and loved and respected them even more.
He hired a young servant with cropped hair
to serve them.
After dusk,
he would always send the servant away.
For condolences or celebrations in the village,
the elder brother would handle them himself,
while the younger brothers remained behind curtains to study.
After half a year,
few had seen their faces.
If guests requested to meet them,
the elder brother would always decline on their behalf.
When people read their essays,
they were astonished and amazed.
Some pushed the door open and forced their way in to see them,
but after a single bow, they would vanish.
Guests who caught a glimpse of their elegant demeanor
were all filled with admiration.
From then on, their fame spread far and wide,
and prominent families vied to have them as sons-in-law.
The elder brother discussed it with them,
but they only smiled faintly.
When pressed further,
they said:
"We are determined to aim for the highest honors,
and until we pass the imperial examinations,
we will not marry."
When the provincial examiner arrived,
both brothers took the exam.
The elder brother failed again.
The younger brother, having placed first in the preliminary exam,
ranked fourth in the Shùntiān prefectural examination;
the following year, he became a jìnshì;
he was appointed magistrate of Tóngchéng County,
where he governed with distinction;
soon he was promoted to the seal-holding censor of the Hénán circuit,
and his residence rivaled those of princes and marquises.
He then feigned illness and requested retirement,
and was granted permission to return to his hometown.
Guests filled his gate,
but he consistently declined to receive them.
Moreover, from his time as a scholar to his rise to prominence,
he never spoke of marriage,
which puzzled everyone.
After returning home,
he gradually acquired maidservants.
Some suspected he had illicit affairs;
but his sister-in-law observed him
and found nothing improper.
Not long after,
the Ming dynasty fell and the Qing rose,
and the world was thrown into chaos.
He then told his sister-in-law:
"To tell you the truth,
I am actually your younger sister-in-law.
Because my husband was incompetent
and unable to stand on his own,
I, out of indignation, took matters into my own hands.
I deeply feared exposure,
which would lead to an imperial summons
and bring ridicule throughout the land."
His sister-in-law did not believe him,
so he took off his boots and showed her his feet,
at which she was stunned;
looking inside the boots,
they were stuffed with worn-out cotton.
She then had her husband assume his official title,
while she resumed her female role and stayed behind closed doors.
However, she never bore children in her lifetime,
so she used her wealth to purchase a concubine.
She said to her husband:
"When ordinary people attain high office,
they buy concubines for their own pleasure;
I served as an official for ten years,
yet remained alone.
How is it that you,
enjoy the company of a beautiful woman without lifting a finger?"
Her husband replied:
"Thirty male attendants,
I leave it to you to arrange."
This became a joke among them.
By this time, her husband's parents
had repeatedly received imperial favors.
When officials paid visits,
they honored her husband with the礼节 of a censor.
But her husband was ashamed to assume his wife's official title,
and contented himself with being a scholar,
never using a carriage or canopy in his lifetime.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"For parents to receive honors through their daughter-in-law is indeed remarkable.
However, censors who are women—
are they not found in every age?
But women who serve as censors are rare.
All those in the world who wear scholars' caps and call themselves men
should die of shame!"
From the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Old Man Dù
was from Yíshuǐ.
Once, as he was leaving the market,
he sat by a wall
to wait for his companions.
Feeling slightly tired,
he dozed off and dreamed
that someone holding a warrant came to arrest him.
He was taken to a government office
he had never seen before.
A man wearing a tile-ridged hat
emerged from inside,
and it turned out to be Zhāng Mǒu from Qīngzhōu,
an old acquaintance of his.
Seeing Dù, Zhāng exclaimed in surprise:
"Brother Dù, how did you end up here?"
Dù replied:
"I don’t know why,
but I was summoned with a warrant."
Zhāng suspected a mistake
and went to investigate.
Before leaving, he instructed Dù:
"Stay right here,
and don’t go anywhere else.
If you get lost,
it will be hard to save you."
With that, he left,
but after a long time, he did not return.
Only the warrant-holder came back,
admitted his error,
and released Dù to go home.
Dù bid farewell and set off.
On the way, he encountered six or seven young women,
all charming and beautiful,
and he was so delighted that he followed them.
Leaving the main road,
he took a small path,
and after walking a dozen steps,
he heard Zhāng shouting behind him:
"Brother Dù,
where are you going?"
But Dù was too captivated to stop.
Soon, he saw the women enter a small, low door,
and he recognized it as the home of the Wáng family who sold wine.
Without thinking, he leaned inside the door
and glanced around,
only to find himself in a pigpen,
lying among several piglets.
Suddenly, he realized
that he had turned into a pig,
though he could still hear Zhāng calling him.
Terrified,
he desperately rammed his head against the wall.
He heard someone say:
"The little pig is having a seizure."
Looking back,
he had become human again.
He hurried out the door,
and there was Zhāng waiting on the road.
Zhāng scolded him:
"I told you not to go anywhere else.
Why didn’t you listen?
You nearly ruined everything!"
Then he took Dù by the hand and escorted him to the market gate
before leaving.
Dù suddenly woke up
and found himself still leaning against the wall.
He went to the Wáng family to inquire,
and indeed, they said a pig had rammed itself to death.
From the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
At the residence of the Ministry Gentleman Jiāng in Wèinán,
there were many ghosts and spirits,
which often bewildered people.
Consequently, he moved away.
He left an old servant to guard the gate, but the servant died.
Several replacements all died as well.
Thus, the place was abandoned.
In the village, there was a scholar named Táo Wàngsān,
who had always been untrammeled and unconventional,
fond of frolicking with courtesans,
and would leave them once the wine was finished.
Friends would deliberately send courtesans to run after him,
and he would laugh and let them in without refusal;
yet in reality, he remained untouched throughout the night.
He once stayed overnight at the Ministry Gentleman’s home,
where a maidservant came to him at night,
but he firmly refused and did not transgress,
earning the Ministry Gentleman’s deep respect for this.
His family was extremely poor,
and he also had
"the sorrow of drumming on a basin" (i.e., the grief of losing his wife),
living in a thatched hut with only a few rafters,
where the humid summer heat was unbearable.
Therefore, he asked the Ministry Gentleman
to lend him the abandoned residence.
The Ministry Gentleman, due to its ominous nature,
refused.
Táo then wrote "A Sequel to the Treatise on the Nonexistence of Ghosts" and presented it to the Ministry Gentleman,
saying:
"What can ghosts possibly do!"
The Ministry Gentleman, seeing his insistence,
agreed.
Táo went to clean the main hall.
As dusk approached,
he placed a book there;
but when he returned to fetch other things,
the book had already vanished.
He found this strange.
Lying on his back on the couch,
he quietly waited to see what would happen.
After about the time it takes to eat a meal,
he heard footsteps,
and glancing sideways,
saw two women emerge from the room,
returning the lost book to the table.
One appeared to be about twenty,
the other perhaps seventeen or eighteen,
both exceptionally beautiful.
They hesitated, standing by the couch,
looking at each other and smiling.
Táo remained still and silent.
The elder one lifted a foot and stepped on his abdomen,
while the younger one covered her mouth and giggled.
Táo felt his heart swaying, almost losing self-control,
but he quickly composed himself with solemn thoughts,
and ultimately paid them no heed.
The woman approached, using her left hand to stroke his beard,
and her right hand to lightly tap his cheeks,
making a soft sound.
The younger one laughed even more.
Táo suddenly rose,
shouting:
"How dare you, ghostly creatures!"
The two women fled in terror and scattered.
Táo feared being tormented at night,
and thought of moving back,
but felt ashamed that his words would not match his actions,
so he lit a lamp and read.
In the darkness, ghostly shadows flickered about,
but he paid them no attention at all.
As midnight approached,
he blew out the candle and went to sleep.
Just as his eyelids were closing,
he felt someone using a thin object to tickle his nose,
causing an intense itch and a great sneeze;
only faint laughter could be heard from the darkness.
Táo did not speak,
pretending to sleep while waiting.
Soon, he saw the younger girl twisting a strip of paper into a thin strand,
moving stealthily like a crane or heron,
and he suddenly rose to scold her,
causing her to float away and flee.
After lying down again,
she tickled his ear.
He endured the disturbance all night.
Once the rooster crowed,
all fell silent,
and Táo finally slept soundly,
seeing and hearing nothing all day.
As the sun set,
the figures vaguely reappeared.
Táo then cooked his evening meal,
intending to stay awake until dawn.
The elder one gradually leaned her elbow on the table,
watching him read;
then she covered his book.
Táo angrily tried to grab her,
but she had already floated away;
a moment later,
she touched him again.
Táo pressed his hand on the book to read.
The younger one stealthily approached from behind,
crossed her hands to cover his eyes,
then vanished in an instant,
standing far away and sneering.
Táo pointed and scolded:
"You little devil heads!
If I catch you, I’ll kill you all!"
The girls, however, showed no fear.
So he teased them:
"Even if you offered yourselves in the bedroom,
I wouldn’t understand,
so pestering me is useless."
The two women smiled slightly,
turned toward the stove,
split firewood and washed rice,
tending the fire for him.
Táo looked at them and praised:
"Aren’t you two better at this
than your mischievous antics?"
Shortly after,
the porridge was ready,
and they vied to place spoons, chopsticks, and earthenware bowls on the table.
Táo said:
"I am grateful for your service,
but how can I repay your kindness?"
The women laughed and said:
"We’ve mixed arsenic and poisoned wine into the rice."
Táo replied:
"I have no enmity with you from the past,
why would you go so far as to do this to me?"
He finished the bowl,
and they served him another,
competing to run errands for him.
Táo enjoyed this,
and it became a regular occurrence.
As days passed and they grew familiar,
they sat close and chatted intimately,
and he inquired about their names.
The elder one said:
"I am Qiūróng,
of the Qiáo family;
she is Xiǎo Xiè of the Ruǎn family."
He further questioned their origins.
Xiǎo Xiè laughed and said:
"Silly man!
You still don’t dare to offer yourself,
who wants you to ask about family backgrounds
as if arranging a marriage?"
Táo said with a serious expression:
"Facing such beauty,
how could I be without affection;
but the energy of the underworld
will surely kill any human it touches.
If you do not wish to live with me,
you may leave;
if you wish to live with me,
you may stay.
If you do not love me,
why tarnish two beauties?
If you do love me,
why cause the death of a reckless scholar?"
The two women looked at each other, visibly moved,
and from then on, they rarely teased or tormented him;
though occasionally they would slip a hand into his bosom
or pull his trousers to the ground,
he no longer found it strange.
One day,
he had gone out before finishing his transcription of a book,
and upon returning, found Xiǎo Xiè leaning over the desk,
holding a brush and transcribing in his stead.
Seeing the scholar,
she tossed the brush aside and looked up with a teasing smile.
He drew closer to look,
and though the characters were poorly formed,
the lines and columns were neatly spaced.
The scholar praised her, saying:
"You are a person of refinement!
If you enjoy this,
I will teach you how to do it."
Then he embraced her,
took her wrist, and taught her to write.
Qiū Róng came in from outside,
her expression suddenly changed,
and she seemed jealous.
Xiǎo Xiè said with a laugh:
"When I was a child, I once learned calligraphy from my father,
but it has been so long since I practiced,
it feels like a dream."
Qiū Róng remained silent.
The scholar understood her feelings,
but pretended not to notice.
He then embraced her and handed her a brush,
saying:
"Let me see if you can do this?"
She wrote a few characters and stood up,
and he said:
"Lady Qiū has a fine hand!"
Qiū Róng was then pleased.
The scholar then folded two sheets of paper as models,
for them to copy together;
he himself lit another lamp and read.
Secretly pleased that each had their own task,
and they did not disturb one another.
After they finished copying,
they stood respectfully before the desk,
listening to the scholar's critique.
Qiū Róng had never learned to read,
and her scribbles were illegible,
so after the judgment was given,
she saw she was not as good as Xiǎo Xiè,
and looked ashamed.
The scholar encouraged and comforted her,
and her expression finally cleared.
From then on, the two girls treated the scholar as their teacher,
sitting to scratch his back,
lying down to massage his legs,
not only not daring to be disrespectful,
but vying to please him.
After a month,
Xiǎo Xiè's writing had become quite neat and proper,
and the scholar occasionally praised her.
Qiū Róng was greatly ashamed,
her makeup streaked with tears,
the tear marks like threads.
The scholar comforted and consoled her in every way,
and only then did she stop.
He then taught her to read,
and she was exceptionally quick-witted,
needing only one explanation,
and never asking again.
She read alongside the scholar,
often staying up all night.
Xiǎo Xiè also brought her younger brother Sān Láng,
to become the scholar's disciple.
He was fifteen or sixteen years old,
with a handsome and elegant appearance.
He presented a golden ruyi scepter as tuition;
the scholar had him and Qiū Róng study a classic together.
The hall was filled with murmuring voices;
the scholar had set up a ghostly school here.
The Vice Minister heard of this and was pleased,
providing a regular salary.
After several months,
Qiū Róng and Sān Láng were both able to compose poetry,
and often exchanged verses.
Xiǎo Xiè secretly urged the scholar not to teach Qiū Róng,
and he agreed; Qiū Róng secretly urged him not to teach Xiǎo Xiè,
and he also agreed.
One day,
the scholar was about to go for the examinations,
and the two girls tearfully saw him off.
Sān Láng said,
"For this trip, you can feign illness to avoid it; otherwise,
I fear you may encounter misfortune."
The scholar considered feigning illness disgraceful,
and so he went.
Previously,
the scholar had enjoyed using poetry to satirize current affairs,
offending the local nobility,
who daily plotted to harm him.
They secretly bribed the education commissioner,
falsely accusing him of misconduct,
and he was imprisoned.
His funds ran out,
and he begged food from fellow prisoners,
resigning himself to the thought that he would not survive.
Suddenly, a person drifted in,
it was Qiū Róng,
bringing food for the scholar.
Facing each other, they wept sorrowfully,
and she said:
"Sān Láng feared misfortune would befall you,
and now it has indeed come true.
Sān Láng and I came together,
and he has gone to the provincial court to plead your case."
After a few words, she left,
unseen by anyone.
The next day,
when the provincial governor went out,
Sān Láng blocked his path and cried out his grievance,
and was taken into custody.
Qiū Róng went to the prison to report to the scholar,
then turned back to investigate,
and did not return for three days.
The scholar, worried, hungry, and bored,
felt each day pass like a year.
Suddenly, Xiǎo Xiè arrived,
grief-stricken and despairing,
saying:
"On her way back, Qiū Róng
passed by the City God Temple,
and was forcibly taken by the Black Judge of the western corridor,
who tried to force her to become his concubine.
Qiū Róng refused to submit,
and is now also imprisoned.
I rushed a hundred li,
the journey was exhausting;
when I reached the northern outskirts,
an old thorn pierced the sole of my foot,
the pain pierced to the bone,
and I fear I may not be able to come again."
Then she showed him her foot,
the blood staining her delicate steps.
She took out three taels of gold,
and limped away, disappearing.
The provincial governor interrogated Sān Láng,
finding he had no prior connection
yet had made a plea on behalf of another for no reason,
and was about to have him beaten,
when he fell to the ground and vanished.
The governor found this strange.
Reading his petition,
the sentiments and wording were mournful and pitiful.
He summoned the scholar for a face-to-face interrogation,
asking:
“Who is Sānláng?”
The scholar pretended not to know.
The provincial governor realized the injustice,
and released him.
After returning home,
there was not a single person all night.
As the night deepened,
Xiǎoxiè finally arrived,
and said sorrowfully:
“Sānláng, at the provincial governor’s office,
was seized by the office deity and taken to the underworld;
the King of the Underworld, considering Sānláng righteous,
ordered him to be reborn into a wealthy and noble family.
Qiūróng has long been imprisoned;
I submitted a petition to the City God,
but it was again suppressed and shelved,
unable to gain entry.
What more can we do?”
The scholar said indignantly:
“How dare that black old demon act like this!
Tomorrow I will topple his statue,
trample it into mud,
and denounce the City God, holding him accountable.
For his subordinate officials to be so violent and tyrannical,
he must be in a drunken stupor!”
Grieving and angry, they faced each other,
unaware that the fourth watch was nearly ending.
Qiūróng suddenly drifted in.
Both were overjoyed,
and urgently asked.
Qiūróng said with tears:
“Now I have suffered ten thousand hardships for you, sir!
The judge daily pressured me with knives and clubs,
but tonight he suddenly released me to return,
saying: ‘I have no other intentions,
originally it was out of love;
since you are unwilling,
I certainly have not defiled you.
Please inform Judicial Officer Táo,
do not condemn me.’”
Hearing this, the scholar felt slightly happier,
and wished to sleep with them,
saying:
“Today I am willing to die for you.”
The two girls said sadly:
“Having received your guidance before,
we have come to understand righteousness and reason somewhat.
How could we bear to kill you, whom we love?”
They firmly refused.
Yet, bowing their heads and leaning close,
their affection was like that of husband and wife.
Because of the hardships they had suffered,
the two girls’ feelings of jealousy completely vanished.
It happened that a Taoist priest encountered the scholar on the road,
looked at him and said:
“You have an aura of ghosts about you.”
The scholar, finding his words strange,
told him everything.
The Taoist priest said:
“These ghosts are very good,
I do not intend to wrong them.”
Then he wrote two talismans and gave them to the scholar,
saying:
“Return and give these to the two ghosts,
let their fortunes decide: if you hear someone outside mourning a daughter,
swallow the talisman and rush out immediately;
the one who arrives first can come back to life.”
The scholar bowed and received them,
returned home and instructed the two girls.
Over a month later,
they indeed heard someone mourning a daughter.
The two girls raced to go.
Xiǎoxiè, in her haste,
forgot to swallow her talisman.
Seeing a funeral procession passing,
Qiūróng went straight out,
entered the coffin and vanished;
Xiǎoxiè could not enter,
and returned weeping bitterly.
The scholar went out to look,
and saw it was the wealthy Hǎo family burying their daughter.
Everyone had seen a girl enter the coffin and disappear;
they were just feeling shocked and suspicious,
when suddenly they heard sounds from the coffin.
Setting down the bier to check,
the girl had already revived.
So they temporarily placed her outside the scholar’s study,
surrounding and watching over her.
Suddenly she opened her eyes and asked for Táo Shēng.
The Hǎo family questioned her closely,
and she replied:
“I am not your daughter.”
Then she told them the whole story.
The Hǎos did not fully believe it,
and wanted to carry her back;
the girl refused,
went straight into the scholar’s study,
lay stiff and would not rise.
The Hǎos then acknowledged him as son-in-law and left.
The scholar went to see her;
though her face was different,
her radiant beauty was no less than Qiūróng’s.
Overjoyed beyond expectation,
they earnestly recounted their lives.
Suddenly they heard a mournful ghostly weeping—
it was Xiǎoxiè crying in a dark corner.
His heart ached for her,
so he immediately took a lamp and went over,
comforting her in her sorrow,
but her sleeves were soaked with tears,
her grief inconsolable.
Near dawn she finally left.
When day broke,
the Hǎos sent maids and elderly women delivering a dowry,
and they were like father- and son-in-law.
At night, entering the bridal chamber,
Xiǎoxiè wept again.
This went on for six or seven nights.
Both husband and wife were deeply saddened,
unable to complete the wedding rites.
The scholar worried, with no solution.
Qiūróng said:
“The Taoist priest
is an immortal.
Go seek him again,
perhaps he will take pity and help.”
The scholar agreed.
Tracking down where the Taoist priest was,
he knelt and kowtowed, explaining himself.
The Taoist priest insisted
he “had no method.”
The scholar pleaded incessantly.
The Taoist priest laughed and said:
“Foolish scholar, so persistent.
It seems we are fated;
I will exhaust my arts for you.”
Then he followed the scholar back,
requested a quiet room,
closed the door and sat,
warning not to disturb him.
For over ten days,
he neither drank nor ate.
Peeking secretly,
he seemed asleep with eyes closed.
One morning as he rose,
a young girl lifted the curtain and entered,
with bright eyes and white teeth,
radiantly beautiful.
Smiling, she said:
“Tramping all day,
I am utterly exhausted!
Because you pestered endlessly,
I rushed over a hundred *li* away,
and finally found a good dwelling.
The Taoist brought me here together.
Now that I see the person,
I will hand her over.”
As dusk gathered,
Xiǎoxiè arrived.
The girl suddenly rose to meet and embrace her,
and with a merging sound, they became one body,
collapsing stiff to the ground.
The Taoist priest came out of the room,
clasped his hands and left directly.
The scholar bowed and saw him off.
Upon his return,
he found the girl had revived.
He helped her onto the bed,
and gradually her breath and body relaxed,
but she held her feet and moaned that her toes and thighs were sore and aching.
It took several days before she could get up.
Later, the young man passed the imperial examinations and obtained an official post.
There was a man named Cài Zǐjīng who was on the same official register as him.
He visited the young man on some business
and stayed for a few days.
When Xiǎo Xiè returned from the neighbor’s house,
Cài caught sight of her
and hurriedly followed her.
Xiǎo Xiè turned aside to avoid him,
secretly angry at his frivolousness.
Cài left the young man and said,
"There is one matter that deeply shocks people.
May I tell you about it?"
When questioned,
he replied,
"Three years ago,
my younger sister died young.
After two nights, her corpse disappeared,
and I have been suspicious and concerned about it ever since.
Just now, when I saw your wife,
why did she look so much like her?"
The young man laughed and said,
"My wife is plain and unrefined.
How could she compare to your sister?
However, since we are on the same official register,
our bond is extremely close.
Why not let me introduce my wife to you?"
He then went inside
and had Xiǎo Xiè come out dressed in the clothes she was buried in.
Cài was greatly astonished and said,
"She really is my sister!"
And he began to weep.
The young man then recounted the whole story from beginning to end.
Cài joyfully said,
"My sister is not dead after all.
I must hurry home
to comfort my strict and caring parents."
He then departed.
After a few days,
the entire family arrived.
From then on, they visited each other just like the Hǎo family.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"A peerless beauty—
to find even one is difficult,
so how could he suddenly obtain two!
Such an event is seen once in a thousand years,
and only those who do not engage in illicit affairs with women can encounter it.
Was that Daoist an immortal?
How divine were his arts!
If one possessed such arts,
even an ugly ghost could be befriended."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
There was a scholar named Fàn
who was staying at an inn.
After eating,
he lit a candle and dozed off.
Suddenly, a maidservant came in,
placed a bundle of clothes on a chair,
and then brought a mirror case and a comb box,
arranging them one by one on the table,
before leaving.
Soon, a young woman emerged from the room,
opened the box and took out the comb,
and faced the mirror to comb her hair.
First, she arranged her hair into a bun,
then inserted hairpins,
and gazed at her reflection, pacing back and forth for a long time.
The maidservant from earlier returned,
bringing a basin for washing.
After washing, she handed her a towel,
and when finished,
took away the washing water.
The woman untied the bundle and took out a skirt and a cape,
which were dazzlingly new,
and put them on.
She adjusted the lapels and straightened the collar,
making sure everything was perfectly arranged.
Fàn remained silent,
but in his heart, he was suspicious and puzzled,
thinking she must be a woman planning to elope,
dressing up meticulously to meet a guest.
Once the woman finished dressing,
she took out a long belt,
hung it over the beam, and tied it.
Fàn was astonished.
The woman calmly stood on tiptoe,
stretched her neck, and hanged herself.
As soon as the belt tightened,
her eyes closed,
her eyebrows raised,
her tongue protruded about two inches from her mouth,
and her complexion turned ghastly, like a ghost.
Fàn, terrified, rushed out,
called the innkeeper,
but when they checked, she had vanished.
The innkeeper said,
"In the past, my daughter-in-law hanged herself here.
Could it have been her?"
Alas,
how strange!
Even after death, she reenacted her appearance.
What is the explanation for this?
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"When injustice reaches its extreme, leading to suicide,
how bitter it is!
Yet, before death, as a person, she was unaware;
after death, as a ghost, she remained unconscious.
What was most unbearable for her
was the moment of dressing and tying the belt.
Thus, after death, she instantly forgot everything else,
but at that moment, in that situation,
she still vividly reenacted it—
this is what she could never forget."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
There was a painter from Wúmén,
whose name has been forgotten.
He loved to paint Lǚ Zǔ,
and every time he imagined him, his spirit would commune with the image,
hoping for the good fortune of meeting him just once.
His devotion was sincere and constant,
never a moment without it.
One day,
he came upon a group of beggars drinking on the outskirts of the city.
Among them was one in tattered clothes with elbows exposed,
yet his bearing was noble and open.
The painter’s heart suddenly stirred,
suspecting it was Lǚ Zǔ.
Looking closely,
he became even more certain.
He grabbed the man’s arm and said:
“You are Lǚ Zǔ.”
The beggar laughed heartily.
The painter insisted it was so,
bowing and refusing to rise.
The beggar said:
“Even if I am Lǚ Zǔ,
what will you do?”
The painter kowtowed,
only begging for guidance.
The beggar said:
“Since you can recognize me,
it can be said we have a connection.
But this is not the place to talk;
we shall meet at night.”
As the painter tried to stop him for more questions,
the beggar vanished in the blink of an eye.
Astonished and sighing, the painter returned home.
That night,
he indeed dreamed that Lǚ Zǔ came and said:
“I am moved by your single-minded devotion,
so I have come to see you.
But your bone structure shows greed and stinginess,
so you cannot become an immortal.
I can let you see someone, though.”
He then waved toward the air,
and a beautiful woman descended from the sky.
Her attire was that of a noble consort,
her radiant appearance and robe
illuminating the entire room.
Lǚ Zǔ said:
“This is Consort Dǒng.
Remember her carefully.”
After a moment, he asked again:
“Do you remember?”
The painter replied:
“I have remembered.”
Lǚ Zǔ said again:
“Do not forget.”
Soon the beautiful woman left,
and Lǚ Zǔ departed as well.
Waking up, the painter found it strange.
He painted the woman he saw in the dream,
keeping the portrait hidden,
but in the end he did not understand the meaning.
Several years later,
he happened to travel to the capital.
It so happened that Consort Dǒng had passed away,
and the emperor, remembering her virtue,
wanted to have a portrait made.
Many painters gathered,
listening to descriptions and imagining,
but none could capture her likeness.
The painter suddenly thought of the woman from his dream—
could it be her?
He presented his painting.
When it was circulated in the palace,
everyone said it was a miraculous likeness.
Thus he was offered a position as a secretary in the Imperial Secretariat,
but he declined;
he was instead bestowed ten thousand taels of gold.
From then on, his fame grew greatly.
Noble families competed to send generous payments,
begging him to paint portraits of their ancestors.
He only needed to paint from memory,
and every one turned out perfectly lifelike.
Within a short time,
he accumulated tens of thousands in wealth.
Zhū Gǒngkuí from Láiwú once met this man.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Jǐ’nán, there was a man named Qī Ānqī,
who was frivolous by nature
and fond of visiting prostitutes.
His wife gently admonished him,
but he would not listen.
His wife, née Lín,
was beautiful and virtuous.
It happened that northern soldiers invaded the region,
and she was captured.
That evening, as they camped on the road,
a soldier tried to assault her.
Lín pretended to consent.
Noticing the soldier’s sword hanging by the bed,
she quickly drew it and slit her own throat;
the soldier then carried her body and discarded it in the wilderness.
The next day,
the troops moved on.
Someone brought word that Lín had died,
and Qī, grieving deeply, went to find her.
Looking at her,
he noticed faint breath.
He carried her home,
and gradually her eyes began to move;
she moaned softly.
Supporting her neck,
he fed her drop by drop through a bamboo tube,
and she could swallow.
Qī stroked her and said:
“If by any chance you live,
may any who betray you meet a violent end!”
After half a year,
Lín recovered as before;
only her head was pulled by the scar on her neck,
often tilting as if looking left.
Qī did not consider her ugly,
and loved her even more than before.
His visits to pleasure quarters
ceased from then on.
Lín felt her appearance was marred
and wanted to arrange a concubine for him;
but Qī firmly refused.
Several years passed,
but Lín had not borne any children,
so she urged Qī to take a maidservant.
Qī said:
"I have sworn not to take a second wife;
surely the gods and spirits have heard this.
Even if I have no heir to continue the family line,
it is simply my fate.
If our line is not meant to end,
how could you, my wife, be too old to bear children?"
Lín then pretended to be ill
and had Qī sleep alone;
she sent the maidservant Hǎitáng
to sleep on a mat beneath his bed.
After some time,
Lín secretly asked the maid in the night whether anything had happened.
The maid said nothing had.
Lín did not believe her.
That night,
she told the maid not to go
and went herself to where the maid usually slept.
After a while,
she heard the sound of breathing from the bed.
She quietly rose,
climbed onto the bed, and touched him.
Qī woke up
and asked who it was.
Lín whispered in his ear:
"It is I, Hǎitáng."
Qī pushed her away and refused, saying:
"I have made a vow
and dare not break it.
If I were like in years past,
would I have needed you to come to me?"
Lín then got down from the bed and left.
From then on, Qī slept alone.
Lín had the maid pretend to be her and go to him.
Qī thought that his wife had never in her life been one to come uninvited,
so he grew suspicious;
he felt her neck
and found no scar,
realizing it was the maid,
and scolded her away.
The maid retreated in shame.
When day broke,
Qī told Lín what had happened
and urged her to quickly marry off the maid.
Lín said with a laugh:
"You need not be so stubborn.
If we could obtain a son,
that would indeed be fortunate."
Qī said:
"If I break my vow,
the ghosts will surely punish me;
how could I then hope to continue the family line?"
The next day, Lín said to Qī with a smile:
"Among farmers,
whether the seedlings will sprout or not is unknown,
but the usual practice of sowing seeds cannot be neglected.
Tonight, the time for plowing has come."
Qī understood her meaning and laughed.
When evening came,
Lín extinguished the lamp and called the maid,
having her sleep under her own quilt.
When Qī came to the bed,
he joked:
"The tenant farmer has arrived.
I am deeply ashamed that my plow is not sharp,
and I may fail this fertile field."
The maid did not speak.
When they began the act,
the maid whispered:
"My private part is slightly swollen,
and I cannot bear too much vigor."
Qī, understanding her meaning, treated her gently and with care.
After the act was done,
the maid pretended to get up to relieve herself
and had Lín take her place.
From then on, whenever it was the time of her monthly period,
they would do this once,
and Qī was unaware of it.
Not long after,
the maid's belly swelled.
Lín often had her sit quietly
and did not let her serve in front of Qī.
She then said to Qī:
"I urged you to take the maid,
but you would not listen.
If on that day she had pretended to be me
and you had mistakenly believed her,
and she had become pregnant from the union,
what would you have done then?"
Qī said:
"Keep the calf and sell the mother."
Lín then said nothing more.
Not long after,
the maid gave birth to a son.
Lín secretly hired a wet nurse
and had the child raised at her mother's home.
Over four or five years,
she bore another son and a daughter.
The eldest son was named Chángshēng;
he was already seven years old
and studied at his maternal grandfather's home.
Every half month, Lín would use the pretext of visiting her parents
to go see them once.
As the maid grew older,
Qī often urged that she be sent away.
Lín would always agree.
The maid missed her children daily,
so Lín granted her wish,
secretly arranged her hair in a married woman's style,
and sent her to her mother's home.
She told Qī:
"You always said I would not marry off Hǎitáng;
my mother's family has an adopted son,
and I have already matched her with him."
Several more years passed,
and the children all grew up.
On the occasion of Qī's birthday,
Lín prepared a feast in advance
to entertain guests and friends.
Qī sighed and said:
"Time flies by;
suddenly half a lifetime has passed.
Fortunately, we are both still healthy,
and our family does not suffer from cold or hunger.
The only regret is
the lack of a child at our knees."
Lín said:
"You were stubborn
and would not listen to me;
whom can you blame?
But if you want a son,
two would not be difficult,
let alone one."
Qī smiled and said:
"Since you say it is not difficult,
tomorrow I will demand two sons."
Lín said:
"Easy,
easy!"
Early the next morning,
she had the carriage prepared and went to her mother's home,
dressed the children in fine clothes,
and brought them back with her.
Upon entering the door,
she had them stand in a line like wild geese
and call out "Father," offering birthday congratulations.
After they finished bowing and rose,
they looked at each other and laughed playfully.
Qī was astonished and did not understand.
Lín said:
"You demanded two sons,
and I have added a daughter."
She then explained the whole story in detail.
Qī said joyfully:
"Why didn't you tell me earlier?"
She replied:
"If I had told you earlier,
I feared you would have cut off ties with their mother.
Now that the children are grown,
can we still cut her off?"
Qī was deeply moved,
and tears flowed uncontrollably.
He then brought the maid back
and they lived together until old age.
Among the virtuous women of ancient times,
one like Lín
can be called sagely!
Based on the manuscript version of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Yìdū, there was a man named Yuè Yújiǔ,
whose home was haunted by a fox spirit.
Cloth, silk, and household utensils
were often thrown over the neighbor's wall.
He had stored some fine linen,
intending to make clothes from it;
he saw the bundles rolled up as before,
but upon untying them for inspection,
he found the edges solid while the centers were hollow,
all having been cut away.
Matters of this sort
made his suffering unbearable.
He cursed and swore at it.
Yuè tried to stop him, saying:
"I fear the fox will hear."
The fox on the beam said:
"I have already heard it."
From then on, the haunting grew even worse.
One day,
while husband and wife were still lying in bed, not yet risen,
the fox snatched their quilt and clothes away.
Each crouched naked on the bed,
gazing into the air and pleading sorrowfully.
Suddenly, they saw a beautiful woman enter through the window,
throwing the clothes onto the bed.
Looking at her,
she was not very tall;
she wore crimson red garments,
with a snowflake-patterned vest over them.
Yuè, putting on his clothes,
bowed to her and said:
"If the exalted immortal intends to favor us with her presence,
please do not trouble us further.
I propose to regard you as my daughter,
how would that be?"
The fox said:
"My age is greater than yours,
how can you presume to act as my elder?"
He then asked to regard her as a sister.
She then agreed.
Thereupon, he ordered the entire household to address her as Hú Dàgū.
At that time, at the home of the eighth young master of the Zhāng family in Yánzhèn,
there was a fox living in the upstairs room,
which often conversed with people.
Yuè asked:
"Do you know her?"
She replied:
"That is my family's Xǐyí,
how could I not know her?"
Yuè said:
"That Xǐyí never troubles people,
why don't you emulate her?"
The fox paid no heed,
and continued her disturbances as before.
She still did not haunt others much,
but focused her hauntings specifically on his daughter-in-law: shoes, socks, and hairpins,
were often discarded on the road;
every time she ate,
the fox would bury a dead mouse or filth in her rice bowl.
The daughter-in-law would then throw the bowl and curse the lascivious fox,
and never prayed for relief.
Yuè prayed, saying:
"The children all call you 'aunt,'
why do you show no respect for the dignity of an elder?"
The fox said:
"Tell your son to divorce his wife,
and I will become your daughter-in-law,
then we will have peace."
The daughter-in-law cursed, saying:
"Shameless, lewd fox,
do you want to compete with a human for a man?"
At that moment, the daughter-in-law was sitting on a clothes chest,
when suddenly thick smoke emerged from beneath her,
scorching hot like an oven.
Opening it to look,
all the stored clothes were reduced to ashes;
only one or two items remained,
which were all garments belonging to her mother-in-law.
The fox again urged Yuè's son to divorce his wife,
but the son did not comply.
After several days,
she pressed him again,
and he still did not comply.
The fox, enraged, struck him with a stone,
splitting his forehead open,
blood flowing,
nearly killing him.
Yuè became even more distressed by this.
In the Western Hills, there was a man named Lǐ Chéngyáo,
skilled in charms and holy water,
so Yuè hired him with money.
Lǐ used mud mixed with gold to write a charm on red silk,
which took three days to complete.
He also tied a mirror to the end of a pole,
holding it as a handle,
and shone it throughout the house.
He had a young boy follow and watch,
instructing that if he saw anything,
he should immediately report it.
When they reached one spot,
the boy said:
"On the wall, there's something like a dog crouching."
Lǐ immediately pointed his fingers like a halberd and wrote a charm on that spot.
Then, performing ritual steps in the courtyard,
he chanted for a while,
and soon saw all the household dogs and pigs come together,
ears flattened and tails tucked,
as if listening to commands.
Lǐ waved his hand and said:
"Away!"
They immediately scattered and left in single file like fish.
He chanted again,
and a flock of ducks came,
and he waved them away too.
Then chickens arrived.
Lǐ pointed at one chicken,
and shouted at it loudly.
The other chickens all left,
but this chicken alone crouched down,
folding its wings and letting out a long cry,
saying:
"I dare not do it again!"
Lǐ said:
"This creature is the Zǐgū that someone in the household made."
The family members all said they had never made one.
Lǐ said:
"The Zǐgū is still here now."
Then they all recalled that three years ago,
they had indeed played this game,
and the strange occurrences had begun from that very day.
They searched everywhere,
and found a straw doll on the stable beam.
Lǐ took it and threw it into the fire.
Then he brought out a wine jar,
chanted three times and shouted three times,
and the chicken rose and went straight away.
They heard a voice from the mouth of the jar say:
"Yuè the Fourth is ruthless!
In a few years,
I will return."
Yuè begged to have it thrown into boiling water or fire;
Lǐ refused,
and took it away with him.
Some people saw dozens of jars hanging on the walls of his home,
all stoppered with foxes inside.
It was said that he released them one by one,
to go out and cause hauntings,
thereby earning his hiring fees,
keeping them as rare commodities.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Chānghuà, there was a scholar named Mǎn,
who set up a school in Yúháng.
Once, while walking through the market streets,
passing under a street-side loft,
suddenly a lychee shell fell on his shoulder.
Looking up,
he saw a young girl leaning over the loft railing,
enchantingly beautiful and graceful,
and he could not help but stare, captivated.
The girl looked down, smiled, and went inside.
Upon inquiry,
he learned she was Xìhóu, the daughter of the Jiǎ family who ran a brothel.
Her reputation and price were quite high,
and he felt he could not fulfill his wish.
Returning to his study, lost in thought,
he lay awake all night.
The next day,
he went and sent in his card,
they met,
talked and laughed very happily,
and his heart grew even more infatuated.
Finding an excuse, he borrowed money from friends,
collected a sum of cash,
and took it to the girl,
where they became intimately close.
Then, on the pillow, he improvised a quatrain and presented it to her:
"The oil lamp's gleam on bronze plate, night not yet done,
Soft whispers by the bed, scent of musk and orchid.
Tomorrow, newly combed, she'll don the phoenix hairpin again,
No more dreams of wandering clouds with the King of Chǔ."
Xìhóu frowned and said:
"Although I am defiled and lowly,
I have always wished to find a kindred spirit to serve.
Since you have no wife,
do you think I could manage your household?"
The scholar was overjoyed,
and immediately made earnest promises,
firmly pledging his commitment.
Xìhóu also said happily:
"As for the art of poetry,
I myself think it is not difficult;
often, in secluded places,
I have wanted to try composing a poem,
but feared it might not turn out well,
and be mocked by those who see or hear it.
If I can follow you,
I hope you will teach me."
Then she asked the scholar:
"How much land and property does your family have?"
The reply was:
"Just a few acres of poor fields,
and a few rafters of a dilapidated house."
Xìhóu said:
"After I marry you,
we should stay together forever,
and you should no longer work as a tutor.
Forty mu of land is enough to support ourselves,
and ten mu can be used to grow mulberry trees,
weave five bolts of silk,
and after paying the taxes for peace, there will still be some left.
We can close the door and face each other,
you reading and I weaving,
and in our leisure time, we can enjoy poetry and wine—
what is so noble about being a marquis with a thousand households!"
The scholar said:
"How much is your price roughly?"
She said:
"Following the greedy intentions of the old woman,
how could it not be high?
At most, two hundred taels of silver would be enough.
It's a pity that I was too young,
and didn't know how to value money;
whatever I got, I gave to my mother,
so the little I have saved privately is not much.
If you can manage a hundred taels,
anything beyond that is not something to worry about."
The scholar said:
"My poverty and obscurity,
you already know;
how could I manage to get a hundred taels on my own?
I have a sworn friend,
who is an official in Húnán,
and has repeatedly invited me;
I was afraid of the long journey,
so I was reluctant to go.
Now, for your sake,
I should go and seek his help.
I estimate it will take three or four months,
and then I can return;
I hope you will wait patiently for me."
Xìhóu agreed.
The scholar immediately left his teaching position and traveled south.
When he arrived, the official had already been dismissed from his post,
and was living in a civilian house due to his mistake,
his official purse empty,
so he could not offer any help.
The scholar, in落魄 and unable to return,
took up teaching in the county.
Three years passed,
and he could not return.
Once, he punished a student,
and the student drowned himself.
The student's father, grieving for his son, sued the teacher,
and so he was arrested and imprisoned.
Fortunately, there were other students
who pitied their teacher for being innocent,
and from time to time sent him gifts,
so he did not suffer too much.
Since parting from the scholar,
Xìhóu shut her door and did not receive any guests.
Her mother found out the reason and questioned her,
but could not change her mind,
so she let her be for the time being.
There was a wealthy merchant who admired Xìhóu's reputation,
and sent a matchmaker to the old woman,
determined to have her,
not sparing any expense.
Xìhóu refused.
The merchant went to Húnán on a trading trip,
and carefully inquired about the scholar's situation.
At that time, the case was about to be resolved,
but the merchant bribed the officials in charge with money,
causing the scholar to be imprisoned for a long time.
He returned and told the old woman:
"The scholar has already died in prison."
Xìhóu doubted the truth of this news.
The old woman said:
"Regardless of whether Mǎn Shēng is dead or not,
even if he is still alive,
would it be better to follow a poor scholar and end up wearing coarse cloth,
or to wear fine clothes and enjoy fine food?"
Xìhóu said:
"Although Mǎn Shēng is poor,
his character is noble;
to stay with a dirty merchant,
is truly not what I wish.
Moreover, rumors on the road,
how can they be trusted!"
The merchant then asked another merchant
to forge a suicide letter from Mǎn Shēng and send it to Xìhóu,
to destroy her hopes.
When Xìhóu received the letter,
she cried mournfully day and night.
The old woman said:
"I raised you since childhood,
and put in a lot of effort to bring you up.
For the two or three years since you became an adult,
the回报 I've received
has not been much daily.
Since you are unwilling to remain in the profession,
and also unwilling to marry,
how do you plan to make a living?"
Xìhóu had no choice,
and so married the merchant.
The merchant provided her with fine clothes and jewelry,
and supplied her lavishly.
After more than a year,
she gave birth to a son.
Not long after,
with the help of his students,
the scholar was cleared of charges and released from prison,
and only then did he learn that the merchant had conspired to imprison him.
However, he thought that they had never had any enmity,
and could not figure out the reason for this反复.
His students righteously helped him with travel expenses to return home.
When he heard that Xìhóu had already married,
his heart was filled with grief and bitterness,
so he entrusted his sufferings
to an old woman selling浆 in the market to convey to Xìhóu.
Xìhóu was greatly saddened,
and only then realized that all the previous events
were the cunning schemes of the merchant.
Taking advantage of the merchant's absence,
she killed the child in her arms,
took all her belongings, and fled back to Mǎn;
as for all the clothing and accessories from the merchant's household,
she took none of them.
When the merchant returned,
he angrily brought the matter to the authorities.
The officials, understanding the circumstances,
did not pursue the matter.
Alas!
How is this different from Shòutíng Hóu's return to Hàn?
Yet, to kill her own child and leave,
she is indeed a狠心 person in the world!
According to the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì"
There was a butcher who was carrying meat home,
and it was already dusk.
Suddenly, a wolf came,
eyeing the meat on the担,
seemingly drooling with greed,
following step by step,
trailing behind for several miles.
The butcher was afraid,
and showed it the knife,
at which it retreated slightly;
but when he started walking again,
it followed him once more.
The butcher had no plan,
and thought to himself that what the wolf wanted was the meat,
so it would be better to暂时 hang it on a tree and fetch it early the next morning.
So he hooked the meat,
raised his foot to hang it between the trees,
and showed the wolf the empty担.
The wolf then stopped.
The butcher went straight home.
At dawn, he went to fetch the meat,
and from afar saw a huge object hanging from the tree,
looking like a person who had hanged himself,
and he was greatly frightened.
Cautiously approaching it,
he found it was a dead wolf.
Looking up and examining it closely,
he saw that it had the meat in its mouth,
and the meat hook had pierced the wolf's jaw,
like a fish swallowing bait.
At that time, wolf pelts were expensive,
worth more than ten taels of silver,
so the butcher became somewhat well-off.
Climbing a tree to seek fish,
the wolf met its demise—
it is also quite laughable!
A butcher was returning home late one evening,
with all the meat in his carrying pole gone,
leaving only some leftover bones.
On the road, two wolves
followed him for quite a distance.
The butcher grew fearful
and threw them a bone.
One wolf got the bone and stopped,
but the other still followed;
he threw another bone,
and the rear wolf stopped while the front one came again;
the bones were all gone,
yet the two wolves continued running side by side as before.
The butcher was in great distress,
afraid of being attacked from both front and rear.
Looking around, he saw a wheat threshing ground in the field,
where the owner had piled up firewood,
covered with a straw mat, forming a hill-like shape.
The butcher then ran over and leaned against it,
put down his carrying pole and held a knife.
The wolves dared not approach,
but glared fiercely at him.
After a short while,
one wolf went straight away;
the other sat in front like a dog,
after a long time,
its eyes seemed to close,
looking very relaxed.
The butcher suddenly sprang up,
chopped the wolf's head with his knife,
and after several more blows, killed it.
Just as he was about to leave,
he turned to look behind the firewood pile,
where the other wolf was digging a hole inside,
intending to tunnel through to attack him from behind.
Its body was already half inside,
only its buttocks and tail exposed.
The butcher cut off its thigh from behind,
and killed it too.
Only then did he realize that the front wolf had pretended to sleep,
likely to lure the enemy.
