Wolves are indeed cunning!
Yet both were killed in an instant.
How much trickery can beasts have?
They only add to the laughter!
A butcher was walking at dusk,
pursued by a wolf.
By the roadside, there was a temporary shelter left by night farmers,
so he rushed in and hid.
The wolf reached its paw through the thatch.
The butcher quickly grabbed it,
preventing it from pulling back.
But he had no way to kill it.
Only a small knife less than an inch long,
so he cut the skin under the paw,
and blew into it using the method for inflating pigs.
After blowing hard for a while,
he felt the wolf barely moving,
so he tied it with a belt.
Going out to look,
he saw the wolf swollen like an ox,
its legs straight and unable to bend,
its mouth open and unable to close.
He then carried it home.
If not for a butcher,
who could devise such a plan!
All three incidents involve butchers;
thus, the cruelty of butchers
can also be used to kill wolves.
According to the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì"
A merchant named Chǔ Shāng was staying in a Beijing lodging.
The lodging was connected to the neighboring house,
separated by a wooden partition;
there was a spot where a pine knot had fallen off the board,
leaving a hole the size of a cup.
her hair styled in a phoenix bun,
extremely beautiful;
then she extended an arm,
white as jade.
Everyone was shocked, thinking she was a demon,
and tried to grab her,
but she had already withdrawn.
A moment later,
she appeared again,
but only on the other side of the partition, her body unseen.
They rushed over,
but she disappeared again.
One merchant took a knife and hid under the partition.
Soon, her head appeared,
and he suddenly chopped it off,
it fell with the stroke,
blood splattering on the dust.
Everyone panicked and told the landlord.
The landlord, fearful, took the head and reported it.
When the merchants were arrested and interrogated,
it all seemed absurd.
They were detained for half a year,
but no evidence emerged,
nor did anyone file a lawsuit for the death,
so the merchants were released,
and the woman's head was buried.
According to the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì"
I heard from Huái Lìrén of Jǐ'nán: Liú Gōng Liàngcǎi
was the reincarnation of a fox.
Initially,
his father lived in the southern mountains,
when an old man visited his home,
claiming the surname Hú.
Asked where he lived,
he said:
"Right here in these mountains.
It's remote with few people,
just the two of us,
so we can spend mornings and evenings together,
that's why I came to pay my respects."
Thus, they conversed,
and his words were eloquent and pleasing,
so Liú grew fond of him.
They drank wine together happily,
and he left after getting drunk.
The next day he came again,
even more intimate and sincere.
Liú said:
"Since we became friends,
our bond has grown deep.
But I don't know where your home is,
how can I inquire about your well-being?"
Hú said:
"I dare not hide it,
I am actually an old fox from the mountains.
I have a predestined connection with you,
so I dared to befriend you.
Certainly, I cannot bring you fortune,
nor will I bring you misfortune,
I hope you trust me and are not alarmed."
Liú did not doubt him either,
and their bond grew even stronger.
They then compared ages,
Hú became the elder brother,
and they interacted like siblings.
If there were minor fortunes or misfortunes,
he would also inform Liú.
At that time, Liú had no heir,
and the old man suddenly said:
"Don't worry, sir,
I will become your descendant."
Liú was surprised by his strange words.
Hú said:
"My allotted lifespan is ending,
and the time for rebirth is near.
Rather than going elsewhere,
why not be born into an old friend's family?"
Liú said:
"Immortals live for ten thousand years,
how could it come to this?"
The old man shook his head and said,
"This is not for you to understand."
Then he left.
That night, Liú indeed dreamed the old man came,
saying:
"I am here now."
After waking up,
his wife gave birth to a boy,
who was Liú Gōng.
After growing up,
he was short in stature,
quick-witted and humorous in speech,
exactly like Hú.
He was talented and renowned from a young age,
and became a Jìnshì in the Rénchén year.
He was chivalrous by nature,
urgently helping those in need,
so guests from Qín, Chǔ, Yān, and Zhào
crowded his door;
wine sellers and cake vendors
formed a market in front of his gate.
According to the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì"
Mǎ Èrhùn
lived inside the eastern gate of Qīngzhōu,
making his living by selling flour.
His family was poor,
he had no wife,
and he and his mother shared a life of hardship.
One day,
while the old woman was alone at home,
a beautiful woman suddenly arrived.
She was about sixteen or seventeen years old,
dressed simply with her hair tied in a knot,
yet her radiance was dazzling.
The old woman, startled, looked her over and questioned her closely.
The girl smiled and said:
"I believe your son is sincere and honest,
and I wish to entrust myself to your household."
The old woman grew even more alarmed and said:
"Young lady, you are a celestial being.
With such words,
you would shorten the lifespans of my son and me by several years!"
The girl insisted.
Suspecting she must be a runaway from some noble household,
the old woman refused even more firmly.
The girl then left.
After three days,
she returned,
lingering and unwilling to leave.
The old woman asked her name.
She said:
"If you agree to accept me,
then I will tell you;
otherwise,
there is no need to ask."
The old woman said:
"We are of humble, servant-class bone,
to have a wife like you
would be neither fitting nor auspicious."
The girl smiled and sat on the edge of the bed,
her attachment seeming very sincere.
The old woman urged her to leave,
saying:
"Young lady, you should leave quickly,
do not bring misfortune upon us."
The girl then went out the door,
and the old woman watched her head west.
A few days later,
an old woman named Lǚ from the western alley came
and said to the mother:
"The neighboring girl, Dǒng Huìfāng,
is orphaned and has no one to rely on.
She wishes of her own accord to become your son's wife.
Why not accept her?"
The mother told her all her doubts and concerns.
Lǚ said:
"How could that be?
If anything goes wrong,
the blame will be on me."
The mother was overjoyed
and agreed.
After Lǚ left,
the old woman swept the room and laid out mats,
planning to wait for her son to return so he could go and marry her.
As dusk approached,
the girl drifted in of her own accord.
Entering the room, she paid respects to the mother,
rising and bowing with full ceremony.
She told the old woman:
"I have two maidservants.
Without your permission,
I did not dare bring them in."
The old woman said:
"My son and I live in this poor hut,
unused to employing maids or servants.
We earn a meager profit each day,
barely enough to support ourselves.
Now with the addition of a new daughter-in-law,
delicate and sitting idle to eat,
I fear we still won't have enough to fill our bellies;
adding two more maidservants—
how could we possibly support them by sipping the wind?"
The girl smiled and said:
"When the maids come,
they will not burden your household expenses;
they can all earn their own food."
The old woman asked:
"Where are the maids?"
The girl then called out:
"Qiūyuè, Qiūsōng!"
Before her voice had faded,
as if two birds had swooped down,
the two maids were already standing before them.
She immediately ordered them to kneel and kowtow to the mother.
Soon after, Mǎ returned home,
and his mother went to meet him and told him the news.
Mǎ was delighted.
Entering the room,
he saw green pillars and carved beams,
rivaling those of a palace;
the tables, screens, curtains, and drapes inside
were so dazzling they hurt the eyes.
Utterly astonished,
he dared not enter.
The girl came down from the bed to greet him with a smile,
looking like an immortal.
Even more terrified,
he retreated.
The girl took his hand,
sat him down, and spoke gently with him.
Mǎ was overjoyed beyond measure,
his body and spirit seeming not to belong together.
He then stood up,
wanting to go out and buy wine.
The girl said:
"No need."
She then ordered the two maids to prepare a feast.
Qiūyuè took out a leather bag,
held it toward the back of the room,
and shook it with a clattering sound.
Then she reached her hand inside
and pulled out a pot of wine,
a platter of roasted meats,
each item steaming hot and fragrant.
After they drank, they retired to sleep,
where flower-patterned rugs and brocade quilts
were exceptionally warm and soft.
At dawn, when he stepped outside,
the thatched hut was as before.
Mother and son both found this strange.
The old woman went to Lǚ's place,
intending to trace the origins of the matter.
Upon entering,
she first thanked her for acting as matchmaker.
Lǚ said in surprise:
"It has been a long time since I visited.
When did I ever recommend a neighboring girl to you?"
The old woman grew even more suspicious
and told her the whole story from beginning to end.
Lǚ was greatly alarmed
and immediately went with the old woman to see the new bride.
The girl smiled and welcomed them,
speaking at length about the principle of forming connections.
Lǚ, seeing her cleverness and beauty,
stared in astonishment for a long while,
then also offered no argument,
merely murmuring in agreement.
The girl gave Lǚ a whitewood backscratcher,
saying:
"I have nothing with which to repay your kindness,
but please accept this for scratching your back, Granny."
Lǚ took it and returned home.
Upon closer inspection, it had turned into white silver.
Since Mǎ had gained this wife,
his old livelihood was suddenly transformed,
and his household was entirely renewed.
His chests held countless sable furs and brocades,
which Mǎ could take and wear as he pleased;
but once he stepped outside the room,
they became plain cloth garments,
though still light and warm.
The clothes the girl wore herself were the same.
After four or five years had passed,
she suddenly said:
"I have been exiled to the mortal world for over ten years.
Because I had a bond with you,
I stayed for a while.
Now I must leave."
Mǎ苦苦 begged her to stay.
The girl said:
"Please choose another good match,
to continue the family line and tend the graves.
I will visit once a year."
Suddenly, she vanished.
Mǎ then married a woman from the Qín family.
Three years later,
on the Qīxī Festival,
as husband and wife were talking together,
the girl suddenly entered
and said with a smile:
"With your new spouse and fine happiness,
do you not think of your old friend?"
Mǎ was startled and rose,
sorrowfully pulling her to sit,
and then poured out his heartfelt feelings.
The woman said:
"I was just sending the Weaving Maiden across the river,
and took a moment to come see you."
They clung to each other,
talking endlessly.
Suddenly, someone in the sky called out
"Huìfāng,"
and the woman hurriedly rose to bid farewell.
Mǎ asked who it was,
and she said:
"I came with my elder sister Shuāngchéng just now,
but she cannot wait long."
Mǎ saw her off.
The woman said:
"Your lifespan is eighty years;
when the time comes,
I will come to collect your bones."
Having said this,
she vanished.
Now Mǎ is over sixty.
This man is merely simple and reticent,
with no other talents.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Mǎ Shēng's name is 'Hùn' (Muddle),
and his profession is lowly—
what did Huìfāng see in him?
From this, we see that immortals value simplicity, honesty, and sincerity.
I once said to a friend: 'If it were you and me,
even ghosts and foxes would abandon us;
the only thing that does not shame us before immortals
is our "muddleheadedness"
alone.'"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Lǐ Huìdǒu from Yìdū
was once traveling in the mountains
when he came upon several people drinking on the ground.
Seeing Lǐ arrive,
they cheerfully rose together,
pulled him to sit,
and vied to toast him.
Looking at their plates of food,
they were arrayed with rare delicacies.
After a while,
they were drinking merrily;
only the wine tasted thin and astringent.
Suddenly, from afar, a person approached,
with a face narrow and long,
perhaps two or three feet in length;
his hat was tall and slender in proportion.
The crowd exclaimed in alarm:
"The mountain god has arrived!"
And immediately scattered in all directions.
Lǐ also hid, crouching in a pit.
After a while, he rose to look,
and found that the food and wine had all vanished,
leaving only broken pottery vessels holding urine
and a few lizard tails on earthenware shards.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Xú Jìcháng,
a man from Línzī,
lived in Mòfáng Zhuāng east of the city.
He studied Confucianism but did not succeed,
so he left to become a clerk.
Once, while visiting relatives by marriage,
he passed by the Yú family's funeral hall.
Returning drunk at dusk,
he passed the place again
and saw a building with numerous splendid towers,
with an old man sitting at the door.
Xú, thirsty from wine, wanted a drink,
so he bowed to the old man and asked for some water.
The old man rose,
invited the guest inside,
led him to the main hall, and gave him a drink.
After drinking,
the old man said:
"It is hard to travel at dusk;
why not stay overnight
and leave early in the morning?"
Xú was also tired and weary,
and gladly accepted the offer.
The old man ordered servants to bring wine for the guest,
and then said to Xú:
"I have a proposal;
do not think it presumptuous:
You, sir, come from a respectable family of good reputation,
and could be joined in marriage.
I have a young daughter, not yet betrothed,
whom I wish to offer as a humble concubine,
hoping you will graciously accept."
Xú was flustered and did not know how to respond.
The old man immediately sent a servant to inform his relatives,
and also sent word for the young lady to dress up.
In a short while,
four or five men in tall hats and broad belts
arrived one after another.
The young lady also came out in dazzling attire,
with beauty surpassing the ordinary.
Then they all sat down together for a feast.
Xú's mind was in a daze,
and he only wished to sleep quickly.
After several rounds of wine,
he firmly declined, saying he could drink no more.
Then a young maid was sent to lead the couple into the bedchamber,
where they stayed together as husband and wife.
Xú asked her family name,
and the woman said:
"My surname is Xiāo,
and I am the seventh daughter."
He inquired further about her family background.
She said:
"Though I am lowly and plain,
matching a clerk should not bring disgrace or loneliness—
why trouble to investigate so thoroughly?"
Xú, infatuated with her beauty,
was tender and affectionate in every way,
and did not suspect anything else.
The woman said:
"We cannot make a home here.
I know your wife at home is very kind and gentle,
and may not object;
go back and clear a room,
and I will come on my own soon."
Xú agreed.
Then she put her arm around him,
and he suddenly fell asleep.
When he awoke,
his embrace was empty.
The sky was bright,
and pine shadows shaded the dawn;
he was lying on a foot-thick bed of sorghum stalks.
Astonished, he sighed and returned home,
and told his wife.
His wife jokingly cleared a room,
set up a bed inside,
closed the door, and left,
saying:
"The bride will arrive tonight."
And they laughed together.
When dusk fell,
his wife playfully pulled Xú to open the door,
saying:
"Could the bride already be inside?"
Upon entering,
they saw the beautiful woman sitting on the bed in splendid attire.
Seeing the two enter,
she rose gracefully to greet them.
Husband and wife were greatly astonished.
The woman covered her mouth and giggled softly,
then bowed respectfully.
The wife then prepared a feast
to celebrate their union.
The woman rose early to work,
never shirking any task.
One day she said to Xú:
"My sisters and aunts all wish to visit our home."
Xú worried that they would have nothing to serve the guests on short notice.
The woman said:
"They all know our family is not well-off,
so they will bring food and drink first;
they only need our sisters to do the cooking."
Xú told his wife,
and she agreed.
After breakfast,
someone indeed arrived carrying wine and meat,
set down the load, and left.
The wife took on the cook's duties.
In the afternoon,
six or seven young women arrived,
the eldest no more than forty or so.
They sat around drinking together,
filling the room with laughter and chatter.
Xú's wife peeked through the window
and saw only her husband and Seventh Sister sitting facing each other;
the other guests were invisible.
When the Big Dipper hung at the corner of the house,
they cheerfully departed.
The woman saw the guests off and had not yet returned.
The wife went in to look at the table
and found the cups and plates all empty.
She laughed and said:
"These girls must have been starving,
and licked the plates clean like dogs."
After a while,
the woman returned,
earnestly expressing thanks for the trouble,
took the utensils to wash herself,
and urged the wife to rest.
The wife said:
"Having guests at our home
and making them bring their own food and drink
is also quite a joke.
After several days,
Xú followed his wife's advice
and had the maidservant summon the guests again.
When the guests arrived,
they ate and drank to their heart's content;
only four dishes were left untouched,
with no spoons or chopsticks added.
The group laughed and said:
"The lady thinks we are wicked,
so she left these for the 'mediator'
Among the guests was a young woman,
around eighteen or nineteen years old,
wearing plain shoes and a white dress,
who was said to be newly widowed;
the wife called her Sixth Sister;
her demeanor was enchanting and coquettish,
skilled at laughter and witty banter.
As she gradually grew closer to Xú,
she often teased him with playful remarks.
When they played drinking games,
Xú acted as the recorder,
forbidding laughter and jesting.
Sixth Sister frequently broke the rules,
and was made to drink over ten cups in a row,
until her face flushed and she fell into a deep drunken stupor.
Her delicate body grew languid,
weak and unable to support itself.
Before long,
she slipped away.
Xú took a candle and searched for her,
only to find her sound asleep behind a dark curtain.
He leaned close to kiss her,
but she remained unaware.
When he reached his hand into her trousers,
he felt the swelling of her private parts.
Just as his heart began to stir,
he heard the guests calling for him from the banquet;
so he hastily straightened her clothes,
noticed a silk handkerchief in her sleeve,
and secretly took it before leaving.
By the middle of the night,
when the guests had all left their seats,
Sixth Sister was still not awake.
Seventh Sister went in and shook her,
and only then did she yawn and rise,
tying her skirt and tidying her hair before leaving with the others.
Xú cherished the memory with deep affection,
unable to let it go from his mind,
and planned to take out the handkerchief she had left behind in a private place to admire it,
but when he searched for it, it was already gone.
Suspecting it had fallen on the road while seeing off the guests,
he took a lamp and carefully examined the steps and courtyard,
but found nothing,
leaving him disheartened and dissatisfied.
When his wife asked about it,
Xú answered vaguely.
His wife laughed and said,
"Don't lie,
the handkerchief has already been taken by someone else,
so there's no use longing for it."
Xú was startled,
and told her the truth,
also expressing his lingering thoughts.
His wife said,
"She has no destined bond with you,
and your connection ends here."
When he asked why,
she replied:
"In her previous life, she was a courtesan;
you were a scholar,
who saw her and fell for her,
but were prevented by your parents,
unable to fulfill your desire,
and fell gravely ill.
You sent someone to tell her: 'I am beyond recovery.
If only you would come,
so I could touch your skin once,
I would die without regret!'
Moved by your sincerity,
she agreed to your request.
But as she was detained by some trivial matters,
she did not go immediately;
when she arrived the next night,
the sick man had already passed away: that was the one-touch bond from your previous life.
Beyond that, there is nothing more to hope for."
Later, when they held another banquet and invited all the women,
only Sixth Sister did not come.
Xú suspected his wife was jealous.
He felt quite resentful.
One day, his wife said to Xú:
"Because of Sixth Sister,
you wrongfully blame me.
She truly refuses to come,
so how is it my fault?
Now that our eight-year bond,
is about to come to an end,
let me do my utmost to arrange something for you,
to clear up your previous doubts.
Even if she won't come,
who can stop me from going to her?
If I go to her doorstep,
perhaps human effort can overcome fate,
who knows?"
Xú was delighted,
and agreed.
His wife took his hand,
and they floated as if walking on air,
arriving at her home in an instant.
The spacious hall was paved with yellow bricks,
with winding doors and passages,
no different from when he first saw it.
Her parents both came out,
and said:
"Our clumsy daughter has long enjoyed your warmth and care.
We, in our old age and frailty,
have been negligent in visiting,
surely you do not hold it against us?"
They then set up a banquet for the gathering.
The wife asked about her sisters.
Her mother said:
"They have all returned to their homes,
only Sixth Sister is here."
She immediately called a maid to fetch Sixth Sister,
but after a long time, she did not appear.
The wife went inside,
and dragged her out.
Sixth Sister kept her head bowed, silent and reserved,
unlike her previous playful self.
After a while,
the couple took their leave.
The wife said to Sixth Sister:
"Sister, you hold yourself too aloof,
making people resent me!"
Sixth Sister gave a faint smile and said:
"Why should a frivolous man be allowed near!"
The wife took the leftover cups from both of them,
forced them to exchange drinks,
and said:
"You've already kissed,
so why put on airs now?"
After a while,
Seventh Sister slipped away,
leaving only the two of them in the room.
Xú suddenly rose and pressed closer,
but Sixth Sister twisted and resisted.
Xú tugged at her clothes, knelt down, and pleaded pitifully,
until her expression gradually softened,
and they went hand in hand into the inner chamber.
Just as he was loosening her garments,
he suddenly heard earth-shaking shouts and cries,
with flames of light shooting through the door.
Sixth Sister was greatly alarmed,
pushed Xú away, and said:
"Disaster has struck suddenly,
what shall we do!"
Xú panicked, not knowing what to do,
and the young woman had already fled without a trace.
Xú sat there disconsolately for a while,
and the house vanished along with everything else.
Over ten hunters,
holding hawks and carrying blades, arrived,
and asked in surprise:
"Who is hiding here at night?"
Xú pretended he had lost his way,
and told them his name.
One of them said:
"We were just chasing a fox,
did you see it?"
He replied:
"No, I didn't."
Upon closer inspection of the place,
he realized it was the Yú family's burial ground.
He returned home dejected,
still hoping Seventh Sister would come again,
consulting morning bird omens for good news,
and evening lamp-wick divinations for signs,
but in the end, there was no news at all.
As told by Dǒng Yùxuán.
Based on the manuscript version of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Tutor Liú Fānghuī,
was a native of the capital.
He had a younger sister who was betrothed to a young man named Dài,
and the wedding day was approaching.
At that time, northern troops invaded the area,
and her father and brother, fearing that the women would be a burden,
planned to send her to the Dài family in her wedding attire.
Before her preparations were complete,
disorderly soldiers swarmed in,
and father and son fled separately.
The girl was captured by a Niúlù.
For several days, she followed him,
but he did not take any liberties with her.
At night, he made her sleep on a separate bed,
and provided her with ample food and drink.
Later, he captured another young man,
about the same age as the girl,
elegant and handsome in appearance.
The Niúlù said to him:
"I have no son,
and I intend to make you my heir.
Are you willing?"
The young man agreed.
Then, pointing to the girl, he said:
"If you agree,
she will be your wife."
The young man was delighted,
and willing to follow his command.
The Niúlù then made them share a bed,
and they became intimate and joyful.
Later, on the pillow, they exchanged surnames,
and it turned out the young man was Dài.
A certain gentleman from Shǎnxī,
who held a salt official position,
did not bring his family with him.
During the rebellion of Jiāng Xiāng,
his hometown fell into the hands of bandits,
cutting off all communication.
After the rebellion was quelled,
he sent someone to inquire,
but for a hundred li, there was no sign of life,
and no way to gather any news.
Later, when he went to the capital to report on his duties,
an old attendant had lost his wife,
and was too poor to remarry,
so the gentleman gave him some money to buy a wife.
At that time, the imperial army was returning in triumph,
having captured countless women,
who were put on the market with tags,
like cattle and horses for sale.
So he took the money to choose one.
Knowing he had little money,
he dared not ask for a young beauty.
Among them was an old woman who was quite neat and clean,
so he ransomed her and brought her home.
The old woman sat on the bed,
looked closely and said:
"Aren't you so-and-so the attendant?"
He asked how she knew,
and she said:
"You served under my son,
how could I not recognize you!"
The attendant was greatly shocked,
and hurriedly informed the gentleman.
The gentleman looked at her,
and indeed it was his mother.
They wept bitterly,
and he repaid the attendant double.
With more money, the attendant
no longer considered an old woman.
He saw a woman in her thirties,
with an extraordinary demeanor,
and ransomed her.
As they walked,
the woman kept looking back and said:
"Aren't you so-and-so the attendant?"
He asked in surprise again,
and she said:
"You served under my husband,
how could you not recognize me!"
The attendant was even more shocked,
and led her to see the gentleman.
The gentleman looked at her,
and indeed it was his wife.
He wept again in sorrow.
In one day, mother and wife were reunited,
and his joy was beyond measure.
So he gave the attendant a hundred taels of silver to marry a beautiful woman.
It must be that the gentleman had great virtue,
so the gods and spirits moved in response.
Unfortunately, the storyteller forgot his name,
but perhaps someone in Qínzhōng can tell it.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"In the calamity of war,
jade and stone are burned together,
truly so.
But as for this gentleman's family,
it is a story worth telling for their reunion.
After Dǒng Ēnbái,
there was only one grandson left,
and now even he cannot continue the sacrifices.
This is also the responsibility of the court officials,
alas!"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
In the mountains of Sìshuǐ,
there was formerly a Buddhist monastery,
with no villages around for miles,
rarely visited by people,
and a Daoist priest lived there.
Some said there were many large snakes inside,
so visitors stayed even farther away.
A young man entered the mountains to catch eagles.
Having gone deep into the mountains,
he had nowhere to stay for the night;
seeing a monastery in the distance,
he hurried toward it.
The Daoist priest exclaimed in surprise:
"Where have you come from, layman?
Fortunately, you were not seen by my children!"
He then invited him to sit and
prepared porridge for him.
Before he finished eating,
a huge snake entered,
over ten arm-spans thick,
raising its head toward the guest,
its angry eyes flashing like lightning.
The guest was terrified.
The Daoist priest struck its forehead with his palm
and shouted:
"Away!"
The snake then lowered its head and entered the eastern chamber.
It wriggled for a while,
before its entire body was inside;
coiling up there,
it filled the whole room.
The guest was even more frightened,
trembling all over.
The Daoist priest said:
"This is what I usually keep.
With me here,
there's no harm;
what I worry about is
if the guest encounters them on his own."
As soon as the guest sat down,
another snake entered,
slightly smaller than the first,
about five or six arm-spans thick.
Seeing the guest, it suddenly stopped,
blinking and flicking its tongue like the previous one.
The Daoist priest scolded it again,
and it also entered the chamber.
The chamber had no space to lie down,
so half of it coiled around the beams,
and the earth on the walls shook and fell with a sound.
The guest grew even more fearful,
and did not sleep all night.
Early in the morning, he wanted to leave,
and the Daoist priest saw him off.
Outside the door,
he saw on the walls and steps,
snakes as large as bowls and cups,
some moving, some lying still.
Seeing a living person,
they all looked ready to devour him.
The guest, terrified,
walked close to the Daoist priest under his arm,
and asked to be escorted out of the valley,
before returning home.
A fellow villager of mine was staying in Zhōngzhōu,
and took up lodging at the Shéfó Temple.
The temple monks prepared supper,
and the meat broth was quite delicious,
but each piece was round,
resembling chicken necks.
Suspicious,
he asked the temple monks:
"How many chickens did you kill to get so many necks?"
The monk said:
"These are snake segments."
The guest was greatly alarmed,
and some rushed out the door to vomit.
After going to bed,
he felt something wriggling on his chest;
feeling it,
it turned out to be a snake.
He immediately jumped up in terror and cried out.
The monk rose and said:
"This is a common occurrence,
nothing to be alarmed about!"
Then, using a torch to illuminate the walls,
they were covered with snakes large and small,
and the bed and floor were full of them as well.
The next day,
the monk led him into the Buddha hall.
Under the Buddha's seat was a huge well,
and in the well was a snake,
as thick as a giant urn,
poking its head over the edge of the well but not coming out.
Lighting a torch to look down,
they saw millions of snake offspring,
living together there.
The monk said,
"In the past, the snake emerged and caused harm,
so the Buddha sat atop it to suppress it,
and the trouble finally ceased."
So it is said.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Mín Zhǔcóngjiǎn from Bózhōu,
his mother was sitting in the house,
when a light rain fell and the sky darkened,
she saw the Thunder God holding a hammer,
flapping his wings as he entered.
Greatly alarmed,
she quickly poured the contents of a chamber pot over him.
The Thunder God, stained with filth,
as if struck by a knife or axe,
turned and fled in haste;
straining to spread his wings and soar,
he could not get away.
Tumbling about in the courtyard,
he bellowed like an ox.
The clouds in the sky gradually lowered,
until they were level with the eaves.
From within the clouds came a whinnying sound like a horse,
answering the Thunder God.
After a while,
rain poured down violently,
washing away all the filth from his body,
and then he departed with a thunderclap.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Hú Dàchéng,
was from Chǔ.
His mother had long been a devout Buddhist.
Chéng studied with a tutor,
and his route passed by the Guānyīn Shrine;
his mother instructed him to always go in and pay respects when passing by.
One day, arriving at the shrine,
he saw a young girl playing with a child inside,
her hair just covering her neck,
and her demeanor graceful and lovely.
At the time, Chéng was fourteen,
and he took a liking to her.
He asked her name,
and the girl smiled and said:
"I am Liǎngjiǎo, daughter of Jiāo the painter, who lives west of the shrine.
What do you want to know for?"
Chéng asked further:
"Do you have a betrothed family?"
The girl blushed and said:
"No, I don't."
Chéng said:
"I could be your husband,
would that be good?"
The girl said shyly:
"I cannot decide for myself."
But her eyes were clear and bright,
glancing up and down at Chéng,
her expression seeming pleased and approving.
Chéng then left.
The girl chased after him and called from a distance:
"Cuī Ěrchéng,
is a friend of my father's,
if you ask him to be the matchmaker,
it will surely succeed."
Chéng said:
"Alright."
Thinking of her cleverness and affection,
he admired her even more.
Returning home,
he honestly told his mother of his wish.
His mother had only this son,
and often feared to oppose him,
so she immediately asked Cuī to act as matchmaker.
Jiāo demanded an extravagant betrothal gift,
and the matter nearly fell through.
Cuī strongly praised Chéng's noble lineage and fine talent,
and Jiāo finally agreed.
Chéng had an uncle,
old and without sons,
who held a teaching post in Húběi.
His wife died at his post,
and Chéng's mother sent him to attend the funeral.
After several months, as he was about to return,
his uncle fell ill,
and also died.
His stay thus prolonged,
it happened that a great bandit occupied Húnán,
and news from home was cut off.
Chéng took refuge among the common people,
left alone and desolate with only his shadow for company.
One day,
an old woman of about forty-eight or forty-nine,
wandered around the village,
lingering until sunset without leaving.
She said of herself:
"Uprooted by war, I have nowhere to return,
and I intend to sell myself."
Someone asked her price,
and she said:
"I disdain to be a slave,
nor do I wish to be a wife,
but if someone will treat me as a mother,
I will follow them,
without haggling over the price."
Those who heard laughed.
Chéng went to see her,
and noticed one or two features in her face somewhat resembled his mother's,
which touched his heart and filled him with great sorrow.
Thinking of himself as alone with no one to mend his clothes,
he invited her home,
treating her with the respect due a son to his mother.
The old woman was pleased,
and cooked meals and wove sandals for him,
toiling like a mother.
If he displeased her, she would scold him;
but if he suffered the slightest illness or hardship,
her care and affection surpassed that of a birth mother.
Suddenly she said to him:
"This place is peaceful,
fortunately free from worries.
But you are grown now,
and though living as a wanderer,
the great bonds of human relations must not be neglected.
In two or three days,
I shall arrange a marriage for you."
Chéng wept and said:
"I already have a wife,
but we are separated north and south."
The old woman said:
"In times of great turmoil,
human affairs are overturned,
how can you stubbornly wait?"
Chéng wept again and said:
"Not only is the vow of marriage not to be broken,
but who would entrust their beloved daughter to a drifting wanderer?"
The old woman did not reply,
but prepared curtains, bedding, and pillows for him,
all very thorough and complete.
He did not know where they came from.
One day,
when the sun had already set,
she admonished Chéng, saying:
"Sit by the candle and do not sleep;
I am going to see if the bride has arrived yet."
With that, she went out the door and left.
When the third watch had passed,
and Wēn had not returned,
he grew very suspicious.
Suddenly, he heard a commotion outside the door.
Going out to look,
he saw a woman sitting in the courtyard,
her hair disheveled, sobbing.
Startled, he asked:
"Who are you?"
She did not reply.
After a long while,
she finally said:
"To marry me here
is not a blessing either,
only death awaits me!"
Chéng was greatly alarmed,
not knowing the reason.
The woman said:
"I was betrothed in my youth to Hú Dàchéng;
unexpectedly, Hú went north,
and news was cut off.
My parents forced me to marry into your family.
My body can be brought here,
but my will cannot be taken away!"
Upon hearing this, Chéng cried out:
"I am that Hú.
Are you, my dear, Língjiǎo?"
The woman stopped weeping and was astonished,
unable to believe it.
They went together into the room,
and by the lamplight, she looked closely,
saying:
"Could this be a dream?"
Thereupon, her sorrow turned to joy,
and they told each other of their hardships of separation.
Previously, after the chaos,
for a hundred lǐ in Húnán,
the land was swept clean, with no one left.
Jiāo took his family and fled to the east of Chángshā,
and there accepted a betrothal from Zhōu Shēng.
Amid the chaos, they could not hold the wedding ceremony,
so it was arranged that she would be sent to his home that evening.
The woman wept and refused to wash or comb her hair;
her family forced her into the carriage.
On the way,
the woman tumbled out of the carriage.
Then four men arrived carrying a sedan chair,
saying they were from the Zhōu family to fetch the bride.
They immediately helped her into the sedan chair,
and it sped along as if flying,
stopping only when they arrived here.
An old woman pulled her inside,
saying:
"This is your husband's home;
just go in and don't cry.
Your mother-in-law
will arrive morning or evening."
Then she left.
Chéng questioned her to understand the situation,
and only then realized the old woman was a divine being.
Husband and wife burned incense and prayed together,
wishing for mother and son to be reunited.
His mother, since the military horses imposed strict security,
had fled with other women to hide in mountain streams and valleys.
One night,
there was a clamor saying bandits were coming,
and they all panicked and scattered to hide.
A youth offered his horse to the mother.
In her haste, she had no time to ask questions;
she leaned on his shoulder and mounted,
and the horse moved swiftly and lightly,
reaching the lake in an instant.
The horse galloped across the water,
its hooves not stirring the waves.
Before long,
he helped her down,
pointing to a house, saying:
"You can live here."
The mother was about to open her mouth to thank him;
turning to look at the horse,
it had transformed into a golden-haired hǒu,
over ten feet tall,
and the youth leaped onto it and rode away.
The mother knocked on the door with her hand,
and it opened wide.
Someone came out to ask,
and she found the voice strangely familiar.
Looking at him,
it was Chéng.
Mother and son embraced and wept.
The wife also woke in surprise,
and the whole family rejoiced and comforted each other.
They suspected the old woman was an incarnation of the Great Being.
From then on, they recited the Guānyīn sūtras and mantras with even greater devotion.
Thus they settled in Húběi,
managing fields and building a home.
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Mǎ Yǒng,
a man from Qí,
was greedy by nature,
and a scoundrel.
His home was repeatedly empty,
and the villagers jokingly named him
"Hungry Ghost."
Over thirty years old,
he grew increasingly impoverished,
wearing tattered clothes like a quail,
his arms crossed over his shoulders,
snatching food in the market.
Everyone shunned him,
not counting him among their kind.
In the county, there was an old man named Zhū,
who in his youth took his wife to live in the markets of the five capitals,
engaging in an unsavory trade.
In his later years, he returned to his hometown,
and was greatly criticized by the scholar class;
but Zhū behaved cleanly and did good deeds,
and people gradually began to treat him with courtesy.
One day,
he encountered Mǎ snatching food without paying,
and being harassed by the shopkeeper.
Taking pity on him,
he paid the money on his behalf.
He took him back home,
gave him a few hundred coins,
so he could use it as capital.
Mǎ left,
but refused to plan any proper work,
sitting idle and eating.
Before long,
his funds were exhausted again,
and he returned to his old ways.
But he often feared meeting Zhū,
so he went to Línyì.
At night, he slept in the Confucian temple,
and on cold winter nights,
he would pluck the tassels from the crowns of the sages' statues and huddle against their tablets for warmth.
The school official found out,
and in anger wanted to punish him.
Mǎ pleaded pitifully for mercy,
offering to make money for the teacher.
The school official was pleased,
and let him go.
Mǎ found out that a certain student was wealthy,
went to his door and forcibly demanded money,
deliberately provoking his anger;
then he cut himself with a knife,
and falsely accused the student to the school.
The school official extorted a heavy bribe,
and only then refrained from reporting and expelling him.
The students were collectively outraged,
and jointly accused him to the county magistrate.
The magistrate investigated and found the truth,
had him beaten forty strokes,
put a cangue around his neck,
and he died after three days.
That night,
Old Man Zhū dreamed that Mǎ entered wearing a cap and sash,
and said:
"I owe you a great debt of gratitude,
and have now come to repay it."
Upon waking,
his concubine gave birth to a son.
The old man knew it was Mǎ,
and named him Mǎ'er.
He was not bright in his youth,
but his father was pleased that he could read.
In his twenties,
he exerted himself in managing affairs,
and managed to enter the county school.
Later, while staying at an inn for an examination,
he lay down on the bed during the day,
and saw that the walls were all pasted with old examination essays;
looking at them,
he saw
"The Nature of Dogs"
as a four-sentence topic,
and felt it was quite difficult;
he read it and memorized it.
Entering the examination hall,
it happened to be that exact topic,
so he copied it,
achieved an excellent grade,
and received a stipend.
In his sixties,
he was appointed as an instructor in Línyì County.
After serving for several years,
he had not made a single friend based on moral principles.
Only when someone took money from their sleeve
would he laugh like a cormorant;
otherwise, his eyelashes would seem an inch long,
and he would glare sternly as if he did not know them.
Once, a magistrate ordered a light punishment for a minor offense by some students,
but he cruelly flogged them as if dealing with bandits.
If someone sued a scholar,
he would immediately come knocking on the door.
With such numerous misdeeds,
the students could no longer endure him.
And as he neared seventy,
he was bloated, deaf, and hunchbacked,
often asking people about black beard dye.
A certain wild student
ground up madder root and deceived him with it.
At dawn, everyone looked,
and he resembled the statue of a temple guardian deity.
Furious,
he detained the student;
but the student had already fled early in the night.
Because of this, anger festered within him,
and he died a few months later.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wén Rénshēng
was from Hénán.
After being ill for days,
he saw a scholar enter,
kneel by his bed,
and bow with utmost courtesy.
Then he invited Wén to take a short walk,
took his arm and spoke at length,
chattering as they walked,
and even after several *lǐ*, still did not say goodbye.
Wén stopped,
cupped his hands, and bid farewell.
The scholar said:
"I must trouble you to go a bit further;
I have a favor to ask."
Wén asked what it was.
He replied:
"All of us scholars are under the jurisdiction of the Examination Corruption Department.
The department head is named King Hollow-Belly Ghost.
At the first meeting,
it is customary to cut a piece of flesh from the thigh;
I beg you to intercede on my behalf."
Wén asked in shock:
"What crime warrants this?"
He said:
"No crime is necessary;
this is an old rule.
If one is rich in bribes,
they can redeem themselves.
But I am poor."
Wén said:
"I am not acquainted with King Ghost;
how can I be of help?"
He said:
"Your grandfather was of the same generation as his grandfather,
so he should listen to you."
As they spoke,
they entered a city.
Arriving at a government office,
the buildings were not very spacious,
but there was a tall, wide hall;
below the hall, two stone tablets stood east and west,
with green characters larger than a basket,
one saying
"Filial Piety, Brotherly Respect, Loyalty, Trustworthiness,"
and the other saying
"Propriety, Righteousness, Integrity, Shame."
Ascending the steps,
he saw a plaque in the hall,
with large characters reading
"Examination Corruption Department."
Between the pillars,
a couplet was carved on a board in green characters:
"Daily schools, daily academies, daily granaries—two words 'virtuous conduct' for hidden instruction;
Upper scholars, middle scholars, lower scholars—one hall of 'ritual and music' for ghostly students."
Before he finished looking around,
the official emerged,
with curly hair and a hunchback,
as if hundreds of years old;
his nostrils pointed upward,
his lips protruded outward,
and did not cover his teeth.
Following him was a registrar,
with a tiger's head and a human body.
More than ten others stood in attendance,
half of them fierce and ugly like mountain spirits.
The scholar said:
"This is King Ghost."
Wén was terrified and wanted to retreat.
But King Ghost had already seen him,
descended the steps, bowed, and invited Wén up,
then asked about his well-being.
Wén only nodded.
He asked again:
"What brings you here?"
Wén explained the scholar's request in full.
King Ghost's expression changed and he said:
"This is an established rule;
even a father's command would not make me relent!"
His demeanor was stern and imposing,
as if not a word could be added.
Wén dared not speak further,
and abruptly rose to take his leave.
King Ghost walked sideways to see him off,
and only turned back after reaching the gate.
Wén did not leave but sneaked back in to see what would happen.
Reaching the hall,
he saw the scholar and several others,
with their arms bound and fingers clamped,
clearly in shackles.
A fierce man came with a knife,
stripped the scholar's thigh,
and cut a piece of flesh,
about three fingers wide.
The scholar howled until he was hoarse.
Wén, young and righteous,
could not contain his anger,
and shouted:
"Such cruelty—what kind of world is this!"
King Ghost rose in surprise,
ordered a temporary halt to the cutting,
and hurried to greet Wén.
But Wén, furious, had already left,
and told everyone in the market,
vowing to appeal to the Heavenly Emperor.
Someone laughed and said:
"How naive!
The vast blue sky—
where would you find the Heavenly Emperor to plead your case?
These people are only close to Yánluó,
so calling him might get a response."
Then he showed Wén the way.
Wén hurried there
and indeed saw a majestic palace with imposing steps,
with Yánluó seated inside.
He knelt on the steps and cried out his grievance.
After Yánluó summoned and questioned him,
he immediately ordered ghosts to take ropes and hammers and go.
Soon after,
King Ghost and the scholar both arrived.
After confirming the truth of the matter,
Yánluó said angrily:
"I pitied you for your past hardships,
and temporarily appointed you to this post,
awaiting your rebirth into a noble family;
how dare you act like this!
I shall remove your good tendons
and add evil bones,
and punish you to never prosper for generations to come!"
The ghosts then beat him,
and he fell to the ground,
losing a tooth.
Then they cut his fingertips with a knife,
pulled out his tendons,
bright and white like silk.
King Ghost screamed in pain,
sounding like a pig being slaughtered.
Soon, the tendons from his feet were also pulled out,
and two ghosts escorted him away.
The scholar bowed and took his leave.
The xiùcai followed him out,
expressing heartfelt gratitude.
As he escorted him through the market,
they passed a house with a crimson curtain hanging in the doorway.
Inside, a girl revealed half her face,
her appearance and makeup utterly beautiful.
The scholar asked,
"Whose house is this?"
The xiùcai replied,
"This is the pleasure quarter."
After they had passed,
the scholar lingered, unable to tear himself away,
and firmly insisted the xiùcai stop.
The xiùcai said,
"You came for my sake,
yet now you leave alone and lonely—
how can my heart bear it?"
The scholar firmly declined,
so the xiùcai departed.
Watching the xiùcai go far away,
the scholar hurriedly slipped inside the curtain.
The girl received him,
delight showing on her face.
Entering the room, they sat close together,
exchanging names.
The girl said of herself,
"My surname is Liǔ,
and my childhood name is Qiūhuá."
An old woman came out
and prepared food and wine for them.
When the wine was finished,
they entered the bed curtains,
their passion and affection intense,
and earnestly pledged to marry.
At dawn,
the old woman entered and said,
"Our funds for daily expenses are exhausted;
we must trouble you, sir, for some money—
what shall we do?"
The scholar, considering his own empty purse,
felt anxious and ashamed, saying nothing.
After a long while,
he said,
"I truly did not bring a single coin with me.
I should write a promissory note as guarantee,
and repay you as soon as I return home."
The old woman’s expression changed as she said,
"Have you ever heard of a night-visiting lady demanding payment on credit?"
Qiūhuá frowned,
not uttering a word.
The scholar temporarily removed his outer garment as a pledge.
The old woman held it and laughed, saying,
"This still can’t even cover the cost of the wine."
Grumbling discontentedly,
she went inside with the girl.
The scholar felt ashamed.
After a while,
he still hoped the girl would come out to bid him farewell
and reaffirm their earlier pledge;
but for a long time there was no sound.
He stealthily crept in to peek
and saw the old woman and Qiūhuá
transformed from the shoulders up into ox-headed demons,
standing opposite each other with gleaming eyes.
Terrified,
he rushed out;
wanting to return home,
he found a hundred branching paths diverging
and had no idea which way to go.
Asking the townspeople,
none knew the name of his village.
Wandering among the shops and stalls,
for two days and nights,
his heart filled with sorrow and bitterness,
his empty stomach growling with hunger,
he could not decide whether to advance or retreat.
Suddenly the xiùcai passed by,
saw him,
and exclaimed in surprise,
"Why haven’t you returned yet,
and why are you in such disarray?"
The scholar flushed with shame and could not reply.
The xiùcai said,
"I see!
Could it be you were beguiled by the flower yācha?"
Then he strode off angrily,
saying,
"Mother and daughter Qiūhuá,
how dare you show so little respect!"
He left for a short while
and then returned with the scholar’s clothes, handing them to him, saying,
"That wanton maid was impertinent;
I have already scolded and berated her."
He escorted the scholar home
before bidding farewell and leaving.
The scholar suddenly fell unconscious for three days and then revived,
recounting the events vividly and in detail.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Lord Xú Xīng of Yízhōu
said of himself that at night he served as Yánluó Wáng.
In the same prefecture, a certain Mr. Mǎ did likewise.
Hearing of this, Lord Xú
visited his home
and asked Mr. Mǎ,
"What matters did you handle in the underworld last night?"
Mr. Mǎ said,
"Nothing much,
only escorting Zuǒ Luóshí as he ascended to heaven.
Lotus flowers fell from the sky,
their blossoms as large as houses, so it is said."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Lǐ Zhìjūn, a Provincial Graduate from Chángshān, was traveling to Qīngzhōu
when he encountered six or seven men along the way.
Their accents resembled those of Yān.
Upon closer inspection,
he noticed that both cheeks of each man
bore scars as large as coins.
Finding this strange,
he asked what illness had caused such identical marks.
The travelers replied: Last year, while sojourning in Yúnnán,
we lost our way at dusk
and entered a great mountain.
With sheer cliffs and jagged rocks,
there was no way out.
So we tethered our horses, unpacked our belongings,
and settled by some trees to rest.
Late into the night,
tigers, leopards, owls, and other creatures
began howling one after another.
We huddled together, knees drawn up,
unable to sleep.
Suddenly, a giant appeared,
standing over ten feet tall.
We crouched in fear,
not daring to breathe.
The giant approached,
seized the horses with his hands, and devoured them;
six or seven were gone in an instant.
Then he broke off a long branch from a tree,
pierced each of us through the cheeks,
stringing us together like fish.
Once strung,
he lifted us and walked a few steps,
but the branch creaked and cracked.
Fearing we might fall,
he bent the two ends of the branch
and weighed them down with a massive rock before leaving.
Sensing he had gone far,
we drew our daggers, cut through the branch,
and fled in agony.
We saw the giant returning with another.
Terrified,
we hid in the thick underbrush.
The newcomer was even larger.
He reached the trees
and paced back and forth, searching,
as if looking for something but failing to find it.
Then he let out a chirping sound,
like the cry of a giant bird,
clearly furious,
likely angry that the first giant had deceived him.
He slapped the first giant across the face with his palm,
and the giant hunched over, submitting meekly,
not daring to protest in the slightest.
Soon, both left.
Only then did we scramble out in panic.
We fled through the wilderness for a long time
until we saw a flickering light atop a ridge in the distance.
We hurried toward it.
Upon arrival, we found a man living in a stone chamber.
We entered, bowed in a circle,
and recounted our ordeal.
The man gestured for us to sit,
saying:
"These creatures are utterly detestable,
but even I cannot restrain them.
Wait until my sister returns;
we can discuss a plan with her."
Before long,
a woman entered from outside, carrying two tigers on her shoulders.
She asked where we had come from.
We knelt and kowtowed, explaining our situation.
The woman said:
"I’ve long known these two were causing trouble,
but I never imagined they were this savage and stubborn!
They must be dealt with immediately."
She fetched a copper hammer from the stone chamber,
weighing three to four hundred hú,
and vanished out the door.
The man cooked tiger meat to feed us.
Before the meat was fully cooked,
the woman had already returned,
saying:
"They tried to flee when they saw me,
but I chased them for dozens of lǐ
and cut off one of their fingers before coming back."
She tossed the finger onto the ground;
it was larger than a shinbone.
We were utterly terrified.
We asked for their names,
but they did not answer.
After a short while,
the meat was ready,
but our wounds hurt too much to eat.
The woman sprinkled medicinal powder over our injuries,
and the pain immediately ceased.
At dawn,
she escorted us back to the trees.
All our luggage was still there.
We shouldered our packs and walked over ten lǐ
until we passed the spot of the previous night’s battle.
The woman pointed it out to us:
in a stone hollow, a basin’s worth of residual blood remained.
Once out of the mountains,
the woman bid us farewell and returned.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Xiàng Gǎo,
courtesy name Chūdàn,
was from Tàiyuán.
He and his elder brother by a concubine, Xiàng Shèng,
were deeply affectionate.
Shèng was intimate with a courtesan,
named Bōsī,
and they had sworn an oath of eternal love;
but because her madam demanded an exorbitant price,
their plans could not be fulfilled.
It happened that the madam wished to leave the profession and reform,
and was willing to send Bōsī away first.
There was a young master of the Zhuāng family,
who had long been fond of Bōsī,
and requested to redeem her to be his concubine.
Bōsī said to her madam:
"Since we wish to escape hardship together,
it is like wanting to leave hell and ascend to heaven.
But if I become someone's concubine,
how much difference is there really!
If you are willing to follow my wish,
Master Xiàng is the suitable one."
The madam agreed,
and conveyed this intention to Shèng.
At that time, Shèng had lost his wife and was unmarried,
he was overjoyed,
and exhausted his resources to betroth Bōsī and bring her home.
When Zhuāng heard of this,
he was furious at having his favorite taken away,
and encountering them by chance on the road,
he hurled great abuse;
Shèng did not submit.
Zhuāng then incited his attendants to beat him with broken canes,
and only left when Shèng was near death.
Gǎo heard and rushed to see,
but his brother was already dead,
and he was overwhelmed with grief and indignation.
He prepared a plaint and went to the prefectural office.
Zhuāng extensively distributed bribes,
causing Gǎo's case to find no redress.
Gǎo's hidden resentment knotted within,
with nowhere to appeal,
he only thought of waylaying Zhuāng on the road to assassinate him.
Daily he carried a sharp blade,
hiding in the thickets of a mountain path.
After a long time,
his plan gradually leaked out.
Zhuāng, knowing of his scheme,
went out with very strict precautions;
hearing that in Fénzhōu there was a man named Jiāo Tóng,
brave and skilled at archery,
he hired him with much gold as a guard.
Gǎo had no stratagem left to employ,
yet still watched for him daily.
One day,
while he lay in ambush,
a violent rainstorm arose,
soaking him from head to toe,
he shivered bitterly from the cold.
Then a fierce wind arose from all sides,
followed by hailstones,
and suddenly his body felt such pain and itching he could no longer bear it.
On the ridge there was an old mountain god temple,
he forced himself up and ran towards it.
Once inside the temple,
he found a Taoist priest he knew was there.
Previously,
this priest had begged for alms in the village,
and Gǎo had always given him food,
so the priest recognized Gǎo.
Seeing Gǎo's clothes soaked,
he gave him a cloth robe,
saying:
"Change into this for now."
Gǎo changed his clothes,
and crouched shivering like a dog,
looking at himself,
he saw fur and hide suddenly grow,
his body had transformed into a tiger.
The Taoist priest had already vanished.
In his heart he was shocked and resentful,
but then it occurred to him that he could get his enemy and eat his flesh,
this plan was also quite good.
He went down the mountain and hid in his old spot,
seeing his own corpse lying in the thicket,
he then realized his former self had died;
still fearing it would be devoured by crows and kites,
he patrolled and guarded it constantly.
The next day,
Zhuāng finally passed this way,
the tiger burst forth violently,
pounced on Zhuāng from his horse, knocking him down,
bit off his head,
and swallowed it.
Jiāo Tóng turned his horse and shot,
hitting the tiger in the belly,
and it stumbled and died.
Gǎo, amidst the brambles,
felt as if awakening from a dream;
after another night,
he was finally able to walk,
and returned listlessly.
His family, because he had not returned for several nights,
were just then all alarmed and suspicious,
seeing him,
they joyfully greeted and inquired after him.
Gǎo only lay down,
sluggish and unable to speak.
After a little while,
hearing news of Zhuāng,
they vied to come to his bedside to congratulate and tell him,
Gǎo then said himself:
"The tiger was me."
And he recounted the strange events.
From this it spread.
Zhuāng's son, pained by his father's terribly cruel death,
heard this and detested it,
and thus sued Gǎo.
The officials considered it fantastical and without evidence,
and set it aside without hearing.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"When a warrior's ambition is fulfilled,
he surely does not return alive,
this is what has been lamented through the ages.
To borrow another's killing to return to life,
the arts of the immortal are indeed divine!
Yet in this world, things enough to make one's hair stand on end are many.
If those with grievances must always remain human,
one cannot help but wish they might temporarily become tigers!"
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Dǒng Shàngshū Kěwèi of Qīngzhōu,
maintained strict discipline in his household,
men and women, inside and out,
did not dare exchange a single word.
One day,
a maidservant and a manservant were flirting outside the middle gate,
the young master saw them and angrily scolded them,
and they each ran off.
When night came,
the master was sleeping in his study with a page boy.
It was then the height of summer,
and the room's door was wide open.
In the deep of the night,
the page heard a very fierce sound from the bed,
and woke with a start.
In the moonlight's shadow,
he saw the former servant carrying something out the door.
Since he was a member of the household,
the page did not think it deeply strange,
and went back to sleep.
Suddenly he heard the thudding sound of boots,
a tall, stalwart man with a red face and long beard,
resembling the image of the Marquis of Shòutíng,
entered holding a human head.
The page was terrified,
and crept snake-like under the bed.
He heard from the bed sounds of creaking and rustling,
as if shaking out clothes,
or rubbing a belly,
and after a while it finally stopped.
The sound of boots rang out again,
and he left.
The page gradually stretched his neck out,
and saw the dawn light on the window lattice.
Reaching his hand to feel the bed,
his hand touched something sticky and wet,
and smelling it, it was the stench of blood.
He cried out for the young master,
who then awoke.
He told him and they lit a light to look,
blood filled the pillow and mat.
Greatly alarmed,
they did not know the reason.
Suddenly, an official runner knocked at the door.
The young master went out to see him.
The runner was astonished,
and could only say it was a strange affair.
When questioned,
he reported:
"Just now, in front of the yamen, there was a man looking dazed and confused.
He shouted loudly: 'I have killed my master!'
Everyone saw bloodstains on his clothes,
so they seized him and reported to the officials.
Upon interrogation, it was learned he was a servant of the young master.
He claimed he had killed the young master,
and buried the head beside the Guān Temple.
We went to verify it,
and the hole in the earth was still fresh,
but the head was nowhere to be found."
The young master was shocked and bewildered.
He hurried to the public court,
and saw that the man was indeed the one who had previously molested the maid.
He then recounted the strange events.
The official was greatly perplexed,
severely punished the servant, and released him.
The young master did not wish to incur the enmity of such a petty man,
so he gave him the former maid as a wife,
and ordered him to leave.
After several days had passed,
their neighbor,
heard a tremendous crash from the servant's room at night, like something splitting apart.
He quickly got up and called out,
but received no response.
Pushing the door open to look inside,
he saw the husband and wife, along with their bed,
all cleanly severed into two halves.
Both the wood and the flesh bore cut marks,
as if sliced through by a single blade.
Guān Yǔ's spiritual manifestations are numerous,
but none are as strange as this one.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Zhāng Tàihuá from Tài'ān,
was a wealthy clerk.
His home was troubled by a fox,
and all attempts to control it were ineffective.
He reported the situation to the prefect,
but the prefect was also powerless to help.
At that time, in the east of the prefecture, a fox also resided in a villager's home.
People commonly saw it as a white-haired old man.
The old man exchanged visits and condolences with the residents,
observing the same etiquette as ordinary people.
He called himself the second son,
so everyone addressed him as
Hú Èryé.
It happened that a scholar was visiting the prefect,
and mentioned this strange affair.
The prefect advised the clerk,
to go and ask the old man.
At that time, someone from the east village was serving as a runner.
The clerk visited him,
and found it was indeed true.
So he went with him.
They set up a feast at the runner's home to invite Hú.
Hú arrived,
exchanging bows, toasts, and drinks,
no different from an ordinary person.
The clerk stated his request.
Hú said:
"I am well aware of it,
but I cannot exert myself on your behalf.
My friend, Zhōu Sān,
resides temporarily at the Yuè Temple.
He should be able to subdue it,
I will make a request on your behalf."
The clerk was pleased,
and expressed his thanks.
Before parting, Hú made an arrangement with the clerk:
tomorrow, prepare a feast east of the Yuè Temple.
The clerk accepted the instruction.
Hú indeed brought Zhōu there.
Zhōu had a curly beard and a stern, iron-like face,
and wore trousers and a jacket.
After several rounds of drinks,
he said to the clerk:
"Just now, Brother Hú Èr conveyed your esteemed intention.
I have fully understood the matter.
But these creatures are truly numerous and have many followers,
they cannot be persuaded with good words,
so using force is unavoidable.
Please allow me to lodge at your home temporarily;
I dare not decline this small effort."
The clerk thought to himself: getting rid of one fox,
only to gain another,
is exchanging one tyranny for another.
He hesitated and did not dare to agree immediately.
Zhōu already knew his thoughts,
and said:
"Do not fear.
I am not like the others,
and moreover, I have a fortunate connection with you.
Please do not doubt."
The clerk agreed.
Zhōu also instructed:
"Tomorrow, gather your family, close the doors, and sit inside the house.
Please do not make any noise."
The clerk returned home,
and followed all the instructions.
Soon, they heard sounds of attack, struggle, and combat in the courtyard,
which lasted for some time before ceasing.
Opening the door to look outside,
they saw bloodstains covering the steps.
In the courtyard were several small fox heads,
as large as bowls or cups.
Looking further at the cleared room,
they saw Zhōu sitting solemnly inside.
He clasped his hands and said with a smile:
"I have received your heavy trust,
the demonic creatures have been completely eradicated."
From then on, he stayed at their home,
and they treated each other like host and guest.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
There are many varieties of pigeons.
In Jìn, there is the Kūn Xīng;
in Lǔ, the Hè Xiù;
in Qián, the Yè Dié;
in Liáng, the Fān Tiào;
in Yuè, the Zhū Jiān: all are rare mountain breeds.
There are also types like Xuē Tóu, Diǎn Zi, Dà Bái, Hēi Shí, Fūfù Què, Huā Gǒu Yǎn, and so on.
Their names are too numerous to count,
and only enthusiasts can distinguish them.
Zhāng Gōngzǐ Dòngliàng from Zōupíng,
was passionately fond of them.
He sought them according to the classics,
striving to collect every breed.
He raised them
like caring for infants;
if they were cold, he treated them with powdered licorice,
if they were hot, he gave them salt grains.
Pigeons are prone to deep sleep,
and if they sleep too much,
they can become paralyzed and die.
When Zhāng was in Guǎnglíng,
he bought a pigeon for ten taels of gold.
Its body was very small,
and it was good at walking.
Placed on the ground,
it would circle endlessly,
not stopping until exhausted,
so it often needed to be held by someone.
At night, placing it among the flock to startle the other pigeons
could prevent the paralysis of their legs.
It was named
"Yè Yóu".
Among pigeon breeders in Qí and Lǔ,
none surpassed the young master;
and the young master also prided himself on his pigeons.
One night,
while sitting in his study,
suddenly a youth in white clothes knocked on the door and entered,
whom he did not recognize at all.
When asked,
he replied:
"I am a wanderer,
what use is there in mentioning my name?
From afar, I have heard that you keep the most splendid pigeons,
and this too is a lifelong passion of mine,
so I wish to feast my eyes upon them."
Zhāng then brought out all he had,
with all five colors present,
shining like brocaded clouds.
The youth smiled and said:
"People's words are indeed not false,
you, sir, may be called a master of pigeon-keeping.
I too have brought a couple with me,
would you care to see them?"
Zhāng was delighted,
and followed the youth away.
The moonlight was dim,
the wild fields desolate,
and in his heart he secretly felt suspicious and fearful.
The youth pointed and said:
"Please press on,
my lodging is not far ahead."
After a few more steps,
they saw a Daoist temple,
with only two pillars.
The youth took his hand and led him inside,
where it was dark without any lamps.
The youth stood in the courtyard,
and made pigeon calls with his mouth.
Suddenly two pigeons emerged: they looked like ordinary pigeons,
but their feathers were pure white;
they flew level with the eaves,
calling and fighting as they went,
and with every swoop,
they would surely turn a somersault.
The youth waved them away with his arm,
and they flew off wing to wing.
Again he pursed his lips and made a strange sound,
and two more pigeons emerged: the larger one was like a duck,
the smaller one only as big as a fist;
they alighted on the steps,
imitating a crane's dance.
The larger one stretched its neck and stood,
spreading its wings like a screen,
twisting and turning, calling and hopping,
as if leading it on;
the smaller one flew up and down, chirping,
sometimes alighting on its head,
its wings fluttering like a swallow landing on a cattail leaf,
its sound fine and fragmented,
like a pellet drum;
the larger one stretched its neck and dared not move,
its calls growing ever more urgent,
its sound changing like a chime stone,
the two harmonizing with each other,
interspersed with rhythmic beats.
After a while, the smaller one flew up,
and the larger one again tumbled about, calling to it.
Zhāng praised and sighed endlessly,
feeling himself dwarfed and ashamed.
Thereupon he bowed to the youth,
begging to be given a share of his treasures;
the youth refused.
Again he firmly pleaded.
The youth then scolded the pigeons away,
still making the earlier sound,
and summoned the two white pigeons,
holding them in his hands,
saying:
"If you do not disdain them,
take these to fulfill my obligation."
Zhāng received them and admired them: their eyes reflected the moonlight with an amber hue,
both pupils clear and transparent,
as if without any barrier,
the black pupils inside rounder than peppercorns;
opening their wings,
the flesh under the wings was crystalline,
their internal organs countable.
Zhāng found them most extraordinary,
but his desire was still not satisfied,
and he deceitfully kept pleading.
The youth said:
"There are still two kinds I have not presented,
but now I dare not ask you to view them anymore."
Just as they were heatedly discussing,
his family came in with hemp torches, searching for their master.
Looking back at the youth,
he had transformed into a white pigeon,
as big as a chicken,
and soared into the sky, flying away.
Moreover, the courtyard and buildings before their eyes all vanished,
revealing a small grave,
with two cypress trees planted.
Together with his family, holding the pigeons,
they returned in astonishment and wonder.
When he tried to make them fly,
they were as tame and extraordinary as before,
and although they were not the finest among them,
they were exceedingly rare in the human world.
Thereupon he cherished them to the utmost.
After two years,
he had bred three males and three females.
Even when relatives and close friends asked for them,
he would not give any away.
There was a certain elder friend of his father's,
a high official.
One day,
he saw the young master Zhāng
and asked:
"How many pigeons do you keep?"
The young master Zhāng answered vaguely and withdrew.
Suspecting that the man was fond of them,
he thought of making a gift of some, but found it hard to part with his favorites.
He also thought that the request of an elder
should not be flatly refused.
Moreover, he dared not offer ordinary pigeons,
so he chose two white ones,
put them in a cage and sent them over,
feeling that he was giving no less than a thousand pieces of gold.
Some days later he saw the official again
and looked rather pleased with himself,
but the other did not say a single word of thanks.
Unable to contain himself,
he asked:
"Were the birds I sent you any good?"
The answer was:
"They were quite plump and tasty."
Zhāng said in surprise:
"You cooked them?"
"Yes,"
said the other.
Zhāng said in great astonishment:
"Those were no ordinary pigeons:
they were what is commonly called 'Dádá'!"
The man thought back and said:
"There was nothing special about the taste."
Zhāng returned home sighing with regret.
That night
he dreamed that a youth in white came to him
and reprimanded him, saying:
"I thought you were capable of loving us,
so I entrusted my offspring to you.
Why did you cast pearls before swine
and cause us to perish in a cooking pot?
Now I am taking my young ones away."
With these words
he turned into a pigeon,
and all the white pigeons that had been raised followed him,
flying off chirping.
At daybreak Zhāng looked:
sure enough, they were all gone.
He was very upset about this,
so he gave away all he had raised
to close friends,
and in a few days they were all gone.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Things always gather around those who appreciate them.
Thus, when Lord Yè was fond of dragons, a real dragon entered his house.
How much more is this true of scholars in regard to good friends and worthy rulers in regard to good ministers?
But of all things, money is what the most people are fond of,
yet it gathers around the fewest.
This shows that ghosts and spirits become angry at greed,
but not at infatuation."
Once a friend gave red carp as a gift to the young master Sūn Yǔnián.
His family had no clever servants,
so he sent an old hired hand.
When the man reached the gate,
he poured out the water, took out the fish
and asked for a plate to serve them on.
By the time he reached his destination,
the fish were dried up and dead.
The young master smiled without a word.
He gave the hired hand wine as a reward
and had the fish cooked to serve at the feast.
When the man returned,
his master asked:
"Was the young master happy to get the fish?"
"Very happy,"
was the answer.
"How do you know?"
"The young master broke into a happy smile at the sight of the fish.
He immediately ordered wine for me
and had several of the fish cooked to reward me."
The master was greatly taken aback.
He thought to himself that the gift he had sent was not at all crude or inferior.
Why would it have been cooked and given to an underling?
So he berated the man:
"You must have acted stupidly and impolitely,
so the young master took his anger out on you."
The hired hand raised his hands and argued vehemently:
"Granted that I am crude and clumsy,
but I am not so inhuman as to go to the young master's gate
without being as careful as possible.
I was afraid the bucket would look inelegant,
so I respectfully asked for a plate, poured them out
and arranged them evenly before presenting them.
What wasn't thorough and careful about that?"
The master cursed him and sent him away.
A certain monk of Língyǐn Temple
was famous for his tea.
His teapot and mortar were both exquisite.
However, the tea he kept was of several grades,
and he always judged the quality of his guests to decide what grade to brew and serve.
He did not serve the best grade
except to distinguished guests and connoisseurs.
One day a high official came.
The monk served him with great deference.
He brought out fine tea
and brewed it personally,
hoping to win praise.
The official said nothing.
Greatly perplexed, the monk
brewed and served tea of the very best grade.
The official finished drinking
without a word of praise.
The monk could wait no longer.
He bowed and asked:
"How is the tea?"
The official picked up the cup, saluted with it and said:
"Quite hot."
These two incidents
can be laughed at along with the young master Zhāng's gift of pigeons.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
The Prince of Lù in Huáiqìng
was given to debauchery.
When he went among the common people,
he would seize any good-looking woman he saw.
The wife of a certain Wáng was seen by the prince,
who sent a carriage and horsemen straight into their home.
The woman wailed and sobbed, refusing to submit,
but she was carried out by force.
Wáng ran away
and hid near the grave of Niè Zhèng,
hoping to catch a last glimpse of his wife as she passed.
Before long his wife arrived.
When she saw her husband,
she threw herself to the ground, weeping loudly.
Wáng was so moved with pity
that he cried out in spite of himself.
The attendants realized he was Wáng
and seized him,
intending to beat him.
Suddenly a man emerged from the grave
holding a gleaming sword.
He was awe-inspiringly majestic.
In a stern voice he said:
"I am Niè Zhèng!
How can you seize a woman from a good family?
Considering that you are not acting of your own free will,
I will pardon you for the time being.
Take this message to your unprincipled prince:
If he does not mend his ways,
I will soon chop off his head!"
The attendants fled in terror,
abandoning the carriage.
The man also disappeared into the grave.
Husband and wife kowtowed before the grave and went home,
still fearing that the prince's men would come again.
After more than ten days
there was still no sign of them,
so they began to feel at ease.
The prince's debauched tyranny was somewhat abated thereafter.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"When I read the Biographies of Assassins,
I admire only the man of Zhì Shēnjǐnglǐ:
In staking his life to repay the one who knew his worth,
he had the righteousness of Yù Ràng;
in butchering a high minister in broad daylight,
he had the courage of Zhuān Zhū;
in disfiguring himself to keep from implicating his sister,
he had the wisdom of Cáo Mò.
As for Jīng Kē,
his strength was not sufficient to plot against the unprincipled King of Qín,
so he brought about his own destruction
by letting the king tear his sleeve and get away.
He lightly made use of General Fán's head:
on what day could it have been returned?
This is cause for regret through the ages
and something that Niè Zhèng would scoff at.
I have heard in an unofficial history
that his grave was dug up by the ghosts of Yáng and Zuǒ.
If this is true,
then he achieved no fame in life
and lost righteousness in death.
How can we compare the worthiness of such a man
with that of Niè, who was moved by righteous indignation to punish debauchery?
Ah!
Niè's worthiness
is all the more believable for this."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In Píngchéng there lived a scholar named Lěng,
who had been extremely dull-witted since childhood.
Even after reaching the age of twenty,
he had not yet mastered a single classic.
Suddenly, a fox came
and stayed with him.
Whenever his brothers heard them talking all night long
and questioned him about it,
he would not reveal anything.
After many days like this,
he suddenly developed a manic illness: whenever he was given a topic to write an essay on,
he would shut himself in and sit blankly;
after a short while,
he would burst into loud laughter.
Peeking in,
they saw his hand never stopping as he wrote,
and in no time, an essay was completed.
Once the draft was finished,
the literary ideas were exquisite and marvelous.
That year, he passed the county-level examination and became a government student,
and the following year, he received a stipend as an advanced scholar.
Whenever he took an examination, he would laugh,
the sound echoing through the hall,
and from then on,
the name "Laughing Scholar"
became widely known.
Fortunately, the education commissioner retired,
and did not hear of it.
Later, when a certain education commissioner who was strict and solemn
sat solemnly in the hall all day,
he suddenly heard laughter,
became angry, and had Lěng seized,
intending to punish him.
The proctor explained his madness on his behalf,
and the commissioner's anger subsided slightly.
He released him,
but stripped him of his scholarly status.
From then on, Lěng pretended to be mad and indulged in wine.
He authored
"Mad Writings"
