in four volumes,
which were outstanding and worth reading.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Shutting the door and laughing—
how different is it from the sudden enlightenment in Buddhism!
Laughing and producing an essay
is also a joyful thing.
Why go so far as to strip him of his status for this?
Such an examiner—
is he not utterly foolish!"
The instructor Sūn Jǐngxià
went to visit a friend.
When he reached outside the window,
he heard no conversation,
but only bursts of laughter,
repeated several times in a short while.
He thought his friend was joking with someone.
Entering to look,
he found him alone in the room.
He found it strange.
His friend then laughed loudly and said:
"Just now, having nothing to do,
I was silently rehearsing some jokes."
In the county, a scholar named Gōng
kept a donkey at home,
which was stubborn and unruly.
Whenever it encountered a pedestrian on the road,
Gōng would clasp his hands and apologize:
"I am in a hurry,
and have no time to dismount.
Please do not take offense!"
Before he finished speaking,
the donkey would already be kneeling on the road,
and this happened every time without fail.
Gōng was deeply ashamed and resentful,
so he plotted with his wife
to have her pretend to be a guest.
He then rode the donkey around the courtyard,
clasped his hands toward his wife,
and spoke as if meeting a guest.
The donkey indeed knelt.
He then used a sharp awl to stab it fiercely.
Just then, a friend came to visit,
and as he was about to knock on the door,
he heard Gōng inside saying:
"I have no time to dismount,
please do not take offense!"
A moment later,
he said it again.
The friend found it very strange,
knocked on the door and asked the reason,
and Gōng told him the truth.
They both burst into laughter.
These two anecdotes
can be attached to the story of Lěng's laughter for transmission.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
A certain scholar bought a new house
and was often troubled by foxes.
All his clothing and belongings
were mostly destroyed by them,
and they often put dust into his soup and noodles.
One day,
a friend came to visit,
but the scholar happened to be out,
and did not return until evening.
The scholar's wife prepared food for the guest,
and afterward, she and the maid ate the leftovers.
The scholar had always been unrestrained
and liked to keep aphrodisiacs,
but no one knew when
the fox had put the medicine into the porridge.
When the wife ate it,
she noticed a scent of musk and brain.
She asked the maid,
but the maid said she did not know.
After eating,
she felt a fiery desire rising within her,
unbearable even for a moment;
she tried hard to suppress it,
but the burning thirst grew more urgent.
Thinking over who in the household she could turn to,
she realized only the guest was there,
so she went and knocked on his door.
The guest asked who it was,
and she truthfully told him.
He asked what she wanted,
but she did not answer.
The guest declined, saying:
"Your husband and I are friends bound by morality and duty;
I dare not commit such a beastly act."
The wife still lingered.
The guest scolded her:
"Your husband's literary reputation and moral character
are being utterly ruined by you!"
He spat at her through the window.
The wife was deeply ashamed
and withdrew.
She then thought to herself: Why did I do this?
Suddenly remembering the fragrance in the bowl,
she wondered if it was aphrodisiac.
Checking the package of medicine,
she found it scattered all over the table,
and the bowl and cup were full of it.
Knowing that cold water could counteract it,
she drank some.
In a moment,
her mind cleared,
but she was so ashamed she could not face anyone.
Tossing and turning for a long time,
the night watch was nearly over.
Fearing even more that daylight would make it impossible to face others,
she untied her belt and hanged herself.
The maid discovered and rescued her,
but her breath was already faint.
After morning,
she began to show slight signs of life.
The guest had fled during the night.
The scholar returned only in the afternoon,
saw his wife lying down,
and asked her what was wrong.
She did not speak,
only shed clear tears.
The maid told him what had happened.
Greatly shocked,
he pressed her for details.
His wife sent the maid away,
and only then told him the truth.
The scholar sighed and said:
"This is the retribution for my lewdness;
how can I blame you?
Fortunately, I have a good friend;
otherwise,
how could I face anyone!"
From then on, he earnestly reformed his ways,
and the foxes also ceased to appear.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"People warn each other at home not to keep arsenic or poison,
but no one warns against keeping aphrodisiacs,
just as people fear weapons but indulge in bedroom pleasures.
Who knows their poison is even greater than arsenic!
Yet they are kept only to please one's wife!
To the point of incurring the jealousy of ghosts and spirits;
how much more so for those who indulge in lewdness
beyond merely keeping such medicine?"
A certain scholar went to take the examinations,
and upon returning from the prefectural capital,
it was already dusk.
He had brought with him lotus seeds, water chestnuts, and lotus roots,
and upon entering his room,
he placed them all on the table.
There was also a fake dildo,
soaked in water in a basin.
Several neighbors, hearing that the scholar had just returned,
brought wine and came to his hall.
In a hurry, the scholar placed the basin under the bed and went out,
instructing his wife to prepare a meal,
while he drank lightly with the guests.
After drinking,
he went inside,
quickly lit a candle to look under the bed,
and found the basin empty.
He asked his wife,
and she said:
"Just now, I took it out along with the water chestnuts and lotus roots to serve the guests.
Why are you still looking for it?"
The scholar recalled that among the dishes, there were black strips mixed in,
and none of the guests knew what they were.
He then laughed and said:
"Silly woman!
What kind of thing is this,
that you could serve it to guests?"
His wife also wondered:
"I was even complaining that you didn't tell me how to cook it.
Its appearance was ugly,
and I didn't know its name,
so I just sliced it up haphazardly."
The scholar then told her what it was,
and they laughed together.
Now that scholar has become prominent,
but his close friends still tease him about it.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
The Mountain Market of Ēshān,
is one of the scenic sights of the county.
It appears only once every several years.
Young Master Sūn Yǔnián,
drinking with friends upstairs,
suddenly saw a solitary pagoda rise atop the mountain,
towering high into the azure sky.
They looked at each other in surprise and doubt,
thinking there was no such monastery nearby.
Before long,
they saw dozens of palaces,
with green tiles and soaring eaves, and realized it was a mountain market.
Soon after,
high walls with battlements appeared,
stretching for six or seven *li*,
forming what seemed like a city.
Within were buildings that looked like towers, halls, and archways,
clearly visible,
countless in number.
Suddenly, a great wind arose,
and a vast haze of dust obscured everything,
leaving the city barely visible.
Then the wind ceased and the sky cleared,
and everything vanished;
only a single tall tower remained,
reaching straight to the heavens.
Its five windows were all wide open;
in a row, there were five bright spots,
which were the sky outside the tower.
Counting layer by layer: the higher the tower,
the fewer the bright spots;
counting up to the eighth layer,
they were as small as stars;
and above that,
it became dim and indistinct,
impossible to count the layers.
People moved about in the tower, bustling,
some leaning, some standing,
in various postures.
After a while,
the tower gradually lowered,
until its top became visible;
then it gradually looked like an ordinary tower;
then like a tall house;
suddenly, it shrank to the size of a fist or a bean,
and finally vanished.
It is also said that early travelers
have seen smoke from households and market stalls on the mountain,
no different from the mortal world,
hence it is also called
"Ghost Market."
So it is said.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Gāo Fān of Línjiāng
was intelligent from a young age,
with a handsome and elegant appearance.
At fourteen, he entered the county school.
Wealthy families vied to marry their daughters to him;
but he was exceedingly picky in his choices,
often disobeying his father's wishes.
His father, Zhòng Hóng,
was sixty years old
and had only this one son,
so he doted on him,
unwilling to oppose him in the slightest.
In the eastern village, there was an old man named Fán,
who taught children in the market,
and moved his family to rent a house from the Gāo family.
The old man had a daughter,
whose childhood name was Jiāngchéng,
the same age as Gāo Fān,
both around eight or nine years old at the time.
They were innocent playmates,
playing together every day.
Later, the old man moved away,
and after four or five years,
they heard nothing more of each other.
One day,
Gāo Fān saw a young lady in a narrow alley,
of stunning beauty,
unlike any ordinary person.
She was followed by a little maid,
only six or seven years old.
He did not dare to look directly at her,
but only glanced sideways.
The girl stopped and gazed,
as if wanting to say something.
Looking closely,
it was Jiāngchéng.
He was immediately overjoyed.
Neither spoke,
they just stood there staring blankly at each other,
and after a while, they parted,
both feeling reluctant.
Deliberately, Gāo Fān dropped a red handkerchief on the ground and left.
The little maid picked it up,
and happily gave it to the girl.
The girl put it in her sleeve,
exchanged it for her own handkerchief,
and pretended to say to the maid:
"Scholar Gāo is no stranger,
but we shouldn't keep something he dropped.
Catch up and return it to him."
The little maid indeed ran after him and gave it to him.
Gāo Fān was overjoyed to receive the handkerchief.
Returning home, he saw his mother
and asked to discuss marriage.
His mother said:
"Our family doesn't even have half a house,
wandering north and south.
How can we be a suitable match?"
He said:
"I want it myself,
and I will certainly have no regrets."
His mother could not decide,
so she consulted Zhòng Hóng;
but Hóng firmly refused.
Upon hearing this, Shēng grew sullen and depressed,
unable to swallow even a grain of rice.
His mother was greatly worried
and said to Gāo:
"Although the Fán family is poor,
they are not to be compared with unscrupulous brokers or ruffians.
I will pay a visit to their home;
if their daughter is suitable for marriage,
it should do no harm."
Gāo said:
"Very well."
His mother used the pretext of going to burn incense at the Black Emperor Temple
and went to see her.
Seeing the girl with bright eyes and lovely teeth,
truly beautiful and graceful,
her heart was filled with great affection and delight.
She then generously presented her with gold and silk,
and frankly told her of her intentions.
Old Mrs. Fán modestly declined at first but later accepted the betrothal.
Upon returning home and describing the situation,
Shēng finally broke into a smile.
A year later,
an auspicious day was chosen to welcome the girl to his home,
and husband and wife got along very happily.
However, the girl was prone to anger,
turning a cold eye as if they were strangers;
her mocking, sarcastic words
often grated on his ears.
Out of love, Shēng
endured it all and bore it patiently.
When the old couple heard of this,
they were not pleased,
and secretly reproached their son.
The girl overheard this,
became furious,
and her scolding and cursing increased all the more.
Shēng began to retort with harsh words of his own,
which made the girl even angrier.
She beat him and drove him out of the house,
shutting the door behind him.
Shēng whimpered outside the door,
not daring to knock,
and spent the night crouching under the eaves.
From then on, the girl regarded him as an enemy.
At first,
kneeling for a long time could still appease her;
gradually, even kneeling on bended knee lost its effect,
and the husband's suffering grew worse.
When his parents mildly reproached her,
the girl's defiance was beyond description.
Enraged,
his parents forced her to return to her natal home.
Fán, ashamed and afraid,
entreated a mutual friend to plead with Zhòng Hóng;
but Zhòng Hóng refused.
Over a year later,
Shēng happened to meet his father-in-law;
Fán invited him to his home,
and apologized profusely.
He then had his daughter dressed up to come out and meet him;
husband and wife looked at each other,
and could not help feeling sorrowful.
Fán then bought wine to entertain his son-in-law,
toasting and urging him to drink with great earnestness.
When night fell,
he firmly insisted they stay overnight,
prepared another bed,
and had the couple sleep together.
At dawn, they bid farewell and returned home,
not daring to tell their parents the truth,
and covered it up with excuses.
From then on, every few days,
they would temporarily stay overnight at her father's home,
unbeknownst to his parents.
One day, Fán personally went to see Zhòng Hóng.
At first, he was not received,
but after pressing, he was finally admitted.
Fán approached on his knees to plead,
but Gāo would not accept responsibility,
shifting it to his son.
Fán said:
"My son-in-law stayed at my house last night,
and I heard no complaints."
Gāo asked in surprise:
"When did he stay over?"
Fán told him everything.
Gāo apologized respectfully, saying:
"I truly did not know.
Since he loves her,
why should I alone bear a grudge?"
After Fán left,
Gāo called his son and scolded him.
Shēng merely bowed his head,
not uttering a word in his own defense.
While they were talking,
Fán had already brought his daughter over.
Gāo said:
"I cannot bear the faults of my children;
it would be better for each to set up their own household.
I will trouble you to oversee the division of the family."
Fán tried to dissuade him,
but he would not listen.
So they moved to live in a separate courtyard,
with a maidservant assigned to serve them.
After more than a month,
things were fairly peaceful,
and the old couple secretly felt relieved.
Not long after,
the girl gradually became unrestrained,
and Shēng's face often bore scratches from her fingernails;
though his parents were well aware,
they endured it and did not inquire.
One day,
unable to bear the beatings and torment,
Shēng fled to his father's place,
looking utterly bewildered, like a bird or sparrow being chased by a hawk.
Just as the old couple was asking in astonishment,
the girl had already charged in wielding a club,
and right beside the old man, she seized Shēng and began beating him.
The old couple cried and shouted,
but she paid them no heed whatsoever,
beating him dozens of times
before finally leaving in a huff.
Gāo drove his son out, saying:
"I divided the household precisely to avoid such turmoil;
since you clearly enjoy this,
why run away from it?"
Driven out, Shēng
wandered about with nowhere to go.
Fearing he might be broken and driven to death,
his mother had him live alone and provided him with food.
She also summoned Fán
to instruct his daughter.
Fán entered her room
and exhorted her in every possible way,
but the girl would not listen,
instead replying with harsh words to torment him.
Fán flung his sleeves and left;
vowing to sever ties with her.
Not long after,
Old Man Fán, angered and distressed, fell ill,
and he and his wife died one after the other.
The girl bore a grudge against them,
and did not even attend the funeral or pay her respects,
only cursing and shouting next door every day,
deliberately to let the old couple hear.
Gāo completely ignored it, pretending not to know.
Since living alone,
Shēng felt as if he had escaped boiling water and fire,
though he also felt desolate and lonely.
Secretly, he bribed the matchmaker, Old Mrs. Lǐ, with money,
and brought a courtesan into his study,
their comings and goings always at night.
After a long time,
the girl got wind of it,
went to the study and railed at him.
Shēng strenuously protested his innocence,
swearing by the sun and sky,
and only then did the girl leave.
From then on,
she watched for Shēng's missteps every day.
When Old Mrs. Lǐ came out of the study
and happened to run into her,
the girl immediately called out to her;
the old woman's expression changed,
making the girl even more suspicious.
She said to the old woman:
"Tell me plainly what you have been doing,
and perhaps I can forgive you;
if you hide anything,
I will pluck out every hair on your head!"
Trembling, the old woman confessed:
"For the past half month,
only the prostitute Lǐ Yúnniáng has come here twice.
Just now, the young master mentioned
that he once saw Mrs. Táo at Yùsì Mountain,
and admired her bound feet;
he told me to summon her here.
Although she is not chaste,
she is not one to become a night-visiting courtesan either,
so whether it will succeed is uncertain."
Believing her words to be true,
the girl reluctantly let her off with a lenient punishment.
As the old woman was about to leave,
she forcibly stopped her.
When dusk fell,
she scolded her, saying:
"First go extinguish the lamp,
then say the potter has arrived."
The old woman did as she was told.
The girl immediately hurried in.
The scholar was overjoyed,
pulled her by the arm and urged her to sit,
fully expressing his longing and desire,
but the girl remained silent.
Groping for her feet in the dark,
he said:
"Ever since catching a glimpse of the immortal visitor on the mountain,
I have been constantly, solely longing for these."
The girl still did not speak.
The scholar said:
"My long-cherished wish,
is only now fulfilled,
how can we meet face to face yet not recognize each other?"
He personally hurried to light a lamp to see,
and it was Jiāng Chéng.
Greatly frightened, his face lost color,
he dropped the candle on the ground,
knelt upright trembling,
as if a blade were at his neck.
She pinched his ear and dragged him home,
pricked both his thighs all over with needles,
then made him sleep on the lower bed,
and would wake him to scold him.
From then on, he feared her like a tiger or wolf;
even if she occasionally showed him a pleasant face,
on the pillow and mat,
he was still too terrified to perform as a man.
She slapped his face and shouted at him to leave,
growing even more disgusted and disdainful, not treating him as a human.
The scholar lived daily amidst orchids and musk,
yet like a prisoner in a cell,
looking up to the jailer's authority.
She had two elder sisters,
both married to scholars.
The eldest sister was gentle and kind,
slow of speech,
and often did not get along with her.
The second sister was married to a Mr. Gě,
she was cunning and clever, skilled in argument,
admiring her own shadow and striking poses,
her looks were not as good as Jiāng Chéng's,
but her fierceness and jealousy were equal.
When the sisters met, they had no other topic,
except each boasting of their domestic authority with great satisfaction.
Therefore, these two got along best.
If the scholar visited relatives or friends,
his wife would immediately get angry;
only when he went to the Gě household,
did she know yet not forbid it.
One day,
he was drinking at the Gěs'.
Already drunk,
Gě mocked him:
"Why are you so afraid of her?"
The scholar laughed and said:
"Many things in this world are hard to explain: my fear,
is fear of her beauty;
yet there are those whose wives are not as beautiful as mine,
but who fear them even more than I do,
isn't that even more perplexing?"
Gě was greatly ashamed,
and could not reply.
A maid overheard,
and told the second sister.
The second sister was furious,
grabbed a stick and rushed out.
Seeing her ferocity,
the scholar slipped on his shoes, wanting to flee.
The stick rose,
and already struck his waist and spine;
three blows, three stumbles, and he could not get up.
A mis-hit struck his head,
blood flowed like a downpour.
The second sister left,
and the scholar staggered home.
His wife, startled, asked him about it.
At first, because he had offended her sister,
he dared not tell her immediately;
after repeated questioning,
he finally related the whole story.
His wife bound his head with cloth,
and said angrily:
"A man of our household,
why should he be subjected to her beating and torture!"
She changed into short sleeves and trousers,
tucked a wooden pestle into her clothes,
and taking a maid, went straight there.
Arriving at the Gě household,
the second sister greeted her with smiling words.
Without a word,
she struck her with the pestle,
knocking her down;
tore her trousers and inflicted pain.
Teeth were knocked out, lips split,
she lost control of her bowels and bladder.
The wife returned,
the second sister, humiliated and enraged,
sent her husband to go complain to Gāo.
The scholar hurried out.
He tried his utmost to be warm and comforting.
Gě whispered to him privately:
"My coming here,
I had no choice.
That shrew is unkind,
luckily you used your hand to punish and discipline her,
what grudge could there be between us two."
His wife had already heard this,
rushed out,
pointed and scolded:
"Filthy scoundrel!
Your wife has been wronged and made to suffer,
yet you secretly cozy up to an outsider!
A man like this,
shouldn't he be beaten to death!"
She quickly called for a stick to be found.
Gě was greatly embarrassed,
forced the door open and fled.
From then on, the scholar had nowhere at all to go.
His classmate Wáng Zǐyǎ visited him,
and he earnestly persuaded him to stay for a drink.
While drinking,
they joked about matters of the inner chambers,
becoming rather lewd and improper.
His wife happened to be spying on the guest,
listened in hiding and heard everything,
secretly put croton seeds into the soup and served it.
Not long after,
he was vomiting and had diarrhea unbearably,
barely clinging to life.
His wife sent a maid to ask him:
"Will you dare be disrespectful again?"
Only then did he realize the source of his illness,
moaned and begged for mercy.
Then mung bean soup was already prepared and waiting.
Drinking it stopped the symptoms.
From then on, his companions warned each other,
not to dare drink at his house.
Wáng owned a wine shop,
in the shop were many red plum blossoms,
he set a banquet to invite his circle of friends.
The scholar used the literary society as a pretext,
reported to his wife and went.
At dusk,
already merry with drink,
Wáng Shēng said:
"It so happens that there is a famous courtesan from Nánchāng,
who has drifted and taken up residence here.
We can summon her to join us for drinks."
The group was greatly delighted.
Only the young man rose from his seat,
and excused himself to leave.
The crowd pulled him back, saying,
"Although the eyes and ears of the inner chambers are long,
they cannot see or hear what happens here."
They then swore to each other to keep their mouths shut.
The young man then sat down again.
After a short while,
the courtesan indeed appeared.
She was seventeen or eighteen years old,
her jade pendants tinkling,
her cloud-like hair elegantly arranged.
When asked her surname,
she said:
"My surname is Xiè,
and my childhood name is Fānglán."
Her words and manner of speaking
were exceedingly refined and elegant,
driving everyone present to a frenzy.
Yet Fānglán still favored the young man,
repeatedly casting meaningful glances at him.
Noticed by the crowd,
they deliberately pulled the two to sit shoulder-to-shoulder.
Fānglán secretly grasped the young man's hand,
and with her finger wrote on his palm
the character
"stay."
At this moment, the young man
wished to leave but could not bear to,
wished to stay but did not dare,
his heart was like tangled silk,
indescribable.
As they leaned their heads together whispering,
their drunken antics grew even wilder,
and the fierce tigress on the bed at home
was completely forgotten.
After a short while,
hearing the night watch drum had sounded,
the tavern's patrons grew even fewer;
only a handsome young man sat at a distant table,
drinking alone by the candlelight,
with a young servant boy holding a towel in attendance.
The crowd privately remarked on his noble elegance.
Before long,
the young man finished drinking,
and went out the door.
The servant boy turned back inside,
and said to the young man:
"My master awaits a word with you."
The others were utterly bewildered,
only the young man's face turned deathly pale,
without even time to bid farewell,
he hurriedly left.
For that young man was none other than Jiāngchéng,
and the servant boy was her household maid.
The young man followed her home,
and prostrated himself to receive a whipping.
From then on, his confinement became even stricter,
and all social visits and celebrations ceased.
When the examiner visited the school,
the young man was demoted to a blue gown for misinterpreting a passage.
One day,
he spoke with a maid,
and his wife suspected an affair,
so she covered the maid's head with a wine jar and beat her.
Afterwards, she bound both the young man and the maid,
and with embroidery scissors cut flesh from their abdomens to exchange and patch each other's wounds,
then released the bindings and ordered them to bandage themselves.
Over a month later,
it was said the wounds actually fused into one.
The wife would often step barefoot on cakes in the dust,
then scold the young man to pick them up and eat them.
Such were the various torments.
The mother, missing her son,
once visited their home,
and seeing her son gaunt as firewood,
returned home weeping bitterly, wishing to die.
That night, she dreamed an old man told
He said:
"Do not worry.
This is due to a cause from a previous life. It is the long-lived rat raised by the monk Yuánjìng of Jiāngchéng.
In your previous life, young master, you were a scholar
who happened to travel to that place
and accidentally killed it.
Now it is bringing you evil retribution;
it cannot be reversed by human effort.
Every morning,
earnestly recite the Guānyīn mantra one hundred times,
and it will surely be effective."
He awoke and told Zhònghóng about it;
they found it strange.
Husband and wife followed the instruction,
and earnestly recited for over two months,
but the girl remained as unruly as before,
even more wildly unrestrained.
Hearing gongs and drums outside the gate,
she would grasp her hair and run out,
foolishly stretching her neck to gaze,
while a thousand people pointed and stared,
yet she remained calm and unperturbed.
Her father- and mother-in-law both felt ashamed of her,
but could not stop her.
Suddenly, an old monk appeared outside the gate proclaiming the fruits of Buddha,
and onlookers crowded like a wall.
The monk blew on the drum's leather, making it sound like an ox.
The girl rushed out,
and seeing the crowd with no gap,
ordered her maid to move a traveling bed,
and stepped up onto it.
All eyes gathered on her,
but she acted as if unaware.
After a while,
as the monk was about to finish his exposition,
he asked for a bowl of clear water,
held it toward the girl, and declared:
"Do not be angry,
do not be angry!
The past life is not false,
the present life is not real.
Begone!
Little rat, shrink your head away,
do not let the cat find you."
After proclaiming this,
he sucked in water and sprayed it onto the girl's face.
Her makeup streamed down,
soaking her collar and sleeves.
The crowd was greatly alarmed,
expecting the girl to burst into rage,
but she did not speak at all,
wiped her face, and returned home by herself.
The monk then also left.
The girl entered her room and sat dazedly,
dejected as if bereaved.
She did not eat all day,
swept the bed and hastily went to sleep.
In the middle of the night,
she suddenly called her husband awake.
He suspected she needed to relieve herself,
and presented the chamber pot.
She refused it,
secretly grasped his arm,
and pulled him under the quilt.
He obeyed her command,
his limbs trembling with fear,
as if receiving an imperial decree.
The girl sighed and said:
"To have made you like this,
how can I face being human!"
Then she used her hand to caress her husband's body,
and whenever she reached a scar from a knife or cane,
she sobbed and whimpered,
using her fingernails to pinch herself,
wishing she could die on the spot.
Seeing her state,
he truly could not bear it,
and comforted her with great kindness.
The girl said:
"I think that monk must be an incarnation of a Bodhisattva.
With one sprinkle of clear water,
it was as if my innards were renewed.
Now, recalling my past actions,
it all seems like a previous life.
Was I not human before?
To have a husband yet not be joyful,
to have parents-in-law yet not serve them—
what kind of heart was that!
Tomorrow we can move our home,
and live again with my parents,
so it will be convenient to attend to them."
They chattered all night,
as if speaking after ten years of separation.
At dawn she rose,
folded clothes and packed utensils,
had the maid carry the trunk,
personally bundled the bedding,
and urged her husband to go ahead and knock on the door.
Her mother came out, startled, and asked;
he explained their intention.
The mother still hesitated with a troubled expression,
but the girl had already entered with the maid.
The mother followed them in.
The girl knelt on the ground weeping sorrowfully,
only begging to be spared death.
Seeing her sincerity,
the mother also wept and said:
"How could I be so severe?"
Her husband gave a detailed account of the previous situation,
and only then did she realize that the dream from before had come true.
Delighted,
she called servants to clean the old rooms.
From then on, the girl served with pleasing demeanor and obedient will,
surpassing even a filial son.
When meeting people,
she was shy like a new bride.
If someone playfully mentioned past events,
her cheeks would flush red.
Moreover, she was diligent and thrifty,
and also skilled at managing and accumulating wealth: for three years, the old couple did not inquire about household accounts,
yet they became exceedingly wealthy.
That year, her husband passed the provincial examination.
She often said to him:
"That day when I saw Fānglán once,
I still remember her now."
Since he had escaped her cruel abuse,
his wishes were already fully satisfied,
and he dared not entertain any improper thoughts,
so he merely assented.
It happened that he went to the capital for the examinations,
and returned after several months.
Entering the chamber,
he saw Fānglán just playing chess with Jiāngchéng.
Startled, he asked about it,
and learned that his wife had spent several hundred taels to redeem her from courtesan status.
This matter was recounted in great detail by Wáng Zǐyǎ of Zhèjiāng.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"In human life, the fruits of karma
must be repaid with every bite and sip;
but among karmic retributions, those within the bedchamber
are like gangrene clinging to the bone—
their poison is especially cruel.
Often we see that among virtuous wives there is one in ten,
while shrewish wives are nine in ten;
this also shows how few in this world can cultivate good karma.
Guānzìzài's vow-power is vast and great—
why does he not sprinkle the water from his bowl over the entire great chiliocosm?"
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Mr. Sūn
married a woman named Xīn, who came from a family of former officials.
When she first entered his home,
she wore a pair of trousers with many ties,
fastened with numerous belts,
which tightly bound her entire body,
and she refused to share a bed with her husband.
She often kept an awl and a bamboo tube by the bedside for self-defense.
Sūn was repeatedly stabbed,
so he moved to sleep on a separate bed.
After more than a month,
he still dared not approach her.
Even when they met during the day,
she never spoke or smiled at him.
A fellow student who knew of this
privately said to Sūn:
"Can your wife drink?"
Sūn replied:
"She drinks a little."
The friend joked:
"I have a method to mediate,
a good and feasible one."
Sūn asked:
"What method?"
The friend said:
"Put a stupefying drug in wine,
trick her into drinking it,
and then you can do as you please."
Sūn laughed it off,
but secretly thought the plan was excellent.
He inquired at a pharmacy
and respectfully boiled aconite in wine,
placing it on the table.
That night,
Sūn strained the wine.
He drank several cups alone and then went to bed.
This went on for three nights,
but his wife never drank.
One night,
after lying down for a while,
Sūn saw his wife still sitting quietly,
so he deliberately pretended to snore;
his wife then got out of bed,
took the wine, and warmed it on the stove.
Sūn secretly rejoiced.
Soon she drank a full cup;
then poured another,
drinking about half a cup,
and poured the remainder back into the pot,
then tidied the bed and went to sleep.
After a long while, there was no sound,
but the lamp was still brightly lit.
Suspecting she was still awake,
he deliberately shouted:
"The tin candlestick is melting!"
His wife did not respond,
and he called again, still no response.
He got up and went to look,
and found her drunk, sleeping like a log.
He lifted the quilt and slipped in,
undoing the layers of ties and knots.
His wife was aware of it,
but could not move,
nor speak,
and had to endure his advances.
When she woke up,
she was disgusted
and tried to hang herself.
Sūn, in his sleep, heard gasping and choking sounds,
got up and rushed to look,
and saw her tongue already protruding about two inches.
Greatly alarmed,
he cut the rope,
laid her on the bed,
and after a while, she revived.
From then on, Sūn deeply loathed her,
and the couple avoided each other,
lowering their heads whenever they met.
For four or five years,
they did not exchange a single word.
Sometimes, when his wife was in the room
laughing and joking with others,
upon seeing her husband arrive,
her expression would immediately change,
cold as frost and snow.
Sūn often stayed at his study,
not returning home for a year;
even if forced to return,
he would face the wall for a while
and silently go to bed.
His parents were very worried.
One day,
an old nun came to their home,
saw the wife,
and repeatedly praised her.
Sūn's mother said nothing,
only sighing deeply.
The nun asked the reason,
and she told her everything.
The nun said:
"This is an easy matter."
The mother said happily,
"If you can change my daughter-in-law's mind,
I will not spare any reward."
Seeing no one else in the room,
the nun whispered:
"Buy a picture of a spring palace,
and in three days,
I will perform a spell for you."
After the nun left,
the mother bought one and waited.
Three days later,
the nun indeed came,
instructing:
"This must be kept very secret,
do not let the couple know."
She then cut out the figures in the picture,
took three needles,
a pinch of mugwort,
wrapped them together in plain paper,
and drew a few worm-like lines on the outside.
She told the mother to lure the wife out,
secretly take her pillow,
open the seam and put the packet inside;
then sew it back up
and return it to its original place.
The nun then left.
That evening,
the mother forced her son to return home to sleep.
An old maidservant went to eavesdrop.
As the second watch was ending,
she heard the wife call Sūn by his childhood name,
but Sūn did not answer.
After a while,
the wife spoke again,
and Sūn responded with an annoyed and disgusted tone.
At dawn,
the mother entered their room
and saw the couple lying back-to-back,
realizing the nun's method had failed.
She called her son to a secluded place
and earnestly advised him.
When Sūn heard his wife's name,
he became angry,
gnashing his teeth.
The mother scolded him angrily,
but he ignored her and left.
The next day,
the nun came,
and was told it had not worked.
The nun was greatly puzzled.
The old maidservant then recounted what she had heard.
The nun smiled and said:
"Earlier, the wife hated her husband,
so I focused the spell on her.
Now the wife's feelings have changed,
but the husband's have not.
Let me perform a dual-targeting method,
and it will surely work."
The mother agreed.
She took her son's pillow and sealed the packet inside as before,
then called him to return to sleep.
After the first watch,
they could still hear tossing and turning from both beds,
occasional coughing,
as if neither could sleep.
After a long time,
they heard the two whispering on one bed,
but the words were indistinct and unclear.
As dawn approached,
they could still hear playful laughter,
giggling incessantly.
The old maidservant reported this to the mother,
who was delighted.
When the nun came,
she richly rewarded her.
From then on, Sūn and his wife were harmonious.
They had a son and two daughters,
and for over ten years, never had a quarrel.
Friends privately asked Sūn the reason,
and he laughed and said:
"Before, the sight of her shadow made me angry;
afterward, the sound of her voice made me happy.
I myself don't understand what changed in my heart."
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"To transform hatred into love—
truly a miraculous art.
Yet what can make people happy
can also make them angry.
The wonder of such arts
is precisely what makes them fearsome.
As the ancient sage said: 'Do not let the six types of old women enter your home.'
There is profound insight in this!"
Based on the Zhuxuezhai manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
There was a scholar named Féng from Líntáo,
who was a descendant of a noble family but had fallen into poverty.
A fisherman owed him money,
and being unable to repay the debt,
he would give Féng any turtles he caught.
One day,
he presented Féng with a huge turtle
that had a white spot on its forehead.
Finding it unusual,
Féng released it.
Later, while returning from his in-laws’ home,
he reached the banks of the Héng River as dusk was falling.
There he saw a drunken man,
followed by two or three servants,
staggering toward him.
Spotting Féng from a distance,
the man asked,
"Who are you?"
Féng replied casually,
"A traveler."
The drunkard angrily said,
"Don’t you have a name?
Why call yourself a traveler?"
Anxious to continue his journey,
Féng ignored him and walked past.
This angered the drunkard even more,
who grabbed Féng’s sleeve to stop him,
his breath reeking of alcohol.
Growing impatient,
Féng tried to break free but couldn’t.
He then asked,
"What is your name?"
The man replied arrogantly,
"I am the former magistrate of Nándū.
What do you want?"
Féng said,
"If there are magistrates like you in this world,
it truly disgraces society!
Fortunately, you’re only a former magistrate;
if you were a new one,
wouldn’t you treat passersby even worse?"
Enraged,
the drunkard seemed ready to resort to violence.
Féng declared loudly,
"I, Féng, am not someone to be beaten!"
Hearing this,
the drunkard’s anger turned to joy.
Staggering, he bowed and said,
"You are my benefactor!
Please forgive my rudeness!"
He then called his servants
and sent them ahead to prepare a feast.
Féng tried to decline but couldn’t.
Hand in hand, they walked several miles
until they reached a small village.
Entering it,
Féng saw magnificent halls and buildings,
resembling the residence of a noble family.
As the drunkard sobered up slightly,
Féng asked for his name.
The man replied,
"Don’t be alarmed when I tell you—
I am the Eighth Great King of the Táo River.
Earlier, I was invited to drink by Qīngtóng from the Western Hills,
and I got drunk without realizing it,
offending you in the process.
I am deeply ashamed."
Realizing he was dealing with a supernatural being,
Féng was not afraid,
as the creature’s words were sincere and warm.
Soon, a lavish feast was set,
and they sat close together, drinking joyfully.
The Eighth Great King was particularly bold,
downing several cups in a row.
Fearing he might get drunk again and cause trouble,
Féng pretended to be intoxicated and asked to rest.
The Eighth Great King understood his concern and said with a smile,
"Are you afraid I might act wildly again?
Please don’t worry.
When drunkards misbehave,
they claim not to remember it the next day—
but that’s just an excuse.
Nine out of ten drunkards misbehave intentionally.
Though I am not considered virtuous among my peers,
I would never dare to act recklessly toward an elder.
Why do you reject me like this?"
Féng sat back down
and earnestly advised him,
"Since you are aware of this,
why not change your ways?"
The Eighth Great King replied,
"When I served as a magistrate,
I was even more addicted to drinking than I am now.
After angering the Emperor,
I was exiled to an island.
For over ten years, I tried to reform,
but now that I am old and nearing the end of my life,
unable to soar high again,
I have relapsed into my old habits.
I don’t even understand it myself.
But now I shall heed your advice."
As they talked,
the distant sound of a bell rang out.
The Eighth Great King stood up,
grasped Féng’s arm, and said,
"Our time together is short.
I have something to repay your great kindness.
However, you must not wear it for long.
Once your wishes are fulfilled,
you must return it to me."
He then spat out a tiny figure,
only about an inch tall.
Using his claw, he pinched Féng’s arm,
causing such pain that the skin split.
He quickly pressed the tiny figure onto the wound,
and when he released his grip,
it had entered beneath the skin,
leaving only a nail mark
that gradually swelled into a lump resembling a tubercle.
Startled, Féng asked what it was,
but the Eighth Great King only smiled without answering.
He simply said,
"You should go now."
After seeing Féng off,
he turned back himself.
When Féng looked back,
the village had completely vanished,
and all he saw was a giant turtle
clumsily slipping into the water and disappearing.
Stunned for a long time,
he realized that what he had received
must be a turtle treasure.
From then on, his eyesight became exceptionally sharp.
He could see jewels hidden deep underground,
and even things he had never known before,
he could name effortlessly.
In his bedroom,
he dug up several hundred strings of cash,
which greatly eased his financial troubles.
Later, when someone was selling an old house,
Féng saw that it contained countless hidden treasures,
so he purchased it at a high price.
From then on, his wealth rivaled that of princes and dukes.
He collected rare gems like huǒqí and mùnán.
Among them was a mirror
with a phoenix-shaped knob on the back
and an engraving of clouds, water, and the Xiāng River goddesses.
Its light could shine over a mile,
making even the finest details visible.
If a beautiful woman looked into it,
her reflection would remain imprinted on the mirror,
unable to be wiped away.
However, if she changed her attire and looked again,
or if another beauty gazed into it,
the previous reflection would vanish.
At that time, the third princess of the Sù Mansion was exceptionally beautiful,
and he greatly admired her reputation.
It happened that the princess was visiting Kōngtóng Mountain,
so he went and hid in the mountains,
waiting for her to descend from her carriage.
He took her picture with the mirror and returned home,
placing it on his desk.
Upon examining it closely,
he saw the beautiful woman within,
holding a handkerchief and smiling softly,
her lips seeming about to speak and her eyes about to move.
Delighted, he hid it away.
Over a year later,
his wife discovered it and leaked the secret,
which was reported to the Sù Mansion.
The prince was furious,
and had him arrested.
The mirror was confiscated,
and he was sentenced to beheading.
The scholar heavily bribed a powerful eunuch,
who spoke to the prince on his behalf:
"If Your Highness grants him pardon,
the greatest treasures under heaven
will not be difficult to obtain.
Otherwise,
he will only die,
and that truly brings no benefit to Your Highness."
The prince intended to confiscate his property and exile him.
The third princess said:
"He has already seen me,
and even ten deaths would not be enough to cleanse this stain.
It would be better to marry me to him."
The prince refused.
The princess shut herself in her room and refused to eat.
The prince's consort grew deeply worried,
and pleaded strongly with the prince.
The prince then released the scholar from prison,
and ordered the eunuch to convey his intentions to him.
The scholar declined, saying:
"One does not abandon one's humble wife,
and I would rather die than accept this command.
If Your Highness allows me to redeem myself,
I am willing to give up my entire fortune."
The prince grew angry again,
and had him arrested once more.
The consort summoned the scholar's wife into the palace,
intending to poison her.
But upon meeting her,
the wife presented the consort with a coral mirror stand,
and her words were gentle and sincere.
The consort took a liking to her,
and had her meet the princess.
The princess also liked her,
and they pledged to become sisters.
She then sent her to persuade the scholar.
The scholar told his wife:
"The daughter of a prince
cannot be treated as a secondary wife based on order of marriage."
His wife did not listen,
and returned home to prepare betrothal gifts to present at the prince's mansion.
The dowry and accompanying procession numbered nearly a thousand people.
As for precious stones and jades,
the prince's household could not even name them all.
The prince was greatly pleased,
released the scholar,
and married the princess to him as a concubine.
The princess still carried the mirror back with her.
One night, as the scholar slept alone,
he dreamed that the Eighth Great King entered majestically and said:
"The object I gave you
should be returned now.
Wearing it for too long
drains one's vital essence and blood,
and shortens one's lifespan."
The scholar agreed,
and immediately invited him to stay for a feast.
The Eighth Great King declined, saying:
"Since I heeded your medicinal advice,
I have abstained from alcohol
for three years now."
He then bit the scholar's arm with his mouth,
causing such intense pain that the scholar awoke.
Looking at it,
he found that the lump had disappeared.
From then on, he became like an ordinary person.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Sober, he is like a man,
but drunk, he is like a turtle—
this is the general state of those who indulge in wine.
Yet, though the turtle may grow accustomed to drunken madness,
he dares not forget kindness,
nor be disrespectful to his elders.
Is the turtle not far superior to some men?
As for a certain someone, sober he is less than a man,
and drunk he is less than a turtle.
The ancients had the 'turtle mirror' for reflection;
perhaps we should take the 'turtle' as our mirror instead.
Thus, I composed the 'Rhapsody of the Wine Drinker.'
The rhapsody reads:
There is a thing that
delights the heart and pleases the palate;
drinking it brings a tipsy, soaring feeling,
and its name is
"jiǔ" (wine).
It has many names,
and its merits have long been known: for feasting honored guests,
for hastening the arrival of fathers and uncles,
for drawing close in intimate joy,
for completing the wedding cup to form a pair;
some regard it as a
"hook for angling poetry,"
others consider it a
"broom for sweeping away sorrow."
Thus, when "Mr. Qu" (wine) visits frequently,
he becomes the sworn friend of the poet;
deep in the land of intoxication,
it becomes the refuge for those fleeing sorrow.
Once the terrace of the dregs hill is built,
the merit of the leather wine-sack is immortal;
a minister of Qí could down one shí,
a scholar also claimed five dǒu.
Thus, wine is certainly passed down through people,
yet people may become infamous because of wine.
Take for instance Mèng Jiā, who lost his cap,
Bó Lún, who carried a spade on his shoulder,
Shān Gōng, who tipped over his headscarf,
Péng Zé, who strained wine through his coarse headcloth.
Sleeping soundly by a beauty's side,
some observed he had no ulterior motive;
immersing his head in ink,
he believed himself inspired.
A scholar lying in a well as if aboard a boat,
a minister with jade ear ornaments tied by the wine vat.
Even imitating a turtle to mock the world,
still does no harm and is not unkind.
As for rainy nights and snowy evenings,
moonlit dawns and flowery mornings,
when the wind is still and dust settles,
with old guests and new courtesans,
shoes and slippers intermingled,
orchid and musk fragrances lingering,
gently critiquing, lightly dabbing,
softly singing, sipping slowly;
suddenly, a clear melody is played,
and all falls silent as if no one is there.
Elegant banter brings blossoms of laughter,
lofty chants ring like jade striking gold.
All are blissfully drunk,
yet souls clear and dreams true.
If so,
even getting drunk once a day,
should not incur the reproach of orthodox teachings.
But then comes clamor without grace,
vulgar words pouring forth;
sitting up and shouting noisily,
babbling forms a din.
Quarreling over a drop,
on the verge of drawing blades;
stretching necks, frowning brows,
gulping cups as if poison;
overturning, smashing goblets,
brushing against lamps, extinguishing embers.
Green grape wine,
spilled recklessly without regret;
sick leaves and wild flowers,
forbidden by the rules of drinking.
With such sentiments,
better not drink at all.
Further, some have wine stuck in the throat,
a gap less than an inch;
mumbling and muttering,
still blaming the host for stinginess,
neither sitting still nor acting,
unable to handle more drink: among wine drinkers lacking character,
this is the worst.
Worse still, under the influence of the maddening drug,
the guest's temper turns rough;
bulging like stone edges,
bristling beard and whiskers;
baring both arms,
leaping with both feet.
Dust clouding the face,
vomit splattering on robes;
mouth like a pig barking wildly,
hair disheveled like a slave.
Groaning to earth and crying to heaven,
like Lǐ Láng vomiting his liver and guts;
throwing down and stamping feet,
like Minister Sū being torn apart by ox carts.
Even one whose tongue produces lotuses
cannot exhaust its description;
one who sketches shadows by lamplight
cannot depict its image.
Defying parents to their faces,
wife and children too weak to support him.
Or a good friend of one's father
pointlessly insulted by a Guàn Fū.
Gentle warnings
only worsen the dizziness.
This is called
"jiǔxiōng" (wine-fiend),
beyond saving.
There is only one method
to sober him up.
What is this method?
Simply a club.
Seize his hands and feet,
treat him like slaughtering a pig.
Only strike his buttocks,
do not injure his head;
beat over a hundred times,
and suddenly he awakens clearly.』」
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain man from the county,
frivolous and shameless.
Once wandering outside the village,
he saw a young woman riding a horse approaching,
and said to his companions:
"I can make her laugh."
The others did not believe him,
and they bet a feast.
The man hurriedly ran forward,
appeared before the horse,
and shouted repeatedly:
"I want to die!"
Then, from the top of a wall, he pulled out a stalk of sorghum,
about a foot long,
untied his belt and hung it on the stalk,
put his neck through it, pretending to hang himself.
The woman indeed passed by and smiled at him,
and the others also laughed heartily.
After the woman had gone far away,
the man still did not move,
and the others laughed even more.
Approaching for a closer look,
they saw his tongue protruding and eyes closed,
and he had truly stopped breathing.
Hanging himself on a sorghum stalk—
isn't that strange?
This can serve as a warning to frivolous and frivolous people.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Luó Zǔ
was from Jímò.
In his youth, he was poor.
When it was the clan's turn to provide one man for garrison duty on the northern frontier,
Luó was sent.
Luó stayed at the frontier for several years
and fathered a son.
The garrison commander treated him quite well.
When the commander was transferred to become a cānjiàng in Shǎnxī,
he wanted to take Luó with him.
Luó entrusted his wife and son to his friend Lǐ Mǒu,
and went west.
From then on, for three years he could not return.
It happened that the cānjiàng needed to send a letter to the northern frontier,
so Luó volunteered,
asking to take the opportunity to visit his wife and son.
The cānjiàng agreed.
When Luó returned home,
his wife and children were safe and sound,
which greatly comforted him.
However, he found a man's discarded shoes under the bed,
and his heart grew suspicious.
Later, he went to Lǐ's place to express his gratitude.
Lǐ served wine with great hospitality;
his wife also spoke of Lǐ's kindness and righteousness,
and Luó felt immensely grateful.
The next day, he said to his wife:
"I am going to deliver my master's orders,
and I won't be able to return by evening,
so don't wait for me."
He went out the door, mounted his horse, and left.
He hid nearby,
and after the night watch had sounded, he returned.
Hearing his wife and Lǐ talking in bed,
he flew into a rage,
and broke down the door.
The two were terrified,
and crawled on their knees, begging for death.
Luó drew his blade,
but then sheathed it again, saying:
"I once thought you were a decent man,
but now that you are like this,
killing you would only stain my blade!
I make this agreement with you: take my wife and children,
assume my name and status,
my horses, weapons, and tools are all here.
I am leaving."
With that, he departed.
The villagers reported the matter to the authorities.
The officials flogged Lǐ,
and Lǐ told the truth.
But as there was no evidence of the incident,
and nothing to verify it,
a widespread search was conducted for Luó,
but he had vanished without a trace.
The officials suspected that he had been killed due to adultery,
and intensified the torture of Lǐ and the wife;
after a year,
both died in shackles.
Their son was then sent by post to Jìmò.
Later, a woodcutter from Shíxiá Camp went into the mountains,
and saw a Daoist priest sitting in a cave,
who never sought food.
People found this strange,
and brought provisions to him.
Some who recognized him
said it was Luó.
Gifts filled the cave,
but Luó never ate,
seeming to dislike the noise,
so visitors gradually dwindled.
After several years,
weeds grew into a forest outside the cave.
Some secretly peeked in,
and saw that he had not moved from his seat.
After a long time,
he was seen wandering on the mountain,
but when approached, he vanished;
when they looked into the cave,
the dust on his clothes remained as before.
People found this even more extraordinary.
A few days later, when they went again,
they saw a jade pillar hanging down,
and he had long since passed away in meditation.
The locals built a temple for him;
every year in the third month,
incense and paper offerings filled the roads.
When his son visited,
people called him "Little Luó Zǔ,"
and all the incense taxes were given to him: even now, his descendants
still go once a year
to collect the tax money.
Liú Zōngyù from Yíshuǐ told me this in great detail.
I laughed and said:
"People in this world,
do not seek to become sages or worthies,
but only hope to become Buddhas or patriarchs.
Let it be known to all: if you wish to become a Buddha instantly,
you must first put down your knife."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
There was a man named Liú in the county,
a tiger in human clothing.
Later, he moved from Zī to Yí,
but his habits remained unchanged,
and the villagers all feared and despised him.
He owned several acres of land,
which bordered the fields of a certain Miáo.
Miáo was diligent,
and had planted many peach trees along the field borders.
When the peaches first bore fruit,
Miáo's son went to pick them;
Liú angrily drove him away,
claiming the peaches as his own.
The son cried and told his father.
Just as the father was shocked and puzzled,
Liú was already at the door, cursing and shouting,
and even threatened to sue.
Miáo smiled and tried to appease him.
But Liú's anger did not subside,
and he left in a rage.
At that time, a fellow townsman named Lǐ Cuìshí was running a pawnshop in Yí,
and Liú, holding his complaint, entered the city,
where he happened to meet him.
As they were acquainted from the same hometown,
Lǐ asked:
"What are you doing here?"
Liú told him.
Lǐ laughed and said:
"Your reputation is well-known to all;
I have long known Miáo as a very honest and kind man,
how would he dare to cheat you?
Perhaps you are saying the opposite of the truth!"
He then tore up the complaint,
dragged Liú into a shop,
and tried to mediate.
Liú remained resentful,
secretly took a brush from the shop,
rewrote the complaint,
hid it in his bosom,
and vowed to sue without fail.
Not long after,
Miáo arrived,
explained the situation in detail,
and begged Lǐ to help resolve the matter,
saying:
"I am a farmer,
and have never seen an official in half my life.
If I can just avoid a lawsuit,
how would I dare to insist on keeping those few peach trees as my own?"
Lǐ called Liú out,
and told him of Miáo's willingness to yield.
But Liú again gestured wildly,
cursing and shouting without end;
Miáo only spoke humbly and gently,
not daring to argue at all.
After the matter was settled,
four or five days passed,
when Lǐ saw someone from that village
spreading word that Liú had died,
which left Lǐ astonished and sighing.
Another day, while going elsewhere,
he saw a man walking with a cane,
and it was unmistakably Liú.
When he approached,
Liú warmly inquired after him
and invited him to visit.
Lǐ hesitated and asked:
"The other day I suddenly heard the sad news of your death;
how could it have been so false?"
Liú did not answer,
but simply pulled him into the village,
to his home,
where he set out wine and refreshments.
Then he said:
"The report the other day
was not false.
Earlier, as I went out the door, I saw two men coming
to seize me and take me to see the officials.
I asked what the matter was,
but they only said they didn't know.
Thinking to myself that I had been in and out of government offices for decades,
and was not one to fear seeing officials,
I wasn't frightened either.
I went along with them,
to the government office,
where I saw the man facing south with an angry expression say:
'So you are such-and-such?
Your crimes are full to overflowing;
you show no sign of remorse.
Moreover, you take others' belongings
and claim them as your own.
Such tyranny and violence
deserve to be thrown into the cauldron!'
One man checked the register and said:
'This man has one good deed;
he should not die.'
The man facing south examined the register,
and his expression softened slightly.
Then he said:
'Send him away for now.'
Dozens of voices shouted in unison to drive me out.
I said:
'For what reason was I brought here?
And for what reason am I being sent away?
I beg you to make it clear.'
A clerk brought the register down
and pointed to one entry to show me.
It recorded: In the thirteenth year of the Chóngzhēn reign,
I used three hundred coins
to save a couple, enabling them to reunite.
The clerk said:
'If not for this,
your life would have ended today,
and you should have fallen into the animal realm.'
Utterly terrified,
I then followed the two men out.
The two men demanded a bribe.
Angrily, I told them:
'Don't you know that Liú so-and-so has been in and out of government offices for twenty years,
specializing in extorting money from people?
How dare you try to get meat from a tiger?'
The two then said nothing more.
They escorted me to the village,
cupped their hands and said:
'For this errand, we didn't even get a sip of water.'
After the two left,
I entered the door and then revived,
though by then I had already been dead for a day.'"
Lǐ heard this and found it strange,
so he asked for the beginning and end of that good deed.
Originally,
in the thirteenth year of the Chóngzhēn reign,
the harvest was terribly bad,
and people ate each other.
Liú was in Zī at the time,
serving as an arresting officer.
He happened to see a man and woman weeping bitterly,
and asked them about it.
They replied:
"We have been married for just over a year,
but this year there is famine,
and we cannot both survive,
so we are grieving."
A little later,
he saw them again in front of an oil shop,
seemingly arguing about something.
He went closer to ask.
The shop owner, surnamed Mǎ, said:
"This couple is starving to death;
every day they beg me for sesame residue to stay alive.
Now they want to sell the wife to me.
I already have more than ten people bought at home.
What's so urgent about this?
If it's cheap, I'll buy her;
otherwise, forget it.
So ridiculous,
coming here to pester me!"
The man then said:
"Now grain is as precious as pearls;
I reckon that without three hundred or so,
it won't be enough to cover the expenses of fleeing the famine.
I originally wanted us both to live,
but if I sell my wife and still cannot escape death,
what's the point?
I dare not haggle over the price,
but only ask you to do a hidden act of virtue."
Liú pitied them,
so he asked Mǎ how much he would offer.
Mǎ said:
"Nowadays, a woman's price
is only about a hundred or so."
Liú asked him not to shortchange them,
and even offered to contribute half the amount.
Mǎ stubbornly refused.
Liú, somewhat indignant,
said to the man:
"That fellow is despicable and not worth discussing;
I will give you the full amount.
If you can flee the famine
and keep your marriage intact,
isn't that even better?"
So he took out his purse and gave it to them.
The couple wept, bowed, and left.
Liú recounted this event,
and Lǐ greatly praised and marveled at it.
From then on, Liú's conduct changed completely,
and now, at seventy, he is still healthy.
Last year,
Lǐ went to Zhōucūn
and encountered Liú arguing with someone;
the crowd surrounded them but couldn't resolve it.
Lǐ laughed and called out:
"Do you want to sue the peach tree again?"
Liú looked blank, his expression changed,
and he stammered, withdrew his hands, and retreated.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Lǐ Cuìshí and his brothers
are all considered well-off commoners.
Yet Cuìshí is also sincere and prudent.
He delights in doing good
and has never flaunted his wealth;
Chái Tíngbīn was from Tàipíng.
His wife, née Jīn,
was not only taciturn,
but also exceptionally jealous.
Chái spent a hundred taels to buy a concubine,
but Jīn treated her with such cruelty
that she died within a year.
Furious, Chái moved out,
sleeping alone for several months
and never setting foot in the inner chambers.
One day,
on Chái’s birthday,
Jīn spoke humbly and performed formal courtesies,
toasting her husband’s longevity.
Chái could not bear to refuse,
and so they began to talk and laugh again.
Jīn set out a feast in the inner bedroom
and invited Chái.
Chái declined, claiming drunkenness.
Jīn, splendidly adorned, went to Chái’s quarters herself and said,
“I have been sincerely attentive all day.
Even if you are drunk,
please have just one cup before we part.”
So Chái went in,
poured wine, and they conversed.
His wife said calmly,
“The other day I mistakenly caused the maid’s death,
and now I deeply regret it.
Why must you hold such enmity and resentment,
as to sever all affection between husband and wife?
Hereafter, I ask you to take in twelve gold hairpins—
I will find no fault with you.”
Chái grew even more pleased.
The candles burned down to their stubs,
and so he stayed the night.
From then on, they were as respectful and loving as before.
Jīn then summoned a matchmaking old woman
and instructed her to seek out a fine secondary wife;
but secretly she told her to delay and not report back,
while she herself deliberately pressed for haste.
A year or more passed like this.
Chái could wait no longer
and asked all his relatives and friends to purchase one for him.
They obtained the adopted daughter of the Lín family.
At first sight,
Jīn’s joy showed on her face.
She shared food and drink with her,
and allowed her to take whatever she wished of cosmetics, flowers, and bracelets.
However, Lín was originally from Yān
and unaccustomed to women’s work;
apart from embroidered slippers,
everything required others to complete.
Jīn said,
“I have always been diligent and frugal—
unlike noble families
who buy women just to look at like paintings.”
Thereupon she gave her fine brocade
and made her learn tailoring,
like a strict teacher instructing a pupil.
At first she scolded and shouted;
later she used whips and rods.
Chái felt the pain in his heart,
but could do nothing about it.
Yet Jīn’s apparent affection for Lín
was even greater than before;
often she would dress her up herself,
applying powder and makeup for her.
But if the heels of her shoes showed the slightest crease,
she would strike her legs with an iron rod;
if her hair was even slightly disordered,
she would slap her cheeks. Lín could not endure such abuse
and hanged herself.
Chái, heartbroken and grief-stricken,
expressed considerable resentment.
His wife angrily said,
“I was teaching your woman on your behalf—
what crime have I committed?”
Only then did Chái realize her treachery.
Thus they quarreled again
and forever ended their marital harmony.
Secretly, he prepared chambers in a separate estate,
intending to purchase a beauty and live apart.
Half a year slipped by,
and he had not found the right person.
He happened to attend a friend’s funeral,
where he saw a sixteen-year-old girl
whose radiant beauty dazzled his eyes.
He stopped and stared, his spirit captivated.
The girl, annoyed by his wild gaze,
cast a sidelong glance at him with her autumn-wave eyes.
He inquired about her from others
and learned she was a Shào.
Shào was a poor scholar
who had only this daughter.
She had been clever since childhood;
when taught to read,
she could grasp everything at a glance.
She especially enjoyed reading the Inner Canon and books on physiognomy.
Her father doted on her;
whenever someone proposed marriage,
he always let her choose for herself.
Yet she found few acceptable, whether rich or poor,
so by seventeen she was still unmarried.
Chái learned the whole story
and knew his hopes were futile,
yet his heart lingered on her.
He also thought that since her family was poor,
perhaps they could be swayed by money.
He consulted several old women,
but none dared to act as matchmaker.
So he lost heart
and gave up all hope.
Suddenly, an old merchant woman
came to Chái’s place to sell pearls.
Chái told her his wish
and bribed her with a heavy sum,
saying:
“I only ask you to convey my sincere intentions;
whether it succeeds or not,
I will not hold you responsible.
If by any chance it can be arranged,
I would not begrudge a thousand pieces of gold.”
The old woman, tempted by the gain,
agreed.
She went to their door
and deliberately chatted with Shào’s wife.
Catching sight of the girl,
she exclaimed in admiration:
“What a beautiful young lady!
If she were in the Zhāoyáng Palace,
how could the Zhào sisters even compare!”
Then she asked:
“Who is her betrothed?”
Shào’s wife replied:
“Not yet.”
The old woman said:
“With such a young lady,
why worry about not having nobles as suitors?”
Shào’s wife sighed:
“We dare not hope for noble families;
we only want a scholarly seed,
that would be fine enough.
Our little troublemaker,
however, keeps picking and choosing,
rejecting nine out of ten,
I don’t understand what she intends.”
The old woman said:
“Madam, you need not fret.
Such a beauty—
who knows what blessings she cultivated in a past life
to be able to enjoy such fortune?
Yesterday there was a big joke: Young Master Chái said that near your family graves,
he caught a glimpse of her beauty,
and is willing to offer a thousand gold as betrothal gift.
Isn’t that a hungry owl dreaming of a swan?
I scolded him and sent him away at once!”
Shào’s wife smiled slightly but did not reply.
The old woman continued:
“But then, for a scholar’s family,
it’s hard to haggle over such matters;
if it were anyone else,
losing an inch to gain a foot—
it might be worth considering.”
Shào’s wife smiled again without speaking.
The old woman clapped her hands:
“If that’s the case,
then my plan is also misguided.
Usually, thanks to your kindness,
I enter your hall and you sit close to offer me wine;
if you obtained a thousand gold,
with carriages and horses going out,
and living in mansions,
when I come to your door again,
the gatekeeper would shout and chase me away.”
Shào’s wife pondered for a long while,
then rose and left,
to speak with her husband.
After a while,
she called their daughter;
after another while,
the three came out together.
Shào’s wife said with a smile:
“This girl is peculiar:
many fine matches she turns down,
yet hearing of becoming a lowly concubine, she agrees.
I only fear she’ll be laughed at by the scholarly community!”
The old woman said:
“If she enters his household
and bears a little son,
how would the great lady regard her then!”
Having said this,
she told them of the plan to live separately.
Shào was even more pleased.
He called his daughter and said:
“Try discussing it with Granny Jiǎ.
This is your own decision;
do not regret it later
and blame your parents.”
The girl said shyly:
“If my parents can enjoy a generous provision,
then your support is secured.
Moreover, I consider my own fate thin;
if I gain a good match,
it must shorten my lifespan.
To suffer less torment—
that might not be misfortune.
Earlier I saw that Young Master Chái also has a fortunate appearance;
his descendants will surely prosper.”
The old woman was overjoyed
and rushed to report.
Chái was delighted beyond expectation.
He immediately set aside a thousand gold,
prepared carriages and horses,
and married the girl in a separate estate,
with none of his family daring to speak of it.
The girl said to Chái:
“Your plan
is like a swallow nesting on a tent—
not planning for morning or evening.
To stop mouths and guard tongues,
hoping nothing leaks out—
how can that be possible?
I suggest you return home early instead;
acting quickly may still bring small misfortune.”
Chái feared destruction.
The girl said:
“Under heaven, there is no person who cannot be transformed.
If I have no fault,
how can anger arise?”
Chái said:
“Not so.
This is an exceptionally fierce person
who cannot be moved by reason or sentiment.”
The girl said:
“As a lowly servant,
I accept that I may be broken.
Otherwise,
living day by day—
how can that last long?”
Chái thought she was right,
but still hesitated and could not decide.
One day,
Chái went elsewhere.
The girl went out in plain blue clothes,
ordered an old servant to lead an old mare,
and had an old woman carry a bundle, following her.
She went straight to the principal wife’s residence,
prostrated herself, and explained.
The wife was angry at first;
then, considering that her confession was forgivable,
and seeing her humble attire and demeanor,
her anger gradually subsided.
She then ordered a maid to bring out brocade clothes for her to wear,
saying:
“That heartless man spread evil among the crowd,
making me bear slander unjustly.
In truth, it’s all because men are unrighteous
and maids are shameless,
provoking such things.
Just think: abandoning his wife to set up another household—
is that even human?”
The girl said:
“Upon careful observation, he seems somewhat remorseful,
but he just won’t humble himself.
As the proverb says: ‘The greater does not submit to the lesser.’
In terms of propriety: a wife to her husband
is like a child to a father,
and a concubine to the principal wife.
If you, madam, would grant him some kindness and warmth,
then accumulated resentment could be entirely abandoned.”
The wife said:
“He himself does not come;
what have I to do with it?”
She then ordered maids and old women to prepare a room for her.
Though unhappy at heart,
she temporarily settled her there.
Chái heard that the woman had returned,
and was so alarmed and fearful that he could not calm down.
He secretly thought that it was like a lamb entering a den of tigers,
and that she must already be in a terrible state.
He rushed over in haste,
but upon seeing the house quiet and still,
his heart finally settled.
The woman met him at the door and urged him,
asking him now to go to the main wife's quarters.
Chái showed a reluctant expression.
The woman shed tears,
and Chái's resolve softened slightly.
The woman went to see the wife and said:
"My husband has just returned,
and is ashamed to have no way to face you, Madam.
I beg you, Madam, to go and tease him a little."
The wife refused to go.
The woman said:
"I have already said: a husband's relation to his wife
is like that of the principal wife to a concubine.
When Mèng Guāng lifted the tray,
no one considered it flattery—
why?
It is because it was in accordance with her proper station."
The wife then followed her,
and upon seeing Chái, said:
"You, with your three burrows like a cunning hare,
why have you come back?"
Chái lowered his head and did not reply.
The woman nudged him with her elbow,
and only then did Chái force a smile.
The wife's expression gradually cleared,
and she was about to leave.
The woman pushed Chái to follow her,
and also instructed the cook to prepare wine.
From then on, husband and wife were reconciled.
The woman rose early, dressed in plain clothes, and went to pay her respects;
after washing,
she handed over the towel,
performing the duties of a maidservant with great deference.
When Chái entered her room,
she firmly declined him,
and only after more than ten nights did she consent once.
The wife also inwardly considered her virtuous;
yet she felt ashamed that she could not match her.
This accumulated shame turned into jealousy.
But as the woman served with care,
there was no flaw to seize upon;
sometimes the wife would lightly scold or reprimand her,
and the woman would only submit and endure.
One night,
the husband and wife had a slight quarrel,
and in the morning while doing her makeup, the wife still wore a look of great anger.
The woman was holding a mirror,
the mirror fell,
and broke.
The wife grew even more furious,
clutching her hair and glaring with eyes wide.
The woman, afraid,
knelt down and pleaded for mercy,
but the anger did not subside,
and she was whipped several dozen times.
Chái could not bear it,
and stormed in angrily,
dragging the woman out.
The wife clamored and chased after them, striking.
Chái, enraged,
snatched the whip and struck back,
until her face split open,
and only then did she retreat.
From then on, husband and wife were like enemies.
Chái forbade the woman from going to see her.
The woman did not listen;
rising early,
she crawled on her knees to wait outside the curtain.
The wife pounded the bed and cursed angrily,
shouting at her to leave,
and would not let her approach.
Day and night, he gnashed his teeth,
waiting for Chái to leave so he could vent his anger on the woman.
Chái learned of this,
declined all social engagements,
and shut his doors, refusing to attend any funerals or celebrations.
His wife could do nothing about it,
and only vented her hatred by daily beating the maids and old women,
making life unbearable for all the servants.
Since the husband and wife had severed their relationship,
the woman also dared not share his bed at night,
so Chái slept alone.
When the wife heard this,
her mind was slightly put at ease.
There was a senior maid who was cunning and sly;
once, when she spoke with Chái,
the wife suspected an affair,
and punished her even more harshly.
The maid would then, in deserted places,
bitterly curse and complain.
One evening,
it was this maid's turn to be on night duty,
and the woman warned Chái,
forbidding him to go,
saying:
"The maid's face shows murderous intent;
her motives are unfathomable."
Chái followed her advice,
summoned the maid,
and questioned her deceitfully:
"What are you up to?"
The maid was frightened,
and could not find words to respond.
Chái grew even more suspicious,
searched her clothes,
and found a sharp knife.
The maid said nothing,
only prostrated herself, begging for death.
Chái wanted to beat her,
but the woman stopped him, saying:
"I fear if the wife hears of this,
this maid will surely not survive.
Her crime is indeed unforgivable,
but it would be better to sell her;
that way, her life is spared,
and we also get some money."
Chái agreed.
Coincidentally, there was someone looking to buy a concubine,
so they hastily sold her.
The wife, because this was done without consulting her,
blamed Chái,
and redirected her anger even more onto the woman,
cursing and insulting her more venomously.
Chái grew furious,
turned to the woman and said:
"This is all your own doing.
If we had killed her earlier,
how could there be today's trouble!"
Having said this, he stormed off.
The wife found his words strange,
questioned everyone around her,
but no one knew anything;
she asked the woman,
but the woman also said nothing.
Her heart grew even more frustrated and angry,
and she grabbed the woman's skirt, wildly cursing.
Chái then returned,
and told her the truth.
The wife was greatly shocked,
and spoke gently to the woman;
but in her heart, she resented her even more for not speaking up earlier.
Chái thought all grievances were resolved,
and no longer took precautions.
When he happened to travel far away,
the wife summoned the woman and rebuked her, saying:
"The crime of attempting to kill one's master is unforgivable;
what were you thinking, letting her go?"
The woman, caught off guard, could not defend herself with words.
The wife heated an iron rod until red-hot and branded the woman's face,
intending to ruin her beauty.
The maids and old women all felt this was unjust.
Every time she cried out in pain,
the entire household wept,
willing to suffer in her place.
The wife then stopped branding her,
but pierced her sides over twenty times with needles,
before finally sending her away.
When Chái returned,
he saw the wounds on her face,
and was furious,
wanting to go confront his wife.
The woman grabbed his lapel and said:
"I knowingly stepped into this fire pit.
When I married you,
did I think your home was a paradise?
I simply recognized my own ill fate,
and resigned myself to venting the wrath of fate.
If I endure patiently,
there may still be an end to this;
but if I provoke her again,
it would be like filling a pit only to dig it up once more."
She then applied medicine to the wounds,
and within a few days, they healed.
Suddenly, she looked in the mirror and joyfully said:
"Today, you should congratulate me,
for she has branded away my unlucky lines!"
Morning and night, she served the wife,
just as before.
Jīn, having earlier seen everyone weeping,
realized she had become like a tyrant,
and felt a slight sprout of remorse,
often calling the woman to help with tasks,
her words and demeanor gentle.
Over a month later,
she suddenly fell ill with nausea,
unable to eat or drink.
Chái wished she would die,
and paid her no attention.
After several days,
her abdomen swelled like a drum,
and she grew weaker day and night.
The woman attended to her tirelessly, without sleep or food,
and Jīn grew even more grateful to her.
The woman offered to treat her with medical knowledge;
but Jīn, feeling her past cruelty had been too severe,
suspected she might seek revenge,
and so declined.
Jīn was strict and orderly in managing the household,
keeping all maids and servants under tight control;
but after falling ill,
they all became idle and neglected their duties.
Chái personally took charge of everything,
toiling arduously,
yet the household's rice and salt
dwindled without being consumed.
Thus, he earnestly considered the need for a proper mistress of the house,
and hired a doctor to treat her.
Jīn would tell everyone she suffered from
"qì gǔ" (a bloating illness),
so when doctors examined her pulse,
they all diagnosed it as depression-induced stagnation.
After changing several doctors,
none proved effective,
