and she was nearing death.
As they were about to prepare another dose of medicine,
the woman stepped forward and said:
"This kind of medicine,
even a hundred doses won't help,
it will only worsen the condition."
Jīn did not believe her.
The woman secretly substituted a different prescription.
After taking the medicine,
within the time it takes to eat a meal, she had three bowel movements,
and her illness vanished as if lost.
She then laughed even more at the woman's earlier claim,
groaning and calling out to her:
"Nǚ Huà Tuó (female Hua Tuo),
what do you say now?"
The woman and all the maids laughed.
Jīn asked why,
and only then did they tell her the truth.
She wept and said:
"Day after day, I received your care and protection without knowing it!
From now on,
I entrust the household affairs to you,
and will follow your guidance."
Not long after,
she recovered from her illness,
and Chái Zhěngshè held a celebration.
The girl stood by the table holding a wine pot;
Jīn got up and snatched the pot away,
pulled her close, and
showed her extraordinary affection.
Late into the night,
the girl made an excuse to leave the table;
Jīn sent two maids to drag her back,
forcing her to share the bed.
From then on,
they discussed everything together,
ate every meal together,
and even sisters were not as harmonious as they.
Not long after,
the girl gave birth to a son.
After childbirth, she fell ill frequently,
and Jīn personally attended to her care,
as if serving her own elderly mother.
Later, Jīn suffered from heart pain,
and when the pain struck,
her face would turn ashen,
and she only wished for death.
The girl hurriedly fetched several silver needles,
and by the time she arrived,
Jīn’s breath was nearly gone.
She pressed on the acupoints and inserted the needles,
and immediately the pain stopped.
After more than ten days, it recurred,
and she was needled again;
after six or seven days, it flared up once more.
Although the treatment was effective each time,
and she did not suffer too greatly,
her heart was constantly filled with dread,
fearing it would return.
One night, she dreamed of arriving at a place
that resembled a temple,
where the deities and spirits in the hall were all in motion.
A deity asked:
“Are you Jīn?
Your sins are numerous,
and your allotted lifespan should be exhausted;
but considering your repentance,
I have merely sent down calamities,
as a slight punishment.
The two concubines you killed earlier,
this is their karmic retribution.
As for Shào, what crime did she commit
that you treated her with such cruelty?
The punishment of whipping
has already been repaid by Chái Shēng on your behalf,
and that can be considered settled;
but the branding you owe her,
and the twenty-two needle pricks—
now, after only three treatments, you have repaid a mere fraction,
and you expect the root of the illness to be eradicated?
Tomorrow, it will strike again!”
She awoke in great fear,
still hoping it was just a deceptive nightmare.
After eating, the illness indeed returned,
and the pain was twice as severe.
When the girl arrived,
she needled her,
and the pain subsided immediately.
The girl said doubtfully:
“My skill ends here,
why is the root of the illness not removed?
Let me apply moxibustion again.
This cannot be cured without severe burning,
but I fear you may not be able to endure it.”
Remembering the words from her dream,
Jīn showed no hesitation.
Yet, as she endured the pain with groans,
she silently thought that she still owed nineteen needle pricks,
and wondered what strange symptoms they might bring;
it would be better to suffer them all at once,
so as to avoid future suffering.
After the moxibustion was finished,
she begged the girl to needle her again.
The girl smiled and said:
“Can needles be used so casually?”
Jīn replied:
“There’s no need to consider the acupoints,
just please give me nineteen pricks.”
The girl smiled but refused.
Jīn pleaded even more insistently,
getting up and kneeling on the bed.
The girl could not bear to refuse.
Jīn then told her the truth about the dream.
The girl then roughly followed the meridians,
and needled her the required number of times.
From then on, she recovered completely,
and indeed never fell ill again.
She repented deeply,
and even when dealing with her subordinates, she showed no harshness.
Her son was named Rìjùn,
and he was exceptionally intelligent and gifted.
The girl often said:
“This child has the appearance of a Hanlin scholar.”
By the age of eight, he was regarded as a child prodigy,
and at fifteen, he passed the imperial examination as a Jìnshì and was appointed to the Hanlin Academy.
At that time, Chái and his wife were forty years old,
while the concubine was only thirty-two or thirty-three.
When she returned to her parents’ home in a carriage,
the villagers regarded it as an honor.
After selling his daughter, Old Shào
suddenly became wealthy,
but scholars were ashamed to associate with him;
only now,
did people begin to interact with him.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
“Women’s cunning and jealousy
are inherent to their nature.
And as for concubines,
they often flaunt their beauty and play tricks,
thereby fueling their mistress’s anger.
Alas!
This is the origin of disaster.
If one could accept fate with peace,
and abide by one’s station,
remaining unwavering despite countless hardships,
how could mere blades and weapons harm them?
Only after being saved from death twice
did repentance begin to sprout.
Alas!
Is this truly human nature?
To repay exactly what was owed,
without adding interest,
is indeed the mercy of the Creator.
Yet to use the art of healing as a means of retribution,
is that not perverse?
I have often seen foolish men and women suffering from illness all day long,
summoning ignorant shamans,
allowing them to prick their flesh and burn their skin without daring to groan,
and I have always found it strange,
but now I understand.”
A man from Mǐn took a concubine,
and in the evening, he went to his wife’s room,
not daring to leave directly,
so he pretended to remove his shoes as if preparing to get into bed.
His wife said:
“Go away!
Stop pretending!”
The husband still hesitated,
and his wife said sternly:
“I am not like those jealous women from other households,
why must you act this way?”
The husband then left.
The wife lay alone in bed,
tossing and turning, unable to sleep,
so she got up,
went and crouched outside the door to eavesdrop.
She could only faintly hear the concubine’s voice,
not clearly enough to make out the words;
only
“lángbà”
these two words
were vaguely discernible.
Lángbà
is what people from Mǐn call their father.
The wife listened for a while,
then choked on phlegm and collapsed,
her head hitting the door with a thud.
The husband was startled and got up,
opened the door,
and her body fell inside.
He called for the concubine to bring a light,
and saw it was his wife.
He quickly helped her up and tried to revive her.
Her eyes slightly opened,
and she immediately groaned:
“Whose father are you calling!”
Such jealousy is laughable.
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
There was a Daoist named Gǒng,
who had no given name,
and no one knew where he was from.
He once sought an audience with the Prince of Lǔ,
but the gatekeeper would not admit him.
When a eunuch came out,
he bowed and pleaded with him.
The eunuch, seeing his shabby appearance,
drove him away;
but he soon returned.
The eunuch grew angry
and chased him off, even hitting him.
When they reached a deserted spot,
the Daoist smiled and produced two hundred taels of gold,
asking the pursuer to relay to the eunuch:
"Tell him I do not wish to see the Prince;
I have only heard that the flowers, trees, towers, and pavilions in the rear garden
are the finest in the mortal world.
If he can guide me on a tour,
my lifelong wish will be fulfilled."
He also bribed the pursuer with silver.
The man, delighted,
returned to report.
The eunuch was also pleased
and led the Daoist in through the Rear Steward's Gate,
showing him all the sights.
They then ascended a tower together.
As the eunuch leaned against the window,
the Daoist gave him a push,
and he felt himself falling outside the tower,
with a thin vine tied around his waist,
suspended in midair.
Looking down,
he saw such height and depth that it made him dizzy,
and the vine seemed to be making faint snapping sounds.
Terrified,
he screamed loudly.
Before long,
several eunuchs arrived
and were utterly shocked.
Seeing him far from the ground,
they went up the tower to look and saw
the end of the vine tied to a root;
they tried to untie it to rescue him,
but the vine was too thin to bear any force.
Searching everywhere for the Daoist,
they found he had vanished without a trace.
Helpless and at a loss,
they reported it to the Prince of Lǔ.
The Prince came to see,
and found it most extraordinary.
He ordered mats and cotton padding to be laid below the tower,
intending to cut the vine then.
As soon as it was done,
the vine snapped on its own,
and he fell barely a foot from the ground.
Everyone laughed in disbelief.
The Prince ordered a search for the Daoist's whereabouts.
Hearing he was staying at Scholar Shàng's house,
they went to inquire,
but he had gone out and not yet returned.
Later,
they met him on the road
and brought him to see the Prince.
The Prince invited him to a banquet and,
once seated, asked him to perform a trick.
The Daoist said:
"I am but a rustic man
with no special talents.
Since I have received such gracious favor,
I dare to offer a troupe of female musicians to celebrate Your Highness."
He then reached into his sleeve and produced a beauty,
placing her on the ground.
She bowed to the Prince.
The Daoist ordered her to perform
"The Feast at Yáochí"
to
wish the Prince ten thousand years of life.
The woman delivered a few lines onstage.
The Daoist then produced another,
who introduced herself as
"the Queen Mother of the West."
Soon after,
Dǒng Shuāngchéng, Xǔ Fēiqióng,
and all the celestial maidens
appeared one after another.
Finally, the Weaving Maid came to pay homage,
presenting a set of heavenly robes
that shimmered with golden brilliance,
filling the room with light.
Suspecting they were fake,
the Prince asked to examine them.
The Daoist urgently said:
"Do not!"
The Prince did not listen
and insisted on looking.
Indeed, it was a seamless garment,
not something made by human hands.
The Daoist said unhappily:
"I served Your Highness with utmost sincerity,
borrowing this temporarily from the Weaving Maid.
Now it is tainted by mortal impurity—
how can I return it to its original owner?"
The Prince also thought the singers must be celestial maidens
and wanted to keep one or two.
Looking closely,
he saw they were all palace musicians.
He then began to doubt that this music
was something they had known before.
When asked,
they were indeed clueless.
The Daoist burned the clothes with fire,
then put the ashes into his sleeve.
Searching again,
they were gone.
The Prince then held the Daoist in high esteem
and asked him to stay in the palace.
The Daoist said:
"A rustic's nature
sees palaces as cages—
I would rather be free at the scholar's house."
Every midnight,
he would return to his place;
if firmly pressed to stay,
he would occasionally spend the night.
At banquets,
he would often amuse everyone by making flowers and plants of the four seasons appear out of order.
The Prince asked:
"I have heard that even immortals cannot forget emotions—
is that true?"
He replied:
"Perhaps some immortals are like that;
but I am no immortal,
so my heart is like withered wood."
One night,
while staying at the palace,
the Prince sent a young courtesan to test him.
Entering his room,
she called several times but got no response. Lighting a candle,
she saw him sitting meditatively on the bed.
Shaking him,
his eyes flashed open and closed again;
shaking him once more,
he began to snore.
Pushing him,
he fell over with her hand still on him,
sleeping soundly like thunder.
Tapping his forehead,
it made a sound like striking an iron pot.
She returned and reported to the Prince.
The Prince ordered needles to be jabbed into him,
but the needles would not penetrate.
Pushing him,
he was too heavy to move;
with over ten people lifting and throwing him off the bed,
he fell like a thousand-pound stone hitting the ground.
In the morning, peeking in,
he was still sleeping on the floor.
Waking up, he laughed and said:
"What a terrible sleep—
I didn't even notice falling off the bed!"
Afterward, the women often amused themselves by pressing on him while he sat or slept:
at first, he felt soft,
but upon pressing again, he became like iron or stone.
The Taoist priest stayed at Xiùcai Shàng’s home,
often not returning until midnight.
Shàng would lock the door,
but by morning when he opened it,
the priest would already be lying in his room.
Earlier,
Shàng had been close to the courtesan Huìgē,
and they vowed to marry.
Huì was skilled in singing,
and her music captivated the entire age.
When King Lǔ heard of her fame,
he summoned her to serve in his palace,
and their bond was severed.
Shàng often thought of her, but had no way to communicate.
One evening,
he asked the priest:
"Have you seen Huìgē?"
The priest replied:
"I have seen all the courtesans,
but I don’t know which one is Huìgē."
Shàng described her appearance,
and told her age,
and the priest then remembered her.
Shàng begged him to convey a message.
The priest smiled and said:
"I am a man beyond this world,
I cannot be your messenger goose."
Shàng pleaded incessantly.
The priest spread his sleeve and said:
"If you must see her,
please enter here."
Shàng peered inside,
and it was as large as a house.
He bent down and entered,
and it was bright and clear,
spacious like a hall;
tables, chairs, and beds,
everything was there.
Staying inside,
he felt no distress at all.
The priest entered the palace,
and played chess with the king.
Seeing Huìgē arrive,
he pretended to dust off his robe sleeve,
and Huìgē was already tucked into his sleeve,
unnoticed by others.
Just as Shàng was sitting alone in deep thought,
suddenly a beauty fell from the eaves,
and looking at her,
it was Huìgē.
They were both surprised and delighted,
and their affection reached its peak.
Shàng said:
"Today’s miraculous encounter,
must be commemorated.
Let us compose a linked verse together."
He wrote on the wall:
"The noble’s gate is like the sea, long without trace."
Huì continued:
"Who would know the wandering lover meets again today."
Shàng said:
"The universe within the sleeve is truly vast."
Huì said:
"It embraces all parted lovers and longing wives."
As soon as they finished writing,
suddenly five people entered,
wearing octagonal hats,
and light red clothes.
Recognizing them,
he had no prior acquaintance with any.
They said nothing,
and seized Huìgē away.
Shàng was terrified,
not knowing the reason.
After the priest returned,
he called Shàng out,
and asked about what happened,
but Shàng concealed the details.
The priest smiled slightly,
took off his robe and turned his sleeve to show him.
Shàng examined it closely,
and faintly there were written characters,
as fine as lice eggs,
which were exactly the lines they had composed.
More than ten days later,
he asked to enter again.
In total, he entered three times.
Huìgē said to Shàng:
"My belly is stirring,
I am very worried,
and often tie a tight cloth around my waist.
There are many eyes and ears in the palace,
if one day I give birth,
where can the baby’s cries be hidden?
Please discuss with Priest Gǒng,
when you see me with three cloths around my waist,
come to my rescue."
Shàng agreed.
Returning to see the priest,
he prostrated himself and would not rise.
The priest pulled him up and said:
"What you said,
I already understand clearly.
But please do not worry.
Your family line depends on this single thread,
how dare I not exert my humble efforts.
However, from now on you need not enter again.
What I repay you for,
originally is not for personal affection."
Several months later,
the priest came in from outside,
smiling and saying:
"I have brought your son.
Quickly fetch swaddling clothes!"
Shàng’s wife was most virtuous,
nearly thirty years old,
had several pregnancies but only one son survived;
she had just given birth to a daughter,
who died after a full month.
Hearing Shàng’s words,
she rushed out in surprise and joy.
The priest reached into his sleeve and brought out an infant,
sleeping soundly as if in a deep slumber,
the umbilical cord still not severed.
Shàng’s wife took and held it,
and it began to cry loudly.
The priest took off his robe and said:
"Birth blood staining clothes,
is most taboo for Taoists.
Now for your sake,
this twenty-year-old garment,
I must discard it at once."
Shàng helped him change clothes.
The priest instructed:
"Do not discard the old garment,
burn a coin’s worth of it,
it can cure difficult labor,
and expel a dead fetus."
Shàng followed his advice.
After residing there for a long time,
he suddenly told Shàng:
"Of the old robe I have stored away,
you should keep a small portion for your own use.
Do not forget this even after I die."
Shàng thought his words were inauspicious.
The Daoist said nothing more and left.
He went in to see the Prince and said:
"Your servant wishes to die!"
The Prince, startled, asked him why.
He replied:
"This is a matter of fate;
what more is there to say?"
The Prince did not believe him
and insisted on keeping him.
After playing a game of chess,
he rose hurriedly;
the Prince again stopped him.
He requested to go to his outer quarters,
and the Prince consented.
The Daoist hastened to lie down,
and when they looked, he was already dead.
The Prince prepared a coffin
and buried him with proper rites.
Shàng attended the funeral and wept with utmost grief,
only then realizing that the earlier words were a forewarning.
The remaining robe was used to aid childbirth,
and it proved as effective as an echo;
those seeking it thronged at his door.
At first, he gave them soiled sleeves;
later, he cut pieces from the collar and lapels,
and all were effective.
Recalling the Daoist's instructions,
he suspected his wife might face a difficult birth,
so he cut a palm-sized piece of the blood-stained cloth
and kept it carefully.
It happened that the Prince of Lǔ had a beloved concubine in labor,
but after three days, she had not yet delivered,
and the doctors had exhausted their skills.
Someone told the Prince about Shàng,
who was immediately summoned.
With one dose, she gave birth.
The Prince was overjoyed,
and offered generous gifts of silver and fine silks,
all of which Shàng declined.
The Prince asked what he desired,
and Shàng said:
"Your servant dares not speak."
When pressed again,
he kowtowed and said:
"If Your Highness wishes to bestow a favor,
granting me the former courtesan Huìgē would suffice."
The Prince summoned her and
asked her age.
She replied:
"I entered the palace at eighteen,
and now it has been fourteen years."
The Prince, considering her advanced age,
ordered all the courtesans to be called,
allowing Shàng to choose freely;
but Shàng showed no interest in any.
The Prince laughed and said:
"What a foolish scholar!
Did you decide on a marriage ten years ago?"
Shàng told him the truth.
The Prince then prepared a lavish carriage and horses,
and used the silks Shàng had declined as Huìgē's dowry,
sending them off.
The son Huìgē had borne
was named Xiùshēng—Xiù meaning "sleeve"—and was then eleven years old.
Shàng daily remembered the immortal's kindness,
and on the Qingming Festival, he would visit his grave.
A traveler who had long been in Chuānzhōng
met the Daoist on the road,
who took out a book and said:
"This belongs to the palace.
When I left, it was in haste,
and I had no time to return it.
Please take it back."
When the traveler returned,
he heard the Daoist had died,
and dared not report to the Prince;
Shàng conveyed the message instead.
The Prince opened it and looked,
and indeed it was the book the Daoist had borrowed.
Suspicious,
he had the grave opened,
but found only an empty coffin.
Later, Shàng's own son died young,
and he relied on Xiùshēng to carry on the family line,
making him even more convinced of the Daoist's foresight.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"A world within a sleeve—
this was but an allegory of the ancients;
could it truly exist?
And yet, how marvelous it was!
Within it were heaven and earth, sun and moon,
where one could marry and have children,
without the hardships of taxes
or the troubles of human affairs.
Then the lice in the sleeve
were no different from the chickens and dogs of Táoyuán.
If a guest could dwell there forever,
he could grow old in that land."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
There was a man surnamed Shāng from Jǔ,
whose elder brother was wealthy while he was poor,
and they lived next door to each other.
During the Kāngxī era,
a year of great famine came,
and the younger brother could not provide for himself day or night.
One day,
as noon approached,
he had not yet lit the stove for cooking,
and with an empty stomach, he paced back and forth,
unable to devise a plan.
His wife told him to go and ask his brother.
Shāng said:
"It's useless.
If my brother pitied my poverty,
he would have helped long ago."
His wife insisted,
so Shāng sent his son instead.
After a short while,
he returned empty-handed.
Shāng said:
"What did I tell you?"
His wife asked in detail what his uncle had said,
and the son replied:
"Uncle hesitated and looked at Aunt;
Aunt told me: 'Brothers live separately now,
each must provide his own meals.
Who can look after the other?'"
Husband and wife fell silent,
and for a time, they exchanged their broken jars and worn-out beds
for a little chaff and husks to survive.
In the village, three or four wicked youths,
seeing that the elder merchant Dà Shāng was well-off,
climbed over the wall at night to break in.
The husband and wife woke up alarmed,
and cried out while banging on washbasins.
The neighbors all resented them,
so no one came to their aid.
Having no alternative,
they desperately called for Èr Shāng.
When Èr Shāng heard his sister-in-law’s cries,
he wanted to rush to their rescue.
His wife stopped him,
and loudly called back to the sister-in-law,
“Brothers live separately now;
each must face his own troubles.
Who can still look out for the other!”
Soon after,
the robbers broke down the door,
seized Dà Shāng and his wife,
and tortured them with hot irons.
Their screams were extremely agonizing.
Èr Shāng said:
“Though they are indeed heartless,
how can I sit by and watch my brother die without helping!”
He led his son over the wall,
shouting loudly and urgently.
Èr Shāng and his son were originally brave and skilled in martial arts,
and people feared them.
Afraid also that the commotion might bring other help,
the robbers then left.
Looking at his elder brother and sister-in-law,
their thighs were scorched.
He helped them onto the bed,
gathered the maids and servants,
and then returned home.
Though Dà Shāng was injured,
none of his money or silk was lost.
He said to his wife:
“What we have left now
is entirely thanks to my brother’s kindness.
We should share it with him.”
His wife said:
“If you had a good brother,
you wouldn’t have suffered this misery!”
Dà Shāng then said nothing more.
Èr Shāng’s household ran out of food,
and he thought his elder brother would surely repay him;
but after a long time,
there was not a word.
His wife couldn’t wait any longer,
and sent their son with a sack to borrow from them.
He returned with only a peck of grain.
The wife was angry it was so little,
and wanted to send it back;
Èr Shāng stopped her.
After two more months,
their poverty and hunger became unbearable.
Èr Shāng said:
“Now we have no way to make a living.
It would be better to sell our house to my brother.
He might fear that if I leave,
he won’t accept the deed but will instead support us out of pity—
that’s possible;
even if not,
getting over ten taels of silver
could also keep us alive.”
His wife agreed,
and sent their son with the deed to Dà Shāng.
Dà Shāng told his wife,
and said:
“Even if my brother is unkind,
he is my own flesh and blood.
If he leaves, I’ll be isolated.
Better to return the deed and help him.”
His wife said:
“Not so.
His talk of leaving
is to pressure us.
If we do as you say,
we’ll just fall into his trap.
Are there no people in the world without brothers?
Do they all die off?
If we raise our walls high,
that’s enough to protect ourselves.
Better to accept the deed,
let him go where he will,
and we can also expand our property.”
Their plan settled,
they had Èr Shāng sign the end of the deed,
paid him the price, and sent him off.
Èr Shāng then moved to a neighboring village.
The unruly men in the area,
hearing that Èr Shāng had left,
attacked again.
They seized Dà Shāng once more,
beating and torturing him severely,
the torment reaching extreme cruelty.
All his gold and assets
were used to ransom his life.
As the robbers were leaving,
they opened the granary and called the poor of the village
to take as they pleased.
In a moment, everything was gone.
The next day,
Èr Shāng finally heard of it.
Rushing to see,
he found his brother already unconscious and unable to speak.
Opening his eyes and seeing his brother,
he could only claw at the bed mat.
Shortly after, he died.
Èr Shāng indignantly brought the case to the county magistrate.
The robber chief had fled,
and could not be captured.
As for the dozen or so who had taken the grain,
they were all poor villagers,
and the prefect could do nothing either.
Dà Shāng left a young son,
only five years old.
The family now impoverished,
the boy often went on his own to his uncle’s place,
staying for several days without returning.
When sent home,
he would cry incessantly.
Èr Shāng’s wife rather looked down on him.
Èr Shāng said:
“His father was unjust,
but what crime has the child committed?”
So he bought several steamed cakes,
and personally took him back.
A few days later,
evading his own wife and son,
he secretly carried a peck of grain to his sister-in-law,
for her to raise the boy.
He continued this regularly.
Several more years passed.
Dà Shāng’s widow sold their fields and house.
With the money, the mother could support herself,
and Èr Shāng no longer visited.
Later, a year of great famine came,
with corpses strewn along the roads.
Èr Shāng’s own household grew larger,
and he could not look after others.
His nephew, now fifteen,
was frail and unable to handle heavy work,
so Èr Shāng had him carry a basket and follow his own son selling flatbreads.
Èr Shāng dreamed his elder brother came to him,
looking sorrowful and distressed, saying:
“I was deluded by my wife’s words,
and lost the duty of brotherhood.
You, brother, did not hold my past faults against me,
adding to my shame.
The old house we sold,
is still vacant now.
You should rent and live there.
Behind the house, under a clump of weeds,
there is hidden buried silver.
Dig it up,
and you can become somewhat well-off.
Let my unworthy son stay with you;
I deeply resent that long-tongued wife of mine—
pay her no mind.”
After waking,
Èr Shāng found it strange.
He offered a high price to the current owner of the house,
and finally secured it.
Sure enough, he dug up five hundred taels of silver.
From then on, he gave up his humble trade,
and had the brothers open a shop in the market.
The nephew was quite clever,
keeping accounts without error;
and he was honest and diligent.
Every trifling sum that came in or went out,
he would report.
Èr Shāng grew even fonder of him.
One day,
the nephew tearfully asked for grain for his mother.
Èr Shāng’s wife wanted to refuse;
but Èr Shāng, moved by his filial piety,
gave him a monthly allowance of grain.
After a few years, the family grew even wealthier.
Dà Shāng’s widow fell ill and died.
Èr Shāng was also old by then,
so he divided the household with his nephew,
giving him half of the family assets.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"I have heard that a great merchant would not lightly take or give even a trifle,
being a man of integrity and self-respect.
Yet he listened only to his wife's words,
muddle-headed, not uttering a single objection,
treating his own flesh and blood with indifference,
and ultimately died because of his stinginess.
Alas!
Is this not indeed strange!
Èr Shāng began with greed,
yet ended as a wealthy commoner.
What was his strength as a person?
Merely that he did not overly follow his wife's instructions.
Alas!
A single difference in conduct,
and thus a man's character becomes distinct."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain scholar from Yíshuǐ
was studying in the mountains.
At night, two beautiful women entered,
smiling without speaking,
each brushed the couch with her long sleeve,
and they sat down together,
their soft garments making no sound.
After a while,
one beauty rose,
spread a white silk scarf on the table,
upon which were three or four lines of cursive script,
though he never examined what words they were.
The other beauty placed a silver ingot,
roughly three or four liǎng;
the scholar picked it up and tucked it into his sleeve.
The beauties took the scarf,
clasped hands, laughed, and went out,
saying:
"Utterly vulgar and unbearable!"
The scholar felt for the silver,
but it was gone.
Lovely ladies present,
offering their fragrant charms,
he paid no heed;
yet he went for the silver—
this is the manner of a beggar,
how could it be endured!
The fox-spirits were delightful creatures,
their elegant demeanor can be imagined.
A friend told this tale,
and thinking of other unbearable things,
I append a record of them here: Facing sour, vulgar guests.
Market-place folk using literary language.
Acting with an air of wealth and nobility.
Scholars pretending to be famous literati.
Observing fawning behavior from the sidelines.
Wearying, glib-tongued lies.
Bowing and seating with painful insistence on precedence.
Forcing others to view or listen to bad poetry or prose.
Miserly rich men complaining of poverty.
Drunkards pestering annoyingly.
Affecting a Mǎnzhōu accent.
Body odor or bad breath oppressively close while speaking.
Vulgar, malicious jokes.
Letting naughty children climb on the banquet table to grab food and fruit.
Hypocrites slowly putting on airs and pretending.
Unqualified degree-holders discussing poetry and prose.
In conversation, frequently mentioning noble relatives.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Fēng Yúntíng
was from Tàiháng.
Once he went to the commandery city,
and was lying down in his rented room by day.
Being young and having lost his wife,
in his solitude,
he was rather given to thought.
As he gazed intently,
he saw the shadow of a woman on the wall,
faintly like a painting.
He thought it must be a product of his imagination.
But it remained motionless for a long time,
and did not fade.
He found it strange.
Getting up to look, it became more distinct;
drawing closer,
it was clearly a young maiden,
her face distressed, tongue protruding,
a noose around her slender neck.
Before his startled gaze ended,
she slowly began to descend.
Knowing she was a ghost of one who hanged herself,
yet emboldened by the daylight,
he was not greatly afraid.
He spoke to her:
"Lady, if you have some grievous injustice,
this humble scholar can exert his utmost efforts."
The shadow actually descended,
and said:
"A chance-met stranger,
how dare I suddenly burden a gentleman with a weighty matter?
Only, this withered skeleton in the springs below,
my tongue cannot retract,
the noose cannot be removed;
I beg you to cut down the roof beam and burn it,
your kindness would be as great as a mountain."
He agreed,
and she vanished.
He called the landlord,
and asked about what he had seen.
The landlord said:
"This was the former residence of the Méi family ten years ago.
At night, a thief entered the house,
was caught by Méi,
and sent to the Diǎnshǐ.
The Diǎnshǐ accepted five hundred coins from the thief,
falsely accused Méi's daughter of having relations with him,
and was about to detain her for interrogation and examination.
The daughter, hearing of it, hanged herself.
Later, Méi and his wife died one after the other,
and the house came to me.
Guests often see strange things,
but there is no way to pacify them."
Fēng told the landlord what the ghost had said.
Considering that tearing down the house and replacing the beam
would cost a great deal,
the landlord found it difficult;
Fēng then joined forces to assist in the work.
Once completed, he lived there again.
Méi's daughter came at night,
and after expressing her thanks,
her face was filled with joy,
her demeanor charming and lovely.
Fēng, loving and delighted by her,
wished to be intimate with her.
She blushed deeply and said with shame:
"My gloomy, wretched aura,
not only brings you no benefit;
if we were to act thus,
then the stain from my life before death,
could not be washed away even by the waters of the Western River.
Our union will have its time,
but today is not yet that day."
He asked:
"When will it be?"
She only smiled and did not answer.
Fēng asked:
"Do you drink?"
She replied:
"I do not drink."
Fēng said:
"Facing a beauty, staring blankly,
what pleasure is there in that either?"
The girl said:
"In my life, the only game I was skilled at
was playing 'Dǎmǎ'.
But with just the two of us, it's lonely,
and late at night, it's hard to have a board.
Now, with the long night and nothing to pass the time,
let me play the string game with you for a while."
Fēng agreed.
Sitting knee to knee, fingers extended like halberds,
they turned and changed the strings for a long time;
Fēng became confused and lost, not knowing what to follow;
the girl would then explain with her mouth and indicate with her chin,
the patterns becoming ever more fantastic,
endless in their variations.
Fēng laughed and said:
"This is a peerless skill of the women's chambers."
The girl said:
"This I figured out myself.
As long as there are two strings,
patterns can be formed;
people just don't notice it."
As the night grew late and they grew rather tired,
he urged her to go to bed,
but she said:
"I am a being of darkness and do not sleep;
please rest yourself.
I know a little of the art of massage,
and wish to use all my skill
to aid your pure dreams."
Fēng complied with her request.
The girl placed her palms together and lightly pressed for him,
from head to heels all over;
wherever her hands passed,
his bones felt intoxicated.
Then she clenched her fingers and kneaded finely,
as if touching him with balls of floss,
his body feeling indescribably relaxed and comfortable: when she kneaded to his waist,
his mouth and eyes grew drowsy;
when she reached his thighs,
he fell into a deep sleep.
When he awoke,
the sun was already approaching the Sì hour (9-11 am),
and he felt his joints light and harmonious,
quite different from usual.
His heart loved and admired her even more,
and he called for her around the room,
but there was no response.
At dusk,
the girl finally arrived.
Fēng said:
"Where do you reside,
that I must call for you everywhere?"
She replied:
"Ghosts have no fixed abode,
but dwell underground."
He asked:
"Are there crevices underground that can accommodate a body?"
She said:
"Ghosts do not see the earth,
just as fish do not see water."
Fēng grasped her wrist and said:
"If you were alive,
I would bankrupt myself to win you."
The girl laughed and said:
"No need to go bankrupt."
They bantered until midnight,
and Fēng pressed her ardently.
The girl said:
"Do not pester me.
There is a courtesan from Zhèjiāng named Àiqīng,
newly residing in the northern neighborhood,
who is quite charming.
Tomorrow night,
I will invite her to come with me,
to serve as my substitute for a while,
how about that?"
Fēng agreed.
The next night,
she indeed arrived with a young woman,
around thirty years old,
with roving eyes,
subtly hinting at a wanton nature.
The three of them sat intimately,
playing a game of mǎdiào.
When the game ended,
the girl stood up and said:
"Your joyous meeting is just beginning,
I shall take my leave."
Fēng tried to detain her,
but she vanished like a wisp.
The two climbed onto the bed,
and their union was exceedingly pleasurable.
When he inquired about her family background,
she evaded and did not fully disclose,
merely saying:
"If you, sir, love me,
tap the north wall with your finger,
and softly call out 'Húlúzi,'
and I will come.
If I do not respond after three calls,
you will know I am occupied,
and you should not summon me again."
At daybreak,
she entered a crevice in the north wall and departed.
The next day,
the girl came.
Fēng asked about Àiqīng.
The girl said:
"She was summoned by Young Master Gāo to accompany him in drinking,
so she could not come."
Then they trimmed the candle and talked together.
Whenever the girl wanted to say something,
her lips would part but then she would stop;
when pressed firmly,
she ultimately refused to speak,
only sighing.
Fēng insisted on frolicking with her,
and she left only at the fourth watch.
From then on, the two women came frequently,
their laughter resounding day and night,
so that the entire city heard of it.
A certain Diǎnshǐ,
also from an old family in Zhèjiāng,
had his principal wife dismissed for an affair with a servant.
He then married a woman named Gù,
and they loved each other deeply;
but within a month she died young,
and he grieved deeply.
Hearing that Fēng had a spirit ghost,
he wanted to inquire about fate in the underworld,
so he rode on horseback to visit Fēng.
At first, Fēng refused to admit it,
but the man insisted earnestly,
so Fēng set out a feast and sat with him,
promising to summon the ghost courtesan.
As dusk fell,
he knocked on the wall and called,
and before three calls were finished,
Àiqīng entered.
Raising her head and seeing the guest,
her face changed and she tried to flee,
but Fēng blocked her way with his body.
The man looked closely,
flew into a rage,
hurled a large bowl at her,
and she vanished instantly.
Fēng was greatly alarmed,
not understanding the reason,
and was about to question him.
Suddenly, an old woman emerged from the dark room,
and cursed loudly, saying:
"You greedy, despicable thief!
You've ruined my money tree!
You must repay the thirty strings of cash!"
She struck him with her cane,
hitting his head.
He clutched his head and wailed:
"This is Gù Shì,
my wife.
She died young,
and I am deeply grieved;
I never imagined she would be unfaithful even as a ghost.
What business is it of yours, old woman?"
The old woman angrily said:
"You were originally a worthless scoundrel from Zhèjiāng,
you bought yourself a black horn belt,
and now your nose bones stick up in arrogance!
What sense of right and wrong did you have as an official?
With three hundred coins in your sleeve,
you'd even call your own father 'sir'!
The gods are angry, the people resent you,
your death is already near.
Your parents pleaded with the underworld judges on your behalf,
willing to send your beloved daughter-in-law into a brothel,
to repay your debts of greed for you.
Didn't you know?"
Having said this,
she struck him again.
He writhed and cried pitifully.
Just as Fēng was shocked and at a loss how to intervene,
he suddenly saw Měi Nǚ emerge from the room,
eyes wide, tongue sticking out,
her face transformed,
approaching to stab his ear with a long hairpin.
Fēng, terrified,
shielded the guest with his body.
The girl's anger did not subside.
Fēng urged:
"Even if he is guilty,
if he dies in my lodgings,
the blame would fall on me.
Please have some consideration for the taboo of 'not smashing the jade while attacking the rat'."
The girl then pulled the old woman, saying:
"Let him breathe a little longer,
for my sake, for Fēng Láng."
The man fled in panic like a rat.
Upon returning to his office,
he suffered from a brain ailment,
and died by midnight.
The next night,
the girl came out smiling and said:
"How satisfying!
The evil anger is vented!"
Fēng asked:
"What enmity was this?"
The girl said:
"I mentioned it before: he took a bribe and falsely accused me of adultery.
I have harbored this hatred for a long time,
and often wanted to ask for your help,
to clear my name.
But feeling ashamed that I had not shown you the slightest kindness,
I would always stop before speaking.
Just now, hearing the commotion,
I secretly listened,
never expecting it was my enemy."
Fēng exclaimed in surprise:
"So this was the one who falsely accused you?"
She said:
"He served as a diǎnshǐ here
for eighteen years;
I have been wrongfully dead for sixteen winters and summers."
He asked:
"Who was the old woman?"
She replied:
"An old procuress."
He asked about Àiqīng,
and she said:
"She is lying ill."
Then, sighing deeply, she said:
"I once said our reunion would come in time,
now it truly is not far off.
You once said you were willing to bankrupt your family to redeem me,
do you remember?"
Fēng said:
"Even today, my heart remains the same."
The girl said:
"To tell you the truth: on the day I died,
I was already reborn into the family of Xiào Lián Zhǎn in Yán'ān.
Only because my great grievance was not redressed,
have I lingered here until now.
Please make a ghost pouch from new silk,
so I may attach myself to you and go with you,
to seek marriage with the Zhǎn family,
I am sure they will agree."
Fēng worried that their statuses were too different,
fearing it would not succeed.
The girl said:
"Just go, do not worry."
Fēng followed her advice.
The girl instructed:
"On the journey, be careful not to call me;
wait until the wedding night,
hang the pouch on the bride's head,
and urgently call out: 'Do not forget, do not forget!'"
Fēng agreed.
As soon as he opened the pouch,
the girl leaped inside.
He carried it to Yán'ān,
inquired,
and indeed there was a Xiào Lián Zhǎn,
who had a daughter,
extremely beautiful in appearance;
but she was foolishly ill,
and often let her tongue hang out of her lips,
like a panting dog in the sun.
At sixteen years old,
no one had come to ask for her hand.
Her parents were so worried they fell ill.
Fēng went to their gate and presented his card,
fully explaining his family background.
After leaving,
he entrusted a matchmaker.
Zhǎn was delighted,
and took Fēng as a live-in son-in-law.
The girl was utterly foolish,
knowing nothing of propriety,
so they had two maids support and drag her to the bridal chamber.
Once the maids left,
the girl opened her robe, exposing her breasts,
and grinned foolishly at Fēng.
Fēng covered her with the pouch and called out.
The girl stopped, stared intently,
as if deep in thought.
Fēng smiled and said:
"Don't you recognize me?"
He raised the pouch to show her.
The girl then understood,
hurriedly closed her robe,
and they joyfully laughed together.
The next morning,
Fēng went to pay respects to his father-in-law.
Zhǎn consoled him, saying:
"My foolish daughter knows nothing,
since you have favored her with your regard,
if you are willing,
our house has no shortage of clever maids,
I will not hesitate to give you one."
Fēng strenuously argued that she was not foolish.
Zhǎn was doubtful.
Not long after,
the girl arrived,
her demeanor entirely proper,
which greatly astonished him.
The girl merely covered her mouth and smiled.
Zhǎn questioned her closely,
the girl hesitated, too shy to speak;
Fēng briefly outlined the story.
Zhǎn was overjoyed,
and loved her even more than before.
He had his son Dà Chéng study together with his son-in-law,
providing ample supplies.
After over a year,
Dà Chéng gradually grew contemptuous of him,
so brother-in-law and brother-in-law did not get along;
the servants also nitpicked his faults.
Zhǎn, influenced by the slander,
treated him somewhat less respectfully.
The girl noticed this,
and said to Fēng:
"We cannot stay long at my father's house;
those who stay long
all become worthless.
Before a major break occurs,
we should return quickly."
Fēng agreed,
and informed Zhǎn.
Zhǎn wanted to keep his daughter,
but she refused.
Father and brother were angry,
and did not provide a carriage or horse.
The girl used her own dowry to hire a horse and return.
Later, Zhǎn summoned her to visit,
but she firmly declined and did not go.
Later, when Fēng passed the provincial examination,
they resumed friendly relations.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"The lower the official rank, the greedier they are;
is this the common nature?
Three hundred coins to falsely accuse someone of adultery—
the innate goodness of the night air is utterly lost.
To seize a good match,
send her to a brothel,
and end up dying a violent death.
Alas!
How terrifying!"
In the jiǎzǐ year of the Kāngxī reign,
the registrar of Bèiqiū was extremely greedy and deceitful,
and the people all resented him.
Suddenly, his wife was seduced by a cunning man and ran away with him.
Someone posted a mock missing-person notice on his behalf, saying:
"Due to his own carelessness,
a certain official has lost one wife.
She carries no other belongings,
only a seven-foot length of red silk
wrapping a single silver ingot.
Its edges are upturned and its grain fine,
with no damage or defect."
This was also a minor, witty report.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A scholar named Guō from Eastern Yuè,
returning from a friend's place one evening,
got lost in the mountains
and wandered into a thicket of brambles.
Around the first watch,
he heard laughter and chatter on a hilltop
and hurried toward it.
He saw over ten people
sitting on the ground drinking.
Spotting Guō,
they exclaimed in unison:
"We were just one guest short at our gathering—
excellent,
excellent!"
After Guō sat down,
he noticed that half of the guests wore scholar's headbands,
so he asked them to show him the way.
One of them laughed and said:
"You are truly pedantic!
Why seek the road when you could enjoy this bright moon instead?"
He immediately sent a goblet flying over.
Guō drank it;
the aroma assailed his nostrils,
and he drained it in one go.
Another person picked up a pot and poured for him.
Guō was originally a good drinker,
and having run until his lips were parched,
he downed ten goblets in a row.
The crowd praised him loudly:
"How heroic!
Truly a friend of ours!"
Guō was unrestrained and fond of joking;
he could imitate bird calls,
each one remarkably lifelike.
Getting up to relieve himself,
he secretly made a swallow's chirp.
The others wondered:
"How can there be such a sound in the middle of the night?"
He then mimicked a cuckoo,
making them even more suspicious.
Guō sat back down,
only smiling without a word.
As they were arguing in confusion,
Guō turned his head and imitated a parrot, saying:
"Scholar Guō is drunk—
send him home!"
Startled, they listened,
but all fell silent, hearing nothing more.
A moment later,
he did it again.
Only then did they realize it was Guō,
and they burst into laughter.
They all puckered their lips to imitate him,
but none succeeded.
One said:
"What a pity Qīngniángzǐ isn't here."
Another added:
"We shall gather here again for the Mid-Autumn Festival—
Master Guō must not fail to come."
Guō respectfully agreed.
One of them stood up and said:
"Our guest possesses an extraordinary skill;
let us also perform the 'shoulder-stepping' game,
what do you say?"
Amidst the clamor, they all rose together.
The first one stood upright and rigid;
immediately, another flew up onto his shoulders,
also standing rigidly upright.
They stacked up to four people,
so high that no one could climb further;
those who followed
climbed by grabbing shoulders and stepping on arms,
as if scaling a ladder. In a moment,
all ten or so people were stacked,
reaching so high they seemed to touch the sky.
Just as Guō was watching in astonishment,
the column suddenly toppled to the ground,
transforming into a long, straight path.
Guō stood terrified for a long while,
then followed that path and made it home.
The next day,
he suffered severe abdominal pain;
his urine was green,
like verdigris,
and could stain anything it touched,
though it had no urine odor.
This lasted three days before it stopped.
He went back to check the spot,
only to find leftover bones scattered about,
surrounded by dense thickets—
there was no path at all.
When Mid-Autumn arrived,
Guō wanted to keep the appointment,
but his friends advised against it.
Had he mustered the courage to go once more and meet Qīngniángzǐ,
something even stranger would surely have happened.
What a pity his resolve wavered!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A certain Dàoshi,
while traveling, found himself at dusk
and sought shelter in a remote temple.
Seeing the monks' quarters locked,
he borrowed a meditation cushion
and sat cross-legged in the corridor.
When night grew quiet,
he heard the sound of a door opening.
Soon, a monk appeared,
covered in blood and filth.
His eyes seemed not to see the Dàoshi,
and the Dàoshi likewise acted as if he did not see him.
The monk went straight into the main hall,
climbed onto the Buddha's seat,
embraced the Buddha's head, and laughed.
After a long while, he left.
At dawn,
the Dàoshi looked at the room—
the door was still locked as before.
Finding this strange,
he went to the village and described what he had seen.
The villagers went to the temple,
opened the lock to investigate,
and found the monk killed on the floor.
The room was in disarray, with mats and boxes overturned,
indicating a robbery.
Suspecting the ghost's laughter had a reason,
they all examined the Buddha's head.
Finding a faint mark on the back of its head,
they gouged it open
and discovered over thirty taels of silver hidden inside.
They then used the money to bury the monk.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"As the proverb says:
'Wealth is tied to life.'
How true!
For a person to hoard wealth through frugality and stinginess,
only to leave it to someone he does not even know,
is already foolish enough;
how much more so for a monk who does not even know who that someone is to hoard it for no one!
Unwilling to enjoy it in life,
he still gazes at it and laughs after death—
such is the lamentable nature of a miser.
The Buddha said:
'Not a single coin can be taken along;
only karma follows the body.'
This surely refers to that monk!"
Gān Yù,
styled Bìrén,
was from Lúlíng.
His parents died early.
He left behind a younger brother named Jué,
styled Shuāngbì,
who was only five years old at the time
and was raised by his elder brother.
Yù was fraternal and affectionate by nature,
caring for his brother as if he were his own son.
Later, as Jué gradually grew up,
his appearance was outstandingly handsome,
and he was also intelligent and skilled in writing.
Yù loved him even more,
often saying:
"My brother is so distinguished;
he cannot be without a good match."
However, his selection criteria were overly strict,
so the marriage never came to fruition.
Once, while studying at a Buddhist temple on Mount Kuāng,
he had just laid down to sleep at night
when he heard the sound of women outside the window.
Peeking out,
he saw three or four young women sitting on the ground,
with several maidservants setting out wine—
all were exceptionally beautiful.
One woman said:
"Lady Qín,
why hasn't Āyīng come?"
The one sitting below replied:
"She came from Hángǔ yesterday,
but was injured on her right arm by a wicked man,
so she cannot join our outing,
and she is still full of regret."
Another woman said:
"I had a terrible dream the night before last,
and I'm still sweating and trembling from it."
The one sitting below waved her hand and said:
"Don't speak of it,
don't speak of it!
Tonight, we sisters are gathered for joy;
speaking of such things is frightening and unpleasant."
The woman laughed and said:
"How can you be so timid, little maid!
Are you afraid a tiger or wolf will carry you off?
If you don't want me to speak of it,
you must sing a song
to accompany our drinking."
The woman softly chanted:
"Peach blossoms on the idle steps bloom one by one,
yesterday's spring outing, the little medicine should not have been missed.
I told my neighbor girl to wait a little, don't rush me,
once I put on my phoenix-head shoes, I'll come right away."
When she finished chanting,
everyone present sighed in admiration.
Amid the talk and laughter,
suddenly a tall, imposing man strode in from outside,
his falcon-like eyes gleaming,
his appearance fierce and ugly.
The women cried out:
"A monster has come!"
In a panic, they scattered in chaos,
almost like birds taking flight.
Only the singer, graceful and hesitant, did not flee in time.
She was seized and wept pitifully,
struggling to resist.
The man roared in anger,
bit off her finger,
and proceeded to chew and eat it.
The young woman fell to the ground as if dead.
Yù, filled with pity and unable to bear it any longer,
quickly drew his sword, pushed open the door, and rushed out.
He swung his sword,
striking the man's thigh;
the thigh was severed,
and the man fled in pain.
Yù helped the woman into his room;
her face was as pale as dust,
blood soaking her sleeves;
examining her hand,
he saw her right thumb was severed.
He tore cloth to bandage it for her.
The woman then moaned and said:
"You have saved my life;
how can I ever repay you?"
From the moment Yù first peeked at her,
he had secretly been planning for his brother,
so he told her his intention.
The woman said:
"A crippled person like me
can no longer manage household duties.
I should find another worthy match for your younger brother."
He asked her surname,
and she replied:
"I am of the Qín family."
Yù then spread out a quilt,
letting her rest temporarily;
he himself took his bedding to another place.
At dawn, when he went to check on her,
the bed was already empty,
and he thought she had returned home on her own.
But when he inquired in nearby villages,
there were very few with that surname;
he broadly sought help from relatives and friends,
but there was no definite news.
Returning home, he told his brother about it,
filled with regret as if he had lost something.
One day, Jué happened to be wandering in the wilderness
when he met a sixteen-year-old young woman.
Her demeanor was graceful and lovely,
and she looked at him with a smile,
as if about to speak.
She glanced around with her autumn-wave eyes and then asked:
"Are you the second young master of the Gān family?"
He replied:
"Yes."
She said:
"Your honored father once made a marriage agreement with me;
why do you now wish to break the former pledge
and arrange another with the Qín family?"
Jué said:
"I lost my parents when I was young,
and have never heard of such an old agreement.
Please tell me your family background,
and I will go home and ask my elder brother."
The woman said:
"There's no need to go into detail;
just give me your word,
and I will come to you on my own."
Jué declined on the grounds that he had not received his elder brother's permission.
The woman laughed and said:
"Silly young man!
Are you so afraid of your elder brother?
I am of the Lù family,
living in Wàng Village in the eastern hills.
In three days,
I will await your gracious reply."
Then she bid farewell and left.
Jué returned home
and told his elder brother and sister-in-law everything.
His elder brother said:
"This is utter nonsense!
When Father died,
I was over twenty years old;
if there had been such an agreement,
how could I not have heard of it?"
Moreover, because she traveled alone in the wilderness
and spoke with a man,
he looked down on her even more.
He then asked about her appearance.
Jué blushed deeply, from face to neck,
and could not utter a word.
His sister-in-law laughed and said:
"She must be a beauty."
Yù said:
"What does a boy know about beauty and ugliness?
Even if she is beautiful,
she surely cannot compare to the Qín girl;
if the match with the Qín family doesn't work out,
it won't be too late to consider her."
Jué silently withdrew.
A few days later,
while Yù was on the road,
he saw a woman walking ahead, weeping.
He lowered his whip, held the reins, and glanced at her slightly—
there was hardly anyone in the world to match her beauty.
He sent a servant to inquire,
and she replied:
"I was formerly betrothed to the second young master of the Gān family;
because my family was poor and moved far away,
we lost contact.
I have only recently returned,
and then I heard that your family is fickle in virtue,
breaking the former pledge.
I am going to ask Elder Brother Gān Bìrén
what he intends to do with me?"
Yù was pleasantly surprised and said:
"Gān Bìrén
is none other than myself.
I truly did not know about
the agreement made by my late father.
My home is not far from here;
please come with me to discuss it."
He then dismounted and handed her the reins,
walking alongside her as she rode back.
The woman said of herself:
"My childhood name is Āyīng,
and I have no brothers,
only an elder cousin, Lady Qín, living with me."
Only then did Yù realize that the beautiful woman was her.
Yù wanted to inform her family,
but the woman firmly stopped him.
Secretly delighted that his brother had found a good wife,
he still feared she might be frivolous and attract gossip.
However, as time passed,
the woman was exceptionally dignified and proper,
and also charming and eloquent.
She served her sister-in-law as a mother would,
and the sister-in-law also genuinely admired and loved her.
It was the Mid-Autumn Festival,
and the couple were just enjoying an intimate feast when
the sister-in-law summoned her.
Jué felt disappointed and frustrated.
The girl sent the messenger ahead,
promising to follow shortly;
yet she remained seated, chatting and laughing for a long time,
with no intention of leaving at all.
Jué feared his sister-in-law would wait too long,
so he repeatedly urged her to go.
The girl merely smiled,
and in the end did not leave.
At daybreak,
just as her morning toilette was finished,
the sister-in-law came herself to inquire with concern:
"Last night when we were together,
why were you so sullen?"
The girl gave a faint smile.
Jué sensed something strange,
and when questioned, their accounts did not match.
The sister-in-law was greatly alarmed:
"If she isn't a demon,
how could she have the art of dividing her body?"
Yù also became afraid,
and speaking from behind the curtain, she said:
"Our family has accumulated virtue for generations,
and we have never had any enemies.
If you are a demon,
please leave quickly,
and I beg you, do not harm my brother!"
The girl said with a bashful expression:
"I am not human by nature,
but only because of your father's old pledge,
that Sister Qín urged me to come.
I know myself incapable of bearing children,
and have often wished to take my leave.
The reason I have lingered with affection
is because you, brother and sister-in-law, have treated me so kindly.
Now that I am suspected,
I ask to bid farewell from this moment."
In the blink of an eye, she transformed into a parrot,
and flew gracefully away.
In the beginning,
when Old Man Gān was alive,
he kept a very clever parrot,
and would often feed it himself.
At that time, Jué was four or five years old,
and asked:
"Why do you feed the bird?"
His father joked:
"I'm going to make her your wife."
Whenever the parrot lacked food,
he would call Jué and say:
"If you don't take food to her,
you'll starve your wife to death!"
The whole family also treated this as a joke.
Later, the parrot broke its chain and fled.
Only then did they realize that the old pledge referred to this.
Yet Jué, though clearly aware she was not human,
could not stop thinking of her;
the sister-in-law missed her even more keenly,
weeping day and night.
Yù regretted it but could do nothing.
Two years later, he arranged a marriage for his brother with a girl from the Jiāng family,
but Jué never felt satisfied in his heart.
He had a cousin who served as a provincial judge in Guǎngdōng,
and Yù went to visit him,
staying away for a long time.
It happened that local bandits caused turmoil,
and the villages nearby
were half reduced to ruins.
Jué was greatly frightened,
and led his family to take refuge in the mountain valleys.
On the mountain, men and women were quite mingled,
and no one knew who was who.
Suddenly, he heard a woman whispering softly,
exactly like Yīng.
The sister-in-law urged Jué to go closer and check,
and it was indeed Yīng.
Jué was overjoyed,
and grabbed her arm, unwilling to let go.
The girl then said to her companion:
"Sister, you go ahead,
I'll wait for my sister-in-law to come."
When she arrived,
the sister-in-law saw her and wept with sorrow.
The girl comforted and urged her repeatedly,
and also said:
"This is no safe place."
She thus advised them to return home.
Everyone feared the bandits would come,
but the girl firmly stated:
"It's no matter."
So they all went back together.
The girl scooped up earth to block the doorway,
instructing them to stay inside peacefully and not go out.
After sitting and speaking a few words,
she turned to leave.
The sister-in-law quickly seized her wrist,
and also had two maidservants grasp her left and right feet.
The girl had no choice,
and stayed.
Yet she seldom returned to the private chamber;
only after Jué entreated her three or four times
did she go there once.
The sister-in-law often said the new bride could not satisfy her brother-in-law's wishes.
So the girl rose early to help Jiāng with her makeup.
After combing her hair,
she carefully applied powder and rouge.
When others saw her,
her beauty had increased severalfold;
after three days like this,
she had become a genuine beauty.
The sister-in-law found it marvelous,
and thus said:
"I have no sons.
I wish to purchase a concubine,
but have not yet had the leisure to do so.
I wonder if the maids can be beautified?"
The woman said:
"There is no one who cannot be transformed,
but those with good natural qualities are easier to work with."
She then examined all the maids,
and only one, who was dark and ugly,
had the appearance of bearing sons.
She called her over and had her washed,
then applied a mixture of thick powder and medicinal herbs to her.
After three days of this,
her complexion gradually turned yellow;
after twenty-eight days,
the ointment had penetrated her skin,
and she became quite presentable.
Every day, they merely closed the door and laughed,
paying no heed to the warfare.
One night,
clamor arose from all sides,
and the whole family did not know what to do.
Suddenly, they heard the noise of men and horses outside the gate,
and they all scattered and left.
When dawn came,
they learned that the village had been almost completely burned and looted;
the bandits had sent groups to search thoroughly,
and all who hid in caves or holes
were either killed or captured.
Thus, they became even more grateful to the woman,
regarding her as divine.
The woman suddenly said to her sister-in-law:
"My coming here
was only because I could not forget your kindness,
and to share in your worries during this chaos.
Now that Elder Brother is about to return,
if I remain here,
as the saying goes,
I am neither plum nor peach,
which would be laughable.
I shall leave for now,
and will surely find an opportunity to visit."
The sister-in-law asked:
"Is the traveler safe?"
She replied:
"There is a great disaster approaching.
This has nothing to do with others,
but Sister Qín has received great kindness,
and is determined to repay it,
so there should be no harm."
The sister-in-law tried to keep her overnight,
but she left before dawn.
When Yù returned from Eastern Yuè,
hearing of the chaos,
he hurried on his journey.
On the way, he encountered bandits,
so he and his servant abandoned their horses,
each tying gold around their waists,
and hid in a thicket of thorns.
A crested myna bird flew and perched on the thorns,
spreading its wings to cover them.
Looking at its feet,
he saw it was missing a toe,
and found it strange.
Soon, bandits surrounded them from all sides,
searching almost everywhere in the undergrowth,
as if looking for them.
The two dared not even breathe.
After the bandits dispersed,
the bird flew away.
After returning home,
each recounted what they had seen,
and they realized that the crested myna was the beautiful woman they had saved.
Later, when Yù was away and did not return,
Yīng would always come at dusk;
she calculated when Yù would return and left early.
Jué sometimes met her at his sister-in-law's place,
and occasionally invited her,
but she would agree but not come.
One evening,
when Yù was away,
Jué thought Yīng would surely come,
so he hid and waited for her.
Before long,
Yīng indeed came,
and he suddenly rose,
blocked her way and took her to his room.
The woman said:
"My romantic bond with you has ended.
Forcing a union
may incur the wrath of the Creator.
If we leave a little room,
and meet occasionally,
how would that be?"
Jué did not listen,
and eventually became intimate with her.
At dawn,
she went to see her sister-in-law,
who found it strange.
The woman smiled and said:
"I was waylaid by strong bandits on the way,
so I've troubled you with worry."
After a few words, she hurried away.
Not long after,
a large wildcat carried a parrot past the bedroom door.
The sister-in-law was terrified,
and suspected it was Yīng.
She was washing her hair at the time,
stopped washing, and cried out urgently.
Everyone rushed to chase and attack,
and finally rescued it.
Its left wing was stained with blood,
barely clinging to life.
She placed it on her lap,
stroking it for a long time,
before it gradually revived.
It used its beak to preen its wing.
After a short while,
it flew around the central room,
calling out:
"Sister-in-law,
farewell!
I resent Jué!"
It then flapped its wings and flew away,
never to return.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Lord Liú of Shǎnxī
served as the magistrate of Xìnghuà.
A Daoist priest came to present a potted tree.
Looking at it,
it was a small tangerine tree,
thin as a finger,
so he declined to accept it.
Liú had a young daughter,
then six or seven years old,
who happened to be celebrating her birthday.
The Daoist priest said:
"This is not worthy of your esteemed appreciation,
but merely to wish the young lady happiness and longevity."
So he accepted it.
The girl saw it
and was exceedingly fond of it.
She placed it in her boudoir,
caring for it day and night, fearing it might be harmed.
When Liú's term ended,
the tangerine tree had grown as thick as a hand's grip.
That year, it bore fruit for the first time.
As they packed to leave,
they found the tangerine tree too heavy and cumbersome,
and considered abandoning it.
The girl hugged the tree and cried pitifully.
The family deceived her, saying:
"We are leaving for now,
but we will return soon."
The girl believed them,
and her tears stopped.
Fearing that someone strong might take it away,
she stood watching as the family transplanted it under the steps,
and then they left.
The girl returned home
and was betrothed to the Zhuāng family.
Zhuāng passed the imperial examination in the Bǐngxū year,
and upon assuming office, became the magistrate of Xìnghuà.
His wife was overjoyed.
Secretly thinking that after more than ten years,
the tangerine tree would no longer exist,
but upon arrival,
she found the tree already ten arm-spans around,
with thousands of fruits hanging in clusters.
Inquiring with the former servants,
they all said:
"After Lord Liú left,
the tree grew luxuriantly but bore no fruit.
This is its first fruiting."
She found it even more marvelous.
Zhuāng served for three years,
and the tree bore abundant fruit without ceasing;
in the fourth year,
it withered and showed no blossoms.
His wife said:
"Your tenure here will not last long."
By autumn,
he was indeed relieved of his post.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Did the tangerine tree have a predestined bond with the girl?
How coincidental their encounter was.
Its fruiting seems like gratitude,
and its lack of blossoms seems like sorrow at parting.
If even plants are like this,
how much more so for humans?"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
On a winter night in the Yǐwèi year of the Shùnzhì era,
fiery red characters appeared in the sky.
The text read:
"Báitiáo dài jìng fǒu fù yì cháo yě chí."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Niú Chéngzhāng was a cloth merchant from Jiāngxī.
He married a woman from the Zhèng family,
and they had a son and a daughter.
Niú died of illness at the age of thirty-three.
His son was named Zhōng,
who was only twelve at the time;
his daughter was only eight or nine years old.
His widow could not remain chaste;
she sold off the family property,
packed up the proceeds,
and remarried, leaving.
She abandoned the two orphans,
who found it difficult to survive.
There was a widowed sister-in-law of Niú's,
already sixty years old,
poor and widowed with nowhere to go,
so she came to live with them.
After a few years,
the old woman died,
and the family's situation declined further.
As Zhōng gradually grew up,
he thought of continuing his father's business but was troubled by the lack of capital.
His sister had married a man named Máo,
who was a wealthy merchant.
The sister pleaded with her husband to lend her brother several dozen taels of silver.
The brother followed someone to Jīnlíng,
but on the way, he encountered bandits,
who robbed him of all his travel funds.
He drifted about, unable to return home.
By chance, he went to a pawnshop,
where he saw that the shopkeeper looked exactly like his father.
He went out and secretly observed him;
even his surname and given name matched.
He was astonished and could not understand the reason.
He just lingered around the shop all day,
trying to discern his intentions,
but the man paid him no attention at all.
After three days like this,
observing his speech, laughter, and mannerisms,
he was truly his father, without a doubt.
Yet he still did not dare to approach and acknowledge him;
instead, he announced himself to the servants,
asking, on account of being from the same hometown,
to be taken on as an employee.
After the contract was signed,
the master looked at his hometown and surname,
and seemed somewhat moved.
He asked where he was from.
Zhōng tearfully told him his father's name.
The master looked despondent, as if he had lost something.
After a long while,
he asked:
"Is your mother well?"
Zhōng still did not dare to say his father was dead,
so he tactfully replied:
"My father left on business six years ago and never returned.
My mother remarried and left.
Fortunately, my aunt took care of us;
otherwise,
we would have been buried in a ditch long ago."
The master said sorrowfully:
"I am your father."
Then they clasped hands and wept in sorrow.
He also led him in to pay respects to his stepmother.
The stepmother, surnamed Jī,
was in her thirties
and had no children of her own.
She was delighted to have Zhōng
and held a banquet at the inner chamber.
Niú, however, remained sighing and unhappy,
and wanted to return to his hometown at once.
His wife worried that the shop would be short-handed,
so she stopped him.
Niú then took his son to manage the shop's affairs.
After living there for three months,
he entrusted all the account books to his son
and packed his bags to return west.
After they parted,
Zhōng truthfully told his stepmother that his father had died.
Jī was greatly shocked
and said:
"He came here as a traveling merchant.
Some old friends from the past
kept him here to run this pawnshop.
He married me six years ago.
How can you say he is dead?"
Zhōng then recounted the details.
They were both puzzled and suspicious,
unable to understand the reason.
After a day and a night,
Niú had already returned,
bringing with him a woman
with hair like a tangled bush.
Zhōng looked at her
and saw it was his birth mother.
Niú grabbed her ear, stamped his feet, and scolded:
"How dare you abandon my son!"
The woman cowered, not daring to move.
Niú bit her neck with his teeth.
The woman cried out to Zhōng:
"Son, save me!
Son, save me!"
Zhōng could not bear it
and threw himself between them to separate them.
Niú was still furious,
but the woman had already vanished.
Everyone was greatly startled,
exclaiming that it was a ghost.
When they turned to look at Niú,
his face had changed to a ghastly hue.
He shed his clothes onto the ground,
transformed into a black vapor,
and soon vanished as well.
Mother and son were terrified and sighed.
They gathered his clothes and hat and buried them.
Zhōng inherited his father's business
and became immensely wealthy, with ten thousand taels of gold.
Later, when he returned home to inquire,
he learned that his remarried mother had died on that very day,
and the whole family had seen Niú Chéngzhāng.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Huò Héng,
courtesy name Kuāngjiǔ,
was from Shānxī.
His father served as a county captain
but died early.
Héng was the youngest child left behind,
exceptionally intelligent and gifted.
At the age of eleven,
he entered the county school as a child prodigy.
But his mother doted on him excessively,
forbidding him from leaving the courtyard,
so that by the age of thirteen, he still could not distinguish between uncles, cousins, or in-laws.
In the same neighborhood lived a military assessor named Wǔ,
who was fond of Daoism
and went into the mountains, never to return.
He had a daughter named Qīng'é,
fourteen years old,
unusually beautiful.
As a child, she secretly read her father's books
and admired the way of life of Immortal He Xiāngū.
After her father retreated into seclusion,
she vowed not to marry.
Her mother could do nothing about it.
One day,
Héng caught a glimpse of her outside the door.
Though still a boy and naive,
he simply felt an extreme fondness for her,
but could not put it into words.
He directly told his mother
to send a matchmaker with betrothal gifts.
His mother knew it was impossible,
so she made it difficult for him.
Héng became depressed and discontented.
His mother, afraid of upsetting her son,
then asked an intermediary to convey their intentions to the Wǔ family.
As expected, it did not succeed.
Héng thought of her while walking and schemed while sitting,
but could think of no plan.
There happened to be a Daoist priest at the gate,
holding a small chisel,
only about a foot long.
Shēng borrowed it to examine,
and asked:
"What is it used for?"
He replied:
"This is a tool for digging up medicinal herbs;
though the object is small,
it can penetrate solid rock."
Shēng did not quite believe him.
The Daoist then used it to strike a stone in the wall,
and it fell away as easily as if it were rotten.
Shēng was greatly astonished,
and fondled it, unwilling to let it go.
The Daoist said with a laugh:
"If the young master loves it,
I shall present it to you."
Shēng was overjoyed,
and offered money in return,
but the Daoist would not accept it and left.
Shēng took it home,
and tried it on bricks and stones,
finding it met with no resistance at all.
He suddenly thought that by boring through a wall he could see the beauty,
not realizing that this was an unlawful act.
After the night watch had sounded,
he climbed over the wall and went out,
straight to Wǔ's mansion;
he bored through two layers of walls,
before reaching the central courtyard.
He saw that in a small side room,
a lamp was still lit,
and peeping in,
he saw Qīng'é removing her evening attire.
After a short while,
the candle went out,
and all was silent.
He bored through the wall and entered,
to find the girl fast asleep.
He gently removed his shoes,
and quietly climbed onto the bed;
fearing that the girl would wake in alarm,
and he would certainly be scolded and driven out,
he then hid himself beside the embroidered quilt,
and catching a faint whiff of her fragrance,
he felt secretly comforted in his heart.
But having labored half the night,
he was quite exhausted,
and as soon as he closed his eyes for a moment,
he unconsciously fell asleep.
The girl woke,
hearing the sound of snoring;
she opened her eyes,
and saw light coming through a hole in the wall.
Greatly alarmed,
she secretly shook her maid awake,
drew back the bolt and went out quietly,
knocked on the window to call the household women,
and together they lit torches and took up sticks to go there.
They saw a young scholar with his hair in a topknot,
sleeping soundly on the embroidered bed;
looking closely,
they recognized him as Huò Shēng.
They pushed him before he awoke,
and he sprang up,
his eyes shining like shooting stars,
and seemed not too frightened,
only looking bashful and saying not a word.
The crowd pointed at him as a thief,
and scolded him threateningly.
Only then did he shed tears and say:
"I am not a thief,
but truly, because I love the young lady,
I wished to be near her fragrant presence."
The crowd also doubted that boring through several layers of walls
was something a youth could accomplish.
Shēng produced the chisel and told of its marvel.
They all tried it,
and were utterly astonished,
marveling that it was a divine gift.
They were about to go together and report it to the mistress.
The girl bowed her head in deep thought,
seeming to feel this was not acceptable.
The crowd, discerning her thoughts,
then said:
"This young man's reputation and family standing
are certainly not disgraceful.
It would be better to let him go,
so that he may again seek a matchmaker.
Tomorrow morning,
we can pretend it was a thief and tell the mistress,
how about that?"
The girl did not reply.
The crowd then urged Shēng to leave.
Shēng asked for the chisel.
They all laughed and said:
"Silly child!
Do you still not forget that weapon?"
Shēng glanced by the pillow,
and saw a phoenix hairpin,
which he secretly tucked into his sleeve.
This had already been seen by a maid,
who hurriedly reported it.
The girl neither spoke nor showed anger.
An old woman patted her neck and said:
"Don't say he's silly,
his little thoughts are quite cunning."
Then she pulled him,
and they went out again through the hole.
After returning home,
he did not dare tell his mother the truth,
but only urged his mother to send a matchmaker again to secure the match.
His mother could not bear to refuse him openly,
so she only asked all the matchmakers far and wide,
to urgently seek another good marriage for him.
Qīng'é learned of this,
and in her heart was anxious and distressed,
secretly sending a trusted person to hint to the old woman.
The old woman was pleased,
and entrusted a matchmaker to go.
But it happened that a young maid leaked the previous affair,
and Madame Wǔ felt insulted,
overcome with indignation.
When the matchmaker arrived,
it further provoked her anger,
and she drew a line on the ground with her staff,
cursing Shēng and even his mother.
The matchmaker fled in fear,
and recounted the situation in full.
Shēng's mother also angrily said:
"The deeds of my unworthy son,
I was completely unaware of.
How could she then treat us with such discourtesy!
When they were lying together,
why didn't she kill both the wanton boy and the licentious girl?"
From then on, whenever she met their relatives,
she would immediately pour out her grievances.
When the girl heard,
she was ashamed and wished to die.
Madame Wǔ greatly regretted it,
but could not stop her from speaking.
The girl secretly sent someone to tactfully convey to Shēng's mother,
and vowed not to marry another,
her words full of sorrow and earnestness.
His mother was moved,
and spoke no more of it;
and the matchmakers discussing marriage
also then ceased.
It happened that Magistrate Ōu from Qínzhōng was governing that district,
and seeing Shēng's writings,
thought highly of him,
often summoning him into the inner office,
and treating him with the utmost favor and kindness.
One day,
he asked Shēng:
"Are you married?"
He replied:
"Not yet."
Questioned in detail,
he answered:
