"I formerly had a slight pledge with the daughter of the late Military Adjudicator Wǔ;
later, due to a minor discord,
it was consequently broken off."
He asked:
"Do you still wish for it?"
Shēng looked bashful and did not speak.
The magistrate said with a laugh:
"I shall accomplish it for you."
He then entrusted the county sheriff and the educational official,
to present betrothal gifts to the Wǔ family.
Madame Wǔ was pleased,
and the marriage was thus settled.
After a year,
he married and brought her home.
When the girl entered the door,
she threw the chisel to the ground and said:
"This bandit's tool,
you may take it away!"
Shēng said with a laugh:
"Do not forget the matchmaker."
He treasured it and wore it,
constantly keeping it on his person.
The woman was gentle, kind, and reserved,
paying respects to her mother three times a day;
the rest of the time she would simply shut herself indoors in quiet solitude,
not paying much attention to household affairs.
If her mother happened to be away visiting elsewhere,
she would manage every matter herself,
and nothing was left in disorder.
Over a year later,
she gave birth to a son named Mèngxiān.
She entrusted everything to the wet nurse and nanny,
seeming not to care for or cherish him much either.
Another four or five years passed,
when she suddenly said to her husband:
"The bond of our joyful love
has lasted eight years now.
Now, the time for parting is long, while that for reunion is short—
what can be done about it?"
Startled, her husband asked her what she meant,
but she had already fallen silent.
Dressed in full attire, she bowed to her mother,
then turned and entered her room.
When he hurried after her to question her,
she was lying on her back on the bed, already breathless and deceased.
Mother and son mourned her painfully,
purchasing fine wood for her coffin and burying her.
Her mother was already frail with age,
and every time she held her grandson, she would think of her daughter,
feeling as if her heart and lungs were being torn apart.
As a result, she fell ill,
growing so weak that she could not rise.
She could not keep food down,
craving only fish soup,
but none was available nearby;
it could only be purchased from a hundred li away.
At the time, all the servants and horses had been dispatched on errands;
being utterly filial by nature,
her son could wait no longer.
Carrying money with him, he set off alone,
traveling day and night without pause.
On his way back through the mountains,
the sun had already set,
his feet were blistered and sore from riding,
and he could barely take a step.
Then an old man approached
and asked:
"Your feet must be blistered, aren't they?"
The son assented.
The old man then pulled him to sit by the roadside,
struck a stone to make fire,
wrapped medicinal powder in paper,
and fumigated his feet with it.
When he tried to walk,
not only was the pain gone,
but he felt even more nimble and strong.
Overwhelmed with gratitude, he expressed his thanks.
The old man asked:
"What urgent matter drives you so?"
He replied that his mother was ill,
and recounted the whole story.
The old man asked:
"Why not marry another?"
He answered:
"I haven't found a suitable one."
The old man pointed to a mountain village in the distance and said:
"There is a beautiful lady there.
If you can come with me,
I will act as your matchmaker."
The son declined, saying he had to hurry back with the fish for his sick mother,
and had no time to spare for now.
The old man then clasped his hands,
arranging to meet in the village another day,
telling him just to ask for Old Wáng,
before bidding farewell and leaving.
The son returned home,
cooked the fish, and offered it to his mother.
His mother ate a little,
and after a few days, she gradually recovered.
He then ordered servants and horses to go seek out the old man.
Arriving at the old place,
he lost track of where the village was.
After wandering for some time,
the evening sun gradually sank;
the mountains and valleys were very tangled,
and he could not see far into the distance.
So he and his servant climbed up a hilltop
to look for the village;
but the mountain path was rugged,
and it was too difficult to ride any further,
so they trudged upward on foot,
as twilight colors veiled the mist.
Pacing back and forth and gazing in all directions,
there were no villages to be seen.
Just as he was about to descend the mountain,
the way back was already lost.
In his heart, a dry fire burned like a blaze.
While fleeing wildly,
he plunged into a sheer cliff in the darkness.
Fortunately, a few feet below there was a narrow, desolate ledge,
and he fell onto it, lying there;
it was only wide enough to hold his body,
and looking down, it was pitch black, bottomless.
Terrified to the extreme,
he dared not move even slightly.
Also fortunately, small trees grew all along the cliff edge,
surrounding his body like a railing.
After a while,
he saw a small cave opening beside his feet;
secretly pleased in his heart,
he pressed his back against the rock,
and wriggled in like a caterpillar.
His mind grew slightly calmer,
hoping that at daybreak he could call for help.
A short while later,
deep inside there was a light like a star’s spark.
Gradually approaching it,
about three or four lǐ or so,
he suddenly saw corridors and buildings,
yet there were no lamps or candles,
but the brightness was like daylight.
A beautiful woman came out from a room,
looking at her,
it was Qīng’é.
Seeing the young man,
she exclaimed in surprise:
“How could you come here, sir?”
The young man had no time to explain,
but embraced her sleeve, weeping sorrowfully.
The woman urged him to stop.
Asking about his mother and child,
the young man recounted all his hardships,
and the woman also looked grieved.
The young man said:
“You died over a year ago,
is this not the underworld?”
The woman said:
“No,
this is an immortal’s abode.
Back then I did not die;
what was buried,
was merely a bamboo staff.
Now that you have come, sir,
you have a share in the immortal fate.”
Thereupon she led him to pay respects to her father,
who was a man with a long beard,
sitting in the hall;
the young man hurried forward and bowed.
The woman announced:
“Young Master Huò has come.”
The old man rose in surprise,
clasped his hand and briefly spoke of ordinary matters.
He said:
“It is excellent that my son-in-law has come,
by fate you should stay here.”
The young man declined, saying his mother was waiting,
and he could not stay long.
The old man said:
“I know that too.
But delaying three or four days,
what harm could there be?”
Then he offered him food and wine,
and immediately ordered a maid to set up a bed in the western hall,
spreading brocade cushions.
After the young man withdrew,
he asked the woman to share the bed with him.
The woman refused him, saying:
“What place is this,
that allows such intimacy?”
The young man grabbed her arm and would not let go.
Outside the window, maidservants giggled with laughter,
and the woman grew even more ashamed.
Just as they were struggling and resisting,
the old man entered,
and scolded:
“Your vulgar bones pollute my cave abode!
You should leave at once!”
The young man had always been proud and spirited,
and ashamed, unable to bear it,
he changed expression and said:
“The feelings between a man and a woman,
are something no one can avoid;
why should an elder spy on me?
It is not difficult to leave,
but let your daughter come with me at once.”
The old man had no reply,
but summoned his daughter to follow him,
opened the back door and sent them out;
luring the young man away from the door,
father and daughter closed the door and left.
Looking back, there were steep cliffs and jagged rocks,
without the slightest crack or seam,
alone with his solitary shadow,
with nowhere to go.
Looking up at the sky, the slanting moon hung high,
and the stars were already sparse.
Disconsolate for a long time,
first sorrowful, then resentful,
he faced the cliff wall, shouting and yelling,
but to the end, no one responded.
In extreme fury,
he took out a chisel from his waist,
chiseled the stone and attacked forward,
attacking while cursing.
In an instant, he had bored three or four feet into the cave,
when faintly he heard someone say:
“What a sinful obstacle!”
The young man exerted himself, chiseling even more fiercely.
Suddenly, at the bottom of the cave, two doors swung open wide,
and they pushed Qīng’é out, saying:
“You may go,
you may go!”
The wall immediately closed again.
The woman complained:
“Since you love me as your wife,
how could you treat your father-in-law like this?
Where did some old Daoist priest
give you that vicious tool,
making people entangled and nearly dead?”
The young man, having obtained the woman,
felt his wish already comforted,
and did not argue further;
he only worried that the road was perilous and hard to return.
The woman broke off two branches,
each mounted one,
and they became like horses,
moving swiftly as they went,
and in a moment they reached home.
By then, the young man had been missing for seven days.
In the beginning,
when Shēng got separated from his servant,
he searched for him but couldn't find him,
so he returned home and told his mother.
His mother sent people to thoroughly search the mountains and valleys,
but there was no trace of him.
Just as she was anxiously worried with nowhere to turn,
she heard that her son had returned on his own,
and joyfully went to welcome him.
Raising her head and seeing the woman,
she was nearly frightened to death.
Shēng briefly explained the situation,
and his mother became even more pleased and comforted.
The woman, because her origins were strange and unusual,
feared it would startle people's ears,
and requested to move immediately.
The mother agreed.
There was another estate in a different commandery,
so they set a date and moved there,
and no one knew about it.
They lived together for eighteen years,
and had a daughter,
who married Lǐ Shì from the same district.
Later, the mother passed away.
The woman said to Shēng:
"In our family's thatched field,
there is a pheasant brooding over eight eggs;
that place can be used for burial.
You and your son should escort the coffin back for interment.
Our son is already grown and established,
so he should stay and guard the hut by the grave;
there is no need for you to return."
Shēng followed her words,
and after the burial, returned alone.
Over a month later,
Mèngxiān went to visit them,
but both his parents had vanished.
He asked the old servant,
who said:
"They went to attend a burial and haven't returned."
In his heart, he knew it was strange,
but could only sigh deeply.
Mèngxiān was very famous for his literary talent,
but struggled in the examination halls,
and for forty years had not succeeded.
Later, as a selected tribute student, he entered the northern examination,
and met a candidate in the same cell,
who was about seventeen or eighteen years old,
with a handsome and elegant demeanor,
and he took a liking to him.
Looking at his examination paper,
it was annotated: "Government student from Shùntiān, Huò Zhòngxiān."
Mèngxiān stared wide-eyed in great shock,
and then stated his own name.
Zhòngxiān also found it strange,
and asked about his hometown,
which Mèngxiān fully told him.
Zhòngxiān said happily:
"When I left for the capital,
my father instructed that if I met anyone surnamed Huò from Shānxī in the examination halls,
they are of our clan,
and I should treat them cordially;
now it has indeed come true.
But why are our names so similar?"
Mèngxiān then inquired about the names of his great-grandparents and grandparents, as well as his parents,
and then exclaimed in surprise:
"These are my parents!"
Zhòngxiān doubted that their ages matched.
Mèngxiān said:
"My parents are both immortals;
how can you judge their age by appearance?"
He then recounted past events,
and Zhòngxiān finally believed him.
After the examination, without time to rest,
they ordered a carriage and returned together.
As soon as they arrived at the gate,
the family came out to greet them and reported
that the old master and his wife had disappeared that very night.
Both men were greatly shocked.
Zhòngxiān went inside and asked his wife,
who said:
"Last night we were still drinking together,
and mother said: 'You young couple are inexperienced in worldly affairs.
Tomorrow when your elder brother arrives,
I will have no more worries.'
In the morning when I entered their room,
it was silent and empty."
When the brothers heard this,
they stamped their feet in sorrow.
Zhòngxiān still wanted to pursue and search for them;
Mèngxiān thought it would be useless,
so they stopped.
That year, Zhòng passed the provincial examination.
Because their ancestral graves were in Shānxī,
he followed his elder brother back.
They still hoped their parents were somewhere in the human world,
and searched everywhere,
but ultimately found no trace.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Drilling holes to share a bed,
his intention was foolish;
chiseling the wall to curse the old man,
his actions were mad;
the immortal who brought them together
only wished to repay his filial piety with long life.
Yet having mingled in the human world,
intimately bearing children,
then living there until the end—
why would that not be acceptable?
But after thirty years, repeatedly abandoning their son—
what, then, was the reason?
Strange indeed!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
The Zhèng brothers of Yìdū
were both scholars of literature.
The elder Zhèng became famous early,
and their parents doted on him excessively,
and because of the son, extended their favor to his wife as well;
the younger Zhèng was down on his luck,
and not much favored by his parents,
so they came to dislike the younger wife,
even to the point of excluding her from proper courtesy: the contrast between cold and warm treatment
left considerable resentment.
The younger wife often said to the younger Zhèng,
"You're a man just like him;
why can't you strive to bring honor to your wife?"
And she refused to share his bed.
Thereupon, the younger Zhèng, stirred by indignation,
applied himself diligently and sharpened his thoughts,
and also became well-known.
His parents began to treat him slightly better,
but he still fell short of his elder brother.
The younger wife watched her husband's progress with intense eagerness.
That year was the great examination,
and secretly on New Year's Eve, she used mirror-listening for divination.
Two people had just gotten up,
pushing each other playfully,
and said:
"You go cool off too!"
The wife returned,
unable to interpret whether it was auspicious or ominous,
and also set it aside.
After the examination,
both brothers returned home.
At that time, the summer heat was still intense,
and the two wives were in the kitchen cooking rice for the farm laborers,
suffering greatly from the heat.
Suddenly, a messenger on horseback arrived at the gate,
announcing that the elder Zhèng had passed.
The mother entered the kitchen and called to the elder wife:
"My elder son has passed the examination!
You can go cool off."
The younger wife, filled with indignation and sorrow,
wept as she continued cooking.
Soon, another messenger arrived announcing that the younger Zhèng had also passed.
The younger wife forcefully threw down her rolling pin and stood up,
saying:
"I'm going to cool off too!"
At that moment, stirred by her inner feelings,
the words unconsciously came out of her mouth;
later, thinking it over,
she realized it was the fulfillment of the mirror-listening divination.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"When one is poor, even parents do not treat him as a son—
there is reason for this!
Within the family curtains,
is certainly not a place for angry outbursts;
yet the younger Zhèng's wife spurred her husband on,
which is also quite different from those who merely complain and act shamelessly.
Throwing down the rolling pin and rising up—
truly a delightfully satisfying event for the ages!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Chén Huáfēng was a man from Méngshān.
One sweltering summer day, he lay down to rest beneath a tree in the wilds.
Suddenly, a man came running up,
his head wrapped in a scarf.
He hurried into the shade of the tree,
gathered some stones to sit on,
and fanned himself incessantly,
sweat pouring down like rain.
Chén sat up and said with a laugh,
"If you remove that scarf, you'll feel cool even without fanning."
The stranger replied,
"It's easy to take off, but hard to put back on."
Chén then engaged him in conversation,
finding him quite refined and knowledgeable.
After a while, the stranger said,
"Right now, I have no other wish
but to have some fine wine chilled with ice.
One taste of that cool fragrance
sliding down my throat
would dispel half this summer heat."
Chén laughed and said,
"That wish is easily granted. I shall fulfill it for you."
He then took the stranger's hand and said,
"My humble home is nearby. Please come with me."
The stranger smiled and followed him.
Upon arriving home,
Chén brought out wine stored in a stone cave;
it was so cold it made one's teeth ache.
The stranger was delighted
and downed ten cups in one go.
As dusk fell,
it suddenly began to rain.
They lit a lamp in the room,
and the stranger finally removed his scarf.
They relaxed together, chatting freely.
During their conversation,
Chén noticed that light from the lamp
seemed to leak from the back of the stranger's head at times,
which puzzled him.
Soon after,
the stranger became heavily intoxicated
and fell asleep on the bed.
Chén moved the lamp closer to take a secret look
and saw a large hole behind the stranger's ear,
as big as a cup.
Several membranes crisscrossed it like a lattice,
with soft skin hanging down outside the lattice,
and the inside seemed hollow.
Shocked,
Chén stealthily pulled out a hairpin
and poked the membrane to peer inside.
A creature resembling a small calf
flew out from the hole,
shattered the window, and fled.
Even more terrified,
Chén dared not probe further.
Just as he was about to turn away,
the stranger woke up.
He exclaimed in alarm,
"You have seen my secret!
You let the niúhuáng out—what am I to do now?"
Chén bowed and asked for an explanation.
The stranger said,
"Since things have come to this, there's no point hiding it.
I'll tell you the truth: I am the plague god of the six domestic animals.
What you just released was the niúhuáng (bezoar).
I fear that within a hundred lǐ, not a single ox will survive."
Chén, who made his living raising oxen,
was horrified upon hearing this
and begged for a remedy.
The stranger said,
"I myself will likely not escape punishment;
what remedy can I offer?
Only kǔshēn powder is most effective.
You must widely disseminate this prescription
and not keep it to yourself."
With these words,
he thanked Chén and left.
He also scooped up some dirt and piled it in a wall niche,
saying,
"Using one hé of this is also effective."
Then, with a bow, he vanished.
Not long after,
the oxen indeed fell ill,
and a great plague broke out.
Chén, wanting to monopolize the profits,
kept the prescription secret
and refused to share it with others,
only telling his younger brother.
His brother tried it and found it miraculously effective.
But when Chén himself prepared and fed the medicine to his oxen,
it had no effect at all.
He had about fifty oxen,
and nearly all of them died;
only four or five old cows remained,
but they too soon perished.
Chén was deeply distressed
and felt utterly helpless.
Suddenly, he remembered the dirt piled in the niche.
Thinking it might not work but trying anyway,
he administered it to the remaining cows.
After one night,
the cows all recovered.
Only then did he realize that the medicine had failed earlier
because the god was punishing him for his selfishness.
A few years later,
the cows bred and multiplied,
gradually restoring his herd to its former size.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Kuàijī, there was a shrine to Méigū.
The deity was originally surnamed Mǎ,
from the Dōngguǎn clan.
She was widowed before marriage
and vowed never to remarry,
dying at the age of thirty.
Her clanspeople built a shrine for her
and called her Méigū.
In the year Bǐngshēn,
a scholar named Jīn from Shàngyú,
passing by on his way to take the imperial examinations,
entered the temple and lingered,
lost in thought.
That night,
he dreamed that a maid in black came
to summon him on Méigū's orders.
He followed her.
Entering the shrine,
he saw Méigū waiting under the eaves.
She smiled and said,
"I am honored by your visit
and feel deeply attached to you.
If you do not嫌弃 my humble self,
I wish to serve you as a concubine."
Jīn murmured his assent.
Méigū saw him off, saying,
"Please go now.
When the seat is prepared,
I will come to welcome you."
He woke up, troubled by the dream.
That same night,
the local villagers dreamed that Méigū said,
"Jīn of Shàngyú is to be my husband.
You should sculpt his statue."
When the villagers compared dreams the next day, they all told the same story.
The clan elders, fearing this would tarnish her chastity,
initially refused.
Soon after,
everyone in one family fell ill.
Terrified,
they sculpted Jīn's statue and placed it to the left of Méigū's.
Once it was completed,
Jīn told his wife,
"Méigū has come for me."
He dressed formally and died.
His wife, grief-stricken and resentful,
went to the shrine and cursed Méigū's statue foully;
she then climbed onto the altar and slapped the statue's face several times
before leaving.
Now, the Mǎ clan refers to him as "Brother-in-Law Jīn."
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"To remain chaste without marrying—this cannot be called unchaste.
Yet after being a ghost for centuries,
she suddenly changes her conduct—how shameless!
Generally, chaste and heroic souls
do not necessarily reside in clay idols.
When temple statues display spiritual power,
startling the world and alarming the common folk,
it is likely ghosts or foxes possessing them."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Cháng Dàzhōng, a jìnshì from Tàiyuán,
was awaiting appointment in the capital.
The night before,
he dreamed that Wénchāng (the God of Literature) sent him a name card.
When he drew his assignment,
he was appointed magistrate of Zǐtóng.
He found this strange.
Later, after returning home for mourning
and completing the mourning period to await a new post,
he had the same dream again.
He wondered silently, "Could I be appointed to Zǐtóng again?"
And indeed, it came to pass.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Lǐ Mǒu was lying down during the day when
he saw a woman emerge from the wall,
her disheveled hair like a basket,
her locks hanging down to cover her face.
When she reached the bed,
she first parted her hair with her hands,
revealing her face,
which was plump, dark, and utterly ugly.
Lǐ was terrified
and wanted to flee.
The woman suddenly climbed onto the bed,
forcefully embraced his head,
and pressed her lips to his,
passing her saliva with her tongue,
cold as an ice block,
slowly seeping into his throat.
He tried not to swallow, but he couldn’t breathe;
when he swallowed, it was thick and sticky, clogging his throat.
As soon as he took a breath,
his mouth filled again,
and in his frantic gasping, he swallowed once more.
This went on for a long time,
until he was suffocating and could bear it no longer.
Hearing footsteps outside the door,
the woman finally released him and left.
From then on, his abdomen swelled, and he panted heavily,
unable to eat for dozens of days.
Someone advised him to induce vomiting with ginseng and reed soup,
and what he vomited was like egg white.
Only then did he recover.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wáng Miǎn,
courtesy name Mǐnzhāi,
was from Língshān.
He was talented and thoughtful,
often excelling in literary examinations,
and his pride was quite high;
he was skilled at mocking and insulting others,
frequently belittling and humiliating them.
Once, he met a Daoist priest,
who looked at him and said:
"Your physiognomy indicates extreme nobility,
but due to your 'frivolous and disrespectful karma,'
it has been almost entirely depleted.
With your intelligence,
if you turn inward and cultivate the Dao,
you may still ascend to the ranks of immortals."
Wáng scoffed:
"Whether blessings and fortune are real, I cannot say,
but how could there be immortals in this world!"
The Daoist said:
"Why is your view so lowly?
Look no further—
I myself am an immortal."
Wáng laughed even more, thinking him deceitful.
The Daoist said:
"I am nothing remarkable.
If you can follow me,
dozens of true immortals
can be seen immediately."
Wáng asked:
"Where are they?"
The Daoist replied:
"Just a stone's throw away."
He then placed his staff between his legs,
handed one end to Wáng,
and told him to do the same.
Instructing him to close his eyes,
he shouted:
"Rise!"
Wáng felt the staff grow as thick as a five-dǒu sack,
soaring through the air,
and secretly touched it—
it was covered in scales, row upon row.
Terrified,
he dared not move again.
After a while,
the Daoist shouted again:
"Stop!"
He then withdrew the staff,
and they landed in a grand mansion,
with towering pavilions and extended halls,
resembling an imperial palace.
There was a platform over ten feet high;
on it stood a hall with eleven pillars,
magnificent and splendid beyond compare.
The Daoist led Wáng up,
and immediately ordered attendants to set up a banquet to welcome guests.
In the hall, dozens of banquet tables were arranged,
their displays dazzling to the eye.
The Daoist changed into formal robes to wait.
After a short while,
guests arrived from the sky,
riding dragons, tigers, or phoenixes,
each different from the others.
They also brought musical instruments.
Some were women,
some were men,
and some had bare feet.
Among them was a particularly beautiful woman,
astride a colorful phoenix;
she was dressed in palace attire,
with a maidservant carrying her musical instrument for her,
which was over five feet long,
neither a qin nor a se,
and its name was unknown.
When the wine began to flow,
rare delicacies were served in abundance,
sweet and fragrant to the taste,
unlike ordinary delicacies.
Wáng sat silently and quietly,
his eyes fixed only on the beautiful woman;
though he admired her,
he also longed to hear her play music,
secretly fearing she might not perform at all.
As the banquet drew to a close,
an old man proposed:
"Thanks to the gracious invitation of Perfected Person Cuī,
today can be called a grand gathering,
and we should all enjoy ourselves to the fullest.
Let those with similar instruments
form groups and play together."
So they all paired up accordingly.
The sounds of strings and bamboo
echoed through the heavens.
Only the woman on the phoenix
had no partner for her music.
When the ensemble ceased,
her maidservant opened an embroidered bag
and laid the instrument horizontally on the table.
The woman then extended her jade-like wrists,
as if playing a zheng,
but the sound was several times brighter than a qin,
powerful enough to open one's chest,
yet soft enough to stir the soul.
After playing for about the time it takes to cook half a pot of rice,
the entire hall fell silent,
with no one coughing.
When she finished,
there was a clear, resonant sound,
like striking a pure qìng.
Everyone praised her:
"What a peerless skill from Lady Yúnhé!"
The crowd all rose to bid farewell,
with crane cries and dragon roars,
and dispersed in an instant.
The Daoist prepared a precious couch with embroidered quilts,
arranging a place for him to sleep.
Upon first seeing the beautiful woman,
Wáng’s heart was already stirred;
after hearing the music,
his thoughts grew even more restless.
Reflecting on his own talent and ability,
he felt it was only natural to effortlessly attain high rank and honor,
thinking that once he achieved wealth and status, what could he not obtain?
In an instant, a hundred thoughts
tangled like wild hemp.
The Daoist seemed to already know this,
and said to him:
"In your previous life, you and I were fellow students,
but later, because your resolve was not firm,
you fell into the dusty world.
It is not that I regard you as an outsider,
but I truly wish to pull you out of this foul mire;
I did not expect that your delusion and obscurity had already sunk so deep,
that you were so dreamily confused, beyond awakening.
Now I must send you on your way.
It is not necessarily that we will never meet again,
but to become a celestial immortal,
you must undergo another kalpa."
He then pointed to a long stone at the foot of the steps,
told him to sit down with his eyes closed,
and sternly instructed him not to look.
Afterward,
he used a whip to drive the stone.
The stone flew up,
the sound of wind filled his ears,
and he had no idea how far they traveled.
Suddenly, he wondered about the scenery below,
unsure what it was like;
secretly, he slightly opened his eyes a crack,
and saw a vast, boundless sea,
with no end in sight.
Greatly frightened,
he immediately closed them again,
but his body had already fallen along with the stone,
with a crashing sound,
sinking into the water like a gull.
Fortunately, having lived near the sea since childhood,
he was somewhat familiar with swimming and floating.
He heard someone clapping and saying:
"What a beautiful fall!"
Just as the danger was most urgent,
a young woman pulled him aboard a boat,
and said:
"Auspicious,
auspicious,
the scholar has 'passed the water'!"
Looking at her,
she appeared to be about sixteen or seventeen years old,
with a radiant and beautiful countenance.
Wáng, emerging from the water, shivered with cold,
and asked for a fire to warm himself.
The young woman said:
"Come with me to my home,
and I will arrange things for you.
If you find it agreeable,
do not forget me."
Wáng said:
"What kind of talk is this!
I am a talented scholar from the Central Plains,
who has accidentally encountered this predicament;
coming here, I intend to repay you with my very person—
how could I merely not forget you!"
The young woman urged the boat forward with her oar,
swift as wind and rain,
and in a moment they were near the shore.
From the cabin, she took a handful of lotus flowers she had gathered,
and led him away with her.
After about half a li, they entered a village,
saw a vermilion gate facing south,
went through several layers of gates,
and the young woman hurried in first.
After a short while,
a man came out,
about forty years old,
bowed to Wáng and invited him up the steps,
ordered attendants to fetch a hat, robe, socks, and shoes,
and had Wáng change his clothes.
Afterward,
he inquired about his family and lineage.
Wáng said:
"I will not deceive you;
my literary reputation is somewhat known.
Dàoist Cuī was deeply attached to me,
and invited me to ascend to the celestial palace.
I considered that achieving fame and fortune would be as easy as turning over my hand,
and therefore had no wish to dwell in seclusion."
The man rose respectfully and said:
"This place is called Xiānrén Dǎo (Immortal Island),
far removed from the human world.
My name is Wénruò,
surname Huán.
Our family has lived in this secluded place for generations;
what fortune to be able to approach such a renowned figure."
Thereupon, he hospitably arranged wine.
Then, leisurely, he said:
"I have two daughters,
the elder named Fāngyún,
now sixteen years old,
who has not yet met a suitable match.
I wish to offer her to serve a man of high standing;
what do you think?"
Wáng thought it must be the lotus-gathering girl,
left his seat and expressed his thanks.
Huán ordered that from among the neighbors,
two or three elders of virtue be invited.
Looking to his attendants,
he immediately called for the young lady.
Before long,
a rich fragrance wafted strongly,
and over ten beautiful maidens,
escorting Fāngyún, came out,
radiant and bright,
like a lotus reflecting the morning sun.
After bowing,
she sat down.
The group of maidens stood in attendance,
and the lotus-gathering girl was among them.
After several rounds of wine,
a young girl with hanging hair came out from within,
only about ten years old,
yet graceful and elegant,
smiling as she leaned against Fāngyún's elbow,
her autumn-wave-like eyes flowing with expression.
Huán said:
"A girl should not be outside the inner chambers;
what business brings you out?"
Then, turning to the guest, he said:
"This is Lǜyún,
my younger daughter.
She is quite clever,
and can already memorize the ancient classics."
Thereupon, he told her to recite a poem for the guest.
So she recited three verses of a "Bamboo Branch Song,"
delicate and charming to hear.
Then he had her sit beside her elder sister in a corner.
Huán then said:
"Wáng Láng is a genius;
his stored compositions must be plentiful.
May this humble person have the honor of hearing your instruction?"
Wáng immediately, with great spirit, recited one of his recent regulated verses,
looking around with self-satisfaction.
Two lines in the middle said:
"All that remains of this body are beard and eyebrows;
a little drink can make the lumps of care dissolve."
The neighboring elders recited them over and over.
Fāngyún quietly told him:
"The first line is Sūn Xíngzhě leaving the Fiery Cloud Cave,
the second line is Zhū Bājiè crossing the Zǐmǔ River."
The whole company clapped their hands.
Huán asked for others.
Wáng recounted a line about waterfowl, saying:
"At the pond's edge, the bird cries 'ge-zhe'..."
Suddenly he forgot the next line.
Just as he was pondering,
Fāngyún whispered into her younger sister's ear,
then covered her mouth and laughed.
Lǜyún told her father:
"She has continued the next line for her brother-in-law.
It says: 'The dog's rear goes "peng-ba."'"
The entire banquet burst into laughter.
Wáng looked ashamed.
Huán glanced at Fāngyún,
and glared at her angrily.
Wáng's expression gradually settled,
and Huán again asked about his literary compositions.
Wáng thought that people outside the mundane world surely would not know the eight-legged essay craft,
so he displayed his championship piece,
the topic being
"How filial was Mǐn Zǐqiān!"
(two lines),
the opening statement said:
"The sage praises the great worthy's filial piety..."
Lǜyún said to her father:
"The sage did not address his disciple by his style name;
the phrase 'How filial...'
is someone else's words."
Wáng heard this,
and his enthusiasm waned.
Huán laughed and said:
"What does a child know!
Let us not dwell on this,
but only discuss the literary composition."
Wáng then recited again.
Every few lines,
the sisters would whisper to each other,
seemingly offering critical comments,
but their murmuring was indistinct.
When Wáng recited to an excellent part,
and also related the examiner's comments,
which included:
"Every word is piercingly poignant."
Lǜyún told her father:
"My elder sister says: 'The character
'qiè'
should be deleted.'"
Everyone was puzzled.
Huán feared her words were disrespectful,
and dared not press for an explanation.
After Wáng finished reciting,
he also recounted the overall critique,
which included:
"With one strike of the war drum,
all flowers fall at once."
Fāngyún again covered her mouth and whispered to her younger sister,
and both of them laughed so hard they couldn't straighten up.
Lǜyún then announced:
"Elder sister says!
'The war drum should be struck four times.'"
Everyone was again puzzled.
Lǜyún opened her mouth to speak,
but Fāngyún, suppressing her laughter, scolded her:
"How dare you, little maid, speak?
You'll be beaten to death!"
Everyone was greatly perplexed,
and they exchanged guesses and theories.
Lǜyún couldn't hold back,
and said:
"Removing the character 'qiè'
makes 'tòng'
then 'bù tōng'
Striking the drum four times,
its sound is like 'bù tōng yòu bù tōng'
Everyone burst into laughter.
Huán angrily scolded her.
He then rose to pour wine all around,
apologizing incessantly.
Wáng had initially prided himself on his literary fame,
and in his eyes, truly regarded no one from the past as worthy;
but at this point,
his spirit was deflated,
and he was merely drenched in sweat.
Huán flattered and comforted him, saying:
"Just now there was a phrase,
I ask those at the banquet to compose a matching couplet:
'Beside the prince, there is not a single point that does not resemble jade.'"
Before anyone could think of a response,
Lǜyún answered immediately:
"On the old turtle's head,
adding half an evening makes it a turtle."
Fāngyún couldn't help laughing,
and, blowing on her hands, pinched Lǜyún's side several times.
Lǜyún broke free and ran away,
looking back and saying:
"What business is it of yours!
You frequently scold him,
and don't consider it wrong;
yet when someone else says one sentence,
you won't allow it?"
Huán shouted at her,
and only then did she laugh and leave.
The old neighbor took his leave.
The maids led the couple into the inner bedroom,
where lamps, candles, screens, and beds
were exquisitely arranged.
Looking into the bridal chamber,
ivory book labels filled the shelves,
and there was no book that was not present.
When Wáng posed a few questions,
the responses were endless.
At this point, Wáng
began to feel ashamed of his own inadequacy.
When Fāngyún called
"Míngdāng,"
the one who picked lotus came hurrying in response,
and from then on, her name was known.
Having been ridiculed and humiliated repeatedly,
Wáng feared he would not be respected in the women's quarters;
fortunately, although Fāngyún's words were harsh,
within the bed curtains,
they still loved each other.
Wáng lived peacefully without incident,
and would often recite poetry again.
Fāngyún said:
"I have a good piece of advice,
I wonder if you will kindly accept it?"
He asked:
"What advice?"
She said:
"From now on, stop writing poetry,
it is also a way to hide one's clumsiness."
Wáng was greatly ashamed,
and thereafter put down his brush.
After a long time,
he gradually became intimate with Míngdāng.
He told Fāngyún:
"Míngdāng once saved my life,
I hope you will show her a little kindness."
Fāngyún then agreed.
Whenever they engaged in bedroom play,
she would summon Míngdāng to join them,
and the affection between the two grew even deeper,
often communicating with glances and gestures.
Fāngyún noticed slightly,
and reproached him repeatedly;
Wáng only chattered on,
trying hard to excuse himself.
One evening,
as they were drinking together,
Wáng thought it too quiet,
and urged her to summon Míngdāng.
Fāngyún refused.
Wáng said:
"You have read every book,
why don't you remember the lines about 'enjoying alone'?"
Fāngyún said:
"I say you are muddled,
and now it's even more evident.
Don't you even know the punctuation?
'To enjoy alone,
one must then enjoy with others;
ask about enjoyment,
who is essential?
The answer: no one.'"
She laughed and let it go.
It happened that Fāngyún's younger sister went to an appointment with a neighbor girl,
and Wáng seized the opportunity,
quickly drew Míngdāng to him,
and was exceedingly affectionate.
That night,
he felt a slight pain in his lower abdomen;
after the pain subsided,
his private parts swelled up completely.
Greatly frightened,
he told Fāngyún.
Fāngyún laughed and said:
"It must be Míngdāng's gratitude repaid!"
Wáng dared not hide it,
and confessed the truth.
Fāngyún said:
"You brought this calamity upon yourself,
there really is no remedy.
Since it's neither painful nor itchy,
just let it be."
After several days without improvement,
he grew worried and unhappy.
Fāngyún knew his thoughts,
but didn't inquire,
only gazed at him intently,
her eyes like autumn waters,
bright as the morning stars.
Wáng said:
"As you said,
'If the heart is upright,
then the pupils are clear.'"
Fāngyún laughed and said:
"As you said, 'If the heart is not upright,
then the clarity is in the pupils.'"
Because
"méiyǒu"
(to not have)
is colloquially pronounced like
"méi,"
which sounds like
"móu" (pupil),
she teased him with this.
Wáng couldn't help laughing,
and begged for a prescription.
She said:
"You didn't listen to good advice,
and before this, you probably suspected me of being jealous.
You didn't know that this maid
originally should not be approached.
I truly loved you before,
but you were like the east wind blowing past a horse's ear,
so I spurned you and showed no pity.
Since there's no other way,
I'll treat it for you.
But a physician must examine the affected area."
Then she reached into his clothes and chanted:
"'Yellow bird, yellow bird,
do not perch on the thorn!'"
Wáng couldn't help laughing out loud,
and after laughing, he was cured.
Several months later,
the king, because his parents were old and his son was young,
was constantly filled with longing and remembrance,
and he told the girl his thoughts.
The girl said:
"Returning is not difficult,
but we will have no day to meet again."
The king's tears flowed down to his cheeks,
and he sorrowfully begged to return together.
The girl pondered repeatedly,
and finally agreed.
Old Huán prepared a feast to bid them farewell.
Lǜyún entered carrying a basket,
and said:
"Sister is going far away,
I have nothing to give as a gift.
I fear that when you reach Hǎinán,
you will have no place to call home,
so I have been preparing a palace day and night,
please do not disdain its rough construction."
Fāngyún bowed and accepted it.
Looking closely and carefully,
it was a building made of fine grass,
as large as a rafter,
and as small as a tangerine,
about twenty or more in number,
each with beams, pillars, rafters, and eaves,
clearly countable;
inside were curtains, beds, and couches,
like sesame seeds.
The king looked at it as if it were a child's toy,
but in his heart he secretly marveled at its craftsmanship.
Fāngyún said:
"Let me tell you the truth: we are all earthly immortals.
Because of a predestined bond,
I was able to accompany you.
Originally, I did not wish to tread the mortal world,
but because you have an old father,
I could not bear to refuse.
Wait until your father passes away naturally,
then I must return."
The king respectfully agreed.
Huán then asked:
"By land?
Or by boat?"
The king, fearing the dangers of wind and waves,
chose land.
When they went out, carriages and horses were already waiting at the gate.
They bid farewell and set off,
their journey swift as if flying.
Soon they reached the seashore,
and the king worried there was no path.
Fāngyún took out a bolt of plain silk,
threw it toward the south,
and it transformed into a long embankment,
its width over ten feet.
In an instant they galloped across,
and the embankment gradually shrank.
They reached a place
where the tidewaters passed,
looking around, vast and distant.
Fāngyún stopped and told them not to go further,
got down from the carriage and took the grass-made items from the basket,
together with several attendants like Míngdāng,
arranged them according to the method,
and in the blink of an eye, they transformed into a grand mansion.
They all entered and unpacked,
finding it no different from their residence on the island,
inside the bridal chamber, the tables and couches were exactly as before,
by then it was already dusk,
so they stayed overnight.
Early the next morning,
she ordered the king to go welcome and care for his father.
The king ordered a horse to hurry to his hometown,
but when he arrived, the family home already belonged to someone else.
He asked the villagers,
and only then learned that his mother and wife had both already passed away,
only his old father was still alive.
His son was fond of gambling,
and all the land and property were gone,
grandfather and grandson had no place to stay,
and were temporarily renting a place in West Village.
When the king first returned,
he still had thoughts of fame and fortune,
and could not let go of them;
but upon hearing this situation,
he was deeply pained and greatly saddened,
thinking to himself that even if wealth and honor could be obtained,
how was it different from empty flowers?
He rode his horse to West Village to see his father,
his clothes dirty and worn,
old and frail, pitiful to see.
When they met,
both cried uncontrollably.
He asked about his unworthy son,
and was told he had gone out gambling and not returned.
The king then took his father back by carriage.
Fāngyún paid her respects in the morning,
prepared hot water for him to bathe,
presented him with brocade clothes,
and had him sleep in a fragrant room.
She also invited old acquaintances from afar to chat and feast with him,
his enjoyment and treatment surpassing that of noble families.
One day, the son found his way to their place,
the king refused him,
not allowing him to enter,
but gave him twenty taels of gold,
and had someone relay the message:
"Take this to buy a wife,
and plan a livelihood.
If you come again,
I will whip you to death on the spot!"
The son left in tears.
Since the king returned,
he did not much engage in social courtesies with others;
however, if old friends happened to visit,
he would certainly invite them in and entertain them,
treating them even more humbly and attentively than before.
Only Huáng Zǐjiè,
who had long been his schoolmate,
and was also a scholar who had experienced hardship,
the king kept him for a very long time,
often speaking with him in private,
and giving him generous gifts.
After three or four years,
Old King passed away,
the king spent ten thousand coins to divine a burial site,
and arranged the funeral with full rites.
By then, the son had already married a wife,
the wife kept her husband under strict control,
and the son's gambling also decreased;
at this time, attending the funeral,
he finally got to meet his parents-in-law.
Fāngyún saw him once,
approved of his ability to manage a household,
and gave him three hundred taels of gold as funds for land and property.
The next day,
Huáng and the son went together to visit,
but the buildings had completely vanished,
and they did not know where they had gone.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"Where beautiful women are,
people would even seek them in hell,
how much more if they could enjoy endless pleasures?
If earthly immortals were allowed to bring along beautiful women,
I fear the imperial court would be empty.
Reducing the official ranks and emoluments of the frivolous,
is indeed reasonable,
but could it be that even immortals do not avoid this?
That woman's mouth,
how cruel it is!"
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
A certain provincial governor's father,
who had previously served as Viceroy of the Southern Provinces,
had passed away long ago.
One night, the governor dreamed that his father came to him,
his countenance sorrowful and trembling,
and told him:
"In my lifetime, I did not commit many sins,
but there was one regiment of garrison troops
that I mistakenly deployed when I should not have.
On the way, they encountered pirates,
and the entire army was annihilated.
Now I am being tried before King Yán,
and the punishments in the prison are cruel and severe—
truly terrifying and dreadful.
This King Yán is none other than
the official who will arrive tomorrow transporting grain supplies—
the one surnamed Wèi.
You must plead for mercy on my behalf—
do not forget!"
Upon waking, the governor found this strange,
but he did not fully believe it.
After falling asleep again,
he dreamed that his father reproached him:
"Your father is suffering calamity,
yet you still do not take it to heart—
are you dismissing it as just an eerie dream?"
The governor was greatly astonished.
The next day,
he paid close attention while reviewing documents,
and indeed there was an official named Wèi,
who had just arrived transporting supplies.
The governor immediately summoned him in,
had two attendants press him into a seat,
and then rose to bow to him,
as if performing a court audience ritual.
After bowing,
he knelt long and tearfully explained the reason.
Wèi did not accept the responsibility,
but the governor remained prostrate on the ground, refusing to rise.
Wèi then said:
"Very well,
such a thing may exist.
But the laws of the underworld
are not like those of the mortal world, where confusion reigns
and one can manipulate matters through underhanded means—
I fear I may not be able to help."
The governor pleaded even more earnestly.
With no alternative,
Wèi agreed.
The governor also begged him to handle it quickly.
Wèi pondered but could think of no quiet place.
The governor offered to clean out a guest hall,
and Wèi consented.
Only then did the governor rise.
He then asked to go and observe secretly,
but Wèi refused.
After repeated insistence,
Wèi instructed him:
"Once you go, do not make a sound.
Moreover, although underworld punishments are cruel,
they differ from those in the mortal world.
Even if someone appears to die temporarily,
they are not truly dead.
If you see something,
do not be alarmed or find it strange."
That night,
the governor hid beside the hall
and saw prisoners below the steps—
some with severed heads, others with broken arms—
crowded in countless numbers.
In the courtyard, a fiery cauldron and an oil wok were set up,
with several men stoking the fire beneath them.
Soon, he saw Wèi emerge in official robes and headdress,
ascend to his seat,
his demeanor imposing and fierce,
utterly different from before.
All the ghosts immediately prostrated themselves,
crying out in unison about their grievances and suffering.
Wèi said:
"Your lives were taken by pirates—
your grievances have their rightful source.
How can you falsely accuse an official?"
The ghosts clamored:
"According to regulations, we should not have been deployed,
yet we were erroneously summoned—
and thus met with disaster.
Who is to blame for our冤?"
Wèi again tried to reason and mediate,
but the ghosts howled with冤,
their voices rising in a tumultuous uproar.
Wèi then called to a ghost attendant:
"Take that official and plunge him into the oil cauldron—
a brief scalding
is only fitting."
Observing his intent,
it seemed he wished to use this to vent the crowd's anger.
Immediately, an ox-headed demon guard
seized the governor's father
and thrust him into the oil cauldron with a sharp fork.
Seeing this,
the governor felt intense sorrow in his heart,
unbearable pain,
and unconsciously let out a loud cry.
The courtyard fell silent,
and all forms vanished.
The governor sighed in dismay and returned home.
By dawn,
when he went to see Wèi,
he found that Wèi had already died in the hall.
This was told by Zhāng Yǔdìng of Sōngjiāng.
As it is not a favorable tale,
the person's name is concealed.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
The Mad Daoist,
whose name is unknown,
lived at Méngshān Temple.
He sang and wept unpredictably,
and no one could understand him.
Some saw him cooking stones for food.
During the Double Ninth Festival,
a local nobleman brought wine for an outing,
traveling by carriage with canopy.
After the banquet, they passed by the temple.
Just as they reached the gate,
the Daoist, barefoot and wearing a tattered robe,
held up a yellow canopy himself
and made sounds like clearing the way for an imperial procession,
seemingly to mock them.
The nobleman felt ashamed and angry,
and ordered his servants to chase and curse him.
The Daoist laughed and retreated.
As the pursuit grew urgent,
he discarded the canopy,
and when they tore it apart together,
the pieces transformed into hawks and falcons,
scattering and flying in all directions.
The crowd was then startled.
The canopy handle turned into a giant蟒,
its red scales dazzling to the eye.
The crowd cried out and wanted to flee,
but one of their companions stopped them, saying:
"This is merely an illusion to dazzle the eyes—
how could it bite anyone!"
He then took up a刀 and charged forward.
The蟒 opened its mouth in fierce resistance
and swallowed the man whole.
The crowd was terrified,
hurriedly escorting the nobleman away,
and rested three miles off.
They sent a few men to cautiously investigate.
Gradually entering the temple,
they found both the man and the蟒 gone.
Just as they were about to return and report,
they heard panting as loud as a donkey's from inside an old locust tree,
and were greatly alarmed.
At first, they dared not approach;
stealthily moving closer,
they saw the tree was rotten and hollow inside,
with an opening as large as a plate.
Trying to climb and peek inside,
they saw the man who had fought the蟒 stuck upside down within,
but the hole was only large enough for two hands—
there was no way to pull him out.
They urgently tried to劈 the tree with a刀,
but by the time the tree split open, the man was already dead.
After a while, he briefly revived,
and they carried him back.
The Daoist was nowhere to be found.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Zhāng Chāi traveled to the mountains,
his weariness with worldly affairs seeped into his very marrow.
The immortal's playful mastery of the art of living,
how laughable indeed!
In my hometown, there was a scholar named Yīn Wénpíng,
who was the brother-in-law of Minister of Revenue Bì.
He was a man who defied worldly conventions.
In Zhāngqiū, there was a certain Mr. Zhōu,
who rose from humble and lowly origins,
yet whenever he went out, he insisted on riding in a sedan chair carried by bearers.
He also had some old connection with Minister Bì.
On the occasion of the Minister's mother's birthday,
Yīn anticipated that Zhōu would certainly come,
so he waited for him on the road beforehand.
He wore pigskin boots,
donned official robes, and held a name card.
When Zhōu arrived,
Yīn bowed deeply by the roadside,
and announced loudly: '
A scholar from Zīchuān,
greets the scholar from Zhāngqiū!'
Zhōu was ashamed,
descended from his sedan chair,
exchanged a few words, and then they parted.
A little later,
they gathered together in Minister Bì's hall.
The place was filled with guests in official caps and robes.
Looking at Yīn's attire,
everyone secretly laughed;
but Yīn remained haughty and composed, utterly unperturbed.
After the banquet ended and everyone was leaving,
each called for their sedan chairs or horses.
Yīn also shouted loudly:
'Where is Master Yīn's single-dragon carriage?'
Two sturdy servants
placed a carrying pole horizontally in front of him.
He leaped up and straddled it.
After bidding farewell and expressing thanks,
he sped away as if flying.
Yīn is also a man akin to those immortals."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Chéng Xiàosī
was from Jiànnán.
From a young age, he was intelligent and skilled in writing.
Both his parents died early,
leaving the family in utter poverty,
with no means of livelihood for food or clothing.
He sought employment as a secretary for the Censor-in-Chief Hú.
Censor Hú tested him with a writing assignment
and was greatly pleased,
saying:
"This man will not remain poor for long;
he is worthy of taking as a son-in-law."
The Censor had three sons and four daughters.
All had been betrothed in infancy to prominent families;
only the youngest daughter, Sìniáng,
was born of a concubine.
Her mother had died early,
and by the age of fifteen, she was still unmarried,
so they took Chéng in as a live-in son-in-law.
Some mocked and laughed at this,
considering it a foolish, senile decision,
but the Censor paid them no heed.
He prepared a separate residence for the scholar
and provided ample supplies.
The other young masters looked down on him and refused to eat with him;
even the maids and servants all teased him.
Chéng remained silent, not disputing right or wrong,
and studied with great diligence.
When others mocked and ridiculed him from the side,
Chéng did not stop reading;
when they clanged gongs and cymbals noisily beside him,
he took his books and left,
reading in the inner chambers instead.
Initially,
before Sìniáng was betrothed,
a spirit medium who could discern people's future nobility or lowliness
observed all the daughters one by one,
but offered no flattering words to any.
Only when it was Sìniáng's turn
did he say:
"This one is truly a noble lady!"
After Chéng was taken in as son-in-law,
all her sisters began calling her
"Noble Lady"
to mock her.
But Sìniáng was dignified and reserved, speaking little,
as if she did not hear them.
Gradually, even the maids and elderly servants
followed suit in addressing her this way.
Sìniáng had a maid named Guì'ér,
who felt quite indignant about this.
She declared loudly:
"How do you know our young master
won't become a high official someday?"
The second elder sister heard this and sneered:
"If Mr. Chéng becomes a high official,
I'll gouge my own eyes out!"
Guì'ér angrily retorted:
"By that time,
I'm afraid you won't be willing to part with your eyes!"
The second sister's maid, Chūnxiāng, said:
"If my mistress goes back on her word,
I'll offer my own two eyes in her place."
Guì'ér grew even angrier.
She clapped her hands and swore an oath:
"I'll make sure both of you go blind!"
The second sister, furious at her insulting words,
immediately slapped her.
Guì'ér wailed loudly.
When the Madame heard about it,
she neither approved nor disapproved,
merely smiling faintly.
Guì'ér went noisily to complain to Sìniáng.
Sìniáng was spinning at the time.
She neither grew angry nor spoke,
but continued spinning as if nothing had happened.
It happened to be the Censor's birthday.
All the sons-in-law had arrived,
and the hall was filled with birthday gifts.
The wife of the eldest son mocked Sìniáng:
"What gift did your family bring?"
The wife of the second son said:
"Two shoulders carrying one mouth!"
Sìniáng remained calm and unruffled,
showing no sign of shame or embarrassment.
Seeing that she acted foolishly in every matter,
people teased her even more.
Only the Censor's beloved concubine, Madame Lǐ,
who was the birth mother of the third daughter,
always treated Sìniáng with respect
and often looked out for her.
She often said to her own daughter, Sānniáng:
"Sìniáng is wise within but simple without.
Her intelligence is profound yet not outwardly displayed.
All those maids are within her grasp,
yet they don't realize it themselves.
Moreover, Mr. Chéng studies hard day and night.
How could he remain subordinate to others for long?
Don't you follow the others' example.
Treat her well,
so that in the future you may meet on good terms."
Therefore, whenever Sānniáng returned to her parental home,
she made a special effort to be friendly.
That year,
thanks to the Censor's influence,
Chéng gained entry into the county school.
The following year,
during the educational commissioner's examination for scholars,
the Censor happened to pass away.
Chéng mourned him like a son, wearing coarse hemp mourning clothes,
and thus could not take the examination.
After the period of mourning beside the grass mat and earthen pillow ended,
Sìniáng gave him money
to enable him to go and register for the supplementary examination.
She admonished him:
"The reason I could stay here so long
without being scolded and driven away
was solely because my old father was alive.
Now that is absolutely impossible!
If you can achieve success and make us proud,
perhaps when you return, there will still be a home for you."
At their parting,
Madame Lǐ and Sānniáng gave him generous gifts of money.
Chéng entered the examination hall,
determined and focused in his studies,
striving to ensure his success.
Not long after,
the results were posted,
but he was ultimately rejected.
His hopes dashed and his spirit disheartened,
he found it difficult to return home.
Fortunately, the funds in his pouch were somewhat sufficient,
so he packed his books and went to the capital.
At that time, many of his wife's relatives held official posts in the capital.
Fearing their ridicule and scorn,
he changed his former name
and falsely reported his hometown,
seeking to hide himself within the household of a high official.
Lǐ Lántái of Dōnghǎi saw him and recognized his talent.
He took him into his retinue,
provided him with living expenses,
and arranged for him to be recommended as a tribute student,
enabling him to take the Shùntiān provincial examination.
He succeeded in consecutive examinations
and was appointed a Hanlin Bachelor.
Only then did he reveal the truth of his circumstances.
Minister Lǐ lent him a thousand taels of silver
and first sent a steward to Jiànnán
to purchase an estate for him.
At that time, the eldest Hú son, due to his father's death and empty coffers,
was selling their fertile villa,
so it was bought.
After the purchase was completed,
Earlier,
after Chéng passed the imperial examination,
a postal messenger arrived with the news,
but the entire household was disgusted to hear it;
moreover, upon verifying that the name did not match,
they scolded and drove him away.
It happened that the third brother was completing his wedding,
and relatives had gathered in the hall for the feast,
with all the sisters and aunts present,
only Sìniáng was not invited by her elder brother and sister-in-law.
Suddenly, a man rushed in,
presenting a letter from Chéng addressed to Sìniáng;
when the brothers opened and read it,
they looked at each other, their faces pale.
The guests at the banquet
then began to request to see Sìniáng.
Her sisters were anxious,
fearing that Sìniáng, bearing a grudge, would not come.
Before long,
she arrived gracefully and unexpectedly.
Those offering congratulations,
those urging her to sit,
those exchanging pleasantries,
filled the room with clamor.
Ears listened,
listening to Sìniáng;
eyes looked,
looking at Sìniáng;
mouths spoke,
speaking of Sìniáng: yet Sìniáng remained as composed as before.
Seeing that she bore no resentment,
everyone gradually settled down,
and then they vied to toast Sìniáng.
Amid the feasting and laughter,
outside the door came urgent cries and wails,
causing everyone to wonder and ask.
Soon, Chūnxiāng was seen rushing in,
her face stained with blood.
When all questioned her,
she wept and could not answer.
Only after Èrniáng scolded her
did she finally say through tears:
"Guì'er demanded my eyes,
if not for freeing myself,
he would have nearly gouged them out!"
Èrniáng was greatly ashamed,
sweat and powder streaming down together.
Sìniáng remained indifferent;
the entire gathering fell silent, not a word spoken,
and the guests began to bid farewell.
Sìniáng, dressed in splendid attire,
solemnly bowed only to Lady Lǐ and her third sister,
then went out the door, boarded her carriage, and departed.
Only then did everyone realize that the buyer of the villa
was Chéng.
When Sìniáng first arrived at the villa,
many necessities were lacking.
Lady Lǐ and the various brothers each sent maids, servants, and utensils as gifts,
but Sìniáng accepted none of them;
only the maid given by Lady Lǐ
did she accept.
Not long after residing there,
Chéng returned on leave to visit the ancestral graves,
with carriages, horses, and attendants like clouds.
He went to his father-in-law's home,
paid respects before Lord Hú's coffin,
and then paid his respects to Lady Lǐ.
After the brothers, dressed in their finest, had competed
and already ascended their carriages.
After Lord Hú's death,
the various sons daily competed for wealth,
neglecting the coffin.
After several years,
gradually turning the splendid house into a burial mound.
Seeing this, Chéng was saddened,
and without consulting the brothers,
he set a date to manage the burial,
handling every matter with full propriety.
On the day of the funeral,
officials and carriages followed one after another,
and everyone in the village praised and sighed in admiration.
For over ten years, Chéng held successive high and illustrious posts,
and whenever encountering urgent difficulties among his fellow villagers,
he did not spare any effort to help.
Èrláng happened to be arrested due to a homicide case,
and the investigating censor on tour,
who was a fellow graduate of Chéng's,
was known for his strict discipline.
Dàláng, through his father-in-law, Inspector Wáng, sent a letter to him,
but received no reply whatsoever,
increasing their fear.
He wanted to go and seek help from his sister,
but felt too ashamed,
so he took a handwritten letter from Lady Lǐ and went.
Arriving in the capital,
he did not dare to approach immediately,
but waited until Chéng had gone to court,
and then went to visit.
Hoping that Sìniáng would remember sibling affection,
and forget past petty grievances.
Once the gatekeeper announced him,
an old maidservant from before came out,
led him into the reception hall,
served wine and food,
though rather hastily.
After eating,
Sìniáng came out,
her expression gentle,
and asked:
"Elder brother is so busy with affairs,
what leisure brings you to visit from afar?"
Dàláng prostrated himself on the ground,
weeping as he explained his purpose.
Sìniáng helped him up and said with a laugh,
"Elder brother is a fine man,
what great matter is this,
to be so distressed?
Your younger sister is but a woman,
when have you ever seen me whimper before others?"
Dàláng then produced Lady Lǐ's letter.
Sìniáng said:
"The wives of my elder brothers
are all extraordinary women,
each can seek help from their own fathers and brothers,
and the matter could be settled,
why trouble yourself to come all this way?"
Dàláng had no words,
only looked at her pleadingly.
Sìniáng changed her expression and said:
"I thought you had traveled here to see your younger sister,
but it turns out you came seeking a powerful person for a major lawsuit!"
She flicked her sleeves and went straight inside.
Dàláng left in shame and anger.
Returning home, he recounted everything in detail,
and everyone, young and old, cursed and reviled her;
Lady Lǐ also said she was heartless.
After a few days,
Èrláng was released and returned home,
to everyone's great joy,
and they laughed at Sìniáng for having only earned herself resentment and slander.
Soon after, Sìniáng sent a servant to inquire after Lady Lǐ.
Summoned inside,
the servant presented gold and coins,
saying:
"My lady, regarding Second Uncle's matter,
acted with great urgency,
and had no time to write a reply.
She sends this small token
in place of a letter."
Only then did everyone realize that Èrláng's return
was due to Chéng's efforts.
Later, when the third sister's family gradually became poor,
Chéng's assistance and repayment exceeded ordinary standards.
And because Lady Lǐ had no sons,
he welcomed and cared for her as if she were his own mother.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Huáng Shēng,
was a son of an old, established family.
His talent and sensibility were quite ample,
and he had long held lofty ambitions.
Outside the village was a Buddhist temple,
where a certain monk resided,
who had always been on close terms with him.
Later, the monk traveled afar,
and after over ten years returned.
Seeing Huáng,
he sighed and said:
"I thought you had achieved success long ago,
but you are still in commoner's clothes?
I suppose your fortune and fate are truly thin.
Let me bribe the underworld officials for you.
Can you provide ten thousand cash?"
Huáng replied:
"I cannot."
The monk said:
"Please try to manage half,
I will borrow the rest for you later.
Three days is the agreement."
Huáng agreed,
and exhausted himself pawning belongings to raise the amount.
Three days later,
the monk indeed brought five thousand coins and gave them to Huáng.
Huáng’s family had an old well for drawing water,
deep and never running dry,
said to connect to rivers and seas.
The monk ordered him to tie the coins and place them by the well,
instructing him:
"Once I reach the temple,
immediately push them into the well.
Wait for the time it takes to cook half a meal,
and when one coin floats up,
you must bow to it."
Then he left.
Huáng did not understand the method,
and thought to himself that it was uncertain whether it would work,
and that ten thousand coins would be a pity to lose.
So he hid nine thousand,
and threw only one thousand into the well.
After a short while,
a huge bubble rose up,
burst with a clanging sound,
and a coin floated out,
as large as a carriage wheel.
Huáng was greatly frightened.
After bowing,
he took the remaining four thousand and threw them in.
As they fell,
they struck with a sound,
but were blocked by the large coin,
unable to sink.
At dusk,
the monk arrived
and scolded him, saying:
"Why didn’t you throw them all in?"
Huáng said:
"I threw them all in."
The monk said:
"The messenger from the underworld only took one thousand away.
Why are you lying?"
Huáng truthfully told him,
and the monk sighed, saying:
"A stingy person is certainly not destined for greatness.
This man’s fate is to end as a Jīngshēng;
otherwise,
he would have immediately attained the highest rank in the imperial examinations."
Huáng deeply regretted it
and begged the monk to perform the ritual again.
But the monk firmly declined and left.
Huáng looked into the well and saw the coins still floating;
he hooked them with a rope,
and the large coin then sank.
That year,
Huáng was selected as a supplementary candidate and granted the status of Gòngshēng,
exactly as the monk had said.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Could it be that the underworld also has a system for selling official titles?
To obtain a degree for ten thousand coins
is indeed cheap.
But who would contribute one thousand coins?
That is still expensive.
A Jīngshēng who fails the examinations—
what is he worth? Not even a single coin!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A certain prominent man often acted unrighteously,
and his wife frequently admonished him with warnings of karmic retribution,
but he paid no heed.
It happened that there was a Daoist adept
who could know a person’s allotted lifespan,
so he went to consult him.
The adept examined him carefully and said:
"You will consume twenty more shí of rice and forty shí of flour,
and then your heavenly allotment will end."
He returned and told his wife.
Calculating that a person eats only two shí of flour in a year,
he still had over twenty years of heavenly allotment left.
How could it be cut off by wicked deeds?
So he continued his tyrannical ways as before.
After a year,
he suddenly fell ill
with "excessive hunger,"
eating a great deal but quickly feeling hungry again,
consuming over ten meals a day and night.
Before a full year had passed,
he died.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Mr. Zhōu
was a descendant of an official family in Shùntiān.
He was good friends with Mr. Liǔ.
Liǔ had received teachings from an extraordinary person
and was skilled in the arts of Yuán Tiāngāng and Xǔ Fù.
He once said to Zhōu:
"You have no share in official rank;
but wealth of ten thousand strings of coins
can still be attained through human effort.
However, your wife has an unfortunate appearance,
and I fear she cannot assist you in achieving success."
Not long after,
his wife indeed passed away.
His household became desolate,
and he had nothing to rely on.
So he went to see Liǔ
to seek divination about marriage.
Entering the guest room,
he sat for a long time,
but Liǔ went inside and did not come out.
After calling him repeatedly,
he finally emerged,
saying:
"I have been seeking a good match for you every day,
and now I have found one.
Just now, I was inside performing a small technique,
asking the Old Man of the Moon to tie the red thread of marriage."
Zhōu was delighted
and asked about it.
Liǔ replied:
"Just now, a man came out carrying a bag.
Did you meet him?"
Zhōu said:
"I met him.
He was dressed in rags like a beggar."
Liǔ said:
"This man is your future father-in-law.
You should treat him with respect."
Zhōu said:
"Because we are close friends,
I came to you to discuss this private matter.
How can you joke with me like this!
Even though my family has declined,
I am still of noble descent.
How could I stoop to marrying into the family of a market haggler?"
Liǔ said:
"Not so.
Even a yak can have offspring—
what harm is there?"
Zhōu asked:
"Have you seen his daughter?"
Liǔ replied:
"Not yet.
I have never had any prior acquaintance with him,
and I only learned his name by asking."
Zhōu laughed and said:
"You don’t even know the yak,
so how do you know its calf?"
Liǔ said:
"I trust in the numbers.
That man is fierce and lowly,
but he is destined to have a daughter of great fortune.
However, if forced together, there will be great calamity.
Let me perform another ritual to avert it."
After Zhōu returned home,
he did not fully believe Liǔ’s words
and searched everywhere,
but in the end, nothing came of it.
One day,
Liǔ Shēng suddenly arrived
and said:
"There is a guest
for whom I have already sent an invitation in your stead."
Zhōu asked:
"Who is it?"
Liǔ said:
"Don't ask for now,
you should quickly prepare a meal."
Zhōu did not understand the reason,
but followed the order to prepare the food.
Soon the guest arrived,
and it turned out to be a soldier surnamed Fù.
Zhōu felt inwardly displeased,
and only superficially engaged in conversation with him;
but Liǔ Shēng treated him with great respect.
After a short while,
wine and dishes were laid out,
and coarse, poor food was served.
Liǔ stood up and told the guest:
"The young master has long admired you,
and often entrusted me to seek you out;
only last night did we finally meet.
Hearing that you will soon be going on a distant campaign,
he immediately invited you—
one could say he is a rather hasty host."
During the drinking,
Fù worried that his horse was sick
and could not be ridden.
Liǔ also bowed his head, pondering the matter for him.
After the guest left,
Liǔ reproached Zhōu, saying:
"A thousand pieces of gold could not buy such a friend—
why do you treat him so coldly?"
He borrowed Zhōu's horse to ride home,
and then, using Zhōu's name,
went to Fù's door and presented the horse to him as a gift.
When Zhōu found out,
he was somewhat displeased,
but there was nothing he could do about it.
After the New Year,
Zhōu was about to go to Jiāngxī
to seek a position as an aide in the judicial commissioner's office.
He went to Liǔ to ask for a divination.
Liǔ said:
"Very auspicious!"
Zhōu laughed and said:
"I have no other intention,
but if I can earn a modest sum,
I will buy a good wife—
I almost hope your previous prediction does not come true—
is that possible?"
Liǔ said:
"Everything will be as you wish."
When he arrived in Jiāngxī,
he encountered a major bandit rebellion,
and for three years he could not return home.
Later, when things had calmed somewhat,
he chose a day to set out on the road.
Midway, he was captured by local bandits;
seven or eight fellow victims
all had their money and valuables taken,
and were released to go;
only Zhōu was taken to the bandits' lair.
The bandit chief questioned him about his family background,
then said:
"I have a daughter,
and I wish to offer her to you in marriage—
you must not refuse."
Zhōu did not reply.
The bandit grew angry
and immediately ordered him beheaded.
Zhōu became afraid,
thinking it better to temporarily comply with the request,
and then find an opportunity to escape later.
So he said:
"The reason I hesitated
is that I am a weak scholar, unable to follow a military life,
and I fear I would only become a burden to you, sir.
If husband and wife could leave together,
your kindness would be immeasurable."
The bandit said:
"I was just worried my daughter would be a burden to others—
why shouldn't you take her with you?"
He led Zhōu inside,
had his daughter dressed and brought out to meet him—
she was about eighteen or nineteen years old,
and was a beauty like a heavenly being.
That night they were wed,
far exceeding his expectations.
Upon carefully inquiring about her surname,
he learned that her father
was the very man who had carried the quiver years ago.
He then recounted Liǔ's words,
and they sighed in amazement.
After three or four days,
they were about to send them on their way,
when suddenly a large army descended upon them,
and the entire family was captured and bound.
Three officers were overseeing the captives;
they had already beheaded the woman's father,
and soon it was Zhōu's turn.
Zhōu resigned himself to the thought that he would not survive.
One officer looked closely at him and said:
"Isn't this Zhōu so-and-so?"
It turned out that soldier Fù had been promoted to deputy general for his military achievements.
He said to his colleagues:
"This is a renowned scholar from a prominent family in my hometown—
how could he be a bandit?"
He untied Zhōu's bonds
and asked where he had come from.
Zhōu deceitfully replied:
"I had just married a wife from the Jiāngxī judicial commissioner's office and was returning home,
when unexpectedly I fell into a bandit lair on the road.
Fortunately, I have been saved by you—
your kindness is as great as a second heaven!
But my wife is now separated from me;
I beg to borrow your great authority
to grant us a chance to survive intact."
Fù ordered the captives to be lined up
and told Zhōu to identify his wife himself,
which he did.
Fù provided them with wine and food,
and gave them travel funds,
saying:
"I have never forgotten
the kindness you showed me in the past by giving me your horse.
But in the midst of this turmoil,
I have no time to observe proper etiquette;
please accept two horses and fifty taels of gold
to assist your journey back north."
He also sent two cavalrymen with a token arrow to escort them.
On the road,
the woman told Zhōu:
"My foolish father would not listen to loyal advice,
and my mother died because of it.
I have long known that today would come.
The reason I clung to life day after day
was that when I was young, a fortune-teller predicted
that one day I would be able to collect my parents' bones.
I have a large amount of gold buried in a certain place;
we can retrieve it to ransom my father's bones.
The remainder we can take back—
it will be enough to plan for our livelihood."
She instructed the escorting cavalrymen to wait by the road,
and the two went to the old place.
The cottage had been reduced to ashes,
but from the ashes she took a dagger and dug about a foot down—
sure enough, they found the gold.
They loaded it all into bags
and returned.
They gave a hundred taels to the cavalrymen
to have the father's body buried;
then she led Zhōu to pay respects at her mother's grave,
and they set off.
When they reached the border of Zhílì,
they richly rewarded the cavalrymen and sent them away.
Zhōu had been away so long
that his family thought he was dead,
and had freely plundered his property—
grain, cloth, and utensils
were all gone without a trace.
Hearing that the master had returned,
they were terrified
and all fled in a panic;
only an old maidservant, a young maid, and an old manservant remained.
Since Zhōu had returned from the brink of death,
he did not pursue the matter further.
When he went to visit Liǔ,
he found that Liǔ had gone, no one knew where.
The woman managed the household better than a man could.
She selected honest and reliable men, gave them capital,
and shared the profits equally.
Whenever the merchants gathered under the eaves to settle accounts,
she would listen from behind a curtain;
if a single bead on the abacus was misplaced,
she would immediately point out the error.
No one inside or outside dared to deceive her.
After a few years,
the number of partner merchants exceeded a hundred,
and the family wealth reached several hundred thousand taels.
She then sent someone to move her parents' bones
and gave them a lavish burial.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"If even the Old Man under the Moon can be bribed and influenced,
no wonder matchmakers are no different from brokers.
But could a bandit have such a daughter?
That 'a small mound cannot grow pines and cypresses'—
this is the opinion of a petty person.
If even women can be misjudged in this way,
how much more so when judging the scholars of the world!"
