Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Mr. Zhū,
a native of Yánggǔ.
In his youth, he was frivolous and unrestrained,
fond of jesting and banter.
Having lost his spouse,
he went to seek out a matchmaker.
Encountering his neighbor's wife,
he glanced at her and found her beautiful.
Jokingly, he said to the matchmaker:
"Just now, I saw your esteemed neighbor—
elegant, youthful, and lovely.
If you could find a partner for me,
she would do."
The matchmaker also joked:
"Please kill her husband,
and I will arrange it for you."
Zhū laughed and said:
"Agreed."
A little over a month later,
the neighbor went out to collect a debt
and was killed in the wilderness.
The county magistrate detained the neighbors and guarantors,
subjecting them to torture to extract the truth,
but no leads were found;
only the matchmaker recounted the jesting exchange,
which aroused suspicion toward Zhū.
Arrested and brought in,
he adamantly refused to confess despite repeated interrogations.
The magistrate then suspected the neighbor's wife of being involved in an illicit affair,
had her flogged,
and subjected her to all manner of tortures.
Unable to endure the suffering,
she falsely confessed.
When Zhū was interrogated again,
he said:
"Her delicate frame cannot withstand harsh torture—
what she said is all false.
Not only is she wrongfully condemned to death,
but she is also branded with a reputation of impropriety.
Even if the gods and spirits remain unaware,
how could my conscience bear it?
Let me confess the truth: wanting to kill the husband and marry his wife—
it was all my doing,
the woman knew nothing of it."
Asked:
"What evidence is there?"
He replied,
"The bloodstained clothing can serve as proof."
But when they searched his home,
they could not find it.
He was tortured again,
dying and reviving twice.
Zhū then said,
"My mother cannot bear to produce the evidence and thus condemn me to death.
Allow me to fetch it myself."
So he was escorted home, where he told his mother:
"Give me the clothing,
and I die;
if you do not give it,
I die as well. Since death is inevitable either way,
it is better to hasten it than delay."
His mother wept,
went into the room for a while,
then brought out the clothing and handed it to him.
The magistrate examined the bloodstains and found them conclusive,
sentencing him to beheading.
After repeated reviews and retrials,
his testimony remained unchanged.
After more than a year,
the day of execution was set.
The magistrate was reviewing the prisoner's case
when suddenly a man strode straight into the courtroom,
glared at the magistrate and shouted:
"Such muddleheadedness—
how can you govern the people!"
Several dozen bailiffs
rushed to seize him.
The man swung his arm once,
and they all fell flat.
Terrified,
the magistrate tried to flee.
The man declared loudly:
"I am General Zhōu, who stands before Lord Guān!
If you, the dim-witted official, make a move,
I will have you executed on the spot!"
The magistrate trembled with fear and listened in trepidation.
The man said:
"The murderer is Gōng Biāo—
what does it have to do with Zhū?"
Having spoken,
he collapsed to the ground,
breath as if cut off.
After a short while, he revived,
his face drained of color.
When questioned about who he was,
it turned out to be Gōng Biāo.
He was flogged,
and he confessed fully to the crime.
It turned out that Gōng had always been a troublemaker;
knowing that the man was returning after collecting a debt,
he assumed he must be wealthy,
but after killing him,
he found nothing.
Hearing that Zhū had been wrongfully convicted,
he secretly felt fortunate.
That day, he entered the yamen
without even realizing it himself.
The magistrate asked Zhū where the bloodstained clothes came from,
but Zhū did not know either.
Summoning his mother for questioning,
it was revealed that she had cut her own arm to stain them;
examining the wound on her left arm,
it had not yet healed.
The magistrate was also astonished.
Later, because of this, he was impeached and dismissed from office,
fined, detained, and died.
Over a year later,
the neighbor's mother wanted to marry off her daughter-in-law;
the woman, moved by Zhū's righteousness,
eventually married him.
The Chronicler of the Tales remarks:
"Lawsuits and trials are the foremost duty of officials.
Nurturing hidden virtue
or destroying heavenly principles—
both lie in this,
and one cannot be careless.
Impatience, corruption, and brutality
certainly violate the harmony of heaven;
procrastination and inaction
also harm the lives of the people.
When one person initiates a lawsuit,
several farmers miss their seasons;
once a case is concluded,
ten households are ruined: how can this be considered trivial!
I have often said that for officials,
not indiscriminately accepting lawsuits
is already a great virtue.
Moreover, unless the circumstances are serious,
there is no need to detain people;
if there are no difficult issues,
why hesitate?
Even if it is a dispute among ignorant villagers
or hot-tempered mountain folk,
arising from quarrels over geese and ducks
and leading to sparrow-like bickering,
this merely requires a word from the official
to settle it peacefully.
There is no need for a full retinue;
only the two parties involved
should be promptly caned or flogged,
and all entanglements severed.
Is this not what is meant by an enlightened official?
I often see those who hear cases today: once a summons is issued,
they seem to forget it intentionally.
The clerks who deliver the documents, unless their hands are filled,
do not allow the cancellation of the summons;
the scribes who draft the judgments, unless their writing brushes are well-lubricated,
refuse to post the hearing notices.
Deceit and procrastination
drag on for months and years.
Before even reaching the magistrate's court,
the people are already worn to skin and bones!
Yet those who sit loftily above the people,
resting comfortably in bed,
remain indifferent as if nothing is amiss.
Do they know that in the fiery depths of the legal system,
there are countless wronged souls,
craning their necks and holding their breath,
hoping for rescue?
As for the wicked and stubborn among the troublemakers,
they certainly deserve no pity;
but what about the innocent commoners who are implicated?
How can they bear it?
Moreover, among those wrongfully entangled,
the troublemakers are often few, while the innocent are many;
and the suffering of the innocent
is often doubled compared to that of the troublemakers.
Why is this?
Because troublemakers are hard to bully,
while the innocent are easy to oppress.
The beatings and curses of the bailiffs,
the demands and extortions of the clerks—
all are inflicted upon the innocent with violence.
Once they enter the yamen,
it is like stepping into boiling water or fire.
Concluding a case one day earlier
means giving them one more day of peace;
what great matter is there
that makes them linger in the courtroom like the dying, as if fearing the ravine of greed will not be quickly filled,
and deliberately prolonging the time?
Even if not cruel or brutal,
their guilt is ultimately the same.
I have seen in a single lawsuit
that the essential and indispensable parties
are no more than three or four people;
the rest are all innocent commoners,
wrongfully ensnared.
Some bear grudges from past minor offenses,
others are accused because they possess something valuable.
Thus, the litigant uses all their strength to pursue the main case
and uses the leftover venom to settle petty vendettas.
Adding a name at the end of a document
becomes like an ulcer clinging to the bone;
suffering countless wrongs in the yamen
truly feels like a pain cutting to the flesh.
When others kneel, they kneel too,
like a flock of crows; when others leave, they leave too,
still bound like monkeys on a leash.
Yet in the end, the official does not question them,
nor do the clerks interrogate them.
They serve no purpose at all,
only enough to bankrupt their families,
filling the greedy pockets of corrupt underlings;
selling their children and pawning their wives,
venting the petty grudges of vile men.
I deeply wish that officials,
whenever a case is submitted,
would briefly examine and question it,
dismissing those who should be dismissed,
and removing those who should be removed.
It takes no more than dipping a brush or moving a wrist,
yet it can preserve so many lives and livelihoods,
and nurture so much vitality.
If those in power never give a thought to this,
why bother with shackles, knives, and saws to kill people!"
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Instructor Zhǎn,
was free-spirited and had the air of a renowned scholar.
However, he was a heavy drinker
and did not adhere to etiquette.
Every time he returned drunk,
he would gallop his horse up the temple steps.
There were many ancient cypress trees on the steps.
One day,
as he rode his horse in,
he struck his head against a tree and split it open.
He said to himself:
"Zǐlù is angry with me for being disrespectful,
and has smashed my skull!"
He died that very night.
A certain Mr. Yǐ from the county,
who was peddling goods in that village,
stayed overnight at an old temple.
When the night was quiet and people were scarce,
he suddenly saw four or five people bringing wine in to drink,
and Zhǎn was among them.
After several rounds of wine,
someone used a character riddle to challenge the group:
"The character 'tián' is not ventilated,
the character 'shí' is in the middle;
push the 'shí' character up,
and the character 'gǔ' wins a cup."
One person said:
"The character 'huí' is not ventilated,
the character 'kǒu' is in the middle;
push the 'kǒu' character up,
and the character 'lǚ' wins a cup."
Another person said:
"The character 'líng' is not ventilated,
the character 'lìng' is in the middle;
push the 'lìng' character up,
and the character 'hán' wins a cup."
Yet another person said:
"The character 'kùn' is not ventilated,
the character 'mù' is in the middle;
push the 'mù' character up,
and the character 'xìng' wins a cup."
When it was finally Zhǎn's turn,
he pondered but could not come up with one.
The others laughed and said:
"Since you cannot command,
you must accept the penalty."
They flew a goblet over to him.
Zhǎn then said:
"I've got it: the character 'yuē' is not ventilated,
the character 'yī' is in the middle; … …"
The others laughed again and said:
"What do you push it up into?"
Zhǎn drained the cup and said:
"Push the 'yī' character up,
and it becomes 'yī kǒu yī dà zhōng' (one mouth, one big cup)!"
They all laughed heartily together,
and soon left through the door.
Mr. Yǐ did not know that Zhǎn had died,
and secretly suspected that he had been dismissed from his post and returned home.
When he returned and inquired about it,
he learned that Zhǎn had been dead for a long time,
and only then realized that those he had encountered were ghosts.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Liú Zhòngkān from Luòchéng,
was dull-witted in his youth but obsessed with ancient texts,
often shutting himself indoors to study diligently,
and not interacting with the world.
One day,
while he was reading,
he suddenly smelled an extraordinary fragrance filling the room;
a moment later,
the sound of jade pendants became very frequent.
Startled, he looked up and saw
a beautiful woman entering,
her hairpins and earrings gleaming brilliantly;
her attendants were all dressed in palace attire.
Liú, frightened, prostrated himself on the ground.
The beautiful woman helped him up and said:
"Why were you so aloof before and now so respectful?"
Liú became even more terrified and said:
"Which celestial immortal are you,
whom I have never had the honor of meeting?
When did I ever show disrespect before?"
The beautiful woman laughed and said:
"How long has it been since we parted,
and yet you are already so forgetful!
The one who sat upright grinding bricks,
was that not you?"
Then she spread out a brocade mat,
set out jade-like wine,
made him sit and drank with him face to face,
discussing matters ancient and modern with him,
displaying extraordinary breadth of knowledge.
Liú was bewildered and did not know how to respond.
The beautiful woman said:
"I have only been to one banquet at the Jade Pond;
you have gone through several lifetimes,
and your intelligence has suddenly vanished!"
She then ordered her attendants
to bring in a crystal paste infused with hot water.
Liú drank it,
and suddenly felt his mind and spirit become clear and pure.
Soon it grew dark,
and the attendants all left.
They extinguished the candles, removed their robes,
and fully enjoyed their passionate union.
Before dawn,
the various maids had already gathered again.
The beautiful woman rose,
her makeup and appearance as before,
her hair neatly arranged,
without needing further attention.
Liú, reluctant to part, pressed her earnestly for her name.
She replied:
"It is no harm to tell you, sir,
but I fear it will only increase your doubts.
I am
Zhēnshì; you,
are the reincarnation of Gōnggàn.
Back then, you incurred punishment because of me,
and my heart truly could not bear it.
Today's meeting
is merely to repay your infatuation."
He asked:
"Where is Wèi Wéndì now?"
She said:
"Cáo Pī
is nothing but the mediocre son of a thieving father.
I merely followed him for a few years of playful wealth and honor,
and once it passed, I never thought of him again.
He, because of Āmán's deeds long ago,
has long been detained in the underworld.
I have not heard of his release,
but instead, Chénsī is in charge of the imperial archives,
and I see him from time to time."
Suddenly, a dragon-drawn carriage stopped in the courtyard.
She then gave Liú a jade-fat box as a gift,
bid farewell, boarded the carriage,
and was carried away by the clouds.
From then on, Liú's literary skills greatly improved.
Yet, he constantly thought of the beautiful woman,
lost in reverie as if in a trance.
After several months,
he gradually became emaciated and near death.
His mother did not know the reason,
and was deeply worried.
There was an old woman in the household,
who suddenly said to Liú:
"Young master, do you perhaps harbor thoughts of someone?"
Liú, feeling her words touched upon his hidden feelings,
told her everything.
The old woman said:
"Young master, try writing a letter,
I can deliver it for you."
Liú was overjoyed and said:
"You possess extraordinary skills,
yet I failed to recognize you before.
If you can truly do this,
I will never forget your kindness."
He then folded a piece of paper into a letter,
handed it to the old woman, and she left.
She returned at midnight and said:
"Fortunately, I did not fail in my task.
When I first arrived at the gate,
the gatekeeper thought I was a demon,
and wanted to bind me.
I then produced your letter,
and he took it away.
After a short while, I was summoned inside.
The lady also sighed with emotion,
saying she could not meet you again.
She was about to write a reply.
I said: 'The young master is weak and exhausted,
a single word cannot cure him.'
The lady pondered for a long time,
then put down her brush and said: 'Please first inform Young Master Liú
that I will send a fine wife to him soon.'
As I was about to leave,
she again instructed: 'What I just said
is a plan for a hundred years;
but do not reveal it,
and it can last forever.'"
Liú was delighted,
and waited.
The next day,
indeed, an old woman led a young lady
to his mother's place.
Her beauty was peerless,
and she said her surname was Chén;
the girl was her daughter,
named Sīxiāng,
and she wished to marry him.
His mother loved her,
and discussed the betrothal;
they did not demand a bride price,
and stayed until the wedding ceremony was completed before leaving.
Only Liú knew this was unusual,
and secretly asked the girl:
"Who is the lady?"
She replied:
"I am a former singing girl of the Tóngquè Terrace."
Liú suspected she was a ghost.
The girl said:
"No.
Both the lady and I are registered among the immortals,
but were temporarily banished to the mortal world due to some fault.
The lady has already been restored to her former position;
my banishment period is not yet over,
so the lady petitioned the heavenly authorities,
temporarily assigning me to serve,
my stay or departure is entirely up to the lady,
thus I am able to serve by your bedside for a long time."
One day,
a blind old woman leading a yellow dog came begging for food at their house,
clapping clappers and singing folk songs.
The girl went out to look,
but before she could stand still,
the dog broke its leash and bit at her.
The girl fled in terror,
and her silk collar was torn.
Liú hurriedly struck the dog with a stick.
The dog was still furious,
biting and tearing her skirt,
shredding it into hemp-like pieces in an instant,
and chewing and swallowing them.
The blind old woman grabbed the dog by the scruff,
tied it up, and left.
Liú went in to see the girl,
her frightened expression not yet settled,
and said:
"You are an immortal,
why are you afraid of a dog?"
The girl said:
"You do not know: the dog is the transformation of Old Cáo,
angry that I did not abide by the 'fragrant division' injunction."
Liú wanted to buy the dog and beat it to death.
The girl would not allow it,
saying:
"It is punished by the Heavenly Emperor,
how can we arbitrarily kill it?"
After two years,
all who saw her were astonished by her beauty,
but upon inquiring about her origins,
it was all vague and unclear,
so everyone suspected she was a demon.
His mother questioned Liú,
and Liú also vaguely mentioned the unusual circumstances.
His mother became greatly afraid,
and ordered him to break off with her.
Liú would not listen.
His mother secretly sought a sorcerer,
who performed rituals in the courtyard.
Just as he was marking out an altar on the ground,
the girl said sorrowfully:
"I originally hoped to grow old together;
now that your mother doubts me,
our bond is severed.
If you want me to leave,
that is also not difficult,
but I fear it is not something a spell can dismiss!"
She then bundled firewood and lit a fire,
throwing it down the steps.
In an instant, smoke obscured the house,
and they lost sight of each other.
Suddenly, there was a sound like thunder.
After the smoke cleared,
they saw the sorcerer dead, with blood flowing from his seven orifices.
Entering the room,
the girl had vanished.
Calling for the old woman to ask,
the old woman was also gone, no one knew where.
Liú then told his mother.
The old woman was actually a fox.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"It began with Yuán,
ended with Cáo,
and later focused on Gōnggàn;
an immortal should not be like this.
But to be fair: the son of the treacherous Cáo,
why must he have a chaste wife?
The dog, seeing the former singing girl,
should have greatly realized the folly of 'dividing the incense and selling shoes,'
yet it still harbored jealousy?
Alas!
The treacherous hero had no time to grieve for himself,
and later generations grieve for him!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wēn Rúchūn
was from an old aristocratic family in Qín.
From a young age, he was obsessively fond of the qin,
and never parted with it, even while traveling.
While traveling in Jìn,
he passed by an ancient temple,
tied his horse outside,
and rested briefly.
Entering, he saw a Daoist in a patched robe,
sitting cross-legged in the corridor,
a bamboo staff leaning against the wall,
and a flower-patterned cloth bag containing a qin.
Wēn, drawn by his own interest,
asked:
"Do you also excel at this?"
The Daoist said:
"I cannot claim mastery,
but wish to learn from a skilled player."
He then took the qin out of the bag and handed it to Wēn.
Looking at it,
the grain was exquisite,
and with a light strum,
it produced an exceptionally clear and resonant sound.
Wēn happily played a short piece.
The Daoist smiled slightly,
as if not fully approving,
so Wēn played with all his skill.
The Daoist chuckled and said:
"Good,
good!
But it is not enough to be my teacher."
Wēn, thinking his words boastful,
asked him to play instead.
The Daoist took the qin and placed it on his knee.
As soon as he plucked the strings,
a gentle breeze seemed to arise;
moments later,
flocks of birds gathered,
filling the courtyard trees.
Wēn was utterly amazed,
and bowed, asking to become his disciple.
The Daoist played the piece three times.
Wēn listened intently with all his heart,
gradually grasping its rhythm.
The Daoist had him try playing it,
correcting his mistakes and smoothing the rhythm,
saying:
"In this mortal world, you now have no equal."
Wēn henceforth practiced with utmost care and refinement,
and eventually became known for his peerless skill.
On the way back,
several dozen li from home,
the sun had already set,
and a torrential rain made it impossible to find lodging.
There was a small village by the roadside,
so he hurried toward it.
Without time to carefully choose,
he saw a gate,
and hastily rushed inside.
Ascending the hall,
it was deserted, with no one around.
Soon, a young lady came out,
seventeen or eighteen years old,
her appearance like that of a celestial being.
Lifting her head and seeing the guest,
she was startled and ran inside.
Wēn at that time was not yet married,
and his feelings were deeply stirred.
Soon an old woman came out to ask the guest,
Wēn gave his name,
and also requested lodging.
The old woman said,
"Lodging should be no problem,
but there are few beds;
if you don't mind bending your body,
you can use straw."
After a short while,
she brought a candle,
spread straw on the ground,
her intentions quite earnest.
He asked her surname,
she replied:
"The surname is Zhào."
He asked again:
"Who is the young lady?"
She said:
"This is Huànniáng,
my niece."
Wēn said:
"Not considering my humble and lowly state,
I wish to seek a marriage connection,
how about it?"
The old woman frowned and said:
"This I dare not agree to."
Wēn asked the reason,
but she only said it was hard to explain,
disappointed, he then gave up.
After the old woman left,
Wēn saw the straw was damp and rotten,
unsuitable for lying on,
so he sat upright playing the qin,
to pass the long night.
When the rain stopped,
he braved the night and returned home.
In the county, there was a retired official, Gě Gōng,
who liked literary men.
Wēn once visited him,
and was asked to play the qin.
Behind the curtain, vaguely, a family member was peeking and listening,
suddenly the wind blew the curtain open,
and he saw a girl of marriageable age,
beautiful beyond compare in the world.
It turned out Gě had a daughter,
pet name Liánggōng,
skilled in poetry and prose,
renowned for her beauty.
Wēn's heart was moved,
he returned and told his mother,
to send a matchmaker;
but Gě, because Wēn's family fortunes had declined,
did not consent.
However, the girl, since hearing the qin,
secretly admired him in her heart,
often hoping to hear his elegant performance again;
but Wēn, because the marriage matter did not succeed,
his will thwarted and spirits low, ceased visiting the Gě household.
One day,
the girl in the garden,
picked up a folded old letter,
on it was written the poem "Xī Yúchūn":
"From resentment comes obsession,
turning thoughts into longing,
every day confused by love.
The crabapple drunk,
the willow grieving spring,
all share the same feelings.
How can new sorrows and old,
cut down yet regrow,
just like green grass.
Since parting,
only in helpless days,
passing dusk and dawn.
Today, frowning damages spring mountains,
gazing wears out autumn waters,
said abandoned, already resolved to abandon!
Fragrant quilts envy dreams,
jade water-clock startles the soul,
wanting to sleep, how can sleep be good?
Don't say the long night is like a year,
to me a year,
is even less than a watch: past the third watch is already three years,
who then does not grow old!"
The girl recited it several times,
liking it in her heart.
Carrying it back,
she took out brocade paper,
solemnly copied it once,
and placed it on the desk;
later searching for it,
could not find it,
secretly thinking it was blown away by the wind.
Just then Gě passed by the boudoir door,
picked it up;
thinking Liánggōng wrote it,
disliked its wanton words,
burned it but could not bear to speak of it,
wishing to quickly marry her off.
The son of Liú Fāngbà from the neighboring county,
came to propose marriage,
he thought well of him,
but still wanted to see the person.
The young master arrived in splendid attire,
handsome and elegant in appearance.
Gě was greatly pleased,
entertained him warmly and generously.
Afterward, as he bid farewell,
under the seat he left a woman's slipper.
Gě immediately disliked his frivolity,
so called the matchmaker and told the reason.
The young master urgently defended himself against the false charge;
Gě would not listen,
and finally broke off the match.
Earlier,
Gě had a variety of green chrysanthemum,
stingy, not passing it on,
Liánggōng planted it in her boudoir.
In Wēn's courtyard, chrysanthemums suddenly had one or two plants turn green,
friends heard of it,
and came to his house to view and admire;
Wēn also treasured them.
At dawn, hurrying to look,
by the flower bed he found a paper with the poem "Xī Yúchūn",
repeatedly reading it over,
not knowing where it came from.
Because
"zhě"
was his own name,
he was even more puzzled,
immediately at the desk carefully added red and yellow marks,
the comments were frivolous.
Just then Gě heard Wēn's chrysanthemums had turned green,
surprised,
personally visited his study,
saw the poem and took it to read.
Wēn, because his comments were frivolous,
snatched it and crumpled it.
Gě had only read a line or two,
but it was exactly the one picked up at the boudoir door.
Greatly suspicious,
and also the green chrysanthemum variety,
guessed it was given by Liánggōng.
Returning home, he told his wife,
making her press and question Liánggōng.
Liánggōng wept, wishing to die,
but there was no evidence of the matter,
nothing to confirm it.
The wife feared the traces would become more obvious,
thought it better to marry the daughter to Wēn.
Gě agreed,
and sent word to Wēn.
Wēn was overjoyed.
That day,
he invited guests for a green chrysanthemum banquet,
burned incense and played the qin,
the beautiful night just ended.
After returning to sleep,
the study boy heard the qin playing by itself,
at first thinking it was a servant's prank;
later knowing it was not human,
he told Wēn.
Wēn went himself to check,
indeed it was true.
The sound was halting and rough,
as if trying to imitate him but not yet able.
Lighting a torch, he rushed in,
but saw nothing.
Wēn took the qin away,
then all night was silent.
Thus thinking it was a fox,
surely knowing it wished to become a disciple,
so every evening he played one piece,
and set the strings, letting it practice as a student,
nightly hiding and listening.
After six or seven nights,
it actually could play a piece,
elegant enough to listen to.
Wēn Jìqīn had already personally welcomed his bride,
and each recounted their past words,
only then realizing the reason for their union,
yet still not knowing where it had come from.
Liáng Gōng heard of the strange sound of the zither,
and went to listen,
saying:
"This is not a fox,
the tune is mournful and sorrowful,
it has the sound of a ghost."
Wēn did not deeply believe it.
Liáng Gōng then said that her family had an ancient mirror,
which could reveal demons and spirits.
The next day,
she sent someone to fetch it,
and when the zither sound began again,
she grasped the mirror and rushed in;
shining it,
indeed there was a woman present,
panicking in the corner of the room,
unable to hide again.
Looking closely at her,
it was Huànniáng of the Zhào family.
Greatly shocked,
they pressed her for an explanation.
Tearfully, she said:
"Acting as a matchmaker for you,
is not without virtue,
why do you press me so harshly?"
Wēn asked to remove the mirror,
promising she would not flee;
she agreed.
Then they put the mirror away.
The woman sat at a distance and said:
"I am the daughter of a prefect,
dead for a hundred years.
In my youth, I loved the qin and zheng;
the zheng I had already mastered quite well,
but this skill alone I could not fully inherit,
even in the underworld I still regret it.
When you visited,
I was able to hear your elegant performance,
and my heart was drawn to it;
but I also regret that as a different being I cannot serve you as a wife,
so in secret I worked to bring together a good match for you,
to repay your kindness and affection.
The embroidered shoes of Liú Gōngzǐ's daughter,
the rustic lyrics of 'Cherish the Remaining Spring,'
were all my doing.
Repaying the teacher cannot be said to be without effort."
Husband and wife both bowed in thanks.
Huànniáng said:
"Your skill,
I have thought over more than half;
but I have not yet grasped its divine principle.
Please play once more for me."
Wēn did as she requested,
and also explained the method in detail.
Huànniáng was greatly pleased and said:
"I have fully understood it now!"
Then she rose and prepared to leave.
Liáng Gōng was skilled at the zheng,
hearing of her expertise,
wished to hear her play.
Huànniáng did not refuse,
her tune and score,
were not of this mortal world.
Liáng Gōng applauded,
and in turn asked to learn from her.
The woman took up a brush and drew eighteen chapters of scores,
then rose to bid farewell.
Husband and wife tried hard to detain her.
Huànniáng said sorrowfully:
"Your marital harmony,
comes from mutual understanding;
a person of ill fortune like me cannot have such happiness.
If there is fate,
we may meet again in another life."
Then she handed a scroll to Wēn, saying:
"This is a small portrait of me.
If you do not forget the matchmaker,
hang it in your bedroom,
and when you are happy, burn a stick of incense,
play a tune facing it,
then I will receive it."
She went out the door and vanished.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Liú Zǐgù from Hǎizhōu,
at fifteen years old,
went to Gài to visit his uncle.
He saw a girl in a sundry goods shop,
beautiful beyond compare,
and his heart loved her.
Stealthily, he went to the shop,
pretending to buy a fan.
The girl called for her father.
Her father came out,
and Liú's spirits fell,
so he haggled over the price and left.
Seeing from afar that her father had gone elsewhere,
he went again.
The girl was about to look for her father,
but Liú stopped her, saying:
"No need,
just tell me the price,
I won't quibble over the cost."
The girl did as he said,
deliberately raising the price.
Liú could not bear to argue,
paid the money and left.
The next day he went again,
and it was the same.
After walking a few steps,
the girl called after him:
"Come back!
I was just lying before,
the price was too high."
So she returned half the money.
Liú was even more moved by her honesty,
seizing every chance to go,
and from then on they became familiar day by day.
The girl asked:
"Where do you live, young master?"
He answered truthfully.
He asked her in turn,
and she said:
"My surname is Yáo."
When leaving,
the things he bought,
the girl wrapped neatly in paper,
and then sealed it with fragrant paper.
Liú took it back and dared not open it again,
fearing to disturb the marks of her tongue.
After half a month,
he was discovered by his servant,
who secretly urged his uncle to insist on his return.
His heart was heavy and discontented.
He secretly placed the perfumed handkerchiefs, rouge, and powder he had bought,
in a box,
and when no one was around,
he would close the door and go through them,
touching each and lost in thought.
The following year,
he went again to Gài,
and as soon as he had unpacked,
he hurried to the girl's place;
but when he arrived, the shop was closed,
and he returned disappointed.
He thought she might have gone out and not returned,
so early the next morning he went again,
but it was still locked.
Asking the neighbors,
he learned that the Yáos were originally from Guǎngníng,
and because trade brought little profit,
they had temporarily returned;
and it was unclear when they might come back.
His spirits were broken.
After staying a few days,
he returned dejectedly.
His mother proposed a marriage for him,
but he repeatedly resisted,
and his mother grew suspicious and angry.
The servant privately told his mother about the past events,
and his mother became even more watchful,
so the road to Gài was thus cut off.
Liú grew listless, losing sleep and appetite.
His mother worried and could think of no plan,
thinking it better to follow his wishes.
So she set a date to prepare his luggage,
and sent him to Gài,
asking his uncle to act as matchmaker.
His uncle immediately went to the Yáos.
After some time, he returned,
and said to Liú:
"It cannot be done!
Ā Xiù is already betrothed to someone from Guǎngníng."
Liú hung his head in dejection,
his heart turned to ashes in despair.
After returning home,
he held the box and wept,
pacing back and forth in longing,
hoping that under heaven there might be someone like her.
Just then a matchmaker came,
and enthusiastically praised the daughter of the Huáng family in Fùzhōu.
Liú, fearing it was not accurate,
ordered the carriage to go to Fùzhōu.
Entering the west gate,
he saw a house facing north,
its two doors half-open,
inside was a young woman,
strangely resembling Ā Xiù;
he fixed his gaze on her,
and as she walked, she glanced back and entered,
truly without error.
Liú was greatly moved,
so he rented the house of its eastern neighbor,
and inquired in detail, learning it was the Lǐ family.
He pondered repeatedly in doubt!
Could there really be someone in the world so strikingly similar?
After staying several days,
he found no opportunity to approach,
and could only stare intently, waiting at her gate,
hoping the girl might come out again.
One day,
as the sun was setting in the west,
the girl indeed came out.
Suddenly seeing Liú,
she immediately turned back to leave,
pointing with her hand behind her;
then again placed her palm on her forehead,
and went in.
Liú was overjoyed,
but could not understand.
After pondering for a while,
he strolled to the back of the house,
and saw a desolate, vast garden,
with a low wall on the west,
roughly shoulder-high.
Suddenly enlightened,
he then crouched and hid in the dew-covered grass.
After a long time,
someone showed their head over the wall,
and whispered:
"Are you coming?"
Liú assented and stood up,
looking closely,
it was truly Ā Xiù.
He was then greatly pained,
tears falling like ropes.
The girl leaned over the wall,
using a handkerchief to wipe his tears,
deeply comforting him.
Liú said:
"After countless attempts without success,
I thought this life was already over,
how could I have expected tonight again?
But how did you come to be here?"
She said:
"The Lǐ family,
is my maternal uncle."
Liú asked to climb over the wall.
The girl said:
"You go back first,
send your attendants to stay elsewhere,
I will come on my own."
Liú did as she said,
and sat waiting.
After a short while,
the girl quietly entered,
her attire not very dazzling,
her robe and trousers still as before.
Liú pulled her to sit,
recounting all his hardships in detail,
then asked:
"You are already betrothed,
why have you not yet married?"
The girl said:
"The talk of me being engaged,
is false.
My father, because the journey is long and far,
did not wish to arrange marriage with the young master,
this was perhaps using my uncle's deceptive words,
to cut off your hopes."
Once they went to bed,
tender and affectionate in countless ways,
the joy of their intimate union,
cannot be described.
At the fourth watch, she quickly rose,
went over the wall and left.
From then on, Liú no longer paid attention to the Huáng family.
Staying at the inn, he forgot to return,
for a month he did not go back.
One night,
the servant got up to feed the horses,
and saw the light in the room still on;
peeping in,
he saw Ā Xiù,
greatly shocked,
but dared not question his master.
In the morning,
he visited the market shops,
then returned and questioned Liú:
"Who is the person you were with last night?"
Liú at first concealed it.
The servant said:
"This place is desolate,
a haunt of foxes and ghosts.
You, young master, should take care of yourself.
That young lady from the Yáo family,
why would she come here?"
Liú, beginning to feel embarrassed, said:
"Her paternal cousin lives in the western neighbor's house,
what is there to doubt or worry about?"
The servant said:
"I have already investigated thoroughly: the eastern neighbor has only a lonely widow,
the western family has a son who is still young,
there are no other close relatives.
The one you encountered must be a ghost or demon;
otherwise,
how could there be clothes from several years ago
that she still hasn't changed?
Moreover, her complexion is excessively pale,
her cheeks are somewhat thin,
and when she smiles, there are no slight dimples—
she is not as beautiful as Ā Xiù."
Liú thought it over repeatedly,
then became greatly afraid and said:
"If so, what should we do?"
The servant planned to wait for her arrival,
then take up weapons and enter together to attack her.
When evening came,
the woman arrived,
and said to Liú:
"I know you suspect me,
but I have no other intentions,
I am merely fulfilling a predestined bond."
Before she finished speaking,
the servant pushed the door open and entered.
The woman scolded him, saying:
"Put down your weapon!
Quickly prepare wine,
I shall bid farewell to your master."
The servant then dropped his weapon as if
it had been snatched away.
Liú grew even more frightened,
and reluctantly set out wine and food.
The woman talked and laughed as usual,
raised her hand toward Liú and said:
"Your concerns,
I was just about to exert my modest efforts to help,
why did you instead lay an ambush?
Although I am not Ā Xiù,
I rather think myself not inferior to her.
Do you still regard me as you did before?"
Liú's hair stood on end,
and he remained silent, not daring to speak.
The woman listened until the third watch,
took up a cup and sipped the wine,
stood up and said:
"I shall leave now.
After the wedding candles are lit,
I will come again to compare who is superior with the new bride."
She turned and then vanished.
Liú believed the fox's words,
and indeed went to Gàizhōu.
Resenting his uncle for deceiving him,
he did not stay at his uncle's house;
instead, he lodged near the Yáo family,
sent a matchmaker to convey his proposal himself,
and offered a substantial betrothal gift.
Yáo's wife then said:
"My younger brother-in-law went to Guǎngníng to find a husband for her,
that is why her father left,
whether it is settled or not is still unknown.
We must wait until he returns before we can discuss it."
Hearing this,
Liú felt anxious and uncertain, unable to decide for himself,
and could only wait steadfastly for her father's return.
After more than ten days,
he suddenly heard news of military unrest,
and still suspected it was a false rumor;
after a long time,
the reports grew increasingly urgent,
so he hurriedly packed and set off.
On the way, he encountered chaos,
and he and his servant became separated.
Liú was captured by scouts.
Because Liú appeared scholarly and weak,
they were lax in guarding him,
and he stole a horse and escaped.
When he reached the border of Hǎizhōu,
he saw a woman,
with disheveled hair and dusty ears,
stumbling along in worn-out shoes,
looking utterly miserable.
Liú rode past her,
when the woman suddenly called out:
"Is the man on horseback not Liú Láng?"
Liú stopped his horse and looked carefully,
and it was indeed Ā Xiù.
In his heart, he still suspected she might be the fox,
and said:
"Are you truly Ā Xiù?"
The woman asked:
"Why do you say that?"
Liú recounted his experiences.
The woman said:
"I am truly Ā Xiù.
My father brought me back from Guǎngníng,
we encountered soldiers and were captured.
They gave me a horse, but I kept falling off.
Suddenly, a woman
grabbed my wrist and urged me to flee.
We fled wildly through the army ranks,
and there was no one to question us.
The woman walked as swiftly as a flying falcon,
and I struggled to keep up,
after a hundred paces, my shoes fell off.
After a long while,
hearing the shouts and cries gradually grow distant,
she released my hand and said: 'Farewell!
The road ahead is all smooth,
you can walk slowly.
The one who loves you will soon arrive,
you should return with him.'"
Liú then knew she was the fox,
and felt grateful to her.
He then explained the reason why he had stayed in Gàizhōu.
The woman said that her uncle had chosen a husband for her from the Fāng family,
but before the betrothal gifts were sent, the turmoil began.
Only then did Liú realize his uncle's words were not false.
He helped the woman onto the horse,
and they rode together, returning home.
Upon entering the house, he found his old mother safe and sound,
and was overjoyed.
After tethering the horse and entering,
he recounted everything that had happened.
His mother was also delighted,
and helped the woman wash and clean up.
Once she was fully dressed and made up,
her beauty shone brilliantly.
His mother clapped her hands and said:
"No wonder my foolish son could not forget her even in his dreams!"
She then prepared bedding,
and had the woman stay with her.
She also sent someone to Gàizhōu,
to deliver a letter to the Yáo family.
Not many days later,
Mr. and Mrs. Yáo both arrived,
they chose an auspicious day for the wedding ceremony, and then departed.
Liú took out the hidden box,
its seal still intact.
Inside was a packet of powder;
upon opening it,
it turned into red earth.
Liú was astonished.
The girl covered her mouth and said:
"The theft from years ago
has only now been discovered.
That day, seeing you let me wrap it up,
you didn't even check its authenticity,
so I played this trick on you."
Just as they were laughing and joking,
someone lifted the curtain and entered, saying:
"So pleased with yourselves,
shouldn't you thank the matchmaker?"
Liú looked at her—
it was another Ā Xiù.
He hurriedly called for his mother.
His mother and the whole household gathered,
but no one could tell them apart.
Even Liú, turning to look, was confused;
after staring for a long while,
he finally bowed and thanked her.
The girl asked for a mirror to look at herself,
then blushed and hurried out,
vanishing without a trace.
The couple, moved by her righteousness,
set up a shrine for her in their room and made offerings.
One evening,
Liú returned home drunk,
the room dark and empty.
Just as he was lighting the lamp,
Ā Xiù arrived.
Liú held her and asked:
"Where have you been?"
She laughed and said:
"Your drunken stench is unbearable!
It's intolerable!
Interrogating me like this—
who would run off to a secret rendezvous?"
Liú laughed and cupped her face in his hands.
The girl said:
"Tell me, who is more beautiful—me or my fox sister?"
Liú said:
"You surpass her.
But those who judge by appearances cannot tell."
Soon they closed the door and became intimate.
Suddenly, there was a knock at the door.
The girl rose, laughing, and said:
"You too judge by appearances."
Liú didn't understand,
but hurried to open the door—
and there stood Ā Xiù.
He was utterly shocked.
Only then did he realize that the one he had just spoken with
was the fox.
From the darkness came laughter again.
Husband and wife prayed into the air,
begging her to appear.
The fox said:
"I do not wish to see Ā Xiù."
They asked:
"Why not take on another form?"
She replied:
"I cannot."
They asked:
"Why can't you?"
She said:
"Ā Xiù
is my younger sister.
In a previous life, she unfortunately died young.
When she was alive,
she and I followed our mother to the Heavenly Palace,
where we saw the Queen Mother of the West.
Secretly admiring her,
we returned and diligently imitated her.
My sister was more clever than I;
in one month, she captured the spirit perfectly.
I studied for three months before succeeding,
but I never matched my sister.
Now, after a lifetime apart,
I thought I had surpassed her,
but unexpectedly, I am still as I was before.
I am moved by the sincerity of you two,
so I visit from time to time.
Now I shall leave."
And she spoke no more.
From then on, she came every three to five days,
resolving all their difficulties.
When Ā Xiù returned to her parents' home,
the fox would often stay for several days,
and the household would fear and avoid her.
Whenever something was lost,
she would sit upright in splendid attire,
wearing a tortoiseshell hairpin several inches long,
and solemnly address the family:
"The stolen item
must be returned to such-and-such place tonight;
otherwise,
a severe headache will strike,
and regret will be too late!"
By dawn,
the item would indeed be found at that place.
After three years,
she stopped coming altogether.
Occasionally, when gold or silk went missing,
Ā Xiù would imitate her appearance
to frighten the household,
and it worked every time.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
A hunter,
lying in ambush in the mountains at night,
saw a small figure,
about two feet tall,
walking alone at the bottom of a ravine.
After a while,
another person came,
of similar height.
Meeting by chance,
they asked each other where they were going.
The first one said:
"I'm going to visit Yáng Bāyǎn.
Earlier, I saw his complexion was dark and gloomy,
likely to meet with misfortune."
The latter said:
"I'm going for the same reason.
What you say is not wrong."
The hunter, realizing they were not human,
shouted at them fiercely,
and both vanished.
That night, he caught a fox
with a scar on its left eye,
as large as a coin.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Wáng Tàicháng,
a man from Yuè,
in his childhood,
was napping on his bed one day.
Suddenly, the sky darkened,
and a great thunderstorm erupted.
A creature larger than a cat
came and crouched beneath him,
refusing to leave.
When the sky cleared after a while,
the creature went straight out.
Looking at it,
he saw it was not a cat
and became frightened,
calling for his brother in the next room.
His brother, hearing this,
said joyfully:
"You are destined for great nobility, brother.
That fox came to you to escape the thunder calamity."
Later, indeed, he passed the imperial examination at a young age
and rose from county magistrate to imperial censor.
He had a son,
named Yuánfēng,
who was extremely foolish;
at sixteen, he still could not tell male from female,
so no one in the village would marry him.
Wáng was worried.
Just then, a woman came to the door with a young girl,
offering her as a bride.
Looking at the girl,
she smiled radiantly—
truly a celestial beauty.
Delighted, he asked their names.
She said:
"My surname is Yú.
My daughter is Xiǎo Cuì,
sixteen years old."
He discussed the bride price with her.
She said:
"She couldn't even get enough chaff to eat with me.
Now that she'll be living in a grand mansion,
attended by maids and servants,
and feasting on rich food,
she'll be content,
and my wish will be fulfilled.
How could I haggle like a vegetable seller?"
The lady of the house was overjoyed
and treated them generously.
The woman immediately told her daughter to bow to Wáng and his wife,
instructing her:
"These are your parents-in-law.
Serve them with care.
I am very busy,
so I'll leave now,
but I'll return in a few days."
Wáng ordered servants and a carriage to escort her.
The woman said:
"The lane is not far;
no need for such trouble."
With that, she went out the door and left.
Xiǎo Cuì showed no sadness or longing
but immediately began rummaging through her trousseau for embroidery patterns.
The lady of the house also grew fond of her.
Several days passed,
but the woman did not come.
When Wáng asked the girl about her residence,
she too was too naive to describe the way,
so he prepared a separate courtyard
and had the couple perform the wedding ceremony.
When the relatives heard that Wáng had picked up a poor girl to be his bride,
they all laughed and ridiculed him;
but upon seeing the girl, they were all astonished,
and the gossip ceased.
The girl was also very clever,
able to discern the moods of her parents-in-law.
Mr. and Mrs. Wáng
doted on her more than usual,
yet they were apprehensive,
fearing only that she might despise their son for his foolishness;
but the girl was exceptionally cheerful and laughing,
showing no sign of aversion.
However, she was fond of teasing:
she would sew cloth into a ball
and kick it around for amusement.
Wearing small leather boots,
she would kick it dozens of steps away,
then trick the young master into running to fetch it,
so that he and the maids were often sweating profusely.
One day,
Wáng happened to pass by,
when the ball came flying
and struck him right in the face.
The girl and the maids all withdrew and hid,
but the young master was still leaping about, chasing after it.
Wáng grew angry,
threw a stone at him,
and only then did he crouch down and cry.
Wáng told his wife about it;
the wife went to reprimand the girl,
who bowed her head with a slight smile,
tracing patterns on the bed with her hand.
After she left,
she frolicked as before,
smearing rouge and powder on the young master,
making his face look like a painted ghost.
When the wife saw this,
she was furious,
and called the girl over to scold her harshly.
The girl leaned against the table, playing with her sash,
neither afraid
nor speaking.
The wife had no way to deal with her,
so she took a rod and beat her son.
Yuánfēng wailed loudly,
and only then did the girl’s expression change:
she knelt down and begged for forgiveness.
The wife’s anger immediately subsided,
and she put down the rod and left.
The girl, smiling, pulled the young master into the room,
dusted off his clothes,
wiped his tears,
rubbed the marks from the rod,
and fed him dates and chestnuts.
The young master then stopped crying and became happy.
The girl closed the courtyard gate,
dressed the young master up as the Conqueror,
and as a desert tribesman;
then she herself put on gorgeous attire,
tied a slender waistband,
and danced gracefully like a performer under a tent;
or she would stick pheasant feathers in her hair,
strum the pipa,
producing delicate, lingering notes,
filling the room with laughter and noise,
and this became a daily routine.
Because his son was foolish, Wáng could not bear to overly blame his daughter-in-law;
even when he heard a little about it,
he acted as if he knew nothing.
In the same lane lived a certain Wáng Jǐjiàn,
separated by more than ten households,
but who had always been on bad terms with Wáng.
At that time, it was the triennial evaluation of officials,
and Jǐjiàn, jealous that Wáng held the seal of Hénán Circuit,
plotted to harm him.
Wáng knew of his scheme,
and was worried, unable to devise a counterplan.
One evening,
he retired early.
The girl put on official robes and hat,
dressed up as the Minister of Personnel,
cut white silk to make a thick beard,
and also dressed two maids in black as attendants,
secretly mounted a horse from the stable,
and went out, joking:
"I’m going to pay a visit to Mr. Wáng."
She galloped to Jǐjiàn’s gate, then whipped her attendants,
and declared loudly:
"I am calling on Attendant Censor Wáng—
why would I visit Jǐjiàn Wáng!"
She then turned her horse and returned.
By the time she reached her own gate,
the gatekeeper mistakenly thought it was real
and rushed to report to Wáng.
Wáng hurriedly rose to receive the guest,
only then realizing it was his daughter-in-law’s prank.
He was furious,
and said to his wife:
"Just when others are trying to find fault with me,
she instead brings the shame of the inner chambers
to their very door and announces it.
Disaster is not far off!"
The wife was angry,
rushed to the girl’s room,
and berated her.
The girl only laughed naively,
not offering a single word in reply.
They thought of beating her, but could not bear to;
of divorcing her, but she had no home:
husband and wife were filled with regret and resentment,
unable to sleep all night.
At that time, a certain Minister of Personnel was extremely powerful,
and his appearance, demeanor, attire, and retinue
were no different from the girl’s disguise,
so Wáng Jǐjiàn also mistook it for real.
He repeatedly spied on Wáng’s gate,
and when the guest had not left by midnight,
he suspected the Minister and Wáng were plotting secretly.
The next morning at court,
he saw Wáng and asked:
"Last night,
did the Minister visit your home?"
Wáng thought he was mocking him,
and replied sheepishly with vague assent,
not answering clearly.
Jǐjiàn grew even more suspicious,
and his scheme was abandoned.
From then on, he became even friendlier with Wáng.
Wáng found out the reason,
secretly rejoiced,
and privately instructed his wife
to advise the girl to mend her ways;
the girl smiled and agreed.
A year later,
the prime minister was dismissed.
It happened that someone sent a private letter to the Duke,
but it was mistakenly delivered to the Censor.
The Censor was overjoyed,
and first sent someone friendly with the Duke to borrow ten thousand taels of silver,
but the Duke refused.
The Censor then personally went to the Duke's residence.
The Duke searched for his official cap and robe,
but could not find them anywhere.
The Censor waited for a long time,
grew angry at the Duke's discourtesy,
and was about to leave in a rage.
Suddenly, he saw the young master dressed in imperial dragon robes and a crown, pushed out from inside the gate by a woman.
He was greatly shocked;
then, laughing, he patted him,
removed his robe and crown, and left.
The Duke hurried out,
but the guest was already far gone.
Upon hearing what had happened,
his face turned ashen with fright,
and he cried out loudly,
"This is a calamitous woman!
She will bring ruin upon our clan any day now!"
He and his wife took up sticks and went to confront her.
The girl already knew of it,
and closed the door, letting them curse and revile her.
The Duke grew furious,
and hacked at the door with an axe.
The girl inside said with a smile:
"Father, do not trouble yourself with anger.
With your daughter-in-law here,
whether it be the knife, saw, axe, or halberd,
I will bear it myself,
and will certainly not let harm come to my parents.
If you act like this, Father,
is it because you wish to kill me to silence me?"
The Duke then stopped.
The Censor returned home,
and indeed submitted a memorial accusing the Duke of treason,
citing the dragon robe and crown as evidence.
The Emperor, shocked, ordered an examination,
and found the crown was made from sorghum stalks and husks,
and the robe was a worn yellow cloth wrapper.
The Emperor was angered by the false accusation.
He also summoned Yuánfēng to court,
and seeing his foolish, simple appearance,
said with a laugh:
"Could this one become an emperor?"
He then handed the case over to the judicial authorities.
The Censor further accused the Duke's household of harboring sorcerers.
The judicial authorities rigorously interrogated the servants,
who all said there was nothing else,
only a mad wife and a foolish son,
who spent their days in play and laughter;
the neighbors also had nothing different to say.
The case was thus settled,
and the Censor was exiled to serve in the Yúnnán army.
The Duke from then on regarded the girl as extraordinary.
Also, because her mother had not come for a long time,
he suspected she was not human.
He had his wife try to sound her out,
but the girl only smiled without speaking.
When pressed further,
she covered her mouth and said:
"Your daughter is the Jade Emperor's daughter,
does Mother not know?"
Not long after,
the Duke was promoted to a high capital ministry post.
He was over fifty,
and often worried about having no grandson.
The girl had lived there for three years.
Every night she slept apart from the young master,
as if they had never been intimate.
The wife had the extra bed removed,
and told the young master to sleep with his wife.
After a few days,
the young master told his mother:
and she bullies me and won't give it back!
Xiǎocuì every night puts her legs and thighs on my belly,
so I can't breathe;
and she's used to pinching my thighs."
The maids and old women all burst out laughing.
The wife scolded him and sent him away.
One day,
the girl was bathing in her room,
and the young master saw her,
and wanted to join her;
the girl laughingly stopped him,
telling him to wait a while.
After she came out,
she then poured more hot water into the vat,
took off his robe and trousers,
and helped him in with a maid.
The young master felt steamed and stifled,
and cried out loudly that he wanted to get out.
The girl paid no heed,
and covered him with a quilt.
After a short while,
there was no sound.
She opened it to look,
and he had already stopped breathing.
The girl remained calm and smiling, unalarmed.
She dragged him onto the bed,
wiped his body dry and clean,
and covered him with another quilt.
When the wife heard of it,
she rushed in crying,
and scolded:
"You mad maid, why did you kill my son!"
The girl said with a radiant smile:
"Such a foolish son,
better not to have had him."
The wife grew even more furious,
and tried to butt the girl with her head;
the maids all pulled and tried to calm her.
Amidst the clamor,
a maid announced:
"The young master is groaning!"
She stopped crying and went to comfort him.
He was breathing steadily,
and great sweat was soaking through,
drenching the mattress and bedding.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
the sweating stopped.
Suddenly he opened his eyes and looked all around,
gazing at each family member,
as if he did not recognize them,
and said:
"Now I recall the past,
it all seems like a dream,
why is that?"
The wife, seeing his speech was not foolish,
found it very strange.
She took him to see his father,
and tested him repeatedly,
and indeed he was no longer foolish.
They were overjoyed,
as if they had obtained a rare treasure.
That evening,
they returned the bed to its original place,
and set up quilts and pillows again to observe them.
The young master entered the room,
and sent all the maids away.
Peeking in early the next morning,
they saw the bed was unused.
From then on, neither foolishness nor madness occurred again,
and they lived in quiet harmony,
as close as body and shadow.
Over a year later,
the Duke was impeached and removed from office by the faction of the Censor,
due to a minor fault.
He had a jade vase, a gift from the Governor of Guǎngxī,
worth a thousand gold pieces,
which he intended to present as a bribe to those in power.
The girl, fond of it, was holding and admiring it
when she accidentally dropped and shattered it.
Ashamed, she went to confess.
The Duke and his wife were already displeased over the dismissal,
and upon hearing this,
they grew angry
and scolded her in unison.
Furious, the girl left
and said to the young master:
"In your household,
what I have preserved is far more than just a vase.
Why then do you show me not the slightest respect?
To tell you the truth: I am not human.
Because my mother suffered the calamity of thunder,
she deeply received your father's protection;
and because the two of us have a predestined bond of five years,
I came to repay his kindness and fulfill that old vow.
I have endured your insults,
more than can be counted by pulling out hairs,
and the reason I did not leave immediately
is that the five years of affection are not yet complete.
Now, how can I stay even a moment longer!"
She stormed out in anger,
and when pursued, she had already vanished.
The Duke felt a sudden emptiness and regret,
but it was too late for remorse.
The young master entered his chamber,
saw her leftover powder and abandoned hairpins,
and wept bitterly, wishing to die;
he could neither eat nor sleep peacefully,
and daily grew thinner and weaker.
The Duke, greatly worried,
hurriedly arranged a remarriage to console him,
but the young master took no pleasure in it.
He only sought a skilled painter to create a portrait of Xiǎocuì,
and day and night he would offer libations and prayers before it,
for nearly two years.
Once, returning from another village on some business,
the bright moon was already shining,
and outside the village was the Duke's garden pavilion.
Riding past outside the wall,
he heard sounds of laughter and talk.
He halted his horse,
had the stable hand hold the reins,
and mounting the saddle to look over,
he saw two young ladies playing within.
The clouds and moon were dim,
making it hard to see clearly,
but he heard one in green clothes say:
"You little maid should be driven out the door!"
One in red clothes said:
"You are in my family's garden pavilion,
yet you want to drive out who?"
The one in green said:
"Aren't you ashamed, little maid?
Unable to be a proper wife,
driven out by others,
and still claiming property as your own?"
The one in red said:
"At least better than an old maid with no one to care for her!"
Hearing her voice,
it sounded exactly like Xiǎocuì's,
so he called out urgently.
The one in green left, saying:
"I won't argue with you now—
your man is here."
Then the one in red came over,
and it was indeed Xiǎocuì.
Overjoyed,
she told him to climb the wall and help her down,
saying:
"Two years apart,
and you're nothing but skin and bones!"
The young master held her hand and wept,
pouring out his longing.
The girl said:
"I know it too,
but I am too ashamed to face the family again.
Now, playing with my elder sister,
we happened to meet again,
which shows that predestined ties cannot be escaped."
He asked her to return with him,
but she refused;
he asked her to stay in the garden,
and she agreed.
The young master sent a servant running to inform the Lady.
The Lady rose in surprise,
took a sedan chair and went there,
unlocked the gate and entered the pavilion.
The girl hurried down to greet and bow;
the Lady grasped her arm, tears flowing,
earnestly confessing her past faults,
almost unable to face her,
saying:
"If you can set aside past grievances,
please come back with us,
to comfort me in my old age."
The girl firmly declined.
The Lady, concerned that the country pavilion was desolate and lonely,
proposed sending many servants to attend her.
The girl said:
"I do not wish to see any of the others,
only the two maids from before to accompany me day and night,
for I cannot help feeling attached to them;
besides, one old servant to answer the gate,
and nothing more is needed."
The Lady complied with all her requests.
She entrusted the young master to recuperate in the garden,
providing only daily food and supplies.
The girl often urged the young master to marry another,
but he would not agree.
After more than a year,
the girl's features, eyes, and voice
gradually became different from before.
Taking out the portrait to compare,
she seemed like a completely different person.
Greatly puzzled,
the girl said:
"Look at me today—
how do I compare to my former beauty?"
The young master said,
"You're only in your twenties—
how could you age so quickly?"
The girl laughed and burned the portrait;
when he tried to save it, it was already ashes.
One day,
she said to the young master:
"In the past, at home,
your father said I would never bear children.
Now your parents are old and you are alone,
and I truly cannot produce offspring,
fearing I will hinder your family line.
Please take a wife into the household,
who can morning and evening serve your parents,
and you can move between the two places,
with no inconvenience."
The young master agreed,
and betrothal gifts were sent to the family of Grand Historian Zhōng.
As the wedding day approached,
the girl made clothes and shoes for the bride,
and sent them to the mother.
When the bride entered the door,
her speech, appearance, and manner
were not the slightest bit different from Xiǎocuì's.
Astonished,
he went to the garden pavilion,
but the girl was nowhere to be found.
He asked the maid,
who brought out a red handkerchief, saying:
"The lady has temporarily returned to her parents' home,
leaving this for the young master."
Unfolding it,
inside was a knotted jade jué pendant.
Knowing in his heart she would not return,
he took the maid and went home.
Though he never forgot Xiǎocuì for a moment,
fortunately, facing the new bride was like seeing his old love.
Only then did he realize that the marriage to the Zhōng family
had been foreseen by the girl,
who had first transformed her appearance
to comfort his future longing.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"A mere fox,
for an unintentional kindness,
still thinks of repaying it;
yet one who has received the blessing of a second life
cries out over a broken pot—
how vulgar indeed!
The moon wanes and becomes full again;
she departs with ease,
showing that the feelings of immortals
are also deeper than those of ordinary folk!"
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Jīn Héshàng was a man of Zhūchéng.
His father was a scoundrel who sold him for a few hundred coins to the Wǔlián Mountain Temple.
As a child, he was dull and obtuse, unable to learn the pure practices of monastic life.
He herded pigs to market like a hired laborer.
After his original master died, he inherited a small sum of money, which he tucked away before leaving the temple to become a traveling peddler.
He was skilled at adulterating goods and monopolizing markets, and his schemes were most cunning.
Within a few years, he had amassed a sudden fortune and bought fields and estates in the village of Gānshuǐpō.
His disciples were numerous, and the mouths to feed numbered in the thousands daily.
Around the village, he owned hundreds of acres of fertile land.
Within the village, he built dozens of residences, all occupied by monks—there were no ordinary people.
If there were any, they were poor and without occupation, renting rooms and farming the land with their wives and children.
Inside each gate, rows of interconnected houses were all occupied by such people.
The monks’ quarters were in the center: at the front was a reception hall, with beams, pillars, and rafters painted in gold and green, dazzling to the eye.
In the main hall, tables and screens gleamed so brightly they could serve as mirrors.
Further inside were the private chambers, with vermilion curtains and embroidered drapes, filled with the overwhelming fragrance of orchids and musk.
The beds were made of inlaid sandalwood, covered with brocade mattresses and cushions folded to a thickness of over a foot.
On the walls, famous paintings of beauties and landscapes were hung so densely there was almost no empty space.
With a single loud call, dozens of people outside would thunderously respond.
Those wearing fine hats and leather boots gathered like crows and stood like pigeons.
When receiving orders, they would cover their mouths and speak in hushed tones, leaning in to listen.
If guests arrived unexpectedly, over a dozen feasts could be prepared in an instant, with rich meats steaming and piled high, scattered like mist and dew.

However, they dared not openly keep singing girls; instead, they had over a dozen clever boys, all witty and charming, with black gauze wrapped around their heads, singing flirtatious tunes—a sight and sound not at all unpleasant.
When Jīn went out, dozens of riders would accompany him front and back, their bows and arrows clattering at their waists.
His servants all addressed him as “Master.”
Even the townspeople and commoners would call him “Grandfather” or “Uncle,” but never “Teacher,” “Venerable,” or by any monastic title.
When his disciples went out, they were slightly less extravagant than Jīn, but with their wind-swept manes and cloud-like reins, they were roughly on par with noble young masters.
Jīn also formed extensive connections, so that even from a thousand miles away, his influence could be felt.
He used this to manipulate local officials, holding their shortcomings over them.
If anyone offended him, they would tremble in fear.
Yet in character, he was vulgar and uncultured, lacking any refinement from head to toe.
In his lifetime, he never recited a single sutra or chant, never set foot in a temple, and never kept a bell or drum in his room.
Such things, his disciples never saw nor heard of.
All those who rented rooms had women as glamorous as those in the capital, their cosmetics and finery all supplied by the monks.
The monks never begrudged this, so in the village, hundreds of people lived as farmers without tilling the land.
Occasionally, a wicked tenant would kill a monk and bury the head under the bed, but this was never thoroughly investigated—they were simply driven out, as was the custom.
Jīn also bought a boy from another family and secretly raised him as his own.
He hired a Confucian tutor to teach him the art of examination essays.
The boy was clever and skilled in writing, so he was enrolled in the county school.
Soon, through a special provision, he became a National University student.
Not long after, he took the provincial examination in the north and passed as a provincial graduate.
From then on, Jīn’s reputation as “Grand Duke” spread far and wide.
Those who once called him “Master” now addressed him as “Grand,” and those who once knelt before him now bowed with their hands at their sides, performing the rites of children and grandchildren.
Before long, Grand Duke the monk passed away.
The provincial graduate mourned in hempen clothes, sleeping on a straw mat and facing north as the bereaved son.
The disciples laid their staffs across the bed, filling it.
Behind the spirit curtain, only the faint sobbing of the provincial graduate’s wife could be heard.
The wives of scholars and officials all came in splendid attire, lifting the curtain to offer condolences, their carriages and horses clogging the roads.
On the day of the funeral, pavilions and tents stretched like clouds, and banners and streamers blotted out the sun.
The burial figurines were adorned with gold and silk.
There were dozens of ceremonial canopies and processional implements, a thousand horses, and a hundred beauties, all lifelike.
The Fangxiàng and Fangxiāng were giant figures made of paper shells, wrapped in black silk with golden embroidery.
They were hollow, with wooden frames inside, carried by living people.
Mechanisms were set to make them move, their beards and eyebrows fluttering, their eyes gleaming as if about to shout.
Onlookers were astonished; some children, seeing them from afar, would cry and run away.
The spirit mansion was as magnificent as a palace, with towers, pavilions, rooms, and corridors spanning dozens of acres.
With a thousand gates and ten thousand doors, those who entered would get lost and be unable to find their way out.
Among the sacrificial offerings and ritual objects, many were difficult to name.
The mourners crowded together, rubbing shoulders.

From high-ranking officials who entered bowing and performed rites as if at court, down to tribute students, supervisors, clerks, and scribes who knelt with their hands on the ground, none dared trouble the young master or the various uncles.
At that time, the entire country gazed in awe.
Men and women panted and sweated along the roads, carrying infants in slings or calling for siblings, their voices rising like a boiling cauldron.
Mixed with the clamor of drums and music and the clanging of various performances, human speech became inaudible.
The crowd was so dense that from the shoulders down, nothing was visible—only ten thousand bobbing heads.
A pregnant woman, gripped by sudden labor pains, was surrounded by female companions who spread their skirts to form a curtain, guarding her closely.
As soon as the baby’s cry was heard, without time to ask whether it was a boy or a girl, they tore a piece of cloth to wrap it, some supporting her, others pulling her, limping away.
What a spectacular sight!
After the burial, the assets Jīn left behind were divided into two parts: one for his son, one for his disciples.
The provincial graduate received half and lived in the southern residence.
The northern, western, and eastern residences were all occupied by the black-robed faction.
Yet they all addressed each other as brothers, sharing joys and sorrows as if closely connected.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"This is a particular school,
not found among the two sects,
nor transmitted by the Sixth Patriarch;
it can be said to have uniquely opened its own Dharma gate.
Moreover, I have heard:
When the five skandhas are all empty,
and the six dusts remain unstained,
this is called a 'true monk' (héshàng).
When one speaks the Dharma with the mouth,
and sits in meditation upon the seat,
this is called a 'monk in form' (héyàng).
When sandals are fragrant from the land of Chǔ,
and the bamboo hat is heavy under the sky of Wú,
this is called a 'roaming monk' (hézhuàng).
When drums and gongs clamor noisily,
and reed pipes and flutes blare loudly,
this is called a 'chanting monk' (héchàng).
When one acts like a dog, fawning and seeking connections,
or like a fly, bustling about in debauchery and gambling,
this is called a 'veiling monk' (hézhàng).
Now, this 'gold' (Jīn, referring to a monk's name or perhaps a metaphor),
is it of the 'true' (shàng) kind?
Or of the 'form' (yàng) kind?
Or of the 'chanting' (chàng) kind?
Or of the 'roaming' (zhuàng) kind?
Or is it the 'veil' (zhàng) of hell?"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Magistrate Xú was the magistrate of Qídōng.
In his yamen, there was a storeroom used for storing food and provisions,
which were often stolen and eaten by some creature,
leaving a mess on the floor.
The servants were repeatedly scolded for this,
so they lay in wait.
They saw a spider as large as a peck measure.
Terrified, they ran to report to the magistrate.
The magistrate found this strange
and daily had maidservants place food for it.
The spider grew even tamer;
when hungry, it would come out and approach people,
leaving only after it was full.
After more than a year,
the magistrate was once reviewing documents
when the spider suddenly came and crouched on his desk.
Thinking it was hungry,
he was about to call servants to bring food
when he suddenly saw two snakes lying on either side of the spider,
as thin as chopsticks.
The spider curled its legs and shrank its belly,
as if overcome with fear.
In an instant,
the snakes violently grew,
becoming thicker than eggs.
Greatly alarmed,
he wanted to flee.
A tremendous thunderclap erupted,
and the entire family was struck dead.
After a while,
the magistrate revived;
but his wife and seven maidservants and servants had been killed.
The magistrate was ill for over a month
and soon died.
He was an upright and incorrupt official who loved the people.
On the day his coffin was carried forth,
the people collected money to send him off,
and the fields were filled with the sound of weeping.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"The 'dragon playing with a spider'—
I always thought it was a baseless rumor from the alleys,
but could it truly exist?
I have heard that thunderbolts strike
only at wicked people.
How then could an honest and good official
suffer such a cruel and poisonous fate?
Is not Heaven's confusion
already excessive enough!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
A certain merchant from Tiānjīn
was about to trade in distant parts
and went to borrow several hundred taels from a rich man.
He was observed by a thief,
who that evening hid in his room in advance, waiting for him to return.
But because the day was auspicious,
the merchant set off directly with the money.
The thief, having hidden for a long time,
only heard the merchant's wife tossing and turning in bed,
as if unable to sleep.
Then a small door in the wall opened,
filling the room with light.
A woman emerged from the doorway,
young and beautiful in appearance.
She held a long belt in her hand,
approached the bed, and offered it to the wife.
The wife pushed it away with her hand.
The woman insisted on giving it to her;
the wife then accepted the belt,
rose, hung it from a beam,
put her neck in it, and hanged herself.
The woman then left,
and the wall door closed.
The thief, greatly shocked,
opened the door and fled.
When day broke,
the family found the wife dead
and reported it to the authorities.
The officials arrested the neighbors and tortured them,
extorting a confession and completing the case.
They were to be executed in a few days.
The thief, indignant at the injustice,
went to the court to confess,
relating what he had seen that night.
Upon interrogation, his account proved true,
and the neighbors were thus spared.
When inquiries were made among the local people,
it was said that a young wife of the former owner of the house had once hanged herself there.
Her age and appearance
perfectly matched the thief's description,
so it was understood to be her ghost.
It is commonly said that those who die a violent death must seek a substitute—
is this indeed so?
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Shào, a scholar from Jìnghǎi,
came from a poor family.
On the occasion of his mother's birthday,
he prepared sacrificial meat and wine and made offerings in the courtyard.
After finishing his bows and rising,
he found the food and wine on the altar had all vanished.
Greatly astonished,
he told his mother what had happened.
His mother suspected he was too impoverished to provide a proper birthday celebration,
and was thus making up a story.
Shào was silent, having no way to justify himself.
Not long after,
the imperial examiner arrived for the examinations.
Shào, troubled by having no travel funds,
borrowed a small sum and set off.
On the road, he met a man
who was crouching by the roadside waiting
and who invited him very earnestly.
Shào followed him
and saw halls, pavilions, towers, and terraces
stretching along the streets.
Once inside,
a kingly figure sat in the main hall.
Shào knelt and bowed.
The king, with a pleasant expression, ordered him to sit
and then bestowed a feast upon him,
saying:
"When I previously passed by your noble residence,
my attendants were hungry and thirsty on the road
and partook of your sumptuous feast."
Shào was startled and did not understand.
The king said:
"I am the King of Wǔguān.
Do you not remember the day your honored mother celebrated her birthday?"
When the feast ended,
he brought out a packet of silver
and said:
"For the disturbance of the pig's trotters (i.e., the humble feast),
let this serve as a token of repayment."
Shào accepted it and left.
Then the palaces, buildings, and people
vanished in an instant;
only a few large trees remained,
standing lonely by the roadside.
Looking at the gift,
he found it was genuine silver.
Weighing it, he found it to be five taels.
By the end of the examinations,
he had spent only half of it
and was still able to take the remainder home to support his mother.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
In Shānxī there was a Doctor Yáng,
skilled in the art of acupuncture and moxibustion;
he could also command ghosts.
Whenever he went out,
those leading his mule and holding his whip
were all ghostly beings.
Once, returning from elsewhere at night,
he was traveling with a friend.
On the road they saw two men approaching,
extraordinarily tall and imposing.
His friend was greatly alarmed.
Yáng then asked:
"Who are you?"
They replied:
"Long-legged Wáng
and Big-headed Lǐ,
respectfully welcoming our master."
Yáng said:
"Go ahead and clear the way for me."
The two turned and walked ahead,
pausing to wait whenever they lagged,
just like slaves.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Xìliǔniáng
was the daughter of a scholar from Zhōngdū.
Some, finding her waist slender and graceful,
playfully called her
"Xìliǔ"
(Slender Willow).
Liǔ was clever from a young age,
understood writing,
and enjoyed reading books on physiognomy.
