Yet in her life she was reserved and taciturn,
never speaking of others' merits or faults;
but whenever a marriage proposal was made,
she insisted on personally observing the man.
She had seen many suitors,
but none were suitable,
and she was already nineteen.
Her parents angrily said to her:
"Has the world truly no good match?
Will you grow old as a spinster?"
The girl said:
"I truly wished for human effort to overcome fate;
but seeing it has long been unsuccessful,
it must be my destiny.
From now on,
I will obey only my parents' commands."
At that time, there was a Mr. Gāo,
a scion of an established family and a renowned scholar,
who, hearing of Xìliǔ's reputation,
sent betrothal gifts.
After the wedding,
husband and wife were very compatible.
There was an orphaned son from Gāo's previous wife,
nicknamed Chángfú,
then five years old,
whom the girl cared for with utmost devotion.
If she ever visited her parents,
Fú would cry and follow her,
unable to be stopped by scolding or sending him away.
Over a year later,
the girl gave birth to a son,
naming him Chánghù.
Gāo asked the meaning of the names,
she replied:
"Nothing special,
only hoping they would long remain by our knees."
The girl was careless with needlework,
often paying it no mind;
but regarding the fields to the southeast,
the amount of taxes,
she would consult the records and inquire,
fearing she might not know the details.
After some time,
she said to Gāo:
"Please set aside household affairs and don't worry about them,
let your concubine manage them herself,
I wonder if I can run the household?"
Gāo did as she said,
and after half a year, no household task was neglected,
and Gāo considered her virtuous.
One day,
Gāo went to a neighboring village to drink,
and it happened that tax collectors pursuing arrears
were pounding on the door and cursing;
she sent a servant to placate them,
but they wouldn't leave.
So she urged a boy to summon Gāo back.
After the clerks left,
Gāo laughed and said:
"Xìliǔ,
now do you know a clever woman is no match for a foolish man?"
Hearing this,
the girl bowed her head and wept.
Startled, Gāo held her and tried to console her,
but she remained unhappy.
Unwilling to burden her with household management,
Gāo still wanted to take it on himself,
but she refused again.
Rising early and retiring late,
she managed affairs even more diligently.
Every year, a year in advance,
she would store up the taxes for the coming year,
so that throughout the year no tax collector ever came to their door;
she also used this method to plan for clothing and food,
so their expenses became even more comfortable.
Then Gāo was greatly pleased,
and once teased her:
"How fine is Xìliǔ: fine brows, fine waist, fine steps,
and happily, her thoughts are even finer."
The girl replied:
"Mr. Gāo is truly lofty: lofty character,
lofty aspirations,
lofty writing,
only may his lifespan be loftier still."
In the village, someone was selling fine timber for a coffin,
the girl spared no expense to acquire it;
when the price couldn't be met,
she borrowed from relatives and neighbors in various ways.
Gāo, considering it an unnecessary item,
firmly tried to stop her,
but she ultimately wouldn't listen.
She stored it for over a year,
when a wealthy family had a funeral,
and offered double the price to buy it from their door.
Gāo, seeing the profit, discussed it with her,
but she wouldn't agree.
He asked the reason,
she didn't speak;
asked again,
her eyes glistened as if about to weep.
He found it strange,
but couldn't bear to strongly oppose her,
so he dropped the matter.
Another year passed,
and Shēng was now twenty-five.
His wife forbade him from traveling far;
if he returned even slightly late,
the servants sent to fetch him
would line the roads one after another.
Because of this, all his friends teased and mocked him.
One day,
Shēng went to drink at a friend’s house.
Feeling unwell, he started home,
but halfway there he fell from his horse
and died.
It was the height of the humid summer,
but fortunately the burial clothes and shroud had been prepared long in advance.
Only then did the villagers begin to admire Xìniáng’s foresight.
Fú was ten years old
when he began his studies.
After his father died,
he grew lazy and unwilling to study,
often running off to play with the shepherd boys.
Scolding did not change him,
and even switching to caning
left him as stubborn and dull as before.
His mother, at her wits’ end,
called him over and admonished him:
"Since you refuse to study,
how can I force you?
But a poor family has no idle members.
Change your clothes, then,
and work alongside the servants.
If not,
don’t regret it when you’re whipped!"
So she dressed him in tattered cotton padding
and set him to tending pigs.
When he returned, he would fetch his own earthenware bowl
and eat gruel with the other servants.
After a few days,
he found it unbearable.
Weeping, he knelt in the courtyard,
begging to return to his studies.
His mother turned her back to the wall
and ignored him.
With no other choice,
he took up his whip and went out sobbing.
As late autumn drew to a close,
he had no clothes on the rack,
no shoes on his feet.
Soaked by the cold rain,
he hunched his shoulders like a beggar.
Seeing this, the villagers pitied him,
and those taking a second wife
all cited Xìniáng as a warning,
grumbling with discontent.
She heard some of this talk,
but remained utterly indifferent.
Unable to bear the hardship,
Fú abandoned the pigs and ran away.
His mother let him go,
not even bothering to pursue him.
After several months,
with nowhere to beg for food,
he returned, haggard and worn.
Not daring to enter directly,
he begged a neighborly old woman to plead his case to his mother.
His mother said:
"If he can endure a hundred strokes,
he may come see me;
otherwise,
he’d best leave again."
Hearing this, Fú
rushed inside
and wept bitterly, willing to accept the beating.
His mother asked:
"Do you now know to repent?"
He said:
"I repent."
She said:
"Since you know to repent,
there’s no need for a whipping.
You may tend the pigs peacefully;
if you offend again, there will be no pardon!"
Fú wailed:
"I’d rather take a hundred strokes
and beg to return to my studies."
His mother would not listen.
Only after the old neighbor urged her on
did she relent.
She washed his hair, gave him fresh clothes,
and had him study under the same teacher as his younger brother, Hù.
Diligent and sharp-minded,
he was utterly transformed from his former self.
After three years, he passed the county examination.
Provincial Surveillance Commissioner Yáng,
impressed by his essays,
granted him a monthly stipend
to aid his studies.
Hù was the dullest;
after years of study, he still could not remember names.
His mother ordered him to put aside his books and farm.
But Hù loved idleness and dreaded hard work.
His mother grew angry:
"Each of the four classes has its proper occupation.
Since you can neither study
nor farm,
would you rather starve to death in a ditch?"
She immediately caned him.
From then on, he led the servants in fieldwork.
If he rose late even once,
she would curse and scold him.
As for clothing and food,
she always gave the finer portions to his elder brother.
Though Hù dared not complain,
he secretly resented it.
When the farming season ended,
his mother provided capital for him to learn petty trade.
But Hù gave himself to debauchery and gambling,
losing everything he touched.
He lied, blaming bandits or fate,
to deceive his mother.
When she discovered the truth,
she caned him nearly to death.
Fú knelt long, pleading tearfully,
offering to take the punishment himself,
and only then did her anger subside.
After this, whenever Hù went out,
his mother would investigate his movements.
Hù’s conduct improved somewhat,
but not from any genuine change of heart.
One day,
he asked his mother
to let him travel to Luò with some merchants—
in truth, to wander far
and indulge his desires.
His heart pounded with anxiety,
fearing she would refuse his request.
But when she heard it,
she showed no suspicion or worry.
She immediately took out thirty taels of broken silver
to prepare his luggage;
then she also gave him one ingot of gold, saying:
"This is a legacy from your grandfather’s official salary.
Do not spend it;
keep it merely to weight your luggage,
for use only in an emergency.
Moreover, as this is your first time traveling such a distance,
I dare not expect great profit—
just do not lose these thirty taels, and that will suffice."
As he left, she admonished him once more.
Hù promised and departed,
overjoyed and pleased with himself.
Arriving in Luò,
he dismissed his traveling companions
and lodged at the house of the famous courtesan Lǐ Jī.
After a dozen or so nights,
his scattered silver was nearly gone.
Thinking he still had the large gold ingot in his bag,
he had not considered the possibility of emptiness.
But when he took it out and examined it,
it turned out to be counterfeit gold.
He was horrified
and turned pale.
Old Madam Lǐ, seeing his state,
taunted him with cold words.
Hù, uneasy at heart
and with an empty purse, had nowhere to turn.
He still hoped Jī, remembering their past affection,
would not cut him off at once.
Suddenly, two men entered with ropes
and swiftly bound his neck.
Terrified, he did not know what to do.
Pleading, he asked the reason,
and learned Jī had already stolen the counterfeit gold and reported him to the authorities.
Brought before the magistrate,
he could offer no defense
and was beaten nearly to death under the rod.
Thrown into prison,
with no money for expenses,
he suffered greatly under the jailers’ abuse.
He begged food from other prisoners,
barely clinging to life.
Earlier, when Hù set out,
his mother had said to Fú:
"Remember that in twenty days,
I will send you to Luòyáng.
My affairs are many,
and I fear I might forget."
Fú did not understand what she meant,
but felt downcast and sorrowful,
not daring to ask further and withdrew.
After twenty days had passed, he inquired.
She sighed and said:
"Your younger brother's current recklessness and dissipation
are just like your past neglect of studies.
If I had not risked a bad reputation,
how could you have achieved what you have today?
People all say I am harsh,
but the tears that soak my pillow and mat
are unknown to others!"
As she spoke, tears fell.
Fú stood respectfully listening,
not daring to question her closely.
When her weeping ceased,
she then said:
"Your younger brother's wayward heart remains unchanged,
so I gave him counterfeit silver to thwart him.
By now, he has likely fallen into the hands of the law.
The Vice Censor-in-Chief treats you well,
go and plead with him.
You may be able to save him from death,
and awaken his shame and remorse."
Fú set off immediately.
By the time he reached Luòyáng,
his brother had already been arrested for three days.
He went to the prison to see him.
Hù looked haggard, his face ghostly,
and upon seeing his elder brother, wept uncontrollably, unable to lift his head.
Fú also wept.
At that time, Fú was highly favored and esteemed by the Vice Censor-in-Chief,
so his name was known far and wide.
The county magistrate, learning that he was Hù's elder brother,
promptly released him.
When Hù returned home,
still fearing his mother's anger,
he approached on his knees.
His mother looked at him and said:
"Have you achieved your wish now?"
Hù shed tears, not daring to make a sound.
Fú also knelt alongside him,
and only then did their mother scold them to rise.
From then on, Hù deeply repented,
diligently managing all household affairs;
even if he occasionally slackened,
his mother did not scold or question him.
For several months,
she did not speak to him about business matters.
He wished to ask himself but did not dare,
so he conveyed his thoughts through his elder brother.
Upon hearing this, his mother was pleased,
pooled resources through loans and entrusted him with capital.
Within half a year, the profit doubled.
That year,
Fú passed the provincial examination in autumn,
and three years later passed the metropolitan examination;
his younger brother's trade and investments amassed immense wealth.
A fellow townsman visiting Luòyáng
caught sight of the Lady Dowager:
though over forty years old,
she still appeared around thirty,
dressed simply and plainly,
resembling a woman from an ordinary family.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Since the appearance of 'The Black-Hearted Talisman,'
tales like 'The Reed Catkins' have arisen.
Ancient and modern times are alike as birds of a feather,
truly lamentable!
Some, to avoid such slander,
often overcorrect to the opposite extreme,
even to the point of sitting idly by while their children run wild without a word of admonition.
How does this differ from mistreatment?
Only when one disciplines one's own child
are they not considered cruel;
but if applied to a stepchild,
criticism follows immediately.
Now, Xìliǔ was certainly not uniquely harsh toward her stepson;
yet had her own son been worthy,
how could she have manifested such intent to justify herself to the world?
But she neither avoided suspicion
nor shunned slander,
ultimately enabling both sons—one to attain wealth, the other honor—
to stand out prominently in the world.
This, regardless of being within the women's quarters,
should also be considered resolute and outstanding among men!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Cuī Shēng of Línqīng
came from a repeatedly impoverished family.
The courtyard walls were in disrepair.
Every morning upon rising,
he would see a horse lying in the dew-covered grass,
black with white markings;
only its tail hairs were uneven,
as if singed by fire.
Driven away,
it would return again at night,
its origin unknown.
Cuī had a good friend
who held office in Shānxī,
and he wished to go join him,
but suffered from lacking a sturdy mount.
So he caught the horse, fitted it with a bridle, and rode off,
instructing his family:
"If someone comes looking for the horse,
tell them I have gone to Shānxī."
Once on the road,
the horse galloped swiftly,
covering a hundred lǐ in an instant.
At night it ate little fodder or beans,
leading him to think it was ill.
The next day he tightened the reins
to keep it from racing,
but the horse stamped, neighed, and foamed at the mouth,
as vigorous and spirited as the day before.
He let it run free again,
and by noon they had reached Shānxī.
When he rode into the marketplace,
onlookers all exclaimed in admiration.
The Prince of Jìn heard of it
and offered a high price to buy it.
Cuī, fearing the owner might come searching,
did not dare sell it.
After half a year
with no news,
he finally sold the horse for eight hundred taels to the princely residence,
and himself bought a sturdy mule to return home.
Later, the prince had urgent business
and dispatched an officer to ride to Línqīng.
The horse bolted,
and the pursuer followed it to the east neighbor of Cuī's home.
It entered the gate
and disappeared.
The officer demanded the horse from the master of the house.
The master, surnamed Zēng,
truly had not seen it.
Upon entering the room,
he saw a painting of horses by Zhào Mèngfǔ hanging on the wall,
and one horse within it closely resembled in color and markings,
with its tail area seemingly burned by incense.
Only then did they realize the horse
was a painting demon.
The officer, unable to fulfill the prince's command,
sued Zēng.
At that time, Cuī, having gained wealth from the horse's sale,
had amassed over ten thousand taels through trade.
He voluntarily lent Zēng the sum to pay the officer,
who then departed.
Zēng felt deeply grateful to him,
unaware that Cuī was the original seller of the horse.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A servant of a certain censor,
happened to be standing in the marketplace,
when a man dressed in splendid attire
approached and struck up a conversation with him.
Gradually, the man inquired about his master's name and official rank,
and the servant told him everything.
The man introduced himself:
"My surname is Wáng,
and I am an inner attendant in the household of a noble princess."
Their conversation grew increasingly cordial,
and the man then said:
"The path of officialdom is treacherous;
those who rise to prominence all attach themselves to the gates of powerful relatives.
To whom does your esteemed master entrust himself?"
The servant replied:
"To no one."
Wáng said:
"This is what they call sparing small expenses while forgetting great calamities."
The servant asked:
"To whom should one entrust oneself?"
Wáng said:
"The princess treats people with courtesy
and is capable of offering protection.
A certain vice-minister was introduced through my efforts.
If you are willing to spare a thousand taels as a gift,
it should not be difficult to gain an audience with the princess."
The servant was delighted
and asked where he lived.
Wáng pointed to a nearby gate and said:
"Do you mean to say you didn't know we live in the same lane?"
The servant returned and reported this to the censor.
The censor was pleased
and immediately prepared a lavish feast,
sending the servant to invite Wáng.
Wáng came gladly.
During the feast, he spoke in great detail about the princess's temperament and daily trivial matters,
and added:
"If not for the bond of living in the same lane,
even if you offered a hundred taels as a reward,
I would not be willing to serve like an ox or a horse."
The censor held him in even higher esteem.
As they parted,
they made an agreement.
Wáng said:
"You just prepare the gifts;
I will find an opportunity to speak on your behalf,
and you should receive a reply soon."
After several days, he finally arrived,
riding a fine horse, very handsome, and said to the Attendant Censor:
"You must quickly pack and go.
The princess's affairs are extremely busy,
with visitors seeking an audience following one after another,
from morning till night,
not a single moment of leisure is to be had.
Now that we have a moment,
you should hurry there;
if you miss it, there will be no chance to meet again."
The Attendant Censor then took out double the gold and heavy currency,
and followed him away.
After winding along for over ten li,
they finally reached the princess's residence,
dismounting and respectfully waiting.
Wáng first took the gifts inside;
after a long while,
he came out
and announced:
"The princess summons such-and-such Censor."
Immediately, several people relayed the call in succession.
The Attendant Censor entered, bowing humbly,
and saw a beautiful woman seated in the high hall,
her appearance like an immortal,
her attire dazzling;
the attending maidens were all dressed in brocade and embroidery,
lined up in rows.
The Attendant Censor prostrated himself and paid full respects;
a command was relayed to grant him a seat under the eaves,
and a golden bowl was presented with tea.
The princess offered a few warm words,
and the Attendant Censor withdrew respectfully.
From inside, a gift of satin boots and a sable hat was bestowed.
After returning,
he deeply felt indebted to Wáng,
and taking his card, went to pay a visit of thanks,
but the gate was shut with no one there.
He suspected that Wáng was still attending the princess and had not returned.
Three times over three days he went,
but never saw him again.
He sent someone to inquire at the noble princess's gate,
only to find the tall gate bolted shut.
Asking the local residents,
they all said,
"There has never been any noble princess here.
Previously, a few people rented the house to live in,
but they left three days ago."
The messenger returned with this report,
and master and servant could only despair.
A certain Deputy General,
carrying funds to the capital,
hoped to secure an official seal,
but painfully lacked the means.
One day,
a man in furs and on horseback came to visit him,
claiming:
"My brother-in-law is a close attendant of the Son of Heaven."
After tea,
he requested a private word, saying:
"Currently, there is a vacancy for a general at a certain place.
If you are not sparing with heavy gold,
I can ask my brother-in-law to speak highly of you before the Sacred Lord;
this appointment can be secured,
and no one, however powerful, can snatch it away."
The man doubted his words were false.
The other said:
"There is no need to hesitate over this.
I merely wish to take a small commission from my brother-in-law;
from you, General, I expect not a single coin.
We agree on a certain sum,
and sign a contract as proof.
Only after you are summoned for an audience
will I ask for the actual payment;
if it proves ineffective,
your gold remains with you—
who could snatch it from your bosom?"
The man then rejoiced
and agreed.
The next day,
he came again to lead the man away,
to see his brother-in-law,
said to be surnamed Tián.
His splendor was like that of a marquis's household.
The man paid his respects,
but the other was extremely haughty and barely returned courtesy.
The fur-clad man held the contract and said to him:
"I have just discussed with my brother-in-law;
roughly, ten thousand gold is indispensable.
Please sign at the end immediately."
The man complied.
Tián said:
"Human hearts are unfathomable;
after the matter, I fear there may be a reversal."
The fur-clad man laughed and said:
"Brother, you worry too much.
If we can give it,
how could we not be able to take it away?
Moreover, among the generals and ministers at court,
there are those who wish to make friends with us but cannot.
The General's future is still long and bright;
he should not be so heartless as to do that."
The man also swore forcefully and left.
The fur-clad man saw him off,
saying:
"In three days, I will bring you a reply."
After two days had passed,
just as the sun was setting in the west,
several men roared and rushed in,
shouting:
"The Sacred Emperor is seated and waiting!"
The man was greatly startled
and hurried into court.
He saw the Son of Heaven seated in the hall,
with fierce guards standing densely.
The man finished his bowing and ceremonial movements.
The Emperor commanded that he be given a seat,
consoled him with earnest concern,
and looking left and right, said:
"I have heard that such-and-such is exceptionally martial and fierce;
now seeing him,
he truly has the talent of a general!"
Then he said:
"A certain place is a strategic location;
now I entrust it to you.
Do not fail my intention;
a marquis's title will come in due time."
The man bowed in gratitude and left.
Immediately, the fur-clad man from before followed him to the guest lodge,
and according to the contract, received payment and left.
Thereupon, the man rested easy on his pillow, awaiting the official seal,
daily boasting of his glory to relatives and friends.
After several days,
he went to inquire,
only to find that the previous vacancy had already been filled by someone else.
Furious,
he argued indignantly in the hall of the Ministry of War,
saying:
"I received the Emperor's selection;
how can it be given to another?"
The Minister found it strange.
When he recounted the favor and encounter he received,
it was half like a dream.
The Minister grew angry
and had him arrested and sent to the Court of Judicial Review.
Only then did he confess the name of the man who had introduced him for the audience,
but there was no such person in the court.
He also lost ten thousand gold,
and only then was he dismissed from his post and left.
How strange!
Although military officers may be foolish,
could even the court gates be faked?
I suspect there was some illusionary art involved;
this is what is called
"the great thief does not carry spear or bow."
Lǐ Shēng from Jiāxiáng,
was skilled at the qin.
Once, he happened to go to the eastern suburbs,
and saw workers digging up earth and finding an ancient qin.
He thus obtained it for a cheap price.
Wiping it, it had an unusual glow;
stringing it and playing,
the sound was exceptionally clear and intense.
Overjoyed,
as if he had obtained a precious jade disc,
he stored it in a brocade bag
and hid it in a secret room,
not showing it even to his closest relatives.
The Assistant Magistrate of the county, surnamed Chéng,
newly arrived at his post,
sent a card to visit Lǐ.
Lǐ originally had few social interactions,
but because the other had initiated the visit,
he returned the courtesy.
After several days,
Chéng again invited him to drink,
and only after persistent urging did he go.
Chéng was a man of unparalleled refinement and elegance,
his conversation free and easy,
and Lǐ was pleased with him.
Another day later,
Lǐ sent an invitation in return,
and their laughter and joy grew even more harmonious.
From then on, whether on moonlit evenings or flowery mornings,
they never failed to be together.
After over a year,
he happened to be in the Assistant Magistrate's office
and saw a qin wrapped in an embroidered bag placed on the table.
Lǐ immediately unfolded it to admire.
Chéng asked:
"Are you also versed in this?"
Lǐ said:
"It has been my lifelong favorite."
Chéng exclaimed in surprise:
"We have been friends for more than a day;
why have I never heard your exceptional skill?"
He stirred the stove, lit some agarwood,
and asked for a small performance.
Lǐ Jìngrú taught him.
Chéng said:
"A great master!
I wish to offer my humble skill,
do not laugh at the lesser shaman."
Then he played
"The Song of Riding the Wind",
its sound was clear and cold,
with a transcendent, otherworldly intent.
Lǐ was even more captivated,
and wished to serve him as a teacher.
From then on, the two became friends through the qin,
their affection growing deeper.
After more than a year,
Chéng had taught him all his skills.
However, whenever Chéng visited Lǐ,
Lǐ would provide an ordinary qin for him to play,
unwilling to reveal his own collection.
One evening,
slightly drunk.
Chéng said:
"I have newly practiced a piece,
would you also like to hear it?"
He played
"The Xiang Consorts",
melancholy and plaintive as if weeping.
Lǐ praised it profusely.
Chéng said:
"What I regret is not having a fine qin;
if I had a fine qin,
the melody would be even more superb."
Lǐ said happily:
"I have stored away a qin,
quite different from ordinary ones.
Now that I have met a Zhōng Zǐqī,
how dare I keep it secret forever?"
Then he opened a chest, carried out a bag, and took it out.
Chéng dusted it off with his sleeve,
leaned on the table and played again,
the firm and gentle notes following the rhythm,
the skill marvelous and divine.
Lǐ could not stop tapping in admiration.
Chéng said:
"My meager, clumsy skill
does not do justice to this fine qin.
If my wife could play it,
there might be a note or two worth hearing."
Lǐ said in surprise:
"Does your wife also excel in this?"
Chéng said with a smile:
"This piece I just played was actually taught to me by my wife."
Lǐ said:
"What a pity she is in the inner chambers,
so I cannot hear her play."
Chéng said:
"We are like family,
so originally we should not be limited by formalities.
Tomorrow,
please bring your qin over,
and I will have her play for you from behind the curtain."
Lǐ was pleased.
The next day,
he carried his qin and went.
Chéng immediately prepared a feast and they drank merrily.
After a while,
he took the qin inside,
and soon came out and sat down.
Suddenly, behind the curtain, there seemed to be a glimpse of beautiful attire,
and shortly after,
fragrance flowed outside the door.
A little later,
the faint sound of strings began,
listening to it,
he did not know what piece it was;
but it felt heart-stirring and enchanting,
making one's soul fly away.
When the piece ended, he peeked behind the curtain,
and saw more than twenty peerless beauties.
Chéng urged him to drink from a large cup,
and inside, they changed the tune to
"The Rhapsody of Carefree Feelings",
Lǐ's mind and spirit grew even more confused.
He drank until he was heavily drunk,
rose from his seat to take leave,
and asked for his qin back.
Chéng said:
"After drinking, I fear you might stumble and fall.
Come again tomorrow,
and I will have the ladies inside play their best for you."
Lǐ returned home.
The next day, he went to visit,
but the official residence was quiet,
with only an old servant answering the door.
When asked,
he said:
"At the fifth watch, he took his family and left,
I don't know what he is doing,
he said he would return in about three days."
Lǐ went to wait as scheduled,
by dusk,
there was still no news.
The clerks and servants all grew suspicious,
and reported to the magistrate,
who broke the lock and peered into the room;
the room was completely empty,
only the table and bed remained.
They reported to the higher authorities,
but no one could guess the reason.
Lǐ, having lost his qin,
could neither eat nor sleep,
and traveled thousands of miles to visit Chéng's hometown.
Chéng was originally from Chǔ,
three years ago,
he donated funds to receive an official post in Jiāxiáng.
When Lǐ inquired about his name and surname,
and asked about his hometown,
no such person existed in Chǔ.
Some said:
"There was a Dàoshi Chéng,
who was skilled at playing the qin;
it was also said he had the art of turning things into gold.
Three years ago,
he suddenly left and was never seen again."
Lǐ suspected it was him.
He further examined his age and appearance,
and they matched without error.
Then he realized that the Dàoshi's becoming an official
was all for the sake of the qin.
They had been friends for over a year,
yet he never spoke of music;
gradually, he brought out the qin,
gradually, he offered his skill,
and gradually, he bewitched him with beautiful women;
slowly soaking for three years.
He obtained the qin and left.
The Dàoshi's obsession
was even greater than Mr. Lǐ's.
In the world, there are many kinds of deceitful schemes,
but a Dàoshi like him
is an elegant one among deceivers.
According to the "Liáozhāi Zhìyì" Zhùxuězhāi manuscript
When Jìnshì Wáng Dòushēng of Chángshān served as a magistrate,
he would often hold court,
and according to the severity of the crime,
order the offenders to pay butterflies as redemption;
in the hall, hundreds would be released together,
like wind-blown scattered brocade,
and Wáng would slap the table and laugh heartily.
One night,
he dreamed of a woman,
dressed in splendid attire,
calmly entering,
saying:
"Suffering under your cruel rule,
many of my sisters have perished.
I shall make you first suffer a small punishment of romantic disgrace."
Having said this,
she transformed into a butterfly,
circled around, and flew away.
The next day,
while drinking alone in his office,
he suddenly received a report that the Zhízhǐshǐ had arrived,
and hurried out in panic,
having playfully placed a plain flower in his cap in the inner chambers,
and forgotten to remove it.
When the Zhízhǐshǐ saw it,
he considered it disrespectful,
and Wáng was severely reprimanded before returning.
From then on, the butterfly penalty order was abolished.
According to the "Liáozhāi Zhìyì" Zhùxuězhāi manuscript
Fújiàn's Zǒngbīng Yáng Fǔ,
had a favorite boy,
whose belly trembled.
When ten months were full,
he dreamed of a deity cutting open his sides and taking them out.
Upon waking,
two boys were crying on his left and right.
Getting up to look at his sides,
the cut marks were clearly visible.
The boys were named Tiān Shě and Dì Shě.
According to the "Liáozhāi Zhìyì" Zhùxuězhāi manuscript
Zhōng Qìngyú was a renowned scholar from Liáodōng.
He went to Jǐnán to take the provincial examination.
Hearing that there was a Taoist priest in the prince's residence who could foretell a person's fortune,
he was deeply intrigued.
After the second session of the exam,
he went to Bàotū Spring,
where he happened to meet the priest.
The priest was over sixty years old,
with a beard that reached past his chest—a venerable Taoist indeed.
A crowd had gathered to inquire about their misfortunes, forming a wall around him,
and the priest gave each of them cryptic advice.
Spotting Zhōng among the crowd,
the priest happily shook his hand and said,
"Your integrity and virtue are truly admirable!"
He then led Zhōng up to a pavilion,
dismissed the others, and spoke privately.
He asked,
"Do you wish to know your future?"
Zhōng replied,
"Yes."
The priest said,
"Your fortune and fate are exceedingly thin,
but you may hope to pass this provincial examination.
However, after your glorious return,
I fear you will no longer see your mother."
Zhōng was extremely filial,
and upon hearing this, he wept
and considered abandoning the exam to return home immediately.
The priest said,
"If you miss this opportunity,
you will not even attain a place on the list."
Zhōng said,
"If I cannot see my mother before she dies,
I cannot continue to live as a human being.
What use is becoming a high minister or prime minister?"
The priest said,
"I have a karmic connection with you from a past life,
so today I must do my utmost to help."
He then gave Zhōng a pill and said,
"Have someone deliver this day and night.
If she takes it, it can prolong her life by seven days.
Finish the exam and then go;
mother and son will still be able to meet."
Zhōng stored the pill,
hurried out,
and was utterly distraught.
Thinking that his mother's final days were numbered,
he believed that returning one day earlier would allow him one more day to care for her.
He hired a donkey with his servant
and immediately set off eastward.
After traveling about a li,
the donkey suddenly turned and bolted back.
Zhōng dismounted, but it remained unruly;
when he tried to control it, it bucked.
Zhōng was at a loss,
sweating profusely.
His servant urged him to stop,
but Zhōng would not listen.
He hired another donkey,
but the same thing happened.
The sun was already setting behind the mountains,
and he had no idea what to do.
His servant again advised,
"The exam will be finished tomorrow.
Why fight over this single morning and evening?
Please let me go ahead first,
and this plan will also work well."
With no other choice,
Zhōng agreed.
The next day,
he hastily completed the exam,
set off immediately without even pausing for a drink,
and raced home like a shooting star.
His mother was critically ill,
but after taking the elixir,
she gradually recovered.
When Zhōng went to see her,
he wept by her bedside.
His mother shook her head to stop him,
held his hand happily, and said,
"I just dreamed of the underworld,
where I saw the king looking kindly.
He said that after reviewing my life,
I had committed no great sins;
now, considering your pure filial piety,
he has granted me an additional twelve years of life."
Zhōng was also overjoyed.
After several days,
his mother was indeed as healthy as before.
Not long after,
Zhōng received news of his success in the exam
and bid farewell to his mother to return to Jǐnán.
He bribed a eunuch
to convey his regards to the Taoist priest.
The priest happily came out,
and Zhōng bowed respectfully.
The priest said,
"You have achieved high honors,
and your mother's lifespan has been extended.
These are all due to your great virtue—
what power does a Taoist have in this?"
Zhōng was further amazed by his foreknowledge
and thus bowed to inquire about his entire life.
The priest said,
"You will not attain great nobility,
but living to a ripe old age will be enough.
In your previous life, you and I were fellow monks.
You threw a stone at a dog
and accidentally killed a frog,
which has now been reborn as a donkey.
According to predetermined fate,
you should have met a violent death;
but your filial virtue moved the gods,
and there is already a star of rescue in your destiny,
so you will certainly be safe.
However, your wife in her previous life was unchaste,
and her fate dictates that she should be widowed young.
Now, because your virtue has extended your lifespan,
she is not your destined match,
and I fear that after a year, the jade tower will collapse."
Zhōng was sorrowful for a long time
and asked where his next wife would be.
The priest said,
"In Zhōngzhōu,
now fourteen years old."
As they parted, he advised,
"If you encounter danger,
you should flee to the southeast."
Over a year later,
Zhōng's wife indeed fell ill and died.
Zhōng's maternal uncle served as a magistrate in Xījiāng,
and his mother sent him to visit him,
passing through Zhōngzhōu on the way
to fulfill the prophecy about his next wife.
He happened to pass by a village
where a theatrical performance was being held by the river,
with a bustling crowd of men and women.
Just as he was about to adjust his reins and hurry past,
a runaway male donkey
followed alongside,
causing his mule to kick out.
Zhōng turned around
and struck the donkey's ear with his whip;
the donkey panicked
and bolted.
At that time, a prince's son, about six or seven years old,
was being held by his wet nurse while sitting on the embankment;
the donkey charged past,
and the attendants were caught off guard,
knocking the child into the river.
The crowd erupted in uproar
and wanted to seize Zhōng.
Zhōng spurred his mule into a gallop
and suddenly remembered the Taoist's words,
heading southeast with all his might.
After about thirty li,
he entered a mountain village
where an old man was at the gate.
Zhōng dismounted and bowed to him.
The old man invited him in,
introduced himself as "surname Fāng,"
and inquired about his origins.
Zhōng knelt and kowtowed on the ground,
telling him everything in detail.
The old man said,
"No matter.
Please stay here for now,
and I will send the pursuers away."
By evening, news arrived
that it was the prince's son,
and the old man was greatly alarmed, saying,
"For others, I might have been able to help,
but this is truly beyond my power!"
Zhōng pleaded desperately.
The old man pondered and said,
"It cannot be done.
Please stay overnight,
and we will see how urgent the situation is;
perhaps we can think of another plan."
Zhōng was filled with anxiety and fear,
unable to sleep all night.
The next day, he learned through inquiries
that warrants had already been issued for investigation,
and those harboring fugitives would be executed in the marketplace.
The old man looked troubled
and went inside without a word.
Zhōng grew suspicious and fearful,
finding no peace within himself.
In the middle of the night, the old man came
and, upon sitting down, asked:
"How old is your wife?"
The student replied that he was a widower.
The old man said happily:
"My plan will succeed."
When asked about it,
he replied:
"My brother-in-law has taken to the Way,
and has hung his staff at Nánshān;
my sister has also passed away.
She left behind an orphaned daughter,
raised by servants,
who is also quite intelligent.
How about having her serve you with broom and dustpan?"
The student was delighted that this matched the Daoist's words,
and moreover hoped that being closely related by marriage,
he could obtain their careful planning,
and said:
"I would indeed be fortunate.
But as a fugitive from afar,
I deeply fear bringing trouble upon you, sir."
The old man said:
"This is for your sake.
My brother-in-law's Daoist arts are quite divine,
but he has long ceased to involve himself in human affairs.
After the wedding,
you can discuss it with your niece yourself,
and she will surely have a plan."
The student was overjoyed,
and became a live-in son-in-law.
The girl was sixteen years old,
peerlessly beautiful.
The student often sighed in her presence.
The girl said:
"Even if I am plain,
why must you so quickly show dislike?"
The student apologized:
"You, lady, are an immortal;
to be paired with you is my fortune.
But with this calamity,
I fear it may lead to separation."
He then told her the truth.
The girl said resentfully:
"My uncle is inhuman!
This is a sky-covering disaster,
impossible to plan for,
yet he did not speak clearly,
but plunged me into this pit!"
The student knelt long and said:
"It was I who begged your uncle with my life at stake;
your uncle was compassionate but his arts were exhausted,
knowing that you could revive the dead and put flesh on bones.
I am truly unworthy to be called a good match,
but my family is fortunately not dishonorable.
If I can live again,
there will be days of offering you incense and flowers."
The girl sighed:
"Since things have come to this,
what more can be said?
But my father has shaved his head at the monastery,
and his love for his children has ended.
There is no other way;
let us go together to beg him,
though I fear we will suffer no small humiliation."
So they stayed awake all night,
making thick knee pads from felt and cotton,
each secretly wearing them under their clothes;
then they called for a sedan chair,
and entered Nánshān for over ten lǐ.
The mountain path was twisting and extremely perilous,
and could no longer be ridden on.
They got out of the sedan,
the girl taking each step with great difficulty;
the student held her arm and supported her,
struggling exhaustedly before they finally ascended.
Not far ahead,
they saw the monastery gate,
and sat together to rest a while.
The girl panted and sweated profusely,
her powder and makeup mingling as they dripped down.
Seeing this,
the student could not bear his feelings,
and said:
"For my sake,
I have made you suffer this hardship!"
The girl said sorrowfully:
"I fear this is not yet the hardship!"
When their fatigue eased slightly,
they went together into the temple,
paid respects to the Buddha, and proceeded.
Winding their way into the meditation hall,
they saw an old monk sitting cross-legged,
his eyes as if closed,
a young attendant standing by with a whisk.
In the abbot's room,
everything was swept clean;
but before the seat were spread sand and gravel,
dense as stars.
The girl did not dare choose,
but entered and knelt upon them;
the student also followed and knelt behind her.
The monk opened his eyes for a glance,
then closed them again.
The girl paid her respects and said:
"It has been long since I came to inquire after your well-being;
now your daughter is married,
so I have come with my husband."
After a long while,
the monk opened his eyes and said:
"You girl are a great burden!"
Then he said no more.
Husband and wife knelt for a long time,
their strength exhausted,
the sand and stones seeming to press into their bones,
the pain unbearable.
After another while,
he finally spoke:
"Have you brought the mule?"
The girl replied:
"No."
He said:
"Husband and wife, leave now,
and quickly bring it here."
The two bowed and rose,
leaving in disarray.
After returning home,
they followed the order,
not understanding its meaning,
but obeyed and waited.
After several days,
word spread that the criminal had been caught,
and executed.
Husband and wife congratulated each other.
Not long after,
a young attendant was sent from the mountain,
delivering a broken staff to the student, saying:
"The one who died in your place,
was this gentleman."
He then instructed them to bury it and offer sacrifices,
to resolve the grievance of the bamboo and wood.
The student looked at it,
and at the broken place were traces of blood.
So he prayed and buried it.
Husband and wife did not dare stay long,
and returned to Liáoyáng by starlight.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In Tài'ān, there was a man named Niè Péngyún
who, along with his wife,
enjoyed a harmonious and loving relationship.
His wife fell ill and passed away.
Niè was consumed by grief and longing,
feeling lost and despondent.
One night, as he sat alone,
his wife suddenly pushed open the door and entered.
Niè asked in surprise:
"Where have you come from?"
She smiled and said:
"I am already a ghost.
Touched by your mourning and remembrance,
I pleaded with the ruler of the underworld,
and was granted a brief reunion with you in the spirit world."
Niè was overjoyed,
took her to bed,
and everything was just as it had been in life.
From then on, they met like stars and the moon,
continuing for over a year.
Niè no longer spoke of remarrying.
His uncles and brothers, fearing the family line would be broken,
privately discussed with the clan
and urged Niè to take a new wife;
Niè agreed
and became engaged to a girl from a good family.
However, fearing his ghost wife would be unhappy,
he kept it secret.
Before long,
the wedding day drew near.
The ghost learned of the situation
and reproached him, saying:
"I risked punishment from the underworld
because I believed in your loyalty;
yet now you break your vow before it is fulfilled—
is this how a devoted lover behaves?"
Niè explained the intentions of his clan.
The ghost remained displeased,
bid farewell, and left.
Though Niè pitied her,
he also felt his plan had succeeded.
On the wedding night,
as the couple lay in bed,
the ghost suddenly appeared,
rushed to the bed and struck the new bride,
shouting loudly:
"How dare you take my place in bed!"
The new bride rose,
and tried to fend her off.
Niè, terrified, crouched naked,
not daring to take either side.
Soon after,
at the crow of the rooster,
the ghost departed.
The new bride suspected Niè's former wife was not actually dead,
thinking he had deceived her,
and tried to hang herself.
Niè recounted the whole story in detail,
and only then did the new bride realize it was a ghost.
The ghost returned day and night.
The new bride, afraid, avoided her.
The ghost no longer slept with Niè,
but only pinched his flesh with her fingers;
then she would glare angrily at him by candlelight,
silent and wordless.
This went on for several nights.
Niè was troubled by it.
In a nearby village, there was a skilled practitioner of magic,
who carved peach wood into stakes
and drove them into the four corners of the grave,
after which the haunting ceased.
According to the Zhūxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
When Huáng Jìngnán Dégōng was still obscure,
he traveled to the capital with two Jǔrén.
On the way, they encountered bandits.
The Jǔrén were terrified,
knelt down, and offered their money.
Huáng was furious;
though he had no weapon,
he grabbed the legs of a mule with both hands,
lifted it, and hurled it at the bandits.
The bandits were caught off guard,
their horses fell, and they tumbled to the ground.
Huáng broke their arms with his fists,
searched them, and returned.
The Jǔrén admired his bravery,
provided funds, and urged him to join the army.
Later, he repeatedly achieved extraordinary military feats,
and eventually wore the robes of a high official.
According to the Zhūxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain Grand Secretary,
a former minister of the Ming dynasty,
had surrendered to the rebel forces,
and was criticized by public opinion.
In his old age, he retired to the countryside.
When his ancestral hall was completed,
several people stayed overnight inside.
At dawn,
they saw a plaque hanging in the hall that read:
"Elder Statesman of Three Reigns."
And a couplet that said:
"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven,
Filial piety, brotherly love, loyalty, trust, propriety, righteousness, integrity."
No one knew when it had been hung.
They found it strange,
but could not understand its meaning.
Someone speculated:
"The first line implies 'forgetting the eighth' (wáng bā, homophone for 'turtle,' a derogatory term),
and the second line implies 'shameless.'"
When Viceroy Hóng led the southern expedition,
he returned victorious.
Arriving in Jīnlíng,
he held a sacrificial ceremony for the fallen soldiers.
An old disciple came to pay his respects;
after bowing,
he presented a literary composition.
Hóng had long grown weary of literary matters,
and declined, citing dim eyesight.
The man said:
"I only ask that you sit and listen,
and allow me to recite it for you to hear."
Then he drew a document from his sleeve,
and read aloud with a clear voice—
it was the sacrificial text written by the late Ming Emperor Sīzōng for Hóng, who had died in Liáoyáng.
After finishing the reading,
he wept loudly and left.
According to the Zhūxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*, with an addendum based on the Shāndōng Provincial Museum manuscript
There was a man named Zhāng,
a poor commoner from Yí.
On the road, he met a Dàoshi,
skilled in physiognomy,
who examined him and said:
"You will become wealthy through a skill or trade."
Zhāng asked:
"What should I pursue?"
The Dàoshi looked at him again,
and said:
"Medicine would be suitable."
Zhāng said:
"I only recognize a few characters—
'zhī' and 'wú'—
how could I manage that?"
The Dàoshi laughed and said:
"How pedantic!
Does a famous doctor need to be highly literate?
Just practice it."
After returning home,
being poor and without a trade,
he collected folk remedies,
cleared a space in the marketplace to set up a stall,
displayed fish teeth and honeycombs,
and made a meager living through his words,
but no one found him remarkable.
It happened that the prefect of Qīngzhōu fell ill with a cough,
and issued an order to his subordinates to recruit doctors.
Yí was a remote mountainous area,
with few skilled physicians;
the magistrate, afraid he would be unable to fulfill his duty,
ordered the villages to report candidates themselves.
So they all recommended Zhāng.
The magistrate immediately summoned him.
Zhāng himself was suffering from phlegm and asthma,
unable to cure his own ailment,
and was terrified upon hearing the order,
firmly refusing.
The magistrate would not listen,
and finally had him sent by post.
On the way through deep mountains,
he grew extremely thirsty,
and his cough worsened.
He searched for water,
but in the mountains, water was as precious as jade nectar;
he begged everywhere,
but no one gave him any.
He saw a woman washing wild vegetables,
with more vegetables than water,
leaving the basin murky and thick like saliva.
Zhāng, parched and desperate,
begged for the leftover dregs to drink.
After a short while,
his thirst was quenched,
and his cough suddenly stopped.
He thought to himself: This must be a good remedy.
By the time he arrived at the prefecture,
the physicians from various towns
had already administered treatments,
but none had brought recovery or relief.
Zhāng entered,
found a secluded place,
falsely wrote out a list of medicines,
and circulated it inside and out;
he then sent someone to gather various wild plants from among the common folk,
processed them according to method,
and offered the juice to the prefect.
After one dose,
the illness was truly cured.
The prefect was greatly pleased,
bestowing generous rewards,
and honored him with a golden plaque.
From this, his fame grew loud,
his door constantly bustling like a marketplace,
and every case he handled was effective without exception.
There was a person suffering from shānghán,
who described his symptoms and sought a prescription.
Zhāng happened to be drunk,
and mistakenly gave him a remedy for malaria.
Upon sobering up and realizing it,
he dared not tell anyone.
Three days later,
someone arrived at his door with lavish gifts to thank him;
upon inquiry,
it turned out to be the shānghán patient,
who had recovered after severe vomiting and diarrhea.
There were many such instances.
Zhāng thus became known as a wealthy man without official rank,
and increasingly valued himself based on his reputation,
so that he would not attend to summons unless heavily paid and provided with a comfortable carriage.
Old Man Hán from Yìdū,
was a renowned physician.
Before he became famous,
he sold medicine throughout the land.
One evening, with nowhere to stay,
he sought lodging at a house,
where the son was dying of shānghán,
and they requested treatment.
Hán thought that if he did not treat him, he had nowhere else to go,
but he truly had no method to cure him.
Pacing back and forth,
he rubbed his body with his hands,
and the sweat and grime formed into clumps,
which he rolled into pellets.
Suddenly, he thought of giving these to deceive them,
reasoning it should cause no harm.
If by dawn the patient was not cured,
he would at least have gained a night's rest and a full meal.
So he gave them.
In the middle of the night,
the host pounded on his door urgently.
Thinking the son had died,
and fearing he would be assaulted and humiliated,
he startled awake,
climbed over the wall, and fled swiftly.
The host chased him for several miles,
and with nowhere to hide,
Hán finally stopped.
Only then did he learn that the patient had sweated profusely and recovered.
They brought him back,
hosting him with a lavish feast;
upon his departure,
they gave him generous gifts.
Based on the Shāndōng Provincial Museum edition of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A certain villager,
once sitting under a tree,
caught a louse,
wrapped it in a scrap of paper,
stuffed it into a tree hollow, and left.
Two or three years later,
passing by the same spot,
he suddenly remembered it,
and saw the paper wrapping still intact in the hollow.
Opening it to examine,
he found the louse thin as bran.
Placing it in his palm, he observed it carefully.
After a short while,
his palm became intensely itchy,
and the louse's abdomen gradually swelled.
He set it aside and returned home.
The itchy spot developed a hard lump,
swollen and painful for several days,
and he died.
Based on the Shāndōng Provincial Museum edition of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Old Man Bái,
a person from Zhílì.
His eldest son, Jiǎ,
had taken office in the southern regions,
and for two years there had been no news.
It happened that a distant relative named Dīng paid a visit,
and the old man entertained him.
Dīng was known to frequently traverse the realms of the living and the dead.
During their conversation,
the old man repeatedly asked about underworld affairs,
and Dīng's replies touched on the fantastical;
the old man did not fully believe him,
merely smiling faintly.
Several days after parting,
while the old man was lying down,
he saw Dīng arrive again,
inviting him to journey together.
He followed him away,
entering a city gate.
After a while,
Dīng pointed to a gate and said:
"Your nephew resides here."
At the time, the old man had a sister's son serving as a magistrate in Jìn,
and he exclaimed in surprise:
"How could he be here?"
Dīng said:
"If you don't believe it,
enter and you will know."
The old man entered,
and indeed saw his nephew,
seated in the hall wearing a cicada-wing hat and a badge embroidered with a mythical beast,
with rows of ceremonial banners,
and no one to announce him.
Dīng pulled him out,
saying:
"Your son's official residence
is not far from here.
Would you like to see him as well?"
The old man agreed.
After a short while,
they arrived at a mansion,
and Dīng said:
"Go in."
Peering through the gate,
he saw a huge wolf blocking the path,
and, terrified,
he dared not enter.
Dīng said again:
"Go in."
Entering another gate,
he saw wolves in the hall, below the hall, sitting and lying,
everywhere.
Looking further into the courtyard,
he saw white bones piled like mountains,
and grew even more afraid.
Dīng then shielded the old man with his body and advanced.
His son, Jiǎ,
just then emerged from inside,
and seeing his father and Dīng, was very pleased.
After sitting briefly,
he called attendants to prepare food.
Suddenly, a huge wolf
entered carrying a dead person in its mouth.
The old man trembled and stood up,
saying:
"What is this for?"
Jiǎ said:
"Merely to supply the kitchen."
The old man urgently stopped him.
His heart pounding with unease,
he wished to take his leave and depart,
but a pack of wolves blocked the way.
As he hesitated, unsure whether to advance or retreat,
he suddenly saw the wolves scattering with howls of avoidance,
some scrambling under beds,
others hiding beneath tables.
Bewildered, he did not understand the reason.
Soon, two fierce warriors in golden armor entered with glaring eyes,
and produced black ropes to bind Jiǎ.
Jiǎ fell to the ground and transformed into a tiger,
with jagged, fierce teeth.
One man drew a sharp sword,
intending to behead him.
The other said:
"Not yet,
not yet.
This is a matter for the fourth month of next year.
Better to just knock out his teeth for now."
So he took out a huge hammer and smashed the teeth,
which fell scattered to the ground.
The tiger roared mightily,
its voice shaking the mountains.
The old man was terrified,
when suddenly he awoke,
and realized it was a dream.
Finding it strange,
he sent someone to summon Dīng,
but Dīng declined and did not come.
The old man recorded his dream in detail,
and sent his second son to visit Jiǎ,
with a letter full of earnest warnings.
Upon arrival,
he saw that his elder brother’s front teeth were all missing: shocked, he asked about it,
and was told they had been broken when he fell from a horse while drunk.
Checking the date,
it turned out to be the very day their father had the dream.
He was even more astonished.
He then presented their father’s letter.
Jiǎ read it and turned pale,
but said:
"This is merely a coincidence with an illusory dream,
nothing to be surprised about."
At the time, he was bribing those in power,
hoping to be recommended for promotion,
so he paid no heed to the ominous dream.
After staying a few days,
the younger brother saw that corrupt clerks filled the hall,
and those delivering bribes and seeking favors came and went incessantly even at midnight;
he tearfully urged his brother to stop.
Jiǎ said:
"You live secluded in a thatched cottage,
so you don’t understand the key to officialdom.
The power of promotion and demotion
lies with the superiors, not with the common people.
If the superiors are pleased,
then you are a good official;
loving the people—
what method can make the superiors happy?"
Knowing he could not dissuade him, the younger brother returned home,
and reported to their father.
Hearing this, the old man wept bitterly.
There was nothing he could do,
so he only donated family wealth to aid the poor,
praying daily to the gods,
hoping that retribution would fall solely on his wayward son,
and not involve his wife and children.
The following year,
news came that Jiǎ had been recommended and appointed to the Ministry of Personnel,
and congratulatory visitors filled the gates;
the old man only sighed and sobbed,
lying on his pillow, feigning illness and refusing to go out.
Not long after,
he heard that his son had encountered bandits on his way home,
and both master and servants had been killed.
The old man then rose and
said to others:
"The wrath of the gods and spirits
stops at his own person,
their protection of our family cannot be said to be insufficient."
He then burned incense to give thanks.
Those who came to console the old man
all believed it to be a false rumor from the road,
but the old man firmly believed it without doubt,
and set a date to prepare a grave.
Yet Jiǎ had not actually died.
Earlier,
in the fourth month,
Jiǎ had been relieved of his post,
and just after leaving the district,
he encountered bandits,
and Jiǎ offered them all his belongings.
The bandits said:
"We have come
to vent the grievances and anger of the entire district’s people,
how could it be solely for this!"
They then cut off his head.
They also asked the servants:
"Is there one named Sī Dàchéng here,
who is he?"
Sī was originally Jiǎ’s confidant,
one who aided a tyrant in his evil deeds.
The servants all pointed him out.
The bandits killed him as well.
There were also four corrupt clerks,
Jiǎ’s henchmen in extortion,
whom he was planning to take to the capital—
all were searched out and executed,
and only then did the bandits divide the loot and put it in their bags,
galloping away.
Jiǎ’s soul lay by the roadside,
and saw an official passing by,
who asked:
"Who is the one killed?"
The attendants ahead replied:
"It is Magistrate Bái of such-and-such county."
The official said:
"This is Bái Mǒu’s son,
it is not fitting for an old man to later see such a ghastly sight,
his head should be reattached."
Immediately, someone picked up the head and placed it on the torso, saying:
"An evil man should not be set straight,
let the shoulder support the chin instead."
They then left.
After a while, he revived.
His wife and children went to collect his body,
and finding him still breathing slightly,
carried him away;
gradually they poured broth into him,
and he was able to swallow.
But they could only lodge at an inn,
too poor to return home.
After about half a year,
the old man finally received definite news,
and sent his second son to bring him back.
Although Jiǎ had come back to life,
he could now see his own back with his eyes,
and was no longer counted among human beings.
The old man’s sister’s son had a reputation for good governance,
and that year was selected to serve as a censor,
fully matching what was seen in the dream.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"I sigh in secret that throughout the world, officials are tigers and clerks are wolves,
and such cases are everywhere.
Even if the official is not a tiger,
the clerks will still be wolves,
let alone those fiercer than tigers!
The trouble is that people worry they cannot see behind themselves;
reviving him and making him see his own back—
the teaching of the gods and spirits is subtle indeed!"
Lǐ Kuāngjiǔ, a Jìnshì from Zōupíng,
served as an official with considerable integrity and wisdom.
Once, a wealthy man was falsely accused,
and a clerk threatened him, saying:
"The official demands two hundred taels from you,
you should prepare it quickly;
otherwise,
you’re ruined!"
The wealthy man was afraid,
and promised to prepare half.
The clerk shook his hand, indicating it wouldn’t do.
The wealthy man pleaded bitterly,
and the clerk said:
"I will do my utmost,
but I’m afraid he won’t agree.
Wait until the hearing,
you’ll see with your own eyes how I plead for you,
whether he agrees or not,
you’ll also understand that my intentions are without ulterior motive."
After a while,
the magistrate heard the case.
The clerk knew that Lǐ had quit smoking,
so he approached and asked:
"Would you like to smoke?"
Lǐ shook his head.
The clerk immediately went down and said:
"I just mentioned the amount,
and the official shook his head in refusal,
did you see that?"
The wealthy man believed him,
became frightened,
and agreed to the full amount.
The clerk knew that Lǐ loved tea,
so he approached and asked:
"Would you like some tea?"
Lǐ nodded.
The clerk pretended to go brew tea,
went down and said:
"It’s settled!
He just nodded in approval,
did you see that?"
Later, when the case was concluded,
the wealthy man was indeed acquitted,
and the clerk not only collected the bribe,
but also demanded a reward.
Alas!
The official considers himself honest,
yet those cursing his greed fill the roads;
this is another case of unleashing wolves without even realizing it.
In this world, there are even more instances like this,
which can serve as a mirror for those in office.
Also, the county magistrate, Lord Yáng,
had a stubborn and unyielding nature.
Those who provoked his anger were sure to die.
He particularly despised yamen runners and constables,
showing no leniency even for minor offenses.
Whenever he sat sternly in the courtroom,
the clerks and underlings
dared not even cough.
If these subordinates had something to report,
he would invariably do the opposite.
It happened that a local man committed a serious crime
and feared death.
A clerk demanded a heavy bribe
to plead for leniency on his behalf.
The local man did not believe him,
and said:
"If you can do it,
why would I begrudge you a reward?"
So they made a pact.
A short while later,
the magistrate interrogated the case.
The local man refused to confess.
The clerk, standing beside him, scolded him, saying:
"If you don't quickly confess the truth,
His Excellency will have you shackled and beaten to death!"
The magistrate angrily said:
"How do you know I will certainly shackle and beat him?
I suspect the bribe hasn't reached you yet."
He then punished the clerk
and released the local man.
The local man then gave the clerk a hundred taels of silver as a reward.
One must know that wolves are cunning in many ways;
if one relaxes vigilance even slightly,
they will be taken advantage of.
This is not just about them baring their claws and fangs to devour people in the countryside.
Such people ruin one's hidden virtue,
and can even lead to the loss of one's life and family.
I don't know what kind of heart and mind those in official positions have,
that they insist on feeding innocent children to the Máhús!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
There was a merchant sailing on the South Sea.
At the third watch,
the boat became as bright as dawn.
He got up to look
and saw a huge creature,
half its body emerging from the water,
towering like a mountain;
its eyes were like two suns rising,
radiating light in all directions,
illuminating the entire land.
He asked the boatmen in alarm,
but none of them knew what it was.
They all crouched down to watch it.
After a while,
it gradually shrank back into the water,
and darkness returned.
Later, when they reached Fújiàn,
people all spoke of a certain night when it became bright and then dark again,
passing it around as a strange occurrence.
Calculating the time,
it was the night they saw the monster on the boat.
According to the twenty-four-volume manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
On the sixth day of the seventh month in the year Dīnghài,
Sūzhōu experienced heavy snow.
The people were terrified,
and together they prayed at the temple of the Great King.
The Great King suddenly possessed someone and said:
"Nowadays, those addressed as 'lǎoye'
all have the character 'big' added;
do you think I, a god, am small,
and not worthy of a 'big' character?"
Everyone was frightened,
and together they cried out
"Great Lǎoye,"
and the snow immediately stopped.
From this, it can be seen
that even gods enjoy flattery.
No wonder those who govern the lower regions get so many carriages!
The Historian of the Strange says:
"The customs of the world have changed;
those below flatter more and more,
while those above grow more and more arrogant.
Even in the more than forty years of the Kāngxī reign,
the way people address each other has become un-ancient,
which is quite laughable.
Jǔrén being called 'yé'
began twenty years ago;
Jìnshì being called 'lǎoye'
began thirty years ago;
Provincial and Metropolitan officials being called 'dà lǎoye'
began twenty-five years ago.
In the past, when a county magistrate visited a provincial governor,
he would only address him as 'lǎo dàrén';
now, this form of address has long been abandoned.
Even if there are gentlemen,
they usually act flatteringly amidst flattery,
not daring to say anything different.
As for the wives of officials being called 'tàitai,'
that has only been a few years.
In the past, only the mothers of officials
had this title;
for a wife to receive this title,
only in licentious stories is there a Qiáo Lín,
I have not seen it elsewhere.
In the Táng dynasty,
the emperor wanted to bestow upon Zhāng Yuè the title of Grand Academician.
Yuè declined, saying: 'Academicians have never had 'grand' in their title,
I dare not accept it.'
Nowadays, who made it 'grand'?
Who made it 'grand'?
Initially, it was due to the flattery of petty men,
and because it pleased the arrogant and noble,
they accepted it without doubt,
and soon it spread everywhere under heaven.
I suspect that in a few years,
those called 'yé' will advance to 'lǎo,'
and those called 'lǎoye' will advance to 'dà,'
but I don't know what honorific will be created above 'dà'?
It is truly unimaginable!"
On the third day of the sixth month in the year Dīnghài,
in Guīdé Prefecture, Hénán, snow fell over a foot deep,
and the crops all froze to death.
It is a pity they did not know the art of flattering the Great King.
How sad!
According to the twenty-four-volume manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Mùdú Town, Sūzhōu,
there was a commoner's daughter sitting in the courtyard at night
when suddenly a falling star struck her head,
and she fell to the ground dead.
Her parents were old and had no sons,
only this daughter.
They cried out in grief and tried to save her.
After a while, she revived,
and said with a laugh:
"I am now a man!"
They checked,
and it was indeed so.
Her family did not consider it demonic,
but secretly rejoiced at gaining a son.
This happened in the year Dīnghài.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
At a certain temple in Tiānjīn,
storks nested on the owl-tail ornaments of the roof.
On the ceiling of the main hall,
a large snake as thick as a basin hid,
and whenever the stork chicks were feathered and ready to fly,
it would come out and devour them all.
The storks would cry mournfully for several days before leaving.
This went on for three years.
People thought they would certainly not return,
but the next year they nested as before.
When the chicks were nearly grown,
the storks flew straight away,
and returned only after three days.
They entered the nest chirping,
and fed their chicks as usual.
The snake again slithered up.
Just as it approached the nest,
the two storks were startled,
flying and crying out in urgent distress,
straight up into the azure sky.
Suddenly, they heard a rushing wind sound,
and in an instant,
heaven and earth seemed to darken.
Everyone was astonished,
and together they saw a huge bird whose wings blotted out the sun,
descending swiftly from the sky,
swift as wind and rain.
It struck the snake with its claws,
and the snake's head immediately fell off,
also breaking off several feet of the temple corner,
before flapping its wings and flying away.
The storks followed behind it,
as if seeing it off.
The nest was overturned,
and both chicks fell,
one alive and one dead.
The monks took the live one and placed it in the bell tower.
After a short while,
the storks returned,
and still fed it,
until its wings grew and it flew away.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"They returned the following year,
probably not expecting the disaster to recur;
nesting in the same place for three years,
shows their resolve for revenge was firm;
not returning for three days,
they must have gone to plead for help like in the Qín court,
that much is clear.
The great bird must have been a sword immortal among the feathered tribes,
coming like a whirlwind,
striking once and leaving.
How could even the skill of Miàoshǒu Kōngkōng surpass this?"
In Jǐnán there was a garrison soldier
who saw a stork passing by.
He shot at it,
and it fell as the bowstring twanged.
In its beak was a fish
it was about to feed its young.
Someone urged him to pull out the arrow and release it,
but the soldier would not listen.
After a short while,
it flew away with the arrow still in it.
Later, it came and went among the city walls
for over two years,
with the arrow still piercing it as before.
One day,
the soldier was sitting under the gate of the military headquarters.
The stork passed by,
and the arrow fell to the ground.
The soldier picked it up and looked at it, saying:
"Is the arrow still intact?"
His ear happened to itch,
so he used the arrow to scratch it.
Suddenly, a strong wind slammed the gate shut,
and the gate closed abruptly,
pushing the arrow through his brain, killing him.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In Tiānjīn, a bird catcher caught a female swan goose.
The male followed to his home,
crying mournfully and circling in the air,
not leaving until dusk.
The next day,
the bird catcher went out early,
and the male goose had already arrived,
flying and calling as it followed him;
then it landed at his feet.
The bird catcher was about to catch it as well.
Seeing it stretch its neck, bowing and raising its head,
it spat out half a gold ingot.
The bird catcher understood its intention
and said:
"This is to ransom its mate."
He then released the female.
The two geese lingered,
as if both sorrowful and joyful,
then flew away together.
The bird catcher weighed the gold,
finding it to be over two liǎng and six qián.
Alas!
What do birds know,
yet they are so deeply attached!
Nothing is sadder than parting in life,
is it the same even for creatures?
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In Guǎngdōng, there was a hunter of wild beasts
who carried arrows into the mountains.
Once, while lying down to rest,
he fell into a deep sleep
and was carried off by an elephant using its trunk.
He thought he would surely be harmed.
Not long after,
it released him under a tree,
bowed its head and trumpeted once,
whereupon many elephants gathered,
circling around on all sides,
as if seeking something.
The first elephant crouched under the tree,
looking up at the tree and down at the man,
seeming to want him to climb.
The hunter understood
and stepped onto the elephant's back,
climbing up.
Even when he reached the treetop,
he still did not know their intention.
After a while,
a suānní came,
and all the elephants prostrated themselves.
The suānní chose a fat one,
intending to seize and devour it.
The elephants trembled in fear,
none daring to flee,
only looking up at the tree together,
as if pleading for pity and rescue.
The hunter understood
and shot an arrow at the suānní from above,
killing it instantly.
The elephants looked up into the air,
as if bowing and dancing in gratitude.
The hunter then climbed down,
and the elephant crouched again,
pulling at his clothes with its trunk,
as if wanting him to ride.
The hunter then mounted it,
and the elephant set off.
They reached a place
where it dug a hole with its hoof,
uncovering countless shed tusks.
The hunter dismounted,
bundled them up, and placed them on the elephant's back.
The elephant then carried him out of the mountains
before returning.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A woodcutter went to the market
and was returning carrying his staff
when he suddenly felt the head of the staff grow heavy.
Looking back,
he saw a headless person hanging from it.
Greatly alarmed,
he threw down the staff and struck wildly at it,
and it vanished.
He fled in terror
to a village.
It was already dusk,
and several people were lighting torches to search the ground,
as if looking for something.
Approaching to ask,
he learned that they had been sitting together
when suddenly a human head fell from the sky,
with disheveled hair and beard,
and vanished in an instant.
The woodcutter told what he had seen,
and together they formed one person,
but they could not figure out where it came from.
Later, someone was walking carrying a basket
when they suddenly saw a human head inside.
People questioned him in surprise,
and only then was he greatly alarmed.
He dumped it on the ground,
and it writhed and disappeared.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In Zhūchéng, there was a scholar named Dīng,
grandson of Lord Yěhè.
A young scholar of repute,
he fell gravely ill and died,
but revived the next night,
saying:
"I have attained enlightenment."
At that time, there was a monk skilled in profound meditation,
whom they invited
to lecture on the Shurangama Sutra by his bedside.
Each time the monk finished a section,
Dīng said it was not correct,
and said:
"If I recover from this illness,
attaining enlightenment will not be difficult.
Only a certain scholar can cure me,
and you should earnestly invite him."
In the county, there was a certain scholar
who was skilled in medicine but did not practice it professionally.
After three invitations, he finally came,
prescribed a formula, and administered medicine,
and Dīng recovered.
After returning home,
a woman entered from outside,
saying:
"I am a maidservant from the household of Minister Dǒng.
The Purple Flower Monk and I have an old enmity,
and now I have pursued him for retribution.
Do you wish to revive him again?
If you go again,
misfortune will befall you."
Having said this,
she vanished.
The scholar was afraid
and declined Dīng's request.
Dīng's illness relapsed,
and he insisted,
so the scholar told him the truth.
Dīng sighed and said:
"This karma is from a past life,
death is my fate."
He soon died.
Later, inquiries were made,
and indeed there was a Purple Flower Monk,
a venerable monk
whom the wife of Minister Dǒng of Qīngzhōu had once supported in her home;
but no one knew the origin of this enmity.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In Huáishàng, there was a senior licentiate named Zhōu Tiānyí,
fifty years old,
with only one son,
named Kèchāng,
whom he dearly loved.
By the age of thirteen or fourteen,
the boy's appearance grew even more handsome;
but he disliked studying
and often skipped school,
playing with other children
and often not returning all day.
Zhōu also let him be.
One day,
when it grew late and he had not returned,
they began to look for him,
but he was nowhere to be found.
The husband and wife wailed in grief,
nearly wishing to die.
After more than a year,
Chāng suddenly returned on his own,
saying:
"I was lured away by a Daoist priest,
but fortunately, I was not harmed.
When he happened to be away,
I managed to escape and come back."
Zhōu was overjoyed,
and did not press for details.
When he was taught to read,
his intelligence and understanding were twice what they had been before.
After another year,
his literary talent greatly advanced,
and after entering the prefectural school for examinations,
he became well-known.
Influential families vied to arrange marriages with him,
but Chāng was quite unwilling.
The daughter of Jìnshì Zhào was beautiful,
and Zhōu forced him to marry her.
After she entered the household,
the couple joked and laughed happily together;
yet Chāng always slept alone,
as if he had no intimate relations.
After another year,
he passed the provincial examination with success.
Zhōu was even more comforted.
However, as his years gradually declined,
he daily hoped to hold a grandchild,
so he often hinted at this to Chāng.
Chāng seemed indifferent and did not understand.
His mother could not bear it,
and morning and night she nagged him with many words.
Chāng’s expression changed,
and he went out, saying:
"I have long wanted to leave,
the reason I have not hastily departed is
only the affection of caring for my parents.
Truly, I cannot engage in marital relations
to fulfill your hopes.
Please allow me to leave again;
the one who complies with your wishes will soon return."
They chased and grabbed him,
but he had already fallen,
his clothes and hat shed like a cicada’s skin.
They were greatly alarmed,
suspecting that Chāng had died,
and that this must have been his ghost.
They could only sigh in sorrow.
The next day,
Chāng suddenly arrived with servants and horses,
and the whole family was terrified.
Approaching to question him,
he also said: he had been seized and sold by wicked men to a wealthy merchant’s household;
the merchant had no son,
so he adopted him as a son.
After obtaining Chāng,
he suddenly had a son of his own.
Chāng missed his home,
so they sent him back.
When asked about his studies,
he was as dull and stupid as before.
Thus, they realized this was the true Chāng;
the one who entered the school and passed the provincial examination
was a ghost’s impersonation.
However, they secretly rejoiced that the matter had not been exposed,
and immediately had him assume the title of Xiàolián.
Entering the bridal chamber,
his wife was very familiar and intimate;
but Chāng appeared bashful and ashamed,
as if newly married.
Just after a year,
they had a son.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Zōng Zǐměi of Tàiyuán,
following his father in traveling for study,
sojourned in Guǎnglíng.
His father was acquainted with old woman Lín beneath the Hóngqiáo bridge.
One day,
father and son passed by Hóngqiáo,
encountered her,
and she firmly invited them to her home,
brewing tea and conversing together.
There was a girl beside her,
of exceptional beauty.
The old man repeatedly praised her.
The old woman looked at Zōng and said:
"The eldest young master is gentle and refined like an unmarried maiden,
a face of good fortune.
If you do not disdain and reject us,
we would offer her in marriage,
how about it?"
The old man laughed,
urged his son to leave his seat,
