and made him bow to the old woman, saying:
"One word is worth a thousand pieces of gold!"
Earlier,
the old woman lived alone,
when the girl suddenly arrived on her own,
telling of her loneliness and hardship.
Asked for her childhood name,
she said it was Cháng'é.
The old woman loved her and kept her,
actually intending to hoard her as a rare commodity.
At that time, Zōng was fourteen,
and seeing the girl, he secretly rejoiced,
thinking his father would certainly arrange the match through a matchmaker;
but his father returned as if forgetting.
His heart burned with anxiety,
and he privately told his mother.
The old man laughed and said:
"That was just a jest with the greedy old woman.
She doesn’t know how much gold she plans to sell her for,
how could this be easily spoken of!"
After a year,
both the old man and his wife passed away.
Zǐměi could not forget his feelings for Cháng'é,
and when the mourning period was nearly over,
he sent someone to convey his intentions to old woman Lín.
The old woman at first did not acknowledge it.
Zōng angrily said:
"In my life, I have never lightly bowed to anyone;
why does the old woman regard me as not worth a single coin?
If you betray the former agreement,
you must return her to me!"
The old woman then said:
"Perhaps there was a playful agreement with your father back then,
it may have happened.
But there was no formal promise,
so it was all forgotten.
Now that you speak thus,
am I keeping her to marry the Heavenly King?
Every day she dresses up,
truly hoping to exchange her for a thousand pieces of gold;
now I ask for half that,
is that acceptable?"
Zōng himself considered it difficult to manage,
and so let the matter drop.
It happened that a widowed old woman rented a house in the western neighborhood,
with a daughter of marriageable age,
whose childhood name was Diāndāng.
By chance, he glimpsed her,
elegant and beautiful, no less than Cháng'é.
Admiring her,
he often used gifts as a stepping stone to approach;
after a long time, they gradually became familiar,
often conveying affection with their eyes,
but with no opportunity to speak.
One evening,
she climbed over the wall to borrow fire.
Zōng happily pulled her in,
and they became intimate.
They agreed to marry,
but she declined, saying her brother was away trading and had not returned.
From then on, they seized opportunities to meet,
their movements careful and secret.
One day,
passing by Hóngqiáo by chance,
he saw Cháng'é just inside the gate,
and hurried past her.
Cháng'é saw him,
beckoned to him with her hand,
and Zōng stopped;
the girl beckoned again,
so he entered.
The girl reproached Zōng for breaking their agreement,
and Zōng explained the reason.
The girl went into the inner room,
took out a ingot of gold and gave it to him,
but Zōng would not accept it,
declining, saying:
"I thought I had permanently severed ties with you,
and so made another agreement.
To accept gold and scheme for you
would be to betray another;
to accept gold and not scheme for you
would be to betray you: I truly dare not betray anyone."
After a long while, the woman said,
"The matter you proposed,
I am well aware of it.
It will certainly not succeed;
even if it does,
I will not resent your unfaithfulness.
You must leave quickly,
my mother will be here soon."
Zōng, caught off guard and unable to decide for himself,
accepted it and returned home.
The next night,
he told Diāndāng about it.
Diāndāng deeply agreed with her words,
but urged Zōng to focus solely on Cháng'é.
Zōng remained silent;
she expressed her willingness to take a subordinate role,
and only then did Zōng become pleased.
He immediately sent a matchmaker with betrothal gifts to Lín's family,
and Lín had no reason to refuse,
so Cháng'é was married to Zōng.
After entering his household,
Zōng recounted everything Diāndāng had said.
Cháng'é smiled slightly,
and pretended to encourage him.
Zōng was delighted,
and eagerly wanted to inform Diāndāng,
but Diāndāng's whereabouts had long been unknown.
Cháng'é knew it was for her sake,
so she temporarily returned to her parents' home,
deliberately creating an opportunity,
and instructed Zōng to secretly take Diāndāng's pouch.
Soon after, Diāndāng indeed arrived,
and when Zōng discussed the plan with her,
she only said not to rush.
As he helped her remove her outer garment and laughed,
he noticed a purple lotus pouch under her arm,
and was about to take it.
Diāndāng's expression changed,
and she stood up, saying:
"You and another are of one heart,
yet with me—
unfaithful man!
Let us part from now on."
Zōng tried his best to appease and explain,
but she would not listen,
and eventually left.
One day,
passing by her door to inquire,
he found another guest from Wú renting the place;
Diāndāng and her mother had moved away long ago,
leaving no trace or clue,
with no way to ask for news.
Since Zōng married Cháng'é,
his family suddenly became wealthy,
with interconnected pavilions and long corridors,
stretching across the streets.
Cháng'é was skilled at jesting and banter;
once, seeing a scroll of beautiful women,
Zōng said:
"I have always thought,
that in all the world, none could match you,
except that I have never seen Fēiyàn or Yángfēi."
The woman laughed and said:
"If you wish to see them,
what difficulty is there in that?"
Then, holding the scroll, she examined it carefully once,
hurried into the room,
faced the mirror to apply her makeup,
imitating Fēiyàn dancing in the wind,
and then learning Yángfēi's drunken demeanor.
Her height, weight, and figure,
changed according to the moment;
her charm and manner,
matched the scroll perfectly.
Just as she was striking a pose,
a maid came in from outside,
unable to recognize her,
and asked her companions in surprise;
then, looking closely and observing,
she suddenly realized and laughed.
Zōng happily said:
"Having obtained one beauty,
all the beauties of ages past
are now within my bedchamber!"
One night,
as he was sound asleep,
several men pried open the door and entered,
the light from their torches illuminating the walls.
The woman hurriedly rose,
exclaiming in alarm:
"Burglars are here!"
Zōng, just waking,
was about to cry out.
One of the men pressed a bright blade against his neck,
and in fear, he dared not even breathe.
Another man seized Cháng'é and carried her off on his back,
and the whole group clamorously departed.
Only then did Zōng begin to wail;
all the household servants gathered,
but the precious curios in the room
were not missing a single item.
Zōng was overcome with grief,
utterly distraught and at a loss,
feeling he had no place left in the world.
He reported it to the authorities for pursuit and capture,
but there was absolutely no news.
As three or four years passed by,
he grew despondent and listless,
and so, on the pretext of taking the examinations, he went to the capital.
Having stayed there half a year,
he consulted divinations and made inquiries,
leaving no method untried.
Once, passing by Yáo Alley,
he encountered a woman,
her face dirty and clothes ragged,
trembling and fearful like a beggar.
He stopped to look at her closely,
and it turned out to be Diāndāng.
Startled, he said:
"How have you become so haggard and worn?"
She replied:
"After we parted, I moved south,
and my old mother passed away.
I was seized by wicked men and sold to a banner household,
subjected to beatings, humiliation, cold, and hunger—
it's too painful to speak of."
Zōng, tears falling, asked:
"Can you be ransomed?"
She said:
"It's difficult.
The expenses are numerous and troublesome;
it's beyond my power."
Zōng said:
"To tell you the truth: in recent years I have become somewhat well-off,
but unfortunately, my funds while traveling as a guest are limited.
Still, I would empty my bags and sell my horse—
I would not dare refuse.
If what is required is too extravagant,
I should return home to raise the money."
The woman arranged to meet him the next day outside the western city,
at a rendezvous under a grove of willow trees;
she instructed him to come alone,
and not to bring anyone with him.
Zōng said:
"Agreed."
The next day,
he went early,
and found the woman already there,
her garments fresh and bright,
completely unlike her previous state.
Startled, he asked her about it,
and she said with a laugh:
"I was just testing your heart.
Fortunately, the sentiment of the silk robe still remains.
Please come to my humble dwelling,
and I will surely find a suitable way to repay you."
Walking north a few paces,
they reached her home.
She then brought out food and wine,
and they conversed and feasted together.
Zōng invited her to return with him.
The woman said:
"I have many mundane burdens,
and cannot follow you.
As for news of Cháng'é,
I have indeed heard quite a bit."
Zōng urgently asked where she was,
and the woman said:
"Her movements are elusive and fleeting,
and I cannot know the details deeply.
In the Western Hills there is an old nun,
blind in one eye.
Ask her,
and you should find out for yourself."
He then stayed overnight at her home.
At daybreak, she showed him the path.
Zōng reached the place,
where there was an ancient temple,
its surrounding walls completely collapsed;
within a thicket of bamboo was half a thatched hut,
where the old nun was mending a robe.
Seeing a guest arrive,
she paid no heed whatsoever.
Zōng bowed to her,
and only then did the nun raise her head to ask his business.
He stated his name,
and immediately explained what he sought.
The nun said:
"An eighty-year-old blind woman,
cut off from the world—
how would I know the whereabouts of a beautiful lady?"
Zōng insisted on pleading.
Then she said:
"I truly do not know.
But two or three relatives
will be visiting tomorrow evening.
Perhaps the young women among them might know her;
it's not certain.
You can come again tomorrow evening."
Zōng then left.
The next day he returned,
but the nun was out elsewhere,
the broken door left ajar.
He waited for a long time;
the night watches were already advancing,
the bright moon hung high,
and he paced about with no plan,
when from afar he saw two or three young ladies entering from outside—
and among them was Cháng'é.
Overjoyed, Zōng
suddenly sprang up,
and urgently seized her sleeve.
Cháng'é said:
"Rash gentleman!
You frightened me to death!
Hateful Diāndāng and her loose tongue—
teaching passions to entangle people."
Zōng pulled her to sit down,
held her hand and spoke earnestly,
recounting all his hardships,
and could not help feeling sorrowful.
The woman said:
"To tell you the truth: I am actually Cháng'é, sent down in banishment,
drifting in the mundane world.
My term has now been fulfilled;
the pretended robbery
was to sever your hopes.
The nun is also a guardian of the Queen Mother's palace.
When I was first banished,
I received her care and support,
so in my leisure time I often pay her a visit.
If you will release me,
I will arrange for Diāndāng to come to you in my stead."
Zōng would not listen,
hanging his head and shedding tears.
The woman looked into the distance and said:
"My sisters are coming."
Just as Zōng looked around,
Cháng'é had already vanished.
Zōng wailed aloud,
no longer wishing to live,
and so loosened his belt to hang himself.
Hazily, he felt his soul had left his body,
drifting disconsolately with nowhere to go.
Suddenly he saw Cháng'é coming,
who grabbed and lifted him,
his feet leaving the ground;
she entered the temple,
took the corpse from the tree and pushed and squeezed it,
calling out:
"Foolish man,
foolish man!
Cháng'é is here."
Suddenly it was as if he awoke from a dream.
After calming down a little,
the woman said angrily:
"That base maid Diāndāng!
Harming me and killing my gentleman—
I cannot forgive her!"
They went down the mountain, hired a carriage, and returned.
After instructing the household to pack their belongings,
he turned and went back out the western city gate,
intending to thank Diāndāng;
but when he arrived, the buildings were completely different,
and he returned in astonishment and sighing.
Secretly, he was glad Cháng'é did not know.
Upon entering his door,
Cháng'é greeted him with a smile and said:
"Have you seen Diāndāng?"
Zōng was stunned and could not answer.
The woman said:
"If you betray Cháng'é,
how can you obtain Diāndāng?
Please sit and wait;
she will come of her own accord."
Before long,
Diāndāng indeed arrived,
flustered, and prostrated herself beneath the couch.
Cháng'é rapped her fingers together and flicked them at her, saying:
"Little imp, you've fallen deep into this!"
Diāndāng kowtowed,
begging only to be spared from death.
Cháng'é said:
"You pushed someone into a pit,
and now you wish to escape beyond the heavens?
The Eleventh Maiden of the Vast Cold Palace is soon to be married,
and a hundred embroidered pillows and a hundred pairs of shoes are needed.
You may come with me,
and we shall work on them together."
Diāndāng respectfully stated:
"I only ask to divide the work,
and deliver it on time."
The lady did not consent,
and said to Zōng:
"If you speak on her behalf,
I will release her immediately."
Diāndāng looked at Zōng,
Zōng smiled and said nothing.
Diāndāng glared at him angrily.
She then begged to return and inform her family,
which was permitted,
and she left.
Zōng asked about her life story,
and then learned she was a fox from the Western Hills.
He prepared a carriage to await her,
and the next day,
she indeed came,
and they returned together.
However, since Cháng'é's return,
she had always been dignified and not given to frivolous laughter.
Zōng insisted on intimate play,
and she secretly taught Diāndāng to do it.
Diāndāng was exceedingly clever,
and skilled in seduction.
Cháng'é preferred to sleep alone,
often declining to spend the night.
One night,
when the water clock had struck three,
they still heard continuous giggling
from Diāndāng's room.
She sent a maid to eavesdrop secretly.
The maid returned,
but did not report,
only asking the lady to go herself.
Peering through the window,
she saw Diāndāng made up to look exactly like herself,
with Zōng embracing her,
calling her Cháng'é.
The lady smiled wryly and withdrew.
Not long after,
Diāndāng suddenly felt a sharp pain in her heart,
hurriedly put on her clothes,
dragged Zōng to Cháng'é's place,
and upon entering, prostrated herself.
Cháng'é said:
"Am I a doctor or a sorcerer who uses curses?
You just want to imitate Xīzǐ clutching her heart."
Diāndāng kowtowed,
only saying she knew her crime.
The lady said:
"It's cured."
She then rose,
could not help laughing, and left.
Diāndāng privately said to Zōng:
"I can make the lady imitate Guānyīn."
Zōng did not believe it,
so they playfully made a bet.
Whenever Cháng'é sat cross-legged,
her eyes seemed half-closed as if in meditation.
Diāndāng quietly placed a jade vase with a willow branch
on the table;
she herself let down her hair, joined her palms,
and stood in attendance beside her,
her cherry lips slightly parted,
her white teeth faintly visible,
her eyes not blinking at all.
Zōng laughed at her.
Cháng'é opened her eyes and asked about it,
Diāndāng said:
"I'm imitating the Dragon Girl attending Guānyīn."
Cháng'é laughed and scolded her,
punishing her by making her imitate a child's bow.
Diāndāng tied up her hair,
then bowed to her from all four sides,
prostrated on the ground and turned over,
displaying all sorts of contortions,
bending left and right,
until her stockings could rub against her ears.
Cháng'é smiled,
sat and kicked her.
Diāndāng raised her head,
and with her mouth caught the phoenix hook,
gently touching it with her teeth.
Just as Cháng'é was laughing playfully,
she suddenly felt a thread of seductive charm,
rising from her toes,
straight to her heart,
her thoughts becoming wanton and lustful,
as if beyond her control.
She quickly collected herself,
and scolded:
"Fox slave, you deserve to die!
Do you not choose whom you bewitch?"
Diāndāng was frightened,
released her mouth and threw herself to the ground.
Cháng'é sternly reprimanded her again,
and the others did not understand.
Cháng'é said to Zōng:
"Diāndāng's fox nature remains unchanged,
just now I was almost fooled by her.
If not for my deep-rooted virtue,
how easy it would be to fall into depravity!"
From then on, whenever she saw Diāndāng,
she treated her with strict control.
Diāndāng felt ashamed and fearful,
and told Zōng:
"I, towards the lady, love every part of her body,
with utmost affection;
loving her to the extreme,
I unconsciously become excessively seductive.
To say I have ulterior motives,
not only would I not dare,
but I could not bear it."
Zōng then told this to Cháng'é,
and Cháng'é treated her as before.
However, because their intimate play knew no bounds,
she admonished Zōng several times,
but Zōng would not listen;
thus, all the maids and servant women,
competed in intimate play.
One day,
two of them were supporting a maid,
imitating Yáng Guìfēi.
The two exchanged glances in understanding,
tricked the maid into relaxing her bones into a drunken pose,
and suddenly released their hands;
the maid fell violently onto the steps,
with a sound like a collapsing wall.
Everyone cried out in alarm;
approaching to check on her,
the imperial consort had already met her end at Mǎwéi.
The crowd was terrified,
and hurriedly reported to their master.
Cháng'é exclaimed in shock:
"Disaster has struck!
What did I say?"
She went to examine her,
but she was beyond saving.
They sent someone to inform her father.
Her father, a certain Jiǎ,
was always ill-behaved,
and came running, wailing,
carrying the corpse into the main hall,
cursing and shouting endlessly.
Zōng closed the doors in fear and anxiety,
not knowing what to do.
Cháng'é went out herself to reprimand him,
saying:
"Even if a master mistreats a maid to death,
the law does not require compensation;
moreover, she died suddenly by chance,
how do you know she won't revive?"
Jiǎ clamored:
"Her limbs are already cold,
how can there be any life left!"
Cháng'é said:
"Stop shouting.
Even if she does not live,
there is still the government office."
She then entered the hall to examine the corpse,
and the maid had already revived,
rising as soon as she touched her.
Cháng'é turned around and angrily said:
"Fortunately, the maid is not dead,
how dare you, thieving slave, behave so outrageously!
Tie him up with a straw rope and send him to the authorities!"
Jiǎ had no words,
and knelt down pleading for mercy.
Cháng'é said:
"Since you admit your guilt,
I will temporarily spare you from investigation.
But a petty man like you is untrustworthy,
and your behavior is fickle;
keeping your daughter here would eventually bring disaster,
so you should take her away immediately.
The original price was such-and-such amount,
you must quickly prepare it and bring it here."
She sent someone to escort him out,
making him ask two or three village elders
to witness and sign the document.
After that,
she called the maid forward,
and had Jiǎ ask her himself:
"Are you unharmed?"
Came the reply:
"Unharmed."
He then let her go.
Afterwards,
she summoned all the maidservants,
scolded and caned each one in turn.
She also called for Diāndāng,
imposing a strict prohibition on her.
She said to Zōng:
"Now I understand that for those in a superior position,
not even a single smile or frown can be taken lightly.
The jest began with me,
and the resulting ill effects could not be stopped.
Generally, sorrow belongs to yīn,
joy belongs to yáng;
when yáng reaches its zenith, yīn is born,
this is the fixed cycle of nature.
The maidservant's misfortune
was a warning from the ghosts and spirits, given gradually.
If one remains lost and unawakened,
then downfall will reach them."
Zōng listened respectfully.
Diāndāng wept, begging to be released.
Cháng'é then pinched her ear;
after a while she let go,
Diāndāng, dazed for a moment,
suddenly seemed to wake from a dream,
prostrated herself on the ground,
overjoyed and about to dance.
From then on, the women's quarters were orderly and quiet,
with none daring to be noisy.
The maidservant, upon reaching her home,
died suddenly without illness.
Jiǎ, unable to repay the ransom money,
entreated the village elder
to plead for mercy and forgiveness on his behalf,
which was granted.
Furthermore, in gratitude for her service,
they bestowed timber upon him and he left.
Zōng often worried about having no sons.
Suddenly, the cry of a child was heard from within Cháng'é's belly,
so she used a blade to cut open her left side and bring it out,
indeed a boy;
not long after,
she was with child again,
and again cut open her right side to bring out a girl.
The boy strongly resembled his father,
the girl strongly resembled her mother,
and both were betrothed to children from prominent families.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Jū Lèrú,
a man from Qīngzhōu.
His wife died,
and he abandoned his home and left.
Several years later,
he arrived dressed in Daoist robes and carrying a meditation cushion.
After staying one night he wished to leave,
but his relatives forcibly kept his robe and staff.
Jū, pretending to take a leisurely stroll, went outside the village,
whereupon his robe and belongings from the room
all flew out softly,
and followed him away.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Chén Xiàolián of Shùntiān,
when he was sixteen or seventeen,
once studied under a tutor at a Buddhist temple,
where the number of fellow students was quite large.
Among them was a student named Chǔ,
who said he was from Shāndōng,
diligent in his studies and seeking understanding,
with no time for rest;
moreover, he lodged at the study,
and was never once seen returning home.
Chén was closest to him,
and so questioned him about it.
He replied:
"My family is poor,
procuring the tuition payment is not easy.
Since I cannot afford to waste an inch of daylight,
by adding the midnight hours,
then my two days
can equal others' three."
Chén was moved by his words,
and wanted to bring his bed to share a room with him.
Chǔ stopped him, saying:
"Not yet,
not yet!
In my view, our tutor here,
his learning is not fit to be my teacher.
At Fùchéngmén there is a Master Lǚ,
although advanced in years,
is worthy to be a teacher.
Let us both transfer to study under him."
It seems that in the capital, those who set up schools often charged by the month;
once the month's tuition was paid in full,
students were free to stay or leave.
So the two students went together to see Lǚ.
Lǚ,
a venerable scholar from Yuè,
down on his luck and unable to return home,
was thus teaching young children,
though it was not truly his aspiration.
He was very pleased to gain these two students;
and Chǔ was especially bright,
understanding everything at a glance,
so Lǚ held him in particularly high regard.
The two became close and affectionate friends,
sharing a desk by day,
and a bed by night.
When the month ended,
Chǔ suddenly returned home on leave,
and for over ten days did not come back.
Everyone was puzzled by this.
One day,
Chén went to Tiānníng Temple to pay a visit,
and encountered Chǔ under the corridor,
splitting hemp and quenching sulfur,
making fire tools.
Seeing Chén,
he appeared awkward and uneasy.
Chén asked,
"Why have you abruptly abandoned your studies?"
Chǔ grasped his hand and asked for a private word,
sadly saying,
"I am too poor to provide gifts for the teacher,
so I must engage in trade for half a month
to afford one month of study."
Chén sighed with emotion for a long while,
then said,
"Just go and study,
I will do my utmost to help."
He ordered his attendant to gather Chǔ's tools,
and they returned together to the school.
Chǔ warned Chén not to reveal the matter,
but to make up some excuse to tell the teacher.
Chén's father was a merchant by trade,
who had amassed wealth through commerce.
Chén secretly took his father's money
to pay the teacher on Chǔ's behalf.
When his father questioned him about the missing gold,
Chén told him the truth.
His father thought him foolish,
and thus made him abandon his studies.
Chǔ was greatly ashamed,
and bid farewell to the teacher, intending to leave.
Lǚ, knowing the reason,
reproached him, saying,
"Since you are poor,
why did you not tell me earlier?"
He then returned all the money to Chén's father,
kept Chǔ studying as before,
and shared meals with him,
treating him like a son.
Although Chén no longer attended the school,
he often invited Chǔ to drink at a tavern.
Chǔ steadfastly avoided going to avoid suspicion;
but Chén insisted even more firmly,
often weeping in his presence.
Chǔ could not bear to sever ties,
and so they continued to meet without interruption.
After two years,
Chén's father died,
and he again sought to resume his studies.
Lǚ, moved by his sincerity,
accepted him;
but having been away from studies for so long,
he was far behind Chǔ.
After half a year,
Lǚ's eldest son came from Yuèzhōu,
begging for food while searching for his father.
The disciples pooled money to help with travel expenses,
but Chǔ could only shed tears and cling to him in sorrow.
Before parting,
Lǚ instructed Chén to regard Chǔ as his teacher.
Chén complied,
and housed Chǔ in his home.
Not long after,
Chǔ entered the county school,
and as a
"supplementary candidate"
took the examinations.
Chén worried he could not complete the paper,
and Chǔ offered to take the exam for him.
When the time came,
Chǔ came with another man,
saying he was his cousin Liú Tiānruò,
and told Chén to go with him for a while.
As Chén was about to leave,
Chǔ suddenly pulled him from behind,
causing him to stumble and nearly fall.
Liú quickly supported him and led him away.
After looking around for a while,
they went together to stay at Liú's home.
There were no women in the household,
so they lodged the guest in the inner quarters.
After staying for several days,
it was suddenly already the Mid-Autumn Festival.
Liú said,
"Today, in Lǐ Huángqīn's garden,
there are many visitors.
We should go to dispel our accumulated gloom,
and I will conveniently see you home."
He had a servant carry a tea stove and drinking set as they went.
They saw only waterside pavilions and plum blossom arbors,
so noisy they could not enter.
Passing a water gate,
under an old willow tree,
lay a painted boat.
They boarded it together.
After several rounds of wine,
they felt the loneliness oppressive.
Liú turned to his servant boy and said,
"At Méihuā Hall, there is a new courtesan.
I wonder if she is at home?"
The boy left for a short while
and returned with the courtesan.
It turned out to be Lǐ Èyún from the brothel.
Lǐ,
a famous courtesan in the capital,
was skilled in poetry and singing.
Chén had once drunk at her place with friends,
so he recognized her.
When they met,
they exchanged a few polite words.
The courtesan looked sorrowful and worried.
Liú asked her to sing,
and she sang "Hāolǐ."
Chén was displeased,
saying,
"Even if the host and guest do not please you,
why sing a song of death to a living person?"
The courtesan rose and apologized,
forcing a cheerful expression,
then sang a romantic song.
Chén was delighted,
grabbed her wrist, and said,
"You once recited 'Huànxīshā' several times for me,
but now I have forgotten it entirely."
The courtesan chanted,
"Tearful eyes gaze upon the dressing mirror,
opening the curtain, I suddenly see my sister-in-law approaching.
Lowering my head, I turn to look at my bow-shaped shoes.
Forcing myself to part my green moth eyebrows into a smiling face,
frequently using my red sleeve to wipe my fragrant cheek,
careful lest others guess my thoughts."
Chén repeated it several times.
Soon they moored the boat,
passed through a long corridor,
and saw many inscriptions and poems on the walls.
Chén immediately took up a brush and wrote the lyrics there.
As dusk approached,
Liú said,
"The examination candidates will soon be coming out."
He then escorted Chén back.
Upon entering the gate,
he took his leave.
Chén found the room dark and empty.
As he lingered,
Chǔ entered the door;
upon closer inspection,
it was not Chǔ at all.
Just as he was puzzled,
the visitor suddenly approached and collapsed.
The family members said,
"The young master is exhausted!"
They helped him up together.
Then he realized the one who had fallen was none other
than himself.
Once he rose,
he saw Chǔ Shēng standing beside him,
feeling dazed as if in a dream.
He dismissed others to investigate the matter.
Chǔ said,
"Do not be alarmed when I tell you: I am actually a ghost.
I should have been reincarnated long ago,
but the reason I lingered here
was that I could not forget your profound friendship.
So I attached myself to your body
to take the exam on your behalf.
Now that the three sessions are over,
this wish is fulfilled."
Chén asked to take the metropolitan examination.
Chǔ said,
"Your ancestors had little fortune;
your bones are marked by stinginess,
unworthy of receiving official honors."
Chén asked,
"Where will you go?"
Chǔ replied,
"Master Lǚ and I share a father-son bond.
I often think of him and cannot let go.
My cousin serves as a registrar in the underworld,
and I have asked him to plead with the ruler of the underworld.
Perhaps there will be a resolution."
He then bid farewell and departed.
Chén found this strange.
At daybreak,
he went to visit Lǐ Jī,
intending to ask about the boating incident,
only to find that Jī had been dead for several days.
He then went to the Imperial Kinsman's Garden,
where he saw the inscribed verse still there,
but the faint ink was indistinct,
as if about to fade away.
Only then did he realize that the one who inscribed it was a soul,
and the one who composed it was a ghost.
By evening,
Chǔ arrived joyfully and said:
"Fortunately, what I planned has succeeded.
I respectfully bid you farewell."
He then extended both palms,
asking Chén to write the character "Chǔ" on them as a memento.
Chén was about to prepare wine for a farewell feast,
but Chǔ shook his head and said:
"No need.
If you do not forget our old friendship,
after the results of the imperial examination are announced,
do not fear the long and difficult journey."
Chén tearfully saw him off.
He saw a man waiting at the gate;
just as Chǔ was lingering reluctantly,
the man pressed his hand on Chǔ's neck,
and it flattened under his touch.
He then scooped it into a bag
and carried it away on his back.
After several days,
Chén indeed passed the examination.
He then prepared his luggage and went to Yuè.
Lǚ's wife had been unable to bear children for decades,
but when she was over fifty,
she suddenly gave birth to a son,
whose hands were tightly clenched and could not be opened.
When Chén arrived,
he requested to see the child
and said that the palms should have the character
"Chǔ" written on them.
Lǚ did not fully believe it.
When the child saw Chén,
its ten fingers opened on their own,
and upon looking, it was indeed so.
Astonished, Lǚ asked the reason,
and Chén told him everything.
They rejoiced together in amazement.
Chén gave them generous gifts
and then returned.
Later, Lǚ went to the capital for the palace examination as a tribute student,
and stayed with Chén.
By then, the child was thirteen years old
and had already entered the county school.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Old Lǚ taught his disciples,
but did not know he was teaching his own son.
Alas!
To do good for others
and bring blessings upon oneself—
is there any gap between them?
As for Chǔ Shēng,
before repaying his teacher with his body,
he first repaid his friend with his soul.
His will and his actions
could shine through the sun and moon.
How could it be considered strange just because he was a ghost?"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
During the Shùnzhì reign,
in the Téng and Yì regions,
seven out of ten people were bandits.
Officials dared not arrest them,
and later, when they accepted amnesty,
the county magistrate separately classified them as
"bandit households."
Whenever disputes arose between them and law-abiding citizens,
he would deliberately side with them,
fearing they might rebel again.
Later, litigants often falsely claimed to be bandit households,
while their opponents strenuously attacked the claim as false.
Whenever both parties presented their cases,
the right and wrong of the matter were set aside,
and instead, the truth or falsity of the bandit status
was repeatedly contested,
troubling the authorities to verify the registers.
It happened that many foxes haunted the government offices,
and the magistrate's daughter was bewitched by one.
He hired a sorcerer,
who captured it with a talisman and put it in a bottle,
intending to burn it with fire.
The fox inside the bottle cried out loudly:
"I am a bandit household!"
Those who heard it could not help but stifle their laughter.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Nowadays, those who rob others openly with torches
are not considered bandits by officials but adulterers;
those who climb walls to commit adultery
often do not admit to adultery but claim to be bandits: the state of the world has changed again.
If there were foxes in government offices today,
they would surely cry out, 'I am a bandit,'
without a doubt."
In Zhāngqiū, the grain tribute, corvée labor,
and the collection of melting fees
were often several times higher for commoners than for gentry,
so landowners vied to have their properties registered under gentry names.
Although this did no harm to state taxes,
it actually reduced the officials' income.
The county magistrate, Zhōng,
submitted a petition to reform these abuses,
which was approved.
At first, he ordered voluntary confessions;
later, cunning people used this to pressure the gentry,
and properties sold decades ago
were falsely claimed as fraudulently registered,
leading to lawsuits against the buyers.
The magistrate consistently sided with them,
so many honest and timid people lost their properties.
A certain Lǐ Shēng was also sued by a certain Jiǎ,
and both went to court for a hearing.
Jiǎ addressed him as
"Xiùcai";
Lǐ vehemently argued,
refusing to accept the title of Xiùcai.
The uproar continued.
The magistrate asked those around him,
and they all pointed out that Lǐ was indeed a Xiùcai.
The magistrate asked:
"Why do you not admit it?"
Lǐ said:
"Let's set aside the title of Xiùcai for now.
After the land dispute is settled,
it won't be too late to be one."
Alas!
When it comes to the name of bandit,
people vie to claim it;
when it comes to the name of Xiùcai,
people vie to reject it: how things have changed!
Someone submitted an anonymous complaint stating:
"The complainant, Yuán Rǎng,
brings a case of resisting the law and seizing property.
Due to old age, I am unable to perform corvée labor.
I have fifty acres of land near the city walls,
which in the first year of Duke Yǐn of Lǔ,
I temporarily registered under the name of the wicked scholar Yán Yuān.
Now that the laws are strict,
I ought to confess.
Unexpectedly, the wicked one long borrowed it without returning it
and seized it as his own.
When I went to reason with him,
he, along with his teacher and seventy-two wicked followers,
beat me severely with rods,
injuring my legs and thighs.
They then locked me in a narrow alley,
giving me only a bowl of food and a gourd of water daily,
imprisoning and starving me nearly to death.
The village head of Hùxiāng can testify.
I beg to have his status revoked and a strict investigation conducted,
so that the property stained with blood may be returned to its owner.
This is my complaint."
This could follow Liǔ Zhí's complaint against Bóyí and Shūqí.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*. The appendix is supplemented from the 24-volume manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
In the western part of the county, there was a certain Mr. Yǐ,
who had formerly been a gentleman of the beams.
His wife deeply feared this,
and repeatedly urged him to stop: Yǐ then completely reformed himself.
After two or three years,
his poverty became unbearable,
and he thought of playing the role of Féng Fù once more before finally stopping.
So, under the pretext of trade,
he went to a skilled diviner
to decide his course.
The diviner said:
"The southeast is auspicious,
favorable for petty men,
unfavorable for gentlemen."
The omen secretly matched his heart's desire,
and he was secretly pleased.
He then traveled south,
reaching the area between Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng.
He roamed villages and towns daily
for several months.
Once, he entered a temple
and saw two or three stones piled in a corner of the wall.
Knowing in his heart it was something unusual,
he also threw a stone among them.
He then went straight to lie down behind a shrine.
When evening fell,
people gathered in the temple to talk,
seeming to be over ten in number.
Suddenly, one person counted the stones,
was surprised there were too many,
and so they searched together.
Behind the shrine, they found Yǐ.
They asked:
"Was it you who threw the stone?"
Yǐ acknowledged.
They questioned his hometown and name.
Yǐ answered deceptively.
They then gave him a weapon
and led him to go with them.
Arriving at a large mansion,
they brought out a soft ladder,
and vied to climb over the wall to enter.
Because Yǐ had come from afar
and was unfamiliar with the paths,
they had him lie hidden outside the wall,
in charge of passing things and guarding the bags.
After a short while,
they threw down a bundle;
after another short while,
they lowered a trunk on a rope.
Yǐ lifted the trunk and knew it contained things.
So he broke open the box,
and with his hands felt around to take out items.
All heavy objects
he put into one bag,
shouldered it, and swiftly ran off,
actually taking the road home.
From this, he built towers and pavilions, bought good farmland,
and became a tribute student by donating grain.
The county inscribed a plaque on his gate saying
"Virtuous Gentleman."
Later, a major case broke out,
and the whole gang of bandits was captured;
only Yǐ's name was not on the register,
and he could not be investigated or questioned,
so he escaped.
After the matter had lain dormant for a long time,
Yǐ would occasionally recount it himself when drunk.
In Cáozhōu, there was a certain great bandit
who, having obtained substantial wealth, returned home
and slept peacefully without a care.
Two or three petty thieves
climbed over his wall and entered,
seized him,
and demanded money.
He refused to give it;
they beat and burned him,
and only after he handed over all he had
did they leave.
He said to people:
"I didn't know the pain of roasting torture was like this!"
He then deeply hated bandits,
and enlisted as a mounted constable,
capturing nearly all the bandits in the county.
When he caught the bandits who had robbed him,
he also inflicted upon them what they had done to him.
According to the twenty-four-volume manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Zhū Dàxīng
was from Zhāngdé.
His family was wealthy but extremely miserly.
Unless it was for his children's weddings,
there were no guests in his seats,
and no meat in his kitchen.
However, he was frivolous and fond of chasing women.
Where women were concerned,
he spared no expense.
Every night,
he would climb over walls and go through villages
to sleep with loose women.
One night,
he encountered a young woman walking alone.
Knowing she was a runaway,
he forced and threatened her,
leading her to come with him back home.
By candlelight,
she was extremely beautiful.
She said herself:
"I am of the Huò family."
He questioned her in detail.
The woman was displeased,
and said:
"Since you have taken me in,
why must you interrogate me further?
If you fear I will bring trouble,
it's better I leave early."
Zhū dared not ask further,
and kept her to sleep with.
However, the woman could not bear coarse food and also disliked seeing meat stew,
requiring bird's nest, chicken hearts, and fish maw cooked into soup
before she could be satisfied.
Zhū had no choice,
and served her with all his effort.
She was also often ill,
needing a bowl of ginseng soup daily.
Zhū at first refused.
The woman moaned as if near death,
and he had no alternative
but to give it to her.
Her illness then vanished as if lost.
So this became routine.
The woman's clothes had to be brocade and embroidery.
After a few days,
she would tire of them and want new ones.
After more than a month like this,
the expenses were incalculable,
and Zhū gradually could not supply her.
The woman sobbed without eating,
asking to leave.
Zhū was afraid,
and again obliged and complied with her.
Whenever she was depressed,
she would have him invite actors to perform a play every ten days or so.
During the plays,
Zhū would set up a stool outside the curtain,
holding his child to watch;
the woman also showed no pleasure,
often scolding and berating him.
Zhū also did not much explain or argue.
After two years,
the family gradually declined.
He gently spoke to the woman,
asking for a slight reduction;
the woman agreed,
and all expenses were cut by half.
After a long time,
it still was not enough,
and the woman also became content with porridge;
gradually, she also wore clothes that were not precious.
Zhū was secretly pleased.
Suddenly one night,
she opened the back door and ran away.
Zhū was disconsolate as if having lost something,
searched everywhere for her,
and then learned she was at the Hé family's home in a neighboring village.
Hé Dàxìng was a man of noble lineage.
He was wealthy and unrestrained, fond of entertaining guests,
with lanterns and candles burning until dawn.
Suddenly, a beautiful woman entered his private chambers in the middle of the night.
When questioned,
she revealed herself to be a runaway concubine from the Zhū family.
Hé had always looked down upon Zhū as a person;
moreover, he was captivated by the woman's beauty,
and ultimately took her in.
After several days of intimacy,
he became even more infatuated with her,
indulging in extreme luxury and desire,
providing for her just as Zhū had done.
When Zhū learned of this,
he came to demand her return,
but Hé paid him no heed.
Zhū then brought the matter before the authorities.
The officials, finding the woman's name and background unclear,
dismissed the case without further action.
Zhū used his wealth to bribe the officials,
and only then did they agree to detain and interrogate her.
The woman said to Hé,
"When I was in the Zhū household,
I was never formally betrothed or married through proper rites—
why should we fear him?"
Hé was pleased and
prepared to face the trial.
A guest present, Gù Shēng, advised him, saying,
"Harboring a fugitive
already violates the laws of the state;
moreover, since this woman entered your household,
her daily expenses have been boundless—
even a family with a fortune of a thousand gold pieces
could not sustain such extravagance."
Hé suddenly realized the truth,
withdrew from the lawsuit,
and returned the woman to Zhū.
After a day or two,
the woman ran away again.
There was a man named Huáng Shēng,
a poor scholar by circumstance,
who had no spouse.
The woman knocked on his door and entered,
explaining where she had come from.
Huáng, seeing such a stunning beauty suddenly throwing herself at him,
was both startled and fearful, unsure of what to do.
Huáng had always been mindful of the law,
and firmly refused her.
The woman did not leave.
In their conversation,
she was delicate, charming, and utterly irresistible.
Huáng's heart was stirred,
and he allowed her to stay,
though he worried she would not be content with poverty.
The woman rose early each morning,
personally undertaking the hardships of household chores,
laboring even more diligently than a long-established wife.
Huáng was a refined and carefree man,
skilled in the art of charming women,
and he regretted that they had not met sooner.
He only feared that word might leak out,
and their happiness would not last long.
As for Zhū, after the lawsuit,
his family grew even poorer;
moreover, he assumed the woman would not remain content,
and so he let the matter drop without further pursuit.
The woman had been with Huáng for several years,
and their affection was very deep.
One day,
she suddenly wanted to return to her parents’ home,
and insisted that Huáng escort her.
Huáng said:
"You said before that you had no family,
why is there such a contradiction?"
She replied:
"I was just speaking carelessly.
I am from Zhènjiāng.
In the past, I followed a wandering man,
drifted about the rivers and lakes,
and ended up here.
My family is quite well-off.
If you exhaust your resources to go there,
you will certainly not suffer any loss."
Huáng followed her words,
hired a carriage and went together.
When they reached the area of Yángzhōu,
they moored the boat by the riverbank.
The woman happened to be leaning by the window,
when the son of a wealthy merchant passed by,
was startled by her beauty,
turned his boat around and followed them,
but Huáng did not know this.
The woman suddenly said:
"Your family is extremely poor.
Now there is a way to cure poverty,
I wonder if you can follow it?"
Huáng asked her about it,
and she said:
"I have been with you for several years,
and have not been able to bear you sons or daughters,
which is also an unresolved matter.
Although I am plain,
fortunately I am not yet old and decrepit.
If there is someone who can give you a thousand taels of silver,
then sell me off.
With this, a wife,
fields, and a house will all be provided.
How about this plan?"
Huáng turned pale,
not knowing the reason.
The woman laughed and said:
"Don’t be anxious.
There are certainly many beautiful women in the world;
who would be willing to buy a concubine for a thousand taels?
I will just jest about it outside,
to see if such a person exists.
Whether to sell or not,
of course still lies with you."
Huáng refused.
The woman herself spoke to the boatman’s wife about it,
the wife glanced at Huáng,
and Huáng casually responded.
Not long after the wife left,
she returned and said:
"The son of a merchant on the neighboring boat
is willing to offer eight hundred."
Huáng deliberately shook his head to make it difficult,
before long,
she came again,
and said he agreed to the price,
and requested to come over to the boat to complete the exchange.
Huáng gave a slight smile.
The woman said:
"Tell him to wait a moment,
I will instruct Huáng-láng,
and then let him go."
The woman said to Huáng:
"I have served you daily with a body worth a thousand taels,
do you only realize it now?"
Huáng asked:
"What words should I use to send him away?"
The woman said:
"Please go immediately to sign the contract,
whether I go or not is of course up to me."
Huáng would not agree,
the woman pressed and urged him,
and Huáng had no choice but to go over.
Immediately the payment was exchanged.
Huáng told them to seal and mark it,
saying:
"Because of poverty,
it has actually come to this,
to cut off and part like this.
If my wife definitely will not consent,
I will still return the original silver to you."
Just as they were moving the silver to the boat,
the woman had already followed the boatman’s wife from the stern onto the merchant’s boat,
glanced back from afar to bid farewell,
without any sorrow or attachment,
Huáng’s soul was startled and left his body,
his throat choked and unable to speak.
Soon the merchant’s boat cast off,
and left like an arrow shot.
Huáng cried out loudly,
wanting to chase and catch up.
The boatman would not comply,
and sailed the boat south across the river.
In an instant they reached Zhènjiāng,
and moved the money ashore.
The boatman hurriedly untied the boat and left.
Huáng guarded his luggage and sat gloomily,
with nowhere to go,
gazing at the surging river water,
like ten thousand knives piercing his body.
Just as he was covering his face and weeping,
he suddenly heard a delicate voice calling
"Huáng-láng."
Startled, he looked back,
and saw the woman already on the road ahead.
Overjoyed,
he shouldered his luggage and followed her,
asking:
"How did you manage to come so quickly?"
The woman laughed and said:
"If I had delayed a few more moments,
then you would have become suspicious."
Huáng then suspected she was no ordinary person,
and firmly questioned her about the situation.
The woman laughed and said:
"In my life, I break those who are stingy,
and deceive those who are wicked.
If I had really discussed it with you,
you certainly would not have agreed;
where could we have obtained a thousand taels?
The money bag is full and bulging,
and the pearl has returned to Hé Pǔ,
you are fortunate enough,
why keep questioning?"
Then she hired a porter to carry the bags,
and they went off together.
Arriving inside the Shuǐmén,
there was a house facing south,
they entered directly.
Soon, old men, old women, men and women,
came out in crowds to welcome them,
all saying:
"Huáng-láng has come!"
Huáng entered and paid respects to the father-in-law and mother-in-law.
Two young men bowed and sat down to talk with him;
they were the woman’s brothers, Dàláng and Sānláng.
At the banquet, there were not many dishes,
four jade plates,
and the square table was already full.
Chicken, crab, goose, fish,
were all sliced into cylinders.
The young men used huge bowls to pass wine; their conversation was bold and unrestrained.
Afterwards, they led him to a separate courtyard,
to let the couple stay together.
The quilts and pillows were smooth and soft,
but the bed used tanned leather instead of rattan.
Daily, a maid would deliver three meals,
and the woman sometimes did not come out all day.
Huáng lived alone, bored and miserable,
repeatedly spoke of returning,
but the woman firmly stopped him.
One day,
she said to Huáng:
"Now I have a plan for you: let’s buy a person,
to plan for an heir.
But buying a maid or concubine would be expensive;
we should pretend she is my elder brother,
and have father discuss marriage for him,
then it won’t be hard to get a girl from a good family."
Huáng would not agree.
The woman did not listen.
There was a daughter of Provincial Scholar Zhāng who had recently been widowed,
the betrothal money discussed was a hundred strings of cash,
the woman insisted on marrying her for him.
The new wife’s childhood name was Āměi,
quite gentle and lovely.
The woman called her sister-in-law;
Huáng felt uneasy and restrained,
but the woman was completely at ease.
Another day,
she said to Huáng:
"I will go with my eldest sister to Nánhǎi,
to visit my aunt,
and return in over a month.
Please, you and your wife live here peacefully."
Then she left.
The husband and wife lived alone in one courtyard,
and were provided with food and drink on time,
which was also quite abundant and well-prepared.
However, since entering the door,
not a single person had ever come to their room again.
Every morning,
Āměi would go to pay respects to Wēn,
and after just a couple of words, she would withdraw.
The sisters-in-law were by her side,
only exchanging glances and smiling.
Even if she lingered and sat for a long time,
they did not engage in intimate conversation.
When Huáng saw the old man,
it was the same.
Occasionally, when the young men gathered to talk,
and Huáng arrived,
they would all fall silent.
Huáng felt suspicious and depressed, with no one to confide in.
Āměi noticed this,
and asked:
"Since you are brothers with the young men,
why has it been like you are a stranger for the past month?"
Huáng was caught off guard and couldn't answer,
stammering as he said:
"I've been away for ten years,
and only now have I returned."
Měi then carefully inquired about the status of the old man and his wife,
and the residences of the sisters-in-law.
Huáng was greatly embarrassed,
unable to hide it any longer,
and the whole truth came out.
The woman wept and said:
"Although my family is poor,
we have never done anything as lowly as being a concubine,
no wonder the sisters-in-law look down on me and treat me with contempt!"
Huáng was terrified and didn't know what plan to make,
only kneeling down for a long time, listening to the woman's decision.
Měi wiped away her tears and pulled him up,
instead asking him what he intended to do.
Huáng said:
"How dare I make any other plans,
my only plan is to leave alone."
The woman said:
"Having married and then returning home,
how could I bear it emotionally?
Although she came first,
it was in secret;
although I came later,
it was publicly acknowledged.
It would be better to wait for her to return,
and ask her, since she came up with this plan,
how does she intend to place me?"
After living there for several months,
the woman still did not return.
One night,
they heard noise and drinking in the guest quarters.
Huáng secretly went to peek,
and saw two guests in military attire sitting in the seats of honor: one was wrapped in leopard skin,
majestic as a heavenly god;
the one sitting to the east,
wore a helmet made of tiger head leather,
with the tiger's mouth biting his forehead,
and the nose and ears all complete.
Startled and amazed, he returned,
and told Āměi about it,
but they couldn't figure out who the Huò father and son were.
The husband and wife were suspicious and fearful,
planning to rent a place elsewhere to live,
but were afraid it would arouse their suspicions.
Huáng said:
"To tell you the truth: even if the person from the South Sea returns,
the matter has already been settled,
I cannot make a home here either.
Now I want to take you away,
but I'm afraid your respected parents might have other objections.
It would be better to part for now,
and I will definitely return within two years.
If you can wait,
wait for me;
if you want to go elsewhere,
that is also up to you."
Āměi wanted to tell her parents and follow him,
but Huáng would not allow it.
Āměi shed tears,
and made him swear an oath,
before they parted and she returned.
Huáng went to bid farewell to the old man and his wife.
At that time, all the young men were out,
and the old man tried to keep him to wait for their return,
but Huáng did not listen and left.
Boarding the boat, he felt desolate,
his spirit and appearance lost.
Arriving at Guāzhōu,
he suddenly turned his head and saw a sail approaching,
sailing as fast as flying;
as it drew closer,
he saw someone sitting at the bow of the boat with a hand on his sword—
it was Huò Dàláng.
From afar, he called out:
"You wanted to send her back,
why didn't you discuss it again?
Sending your wife away,
who can wait two or three years?"
As he spoke,
the boat had already drawn near.
Āměi came out from the boat,
and Dàláng helped her board Huáng's boat,
then jumped and went straight away.
Earlier,
after Āměi had returned,
she was just crying and telling her parents about it,
when suddenly Dàláng arrived at the door with a carriage,
pressed his sword to threaten them,
and forced the woman to leave quickly.
The whole family was terrified and held their breath,
not daring to stop or question.
The woman recounted the situation,
and though Huáng didn't understand the meaning,
he was very happy to have Měi,
and they set sail and departed.
Arriving home,
they used their funds to start a business,
and became quite wealthy.
Āměi often missed her parents,
and wanted Huáng to go visit them;
but she was afraid that if Huò's daughter came,
there would be disputes between the wife and concubine again.
Not long after,
Old Man Zhāng came to visit,
and seeing the house well-kept and tidy,
he felt quite comforted,
and said to his daughter:
"After you left,
I went to the Huò family to inquire,
and saw the door already locked,
and even the landlord didn't know about it,
so for half a year there was no news at all.
Your mother cried day and night,
saying you had been tricked away by a villain,
not knowing where you had drifted to.
Now, fortunately, you are safe and sound?"
Huáng truthfully told him the situation,
and they guessed that they were deities.
Later, Āměi gave birth to a son,
and named him Xiāncì.
When he was over ten years old,
his mother sent him to Zhènjiāng.
Arriving at the boundary of Yángzhōu,
he rested at an inn,
and all his attendants went out.
A woman came,
took the child into another room,
lowered the curtain,
held him on her lap,
smiled and asked his name,
and the child told her.
She asked:
"What is the meaning of the name?"
He replied:
"I don't know."
The woman said:
"Go back and ask your father, and you will know."
Then she tied his hair into a bun,
took a flower from her own hairpin and put it in his hair for him;
took out a gold bracelet and put it on his wrist.
Then she put some gold into his sleeve,
and said:
"Take it to buy books to read."
The child asked who she was,
and she said:
"Child, don't you know you have another mother?
Go back and tell your father: Zhū Dàxīng died without a coffin,
you should help him,
don't forget."
The old servant returned to the room,
and found the young master missing;
searching until he reached another room,
he heard him talking with someone,
peeked in,
and it was the former mistress.
Outside the curtain, he coughed lightly,
intending to speak.
The woman pushed the child onto the bed,
and in a daze, she had already vanished.
He asked the innkeeper,
but no one knew about it.
A few days later,
returning from Zhènjiāng,
he told Huáng,
and also showed the gifts he had received.
Huáng sighed endlessly.
When he inquired about Zhū,
he had died just three days before,
his body exposed and not yet buried,
so Huáng gave generous assistance for his funeral.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Was the woman an immortal?
She changed masters three times, which does not count as chaste.
However, she broke the miser's stinginess,
and hastened the debauchery of the lecher.
She was not without intent.
Yet, having broken them, there was no need for her to pity them.
As for the bones of the greedy, lecherous, vulgar, and miserly,
why regret them being cast into ditches and gullies?"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*:
Yù Píngzǐ from Píngyáng
went to take the provincial examination in the northern capital
and rented lodgings at Bàoguó Temple.
A scholar from Yúháng was already staying at the temple,
and since Wáng was living next door,
he sent over his name card.
The scholar did not reply.
Morning and evening, whenever they met,
he was often very rude.
Wáng was angered by his arrogance and perversity, and thus their interaction ceased.
One day,
a young man was visiting the temple.
Dressed in white robes, skirt, and hat,
he appeared imposing from a distance.
Approaching and conversing with him,
Wáng found his speech witty and marvelous,
and grew fond and respectful of him.
Upon inquiring about his background and clan,
he said:
"The surname is Zhū, from Dēngzhōu."
Wáng then ordered his servant to set a seat,
and they sat facing each other, laughing and talking.
The Yúháng scholar happened to pass by,
and they both rose to defer the seat to him.
The scholar presumptuously took the seat of honor,
and without any modesty, abruptly asked Zhū:
"Are you also sitting for the examination?"
He replied,
"No.
With my nag's talent,
I have long had no ambition to gallop ahead."
He asked further:
"From which province?"
Zhū told him.
The scholar said:
"You don't even pursue advancement;
that shows your discernment.
To the left and right of the mountains, there isn't a single literate person."
Zhū said:
"Northerners certainly have few literate ones,
but the illiterate one isn't necessarily me;
Southerners certainly have many literate ones,
but the literate one isn't necessarily you."
Having said this,
he clapped his hands.
Wáng joined in,
causing an uproar of laughter in the room.
The scholar, ashamed and angry,
raised his eyebrows, rolled up his sleeves, and boasted:
"Do you dare to accept a topic set on the spot,
to compare literary skill?"
Zhū looked away and said with a scornful laugh:
"What is there to dare!"
He then hurried to his lodgings,
brought out a Confucian classic, and handed it to Wáng.
Wáng flipped through it at random,
pointed, and said:
" 'The boy from the Que Dang clan was sent with a message.'"
The scholar stood up,
asking for brush and paper.
Zhū pulled him and said:
"You can compose orally.
My 'breakdown' is already done:
'In a place where guests come and go,
one sees a person who knows nothing.'"
Wáng held his belly laughing.
The scholar angrily said:
"Completely incapable of writing,
only engaging in abuse,
how can this be considered human conduct!"
Wáng tried hard to mediate the dispute,
asking for another, better topic to be set.
He flipped again and said:
" 'Yin had three men of benevolence.'"
Zhū immediately responded:
"The three men took different paths,
but their direction was the same.
What is that one thing?
It is said: benevolence.
A gentleman only needs benevolence,
why must they be the same?"
The scholar then did not compose,
stood up and said:
"He is a man of some small talent."
And then left.
Because of this, Wáng esteemed Zhū even more.
He invited him into his room,
and they talked cordially for a long time.
Wáng took out all his writings for Zhū to evaluate.
Zhū skimmed through them with extreme speed,
and in a short while had finished a hundred pieces.
He said:
"You are also deeply immersed in this path?
However, when you put brush to paper,
while you have no thought of necessarily succeeding,
you still harbor a mind hoping for lucky success.
This alone already places you in the lower grade."
He then took the ones he had read
and explained them one by one.
Wáng was greatly pleased,
and treated him as a teacher.
He had the cook make *shuǐjiǎo* with sugarcane sugar.
Zhū ate them and found them sweet,
saying:
"In my life, I have never tasted such flavor.
Please make them again another day."
From then on, they got along very happily.
Zhū would come every three to five days,
and Wáng would always prepare *shuǐjiǎo* for him.
The Yúháng scholar occasionally met him.
Although they did not converse deeply,
his air of arrogant disdain diminished considerably.
One day,
he showed Zhū his examination practice essays.
Zhū saw that his friends had already marked them with many circles and praises.
He glanced over them once,
pushed them aside on the desk,
and did not say a word.
The scholar suspected he hadn't read them,
and urged him again.
Zhū replied he had already finished looking.
The scholar again suspected he didn't understand them.
Zhū said:
"What's difficult to understand?
They're just not good!"
The scholar said,
"You only glanced at the red markings;
how can you know they're not good?"
Zhū then recited his essay
as if he had read it long ago.
And as he recited, he criticized it.
The scholar, cramped and sweating,
left without a word.
After a while,
Zhū left.
The scholar entered
and insistently asked Wáng to show his own work.
Wáng refused.
The scholar forcibly searched and found it.
Seeing the many circles and dots on the essay,
he laughed and said:
"This looks a lot like *shuǐjiǎo*!"
Wáng was by nature simple and reticent,
and just blushed.
The next day,
when Zhū arrived,
Wáng told him everything.
Zhū angrily said:
"I thought 'the southerners would not revolt again,'
how dare this northern bumpkin act like this!
I must certainly repay him for this!"
Wáng earnestly advised him with warnings against frivolity and disrespect,
After the examination,
Wáng showed his essays to Sòng,
who praised them highly.
Once, while strolling through the temple halls,
they saw a blind monk sitting in the corridor,
selling medicine and offering medical consultations.
Sòng exclaimed in surprise:
"This is an extraordinary man!
He is most skilled at judging essays;
we must seek his advice."
So he told Wáng to go back and fetch his essays.
On the way, they met Yúháng Shēng,
and so they all went together.
Wáng called out to the monk and paid his respects.
The monk, suspecting he was a patient seeking medical advice,
inquired about his symptoms.
Wáng explained that he had come to seek his judgment on essays.
The monk laughed and said:
"Who has been talking so much?
Without eyes, how can I discuss essays?"
Wáng asked him to use his ears instead of his eyes.
The monk said,
"Three essays, over two thousand words—
who has the patience to listen to all that!
Better to burn them,
and I will judge them with my nose."
Wáng agreed.
Each time he burned one essay,
the monk sniffed and nodded, saying:
"You have begun by imitating the great masters;
though not yet perfectly true to them,
you are close.
I have just taken this in through my spleen."
Wáng asked:
"Could it pass the examination?"
The monk replied:
"It could pass."
Yúháng Shēng, not fully convinced,
first burned an essay by an ancient master to test him.
The monk sniffed again and said:
"Excellent!
This essay, I take it in through my heart.
Who but Guī Yǒuguāng or Hú Yǒurén could have written this!"
Shēng was greatly astonished
and then burned his own essay.
The monk said:
"Just now I sampled one piece;
I haven't seen the whole picture yet.
Why have you suddenly switched to another person?"
Shēng pretended, saying:
"That was a friend's work;
only this one piece.
This is my own writing."
The monk sniffed the remaining ashes,
coughed violently several times,
and said:
"Don't offer any more!
It's so grating I can't swallow it;
I had to force it down past my diaphragm.
If you burn another,
it will make me retch."
Shēng left in shame.
A few days later, the results were posted:
Shēng actually came out on top;
Wáng failed.
Shēng and Wáng went together to tell the monk.
The monk sighed and said:
"Though I am blind in my eyes,
I am not blind in my nose.
The examiners behind the curtain must be blind in their noses as well."
Soon after, Yúháng Shēng arrived,
swaggering with pride,
and said:
"Blind monk,
did you also get a taste of humble pie?
How do you explain this now?"
The monk replied:
"What I discussed was the writing itself;
I did not presume to discuss fate with you.
If you try to find the essays of the various examiners,
take one from each and burn them,
I will know which one is your teacher."
Shēng and Wáng searched together
and found only eight or nine.
Shēng said:
"If you are mistaken,
what shall be your penalty?"
The monk said angrily:
"Gouge out my blind eyes!"
Shēng began burning them.
For each essay,
the monk said it was not the one;
when they reached the sixth,
the monk suddenly turned toward the wall and vomited violently,
with gas passing like thunder.
Everyone burst out laughing.
The monk wiped his eyes and said to Shēng:
"This is truly your teacher!
At first, not knowing, I sniffed it abruptly—
it stabbed my nose,
pierced my belly,
and my bladder couldn't contain it;
it went straight out from below!"
Shēng flew into a rage,
left,
and said:
"We'll see tomorrow—
don't regret it,
don't regret it!"
After two or three days,
he still hadn't come;
when they went to look,
he had already moved away.
Then they realized he was that examiner's student.
Sòng comforted Wáng, saying:
"All of us scholars
should not blame others,
but should discipline ourselves:
not blaming others increases our virtue,
and disciplining ourselves advances our learning.
Your current setback
is indeed due to an unlucky fate;
but to be fair,
your writing is not yet at its peak.
If you continue to hone it,
the world will surely have those who recognize it without being told."
Wáng rose respectfully, filled with awe.
Hearing that the provincial examination would be held again the following year,
he decided not to return home,
but to stay and receive instruction.
Sòng said:
"In the capital, firewood is as costly as cassia and rice as precious as pearls;
don't worry about funds.
Behind my house, there is a stash of buried silver
that you can use."
He then showed him the spot.
Wáng declined, saying:
"In the past, Dòu Yí and Fàn Zhòngyān remained incorruptible even in poverty.
Now that I am fortunate enough to support myself,
how dare I taint myself?"
One day, Wáng fell asleep drunk,
and his servant and the gatekeeper secretly went to dig it up.
Wáng suddenly awoke
and heard noises behind the house;
stealing out to look,
he saw gold piled on the ground.
With their scheme exposed,
they both knelt in fear.
Just as Wáng was scolding them,
he noticed a gold cup
with many inscriptions;
upon closer inspection,
they were all his grandfather's name and style.
It turned out that Wáng's grandfather had once served as a郎官 in the southern ministry,
came to the capital and stayed here,
died suddenly of illness,
and this gold was what he left behind.
Wáng was overjoyed,
weighed the gold, and found it to be over eight hundred taels.
The next day, he told Sòng
and showed him the cup,
intending to share the gold with him,
but Sòng firmly declined, so he gave up.
He took a hundred taels to give to the blind monk,
but the monk had already left.
After several months of accumulation,
he studied with even greater diligence.
When the examination approached,
Sòng said:
"If you don't succeed in this battle,
then it truly is fate!"
Soon, he was disqualified for violating the rules.
Wáng remained silent;
Sòng wept bitterly,
unable to stop.
Wáng, on the contrary, comforted and consoled him.
Sòng said:
"I am hated by the Creator,
and have been troubled and distressed my entire life.
Now I have even implicated my good friend.
Such is fate!
Such is fate!"
Wáng said:
"Everything in life is governed by fate,
but as for you, sir, you have no ambition to advance—
that is not fate."
Sòng wiped away his tears and said:
"I have long wanted to speak,
but feared it would startle and alarm you.
I am not a living person,
but a wandering, drifting ghost.
In my youth, I was known for my talent,
but never succeeded in the examination halls.
Feigning madness, I went to the capital,
hoping to find someone who understood me,
to transmit my writings.
In the year of Jiǎshēn,
I unexpectedly met with disaster,
and have drifted like tumbleweed year after year.
Fortunately, you understood and cared for me,
so I exerted all my efforts to be your 'other mountain,'
a whetstone for your improvement.
My lifelong unfulfilled wish
was truly to borrow a good friend to achieve a moment of joy.
Now that literary fortune has met such misfortune,
who can remain indifferent!"
Wáng was also moved to tears,
and asked:
"Why have you lingered here?"
He said:
"Last year, the Heavenly Emperor issued an order,
entrusting Xuānshèng and Yánluówáng to investigate the ghosts of the calamity,
the superior ones to be assigned to various offices for employment,
the rest to be sent for reincarnation.
My humble name was already recorded,
but I had not yet reported for duty,
wishing first to witness the joy of your success.
Now I must bid farewell!"
Wáng asked:
"What position were you examined for?"
He said:
"In the Zǐtóng Prefecture, there is a vacancy for a Sīwénláng,
temporarily filled by a deaf and ignorant fellow,
which is why literary fortune has been turned upside down.
If by chance I obtain this post,
I will surely make the teachings of the sages flourish."
The next day,
he arrived joyfully,
saying:
"My wish is fulfilled!
Xuānshèng ordered me to write an 'Essay on Nature and the Way,'
and seeing it, he looked pleased,
saying I was fit to oversee literature.
Yánluówáng checked the register,
and wanted to reject me for 'verbal sins,'
but Xuānshèng argued on my behalf,
and I was able to take the post.
I bowed in gratitude,
and he called me closer to the desk,
instructing me:
'Now, out of pity for your talent,
I promote you to a pure and important post;
you must cleanse your heart and serve diligently,
and not repeat past transgressions.'
From this, one can see that the underworld values virtue and conduct even more than literary talent.
You must cultivate your conduct further,
but if you accumulate good deeds without slacking, it will suffice."
Wáng said:
"If that is so,
where is the virtue and conduct of that fellow from Yúháng?"
He said:
"I do not know.
But the rewards and punishments of the underworld
are never the slightest bit off.
Even that blind monk from the other day
was also a ghost,
a famous scholar of a previous dynasty.
Because in life he discarded too many papers with writing,
he was punished with blindness.
He himself wished to heal people's sufferings,
to atone for his past transgressions,
hence he roamed the marketplace in disguise."
Wáng ordered wine to be set out.
Sòng said:
"No need.
The disturbance of a whole year
ends at this moment;
just prepare some boiled dumplings for me, and that will suffice."
Wáng, sad and distressed, did not eat,
but sat and let him eat alone.
In a moment,
he had already finished three servings,
and holding his belly, said:
"This meal can fill me for three days;
I do this to remember your kindness.
What I ate before
is all behind the hut,
and has already turned into mushrooms.
Keep them as medicinal ingredients,
they can increase a child's intelligence."
Wáng asked about meeting again,
and he said:
"Since I now have official duties,
I must avoid suspicion."
Wáng asked again:
"If I offer a libation and pray at the Zǐtóng Temple,
will it reach you?"
He said:
"That is all useless.
The Ninth Heaven is very far,
but if you purify yourself and act diligently,
the earthly offices will report it,
and I will surely know."
Having said this,
he bid farewell and vanished.
Wáng looked behind the hut,
and indeed, purple mushrooms had grown.
He picked and stored them.
Beside them, a mound of fresh earth had risen,
and the boiled dumplings were clearly there.
Wáng returned home,
and disciplined himself even more strictly.
One night,
he dreamed that Sòng arrived in a carriage with a canopy,
saying:
"You once, in a fit of anger,
mistakenly killed a maidservant,
and were stripped of your official rank;
now your sincere conduct has redeemed it.
However, your fate is too thin to bear an official career."
That year,
he passed the provincial examination;
the next year,
he passed the metropolitan examination in spring.
After that, he did not take up an official post again.
He had two sons,
one of whom was extremely dull;
he fed him the mushrooms,
and the boy became greatly intelligent.
Later, on business, he went to Jīnlíng,
and met the scholar from Yúháng at an inn.
They spoke of their long separation,
and the scholar from Yúháng was deeply humble and self-effacing,
but his temples were already streaked with gray.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Mù Shēng
was a man of Chángshā.
His family was poor and pure,
and in winter, they had no padded clothes.
One evening, as he sat despondently,
a woman entered,
her clothes dazzling and beautiful but her face dark and ugly.
She smiled and said:
"Aren't you cold?"
Startled, he asked who she was.
She said:
"I am a fox immortal.
I pity your lonely desolation,
and wish to share warmth on your cold bed."
He feared she was a fox,
and was repelled by her ugliness,
so he cried out loudly.
The woman placed a silver ingot on the table,
saying:
"If you agree to be harmonious and good with me,
I will give you this."
Pleased, he complied.
The bed had no mattress or bedding,
so she used her robe instead.
As dawn approached,
she rose and instructed him:
"With what I gave you,
quickly buy soft silk to make bedding;
with the rest, make padded clothes and quilts,
and that will be enough.
If we can be together forever,
do not worry about poverty."
Then she left.
He told his wife,
and she was also pleased.
They immediately bought silk and sewed the bedding.
When the woman came at night,
she saw the new bedding and said happily:
"Your wife has worked hard!"
She left gold to repay her.
From then on, she came every night without fail.
Each time she left,
she would leave something behind.
Over a year later,
the house was repaired and tidy,
both inside and out everyone wore brocade and embroidered silks,
truly living like a wealthy family without an official title.
The woman gradually gave fewer gifts,
and from this, the student grew weary of her.
He hired a sorcerer to come,
who drew talismans on the door.
The woman bit them off, broke them, and threw them away,
then entered and pointed at the student, saying:
"To betray virtue and be ungrateful—
you have reached the extreme!
But how can this harm me?
If you are tired of me and look down on me,
I will leave on my own.
However, since affection and righteousness are now severed,
what you received from me
must be repaid!"
She left in anger.
The student was afraid
and told the sorcerer.
The sorcerer set up an altar,
but before the arrangements were complete,
he suddenly fell to the ground,
blood flowing all over his face.
Looking at him,
one of his ears had been cut off.
Everyone was terrified,
and they scattered in flight.
The sorcerer also covered his ear and fled.
Stones as big as basins were thrown inside the room,
and the doors, windows, pots, and steamers
were no longer intact.
The student hid under the bed,
trembling, shrinking, sweating, and shaking.
Soon he saw the woman enter carrying something,
with a cat's head and a puppy's tail.
She placed it before the bed
and urged it, saying:
"Xīxī,
go chew the feet of this treacherous man."
The creature immediately bit his shoe,
its teeth sharper than blades.
The student was terrified
and wanted to curl up and hide his feet,
but his limbs could not move.
The creature chewed his toes,
making crisp, crunching sounds.
The student, in extreme pain,
pleaded and prayed.
The woman said:
"Bring out all the gold and pearls—
hide nothing."
The student agreed.
The woman said:
"Hēhē!"
The creature then stopped.
The student could not get up,
so he just told her where they were.
The woman went to search herself,
and aside from pearl hairpins and clothes,
she found only a little over two hundred taels of silver.
The woman thought it too little
and said again:
"Xīxī!"
The creature resumed chewing.
The student wailed and begged for mercy.
The woman set a limit of ten days
to repay six hundred taels of silver.
The student promised,
and the woman then carried the creature away.
After a while,
the family gradually gathered,
pulled the student out from under the bed,
his feet dripping with blood,
having lost two toes.
Looking around the room,
all the valuables were gone,
only the tattered quilt from back then remained.
They used it to cover the student
and had him lie down.
Fearing she would return in ten days,
he sold maidservants and clothes
to make up the amount.
When the time came,
the woman indeed arrived.
He hurriedly gave it to her,
and she left without a word.
From then on, she never came again.
The student's foot wounds
took half a year of medicine to heal,
and his family was as poor as before.
The fox then went to a nearby village to a man named Yú.
Yú worked as a farmer,
and his family was not well-off.
Within three years,
he followed the precedent of donating grain for an official title,
and his grand houses spread continuously.
The fine clothes he wore
were half from the student's household.
When the student saw him,
he dared not ask.
Once, by chance, he went to the countryside
and met the woman on the road.
He knelt for a long time by the roadside.
The woman said nothing,
but wrapped five or six taels of silver in a plain handkerchief,
threw it to him from afar,
turned around, and went straight away.
Later, Yú died early,
and the woman still occasionally came to his home.
Whenever she did, gold and silk would disappear from the house.
Yú's son, seeing her come,
bowed and paid respects to her,
praying from afar:
"Even though my father has passed away,
we, your children, are all like your own sons.
Even if you do not care for us,
how can you bear to sit by and let us live in poverty?"
After the woman left,
she never came again.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"When evil beings come,
killing them is also a brave act.
But once you have received their kindness,
even a ghost or spirit should not be betrayed.
To become noble and then kill Zhào Mèng—
even the worthy and heroic would condemn this.
If a person does not truly desire something in their heart,
how could ten thousand measures of grain move them?
