Observing how his face lit up at the sight of gold,
it seems that where profit lies,
people are willing to risk their lives and disgrace their conduct without regret.
How pitiful are the greedy—
they end up bringing ruin upon themselves!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Gōngzǐ Sūn of Luòyáng,
named Qí,
married the daughter of Prefect Jiǎng,
and they were very compatible.
At twenty, she died young,
and he was overwhelmed with grief.
He left home
and lived in a mountain villa.
Once during rainy weather,
he was lying down during the day,
and there was no one in the room.
Suddenly, from behind the inner room's curtain,
he saw a woman's feet exposed.
Suspicious, he asked about it.
A woman lifted the curtain and entered,
around eighteen or nineteen years old,
her clothes simple and clean,
but slightly dark-skinned and pockmarked,
like a girl from a poor family.
Thinking she must be someone from the village renting a room,
he scolded her:
"If you need something, you should tell the family—
how dare you enter so lightly!"
The woman smiled and said:
"I am not from this village;
my ancestral home is in Shāndōng,
and my surname is Lǚ.
My father was a literary scholar.
My childhood name is Wúbìng.
I followed my father as a guest traveler,
and lost my parents early.
I admire you, sir, as a scion of a distinguished family and a renowned scholar,
and wish to serve as a literary maid like Zhèng Xuán's."
Sūn laughed and said:
"Your intention is most kind.
However, we live here in mixed company,
which is truly inconvenient.
Allow me, upon returning home,
to send a carriage to formally engage you."
The girl hesitated and said:
"I consider myself crude and unworthy;
how dare I aspire to be an equal partner?
I merely wish to serve at your desk,
and I surely won't hold the books upside down."
Sūn said:
"Even taking a maid requires an auspicious day."
He then pointed to the bookshelf,
telling her to fetch the fourth volume of the almanac—
this was to test her.
The girl searched through it and found it.
She first looked through it herself,
then presented it to him,
smiling and saying:
"Today, the 'Hékuí' star is not in the chamber."
Sūn's mind was slightly moved,
and he let her stay hidden in his room.
With nothing to do while idle,
she dusted his desk and tidied his books,
lit incense and cleaned the censers,
making the whole room bright and clean.
Sūn was pleased with her.
When evening came,
he sent his servant to sleep elsewhere.
The girl, with lowered brows and submissive eyes,
attended to him with utmost diligence.
Ordered to retire,
she first took the candle and left.
In the middle of the night, waking from sleep,
he felt as if there was someone lying by the bed;
reaching out to feel,
he realized it was the girl,
and grabbed and shook her.
The girl startled awake,
and stood by the bed.
Sūn said:
"Why aren't you sleeping elsewhere?
Is the bedside your place to sleep?"
The girl said:
"I am terribly afraid."
Sūn took pity on her,
and placed a pillow for her inside the bed.
Suddenly, he noticed her breath,
fresh as lotus stamens,
and found it extraordinary;
he called her to share his pillow,
and could not help but feel his heart stirred;
gradually they shared the same quilt,
and he was greatly delighted.
Considering that hiding her was not a good plan,
and fearing criticism if they returned together,
Sūn had a maternal aunt
living nearby, just over a dozen doors away.
He planned to have her escape to her house first,
and then bring her back later.
The girl agreed it was good,
and then said:
"Auntie,
I am well acquainted with her;
there's no need to inform her first,
I'll go right away."
Sūn saw her off,
and she climbed over the wall and left.
Sūn's maternal aunt
was a widowed old lady.
Early in the morning, opening her door,
the girl slipped in.
The old lady questioned her,
and she replied:
"Your nephew sent me to inquire after you, Auntie.
The young master wishes to return home,
but the road is long and he lacks a mount,
so he left me here temporarily."
The old lady believed her.
So she stayed there.
When Sūn returned home,
he falsely claimed that his aunt had a maid
whom he wished to be given to him,
and sent someone to carry her back in a sedan.
She attended to him whether he sat or lay down.
Over time, he grew even fonder of her,
and took her as his concubine.
When distinguished families proposed marriages,
he refused them all,
seemingly determined to stay with her for life.
The girl learned of this,
and earnestly urged him to marry;
so he married a woman from the Xǔ family,
yet remained deeply fond of Wúbìng.
Lady Xǔ was very virtuous,
and hardly contended for his attention at night;
Wúbìng served Lady Xǔ with even greater respect: thus, wife and concubine lived in harmony.
Lady Xǔ bore a son named Ājiān,
and Wúbìng loved and held him as if he were her own.
When the boy was just three years old,
he would leave his wet nurse
to sleep with Wúbìng,
and would not go when Lady Xǔ called him.
Not long after,
Lady Xǔ fell ill and passed away.
On her deathbed,
she entrusted Sūn, saying:
"Wúbìng loves our son the most;
you may let her be his mother;
you may even make her your principal wife."
After the burial,
Sūn intended to carry out her words,
and informed his clan relatives,
but they all said it was not permissible;
the girl also firmly declined,
so he stopped.
In the county there was a daughter of the Minister of Personnel, Wáng Tiāngōng,
newly widowed,
who came to propose marriage.
Sūn was quite unwilling to marry her,
but Wáng repeatedly requested it.
The matchmaker praised her beauty,
and the clan admired her family's influence,
so they all urged him on.
Sūn became confused,
and married her again.
Her appearance was indeed stunning;
but she was excessively arrogant,
regarding clothes and utensils,
she often found them displeasing,
and would immediately destroy or discard them.
Out of love and respect, Sūn
could not bear to oppose her.
Within a few months of entering the household,
she monopolized favor and the master's chambers,
and when Wúbìng came before her,
whether she laughed or cried, it was considered a fault.
She often vented her anger on her husband,
and frequently quarreled and fought with him.
Sūn suffered bitterly from this,
and often slept alone.
The wife grew angry again.
Sūn could not endure it,
so he found a pretext to go to the capital,
fleeing from his wife's torment.
The wife blamed Wúbìng for his distant journey.
Wúbìng bowed humbly and held her breath,
anxiously watching her expression,
but the wife remained displeased.
At night, she made Wúbìng keep watch at the foot of the bed,
and the child ran to join her.
Whenever she called Wúbìng to serve her,
the child would cry.
The wife cursed her in annoyance.
Wúbìng hurriedly called the wet nurse to take the child,
but he wouldn't leave;
when forced,
he cried even louder.
The wife angrily got up,
and savagely beat him countless times,
before he finally went with the wet nurse.
Because of this, the child fell ill with fright,
and refused to eat.
The wife forbade Wúbìng from seeing him.
The child cried all day long,
and the wife scolded the wet nurse,
ordering her to throw him on the ground.
The child, breathless and hoarse,
cried out asking for water;
the wife forbade giving him any.
As dusk fell,
Wúbìng, seeing the wife was not around,
secretly gave the child water.
When the child saw her,
he pushed the water aside, grabbed her lapel,
and wailed uncontrollably.
Hearing this, the wife
stormed out in a furious rage.
The child, hearing her voice, stopped crying,
gave one leap, and then died.
Wúbìng wept bitterly.
The wife angrily said:
"Vile slave, putting on an ugly show!
Do you think you can threaten me with the child's death?
Never mind that it's just a swaddling thing of the Sūn family;
even if I killed a prince's heir,
I, the daughter of Minister Wáng Tiāngōng, could handle it!"
Wúbìng then stifled her sobs and held back tears,
asking for burial items.
The wife refused,
and immediately ordered the body discarded.
After the wife left,
Wúbìng secretly felt the child,
and found his limbs still warm.
She whispered to the wet nurse:
"Quickly take him away,
wait a little in the wilds,
I will follow shortly.
If he is dead,
we will discard him together;
if alive,
we will raise him together."
The wet nurse said:
"Yes."
Wúbìng went into the room,
took out hairpins and earrings,
and caught up with her.
Together they looked at the child,
who had already revived.
The two were overjoyed,
and planned to hurry to a separate estate,
to rely on an aunt.
The wet nurse worried that Wúbìng's delicate steps would be a burden,
but Wúbìng went ahead to wait for her,
swift as the whistling wind.
The wet nurse had to run with all her might to keep up.
Around the second watch,
the child's condition became critical,
and they could go no further.
So they turned sideways into a village,
reaching an old farmer's house.
They waited by the door until dawn,
then knocked to borrow a room.
They traded hairpins and earrings for funds,
summoned both shamans and doctors,
but the illness ultimately did not improve.
Wúbìng, covering her face, wept and said:
"Nurse, take good care of the child,
I will go find his father."
As the wet nurse was startled by her absurdity,
Wúbìng had already vanished.
The nurse was utterly shocked and bewildered.
That day,
Sūn was in the capital,
just resting on his bed,
when Wúbìng quietly entered.
Sūn rose in shock and said:
"I just fell asleep and am already dreaming!"
Wúbìng grasped his hand, choked with sobs,
stamping her feet but unable to utter a sound.
After a long, long time,
she finally cried out and said:
"I endured countless hardships,
and fled with the child to Yáng—"
Before finishing the sentence,
she burst into loud weeping,
fell to the ground, and vanished.
Sūn was terrified out of his wits,
still suspecting it was a dream;
he called his attendants to look together,
but her clothes and shoes were clearly there,
leaving him greatly perplexed and unable to understand.
He immediately packed his luggage,
and raced back like a shooting star.
Upon hearing that the child had died and the concubine had fled,
he beat his chest in great sorrow.
He spoke reproachfully to his wife,
who retorted with sharp words.
Sūn grew furious,
drew a knife;
maids and old women blocked and tried to rescue,
unable to get close,
he threw it from a distance.
The back of the blade struck her forehead,
breaking the skin and causing blood to flow,
she rushed out with disheveled hair, howling,
intending to run and inform her family.
Sūn caught her and dragged her back,
beat her countless times with a stick,
her clothes were torn to shreds,
the pain from her injuries made it impossible for her to turn over.
Sūn ordered her carried to a room to be nursed,
planning to wait until she recovered before divorcing her.
The wife's brothers heard of this,
were enraged,
led many horsemen to his gate;
Sūn also gathered strong servants, armed to defend,
both sides shouted and cursed,
only dispersing at the end of the day.
Wáng, still unsatisfied,
filed a lawsuit.
Sūn defended himself and entered the city,
personally went to present his case for trial,
accusing his wife of her wicked conduct.
The magistrate could not subdue him,
sent him to the educational official for punishment to please Wáng.
Educational official Zhū Xiānshēng,
a descendant of an official family,
upright and unyielding.
Upon investigating and learning the truth,
angrily said:
"Does the magistrate in the hall think I am one of those filthy instructors in the world,
extorting money that harms heaven and reason,
one who sucks people's sores and piles?
Such beggarly behavior,
I cannot do!"
In the end, he did not accept the order.
Sūn returned openly.
Wáng had no recourse against him,
then signaled to friends,
to mediate for him,
hoping to have Sūn apologize at his home.
Sūn refused,
after ten attempts no resolution could be reached.
The wife's wounds gradually healed,
he wanted to divorce her,
but feared the Wáng family would not accept her back,
so he delayed and let things remain.
The concubine gone, the child dead,
day and night his heart grieved,
he wished to find the wet nurse,
to ask her about the circumstances.
Recalling Wúbìng's words
"fled to Yáng,"
there was a village called Yángjiātuǎn nearby,
he suspected she was there;
went to inquire,
but no one knew.
Someone said there was a Yánggǔ fifty li away,
he sent a horseman to ask,
and indeed found her,
the child gradually recovered;
meeting each other, both were joyful,
he brought her back with him.
The child, seeing his father,
wailed loudly,
Sūn also shed tears.
The wife, hearing the child was still alive,
rushed out in a rage,
intending to berate and scold.
The child was crying,
opened his eyes and saw the wife,
startled, threw himself into his father's arms,
as if seeking to hide.
Sūn held him and looked,
the child had already stopped breathing.
He urgently called to him,
after a while he revived.
Sūn angrily said:
"I don't know what cruel abuse
could have driven my child to this!"
Then he immediately wrote a divorce document,
and sent the wife back.
The Wáng family indeed would not accept her,
and carried her back to Sūn.
Sūn had no choice,
father and son moved to a separate courtyard,
cutting off contact with the wife.
The wet nurse then fully recounted Wúbìng's circumstances,
and Sūn realized she had been a ghost.
Moved by her righteousness,
he buried her clothes and shoes,
and inscribed the tombstone:
"Tomb of ghost wife Lǚ Wúbìng."
Not long after,
the wife gave birth to a son,
but strangled him with her own hands.
Sūn grew even more furious,
again divorced her;
Wáng again sent her back.
Sūn then prepared a petition,
appealing to higher authorities,
but all, because of the celestial official's influence,
set it aside without action.
Later, the celestial official died,
Sūn persisted in his appeal,
and finally a judgment was made ordering her permanent return to her natal family.
From then on, Sūn did not marry again,
but took a maid as concubine.
The wife, having returned home,
her shrewish reputation became widely known,
for three or four years no one asked for her hand.
The wife suddenly repented,
but it was already irreparable.
There was an old woman from the Sūn family,
who happened to visit her home.
The wife treated her well,
shedding tears in her presence;
gauging her feelings,
she seemed to miss her former husband.
The old woman returned and told Sūn,
Sūn laughed and dismissed it.
Another year or so later,
the wife's mother also died,
leaving her alone with no one to rely on,
her sisters-in-law quite despised and envied her;
the wife became even more displaced,
weeping daily.
A poor scholar lost his spouse,
her elder brother proposed giving her a generous dowry and sending her off,
but the wife refused.
Often she secretly asked intermediaries to convey her feelings to Sūn,
tearfully telling of her repentance,
but Sūn would not listen.
One day,
the wife, leading a maid,
stole a donkey and mounted it,
and actually ran to Sūn.
Sūn was just coming out from inside,
she knelt before him at the steps,
weeping uncontrollably.
Sūn wanted to send her away,
she tugged at his clothes and knelt again.
Sūn firmly declined, saying:
"If we were to live together again,
it would be fine if there were never any discord;
but once something else happens,
your brothers are like tigers and wolves,
to seek separation again,
how could it be possible!"
The wife said:
"I have secretly run to you,
there is absolutely no reason to return.
Keep me if you will,
otherwise I shall die!
Moreover, from twenty-one I followed you,
at twenty-three I was cast out,
even if I were ten parts wicked,
could there not be one part of affection?"
Then she removed a bracelet from her wrist,
and bound it around both her feet,
covering it with her sleeve,
saying:
"At this moment, the vow before the incense and fire,
do you not remember it?"
Sūn then felt his eyes grow moist with tears,
had someone help her into the room;
yet he still suspected Wáng Shì of deceit,
wanting a word from her brothers as proof.
The wife said:
"I left home in secret,"
"how can I face my brothers again?
If you do not believe me,
I have the means of death here with me.
Allow me to cut off a finger to prove my sincerity."
Then she drew a sharp blade from her waist,
extended the little finger of her left hand by the bedside and severed it,
blood gushing forth like a fountain.
Sūn was greatly alarmed,
and hurriedly bandaged it for her.
The woman's face changed with the pain,
yet she did not utter a single groan.
Instead, she smiled and said:
"Today, my dream of yellow millet has awakened.
I only wish to borrow a humble room to plan my renunciation of the world.
Why must you suspect me?"
Sūn then had his son and concubine live in separate quarters,
while he himself went back and forth between the two places day and night.
He also sought good medicine daily to treat her finger wound,
which healed after a little over a month.
From then on, the woman abstained from meat and wine,
merely shutting herself in to chant Buddhist sutras.
After living there for a long time,
seeing the household affairs neglected and in disarray,
she said to Sūn:
"When I came here,
I originally intended to disregard all other matters;
but now, seeing such extravagance in expenses,
I fear your descendants may face starvation.
Having no other choice,
I will shamelessly manage things once more."
She then gathered the maids and elderly servant women,
holding them accountable daily for their spinning and weaving.
The family members, thinking she had imposed herself,
treated her with disrespect,
secretly mocking and ridiculing her,
but the woman acted as if she did not hear.
Later, when she inspected their work,
she whipped those who were lazy without leniency,
and only then did everyone begin to fear her.
She also sat behind a curtain to oversee the stewards in charge of accounts,
managing everything meticulously and in detail.
Sūn was greatly pleased,
and had his son and concubine pay their respects to her every morning.
Ā Jiān was already nine years old,
and the woman treated him with extra warmth and care.
When he went to school in the morning,
she often saved sweet treats for his return;
the child also gradually grew fond of her.
One day,
the boy threw a stone at a sparrow,
and as the woman happened to be passing by,
it struck her forehead and she fell,
remaining silent for a long while.
Sūn was furious,
and beat the child.
When the woman regained consciousness,
she strenuously stopped him,
and even said happily:
"In the past, I abused the child,
and my heart was never at ease.
Now, fortunately, one sin has been redeemed."
Sūn loved her even more dearly,
but the woman often refused him,
sending him to sleep with the concubine.
After several years,
she gave birth multiple times but each child died young.
She said:
"This is retribution for killing the child in the past."
After Ā Jiān married,
she entrusted external affairs to her son,
and internal affairs to her daughter-in-law.
One day, she said:
"I shall die on such-and-such a day."
Sūn did not believe her.
The woman prepared her own burial items,
and when the day arrived,
she changed her clothes, entered the coffin, and passed away.
Her complexion was as if she were alive,
and a strange fragrance filled the room;
only after she was encoffined
did the fragrance gradually fade.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"What the heart favors
originally does not lie in beauty or ugliness.
How do we know that Máo Qiáng and Xī Shī
were not considered beautiful by those who loved themselves?
Yet, had she not encountered jealousy and harshness,
her virtue would not have been revealed,
almost making people laugh alongside those who delight in scabs.
As for the lady behind the brocade screen,
her innate roots were originally deep,
thus with a sudden awakening,
she immediately attained Bodhi;
whereas in the path of hell,
are all those who enjoyed wealth and honor without enduring hardship."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Xià Shāng
was a man from Héjiān.
His father, Dōnglíng,
was extremely wealthy and extravagant.
Whenever he ate steamed buns,
he would discard the corners,
littering them all over the ground.
Because he was fat and heavy,
people called him
"The Corner-Discarding Grand Marshal."
In his later years,
his family became extremely poor,
often lacking food for the day;
his two arms grew thin,
with skin hanging loose like empty bags,
so people called him
"The Alms-Seeking Monk"
— meaning he was like a hanging bag.
On his deathbed,
he said to Shāng:
"In my life, I recklessly wasted the gifts of nature,
offending Heaven's wrath,
and thus came to die of hunger and cold.
You must cherish blessings and strive diligently,
to atone for your father's transgressions."
Shāng strictly followed his father's dying instructions,
remaining honest and simple without fail,
farming by himself to support his livelihood.
All the villagers loved and respected him.
A certain wealthy old man pitied his poverty,
lent him capital,
and had him learn trading as a peddler,
but he often lost the principal.
Ashamed and unable to repay,
he asked to work as a laborer.
The old man refused.
Shāng, uneasy and startled,
sold all his fields and house,
and went to repay the old man.
When the old man learned the truth,
he pitied him even more,
and forcibly redeemed his former property for him;
he also lent him a large sum of money,
to engage in commerce.
Shāng declined, saying:
"I still cannot repay a dozen or so taels of gold,
how can I incur a donkey or horse debt for the next life?"
The old man then invited another merchant to accompany him.
After several months, they returned,
barely managing not to incur losses;
the old man did not collect interest,
and had him trade again.
Over a year later,
the goods and capital filled a cart.
On the way back, crossing the river,
they encountered a hurricane,
the boat nearly capsized,
and half the goods were lost.
Calculating what remained upon returning,
it was roughly enough to repay the principal,
so he said to the merchant:
"When Heaven impoverishes someone,
who can save them?
All this is because I have burdened you!"
He then checked the account book and handed it to the merchant,
withdrawing himself.
The old man urged him strongly again,
but he absolutely refused,
and continued farming as before.
He often sighed to himself:

It happened that a sorceress from elsewhere arrived,
who practiced divination with coins
and knew all about people's fortunes.
Shāng Jìng went to visit her.
The sorceress
was an old woman.
Her dwelling was neat and clean,
with a shrine set up in the middle
where incense was constantly burning.
After the merchant bowed in worship,
the sorceress demanded payment.
Shāng handed over a hundred coins,
which the sorceress placed entirely into a wooden tube.
Holding it, she knelt before the shrine,
shaking it as if in prayer.
After a while, she stood up,
poured the coins into her hand,
and then arranged them in order on the table.
Her method considered the inscribed side as unfavorable
and the reverse side as auspicious.
Up to the fifty-eighth coin, all were inscribed,
but after that, all were reverse.
She then asked:
"How old are you?"
He replied:
"Twenty-eight years old."
The sorceress shook her head and said:
"Too early!
Too early!
Sir, you are currently under the fortune of your ancestors,
not your own.
At fifty-eight,
you will begin your own fortune,
and only then will there be no complications."
He asked:
"What is meant by the fortune of ancestors?"
She said:
"If ancestors did good deeds,
and their blessings are not yet exhausted,
then their descendants enjoy them;
if ancestors did wrong,
and their misfortunes are not yet exhausted,
then their descendants also suffer them."
Shāng counted on his fingers and said:
"Another thirty years,
and my teeth will be old and worn,
nearing the grave."
The sorceress said:
"Before fifty-eight,
there will be five years of respite,
allowing some planning;
but it will only spare you from hunger and cold.
In your fifty-eighth year,
a great sum of money will come to you on its own,
requiring no effort.
Sir, you have committed no wrongs in this life,
and in the next life, you will enjoy endless blessings."
He bid farewell to the sorceress and returned,
half in doubt, half in belief.
Yet he remained content in poverty and kept to himself,
not daring to seek recklessly.
Later, when he reached fifty-three,
he paid attention to verify it.
At that time, during the spring plowing,
he fell ill with malaria and could not farm.
After recovering,
there was a great drought,
and the early crops all withered.
Near autumn, it finally rained,
but his family had no other seeds,
so he planted millet on all his few acres of land.
Then another drought came,
and half the buckwheat and beans died,
but the millet remained unharmed;
later, rain fell abundantly,
and the harvest doubled.
The following spring, there was a great famine,
but he managed to avoid starvation.
Shāng thus believed the sorceress,
borrowed capital from an old man,
and engaged in small-scale lending,
often making small profits;
some urged him to become a big merchant,
but Shāng refused.
When he reached fifty-seven,
he happened to be repairing a wall
and dug up an iron pot from the ground;
when he lifted the lid,
white vapor like cotton floss emerged,
and he was too afraid to open it further.
After a while,
the vapor dissipated,
and the pot was full of silver ingots.
He and his wife moved it together,
and upon weighing, it totaled one thousand three hundred and twenty-five taels.
They secretly remarked that the sorceress's prediction was slightly off.
The neighbor's wife entered Shāng's house
and caught a glimpse of it;
she returned and told her husband.
The husband was envious
and secretly reported it to the county magistrate.
The magistrate was extremely greedy
and detained Shāng, demanding the gold.
Shāng's wife wanted to hide half of it,
but Shāng said:
"What is not rightfully ours,
keeping it will invite disaster."
He handed it all over.
After obtaining the gold,
the magistrate feared there might be more hidden,
so he also seized the container
and filled it with the gold;
it was full,
and only then did he release Shāng.
Not long after,
the magistrate was promoted to assistant prefect of Nánchāng.
A year later,
Shāng traveled to Nánchāng for trade,
only to find that the magistrate had already died.
The magistrate's wife and children were preparing to return home
and were selling off their heavy belongings;
among them were several baskets of tung oil,
and Shāng, finding the price cheap,
bought them and brought them home.
Upon arriving home,
he found the containers leaking,
so he poured the oil into other vessels,
only to discover two silver ingots inside;
checking all of them, they were all the same.
Exchanging them for currency,
he happened to obtain the exact amount of the previously dug-up silver.
Shāng thus suddenly became wealthy,
and he increasingly aided the poor,
generous and unstinting.
His wife urged him to save for their descendants,
but Shāng said:
"This is precisely how I leave something for my descendants."
The neighbor had become utterly destitute, reduced to begging,
and though he wanted to ask for help,
he felt ashamed in his heart.
Shāng heard of this and told him:
"What happened in the past
was because my time had not yet come,
so the ghosts and spirits used your hand to thwart it;
what fault is it of yours?"
He then provided for him generously.
The neighbor was moved to tears.
Later, Shāng lived to eighty,
and his descendants carried on his legacy,
remaining prosperous for generations.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Extravagance and excess,
even kings and nobles cannot avoid,
let alone commoners!
In life, they waste the gifts of heaven;
in death, they have no rice for their mouths—
how pitiable!
Fortunately, like a dying bird's mournful cry,
the son was able to rectify his father's errors,
and after seventy years of decline and ruin,
he ultimately restored the family's fortunes;
otherwise,
the father's misdeeds would burden the son,
and the son would in turn burden the grandson,
until the line ended in beggary.
What kind of old sorceress was this,
who could unveil heaven's secrets?
Alas!
How strange!"
Based on the twenty-four-volume manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Yáo Ān
was a man from Líntáo
with handsome features and graceful bearing.
In the same village lived a man named Gōng,
who had a daughter named Lǜ'é,
a beautiful girl who was well-read.
She was selective in choosing a husband and remained unmarried.
Her mother said to people:
"Only a man of distinguished family and elegant appearance
like Mr. Yáo will I give my daughter to in marriage."
Upon hearing this,
Yáo deceived his wife into looking into a well
and pushed her in, drowning her.
He then married Lǜ'é.
They were very affectionate with each other.
However, because she was so beautiful,
he became suspicious of her.
He kept her confined indoors,
following her every step;
if she wanted to visit her parents,
he would use his elbows to hold her robe,
covering her as they went out.
Upon entering the carriage, he would seal it shut,
then ride closely behind.
After staying overnight,
he would hurry her to return with him.
Lǜ'é could not bear this,
and angrily said:
"If I had a secret lover,
how could such petty restrictions stop me!"
When Yáo had to go elsewhere,
he would lock her in the room.
She grew increasingly resentful.
Waiting for him to leave,
she deliberately placed another key outside the door to arouse his suspicion.
When Yáo saw it, he flew into a rage,
demanding to know where it came from.
Lǜ'é angrily replied:
"I don't know!"
Yáo grew even more suspicious
and watched her even more closely.
One day,
returning from outside,
he eavesdropped for a long time,
then unlocked and opened the door,
careful not to make a sound,
and quietly slipped inside.
He saw a man wearing a marten-fur hat lying on the bed.
Enraged,
he grabbed a knife and rushed in,
hacking at the man with all his might.
Drawing closer to look,
he realized it was his wife, napping during the day and feeling cold,
so she had covered her face with marten fur.
Horrified,
he stamped his feet in regret.
Old Man Gōng angrily brought the case to the authorities.
Yáo was arrested,
stripped of his scholar's robe, and tortured with instruments.
Yáo went bankrupt,
using a huge sum of money to bribe officials high and low,
and thus escaped death.
From then on, he became mentally confused,
as if he had lost something.
Once, while sitting alone,
he saw his wife and a bearded man
being intimate on the bed.
Disgusted,
he grabbed a knife and rushed over,
but they vanished.
Returning to sit down,
he saw them again.
Furious,
he struck the bed with his knife,
splitting the mat and bedding.
In a rage, he gripped the knife,
approached the bed, and waited.
He saw his wife standing facing him,
looking at him and laughing.
He suddenly slashed at her,
immediately cutting off her head.
After sitting down again,
his wife remained in the same spot,
still laughing as before.
At night, when the candles were extinguished,
he would hear sounds of wanton intimacy,
too indecent to describe.
This happened every day,
until he could bear it no longer.
So he sold his fields and house,
planning to move elsewhere.
That night,
thieves tunneled through the wall and entered,
robbing him of his money and fleeing.
From then on, he was destitute, without even a place to stand an awl.
He died in anger and resentment.
The villagers buried him in a rough coffin.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"To love the new and kill the old—
how cruel!
People only know that the new ghost can become a vengeful spirit,
but they do not realize that the old ghost can steal one's soul.
Alas!
To cut off one's toes to fit the shoes—
how can one avoid ruin!"
Based on the twenty-four-volume manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
When the Ming dynasty was overthrown,
the flames of war rose high.
A certain Mr. Liú Zhīshēng of Wūlíng
gathered a following of tens of thousands
and was about to cross the river to the south.
Suddenly a stout man came to the gate of his stockade,
wearing tattered clothes that left his belly exposed,
and requested an audience with the commander.
Mr. Liú invited him in and spoke with him,
and was greatly pleased.
He asked his name,
and the man called himself Cǎiwēi Wēng.
Liú kept him on as a staff advisor
and presented him with a sword.
The old man said:
"I have my own sharp weapons;
I have no need for spears or halberds."
Liú asked:
"Where are your weapons?"
The old man then pulled aside his clothes to expose his belly;
his navel was large enough to hold a chicken egg.
He held his breath and puffed it out,
when suddenly the skin around his navel made a tearing sound,
and the hilt of a sword protruded.
He grasped it and drew it out—
the gleaming blade was like frost.
Liú was greatly astonished
and asked:
"Is that all?"
The old man laughed, pointed to his belly, and said:
"This is an arsenal;
what is there that it does not contain?"
Liú ordered him to produce a bow and arrows,
and again as before,
a carved bow emerged.
With a slight holding of his breath,
an arrow flew out and fell,
and they emerged without end.
Afterward, he inserted the sword into his navel,
and it all vanished.
Liú regarded him as supernatural,
shared quarters with him,
and treated him with the utmost respect and courtesy.
Though orders in the camp were strict,
the ragtag crowd
still occasionally went out to plunder.
The old man said:
"Discipline is the essence of an army;
now you command tens of thousands of men,
yet you cannot awe and control their hearts—
this is the path to defeat and ruin."
Liú was pleased with him,
and so he began to inspect the troops.
Those who seized women or property
were beheaded as a warning to all.
The army became somewhat more orderly,
but the problem could not be entirely eradicated.
From time to time, the old man would ride out
and roam among the troops,
and then the army's fierce generals and arrogant soldiers
would suddenly find their heads falling to the ground,
for no apparent reason.
Thus they all grew suspicious of the old man.
Earlier, his strict disciplinary measures
had already made the soldiers fear and resent him;
now their hatred and resentment grew even stronger.
The various unit commanders slandered him to Liú, saying:
"Cǎiwēi Wēng
practices sorcery.
Since ancient times, famous generals
have been known for their wisdom,
not for sorcery.
Followers of Fúyún and Báiquè
ultimately brought about their own destruction.
Now innocent officers and soldiers
often lose their heads for no reason,
and morale is turbulent and fearful;
for you, General, to keep company with him
is also a dangerous path.
It would be better to deal with him."
Liú followed their advice
and plotted to kill him while he slept.
He sent someone to spy on the old man;
the old man was lying on his back with his belly exposed,
snoring like thunder.
The men were overjoyed,
surrounded his quarters with soldiers,
and two men entered with swords
and cut off his head.
But when they raised their swords,
his head had already rejoined his body,
and he was snoring as before.
They were greatly shocked.
They then hacked at his belly;
it split open without bleeding,
and inside were dense clusters of spears and halberds,
all with their points exposed.
The men were even more terrified
and dared not approach.
From a distance, they prodded him with a lance,
and iron crossbows suddenly fired,
shooting several of them.
The men scattered in panic
and reported to Liú.
Liú hurried to the spot,
but the old man had already vanished without a trace.
Based on the twenty-four-volume manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Cuī Měng,
courtesy name Wùměng,
was the son of an aristocratic family in Jiànchāng.
His nature was resolute and firm.
When young and studying in school,
if any of the other children offended him even slightly,
he would immediately raise his fists and beat them,
and his teacher repeatedly admonished him without effect.
His given name and courtesy name
were both bestowed by his teacher.
By the age of sixteen or seventeen,
he was exceptionally strong and skilled in martial arts,
and could also use a long pole to leap onto high roofs.
He delighted in righting injustices,
and for this reason, the local people all respected him,
and those seeking to lodge complaints or appeals filled his home, crowding the steps and rooms.
Cuī suppressed the strong and supported the weak,
without avoiding grudges or suspicion.
If anyone slightly opposed him,
stones and clubs would fly,
and limbs would be broken.
Whenever he was in a great rage,
no one dared to move.
He was filial only to his mother,
and when she arrived, he would calm down.
If his mother reprimanded him severely,
Cuī would listen obediently,
but once out the door, he would forget.
A neighbor had a fierce wife
who daily abused her mother-in-law.
The mother-in-law was starving and near death,
and her son secretly gave her food.
When the wife found out,
she cursed and railed endlessly,
and her voice was heard throughout the neighborhood.
Cuī grew angry,
leapt over the wall,
cut off her nose, ears, lips, and tongue,
and she died on the spot.
When his mother heard, she was greatly alarmed,
called the neighbor's son and comforted him with utmost kindness,
and provided him with a young maidservant as a wife,
and the matter was settled.
His mother wept in anger and refused to eat.
Cuī was afraid,
knelt and asked to be beaten,
and confessed his remorse.
His mother wept and paid him no heed.
Cuī's wife, Zhōu,
also knelt beside him.
His mother then beat her son
and also pricked his arm with a needle,
making a cross-shaped mark,
which she painted with vermilion,
so that it would not fade.
Cuī endured it all.
His mother then ate.
His mother was fond of feeding Buddhist monks and Daoist priests,
often satisfying them to the full.
It happened that a Daoist priest was at the gate,
and as Cuī passed by,
the priest looked at him and said:
"Young master, you have much fierce and violent energy,
I fear it will be difficult for you to preserve your life to a good end.
In a family that accumulates good deeds,
there should not be such a one."
Cuī had just received his mother's admonition,
and hearing this,
he rose respectfully and said:
"I am aware of this myself;
but whenever I see injustice,
I find it hard to restrain myself.
If I strive to change,
might I possibly avoid it?"
The priest smiled and said:
"Do not ask for now whether you can avoid it or not;
first ask yourself whether you can change or not.
Only you must earnestly restrain yourself;
if there is even the slightest chance,
I will tell you a method to resolve death."
Cuī had never believed in exorcisms and spells,
so he smiled and said nothing.
The priest said:
"I knew you would not believe.
But what I speak of
is not like the practices of sorcerers;
to act on it would also be a great virtue;
even if it proves ineffective,
it will do no harm."
Cuī asked for instruction,
and the priest then said:
"Just now outside the gate there was a young man;
you should form a deep bond with him,
for even if you commit a capital crime,
he will be able to save you."
Calling Cuī out,
he pointed out the person.
It was the son of the Zhào family,
named Sēnggē.
Zhào,
a man from Nánchāng,
due to famine in a year of poor harvest,
had taken up temporary residence in Jiànchāng.
From then on, Cuī formed a deep friendship with him,
invited Zhào to stay in his home,
and provided for him generously.
Sēnggē was twelve years old,
entered the hall to pay respects to Cuī's mother,
and they pledged to be as brothers.
Over a year later, at the start of spring plowing,
Zhào took his family and left.
News then ceased.
Since the death of the neighboring woman,
Cuī's mother admonished her son even more strictly;
when people came with complaints,
she would always turn them away.
One day,
Cuī's maternal uncle died,
and he followed his mother to offer condolences.
On the road they encountered several men,
binding a man,
shouting, cursing, and hurrying him along,
beating him as well.
Onlookers blocked the road,
and the carriage could not advance.
Cuī asked about it,
and those who recognized Cuī vied to crowd around and tell him.
Previously,
there was a certain Jiǎ, son of a powerful gentry,
who tyrannized the entire village.
Seeing that Lǐ Shēn's wife was beautiful,
he wanted to seize her,
but had no pretext.
So he ordered his servants to lure Shēn into gambling,
lending him money at high interest,
forcing him to sign a bond pledging his wife as collateral,
and when the funds were exhausted, lending him more.
By the end of the night,
Shēn owed several thousand;
after half a year,
the total principal and interest exceeded thirty thousand.
Shēn could not repay,
so [Jiǎ] forcibly seized his wife with a gang of men.
Shēn went weeping to his gate.
Enraged,
[Jiǎ] had him dragged and tied to a tree,
flogged, stabbed, and cut,
forcing him to sign
a "statement of no regret."
Hearing this,
Cuī's anger surged like a mountain,
and he whipped his horse forward,
intending to use force.
His mother lifted the carriage curtain and called out:
"Ah!
Are you going to do this again!"
Cuī then stopped.
After offering condolences and returning home,
he neither spoke nor ate,
sitting rigidly and staring straight ahead,
as if enraged about something.
His wife questioned him,
but he did not answer.
When night came,
he lay on the bed fully clothed,
tossing and turning until dawn.
The next night was the same,
when suddenly he opened the door and went out,
only to return and lie down again.
This happened three or four times;
his wife dared not question him,
and could only listen with bated breath.
After a long while he finally returned,
closed the door, and fell into a deep sleep.
That night,
someone killed Jiǎ in his bed,
disemboweling him so that his intestines spilled out;
Shēn's wife was also found naked, dead beneath the bed.
The officials suspected Shēn,
arrested and tried him.
He was brutally tortured,
his ankle bones exposed,
yet he had nothing to confess.
After more than a year,
unable to endure the torture,
he falsely confessed,
and was sentenced to execution.
It happened that Cuī's mother died.
After the burial,
he told his wife:
"The one who killed Jiǎ
was actually me.
Only because I had an elderly mother,
I dared not reveal it.
Now the great matter is settled;
how can I let another suffer for my crime?
I will go to the authorities and die!"
His wife, shocked, tried to hold him back,
but he tore his sleeve away and left,
surrendering himself at the court.
The officials were astonished,
shackled him and sent him to prison,
releasing Shēn.
Shēn refused,
firmly insisting on taking the blame himself.
The officials could not decide,
so they imprisoned both.
Relatives all reproached Shēn.
Shēn said:
"What the young master did
is what I wished to do but could not.
He did it for me;
how could I bear to sit by and watch him die?
Today, you might as well say the young master never came forward."
He stubbornly maintained this without variation,
firmly contending with Cuī.
After a long time,
everyone in the yamen learned the truth,
and they forced Shēn out,
holding Cuī accountable for the crime.
He was on the verge of execution
when the reviewing official, Vice Minister Zhào from the Board of Punishments,
came to inspect the prisoners.
When he reached Cuī's name,
he dismissed the others and summoned him.
Cuī entered,
looked up at the hall,
and it was Sēnggē.
He told his story with mixed sorrow and joy.
Zhào paced back and forth for a long while,
then still ordered him back to prison,
instructing the jailers to treat him well.
Soon, due to his surrender, his sentence was reduced,
and he was exiled to serve in the army in Yúnnán.
Shēn went along to serve him,
and before a year had passed,
they were pardoned and returned: all due to Zhào's efforts.
After returning home,
Shěn Zhōng never left his side,
managing his household affairs on his behalf.
When offered money,
he refused to accept it.
He showed great interest in
pole-climbing and martial arts.
Cuī Měng treated him generously,
buying him a wife and granting him land.
From then on, Cuī Měng earnestly reformed his former ways,
and whenever he stroked the scar on his arm,
he would shed tears of remorse.
Thus, whenever disputes arose among the villagers,
Shěn Zhōng would take it upon himself to mediate,
without seeking Cuī Měng’s permission.
There was a certain Imperial Student Wáng,
whose family was wealthy and powerful,
and all manner of unscrupulous and lawless individuals
frequented his household.
Many of the well-off families in the county
were subjected to plunder;
if anyone dared to resist,
he would send bandits to kill them on the road.
His son was equally depraved and violent.
Wáng had a widowed aunt,
whom both father and son violated.
His wife, Qiú Shì,
repeatedly tried to dissuade him,
so Wáng strangled her to death.
Qiú’s brothers brought the case before the authorities,
but Wáng bribed and influenced the officials,
resulting in the accusers being convicted of false accusation.
The brothers, filled with unavenged grievance and indignation,
went to Cuī Měng to plead for help.
Shěn Zhōng turned them away and sent them off.
A few days later,
when guests arrived
and there happened to be no servants available,
Cuī Měng asked Shěn Zhōng to brew tea.
Shěn Zhōng left silently,
and told others:
"I am Cuī Měng’s friend,
and I followed him across thousands of miles—
surely that counts as utmost loyalty!
Yet I have never received any regular support,
and now I am treated like a common servant—
this is something I cannot accept!"
He then left in anger.
Someone reported this to Cuī Měng.
Cuī was surprised by his change in attitude,
but did not find it particularly remarkable.
Suddenly, Shěn Zhōng filed a lawsuit against Cuī,
claiming that Cuī had not paid him wages for three years.
Cuī was greatly astonished,
and personally confronted him in court,
where Shěn Zhōng argued angrily.
The magistrate ruled against him,
reprimanded him, and drove him away.
A few days later,
Shěn Zhōng suddenly broke into the Wáng household at night,
killing the father, son, aunt, and wife,
and pasted a paper on the wall,
inscribing his own name on it.
When the authorities pursued and arrested him,
he had already fled without a trace.
The Wáng family suspected Cuī Měng of masterminding the killings,
but the officials did not believe it.
Only then did Cuī realize that Shěn Zhōng’s earlier lawsuit
was likely intended to prevent himself from being implicated in the murders.
Warrants were issued to nearby prefectures and counties,
and the pursuit was intense.
At that time, the rebel forces of Lǐ Zìchéng were causing chaos,
and the matter was eventually dropped.
After the Ming Dynasty fell and the Qing Dynasty was established,
Shěn Zhōng returned home with his family,
and remained as close to Cuī Měng as before.
At that time, local bandits were gathering in large numbers.
Wáng had a nephew named Wáng Dérén,
who rallied the lawless men his uncle had once recruited,
occupied a mountain as a bandit stronghold,
and plundered and burned villages.
One night,
they launched a full-scale attack,
claiming to seek revenge.
Cuī Měng happened to be away; Shěn Zhōng only realized what was happening when the gate was broken down,
and he leaped over the wall, hiding in the darkness.
The bandits searched for Cuī.
Unable to find him,
they abducted Cuī’s wife
and looted all the valuables before leaving.
When Shěn Zhōng returned,
he found only one servant remaining.
Filled with rage,
he cut dozens of lengths of rope,
giving the shorter ones to the servant
and keeping the longer ones for himself.
He instructed the servant to go to the bandits’ lair,
climb halfway up the mountain,
light the ropes on fire,
scatter them among the thorns,
and then return without looking back.
The servant agreed and left.
Shěn Zhōng observed that the bandits all wore red sashes around their waists
and red silk ribbons on their hats,
so he dressed himself in the same manner.
There was an old mare that had just given birth to a foal,
which the bandits had left outside the gate.
Shěn Zhōng then tied up the foal, mounted the mare,
and rode out silently,
heading straight for the bandits’ lair.
The bandits occupied a large village,
and Shěn Zhōng tied the horse outside,
then climbed over the wall to enter.
He saw the bandits bustling about,
still armed and not yet at rest.
Shěn Zhōng discreetly inquired among them
and learned that Cuī’s wife was held in Wáng’s quarters.
Soon, an order was issued
for everyone to rest,
and the bandits responded with a loud clamor.
Suddenly, someone reported that there was a fire on the eastern mountain,
and all the bandits looked in that direction;
at first, there were only one or two points of light,
but soon they multiplied like stars.
Shěn Zhōng, panting heavily, urgently shouted that there was trouble on the eastern mountain.
Wáng was greatly alarmed,
gathered his gear, and led his men out.
Seizing the opportunity, Shěn Zhōng slipped out from the right side,
turned back, and entered the inner quarters.
He saw two bandits guarding the tent,
and deceived them by saying:
"General Wáng has sent his sword."
The two bandits scrambled to look for it.
Shěn Zhōng struck from behind,
and one bandit fell;
the other turned around,
and Shěn Zhōng cut him down as well.
He then carried Cuī’s wife on his back, climbed over the wall, and escaped.
Untying the horse and handing her the reins,
he said:
"Madam, since you do not know the way,
just let the horse run freely."
The horse, longing for its foal, galloped swiftly,
and Shěn Zhōng followed.
Once they passed through a narrow pass,
Shěn Zhōng lit the ropes on fire,
scattered them all around,
and then returned home.
The next day,
Cuī Huán,
considering it a great humiliation,
was agitated in body and spirit,
and wished to ride alone to suppress the bandits.
Shěn advised against it.
He gathered the villagers to discuss together,
but the crowd was timid and none dared respond.
After repeated explanations and persuasions,
he obtained over twenty men willing to go,
but they were troubled by having no weapons.
It happened that from a clan member of Dé Rén’s family, two spies were captured.
Cuī wanted to kill them,
but Shěn would not allow it;
he ordered the twenty men each to hold a white club,
and arranged them in a row in front,
then cut off the spies’ ears and released them.
The crowd complained, saying:
"With such troops,
we should fear the bandits knowing,
yet you instead show them.
If they bring their whole force here,
the entire village will not be preserved!"
Shěn said:
"I precisely want them to come."
He arrested and executed those who had hidden the thieves.
He sent men out in all directions,
each borrowing bows, arrows, and firearms,
and also went to the county to borrow two large cannons.
At dusk,
he led strong men to the narrow pass,
placing the cannons to block the path;
he had two men hide fire and lie in ambush,
instructing them to fire only upon seeing the bandits.
He also went to the eastern mouth of the valley,
cut down trees and placed them on the cliff.
Afterwards, he and Cuī each led over ten men,
ambushing on both sides.
As the first watch was about to end,
from afar came the sound of horses neighing,
the bandits indeed arrived in great force,
stretching on without end.
Waiting until they had all entered the valley,
they then pushed down the trees,
cutting off their retreat.
Soon the cannons fired,
the clamor and cries
shook the mountains and valleys.
The bandits suddenly retreated,
trampling each other;
reaching the eastern mouth,
they could not get out,
gathering with no empty space.
From both sides, firearms and arrows attacked in a pincer,
with the force of wind and rain,
those with severed heads and broken legs
lay piled in the ditch.
Over twenty survivors
knelt and begged for their lives.
He then sent men to bind and send them back.
Riding the victory, they went straight to their lair.
Those guarding the lair, hearing the news, fled and scattered;
they searched their supplies and returned.
Cuī was overjoyed,
and asked about the strategy of setting fires.
He said:
"Setting fires in the east,
was to fear they would chase westward;
short,
wishing them to quickly exhaust,
fearing they would detect there were no men;
then setting them at the valley mouth,
the mouth is very narrow,
one man can block it,
even if they chase here,
seeing the fires they will surely fear: all were risky stratagems of the moment."
Capturing the bandits and interrogating them,
they indeed had chased into the valley,
saw the fires and retreated in alarm.
The over twenty bandits
all had their noses cut off and were released.
From this, his might and fame greatly shook,
those far and near fleeing chaos followed him like a market,
obtaining a local militia of over three hundred men.
Various places' strong bandits dared not offend,
the region relied on this for peace.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"A swift ox will surely break the cart,
this describes Cuī!
His will and spirit were lofty and generous,
indeed few could match.
Yet wishing that under heaven there be no unjust matters,
is this not an intention exceeding reason?
Lǐ Shěn,
a common man of humble status,
was thus able to achieve excellence.
Climbing poles to fly in,
he cut down beasts in the deep boudoir;
blocking roads with pincer attacks,
he swept away demons in narrow valleys.
Had he been given a five-zhang banner,
to serve the country with his life,
why would he not face south and be king!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
A resident of Qīngzhōu, Fàn Xiǎoshān,
made his living selling brushes,
and was away on business.
In the fourth month,
his wife, Héshì, lived alone,
and at night was killed by a thief.
That night there was light rain,
and in the mud was left a fan with a poem,
which was Wáng Shèng’s gift to Wú Fēiqīng.
Shèng,
was unknown who he was;
Wú,
a wealthy man of Yìdū,
lived in the same neighborhood as Fàn,
and usually had rather frivolous conduct,
so the local community all believed it.
The prefecture and county arrested and interrogated him,
he firmly would not confess,
was cruelly tortured with instruments,
and falsely accused to close the case;
reviews and transfers back and forth,
passed over ten officials,
with no differing opinions.
Wú himself thought he must die,
instructed his wife to exhaust all they had,
to aid the widowed and solitary.
To those who chanted Buddha’s name a thousand times at his door,
he gave cotton trousers;
to those who chanted ten thousand times, cotton jackets: thus beggars came like a market,
the sound of Buddha’s name heard for over ten lǐ.
Consequently, the family suddenly became poor,
only daily selling land to provide travel funds.
Secretly bribing the jailer to buy poison.
At night he dreamed a divine person told him:
"Do not die,
formerly 'outside fierce',
now 'inside auspicious'."
Sleeping again,
he spoke again,
thus he did not die.
Not long after,
Mr. Zhōu Yuánliàng was assigned to oversee this circuit,
reviewing prisoners, when he came to Wú,
he seemed thoughtful.
Thus he asked:
"Wú so-and-so killing someone,
what solid evidence is there?"
Fàn answered with the fan.
The gentleman examined the fan carefully,
then asked:
"Who is Wáng Shèng?"
And said he did not know.
He then carefully read through the legal documents once,
immediately ordered his death cangue removed,
and moved him from prison to a granary.
Fàn strongly objected.
Angrily he said:
"Do you want to wrongly kill one person and be done?
Or will you be satisfied only upon getting the true enemy?"
The crowd suspected the gentleman favored Wú,
but none dared speak.
The gentleman issued a red warrant,
immediately arresting the owner of a certain shop in the southern suburb.
The owner was afraid,
not knowing why.
When he arrived, he was asked:
"On your shop wall is a poem by Lǐ Xiù of Dōngguǎn,
when was it inscribed?"
He replied:
"Last year when the education commissioner held examinations,
two or three scholars from Rìzhào,
drank drunk and left this inscription,
I do not know where they lived."
He then sent an officer to Rìzhào,
sitting to arrest Lǐ Xiù.
After several days,
Xiù arrived.
Angrily he said:
"Since you are a scholar,
how could you plan murder?"
Xiù kowtowed, startled and confused,
and said:
“No!”
The magistrate threw the fan down,
telling him to look at it himself,
and said:
“It is clearly your work,
why falsely attribute it to Wáng Shèng?”
Xiù examined it carefully,
and said:
“The poem is indeed mine,
but the calligraphy is certainly not my hand.”
The magistrate said:
“Since we know it is your poem,
it must be your friend.
Who wrote it?”
Xiù said:
“The handwriting resembles that of Wáng Zuǒ from Yízhōu.”
So he sent an officer with a warrant to arrest Wáng Zuǒ.
When Zuǒ arrived,
he was interrogated in the same manner as Xiù.
Zuǒ testified:
“This was written by me at the request of Zhāng Chéng, an iron merchant from Yìdū,
who said Wáng Shèng was his cousin.”
The magistrate said:
“The thief is here.”
Shèng was arrested and brought in,
and with a single interrogation he confessed.
Previously,
Shèng had spied on Hè and found her beautiful,
and wanted to proposition her,
but feared she would not consent.
Thinking that if he pretended to be Wú,
he would certainly be believed by everyone,
he therefore forged a fan in Wú’s name,
and went holding it.
If she consented, he would claim it himself;
if she did not, he would shift the blame onto Wú,
but he truly did not expect it to lead to murder.
He climbed over the wall and entered,
and forced himself upon the woman.
As the woman lived alone,
she often kept a knife for self-defense.
Once she realized,
she grabbed Shèng’s clothes,
and picked up the knife to rise.
Shèng, afraid,
snatched the knife from her.
The woman clung to him with all her strength,
not letting him escape,
and screamed.
Shèng grew even more desperate,
and so killed her,
dropped the fan, and left.
A three-year wrongful conviction,
cleared in a single day—
there was no one who did not praise the magistrate’s divine insight.
Only then did Wú realize
that “inside auspicious”
was
the character “Zhōu.”
Yet he never understood the reason.
Later, a local gentryman seized an opportunity to ask him,
and he laughed and said:
“This is easiest to know.
Looking carefully at the court records,
Hè was killed in the first ten days of the fourth month;
that night was overcast and rainy,
the weather still cold—
a fan is not an urgent item.
How could there be, in a moment of haste and urgency,
someone who would instead carry this to add to their burden?
From this, the shifting of blame could be known.
Earlier, while sheltering from rain in the southern suburbs,
I saw a poem inscribed on a wall and the one on the fan—
the style of expression was similar,
so I rashly surmised it was Mr. Lǐ,
and indeed through this the true thief was found.”
Those who heard sighed in admiration.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
“For matters under heaven, those who delve deeply into them
can make use of what seems to have no use.
Poetry and literary compositions
are tools to adorn the state,
yet the magistrate used them to evaluate scholars of the world,
and was called a Sūn Yáng.
Is this not delving deeply into them?
And who would have thought that the way of evaluating scholars
could be transferred to deciding legal cases.
The *Book of Changes* says: ‘To know the subtle signs is to be divine.’
The magistrate possessed this.”
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Beyond the pass, in the mountains, there are many deer.
The locals put on deer heads,
hide in the grass,
and curl leaves to make sounds,
and the deer come in herds.
However, there are few males and many females.
A male mates with the whole herd of females,
covering every one of the hundreds or thousands,
and once done, he dies.
The females sniff him,
know he is dead,
and scatter into the valleys,
carrying a special herb in their mouths to place by his snout and revive him with its scent,
and in a moment he comes back to life.
If you quickly sound a gong or fire a gun,
the herd of deer flees in alarm.
Then you can take that herb,
which can bring the dead back to life.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In Tiānjīn, there was a certain boatman
who dreamed at night that someone instructed him, saying:
“Tomorrow there will be someone carrying a bamboo trunk who hires a boat—
demand a thousand taels from him;
if not,
do not ferry him.”
The man woke,
and did not believe it.
When he slept again,
he dreamed once more,
and the person wrote
three characters on the wall,
instructing him:
“If he is stingy with the price,
immediately write these and show him.”
The boatman found it strange.
But he did not recognize the characters,
nor did he understand their meaning.
The next day,
he paid attention to travelers.
When the sun was in the west,
sure enough, a man came driving a mule carrying a trunk,
asking for a boat.
The boatman demanded the price as in the dream.
The man laughed at him.
After going back and forth for a long time,
the boatman took his hand
and traced the previous characters with his finger.
The man was greatly startled,
and vanished on the spot.
Searching his load,
they found over ten thousand small coffins,
each only about the length of a finger,
each containing only a drop of blood.
The boatman showed the three characters far and wide,
but no one knew them.
Not long after,
when Wú Sānguì’s rebellious plot was exposed,
his followers were all executed,
and the corpses laid out numbered almost as many as the coffins.
Told by Xú Báishān.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In Téng County there was a certain Yáng,
who was a follower of the White Lotus Sect
and had learned the arts of sorcery.
After Xú Hóngrú was executed,
Yáng was fortunate to escape capture
and thus used his arts to swindle people.
His home had fields, gardens, towers, and pavilions,
and was quite wealthy.
Once, at the home of a certain gentleman in Sìshàng,
he performed magical tricks as entertainment.
The women of the household came out to watch,
and Yáng, seeing that the gentleman's daughter was beautiful,
returned home and plotted to abduct her.
His second wife, Madame Zhū,
was also charming and graceful.
He dressed her in splendid attire,
disguising her as a celestial maiden;
then he gave her a wooden bird
and taught her how to use it.
He then pushed her from the top of a tower.
Madame Zhū felt her body become as light as a leaf,
floating and soaring through the clouds.
Before long,
she reached a place
where the clouds stopped and would not go further.
She knew she had arrived.
That night,
the moonlight was clear and bright,
and looking down, she could see everything distinctly.
She took the wooden bird and threw it,
and the bird flapped its wings and flew away,
straight to the young lady's chamber.
The young lady saw a colorful bird fly in,
and called her maid to catch it,
but the bird had already dashed out through the curtain.
The young lady chased it,
and the bird fell to the ground with a flapping sound.
As she approached and tried to seize it,
it darted under her skirt. In the struggle,
it lifted the young lady and flew up,
soaring straight into the heavens.
The maid screamed loudly.
Madame Zhū, from within the clouds, said:
"Mortals below need not be alarmed.
I am Héng'é from the Moon Palace.
She is the ninth daughter of the Queen Mother of the West,
who was temporarily banished to the mortal world.
The Queen Mother misses her dearly every day,
and has summoned her for a brief reunion.
She will be returned shortly."
Then she took the young lady by the hand and flew away.
Just as they reached the boundary of Sìshuǐ,
it happened that someone was setting off a firecracker,
which struck the bird's wing at an angle.
The bird, startled, fell,
pulling Madame Zhū down with it,
and they landed in the home of a scholar.
The scholar, Xíng Zǐyǐ,
was extremely poor but upright and stubborn in character.
Once, a neighbor's wife came to him at night,
but he refused to let her in.
The woman left in resentment
and slandered him to her husband,
accusing him of making advances.
Her husband was a scoundrel,
and morning and evening he came to Xíng's door to curse and insult him.
Xíng therefore sold his property
and rented a house in another village.
There was a fortune-teller named Gù,
skilled at determining people's fortune and longevity.
Xíng went to his door to consult him.
Gù looked at him and laughed, saying:
"Your destiny holds wealth of a thousand measures,
so why do you appear before others in tattered clothes?
Do you think I have no eyes?"
Xíng scoffed, thinking him delusional.
Gù examined him carefully and said:
"It is so.
Although you are currently destitute,
a gold mine is not far away."
Xíng again thought him absurd.
Gù said:
"Not only will you suddenly become rich,
but you will also obtain a beautiful wife."
Xíng still did not believe him.
Gù pushed him out,
saying:
"Go now, go now.
After it comes true, then you may come to thank me."
That night,
Xíng was sitting alone under the moonlight
when suddenly two women descended from the sky.
Looking at them,
he saw they were both beautiful ladies.
Thinking they were demons,
he questioned them,
but at first they refused to speak.
Xíng was about to call the villagers,
and Madame Zhū, afraid,
finally told him the truth,
and urged him not to reveal it,
expressing her wish to stay with him forever.
Xíng thought that a daughter from a respectable family was not the same as the wife of a sorcerer,
so he sent someone to inform her family.
Her parents, since their daughter had flown away,
had been weeping and bewildered.
Suddenly receiving the message,
they were overjoyed beyond expectation,
and immediately ordered a carriage to rush there at top speed.
They rewarded Xíng with a hundred taels of gold
and took their daughter home.
Xíng had gained a beautiful wife,
but was worried about his poverty.
Receiving the gold greatly comforted him.
He went to thank Gù.
Gù examined him again and said:
"Not yet, not yet.
Your time of prosperity has just begun.
A hundred taels of gold is nothing to speak of!"
Thus he refused the thanks.
Earlier,
when the gentleman returned home,
he requested the authorities to arrest Yáng.
Yáng had fled in advance,
and no one knew where he had gone,
so his property was confiscated,
and a warrant was issued for Madame Zhū's arrest.
Madame Zhū was afraid
and clung to Xíng, weeping.
Xíng was also at a loss,
so he finally bribed the officer serving the warrant,
hired a carriage, and took Madame Zhū to see the gentleman,
pleading for her release.
The gentleman, moved by his righteousness,
exerted himself to scheme on their behalf,
and managed to have her ransomed and pardoned.
He accommodated the couple in a separate lodge,
treating them as happily as close relatives.
The gentleman's daughter had been betrothed in childhood to a man named Liú.
Liú
held a high official position.
Hearing that the young lady had stayed at Xíng's home for two nights,
he considered it a disgrace,
returned the marriage contract,
and broke off the engagement.
The gentleman planned to arrange another marriage for her with another family,
but the young lady told her parents
that she was determined to marry Xíng.
Xíng was delighted to hear this;
Madame Zhū was also pleased
and willingly agreed to take a secondary position.
The gentleman worried that Xíng had no home.
At that time, Yáng's residence was being sold by the authorities,
so he purchased it on Xíng's behalf.
The couple then returned home,
took out the previous gold,
roughly furnished the house,
and hired maids and servants.
Within ten days, the money was all spent.
They only hoped that when the young lady came,
they would again receive financial support.
One evening,
Madame Zhū said to Xíng:
"That wicked husband of mine, Yáng,
once buried a thousand taels of gold under the building.
Only I know about it.
I just checked the spot,
and the bricks and stones are still in place.
Perhaps the hidden treasure is intact."
They went together to dig it up,
and indeed found the gold.
Xíng then believed in the accuracy of Gù's art,
and rewarded him generously.
Later, when the young lady married and came to his home,
her dowry was abundant.
Within a few years,
he became the wealthiest man in the entire prefecture.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"The White Lotus Sect was exterminated, yet Yáng alone did not die.
Moreover, he added to his wicked deeds.
One might almost suspect that the net of heaven is wide-meshed and full of holes.
Who would have known that heaven spared him
for the sake of Xíng?
Otherwise,
even if Xíng's misfortune had turned to fortune,
how could he have suddenly built towers and pavilions and amassed great wealth?
He did not covet a single beauty,
yet heaven rewarded him with two.
Alas!
The Creator does not speak,
but his intent can be known."
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Shànghé County, there was a scholar named Lǐ who was fond of Daoism.
About a mile outside the village,
there was a Buddhist temple;
he built a three-room meditation hut there
and sat in meditation inside.
Traveling monks and Daoist priests
who came to stay overnight
would always engage in deep conversations with him,
and he never tired of providing for them.
One day,
during heavy snow and bitter cold,
an old monk arrived carrying a bag and asked for lodging.
His words were profound and mysterious.
After staying for two nights, he prepared to leave,
but Lǐ firmly urged him to stay,
and he remained for a few more days.
It happened that Lǐ had to return home for some reason,
and the monk asked him to come back early,
intending to bid him farewell.
Lǐ went at the crow of the rooster,
but knocking on the gate brought no response.
He climbed over the wall to enter
and saw a faint flickering light inside,
suspecting the monk was up to something,
he secretly peeked in.
The monk was hurriedly packing his belongings,
and a skinny donkey was tied to the lamp stand.
Upon closer inspection,
it did not seem like a real donkey,
but rather resembled a burial object;
however, its ears and tail occasionally twitched,
and it breathed heavily.
Soon, the packing was done,
and the monk opened the door and led the donkey out.
Lǐ secretly followed him.
Outside the gate, there was originally a large pond.
The monk tied the donkey to a tree by the pond,
stripped naked, and entered the water,
washing his entire body thoroughly;
then he put on his clothes, led the donkey in,
and washed it as well.
Afterward, he loaded the donkey and mounted it,
and it galloped away with incredible speed.
Only then did Lǐ call out to him.
The monk merely bowed from afar in thanks.
His words could not be heard,
and he was already far away.
Wáng Méiwū said: Lǐ was his friend.
He had once visited his home
and saw a plaque in the hall inscribed
"Hall of Awaiting Death,"
showing that he was also a man of profound insight.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Lord Zhào,
a native of Wǔlíng in Húguǎng,
served as an official in the palace
and retired to return home.
A young man waited at his gate,
seeking employment as a secretary.
Lord Zhào summoned him inside
and saw that he was elegant and refined;
he asked for his name,
and the young man said he was Lù Yāguān.
He did not ask for wages.
Lord Zhào kept him,
and he was far more intelligent than ordinary servants.
In handling correspondence and memorials,
he drafted replies as he pleased,
and all were exquisite and skillful.
When his master played chess with guests,
Lù would watch and offer pointers,
and they would always win.
Lord Zhào treated him with even greater favor.
The other servants, seeing how highly their master regarded him,
jokingly asked him to host a banquet.
Yāguān agreed
and asked,
"How many colleagues are there?"
At that time, the estate's stewards numbered over thirty,
and they all told him the number to make things difficult for him.
Yāguān said,
"This is very easy,
but there are many guests,
and it would be too hasty to prepare it here.
We can go to a restaurant."
So he invited all his companions
to a street-side inn.
Everyone sat down.
Just as the wine was being served,
someone stood up with a wine pot and said,
"Gentlemen, please don't drink yet.
May I ask who is hosting today?
The host should first put up the money as a guarantee,
so we can drink and eat freely;
otherwise,
after spending thousands in one go,
if everyone scatters in an uproar,
who will pay the bill?"
Everyone looked at Yāguān.
Yāguān smiled and said,
"Are you worried that I have no money?
I certainly have money."
Then he stood up,
took a fist-sized lump of wet dough from a basin,
pinched it into pieces and placed them on the table;
as he tossed them,
they turned into mice,
scurrying all over the table.
Yāguān grabbed one of them,
tore it open,
and with a squeak, its belly split,
revealing a small piece of gold;
he grabbed another,
and it was the same.
In an instant, all the mice were gone,
and broken pieces of gold lay scattered before them.
He then said to everyone,
"Isn't this enough to pay for the drinks?"
Everyone was amazed
and drank to their hearts' content.
After the meal,
the bill came to over three taels of silver.
They weighed the gold,
and it exactly matched the amount.
Someone took one piece of gold and brought it home,
telling their master about the strange event.
The master ordered the gold to be brought to him,
but when they searched for it, it had already disappeared.
When they questioned the innkeeper,
it turned out the payment had all turned into thorns.
The servant reported this to Lord Zhào,
and Lord Zhào questioned Yāguān.
Yāguān said,
"My friends pressured me to treat them to food and drink,
but my pockets were empty and I had no money.
When I was young, I learned a little magic trick,
so I tried it out."
The others demanded payment again.
Yāguān said,
"In the wheat straw at such-and-such village,
if you winnow it once more,
you can get two dàn of wheat,
which is more than enough to pay for the wine."
So he took one person with him to go there.
The steward of that village was about to return,
so he went along with them.
When they arrived, several hú of clean wheat
were already piled in the threshing ground.
From then on, everyone regarded Yāguān as even more extraordinary.
One day,
Lord Zhào attended a friend's banquet,
where there was a pot of orchids in the hall, lush and thriving,
and he admired it greatly.
Even after returning home, he kept praising it.
Yāguān said,
"If you truly love these orchids,
it is not difficult to obtain them."
Lord Zhào did not believe him.
Early the next morning, when he went to his study,
he suddenly smelled a rich, extraordinary fragrance.
There was a pot of orchids,
with the same number of stems and leaves
as the one he had seen.
Suspecting that Yāguān had stolen it,
he questioned him.
Yāguān said,
"My family has hundreds, if not thousands, of orchids.
Why would I need to steal?"
Lord Zhào did not believe him.
Just then, his friend arrived,
saw the orchids, and exclaimed in surprise,
"How strikingly similar to the ones in my home!"
Lord Zhào said:
"I just bought it,
and I don't know where it came from either.
But when you left the house,
did you see if the orchid was still there?"
The man said:
"I actually never went to the study,
so whether it was there or not, I certainly wouldn't know.
But how did it get here?"
Zhào looked at Yāguān,
and Yāguān said:
"This isn't hard to distinguish.
The pot in your home is broken,
and has a mended spot;
this pot does not."
Upon inspection, they were convinced.
That night, Yāguān said to his master:
"Earlier I mentioned that a certain family has quite a lot of flowers and plants.
Now, if you would condescend to go,
we can visit them by moonlight.
But none of the others can come along,
only Ā Yā is fine."
—Yā
was a page of the Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
So they went as requested.
When the master went out,
there were already four men carrying a sedan chair,
kneeling by the roadside waiting.
Zhào got in,
and it sped along faster than a galloping horse.
In a moment they entered the mountains,
where they only smelled an extraordinary fragrance that penetrated to the bone.
They arrived at a cave dwelling,
and saw that the buildings were splendid and dazzling,
completely different from the human world;
everywhere were arranged flowers and rocks,
exquisite pots and fine plants,
shimmering light and scattered fragrance.
Just the orchid variety alone,
numbered several dozen pots,
all thriving luxuriantly.
After viewing them,
they returned as before by sedan chair.
Yāguān served Zhào for over ten years.
Later, Zhào died without illness,
and then Yāguān left together with Ā Yā,
and no one knows where they went.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Grand Historian Jiǎng Chāo,
recorded that in a previous life he was a monk on Éméi Mountain,
and often dreamed of going to the pond in front of his former temple to wash his feet.
As a person, he was deeply devoted to Buddhist scriptures,
wholeheartedly to the Tiāntái school,
and although he early on entered the Imperial Forest Academy,
he often harbored thoughts of renouncing the world.
On leave returning to Jiāngnán,
upon reaching Qínyóu,
he did not wish to go home.
His son wept and tried to dissuade him,
but he would not listen.
So he entered Shǔ,
residing at Jīnshā Temple in Chéngdū;
after a long time,
he went again to Éméi,
residing at Fúhǔ Temple,
where he manifested illness and passed away peacefully.
He himself wrote a verse saying:
"Carefree, the apes and cranes naturally draw near,
this old monk for no reason fell into the dust of karma.
Vainly seeking to escape the heat by heading towards the cauldron's boiling soup,
how then from the vast sea to turn over?
Fame and fortune are but things within the puppet theater,
wife and children merely people among the ranks of skeletons.
Only towards sovereign and parents is there gratitude left unrequited,
life after life I shall constantly pray to the Able One."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Presented Scholar Shào,
named Shìměi,
was from Jìníng.
Initially appointed Instructor of Dēngzhōu,
two elderly Xiùcai came presenting their cards.
Upon seeing their names,
they seemed very familiar;
after pondering for a long while,
he suddenly realized his previous life.
He then asked the janitor:
"Does a certain student live in a certain village?"
He also described his appearance and demeanor,
and everything matched perfectly.
Soon the two students entered,
and grasping hands they poured out conversation,
joyful as if lifelong friends.
During the talk,
he asked about the situation of Gāo Dōnghǎi.
The two students said:
"He died in prison over twenty years ago,
and now one son still survives.
He was a commoner in this village,
how did you come to know of him?"
Shào smiled and said:
"He is an old relative of mine."
Previously,
Gāo Dōnghǎi had been unruly and shiftless;
however, his nature was bold and straightforward,
he disregarded wealth and was fond of righteousness.
There was a man who, unable to pay his rent, was selling his daughter;
Gāo emptied his purse to redeem her for him.
He had a secret affair with an old woman,
