and the old woman was implicated for concealing stolen goods;
the officials were pursuing her very urgently,
and she fled and hid in Gāo's home.
The officials found out,
arrested Gāo,
and subjected him to extreme torture,
but he never confessed,
and soon died in prison.
The day of his death
was the very day of Shào's birth.
Later, when Shào went to that village,
he provided relief to Gāo's wife and son,
and far and wide everyone knew of this strange affair.
This was told by Vice Minister of Personnel Gāo,
that is, Gāo Gōngzǐ Jìliáng, who passed the imperial examination in the same year.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A gentleman from Jiāngnán named Gù,
while staying in Jìxià,
suffered a sudden and severe swelling of his eyes.
He groaned day and night,
with no medicine or treatment to relieve him.
After more than ten days,
the pain subsided somewhat.
But whenever he closed his eyes,
he would see a huge mansion: four or five courtyards deep,
with all its gates wide open;
in the innermost part, people were coming and going,
but he could only glimpse them from afar, unable to make out details.
One day,
as he was intently watching,
he suddenly felt himself entering the mansion.
Passing through three gateways,
he found no trace of anyone.
There were north and south halls,
their interiors carpeted with red felt.
Peering inside,
he saw the rooms filled with infants—
some sitting, some lying, some crawling on their knees—
too many to count.
While he stood there astonished and bewildered,
a person emerged from behind the building.
Upon seeing Gù, he said:
"The young prince said there was a visitor from afar at the gate,
and indeed it is so."
He then invited Gù inside.
Gù dared not enter,
but after being urged, he finally went in.
He asked:
"What place is this?"
The man replied:
"This is the residence of the Ninth Prince's heir.
The heir has just recovered from malaria,
and today relatives and friends are here to congratulate him.
You, sir, are fortunate to have this opportunity."
Before he finished speaking,
someone came running up,
urging them to hurry.
Soon they arrived at a place
with carved pavilions and vermilion railings.
A hall faced north,
with nine pillars in total.
Ascending the steps,
they found the guests already filling the seats.
Seeing a young man sitting facing north,
Gù knew it was the prince.
He immediately prostrated himself at the foot of the hall.
All the guests in the hall rose.
The prince pulled Gù to sit facing east.
Once the wine began to flow,
drums and music suddenly started playing.
Several female entertainers ascended the hall
and performed
"The Huáfēng Blessing."
Just after three acts,
the innkeeper and his servant came to call him for lunch,
repeatedly calling by his bedside.
Gù heard them very clearly.
Fearing the prince might notice,
he excused himself to go relieve himself and left.
Looking up, he saw the sun was already setting.
Then he saw his servant standing by his bed
and realized he had never left the inn.
Wishing to return quickly,
he sent the servant away and closed the door.
As soon as his eyelids met,
he saw the palace buildings just as before.
He hurriedly followed the previous path inside.
Passing by the place where the infants had been,
he found no infants there now,
but several dozen old women with disheveled hair and hunched backs,
sitting and lying about.
Upon seeing Gù,
they shouted harshly:
"Whose good-for-nothing is this,
coming here to spy!"
Startled and frightened,
Gù dared not argue.
He hurried to the rear courtyard
and ascended the hall to take his seat.
He saw the prince now had a beard over a foot long beneath his chin.
Seeing Gù,
he asked with a smile:
"Where did you go?
The play has already passed seven acts."
He then showed a huge goblet to indicate a penalty drink.
After a while, the performance ended,
and a new playbill was presented.
Gù pointed to
"Péngzǔ Takes a Wife."
The entertainers then used a coconut dipper to serve wine,
which could hold about five dǒu.
Gù rose from his seat and declined, saying:
"Your subject has an eye ailment
and dares not get too drunk."
The prince said:
"Since you suffer from eye trouble,
there is a royal physician here.
He should examine you."
A guest sitting in the east seat
immediately rose and came over.
Using two fingers, he opened Gù's eyelids
and applied a white ointment like grease with a jade hairpin,
instructing him to close his eyes and sleep a little.
The prince ordered an attendant to lead Gù to a side chamber
and had him lie down.
After lying there a short while,
he felt the bed curtains were fragrant and soft,
and thus fell into a deep sleep.
Not long after,
he suddenly heard the clanging and clamor of gongs,
and immediately woke up again.
Thinking it might be the performers' show not yet finished,
he opened his eyes to look,
but it was a dog in the inn licking an oil pot.
However, his eye ailment seemed to have vanished.
Closing his eyes again,
he saw nothing at all.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Chén Xījiǔ
was from Pī.
His father, Zǐyán,
was a renowned scholar in the county.
A wealthy man named Zhōu,
admiring his reputation,
arranged a marriage alliance with him.
Chén repeatedly failed the imperial examinations,
and the family's fortunes declined.
He traveled to study in Qín,
and for years there was no news from him.
Zhōu secretly began to regret the match.
He married his younger daughter to Jǔrén Wáng as a second wife;
Wáng's betrothal gifts were lavish,
and his servants and horses were very fine.
Because of this, Zhōu grew even more disdainful of Xījiǔ's poverty
and firmly resolved to break off the engagement.
When he asked his daughter,
she refused.
Angered,
he sent her to Xījiǔ dressed in shabby clothes.
They often had no fire to cook meals,
but Zhōu showed no concern or pity.
One day,
he sent a maidservant with a hamper of food to his daughter.
Entering the door, she said to the mother:
"My master sent me to see if the young lady has starved to death yet."
Fearing her mother would be ashamed,
the daughter forced a laugh to divert the conversation.
She then took out the food from the hamper
and set it before her mother.
The maidservant stopped her, saying:
"No need for that!
Since the young lady entered this household,
when have we ever received even a cup of warm or cool water in return?
Our family's things—
I reckon you, granny, wouldn't have the face to eat them either."
The mother was greatly enraged,
her expression and voice both changing.
The maidservant was unyielding
and hurled abusive words at her.
Amid the commotion,
Xījiǔ came in from outside.
Upon learning what happened, he was furious.
He grabbed her hair and slapped her face,
then drove her out the door.
The next day,
Zhōu came to fetch his daughter,
but she refused to return.
The day after, he came again,
increasing the number of people with him.
With many mouths clamoring,
it seemed they intended to start a fight.
The mother strongly urged her daughter to go.
The daughter tearfully bowed to her mother
and got into the carriage to leave.
After several days,
Zhōu again sent someone to press for a divorce document.
The mother forced Xījiǔ to give it.
She only hoped Zǐyán would return,
so they could plan something else.
Someone from the Zhōu family who had come from Xī'ān
reported that Zǐyán had died.
Chén's mother, grief-stricken and indignant, fell ill and passed away.
In his grief and desperation, Xījiǔ still hoped his wife would return;
but as time passed without a trace of her,
his sorrow and indignation grew even more intense.
He sold his few acres of thin farmland
to prepare for the burial.
After the funeral,
he begged his way to Qín,
seeking his father's remains.
Arriving in Xī'ān,
he inquired among all the local residents.
Some said that several years ago, a scholar had died at an inn
and was buried in the eastern suburbs,
but his family was now gone.
Xījiǔ was at a loss;
his only plan was to beg in the marketplaces by day
and lodge in wild temples at night,
hoping to find someone who knew.
One evening, as he passed through a cluster of graves,
several men blocked his path,
demanding payment for a meal.
Xījiǔ said,
"I am a stranger here,
begging for food within the city walls.
Where would I owe anyone for a meal?"
They grew angry together,
seized him and threw him to the ground,
stuffing his mouth with the rotten cotton wadding used to bury a child.
His strength exhausted and his voice hoarse,
he was gradually nearing a critical state.
Suddenly, they all cried out in alarm:
"Where did this official come from!"
They released him and fell silent.
Soon, a carriage and horses arrived,
and someone asked,
"Who is that lying there?"
Immediately, several men helped him to the carriage.
The person in the carriage said,
"This is my son.
How dare you wicked ghosts act like this!
Tie them all up and bring them here,
don't let any escape."
Xījiǔ felt someone remove the stuffing from his mouth.
After calming down a little,
he looked closely and recognized
that it was truly his father.
He wailed,
"Your son has suffered greatly for your remains.
So you are still in the world of the living after all!"
His father said,
"I am not a living person;
I am the Commander of Tàiháng.
I came here also for my son."
Xījiǔ wept even more mournfully,
and his father comforted and instructed him.
Xījiǔ tearfully recounted how his father-in-law's family had divorced him.
His father said,
"Do not worry.
Your new wife is now also at your mother's place.
Your mother misses you terribly;
you should go see her for a while."
So he rode in the same carriage with him,
speeding like wind and rain.
After a while,
they reached an official residence.
Alighting and passing through several gates,
he saw his mother there.
Xījiǔ was overcome with grief,
but his father stopped him.
Xījiǔ sobbed and obeyed.
Seeing his wife beside his mother,
he asked his mother,
"My wife is here;
could it be she is also in the underworld?"
His mother said,
"No, she is not.
Your father brought her here.
We will send her back when you return home."
Xījiǔ said,
"Your son wishes to serve his parents
and does not want to return."
His mother said,
"You traveled here through such hardship and toil
for your father's remains.
If you do not return,
what was your original purpose?
Moreover, your filial conduct has already reached the Heavenly Emperor,
who has granted you ten thousand catties of gold.
You and your wife have a long life of enjoyment ahead;
how can you speak of not returning?"
Xījiǔ wept with bowed head.
His father repeatedly urged him to depart,
and Xījiǔ cried out loud.
His father said angrily,
"You refuse to go?!"
Xījiǔ, afraid,
stifled his sobs
and finally asked about the burial site.
His father, pulling him along, said,
"Go, and I will tell you:
About a hundred paces from the cluster of graves,
there is a pair of white elms, mother and son. That is the place."
He pulled him urgently,
so that Xījiǔ had no time to bid farewell to his mother.
Outside the gate, a sturdy servant
was holding a horse, waiting for him.
Once he had mounted,
his father instructed him:
"At the place where you stayed last night,
there is a small amount of travel funds.
Use it quickly to prepare for your journey home,
and go to your father-in-law to demand your wife back.
Do not stop until you have your wife."
Xījiǔ assented and set off.
The horse galloped with extreme speed;
they reached Xī'ān at cockcrow.
The servant helped him dismount,
and just as he was about to bow and convey his respects to his parents,
the man and horse had vanished.
He found his way to his old lodging place,
leaned against the wall, and dozed off,
waiting for daybreak.
Where he sat, a fist-sized stone was pressing against his thigh;
at dawn, he looked at it—
it was white silver.
He bought a coffin, hired a cart,
sought out the twin elms,
retrieved his father's remains, and returned home.
After the joint burial was completed,
his household was left with nothing but bare walls.
Fortunately, the villagers, moved by his filial piety,
provided him with food.
He planned to go demand his wife back,
but considering he could not use force himself,
he went with his clansman, Nineteenth Brother.
Arriving at the gate,
the gatekeeper refused them entry.
Nineteenth Brother, always a scoundrel,
spewed foul and obscene language.
Zhōu sent someone to persuade Xījiǔ to return home,
promising to send his daughter immediately.
Xījiǔ went back.
At the beginning,
when the daughter returned home,
Zhōu cursed her husband and mother-in-law to her face,
but the daughter remained silent,
only turning toward the wall and shedding tears.
When Chén's mother died,
he did not let her know.
After receiving the divorce letter,
he threw it at the daughter, saying:
"The Chén family has cast you out!"
The daughter replied:
"I have never been fierce or rebellious—
why would they cast me out?"
She wanted to return and inquire about the reason,
but he confined her.
Later, when Xījiǔ went to Xī'ān,
he fabricated news of his death,
to sever the daughter's hopes.
Once this news spread,
a certain Dù Hànlín came to propose marriage,
and Zhōu agreed.
When the wedding day was set,
the daughter found out,
and wept, refusing to eat,
covering her face with a quilt,
her breath as faint as a thread.
Just as Zhōu was at a loss,
he suddenly heard that Xījiǔ had arrived,
and spoke insolently.
Expecting his daughter to die soon,
he sent her back to Xījiǔ,
intending to vent his anger after her death.
When Xījiǔ returned home,
those escorting the daughter had already arrived;
fearing Xījiǔ would see her illness and refuse to take her in,
they barely entered the door
before abandoning her and leaving.
The neighbors, concerned,
planned together to carry her back;
but Xījiǔ refused,
and helped her onto the bed,
only to find she had stopped breathing.
He was then greatly frightened.
In the midst of his panic,
Zhōu's son led several men armed with weapons inside,
smashing all the doors and windows.
Xījiǔ hid and fled,
while they searched for him relentlessly.
All the villagers were indignant;
Shíjiǔ gathered over ten men who bravely stepped forward to help in the crisis,
and Zhōu's sons and brothers were all wounded,
before they fled like rats.
Zhōu grew even angrier,
sued at the official court,
and had Xījiǔ, Shíjiǔ, and others arrested.
As Xījiǔ was about to leave,
he entrusted his wife's body to an elderly neighbor.
Suddenly, he heard a faint breath from the bed,
and upon closer look,
her eyes showed a slight movement;
after a short while,
she was already able to turn over.
Overjoyed,
he went to the official to explain himself.
The magistrate was angry at Zhōu's false accusation.
Zhōu, afraid,
bribed him heavily,
and only then was spared.
When Xījiǔ returned home,
he and his wife met again,
mingling sorrow and joy.
Earlier,
when the daughter stopped eating and lay near death,
she vowed to die.
Suddenly, someone lifted her up, saying:
"I am from the Chén family.
Come with me quickly,
and you can see your husband;
otherwise,
it will be too late!"
Unaware, she found herself outside the door,
and two people helped her into a sedan chair.
In moments, they arrived at an official residence,
where she saw her father-in-law and mother-in-law both present.
She asked:
"Where is this?"
Her mother-in-law said:
"No need to ask,
we will send you back soon."
One day,
she saw Xījiǔ arrive,
and was very happy.
But after seeing him, he quickly left,
which puzzled her greatly.
Her father-in-law was often away for days,
not knowing what he was doing.
Last night, he suddenly returned, saying:
"I was in Wǔyí,
and delayed returning for two days,
which must have been hard on Bǎo'ér.
We must send her back quickly."
So they sent her back by carriage.
Suddenly seeing her home's gate,
she felt as if waking from a dream.
She and Xījiǔ recounted their past experiences,
and were both astonished and delighted.
From then on, husband and wife lived together,
but had no means to support themselves day and night.
Xījiǔ set up a school for children in the village,
while also studying hard himself.
He often whispered to himself:
"Father said heaven would bestow gold,
but now the house is empty—
how can teaching and reading bring fortune?"
One day,
on his way back from school,
he met two men,
who asked him:
"Are you Mr. Chén?"
Xījiǔ replied:
"Yes."
The two immediately took out iron chains and bound him.
Xījiǔ did not understand why.
After a short while,
the villagers gathered,
and after questioning,
learned he was implicated by a gang of thieves.
Pitying his injustice,
they pooled money to bribe the officers,
so he suffered no hardship on the journey.
When he met the prefect at the prefecture,
he recounted his family background.
The prefect was astonished, saying:
"This is the son of a renowned scholar—
gentle and refined—
how could he be a thief!"
He ordered the chains removed,
and had the thieves severely interrogated,
who then confessed they were bribed by a certain Zhōu.
Xījiǔ also explained the reason for the falling out with his father-in-law,
and the prefect grew even angrier,
immediately ordering Zhōu's arrest.
He then invited Xījiǔ to his office,
and spoke of their family friendship,
as the prefect was the son of former Pī County Magistrate Hán,
who had been a student of Zǐyán.
He gave Xījiǔ a hundred taels for study expenses;
and also provided two mules for transportation,
so he could travel to the prefecture from time to time
to discuss literary studies.
The prefect further praised his filial piety to higher officials,
and from the governor-general down,
all sent gifts.
Xījiǔ rode the mules home,
and husband and wife were greatly comforted.
One day,
his wife's mother arrived in tears,
and upon seeing her daughter, knelt on the ground, refusing to rise.
The daughter, alarmed, asked why,
and learned that Zhōu had been shackled and imprisoned.
The daughter wept in sorrow and blamed herself,
wanting only to die.
Xījiǔ had no choice
but to go to the prefecture to plead for leniency.
The prefect released Zhōu on condition of self-redemption,
fining him a hundred piculs of grain,
which he awarded to the filial son Chén Xījiǔ.
After Zhōu was released,
he took grain from the granary,
mixed it with chaff, and transported it.
Xījiǔ said to his wife:
"Your father measures a gentleman's heart with a petty man's mind.
How did he know I would accept it,
and bother to mix chaff with the grain?"
He then smiled and refused it.
Although the Xī family was somewhat well-off,
their walls were low and dilapidated.
One night,
a group of thieves broke in.
The servant woke up
and shouted loudly,
but the thieves only stole two mules and left.
More than half a year later,
Xī Jiǔ was reading at night
when he heard knocking at the door.
He asked who it was, but there was no response.
He called his servant to get up and check,
and as soon as the door was opened,
two mules leaped inside—
they were the ones that had been stolen earlier.
They ran straight under the poplar tree,
panting and sweating heavily.
When examined by candlelight,
each was carrying a leather bag.
Upon opening them,
they were found to be filled with silver.
Greatly astonished,
he had no idea where they had come from.
Later, he heard that on that night, a major robbery had occurred at the Zhōu family’s home.
The thieves, laden with plunder,
were being hotly pursued by the local guards.
In their haste, they abandoned their bundles and fled.
The mules, recognizing their former master,
ran straight to his home.
After Zhōu returned from prison,
his wounds from the punishment were still severe;
now, having been robbed,
he fell seriously ill and died.
That night, his daughter dreamed that her father, still in prison garb, came to her
and said:
"In my lifetime, what I did
is now beyond regret.
Now I am suffering punishment in the underworld,
and only your father-in-law can save me.
Plead with my son-in-law on my behalf
to deliver a letter for me."
She woke up weeping.
When questioned,
she told him everything.
Xī Jiǔ had long wanted to visit Tàiháng,
and so he set out that very day.
Upon arriving,
he prepared sacrificial offerings and prayed,
then slept outdoors at the site,
hoping to see something.
But the whole night passed without incident,
so he returned home.
After Zhōu’s death,
his wife and daughter grew even poorer,
relying on support from the second son-in-law.
The Provincial Graduate Wáng, who had been appointed as a county magistrate,
was dismissed for corruption,
and his entire family was exiled to Shěnyáng,
leaving them with nowhere to turn.
Xī Jiǔ often looked after and assisted them.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"No virtue is greater than filial piety;
spirits and gods are moved by it,
as is only right.
If one is a virtuous and enlightened person,
even if they remain poor to the end,
they will still be chosen—
how much more so when prosperity is destined to follow?
Some people, with their beloved daughters in their laps,
hand them over to white-haired old men
and boast proudly:
'Such-and-such a high official is my son-in-law.'
Alas!
The gentle, delicate girl remains as before,
but her high-ranking husband returns for burial,
which is tragic enough;
how much worse is it for a young wife to follow the army?"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
The daughter of a certain old man from Línzī
was the wife of a National University student named Lǐ.
Before she was married,
a fortune-teller read her fate
and predicted that she would surely suffer official punishment.
The old man was angry at this,
but then laughed and said:
"What nonsense to go this far!
Not only would a girl from a respectable family never appear in court,
but how could a National University student fail to protect his own wife?"
After she married,
she was extremely fierce,
and beating and cursing her husband became routine.
Lǐ could not endure her abuse,
and in anger, he brought a complaint to the authorities.
The county magistrate, Shào, accepted his petition
and immediately issued a warrant for her arrest.
When the old man heard of this,
he was greatly alarmed.
Leading his sons and nephews, he went to the magistrate’s hall
and begged for the matter to be dropped.
But the magistrate refused.
Lǐ himself also regretted it
and asked to withdraw the complaint.
The magistrate angrily said:
"Do you think the court’s business can be started and stopped at your whim? She must be brought for trial!"
Once she arrived,
after asking a few questions,
he declared:
"Truly a shrew!"
He sentenced her to thirty strokes of the rod,
and the flesh of her buttocks was completely torn.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Could it be that the magistrate had some personal grievance regarding women?
How fierce his anger was!
Yet when a county has a wise magistrate,
there will be no shrews in the villages.
I record this
to supplement what is missing in the 'Biographies of Upright Officials.'"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Táo Shèngyú of Běipíng
was a scholar of some renown.
During the Shùnzhì reign,
while on his way to take the provincial examination,
he lodged in the outskirts of the city.
Once, as he stepped outside,
he saw a man carrying a book bag, looking hesitant,
as if he had not yet found a place to stay.
After a brief inquiry,
the man set down his burden by the roadside,
and they engaged in conversation.
His words and demeanor were those of a refined scholar.
Táo was greatly pleased with him
and invited him to live together.
The guest was delighted,
brought his belongings inside,
and so they shared the lodging.
The guest introduced himself:
"A native of Shùntiān,
surnamed Yú,
courtesy name Qù'è."
Because Táo was older,
he regarded him as an elder brother.
By nature, he disliked going out to sightsee,
often sitting alone in his room,
yet there were no books on his desk.
If Táo did not speak with him,
he would simply lie silently.
Táo grew suspicious of him,
searched his bags and boxes,
but aside from brushes and inkstones,
there were no other possessions.
Perplexed, he asked him about it,
and he laughed, saying:
"When we scholars read,
do we wait until we are thirsty to start digging a well?"
One day,
he borrowed a book from Táo and left,
shut his door and copied it with great speed,
producing over fifty pages in a single day,
yet he was never seen folding them into volumes.
Peeking secretly,
Táo saw that each time he finished a draft,
he would burn it to ashes and swallow them.
This made Táo even more puzzled.
Questioning him about the reason,
he said:
"I use this method in place of reading."
He then recited the book he had copied,
several chapters in an instant,
without a single error.
Táo was delighted,
and wanted to learn his method;
Yú considered it improper.
Táo suspected he was being stingy,
and his words carried a tone of reproach.
Yú said:
"Brother, you truly do not understand me deeply enough.
If I do not speak,
my heart cannot be laid bare;
if I speak abruptly,
I fear you will be shocked and deem it strange.
What should I do?"
Táo insisted, saying:
"It is no matter."
Yú said:
"I am not human,
but actually a ghost.
Now, in the underworld, official posts are granted through examinations;
on the fourteenth day of the seventh month, an edict was issued to examine the examiners,
on the fifteenth, the scholars enter the examination halls,
and by the end of the month, the results are posted."
Táo asked:
"What is the examination of examiners?"
He said:
"This is the Lord on High's way of being cautious;
regardless of whether they are bird officials or turtle officials,
all are examined.
Those skilled in writing are appointed as inner examiners,
those who are incompetent are not allowed to participate.
For in the underworld, there are various deities,
just as in the mortal world there are prefects and magistrates.
Those who have achieved success, their eyes have never seen the classics,
they merely wield a 'door-knocking brick' in their youth,
hunting for fame and rank;
once the door is opened,
they discard it;
after managing documents for over a decade,
even if they are literary scholars,
do they still have any words left in their minds!
The reason why the mortal world is filled with the unworthy advancing by luck,
while heroes lose their aspirations,
is solely because they lack this one examination."
Táo deeply agreed with him,
and from then on, he held him in even greater awe and respect.
One day,
he came in from outside,
looking troubled,
and sighed, saying:
"I was born poor and lowly,
and thought I could escape it after death;
I never expected that Mister Zhūnzhān,
would follow me underground."
Táo asked the reason,
and he said:
"Wén has been appointed to confer the title of king in the State of Dōuluó,
so the exam for the curtain officials has been suspended.
For decades, wandering spirits and wasted ghosts
have mingled in evaluating the essays—
how can people like us have any hope?"
Táo asked:
"Who are these people?"
He said:
"Even if I tell you,
you wouldn’t know them.
Let me mention one or two,
and you’ll get the general idea: Yuèzhèng Shī Kuàng and Sīkù Hé Qiáo are among them.
I’ve come to think that fate cannot be relied upon,
nor can literary talent be depended on—
it’s better to give up."
Having said this, he looked disheartened,
and prepared to pack his belongings.
Táo held him back and comforted him,
so he stayed.
On the night of the Ghost Festival,
he said to Táo:
"I’m going to enter the examination hall.
Please, at dawn,
hold an incense stick in the eastern wilderness,
call out 'Qù'è' three times,
and I will arrive."
Then he went out the door and left.
Táo bought wine and cooked fresh delicacies to await him.
When the east grew bright,
he reverently followed the instructions.
Before long,
Yú arrived with a young man.
Táo asked his name,
and Yú said:
"This is Fāng Zǐjìn,
a good friend of mine.
We happened to meet in the examination hall.
Hearing of your esteemed reputation,
he deeply wished to pay his respects and make your acquaintance."
They went together to the lodging,
lit a candle, and performed the formal greetings.
The young man stood gracefully like jade,
with a modest and gentle demeanor.
Táo liked him very much,
and asked:
"Zǐjìn’s fine compositions
must have brought great satisfaction."
Yú said:
"It’s laughable to speak of it!
In the hall, there were seven sections;
he had completed more than half,
but upon carefully examining the examiner’s name,
he packed his things and left directly.
What an extraordinary man!"
Táo fanned the stove to warm the wine,
and asked:
"What were the topics in the hall?
Did Qù'è come out first in the provincial exam?"
Yú said:
"One on calligraphy and art, one on classical discourse—
anyone could handle those.
The policy question was:
'Since ancient times, there have been many wicked and depraved people,
but today’s social customs
are filled with treacherous affairs and ugly behaviors
that are increasingly indescribable.
Not only are the eighteen layers of hell insufficient to contain them all,
but they may not even be able to hold them.
What method, then, can be used?
Some say we should add one or two more layers of hell,
but that would greatly violate the Lord of Heaven’s compassionate heart for all living beings.
Should they be increased or not?
Or is there another way to cleanse the source?
You scholars, speak fully and do not conceal your thoughts.'
My younger brother’s policy essay wasn’t excellent,
but it was quite forthright.
The memorial topic: 'On the proposal to exterminate the demon king,
bestowing dragon-horses and celestial robes upon the ministers in varying degrees.'
Next was 'Poem Composed by Imperial Command at the Jasper Terrace'
and 'Rhapsody on the Peach Blossoms of the Western Pool.'
For these three,
I believe no one in the hall could match me!"
Having said this, he clapped his hands.
Fāng said with a smile:
"You’re pleased now,
and think you’re unmatched, brother;
but in a few days,
if you don’t weep bitterly, then you’ll truly be a man."
When day broke,
Fāng wanted to take his leave.
Táo urged him to stay and share the lodging,
but Fāng declined,
only promising to return at dusk.
Three days passed,
and he still hadn’t come back.
Táo sent Yú to look for him.
Yú said:
"No need.
Zǐjìn is sincere and earnest—
he’s not one to be indifferent."
When the sun set in the west,
Fāng indeed came.
He took out a scroll and handed it to Táo,
saying:
"I broke our appointment for three days,
but I respectfully copied over a hundred of my old compositions,
hoping you would evaluate them."
Táo took it and read with great delight,
praising it line by line.
After going through one or two pieces briefly,
he stored them in a bamboo case.
They talked until late into the night,
and Fāng stayed over,
sharing a bed with Yú.
From then on, it became routine.
There wasn’t an evening when Fāng didn’t come,
and Táo was never unhappy when Fāng was around.
One evening,
Fāng hurried in,
and said to Táo:
"The underworld rankings have been posted,
and Brother Yú has failed the exam!"
Yú was lying down,
but upon hearing this, he startled up,
tears streaming down his face.
The two of them comforted him with all their might,
and only then did his tears stop.
Yet they sat facing each other in silence,
finding it almost unbearable.
Fāng said:
"I just heard that the Grand Circuit Inspector Zhāng Huánhóu is about to arrive,
fearing it might be a rumor spread by those who have lost their ambitions;
otherwise,
the literary field may still see upheavals."
Yú Wénzhī, upon hearing this,
showed a pleased expression.
Táo Wàngsān inquired about the reason,
and Yú said:
"Huánhóu Yìdé,
inspects the underworld once every thirty years,
and the mortal world once every thirty-five years.
The injustices between these two realms
await this elder to resolve them."
He then stood up,
pulling Fāng Zǐjìn along to leave.
They returned after two nights,
and Fāng joyfully said to Táo:
"Aren't you going to congratulate your fifth brother?
Huánhóu arrived the night before last,
tore up the earthly examination roster,
and of the names on the roster,
only one-third remained.
After thoroughly reviewing the discarded papers,
he was very pleased to find your fifth brother's;
he recommended him as the Inspector of the Southern Seas in Jiāonán,
and carriages and horses will arrive any day now."
Táo was overjoyed,
and prepared wine to celebrate.
After several rounds of wine,
Yú asked Táo:
"Do you have any spare rooms at your home?"
Táo asked:
"What for?"
Yú replied:
"Zǐjìn is alone and has no hometown,
nor can he bear to part from you so abruptly.
I was thinking of borrowing a place for him to stay with you."
Táo happily said:
"If so,
it would be a great fortune.
Even if there aren't many rooms,
sharing a bed is no hindrance.
However, I have a strict father,
so I must inform him first."
Yú said:
"I know your esteemed father is kind and dependable.
Since your examination is approaching,
if Zǐjìn cannot wait,
why not let him go first?"
Táo kept him as a companion at the inn,
waiting to return together.
The next day,
as evening fell,
carriages and horses arrived at the gate,
to escort Yú to his post.
Yú stood up,
shook hands and said:
"We part from here.
There is one thing I wish to say,
but I fear it may dampen your determined spirit."
Táo asked:
"What is it?"
Yú said:
"Your fate is fraught with delays,
and you were born at an inopportune time.
Your chances in this examination are one in ten;
in the next examination, when Huánhóu visits the mortal world,
justice will begin to prevail,
and your chances will be three in ten;
only by the third examination can you have hope."
Táo, upon hearing this,
wanted to withdraw.
Yú said:
"No,
this is all fate.
Even if you clearly know it's impossible,
the hardships destined for you
must still be endured."
He then turned to Fāng and said:
"Do not linger,
today's year, month, day, and hour are all auspicious,
so I will send you back by carriage.
I will ride off on horseback myself."
Fāng joyfully bid farewell.
Táo was confused at heart,
not knowing what to say,
and could only weep as he saw them off.
He watched as the carriages and horses went their separate ways,
and in a moment, they were all gone.
Only then did he regret that he had not sent a single word with Zǐjìn as he headed north,
but it was already too late.
After the three sessions of the examination,
Táo was not very satisfied,
and returned home after much奔波.
Upon entering the door, he asked about Zǐjìn,
but no one at home knew anything.
He then told his father about it,
and his father happily said:
"If that's the case,
then the guest has been here for a long time."
Earlier, Old Man Táo had been napping during the day,
and dreamed that a carriage stopped at his gate.
A handsome young man stepped out of the carriage,
entered the hall, and bowed.
Surprised, the old man asked where he came from,
and the young man replied:
"Elder brother promised to lend me a room,
but he couldn't come with me because he had to take the examination.
I have arrived first."
After saying this,
he asked to go in and pay respects to the mother.
Just as the old man was modestly declining,
a maid entered and said:
"The mistress has given birth to a young master."
He woke up with a start,
and found it very strange.
On this day, Táo's story
matched the dream exactly,
and they realized that the child was the reincarnation of Zǐjìn.
Father and son were both delighted,
and named the child Xiǎojìn.
When the child was first born,
he often cried at night,
troubling his mother.
Táo said:
"If this is Zǐjìn,
let me see him,
and the crying will stop."
It was customary to avoid exposing newborns to strangers,
so Táo was not allowed to see him.
The mother, unable to bear the crying any longer,
called Táo in.
Táo soothed him, saying:
"Zǐjìn, don't cry!
I am here!"
The child was crying intensely,
but upon hearing the voice, he stopped immediately,
staring without blinking,
as if carefully examining him.
Táo patted his head and left.
From then on, the child never cried again.
A few months later,
Táo did not dare to see him:
if he saw him once,
the child would bend over, asking to be held;
if Táo walked away,
the child would cry uncontrollably.
Táo also grew fond of him.
At four years old,
he would leave his mother to sleep with his brother;
if his brother went out,
he would pretend to sleep, waiting for his return.
His brother taught him
the "Book of Songs"
on the pillow,
and he would murmur the verses,
reciting over forty lines by night.
When given Zǐjìn's leftover writings to study,
he happily read them,
memorizing them after a single recitation;
but when tested on other texts,
he could not do it.
By eight or nine years old,
his features were clear and bright,
exactly like Zǐjìn.
Táo took the examination twice,
but did not pass.
In the year Dīngyǒu,
a scandal erupted in the examination hall,
and many examiners were executed or exiled.
The path for imperial examinations was cleansed,
all thanks to the efforts of Inspector Zhāng.
In the next examination, Táo passed as a deputy candidate,
and soon became a tribute scholar.
He then lost interest in pursuing an official career,
and retired to teach his younger brother.
He once told people:
"With this joy,
I would not exchange it for a position in the Imperial Academy."
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Every time I visit the temple of Master Zhāng,
I gaze upon his beard and eyebrows,
which are awe-inspiring and full of vitality.
Moreover, his voice in life was like thunder,
and wherever his spear and horse went,
it brought great satisfaction,
beyond expectations.
The world, thinking the general was fond of martial arts,
placed him alongside Jiàng and Guàn;
but who knew that the affairs of Wénchāng are numerous,
and many marquises are needed!
Alas!
Thirty-five years,
why does it come so late!"
Scholar Liú recounted:
"In Jìníng there was a certain mad scholar,
skilled at drinking;
his household lacked even a peck of grain,
yet whenever he got money he would buy wine,
never once considering his poverty and hardship.
It happened that a new prefect arrived to take up his post,
who was skilled at drinking but had no match.
Hearing of the scholar's reputation,
he summoned him to drink and was delighted with him,
often sharing conversation and feasts.
The scholar, relying on this familiarity,
whenever someone involved in a minor lawsuit sought a favorable judgment,
would accept a small bribe to intercede on their behalf;
the prefect would often grant his requests.
The scholar grew accustomed to this as normal,
and the prefect grew weary of it in his heart.
One day during the morning court session,
the scholar presented his name card and entered the hall.
The prefect read it and smiled faintly.
The scholar said in a stern voice:
'If you grant the request,
approve it;
if you do not grant the request,
reject it.
Why are you laughing!
I have heard it said: a scholar can be killed but not humiliated.
Other things I may not be able to repay,
but can I not repay even a single laugh?'
Having said this,
he laughed loudly,
the sound shaking the hall's walls.
The prefect angrily said:
'How dare you be so disrespectful!
Have you not heard of the magistrate who wipes out families?'
The scholar swung his sleeves and strode down,
shouting loudly: 'This scholar has no family gate to be wiped out!'
The prefect grew even angrier
and had him seized.
Investigating his home situation,
it was found he had neither fields nor property,
only that he lived with his wife atop the city wall.
Hearing this, the prefect released him,
but only banished him, not allowing him to reside within the city walls.
Friends, pitying his madness,
bought a few feet of land for him,
and built a tiny room there.
Entering to live in it, he sighed:
'From now on, I fear the magistrate!'"
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"A scholar-gentleman upholds the law and observes propriety,
not daring to rob people in the marketplace;
what can those in authority do to me!
Yet the reason enemies can still inflict harm
is merely because one has a family gate.
When one reaches the point of having no gate to wipe out,
then the angry have nothing left to inflict.
Ah!
Is this not what is called 'the poor and lowly being arrogant'?
However, a gentleman, though poor,
does not lightly impose on others.
To, for the sake of filling one's belly,
chatter incessantly in the official hall,
is truly low behavior.
Even so,
his madness is unmatched."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Chéngzhōu, many people transform into creatures
and leave their courtyards to seek food.
A traveler lodging at an inn
often saw a group of rats enter a rice jar;
when driven away, they would flee.
The traveler waited for them to enter,
suddenly covered the jar,
and poured gourdfuls of water inside;
in a moment, they were all dead.
The innkeeper's entire family suddenly died,
only a single son remained.
He brought a lawsuit to the authorities;
the official investigated the cause and pardoned him.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Liú Chìshuǐ,
a native of Pínglè,
was exceptionally bright and talented from a young age.
At fifteen, he entered the prefectural school.
His parents died early,
and so he abandoned himself to a life of idle wandering.
His family was not well-off,
yet he had a penchant for refinement,
and his bed and bedding were all exquisite.
One evening,
he was invited out for a drink,
and left forgetting to extinguish the candle.
After several rounds of wine,
he finally remembered,
and hurried back.
Hearing whispers inside his room,
he peeked in secretly,
and saw a young man embracing a beautiful woman sleeping on his bed.
His house bordered the abandoned mansion of a noble family,
where strange occurrences were frequent.
Knowing in his heart they were foxes,
he was not afraid.
He entered and shouted:
"How can you snore and sleep on another's bed!"
The two were flustered,
grabbed their clothes and fled naked.
They left behind a pair of purple silk trousers,
with a needle pouch attached to the belt.
Greatly pleased,
and fearing they might steal them back,
he hid them under the quilt and held them tight.
Soon, a disheveled maid entered through a crack in the door,
and asked Liú for them back.
Liú laughed and demanded compensation.
The maid offered wine,
he refused;
she offered gold,
he refused again.
The maid left with a laugh.
She returned shortly and said:
"The eldest young lady says: if you return them,
she will repay you with a fine match."
Liú asked:
"Who is she?"
She replied:
"Our family name is Pí.
The eldest young lady's pet name is Bāxiān;
the one sleeping with her is Master Hú.
The second young lady is Shuǐxiān,
married to Master Dīng of Fùchuān;
the third young lady is Fèngxiān,
even more beautiful than her two sisters,
and surely one you would find agreeable."
Fearing they might break their promise,
Liú asked her to wait for good news.
The maid left and returned again, saying:
"The eldest young lady sends word: how can a good match be arranged so hastily?
I just spoke to her about it,
and instead received harsh words.
But give us some time to wait,
our family is not one to make promises lightly or break faith."
Liú gave her the trousers.
Several days passed,
with no news at all.
At dusk,
returning from outside,
he had just sat down after closing the door,
when suddenly the double doors opened by themselves.
Two people carried a young lady on a quilt,
holding its four corners, and entered,
saying:
"We've delivered the bride!"
They laughingly placed her on the bed and left.
Looking closely,
he saw she was sound asleep, not yet awake,
her breath still fragrant with wine,
her flushed face and drunken demeanor
were utterly captivating.
Overjoyed,
he held her feet, removed her stockings,
and embraced her, slowly undressing her.
By then, the girl was slightly awake.
Opening her eyes and seeing Liú,
her limbs were not under her control.
She could only say resentfully:
"That lewd maid Bāxiān has sold me!"
Liú held her intimately.
The girl disliked his cold skin,
and said with a faint smile:
"What night is this tonight,
that I meet this chilly man!"
Liú replied:
"Oh you, oh you,
what is to be done with such a chilly man!"
Thereupon they loved each other joyfully.
Afterwards, she said:
"That maid is shameless,
defiling someone's bed,
and trading me for a pair of trousers!
I must get a little revenge!"
From then on, she came every night without fail,
their affection was very deep.
She took a gold bracelet from her sleeve,
and said:
"This belongs to Bāxiān."
A few days later,
she brought a pair of embroidered shoes in her bosom,
inlaid with pearls and embroidered with gold,
exquisitely crafted,
and she instructed Liú to display them publicly.
Liú took them out to show off to relatives and guests.
Those who wanted to see them all paid for wine as a fee,
and from then on he treated them as rare treasures.
One night when the girl came,
she spoke words of farewell.
Surprised, he asked why,
and she replied:
"My elder sister hates me because of the shoes,
and wants to take the family far away,
to separate me from my love."
Liú was afraid,
and offered to return them.
The girl said:
"No need.
She is using this to pressure me.
If I return them,
I'll fall right into her trap."
Liú asked:
"Why not stay behind alone?"
She said:
"My parents are going far away,
the whole family of over ten people
all rely on Master Hú to manage affairs.
If I don't go with them,
I fear that long-tongued woman will spread rumors."
From then on, she did not come again.
After more than two years,
he missed her intensely.
Once on the road,
he encountered a young woman riding a slow-paced horse,
with an old servant holding the reins.
They brushed shoulders as they passed;
she turned and lifted her veil to peek at him,
revealing a stunningly beautiful appearance.
A moment later,
a young man arrived from behind.
He said:
"Who is that woman?
She seems quite lovely."
Liú praised her enthusiastically.
The young man clasped his hands and laughed:
"You flatter her too much!
This is my humble wife."
Liú, flustered and ashamed, apologized for his mistake.
The young man said:
"No harm done.
But among the three Zhǔs of Nányáng,
you obtained the dragon;
what is my insignificant self worth mentioning!"
Liú was puzzled by his words.
The young man said:
"Do you not recognize the one who secretly slept on your couch?"
Only then did Liú realize it was Hú.
They spoke of their bond as brothers-in-law,
joking and bantering very merrily.
The young man said:
"My father-in-law has just returned,
and I am going to pay him a visit.
Would you like to come along?"
Liú was delighted
and followed him into the winding mountains.
On the mountain was an old estate where local people had taken refuge from turmoil.
The woman dismounted and went inside.
After a short while,
several people came out to look,
saying:
"Official Liú has come too."
He entered the gate and paid his respects to the old man and his wife.
Another young man was already there,
his boots and robes dazzlingly fine.
The old man said:
"This is my son-in-law Dīng from Fùchuān."
They all bowed and took their seats.
Soon after,
wine and roasted meats were served in abundance,
and the conversation and laughter were quite congenial.
The old man said:
"Today, with all three sons-in-law present,
it can be called a fine gathering.
Since there are no outsiders,
we can call the children to come
and have a family reunion."
In a moment,
the sisters all came out.
The old man ordered seats to be set,
each beside her own husband.
When Bāxiān saw Liú,
she only covered her mouth and laughed;
Fèngxiān teased and mocked him;
Shuǐxiān's looks were slightly inferior,
but she was dignified, gentle, and reserved.
While the whole table engaged in lively conversation,
she merely held her wine and smiled.
Thus, shoes and slippers intermingled,
the fragrance of orchids and musk perfumed the air,
and they drank wine with great joy.
Liú noticed that musical instruments were fully prepared by the bedside,
so he took a jade flute
and offered to play for the old man's longevity.
The old man was pleased
and ordered those skilled to each take up an instrument.
Thereupon, everyone at the table vied to take one;
only Dīng and Fèngxiān did not take any.
Bāxiān said:
"It's fine if Young Master Dīng is not proficient,
but how can you, with your fingers curled, not stretch them out?"
She then threw the clappers into Fèngxiān's lap.
And so they played a medley of tunes.
The old man said happily:
"Our family's joy is at its peak!
Since the children can all sing and dance,
why not each display their best skills?"
Bāxiān stood up,
grabbed Shuǐxiān, and said:
"Fèngxiān has always treated her voice as gold and jade,
not daring to trouble her;
the two of us can sing
the song 'Luòfēi'."
Just as the two finished singing and dancing,
a maid happened to bring in fruit on a golden tray,
but no one knew what it was called.
The old man said:
"This was brought from Zhēnlà,
what is called
'tián pó luó'."
He then scooped up several and offered them to Dīng.
Fèngxiān said unhappily:
"Does father-in-law base his affection on wealth and poverty?"
The old man gave a slight smile and did not speak.
Bāxiān said:
"Father treats Young Master Dīng as a guest because he is from another county.
If we talk about seniority,
is Fèngxiān the only one with a sour-faced husband the size of a fist?"
Fèngxiān remained displeased.
She removed her splendid attire,
handed the drumsticks to a maid,
and sang
the act
"The Dilapidated Kiln",
her voice filled with tears.
When she finished,
she flicked her sleeves and left directly,
casting a pall over the whole gathering.
Bāxiān said:
"That girl's willful temper is as it always was."
She went after her,
but did not know where she had gone.
Liú, feeling ashamed,
also took his leave and returned.
Halfway there,
he saw Fèngxiān sitting by the roadside.
She called him to sit beside her,
saying:
"You are a man;
can you not bring honor to the one at your bedside?
The golden house lies within the books;
I hope you will strive diligently."
Lifting her foot, she said:
"I left in such a hurry
that thorns tore my embroidered shoes.
Is the thing I gave you
still with you?"
Liú took it out.
She took it and changed into it.
Liú asked for her worn-out pair.
She laughed and said:
"You are really quite shameless!
When have you seen someone wanting to keep
their own beddings and pillows?
If you truly care for me,
I can give you one thing."
She immediately took out a mirror and handed it to him, saying:
"If you wish to see me,
you must look for me among the books;
otherwise,
there will be no chance for us to meet."
Having said this,
she disappeared.
He returned feeling disconsolate.
Looking into the mirror,
he saw Fèngxiān standing with her back to him inside it,
as if she were a person seen from a hundred paces away.
Remembering her instructions,
he declined visitors and secluded himself behind lowered curtains.
One day,
he saw the figure in the mirror suddenly turn to face him,
her smile brimming as if about to laugh,
and he cherished her even more.
When no one was around,
he would often gaze at her together with his reflection.
After more than a month,
his determination gradually waned,
and he frequently went out wandering, forgetting to return.
Coming home and seeing the image in the mirror,
it looked sorrowful as if weeping;
looking again the next day,
she was standing with her back to him as before: he then realized it was because he had neglected his studies.
So he shut his door and studied diligently,
day and night without cease;
after more than a month,
the image turned outward again.
From then on, he tested it:
whenever he neglected his duties,
her expression would be sad;
after several days of hard work,
her expression would be smiling.
Thus, he hung the mirror morning and evening,
as if facing a teacher or guardian.
Continuing like this for two years,
he passed the examination in one attempt.
Overjoyed, he said:
"Now I can face my Fèngxiān!"
Taking up the mirror to look,
he saw painted eyebrows long and curved,
teeth like melon seeds slightly revealed,
a joyful expression as if it could be scooped up,
as if she were right before his eyes.
Loving her to the extreme,
he gazed without stopping.
Suddenly, the figure in the mirror laughed and said:
"'The lover in the reflection,
the beloved in the painting'—
that describes us now."
Startled and delighted, he looked all around,
and Fèngxiān was already seated beside him.
Holding her hand, he asked after her parents' well-being.
She said:
"Since I parted from you,
I have not returned home,
but stayed hidden in a mountain cave,
sharing your hardships from afar."
When Liú went to a banquet in the commandery,
the girl asked to go with him;
they rode together in the carriage,
yet people facing them could not see her.
Later, when about to return,
she secretly plotted with Liú
to pretend he had married someone from the commandery.
Once the girl had returned,
she began to receive guests
and manage household affairs.
Everyone marveled at her beauty,
but did not know she was a fox.
Liú was a protégé of the magistrate of Fùchuān,
and went to pay his respects.
He met Dīng,
who warmly invited him to his home,
treating him with generous hospitality.
He said:
"My parents-in-law have recently moved elsewhere.
My wife has gone to visit her family,
and will return soon.
I will send a letter to inform them,
and also come to offer congratulations."
Liú initially suspected Dīng was also a fox,
but after carefully inquiring about his family background,
learned he was the son of a wealthy merchant from Fùchuān.
Earlier,
Dīng was returning from his country estate at dusk
when he met Shuǐxiān walking alone.
Seeing her beauty,
he glanced at her subtly.
The girl asked to ride with him.
Dīng was pleased,
took her to his study,
and they slept together.
When she could enter through the window lattice gaps,
he realized she was a fox.
The girl said:
"Do not doubt me, sir.
It is because of your sincere devotion
that I wished to entrust myself to you."
Dīng doted on her,
and ultimately did not marry anyone else.
When Liú returned,
he borrowed a spacious house from a wealthy family,
prepared guest rooms and a bridal chamber,
cleaned and polished until it was spotless,
but worried about lacking furnishings;
looking the next night,
it was already splendidly decorated.
After several days,
indeed over thirty people arrived,
carrying banners, bringing wine and gifts,
carriages and horses in great profusion,
filling the steps and lanes.
Liú ushered the old man and Dīng and Hú into the guest quarters,
while Fèngxiān welcomed the old woman and her two sisters into the inner chambers.
Bāxiān said:
"Now that our little sister is noble,
she won't blame the matchmaker anymore.
Are the bracelet and shoes still there?"
The girl searched and handed them to her,
saying:
"The shoes are still here,
but they've been seen through by a thousand people."
Bāxiān hit her back with the shoe,
saying:
"I strike you for sending them to Liú."
Then she threw them into the fire,
chanting:
"When new, like a flower blooming;
when old, like a flower withering;
treasured, never worn—
may Cháng'é come to borrow them."
Shuǐxiān also chanted for her:
"Once cradling jade bamboo shoots,
worn, praised by ten thousand;
if Cháng'é were to see them,
she would pity them for being too slender."
Fèngxiān poked the fire and said:
"Nightly ascending the blue sky,
one morning leaving the beloved;
leaving behind a slender shadow,
for all the world to see."
Then she mixed the ashes in a tray,
heaping them into over ten portions.
Seeing Liú approach,
she presented them to him as a gift.
All he saw were embroidered shoes filling the tray,
all in the original style.
Bāxiān hurried out,
pushed the tray to the ground;
one or two shoes still remained on the ground,
and she bent down to blow on them,
until their traces finally vanished.
The next day,
because the journey was long,
Dīng and his wife returned first.
Bāxiān, indulging in play with her sister,
was urged repeatedly by the old man and Hú,
and only emerged at noon,
leaving with the others.
When they first arrived,
their procession was overly grand,
drawing crowds of onlookers like a market.
Two bandits caught sight of the beautiful women,
lost their souls,
and plotted to rob them on the road.
Watching them leave the village,
they followed behind.
Though separated by less than a foot,
their horses galloped at full speed,
yet could not catch up.
Reaching a place
where cliffs narrowed the road on both sides,
the carriage slowed slightly;
catching up,
they brandished knives and roared,
and the crowd all fled.
Dismounting and lifting the carriage curtain,
they found an old woman sitting inside.
Suspecting they had mistakenly seized her mother;
just as they looked away,
a weapon wounded the right arm,
and in moments they were bound.
Staring intently,
the cliffs were not cliffs at all,
but the city gate of Pínglè;
in the carriage was the mother of Jìnshì Lǐ,
returning from the countryside.
The other bandit arriving later
also had his horse's leg cut and was captured.
The gate guards seized and delivered them to the prefect,
and they confessed after one interrogation.
At the time, a major robber had not been caught;
questioning them,
it turned out to be them.
The following spring,
Liú passed the highest imperial examination.
Fèngxiān, because her beauty had invited trouble,
declined all congratulations from her relatives.
Liú also never married anyone else.
When he became a court official,
he took a concubine,
and they had two sons.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Alas!
The attitudes of warmth and coldness
are indeed no different between immortals and mortals!
'If one does not exert oneself in youth,
in old age one will only lament in vain.'
It is a pity that there are no competitive beauties
to serve as mirror reflections of sorrow and laughter.
I wish that the countless immortals of the Ganges sands
would all send their lovely daughters to marry in the mortal world;
then in the sea of poverty,
sentient beings would have less suffering."
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Dǒng Shēng,
a man from Xúzhōu,
was fond of swordsmanship
and often considered himself gallant and heroic.
Once on the road, he met a traveler
riding a lame donkey and traveling together.
Speaking with him,
his conversation was bold and unrestrained.
Asked his name,
he said:
"My surname is Tóng, from Liáoyáng."
Dǒng asked:
"Where are you going?"
He replied:
"I have been away from home for twenty years,
and have just returned from overseas."
Dǒng said:
"You have roamed the four seas,
and seen many people;
have you ever encountered extraordinary individuals?"
Tóng said:
"What kind of extraordinary individuals?"
Dǒng then described his own interests,
expressing regret at not having received teachings from extraordinary individuals.
Tóng said:
"Extraordinary individuals can be found everywhere;
but only those who are loyal ministers and filial sons
can receive their arts."
Dǒng again declared himself resolutely;
then drew his sword,
flicked it and sang;
and also cut down a small tree by the roadside,
to show off its sharpness.
Tóng stroked his beard and smiled slightly,
then asked to borrow it for a look.
Dǒng handed it to him.
After examining it once,
he said:
"This is forged from armor iron,
steamed by sweat and odor,
and is of the lowest quality.
Although I have not studied swordsmanship,
I have a sword
that is quite usable."
He then drew a short blade about a foot long from under his clothes,
and used it to slice Dǒng's sword,
which fell apart like a melon or gourd,
breaking diagonally with a single stroke,
like a horse's hoof.
Dǒng was utterly astonished,
and also asked to handle it;
after repeatedly wiping it, he returned it.
He invited Tóng to his home,
and insisted on hosting him for two nights.
When asked about swordsmanship,
Tóng declined, saying he knew nothing.
Dǒng talked boldly with his hands on his knees,
while Tóng only listened respectfully.
Late into the night,
they suddenly heard commotion in the neighboring courtyard.
The neighboring courtyard was where Dǒng's father lived,
and he grew alarmed and suspicious.
He pressed close to the wall and listened intently,
hearing only an angry voice saying:
"Tell your son to come out quickly for punishment,
and we will spare you!"
After a moment,
it seemed like someone was being beaten,
with continuous groaning;
it was indeed his father.
Dǒng seized a spear and wanted to go.
Tóng stopped him, saying:
"Going there would likely mean no chance of survival;
you should consider the safest course."
Dǒng anxiously asked for advice.
Tóng said:
"The bandits are demanding you by name;
they are determined to have their way.
You have no other close relatives,
so you should entrust your affairs to your wife;
I will open the door
and alert the servants for you."
Dǒng agreed,
and went in to tell his wife.
His wife clung to his clothes and wept.
Dǒng's heroic resolve instantly vanished,
and they both went upstairs,
searching for bows and arrows
to prepare for the bandits' attack.
In the midst of their panic,
they heard Tóng laughing on the eaves of the building:
"The bandits have fortunately left."
When they lit a candle to look,
he had already vanished.
Hesitantly, they went out
and saw the old man returning from drinking with neighbors,
carrying a lantern;
only in the courtyard were there traces of burnt straw ashes.
Then they realized Tóng was an extraordinary being.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Loyalty and filial piety
are the very lifeblood of a person;
throughout history, subjects and sons who failed to die for their rulers or fathers
—did they not initially have moments of heroic resolve to take up arms?
It is all because a single change of thought led them astray.
In the past, Xiè Jìn and Fāng Xiàorú pledged to die together,
but in the end, Xiè broke his word;
who knows if, after returning from making the vow,
he did not listen to his wife weeping by the bedside?"
In the county, there was a certain swift constable
who often did not return home for several days,
so his wife had an affair with a local rogue.
One day, upon returning,
he encountered the young man coming out of the room,
and grew highly suspicious,
questioning his wife intensely.
His wife denied it.
Then, finding the young man's belongings by the bedside,
his wife was cornered and speechless,
only kneeling and begging for mercy.
The constable was furious,
threw her a rope,
and forced her to hang herself.
His wife asked to dress up before dying,
and he agreed.
His wife then went into the room to tidy her appearance;
he poured himself a drink and waited,
scolding and urging her repeatedly.
Soon, his wife came out in dazzling attire,
tearfully bowing and saying:
"Do you truly have the heart to make me die?"
The constable angrily rebuked her.
His wife turned and ran back into the room;
just as she was about to tie the noose,
he threw down his cup and shouted:
"Hey,
come back!
A green hat
might not be enough to crush a person to death."
Thus, they resumed their relationship as husband and wife.
This is also a case similar to that of the great official,
a laughable matter.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
A certain man from Yíshuǐ,
during the late Ming, served in the Liáoyáng army.
When Liáoyáng city fell,
he was killed by chaotic soldiers;
though his head was severed,
he was not entirely dead.
By night,
a person holding a register came
and checked the names of the ghosts.
When he reached this man,
he said he should not have died,
and ordered his attendants to reattach his head and send him back.
So they took the head and placed it on his neck,
supported him together,
with the wind rustling,
and after moving for a while,
set him down and left.
Looking at the place,
it was his hometown.
The local magistrate heard of this
and suspected he had escaped secretly.
After detaining and interrogating him, he learned the truth,
but remained quite skeptical;
further examining his neck and finding no trace of severance,
he was about to punish him.
The man said:
"My words are unreliable,
but I ask to be held in prison temporarily.
A severed head can be faked,
but a fallen city cannot.
If Liáoyáng city remains unharmed,
then it will not be too late to receive punishment."
The magistrate agreed.
A few days later,
news from Liáoyáng arrived,
and the timing matched exactly what he had said,
so he was released.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Scholar Zhāng from Ānqiū,
lying ill in bed,
was reclining with his head propped up.
Suddenly, he saw a tiny man emerge from his chest,
only half a foot tall;
wearing a scholar's cap and robes,
he performed like an actor.
He sang a Kūnshān opera tune,
his voice clear and pure,
and in his spoken parts, he introduced himself by name and origin,
which were exactly the same as Zhāng's own;
the events he sang about,
were all the experiences of Zhāng's life.
After four acts were completed,
he recited a poem and vanished.
Zhāng still remembered the gist of it,
and recounted it to others.
According to the twenty-four volume manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Scholar Xú from Héjiān,
was teaching in Ēn.
At the start of winter, he was returning home,
when he met an old man on the road,
who looked him over and said:
"Master Xú has concluded his teaching term.
Where will you teach next year?"
Xú replied:
"The same as before."
The old man said:
"My name is Shī Jìngyè.
I have a nephew who is seeking a good teacher,
and I was just entrusted to go to Dōngtuǎn to hire Lǚ Zǐlián,
but he has already accepted payment in Jìmén.
If you would be willing to take the position,
the salary would be double what you receive in Ēn."
Xú declined, citing his prior commitment.
The old man said:
"You are a man of your word.
However, the new year is still far off,
I respectfully offer one tael of gold as payment,
for you to teach him temporarily,
and we can discuss next year separately, how about that?"
Xú agreed.
The old man dismounted and presented a gift box,
and said:
"My humble home is not far.
The residence is quite cramped,
and it's difficult to keep livestock,
please send your servant and horse away now: walking would be fine."
Xú complied,
placing his luggage on the old man's horse.
After walking three or four *lǐ*,
as dusk fell,
they finally reached the residence,
with riveted nails and beast-head knockers,
it clearly resembled an old, established family's home.
He called his nephew out to pay respects,
a boy of thirteen or fourteen.
The old man said:
"My brother-in-law Jiǎng Nánchuān,
formerly served as a Commander.
He left only this son,
who is quite bright,
but somewhat spoiled.
With a month of your good guidance,
it should be worth ten years."
Before long,
a banquet was set,
extremely lavish and sumptuous;
and serving wine and food,
were all maids and elderly women.
One maid stood holding a wine pot,
about fifteen or sixteen years old,
with an exceptionally charming and graceful demeanor,
and Xú secretly felt stirred.
After the banquet ended,
the old man arranged for a bed to be prepared for him to sleep,
then took his leave and departed.
Before dawn,
the boy came out for his studies.
Just as Xú got up,
a maid came to hold a towel and assist with washing,
it was the same maid who had held the wine pot.
She provided three meals a day,
all handled by this maid;
in the evening,
she came again to make the bed.
Xú asked:
"Why are there no male servants?"
The maid smiled without answering,
spread the quilt and left directly.
The next evening she came again.
Xú made flirtatious remarks to her,
the maid smiled without refusing,
so he became intimate with her.
She then told him:
"My family has no men at all,
external matters are entrusted to Uncle Shī.
My name is Àinú.
The mistress deeply respects you,
fearing the other maids might not be clean,
so she sent me.
Now we must keep this secret,
if discovered,
we would both lose face."
One night,
sleeping together, they forgot the dawn,
and were encountered by the young master,
Xú felt ashamed and uneasy.
That evening,
the maid came and said:
"Fortunately, the mistress values you,
otherwise it would be ruined!
The young master went to tell her,
the mistress quickly covered his mouth,
as if afraid you might hear.
She only warned me not to stay long in the study."
Having said this,
she left.
Xú was very grateful to her.
However, the young master did not study well,
and when Xú scolded him,
the mistress would always intercede on his behalf.
At first, she sent the maid to relay messages;
gradually, she came in person,
speaking with the teacher through the door,
often shedding tears.
But every evening she would ask about the young master's daily lessons.
Xú grew quite impatient,
and with a stern expression said:
"You indulge your son's laziness,
yet blame his lack of diligence,
I am not accustomed to being such a teacher!
I request to resign."
The mistress sent the maid to apologize,
and Xú then stayed.
Since entering the household,
whenever he wanted to go out for a stroll,
he was always confined.
One day,
feeling depressed while drunk,
he called the maid to ask the reason.
The maid said:
"No other reason,
just fearing it would disrupt studies.
If you must go out,
please only do so at night."
Xú angrily said:
"Having received a few taels of gold,
must I be imprisoned here until I die!
You tell me to sneak out at night, but where would I go?
I have long been ashamed of idly eating without working,
the payment is still in my bag anyway."
So he took out the gold and placed it on the table,
packed his belongings, and prepared to leave.
The mistress came out,
gazing silently without speaking,
only covering her face with her sleeve and sobbing,
had the maid return the gold,
unlocked the door, and saw him off.
Xú felt the doorway was narrow and cramped;
after walking a few steps,
sunlight shone in,
and he found himself emerging from within a burial mound,
looking around at the desolate scene,
it was an ancient tomb.
He was greatly shocked.
However, moved by their kindness,
he sold the gold he had been given,
and had the mound repaired and trees planted before leaving.
After a year had passed,
I passed by that place again,
paid my respects at the tomb, and then continued on my way.
From afar, I saw Old Man Shī,
who greeted me with a warm smile,
and earnestly invited me.
Though I knew he was a ghost,
I wanted to inquire about Madame Jiǎng’s well-being,
so I accompanied him into the village,
where we bought wine and drank together.
Unaware that dusk had fallen,
the old man rose to pay for the wine,
and then said:
“My humble home is not far from here.
My younger sister has also just returned for a visit.
I hope you will grace us with your presence,
to help dispel any inauspiciousness for this old man.”
We left the village and walked a short distance,
then came upon another hamlet.
He knocked on the door and we entered,
and he lit a candle for his guest.
Shortly after,
Madame Jiǎng came out from within,
and upon closer inspection,
she appeared to be a beautiful woman of about forty.
She bowed in gratitude and said:
“Our family has declined,
and our household is scattered and desolate.
Yet you, sir, have shown kindness even to dry bones—
truly, there is no way we can repay you.”
Having said this,
she began to weep.
Then she called for Àinú,
and said to Xú:
“This maid
is someone I dearly love.
I now give her to you,
hoping she may bring some comfort to your solitude while away from home.
Whatever you may need,
she can also somewhat understand your intentions.”
Xú assented.
After a short while,
both the brother and sister departed,
leaving the maid to attend to him for the night.
At the first crow of the rooster,
the old man came to urge him to pack and see him off;
Madame Jiǎng also came out,
instructing the maid to serve the gentleman well.
She also said to Xú:
“From now on, you must be especially discreet.
Our encounter has been strange and unusual,
and I fear that busybodies may spread rumors.”
Xú agreed and bid farewell,
then rode off together with the maid.
Upon arriving at his lodging,
he occupied a separate room,
where they lived together.
Sometimes when guests came,
the maid did not hide,
yet others could not see her.
Occasionally, if he desired something,
the thought would just arise,
and the maid would already have brought it.
She was also skilled in witchcraft;
with a gentle rub, ailments would be cured instantly.
During the Qingmíng Festival, he returned home,
and when they reached the tomb site,
the maid took her leave and descended.
Xú asked her to convey his gratitude to Madame Jiǎng.
She replied:
“Yes.”
And then she vanished.
A few days later, when he returned,
just as he was about to visit the tomb again,
he saw the maid sitting under a tree in splendid attire,
so they set off together.
Throughout the year, they came and went like this,
and it became their usual routine.
He wanted to take her back with him to his home,
but she firmly refused.
At the end of the year,
he resigned from his teaching position and returned home,
and they agreed to meet again later.
The maid accompanied him to the place where they had previously sat,
pointed to a pile of stones, and said:
“This is Jiāng’s tomb.
Before Madame was married,
I served her,
and when I died young, I was buried here.
If you pass by again,
burn a stick of incense in mourning,
and we will surely meet again.”
They parted, and he returned home,
longing for her with deep sorrow.
He respectfully went to offer prayers,
but there was no sign of her at all.
So he bought a coffin and opened the tomb,
intending to take her bones back for burial,
as a way to express his affection and longing.
When the tomb was opened, he entered,
and saw that her complexion was as if she were alive.
Though her skin had not decayed,
her clothes had turned to dust;
the jade ornaments and gold bracelets on her head
all looked as if they were newly made.
Looking at her waist,
he found several ingots of gold wrapped there,
which he took and kept.
Then he removed his robe to cover the corpse,
carried it into the coffin,
hired a carriage to transport it back;
placed it in a separate residence,
adorned it with embroidered garments,
and slept alone beside it,
hoping for some spiritual response.
Suddenly, Àinú entered from outside,
and said with a laugh:
“So the grave robber is here!”
Xú was both startled and overjoyed, and greeted her warmly.
The maid said:
“I went with Madame to Dōngchāng,
and when we returned after three days,
the house was already empty.
Though you invited me many times,
the reason I refused to follow you
was that I had received great kindness from Madame,
and could not bear to leave her.
But now that you have taken me by force,
quickly bury me,
and that will be a great kindness.”
Xú asked:
“There are stories of people reviving after a hundred years.
Since your lovely body remains as before,
why not try to revive?”
She sighed and said:
“This is a matter of fate.
The miraculous tales passed down in the world
are often half illusory and false.
If I wanted to rise and move about again,
would that really be so difficult?
But I cannot be like a living person,
so it is unnecessary.”
Then she opened the coffin and entered,
and the corpse immediately rose,
standing gracefully and lovely.
Feeling her chest,
it was as cold as ice and snow.
She was about to lie back down in the coffin,
but Xú insisted she stay.
The maid said:
“I was excessively favored by Madame.
When my master returned from a foreign land,
he brought back tens of thousands in gold,
and I secretly took some of it.
He did not pursue the matter much.
Later, when I was critically ill,
and had no relatives,
I hid it to take with me in death.
Madame grieved over my early death,
and also buried me with precious ornaments.
The reason my body has not decayed
is simply due to the lingering energy of the gold and treasures.
If I were among the living,
how could this last long?
If you insist on keeping me like this,
you must never force me to eat or drink;
if my spiritual energy disperses,
then my wandering soul will also vanish.”
So Xú built a refined dwelling,
where they lived together.
Her laughter and conversation were just like an ordinary person’s;
but she did not eat or breathe,
and did not appear before living people.
After more than a year,
Xú drank until slightly intoxicated,
and insisted on pouring the dregs of the wine down her throat;
she immediately collapsed to the ground,
blood and water flowing from her mouth,
and by the end of the day, her corpse had already decomposed.
He was filled with grief and regret, but it was too late,
so he buried her with great ceremony.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
“Madame’s way of educating her son
was no different from that of the human world;
yet how generous she was in her treatment of the tutor!
Is she not virtuous indeed!
I say that a beautiful corpse is not as good as an elegant ghost.
Yet because of the crude recklessness of a poor scholar,
a spiritual being was unable to enjoy longevity—
what a pity!”
In Zhāngqiū there was a scholar named Zhū,
who was upright and stubborn.
He was hired as a tutor in the home of a certain provincial graduate.
Whenever he disciplined his students,
the lady of the house would send a maid to plead for mercy,
but he would not listen.
One day,
the lady herself came to the window
to argue with Zhū.
Zhū became angry,
grabbed a ruler, and rushed out, cursing loudly.
The lady fled in fear;
Zhū chased her,
and from behind struck her buttocks and thighs horizontally,
producing a clanging sound like flesh and skin.
It was absolutely laughable!
A certain man from Chángshān,
whenever he hired a tutor,
would take the year's tuition,
combine the total for the entire year's vacancies and full days,
and calculate the amount due per day;
furthermore, he would record in detail in a ledger the days the tutor left the study and returned to the study;
he kept a detailed record in a ledger;
at the end of the year,
he would publicly calculate together, multiplying and dividing by the days.
A scholar named Mǎ was hired at his home,
and when he first saw him bringing the abacus,
he was very startled to learn the reason;
but then he secretly devised a plan,
turning anger into joy,
and allowed him to recalculate without any argument.
The old man was greatly pleased,
and firmly insisted on renewing the contract for the next year.
Mǎ declined for some reason.
He then recommended a very eccentric scholar to replace himself.
When he took up the position,
he would scold and curse at every turn,
and the old man had no choice
but to endure it all.
At the end of the year,
he brought the abacus.
The scholar became extremely furious,
but reluctantly allowed him to calculate.
The old man also counted the days on the road,
and credited them all to the east;
the scholar would not accept,
and moved the beads back to the west.
The two argued without resolution,
and took up weapons to confront each other;
both ended up with broken heads and bloody faces, and went to court.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain commoner from Qīngzhōu,
over fifty years old,
remarried a young woman.
His two sons feared she would bear more children,
so when their father was drunk,
they secretly cut off his testicles and applied medicine to the wound.
The father awoke,
pretended to be ill and said nothing.
After a long time,
the wound gradually healed.
Suddenly, one day he entered the room,
the sutures split open,
blood gushed out uncontrollably,
and he soon died.
