His wife learned the reason,
and sued the sons in court.
The official interrogated the sons under torture,
and they indeed confessed.
The official exclaimed in shock:
"Now I am the 'Magistrate of Dānfù'
He executed them both.
In the county, there was a scholar named Wáng,
who divorced his wife after just over a month of marriage.
His wife's father sued him.
At that time, the magistrate of Zī, Lord Xīn,
asked Wáng:
"Why did you divorce your wife?"
He replied:
"It's unspeakable."
Pressed firmly,
he said:
"Because she cannot bear children."
Lord Xīn said:
"Nonsense!
A bride of just over a month,
how can you know she won't bear children?"
After hemming and hawing for a long time,
he confessed:
"Her private parts are very lopsided."
Lord Xīn laughed and said:
"So it is the harm of being lopsided,
that causes the family to be disharmonious."
This story can be
passed down together with
the "Magistrate of Dānfù."
A laugh.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Sūn Bìzhēn was crossing the river,
when he encountered a great storm with wind and snow,
the boat rocked violently,
and everyone on board was terrified.
Suddenly, they saw a golden-armored god standing in the clouds,
holding a golden plaque down for them to see;
everyone looked up together,
and on it was written
"Sūn Bìzhēn"
three characters,
very clearly.
The crowd said to Sūn:
"You must have offended heaven and are being punished,
please take a separate boat,
do not implicate us."
Sūn had not yet spoken,
but the crowd did not wait for his consent,
seeing a small boat nearby,
they pushed him onto it.
After Sūn boarded the boat,
he looked back,
and saw the previous boat capsize.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In the county, there was a villager
who was always a rogue.
One day,
he got up in the morning,
and two men seized him and took him away.
When they reached the market,
he saw a butcher hanging half a pig on a rack,
the two men pushed and squeezed him hard against it,
and he felt his body merge with the meat,
and the two men left directly.
After a while,
the butcher began selling meat,
wielding a knife to cut it,
and he felt pain with each cut,
piercing to the marrow.
Later, an old neighbor came to buy meat,
haggling bitterly over the price,
adding fat and extra meat,
cutting piece by piece into fragments,
his suffering was even more severe.
When the meat was all sold,
he then found his way home;
by the time he returned,
the sun was already high in the morning.
His family thought he had gotten up late,
so he recounted in detail what he had experienced.
They called the neighbor to ask,
who had just returned from buying meat,
and the number of pieces and weight of meat he mentioned
matched exactly without the slightest error.
Within a single morning,
he had already suffered a dismemberment once,
isn't that strange!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
On the steep cliffs of the riverbank in Guǎngdōng,
there were often silver ingots embedded in the rocks.
Below the cliff, waves surged,
making it impossible for boats to dock.
Some would row close to pick them,
but they were firmly stuck and immovable;
if a person was destined to obtain it,
then with one pick it would fall off,
and looking back, it would have already regrown.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wáng Zhòngchāo said:
"On Jūnshān in Dòngtíng, there is a stone cave,
high enough to accommodate a boat,
deep and dark, unfathomable,
with lake water flowing in and out.
Once, holding a torch, we rowed a boat in,
and saw that both walls were black stones,
their color like lacquer,
touching them felt soft;
taking a knife to cut them,
it was like cutting hard bean curd.
We could shape them into inkstones at will,
once taken out,
exposed to wind, they would harden and solidify more than other stones.
Testing them with ink,
they were excellent.
Merchant boats and pleasure craft,
come and go in great numbers,
yet among them are fine stones,
but they do not know to take and use them,
relying instead on the appraisal of the curious."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
At Wǔyí Shān there is a sheer cliff a thousand ren high.
People often pick up pieces of fragrant aloeswood and jade at its base.
The prefect heard of this,
and supervised several hundred men in constructing a cloud ladder,
intending to reach the summit to observe the marvel.
It took three years to complete.
The prefect ascended it.
Just as he was about to reach the peak,
he saw a huge foot extending downwards,
its big toe thicker than a clothes-pounding pestle.
A loud voice said:
"If you do not descend,
you will fall!"
Greatly alarmed,
he hurried down.
Just as he reached the ground,
the wooden framework decayed and snapped,
collapsing and falling without a trace remaining.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
During the Wànlì period,
there was a rat in the palace,
as large as a cat,
which caused severe harm.
Fine cats from among the people were sought everywhere to catch and subdue it,
but they were invariably devoured by it.
It happened that a lion cat was offered as tribute from a foreign country,
its fur white as snow.
It was carried and released into the rat's room,
the door was closed,
and they secretly watched it.
The cat crouched for a long time.
The rat hesitantly emerged from its hole,
saw the cat,
and angrily charged at it.
The cat avoided it by leaping onto a table,
the rat also climbed up,
and the cat then jumped down.
Repeating this back and forth,
it happened no less than a hundred times.
Everyone said the cat was timid,
thinking it was incapable.
After a while, the rat's leaps and bounds gradually slowed,
its bulging belly seeming to pant,
and it crouched on the ground to rest briefly.
The cat immediately swiftly descended,
claws seizing the fur on its head,
mouth biting its neck,
they tussled and struggled,
the cat growling,
the rat squeaking.
They opened the door and looked urgently:
the rat's head was already chewed to pieces.
Only then did they realize the cat's avoidance
was not timidity,
but waiting for the rat to tire.
When it came out, it retreated;
when it retreated, it came out again—
it was using this strategy.
Alas!
A common man grasping his sword in anger—
how is he different from this rat!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A certain merchant,
reaching the border of Zhílì,
was suddenly caught in heavy hail.
He took cover among the crops.
He heard a voice in the sky say:
"This is Zhāng Bùliàng's field;
do not harm his grain."
The merchant privately thought: since the Zhāng family is called
"Bùliàng" (No Measure/Not Good),
why is it instead protected?
When the hail stopped,
he entered the village,
inquired about that man,
and also asked the meaning of his name.
It turned out Zhāng was long wealthy,
and had accumulated a great store of grain.
Every spring when poor people came to borrow,
he did not scrutinize how much they repaid;
he accepted it all,
never insisting on using the measuring scoop to get a full measure.
Hence he was named
"Bùliàng" (Does Not Measure),
not "Bùliáng" (Not Good).
The crowd hurried to the fields
and saw stalks and ears broken like hemp,
but only the various fields of the Zhāng family were unharmed.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Two shepherd boys entered the mountains and came to a wolf's den.
The den had two wolf cubs.
They plotted to catch them separately.
Each climbed a tree,
several tens of paces apart.
After a short while,
the big wolf arrived.
Entering the den and finding its young missing,
it appeared very frantic.
A boy in the tree pinched the cub's legs and ears, deliberately making it howl.
The big wolf heard the sound and looked up,
then angrily ran beneath the tree,
howling and clawing.
The other boy then made the cub in that tree cry urgently.
The wolf stopped its noise and looked around in all directions,
finally spotting it,
then left this one and rushed to that one,
running and howling as before.
The cub in the former tree cried again,
and it turned and ran back.
Its mouth never ceased sound,
its feet never stopped moving.
After several tens of trips back and forth,
its running gradually slowed,
its sounds gradually weakened.
Then, barely breathing, it stiffly lay down,
and after a long time did not move.
The boys climbed down to look:
its breath had already ceased.
Now there are sons of the powerful and bullying,
glaring angrily and gripping their swords,
as if about to pounce and devour.
Those who are the object of their anger
simply close their doors and leave.
The bully exhausts his strength and strains his voice,
but finds no opponent.
Does he not then feel supremely self-satisfied?
He does not know that this is the ferocity of a beast,
and people are merely toying with him for amusement.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A certain rich old man:
many merchants borrowed capital from him.
One day as he went out,
a young man followed behind his horse.
He asked him,
and he too was one seeking to borrow capital.
The old man agreed.
When they reached home,
there happened to be several tens of coins on the table.
The young man immediately began stacking the coins with his hand,
piling them high and low.
The old man saw him off,
but in the end did not give him the capital.
Someone asked the reason.
The old man said:
"This man must be skilled at gambling,
he is not an upright person.
The skill he is familiar with
unconsciously manifests in his hands and feet."
Inquiries proved it indeed so.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
When Wáng Jìyǔ, the Grand Marshal of Xīnchéng, was guarding the northern frontier,
he often had craftsmen cast a large pole-blade,
a full foot wide,
weighing a hundred jun.
Whenever he inspected the border,
he would have four men carry it.
Wherever his procession halted,
it was placed on the ground.
Therefore, northerners, grabbing it, found that human strength could not move it in the slightest.
The Marshal secretly had a replica made of paulownia wood,
identical in width, narrowness, and size,
covered with silver foil.
He would often brandish it while on horseback.
The various tribes, seeing it from afar,
were all shocked and awed.
He also buried reed mats beyond the border to mark a boundary,
running diagonally for over ten li.
They looked like a fence.
He proclaimed:
"This is my Great Wall."
When northern troops arrived,
they pulled them all up and burned them.
The Marshal set them up again.
After they were burned three times,
he then placed artillery stones and hidden mechanisms beneath them.
When the northern troops burned the mats,
the explosives and stones all discharged,
causing many casualties.
After they fled,
the Marshal set up the mats as before.
The northern troops, seeing them from afar, all retreated and ran,
and therefore submitted as if to a god.
Later, the Marshal requested retirement and returned home.
An alarm arose again on the frontier.
He was summoned to serve once more.
The Marshal was then eighty-three years old.
Summoning his strength despite illness, he took leave of the emperor.
The emperor consoled him, saying:
"We merely trouble you, Minister, to govern while reclining."
Thereupon the Marshal returned to the frontier.
Wherever he stopped,
he would lie within a curtained enclosure.
When the northerners heard the Marshal had arrived,
they all disbelieved it.
Therefore, under the pretext of discussing peace,
they intended to verify the truth.
They lifted the curtain
and saw the Marshal merely lying there.
They all gazed at the couch, prostrated in worship,
stuck out their tongues in awe, and withdrew.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Yángzhōu Assistant Prefect Tí
dreamed at night that the Mountain God summoned him,
with an angry expression and harsh words.
Looking up, he saw a man standing by the god’s side,
who spoke a few words to ease the situation.
Upon waking, he felt disturbed by the dream.
Early in the morning, he went to the Mountain God Temple,
silently praying for deliverance.
After leaving,
he saw a person at a pharmacy,
who looked exactly like the man he had seen in the dream.
He inquired about him
and learned he was a doctor.
Upon returning home,
he suddenly fell ill.
He specifically sent someone to hire the doctor.
When the doctor arrived, he prescribed medicine.
He took it in the evening,
and died by midnight.
Some say: The King of Hell and the Emperor of the Eastern Peak
daily dispatch 108,000 male and female attendants,
scattered across the world to act as shamans and doctors,
named
"Soul-Snatching Envoys."
Those who use medicine must be cautious!
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Wáng Mùzhēn of Méngyīn
was from an old and prominent family.
Once while traveling in Jiāngzhè,
he saw an old woman crying by the roadside
and asked her why.
She said:
"My late husband left only one son,
who is now sentenced to death.
Is there anyone who can save him?"
Wáng, being generous by nature,
took note of the name
and used money from his purse to intervene on his behalf.
Eventually, the man’s crime was pardoned.
After the man was released,
he heard that Wáng had saved him
but was utterly puzzled as to the reason.
He visited Wáng at his inn,
expressing gratitude and asking for an explanation.
Wáng said:
"It’s nothing.
I just pitied your mother’s old age."
The man was shocked and said:
"My mother has been dead for a long time."
Wáng also found this strange.
By evening,
the old woman came to thank him.
Wáng reproached her for lying.
The old woman said:
"To tell you the truth, I am an old fox from the Eastern Hills.
Twenty years ago,
I had a brief affair with the man’s father,
so I couldn’t bear to see his ghost go hungry."
Wáng rose in awe and respect.
When he tried to question her further,
she had already vanished.
Earlier,
Wáng’s wife was virtuous and devoutly Buddhist.
She abstained from meat and wine;
she kept a clean room
with an image of Guānyīn hanging
and, having no son,
burned incense and prayed there daily.
The deity was very responsive,
often giving her dreams
to guide her on what to do or avoid,
so family matters were all decided based on these.
Later, she fell ill,
and her condition became critical.
She moved her bed into that room;
she also set up a brocade mattress in the inner chamber and locked the door,
as if waiting for someone.
Wáng thought this odd,
but since her illness had made her confused,
he couldn’t bear to upset her.
She had been bedridden for two years,
disliking noise,
and often dismissed others to sleep alone.
Listening secretly,
it seemed she was talking to someone;
but when the door was opened to look,
all was silent.
During her illness, she had no other worries
except her fourteen-year-old daughter,
whom she urged daily to prepare for marriage.
After the daughter was married,
she called Wáng to her bedside,
took his hand, and said:
"Now we must part!
When I first fell ill,
the Bodhisattva told me my life would end soon: what troubled me
was that my daughter was not yet married,
so she gave me some medicine
to prolong my life until then.
Last year,
when the Bodhisattva was returning to the Southern Sea,
she left her attendant Xiǎo Méi before the altar
to serve me.
Now that I am about to die,
I, an ill-fated woman, have no offspring.
Bǎo’ér,
whom I love dearly,
I fear will marry a fierce and angry wife,
leaving him and his mother with no place.
Xiǎo Méi is beautiful and graceful,
gentle and virtuous,
so she can be your second wife."
It turned out Wáng had a concubine
who bore a son,
named Bǎo’ér.
Wáng thought her words absurd
and said:
"You have always revered the gods,
but now you speak like this—
isn’t it blasphemous?"
She replied:
"Xiǎo Méi has served me for over a year,
and we’ve become close as one.
I have already earnestly asked her."
Wáng asked:
"Where is Xiǎo Méi?"
She said:
"Isn’t she in the room?"
Just as he was about to ask more,
she closed her eyes and passed away.
Wáng kept vigil by the spirit curtain at night,
when he heard faint sobbing from the room.
Greatly alarmed,
he suspected it was a ghost.
He called for the maids and concubines to unlock the door and look inside,
and there was a beautiful sixteen-year-old girl,
dressed in mourning clothes, inside the room.
Everyone thought she was a deity,
and they all knelt and bowed to her.
The girl wiped away her tears and helped them up.
Wáng stared intently at her,
but she merely bowed her head.
Wáng said:
"If the words of the deceased Madam are not false,
please ascend to the main hall at once,
and receive the homage of your children;
if this is not possible,
I dare not entertain any wild hopes,
lest I incur blame."
The girl rose gracefully,
and went straight to the north hall.
Wáng had a maid set up a seat facing south for her,
and Wáng bowed first,
to which the girl returned the bow;
then, from the eldest to the youngest, from the humble to the lowly,
they all knelt and kowtowed in turn,
and the girl sat solemnly and received their homage;
only when the concubine came forward,
did she pull her up.
Ever since the Madam fell ill,
the maids had been lazy and the servants thievish,
and the household had long been in decline.
After everyone had paid their respects,
they stood in orderly rows.
The girl said:
"I am moved by Madam's great kindness,
and have lingered in the mortal world,
and she has also entrusted me with this great responsibility.
You should all cleanse your hearts,
and exert yourselves for your master;
as for past faults,
I will not hold them against you;
otherwise,
do not think there is no one in charge here!"
Everyone looked at the seat,
and it truly seemed as if a portrait of Guānyīn was hanging there,
occasionally stirred by a gentle breeze.
Hearing her words, they were awed and vigilant,
and all agreed in unison.
The girl then arranged the funeral affairs,
and everything was done in perfect order.
From then on, no one, great or small, dared to be negligent.
The girl managed both internal and external affairs all day long,
and whenever Wáng intended to do something,
he would also report to her before acting;
yet although they met several times a day,
they never exchanged a single private word.
After the burial,
Wáng wanted to bring up the previous agreement,
but did not dare to speak directly,
so he asked the concubine to hint at it subtly.
The girl said:
"I received Madam's earnest instructions,
and in duty I cannot refuse;
but the great ceremony of marriage,
cannot be done hastily.
Your father's friend, Elder Huáng,
is of high rank and great virtue,
if you ask him to preside over the marriage alliance,
then I will obey your command."
At that time, Huáng, the former Grand Coachman of Yíshuǐ,
was retired and living in leisure,
and was a close friend of Wáng's father,
so they were on the best of terms.
Wáng went to visit him in person,
and told him the truth.
Huáng found it strange,
and immediately came with him.
When the girl heard,
she came out and bowed.
Huáng saw her once,
and was astonished, thinking her a celestial being,
and modestly declined, not daring to accept her courtesy;
later, he provided generous dowry assistance,
and left only after the ceremony was completed.
The girl sent gifts of pillows and shoes,
as if serving her parents-in-law,
and from then on, their relationship grew even closer.
After the wedding,
Wáng, still thinking her a deity,
treated her with reverence amidst intimacy,
and often inquired about the Bodhisattva's daily life.
The girl laughed and said:
"You are too foolish;
how could a righteous deity descend to marry in the mortal world?"
Wáng insisted on knowing her origin.
The girl said:
"There is no need to investigate thoroughly; since you consider me a deity,
just make offerings morning and evening,
and naturally there will be no calamity."
The girl was always lenient in managing her subordinates, and would not speak unless she smiled;
but when the maids and servants were joking and playing around,
if they saw her from afar,
they would fall silent.
The girl smiled and explained:
"Do you still think I am a deity?
What deity am I!
I am actually Madam's cousin,
and we were close since childhood;
when my elder sister fell ill, she missed me,
and secretly sent Granny Wáng from the southern village to summon me here.
But because I would be near my brother-in-law daily,
and there are proprieties between men and women,
I pretended to be a deity and secluded myself in the inner room.
What deity am I, really?"
The crowd still did not believe her.
But as they attended her daily,
and observed her actions,
they found nothing different from an ordinary person,
and the rumors gradually died down.
Yet even the most stubborn slaves and dull-witted maids,
whom Wáng had never been able to reform even with beatings,
would happily obey her with a single word.
They all said:
"We don't even know why.
It's not that we fear her;
but whenever we see her face,
our hearts soften on their own,
so we cannot bear to go against her wishes."
Thus, all neglected affairs were revived.
In a few years,
their fields stretched far and wide, and their granaries held ten thousand bushels.
A few more years later,
the concubine gave birth to a daughter.
The girl gave birth to a son—when the son was born,
there was a red dot on his left arm,
so they named him Xiǎohóng.
When the child was one month old, the girl had Wáng prepare a grand feast and invite Huáng.
Huáng sent generous congratulatory gifts,
but declined on account of his old age,
saying he could not travel far;
the girl sent two sedan chairs to insistently invite him,
and Huáng finally came.
She carried the child out,
bared his left arm,
and showed him the meaning behind the name.
She also repeatedly asked about the child's fortune.
Huáng smiled and said,
"This is a joy-red mark,
so you can add a character,
and name him Xǐhóng."
The girl was overjoyed,
and came out again to bow and kowtow.
That day,
drums and music filled the courtyard,
and noble relatives crowded like a market.
Huáng stayed for three days before leaving.
Suddenly, a carriage and horses arrived outside the gate,
to welcome the girl back to her maiden home.
For over ten years,
there had been no contact,
so everyone discussed it,
but the girl acted as if she did not hear.
After finishing her makeup,
she held the child in her arms,
and asked Wáng to see her off,
and Wáng complied.
After about twenty or thirty lǐ,
where it was quiet and there were no pedestrians,
the girl stopped the carriage,
called for Wáng to dismount from his horse,
dismissed the attendants, and spoke with him:
She said:
"Wáng láng, Wáng láng,
our meetings are short, our partings long—
isn't this sad?"
Wáng asked in surprise why she said this,
and the girl said:
"Who do you think I am?"
He replied:
“I don’t know.”
The woman said,
“In Jiāngnán, you once saved someone from a death sentence—
is that true?”
He replied:
“Yes.”
She said:
“The one weeping by the roadside was my mother.
Moved by your righteousness and wishing to repay you,
she took advantage of your wife’s devotion to Buddhism
and attached herself as a deity,
all so that I could repay you.
Now, fortunately, I have given birth to this child in swaddling clothes,
and this wish is fulfilled.
I see that misfortune is about to befall you.
If this child remains at home,
I fear he cannot be raised safely.
Therefore, I am taking advantage of visiting my parents
to save the child from danger.
Remember this: when there is a death in your household,
at the first crow of the morning rooster,
go to the willow embankment by the West River.
When you see someone carrying a sunflower lantern approaching,
block the road and plead bitterly—
then you may avoid disaster.”
Wáng said:
“Yes.”
He then asked when she would return.
The woman said:
“It cannot be predetermined.
But you must firmly remember my words.
Our reunion will not be far off.”
At parting, they held hands,
shedding tears in sorrow.
In a moment, she mounted the carriage,
swift as the wind.
Wáng watched until she disappeared from sight,
then returned home.
Six or seven years passed,
with absolutely no word from her.
Suddenly, a plague broke out in the surrounding villages,
and many died.
One maidservant fell ill and died after three days.
Wáng recalled the earlier instruction
and grew quite concerned.
That day, he was drinking with guests
and fell into a deep, drunken sleep.
When he awoke,
he heard the rooster crow.
He hurriedly got up and went to the embankment,
where he saw a flickering lantern light
that had just passed by.
He chased after it urgently,
but though it was only about a hundred paces away,
the more he chased, the farther it went,
until gradually it vanished from sight.
He returned in frustration and regret.
A few days later, he fell violently ill
and soon died.
The Wáng clan had many ruffians
who together bullied the orphaned and widowed,
openly cutting down and taking
the fields, crops, and trees,
causing the family to decline daily.
After a year,
Bǎo’ér also died young,
leaving the household without any master.
The clansmen grew even more aggressive,
dividing up the farmland and property.
The oxen and horses in the stables were all gone;
they then wanted to split up the residence.
Because the concubine still lived there,
several men came
and forcibly seized her to sell her off.
The concubine clung to her young daughter,
and mother and child wept together,
their misery moving the neighbors.
Just as they were in this crisis,
suddenly they heard the sound of a sedan chair outside the gate.
Everyone looked,
and saw the woman stepping out of the carriage with a young boy.
She glanced around at the bustling crowd and asked:
“Who are these people?”
The concubine tearfully recounted what had happened.
The woman’s face turned pale with distress.
She immediately called the servants who had come with her,
closed the gate, and locked it.
The ruffians tried to resist,
but their limbs went limp as if paralyzed.
The woman ordered them all tied up,
bound to the corridor pillars,
and given only three bowls of thin gruel a day.
She then sent an old servant running to inform Huáng Gōng,
after which she entered the house and wept mournfully.
When her tears subsided,
she said to the concubine:
“This is fate.
I was originally due to come last month,
but my mother’s illness delayed me,
and so it has come to this.
Who would have thought that in the blink of an eye, it would become ruins!”
She asked about the former maids and nannies,
only to learn they had all been seized by the clansmen,
which made her sigh even more.
The next day,
when the maids and servants heard the woman had returned,
they all slipped back on their own.
At the reunion, everyone wept.
The captured clansmen
all clamored that the boy was not Mùzhēn’s true heir,
but the woman did not bother to argue.
Soon after, Huáng Gōng arrived.
The woman led the boy out to greet him.
Huáng grasped the boy’s arm,
rolled up his left sleeve,
and saw the vermilion birthmark clearly there.
He then bared it to show everyone,
proving it was indeed true.
He then carefully checked the missing items,
recorded them in a ledger by name,
and personally went to see the county magistrate.
The magistrate detained the ruffians,
gave each forty lashes,
and imprisoned them under strict orders to recover everything.
Within a few days,
the fields, land, oxen, and horses
were all returned to their original owner.
When Huáng was about to leave,
the woman led the boy in tearful homage and said:
“I am not of this world,
as you, Uncle, know.
I now entrust this child to you.”
Huáng said:
“As long as this old man has a breath left,
I will do everything I can to manage things.”
After Huáng left,
the woman settled all accounts and arrangements,
entrusted the boy to the concubine,
and then prepared offerings to sweep her husband’s grave.
Half a day passed, and she did not return.
They went to look,
and found the wine cups and offerings still laid out,
but she had vanished without a trace.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
“One who does not cut off another’s line
will not have his own line cut off—
this seems like human action, yet it is truly heavenly.
As for having good friends in one’s circle,
sharing carriages and furs;
but once the weeds grow over the grave
and wife and children are oppressed,
then those in the carriage look coldly and depart.
To not forget a friend even in death,
to feel gratitude and seek to repay it—
what kind of person is this!
A fox!
If you had great wealth,
I would serve as your steward.”
From the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A certain man from Jìníng
happened to see a wandering monk outside a country temple,
who was sunning himself and catching lice.
The monk carried a gourd on his staff,
like a medicine seller.
The man jokingly said,
"Monk, do you also sell bedroom pills?"
The monk replied,
"Yes.
The weak can become strong,
the small can become large,
with immediate effect,
without waiting overnight."
The man was delighted
and asked for some.
The monk untied a corner of his robe,
took out a pill the size of a millet grain,
and told him to swallow it.
After about half the time it takes to cook a meal,
his lower part suddenly grew;
after another moment, he felt it himself—
it had increased by one-third compared to before.
Still unsatisfied,
he watched as the monk got up to relieve himself,
secretly untied the robe,
took two or three pills, and swallowed them all.
Soon he felt as if his skin were splitting,
his tendons being pulled,
his neck shrinking and his waist bending,
while his private part kept growing.
Terrified,
he had no solution.
When the monk returned
and saw his condition,
he exclaimed in alarm,
"You must have stolen my medicine!"
He quickly gave him one pill,
and only then did it stop.
Undressing to look at himself,
he found it had grown almost as long as his two thighs, forming a tripod.
With his neck shrunk, he staggered home,
and even his parents could not recognize him.
From then on, he became a useless creature,
lying on the street all day,
seen by many.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Viceroy Yú Chénglóng
was inspecting the region and arrived at Gāoyóu.
It happened that a wealthy family was about to marry off their daughter,
with a rich dowry,
which was stolen overnight by thieves who took everything.
The local magistrate was at a loss.
Lord Yú ordered all city gates closed,
leaving only one open for pedestrians to come and go,
with officers guarding it
and strictly searching all loads.
He also issued a notice,
instructing all households in the city to return to their homes,
to await a search the next day,
ensuring the stolen goods would be found.
He then secretly instructed the officers:
if anyone passed through the gate more than once,
arrest them.
After noon, two such men were caught,
carrying nothing but themselves.
Lord Yú said,
"These are the real thieves."
The two men argued incessantly.
Lord Yú ordered them stripped and searched,
and under their robes were found two sets of women's clothing,
all from the dowry.
It turned out they feared the next day's search,
and were in a hurry to move the goods,
but there was too much to carry,
so they secretly wore them and made multiple trips.
Also, when Lord Yú was a county magistrate,
he once went to a neighboring county.
Early in the morning,
passing outside the city walls,
he saw two men carrying a sick person on a bed,
covered with a large quilt;
hair was visible on the pillow,
with a phoenix hairpin stuck in it,
and the person lay sideways on the bed.
Three or four strong men accompanied them,
taking turns pressing the quilt
under the body,
as if afraid of wind getting in.
After a while,
they rested by the roadside,
and had two others take over carrying the bed.
As Lord Yú passed,
he sent a clerk back to ask,
and was told it was a critically ill younger sister
being taken back to her husband's home.
After walking two or three miles,
Lord Yú sent the clerk back again
to see which village they entered.
The clerk followed them
to a village house,
where two men came out to meet them and they went inside.
The clerk returned and reported to Lord Yú.
Lord Yú asked the county magistrate,
"Has there been any robbery in the city?"
The magistrate replied,
"None."
At the time, laws were strict,
and both superiors and subordinates avoided mentioning robbery,
so even if people were robbed or killed,
they endured it and dared not speak up.
Lord Yú went to his lodgings
and instructed his men to investigate carefully.
Sure enough, a wealthy family had been invaded by robbers,
and the owner had been tortured to death.
Lord Yú summoned the son
and questioned him about the situation.
The son stubbornly denied it.
Lord Yú said,
"I have already captured the major thieves;
there is nothing else."
The son then kowtowed, weeping bitterly,
and begged for justice for the deceased.
Lord Yú went to see the county magistrate,
and dispatched strong officers at the fourth watch to leave the city,
go straight to the village house,
and arrest eight men,
who confessed after one interrogation.
When asked who the sick woman was,
the thieves confessed:
"That night we were all in the brothel,
so we conspired with a prostitute,
placed the money on the bed,
and had her lie on it until we reached the hideout to divide the loot."
Everyone admired Lord Yú's divine insight.
When asked how he knew,
Lord Yú said,
"This is very easy to explain,
but people just don't pay attention.
How could a young woman on a bed
allow men to put their hands under the quilt?
Moreover, when changing shoulders while carrying her,
they were very careful;
with hands guarding it,
it was clear there must be something inside.
If it were a sick woman in a daze,
there would surely be women waiting at the door to welcome her;
but only men were seen,
and they didn't even ask a single surprised question—
that's how I knew for sure they were thieves."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
During the Wànlì reign,
the magistrate of Lìchéng dreamed that the city god demanded servants.
He wrote the names of eight yamen runners on a document,
sealed it with his official seal, and burned it in the temple.
That night,
all eight men died.
East of the temple was a wine shop,
whose owner was previously acquainted with one of the runners.
That night, the runner came to buy wine.
The shopkeeper asked,
"What guests are you entertaining?"
He replied,
"I have many colleagues;
I'm buying a jar to share a drink and chat."
At dawn,
when the shopkeeper saw other runners,
he learned that the man had already died.
He went to the temple and opened the door,
and found the wine jar there,
still full of wine as before.
Returning home, he looked at the money he had been given—
it was all paper ashes.
The magistrate had statues of the eight men made for the temple.
Whenever runners were assigned duties,
they would first make offerings to them before leaving;
otherwise,
they would surely be beaten or reprimanded.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Shàoxīng, there was a widowed old woman spinning at night,
when suddenly a young girl pushed the door open and entered.
Smiling, she said:
"Old granny, aren't you toiling too hard?"
Looking at her,
she appeared about eighteen or nineteen,
with elegant and beautiful features,
and wearing a dazzlingly splendid robe.
The old woman, startled, asked,
"Where have you come from?"
The girl said:
"I pitied you living alone,
so I came to keep you company."
The old woman suspected she was a fugitive from a noble household,
and pressed her with questions.
The girl said:
"Don't be afraid, granny.
My being orphaned,
is just like your widowhood.
I admire your purity and integrity,
so I came to join you.
Wouldn't it be nice for both of us to avoid loneliness?
Isn't it indeed a good thing?"
The old woman then suspected she was a fox spirit,
and fell silent, hesitating.
The girl, however, climbed onto the bed and began spinning in her place,
saying:
"Don't worry, granny.
This kind of work,
I am quite skilled at,
and I certainly won't be a burden on you for food and drink."
Seeing her gentle, sweet, and lovely,
the old woman settled down.
Late at night,
the girl said to the old woman:
"The bedding and pillow I brought,
are still outside the door.
When you go out to relieve yourself,
please fetch them for me."
The old woman went out
and indeed found a bundle of clothing.
The girl unpacked and laid it out on the bed.
It was impossible to tell what kind of brocade it was,
but it was incredibly fragrant and smooth.
The old woman also spread out her own cotton quilt
and shared the bed with the girl.
As soon as the girl loosened her silk garments,
an extraordinary fragrance filled the room.
After they lay down,
the old woman thought to herself:
"To encounter such a beauty,
it's a pity I'm not a man."
The girl laughed by the pillow and said:
"Granny, you're seventy years old,
and still having such fanciful thoughts?"
The old woman said:
"I don't have any."
The girl said:
"If you're not having fanciful thoughts,
then why do you wish you were a man?"
The old woman became even more certain she was a fox,
and was greatly frightened.
The girl laughed again and said:
"What kind of heart is it that wishes to be a man,
yet fears me?"
The old woman grew even more terrified,
her thighs trembling so much the bed shook.
The girl said:
"Alas!
With such a big heart (for desires),
you still wish to be a man!
Let me tell you the truth: I am truly an immortal,
but I am not here to harm you.
You just need to be discreet in your speech,
and you'll have ample food and clothing."
The old woman rose early,
and bowed before the bed.
The girl reached out her arm to help her up.
Her arm was smooth as lard,
exuding a warm, fragrant scent;
once her skin touched a person,
one felt their own skin relax and become comfortable.
The old woman felt her heart stir,
and her thoughts wandered into fanciful realms again.
The girl smiled mockingly and said:
"Old woman, your trembling has just stopped,
where has your heart wandered off to again!
If you were a man,
you would surely die for love."
The old woman said:
"If I were a man,
how could I not die tonight!"
From then on, the two became deeply harmonious,
working together daily.
Looking at the thread she spun,
it was even, fine, and glossy;
woven into cloth,
it was lustrous and radiant like brocade,
fetching a price three times the usual.
When the old woman went out,
she would lock the door;
if someone came to visit the old woman,
she would receive them in another room.
After half a year,
no one knew about it.
Later, the old woman gradually leaked the secret to a close relative,
and the sisters in the neighborhood all entreated the old woman to arrange a meeting.
The girl reproached her, saying:
"You were not discreet with your words,
I will not be able to stay here long now."
The old woman regretted her slip of the tongue,
and deeply blamed herself;
but those seeking to meet the girl grew more numerous by the day,
to the point where some even used pressure to force the old woman.
The old woman wept and explained the situation herself,
The girl said:
"If it's those female companions,
meeting them is harmless;
I fear there might be frivolous young men,
who would act disrespectfully and take liberties."
The old woman again pleaded earnestly,
and only then did she agree.
The next day,
old women and young girls,
came in an endless stream like a line of incense smoke along the road.
The girl grew weary of the bother,
and regardless of whether visitors were noble or common,
she did not exchange a single word with any;
she only sat silently upright,
listening to their morning audience as if receiving homage.
The young men in the village, hearing of her beauty,
were utterly captivated, their souls stirred,
but the old woman refused them all.
There was a certain Fèi Shēng,
a renowned scholar of the county,
who exhausted his property
to offer the old woman a large sum of money as a bribe.
The old woman agreed
and made the request to the girl on his behalf.
The girl already knew about it,
and reproached her, saying,
"Have you sold me?"
The old woman threw herself on the ground in apology.
The girl said:
"You covet his bribe,
but I am moved by his infatuation.
He may see me once.
However, our缘分 (fateful connection) will then be exhausted."
The old woman again kowtowed on the ground.
The girl arranged for the meeting to be the next day.
Fèi Shēng heard this,
was overjoyed,
prepared incense and candles and went there,
entering the door and making a deep bow.
The girl spoke to him from behind the curtain,
asking:
"You have bankrupted yourself to see me,
what instruction do you have for me?"
Fèi Shēng said:
"I truly dare not make any other request.
I only wish to see Wáng Qiáng and Xīzǐ,
of whom I have merely heard tales;
if you do not reject me for my dullness,
and allow me to broaden my horizons,
my humble wish will be satisfied.
As for fortune or misfortune, they are predetermined,
and I have no desire to hear of them."
Suddenly, from within the cloth curtain,
a radiant glow shone through,
revealing dark brows and red lips,
all clearly visible,
as if there were no curtain or screen separating them.
The scholar felt dazzled and entranced,
and unconsciously bowed deeply.
After bowing, he rose,
but the thick curtain hung heavily again,
and though he could hear sounds, he could no longer see.
In his regret and longing,
he secretly lamented not having seen her lower body;
suddenly, he saw a pair of embroidered shoes peeking from beneath the curtain,
so slender they seemed less than a finger's width.
The scholar bowed again.
A voice from behind the curtain said:
"Please return now!
I am weary."
The old woman led the scholar to another room,
where she brewed tea for him.
The scholar inscribed a lyric to the tune of "Nánxiāngzǐ" on the wall:
"Vaguely before the painted curtain,
three-inch lotus steps, jade bamboo shoots in the dust;
touching the ground, clearly lotus petals fall,
delicate and fine,
adorned again, even more pitiable.
Flowers set off phoenix-head curves,
in hand, they should feel soft as cotton;
I only wish to turn into a butterfly and go,
by her skirt's edge,
to catch a whiff of lingering fragrance, even death would be sweet."
After finishing the inscription, he left.
The maiden, upon reading it, was displeased,
and said to the old woman:
"I said our fate was exhausted,
and now it proves true."
The old woman knelt and begged for forgiveness.
The maiden said:
"The fault is not entirely yours.
I momentarily fell into the snare of passion,
revealing my physical form to a man,
and was thus defiled by licentious words.
This is all my own doing;
how can I blame you?
If I do not leave quickly,
I fear I will sink into the abyss of passion,
and find it difficult to escape in future rebirths."
So she gathered her bedding and left.
The old woman chased after her, trying to hold her back,
but in an instant, she had vanished.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
The country of the Red Hairs,
was formerly permitted to trade with China.
The border commander, seeing their numbers,
forbade them from coming ashore.
The Red Hairs insisted:
"Just grant us a piece of land the size of a felt rug."
The commander thought a felt rug could not hold many,
and agreed.
They placed the felt rug on the shore,
which only accommodated two people;
they pulled it,
and it held four or five;
as they pulled and climbed,
in moments the rug expanded to over an acre,
and already held several hundred people.
Short blades were drawn simultaneously,
catching them off guard,
and they plundered several miles before leaving.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
A certain commoner from Láiyáng was napping during the day,
when he saw a man and a woman holding hands enter.
The woman was sallow and swollen,
her waist so thick she seemed about to topple backward,
her expression sorrowful and pained.
The man urged her:
"Come,
come!"
The man thought they were engaging in illicit relations,
so he pretended to sleep to spy on their actions.
Once inside,
they seemed not to notice anyone on the bed.
The man urged again:
"Hurry up!"
The woman then bared her chest,
exposing her belly,
which was as large as a drum.
The man took out a butcher's knife,
thrust it forcefully into her,
slicing straight from below the heart down to the navel,
making a hissing sound.
The man was terrified,
not daring to breathe.
Yet the woman furrowed her brows and endured,
without uttering a single groan.
The man held the knife in his mouth,
reached into her belly with his hand,
pulled out the intestines and hung them on his elbow;
as he hung them, he kept pulling,
and in moments his arm was full.
He then cut them off with the knife,
placed them on a small table,
and went back to pull more,
until the table was full,
then hung them on a chair;
when the chair was full,
he piled dozens of plates,
like a fisherman hauling in a net,
and tossed them toward the man's head.
He felt a wave of hot, fishy odor,
covering his face, eyes, throat, and chest without a gap.
The man could no longer bear it,
pushed the intestines away with his hands,
let out a loud cry, and ran.
The intestines fell before the bed,
entangling his feet,
and he fell unconscious.
His family rushed to see,
and found him wrapped in pig entrails;
upon closer inspection,
there was nothing there at all.
Everyone thought their eyes were playing tricks,
and were not particularly alarmed.
Only when the man recounted what he had seen
did they find it strange.
Yet there were no traces in the room,
except for a fishy smell that lingered for several days.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Zhāng Hóngjiàn
was a native of Yǒngpíng.
At eighteen,
he was a renowned scholar in the commandery.
At that time, Magistrate Zhào of Lúlóng was greedy and cruel,
and the people suffered greatly under him.
A scholar named Fàn had been beaten to death,
and his classmates, angered by the injustice,
planned to appeal to the provincial authorities,
asking Zhāng to draft the legal petition,
and inviting him to join their cause.
Zhāng agreed.
His wife, Fāng shì,
beautiful and virtuous,
heard of their plan,
and advised him:
"Generally, when scholars undertake something,
they can share success,
but not failure: if they succeed, everyone claims credit for heaven's work,
but if they fail, they scatter like falling tiles,
unable to regroup.
In this world of power and influence,
right and wrong are hard to determine by reason alone;
you are isolated,
and if things go awry,
who will come to your aid in times of crisis?"
Zhāng heeded her words,
regretted his decision,
and politely declined the other scholars,
only drafting the petition before leaving.
After a single hearing,
no verdict was reached.
Zhào bribed high officials with a large sum of gold,
and the scholars were arrested on charges of forming a faction,
while the petition writer was also pursued.
Zhang was afraid and
fled.
He reached the boundary of Fèngxiáng,
where his travel funds ran out.
As the day grew dark,
he wandered aimlessly in the wilderness,
with nowhere to go.
Suddenly, he saw a small village
and hurried toward it.
An old woman was just closing the gate,
and upon seeing the scholar,
asked what he wanted.
Zhang told her the truth,
and the old woman said:
"Food, drink, and a bed—
these are all minor matters;
but there are no men in this household,
so it is inconvenient to host a guest."
Zhang said:
"I dare not hope for too much,
but if you would allow me to lodge inside the gate,
it would be enough to shelter me from tigers and wolves."
The old woman then let him in,
closed the gate,
gave him a straw mat,
and instructed him:
"I pity that you have nowhere to go,
and am secretly allowing you to stay overnight.
You should leave early before dawn,
for fear that my young mistress will find out,
and then I will be blamed."
The old woman left,
and Zhang leaned against the wall to doze.
Suddenly, a lantern shone brightly,
and he saw the old woman leading a young lady out.
Zhang quickly hid in the shadows,
peeking slightly.
She was a beauty of about twenty.
Upon reaching the gate,
she saw the straw mat
and questioned the old woman.
The old woman told her the truth,
and the young lady angrily said:
"Our household is delicate and weak,
how could we harbor a suspicious person!"
She immediately asked:
"Where is this man?"
Zhang, terrified,
came out and prostrated himself at the foot of the steps.
The young lady carefully inquired about his family and background,
and her expression softened slightly.
She said:
"Fortunately, you are a refined scholar,
so it is no harm to let you stay.
However, the old servant did not inform me at all—
such a hasty arrangement
is no way to treat a gentleman."
She ordered the old woman to lead the guest inside.
Soon after,
wine and food were laid out,
all exquisite and clean;
then a brocade mattress was spread on the bed.
Zhang was very grateful to her,
and privately inquired about her surname.
The old woman said:
"Our family name is Shī.
The old master and his wife have both passed away,
leaving only three daughters.
The one you just saw
is the eldest, Shùnhuá."
The old woman left.
Zhang saw a copy of the *Zhuāngzǐ* with annotations on the table,
so he took it and,
leaning on the bed, began to flip through it.
Suddenly, Shùnhuá pushed the door open and entered.
Zhang put down the book
and searched for his hat and shoes.
The young lady pressed him to sit on the bed and said:
"No need,
no need!"
She then sat close to the bed
and said shyly:
"I consider you a talented and romantic scholar,
and wish to entrust my household to you, though it risks suspicion.
Would you not reject me?"
Zhang was flustered and did not know how to respond,
only saying:
"I dare not deceive you—
in my home,
I already have a wife."
The young lady laughed and said:
"This shows your honesty,
but it does not matter.
Since you do not dislike me,
tomorrow I will ask a matchmaker to arrange things."
Having said this,
she prepared to leave.
Zhang reached out to hold her back,
and she stayed.
Before dawn, she rose,
gave Zhang some gold, and said:
"Take this for your sightseeing expenses;
toward evening,
you should come late,
for fear that others might see."
Zhang followed her instructions,
leaving early and returning late,
and this became routine for half a year.
One day,
he returned quite early,
and when he reached the spot,
the village houses were completely gone,
leaving him utterly astonished.
As he was hesitating,
he heard the old woman say:
"Why have you come so early!"
In the blink of an eye,
the courtyard appeared as before,
and he found himself already inside the room,
which only deepened his bewilderment.
Shùnhuá came out from within,
smiled, and said:
"Do you doubt me?
To be honest with you: I,
am a fox immortal,
and with you, I have a predestined bond.
If you must find this strange,
I shall take my leave at once."
Zhāng, captivated by her beauty,
accepted it calmly.
At night, he said to the woman:
"Since you are an immortal,
you must be able to travel a thousand li in a single breath.
I have been away from home for three years,
and thoughts of my wife and children never leave my heart.
Could you take me back for a visit?"
The woman seemed displeased,
and said:
"In terms of marital affection,
I have certainly been devoted to you;
yet you cling to thoughts of her while with me—
this means all our tender moments together
have been in vain!"
Zhāng apologized, saying:
"Why do you say such things?
As the proverb goes:
'One day as husband and wife,
brings a hundred days of kindness.'
In the future, when I think of you,
it will be just like how I think of her now.
If I were to forget the old for the new,
what would you see in me?"
The woman then smiled and said:
"I have a selfish heart: for myself,
I wish you would never forget me;
for others,
I wish you would forget them.
However, if you wish to return briefly,
what difficulty is there? Your home is only a footstep away."
She then took him by the sleeve and went out the door.
Seeing the road dark and gloomy,
Zhāng hesitated and did not advance.
The woman pulled him along,
and before long,
she said:
"We have arrived.
You go in, and I shall leave."
Zhāng stopped to look carefully,
and indeed saw his own gate.
He climbed over the low wall and entered,
seeing a faint light still glowing in the room.
He approached and tapped on the door with two fingers.
From inside came the question, "Who is it?"
Zhāng explained where he had come from.
Inside, a candle was lit, and the door was opened—
it was indeed Fāng Shì.
Both were startled and overjoyed,
and they held hands as they entered the curtained bed.
Seeing their child lying on the bed,
he sighed with emotion and said:
"When I left, the child was only knee-high,
and now he has grown so tall!"
Husband and wife leaned against each other,
as if in a dream.
Zhāng recounted all that had happened to him.
When he asked about the lawsuit,
he learned that some of the scholars had died in prison,
while others had been exiled to distant places,
making him admire his wife's foresight even more.
Fāng Shì nestled into his embrace and said:
"With such a lovely companion,
I suppose you no longer think of the lonely woman weeping beneath the solitary quilt!"
Zhāng said:
"If I did not think of you,
why would I have come here?
Although I share affection with her,
she is, after all, not of the same kind;
it is only her kindness that is hard to forget."
Fāng Shì said:
"Who do you think I am?"
Zhāng looked closely—
it was not Fāng Shì at all,
but Shùnhuá.
He reached out to touch the child,
only to find it was a bamboo wife.
Greatly ashamed, he fell silent.
The woman said:
"Your heart is clear to see!
Our bond should end here;
yet it is fortunate that you have not forgotten kindness,
which somewhat redeems you."
After two or three days,
she suddenly said:
"I have been thinking—clinging to someone with foolish affection
is ultimately meaningless.
You often complain that I do not see you off,
but now I happen to be going to the capital,
and we can go together along the way."
She then took the bamboo wife from the bedside, and they straddled it together.
She told him to close both eyes,
and he felt himself rise not far from the ground,
with the wind whistling past.
After a while,
they landed.
The woman said:
"We part here."
Just as he was about to ask for instructions,
she had already vanished into the distance.
He stood there disconsolately for a moment,
then heard village dogs barking.
In the dim light, he saw trees and houses—
all the familiar scenery of his hometown.
He followed the road back,
climbed over the wall, and knocked on the door,
just as before.
Fāng Shì rose in surprise,
unable to believe her husband had returned.
Only after questioning and confirming the truth
did she light a lamp and come out, sobbing.
When they met,
her tears could not be held back.
Zhāng still suspected it might be another illusion conjured by Shùnhuá;
but then he saw a child lying on the bed,
just like the previous night,
and he smiled and said:
"Has the Bamboo Wife taken another man?"
Fāng shì did not understand,
and her expression changed as she said:
"I have longed for you as if for the turning of the year;
the tear stains on the pillow are still there.
Barely have we met,
yet you show no trace of sorrow or affection—
how can this be in your heart!"
Zhāng, seeing her feelings were genuine,
at last took her arm and sighed tearfully,
telling her the whole story in detail.
When he asked how the lawsuit had concluded,
it was exactly as Shùnhuá had said.
As they were sharing their emotions,
they heard footsteps outside the door.
They called out but received no answer.
It turned out that in the village there was a wicked young man, Jiǎ,
who had long been coveting Fāng's beauty.
That night, returning from another village,
he saw from afar a man climbing over the wall and leaving,
and assumed he must be someone keeping a secret tryst.
He followed him in.
Jiǎ did not really know Zhāng well,
so he just crouched and listened.
When Fāng urgently asked who was there,
he then said:
"Who is in the room?"
Fāng tried to conceal it, saying:
"No one."
Jiǎ said:
"I have been eavesdropping for a long time,
and I respectfully intend to catch the lovers."
Fāng, having no choice,
told him the truth.
Jiǎ said:
"Zhāng Hóngjiàn's major case is still unresolved;
even if he has returned home,
he should be bound and sent to the authorities."
Fāng pleaded bitterly with him,
but Jiǎ's words grew increasingly lewd and threatening.
Zhāng, his anger blazing within,
grabbed a knife and rushed out,
striking Jiǎ on the head.
Jiǎ fell,
but still cried out;
Zhāng struck him several more times,
and he died.
Fāng said:
"Since things have come to this,
your crime is even heavier.
You must flee quickly,
and I will take responsibility for the guilt."
Zhāng said:
"A true man would rather die
than bring shame upon his wife and burden his child to save his own life!
Do not worry about me,
only ensure that our son does not break the family's scholarly tradition—
then I can close my eyes in peace."
At daybreak,
he went to the county office to surrender himself.
Magistrate Zhào, because it involved a case under imperial review,
only gave him a light punishment for the time being.
Soon he was transferred from the prefecture to the capital,
where he was shackled and imprisoned, suffering greatly.
On the road, he encountered a woman riding a horse,
with an old woman holding the bridle—
it was Shùnhuá.
Zhāng called to the old woman, wanting to speak,
tears falling with his voice.
The woman turned her horse,
lifted her veil with her hand,
and exclaimed in surprise:
"Cousin,
how have you come to this?"
Zhāng briefly recounted what had happened.
The woman said:
"Based on your past actions, brother,
I should turn my head and ignore you;
but I cannot bear to.
My humble home is not far;
I will invite the officers to come along,
and can also provide a little travel money."
After going two or three lǐ,
they saw a mountain village,
with tall, well-ordered buildings and pavilions.
The woman dismounted and went inside,
ordering a maid to open the door and invite the guests in.
Soon, wine and roasted meats, rich and delicious, were served,
as if prepared long in advance.
She then sent the maid out to say:
"There happen to be no men at home right now.
Official Zhāng should urge the officers to drink a few more cups;
you will rely on them greatly on the road ahead.
Someone has been sent to arrange for several dozen taels of silver for Official Zhāng's expenses,
and also to reward the two guests—
they have not arrived yet."
The two officers secretly rejoiced,
drank freely,
and no longer spoke of the journey.
As the day grew late,
the two officers became thoroughly drunk.
The woman came out,
pointed her finger at the shackles.
The shackles immediately fell off;
she pulled Zhāng to mount a horse together with her,
and they sped off like a dragon.
After a short while,
she urged him to dismount,
saying:
"Stop here.
I have an appointment with my sister at the Green Sea,
and have already lingered here for your sake a while,
keeping her waiting long."
Zhāng asked:
"When will we meet again?"
The woman did not answer;
when he asked again,
she pushed him off the horse and left.
When dawn came,
he asked about the place,
and found it was Tàiyuán.
So he went to the prefectural city,
rented a house, and took on students.
He assumed the name Gōng Zǐqiān.
After living there for ten years,
he learned that the search for him had gradually slackened,
and so he cautiously headed east again.
When he neared his village gate,
he did not dare enter immediately,
but waited until deep into the night before going in.
Upon reaching the door,
he found the walls high and solid,
impossible to climb over again,
so he could only knock with his whip.
After a long time,
his wife finally came out to ask who it was.
Zhāng whispered to her.
Overjoyed,
she let him in,
making scolding noises,
saying:
"If funds in the capital are short,
you should return early;
how could they send you here in the middle of the night?"
Once inside,
they each told their stories,
and only then did he learn that the two officers had fled and not returned.
As they were talking,
a young woman outside the curtain kept coming by.
Zhāng asked who she was,
and was told:
"Your daughter-in-law."
He asked:
"Where is our son?"
The reply was:
"He went to the prefectural city for the imperial examinations and has not returned yet."
Zhāng shed tears and said:
"After years of wandering and hardship,
our son is already grown and established;
I never thought he could continue the family's scholarly tradition—
you have nearly exhausted your heart's blood!"
Before he finished speaking,
the daughter-in-law had already warmed wine and cooked a meal,
laying it out in abundance on the table.
Zhāng was overjoyed and comforted beyond expectation.
After staying a few days,
he hid himself in the inner rooms,
fearing others might find out.
One night,
as he was lying down,
he suddenly heard a clamor of voices,
and fierce pounding on the door.
Terrified,
they both got up.
They heard someone say:
"Is there a back door?"
Even more frightened,
they quickly used a door panel as a ladder,
helping Zhāng escape over the wall at night;
only then did they go to the door to ask what was the matter—
it turned out to be news of the new successful candidate.
Fāng was overjoyed,
but deeply regretted that Zhāng had fled,
and could not be caught and brought back.
That night, Zhāng pushed through brambles and thickets,
rushing without choosing a path;
by dawn,
he was utterly exhausted.
His initial intention had been to head west,
but when he asked a passerby,
he found he was not far from the main road to the capital.
So he entered a village,
intending to pawn his clothes for food.
He saw a grand gatehouse with a notice pasted on the wall;
looking closely,
he learned it belonged to the Xǔ family,
who had a new Provincial Graduate.
Shortly after, an old man came out from inside.
Zhāng approached, bowed, and told him his situation.
The old man saw that the guest was dignified and refined,
knowing he was not someone who came to freeload a meal,
invited him in to entertain him.
He then asked where he was going,
and Zhāng made up a story:
"I was teaching in the capital,
and on my way back, I encountered bandits."
The old man kept him to tutor his youngest son.
Zhāng inquired briefly about his official background,
and learned he was a retired high-ranking official from the capital;
the Xiàolián,
was his nephew.
After more than a month,
the Xiàolián returned with a fellow candidate,
said to be surnamed Zhāng from Shuǐpíng,
a youth of eighteen or nineteen.
Since their ancestral hometowns matched,
Zhāng secretly suspected it was his son;
but there were many with this surname in the county,
so he kept silent for the time being.
In the evening, when they unpacked,
he took out
the "Register of Successful Candidates,"
and eagerly borrowed it to read—
it truly was his son.
He couldn't help but shed tears.
Everyone asked in surprise,
and he pointed to the name, saying:
"Zhāng Hóngjiàn,
that is me."
He explained everything in detail,
and Zhāng the Xiàolián embraced his father and wept bitterly.
Xǔ, as uncle and nephew, comforted and persuaded them,
and only then did their sorrow turn to joy.
Xǔ immediately sent a letter with gold and silk:
reporting to the Provincial Surveillance Commissioner;
and father and son returned together.
Just when his wife had heard the news,
grieving daily over Zhāng's uncertain fate,
she suddenly heard that the Xiàolián had returned,
and her sorrow deepened even more.
A short while later,
father and son entered together,
astonishing her as if they had descended from heaven.
After learning the reason,
they all shared in the mix of grief and joy.
Jiǎ's father, seeing his son now honored,
no longer dared to harbor any malicious intentions.
Zhāng treated him even more generously,
and recounted the events of that year in detail.
Jiǎ's father felt both grateful and ashamed,
and they thus became good friends.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
During the Wànlì reign,
Sūn the Investigating Secretary was orphaned young,
and his mother became a widow at nineteen.
By the time Sūn passed the imperial examination as a Jìnshì,
his mother had already died.
He once told people:
"I must earn an imperial honorific title to bring glory to her in the netherworld,
so as not to betray her bitter chastity in the grave."
Suddenly he fell seriously ill,
critically so.
He had long been on good terms with the imperial physician,
so he sent someone to summon him;
but as the messenger went out the door,
his illness grew even more severe.
He stared wide-eyed and said:
"If I cannot gain fame in life to honor my parents,
how can I face my old mother in the underworld!"
And so he died,
his eyes unclosed.
Not long after,
the imperial physician arrived,
heard the crying,
and immediately entered to pay his condolences.
Seeing his condition,
he found it strange.
The family told him the reason,
and the imperial physician said:
"If you want an imperial honorific title,
it is not difficult.
The empress will give birth any day now,
if he can just live another ten days or so,
the honorific title can be obtained."
He immediately ordered moxa to be fetched,
and applied moxibustion to the corpse at eighteen points.
As the moxa cones were nearly burnt out,
groans already came from the bed;
medicine was hastily administered,
and he actually revived.
The physician instructed:
"Be sure not to eat bear or tiger meat."
Everyone noted this;
but since such things were not commonly available,
they paid little attention to it.
After three days, he recovered fully,
and still attended court celebrations.
Six or seven days later,
the empress indeed gave birth to a crown prince,
and the emperor summoned the officials for a feast.
A eunuch brought out rare delicacies,
distributing them to all civil and military officials.
White slices with red streaks,
incredibly sweet and delicious.
Sūn ate it,
not knowing what it was.
The next day,
he asked his colleagues,
and they said:
"It was bear's paw."
He turned pale with shock;
fell ill on the spot,
and upon returning home, died.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain man from the county
bought an ox,
quite robust.
One night he dreamed the ox grew two wings and flew away,
considering it an ill omen,
he feared he would suffer a loss.
He led it to the market and sold it at a reduced price.
He wrapped the money in a cloth,
and tied it around his arm.
On his way back halfway,
he saw an eagle eating the remains of a rabbit,
and as he approached, it was very tame.
So he used the cloth ends to tie its leg,
and carried it on his arm.
The eagle struggled repeatedly,
and as his grip slackened slightly,
it flew away with the cloth.
Although this was fate,
had he not been suspicious of the dream,
nor greedy to pick up something left behind,
then how could something walking have flown away?
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wáng Zǐ'ān
was a famous scholar from Dōngchāng
who repeatedly failed the imperial examinations.
After entering the examination hall,
he held high hopes.
As the results were about to be announced,
he drank heavily and got drunk,
then returned to his bedroom to sleep.
Suddenly, someone announced:
"The messenger has arrived!"
Wáng staggered to his feet and said:
"Give him ten thousand in reward!"
Seeing him drunk,
his family tricked him to calm him down, saying:
"Just go to sleep,
the reward has already been given."
Wáng then went back to sleep.
Soon, another person came and said,
"You have passed the jìnshì examination!"
Wáng said to himself,
"I haven't even gone to the capital yet,
how could I have passed?"
The person replied:
"Have you forgotten?
You've already finished all three sessions!"
Overjoyed,
Wáng got up and shouted:
"Give him ten thousand in reward!"
His family tricked him again as before.
After a while,
someone rushed in and said:
"You've been appointed to the Hànlín Academy after the palace examination,
and your attendants are here."
Sure enough, he saw two men bowing at the foot of his bed,
dressed neatly and cleanly.
Wáng called for wine and food to be given to them,
and his family pretended to comply,
secretly laughing at his drunkenness.
After a long time,
Wáng thought he must go out and show off to his hometown,
so he shouted for his attendants;
he called dozens of times,
but no one answered.
His family laughed and said:
"Lie down for a while and wait,
they've gone to look for something."
After another long while,
the attendants indeed returned.
Wáng pounded the bed and stamped his feet,
cursing loudly:
"Where have you stupid slaves been?!"
The attendants angrily said,
"You wretched scholar, how shameless!
We were just joking with you earlier,
and now you're really cursing us?"
Enraged,
Wáng suddenly lunged at them,
knocking off one's hat.
Wáng also stumbled and fell.
His wife entered,
helped him up, and said:
"How could you get so drunk!"
Wáng said:
"The attendants are detestable,
so I punished them.
What does being drunk have to do with it?"
His wife laughed and said:
"We only have one old maid at home,
who cooks for you during the day
and warms your feet at night.
Where would we get attendants
to serve a poor man like you?"
The children all laughed.
Wáng's drunkenness gradually subsided,
and he suddenly felt as if waking from a dream,
realizing that everything before had been an illusion.
But he still remembered the attendant's hat falling off: he searched behind the door
and found a tasseled hat as small as a cup,
which puzzled everyone.
He laughed at himself and said:
"In the past, people were mocked by ghosts;
today, I have been ridiculed by a fox."
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"When a scholar enters the examination hall,
he resembles seven things.
Upon entering,
barefoot and carrying a basket,
he resembles a beggar.
During roll call,
scolded by officials and cursed by clerks,
he resembles a prisoner.
When he returns to his examination cell,
sticking his head out of each hole,
exposing his feet from every compartment,
he resembles a cold bee in late autumn.
Upon leaving the examination hall,
his spirit dazed,
the world seeming different,
he resembles a sick bird released from its cage.
While awaiting the results,
every rustle of grass and trees startles him;
his dreams become illusions.
At times, he imagines success,
and in an instant, towers and pavilions rise before him; when he imagines failure,
in a flash, his bones seem to have decayed.
During this time, restless whether sitting or standing,
he resembles a monkey tied to a stake.
Suddenly, a messenger on horseback arrives,
but the announcement does not include his name.
At this moment, his expression changes drastically,
and he slumps as if dead,
resembling a fly poisoned by bait;
even poking him would not rouse him.
Initially, in his disappointment,
he becomes disheartened and defeated,
cursing the examiners for their blindness,
and blaming his writing for lacking power.
He is determined to burn all the books on his desk;
if burning is not enough,
he will stomp on them;
if stomping is not enough,
he will throw them into the muddy river.
From then on, he will let his hair down and retreat to the mountains,
facing a stone wall in meditation.
If anyone dares to present him with essays beginning with 'Moreover'
or 'It is said',
he will surely take up arms and chase them away.
But before long,
as days pass,
his anger subsides,
and his itch for writing returns.
Then, like a dove whose eggs have broken,
he can only gather twigs to rebuild his nest,
starting all over again.
In such a state,
the person involved may weep bitterly and wish to die;
but from an outsider's perspective,
could anything be more laughable?
In Wáng Zǐ'ān's mind,
a thousand thoughts arose in an instant.
The ghosts and foxes must have been secretly laughing at him for a long time,
so they took advantage of his drunkenness to play tricks on him.
When the person by his bedside wakes him,
how can one not burst into laughter?
Yet the taste of success
lasts only a moment;
the esteemed scholars in the literary world
experience only two or three such moments.
Wáng Zǐ'ān tasted them all in a single morning,
so the fox's kindness is equal to that of a recommender."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
There was a man named Diāo
who had no means of livelihood at home
and often went out to practice the art of fortune-telling—though in reality, he had no such art. Every few months, when he returned home,
his bags were filled with gold and silk.
Everyone found this strange.
Once, a fellow villager who was traveling afar
saw from a distance a man inside a grand gate,
wearing a Huáyáng cap,
chattering away,
surrounded by a crowd of women.
Drawing closer for a look,
he realized it was Diāo
and secretly observed what he was doing.
He saw someone ask:
"Among all of us here,
there is a noble lady.
Can you identify her?"
It turned out that a noblewoman was among them in plain clothes,
intending to test his skills.
The fellow villager felt embarrassed for Diāo.
But Diāo calmly pointed into the air and said:
"What's so hard about that?
Just look—above the noble lady's head,
there is an aura of clouds circling."
Everyone unconsciously turned their eyes to one person,
trying to see the cloud aura.
Diāo then pointed at that person and said:
"This is the true noble lady!"
The crowd was amazed, thinking him divine.
When the fellow villager returned,
he recounted Diāo's cunning trick.
From this, we learn that even in minor arts,
one must possess extraordinary talent;
otherwise,
how could one deceive people's eyes and ears, swindle money,
and prosper without any real foundation?"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
West of the county town, in Cíyáowù, there was a farmer's wife
who was as brave and strong as a man
and often mediated disputes and resolved difficulties in the village.
She lived in a different county from her husband.
Her husband's family was in Gāoyuàn,
over a hundred li from Zī;
he would occasionally come to visit,
stay for a couple of nights, and then leave.
The woman herself went to Yánshān
to trade pottery for a living.
If she had any surplus,
she would give it to beggars.
One evening, while talking with a neighbor woman,
she suddenly stood up and said:
"I have a slight pain in my abdomen;
I think the little troublemaker is about to leave my body."
She then left.
At dawn, when they went to check on her,
they saw her carrying two large wine-making jars on her shoulders,
just about to enter the door.
Following her into her room,
they saw an infant swaddled and lying there.
Astonished, they asked her about it,
and it turned out that after giving birth, she had already carried a heavy load for a hundred li.
She had been friends with a nun from the North Convent,
and they had sworn to be sisters.
Later, when she heard that the nun had engaged in immoral behavior,
she angrily took up a stick
and was about to go and beat her,
but was stopped by the persuasion of many people.
One day,
she met the nun on the road,
and immediately slapped her.
The nun asked:
"What crime have I committed?"
She did not answer.
Fists and stones flew together,
until the nun could no longer cry out,
and then she released her and left.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"People speak of a woman among men,
but she still knows she is not a man;
this woman even forgot she was a woman.
Her forthright and carefree nature
is no different from the ancient sword immortals.
Could it be that her husband is also one of those who polishes mirrors?"
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In Jinlíng, there was a certain wine seller,
who, every time he finished brewing,
would add water and put poison in it;
even those who could hold their liquor well
would become dead drunk after no more than a few cups.
Because of this, he gained
the reputation of
"Zhōngshān"
and
amassed great wealth.
One morning, getting up early,
he saw a fox lying drunk by the trough;
he tied up its four limbs,
and was about to look for a knife,
when the fox woke up
and pleaded:
"Do not harm me,
I will grant whatever you ask."
So he released it,
and after turning over, it had already transformed into a human.
At that time, in the alley, the Sun family
had their eldest daughter-in-law troubled by a fox spirit,
so he asked the fox about it.
It replied:
"That is me."
The wine seller, seeing that the younger sister-in-law was even more beautiful,
asked the fox to take him there.
The fox was reluctant.
The wine seller insisted.
The fox invited him to go,
entered a cave,
took out a brown garment and gave it to him,
saying:
"This was left by my late elder brother;
wearing it, you should be able to go."
After putting it on and returning home,
his family could not see him;
when he put on his clothes and went out,
they could see him.
Greatly pleased,
he went with the fox to the Sun family home.
Seeing a large talisman pasted on the wall,
drawn winding like a dragon,
the fox said fearfully:
"The monk is truly wicked,
I will not go there!"
And so it left.
The wine seller hesitantly approached,
and saw a real dragon coiled on the wall,
raising its head as if about to fly.
Terrified, he also left.
It turned out that Mr. Sun had sought out a foreign monk
to perform exorcism for him,
and had been given the talisman to bring back first,
while the monk had not yet arrived.
The next day,
the monk came
and set up an altar to perform his rites.
The neighbors all came to watch,
and the wine seller also mingled among them.
Suddenly, he changed color and ran hurriedly,
as if being caught: when he reached outside the door,
he fell to the ground and transformed into a fox,
its four limbs still clad in human clothes.
They were about to kill it.
His wife and children knelt and begged.
The monk ordered it to be taken away,
and gave it food and drink daily,
but after a few months, it died.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Sūn Wǔlì
had a servant boy who slept alone in one room,
and in a daze, he felt as if someone had taken him away.
He arrived at a palace,
saw Yánluó seated above,
who looked at him and said:
"A mistake,
this is not the one."
And so he was sent back.
After returning,
he was greatly afraid,
and moved to sleep elsewhere;
then there was a fellow servant named Guō Ān,
who, seeing the bed empty,
went to sleep in it.
Another servant, Lǐ Lù,
had a long-standing grudge against the boy,
and had long wanted to settle the score;
that night, he took a knife and entered,
felt around,
thinking it was the boy,
and ended up killing him.
Guō's father appealed to the authorities.
At that time, Chén Qíshàn was the county magistrate,
and he did not trouble himself much over it.
Guō wailed in sorrow,
saying:
"I have only this one son in my half a lifetime;
now, how am I to live!"
Chén then made Lǐ Lù his son.
Guō, bearing his grievance, withdrew.
This is not so strange because the boy saw a ghost,
but because of Chén's judgment in the case.
In a western county of Jì, there was a murderer,
whose wife brought a lawsuit against him.
The magistrate was angry,
immediately had the criminal brought in,
slapped the table and scolded:
"A good couple in a household,
and you make her a widow!
I will have you marry her,
and also make your wife a widow."
