So he sentenced them to marry.
Such clear and decisive judgments
are all the work of those who passed the highest imperial examination,
others cannot do it.
Yet Chén was also like this;
in what path is there no talent!
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In Xīyá Zhuāng, west of the county town,
a merchant named Jiǎ was killed on the road;
the next night,
his wife also hanged herself.
Jiǎ's younger brother appealed to the authorities.
At that time, Fèi Gōng Yīzhì from Zhèjiāng was the magistrate of Zī,
and he personally went to investigate.
He saw a cloth bundle containing a little over five qian of silver,
still at the waist,
and knew it was not for money.
He detained the neighbors and guarantors from the two villages for questioning once,
but found very few clues,
and without even using torture,
released them to return to farming;
he only ordered the local headmen to investigate carefully,
and report every ten days.
After more than half a year,
the matter gradually slackened.
Jiǎ's younger brother resented the magistrate's leniency,
and went to the hall repeatedly to complain.
The magistrate angrily said:
"Since you cannot name anyone,
do you want me to put shackles on innocent people!"
He scolded him and drove him out.
Jiǎ's younger brother had nowhere to appeal,
and resentfully buried his brother and sister-in-law.
One day,
due to unpaid taxes,
several people were arrested and brought in.
Among them was one named Zhōu Chéng,
who, fearing punishment,
stepped forward and claimed that the money and grain had already been fully prepared.
He then took out a silver bundle from his waist,
presenting it for the magistrate’s inspection.
After inspecting it,
the magistrate asked:
"Where is your home?"
He replied:
"In such-and-such village."
The magistrate asked further:
"How many li is it from Xīyá?"
He answered:
"Five or six li."
"Jiǎ Mǒu, who was killed last year,
what relation was he to you?"
He replied:
"I don’t know that person."
The magistrate suddenly flared up and said:
"You killed him,
and you still say you don’t know him!"
Zhōu strenuously protested,
but the magistrate paid no heed;
he was severely tortured,
and indeed confessed to the crime.
Earlier,
Jiǎ’s wife, Wáng Shì,
was about to visit relatives,
but felt ashamed for lacking hairpins and ornaments.
She nagged her husband to borrow some from the neighbors.
Her husband refused;
so she borrowed them herself,
and treasured them greatly.
On the way back,
she took them off and wrapped them in a bundle,
placing it in her sleeve;
but upon arriving home,
she found upon checking that they were lost.
She dared not tell her husband,
nor could she afford to compensate the neighbor,
and was so distressed she wished to die.
That day,
Zhōu happened to pick them up,
and knowing they were lost by Jiǎ’s wife,
he watched for Jiǎ to go out,
then climbed over the wall at midnight,
intending to use them to force her into intimacy.
It was the height of summer,
and Wáng Shì was sleeping in the courtyard.
Zhōu stealthily approached and raped her.
Wáng Shì woke up,
and screamed loudly.
Zhōu hastily stopped her,
leaving the bundle and giving her the hairpins.
After the deed,
the woman urged him:
"Don’t come again later.
The man in my house is fierce;
if he catches you, we’ll both die."
Zhōu angrily said:
"I’ve spent enough to keep a courtesan for several nights;
how can one time repay it?"
The woman soothed him, saying:
"It’s not that I don’t wish to be with you,
but he is often sickly;
it would be better to wait patiently for his death."
Zhōu then left,
and so he killed Jiǎ.
That night, he went to the woman and said:
"Your husband has already been killed by someone,
as we agreed."
Upon hearing this, the woman wailed loudly.
Zhōu, frightened, fled.
By daybreak, the woman was dead.
The magistrate ascertained the truth,
and sentenced Zhōu to death for the crime.
Everyone admired his supernatural insight,
but did not know how he was able to detect it.
The magistrate said:
"Matters are not difficult to discern;
the key is to be attentive everywhere.
When I first examined the corpse,
I saw the silver bundle embroidered with a swastika pattern;
Zhōu’s bundle was the same,
showing they came from the same source.
And when questioned,
he claimed to have no prior connection,
but his words and expression were evasive and shifting,
so I was certain he was the true murderer."
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Those in the world who adjudicate cases
either idly neglect them,
or shackle dozens of people and treat them brutally.
In the hall, the sound of flesh being beaten
resounds in all directions,
and they frown and say:
'I am laboring for the people’s affairs.'
When the dismissal board is struck three times,
they indulge in music and women,
and difficult judgments
are no longer given any thought;
they only await the time to ascend the hall,
to burn the old turtle by scorching the mulberry tree.
Alas!
How can the people’s sentiments be understood?
I often say:
'The wise need not be benevolent,
but the benevolent must be wise;
for when one’s efforts are earnest, ingenuity emerges.'
The words 'be attentive everywhere'
can instruct all those in the world who govern the people."
A fellow townsman named Hú Chéng,
lived in the same village as Féng Ān,
and their families had been feuding for generations.
Hú and his son were strong and domineering,
so Féng, suppressing his true feelings, tried to befriend them,
but Hú remained suspicious of him.
One day,
they drank together until slightly intoxicated,
and became quite candid with each other.
Hú boasted:
"Don't worry about poverty—
amassing a fortune of a hundred taels is not difficult."
Féng, knowing Hú's family was not wealthy,
scoffed at him.
Hú said with a serious expression:
"To tell you the truth: yesterday I met a wealthy merchant on the road,
carrying a heavy load of goods.
I knocked him into a dry well on South Mountain."
Féng laughed at him again.
At that time, Hú had a brother-in-law named Zhèng Lún,
who had entrusted him with negotiating the purchase of some land,
and had left several hundred taels of silver at Hú's house.
Hú then brought out all the money to show off to Féng.
Féng believed him.
After they parted,
Féng secretly reported the matter to the county authorities.
The magistrate had Hú arrested for questioning.
Hú told the truth,
and when Zhèng and the landowner were questioned, their accounts matched.
So they all went to inspect the dry well.
A constable was lowered down on a rope,
and indeed, there was a headless corpse inside.
Hú was greatly alarmed,
unable to offer any defense,
and could only cry out his innocence and misery.
The magistrate grew angry,
struck him several dozen times with the jaw-squeezer,
and said:
"There is clear evidence—
how dare you still cry injustice!"
He then had Hú confined with the instruments used for death row prisoners.
The corpse was ordered not to be removed,
but a notice was posted in the villages,
calling for the family of the deceased to come forward.
The next day,
a woman came with a petition,
claiming to be the wife of the deceased,
and said:
"My husband, Hé Jiǎ,
took several hundred taels to go trading,
and was killed by Hú."
The magistrate said:
"There is a dead man in the well,
but it may not necessarily be your husband."
The woman insisted firmly.
The magistrate then ordered the corpse to be brought out of the well.
Upon seeing it,
it indeed was not mistaken.
The woman dared not approach,
but stood back wailing.
The magistrate said:
"The true criminal has been caught,
but the corpse is incomplete.
You may return home for now.
Once the deceased's head is found,
we will summon you to report so he can pay with his life."
He then had Hú brought out from prison,
and scolded him:
"If you do not bring the head tomorrow,
I will break your legs with the cangue!"
Hú was taken away and returned at the end of the day.
When questioned,
he could only weep.
The magistrate then placed the cangue in front of him, threatening punishment,
but did not actually punish him,
saying:
"I imagine you were in a hurry carrying the corpse that night,
and did not notice where the head fell.
Why not search more carefully?"
Hú begged pitifully for time to search.
The magistrate then asked the woman:
"How many children do you have?"
She replied:
"None."
He asked:
"What relatives does Hé Jiǎ have?"
"Only one paternal uncle."
The magistrate said sympathetically:
"Losing your husband at such a young age,
so alone and helpless—
how will you make a living!"
The woman wept,
kowtowing and begging for pity.
The magistrate said:
"The murder charge is already settled.
Once the complete corpse is found,
this case will be closed.
After it is closed,
you may remarry quickly.
You are a young woman—
do not come to the yamen again."
The woman wept with gratitude,
kowtowed, and left.
The magistrate then issued a notice to the villagers,
asking them to help search for the head.
After one night,
a fellow villager named Wáng Wǔ
reported that he had found it.
After questioning and verification,
he was rewarded with a thousand cash.
The magistrate summoned Hé Jiǎ's uncle and said:
"The major case is settled;
however,
a murder case is serious,
and it may take years to fully conclude.
Since your nephew has no heirs,
and the young widow will struggle to survive,
let her remarry early.
After this, there will be no other matters,
except if higher authorities review the case,
you will only need to respond."
Hé Jiǎ's uncle refused,
so the magistrate threw down two warrants;
when he argued further,
another warrant was thrown down.
Hé Jiǎ's uncle grew afraid,
agreed, and left.
When the woman heard,
she came to thank the magistrate.
The magistrate comforted her warmly.
He then announced:
"If anyone wishes to marry this woman,
they must declare it in court."
After she left,
someone immediately submitted a marriage petition—
it was none other than Wáng Wǔ, who had reported finding the head.
The magistrate called the woman forward and said:
"Do you know
who the true murderer is?"
She replied:
"Hú Chéng."
The magistrate said:
"No.
You and Wáng Wǔ are the true criminals."
The two were terrified,
and vehemently protested their innocence.
The magistrate said:
"I have long known the truth.
The reason I delayed revealing it
was for fear there might be the slightest injustice.
Before the corpse was brought out of the well,
how could you be so certain it was your husband?
You must have known he was dead already.
Moreover, Hé Jiǎ was wearing tattered clothes when he died—
where would several hundred taels have come from?"
He then said to Wáng Wǔ:
"How did you know so precisely
where the head was?
The reason you were in such a hurry
was because you wanted to marry quickly."
The two turned pale with fright,
unable to utter a single word in defense.
They were both put in cangues,
and indeed confessed the truth.
It turned out Wáng Wǔ and the woman had been having an affair for a long time,
and had plotted to kill her husband.
They happened to take advantage of Hú Chéng's joke.
Hú was then released.
Féng, for false accusation,
was heavily caned
and sentenced to three years of penal servitude.
The case was concluded
without wrongly punishing a single person.
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Zhōucūn there was a merchant named Jiǎ,
who traded in Wúhú
and earned a great fortune.
He hired a boat to return home,
and saw on the embankment a butcher tying up a dog.
He redeemed it at double the price
and kept it on the boat.
The boatman was actually a long-time bandit;
he eyed the passenger’s belongings,
rowed the boat into the reeds,
and raised a knife to kill him.
Jiǎ pleaded to be granted a whole corpse,
so the robber wrapped him in a felt blanket and threw him into the river.
The dog saw this,
howled mournfully and leaped into the water,
gripping the blanket bundle in its mouth,
floating and sinking together with him.
Drifting for who knows how many miles,
they reached a shallow bank and stopped.
The dog swam ashore,
went to where there were people,
and barked mournfully and incessantly.
Some thought it strange
and followed it,
finding the felt bundle in the water.
They pulled it out and cut the rope.
The passenger was not yet dead
and began to tell his story.
He then entreated the boatmen
to take him back to Wúhú,
intending to wait for the robber boat’s return.
Upon boarding the boat, he found the dog missing,
and felt deeply sorrowful.
After arriving at the customs post for three or four days,
with merchant vessels as dense as a forest,
the robber boat was nowhere to be seen.
Just then, a fellow townsman merchant was about to take him back together,
when suddenly the dog came on its own,
gazed at the passenger and barked loudly,
but when called, it ran away.
The passenger disembarked and chased it.
The dog ran onto a boat,
bit a man on the leg,
and would not let go even when beaten.
The passenger approached and shouted at it,
only to find that the man bitten was the former robber.
His clothes and boat had been changed,
so he could not be recognized.
They tied him up and searched him,
and the wrapped gold was still there.
Alas! A mere dog,
yet it repaid kindness in such a way.
Those in the world without a conscience,
should they not feel ashamed before this dog!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Great Master Yáng Lián of Dàhóng,
in his humble days, was a renowned scholar of Chǔ,
and considered himself extraordinary.
After the imperial examination,
he heard the announcement of the top candidates.
At the time, he was eating,
and with food in his mouth, he went out to ask:
“Is there a certain Yáng?”
The reply was:
“No.”
Unconsciously, he fell into dejection,
swallowed the food into his diaphragm,
and it formed a hard lump,
causing severe obstruction and suffering.
Everyone urged him to take the supplementary examination;
he worried about lacking funds,
so everyone pooled ten taels of gold to send him off,
and he reluctantly set out.
At night, he dreamed of someone telling him:
“Ahead, there is someone who can cure your illness;
you should earnestly seek him.”
Before leaving,
the person gave him a poem,
which included the lines:
“By the river, under the willow, three tunes on the flute,
cast into the river’s heart, sigh not in regret.”
The next day on the journey,
he indeed saw a Daoist priest sitting under a willow tree,
so he approached and pleaded.
The Daoist priest said with a smile:
“You are mistaken;
how can I cure illness?
I can only play three tunes for you.”
Then he took out a flute and played it.
Yáng, reminded of his dream,
bowed and pleaded even more earnestly,
and even emptied his purse to offer it.
The Daoist priest took the gold
and threw it into the river.
Yáng, thinking how hard it was to come by,
was struck dumb with shock and regret.
The Daoist priest said:
“Sir, are you unable to be indifferent?
It is all by the river;
please take it yourself.”
Yáng went to look and indeed it was there.
He found it even more marvelous,
and called him an immortal.
The Daoist priest casually pointed and said:
“I am not an immortal;
the immortal has come over there.”
Tricking Yáng to look back,
he forcefully slapped his neck and said:
“How vulgar!”
Yáng, receiving the slap,
opened his mouth and made a sound,
vomiting something from his throat,
which fell to the ground with a thud.
He bent down and broke it open,
and inside the red fibers, the rice was still there.
His illness seemed to vanish.
Looking back, the Daoist priest had already disappeared.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
“In life, he was a river and mountain;
in death, he became the sun and stars.
Why must one live long to be considered immortal?
Some say he could not avoid vulgarity,
and thus did not become a celestial immortal,
and for this they mourn and regret for him.
I say: better one more sage in the world
than one more immortal in heaven.
Those who understand will surely not criticize my words as absurd.”
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
In Zhāngqiū, at Cháyá Mountain,
there is a stone cave like a well,
several feet deep.
On the northern wall is a cave entrance;
crouching and stretching one’s neck, one can see it.
Once, several people from a nearby village,
climbing on the Double Ninth Festival,
drank at that spot
and together planned to explore it.
Three of them took lanterns
and were lowered down by rope.
The cave's height and spaciousness were comparable to a grand summer house;
after advancing several paces inside,
it gradually narrowed,
and then abruptly reached a bottom.
At the base's edge was a small opening,
through which one could crawl in like a snake.
Holding a candle to it,
it appeared pitch-black and unfathomably deep.
Two men, daunted, retreated in fear;
one man snatched the torch and scoffed at them,
boldly squeezing himself through the opening to advance.
Fortunately, the narrowest part was only slightly thicker than a wall,
and then it suddenly became high and wide again,
allowing him to stand,
and then walk.
The stones on the ceiling jutted out precariously, seemingly on the verge of falling.
The walls on both sides were rugged and jagged,
resembling the clay sculptures found in mountain temples,
all taking the shapes of birds, beasts, humans, and ghosts: birds as if flying,
beasts as if running,
humans as if sitting or standing,
ghosts and specters appearing wrathful;
strange and bizarre,
mostly ugly with few beautiful forms.
His heart grew fearful and apprehensive.
He was glad the path was level,
without any slopes.
After cautiously proceeding several hundred steps,
a stone chamber opened in the western wall,
with a grotesque stone ghost to the left of the entrance,
standing facing him,
eyes bulging,
mouth gaping wide,
teeth and tongue fierce and hideous;
left hand clenched in a fist,
pressed against its waist;
right hand splayed with five fingers,
as if about to pounce on someone.
Greatly terrified,
his hair stood on end.
Looking into the distance within the doorway, he saw ashes of a burnt fire,
realizing someone had been there before,
so his courage slightly bolstered,
and he forced himself to enter.
He saw bowls and cups arranged on the ground,
caked with mud and grime;
however, they were all recent items,
not ancient kiln ware.
Beside them lay four tin pots,
coveting them,
he untied his belt, fastened them around his neck, and tied them at his waist.
Then, glancing aside again,
he saw a corpse lying in the western corner,
with its two arms and legs splayed out horizontally.
Utterly horrified.
Gradually examining it closely,
the feet wore pointed shoes,
the plum blossom pattern on the soles still visible,
he knew it was a young woman.
No one knew which village she was from,
nor in which year she had died.
Her clothes were faded and decayed,
indistinguishable between blue or red;
her hair was a tangled mess, about the size of a basket,
with stray strands sticking to the skull;
two eyes, two nostrils;
two rows of gourd seed-like teeth,
starkly white,
suggesting the mouth's location.
Imagining there might be gold or pearl ornaments on her head,
he brought the flame close to her skull,
when it seemed as if a breath of air exhaled onto the lamp,
causing the lamp to flicker unsteadily,
the flame turning orange-yellow,
and her clothes fluttering slightly.
Again seized with great fear,
his hand trembled,
and the lamp suddenly went out.
Recalling the way, he dashed back in panic,
not daring to feel along the walls with his hands,
afraid of touching ghostly things.
His head struck a rock,
he fell,
but immediately got up again;
a cold, wet sensation soaked his chin and cheeks,
realizing it was blood,
yet feeling no pain,
nor daring to groan;
gasping for breath, he ran to the opening,
just about to crouch down,
when it felt as if someone grabbed his hair and held him fast,
and he fainted into unconsciousness.
The others sat by the well above, waiting for a long time,
grew suspicious,
and lowered two more men down.
Leaning into the opening to investigate,
they saw his hair caught on a rock,
blood oozing, already stiff.
The two men turned pale,
not daring to enter,
sat down worried and sighing.
Soon, two more men were sent down from above;
among them was a brave one,
who finally ventured in boldly,
and dragged him out.
Placed on the mountain,
he only regained consciousness after half a day,
recounting the events in detail,
regretting only that he had not explored to the very end;
if explored fully,
there surely would have been even more wondrous sights.
Later, Magistrate Zhāng heard of this,
and sealed the opening with clay pellets,
making it impossible to enter again.
During the 26th and 27th years of the Kāngxī reign,
south of Yǎngmǔ Valley, a cliff collapsed,
revealing a cave entrance;
looking inside,
stalactites stood densely like thick bamboo shoots.
However, it was deep and perilous,
and no one dared to enter.
Suddenly, a Daoist priest arrived,
claiming to be a disciple of Zhōnglí,
saying:
"My master sent me ahead,
to clean and prepare the cave abode."
The local residents provided him with oil and torches,
the Daoist took them and descended,
but fell onto a stone stalagmite,
which pierced his abdomen, causing his death.
Reported to the magistrate,
who ordered the cave sealed.
There must certainly be extraordinary sights within,
it is a pity the Daoist achieved liberation through death,
leaving no further word.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Liú Hóngxùn, Grand Secretary of Chángshān,
together with a certain military envoy, was dispatched to Cháoxiǎn.
Hearing that Ānqī Island was where immortals resided,
he wished to command a boat to visit.
All the ministers and officials of the country unanimously advised against it,
telling him to wait for Xiǎo Zhāng.
For Ānqī did not communicate with the mortal world,
only having a disciple named Xiǎo Zhāng,
who would come once or twice a year.
Those wishing to go to the island
must first state their intention to him.
If he deemed it permissible,
then a smooth sail would take them there;
otherwise, a hurricane would capsize the boat.
After one or two days,
the king summoned them for an audience.
Entering the court,
they saw a man wearing a sword,
a palm-leaf hat on his head,
sitting in the hall;
about thirty years old,
with dignified and clean appearance.
Upon inquiry,
it was Xiǎo Zhāng.
Liú then expressed his longing desire,
and Xiǎo Zhāng consented.
But he stated:
"The deputy envoy may not go."
Then coming out,
he looked over all the attendants,
and said only two could accompany the journey.
Thereupon, he commanded a boat and guided Liú to go together.
The journey by water was of unknown distance,
but it felt as if soaring through clouds and mist,
and in no time, they had reached their destination.
At the time, it was bitterly cold,
but upon arrival,
the climate was warm and pleasant,
with mountain flowers blooming all over the cliffs and valleys.
Guided into the cave dwelling,
they saw three old men sitting cross-legged.
The ones to the east and west paid no attention to the guests' entry,
as if completely unaware;
only the one sitting in the middle rose to greet them,
exchanging courtesies.
Once seated,
he called for tea.
A boy took a tray away.
Outside the cave, on the stone wall, there was an iron awl,
its sharp tip embedded in the rock;
the boy pulled out the awl,
and water immediately gushed forth,
which he caught in a cup;
when it was full,
he plugged it again.
Soon, the tea was brought,
its color a pale green.
Upon tasting it,
its coldness chilled the teeth.
Liú, fearing the cold, did not drink.
The old man glanced at the boy and gestured with his chin.
The boy took the cup away,
sipped the remaining tea;
then, from the same spot, he pulled out the awl again,
caught the overflowing water and returned,
and the tea was now fragrant, steaming hot,
as if freshly brewed.
Liú secretly marveled at this.
He asked about fortune and misfortune,
but the old man laughed and said:
"We who dwell beyond the world know not the passage of years,
how could we understand human affairs?"
When asked about the art of prolonging life,
he said:
"This is not something a man of wealth and honor can achieve."
Liú rose to take his leave,
and Xiǎo Zhāng escorted him back.
Upon returning to Cháoxiǎn,
he recounted the strange events in detail.
The king sighed and said:
"What a pity you did not drink the cold tea.
That is the primordial jade nectar,
a single cup of which can extend one's life by a hundred years."
When Liú was about to return home,
the king gave him a gift,
wrapped in layers of paper and silk,
with instructions not to open it until he was far from the sea.
Once away from the sea,
he eagerly unwrapped it,
removing hundreds of layers,
until he finally saw a mirror;
upon examining it,
he saw the palaces of the mermaids and the clans of dragons,
all vividly before his eyes.
As he was gazing intently,
he suddenly saw a tidal wave taller than the towers,
raging and approaching.
Terrified,
he fled at full speed;
the tide pursued him.
Swift as wind and rain.
In great fear,
he threw the mirror into the tide,
and the wave immediately subsided.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Lǐ Jìlín took up his post as acting magistrate of Yuánjiāng,
and upon assuming office,
he saw cats and dogs filling the hall,
which surprised him.
His subordinates said:
"These are the common folk of the countryside,
coming to behold your esteemed presence."
After a while,
half of them had turned into humans;
a little later,
all had become human again,
and they dispersed in a flurry.
One day,
while out visiting a guest,
he was traveling in a sedan chair.
Suddenly, one of the bearers cried out urgently:
"I am harmed!"
He immediately asked another servant to take his place,
and knelt on the ground begging for leave.
Lǐ angrily scolded him,
but the servant paid no heed,
and hurried away.
Lǐ sent someone to follow him.
The servant rushed into the market,
found an old man,
and begged him to examine him.
The old man looked at him and said:
"You have indeed been harmed."
He then used his hands to feel the servant's skin and flesh,
pushing forcefully from top to bottom;
when he reached the lower thigh,
he saw a swelling under the skin,
and with a sharp knife, he cut it open,
extracting a small stone,
and said:
"You are healed."
The servant then ran back.
Later, Lǐ heard that it was a local custom for someone to lie in their room,
while their hand would fly out,
enter another's bedroom,
and steal valuables.
If discovered by the owner,
and the hand was caught and not allowed to leave,
then that person's arm would become useless.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Ān Dàyè was a native of Lúlóng.
He could speak as soon as he was born,
and only stopped after his mother made him drink dog’s blood.
As he grew up,
he was handsome and graceful,
and when he looked at his own shadow, he felt he had no equal.
Intelligent and studious,
prominent families vied to arrange marriages with him.
His mother dreamed someone told her,
“Your son is destined to marry a princess.”
She believed it.
By the time he was fifteen or sixteen,
there was still no sign of it,
and she gradually began to regret having believed the dream.
One day,
as Ān was sitting alone,
he suddenly smelled an unusual fragrance.
Soon, a beautiful maidservant rushed in
and said,
“The princess has arrived.”
She then laid a long felt rug on the ground,
stretching from outside the door all the way to the front of his couch.
While he was still shocked and puzzled,
a young lady entered, leaning on the maid’s shoulder.
The color of her clothes and the radiance of her face
illuminated the four walls.
The maid immediately placed an embroidered cushion on the couch
and helped the young lady sit down.
Ān was flustered and did not know what to do.
Bowing, he asked,
“What immortal are you,
that you have troubled yourself to descend here?”
The young lady smiled
and covered her mouth with her sleeve.
The maid said,
“This is Princess Yúnluó from the palace of the Holy Empress.
The Holy Empress has taken a liking to you, sir,
and wishes to marry the princess to you.
That is why she has come herself to inspect your residence.”
Ān was both surprised and delighted,
but he could not find words to reply.
The young lady also lowered her head,
and they sat facing each other in silence.
Ān had always been fond of chess,
and a chessboard was often placed beside his seat.
One of the maids dusted it off with a red handkerchief,
moved it onto the table,
and said,
“My lady is addicted to this game.
I wonder who would win between her and the powder marquis?”
Ān moved his seat closer to the table,
and the princess smiled and followed suit.
After only thirty-some moves,
the maid deliberately scrambled the pieces
and said,
“The imperial son-in-law has lost!”
She gathered the pieces into the box
and said,
“The imperial son-in-law must be a master among mortals.
My lady can only give you a handicap of six stones.”
She then placed six black stones on the board,
and the princess agreed.
While the princess was seated,
she often had a maid kneel beneath her seat
to support her feet with her back.
When her left foot touched the ground,
another maid would kneel on the right.
Two young attendants also stood by her side.
Whenever Ān was deep in thought,
one of them would bend an elbow and lean on his shoulder.
Before the game was finished,
one of the young attendants laughed and said,
“The imperial son-in-law has lost by one stone.”
She then added,
“My lady is tired.
It would be best to retire now.”
The young lady then leaned over and whispered into the maid’s ear.
The maid went out
and returned after a short while,
placing a thousand taels of gold on the couch.
She told Ān,
“Just now, my lady said your residence is cramped and humble.
Please use this to make some renovations,
and she will meet you again once the construction is complete.”
Another maid said,
“This month is afflicted by heavenly punishment,
so it is not suitable for construction.
The month after next will be auspicious.”
The young lady stood up.
Ān blocked her way
and closed the door.
The maid took out an object
that looked like a leather bellows
and pumped it on the ground.
Clouds of mist suddenly burst forth,
and in a moment, they enveloped everything.
It grew dark, and nothing could be seen.
When he searched for them, they had already vanished.
His mother learned of this
and suspected it was the work of demons.
But Ān’s thoughts were captivated,
and he could not let go of the memory.
Eager for the renovations to be completed,
he paid no attention to taboos or restrictions.
He set a strict deadline and urged the workers on,
Previously,
there was a scholar from Luánzhōu named Yuán Dàyòng,
who was lodging in the neighboring district.
He sent his calling card to the gate;
the scholar had always been unsociable,
so he excused himself by claiming to be out,
and when he saw Yuán was away, he returned the visit.
Over a month later,
they happened to meet outside the gate.
Yuán was a young man of about twenty,
wearing a plain silk robe,
a silk sash, and black shoes,
with an elegant and refined demeanor.
After a brief conversation,
he appeared gentle and prudent.
The scholar took a liking to him,
bowed, and invited him inside.
He asked Yuán to play a game of chess with him,
and they each won and lost some games.
Later, he set out wine and kept Yuán as a guest,
and they talked and laughed joyfully.
The next day,
Yuán invited the scholar to his lodgings,
where rare delicacies were served in abundance,
and he treated the scholar with great warmth and hospitality.
There was a young servant boy of about twelve or thirteen,
who clapped time and sang clear melodies,
and also jumped and performed tricks.
The scholar became heavily intoxicated
and was unable to walk,
so Yuán ordered the boy to carry him.
The scholar, seeing how slender and weak the boy was,
feared he would not be able to bear the weight.
But Yuán insisted.
The boy had more than enough strength,
and carried him back on his shoulders.
The scholar found this extraordinary.
The next day,
he rewarded the boy with money,
which the boy declined several times before accepting.
From then on, their friendship grew close and intimate,
and they visited each other every few days.
Yuán was a man of few words,
but generous and fond of giving.
When he saw someone in the market who was in debt and selling his daughter,
he would open his purse and redeem her for them,
without a hint of reluctance.
The scholar respected him all the more for this.
A few days later,
Yuán visited the scholar to bid farewell,
and presented him with over ten items, including ivory chopsticks and nánmù beads,
as well as five hundred taels of silver,
to help with his wedding preparations.
The scholar returned the silver but accepted the gifts,
and in return gave Yuán a bolt of silk.
Over a month later,
an official returning home to Lètíng,
with his bags full of money,
was robbed by bandits at night.
They seized the master of the house,
heated iron tongs and burned him,
and plundered everything.
The family recognized Yuán,
and a warrant was issued for his arrest.
A butcher named Tú in the neighboring courtyard,
who had long been at odds with the scholar’s family,
became suspicious and jealous
when he saw the scholar undertaking major construction work.
It happened that a young servant stole an ivory chopstick
and sold it to Tú’s household.
When Tú learned it was a gift from Yuán,
he reported it to the magistrate.
The magistrate sent soldiers to surround the scholar’s house.
At the time, the scholar and his servant were away,
so they seized his mother and took her away.
The elderly mother, frightened and shocked,
was barely breathing,
and for two or three days could neither eat nor drink.
The magistrate released her.
When the scholar heard of his mother’s ordeal,
he rushed home in haste,
only to find his mother critically ill.
She passed away the following night.
Just as the funeral arrangements were completed,
he was arrested by constables.
The magistrate, seeing that he was young and gentle-mannered,
secretly suspected he might be falsely accused,
and so tried to intimidate him.
The scholar truthfully recounted the circumstances of his association with Yuán.
The magistrate asked:
"How did you suddenly become so wealthy?"
The scholar replied:
"My mother had hidden savings,
and because I wished to marry,
I prepared the wedding chamber."
The magistrate believed him,
and prepared documents to send him to the prefecture.
The neighbor, knowing the scholar was innocent,
bribed the jailers heavily
to kill him along the way.
As they passed through deep mountains,
he was dragged near a steep cliff
and was about to be pushed over.
In this desperate and perilous situation,
just as the crisis was at its peak,
suddenly a tiger emerged from the thick undergrowth,
bit the two jailers to death,
and carried the scholar away.
They arrived at a place
with towering pavilions and layered halls.
The tiger entered
and set him down.
He saw Yúnluó supporting a maid as she came out,
and she sorrowfully consoled him:
"I wished to keep you here,
but your mother’s burial place is yet to be determined.
You may take the documents with you,
go to the prefecture and surrender yourself,
and you will surely be safe."
She then took the sash from his chest,
tied over ten knots in it,
and instructed him:
"When you see the official,
hold these knots and untie them,
and you can avert disaster."
The scholar followed her advice,
went to the prefecture, and surrendered himself.
The prefect was pleased with his honesty,
and after examining the documents, recognized his innocence.
He cleared his name and ordered him to return home.
On the way back,
he encountered Yuán,
who dismounted and grasped his hand.
The scholar recounted everything in detail.
Yuán grew angry, his face darkening,
but remained silent.
The scholar said:
"With your noble bearing,
why do you stoop to such disgrace?"
Yuán replied:
"Those I kill are all unrighteous people,
and what I take is all ill-gotten wealth.
Otherwise,
even if it were dropped on the road,
I would not pick it up.
Your advice is well-intentioned,
but how can someone like your neighbor
be allowed to remain in this world!"
With these words,
he leaped onto his horse and rode away.
The scholar returned home,
and after burying his mother,
he shut his door and declined visitors.
Suddenly one day,
bandits broke into the neighbor’s house,
and over ten members of the family, father and sons,
were all slaughtered,
leaving only a maidservant alive.
They gathered all the valuables,
and the servant boy helped carry them away.
Before leaving,
holding a lamp, he said to the maidservant:
"Remember this:
I am the one who killed them.
It has nothing to do with anyone else."
Without even opening the gate,
they leaped over the eaves and walls and vanished.
The next day,
the incident was reported to the authorities.
Suspecting the scholar had prior knowledge,
they arrested him again.
The county magistrate interrogated him with harsh words and a severe expression.
The scholar stepped forward, grasped his sash,
and defended himself while untying the knots.
The magistrate could not press him further,
and released him once more.
After returning home,
he kept an even lower profile,
devoting himself to study and staying indoors,
with only a lame old woman cooking for him.
When the mourning period ended,
he swept the courtyard daily,
awaiting good news.
One day,
a strange fragrance filled the courtyard.
He climbed the pavilion to look,
and found the interior and exterior newly and splendidly furnished.
Quietly lifting the painted curtain,
he saw the princess sitting in full attire.
He hurriedly bowed to her.
She took his hand and said:
"You did not trust in fate,
and so brought about the disaster of construction,
and with the grief of mourning,
delayed our union for three years. Thus, by rushing, you instead caused delay—
such is the way of things in this world."
The scholar was about to fetch funds to prepare a feast.
She said:
"There is no need."
The maid reached into a chest,
There were dishes and soups as hot as if they had just come from the cauldron,
and the wine was fragrant and clear; they drank for a long time.
The sun had already set,
and the maids he had been stepping on
gradually all vanished.
The woman’s limbs grew languid and delicate,
her legs bending and stretching
as if they had nothing to rest on.
The scholar embraced her intimately.
The woman said:
"Please release your hands for a moment.
Now there are two paths,
I ask you to choose one."
The scholar held her by the neck and asked why,
she said:
"If we remain as companions in chess and wine,
we can be together for thirty years;
if we indulge in the pleasures of the bed,
we can only be harmoniously united for six years.
Which do you choose?"
The scholar said:
"We can discuss it again after six years."
The woman then fell silent,
and they proceeded to enjoy intimate relations.
The woman said:
"I knew you could not avoid worldly ways,
this is also fate."
She then had the scholar keep maids and old women,
living separately in the southern courtyard,
where they cooked, spun, and wove,
to make a living.
In the northern courtyard, there was no cooking fire,
only a chessboard and wine utensils.
The door was always closed,
but when the scholar pushed it, it would open by itself,
and no one else could enter.
However, whether the people in the southern courtyard worked diligently or lazily,
the woman always knew about it,
and often sent the scholar to reprimand them,
and none failed to admit their faults.
The woman did not speak much,
nor did she laugh loudly;
when she had something to discuss,
she would only lower her head and give a slight smile.
Whenever they sat shoulder to shoulder,
she liked to lean against him.
The scholar would lift her and place her on his knee,
light as holding an infant.
The scholar said:
"You are so light like this,
you could dance on the palm of a hand."
She said:
"What’s so difficult about that!
But it is something a maid does,
and I disdain it.
Fēiyàn was originally the ninth sister’s maid,
who repeatedly offended due to her frivolity,
and was angrily banished to the mortal world,
and she did not preserve a woman’s chastity;
now she has already been imprisoned."
The chamber was fully covered with brocade mats,
so it never felt cold in winter,
nor hot in summer.
Even in severe winter, the woman wore only light silk;
the scholar made her bright-colored clothes,
and insisted she wear them.
After a while she would take them off,
saying:
"These dusty, impure things
almost crush the bones with their burden!"
One day,
he held her on his knee,
and suddenly felt she was much heavier than before,
and found it strange.
She smiled and pointed to her belly, saying:
"There is a worldly seed in here."
After a few days,
she frowned and did not eat,
saying:
"Lately I suffer from morning sickness,
and I rather crave the taste of cooked food."
The scholar then prepared delicious dishes for her.
From then on, her eating and drinking were no different from ordinary people.
One day she said:
"My constitution is frail,
I cannot endure childbirth.
The maid Fán Yīng is quite robust,
she can take my place."
She then took off her undergarment and put it on Yīng,
and shut her in a room.
After a short while,
the sound of a baby crying was heard.
Opening the door to look,
it was a boy.
She said happily:
"This child has the appearance of good fortune,
he will be a great vessel!"
Thus they named him Dàqì.
Wrapping him up, she placed him in the scholar’s arms,
telling him to hand him to a wet nurse,
and raise him in the southern courtyard.
After the woman gave birth,
her waist was as slender as before,
and she no longer ate cooked food.
Suddenly she bid farewell to the scholar,
wishing to temporarily return to her parents.
Asked when she would return,
she answered
"three days."
She beat the leather bag as before,
and then vanished.
When the time came, she did not return;
after more than a year had passed,
there was no news at all,
and he had already given up hope.
The scholar locked his door and lowered the curtains,
and then passed the provincial examination.
He still refused to marry;
often staying alone in the northern courtyard,
bathing in its lingering fragrance.
One night,
as he tossed and turned on the bed,
he suddenly saw lamplight shining through the window,
and the door opened by itself,
with a group of maids escorting the princess inside.
The scholar was delighted,
rose and asked about her breaking the promise.
The woman said:
"I did not miss the date,
it was only two and a half days in heaven."
The scholar proudly boasted,
telling her of his success in the autumn examination,
thinking she would surely be pleased.
The woman said with a sad expression:
"What use is such a fortuitous thing!
It brings neither honor nor disgrace,
only shortens one’s lifespan.
Not seeing you for three days,
you have sunk another layer into worldly obstructions."
From then on, the scholar no longer pursued official advancement.
After a few months,
she again wanted to return to her parents.
The princess was deeply sorrowful and attached.
The woman said:
"This time I will certainly return early,
do not trouble yourself to watch and wait.
Moreover, the meetings and partings in human life
are all predetermined by fate;
if restrained, they are long,
if indulged, they are short."
After she left,
she returned after just over a month.
From then on, she would leave once every year or half a year,
often staying for several months before returning;
the scholar grew accustomed to it,
and did not find it strange.
She gave birth to another son.
The woman lifted him and said:
"A wolf!"
Immediately ordered him to be abandoned.
The scholar could not bear it and stopped her,
naming him Kěqì.
As soon as he reached his first birthday,
she urgently arranged a marriage for him.
Matchmakers came one after another,
but when she asked their birth dates,
she said none were suitable.
She said:
"I wanted to prepare a deep pen for this wolf cub,
but in the end could not find one;
he will surely bring ruin in six or seven years,
this is also fate."
She instructed the scholar, saying:
"Remember, four years from now,
the Hóu family will have a daughter,
with a small wart on her left side,
she is this boy’s wife.
You must marry her to him,
do not consider their family status."
She then had him write it down and remember it.
Later she again returned to her parents,
and never came back.
Shēng often told his relatives and friends about his mother's dying wish.
There was indeed a daughter of the Hóu family,
who was born with a wart.
The Hóu family was of low status and their conduct was vile,
so everyone looked down on them.
Nevertheless, Shēng arranged the match for his son.
Dàqì passed the imperial examination at seventeen,
married a woman from the Yún family,
and both husband and wife were filial and friendly.
Their father doted on them.
Kěqì gradually grew up,
disliked studying,
and would secretly gamble with ruffians,
often stealing things to pay his gambling debts.
His father was furious,
beat him,
but he never reformed.
The family took precautions,
not letting him get his hands on anything.
So he went out at night,
and did some minor burglary.
The owner caught him,
tied him up, and sent him to the county magistrate.
The magistrate inquired about his surname and family,
and sent him home with a calling card.
His father and brother tied him up together,
beat him cruelly and severely,
nearly killing him.
His elder brother pleaded for mercy on his behalf,
and only then was he released.
His father, filled with anger and resentment, fell ill,
and his appetite sharply decreased.
So he drew up a property division document for his two sons,
with the buildings and fertile fields
all going to Dàqì.
Kěqì was resentful and angry,
and one night, holding a knife, he entered the chamber,
intending to kill his elder brother,
but mistakenly struck his sister-in-law.
Previously,
the princess had left behind a soft garment,
extremely light and thin,
which Yún had picked up and made into a sleeping robe.
When Kěqì slashed at it,
sparks flew in all directions,
and he fled in great terror.
When his father learned of this,
his illness worsened,
and he died a few months later.
Hearing of his father's death, Kěqì
finally returned home.
His elder brother treated him well,
but Kěqì became even more unrestrained.
After over a year,
the land and property he had received were nearly exhausted,
so he went to the prefecture to sue his brother.
The official, after investigating and learning what kind of man he was,
drove him out.
Thus, the brotherly bond was severed.
Another year passed,
Kěqì was twenty-three,
and the Hóu girl was fifteen.
Remembering his mother's words, the elder brother
wanted to hasten the marriage.
He summoned Kěqì home,
prepared a fine house for him to live in;
welcomed the bride into the household,
and taking the good fields left by their father,
registered them all and handed them over,
saying:
"These few acres of meager property,
I have guarded them as if facing death,
and now I entrust them all to you.
My younger brother is dissolute;
if you give him even a blade of grass,
he will squander it.
Henceforth, success or failure
lies with the new bride: if you can make him reform his ways,
you need not worry about cold and hunger;
otherwise,
not even I can fill a bottomless pit."
Although Miss Hóu came from a humble family,
she was clever and beautiful,
and Kěqì both feared and loved her deeply,
not daring to disobey anything she said.
Every time he went out,
she set a strict time limit;
if he exceeded it,
she would scold him severely and withhold food and drink.
Because of this, Kěqì restrained himself somewhat.
Over a year later,
she gave birth to a son.
The wife said:
"From now on, I have no need to rely on others.
With several acres of fertile land,
why should mother and son fear lack of warmth and food?
Even without a husband,
it would be fine."
Once, Kěqì stole grain to go gambling,
his wife found out,
and stood at the door with a drawn bow to bar his entry.
Terrified,
he fled.
Watching his wife enter,
he hesitantly followed.
His wife picked up a kitchen knife.
Kěqì turned and ran,
his wife chased and slashed at him,
cutting his robe and wounding his buttock,
blood staining his socks and shoes.
Furious,
he went to complain to his elder brother,
but his brother paid him no heed,
so he left feeling wronged and ashamed.
The next day he came again,
knelt before his sister-in-law weeping pitifully,
begging her to plead his case with his wife first,
but his wife resolutely refused to take him back.
Enraged, Kěqì
threatened to go kill his wife,
but his brother remained silent.
Kěqì sprang up in anger,
grabbed a spear and stormed out.
His sister-in-law was startled,
and wanted to stop him.
Her husband stopped her with a look.
After Kěqì left,
he said:
"He's just putting on an act,
he actually doesn't dare go home."
He sent someone to spy on him,
and he had indeed entered his own house gate.
Only then did the elder brother's expression change,
and he was about to rush over,
when Kěqì came panting in.
It turned out that when Kěqì entered his home,
his wife was playing with their child.
Seeing him,
she threw the child on the bed,
and went to fetch the kitchen knife;
Kěqì was afraid,
turned dragging his spear and ran,
and his wife chased him out the gate before returning.
Having learned the truth, his elder brother
questioned him,
but Kěqì said nothing,
only wept facing the corner,
his eyes completely swollen.
Taking pity on him, his elder brother
personally led him back,
and only then did his wife let him in.
After his brother left,
she made him kneel for a long time as punishment,
forced him to swear a solemn oath,
and then gave him food in an earthen bowl.
From then on, he reformed and did good.
His wife managed the accounts and calculations,
daily increasing their wealth,
while Kěqì merely enjoyed the fruits of her labor.
In later years, when he was seventy,
with children and grandchildren gathered before him,
his wife would still sometimes pull his white beard,
making him walk on his knees.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"A fierce wife or a jealous woman,
encountering one is like a carbuncle attaching to the bone,
ceasing only upon death—
is that not vicious indeed!
However, arsenic and aconite,
the most poisonous things under heaven,
if used appropriately,
can cause dizziness but effect a great cure,
something ginseng and poria cannot match.
And if not for the immortal's insight into one's very innards,
who would dare bequeath such poison as medicine to their descendants!"
In Zhāngqiū County, there was a Provincial Graduate named Lǐ Shànqiān,
who, from a young age, was free-spirited and unconventional.
He excelled in all forms of music, poetry, and song.
Both of his elder brothers had passed the highest imperial examinations,
but Shànqiān grew even more frivolous and unrestrained.
He married a woman named Xiè,
who gradually began to impose restrictions on him.
So he ran away,
and for three years did not return,
with no trace of him found anywhere.
Later, he was discovered in a pleasure quarter in Línqīng.
When his family entered,
they saw him sitting facing south,
with more than ten young courtesans attending to him on either side—
all of whom had become his disciples to learn music and arts.
As he was about to leave,
he had accumulated piles of clothes and bamboo tubes,
all gifts from the courtesans.
After returning home,
his wife confined him to a single room,
filling the desk with books.
She tied a long rope to the foot of his bed,
threaded the other end through the window lattice,
strung it with a large bell,
and fastened it in the kitchen.
Whenever he needed anything,
he would step on the rope;
the rope would move, the bell would ring,
and someone would respond.
His wife personally managed a pawnshop,
receiving items from behind a curtain and estimating their value;
in her left hand, she held an abacus,
in her right, a writing brush—
with only an old servant running errands for her. Thus, through accumulation, she grew wealthy.
She often felt ashamed that she was not as esteemed as her sisters-in-law.
After three years of confinement,
Shànqiān passed the provincial examination.
Overjoyed, she said:
"Three eggs, two hatched—
I thought you were the rotten one,
but now it seems you're not?"
Additionally,
there was Jìnshì Gěng Sōngshēng,
also from Zhāngqiū.
His wife often spun thread by lamplight to support his studies:
the spinner never ceased,
and the reader dared not rest.
If friends or old acquaintances visited,
she would secretly listen: if they discussed scholarly matters, she would prepare tea and cook millet;
but if they indulged in jesting and banter,
she would scold them and drive them away.
Whenever he achieved only an average grade in exams,
he dared not enter the house;
only if he surpassed others
would she smile and welcome him.
If he earned money from teaching,
he would hand it all over to her,
not daring to conceal even the slightest amount.
Thus, when his employer gave gifts,
she would openly scrutinize every penny.
Some people mocked and laughed at her,
not realizing how difficult it was for her to manage the accounts.
Later, he was invited by his father-in-law to teach his younger brother-in-law.
That year, the brother-in-law passed the county examination,
and the father-in-law gave ten taels of silver as a token of gratitude.
Gěng accepted the gift basket but returned the money.
When his wife found out, she said:
"Although he is a close relative,
what about the labor of teaching?"
She chased after him to retrieve the money and accepted it.
Gěng did not dare argue,
but in his heart, he felt uneasy,
and thought of secretly compensating his father-in-law.
So, each year, he would report a smaller amount of his teaching earnings to his wife.
After more than two years,
he had saved a certain sum.
Suddenly, he dreamed of someone telling him:
"Tomorrow, if you climb to a high place,
the amount of money will be complete."
The next day,
he tried climbing to a vantage point,
and indeed found lost silver,
exactly matching the missing amount.
He then compensated his father-in-law.
Later, when he became a Jìnshì,
his wife still scolded and reprimanded him.
Gěng said:
"Now that I am an official,
how can you still treat me like this?"
His wife replied:
"As the proverb says:
'When the water rises, the boat goes up with it.'
Even if you become a prime minister,
does that make you so great?"
Based on the manuscript version of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*, with missing text supplemented from the Zhùxuězhāi抄本.
In Zhōngzhōu, there was a Dàoshi
who begged for food in the villages.
After eating,
he heard an oriole singing;
he then warned the host to be cautious of fire.
When asked why,
he replied:
"The bird says:
'A great fire is hard to extinguish,
terrifying!'"
Everyone laughed at him,
and no preparations were made.
The next day,
a fire indeed broke out,
spreading to several households,
and only then did people marvel at his divine insight.
Some curious individuals caught up with him,
calling him an immortal.
The Dàoshi said:
"I merely understand bird language;
how could I be an immortal?"
Just then, a皂花雀 (black-and-white sparrow) chirped in a tree,
and the crowd asked what it was saying.
He said:
"The sparrow says: 'On the sixth day, raise them;
on the sixth day, raise them;
on the fourteenth and sixteenth days, they will die.'
It seems this family has twins.
Today is the tenth;
within five or six days,
they will both die."
Upon inquiry,
it was indeed true that twins had been born;
not long after,
both died, and the dates matched exactly.
The county magistrate, hearing of his extraordinary ability,
summoned him
and invited him to be a guest.
At that moment, a flock of ducks passed by,
so the magistrate asked him about them.
He replied:
"Your Excellency's inner chambers
must be embroiled in a dispute.
The ducks are saying:
'Enough, enough!
You favor her!
You favor her!'"
The magistrate was greatly impressed,
for indeed his wife and concubine had been quarreling,
and he had just left the noisy commotion.
He thus kept the man in the yamen,
treating him with great courtesy.
The man often interpreted bird calls,
and many of his interpretations proved remarkably accurate.
However, the Daoist priest was rustic and straightforward,
speaking freely without restraint or caution.
The magistrate was extremely greedy;
all supplies and goods provided
were converted into money and pocketed by him.
One day,
as they were sitting,
the flock of ducks came again,
and the magistrate once more questioned him about them.
He answered:
"What they say today
is different from before;
now they are calculating accounts for Your Excellency."
Asked,
"What accounts?"
He said:
"They say:
'One hundred and eight candles,
one thousand eight hundred units of vermilion.'"
The magistrate felt ashamed,
suspecting he was being mocked.
The Daoist priest requested to leave,
but the magistrate would not allow it.
A few days later,
while hosting a banquet for guests,
they suddenly heard a cuckoo.
The guests asked about it,
and he replied:
"The bird says:
'Lose your office and depart.'"
Everyone was stunned and turned pale.
The magistrate flew into a rage
and immediately drove him out.
Not long after,
the magistrate indeed lost his position due to corruption.
Alas!
This was a warning from an immortal,
but alas, those consumed by perilous greed
fail to realize it.
In the custom of Qí, cicadas are called
"Shāoqiān" (slightly promoted),
and the green ones are called
"Dūliǎo" (all finished).
In the county, there was a father and son,
both Xiùcai of the first and second grades,
who were about to take the annual examination.
Suddenly, a cicada alighted on the father's lapel.
The father joyfully said:
"Shāoqiān—
an auspicious omen."
A young servant looked at it
and said:
"What Shāoqiān?
It's just Dūliǎo."
Guō Shēng,
a native of the capital,
was over twenty years old,
with a handsome and elegant appearance.
One day,
at dusk,
an old woman presented him with a jar of wine.
He found it strange that she had no reason to do so.
The old woman smiled and said:
"There's no need to ask.
Just drink it,
and you will naturally enter a wonderful realm."
Then she left directly.
He lifted the jar and gave it a slight sniff;
a strong, fragrant aroma burst forth,
so he drank it.
Suddenly, he became heavily intoxicated,
falling into a deep, unconscious slumber.
When he awoke,
he found himself lying side by side with someone on a pillow.
Touching the person,
the skin was as smooth as lard,
exuding a scent of musk and orchids;
it was indeed a woman.
He asked her,
but she did not answer.
So he engaged in intimacy with her.
After they were done,
he felt the wall with his hand;
the wall was all stone,
damp and earthy,
very much like a tomb.
Greatly alarmed,
he suspected he had been bewitched by a ghost,
and thus asked the woman:
"What kind of deity are you?"
The woman said:
"I am not a deity,
but rather an immortal.
This is a cave abode.
You and I have a predestined connection,
do not be surprised,
just endure and stay here.
Through another door,
there is a place with some light filtering through,
where you can relieve yourself."
Soon after, the woman got up,
closed the door, and left.
After a long while,
he felt hungry: then a young maid came,
bringing him wheat cakes and duck stew,
letting him feel around to eat.
It was pitch black, and he could not tell day from night.
Not long after,
the woman came to sleep,
and only then did he know it was night.
Guō said:
"During the day, there is no sunlight,
at night, there are no lamps or candles,
when eating roasted food, I don't even know where to put it in my mouth;
if it is always like this,
then how is Cháng'é any different from a rākṣasa,
and how is heaven any different from hell!"
The woman smiled and said:
"Because you are a mundane person,
talkative and prone to revealing secrets,
I did not wish to let you see my form and appearance.
Moreover, when groping in the dark,
beauty and ugliness should still be distinguishable,
why must there be lamps and candles!"
After living there for several days,
he felt exceptionally gloomy and bored,
and repeatedly requested to return home temporarily.
The woman said:
"Tomorrow night, I will take you on a tour of the celestial palace,
and then we shall part."
The next day,
suddenly a young maid entered carrying a lantern,
saying:
"The lady has been waiting for you for a long time."
He followed her out.
Amidst the starlight,
he saw countless towers and pavilions.
Passing through several winding painted corridors,
they finally arrived at a place,
where pearl curtains hung in the hall,
and huge candles burned as bright as day.
Entering,
he saw a beautiful woman sitting facing south in splendid attire,
about twenty years old;
her brocade robe dazzled the eyes;
the pearls on her head,
raised and trembling, hung down on all sides;
short candles were placed on the ground,
illuminating the hem of her skirt: truly a celestial being.
Guō, bewildered and flustered,
unconsciously knelt down.
The woman ordered the maids to help him up and seat him.
Shortly after,
a feast of delicacies was laid out.
The woman offered a toast, saying:
"Drink this to send you off."
Guō bowed and said:
"Earlier, I met you face to face but did not recognize you as an immortal,
for which I am truly regretful and ashamed;
if you would allow me to redeem myself,
I wish to be accepted as your lifelong, unwavering servant."
The woman glanced at the maid and smiled,
then ordered the feast to be moved to the bedroom.
In the room, there were tasseled embroidered bed curtains,
and fragrant, soft quilts and bedding.
She had Guō sit on the bed.
While drinking,
the woman repeatedly said:
"You have been away from home for a long time,
it would be no harm for you to return temporarily."
After another round of drinking,
Guō did not speak of leaving.
The woman called the maid to carry the lantern and see him off.
Guō did not speak,
pretending to be drunk and asleep on the bed,
and when pulled, he did not move.
The woman had several maids undress him.
One maid patted his private parts and said:
"This man's appearance is gentle and elegant,
but this thing is so uncivilized!"
They lifted him and placed him on the bed,
then left laughing loudly.
The woman also went to bed,
and Guō then turned over.
The woman asked:
"Are you drunk?"
He said:
"How could I, a humble scholar, be drunk!
It is just that upon seeing an immortal,
my mind became utterly confused."
The woman said:
"This is the celestial palace.
Before dawn,
you should leave early.
If you find the cave dreary and stifling,
it would be better to part sooner."
Guō said:
"Suppose someone obtains a famous flower at night,
smelling its fragrance and feeling its stem,
but suffers from having no lamp or candle;
how can such a situation be endured?"
The woman laughed,
and agreed to provide lamps and candles.
When the water clock indicated the fourth watch,
she called the maid to carry the lantern,
and holding his clothes, she saw him off.
Entering the cave,
he saw it was exquisitely decorated with red and white plaster;
the sleeping area had a leather mattress and a palm-fiber felt about a foot thick.
Guō took off his shoes and wrapped himself in the quilt,
while the maid lingered and did not leave.
Guō gazed at her intently;
she was graceful and lovely.
Teasingly, he said:
"The one who said I was uncivilized,
was it you?"
The maid smiled,
kicked the pillow with her foot, and said:
"You should lie still!
Don't say any more."
He saw pearls as large as beans embedded in the tips of her shoes.
He grabbed and pulled her;
the maid fell into his embrace,
and they began to frolic,
but she moaned and winced, unable to bear it.
Guō asked:
"How old are you?"
She replied:
"Seventeen."
He asked:
"Does a virgin also know about passion?"
She said:
"I am not a virgin,
but it has been three years since I was last intimate."
Guō pressed for the immortal's surname and name,
as well as her background and honorable lineage.
The maid said:
"Don't ask!
Even if this is not heaven,
it is still different from the mortal world.
If you must know the exact details,
I fear you will have nowhere to seek death."
So Guō did not dare to ask again.
The next night,
the woman indeed came with candles,
and they slept and ate together,
making this their regular routine.
One night,
the woman came and said:
"I had hoped for an everlasting bond;
but unexpectedly, human feelings have turned sour,
and now the celestial palace is to be cleansed,
and I can no longer keep you here.
Please take this farewell wine as our parting."
Guō wept,
begging to be allowed to take some cosmetics as a keepsake.
The woman refused,
but gave him a catty of gold and a hundred pearls.
After three cups of wine were finished,
he suddenly felt dizzy and drunk.
When he awoke,
he felt his limbs bound tightly,
entangled so densely
that his legs could not stretch,
nor his head emerge.
Struggling to turn,
he fell dizzily from the bed.
Reaching out to feel around,
he found himself wrapped in a brocade quilt,
tied with fine ropes.
Sitting up, he pondered intently,
and glimpsed the bed railings—
only then did he realize he was in his own study.
By then, he had been away from home for three months,
and his family believed he was already dead.
At first, Guō dared not speak openly,
fearing punishment from the immortal,
yet his heart was filled with doubt and wonder.
He secretly confided in a close friend,
but none could guess the reason.
The quilt was placed by the bedside,
filling the room with fragrance;
upon opening it to inspect,
he found it was made of Húzhōu silk mixed with powdered incense,
so he treasured it carefully.
Later, a certain high official heard of this and questioned him,
then laughed and said:
"This is the old trick of Empress Jiǎ.
How could an immortal act like this?
Even so,
this matter should be kept secret;
if it leaks out,
your clan will be wiped out!"
There was a shaman who often visited noble households,
and described the shape of the pavilions and towers,
exactly resembling those of Yán Dōnglóu's home.
When Guō heard this,
he was greatly terrified,
and fled with his family.
Not long after,
Yán was executed,
and only then did he return.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Lofty pavilions, hazy and indistinct,
fragrance filling embroidered curtains;
young servants bustling about,
shoes adorned with bright pearls—
were it not for the wanton indulgence of treacherous officials,
the arrogance and extravagance of the powerful,
how could such things exist?
Yet with a single throw of the lustful dice,
the golden chamber turns into the Chángmén Palace;
before the spittoon dries,
the field of love is overgrown with weeds.
An empty bed wounds the heart,
dim candles consume the soul.
Frowning before the jade terrace,
gazing intently within the precious canopy—
thus, on the platform of the wine dregs mound,
the path leads to the heavenly palace;
in the land of tenderness,
one suspects a fairy maiden.
Though the debauchery of boorish men is hardly worth shame,
those who let their vast fields lie fallow
should also take warning!" According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Píngyuán County lived a man named Qiáo,
who had a daughter, dark and ugly: with a sunken nose,
and a lame foot.
By the age of twenty-five or six,
no one had come to ask for her hand.
In the same county lived a man named Mù,
over forty years old,
whose wife had died,
and who was too poor to remarry,
so he engaged her.
After three years,
she bore a son.
Not long after,
Mister Mù died,
and the family became even more destitute;
in great hardship,
she begged for pity from her mother.
Her mother grew quite impatient with her.
The daughter, also resentful, never returned,
relying solely on spinning and weaving to support herself.
There was a man named Mèng who had lost his spouse,
leaving behind a son named Wūtóu,
just a year old,
and with no one to nurse him,
he was anxious to find a new wife;
however, though matchmakers spoke of many,
none suited him.
Suddenly seeing the woman,
he was greatly pleased with her,
and secretly sent someone to hint his intentions to her.
The woman declined,
saying:
"Though I suffer hunger and cold like this,
and following a gentleman would bring warmth and fullness,
how could I not wish for it?
But I am crippled and ugly, inferior to others;
the only thing I can trust in myself
is my virtue.
Moreover, to serve two husbands—
what would you, sir, gain from that!"
Mèng admired her even more for this,
and his admiration grew especially fervent,
sending a matchmaker with a letter containing money and gifts to persuade her mother.
The mother was pleased,
and went herself to her daughter's place,
firmly urging her;
but the woman's resolve remained unshaken.
The mother felt ashamed,
and offered her younger daughter to Mèng instead;
the family was all delighted,
but Mèng was utterly unwilling.
Not long after,
Mèng suddenly fell ill and died,
and the woman went to mourn and weep with utmost grief.
Mèng had no close relatives,
and after his death,
the local ruffians all took advantage,
carrying off all the furniture,
and were planning to divide his land and property.
The servants also each stole what they could and left,
leaving only an old nurse holding the child and weeping inside the curtains.
The woman inquired and learned the reason,
and felt great injustice.
Hearing that a Mister Lín had been on good terms with Mèng,
she went to his door and told him:
"Husband and wife,
and friends,
are among the great human relationships.
I, with my extraordinary ugliness,
am despised by the world,
yet only Mèng was able to understand me;
though I firmly refused him before,
I had already pledged my heart to him.
Now he is dead and his son young,
I surely must repay my understanding friend.
But preserving an orphan is easy,
defending against insults is hard;
if, having no brothers or parents,
one sits by and watches his son die and his family perish without offering any help,
then among the five relationships, friends might as well not exist.
I ask nothing more of you, sir,
only that you send a note to inform the county magistrate;
as for raising the orphan,
I dare not decline."
Lín said:
"Agreed."
The woman bid farewell and returned.
Lín was about to do as she instructed;
the ruffians grew angry,
all wanting to take revenge with blades.
Lín became greatly afraid,
shut his door and dared not go out again.
The woman waited several days,
but there was no news;
upon inquiring,
she found that the Mèng family's land and property had already been completely taken.
The woman was extremely indignant,
and resolutely went herself to the authorities.
The official questioned her about her relation to Mèng,
and she said:
"You, sir, govern this county,
relying on principle.
If my words are false,
then even the closest kin cannot escape punishment;
if they are not false,
then even a stranger on the road should be heard."
The official was angered by her blunt words,
and scolded and drove her out.
The woman, with no way to redress her grievance and indignation,
went weeping to plead at the gates of the gentry.
A certain gentleman, hearing of it and considering her righteous,
interceded on her behalf with the magistrate.
The magistrate investigated,
and found it true,
severely punishing the ruffians,
and returning all that had been taken.
Some suggested that the woman stay at the Mèng residence,
to care for the orphan;
but she refused.
She locked its doors,
had the nurse carry Wūtóu,
and followed them back to her home,
housing them separately.
For all of Wūtóu's daily needs,
she would open the door with the nurse to take out grain,
and manage things for him;
she herself took not a penny,
living in poverty with her own son,
just as before.
After several years,
Wūtóu gradually grew up,
and she hired a tutor to teach him to read;
her own son she made learn manual work.
The nurse urged her to have both study,
but the woman said:
"The expenses for Wūtóu
come from what is rightfully his;
if I spend another's wealth to educate my own son,
how could my heart be clear?"
After several more years,
she had accumulated several hundred dan of grain for Wūtóu,
then arranged a marriage for him with a renowned family,
repaired his house,
and urged him to return.
Wūtóu tearfully begged to live together,
and only then did she agree;
but she continued spinning as before.
Wūtóu and his wife tried to take her tools away,
but she said:
"For my son and me to sit and eat idly,
how could my heart be at peace?"
So she managed things for them morning and night,
sending her son to patrol the fields,
as if he were a hired laborer.
If Wūtóu and his wife made small mistakes,
she would scold and reprimand without leniency;
if they showed slight neglect,
she would angrily wish to leave.
The couple would kneel and plead with words of remorse,
and only then would she stop.
Not long after,
Wūtóu entered the county school,
and she again wished to leave and return home.
Wūtóu would not allow it,
and contributed betrothal gifts,
to arrange a marriage for Mister Mù's son.
Only then did she urge her son to return.
Wūtóu could not keep her,
so secretly had someone buy a hundred mu of permanent farmland in a nearby village before sending her off.
Later, when she fell ill and asked to return,
Wūtóu would not listen.
As her illness grew critical,
she instructed:
"You must bury me back home!"
Wūtóu agreed.
After her death,
he secretly gave money to Mister Mù's son,
to have her buried together with Mèng.
When the time came,
the coffin became heavy,
and thirty men could not lift it.
Mister Mù's son suddenly collapsed,
bleeding from all seven orifices.
He said himself:
"Unworthy son,
how could you sell your mother!"
Wūtóu was afraid,
prayed and made vows,
and only then did he recover.
So they delayed several more days,
repaired Mister Mù's grave,
and only then buried them together.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"The feeling of having an understanding friend,
pledging one's self in return—
this is what a heroic man would do.
What does a woman know,
yet to be so extraordinary and great?
If she had met a Jiǔfāng Gāo,
he would surely have seen her as a stallion."
According to the manuscript of "Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio"
In the Eastern Sea there is a clam
that floats to the shore when hungry,
opening its two shells;
a small crab emerges from within,
tethered by a red thread,
and ventures several feet away from the shell,
hunting until satiated,
then returns,
and the shell closes.
If someone secretly severs the thread,
both creatures die.
This is indeed a strange natural phenomenon.
According to the manuscript of "Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio"
There was a scholar named Lián,
a native of Zhāngdé.
In his youth, he was devoted to studies;
however, he was orphaned early
and his family was extremely poor.
One day, while he was out,
he lost his way returning at dusk.
Entering a village,
an old woman came and said to him:
"Where is Young Master Lián headed?
Is the night not too deep?"
Lián, feeling both alarmed and fearful,
had no time to ask who she was,
and simply requested a place to rest.
The old woman led him away
into a large mansion.
A maid with double buns, holding a lantern,
guided a lady out,
who appeared over forty years old
and carried herself with noble grace.
The old woman greeted her, saying:
"Young Master Lián has arrived."
Lián hurried forward and bowed.
The lady said joyfully:
"The young master is so talented and handsome,
why settle for merely becoming a wealthy man!"
She then set out a feast,
sitting to the side,
and urged him to drink with great enthusiasm,
though she herself never drank from her cup
nor ate with her chopsticks.
Lián felt bewildered
and repeatedly inquired about her family background.
She smiled and said:
"After three more cups, I will tell you."
Lián complied as instructed.
The lady then said:
"My late husband, surnamed Liú,
was a merchant in Jiāngyòu
and met with a sudden disaster, passing away.
I, a widow, live alone in this desolate and remote place,
and our fortunes decline day by day.
Although I have two grandsons,
they are either like owls
or like worn-out nags.
Though you, young master, are of a different surname,
you are like flesh and bone from three lifetimes;
moreover, your nature is sincere and devoted,
so I have boldly met with you.
There is no other trouble—
I have a modest sum of money
and wish to entrust you, young master, to take it on a trading journey,
sharing the profits,
which is better than letting it lie idle and wither away like fireflies on a desk."
Lián declined, citing his youth and bookish nature,
fearing he might fail such an important task.
The lady said:
"The plan of studying
comes after securing a livelihood.
You are intelligent, young master—
what can you not accomplish?"
She ordered a maid to bring out the funds,
handing over over eight hundred taels of silver.
Lián, alarmed, firmly declined.
The lady said:
"I know you are not accustomed to trade, young master,
but just try it,
and surely nothing will go wrong."
Lián worried that such a large sum was too much for one person to manage
and suggested finding partners.
The lady said:
"No need.
Just find an honest, experienced servant
to serve you, and that will suffice."
She then counted on her slender fingers and divined,
saying:
"Someone with the surname Wǔ is auspicious."
She ordered a servant to prepare a horse, pack the silver, and see Lián off,
saying:
"When the year ends and the cups are washed,
I will await your triumphant return."
Then, turning to the servant, she said:
"This horse is well-trained
and suitable for riding;
I give it to you, young master,
no need to bring it back."
Lián returned home;
it was only the fourth watch of the night,
and the servant tied up the horse and left on his own.
The next day,
Lián searched extensively for a servant
and indeed found one surnamed Wǔ,
whom he hired at a generous wage.
Old Wǔ was experienced in travel
and was honest and meticulous,
so Lián entrusted all the funds to him.
They traveled to Jīngxiāng,
returning only at the end of the year,
with profits tripling the capital.
Lián felt that Old Wǔ had contributed greatly,
so beyond the usual share,
he gave him additional rewards,
planning to share the extra secretly
without letting the lady know.
As soon as they arrived home,
the lady had already sent someone to welcome them,
and they went together.
They saw a lavish feast already set in the hall;
the lady came out
and offered warm greetings.
Lián handed over the capital,
presenting the account books;
the lady set them aside without a glance.
Shortly after, they took their seats,
with songs and music resounding;
Wǔ was also feasted in an outer room,
getting thoroughly drunk before returning.
Since Wǔ had no family,
he stayed to celebrate the New Year.
The next day,
Lián again requested an audit.
The lady smiled and said:
"No need for that in the future;
I have already accounted for everything."
She then showed him a ledger,
which recorded everything in detail,
including the rewards given to the servant,
all noted therein.
Lián exclaimed in astonishment:
"Madam, you are truly divine!"
A few days later,
he was treated to lavish hospitality
as if he were her own son or nephew.
One day,
a feast was set up in the hall,
with one seat facing east,
and another facing south;
below the hall, a mat was laid facing west.
She said to the young man:
"Tomorrow, the God of Wealth will shine upon you,
