so it is an auspicious time for a long journey.
Today, as your host, I have prepared a simple farewell feast,
to add grandeur to your departure."
After a short while,
Wǔ was also summoned,
and was given a seat below the hall.
For a time, drums and gongs blared noisily.
Actresses presented the list of songs,
and the young man requested them to sing
"Táo Zhū"
The woman laughed and said:
"This is an omen,
you will surely gain Xīshī as your helpmate."
After the banquet,
she again gave the young man the full amount of gold,
saying:
"This journey cannot be measured in months or years,
do not return until you have gained immense wealth.
I and you, young master,
rely on fortune and fate,
and trust in our sincere hearts.
Do not trouble yourself with calculations;
the profits from distant lands,
I will know of them myself."
The young man assented and withdrew.
He went to stay in Huáishàng,
and became a salt merchant,
after more than a year,
his profits multiplied several times over.
However, the young man was fond of reading,
and even while managing accounts, he never forgot his books;
those he associated with were all scholars.
Having already gained ample wealth,
he secretly thought of stopping and being content,
and gradually withdrew from his responsibilities to Wǔ.
Xuē Shēng from Táoyuán was his closest friend;
he happened to visit him,
but the entire Xuē family had gone to their country estate,
and as dusk fell with nowhere else to go,
the gatekeeper invited the young man in,
swept a bed for him and prepared a meal.
He inquired in detail about the master's circumstances,
for at that time, rumors were spreading that the court intended to select daughters from good families,
to reward the border troops,
causing unrest among the people.
Hearing that there were young men without wives,
without going through matchmakers,
they simply sent their daughters to their homes,
to the extent that some gained two wives in a single night.
Xuē had also recently married into a prominent family,
and fearing that the commotion of carriages and horses
might be heard by the county magistrate,
he had temporarily moved to the countryside.
As the first watch of the night was nearing its end,
and he was about to tidy the bed and retire,
he suddenly heard several people pushing the door open and entering.
The gatekeeper did not know what was said,
but only heard one person ask:
"Since the master is not at home,
who is the one holding the candle?"
The gatekeeper replied:
"It is Young Master Lián,
a guest from afar."
Soon, the questioner had entered.
His robe and hat were neat and clean,
and with a slight raise of his hand,
he immediately inquired about the young man's family and origins.
The young man told him.
Delighted, the man said:
"We are from the same hometown.
Which family is your wife from?"
The young man replied:
"I have no wife."
Even more pleased,
he hurried out,
quickly called in a young man to join them,
and respectfully greeted him.
Abruptly, he said:
"To be honest with you, young master: my surname is Mù.
Coming here tonight,
I intended to send my younger sister to Master Xuē,
but only upon arriving did I realize it was futile.
At this moment of being caught in a dilemma,
I happened to meet you, young master—
is this not fate!"
Since the young man did not know him well,
he hesitated and did not dare to respond.
Mù, however, paid no heed to his hesitation,
and urgently called for those escorting the girl.
After a short while,
two elderly women supported a young lady inside,
and seated her on the young man's bed.
Glancing at her,
she appeared fifteen or sixteen years old,
exquisitely beautiful beyond compare.
The young man was delighted,
and finally straightened his attire and bowed to Mù in thanks;
he also instructed the gatekeeper to buy wine,
to show some hospitality.
Mù said:
"Our ancestors were from Zhāngdé;
my mother's family was also an established lineage,
but now it has declined.
I heard that my maternal grandfather left behind two grandsons,
but I do not know how their family circumstances are."
The young man asked:
"Who are they?"
Mù said:
"My maternal grandfather was named Liú,
courtesy name Huīruò,
and I heard he lived thirty lǐ north of the commandery."
The young man said:
"I am from the southeast of the commandery city,
quite far from the northern villages;
moreover, I am young,
and do not have many acquaintances.
This surname is very numerous in the commandery,
I only know that north of the commandery there is a Liú Jīngqīng,
also a literary scholar,
but I am not sure if it is him,
though he is poor."
Mù said:
"My ancestral graves are still in Zhāngjùn,"
"and I have long wanted to bring the two coffins back to be buried in our hometown."
"However, I have not yet managed to gather the travel funds,"
"so I have been delaying it."
"Now that my daughter is going with you,"
"my resolve to return is even firmer."
Upon hearing this,
the young man eagerly took on the responsibility.
Both Mùs were delighted.
After several rounds of wine,
they took their leave.
The young man dismissed his servant and moved the lamp,
and the love between them
was beyond words.
The next day,
Xuē already knew about it,
hurried into the city,
and arranged a separate courtyard to accommodate the young man.
The young man went to Huái,
completed the handover of accounts,
and left Wǔ to manage the shop;
he then packed his belongings and returned to Táoyuán,
and together with the two Mùs, he collected the remains of his wife's parents.
The families, including all the young and old,
were loaded onto the carts and returned with him.
Once they entered the gate and settled down,
he took the money from his bag to see the hostess.
The former servant was already waiting on the road.
He followed him,
and the woman came out to meet him.
With a pleased expression, she said:
"Tàozhūgōng has brought Xīzǐ back with him!"
"The other day you were a guest,"
"but today you are my nephew-in-law."
She prepared wine to welcome him,
and they became even closer and more affectionate.
The young man admired her foreknowledge,
so he asked:
"How are you related to my mother-in-law?"
The woman said:
"Don't ask,"
"you'll know in time."
Then she piled the gold on the table,
dividing it into five portions;
she took two for herself,
and said:
"I have no use for these,"
"so I'll give them to my eldest grandson."
The young man felt it was too much,
and declined to accept it.
Sadly, she said:
"My family has fallen into decline,"
"the tall trees in the courtyard"
"have been cut down for firewood by others;"
"my grandson lives quite far from here,"
"and the household is desolate."
"I must trouble you, young master, to take care of it."
The young man agreed,
but only accepted half of the gold.
The woman insisted on giving it all to him.
She saw him off,
and with tears in her eyes, she returned.
As the young man was feeling puzzled and strange,
he looked back at the mansion,
only to find it had turned into a desolate grave.
Only then did he realize that the woman was his wife's maternal grandmother.
After returning,
he redeemed an acre of grave land,
and built a magnificent tomb with grand plantings.
Liú had two grandsons,
the elder was Jīngqīng;
the younger was Yùqīng,
a good-for-nothing who indulged in drinking and gambling,
and both were poor.
The brothers went to the young man to express their thanks,
and he gave them generous gifts.
From then on, they became very familiar and visited frequently.
The young man often spoke of the reason for his business success,
and Yùqīng secretly thought that there must be a lot of gold in the grave.
One night, he gathered a group of gamblers,
dug up the grave and searched it,
opened the coffin and exposed the corpse,
but found nothing at all,
and left disappointed.
When the young man learned that the grave had been dug up,
he told Jīngqīng.
Jīngqīng went with the young man to inspect it,
and upon entering the burial chamber,
they saw piles of gold on the table,
with all the previously divided gold still there.
Jīngqīng wanted to take it together with the young man.
The young man said:
"The lady originally left this for you, brother."
So Jīngqīng packed it up and took it home,
reported it to the county magistrate,
who launched a strict investigation to apprehend the culprits.
Later, someone tried to sell a jade hairpin from the grave,
was caught,
and under intense interrogation,
it was revealed that Yùqīng was the ringleader.
The magistrate was about to sentence him to death;
but Jīngqīng pleaded on his behalf,
and he was only spared from execution.
The two families worked together to repair the grave,
making it even sturdier and more beautiful than before.
From then on, both the Lián and Liú families became wealthy,
except for Yùqīng, who remained as before.
The young man and Jīngqīng often helped him financially,
but it was never enough to cover his gambling losses.
One night,
robbers broke into the young man's house,
and demanded money and valuables.
The gold that the young man had stored
was all in ingots of fifteen hundred each,
and he showed it to them.
The robbers took two of them,
and there was only a ghost horse in the stable,
which they used to carry the gold away.
They made the young man escort them to the wilderness,
and then released him.
The villagers saw that the robbers' torches were not far away,
and chased after them with shouts;
the robbers fled in panic.
When everyone reached the spot,
they found the gold discarded by the roadside,
and the horse had already turned to ashes.
Only then did they realize that the horse was also a ghost.
That night, only one gold bracelet was lost.
Earlier,
when the robbers captured the young man's wife,
they were attracted by her beauty,
and were about to assault her,
when one robber wearing a mask
sternly stopped them,
and his voice sounded like Yùqīng's.
The robbers released the young man's wife,
but took the bracelet from her wrist and left.
Because of this, the young man suspected Yùqīng,
but in his heart, he felt grateful to him.
Later, when the robber tried to pawn the bracelet to gamble,
he was caught by the constables,
and when they interrogated his accomplices,
Yùqīng was indeed among them.
The magistrate was furious,
and subjected him to extreme torture.
His brother and the young man discussed
trying to bribe heavily to get him released,
but before their plan could be carried out, Yùqīng had already died.
The young man still often provided for his wife and children.
Later, the young man passed the imperial examination,
and for several generations, his family remained wealthy without holding official posts.
Alas!
The character for "greed"
in its strokes and form
is very close to
the character for "poverty."
Someone like Yùqīng
can serve as a warning:
According to the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì"
In the household of Grand Historian Lǐ in Língxiàn,
they often found antique vases, tripods, and curios
moved to the edge of the table,
in a precarious position about to fall.
Suspecting it was the work of the servants,
they would angrily reprimand them.
The servants claimed innocence,
but no one knew the reason,
so they locked the study door tightly,
yet by morning, it would happen again.
Realizing it was something strange,
they secretly kept watch.
One night,
the room was filled with light,
and they were surprised, thinking it was thieves.
Two servants approached to peek,
and saw a fox lying on the table,
with light emanating from its eyes,
shining brightly in all directions.
Afraid it would escape,
they rushed in to catch it.
The fox bit the servant's wrist in an attempt to break free,
but the servant held on even tighter,
and together they tied it up.
When they lifted it to look,
they saw that all four of its legs were boneless,
swaying limply like hanging ribbons when shaken.
The Grand Historian, considering its spiritual nature,
could not bear to kill it;
he covered it with a willow basket,
and the fox could not get out,
so it ran off with the basket on its head.
Then they enumerated its offenses and released it,
and the strange occurrences ceased.
According to the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì"
In Jǐnán, there was an old man who made his living selling wine.
He sent his son, Xiǎo Èr, to Qíhé to collect a debt.
As Èr passed through the west gate,
he saw his elder brother, Ā Dà.
Dà had been dead for a long time.
Startled, Èr asked,
"Brother, how did you get here?"
Dà replied,
"There's a doubtful case in the underworld,
and I need you to testify."
Èr's expression changed to one of resentment and complaint.
Dà pointed to a man behind him dressed like a yamen runner and said,
"The official's servant is here,
how could I act freely?"
He merely reached out and beckoned,
and Èr unconsciously followed.
They ran wildly day and night
until they reached the foot of Mount Tài.
Suddenly, they saw an official yamen.
Just as they were about to enter together,
they saw a crowd of people pouring out.
The runner clasped his hands and asked,
"How did things go?"
One person said,
"No need to go in anymore,
it's settled."
The runner then released Èr and told him to go home.
Dà worried that his brother had no travel money.
The runner thought for a long time,
then led Èr away.
After walking twenty or thirty *li*,
they entered a village
and reached the eaves of a house.
The runner instructed,
"If someone comes out,
ask them to escort you;
if they refuse,
just say Wáng Huòláng told you to say so."
He then left.
Èr fell unconscious and rigid.
At dawn,
the master of the house came out
and saw a man dead outside his door,
greatly alarmed.
He watched over him for a while,
and Èr gradually revived;
he helped him inside and gave him food.
Èr then stated where he lived
and asked for help to get back.
The host was reluctant.
Èr repeated what the runner had said.
The host was utterly astonished
and hastily hired a horse to send him home.
Èr offered payment,
but the host wouldn't accept it;
when asked the reason,
he also wouldn't say.
They parted and went their separate ways.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Imperial Censor Yù from Jiāozhōu
was sent on a mission to Liúqiú.
While sailing on the sea,
suddenly, a huge dragon fell from the clouds,
splashing water several *zhàng* high.
The dragon floated half-submerged,
lifting its head
so that the boat rested against its jaw;
its eyes were half-closed,
looking dazed and despondent.
Everyone on the boat was terrified,
stopping the oars and not daring to move at all.
A boatman said,
"This is a rain-weary dragon from heaven."
Yù hung the imperial edict above
and burned incense, offering prayers together.
After a while,
the dragon leisurely departed.
Just as the boat started moving again,
another dragon fell,
exhibiting the same behavior as before.
This happened three or four times a day.
Another day later,
the boatmen ordered everyone to prepare plenty of white rice,
warning them:
"We are not far from the Qīngshuǐ Tán.
If you see anything,
just sprinkle rice into the water
and remain absolutely silent."
Soon they reached a place
where the water was crystal clear to the bottom.
Below were groups of dragons,
multicolored,
as large as basins or jars,
each lying prostrate.
Some were coiled,
their scales, manes, claws, and teeth
clearly countable.
Everyone's souls were frightened out of them;
they held their breath and closed their eyes,
not only not daring to look,
but also unable to move.
Only the boatmen grasped rice and scattered it themselves.
After a long time,
when they saw the sea waves turn deep black,
someone finally dared to groan.
They asked the reason for throwing the rice,
and the boatmen replied:
"Dragons fear maggots,
worried they might get under their scales.
White rice resembles maggots,
so when dragons see it, they immediately prostrate themselves.
Sailing over them,
we can avoid harm."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Cháng'ān, there was a scholar named Jiǎ Zǐlóng.
Once, passing through a neighboring alley,
he saw a guest with an elegant and free-spirited demeanor.
Upon inquiry, it was Zhēn Shēng,
a man from Xiányáng lodging there.
Zǐlóng admired him in his heart.
The next day,
he went to present his card,
but happened to find him away;
he visited three times in total,
but never met him.
So he secretly had someone watch for when Zhēn was home and then went to visit,
but Zhēn avoided him and wouldn't come out;
only after Jiǎ searched for him did he emerge.
They sat close and talked heart-to-heart,
finding great mutual understanding and joy.
Jiǎ went to the inn
and sent a servant boy to buy wine.
Zhēn was also a good drinker
and skilled at elegant banter,
so they were very merry.
When the wine was almost finished,
Zhēn searched his trunk and brought out a drinking vessel—
a jade *zhī* without a bottom.
He poured a cup of wine into it,
and it became brimming full;
when he ladled it out with a small cup into the pot,
the wine in the *zhī* didn't decrease at all.
Jiǎ found this strange
and persistently begged to learn the art.
Zhēn said:
"The reason I didn't want to meet you
is not that you have other faults,
but that your greed is not yet pacified.
This is an esoteric art of the immortals;
how could I teach it to you?"
Jiǎ said:
"What injustice!
How am I greedy?
If I occasionally entertain extravagant thoughts,
it's only because of poverty."
They parted with a laugh.
From then on, they visited each other without restraint,
forgetting all formalities.
Whenever Jiǎ was in financial difficulty,
Zhēn would take out a black stone,
blow on it while reciting a spell,
and rub it against tiles or gravel,
which would instantly turn into silver,
which he then gave to Jiǎ;
it was always just enough for his needs,
never any surplus.
Whenever Jiǎ asked for more,
Zhēn would say:
"I said you were greedy—
see,
see!"
Jiǎ thought that openly asking would certainly not succeed,
so he planned to wait until Zhēn was drunk and asleep,
steal the stone, and force him to teach the art.
One day,
after drinking, they lay down to sleep.
Jiǎ quietly got up
and searched under Zhēn's clothes.
Zhēn sensed it and said:
"You truly have lost your mind;
we can no longer stay together!"
He then bid farewell
and moved away.
More than a year later,
Jiǎ was walking by the riverbank
when he saw a stone, lustrous and pure,
that looked exactly like the real creature.
He picked it up
and treasured it like a precious gem.
A few days later,
Zhēn suddenly arrived,
looking as if he had lost something.
Jiǎ asked him what was wrong.
Zhēn said:
"What you saw before,
was an immortal's philosopher's stone.
I once traveled with Bàozhēnzǐ:
he took pity on my uprightness,
and gave it to me.
After getting drunk, I lost it,
and through divination, I sensed it must be with you.
If you could return it with the kindness of returning a lost belt,
I would not dare forget to repay you."
Jiǎ laughed and said:
"I have never dared deceive a friend in my life.
It is indeed as you divined.
But those who know Guǎn Zhòng's poverty best
are none other than Bào Shū.
What do you intend to do?"
Zhēn offered to give him a hundred taels of gold.
Jiǎ said:
"A hundred taels is not little,
but if you teach me the incantation,
and let me try it once myself,
I would have no regrets."
Zhēn feared he might not keep his word.
Jiǎ said:
"You are an immortal yourself,
surely you know that I, Jiǎ, would never break faith with a friend!"
Zhēn taught him the incantation.
Jiǎ saw a large stone on the steps,
and was about to try it.
Zhēn grabbed his elbow,
not letting him proceed.
Jiǎ then bent down, scooped up half a brick and placed it on the stone, saying:
"Like this,
isn't it too much?"
Zhēn then let him proceed.
Jiǎ did not rub the brick but rubbed the stone;
Zhēn changed color and was about to argue,
but the stone had already turned into solid gold.
Jiǎ returned the stone to Zhēn.
Zhēn sighed and said:
"Since things have come to this,
what more is there to say.
But recklessly bestowing fortune and wealth upon others
will surely bring heavenly punishment.
If you wish to absolve me of my crime,
provide a hundred coffins and a hundred padded garments—
would you agree?"
Jiǎ said:
"The reason I wanted money
was never to hoard it away.
Do you still see me as a miserly money-hoarder?"
Zhēn left happily.
Jiǎ obtained the gold,
and both gave alms and traded;
within three years,
he had fulfilled the promised number.
Zhēn suddenly arrived,
grasped his hand and said:
"You are truly a man of trust and righteousness!
After we parted, the God of Fortune reported me to the Emperor,
and I was stripped of my immortal status;
thanks to your extensive charity,
I have now fortunately atoned for my crime through merit.
I urge you to continue,
and not to cease."
Jiǎ asked Zhēn:
"What office do you hold in heaven?"
He said:
"I am actually a fox with spiritual attainment.
My origins are extremely humble,
unable to bear heavy karmic burdens,
so throughout my life I have cherished myself,
not daring to act recklessly in the slightest."
Jiǎ prepared wine for him,
and they drank joyfully as before.
Jiǎ lived to over ninety,
and the fox still visited his home from time to time.
A certain man from Chángshān
sold an antidote for poison,
and even if someone was near death,
if administered, they would always revive;
however, he kept the formula secret,
not even passing it to relatives or close friends.
One day,
he was arrested due to involvement in a case.
His brother-in-law brought him food in prison,
secretly hiding the antidote in it.
He waited until the meal was finished
before telling him.
The man did not believe it.
After a short while,
his stomach began to churn violently,
and only then was he greatly alarmed,
cursing:
"You beast, hurry and go!
Although there is medicinal powder at home,
I fear the road is too far to wait;
quickly find Ficus pumila in the city to grind into powder,
with a cup of clear water,
bring it quickly!"
His brother-in-law followed his instructions.
By the time he found it and returned,
the man was already vomiting and purging, nearly dead.
He urgently administered it,
and he immediately recovered.
The formula was thus passed down from then on.
This is also like the fox keeping his stone secret.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A cloth merchant
traveled to the Qīngzhōu region,
and happened to enter an abandoned temple.
Seeing its courtyards and buildings dilapidated,
he sighed and lamented endlessly.
A monk at his side said:
"If now there were a benevolent believer
to temporarily restore the temple gate,
it would also bring glory to Buddha's face."
The traveler generously took it upon himself.
The monk was pleased,
invited him into the abbot's quarters,
and treated him with great hospitality.
Then he mentioned the inner and outer halls and pavilions,
and requested that they all be renovated;
the traveler declined, saying he could not.
The monk insisted forcefully,
his words and expression fierce and angry.
The traveler became afraid,
and offered to empty his purse right away.
So he turned his bag inside out,
and gave everything to the monk.
As he was about to leave,
the monk stopped him, saying:
"You exhausting your funds was not truly your wish,
could it be that you bear a grudge against me?
Better to act first."
He then grabbed a knife and confronted him.
The traveler pleaded desperately,
but he would not listen;
he asked to hang himself,
and the monk agreed.
He forced him into a dark room and urged him on.
It happened that a coastal defense general was passing outside the temple,
and from afar, through a gap in the wall, he saw a woman in red entering the monk's quarters.
He became suspicious.
Dismounting, he entered the temple,
and searched thoroughly from front to back,
but could not find her.
Reaching the dark room,
he found the double doors tightly locked.
The monk refused to open them,
claiming there were evil spirits inside.
The general grew angry,
broke down the door and entered,
only to see the traveler hanging from a beam.
He rescued him,
and after a short while he revived.
Upon questioning, he learned the truth.
He then interrogated the monk under torture about the woman's whereabouts,
but in reality, there was none—
it must have been a manifestation by gods or Buddhas.
He killed the monk,
and returned the property to the traveler.
The traveler further raised funds to repair the temple,
and from then on, the incense offerings flourished greatly.
Xiàoyuán, the Provincial Graduate Zhào Fēng, recounted this in the most detail.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Hán Gōngfǔ of Yǔchéng said himself:
"I was walking on the road with Péng Èrzhēng, a fellow townsman,
when suddenly I turned my head and he was gone,
only his empty donkey following along.
But I heard urgent cries for help,
and upon listening carefully, they came from inside the saddlebag.
Looking closely at the bag, it was bulging,
and though it was lopsidedly heavy,
it did not fall off.
I wanted to get him out,
but the bag's opening was sewn very tightly;
I cut the thread with a knife,
and only then saw Péng lying inside like a dog.
After he came out,
I asked how he got in,
but he was utterly unaware himself.
It seems there was a fox causing trouble in his home,
and there were many incidents like this, so it is said."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Chángshān, there was a gentleman named Wáng Ruìtíng,
who was skilled in divination using a planchette.
The spirit that descended through the planchette called itself Immortal Hé,
and claimed to be a disciple of Chúnyáng,
though some said it was actually the crane ridden by Patriarch Lǚ.
Whenever it descended,
it would discuss literature and compose poetry with people.
Grand Historian Lǐ Zhìjūn revered it as his teacher,
who would correct his essays with red and yellow ink,
clarifying his thoughts with precision;
the Grand Historian’s mastery of literary composition
was largely due to the power of Immortal Hé,
and as a result, many literary scholars came to follow it.
However, when resolving people’s doubts and difficulties,
it mostly relied on reason,
and seldom spoke of fortune or misfortune.
In the year Xīnwèi,
when Chief Examiner Zhū came to Jǐnán to oversee the examinations,
after the tests,
several friends gathered to predict the results.
Immortal Hé requested the examination essays,
and evaluated them all.
Among those present was someone who was friends with Lǐ Biàn from Lèlíng,
who was a diligent and thoughtful scholar,
and everyone had high hopes for him,
so they presented his essay,
and requested an evaluation on his behalf.
The planchette wrote:
"First class."
A moment later,
it wrote again:
"Just now, when evaluating Scholar Lǐ,
I judged based on his essay,
but this student’s fortune is extremely unlucky,
and he should suffer punishment.
How strange!
His essay and his fortune do not align at all.
Could it be that the chief examiner does not judge based on the essay?"
Gentlemen, wait a moment,
let me go and investigate."
After a short while,
it wrote again:
"I just went to the education commissioner’s office,
and saw that the chief examiner was overwhelmed with official duties,
and his concerns were not at all focused on the essays.
He left everything to six or seven assistants,
who were all students who had purchased their degrees.
They were all among them,
and in their previous lives, they had no foundation at all,
most of them were wandering souls from the realm of hungry ghosts,
begging for food in all directions.
They had been in the dark prison for eight hundred years,
which damaged the essence of their eyes,
like someone who has been in a cave for a long time—
when they first come out, the world appears in strange colors,
and they cannot see clearly.
Among them, one or two were transformed from human bodies,
but when grading essays and assigning rankings,
I fear they will not be able to do it properly."
Everyone asked if there was a way to reverse this,
and it wrote:
"The method is extremely simple,
and everyone knows it—
why bother asking?"
Everyone understood its meaning,
and informed Lǐ.
Lǐ was afraid,
so he took his essay to Grand Historian Sūn Rénshǐ Zǐwèi for evaluation,
and also told him about the omen.
The Grand Historian praised his essay,
and tried to dispel his doubts.
Lǐ, considering the Grand Historian a master of the literary world,
felt more confident,
and no longer worried about the planchette’s words.
Later, when the results were announced,
he was placed in the fourth class.
The Grand Historian was greatly shocked,
and took his essay to review again,
finding no flaws at all.
He commented,
"Examiner Shímén,
who has long been renowned for his literary talent,
would certainly not make such a mistake.
This must have been done by a drunk assistant
who does not even understand punctuation."
Thus, everyone admired Immortal Hé even more,
and burned incense to thank it.
The planchette wrote:
"Scholar Lǐ, do not let this temporary setback
make you feel ashamed or discouraged.
You should write more examination essays
and make them even more outstanding—
next year, you can achieve a high rank."
Lǐ followed its advice.
After some time, word spread in the office,
and a special notice was posted to console him.
The following year, he indeed achieved a high rank,
demonstrating the spirit’s efficacy.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"With so many such assistants in the offices,
it is no wonder that in the capital’s alley of ugly women,
by evening, there are no empty beds.
Alas!"
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
(the preceding part is missing) Niú entered his father’s room,
and saw the old man lying on the bed, still asleep.
From this, he knew it was a fox,
and angrily said:
"Foxes can be tolerated,
but how dare you disrupt our human relations!
Guān Shèng is called the ‘Demon Subduer’—
where is he now,
allowing such creatures to run rampant!"
He then wrote a petition to the Jade Emperor,
subtly accusing Guān Dì of neglecting his duties.
After some time,
(Guān Dì suddenly heard a shouting voice from the sky—
it was Guān Dì.
He angrily scolded:
"How dare a scholar be so disrespectful!
Am I solely responsible for driving away foxes from your house?
If your petition had not been acted upon,
how could you complain?"
He immediately ordered Niú to be beaten twenty times with a rod,
nearly tearing the flesh from his thighs.
A moment later,
a black-faced general bound a fox and led it away,
and the strange occurrences ceased.
Three years later,
the daughter of the Jǐnán garrison commander was bewitched by a fox,
and no method could drive it away.
The fox said to the girl:
"In my entire life, the only one I fear
is Niú Tóngrén."
The garrison commander did not know where Niú was from,
and had no way to find him.
Just then, the education commissioner arrived for the examinations,
and Niú came to take the test.
While in the provincial capital, he happened to be insulted by a soldier,
and angrily went to complain at the garrison commander’s gate.
As soon as the garrison commander heard his name,
he was overjoyed and surprised,
and bowed respectfully.
He immediately had the soldier arrested
and punished severely according to the law.
Afterward,
he explained the situation truthfully.
Niú had no choice
but to petition Guān Dì on his behalf.
In an instant,
a golden-armored god descended to his home.
The fox was in the room at the time,
and its face suddenly changed color,
transforming into the shape of a dog,
running around the room howling.
It soon rushed out
and threw itself at the foot of the steps.
The god said:
"The Emperor showed mercy last time and did not execute you,
but if you offend again,
you will not be pardoned!"
He tied it to the neck of his horse and left.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
There was a scholar named Mǐ, a native of Fújiàn,
whose name and hometown have been forgotten by the storyteller.
Once, he happened to enter the prefectural city
and, while drunk, passed by a marketplace.
He heard the sound of pipes and drums like thunder coming from a grand house.
He asked the local residents about it,
and they said it was a birthday celebration,
yet the gate and courtyard appeared unusually quiet and deserted.
Listening to the lively music and singing,
he, in his drunken state, quite enjoyed the melodies.
Without even asking whose house it was,
he immediately bought a congratulatory gift from the street vendor
and sent in a visiting card under the humble title of "junior."
Someone, seeing his plain and shabby attire,
asked him,
"What relation are you to the old gentleman?"
He replied,
"None."
The person then said,
"This is a sojourner living here temporarily.
It's unclear what official position he holds,
but he is very haughty and aloof.
Since you are not a relative,
what are you seeking?"
Upon hearing this, Mǐ regretted his actions,
but his card had already been delivered.
Before long,
two young men came out to greet the guest.
Their splendid robes dazzled the eyes,
and their demeanor was elegant and refined.
They bowed and invited Mǐ inside.
He saw an old man sitting facing south,
with several banquet tables arranged to the east and west.
There were six or seven guests,
all seemingly of noble lineage.
When they saw Mǐ arrive,
they all stood up to salute him,
and the old man also rose with the aid of his cane.
Mǐ stood for a long time,
waiting to exchange courtesies,
but the old man never left his seat.
The two young men addressed him, saying,
"Our father is frail with age,
and rising to bow is quite difficult for him.
We brothers thank you on his behalf for honoring us with your presence."
Mǐ modestly declined their thanks, and the matter ended there.
Then, an additional table was set above,
next to the old man's seat.
Not long after,
female musicians began performing below.
Behind the seats was a glass screen
to shield the women of the household from view.
The music and drums swelled loudly,
making conversation among the guests impossible.
As the banquet neared its end,
the two young men stood up
and urged each guest to drink from a huge cup,
which could hold three dǒu.
Mǐ showed a reluctant expression,
but seeing the other guests accept,
he did the same.
In a moment, looking around,
he saw that both hosts and guests had drained their cups.
With no alternative,
Mǐ also forced himself to finish his.
The young men poured again;
Mǐ felt utterly exhausted
and stood up to take his leave.
The young men firmly grabbed his sleeve to stop him.
Mǐ, heavily drunk, collapsed to the ground.
He only felt someone sprinkling cold water on his face,
and then he seemed to wake up as if from a dream.
Getting up and looking around,
he found that all the guests had dispersed.
Only one young man held his arm and escorted him out,
and so they parted, and Mǐ returned home.
Later, when he passed by that house again,
it had already been vacated.
After returning from the prefectural city,
he happened to go to the market one day.
A man came out of a shop
and invited him for a drink.
Mǐ looked at him but did not recognize him;
nevertheless, he followed him inside.
There, he found his fellow villager Bào Zhuāng already seated.
He asked the man who he was,
and learned his surname was Zhū,
a mirror polisher from the market.
Mǐ asked,
"How do you know me?"
Zhū replied,
"The other day at the birthday celebration,
do you recognize that host?"
Mǐ said,
"I do not."
Zhū said,
"I am very familiar with that household, coming and going frequently.
The old man
has the surname Fù,
but I don't know which province he is from or what official position he holds.
When you, sir, attended the birthday celebration,
I was below the steps,
so I recognized you."
As evening fell,
they finished drinking and parted.
That night, Bào Zhuāng died on the road.
Bào's father did not know Zhū
and, based on names, brought a lawsuit against Mǐ.
An examination revealed severe injuries on Bào Zhuāng's body.
Mǐ was convicted of murder and sentenced to death,
enduring all manner of torture and shackles.
Because Zhū had not been captured,
there was no conclusive evidence for the crime,
so Mǐ was kept imprisoned.
Over a year later,
an imperial inspector came on a tour,
ascertained the injustice of the case,
and released him.
Having lost all his family's farmland and property,
his scholar's attire and cap were stripped away.
Hoping to have them restored,
he then carried his bag and entered the prefectural city.
As the day was nearing dusk,
his steps were quite weary,
and he rested by the roadside.
From afar, he saw a small carriage approaching,
with two maidservants flanking it.
After it passed,
he suddenly heard an order to halt the carriage.
He could not make out what was said inside the carriage,
but soon one of the maidservants approached and asked him,
"Are you not of the surname Mǐ?"
Startled, he rose and affirmed it.
She asked:
"Why are you so impoverished?"
He told her the reason.
She asked again:
"Where are you going?"
He told her that as well.
The maidservant left
and spoke to someone in the carriage;
soon she returned,
inviting Mǐ to approach the carriage.
From within the carriage, a delicate hand lifted the curtain,
and she glanced at him slightly—
she was a beauty of unparalleled grace.
She said to him:
"You have unfortunately suffered an unjust calamity,
and hearing of it makes me sigh deeply.
Today, at the Education Commissioner's office,
one cannot enter empty-handed.
On the road, I have nothing to offer you...
Then she took a pearl flower from her hair,
handed it to him, and said:
"This item can be sold for a hundred taels of silver.
Please keep it safely hidden."
Mǐ bowed deeply,
wishing to ask about her official family,
but the carriage moved swiftly,
and she had already gone far away,
leaving him unsure of who she was.
Holding the flower, he pondered it;
it was adorned with luminous pearls,
no ordinary object.
He treasured it and continued on his way.
Upon reaching the prefectural city,
he submitted his petition,
but officials at all levels demanded heavy bribes;
taking out the flower to look at it,
he could not bear to part with it,
and so he returned home.
Returning with no home of his own,
he relied on his elder brother and sister-in-law.
Fortunately, his brother was virtuous,
managing affairs for him,
and despite poverty, he did not abandon his studies.
The following year,
he went to the prefectural city to take the child scholar examination,
but mistakenly entered deep into the mountains.
It happened to be the Qingmíng Festival,
and there were many visitors.
Several women on horseback approached,
and among them was a young lady
who turned out to be the person from the carriage that year.
Seeing Mǐ, she halted her horse
and asked where he was going.
He told her everything.
Startled, she said:
"Have your scholar's attire and cap not been restored yet?"
With a pained expression, Mǐ took out the pearl flower from beneath his clothes and said:
"I could not bear to part with this,
so I am still a child scholar."
The young lady's cheeks flushed crimson,
and she instructed him to sit and wait by the roadside.
Then she rode away at a leisurely pace.
After a long while,
a maidservant galloped over on horseback,
handed him a wrapped object, and said:
"The young lady says: today, the Education Commissioner's gate is as crowded as a marketplace. She gives you two hundred taels of silver
as funds for your advancement."
Mǐ declined, saying:
"The young lady has already shown me great kindness!
I believe passing the examination is not difficult for me,
but I dare not accept such a large sum of money.
If only she would tell me her name,
I would paint a small portrait of her,
burn incense, and offer it in reverence—
that would be enough."
The maidservant paid no heed,
dropped the package on the ground, and left.
From then on, Mǐ had ample means for his expenses,
but he remained unwilling to seek favor through connections.
Later, he placed first in the county-level examination.
He gave the silver to his elder brother;
his brother was skilled in managing wealth,
and within three years, their former family estate was fully restored.
It so happened that the Provincial Governor of Fújiàn was a former student of Mǐ's grandfather,
and he provided generous support,
making the brothers a wealthy family.
However, Mǐ was by nature upright and unyielding;
although he was connected to high officials through family ties,
he never sought personal favors from them.
One day,
a visitor arrived at the gate, dressed in furs and riding a fine horse,
but no one recognized him.
He went out to look,
and it was Fù Gōngzǐ.
They bowed and entered,
each inquiring after the other's well-being.
Food and drink were prepared to entertain him,
but the guest declined, citing busyness,
yet he did not insist on leaving.
Soon, when wine and dishes were laid out,
Gōngzǐ rose and requested a private word;
they went inside together,
and he prostrated himself on the ground.
Shēng, startled, asked what the matter was.
With sorrow, he said:
"My father has just suffered a great calamity,
and I wish to seek help from the Provincial Governor,
which only you, brother, can do."
Shēng declined, saying:
"Although he is a family friend,
to trouble others for private matters
is something I have never done in my life."
Gōngzǐ knelt on the ground, weeping pitifully.
Shēng said sternly:
"I and you, Gōngzǐ,
are merely acquaintances who shared a drink;
how can you force someone to compromise their integrity!"
Gōngzǐ was greatly ashamed,
rose, and took his leave.
The next day,
while sitting alone,
a servant in dark clothing entered.
Looking at her,
it was the one who had given him gold in the mountains.
Just as Shēng rose in surprise,
the servant said:
"Have you forgotten the pearl flower?"
Shēng said:
"Indeed, indeed,
I dare not forget."
She said:
"Yesterday's Gōngzǐ
is the young lady's own brother."
Hearing this,
Shēng secretly rejoiced,
but pretended:
"This is hard to believe.
If I could hear a word from the young lady herself,
I would even tread into a cauldron of boiling oil;
otherwise,
I dare not accept the task."
The servant went out,
galloped away on horseback.
After half a watch, she returned,
knocked on the door, and entered, saying:
"The young lady has come."
Before she finished speaking,
the young lady entered sorrowfully,
faced the wall and wept,
not uttering a word.
Shēng bowed and said:
"If not for you,
I would not have what I have today.
If there is any task to be done,
how dare I not obey your command!"
The young lady said:
"Those who receive requests often act arrogantly,
while those who make requests often feel fearful.
Running about in the middle of the night—
how could you understand this hardship in your life?
It is only because I fear others that I do so;
what more is there to say!"
Shēng comforted her, saying:
"The reason I did not immediately agree
was fear that after this meeting, it would be difficult to see you again.
To have you endure dew day and night—
I know I am at fault!"
He then took hold of her sleeve,
secretly pressing and caressing it.
The young lady angrily said:
"You truly are a base man!
Not remembering the kindness of the past,
but seeking to take advantage of another's distress.
I was wrong!"
Furious, she went out,
mounted the carriage and prepared to leave.
Shēng chased after her to apologize,
kneeling long to block her way.
The servant also pleaded on his behalf.
The young lady's anger slightly subsided,
and from the carriage, she said to Shēng:
"To tell you the truth: I am not human,
but a goddess.
My father serves as the Dūlǐsī of Nányuè,
but he accidentally offended the Earth Official,
and the matter will be reported to the Emperor;
without the official seal of the local Dūrén official,
it cannot be resolved.
If you have not forgotten our past bond,
take a sheet of yellow paper
and seek it for me."
Having said this,
the carriage departed and left.
Shēng returned home,
trembling with fear.
He then pretended to perform an exorcism,
and went to see the Provincial Governor.
The Governor said the matter resembled sorcery,
and refused.
Shēng bribed the Governor's confidant heavily with gold,
and he agreed,
but had not found an opportunity.
After returning,
the servant was waiting at the door.
Shēng told her everything,
and she silently left,
seeming to resent his lack of sincerity.
Shēng chased after her and said:
"Go back and tell the young lady:
if the matter cannot be accomplished,
I will give my life for it!"
After returning,
he tossed and turned all night,
unable to think of a plan.
It happened that the Governor's favorite concubine was buying pearls,
so Shēng presented the pearl flower to her.
The concubine was greatly pleased,
and secretly stamped the seal for him.
Carrying it back,
he met the servant just arriving.
Smiling, she said:
"Fortunately, I have not failed in my mission.
But for years, even when impoverished and begging, I could not bear to sell it;
now it has been discarded by its owner!"
He then explained the situation.
And said:
"Even if gold were cast aside,
I would not regret it.
But tell the young lady: the pearl flower must be repaid."
Several days later,
Young Master Fù came to his home to express thanks
and presented him with a hundred taels of gold.
The scholar said with a stern expression:
"The reason I did what I did
was because your younger sister treated me with selfless kindness.
Otherwise,
even ten thousand taels of gold would not be enough to exchange for one's reputation and integrity!"
When the young master insisted further,
the scholar's tone and expression grew even more severe.
The young master left in shame,
saying:
"This matter is far from settled!"
The next day,
a maidservant, following the young lady's orders,
presented a hundred luminous pearls,
saying:
"Is this enough to repay the pearl flower?"
The scholar said:
"What I valued about the flower
was not the pearls.
If you had given me a treasure worth ten thousand yì that day,
I would have simply sold it to become a rich man.
Why would I have cherished it and willingly remained in poverty?
What would have been the point?
The young lady is a divine being.
How dare I, a mere student, have any other hopes?
If I am fortunate enough to repay even a ten-thousandth part of her great kindness,
I would die without regret!"
The maidservant placed the pearls on the table.
The scholar bowed toward them and then declined them.
A few days later,
the young master came again.
The scholar ordered food and wine to be prepared.
The young master had his attendants enter the kitchen
and cooked the meal himself.
They drank freely facing each other,
as joyfully as if they were family.
A guest had presented some bitter glutinous rice wine.
The young master drank it and found it delicious.
He drank a hundred cups in succession,
until his cheeks were slightly flushed.
He then said to the scholar:
"You are a truly upright and principled gentleman.
My brother and I failed to recognize your worth earlier,
and we feel far more ashamed than the womenfolk.
My father is deeply grateful for your great virtue,
but has no way to repay you.
He wishes to have my younger sister join you in marriage,
but fears you might disdain her because she belongs to the realm of spirits."
The scholar was both overjoyed and apprehensive,
and did not know how to respond.
The young master took his leave and departed,
saying:
"Tomorrow night is the ninth day of the seventh month.
The new moon will be like a hook beside the stars.
It is an auspicious time for the Weaving Maid's youngest daughter to descend and marry.
It is a propitious date.
You should prepare the wedding chamber."
The following evening,
they indeed sent the young lady over.
In every way, she was no different from an ordinary person.
Three days later,
the young lady gave gifts to everyone, from her elder brother and sister-in-law down to the maids and servants, young and old.
She was also extremely virtuous,
serving her sister-in-law as if she were her own mother.
After several years without bearing children,
she urged her husband to take a concubine,
but the scholar refused.
It happened that his elder brother was trading in the Jiāng-Huái region,
and he bought a young maiden and brought her back.
The maiden's surname was Gù,
and her childhood name was Bóshì.
Her appearance was also delicate and graceful.
Both husband and wife were pleased.
Seeing a pearl flower inserted in her hairpin,
it looked very much like the one from years past.
She took it off to look,
and indeed it was the same.
Astonished, they questioned her about it.
She replied:
"Long ago, a governor's beloved concubine died.
Her maidservant stole it and sold it in the market.
My late father, considering the price fair,
bought it and brought it home.
I loved it.
My late father had no sons,
only me, his daughter.
Therefore, whatever I asked for, I received.
Later, after my father died, the family declined.
I was sent to live with the Gù family.
Madam Gù was like an aunt to me.
When she saw the pearl,
she repeatedly wanted to sell it.
I threw myself into a well seeking death,
so it has survived until now."
The husband and wife sighed and said:
"For an object from ten years ago
to return to its original owner—
is this not fate?"
The young lady took out another pearl flower
and said:
"This object has long been without its mate!"
She then bestowed both upon her
and personally pinned them in her hair.
After Bóshì withdrew,
she inquired very thoroughly about the young lady's family background,
but the household members all avoided speaking of it.
She said privately to the scholar:
"In my observation, the young lady
is not of the human world.
There is a divine aura between her brows and eyes.
Yesterday, when she was pinning the flowers, I was able to look at her closely.
Her beauty emanates from within her skin and flesh,
unlike ordinary people whose charm lies merely in the arrangement of black and white features."
The scholar laughed at her.
Bóshì said:
"Don't say anything.
I will test her.
If she is indeed divine,
then whenever I need something,
I will burn incense and pray for it in a place with no one around,
and she will surely know."
The young lady's embroidered socks were exquisitely crafted.
Bóshì admired them
but did not dare to say so.
She then burned incense in her inner chamber and prayed for them.
The young lady rose early
and suddenly, checking her chest,
took out a pair of socks
and sent a maidservant to give them to Bóshì.
The scholar saw this and laughed.
The young lady asked the reason,
and he told her the truth.
The young lady said:
"How clever this maid is!"
Because of her intelligence,
she loved her even more.
However, Bóshì became even more respectful.
At dawn every day,
she would bathe and perfume herself before paying her respects.
Later, Bóshì gave birth to twin boys at once,
and the two women each raised one.
When the scholar reached the age of eighty,
the young lady's appearance was still like that of a maiden.
When the scholar fell ill,
the young lady gathered carpenters to make a coffin,
ordering it to be twice as large as usual.
After he died,
the young lady did not weep.
When the others had gone elsewhere,
she had already entered the coffin and died.
Thus they were buried together.
To this day, it is called
the "Large Coffin Tomb."
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"The young lady was indeed divine.
But for Bóshì to be able to perceive this—
by what method did she follow?
Thus we know that human intelligence
can indeed surpass that of the divine!"
Based on the manuscript edition of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Yàn Zhòng was from Yán'ān in Shǎnxī.
He lived together with his elder brother Bó,
and their affection for each other was deep and sincere.
Bó died at the age of thirty,
leaving no heir;
his wife also passed away soon after.
Zhòng grieved bitterly for them,
and often thought that if he had two sons,
he would give one to continue his brother's line.
He had just had a son
when his own wife died as well.
Fearing that a new wife might not care for his child,
Zhòng decided to buy a concubine.
In a neighboring village, someone was selling a maidservant.
Zhòng went to look her over,
but was not at all satisfied.
Feeling disheartened and listless,
he was kept by a friend for drinks and returned home drunk.
On the way, he met an old schoolmate, Liáng Shēng,
who shook his hand warmly
and invited him to his home.
In his drunkenness, Zhòng forgot that Liáng was already dead
and followed him.
Entering the gate,
he saw it was not the old residence
and asked suspiciously.
The reply was:
"We've just moved here."
Going inside to prepare wine,
Liáng found the home-brewed liquor exhausted,
so he asked Zhòng to sit and wait
while he took a bottle to buy more.
Zhòng went out and stood by the gate to wait.
He saw a woman riding a donkey pass by,
followed by a boy
about eight or nine years old,
whose face and expression
were exactly like his brother's.
His heart stirred with pity,
and he hurried after them,
asking:
"What is your surname, child?"
The boy replied:
"Surname Yàn."
Zhòng was even more startled,
and asked again:
"What is your father's name?"
The answer was:
"I don't know."
As they spoke,
they reached the boy's gate,
and the woman dismounted and went inside.
Zhòng took the boy's hand and said:
"Is your father at home?"
The boy nodded and went in.
After a moment,
an old woman came out to look—
it was truly his sister-in-law.
She was surprised to see her brother-in-law there.
Zhòng was greatly saddened
and followed her inside.
He saw the house was also tidy and well-kept,
and asked:
"Where is my brother?"
She said:
"He's out collecting debts and hasn't returned."
Zhòng asked:
"Who was the one on the donkey?"
She replied:
"That is your brother's concubine, Gān Shì.
She has borne two sons.
The elder, Ā Dà,
has gone to the market and isn't back yet;
the one you saw is Ā Xiǎo."
After sitting for a long time,
the wine gradually wore off,
and Zhòng began to realize that all he saw were ghosts.
But because of his deep fraternal affection,
he was not afraid.
His sister-in-law warmed wine and prepared food.
Eager to see his brother,
Zhòng urged Ā Xiǎo to go find him.
After a long while,
Ā Xiǎo returned crying and said:
"The Lǐ family won't repay what they owe,
and are even quarreling with Father."
Hearing this,
Zhòng rushed out with Ā Xiǎo
and saw two men throwing his brother to the ground.
Furious,
Zhòng charged in with clenched fists,
knocking down everyone in his way.
He quickly helped his brother up;
the opponents had all fled.
Chasing and catching one of them,
he pummeled him countless times
before letting him go.
Holding his brother's hand,
he stamped his feet and wept bitterly;
his brother also wept.
Returning home,
the whole family offered comfort,
then prepared wine and food
for the brothers to celebrate their reunion.
Not long after,
a youth entered,
about sixteen or seventeen years old.
Bó called him Ā Dà
and told him to bow to his uncle.
Zhòng pulled him up
and said tearfully to his brother:
"Elder Brother, you have two sons in the underworld,
yet your grave remains untended;
your younger brother has but one son and is a widower—
what are we to do?"
Bó was also deeply saddened.
His wife said to Bó:
"Let Ā Xiǎo go with his uncle—
that would be fine."
Hearing this,
Ā Xiǎo clung to his uncle's side,
unwilling to leave.
Zhòng stroked his head,
feeling even more heartache.
He asked:
"Are you willing to come with me?"
The boy replied:
"I am willing."
Zhòng thought that though ghosts are not human,
having some comfort is better than none,
and so his expression softened.
Bó said:
"Let him go with you,
but don't spoil him.
You must feed him flesh and blood,
and drive him to bask in the sun—
only stop after noon.
A child of six or seven,
from spring through summer,
will regenerate flesh and bone,
and can then marry and have children;
only I fear he may not live long."
As they spoke,
a young girl was peeping and listening outside the door,
her demeanor gentle and graceful.
Zhòng suspected she was his brother's daughter
and asked his brother,
who said:
"Her name is Xiāng Qún,
the younger sister of my concubine.
She is orphaned and has nowhere to go,
so she has been living with us for ten years."
Zhòng asked:
"Is she betrothed?"
Bó said:
"Not yet.
Recently, a matchmaker proposed the Tián family from the east village."
The girl whispered outside the window:
"I won't marry that cowherd from the Tián family."
Zhòng felt somewhat stirred within,
but did not speak openly.
Soon after, Bó rose,
set up a bed in the study,
and had his brother stay the night.
Zhòng did not wish to stay,
yet his heart was attached to Xiāngqún.
He intended to devise a way to gauge his elder brother’s feelings,
so he bid his brother farewell and went to bed.
It was early spring at the time,
and the weather was still cold.
The study had long lacked a fire,
making it so chilly it raised goosebumps.
Facing the candle, he sat in the cold,
thinking of having a little drink.
Suddenly, Ā Xiǎo pushed the door open and entered,
placing a cup of broth and a jug of wine on the table.
Zhòng was overjoyed,
and asked:
“Who did this?”
The reply was:
“Aunt Xiāng.”
When the wine was nearly finished,
she also covered the brazier fire with ashes
and placed it under the bed.
Zhòng asked:
“Have Father and Mother gone to bed?”
He said:
“They’ve been asleep for a long time.”
“Where do you sleep?”
He said:
“I share a bed with Aunt Xiāng.”
Ā Xiǎo waited until his uncle had fallen asleep
before closing the door and leaving.
Zhòng thought of Xiāngqún’s kindness and understanding,
and his admiration for her grew even stronger;
moreover, seeing that she could care for Ā Xiǎo,
his desire to have her became even firmer.
Tossing and turning in bed,
he stayed awake all night.
Early the next morning,
he told his elder brother:
“I am alone without a partner;
I trouble you, elder brother, to keep an eye out for me.”
Bó said:
“Our family is not one of those with only a single gourd and a carrying pole;
there should be someone suitable to choose from.
Even if there are beautiful women in the underworld,
I fear they would be of no benefit to you.”
Zhòng said:
“The ancients also had ghost wives;
what harm is there?”
Bó seemed to understand his meaning,
and then said:
“Xiāngqún is also good,
but if a large needle is used to prick the rén yíng point and the blood does not stop flowing,
then she can become a living man’s wife.
How can this be done carelessly?”
Zhòng said:
“If I can have Xiāngqún to care for Ā Xiǎo,
that would be fine.”
Bó only shook his head.
Zhòng kept pleading without cease,
until his sister-in-law said:
“Try catching Xiāngqún and forcefully pricking her to test it;
if it doesn’t work, then forget it.”
So she took the needle and went outside,
where she encountered Xiāngqún.
She quickly grabbed her wrist,
and found the bloodstain was still wet.
It turned out that when she heard Bó’s words earlier,
she had already tested it on herself.
The sister-in-law released her hand and laughed,
then went back and told Bó:
“She has been playing the part of a clever one for a long time now;
why should we still worry on her behalf?”
The concubine heard this and became angry,
rushed up to Xiāngqún,
pointed at her eye sockets and scolded:
“Shameless, wanton maid!
Do you want to run off with your uncle?
I will certainly not let you have your wish!”
Xiāngqún felt ashamed and indignant,
crying and wanting to seek death,
throwing the whole household into an uproar.
Zhòng then felt greatly ashamed,
bid farewell to his elder brother and sister-in-law,
and led Ā Xiǎo away.
His elder brother said:
“Brother, go for now;
do not let Ā Xiǎo come back again,
for fear it will harm his vitality.”
Zhòng agreed.
After returning home,
he falsely increased Ā Xiǎo’s age,
claiming he was the posthumous child of a maid sold by his elder brother.
Everyone thought his appearance strikingly resembled Bó’s,
and so believed he was Bó’s offspring.
Zhòng taught him to read,
often sending him to hold a book and recite it in the sunlight.
At first, he found it hard,
but gradually became accustomed and at ease.
In the sixth month,
when the tables and desks were scorching hot,
the boy played and studied,
showing not the slightest complaint.
The boy was very bright,
finishing half a volume each day.
At night, sharing a bed with his uncle,
he would often recite from memory.
His uncle was greatly comforted.
Moreover, because he could not forget Xiāngqún,
he no longer entertained
thoughts of
“Yànlóu.”
One day,
two matchmakers came to discuss a marriage for Ā Xiǎo.
With no one to manage the household,
his heart grew very anxious and impatient.
Suddenly, Sister-in-law Gān entered from outside and said:
“Uncle, do not blame me;
I have brought Xiāngqún to you.
Because this maid did not know shame,
I deliberately humiliated and punished her.
With you, Uncle, being such an outstanding man,
if she does not follow you,
whom else would she willingly follow?”
Seeing Xiāngqún standing behind her,
his heart was filled with joy.
He respectfully invited his sister-in-law to sit;
explaining that there were guests in the hall,
he hurried out.
After a short while, he returned inside,
and found that Gān shì had already left.
Xiāngqún removed her makeup and entered the kitchen,
and soon the sounds of chopping and cutting filled the air.
Shortly after, an array of dishes and delicacies were presented,
cooked to perfection.
After the guests left,
Zhòng entered,
and saw Xiāngqún sitting in the room in full makeup.
So they performed the ceremonial bows and completed the wedding rites.
When evening came,
she still wanted to sleep with Ā Xiǎo.
Zhòng said:
“I want to warm him with my yang energy;
he cannot be separated from me.”
So he placed the woman in a separate room,
only visiting her in the evenings for a cup of wine and joyful meetings.
Xiāngqún cared for the former child as if he were her own,
and Zhòng esteemed her even more for it.
One evening,
as husband and wife were being intimate and harmonious,
Zhòng playfully asked:
“Are there beauties in the underworld?”
The woman thought for a long time,
then replied:
“I haven’t seen any.
Only the neighbor girl, Wēilíngxiān,
is considered beautiful by many;
but her appearance is still just like any other person’s,
it’s just that she is skilled at adornment.
She has associated with me the longest,
but in my heart, I secretly despise her wantonness.
If you wish to see her,
she can be summoned in an instant.
But such a person
should not be provoked.”
Zhòng urgently wanted to see her once.
The woman picked up a brush as if to write a letter,
but then threw down the brush and said:
“No,
no!”
He pressed her again and again,
and finally she said:
"Do not be beguiled by her."
Zhòng promised.
He then tore a piece of paper and drew several strokes resembling talismanic symbols,
burning them outside the door.
After a short while,
the curtain stirred and the hook jingled,
followed by a giggling laugh.
The woman rose and pulled her inside;
she wore her hair in a high chignon like a cloud,
almost resembling a painting.
She helped her sit by the bedside,
and they drank wine together, recounting their long separation.
At first, upon seeing Zhòng,
she still covered her mouth with her red sleeve,
not speaking freely;
after several cups,
she grew playful and uninhibited,
gradually stretching out a foot to press against Zhòng's robe.
Zhòng's mind became confused and agitated,
not knowing where his soul had gone.
The only obstacle before his eyes was Xiāngqún;
Xiāngqún also deliberately guarded against it,
never leaving his side for a moment.
Wēilíngxiān suddenly rose,
lifted the curtain, and went out;
Xiāngqún followed her,
and Zhòng also followed.
Wēilíngxiān took hold of Zhòng,
and hurried into another room.
Xiāngqún was deeply resentful,
but could do nothing about it,
and returned to her room in anger,
merely listening to what they did.
After a while, Zhòng came in,
and Xiāngqún reproached him, saying:
"If you do not heed my words,
I fear later you will not be able to refuse her."
Zhòng suspected her of jealousy,
and they parted unhappily.
The next evening,
Wēilíngxiān came unsummoned.
Xiāngqún was very disgusted to see her,
and treated her arrogantly without courtesy;
Wēilíngxiān actually went off with Zhòng.
This continued for several nights.
Whenever the woman saw her coming,
she would insult and abuse her,
but still could not drive her away.
After more than a month,
Zhòng fell ill and could not rise,
and only then did he greatly regret it.
He called Xiāngqún to stay with him,
hoping to avoid Wēilíngxiān;
but if their vigilance slackened day or night,
the human and ghost were already in the bedchamber.
Xiāngqún took a stick and chased her away,
but the ghost angrily fought back,
and Xiāngqún, being delicate and weak,
was wounded on her hands and feet.
Zhòng gradually sank into a critical condition.
Xiāngqún wept and said:
"How can I face my elder sister now!"
After a few more days,
Zhòng passed away quietly.
At first, he saw two officers holding a warrant enter,
and unconsciously followed them.
On the road, he worried about having no travel funds,
and invited the officers to pass by his elder brother's place on the way.
When his elder brother saw him,
he was shocked and turned pale,
asking:
"What have you been doing lately, brother?"
Zhòng said:
"Nothing else,
only suffering from a ghostly illness."
He told him the truth.
The elder brother said:
"So it is."
He then took out a packet of silver,
and said to the officers:
"Please accept this for now.
My brother's crime does not warrant death,
I ask you to release him and let him return.
I will send my son to go with you,
perhaps there will be no problem."
He then called Ādà to accompany the officers for a drink.
Turning back into the house,
he explained the situation to everyone.
He then had Gān shì call Wēilíngxiān from next door.
She arrived shortly,
and upon seeing Zhòng, tried to flee.
The elder brother grabbed her back and scolded her:
"Lewd wench!
In life you were a wanton woman,
in death a base ghost,
long shunned by all;
and now you corrupt my brother!"
He immediately slapped her,
her cloud-like hair flying in disarray,
and her seductive appearance instantly diminished.
After a while,
an old woman came,
kneeling on the ground and pleading pitifully.
The elder brother also reproached the old woman for allowing her daughter to indulge in debauchery,
scolding and berating her for some time,
before finally ordering her to leave with her daughter.
The elder brother then escorted Zhòng out,
and in a fleeting moment, they had already reached his home's gate.
Going straight to the bedroom,
he suddenly awoke as if from a dream,
only then realizing that he had just died.
The elder brother reproached Xiāngqún, saying:
"My sister and I,
thinking you virtuous and capable,
therefore had you accompany my brother;
yet you instead sought to hasten his death!
If it were not for the impropriety of our relationship,
I would have beaten you!"
Xiāngqún, ashamed and fearful, sobbed,
and bowed to the elder brother in apology.
The elder brother looked at Āxiǎo happily and said:
"The child is actually a living person now!"
Xiāngqún wanted to go out to prepare millet,
but the elder brother declined, saying,
"My brother's affairs are not yet settled,
I have no leisure."
Āxiǎo was thirteen years old,
and gradually knew to miss his father; seeing his father leave,
he tearfully followed him.
His father said:
"Following your uncle is the happiest;
I will go and come back again."
Turning around, he then vanished,
and from then on, no more news was heard of him.
Later, Āxiǎo took a wife,
and they had a son,
who also died at the age of thirty.
Zhòng raised his orphaned child,
as if his nephew were still alive.
When Zhòng was eighty years old,
his son was over twenty,
and he then divided the property with him.
Xiāngqún had no children of her own.
One day,
she said to Zhòng:
"May I go ahead to drive away the foxes underground?"
She dressed in fine attire, lay on the bed, and passed away.
Zhòng also did not grieve,
and half a year later, he too passed away.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"In all the world, how many are as fraternal as Zhòng!
It is fitting that he did not die and was granted additional years.
The yang line cut off but the yine line continued,
this is all due to the sincere heart that could not bear the death of his brother moving the spirits;
among humans, there is no such principle,
but in heaven, could there be such a fate?
Those who bear sons in the underworld,
wishing to continue the ancestral line,
are likely not few: I fear that those virtuous elder and younger brothers who inherit the extinct property
are unwilling to take in and care for them!"
According to the manuscript version of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
A certain man from Húnán,
could remember his previous three lifetimes.
In his first life, he was a magistrate,
and served as an examiner in the imperial examinations.
A renowned scholar named Xìng Gāntáng was failed,
and died of indignation and resentment.
He went to the underworld and filed a complaint with his examination paper.
Once this complaint was submitted,
thousands upon thousands of those who had died from similar grievances
elected Xìng as their leader,
gathering and dispersing in groups.
The man was summoned,
and they confronted each other for cross-examination.
King Yán asked:
"Since you were evaluating essays,
how could you fail an excellent scholar and promote mediocre ones?"
The man argued:
"There were chief examiners above me,
I was merely carrying out orders."
King Yán immediately issued a warrant,
to summon the chief examiner.
After a long time,
he was brought in.
King Yán then repeated the man's words.
The chief examiner said:
"I was only overseeing the overall process;
even if there were excellent essays,
if the assistant examiners did not recommend them,
how could I have seen them?"
King Yán said:
"You cannot shift blame onto each other,
you are equally derelict in your duties,
and according to the rules, you both deserve flogging."
Just as they were about to administer the punishment,
Xìng was dissatisfied,
and let out a loud cry;
the ghosts on both sides of the hall,
echoed with tens of thousands of voices.
King Yán asked the reason,
and Xìng declared loudly:
"Flogging is too light a punishment,
they must have their eyes gouged out,
as retribution for failing to recognize good writing."
King Yán refused,
but the crowd shouted even more fiercely.
King Yán said:
"It is not that they did not want to select good essays,
but that their judgment was poor."
The crowd then demanded their hearts be cut out.
King Yán had no choice,
and ordered their official robes removed,
and a white blade plunged into their chests.
The two men screamed as their blood poured out.
Only then was the crowd greatly satisfied,
and all said:
"We have been depressed in the underworld,
with no one able to vent this grievance;
now, thanks to Mr. Xìng,
our resentment is finally dispelled."
With a clamor, they dispersed.
After the man had his heart cut out,
he was sent to be reborn as the son of a commoner in Shǎnxī.
When he was over twenty years old,
a great bandit uprising occurred,
and he was captured among the rebels.
A military inspector was sent to suppress the bandits,
and many captives were taken,
including the man.
He still believed he was not a bandit,
hoping he could explain and be released.
When he saw the official in the hall,
who was also over twenty years old,
and looked closely,
it turned out to be Xìng.
He exclaimed in shock:
"I am doomed!"
Soon after, all the captives were released,
but the man was brought last,
and was not allowed to explain himself,
and was ultimately beheaded.
The man went to the underworld and filed a complaint against Xìng.
King Yán did not summon him immediately,
but waited until his official salary was exhausted.
After thirty years,
Xìng finally arrived,
and they confronted each other face to face.
Xìng was punished for treating human life as worthless,
and sentenced to be reborn as an animal.
Upon investigating the man's deeds,
it was found he had once beaten his parents,
and his crime was equally severe.
The man, fearing retribution in the next life,
requested to be reborn as a large animal.
King Yán sentenced him to be reborn as a large dog,
and Xìng as a small dog.
The man was born in the market streets of Shùn Tiānfǔ in the north.
One day,
while lying on the street,
a traveler from the south arrived,
carrying a golden-haired dog,
as large as a wildcat.
The man looked at it,
and it was Xìng.
Thinking it was small and easy to handle,
he bit it.
The small dog bit his throat,
hanging from it like a bell;
the large dog thrashed and howled as it fled.
The people in the market could not separate them,
and soon both died.
They arrived together in the underworld,
arguing with each other.
King Yán said:
"If grievances are repaid with grievances,
when will it ever end?
I will now resolve this for you."
He then sentenced Xìng to be reborn as the man's son-in-law in his next life.
The man was reborn in Qìngyún,
and passed the provincial examination at twenty-eight.
He had a daughter,
gentle, quiet, and beautiful,
and many prominent families sought her hand in marriage.
But the man refused them all.
Once, while passing through a neighboring prefecture,
he happened to witness the education commissioner announcing the results of the examinations,
and the top candidate, surnamed Lǐ—was actually Xìng.
He then invited him to his inn,
and treated him generously.
He asked about his family,
and finding he was still unmarried,
arranged a marriage alliance.
People all thought the man admired talent,
not knowing there was a past cause.
Later, Xìng married the daughter,
and they were very happy together.
However, the son-in-law, relying on his talent, often insulted his father-in-law,
and would not visit his home for years at a time.
The father-in-law tolerated it.
Later, the son-in-law encountered difficulties in middle age,
struggling to advance in the examinations.
The father-in-law used every means to help him,
and he finally succeeded in the scholarly world.
From then on, they were as close as father and son.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"To hold a grudge for three lifetimes over one failure—
how deep can resentment go!
King Yán's mediation was certainly skillful;
but among the thousands in the hall,
with such chaos,
could it be that all the beloved sons-in-law in the world
are those who wailed and clamored in the underworld?"
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Shí Tàipú,
a man from Tàishān,
was fond of exorcism and magical arts.
A Taoist priest met him,
admired his intelligence,
and took him as a disciple.
He opened a case of bamboo slips,
and took out two scrolls—the first on driving away foxes,
the second on driving away ghosts.
He then gave him the second scroll,
saying:
"Devoutly follow this book,
and you will have clothing, food, and beautiful women."
Shí asked his name,
and he said:
"I am Wáng Chìchéng from Yuándì Temple in the northern village of Biànchéng."
He stayed for several days,
and taught him all the secrets.
From then on, Shí became skilled in talismanic arts,
and those seeking his services flocked to his door.
One day,
an old man came,
claiming his surname was Wēng,
and presented lavish gifts of silk and money,
saying his daughter was critically ill from a ghostly affliction,
and he must beg him to come in person.
Shí, hearing the illness was dangerous,
declined and would not accept the gifts,
but went along with him anyway.
After over ten lǐ,
they entered a mountain village,
arriving at his home,
where the corridors and buildings were splendid and fine.
Entering the chamber,
he saw a young girl lying behind a gauze curtain,
a maid using a hook to hold it open.
Looking at her,
she appeared about fourteen or fifteen,
propped up on the bed,
her appearance already withered.
As he drew near to examine her,
she suddenly opened her eyes and said:
"The good doctor has arrived."
The whole family rejoiced,
saying she had not spoken for several days.
Shí then withdrew,
and inquired about the symptoms of the illness.
The old man said:
"During the day, a young man appears,
shares her bed,
but when grasped, he vanishes;
after a short while he returns again,
we suspect he is a ghost."
Shí said:
"If it is a ghost,
exorcising it is not difficult;
but I fear it might be a fox,
then it is beyond what I dare to handle."
The old man said:
"It definitely is not, definitely not."
Shí gave him a talisman,
and that evening stayed at their home.
At midnight,
a young man entered,
his clothes and cap neat and proper.
Shí suspected he was a member of the host's family,
rose and asked him.
He said:
"I am a ghost.
The Wēng family are all foxes.
I happened to fancy their daughter Hóngtíng,
so I lingered here.
A ghost haunting foxes
does no real harm to their hidden virtue;
why must you, sir, sever another's bond and protect them?
The girl's elder sister Chángtíng
is even more stunningly beautiful.
I respectfully leave her untouched,
awaiting a worthy gentleman.
If they promise her to you,
then you may proceed with the cure;
at that time, I will depart of my own accord."
Shí agreed.
That night,
the young man did not return,
and the girl immediately awoke.
At daybreak,
the old man was delighted,
told Shí,
and asked Shí to come examine her.
Shí burned the old talisman,
then sat to diagnose her.
He saw behind an embroidered curtain a young lady,
beautiful as a celestial being,
and knew in his heart it was Chángtíng.
After the examination,
he asked for water to sprinkle the curtain.
The young lady hastily handed him a bowl of water;
in her hurried steps,
her intent stirred and spirit flowed.
At this moment, Shí's
mind was no longer on the ghost at all.
He went out and took leave of the old man,
excusing himself to prepare medicine,
and did not return for several days.
The ghost grew even more unrestrained;
except for Chángtíng,
the daughters-in-law and maidservants
were all seduced and bewitched.
They again sent a servant and horse to fetch Shí,
but Shí feigned illness and did not go.
The next day,
the old man came himself.
Shí deliberately pretended his leg was ailing,
and came out leaning on a cane.
The old man bowed,
asked the reason,
and Shí said:
"This is the hardship of a widower!
The other night a maidservant climbed onto the bed,
stumbled and fell,
spilling the Lady of the Soup's brew and scalding both my feet."
The old man asked:
"Why have you not remarried for so long?"
Shí said:
"I only wish I could find a pure family like yours, sir."
The old man left silently.
Shí hurried to see him off, saying:
"When I recover, I will come myself,
no need to trouble your noble steps."
After several more days,
the old man came again,
and Shí met him limping.
After the old man offered a few words of consolation,
he said:
"I just spoke with my wife;
if you, sir, drive the ghost away,
allowing our whole family to sleep peacefully,
my younger daughter Chángtíng,
now seventeen years old,
we are willing to send her to serve you, sir."
Shí was overjoyed,
and kowtowed to the ground.
Then he said to the old man:
"With such gracious intent,
how dare this sickly body cherish itself further?"
He immediately went out the door,
and they rode off together.
After entering and finishing his inspection of the afflicted,
Shí, fearing they would break the agreement,
asked to make a pledge with the old woman.
The old woman hurried out and said:
"Why does the gentleman doubt us?"
She then took the gold hairpin worn by Chángtíng
and gave it to Shí as a pledge.
Shí bowed to her in the morning fashion,
then gathered all the family members,
and performed exorcisms for all of them.
Only Chángtíng remained deeply hidden without a trace;
so he wrote a talisman to be worn,
