and had someone take it to her.
That night was quiet,
all ghostly shadows vanished,
only Hóngtíng still moaned incessantly;
he applied the ritual water to her,
and her affliction vanished as if lost.
Shí wished to take his leave,
but the old man earnestly urged him to stay.
By evening,
a lavish spread of food and wine was laid out,
and they urged each other to drink most earnestly.
When the water clock struck the second watch,
the host then bade the guest farewell.
Just as Shí was settling onto his pillow,
he heard urgent knocking at the door;
rising to look,
it was Chángtíng slipping in,
her words hurried and flustered,
saying:
"My family intends to take revenge on you with blades,
flee quickly!"
Having spoken,
she turned and left directly.
Shí trembled with fear, his face pale,
and hastily fled over the wall.
In the distance he saw firelight,
ran swiftly towards it,
and found it was villagers on a night hunt.
He was relieved.
He waited for the hunt to end,
then returned with them.
His heart harbored resentment and indignation,
with nowhere to vent it;
he thought of going to Biàn to seek Chìchéng,
but at home he had an old father,
long ill and incapacitated;
day and night he pondered,
unable to decide whether to go or stay.
One day,
two carriages arrived at the gate.
It was the old man and woman sending Chángtíng over.
They said to Shí:
"When you returned that night,
why didn't you come back to discuss things?"
When Shí saw Chángtíng,
all his resentment vanished,
so he also kept silent and didn't bring it up.
The old woman urged the two to bow in the courtyard, and once finished,
Shí prepared to set out a feast.
They declined, saying:
"I am not an idle person;
I cannot sit and enjoy fine delicacies.
Our old man is muddle-headed;
if there is any negligence,
if you, sir, would think of this old woman for Chángtíng's sake,
it would be a great fortune."
They boarded the carriage and left.
It turned out that the plot to kill the son-in-law
was unknown to the old woman;
and when they chased after him but failed to catch him and returned,
the old woman only then learned of it.
She was quite displeased,
and quarreled with the old man daily.
Chángtíng also wept and refused to eat.
The old woman forced herself to send the girl here;
it was not the old man's wish.
After Chángtíng entered the household,
upon questioning her,
Shí learned the reason.
After two or three months,
the old man's family came to take the girl back for a visit.
Shí reckoned she would not return,
and forbade it.
From this time on, the girl wept constantly.
Over a year later,
she gave birth to a son,
named Huì'ér,
and they hired a wet nurse to feed him.
However, the child was prone to crying,
and at night he always had to return to his mother.
One day,
the old man's family again sent a carriage,
saying the old woman missed her daughter terribly.
Chángtíng grew even more sorrowful,
and Shí could not bear to keep her any longer.
She wanted to take the child with her,
but Shí would not allow it,
so Chángtíng went back alone.
At parting,
they set one month as the time limit,
but then half a year passed without any news.
He sent someone to inquire,
only to find the house they had rented long empty.
After another two years or more,
all hope was lost;
and the child cried all night long,
cutting Shí's heart to pieces.
Then Shí's father fell ill and died,
doubling his grief;
as a result, he became ill and exhausted,
lingering on his mourning mat,
unable to receive condolences from guests and friends.
Just as he was in a daze,
he suddenly heard a woman weeping as she entered.
Looking,
it was Chángtíng in mourning clothes.
Shí was overwhelmed with sorrow,
and with one burst of grief, he fainted.
The maids cried out in alarm,
and only then did the girl stop weeping.
She tended to him for a long time,
and he gradually revived.
Suspecting he was already dead,
he thought they were reunited in the underworld.
The girl said:
"No.
I, your concubine, am unfilial;
I could not win my strict father's heart.
For three years I was prevented from returning,
truly I have failed in my duty.
Just now, our family passed by here on their way from Hǎidōng,
and I learned of my father-in-law's death.
I obeyed my strict father's command and severed my feelings as wife and mother,
but I dared not follow a disordered command and neglect the rites between father-in-law and daughter-in-law.
When I came,
my mother knew but my father did not."
As she spoke,
the child threw himself into her arms.
After speaking,
she finally caressed him,
and wept, saying:
"I have a father,
but my child has no mother!"
The child also wailed loudly,
and everyone in the room wept.
The girl rose,
managed the household affairs,
and prepared clean and ample sacrificial offerings before the coffin,
which greatly comforted Shí.
But having been ill for a long time,
he could not rise urgently.
The girl then asked Shí's cousin to receive the mourning guests.
After the funeral was concluded,
Shí was finally able to rise with a cane,
and together they planned the burial and mourning rites.
After the burial,
the girl wished to bid farewell and return,
to receive her father's reproach for disobeying him.
Her husband held her back and the child cried,
so she restrained herself and stayed.
Not long after,
someone came to report her mother's illness,
and she said to Shí:
"I came for your father's sake;
will you not let me go for my mother's sake?"
Shí agreed.
The girl had the wet nurse take the child elsewhere,
and left in tears.
After she left,
she did not return for several years.
Shí and his son gradually forgot her.
One day,
at dawn as he opened the door,
Chángtíng drifted in.
Shí was just about to ask in astonishment,
when the girl sat sorrowfully on the bed,
sighed, and said:
"Raised in the women's quarters,
I considered one li a great distance;
now I have traveled a thousand li in a day and a night—
it was nearly the death of me!"
When he questioned her closely,
she wanted to speak but stopped.
He pressed her repeatedly,
and she wept, saying:
"Now that I tell you,
I fear what saddens me
will please you.
In recent years we moved to the Shānxī border,
renting a residence from a gentry named Zhào.
Host and guest became very close,
and he married Hóngtíng to the gentleman's son.
The young master was often wayward and dissolute,
causing much discord in the family.
My sister returned and told our father;
Father kept her there,
not letting her return for half a year.
The young master grew resentful and angry,
and from somewhere hired a wicked man,
who dispatched divine chains and shackles
to bind our old father and take him away.
The whole household was terrified,
and in an instant, everyone scattered."
Hearing this,
Shí could not help but laugh.
The girl angrily said:
"Though he is unkind,
he is my father.
I have been your wife for several years,
with only mutual affection and no mutual blame.
Now our family is ruined and our people lost,
a hundred mouths scattered and displaced.
could you not at least mourn for my sake?
Hearing this, you dance with joy,
without a single word of comfort—
how heartless!"
She flicked her sleeves and left.
Shí chased after her to apologize,
but she was already gone.
Regretful and remorseful,
he thought the break was final.
After two or three days,
the old woman and the girl both came.
Shí was delighted and greeted them.
Mother and daughter both knelt.
Startled, he asked them,
and both mother and daughter wept.
The girl said:
"I left in anger,
and now, unable to stand firm on my own,
I come again to seek help from others—
what face do I have left!"
Shí said:
"Yue is indeed not human;
your mother's kindness,
and your affection,
I shall never forget.
However, to take pleasure upon hearing of misfortune
is also human nature.
Why can you not endure it for a moment?"
The woman said:
"Just now on the road I encountered Mother,
and only then learned that the one who captured my father
is actually your master."
Shí said:
"If that is indeed the case,
it is also very easy.
However, if the old man does not return,
then you and your father will be separated;
I fear that if the old man returns,
then your husband will weep and your child will grieve."
The old woman swore to prove her sincerity,
and the woman also vowed to repay him.
Shí then immediately packed his belongings and went to Biàn.
He inquired and arrived at the Yuándì Temple,
where Chìchéng had returned not long ago.
He entered and paid his respects,
and [Chìchéng] asked:
"What brings you here?"
Shí saw an old fox in the kitchen,
with a hole pierced through its front leg and tied up.
He laughed and said:
"Your disciple has come
for the sake of this old monster."
Chìchéng questioned him,
and he said:
"This is my father-in-law."
He then told him the truth.
The Daoist priest said he was cunning and deceitful,
and was unwilling to release him lightly.
After Shí insisted on his request,
he finally agreed.
Shí then fully described his deceitfulness.
The fox, hearing this,
hid its body in the stove,
appearing ashamed.
The Daoist priest laughed and said:
"Its sense of shame and aversion
is not yet completely lost."
Shí stood up,
led it out,
and cut the rope with a knife, pulling it out.
The fox was in extreme pain,
its teeth grinding audibly.
Shí did not pull it out quickly,
but did so in a halting manner,
and asked with a laugh:
"Does it pain you, old man?
Should I not pull it out?"
The fox's eyes flashed,
seeming to show a look of resentment.
Once released,
it wagged its tail and left the temple.
Shí bid farewell and returned.
Three days earlier,
someone had already brought news of the old man,
the old woman had gone ahead,
leaving the woman to wait for Shí.
When Shí arrived,
the woman came to meet him and knelt.
Shí helped her up and said:
"If you do not forget the affection between husband and wife,
that is gratitude enough."
The woman said:
"Now we have moved back to our old residence;
the village houses are nearby,
so news need not be obstructed.
I wish to return home for a visit,
and will be back in three days.
Do you believe me?"
He said:
"Our child was born without a mother,
yet did not die prematurely.
I have lived alone day after day,
and have grown accustomed to it.
Now I am not like that young master Zhào,
but instead repay kindness with virtue.
I have done all I can for you.
If you do not return,
it would be you who is ungrateful.
Although the distance is short,
I will certainly not inquire further.
Why would I not believe you?"
The woman left the next day,
and returned after two days.
He asked:
"Why so quickly?"
She said:
"Father said that since you teased him in Biàn,
he cannot forget it,
and kept talking about it incessantly;
I did not wish to hear it again,
so I came back early."
From then on, their interactions in the inner chambers were uninterrupted,
but between father-in-law and son-in-law, there was still no exchange of condolences or congratulations.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"The fox's feelings are fickle,
and its deceitfulness is extreme.
The matter of breaking off the engagement
followed the same pattern with both daughters,
showing how cunning it was.
However, to force the marriage upon them
was to plant the seeds of regret from the very beginning.
Moreover, since the son-in-law loved the daughter and saved her father,
he should have let go of past grievances and treated him with benevolence;
yet he again teased and played with him in a moment of crisis.
No wonder the fox never forgot it for the rest of its life!
In the world, when ice and jade are incompatible,
it is often like this."
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Xí Fāngpíng
was from Dōng'ān.
His father's name was Lián,
and he was honest and simple-minded.
Because he had a feud with a wealthy family named Yáng in the village,
Yáng died first.
Several years later,
Lián fell critically ill,
and said to people:
"That Yáng is now bribing underworld officials to torture me."
Soon, his body became red and swollen,
and he screamed and died.
Xí was grief-stricken and refused to eat,
saying:
"My father was simple and inarticulate;
now he is being bullied by a powerful ghost.
I will go to the underworld
to seek justice on his behalf."
From then on, he spoke no more,
sometimes sitting, sometimes standing,
appearing like an idiot,
for his soul had already left his body.
Xí felt that as soon as he left the door,
he did not know where to go,
but seeing travelers on the road,
he asked for the city.
After a short while,
he entered the city.
His father had already been imprisoned.
Arriving at the prison gate,
he saw from afar his father lying under the eaves,
looking quite wretched.
Raising his eyes and seeing his son,
tears streamed down his face,
and he said:
"The prison guards all accepted bribes and instructions,
beating and torturing him day and night,
to the point where his shins and thighs were severely broken!"
Xí was furious,
cursing the prison guards loudly:
"If my father is guilty,
there are laws to judge him,
how can you dead demons decide his fate!"
He then left,
took up a brush, and wrote a petition.
Just as the City God was holding his morning court,
Xí shouted his grievance and submitted it.
Yáng was afraid,
bribed both inside and outside,
and only then did he come out to face the trial.
The City God, claiming there was no evidence for the accusations,
was rather unfair to Xí.
Xí, with his indignation still unvented,
walked over a hundred li in the underworld,
reached the prefecture,
and reported the private misconduct of the officials to
the Prefectural Judge.
After a delay of half a month,
he finally got a hearing.
The Prefectural Judge had Xí beaten,
and still ordered the City God to reinvestigate the case.
Xí returned to the county,
suffered all kinds of shackles and torture,
his bitter grievance unable to find relief.
The City God, fearing he would sue again,
sent officers to escort him home.
The officers left him at his gate and departed.
Xí refused to enter,
instead fled to the Underworld Court,
to accuse the prefectural and county officials of their cruelty and corruption.
The King of the Underworld immediately summoned them for a confrontation.
The two officials secretly sent their confidants to negotiate with Xí,
offering a thousand taels of gold.
Xí would not listen.
After a few days,
the innkeeper warned him:
"You are too stubborn,
the officials seek peace but you obstinately refuse.
Now I hear they have each sent letters ahead to the King,
I fear things are in peril."
Xí, considering this just roadside talk,
did not fully believe it.
Soon a man in black summoned him inside.
Ascending the hall,
he saw the King of the Underworld wore an angry expression,
not allowing him to speak,
and ordered him beaten twenty times.
Xí asked sternly:
"What crime have I committed?"
The King of the Underworld ignored him as if he hadn't heard.
As Xí was being beaten,
he shouted:
"I deserve this beating,
who told me I had no money!"
The King of the Underworld grew even angrier,
and ordered him placed on the fire bed.
Two demons dragged Xí down,
and he saw an iron bed on the eastern steps,
with a blazing fire beneath it,
the bed's surface glowing red-hot.
The demons stripped Xí's clothes,
lifted him and placed him on it,
turning and pressing him over and over.
The pain was extreme,
his flesh and bones charred black,
yet he could not die from the agony.
After about an hour,
a demon said:
"Enough."
They then helped him up,
urged him to get off the bed and dress,
and he was fortunate to still be able to walk, though limping.
Returning to the hall,
the King of the Underworld asked:
"Do you dare sue again?"
Xí said:
"My great grievance remains unredressed,
my heart will not rest until it is.
To say I will not sue
would be to deceive Your Majesty.
I will sue!"
The King said:
"What will you sue about?"
Xí said:
"I will speak of everything
that I have suffered."
The King of the Underworld grew angry again,
and ordered his body sawn apart.
Two demons dragged him away,
and he saw a standing post about eight or nine feet tall,
with two wooden boards,
placed face-up beneath it,
smeared with clotted blood above and below.
Just as he was about to be bound,
suddenly a great shout came from the hall:
"Xí Mǒu!"
The two demons immediately brought him back.
The King of the Underworld asked again:
"Do you still dare to sue?"
He answered:
"I will sue!"
The King of the Underworld ordered them to take him away and saw him quickly.
Once below,
the demons clamped Xí between the two boards,
and bound him to the post.
As the saw began to descend,
he felt the top of his skull gradually splitting,
the pain unbearable,
yet he endured it and did not cry out.
He heard a demon say:
"What a stout fellow this man is!"
The saw rumbled down to below his chest.
Then he heard another demon say:
"This man is greatly filial and innocent,
let the saw deviate slightly,
do not damage his heart."
Then he felt the saw blade curve and descend,
the pain doubling in intensity.
In a moment,
half his body was split apart.
The boards were loosened,
and both halves of his body fell.
A demon went up to the hall and reported loudly.
A call came from the hall,
ordering him to come see them with his body whole.
The two demons then pushed the halves together to reunite them,
and dragged him to make him walk.
Xí felt the line of the saw cut,
the pain threatening to split him open again,
and after half a step he stumbled and fell.
One demon took a silk belt from his waist and gave it to him,
saying:
"I give you this to reward your filial piety."
Xí took it and tied it around himself,
and his body suddenly felt strong and healthy,
with no pain at all.
He then ascended the hall and prostrated himself.
The King of the Underworld asked again as before;
Xí, fearing he would suffer cruel torture again,
answered:
"I will not sue."
The King of the Underworld immediately ordered him sent back to the world of the living.
The bailiffs led him out the north gate,
pointed out the way back,
and turned to leave.
Xí thought that the darkness of the underworld was even worse than that of the world of the living,
but there was no way to bring his case to the attention of the Emperor of Heaven.
It was said in the world that the Er Láng of Guànkǒu was a meritorious relative of the Emperor,
and that this deity was intelligent and upright;
if he were to appeal to him, there should be a miraculous response.
Secretly glad that the two bailiffs had left,
he turned and headed south.
While running,
two men caught up with him,
saying:
"The King suspected you would not return,
and now it is indeed so."
They dragged him back to see the King of the Underworld.
Xí thought that the King of the Underworld would be even more furious,
and the calamity would certainly be more severe;
but the King showed no stern expression at all,
and said to Xí:
"Your intention is truly filial.
But as for your father's grievance,
I have already avenged it for you.
He has now been reborn into a wealthy and noble family;
what need is there for you to cry out?
Now I will send you back,
and grant you a fortune of a thousand in gold and a lifespan of a hundred years—
is this enough to satisfy your wishes?"
He then recorded it in the register,
stamped it with a large seal,
and had Xí look at it himself.
Xí thanked him and descended.
The ghosts went out with him,
and upon reaching the road,
drove him forward, cursing:
"Treacherous and cunning thief!
Repeatedly turning back and forth,
you make us run about until we're nearly dead!
If you offend again,
we'll catch you and put you into the great mill,
and grind you up finely!"
Xí glared and shouted at them:
"What are you ghosts doing!
My nature can endure the saw and the knife,
but not flogging and beating.
Let's go back to see the King;
if the King now orders me to return on my own,
what need is there for you to trouble yourselves to escort me?"
He then turned and ran back.
The two ghosts were afraid,
and gently persuaded him to return.
Xí deliberately walked slowly and haltingly,
taking a few steps,
then resting by the roadside.
The ghosts, filled with anger, dared not speak again.
After about half a day,
they reached a village,
where one door was half-open;
the ghosts led him in and sat with him;
Xí then sat on the threshold.
The two ghosts, taking advantage of his unpreparedness,
pushed him through the door.
When he recovered from the shock and looked at himself,
he had already been reborn as an infant.
Furious, he cried and refused to nurse,
and died after three days.
His soul, wavering and unsteady, still remembered Guànkǒu,
and after running for several dozen lǐ,
he suddenly saw a feather canopy approaching,
with banners and halberds blocking the road.
He tried to cross the road to avoid it,
but thereby trespassed into the imperial procession,
and was seized by the outriders,
who bound him and brought him before the carriage.
Looking up, he saw a young man in the carriage,
of majestic and imposing appearance.
He asked Xí:
"Who are you?"
Xí's resentment and indignation had nowhere to vent,
and he thought that this must be a high official,
who might be able to wield authority,
so he recounted in detail his suffering and pain.
The man in the carriage ordered his bonds to be released,
and had him follow the carriage.
Soon they arrived at a place,
where over ten officials
greeted and bowed by the roadside;
the man in the carriage exchanged greetings with each of them.
Then, pointing to Xí, he said to one official:
"This is a man from the world below,
who was just on his way to lodge a complaint;
you should immediately adjudicate his case for him."
Xí inquired of the attendants,
and only then learned that the man in the carriage was the Ninth Prince, a son of the Emperor of Heaven,
and the one he had instructed was Er Láng.
Xí looked at Er Láng:
he was tall and had a full beard,
unlike what was said in the world.
After the Ninth Prince had left,
Xí followed Er Láng to an official residence,
where his father and the man named Yáng, along with the yamen bailiffs, were all present.
After a short while,
prisoners emerged from a caged cart—
they were the King of the Underworld, the prefectural judge, and the city god.
They were cross-examined in the hall,
and everything Xí said was found to be true.
The three officials trembled with fear,
looking like crouching mice.
Er Láng took up a brush and immediately pronounced judgment;
in a moment,
the judgment was passed down,
and all those involved in the case were ordered to look at it.
The judgment read:
"It is found that the King of the Underworld: holding the title of king,
he receives the grace of the emperor.
He should have been pure and upright to set an example for his officials,
and should not have been corrupt to invite public censure.
Yet with his ornate chariots and ceremonial halberds,
he merely flaunts the dignity of his rank;
as cruel as a wolf and as greedy as a sheep,
he has indeed tarnished the integrity of a minister.
The axe strikes the chisel,
the chisel enters the wood,
leaving the skin and bones of women and children utterly hollow;
the whale swallows the fish,
the fish eats the shrimp,
pitiable are the tiny lives of ants and insects.
We should scoop up the waters of the Western River
to cleanse your intestines;
then heat the bed of the Eastern Wall,
and invite you to enter the jar.
The City God and the Prefectural Judge,
as officials who are the parents of the common people,
are entrusted with the care of the emperor's flock.
Although their positions are lowly,
those who are diligent do not refuse to bow;
even if pressured by higher officials,
those with integrity should stand firm.
Yet they raise their hawk-like hands high and low,
showing no concern for the poverty of the people;
and they flaunt their cunning and deceitful tricks,
not even minding that the ghosts are emaciated.
They accept bribes and pervert the law,
truly having human faces but the hearts of beasts!
They should have their marrow scraped and their hair plucked,
and be temporarily sentenced to death in the underworld;
they should be skinned and their hides changed,
and then reborn as humans.
As for the underlings: since they are among the ghostly ranks,
they are no longer human.
They should only cultivate virtue in the public office,
so as to regain their human form in the next life;
why stir up waves in the sea of suffering,
adding to the boundless sins?
Arrogant and domineering,
their dog-like faces are as cold as the frost of June;
rampaging and shouting,
their tiger-like authority blocks the roads of the nine thoroughfares.
They wield their tyranny in the underworld,
all knowing that the prison guards are supreme;
aiding cruel and oppressive officials,
all fear them as butchers.
They should be taken to the execution ground,
where their limbs are to be chopped off;
and then thrown into the boiling cauldron,
to have their sinews and bones fished out.
As for Mr. Yáng: wealthy but unkind,
cunning and deceitful.
His golden light covers the earth,
causing the halls of Yánluó to be filled with gloom;
the stench of his copper coins fills the sky,
making the city of the dead devoid of sunlight and moonlight.
The lingering stench of his wealth can still command ghosts,
and his great power can even reach the gods.
The property of the Yáng family should be confiscated,
to repay the filial piety of Xí Shēng.
He is to be taken to Dōngyuè for execution."
Then he said to Xí Lián:
"In consideration of your son's filial piety and righteousness,
and your own good and gentle nature,
you are granted an additional thirty-six years of life."
He then sent two men to escort them back to their hometown.
Xí copied the judgment,
and on the way, father and son read it together.
When they arrived home,
Xí revived first;
he ordered his family to open the coffin to see his father,
whose corpse was still cold as ice.
They waited all day,
and gradually he warmed and came back to life.
When they looked for the copied judgment,
it was already gone.
From then on,
their family fortunes grew daily,
and within three years, fertile fields spread everywhere;
while the descendants of the Yáng family declined,
their mansions and lands
all became the property of Xí.
Some villagers who bought Yáng's land
dreamed at night of a deity scolding them:
"This is the property of the Xí family,
how dare you take it!"
At first, they did not believe it;
but when they planted crops,
they harvested nothing all year,
so they sold the land back to Xí.
Xí's father lived to over ninety before passing away.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"Everyone speaks of the Pure Land,
but they do not know that life and death are separated by worlds,
and thoughts and consciousness are all confused;
they do not even know where they come from,
let alone where they go;
and how much more so for those who die and die again,
or are born and reborn?
With unwavering loyalty and filial piety,
unchanged through countless calamities,
how extraordinary is Xí Shēng,
how great he is!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Yǔ Shèn,
courtesy name Jǐn'ān,
was from an old family in Shùntiān.
He went to the capital for the examinations,
and stayed in the suburbs,
where he often saw a young man across the street,
as handsome as a jewel,
and took a liking to him.
Gradually, he approached and spoke with him,
finding him exceptionally refined and elegant.
Greatly pleased,
he took him by the arm and invited him to his lodging,
where they feasted together.
When asked his name,
the young man said he was from Jīnlíng,
surnamed Yǔ, named Shìchén,
courtesy name Xúnjiǔ.
The young master, hearing they shared the same surname,
felt even closer to him,
and so they swore brotherhood;
the young man then used his given name, omitting his courtesy name, as Chén.
The next day,
Yǔ Shèn visited his home,
where the study was clean and bright;
but the courtyard was desolate,
with no servants in sight.
He led the young master inside,
and called his younger sister to come out and greet him.
She was about thirteen or fourteen,
with skin as clear as crystal,
whiter than powdered jade.
After a while,
she brought tea for the guest,
and there were no maids or elderly women in the house either.
The young master found this strange,
and after a few words, he left.
From then on, they were as close as brothers.
Xúnjiǔ came to the lodging every day,
and when asked to stay overnight,
he would decline, saying his young sister had no one to keep her company.
The young master said:
"My brother, you reside a thousand miles away,
with no servant to answer the door,
and your sister is delicate and frail.
How will you make a living?
I think it would be better for you to come with me;
I have a small house where we can live together.
What do you say?"
Xúnjiǔ was delighted
and agreed to go after the examination.
When the exam was over,
Xúnjiǔ invited the young master to his home,
saying:
"The moonlight on Mid-Autumn Festival is as bright as day.
My younger sister, Sùqiū,
has prepared some vegetables and wine.
Do not disappoint her."
He then pulled him inside.
Sùqiū came out,
exchanged a few polite words,
and then went into an inner room,
lowering the curtain to prepare the meal.
After a short while,
she came out herself to serve the food.
The young master stood up and said:
"For my sister to be bustling about like this—
how can I bear it in good conscience?"
Sùqiū smiled and went back inside.
A moment later,
the curtain was lifted,
and a maid in black clothes came out carrying a wine pot;
then an old woman brought in a tray with a cooked fish.
The young master exclaimed in surprise:
"Where did these people come from?
Why didn't they take care of things earlier,
and trouble my sister instead?"
Xúnjiǔ smiled faintly and said:
"Sùqiū is up to her tricks again."
Just then, a giggling sound was heard from behind the curtain,
but the young master did not understand what was going on.
After the banquet ended,
the maid and the old woman cleared away the dishes.
The young master happened to cough,
and accidentally spat on the maid's clothes;
the maid immediately fell over with the spittle,
breaking the bowl and spilling the food.
Looking at the maid,
she turned out to be a paper-cut figure,
only about four inches tall.
Xúnjiǔ laughed heartily,
and Sùqiū came out smiling,
picked it up, and left.
Soon after, the maid reappeared,
bustling about as before.
The young master was greatly astonished.
Xúnjiǔ said:
"This is just a little trick my sister learned in her childhood
when she used to divine with the goddess Zǐgū."
The young master then asked:
"Both you and your sister are already grown up.
Why haven't you married yet?"
He replied:
"Our parents have passed away,
and we have no fixed place to stay,
so we have delayed it."
They then agreed on a date for the journey,
sold the house,
and, taking his sister, went west with the young master.
After they returned,
the young master cleared out a house for them to live in;
he also sent a maid to serve them.
The young master's wife,
who was the niece of Vice-Minister Hán,
also loved Sùqiū dearly,
and they ate and drank together.
The young master and Xúnjiǔ were the same.
Moreover, Xúnjiǔ was extremely intelligent,
able to read ten lines at a glance,
and when he wrote an essay,
even seasoned scholars could not match him.
The young master urged him to take the child examination.
Xúnjiǔ said:
"I have been studying for this profession
merely to share your hardships.
I know my own fortune is thin,
and I am not suited for an official career;
moreover, once one enters this path,
one cannot help but worry about success and failure,
so I have not pursued it."
After three years,
the young master failed the examination again.
Xúnjiǔ was deeply distressed,
and said with determination:
"To have one's name on the list—
how can it be so difficult!
At first, I did not want to be troubled by success or failure,
so I preferred to remain obscure.
But now, seeing that my elder brother cannot achieve his aspirations,
I cannot help but feel agitated.
Though I am a nineteen-year-old candidate,
I will now strive like a galloping steed."
The young master was pleased,
and when the examination period arrived, he sent him into the examination hall.
Xúnjiǔ placed first in the county, prefecture, and circuit examinations.
He then studied even harder with the young master.
The following year, in the provincial examination,
they both came first in the prefecture and county.
Xúnjiǔ's fame spread far and wide,
and people from near and far vied to marry him,
but Xúnjiǔ refused them all.
The young master urged him strongly,
and he used the upcoming examination as an excuse to delay.
Not long after,
when the examination was over,
his admirers rushed to copy his essays,
praising and circulating them;
Xúnjiǔ himself felt that he did not deserve to be second to anyone.
When the results were posted,
both brothers had failed.
At the time, they were drinking together,
and the young master was still forcing himself to joke;
but Xúnjiǔ turned pale,
dropped his wine cup,
and collapsed under the table.
They helped him onto the bed,
but his condition was already critical.
The young master hurriedly called Sùqiū over.
Xúnjiǔ opened his eyes and said to the young master:
"Although our bond is as close as brothers,
we are not actually of the same clan.
I know that my name is already on the register of the dead.
I have no way to repay your kindness,
but Sùqiū is now grown up.
Since she has received the care of your wife,
you may take her as a concubine."
The young master said sternly:
"This is truly the confused command of my brother!
Do you think I am a beast in human form?"
Xúnjiǔ wept.
The young master immediately spent a large sum to buy a fine coffin.
Xúnjiǔ had it carried in,
and, mustering his strength, he entered it,
instructing his sister:
"After I die,
close the coffin immediately,
and do not let anyone open it to look."
The young master still wanted to say something,
but Xúnjiǔ had already closed his eyes.
The young master was grief-stricken,
as if he had lost a brother.
However, he was secretly puzzled by the strange instruction,
and when Sùqiū went out,
he opened the coffin to look.
Inside, the robe and clothes lay like an empty shell;
when he lifted them,
he found a silverfish a foot long,
lying stiff inside.
While he was still astonished,
Sùqiū hurried in,
and said sadly:
"What barrier is there between brothers?
The reason for this
was not to avoid you;
I was only afraid that if word spread,
I would not be able to stay here long either."
The young master said:
"Rituals are established based on feelings.
Where true feelings exist,
what difference does it make if we are of different clans?
Do you not know my heart, sister?
Even my wife will not breathe a word of this,
so please do not worry."
He then quickly chose an auspicious date
and buried Xúnjiǔ with full honors.
In the beginning,
the young master wished to arrange a marriage for Sùqiū with a prominent family,
but Xúnjiǔ was unwilling.
After his death,
the young master discussed the matter with Sùqiū,
but she did not respond.
The young master said:
"My sister is already twenty years old.
To remain unmarried at such an age—
what will people say of me?"
She replied:
"If that is the case,
I will follow my brother's command.
However, I consider myself lacking in fortune and appearance,
and do not wish to enter the gates of nobility.
A poor scholar would suffice."
The young master said:
"Very well."
Within a few days,
matchmakers came one after another,
but in the end, none were suitable.
Earlier,
the young master's brother-in-law, Hán Quán, had come to offer condolences,
and upon catching a glimpse of Sùqiū,
he was captivated,
desiring to purchase her as a concubine.
He consulted his sister,
who urgently warned him not to speak of it,
fearing the young master would find out.
After Hán left,
he could not let go of the matter,
and sent a matchmaker to hint at his intentions to the young master,
promising to buy him a pass in the provincial examination.
Upon hearing this,
the young master flew into a rage and cursed,
driving the messenger out with blows.
From then on, their association ceased.
It happened that a certain Jiǎ, grandson of a former minister,
was about to marry when his bride suddenly died,
and he also sent a matchmaker.
His mansion was grand and imposing,
and the young master was familiar with it,
but he wished to meet the man in person.
Thus, he arranged with the matchmaker
for Jiǎ to pay a visit.
When the day arrived,
a curtain was hung inside,
and Sùqiū was told to observe him herself.
When Jiǎ arrived,
his furs, horses, and attendants
dazzled the neighborhood;
he was also elegant and refined, like a young maiden.
The young master was greatly pleased,
and all who saw him praised his appearance,
but Sùqiū was not at all happy.
The young master paid no heed,
and eventually agreed to the match,
preparing a lavish dowry
at great expense.
Sùqiū firmly tried to stop him,
asking only for an elderly maidservant
to attend to her needs.
But the young master would not listen,
and in the end, gave her a generous dowry.
After her marriage,
the couple was deeply affectionate.
However, her brother and sister-in-law often missed her,
and she would return to visit them once a month.
Each time she came,
she would bring several items of jewelry and embroidery from her dowry
and hand them to her sister-in-law for safekeeping.
Her sister-in-law did not understand her intention,
but humored her nonetheless.
Jiǎ had lost his father young,
and his widowed mother doted on him excessively.
He associated with unsavory characters,
who gradually lured him into debauchery and gambling.
The family heirlooms—paintings, calligraphy, bronzes, and antiques—
were all sold to pay his gambling debts.
Hán Quán, who had some connection with him,
invited him for a drink and secretly broached the subject,
offering to exchange two concubines and five hundred taels of gold for Sùqiū.
At first, Jiǎ refused;
but Hán persisted,
and Jiǎ began to waver,
though he feared the young master would not accept it.
Hán said:
"I am a close relative of his,
and she is not even of his own lineage.
Once the matter is settled,
what can he do about it?
If anything goes wrong,
I will take full responsibility.
With my father around,
why fear a single Yǔ Jǐn'ān?"
He then dressed up two concubines and brought them out to serve wine,
saying:
"If our agreement holds,
these will be members of your household."
Jiǎ was swayed
and set a date before departing.
When the day arrived,
fearing Hán might deceive him,
he waited by the roadside at night.
Sure enough, a sedan chair arrived.
He lifted the curtain and verified it was indeed Sùqiū,
then led the way
and temporarily placed her in a study.
Hán's servant handed over the five hundred taels of gold, completing the transaction.
Jiǎ rushed inside
and deceitfully told Sùqiū,
saying:
"Your brother has suddenly fallen ill and is calling for you."
Sùqiū had no time to dress properly
and hastily went out.
Once the sedan chair set off,
they lost their way in the darkness,
traveling a great distance
without reaching their destination.
Suddenly, they saw two giant torches approaching.
Secretly delighted, they thought they could ask for directions.
Before long,
they drew near,
only to realize the "torches" were the eyes of a giant serpent.
Terrified,
the men and horses scattered in panic,
abandoning the sedan chair by the roadside.
At dawn, they regrouped
and found only an empty sedan chair.
Assuming she must have been devoured by the serpent,
they returned to report to their master,
utterly dejected.
A few days later,
the young master sent someone to visit his sister,
only to discover she had been tricked away by villains.
At first, he did not suspect her husband's treachery.
He brought the maidservant back
and questioned her in detail about the circumstances,
gradually uncovering the truth.
Furious,
he filed complaints throughout the prefecture and county.
Jiǎ grew fearful
and sought help from Hán.
Hán, having lost both his gold and concubines,
was already filled with regret and frustration,
and refused to assist him.
Jiǎ, foolish and at a loss,
received summons from various authorities,
but managed to avoid appearing by bribing them.
After over a month,
his gold, pearls, clothing, and ornaments
were all pawned or sold.
The young master pressed the case urgently with the provincial authorities,
and county officials, under strict orders,
left Jiǎ with no place to hide.
He finally appeared
and confessed the entire truth in court.
A warrant was issued to summon Hán for confrontation.
Hán, afraid,
told his father everything.
His father, then retired from office,
was enraged by his unlawful conduct
and handed him over to the authorities.
When brought before the officials,
Hán mentioned the incident with the serpent,
but everyone thought his story was fabricated.
His servants were tortured extensively,
and Jiǎ was also repeatedly beaten.
Fortunately, his mother sold off land and property daily,
bribing officials at all levels to intervene,
and the punishment was lightened, sparing his life.
However, Hán's servant had already died in prison.
Hán, long imprisoned,
offered to help Jiǎ bribe the young master with a thousand taels of gold,
pleading for the lawsuit to be dropped.
The young master refused.
Jiǎ's mother then offered two additional concubines,
asking only to leave the case unresolved for the time being,
pending further investigation.
Meanwhile, the young master's wife, acting on her aunt's behalf,
pleaded with him day and night to relent.
Finally, the young master agreed.
Jiǎ's family was extremely poor,
and they put their house up for sale to raise the money,
but could not find a buyer quickly.
They sent the concubines first,
begging for an extension.
After several days had passed,
the young master was sitting in his study one night
when Sùqiū entered suddenly with an old woman.
The young master asked in alarm,
"Are you all right, sister?"
She said with a smile,
"The python transformation was just a little trick of mine.
That night I slipped into the home of a scholar
and stayed with his mother.
He said he knew you, brother,
and he is now outside the gate.
Please invite him in."
The young master hurried out to welcome him,
and by lamplight saw that it was none other
than Zhōu Shēng,
a well-known scholar from Wǎnpíng,
with whom he had always been on good terms.
They entered the study arm in arm
and conversed with the utmost cordiality.
After talking for a long time,
the young master learned the whole story.
Earlier, Sùqiū had knocked on Zhōu's door at daybreak;
his mother let her in
and, upon questioning,
learned she was the young master's sister.
She wanted to send word immediately,
but Sùqiū stopped her
and stayed with the mother instead.
She was intelligent and understanding,
and the mother grew fond of her.
Since her son was unmarried,
the mother secretly had Sùqiū in mind
and hinted at it.
Sùqiū declined on the grounds that she had not received her brother's permission.
Zhōu Shēng, too, because of his friendship with the young master,
was unwilling to enter into a match without a proper go-between,
but he kept making inquiries.
When he learned that the lawsuit had been settled through mediation,
Sùqiū told the mother she wished to return home.
The mother sent Zhōu Shēng with an old woman to escort her
and instructed the old woman to act as matchmaker.
The young master had already been secretly considering the matter,
since Sùqiū had stayed so long at Zhōu's house,
but had not spoken of it.
Hearing the old woman's proposal,
he was delighted
and immediately arranged the match with Zhōu Shēng in person.
Earlier, when Sùqiū returned at night,
she had intended to wait until the young master received the money before revealing herself.
The young master would not hear of it,
saying,
"I was angry before and had no way to vent it,
so I demanded money just to ruin them.
Now that I have my sister back,
what could ten thousand taels of gold possibly replace?"
He immediately sent word to both families
and dropped the matter at once.
Considering that Zhōu's family was not well-off
and the journey was long,
making the wedding procession difficult,
he had Zhōu's mother brought over
to live in Xúnjiǔ's former residence.
Zhōu Shēng also prepared betrothal gifts, music, and drums,
and the wedding was duly celebrated.
One day, the sister-in-law teased Sùqiū,
"Now that you have a new husband,
do you still remember the love from your pillow and mat in earlier years?"
Sùqiū smiled
and, turning to her maid, asked,
"Do you remember?"
The sister-in-law did not understand
and pressed for an explanation.
It turned out that for three years in the marriage bed,
everything had been done by the maid.
Every night, Sùqiū would paint the maid's eyebrows with a brush,
send her off,
and then sit alone by the candle,
and her husband never noticed the difference.
The sister-in-law found this even more astonishing
and asked to learn the art,
but Sùqiū only smiled and said nothing.
The following year, during the provincial examinations,
Zhōu Shēng planned to go with the young master.
Sùqiū said,
"There's no need."
But the young master insisted and dragged him along.
In that examination,
the young master passed,
but Zhōu Shēng failed and returned home,
secretly inclined to give up scholarly pursuits.
A year later, his mother passed away,
and he never spoke of advancement again.
One day, Sùqiū told her sister-in-law,
"When you asked me about my art before,
I was unwilling to startle people with it.
Now we are about to part for a long time,
and the day of departure is near.
Let me secretly teach it to you;
it can also help you avoid the ravages of war."
The sister-in-law asked in surprise.
Sùqiū replied,
"Three years from now,
this place will be deserted.
I am too delicate to endure such fright
and plan to go into seclusion by the seaside.
Elder brother is a man of wealth and status
and cannot come with me,
so I must say farewell."
She then taught her art in full to the sister-in-law.
A few days later, she also informed the young master.
He could not persuade her to stay
and wept, asking,
"Where will you go?"
But she would not say.
At cockcrow, she rose early,
took along a white-bearded servant,
and rode off on two donkeys.
The young master secretly sent someone to follow them.
When they reached the border of Jiāolái,
a dust storm blotted out the sky.
Once it cleared,
they had already lost track of where she went.
Three years later,
when the rebel bandits rose in revolt,
the village houses were reduced to ruins.
Lady Hán cut a piece of silk and placed it inside the gate.
When the bandits arrived,
they saw clouds swirling around a statue of Wéituó over ten feet tall
and fled in terror.
Thus, the household remained unharmed.
Later, a merchant from the village went to the seacoast
and met an old man who resembled the white-bearded servant,
except that his beard and hair were completely black,
so he could not recognize him at once.
The old man stopped and said with a smile,
"Is my family's young master still well?
Please take this message:
Miss Qiū is also very happy and safe."
When asked where he lived,
he said,
"Far, far away!"
and hurried off.
When the young master heard of this,
he sent people to search everywhere,
but they found no trace.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"That the brush-wielder has no prospect of high office
is an old story indeed.
His initial resolve was clear enough,
yet he failed to hold fast to it.
How could he know that the muddle-eyed examiners
judge fate, not essays?
One failed attempt,
and he died in obscurity—
the folly of a bookworm,
how pitiable!
Alas, better to lie low as a hen
than to soar as a rooster and come to grief."
Based on the manuscript version of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*, with missing text supplemented from the Zhuxuezhai transcription.
Jiǎ Fèngwéi
was a man from Píngliàng.
His talent and reputation were unmatched in his time,
yet he repeatedly failed the imperial examinations.
One day,
he met a scholar on the road,
who said his surname was Láng.
His demeanor was carefree and elegant,
and his conversation, though subtle, always hit the mark.
Jiǎ therefore invited him home,
and brought out his own examination essays for correction.
After reading them,
Láng did not praise them much,
saying:
"Sir, your writing
is more than sufficient to take first place in the preliminary exams,
but not enough to even make the bottom of the list in the provincial examinations."
Jiǎ said:
"What is to be done?"
Láng said:
"In all matters under heaven,
striving for them by looking up is difficult,
but attaining them by stooping down is very easy.
Why would this require my saying so!"
He then pointed to one or two individuals and one or two essays as examples,
which were largely the sort Jiǎ despised and disdained to mention.
Hearing this, Jiǎ laughed and said:
"When a scholar establishes his words,
their value lies in being immortal.
Even if they contain the flavors of the eight delicacies,
they should not be considered excessive by the world.
To hunt for fame and rank in such a manner,
even if one ascends to the highest ministries,
is still base."
Láng said:
"Not so.
Though an essay may be beautiful,
if its author remains lowly, it will not be transmitted.
If you wish to cling to your scrolls and end your days that way, then so be it;
if not,
the various officials inside the examination halls
all advanced their positions using precisely this sort of material.
I fear they cannot, for the sake of reading your essays,
change to a different set of eyes and innards."
Jiǎ fell silent in the end.
Láng stood up, laughed, and said:
"The lofty spirit of youth!"
Then he took his leave and departed.
That autumn, Jiǎ entered the provincial examinations and failed again,
feeling depressed and unfulfilled.
He thought considerably about Láng's words,
and so took up the writings previously indicated and forced himself to read them.
Before he reached the end of a single piece,
he was drowsy and ready to sleep,
his mind bewildered and unable to find its own master.
Another three years passed,
and as the time for the provincial examinations drew near,
Láng suddenly arrived.
They met with great joy.
Láng produced seven practice examination topics he had prepared,
and had Jiǎ write essays on them.
The next day,
he asked for the essays to read,
found them unsatisfactory,
and had Jiǎ write them again;
when they were done,
he criticized them once more.
Jiǎ, in jest, gathered from among his failed drafts
the most clichéd, hackneyed, and unspeakable phrases,
strung them together into an essay,
and waited for Láng's arrival to show him.
Láng was delighted and said:
"You've got it!"
He then made Jiǎ memorize it thoroughly,
firmly instructing him not to forget it.
Jiǎ laughed and said:
"To tell the truth, these words do not come from my heart.
They will be gone in the blink of an eye,
and even if I were beaten with the rod,
I would not be able to recall them again."
Láng sat at the desk,
and insisted he recite it once himself;
then he made Jiǎ bare his back,
drew a talisman on it with a brush, and departed,
saying:
"This alone is sufficient;
you can bundle up all your other books and put them away."
Examining the talisman,
Jiǎ found it would not wash off,
having sunk deep into his skin.
When he entered the examination hall,
not one of the seven topics was missed.
Thinking back on all his other compositions,
they were a blur, impossible to remember.
Only the playfully patched-together essay
was clear and vivid in his mind.
Yet, taking up his brush, he ultimately felt ashamed;
he wanted to make a few alterations,
but though he racked his brains, turning it over and over,
he actually could not change a single word.
The sun had already set in the west,
so he simply copied it out and left.
Láng had been waiting for him for a long time,
and asked:
"Why so late?"
Jiǎ told him the truth,
and immediately asked him to wipe off the talisman;
looking at it,
it had already faded away.
Recalling the essay from the examination hall,
it was as if it were from a past life.
Greatly astonished by this,
he therefore asked:
"Why don't you seek office for yourself?"
Láng laughed and said:
"It is precisely because I do not entertain such thoughts
that I am able not to read such essays."
He then arranged to meet Jiǎ the next day at his lodgings.
Jiǎ agreed.
After Láng had left,
Jiǎ took out his examination manuscript and read it himself.
It was utterly contrary to his true feelings,
leaving him disgruntled and dissatisfied.
He did not go to visit Láng again,
but returned home dejected and dispirited.
Not long after,
the results were posted,
and he had actually placed among the top candidates.
Reading his old draft again,
with each line he broke into a sweat.
When he finished reading,
even his layered robes were completely soaked.
He said to himself:
"Once this essay is published,
how will I face the scholars of the world!"
Just as he was wallowing in shame,
Láng suddenly arrived,
saying:
"You sought to pass, and you have passed.
Why so troubled?"
Jiǎ said:
"I was just thinking to myself
that using a golden basin and jade bowl to hold dog excrement—
I truly have no face to appear before my peers.
I am about to withdraw to the hills and forests,
and sever all ties with the world forever."
Láng said:
"This too is a highly lofty aim,
but I fear you cannot do it.
If you truly can,
I will introduce you to someone
from whom you may obtain immortality.
Then even a fame lasting a thousand years
would not be worth clinging to,
let alone this accidental wealth and honor!"
Jiǎ was pleased,
and asked Láng to stay and share his quarters for the night,
saying:
"Allow me to think it over."
At daybreak,
he said to Láng:
"My resolve is firm!"
Without informing his wife and children,
he drifted away like a wisp of cloud.
Gradually they entered deep into the mountains,
arriving at a cave dwelling.
Within, there was a world of its own.
The old man sat in the hall,
and Láng made Jiǎ pay his respects,
calling him "Master."
The old man said:
"Why have you come so early?"
Láng said:
"This man's resolve on the path is already firm,
I hope you will accept him."
The old man said:
"Since you have come,
you must put aside all concern for this body,
only then can you succeed."
Jiǎ respectfully obeyed.
Láng escorted him to a courtyard,
settled him in his sleeping quarters,
and gave him some food,
before leaving.
The room was also clean and refined;
only, the door had no panel,
the window no lattice,
inside there was only a small table and a bed.
Jiǎ took off his shoes and climbed onto the bed,
moonlight pierced through;
he felt slightly hungry,
took the food and ate it,
it was sweet and easily filled him up.
Secretly he thought Láng would come again.
He sat for a long time in silence,
with no sound at all,
only feeling a pure fragrance filling the room,
his internal organs clear and empty,
his veins and arteries all countable.
Suddenly he heard a very fierce sound,
like a cat scratching an itch,
peering through the window,
he saw a tiger crouching under the eaves.
At first sight,
he was greatly alarmed;
but remembering his master's words,
he immediately gathered his spirit and sat still.
The tiger seemed to know there was someone there,
soon it entered and approached the bed,
breathing heavily,
sniffing all over his feet and legs.
After a short while,
he heard a commotion of cries in the courtyard,
like a chicken being tied up,
and the tiger hurried out.
After sitting a little longer,
a beautiful woman entered,
the scent of orchids and musk wafting from her,
quietly she climbed onto the bed,
leaned close to his ear and whispered:
"I have come."
As she spoke these words,
the fragrance of her lip rouge scattered.
Jiǎ kept his eyes closed and did not move at all.
She said again in a low voice:
"Are you asleep?"
Her voice was quite like his wife's,
his heart stirred slightly.
But then he thought:
"These are all illusions conjured by the master to test me."
He kept his eyes closed as before.
The beautiful woman laughed and said:
"The little mouse is stirring!"
Earlier,
he and his wife shared a room with a maid,
intimate moments were always afraid the maid would hear,
so they privately agreed on a code phrase:
"The little mouse stirs,
then we can be intimate."
Suddenly hearing these words,
he could not help but be greatly stirred,
opened his eyes and stared intently,
it really was his wife.
He asked:
"How could you come?"
She replied:
"Láng shēng feared you would be lonely and think of returning,
so he sent an old woman to guide me here."
As she spoke,
because Jiǎ had left without telling her,
while nestling close to him,
she showed some resentment.
Jiǎ comforted her for a long time,
before she finally smiled and they enjoyed themselves.
After they finished,
the night was nearing dawn,
when they heard the old man's scolding voice,
gradually approaching the courtyard.
His wife hurriedly got up,
with nowhere to hide,
so she leaped over the low wall and left.
A moment later,
Láng entered with the old man.
The old man, facing Jiǎ, caned Láng,
then ordered the guest to be expelled.
Láng also led Jiǎ out through the low wall,
saying:
"I had high hopes for you,
and could not help but be hasty;
I did not expect your emotional ties were not yet severed,
causing me repeated beatings and reprimands.
From now on, leave for a while,
we will meet again in due time."
He pointed out the way back,
cupped his hands in farewell, and they parted.
Jiǎ looked down at his old village,
which was still within sight.
He thought that his wife, with her weak steps,
must have lagged behind on the road.
He hurried along for over a li,
and soon arrived at his own gate.
But all he saw were crumbling walls and scattered houses,
with none of the old scenery remaining.
Among the old and young in the village,
not a single one was familiar to him.
His heart began to tremble with shock and bewilderment.
Suddenly he recalled the story of Liú Chén and Ruǎn Zhào returning from Tiāntāi,
and the scene truly seemed similar.
Not daring to enter the gate,
he sat down to rest opposite the house.
After a long while,
an old man came out leaning on a cane.
Jiǎ bowed to him
and asked,
"Where is the residence of Jiǎ Fèngzhí?"
The old man pointed to the house and said,
"This is it.
Could it be that you wish to inquire about the strange affair?
I know all about it.
It is said that after this gentleman heard of his success in the examinations, he fled;
at the time of his flight,
his son was only seven or eight years old.
Later, when the son reached fourteen or fifteen,
his mother suddenly fell into a deep sleep and did not wake.
While the son was alive,
he changed her clothes according to the seasons;
after his death,
the two grandsons were impoverished,
the house was dismantled,
and they only used wooden frames covered with thatch to shelter her.
A month ago,
the lady suddenly awoke,
and by counting on her fingers, it had been over a hundred years.
People from near and far, hearing of this marvel,
all came to visit and see for themselves,
but recently it has become somewhat less frequent."
Jiǎ suddenly understood everything clearly,
and said,
"Old sir, you do not realize that I am Jiǎ Fèngzhí."
The old man was greatly startled
and hurried to report to the family.
At that time, the eldest grandson had already died;
the second grandson, Xiáng, came forward—
he was over fifty years old.
Seeing Jiǎ so young,
he suspected deception.
After a short while,
the lady came out
and only then recognized him.
Tears streamed down her face,
and she called him to go with her.
They had no house to live in,
so they temporarily moved into their grandson's dwelling.
Men and women, young and old,
came rushing in and crowded around—
they were all his great-grandchildren and great-great-grandchildren,
mostly crude and lacking refinement.
The wife of the eldest grandson, Wú shì,
bought wine and prepared simple meals of wild herbs;
she also had her younger son, Gǎo, and his wife
share a room with her,
vacating a room for their grandparents.
When Jiǎ entered the room,
he found it filled with smoke, dust, and the smell of children's urine—
a foul mixture that assailed the senses.
After living there for several days,
he felt deeply regretful and could hardly bear it.
The two grandsons took turns providing meals,
but the cooking was especially poor.
The villagers, hearing of Jiǎ's return,
invited him to drink every day;
yet his wife often could not get a full meal.
Wú shì, being the daughter of a scholar,
was quite well-versed in household duties
and continued to serve them respectfully without fail.
Xiáng's family gradually provided less and less,
sometimes even calling out rudely when giving them things.
Jiǎ grew angry,
took his wife, and left,
setting up a school in the eastern part of the village.
He often said to his wife,
"I deeply regret returning this time,
but it is too late now.
Having no other choice,
I have taken up my old profession again.
If one has no shame or guilt in their heart,
wealth and honor are not hard to attain."
After living there for over a year,
Wú shì still occasionally sent them provisions,
but Xiáng and his son never showed up again.
That year,
Jiǎ passed the county-level examination and entered the county school.
The county magistrate valued his literary talent
and generously rewarded him,
so from then on, the family became somewhat better off.
Xiáng gradually began to approach and seek him out again.
Jiǎ called him in,
calculated the expenses he had previously incurred,
paid him with silver,
and drove him away, cutting off all ties.
He then bought a new house
and moved Wú shì in to live with them.
Wú shì had two sons:
the elder stayed to manage the old property;
the younger, Gǎo, was quite clever,
so Jiǎ had him study with his own students.
Since returning from the mountains,
Jiǎ's mind had become even clearer and more perceptive,
and he passed the higher examinations in succession, earning the jìnshì degree.
A few years later,
he was appointed as an imperial censor and sent to inspect Liǎngzhè,
where his reputation became illustrious and grand.
With singing, dancing, towers, and pavilions,
his lifestyle was celebrated as magnificent for a time.
Jiǎ was upright and stern by nature,
unafraid of powerful officials,
so the high-ranking ministers at court
sought to harm him.
Jiǎ repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to retire,
but his requests were not approved by the emperor.
Before long, disaster struck.
Earlier,
Xiáng's six sons were all scoundrels.
Although Jiǎ had disowned and disdained them,
they all secretly used his remaining influence to abuse their power,
forcibly seizing fields and houses,
so the villagers all suffered because of them.
There was a certain man, Yǐ, who had just married a new wife,
and Xiáng's second son forcibly took her as his concubine.
Yǐ was cunning and deceitful by nature,
so the villagers pooled money to help him file a lawsuit,
and the matter became known in the capital.
High officials submitted memorials one after another attacking Jiǎ.
Jiǎ had no way to defend himself,
and was imprisoned for a year.
Xiáng and his second son both died in prison.
Jiǎ was sentenced by imperial decree to serve in the army in Liáoyáng.
By then, Gǎo had already entered the county school for some time;
he was quite kind and honest by nature,
and had a reputation for virtue.
Jiǎ's wife had given birth to a son,
who was now sixteen years old,
so they entrusted him to Gǎo's care.
Husband and wife, accompanied by one servant and one maidservant, set off.
Jiǎ said,
"Over ten years of wealth and honor
were not even as long as a dream.
Now I finally understand that the realm of glory and splendor
is nothing but a state of hell.
I regret that, compared to Liú Chén and Ruǎn Zhào,
I have created an additional layer of sinful karma."
A few days later, they reached the seashore.
In the distance, they saw a large boat approaching,
with drums and music resounding grandly.
The attendants all looked like heavenly deities.
As it drew near,
a person emerged from the boat,
smiled, and invited the censor to come aboard for a short rest.
When Jiǎ saw him, he was both startled and delighted,
leaped across,
and the escorting officers dared not stop him.
His wife anxiously tried to follow,
but the distance was already too great,
so in despair, she threw herself into the sea.
After drifting a few paces,
she saw someone lower a white silk ribbon into the water,
pulled her up, and rescued her.
The officers ordered the boatmen to row quickly,
chasing after them while shouting,
but all they heard was thunderous drumming,
mingled with the roaring waves,
and in an instant, they vanished.
The servant recognized the person—
it was none other than Láng shēng.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"It is said that Chén Dàshì, while in the examination hall,
after completing his examination essay, recited it several times
and sighed, saying, 'Who else could understand this?'
He then discarded it and wrote another,
which is why his published examination essay was inferior to his other drafts.
Mr. Jiǎ, ashamed, fled and hid away—
herein lies the bone of an immortal.
Yet when he returned to the human world again,
he debased himself for the sake of food and livelihood.
How deeply poverty and lowliness can affect a person!"
Based on the manuscript version of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Dōngchāng, there was a man named Biàn,
who practiced as a cattle doctor.
He had a daughter whose childhood name was Yānzhī,
talented and graceful, intelligent and beautiful.
Her father treasured and loved her,
wishing to marry her into a respectable family,
but prominent clans looked down on their humble and lowly status,
disdaining to form an alliance,
so she remained unmarried as she reached the appropriate age.
Across the street lived a woman named Wáng, the wife of a man surnamed Gǒng,
frivolous and fond of jesting,
and a close friend of the girl, often chatting in her boudoir.
One day,
after seeing her to the door,
they saw a young man passing by,
dressed in white robes, skirt, and hat,
with an exceptionally handsome demeanor.
The girl seemed moved,
her autumn-wave-like eyes lingering and turning toward him.
The young man lowered his head and hurried away.
After he had gone far,
the girl still gazed intently.
Wáng, sensing her feelings,
teased her, saying:
"With your talent and beauty,
if you could be matched with such a man,
you would likely have no regrets."
The girl blushed,
silently, without uttering a word.
Wáng asked:
"Do you know this young man?"
The girl replied:
"No."
Wáng said:
"This is the scholar È Qiūsǔn from the southern lane,
the son of a former Xiàolián.
I used to live in the same neighborhood,
so I know him.
There is no man in the world as gentle and refined as he.
Now he is dressed in plain clothes
because he is still in mourning for his wife.
If you are interested,
I can send word to him to arrange a matchmaker."
The girl remained silent,
and Wáng laughed as she left.
Several days passed without any news,
and the girl began to suspect that Wáng had not found the time to go,
or that the descendant of an official family would not stoop to pick her up.
Depressed and restless,
she was tormented by her thoughts,
gradually losing her appetite,
falling ill and becoming weak and weary.
Wáng happened to come for a visit,
and inquired about the cause of her illness.
The girl replied:
"I don't know myself.
But since the day we parted,
I have felt listless and unhappy,
barely clinging to life,
as if I might die at any moment."
Wáng whispered:
"My husband
is away on business and hasn't returned yet,
so no one has yet sent word to young È.
Is your delicate health out of sorts
because of this?"
The girl blushed for a long time.
Wáng teased her:
"If it really is because of this,
and you're already this ill,
what is there to fear?
Why not first let him come one night for a meeting?
Would he really refuse?"
The girl sighed:
"Things have come to this,
I can no longer be shy.
If he does not disdain my humble and lowly status,
and sends a matchmaker,
my illness will surely heal;
but a secret rendezvous—
that is absolutely unacceptable!"
Wáng nodded,
and then left.
When Wáng was young, she had an affair with a neighbor named Sù Jiè.
After she married,
whenever Sù found out her husband was away,
he would seek out their old relationship.
That night, Sù happened to come,
and she recounted the girl's words as a joke,
playfully urging him to convey her feelings to young È.
Sù had long known of the girl's beauty,
and hearing this, he secretly rejoiced,
glad that there was an opportunity he could exploit.
He considered discussing it with Wáng,
but feared her jealousy,
so he pretended to speak casually,
asking in detail about the layout of the girl's boudoir.
The next night,
he climbed over the wall,
went straight to the girl's room,
and tapped on the window with his finger.
From inside came the question:
"Who is it?"
He replied,
"It's È."
The girl said:
"The reason I long for you
is for a lifetime,
not for a single night.
If you truly love me,
you should quickly arrange for a matchmaker;
if you speak of a secret union,
I dare not comply."
Sù pretended to agree,
but pleaded to hold her slender wrist as a token.
The girl could not bear to refuse too harshly,
and with great effort, opened the door.
Sù rushed in,
immediately embracing her and seeking intimacy.
The girl, too weak to resist,
collapsed to the ground,
breathless.
Sù hurriedly pulled her up.
The girl said:
"Where did this ruffian come from?
You are certainly not young È: if it were really young È,
he is gentle and kind,
and knowing the cause of my illness,
would surely pity and care for me.
How could he act so violently!
If you continue like this,
I will cry out,
and both our reputations will be ruined,
with no benefit to either!"
Sù, afraid his disguise would be exposed,
dared not force her further,
but only asked for a future meeting.
The girl said it would be when he came to fetch her in marriage.
Sù thought that was too far off,
and pleaded again.
The girl, annoyed by his persistence,
agreed to meet after she recovered from her illness.
Sù asked for a keepsake,
but the girl refused.
Sù grabbed her foot, removed an embroidered slipper, and left.
The girl called him back,
saying:
"I have already promised myself to you,
what more is there to begrudge?
But I fear 'drawing a tiger only to produce a dog,'
leading to slander and disgrace.
Now that this intimate item is in your hands,
I suppose it cannot be returned.
If you betray me,
I have only death!"
After Sù left,
he went to stay at Wáng's place.
Once in bed,
his mind still on the slipper,
he secretly felt his sleeve,
only to find it gone.
He quickly got up and lit the lamp,
shaking out his clothes and searching in the dark.
When questioned,
Wáng did not respond.
Suspecting she had hidden it,
Wáng deliberately laughed to make him doubt.
Sù could no longer hide it,
and truthfully told her what had happened.
After speaking,
he searched everywhere outside with a candle,
but could not find it.
Regretful and resentful, he went back to bed,
still thinking that in the deep night with no one around,
it must have fallen on the road.
He got up early to search for it,
but it was nowhere to be found.
Prior to this,
in the alley there was a man named Máo Dà,
an idle loafer without a fixed occupation.
He had once tried to seduce Wáng Shì but failed,
and knowing that Sù Xiànghé was intimate with her,
he thought to catch them together and use it to threaten her.
That night,
passing by her door,
he pushed it and found it unbolted,
so he slipped inside.
Just as he reached the window,
he stepped on something,
soft like cotton or silk,
picked it up to look,
and found it was a woman’s shoe wrapped inside.
Crouching to listen,
he heard Sù recount everything in detail,
and was overjoyed,
holding his breath as he slipped away.
After several nights,
he climbed over the wall into the girl’s house,
but not knowing the layout well,
he mistakenly went to the old man’s room.
The old man peered through the window,
saw a man,
and from his voice and movements,
knew he had come for the girl.
Furious,
he grabbed a knife and rushed straight out.
Máo Dà was terrified,
and turned to flee.
Just as he tried to climb the wall,
Biàn was already close behind,
and in his panic with nowhere to escape,
he turned and wrested the knife away;
the old woman got up and shouted loudly,
Máo could not get away,
and so he killed him.
The girl, somewhat recovered,
heard the commotion and finally got up.
Together they lit a candle to look,
the old man’s skull was split and he could not speak,
and in a moment he was dead.
Under the wall they found an embroidered slipper,
the old woman looked at it,
and it was Yānzhī’s.
Pressing the girl,
she wept and told the truth;
but she could not bear to implicate Wáng Shì,
and only said that È Shēng had come on his own.
At daybreak,
they brought a lawsuit in the county.
The county magistrate had È arrested.
È was a cautious and reticent person.
Nineteen years old,
when meeting guests he was as shy and bashful as a child.
When seized,
he was utterly terrified,
and in the court he did not know how to defend himself,
only trembling.
The magistrate became even more convinced of his guilt,
and harshly applied torture instruments.
The young man could not endure the pain,
and so falsely confessed.
After being sent to the prefecture,
the beatings were the same as in the county.
Filled with resentment and injustice,
he often wanted to confront the girl face to face;
but when they met,
the girl would revile and curse him,
so he became tongue-tied and unable to defend himself,
and thus was sentenced to death.
The case went back and forth for repeated interrogations,
passing through several officials without any differing opinions.
Later it was assigned to the Jǐnán Prefecture for reinvestigation.
At that time, Lord Wú Nándài was the prefect of Jǐnán,
and upon first seeing È Shēng,
he suspected he did not seem like a murderer,
so he secretly sent someone to question him calmly in private,
allowing him to fully express himself.
From this, the lord became even more convinced of È Shēng’s innocence.
After pondering for several days,
he began the trial.
First he questioned Yānzhī:
“After making the agreement,
was there anyone who knew?”
She replied:
“No one.”
“When you met È Shēng,
was there anyone else present?”
She also replied:
“No one.”
Then he called the young man forward,
and spoke to him gently to comfort him.
The young man said himself:
“I once passed by her door,
but only saw my former neighbor Wáng Shì and a young girl come out,
so I hurriedly avoided them,
and beyond that, not a word was spoken.”
Lord Wú rebuked the girl, saying:
“You just said there was no one else beside you,
so how is it there was a neighbor woman?”
He intended to apply torture.
The girl, frightened, said:
“Although there was Wáng Shì,
she truly had nothing to do with it.”
The lord ended the questioning and ordered Wáng Shì arrested.
After several days she was brought in,
and she was kept isolated without contact with the girl,
then brought out immediately for interrogation,
and he asked Wáng:
"Who is the murderer?"
The king replied:
"I do not know."
The magistrate feigned and said:
"Yānzhī testified that
you knew all about the murder of Biàn Mǒu,
how could you conceal it?"
The woman cried out:
"How unjust!
That wanton maid herself longed for a man;
although I had words of matchmaking,
I was merely joking with her.
She herself led the adulterer into the courtyard;
how would I know anything about it!"
The magistrate interrogated her in detail,
and she then recounted the words of their previous banter.
The magistrate summoned the girl forward,
and angrily said:
"You said she knew nothing of it,
so why does she now confess to matchmaking?"
The girl wept and said:
"I myself am unworthy,
causing my father's tragic death;
the lawsuit may drag on for who knows how many years,
and now I have implicated others—
I truly cannot bear it."
The magistrate asked Wáng Shì:
"After the jest,
to whom did you speak of it?"
Wáng testified:
"To no one."
The magistrate angrily said:
"Husband and wife in bed
surely speak of everything;
how can you say 'to no one'?"
Wáng testified:
"My husband has been away traveling for a long time and has not returned."
The magistrate said:
"Even so,
those who jest with others
all laugh at people's foolishness
to show off their own cleverness;
if you did not speak of it to a single person,
whom were you trying to deceive?"
He ordered her fingers to be crushed.
The woman, having no alternative,
truthfully testified:
"I did speak of it to Sù."
The magistrate then released È and detained Sù.
When Sù arrived,
he testified:
"I do not know."
The magistrate said:
"One who frequents prostitutes is certainly no good man!"
He subjected him to severe torture.
Sù testified:
"Deceiving the girl is true.
After losing the shoe,
I dared not go again;
I truly know nothing of the murder."
The magistrate angrily said:
"One who climbs over walls is capable of anything!"
He tortured him again.
Sù could not endure the torment;
thus he confessed.
The confession was completed and reported upward;
all praised Magistrate Wú's divine insight.
The case was ironclad as a mountain;
Sù then stretched his neck awaiting the autumn execution.
However, although Sù was unrestrained and lacking in conduct,
he was originally a famous scholar of the eastern region.
Hearing that the Education Commissioner Shī Yúshān was renowned as the most virtuous and capable,
and moreover had a reputation for cherishing talent and sympathizing with scholars,
he therefore submitted a petition pleading his injustice,
the language full of sorrow and distress.
The commissioner examined his confession,
pondered it over and over,
and slapped the table, saying:
"This scholar is wronged!"
He then petitioned the Provincial Administration Commission and Surveillance Commission,
and transferred the case for retrial.
He asked Scholar Sù:
"Where did you lose the shoe?"
Sù replied:
"I forgot.
But when I knocked on the woman's door,
it was still in my sleeve."
Turning to interrogate Wáng Shì:
"Besides Sù Jiè,
how many adulterers were there?"
She testified:
"There were none."
The commissioner said:
"How could a licentious person be devoted to only one?"
She testified:
"I had a youthful affair with Sù Jiè,
and thus could not refuse him;
though others have since propositioned me,
I have truly not dared to comply."
The magistrate then had her point out the man to verify her statement,
and she testified:
"It was Máo Dà from the same neighborhood,
who propositioned me repeatedly but was always refused."
The magistrate said:
"How did you suddenly become so chaste and pure?"
He ordered her to be beaten.
The woman kowtowed until her forehead bled,
strenuously protesting her innocence,
and so he released her.
He then questioned further:
"With your husband away,
surely there were those who came on some pretext?"
She replied:
"There were.
A certain Jiǎ and a certain Yǐ,
both came to my humble home once or twice,
on the pretext of borrowing money or bringing gifts."
Now, Jiǎ and Yǐ were both idlers in the alley,
who had designs on the woman but had not yet acted.
The magistrate recorded all their names,
and had them all arrested.
Once assembled,
the magistrate went to the City God Temple,
and made them all drink before the altar.
He then declared:
"Previously, a deity appeared to me in a dream and said
the murderer is among you four or five.
Now, before the divine presence,
you must not speak falsely.
If you are willing to confess,
you may still be pardoned;
but if you lie,
once discovered, you will not be spared!"
