They all claimed they had not committed murder.
The magistrate had the three wooden instruments of torture laid on the ground,
intending to apply them to all;
they were bound, their hair gathered, and stripped naked,
all crying out in grievance and misery.
The magistrate ordered them released,
and said:
"Since you will not confess to the officials,
I shall have the ghosts and spirits point you out."
He had men use felt mats to cover all the temple windows completely,
leaving not the slightest gap;
he bared the prisoners' backs,
drove them into the darkness,
then gave them a basin of water—
ordering them to wash their hands;
he then tied them against the wall,
commanding them
"face the wall and do not move;
the murderer
will have his back written on by a god."
After a short while,
he called them out to be examined,
pointed at Máo and said:
"This is the true murderer!"
For the magistrate had first had men coat the wall with ash,
and had also soaked their hands in soot: the murderer, fearing the god would write on his back,
therefore pressed his back against the wall and got ash on it;
when about to leave,
he protected his back with his hands,
and thus got soot on it.
The magistrate had already suspected it was Máo,
and now was even more convinced.
Applying severe torture,
Máo confessed everything.
The judgment read:
"Sù Jiè: You trod the path that led Péng Chéng Kuò to his death,
and achieved the reputation of a Dēngtúzǐ for lechery.
Only because of an innocent childhood friendship,
did a wild duck become like a domestic fowl in affection;
because of a single careless word,
you conceived the mind to covet Shǔ after obtaining Lǒng.
You scaled the garden wall like Zhòngzǐ,
dropping down like a bird;
impersonating Liú Láng, you reached the cave entrance,
and actually tricked the door open.
You startled the sash and alarmed the dragon—
does a rat have skin to behave thus?
Climbing for flowers and breaking branches—
what can be said of a scholar without virtue!
Fortunately, you heeded the delicate cry of the ailing swallow,
still showing regard for the jade;
you were not as wild as an oriole.
And releasing the tiny phoenix from the net
still showed a scholar's intent;
yet to seize a fragrant pledge from beneath a stocking—
is this not the height of rascality!
The butterfly flew over the wall,
but ears were listening outside the window;
the lotus petal fell,
dropping to the ground without a trace.
Falsehood within falsehood arose,
who would believe injustice beyond injustice?
Heaven sent down calamity,
cruel torture brought you near death;
you filled the measure of your own misdeeds,
your head nearly severed beyond rejoining.
You, scaling walls and peeping through cracks,
certainly brought disgrace upon the scholar's cap;
but to have the plum wither in place of the peach—
truly it is hard to dispel your sense of grievance.
Therefore, it is fitting to slightly lessen the flogging,
to reduce the severity you have already suffered;
let you be demoted to a blue-gowned scholar,
to open a path for self-renewal.
As for Máo Dà: cunning and crafty, without registration,
a violent ruffian of the marketplaces.
Struck by the neighbor girl's shuttle,
his lustful heart did not die;
watching the wild youth enter the lane,
a thief's cunning suddenly arose.
Opening the door to the wind,
he joyfully trod in Zhāng Shēng's footsteps;
seeking broth, he found wine,
wildly thinking to steal Hán Yuàn's fragrance.
How could he have thought his spirit would be seized by heaven,
his soul captured by ghosts?
Recklessly riding a raft of wood,
he went straight into the Guanghán Palace;
directly sailing a fishing boat,
he mistook the way to the Peach Blossom Spring.
Thus causing the flame of passion to die,
and waves to rise in the sea of desire.
Knife held straight forward,
he threw himself at the rat without a thought for anything else;
the bandit at bay, where could he go?
The desperate hare turned to bite back.
Scaling the wall into another's house,
he only hoped to borrow Lǐ's cap while wearing Zhāng's;
seizing the weapon and dropping the embroidered slipper,
he thus taught the fish to escape the net while the swan was caught.
That such a demon should arise on the path of romance,
that such a ghostly creature should exist in the land of tenderness!
He shall be beheaded immediately,
to satisfy the people's hearts.
Yānzhī: Though not yet betrothed,
she has reached the age of hair-pinning.
Being a fairy from the moon palace,
she naturally should have a jade-like husband; originally of the old troupe of Nícháng dancers,
why worry about lacking gold to fill the house?
Yet stirred by the 'Guān Jū', she longed for a good mate,
and actually became entangled in Chūnpó's dream;
lamenting the 'Biāo Méi', she thought of a fine gentleman,
and thus the soul of the lovely maiden wandered.
Because of a single thread of longing,
a host of demons came in succession.
Competing for a woman's beauty,
they feared to lose 'Yānzhī';
inciting the mandarin ducks to fly in confusion,
they all claimed to be 'Qiū Sǔn'.
The lotus hook taken away,
it was hard to preserve the fragrance of a single petal;
the iron threshold knocked upon,
the priceless jade was nearly shattered.
Inlaying red beans into dice,
the bones of相思 actually became steps to calamity;
felling the tall tree with axe and hatchet,
the hateful talent truly became a flood of disaster.
Maintaining her delicate reserve,
she was fortunate that the white jade remained flawless;
struggling bitterly in bonds,
she rejoiced that the brocade quilt could cover her.
Praising her resistance at the door,
she was still a lover of unsullied purity;
is also an elegant affair of romance.
Let the magistrate of that district
act as your matchmaker."
Once the case was concluded,
it was circulated and praised far and wide.
After Magistrate Wú's interrogation,
the girl finally knew of È Shēng's innocence.
Meeting under the hall,
she bashfully held back tears,
seeming to have words of painful regret,
but unable to speak them.
The young man, moved by her affectionate attachment,
felt intense love and admiration;
yet he also considered her humble origins,
and that she had appeared daily in the public court,
seen and pointed at by a thousand people—
he feared marrying her would bring ridicule,
and day and night he was entangled in thought,
unable to decide for himself.
Once the judgment was issued,
his mind was finally set at ease.
The district magistrate acted as matchmaker for him,
and provided a wedding procession with musicians.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"How true it is!
One cannot but be cautious when hearing legal cases!
Even if one can recognize that Lǐ Dài was wronged,
who would further consider that Táo Jiāng was also unjustly accused?
Yet, though matters may be obscure,
there must be gaps in them;
unless one examines and investigates carefully,
one cannot uncover the truth.
Alas!
People all admire the wisdom of the sage in adjudicating cases clearly,
but they do not know the painstaking effort of the skilled artisan.
Those who occupy positions above the people,
passing their days with chessboards,
lingering idly in their offices,
are even more unwilling to trouble their minds
with the hardships and grievances of those below.
When the drums sound and the court opens,
they sit loftily in the hall,
using shackles and fetters to silence those who clamor—
no wonder so many injustices lie buried beneath overturned basins!"
Mr. Yúshān
was my teacher.
When he first recognized my talent,
I was still a child.
I secretly observed how he encouraged and advanced scholars,
earnestly, as if fearing he had not done enough.
If there was the slightest injustice or grievance,
he would go to great lengths to protect them,
never using his authority in the school
to curry favor with the powerful.
He was truly a guardian of the teachings of Confucius,
not merely an arbiter of literature who never wronged a scholar.
Moreover, his love for talent was as strong as life itself,
far surpassing those later educational commissioners who merely went through the motions.
Once, a renowned scholar entered the examination hall
and wrote an essay
on "The Treasure Bursting Forth,"
but mistakenly wrote
"underwater"
instead.
After finishing the transcription, he realized his error,
and thought there was no chance he would not be failed.
He composed a verse:
"The treasure lies in the mountains,
but I mistakenly thought it was by the water's edge.
A crystal palace built atop the mountain peak,
coral growing on the summit,
pearls hanging from the treetops;
this time, the boatman will fall to his death from the cliff!
I beg Heaven: leave a little stem,
so my friends may see."
When the teacher read the essay and reached this point, he responded with a verse:
"The treasure boasts of the mountain,
but suddenly appears by the water's edge.
The woodcutter idly speaks the fisherman's words.
Though the topic is mistaken,
the writing is excellent—
how could I place it below others?
I have seen him
afraid of heights when climbing;
when have I ever seen
a swimmer drown?"
This is also a glimpse of his refinement and an example of his compassion for talent.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*:
Xī Shān
was from Gāomì.
He made his living as a traveling merchant,
often staying in the area between Méng and Yí.
One day,
he was delayed by rain on the road,
and by the time he reached his usual lodging place,
the night was already deep.
He knocked on the doors of several inns,
but no one answered.
He paced back and forth under the eaves.
Suddenly, two doors swung open,
and an old man emerged,
inviting him inside.
Xī Shān gladly followed him.
He tied up his donkey and entered the hall,
but there were no tables or couches in the hall.
The old man said:
"I pitied you, traveler, with nowhere to go,
so I took you in.
I am not actually in the business of selling food or drink.
There are not many hands in my household—
only my old wife and a frail daughter,
who are already fast asleep.
Though I have some leftover dishes,
I lack the means to heat them properly.
Please do not mind eating them cold."
With these words,
he went inside.
After a short while,
he brought out a footstool and placed it on the ground,
urging the guest to sit;
then he brought a short-legged table.
He bustled back and forth,
treading busily and laboriously.
Xī Shān rose from his seat, feeling uneasy,
and pulled at him to rest for a while.
After a short time,
a young woman came out to serve wine.
The old man looked at her and said:
"Our Ā Xiān is up."
Looking at her,
she was about sixteen or seventeen years old,
slender, delicate, and graceful,
with a charming demeanor.
Xī Shān had a younger brother who was unmarried,
and he secretly took a liking to her.
He then asked the old man about his background and family,
to which the old man replied:
"My name is Shìxū,
surname Gǔ.
My sons and grandsons all died young,
leaving only this daughter.
I could not bear to disturb her deep sleep earlier,
but I suppose my old wife has woken her up now."
Xī Shān asked:
"To whom is she betrothed?"
The old man replied:
"She is not yet engaged."
Xī Shān secretly rejoiced.
Soon, an assortment of dishes was laid out,
as if prepared in advance.
After the meal,
Xī Shān respectfully said:
"A chance encounter like duckweed on water,
yet I have received such generous hospitality—
I will never dare forget it for the rest of my life.
Because of your great virtue, sir,
I dare to speak bluntly:
I have a younger brother named Sānláng,
seventeen years old.
He studies and applies himself to his work,
and is not at all foolish.
I wish to seek a marriage alliance—
would you disdain our humble and lowly status?"
The old man happily said:
"I, an old man, am also living here as a sojourner.
If we can be entrusted to each other,
we could borrow a cottage,
move our family here,
and thus avoid worries."
Xī Shān agreed to everything,
then rose and bowed in thanks.
The old man diligently arranged accommodations and then left.
When the rooster crowed,
the old man had already come out,
calling the guest to wash up.
After packing his belongings,
Xī Shān offered payment for the meal.
The old man firmly declined, saying:
"A guest staying for a meal—
there is absolutely no reason to accept money;
how much more so when we are to become relatives by marriage?"
After parting,
Xī Shān was away for over a month
before returning.
About a li from the village,
he met an old woman leading a young woman,
both dressed entirely in white.
As they drew near,
he suspected it was Ā Xiān.
The young woman also frequently glanced back,
then tugged at the old woman's sleeve
and whispered something in her ear.
The old woman stopped walking
and said to Xī Shān:
"What is your surname, sir?"
Shān Wéiwei responded.
The old woman said with a sorrowful expression:
"Unfortunately, my old husband was crushed under a collapsed wall,
and now I am going to visit his grave.
The house is empty with no one around,
please wait a little by the roadside,
I will return shortly."
She then went into the woods,
and only returned after some time.
The road was already dark,
so they set off together.
As she spoke of her loneliness and helplessness,
she couldn't help but weep sadly;
Shān Wéiwei also felt sorrowful.
The old woman said:
"The people here are not very kind,
it is difficult for a lonely widow to get by.
Since Ā Xiān is already your family's daughter-in-law,
staying here might cause delays,
it would be better to return together early in the morning."
Shān Wéiwei agreed.
When they arrived home,
the old woman lit a lamp to serve the guest,
then said to Shān Wéiwei:
"I thought you would come,
so I had already sold off the stored grain;
there are still over twenty dan left,
but it's too far to transport.
Four or five li to the north,
at the first gate in the village,
there is a man named Tán Èrquán,
who is the buyer.
Please do not mind the trouble,
first use your honorable mount to carry one sack there,
knock on the door and tell him,
just say that the old woman from the southern village has several dan of grain,
selling it for travel expenses,
and ask him to send a cart to fetch it."
She then handed a sack of grain to Shān Wéiwei.
Shān Wéiwei rode his donkey there,
knocked on the door,
and a pot-bellied man came out.
After explaining the situation,
he emptied the sack and returned first.
Soon, two men arrived with five mules.
The old woman led Shān Wéiwei to where the grain was stored,
which was in a cellar.
Shān Wéiwei helped measure and scoop the grain,
the mother poured while the daughter collected,
and in no time, the sacks were filled,
handed over, and they left.
After four trips, all the grain was gone.
Then, the money was given to the old woman.
The old woman kept one man and two animals,
packed their belongings, and headed east.
After traveling twenty li,
dawn finally broke.
They arrived at a market.
At the market, they rented horses,
and Tán's servant returned.
After returning home,
Shān Wéiwei told his parents the whole story.
They were very pleased to meet,
and immediately arranged a separate residence for the old woman,
choosing an auspicious day for Sānláng to complete the wedding.
The old woman prepared a very complete dowry.
Ā Xiān spoke little and rarely showed anger,
if someone spoke to her,
she would only smile slightly;
day and night, she spun and wove,
never stopping.
Because of this, everyone in the household loved and admired her.
She said to Sānláng:
"Please tell your eldest brother: if he passes by the western road again,
do not mention me and my mother."
After three or four years,
the Xī family grew even richer,
and Sānláng entered the county school.
One day,
Shān Wéiwei stayed at an old neighbor's place,
and by chance, the conversation turned to the time years ago when he had nowhere to go
and sought shelter with an old couple.
The host said:
"You are mistaken, guest.
The eastern neighbor is your eldest brother's other residence,
three years ago,
those living there kept seeing strange things,
so it has been empty and abandoned for a long time,
how could there have been an old couple hosting you?"
Shān Wéiwei was very surprised,
but did not fully believe it.
The host continued:
"This house has been empty for ten years,
no one dared to enter.
One day,
the back wall of the residence collapsed,
he saw a huge rat, as big as a cat, crushed under a stone,
its tail still wagging outside.
He hurried back,
called everyone to go together,
but it had already disappeared.
Everyone suspected that creature was a monster.
More than ten days later,
they went in to check again,
but it was quiet with no sign or sound;
another year or so later,
people finally started living there again."
Shān Wéiwei found it even more strange.
Returning home, he spoke privately,
secretly suspecting that the new bride was not human,
and worried in secret for Sānláng;
but Sānláng loved her as deeply as ever.
After a long time,
the family members began to gossip and speculate,
and the woman noticed it slightly.
One night, she said to Sānláng:
"I have been with you for several years,
and have never failed in my duties as a wife;
now you treat me as if I am not even human,
please grant me a divorce paper,
and choose a good match for yourself."
As she spoke, tears fell.
Sānláng said:
"My sincere heart,
you should have known long ago.
Since you entered our home,
the family has grown richer day by day,
everyone attributes the blessings to you,
how could there be any strange talk?"
The woman said:
"I know you have no second thoughts,
how could I not know;
but with everyone gossiping,
I fear I may eventually be cast aside like a fan in autumn."
Sānláng comforted and reassured her repeatedly,
and only then did she calm down.
Shān Wéiwei, however, remained unconvinced,
and every day sought a good mouser cat
to test her reaction.
Although the woman was not afraid,
she felt uneasy and unhappy.
One evening,
she said her mother was slightly ill,
and bid farewell to Sānláng to go attend to her.
By daybreak,
when Sānláng went to check,
the room was already empty.
Terrified,
he sent people to search for her on all roads,
but there was no news.
His heart was restless,
and he could neither eat nor sleep.
But his father and brother thought it was fortunate,
comforting him one after another,
and planning to arrange another marriage for him;
but Sānláng was deeply unhappy.
He waited for over a year,
but there was still no news.
His father and brother began to blame and pressure him,
and with no other choice,
he bought a concubine with a large sum of money;
but his longing for Ā Xiān never faded.
Several more years passed,
and the Xī family gradually grew poorer,
so they began to miss Ā Xiān.
There was a younger cousin named Lán,
who happened to go to Jiāo,
and took a detour to stay at the home of a relative, Mr. Lù.
At night, he heard a neighbor crying very sorrowfully,
but did not have time to ask about it.
After returning,
he heard it again,
so he asked the host.
The host replied:
"Several years ago,
a widowed mother and her solitary daughter
rented and lived here.
Then, a month ago,
the old woman died,
leaving the daughter alone,
without a single thread of kin,
hence the sorrow."
He asked:
"What is their surname?"
The reply was:
"Surname Gǔ.
They often kept their door shut and did not interact with the village community,
so I am not fully aware of their family background."
Lán exclaimed in surprise:
"That is my sister-in-law!"
He then went and knocked on the door.
Someone came out wiping tears,
and responded from behind the door:
"Who are you, guest?
Our household has never had any men."
Lán peeked through a crack and scrutinized from a distance,
and indeed it was his sister-in-law.
He then said:
"Sister-in-law, please open the door,
I am Ā Suì from your brother-in-law's family."
Upon hearing this,
the woman unlatched the door and let him in,
pouring out her loneliness and hardship,
her mood desolate and sorrowful.
Lán said:
"Third Brother misses you bitterly;
even if there were discord between husband and wife,
why did you flee so far away to this place?"
He immediately wanted to hire a carriage to return together.
The woman said sorrowfully:
"Because I was looked down upon by others,
I went into seclusion with my mother;
now if I return to depend on others again,
who would not treat me with disdain?
If I must go back,
we must live separately from Eldest Brother;
otherwise,
I would rather take poison and seek death!"
After Lán returned,
he told Sānláng.
Sānláng rushed there overnight.
Husband and wife met,
both shedding tears.
The next day,
they informed the house owner.
The house owner, Xiè the Imperial Student,
had noticed the woman's beauty,
and secretly intended to make her his concubine.
For several years he had not taken rent,
frequently hinting to the old woman,
but she refused him.
After the old woman died,
he secretly rejoiced, thinking he could scheme,
when suddenly Sānláng arrived.
He calculated the total rent to create difficulties.
Sānláng's family was originally not well-off,
and hearing the large sum of money,
he looked quite worried.
The woman said:
"It's no matter."
She led Sānláng to see the stored grain,
roughly over thirty *dan* of millet,
more than enough to pay the rent.
Sānláng was pleased,
and told Xiè,
but Xiè would not accept the millet.
He insisted on demanding silver.
The woman sighed and said:
"This is all the evil karma of my humble self!"
She then told Sānláng the whole situation.
Sānláng was furious,
and was about to sue at the county office.
Lù shì stopped him,
distributed the millet among the village neighbors,
collected funds to repay Xiè,
and sent the couple back by carriage.
Sānláng truthfully told his parents,
and separated from his elder brother to live apart.
Ā Xiān brought out her private funds,
and daily built granaries,
yet the household still had not a peck or bushel of grain;
everyone found it strange.
After over a year of checking,
the granaries were found full.
Within a few years,
the household became very wealthy;
while Shān remained bitterly poor.
The woman moved her parents-in-law to support them herself;
she regularly provided money and grain to assist her brother-in-law,
making it a customary practice.
Sānláng said happily:
"You can truly be said to bear no grudge for past wrongs."
The woman said:
"He himself loved his younger brother.
Moreover, if not for him,
how would I have had the chance to meet you, Sānláng?"
Afterwards, nothing particularly strange occurred.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Ruìyún,
a famous courtesan of Hángzhōu,
unparalleled in beauty and talent.
At fourteen years old,
her mother, Cài the old woman,
was about to have her receive guests.
Ruìyún said:
"This is the beginning of my lifelong journey,
it cannot be done carelessly.
The price shall be set by mother,
but the guests I shall choose myself."
The old woman said:
"Agreed."
So the price was set at fifteen taels of silver,
and she began receiving guests daily.
Guests seeking an audience must bring a gift: those with generous gifts
were entertained with a game of Go,
and repaid with a painting;
those with meager gifts,
were merely served a cup of tea.
Ruìyún's fame had long been widespread,
and from then on, wealthy merchants and noble youths,
came daily to her door.
Hè Shēng of Yúháng,
long renowned for his literary talent,
but whose family was only moderately wealthy.
He had long admired Ruìyún,
yet never dared to dream of being her match,
but he also exhausted his meager resources for a gift,
hoping for a glimpse of her beauty.
Secretly fearing that having seen many people,
she would not care for a poor scholar;
but when they met and talked,
she received him with exceptional warmth.
They sat and talked for a long time,
her eyes and brows filled with affection.
She composed a poem for Shēng, saying:
"For what does the seeker of nectar
knock at Lán Bridge at dawn?
If one has the heart to seek the jade pestle,
it is truly only among mortals."
Shēng obtained it and was ecstatic.
Just as he wished to say more,
suddenly a young maid came to announce
"A guest has arrived"
and Shēng hastily took his leave.
After returning home,
he recited and savored the poem,
his soul entangled in dreams.
After a day or two,
unable to control his feelings,
he prepared another gift and went again.
Ruìyún received him with great joy.
Moving her seat closer to Shēng,
she quietly said:
"Can we arrange to spend a night together?"
Shēng said:
"I am but a poor and humble scholar,
only able to offer my sincere feelings to a kindred spirit.
The meager gift I brought,
has already exhausted my limited means.
To be near your fragrant presence,
my wish is already fulfilled;
as for intimate physical closeness,
how dare I harbor such a dream."
Upon hearing this,
Ruìyún became sorrowful and unhappy: facing each other, they then fell silent.
Shēng sat for a long time without leaving,
the old woman repeatedly called Ruìyún to urge him,
and Shēng then departed.
His heart was deeply troubled,
thinking of exhausting his family wealth for one moment of joy,
but to part at the end of the night,
how could such feelings be endured again?
Contemplating this,
his ardent thoughts all dissipated,
and from then on, communication ceased.
Ruìyún had been selecting a husband for several months,
but had not found a single suitable match.
The madam was quite angry,
and was about to force her to marry someone,
but had not yet acted.
One day,
a scholar came to pay his respects.
After sitting and talking for a short while,
he stood up,
and with one finger pressed on the girl’s forehead, said:
"What a pity,
what a pity!"
Then he left.
After Ruìyún saw the guest off and returned,
everyone saw a black fingerprint like ink on her forehead.
Washing it only made it more distinct.
After a few days,
the ink mark gradually spread wider.
After more than a year,
it extended from her cheeks to her nose.
Those who saw her would laugh,
and the tracks of carriages and horses ceased to come.
The madam stripped her of her ornaments,
and made her work among the maids.
Ruìyún was also delicate and weak,
unable to bear the heavy tasks,
and grew increasingly haggard.
Hè heard about this and went to visit her.
He saw her with disheveled hair in the kitchen,
looking as ugly as a ghost.
She raised her head and saw Hè,
then turned to face the wall to hide herself.
Hè pitied her,
so he spoke with the madam,
expressing his wish to redeem her as his wife.
The madam agreed.
Hè sold his land and emptied his belongings,
bought her, and brought her home.
Upon entering the door,
she tugged at his clothes and wiped her tears,
not daring to consider herself his wife,
but willing to serve as a concubine,
awaiting a future wife.
Hè said,
"What matters most in life is a true friend who understands you: when you were in your prime, you were still able to recognize my worth.
How could I forget you now that you are in decline!"
Thus, he did not marry again.
Those who heard this all mocked him,
but his affection grew even deeper.
After living together for over a year,
he happened to go to Sūzhōu.
There was a man named Héshēng staying at the same inn.
Suddenly, Hé asked:
"In Hángzhōu, there is a famous courtesan named Ruìyún.
How has she been lately?"
Hè replied that she had married someone.
Hé asked again:
"Who is the man?"
Hè said:
"That person is roughly on the same level as me."
Hé said:
"If he is truly like you,
then she has found a good match.
I wonder how much the price was?"
Hè said:
"Because she had a strange illness,
she was sold cheaply.
Otherwise,
someone like me
could never afford to buy such a beauty from a brothel!"
Hé asked again:
"Is that man really like you?"
Hè found his questioning strange,
so he asked him in return.
Hé smiled and said:
"To tell you the truth: I once saw her beautiful appearance,
and deeply regretted that such a peerless beauty
should fall into misfortune and not find a good match.
So I used a small trick to dim her radiance and preserve her purity,
leaving her for a true connoisseur of talent to recognize."
Hè eagerly asked:
"Since you could mark her,
can you also wash it away?"
Hé smiled and said:
"How could I not be able to?
But it requires a sincere request from the person involved."
Hè stood up and bowed, saying:
"Ruìyún’s husband
is none other than me."
Hé happily said:
"Only a truly talented person in the world can be so deeply affectionate,
not changing their feelings based on beauty or ugliness.
Please allow me to return with you,
and I will present you with a beauty."
So he returned with Hè.
Upon arriving,
Hè was about to order wine.
Hé stopped him, saying:
"First, let me perform my method.
We should first make the one preparing the meal happy."
He immediately ordered a basin to be filled with water,
pointed his finger like a halberd and wrote on it,
saying:
"Washing with this will cure her.
But she must personally come out to thank the doctor."
Hè smiled, took the basin, and left.
He stood waiting for Ruìyún to wash her face with it.
Instantly, her skin became smooth and clean,
and her beauty was as radiant as in her prime.
The couple both felt grateful to him,
and together went out to express their thanks,
but the guest had already vanished.
They searched everywhere but could not find him.
Could he have been an immortal?
Based on the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì."
Qiú Zhòng,
a man from Jìn,
though his prefecture and county are forgotten.
During a great rebellion,
he was captured by bandits.
His two sons, Fú and Lù, were both young.
His second wife, Shào shì,
raised the two orphans,
and fortunately, the family property allowed them to live in warmth and comfort.
However, years of poor harvests
and the bullying by powerful local tyrants
brought them to the brink of starvation.
Qiú Zhòng’s uncle, Lián, saw an advantage in marrying her off,
and repeatedly urged her to remarry,
but Shào shì remained steadfast in her resolve.
Lián secretly made an agreement with a wealthy family,
intending to force her into marriage.
The arrangement was already settled,
but no one else knew about it.
A fellow villager named Wèi Míng,
who had always been cunning,
had long been at odds with the Qiú family,
and constantly sought ways to harm them.
Taking advantage of Shào’s widowhood,
he spread false rumors to slander and disgrace her.
When the wealthy family heard this,
they were disgusted by his lack of virtue and stopped the arrangement.
After some time,
Lián’s secret plot and the spreading rumors
gradually reached Shào’s ears.
Grief and resentment filled her heart,
and she wept day and night.
Gradually, her limbs grew numb,
and she became bedridden.
Fú was just sixteen years old,
and since there was no one to manage the household chores,
he hastily arranged a marriage.
His wife
was the daughter of Scholar Jiāng Qǐzhān,
and was quite virtuous and capable.
All matters relied on her management.
From then on, their circumstances gradually improved,
and they still sent Lù to study with a teacher.
Wèi Jì was jealous of him,
but outwardly acted friendly,
frequently inviting Fú to drink,
and Fú came to rely on him as a close confidant.
Wèi seized an opportunity to tell him:
"Your mother is ill and incapacitated,
unable to manage the household or its livelihood;
your brother sits idle,
doing nothing at all.
Why should you and your wife toil like oxen and horses!
Moreover, when your brother buys a wife,
it will cost a great deal of money.
For your sake,
it would be better to divide the family early,
so that poverty falls on your brother and wealth remains with you."
Fú returned home,
discussed it with his wife;
his wife rebuked him.
But Wèi daily insinuated subtle words,
and Fú became confused,
directly telling his mother his own thoughts.
His mother grew angry,
and scolded him.
Fú became even more resentful,
and began to regard the family's money and grain as belonging to others, squandering them carelessly.
Wèi seized the chance to lure him into gambling,
and the granary's stores gradually emptied.
His wife knew but did not dare speak of it,
until it came to the point where they ran out of food,
and when his mother asked in alarm,
she finally told the truth.
His mother was furious,
but could do nothing about it,
and so divided the family.
Fortunately, Jiāngnǚ was virtuous,
morning and evening cooking for her mother-in-law,
serving her just as in ordinary times.
After Fú's family was divided,
he became even more unrestrained,
indulging recklessly in debauchery and gambling.
Within a few months,
his fields and house were all lost to gambling debts,
and his mother and wife knew nothing of it.
Once Fú's resources were exhausted,
he had no plan,
so he mortgaged his wife to borrow money,
but struggled to find anyone willing to accept.
A man in the county, Zhào Yánluó,
originally a major bandit who had slipped through the net,
tyrannized the entire village,
and certainly was not afraid that Fú would renege on his word,
so he generously lent him money.
Fú took it and left,
and within a few days it was all gone again.
He hesitated in his thoughts,
considering breaking the mortgage agreement.
Zhào glared at him fiercely.
Fú became afraid,
and tricked his wife into being handed over.
Wèi heard of this and secretly rejoiced,
rushing to tell Jiāng,
actually intending to ruin his enemy.
Jiāng was angry,
and a lawsuit arose.
Fú was terrified,
and fled.
When Jiāngnǚ arrived at Zhào's house,
she realized she had been sold by her husband,
wept bitterly,
and only wanted to find a way to die.
Zhào at first tried to comfort and persuade her,
but she would not listen;
then he threatened her,
and she cursed him even more;
enraged,
he whipped her,
but she still refused to submit.
So she pulled out a hairpin and stabbed her own throat,
and though they rushed to save her,
it had already pierced her esophagus,
and blood gushed out.
Zhào hurriedly bound her neck with cloth,
still hoping to break her spirit over time.
The next day,
the arrest warrant had arrived,
but Zhào went about unconcerned.
The official examined the woman's severe injuries,
ordered him to be caned,
but the attendants looked at each other, not daring to use the punishment.
The official had long heard of his tyranny and violence,
and now believed it even more,
grew furious,
called his own servants out,
and had him beaten to death on the spot.
Jiāng then carried his daughter home.
Since Jiāng's lawsuit,
Shào shì first learned of Fú's unworthy behavior,
she wailed once and nearly fainted,
falling into a deep decline.
Lù was fifteen at the time,
left alone with no good master to rely on.
Before this,
Zhòng had a daughter from his previous marriage named Dàniáng,
who was married in a distant commandery,
and had a fierce and stubborn temperament.
Whenever she returned home to visit,
if the gifts she received did not satisfy her desires,
she would often defy her parents,
and would leave in anger,
so Zhòng grew to dislike her;
also because the journey was long,
she had not visited for several years.
When Shào shì was critically ill,
Wèi wanted to summon her to stir up conflict.
Coincidentally, there was a traveling merchant
from the same village as Dàniáng,
so he entrusted him to pass a message to Dàniáng,
enticing her with the prospect of seizing the family property.
A few days later,
Dàniáng indeed arrived with her younger son.
Upon entering the house,
she saw her young brother tending to their sick mother,
the scene bleak and desolate,
and she couldn't help but feel sorrowful.
She then asked her brother about Fú,
and Lù told her everything.
When Dàniáng heard this,
anger choked her throat,
and she said:
"With no adults in the family,
they've let people trample us to this extent!
How dare those thieves swindle away our family's fields and property!"
She then went into the kitchen,
lit a fire to cook porridge,
first served her mother,
and then called her brother and son to eat.
After eating,
she went out angrily,
went to the county office to submit a petition,
and sued the gamblers.
The gamblers were afraid,
and pooled money to bribe Dàniáng.
Dàniáng accepted their money,
but still proceeded with the lawsuit.
The county magistrate detained Jiǎ, Yǐ, and others,
and punished each with caning,
but did not address the matter of the fields and property.
Dàniáng, still furious,
took her son to the commandery office.
The commandery governor detested gamblers the most.
Dàniáng forcefully described her orphaned and suffering situation,
and how the villains had cheated them,
her words passionate and moving.
The governor was moved,
and ordered the county magistrate to recover the fields and return them to their owner;
he also punished Chóu Fú,
to serve as a warning to the unworthy.
After returning,
the county magistrate, following orders, pressed for restitution,
and thus all the original property was returned.
Dàniáng had long been widowed,
so she sent her younger son back,
instructing her cousin to focus on his work,
and not to come again.
From then on, Dàniáng stayed at her mother's home,
caring for her mother and teaching her brother,
managing everything inside and out in an orderly manner.
Her mother was greatly comforted,
her illness gradually improved,
and all household affairs were entrusted to Dàniáng.
If the local bullies
showed the slightest aggression,
she would take a knife and go to their doors,
arguing firmly and confidently,
and none could resist her.
After living there for over a year,
the fields and property increased daily,
and she often bought medicines and delicacies
to send to Jiāng's daughter.
Seeing that Lù was gradually growing up,
she frequently urged matchmakers to find him a wife.
Wèi told people:
"The Chóu family's property
all belongs to Dàniáng now,
I'm afraid it will never be returned."
Everyone believed this,
so no one was willing to discuss marriage with them.
There was a Master Fàn Zǐwén,
whose famous garden
was considered the best in Jìn.
In the garden, famous flowers lined the paths,
leading straight to the inner chambers.
If someone unknowingly wandered in,
and encountered the master holding a private banquet,
he would angrily seize them as thieves,
and cane them nearly to death.
During the Qingmíng Festival,
Lù was returning from school,
when Wèi led him on an excursion,
and they arrived at the garden.
Wèi was previously acquainted with the gardener,
who let them in,
and they toured the pavilions and terraces.
Soon they reached a place
where a stream rushed fiercely,
with a painted bridge and red railings,
leading to a lacquered door;
looking into the distance inside the door,
they saw flowers blooming like brocade—
this was the master's inner study.
Wèi deceived him, saying:
"Please go in first,
I need to relieve myself."
Lù believed him,
crossed the bridge and entered the door,
arriving at a courtyard,
where he heard the laughter of women.
As he stopped in his tracks,
a maidservant came out,
saw him,
and immediately turned back.
Lù, startled, began to run.
Before long,
the master came out,
shouting for his servants to tie him up and chase him.
Lù, in great distress,
threw himself into the stream.
The master, instead of being angry, laughed,
and ordered his servants to pull him out.
Seeing that his appearance and attire were elegant,
he had him change his clothes and shoes,
led him into a hall,
and asked his name.
With a kind expression and gentle words,
he seemed very friendly.
Soon he hurried inside;
then came out,
smiling, took Lù's hand,
crossed the bridge,
and gradually reached the previous place.
Lù did not understand his intention,
and hesitated, not daring to enter.
The master forcefully pulled him in,
and behind a flower fence, they vaguely saw a beautiful woman peeking.
After sitting down,
maidservants served wine.
Lù declined, saying:
"I, a mere youth, was ignorant,
and mistakenly trespassed into your inner chambers.
To receive your pardon
is already beyond my hopes.
I only ask to be released to return early,
and I will be deeply grateful."
The master did not listen.
Soon after,
dishes of meat and delicacies were served in abundance.
Lù stood up again,
excusing himself, saying he was full and drunk.
The master pressed him to sit,
and said with a smile:
"I have the name of a musical piece,
if you can match it with a couplet,
I will let you go."
Lù respectfully asked for the instruction.
The master said:
"The piece is called 'Hún Bù Sì' (Utterly Unlike)."
Lù thought silently for a long time,
and replied:
"Silver becomes 'Mò Nàihé' (Helpless)."
The master laughed heartily and said:
"Truly a Shí Chóng!"
Lù did not understand at all.
It turned out the master had a daughter named Huìniáng,
beautiful and well-educated,
who was daily choosing a good match.
One night, she dreamed of someone telling her:
"Shí Chóng,
is your husband."
She asked:
"Where is he?"
The reply was:
"Tomorrow, he will fall into the water."
She told her parents early in the morning,
and they all found it strange.
Lù happened to match the dream's omen,
so the master invited him into the inner quarters,
to let his wife and daughter observe him.
The master was delighted upon hearing his couplet,
and then said:
"The name of the piece was devised by my daughter,
she has thought about it many times but could not find a matching couplet,
now you have provided the pair."
There was also a predestined match from heaven.
I wish to offer my humble daughter to serve you with dustpan and broom;
my humble home is not lacking in houses and estates,
and there is no need for you to trouble yourself with the bridal procession.”
Lù was flustered and declined with modesty,
using his mother’s illness as an excuse for not being able to marry into the family.
The young master told him to go home and discuss it first,
then sent a stableman to carry his wet clothes
and escorted him with a horse.
After returning home and telling his mother,
she was alarmed, considering it inauspicious.
Only then did they realize how treacherous the Wèi family was;
however, because misfortune had turned into good fortune,
they also set aside any enmity,
merely warning their son to stay far away from them.
After several days,
the young master again sent someone to convey his intentions to the mother,
but she still did not dare to agree.
Dàniáng agreed to it,
and immediately engaged two matchmakers to present the betrothal gifts.
Not long after,
Lù married into the young master’s family.
A year later, he entered the county school,
and his talent and reputation became widely known.
When his wife’s younger brother grew up,
his respect for Lù somewhat slackened;
Lù became angry,
took his wife and returned home,
by which time his mother could already walk with a cane.
Over the years, they had relied on Dàniáng to manage affairs,
and the house and estate were quite well-maintained.
After the new bride returned,
with servants and attendants like clouds,
it truly had the air of a great household.
Wèi, seeing himself cut off,
became even more jealous and resentful,
hating that there was no flaw to exploit,
so he instigated a fugitive under the banner to falsely accuse Lù of harboring assets.
At the beginning of the dynasty, the laws were most severe,
and Lù, according to the decree, was exiled beyond the passes.
Young Master Fàn used connections and bribes up and down,
only managing to exempt Huìniáng from going;
their fields and properties were all confiscated by the government.
Fortunately, Dàniáng held the property division document,
and boldly brought a lawsuit,
so the newly added fertile lands, amounting to several thousand qǐng,
were all registered under Fú’s name,
and mother and daughter were able to live in peace.
Lù, thinking he would never return,
wrote a divorce document and gave it to his wife’s family,
then set off alone in desolation.
After traveling for several days,
he reached the north of the capital,
and ate at an inn.
There was a beggar lingering outside the door,
whose appearance greatly resembled his elder brother;
approaching to inquire,
it was indeed his brother.
Lù then told his own story,
and the brothers were filled with sorrow.
Lù took off an extra garment,
divided some silver,
and urged him to return home.
Fú tearfully accepted and parted.
Lù reached beyond the passes,
and was placed under a general’s tent as a slave.
Because Lù was scholarly and weak,
he was put in charge of accounts and records,
and lived together with the other servants.
The servants inquired about his family background,
and Lù told them everything.
One among them exclaimed in surprise:
“This is my son!”
It turned out that Chóu Zhòng had initially herded horses for bandits,
and later, when the bandits surrendered,
sold Zhòng under the banner,
and at that time he followed his master to garrison beyond the passes.
After Zhòng recounted the past to Lù,
they finally knew they were truly father and son,
embracing each other in grief,
filling the room with sorrow.
After a while, Zhòng said angrily:
“What kind of fugitive scoundrel,
to falsely accuse my son like this!”
He then tearfully reported to the general.
The general immediately appointed Lù to act as secretary;
sent a letter to the prince,
and entrusted Zhòng to go to the capital.
Zhòng waited for the prince’s carriage to come out,
and first submitted his grievance petition.
The prince intervened on his behalf,
and thus he obtained redress,
with orders for the local officials to redeem the property and return it to the Chóu family.
Zhòng returned,
and father and son were both overjoyed.
Lù inquired in detail about the family members,
planning to redeem their freedom.
Only then did he learn that after Zhòng entered the banner,
he had married twice but had no children,
and was now a widower.
Lù then prepared to return.
Earlier,
when Fú parted from his younger brother and returned home,
he crawled forward and threw himself on the ground.
Dàniáng, serving their mother seated in the hall,
grasped a cane and questioned him:
“If you are willing to receive a beating as punishment,
you may stay for now;
otherwise,
since your fields and properties are all gone,
there is also no place for you to eat,
please leave again.”
Fú wept and prostrated on the ground,
willing to receive the flogging.
Dàniáng threw down the cane and said:
“A man who sells his wife
is not worth punishing.
But since the old case is not yet closed,
if you offend again, you can be reported to the authorities.”
She immediately sent someone to inform Jiāng.
Jiāng’s daughter scolded:
“What relation am I to the Chóu family,
that you come and tell me this!”
Dàniáng frequently reported Fú's situation while mocking him,
and Fú felt ashamed, not daring to utter a word.
After half a year,
although Dàniáng provided for him adequately,
she treated him like a servant.
Fú worked without complaint,
and whenever entrusted with money, he handled it with utmost care.
Dàniáng observed that he had no ill intentions,
so she informed her mother,
requesting that Jiāngnǚ return.
Her mother believed it was impossible to reconcile.
Dàniáng said:
"Not necessarily.
If she were willing to serve two masters,
why would she have inflicted such torment upon herself?
It’s just that she couldn’t help but harbor this resentment."
She led her brother to personally go and apologize.
Jiāngnǚ’s parents reproached them severely,
and Dàniáng scolded Fú, making him kneel for a long time,
before requesting to see Jiāngnǚ.
After repeated pleas,
Jiāngnǚ stubbornly refused to come out;
Dàniáng searched for her and dragged her out.
Jiāngnǚ then pointed at Fú, spitting and cursing,
and Fú was so ashamed and sweating that he wished he could disappear.
Jiāngnǚ’s mother finally pulled her up.
Dàniáng asked when she would return,
and Jiāngnǚ said:
"I have received many kindnesses from you before,
and now, following your esteemed command,
how could I dare to object?
But I fear I cannot guarantee that I won’t be sold again!
Moreover, our bond of affection has already been severed,
how could I have the face to live with such a black-hearted scoundrel?
Please prepare a separate room for me,
and I will go serve my elderly mother,
which is better than shaving my head and becoming a nun."
Dàniáng conveyed her remorse on her behalf,
and they parted after agreeing to meet the next day.
The following morning,
they brought her back in a carriage,
and her mother knelt and bowed to her at the gate.
Jiāngnǚ fell to the ground, weeping bitterly.
Dàniáng consoled her and stopped her tears,
then set out wine to celebrate,
ordering Fú to sit beside the table.
She raised her cup and said:
"My struggles were not for my own benefit.
Now that my brother has repented,
and the chaste wife has returned,
I ask to hand over the household accounts;
I came alone,
and I shall leave alone."
The couple both rose from their seats, their expressions changed,
and they knelt and wept sorrowfully,
so Dàniáng stayed.
Not long after,
the order for rehabilitation arrived,
and within a few days,
all the fields and properties were returned to their original owner.
Wèi was greatly shocked,
not knowing how this had happened,
and regretted that he had no means to act again.
Just then, a fire broke out at the western neighbor’s house,
and Wèi went under the pretense of helping to put out the fire,
secretly setting fire to Lù’s residence with a bundle of reeds.
The wind blew fiercely,
and the fire spread, burning almost everything;
only two or three rooms where Fú lived remained,
and the whole family gathered there.
Before long,
Lù arrived,
and they met with mixed emotions of sorrow and joy.
Earlier,
when Fàn Gōngzǐ received the divorce letter,
he discussed it with Huìniáng.
Huìniáng wept bitterly,
tore the letter to pieces, and threw it on the ground.
Her father respected her wishes,
and did not force her.
When Lù returned,
hearing that she was still unmarried,
he joyfully went to his father-in-law’s house.
Knowing of his misfortune, Gōngzǐ wanted to keep him;
but Lù refused,
and so he took his leave and departed.
Fortunately, Dàniáng had hidden some gold,
and she used it to repair the damaged walls.
Fú carried a shovel to help with the construction,
and while digging, they discovered a cellar of silver.
That night, he and his brother opened it together,
and found a stone pool over ten feet deep,
filled with unmovable wealth.
From then on, they hired workers and began large-scale construction,
with buildings rising in clusters,
as magnificent as those of noble families.
Lù was moved by the General’s righteousness,
and prepared a thousand taels of silver to ransom his father.
Fú requested to go,
so they sent strong servants to accompany him on the journey.
Lù then welcomed Yìniáng back.
Not long after,
his father and elder brother returned together,
and the whole household rejoiced.
Dàniáng had been living at her mother’s home,
forbidding her son to visit,
fearing that people would gossip about her partiality.
After her father returned,
she firmly insisted on leaving.
Her brothers could not bear it.
Their father then divided the property into three parts: the sons received two shares,
and the daughter received one.
Dàniáng firmly declined.
Her brothers both wept and said:
"If not for you, sister,
how could we have today!"
Dàniáng then accepted and settled down.
She sent for her son,
and moved the family to live together.
Someone asked Dàniáng:
"They are half-brothers from different mothers,
why do you care for them so deeply?"
Dàniáng said:
"Only beasts know their mother but not their father.
How could a human imitate that?"
When Fú and Lù heard this, they both wept,
and had workers build her residence,
making it equal to their own.
Wèi reflected that over more than a decade,
his attempts to harm them had only brought them more fortune,
and he felt deeply ashamed and remorseful.
Moreover, he admired their wealth,
and wanted to befriend them,
so he used Zhòng as an intermediary,
bringing gifts to visit.
Fú wanted to refuse him;
but Zhòng could not bear to turn him away,
and accepted the chicken and wine.
The chicken’s legs were tied with cloth strips,
and it escaped into the kitchen;
the kitchen fire ignited the cloth,
and the chicken fled to a pile of firewood.
The servants saw it but paid no attention.
Soon, the firewood caught fire and spread to the house,
alarming the whole family.
Fortunately, there were many hands,
and they extinguished it quickly,
but everything in the kitchen was destroyed.
The brothers both said the gifts were inauspicious.
Later, on their father’s birthday,
Wèi again sent a gift of a sheep.
They could not refuse it,
so they tied the sheep to a tree in the courtyard.
That night, a servant boy, beaten by another servant,
angrily went to the tree,
untied the rope, and hanged himself.
The brothers sighed and said:
"His blessings are not as good as his misfortunes!"
From then on, although Wèi was diligent in his efforts,
they dared not accept even a thread from him,
and only repaid him generously.
Later, when Wèi grew old,
impoverished and begging,
the Qiú family often gave him cloth and grain, treating him with kindness.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Alas!
The ways of creation are not governed by man!
The more one tries to harm them, the more fortune they receive—
how utterly meaningless are the schemes of the cunning!
Yet, to accept their affection and respect,
only to bring misfortune upon oneself—
is that not even more strange?
From this, we know that even a single handful of water from a stolen spring
can stain one’s purity."
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Outside the city of Xǔ, there was a river with turbulent waters,
deep and dark near the cliff.
During the height of summer,
someone went in to bathe
and suddenly felt as if struck by knives and axes.
His severed corpse floated to the surface.
Another person later suffered the same fate.
People began to spread the alarming news in fear.
The county magistrate heard of this
and dispatched many men to dam the upstream flow,
draining the water.
They saw a deep cave beneath the cliff,
inside which was placed a rotating wheel,
lined with sharp blades as bright as frost.
Removing the wheel and advancing further,
they found a small stele,
inscribed with characters in Hàn seal script.
Upon closer inspection,
it turned out to be the tomb of Cáo Mèngdé.
They broke open the coffin, scattered the bones,
and took all the gold and treasures buried with him.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"A later worthy wrote in verse: 'If one digs up all seventy-two decoy tombs,
surely one will contain your lordship's corpse.'
Who would have thought it lay outside those seventy-two tombs?
How cunning was Mán!
Yet after over a thousand years, his decayed bones could not be preserved—
what good did all his deceit and trickery do him?
Alas,
Mán's cleverness
was precisely his folly!"
Based on the manuscript version of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Ānqìng, there was a scholar named Dài,
who in his youth was frivolous in conduct,
lacking restraint.
One day,
returning drunk from elsewhere,
he encountered on the road his late cousin, Jì.
In his drunken stupor,
he also forgot that Jì was dead
and asked:
"Where have you been lately?"
Jì replied:
"I have already become a different being—
have you forgotten?"
Only then did Dài realize,
but in his drunken state, he felt no fear.
He asked:
"What do you do in the underworld?"
The answer came:
"Lately, I serve as a registrar under His Highness King of the Wheel of Rebirth."
Dài said:
"Then you must know the fortunes and misfortunes of the human world?"
Jì said:
"That is my duty—
how could I not know?
But it is overly burdensome;
unless it is of great concern,
I cannot remember everything.
Three days ago, I happened to check the register
and still saw your name."
Dài urgently asked what it said.
Jì replied:
"I dare not deceive you—
your esteemed name is listed in the Dark Prison."
Dài was greatly terrified,
and his drunkenness also sobered.
He bitterly pleaded for rescue.
Jì said:
"This is not within my power to assist.
Only good deeds can remedy it.
However, your record of misdeeds fills the fingers—
without great goodness, it cannot be reversed.
What great power does a poor scholar possess?
Even if you performed one good deed daily,
it would take over a year to balance the account.
Now it is already too late.
But if from now on you diligently cultivate virtue,
then perhaps there may be a time when you escape hell."
Hearing this, Dài wept,
prostrated himself, and pleaded sorrowfully.
When he lifted his head,
Jì had already vanished.
He returned home dejected.
From then on, he reformed his heart and mended his ways,
daring not to make a single misstep.
Previously,
Dài had an affair with his neighbor's wife,
and though the neighbor heard of it, he was unwilling to expose it,
so Ēn seized him by surprise.
Dài then reformed his conduct,
and permanently broke off with the woman;
the neighbor, having spied on him without success,
bore a grudge.
One day,
they met in the fields,
and the neighbor pretended to speak with him,
luring him to look into a dry well,
and thus causing him to fall in.
The well was several zhang deep,
and he reckoned he would surely die.
But Dài revived in the middle of the night,
and sat in the well, crying out loudly,
yet no one knew of it.
The neighbor, fearing he might come back to life,
went to listen the next day;
hearing his voice,
he hastily threw stones.
Dài moved and hid in a cave,
not daring to make another sound.
The neighbor, knowing he was not dead,
dug earth to fill the well,
nearly filling it completely.
Inside the cave, it was pitch dark,
truly no different from hell.
The cave was empty, with nothing to eat,
and he thought there was no chance of survival.
Crawling slowly inward,
he found that three steps ahead was all water,
with nowhere else to go,
so he returned to sit where he had been.
At first, he felt hungry,
but after a long time, he forgot about it.
Thinking that in the depths of the earth there was no good deed he could do,
he only chanted the Buddha's name repeatedly.
Then he saw will-o'-the-wisps floating about,
flickering all over the cave,
and so he prayed to them:
"I have heard that blue phosphorescence is all from wronged ghosts;
though I am temporarily alive,
I certainly cannot return,
if we could talk together,
it would also comfort my loneliness."
Then he saw the flames gradually floating over the water;
within each phosphorescence was a person,
about half the height of a human.
He asked where they came from,
and they replied:
"This is an ancient coal mine.
The owner was mining coal,
and disturbed an ancient tomb,
so Lord Lóngfēi diverted the waters of the underground sea,
drowning forty-three people.
We are all ghosts."
He asked:
"Who is this lord?"
They said:
"We do not know.
But the lord is a literary scholar,
and now serves as an assistant to the City God,
and he also pities us for being innocent,
so every three to five days, he gives us water and porridge.
Thinking of us soaked in cold water, our bones chilled,
with no hope of deliverance.
If you, sir, ever return to the human world,
we beg you to gather our remaining bones and bury them in a charitable cemetery.
Then your kindness will reach many in the underworld."
Dài said:
"If there is even one chance in ten thousand,
this would not be difficult.
But I am deep in the ninth layer of earth,
how can I hope to see the light of day again!"
So he taught the ghosts to chant the Buddha's name,
using clumps of earth as prayer beads,
and keeping count of the recitations.
He did not know whether it was day or night,
when tired, he slept,
and when awake, he sat.
Suddenly, he saw a lantern deep inside,
and the ghosts joyfully said:
"Lord Lóngfēi is distributing food!"
They invited Dài to go with them.
Dài worried about the water hindering him,
but the ghosts forcefully dragged and supported him along,
floating as if walking on air.
After winding about half a li,
they reached a place,
where the ghosts released him to walk on his own;
the steps went upward,
like climbing a staircase several ren high.
At the top of the stairs,
he saw buildings and corridors,
and in the hall, a bright candle was burning,
as thick as an arm.
Having not seen firelight for a long time,
Dài was overjoyed and hurried forward.
An old man sat above,
dressed in scholar's robes and hat.
Dài halted, not daring to advance.
The old man had already seen him,
and asked in surprise:
"Where does this living person come from?"
Dài went forward,
and prostrated himself, explaining his situation.
The old man said:
"You are my descendant."
He then told him to rise,
and gave him a seat.
He said of himself:
"I am Dài Qián,
courtesy name Lóngfēi.
Previously, because of my unworthy descendant Táng,
who associated with bandits,
and dug a well near the tomb,
causing me unrest in my nocturnal abode,
I flooded it with seawater,
how are his descendants now?"
It turned out that among Dài's close clan, there were five branches,
and Táng was the eldest.
Initially,
a powerful family in the town bribed Táng,
to mine coal beside their ancestral graves.
His younger brothers feared his strength,
and did not dare to oppose.
Not long after,
underground water suddenly surged,
and all the coal miners died in the well.
The families of the deceased
collectively filed a major lawsuit,
and both Táng and the powerful family were impoverished by this;
Táng's descendants were left without even a place to stand.
Dài was a descendant of Táng's younger brother.
He had heard his ancestors tell of this matter,
and so informed the old man.
The old man said:
"Such unworthy descendants,
how can their line prosper!
Since you have come here,
you must not neglect your studies."
He then served him wine and food,
and placed volumes on the desk,
all containing the eight-legged essays of the Chéng and Hóng periods,
forcing him to study them.
He also assigned topics for essays,
like a teacher instructing a pupil,
and the candle in the hall was always bright,
needing neither trimming nor extinguishing.
When tired, he would sleep,
unable to distinguish morning from evening.
When the old man went out,
he would leave a servant boy to attend to him.
After what felt like several years had passed,
he was fortunate to suffer no hardship.
But there were no other books to read,
only a hundred eight-legged essays,
each read over four thousand times.
One day, the old man said to him:
"Your karmic retribution is now complete,
and you should return to the human world.
My tomb is adjacent to the coal mine,
and the yin wind pierces the bones,
after you achieve success,
you must move me to the eastern plain."
Dài respectfully agreed.
The old man then summoned the group of ghosts,
and sent him back to his original seat.
The ghosts bowed in a circle and urged him again.
Dài also did not know how he could get out.
Earlier,
the Dài family had lost Mr. Dài,
and after an exhaustive search yielded no results,
his mother reported it to the authorities.
Many people were imprisoned,
but there were still no clues.
After three or four years,
the official left his post,
and the investigation also slackened.
Dài’s wife, unable to remain in the household,
was sent away to remarry.
It happened that people from the village were cleaning out an old well again,
and upon entering the cave, they found Dài.
When they touched him, he was not dead.
Greatly alarmed,
they reported it to his family.
They carried him back, and after a full day,
he was finally able to speak about what had happened.
After Dài fell into the well,
a neighbor beat his wife to death,
and was sued by the wife’s father.
After over a year of trials and retrials,
he returned with only skin and bones left.
Hearing that Dài had come back to life,
he was terrified and fled.
The clan members discussed pursuing and punishing him,
but Dài would not allow it;
he said that in the past, it was truly his own fault,
and this was a punishment from the underworld—
what did it have to do with him?
The neighbor, seeing that he bore no ill will,
finally returned hesitantly.
After the well water dried up,
Dài hired people to enter the cave and collect the bones,
having each set prepared separately,
purchased coffins and arranged burial grounds,
and buried them in a mass grave.
He also checked the clan genealogy and found the name Qián,
courtesy name Lóngfēi,
so he first set out offerings and sacrificed at his grave.
The education commissioner heard of this strange event,
and also admired his literary talent,
so that year he entered the provincial examination with high honors,
and succeeded in passing it.
After returning,
he prepared a burial site in the eastern plains and moved Lóngfēi there for a proper burial;
he visited the grave in spring and autumn,
and did so year after year without fail.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"In my hometown, there were coal miners,
and the tunnel was flooded,
with over ten people trapped inside.
They drained the water to retrieve the bodies,
and after more than two months, it finally dried up,
but none of the over ten people had died.
It seems that when the water rushed in,
they all swam to a high spot,
and thus avoided drowning.
They were pulled up by rope,
and only after being exposed to the wind did they faint,
and after a day and a night, they gradually revived.
Then we learned that when people are underground,
they hibernate like snakes or birds,
and cannot die quickly.
However, none had been there for several years.
If not for utmost goodness,
after three years in hell,
how could there still be a living person!"
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Ān Shēng Dàchéng,
a native of Chóngqìng,
his father was a provincial graduate,
who died early.
His younger brother, Èrchéng,
was still young.
Shēng married a woman from the Chén family,
whose childhood name was Shānhú,
and who was gentle and virtuous.
But Shēng’s mother, Shěn,
was fierce, unreasonable, and unkind,
and treated her harshly,
yet Shānhú showed no resentment.
Every morning,
she would dress neatly and go to pay her respects.
Once, when Shēng was ill,
his mother accused her of leading him astray,
and scolded and berated her.
Shānhú withdrew,
removed her makeup, and went to see her again.
Her mother grew even angrier,
banging her head and slapping herself.
Shēng, being filial by nature,
beat his wife,
and only then did his mother calm down a little.
From then on, she hated her daughter-in-law even more,
and although Shānhú served her with utmost care,
she never spoke a word to her.
Shēng, knowing his mother was angry,
also stayed elsewhere,
to show he had cut ties with his wife.
After a long time,
his mother remained unhappy,
and would curse at anything,
always meaning Shānhú.
Shēng said:
"I took a wife to serve my parents,
but now it’s like this—
what use is a wife!"
So he sent Shānhú away,
having an old woman escort her back to her family.
Just as they left the village gate,
Shānhú wept and said:
"As a woman, I cannot be a proper wife—
how can I face my parents when I return?
Better to die!"
She took a pair of scissors from her sleeve and stabbed her throat.
They rushed to save her,
blood gushed and soaked her clothes,
and they helped her back to the home of Shēng’s clan aunt.
The aunt, Wáng shì,
was widowed and alone,
so Shānhú stayed there.
When the old woman returned,
Shēng told her to keep it secret,
but secretly feared his mother would find out.
After a few days,
he learned that Shānhú’s wound was gradually healing,
so he went to Wáng’s door,
telling her not to keep Shānhú.
Wáng called Shēng in;
he refused to enter,
but angrily demanded Shānhú leave.
Not long after,
Wáng led Shānhú out to see Shēng,
and asked directly:
"What crime has Shānhú committed?"
Shēng blamed her for failing to serve his mother.
Shānhú gazed silently without a word,
only bowing her head and sobbing,
her tears all red,
staining her plain gown completely.
Shēng, heartbroken, could not finish his words and left.
A few more days later,
his mother had heard about it,
and angrily went to Wáng,
hurling harsh accusations.
Wáng, proud and unyielding,
instead listed her faults,
and said:
"The wife has already been sent away—
what relation does she still have to the Ān family?
I am keeping the Chén family’s daughter,
not the Ān family’s daughter-in-law,
why trouble yourself meddling in others’ affairs!"
His mother was furious but had no retort,
and seeing her aggressive demeanor,
she left in shame and frustration, weeping loudly.
Shānhú felt uneasy,
and thought of going elsewhere.
Earlier,
Shēng had a maternal aunt, Old Woman Yú,
who was Shěn’s elder sister.
She was over sixty,
her son had died,
leaving only a young grandson and a widowed daughter-in-law;
and she had always treated Shānhú well.
So Shānhú bid farewell to Wáng,
and went to seek refuge with the old woman.
The old woman asked for the reason,
and strongly criticized her younger sister’s foolish tyranny,
and wanted to send Shānhú back immediately.
Shānhú insisted it was not possible,
and also urged her not to speak of it.
So she lived with Old Woman Yú,
like mother-in-law and daughter-in-law.
Shānhú had two elder brothers,
who heard of this and pitied her,
wanting to take her back and remarry her.
Shānhú firmly refused,
and only spun and wove with Old Woman Yú to support herself.
After Shēng divorced his wife,
his mother tried in every way to arrange a marriage for him,
but the reputation of her own shrewishness had spread far and wide,
so no one, near or far, would match with him.
After three or four years had passed,
Èrchéng gradually grew up,
and so they arranged his marriage first.
Èrchéng’s wife, Zānggū,
was arrogant, fierce, and quarrelsome,
even more so than his mother by several times.
If his mother showed anger in her expression,
then Zānggū would vent her anger with her voice.
Èrchéng was also cowardly,
not daring to take sides.
Thus, his mother’s authority suddenly diminished,
and she dared not provoke her,
instead looking at her expression and smiling to curry favor with her,
yet still unable to win Zānggū’s affection.
Zānggū treated his mother like a servant;
Shēng did not dare speak out,
but only took on his mother’s tasks himself,
handling chores like washing utensils and sweeping.
Mother and son often, in places with no one around,
faced each other and wept in silence.
Not long after,
his mother, due to pent-up depression, fell ill,
lying weak and exhausted in bed,
where turning over and relieving herself all required Shēng’s help;
Shēng could not sleep day or night,
and both his eyes turned completely red.
He called his younger brother to take over the duties,
but as soon as he entered the door,
Zānggū would summon him away.
Shēng then rushed to inform the old woman,
hoping she would come to visit and console.
Upon entering her door,
he wept as he told his story.
Before he finished his tale,
Shānhú emerged from behind the curtain,
and Shēng was greatly ashamed,
falling silent and wanting to leave,
but Shānhú blocked the door with both hands.
Shēng, in extreme distress,
slipped out under her arm and returned home,
not daring to tell his mother either.
Not long after,
the old woman arrived,
and his mother, overjoyed, urged her to stay.
From then on, the old woman’s household sent someone over every day,
and whenever they came, they brought delicious food for the old woman.
The old woman sent a message to her widowed daughter-in-law:
"I’m not hungry here,
don’t do this again in the future."
But the gifts from home
never ceased, not even slightly.
The old woman refused to taste even a little of the food,
instead sealing it and saving it to serve to the sick woman.
His mother’s illness gradually improved.
The old woman’s young grandson also came, on his mother’s orders, bringing fine snacks to inquire after her health.
Shěn sighed and said:
"What a virtuous woman!
What good deeds did my elder sister do to deserve this!"
The old woman said:
"What kind of person does my younger sister think the divorced wife was?"
She replied:
"Alas!
She certainly wasn’t as bad as that woman of mine!
But how could she compare to the virtue of my nephew’s wife?"
The old woman said:
"When the wife was here,
you didn’t know hardship;
when you were angry,
the wife bore no resentment: in what way was she not as good?"
Shěn then shed tears,
and told her of her regret,
saying:
"Has Shānhú remarried yet?"
She replied:
"I don’t know,
let me inquire."
After several more days,
her illness was fully recovered,
and the old woman wanted to leave.
Shěn wept and said:
"I fear if my elder sister leaves,
I will still die!"
The old woman then discussed with Shēng,
to separate Èrchéng’s household.
Èrchéng told Zānggū.
Zānggū was unhappy,
her words offending her elder brother,
and also involving the old woman.
Shēng was willing to give all the good farmland to Èrchéng,
and only then was Zānggū pleased.
Once the property division deed was established,
the old woman finally left.
The next day,
she came with a carriage to fetch Shěn.
When Shěn arrived at her home,
she first asked to see her nephew’s wife,
repeatedly praising her nephew’s wife’s virtue.
The old woman said:
"With a hundred good qualities in a young woman,
how could there not be a single flaw?
I can certainly tolerate her.
Even if you had a daughter-in-law like my daughter-in-law,
I’m afraid you wouldn’t be able to enjoy her either."
Shěn said:
"Alas, how unjust!
Do you think I’m a block of wood, a stone, a deer, or a pig!
I have a mouth and a nose,
how could I not know when I encounter fragrance or stench?"
The old woman said:
"When she was divorced, like Shānhú,
I wonder what she thought of you?"
She replied:
"She cursed me."
The old woman said:
"If upon self-reflection there was nothing to curse,
then why would she curse you?"
He said:
"Faults are something people always have.
It is precisely because she is not virtuous
that I know she is being scolded."
The old woman said:
"When one does not resent those who deserve resentment,
then one can know the virtue of the one who shows kindness;
when one does not leave those who should be left,
then one can know the care of the one who comforts.
As for the one who previously sent gifts and served you;
she was certainly not your daughter-in-law,
and yet she was your daughter-in-law."
Shěn was startled and said:
"How so?"
She said:
"Shānhú has been staying here for a long time.
What was provided before,
were all things she earned by spinning at night."
When Shěn heard this,
he shed tears in streams,
saying:
"How can I face my wife now!"
The old woman then called Shānhú.
Shānhú came out with tears in her eyes,
and prostrated herself on the ground.
The mother, ashamed and pained, began to strike herself,
and only stopped after the old woman strongly urged her to,
thus they became mother-in-law and daughter-in-law as before.
After more than ten days, they returned together.
The family had only a few mu of poor land,
insufficient to support themselves,
relying solely on the husband's writing for a living,
and the wife's needlework.
Èrchéng was said to be well-off,
but the elder brother did not seek help from him,
nor did the younger brother show any concern for him.
Zānggū despised her sister-in-law for having been driven out;
the sister-in-law also detested her fierceness,
and treated her as beneath contempt.
The brothers lived in separate courtyards.
Zānggū often bullied and mistreated others,
and the whole family covered their ears to avoid hearing it.
Zānggū, having no one else to mistreat,
turned her abuse on her husband and the maidservant.
One day, the maidservant hanged herself.
The maidservant's father sued Zānggū,
Èrchéng appeared in court on behalf of his wife,
was severely beaten and reprimanded,
and Zānggū was still detained.
Dàchéng went up and down trying to secure her release,
but ultimately failed.
Zānggū had her fingers clamped in the cangue,
until the flesh was completely stripped off.
The official was greedy and cruel,
and his demands for bribes were exorbitant.
Èrchéng mortgaged the land to borrow money,
and after paying the full amount,
she was finally released and returned home.
But the creditors pressed for repayment daily,
and having no choice,
he sold all the good land to Old Man Rén in the village.
Since half the land originally belonged to Dàchéng, who had yielded it,
the old man insisted that Dàchéng sign the deed.
Dàchéng went,
and the old man suddenly said:
"I am Ān Xiàolián.
Who is this Rén,
that he dares to buy my property!"
Then he turned to Dàchéng and said:
"In the underworld, we were moved by the filial piety of you and your wife,
so I was allowed to return briefly to see you."
Dàchéng shed tears and said:
"If father has spiritual power,
please quickly save my younger brother!"
He said:
"An unfilial son with a fierce wife,
is not worth pitying!
Return home quickly and prepare money,
to redeem the property bought with my blood and sweat."
Dàchéng said:
"Mother and I are barely surviving,
how can we have so much money?"
He said:
"Under the crape myrtle tree, there is hidden gold,
you can take it and use it."
Dàchéng wanted to ask more,
but the old man had already stopped speaking;
after a short while, he woke up,
bewildered and unaware of what had happened.
Dàchéng returned and told his mother,
but she did not fully believe it.
Zānggū had already led people to dig for the treasure,
digging four or five feet into the ground,
but only found bricks and stones,
with no sign of any gold,
and left disappointed.
When Dàchéng heard they were digging for treasure,
he warned his mother and wife not to go and look.
Later, when he learned they had found nothing,
his mother secretly went to peek,
saw bricks and stones mixed in the soil,
and returned.
Shānhú went afterward,
and saw that the soil was full of silver ingots;
she called Dàchéng to verify,
and indeed it was so.
Dàchéng, considering it left by his ancestors,
could not bear to keep it for himself,
so he called Èrchéng to divide it equally.
The amount happened to be exactly divisible by two,
and each took their share home.
Èrchéng and Zānggū examined it together,
but when they opened the bag, it was full of tiles and rubble,
and they were greatly alarmed.
Suspecting that Èrchéng had been fooled by his elder brother,
she sent Èrchéng to spy on him,
and saw Dàchéng displaying the gold on the table,
celebrating with his mother.
Èrchéng then truthfully told his elder brother,
who was also shocked,
and felt great pity for him,
so he gave him all the gold,
which made Èrchéng happy.
He went to repay the debts:
and felt very grateful to his elder brother.
Zānggū said:
"This only proves how cunning your elder brother is.
If he didn't feel guilty in his heart,
who would give up their share after dividing it?"
Èrchéng was half-convinced and half-doubtful.
The next day,
the creditor sent a servant,
saying that the money repaid was all counterfeit,
and they would take it to the authorities,
leaving the couple pale with fear.
Zānggū said:
"See!
I always said your elder brother wasn't that virtuous—
this is to get you killed!"
Èrchéng was terrified,
and went to beg the creditor, but his anger would not subside.
Èrchéng then mortgaged the land to the creditor,
letting him sell it himself,
and only then got the original gold back.
Upon closer inspection,
they saw two broken gold ingots,
with only a leek-leaf-thick layer of real gold on the outside,
and the inside was all copper.
Zānggū then plotted with Èrchéng: to keep the broken ones,
and return the rest to his elder brother to test him.
And she taught him to say:
"I have repeatedly received your generous yielding,
and truly cannot bear it.
I will keep only two ingots,
to show the meaning of your kindness.
As for the remaining property,
it is still equal to yours,
and I have no need for more land.
Since it has already been sold,
whether to redeem it is up to you."
