Dàchéng did not understand their intention,
and firmly insisted on yielding.
Èrchéng refused decisively,
so Dàchéng accepted.
Weighing it, he found it was short by over five taels,
so he had Shānhú pawn her jewelry to make up the amount,
and took it to the creditor.
The creditor suspected it was the old gold,
and tested it by cutting with scissors,
finding the pattern and color perfect,
with no discrepancy,
so he accepted the gold,
and exchanged the deed with Dàchéng.
After Èrchéng returned the gold,
he thought there would surely be trouble;
but when he heard the old property had been redeemed,
he was greatly surprised.
Zānggū suspected that when digging,
the elder brother had hidden the real gold first,
and angrily went to his place,
scolding and insulting him,
so Dàchéng finally understood why the gold had been returned.
Shānhú met her with a smile and said:
"The property is still here,
why be angry?"
She had Dàchéng take out the deed and give it to them.
One night, Èrchéng dreamed that his father scolded him:
"You are unfilial and disrespectful to your elder brother,
your time in the underworld is near,
not an inch of land belongs to you—
what use is it to occupy and cling to it!"
He woke and told Zānggū,
wanting to return the land to his elder brother.
Zānggū laughed at his foolishness.
At that time, Èrchéng had two sons,
the elder seven years old,
the younger three.
Not long after,
the elder son died of smallpox.
Only then did Zānggū become afraid,
The two younger brothers had the deeds returned to their elder brother.
They insisted repeatedly,
but Shēng would not accept them.
Not long after,
the second son also died.
Zàng Gū became even more fearful
and personally placed the deeds in her sister-in-law's quarters.
As spring was nearing its end,
the fields lay wild and untilled.
Shēng had no choice
and began to cultivate them.
From then on, Zàng Gū reformed her conduct,
attending to her parents-in-law with the devotion of a filial son;
she also respected her sister-in-law to the utmost.
Before half a year had passed, the mother fell ill and passed away.
Zàng Gū wept for her with intense grief,
to the point where she could not even swallow a spoonful of water.
She said to others:
"My mother-in-law died early,
preventing me from serving her.
This is Heaven not allowing me to redeem myself!"
She bore ten children but none survived,
so she adopted her brother-in-law's son as her own.
Both husband and wife lived to a ripe old age.
Shēng had three sons, two of whom became Jìnshì.
People considered this the reward for their filial piety and fraternal love.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Without encountering the tyranny of the domineering,
one does not recognize the loyalty of the peaceful and devoted.
Is there not a shared sentiment between family and state?
When the rebellious daughter-in-law reformed, the mother died.
It seems that with a whole household practicing filial piety,
there was no virtue left to sustain her.
Zàng Gū blamed herself,
saying Heaven did not permit her self-redemption.
If not one who has comprehended the Way, who could utter such words?
Yet, though she deserved a premature death,
she lived to a ripe old age.
Heaven had indeed already forgiven her.
'Born through sorrow and hardship'—
there is truth in this saying!"
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In the south, there are Wǔtōng,
just as in the north there are foxes.
However, while fox hauntings in the north
can still be driven away by various means,
in Jiāngzhè, the Wǔtōng
would forcibly debauch and seize any beautiful woman from common households.
Parents and brothers
dared not utter a word,
making their harm especially severe.
There was a man named Zhào Hóng,
a pawnbroker from Wú.
His wife, Yán shì,
was quite graceful.
One night,
a man strode imposingly in from outside,
hand on his sword, looking all around.
The maids and old women all fled.
When Yán tried to leave,
the man blocked her way
and said:
"Do not be afraid.
I am the Fourth Lord of the Wǔtōng spirits.
I fancy you;
I will not bring you harm."
Then he lifted her by the waist as if she were a baby,
placed her on the bed,
her skirt sash came undone by itself,
and he violated her.
His stature was so immense it was unbearable;
in her dazed state, she moaned in agony, feeling near death.
The Fourth Lord also took pity,
and did not fully exert himself.
Afterward, he got off the bed
and said:
"I shall return in five days."
Then he left.
Hóng ran his pawnshop outside the gate.
That night, a maid rushed to tell him.
Knowing it was a Wǔtōng,
Hóng dared not intervene.
At dawn, he went to see his wife,
who was exhausted and could not rise.
He felt deeply ashamed
and warned the household not to spread the news.
After three or four days, the woman began to recover,
but she feared he would come again.
The maids did not dare sleep in the inner chambers,
all retreating to the outer quarters;
only the wife remained, facing the candle with sorrow, waiting.
Before long,
the Fourth Lord arrived with two others,
both refined young men.
A servant boy laid out food and wine,
and they drank with the woman.
She shrank back in shame, head bowed;
even when pressed to drink, she would not.
Her heart was filled with dread,
fearing they would take turns violating her,
which would mean her life was surely over.
The three urged each other to drink,
addressing one another as Eldest Brother or Third Brother.
Drinking until midnight,
the two guests in the seats of honor stood up together
and said:
"Today, Fourth Brother has summoned us to meet a beauty.
We should invite Second Brother and Fifth Brother to pool money for wine in celebration."
Then they took their leave and departed.
The Fourth Lord pulled the woman into the bed curtains.
She pleaded pitifully to be spared;
the Fourth Lord forced himself upon her.
Blood flowed freely,
and she fell unconscious.
Only then did the Fourth Lord leave.
The woman lay weakly on the bed,
overwhelmed by shame and indignation.
She thought of ending her own life,
but whenever she tried to hang herself, the belt would break of its own accord.
She tried repeatedly, with the same result,
suffering bitterly, unable to die.
Fortunately, the Fourth Lord did not come often,
promising to visit only once after she recovered.
After two or three months had passed,
the whole family was living in misery.
There was a man from Kuàijī named Wàn shēng,
a cousin of Zhào Hóng's,
who was fierce, brave, and skilled in archery.
One day, he visited Zhào.
As it was already evening,
and Zhào's guest quarters were occupied by family members,
he led his guest to stay in the inner courtyard.
Wàn lay awake for a long time
when he heard footsteps in the courtyard.
Peering through the window,
he saw a man enter the woman's chamber.
Suspicious,
he grabbed his knife and stealthily went to look.
He saw the man sitting shoulder to shoulder with Yán shì,
with food laid out on the table.
Flames of rage surged within him,
and he rushed inside.
The man sprang up in alarm,
hastily searching for his sword;
but Wàn's blade had already struck his skull,
splitting it open, and he fell dead.
Looking at him,
it was a small horse,
the size of a donkey.
Astonished, he questioned the woman;
she told him everything
and said:
"The other spirits will surely come.
What shall we do?"
Wàn waved his hand,
signaling her to keep silent.
He extinguished the candle, took his bow and arrows,
and hid in the darkness.
Before long,
four or five figures descended from the sky.
Wàn swiftly shot an arrow,
and the leader fell dead.
The other three roared in anger,
drawing their swords to search for the archer.
Wàn gripped his blade behind the door,
remaining perfectly still.
One of them entered;
Wàn chopped at his neck, and he too fell dead.
Still leaning against the door,
he waited a long time without hearing any sound,
then came out
and knocked to inform Zhào.
Zhào was greatly alarmed.
They lit candles and examined the scene:
one horse and two pigs lay dead in the room.
The whole family celebrated together.
Still fearing the creatures might seek revenge,
they kept Wàn at their home,
cooking the pig and horse to feed him;
the flavor was delicious,
different from ordinary delicacies.
Wàn shēng's fame
thus spread far and wide.
After staying for over a month,
with the strange occurrences completely ceased,
he prepared to take his leave.
A certain timber merchant earnestly entreated him to stay.
Previously,
Mù had a daughter who was not yet married.
Suddenly, the Wǔtōng spirit descended during the day,
appearing as a handsome man in his twenties,
saying he intended to take her as his wife.
He left a hundred taels of gold as betrothal gifts,
set an auspicious date, and departed.
As the appointed date drew near,
the entire family was terrified and fearful.
Hearing of Wàn Shēng’s reputation,
they firmly invited him to their home.
Fearing Wàn might refuse,
they concealed the true reason and did not tell him.
After a lavish banquet was concluded,
they dressed their daughter and had her come out to greet the guest.
She was sixteen or seventeen years old,
a beautiful young woman.
Wàn was startled and puzzled, not understanding the reason,
and rose from his seat to bow.
Mǜ pressed him to sit and truthfully informed him.
Wàn was initially shocked upon hearing this,
but as he had always prided himself on his courage,
he did not decline.
On the day,
Mǜ still hung colorful decorations at the door
and had Wàn sit inside the room.
As the sun set and the groom had not arrived,
they secretly thought the bridegroom was already among the doomed.
Not long after,
they saw something suddenly drop from the eaves like a bird,
and a youth in splendid attire entered.
Upon seeing Wàn,
he turned and fled.
Wàn chased him out,
and saw only a black vapor about to fly away.
He leaped and swung his knife at it,
cutting off one of its feet.
It let out a great howl and departed.
Looking down,
they saw a huge claw as large as a hand,
not knowing what creature it was;
following its trail of blood,
it led into the river.
Mǜ was overjoyed,
and hearing that Wàn was unmarried,
that very night he prepared the bridal chamber
and had him marry the daughter.
From then on, all those who had long suffered from the Wǔtōng
came to bow and request that he spend a night at their homes.
After residing there for over a year,
he finally took his wife and left.
From then on, in Wúzhōng there remained only one Wǔtōng,
which did not dare to openly cause harm.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"The Wǔtōng and the green frogs
have long deluded the common folk,
leading to rampant debauchery,
with no one daring to privately discuss
a single word of it.
Wàn Shēng is truly a man of heroic spirit in the world!"
According to the manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Jīn Shēng,
styled Yùsūn,
was from Sūzhōu.
He set up a school in Huái,
residing in the garden of a local gentry.
The garden had few buildings,
but was overgrown with flowers and trees.
When night grew deep,
the servants all dispersed,
leaving him alone and desolate,
his thoughts and feelings deeply troubled.
One night,
as the third watch was about to end, someone suddenly tapped on the door with a finger.
He hurriedly asked who it was,
and the reply was
"to borrow a light,"
the voice resembling that of the young servant from the school.
Opening the door to let them in,
he saw a beautiful girl of about sixteen,
with a maid following behind her.
Suspecting she was a demon or spirit,
he questioned her thoroughly.
The girl said:
"I thought you were a man of refined taste,
lonely and pitiable,
and unafraid of the heavy dew,
so I came to spend this fine night with you.
If I were to speak of the reason,
I would not dare to come,
and you would not dare to accept me either."
Jīn Shēng then thought she was a girl from the neighborhood eloping,
and fearing to compromise his conduct,
politely declined her.
The girl cast a sidelong glance,
and Jīn Shēng felt his soul utterly captivated.
Suddenly, he was overwhelmed and could no longer control himself.
The maid, already aware of this,
then said:
"Xiá Gū,
I shall leave now."
The girl nodded.
Then she scolded:
"If you're leaving, then leave!
What's with all this 'cloud' and 'mist' talk!"
After the maid left,
the girl laughed and said:
"Just now, there was no one in the room,
so I brought the maid along.
How foolish of me,
to let you hear my childhood name."
Jīn Shēng said,
"You are so deep and subtle,
that I fear there may be hidden dangers."
The girl said:
"In time you will know,
I assure you I will not ruin your conduct,
do not worry."
She went to the bed and loosened her garments,
revealing bracelets on her arms,
made of gold strips set with fire opals,
and adorned with twin pearls.
Once the candle was extinguished,
their light illuminated the entire room.
Jīn Shēng was even more astonished,
but could never discern where she came from.
After their intimacy,
the maid came knocking at the window.
The girl rose,
and using the bracelet's light to illuminate the path,
disappeared into the thicket of trees.
From then on, she came every night without fail.
Once, as she was leaving,
Jīn Shēng followed her from afar;
the girl seemed to have noticed,
and abruptly concealed her light.
The trees were dense and lush,
and in the darkness where he could not see his own hand, he returned.
One day,
Jīn Shēng went north of the river.
The strap of his bamboo hat broke,
and the wind threatened to blow it off,
so he repeatedly pressed it down with his hand while on horseback.
Upon reaching the river,
he boarded a small boat.
A gust of wind blew his hat off,
and it drifted away with the waves.
He felt quite disheartened.
After crossing the river,
he saw a strong wind blowing his hat,
spinning in the air;
gradually it descended,
and as he caught it with his hand,
he found the strap had been repaired.
He found this strange.
Returning to his study, he recounted the incident to the girl in detail. She said nothing,
only smiling faintly.
Jīn Shēng suspected it was her doing,
and said:
"If you are indeed a divine being,
you should clearly tell me,
to dispel my confusion and worry."
The girl said:
"In your solitude,
to have such a devoted lover to relieve your boredom,
I thought I was not doing badly.
Even if I could do such things,
it is out of love for you.
If you insist on questioning and challenging me,
do you wish to sever our ties?"
Jīn Shēng dared not speak further.
Previously,
the scholar had raised his niece.
After she married,
she was bewitched by a Wǔtōng spirit,
which troubled her heart, but she dared not tell anyone.
Since the scholar and the girl had been intimate for a long time,
they confided in each other without reservation.
The girl said:
"Such creatures
can be driven away by my father.
But how dare I tell my strict father about a lover's private affairs?"
The scholar pleaded desperately for a solution.
The girl thought for a moment and said:
"This is also easy to deal with,
but I must go in person.
Those creatures are all slaves of my family.
If even one of them touches my skin,
then this shame could not be washed away even with the waters of the West River."
The scholar continued to plead earnestly.
The girl said:
"I will plan it immediately."
The next evening she came
and told him:
"I have sent a maid south for you.
The maid is weak,
I fear she may not be able to kill it outright."
The following night, as they were about to sleep,
the maid came knocking at the door.
The scholar hurriedly let her in.
The girl asked:
"How did it go?"
She replied:
"I was not strong enough to capture it,
so I castrated it instead."
The girl laughed and asked for details.
She said:
"At first I thought it was the scholar's home;
after arriving,
I realized it was not.
When I reached the husband's house,
the lamps were already lit.
I entered and saw the young lady sitting under the lamp,
leaning on a table as if asleep.
I gathered her soul and covered it in a jar.
After a while,
the creature arrived.
It entered the room but quickly retreated,
saying: 'How can there be a living person here!'
After examining and finding nothing amiss,
it entered again.
I pretended to be unconscious.
It lifted the bedcovers to enter,
then cried out in alarm: 'How can there be the aura of a weapon!'
I originally did not want to dirty my fingers with such filth,
but fearing delay might lead to trouble,
I quickly seized and castrated it.
The creature screamed in terror
and fled.
Then I got up and opened the jar,
the young lady seemed to wake,
and I left."
The scholar joyfully thanked her,
and the girl left with the maid.
More than half a month later,
she still had not returned,
and he had already given up hope.
At the end of the year,
as he was preparing to leave the school and return home,
the girl suddenly appeared.
The scholar happily welcomed her,
saying:
"You have abandoned me for so long,
I thought I must have offended you somewhere;
are you fortunate enough not to sever ties completely?"
The girl said:
"After a year of affection,
to part without a word
would indeed be an incomplete affair.
Hearing that you are packing up,
I secretly came to bid farewell."
The scholar asked her to return with him.
The girl sighed and said:
"It is hard to explain!
Now that we are parting,
I cannot bear to hide the truth: I am actually the daughter of the Great King Jīnlóng,
because I had a predestined bond with you,
I came to be with you.
It was improper for me to send a maid to the south,
causing rumors to spread along the rivers and lakes,
saying that I had you castrate a Wǔtōng.
When my father heard of it,
he considered it a great disgrace,
and in anger wanted to have me put to death.
Fortunately, the maid took responsibility herself,
and his anger subsided somewhat;
he gave the maid over a hundred lashes.
Every step I take,
is accompanied by a governess.
I seized a moment to come here,
but cannot fully express my heartfelt feelings,
what can I do!"
Having said this,
she prepared to leave.
The scholar held her back and wept.
The girl said:
"Do not be like this,
after thirty years we can meet again."
The scholar said:
"I am already thirty years old,
in another thirty years,
I will be a white-haired old man,
how could I have the face to see you again?"
The girl said:
"Not so,
there are no white-haired old men in the dragon palace.
Moreover, the length of a person's life
is not reflected in their appearance.
If you only seek to preserve your youthful looks,
that is actually very easy."
Then she wrote a prescription on a scroll and left.
The scholar returned to his hometown,
and his niece then spoke of the strange event,
saying:
"That night it was like a dream,
I felt someone grab me and stuff me into a jar;
when I woke up,
the bed was stained with blood,
and the monster was gone."
The scholar said:
"I once prayed to the River God."
Everyone's doubts were then resolved.
Later, when the scholar was over sixty,
he still looked like a man in his thirties.
One day,
while crossing the river,
he saw from afar a lotus leaf floating upstream,
as large as a mat,
with a beautiful woman sitting on it.
As he looked closer,
it was the goddess.
He leaped to follow her,
and as he did, the lotus leaf grew smaller,
gradually shrinking to the size of a coin before vanishing.
This incident and the one about Zhào Hóng
both occurred in the late Ming dynasty,
though it is unclear which came first.
If it happened after Wàn Shēng used force,
then only half a Tōng remained in Wúxià,
so it was naturally insufficient to cause harm.
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
By the side of the Jīng River,
there was a scholar’s son named Shēn,
whose family was extremely poor,
and who often went all day without lighting a cooking fire.
Husband and wife faced each other,
with no plan to rely on.
His wife said:
“There’s no other way—
could you perhaps become a thief?”
Shēn replied:
“A scholar’s son,
unable to uphold the family honor,
yet to disgrace the household and shame his ancestors—
better to live as a bandit,
than to die as a righteous man!”
His wife angrily said:
“You want to live but hate disgrace?
In this world, those who do not farm yet must eat
have only two paths: since you cannot steal,
I would rather be a prostitute!”
Shēn grew furious,
and they exchanged harsh words.
His wife went to bed seething with anger.
Shēn thought: “As a man, I cannot provide two meals a day,
to the point that my wife wishes to become a prostitute—
truly better to die!”
He quietly rose,
and hanged himself from a tree in the courtyard.
Then he saw his father approach,
who exclaimed in alarm:
“Foolish child,
how could it come to this!”
He cut the rope,
and instructed him:
“You can become a thief,
but you must hide in deep patches of grain.
This venture can bring wealth,
no need to do it again.”
His wife heard the sound of something falling to the ground,
and woke with a start;
she called her husband but got no reply;
lighting a torch to search,
she saw the noose broken on the tree,
and Shēn lying dead beneath it.
She was greatly terrified.
Rubbing and pressing him,
after a while he revived,
and she helped him lie down on the bed.
Her anger subsided somewhat.
When day broke,
using her husband’s illness as a pretext,
she begged the neighbors for some thin gruel to feed Shēn.
After Shēn finished sipping it,
he went out and left.
By noon,
he returned carrying a sack of rice.
His wife asked where it came from,
and he said:
“My father’s friends are all from established families;
previously, I considered begging shameful,
so I disdained to ask them for help.
The ancients said: ‘When one is in dire straits, there is nothing one may not do.’
Now I am about to become a thief—
why should I care about that!
Quickly cook this,
I will follow your advice,
and go commit robbery.”
His wife suspected he had not forgotten his earlier anger at her words,
and bore it in silence.
She then washed the rice to make porridge.
After Shēn ate his fill,
he urgently sought a sturdy piece of wood,
fashioned it with an axe into a club,
and prepared to go out holding it.
His wife, observing that his intention seemed genuine,
pulled him back to stop him.
Shēn said:
“You taught me to do this.
If the affair fails and implicates you,
do not regret it!”
He tore himself free and left.
At dusk,
he reached a neighboring village,
and hid about a li away from the village.
Suddenly a heavy rain fell,
drenching him from head to toe.
Gazing into the distance at a dense grove of trees,
he decided to head there for shelter.
But with a flash of lightning,
he saw he was already near the village wall.
Far off, there seemed to be a traveler;
fearing he might be spotted, and noticing dense grain growing beneath the wall,
he hurried over and entered it,
crouching to hide inside.
Not long after,
a man came along,
very tall and robust,
and also ducked into the grain.
Shēn was afraid,
and dared not move at all.
Fortunately, the man went off at an angle.
Peering cautiously,
Shēn saw him enter through the wall.
Silently recalling that inside the wall was the mansion of the wealthy Kàng family,
he thought this must be a gentleman of the beams (a thief),
and if he waited for him to come out with his heavy haul,
he ought to get a share.
Then he thought again: this man was strong and vigorous;
if he took the loot by force and refused to share,
it would surely come to blows.
Judging that his own strength was no match,
it would be better to take him by surprise and knock him down.
His plan settled,
he lay in wait with full concentration.
Just before the rooster crowed,
the man finally climbed over the wall and emerged.
Before his feet touched the ground,
Shēn sprang up violently,
striking him in the waist and spine with his club,
and the man toppled with a thud.
It turned out to be a giant turtle,
its mouth gaping like a basin.
Greatly shocked,
Shēn struck it several more times in succession,
and it died.
Earlier,
Old Man Kàng had a daughter,
exceedingly clever and beautiful,
whom her parents both dearly loved.
One night,
a man entered her chamber,
molested and forced himself on her.
When she tried to scream,
his tongue was already in her mouth,
and she fell unconscious,
letting him do as he pleased before he left.
Ashamed to tell anyone,
she only gathered more maids and elderly women,
and secured the doors and windows tightly.
Yet at night after they had gone to bed,
they did not know how the door opened by itself: when he entered the room, everyone became dazed,
and the maids and elderly women were all violated.
So they told each other in alarm,
and reported it to the old man;
the old man ordered the household to take up weapons and surround the embroidered chamber,
while the people inside sat by candlelight.
Around midnight,
everyone inside and outside suddenly fell into a stupor,
then as if waking from a dream,
they saw the girl lying naked,
appearing dazed,
and only after a long while did she come to.
The old man deeply resented this,
but could do nothing about it.
After several months,
the girl became as thin as firewood and was near death.
He often told people:
“If anyone can drive this away,
I will reward them with three hundred in gold.”
Shēn had also heard of this before.
That night, having obtained the turtle,
he realized the thing haunting the old man’s daughter
must be this creature.
So he knocked on the door to claim the reward.
The old man was delighted,
invited him to the seat of honor,
had people carry the turtle into the courtyard,
and cut it into pieces.
He kept Shēn overnight,
and indeed the monster ceased to appear,
so he gave him the promised sum.
Shēn carried the gold home.
His wife, because he had not returned the previous night,
was just then anxiously watching for him;
seeing Shēn enter,
she hurriedly asked him about it.
Shēn did not speak,
but placed the silver on the bed.
His wife opened it and looked,
nearly dying of fright.
She said:
"Did you really become a thief?"
Shēn said:
"You forced me into this,
and now you say such words!"
His wife wept and said:
"Before, I was only joking with you.
Now you have committed a crime punishable by beheading;
I cannot bear to be implicated as a thief's wife.
Let me die first!"
Then she ran out.
Shēn chased after her,
laughed, pulled her back, and returned her inside,
fully telling her the truth.
His wife then rejoiced.
From then on, they planned their livelihood
and became known as wealthy commoners.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"People should not worry about poverty,
but about lacking virtue.
Those whose conduct is upright,
even if they starve, will not die;
even if they are not pitied by others,
they will still have the protection of ghosts.
Among the poor of this world,
where profit lies, they forget righteousness;
where food lies, they forget shame.
Others dare not entrust them with even a single coin,
so how can they expect understanding from ghosts and spirits?"
In the county, there was a certain poor man, Yǐ,
as the end of the year approached,
he had no whole garment on his body.
He thought to himself: How will I see out the year?
Not daring to speak with his wife,
he secretly took a white club,
went out and hid in a graveyard,
hoping that someone traveling alone would pass by,
so he could rob them of their possessions.
He waited with great hardship,
but there was not a trace of anyone;
the pine wind pierced his bones,
and he could no longer endure it.
Just as he was on the verge of giving up,
he suddenly saw a hunched figure approaching.
His heart secretly rejoiced,
and he rushed out with his club.
It was an old man carrying a bag by the roadside,
who pleaded:
"I truly have nothing of value on me.
My family has no food,
and I have just begged five sheng of rice from my son-in-law's house."
Yǐ seized the rice,
and also wanted to strip off the old man's padded jacket.
The old man bitterly pleaded.
Yǐ took pity on his age,
released him,
and carried the rice home.
His wife questioned where it came from,
and he deceitfully
replied, "gambling debts."
Secretly, he thought this method was quite good.
The next night, he went again.
Not long after,
he saw a man carrying a club approach,
also entering the graveyard,
squatting down to look around,
seeming to be of the same profession.
Yǐ then cautiously emerged from behind a grave mound.
The man asked in surprise:
"Who is it?"
He replied:
"A traveler."
The man asked:
"Why aren't you traveling?"
He said:
"Waiting for you."
The man laughed.
Each understood the other's intent,
and they spoke of the hardships of hunger and cold.
The night grew deep,
and they had caught nothing.
Yǐ wanted to return,
but the man said:
"Although you are in this line of work,
you are still a novice.
In the village ahead, there is a family marrying off their daughter;
they are busy preparing late into the night,
and the whole family must be exhausted.
Come with me,
and we'll share whatever we get fairly."
Yǐ was pleased
and followed him.
They reached a gate,
and through the wall heard the sound of steam-bread being made,
knowing they were not yet asleep.
They hid and waited.
Before long,
a person opened the gate, shouldered a pole, and went out to fetch water.
The two seized the opportunity to slip in.
They saw lamplight shining in the northern room,
while the other rooms were all dark.
They heard an old woman say:
"Eldest daughter,
go take a look in the eastern room.
Your dowry is all in the chest;
have you forgotten to lock it or not?"
They heard a young girl's voice, lazy and coquettish.
The two secretly rejoiced
and stealthily headed to the eastern room,
groping in the dark until they found a sleeping chest.
They opened the lid and felt inside,
but it was deep and they could not reach the bottom.
The man said to Yǐ:
"Go in!"
Yǐ indeed went in
and found a bundle,
passing it out.
The man asked:
"Is that all?"
Yǐ said:
"That's all."
The man tricked him, saying:
"Search again."
Then he closed the chest
and locked it before leaving.
Yǐ was inside,
in desperate straits with no plan.
Before long,
lamplight entered the room,
first shining on the chest.
They heard the old woman say:
"Who has already locked it?"
Then the mother and daughter got onto the bed and extinguished the candle.
Yǐ grew extremely anxious
and made the sound of a mouse gnawing on something.
The girl said:
"There's a mouse in the chest!"
The old woman said:
"Don't let it ruin your clothes.
I am utterly exhausted;
you should go check it yourself."
The girl shook out her clothes and got up,
unlocked and opened the chest.
Yǐ suddenly leaped out,
and the girl collapsed in fright.
Yǐ unbolted the gate and fled.
Although he had gained nothing,
he secretly rejoiced at having escaped.
The family marrying off their daughter had been robbed,
and news spread in all directions.
Some suspected Yǐ.
Yǐ, afraid,
fled east for a hundred li
and became a hired laborer for an innkeeper.
After over a year,
rumors gradually subsided.
He then brought his wife to live with him
and no longer practiced the white club trade.
This is his own account,
and because it resembles Shēn's story,
it is appended here.
Based on the manuscript version of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Hóng Dàyè,
a man from the capital,
had a wife named Zhū shì,
who was quite beautiful,
and the two loved each other dearly.
Later, Hóng took a maid named Bǎodài as his concubine.
Though her looks were far inferior to Zhū’s,
Hóng doted on her.
Zhū was displeased,
and they often quarreled over this.
Though Hóng dared not openly stay with his concubine,
he only doted on Bǎodài more,
and grew distant from Zhū.
Later, they moved to a new residence,
and became neighbors with a silk merchant surnamed Dí.
Dí’s wife, Héngniáng,
first came over to visit Zhū.
Héngniáng was around thirty,
with only average looks,
but her light and charming speech pleased Zhū.
The next day,
Zhū returned the visit,
and saw that in her household there was also a young concubine,
around twenty years old,
very lovely.
They had been neighbors for almost half a year,
yet never once heard any quarrelsome words from them;
and Dí loved only Héngniáng,
while the concubine was merely an empty title.
One day, Zhū saw Héngniáng and asked her:
"I used to think that a husband’s love for his concubine
was because she was a concubine,
and I often wished to exchange the titles of wife and concubine,
but now I know it is not so.
What method do you have?
If it can be taught,
I would gladly become your disciple."
Héngniáng said:
"Ha!
You are the one who distances yourself,
yet you blame the man?
Nagging him morning and night,
is like driving sparrows into the thicket—
it only makes the separation worse!
Go back and indulge him even more,
and even if the man comes to you,
do not accept him.
After a month,
I will plan for you again."
Zhū followed her words,
dressing Bǎodài even more finely,
and having her sleep with her husband.
When serving meals,
she also had Bǎodài join them.
Whenever Hóng tried to attend to Zhū,
Zhū refused him even more firmly,
so everyone praised Zhū shì as virtuous.
After more than a month like this,
Zhū went to see Héngniáng.
Héngniáng said happily:
"You have it!
Go back and ruin your makeup,
wear no fine clothes,
no rouge or powder,
dirty your face and wear worn-out shoes,
and mix with the servants in their work.
After a month,
you may come again."
Zhū obeyed: she wore patched, worn clothes,
deliberately kept herself unclean,
and did nothing but spin and weave.
Hóng pitied her,
and had Bǎodài share her labor;
Zhū would not accept it,
and often scolded her away.
After a month like this,
she went again to see Héngniáng.
Héngniáng said:
"You truly can be taught!
The day after tomorrow is the Shangsi Festival,
I wish to invite you to stroll in the spring garden.
You must discard all your worn clothes,
your robe, trousers, socks, and shoes
must be brand new,
and come to me early."
Zhū said:
"Yes."
On that day,
she looked in the mirror and carefully applied makeup,
exactly as Héngniáng had taught.
After finishing her makeup,
she went to Héngniáng.
Héngniáng said happily:
"Good!"
She then helped her tie a phoenix bun,
so glossy it could reflect a shadow.
Her robe sleeves were not in fashion,
so she unpicked the seams,
and remade them;
said her shoe style was clumsy,
took a pair of ready-made shoes from her box,
and finished them together.
When done,
she had Zhū change into them at once.
At parting,
she gave her wine to drink,
and instructed:
"When you return and see your man,
close the door early and sleep.
If he comes knocking,
do not answer.
Only on the third call,
may you let him in once.
If he seeks kisses with his mouth,
or seeks with his hands and feet,
be stingy with them all.
After half a month,
come again."
Zhū returned,
and showed off her makeup to Hóng.
Hóng stared at her up and down,
his joy and laughter different from usual.
Zhū spoke a little about her stroll,
then rested her chin on her hand, acting coy;
before dusk had fallen,
she rose and entered her room,
closed the door and slept.
Not long after,
Hóng indeed came knocking,
but Zhū lay firmly, not rising,
and Hóng left.
The next evening was the same.
The following day,
Hóng reproached her.
Zhū said:
"I am used to sleeping alone,
and cannot bear disturbance again."
When the sun had set,
Hóng entered her chamber and sat waiting.
They put out the candle and went to bed,
like newlyweds,
intimate and very happy.
He tried to make a date for the next night,
but Zhū refused;
finally making an agreement with Hóng
to meet once every three days.
About half a month later,
she visited Héngniáng again.
Héngniáng closed the door and said to her:
"From now on, you can monopolize his affection.
However, although you are beautiful,
you lack charm.
With your looks,
a single charming glance could snatch away Xīshī's favor,
let alone those lesser ones!"
So she tried making her squint,
and said:
"No!
The flaw lies in the outer corner of the eye."
She tried making her smile,
and again said:
"No!
The flaw lies in the left cheek."
Then she demonstrated a charming glance with autumn-wave eyes,
and a radiant smile revealing the fine teeth slightly,
making Zhū imitate her.
After dozens of attempts,
she finally grasped a rough approximation.
Héngniáng said:
"Go home now,
practice in front of the mirror until you are proficient,
and there will be no more techniques left.
As for matters within the bedchamber,
act according to the situation,
cater to his preferences,
these cannot be conveyed in words."
Zhū returned,
and followed Héngniáng's teachings exactly.
Hóng was greatly delighted,
utterly captivated in body and spirit,
fearing only that she might reject him.
As dusk approached,
they would flirt and joke together,
never leaving the inner chambers even a step,
making it a daily routine,
and he could not bring himself to send her away.
Zhū treated Bǎodài even better,
whenever there was a feast in the room,
she would call her to sit together on the couch;
but Hóng found Bǎodài increasingly ugly,
and before the feast ended,
he would send her away.
Zhū tricked her into Bǎodài's room,
locked the door,
so Hóng had no contact with her all night.
Thus Bǎodài grew to resent Hóng,
complaining and slandering him to others.
Hóng became even more disgusted and angry with her,
gradually resorting to whipping and beating.
Bǎodài, filled with resentment,
neglected her appearance,
wearing tattered, dirty shoes,
her hair like tangled weeds,
no longer resembling a human being.
One day, Héngniáng said to Zhū:
"How is my technique?"
Zhū said:
"The method is extremely subtle;
but although your disciple can follow it,
she still cannot fully understand it.
Letting him indulge,
why is that?"
She said:
"Have you not heard: human nature tires of the old and delights in the new,
values what is hard to get and takes lightly what is easy?
A husband's love for a concubine,
is not necessarily because she is beautiful,
but because he relishes what he has newly obtained,
and treasures what is hard to come by.
If you let him indulge to satiety,
even delicacies become tiresome,
let alone coarse food!"
"Why ruin her and then show her off again?"
She said:
"If you keep something out of sight,
it seems like a long separation;
suddenly seeing her in gorgeous attire,
it feels like a new arrival: like a poor man suddenly getting fine grain and meat,
then coarse rice seems tasteless.
And if you are not easily attainable,
then she is old and you are new,
she is easy and you are hard to get,
this is the method of changing a wife into a concubine."
Zhū was greatly pleased,
and they became close friends in the inner chambers.
After several years,
she suddenly said to Zhū:
"Our feelings are like one body,
I should not hide my origins from you.
I wanted to tell you earlier but feared you would doubt;
now that we are about to part,
I dare to tell you the truth: I am a fox spirit.
In my youth, I suffered a change due to my stepmother,
and was sold in the capital.
My husband treated me well,
so I could not bear to leave abruptly,
lingering until now.
Tomorrow my old father will undergo liberation of the corpse,
I am going to visit him,
and will not return."
Zhū held her hand and sighed.
Early the next morning, she went to see her,
only to find the whole household in panic,
Héngniáng had vanished without a trace.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"Those who buy pearls do not value the pearl but the box: the feelings of new versus old, easy versus hard,
for millennia cannot break their delusion;
and the technique of turning hatred into love,
thus finds its place among them.
In ancient times, treacherous ministers serving their lord,
would not let him see people,
nor let him read books.
From this we know that preserving one's position and securing favor,
all have their secret transmissions."
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Cháng Dàyòng,
was from Luòyáng.
He had a passion for peonies.
Hearing that Cáozhōu peonies were the best in Qí and Lǔ,
his heart yearned to see them.
It happened that he had business in Cáozhōu,
so he borrowed a garden from a local gentry to stay.
It was then the second month,
and the peonies had not yet bloomed,
so he could only wander in the garden,
gazing intently at the sprouting buds,
hoping they would burst open.
He composed a hundred quatrains longing for the peonies.
Before long,
the flowers gradually formed buds,
but his travel funds were nearly exhausted;
he pawned his spring clothes,
lingering and reluctant to leave.
One day,
he went to the flower garden at dawn,
and found a young lady and an old woman there.
Suspecting they were from a noble family,
he quickly turned back.
In the evening, he went again,
and saw them once more,
he discreetly avoided them.
Peeking slightly,
she was dressed in palace attire, stunningly beautiful.
In his dazzled confusion,
a sudden thought occurred: she must be an immortal,
for how could such a woman exist in this world!
He hurriedly turned to search for her,
rushing past the rockery,
and happened to meet the old woman.
The young lady was sitting on a rock,
they looked at each other in surprise.
The old woman shielded the girl with her body,
and scolded:
"What does this madman want!"
The scholar knelt down and said:
"This lady must be a celestial being!"
The old woman rebuked him:
"Such wild talk,
you should be bound and sent to the magistrate!"
The scholar was terrified.
The young lady smiled and said:
"Let him go!"
Then they went over the hill and left.
The scholar returned,
unable to walk steadily,
thinking the young lady would tell her father and brothers,
and they would surely come to insult him: he lay down in his empty study,
regretting his rashness.
Secretly glad that the young lady showed no anger,
perhaps she would not hold it against him.
Regret and fear mingled,
and by nightfall he fell ill.
By mid-morning the next day,
relieved that no punitive force had come,
his mind gradually calmed.
But recalling her voice and appearance,
his fear turned to longing.
After three days like this,
he was haggard and near death.
Holding a candle late at night,
when his servant was sound asleep,
the old woman entered,
holding a bowl and offering it, saying:
"Our Lady Gějīn has personally prepared a poisoned soup;
drink it quickly!"
The scholar was shocked upon hearing this,
but then said:
"I and the lady have never had any enmity or grievance;
why must I be sentenced to death?
Since it was personally prepared by the lady,
rather than suffer lovesickness and illness,
I would prefer to drink the poison and die!"
He then raised the bowl and drank it all.
The old woman laughed,
took the bowl, and left.
The scholar felt the medicine's aroma cool and fragrant,
unlike poison.
Soon he felt his chest and diaphragm relax and clear,
his head light and refreshed,
and fell into a deep sleep.
When he awoke,
the bright sun filled the window.
He tried to rise,
and his illness seemed to have vanished.
His heart grew more convinced she was an immortal.
With no way to seek her out,
he could only, when no one was around,
visualize the places where she had stood or sat,
and bow reverently in silent prayer.
One day,
as he was walking,
he suddenly met the young lady face-to-face amidst the deep trees.
Fortunately, there were no others around.
Overjoyed,
he threw himself to the ground.
The young lady approached and pulled him up.
Suddenly, he smelled an extraordinary fragrance enveloping her body.
He immediately grasped her jade-like wrist and rose.
Her skin felt soft and smooth to the touch,
making his very bones feel as if they would melt.
Just as he was about to speak,
the old woman suddenly arrived.
The young lady told him to hide behind a rock,
pointed south, and said:
"Tonight, use a ladder of flowers to climb over the wall.
The room with red windows on all four sides is where I live."
Then she hurried away.
The scholar was disconsolate,
his soul seemed to scatter,
not knowing where she had gone.
That night,
he moved a ladder and climbed the southern wall,
only to find a ladder already placed below.
Delighted, he descended.
Sure enough, there were red windows,
and from inside the room came the sound of chess pieces being played.
He stood still, not daring to proceed further,
and reluctantly climbed back over the wall to return.
After a short while,
he went back again.
The sound of chess pieces was still frequent.
Gradually approaching to peek inside,
he saw the young lady playing chess opposite a beauty dressed in white.
The old woman was also seated there,
with a maidservant in attendance.
He turned back again.
After going back and forth like this three times,
the third watch of the night was already urging.
Crouching on the ladder,
he heard the old woman come out and say:
"A ladder!
Who placed this here?"
She called the maidservant, and together they moved it away.
The scholar, now on top of the wall,
wanted to descend but had no steps.
Full of resentment and melancholy, he returned.
The next night, he went again,
and the ladder was already set up beforehand.
Fortunately, it was quiet with no one around.
He entered and found the young lady sitting alone,
as if lost in thought.
Seeing the scholar, she rose in surprise,
standing sideways with a shy expression.
The scholar bowed and said:
"I had thought myself lacking in fortune,
fearing I had no share with a heavenly being.
Yet I have this night!"
He then embraced her intimately.
Her slender waist was just a handful,
her breath fragrant like orchids.
Pushing him away, she said:
"Why so sudden!"
The scholar said:
"Good things face many obstacles;
delay invites the envy of ghosts."
Before he finished speaking,
they heard voices in the distance.
The young lady said urgently:
"My younger sister Yùbǎn is coming!
You can hide under the bed for now."
The scholar complied.
Shortly after,
a young woman entered,
laughing and saying:
"A defeated general,
dare you speak of battle again?
I've already brewed tea,
and venture to invite you for a night of revelry."
The young lady declined, pleading fatigue.
Yùbǎn insisted on inviting her,
but the young lady firmly remained seated, refusing to go.
Yùbǎn said:
"So reluctant to leave,
could you be hiding a man in your room?"
She forcibly pulled her out the door and left.
The scholar crawled out from under the bed,
utterly frustrated.
He then searched the pillows and mats,
hoping to find some keepsake she had left behind.
There was no vanity case in the room,
only a crystal ruyi scepter by the bedside,
tied with a purple scarf,
fragrant and clean, lovely to behold.
He tucked it into his robe,
climbed back over the wall, and returned home.
Adjusting his lapels and sleeves,
the fragrance of her body still lingered upon him.
His admiration grew even more intense.
However, the fear from hiding under the bed
brought with it the apprehension of facing punishment.
He pondered and dared not go again,
but only treasured the ruyi scepter,
hoping she would come looking for it.
The night after next,
the young lady indeed came.
Laughing, she said:
"I once thought you a gentleman,
but now I know you are a thief."
The scholar said:
"Indeed, I am.
The reason I occasionally do not act like a gentleman
is solely in the hope of obtaining your ruyi."
He then drew her into his embrace
and began to untie the fastenings of her skirt.
As her jade-like skin was first revealed,
a warm fragrance flowed all around.
In their close embrace,
he felt her breath and the scent of her perspiration—
every exhalation was fragrant.
Therefore, he said:
"I always believed you were an immortal,
and now I am even more certain it is true.
Fortunately, you have favored me with your regard;
our bond spans three lifetimes.
Yet I fear that even if Dù Lánxiāng were to marry a mortal,
it would ultimately end in parting sorrow."
The young lady laughed and said:
"Your worries are excessive.
I am merely a lovesick maiden like the soul-separated Qiàn Nǚ,
momentarily moved by passion.
This matter must be kept secret and discreet.
I fear wagging tongues
that fabricate black and white.
You cannot grow wings,
nor can I ride the wind."
Then the calamity of separation would be even more unbearable than the pain of parting."
The scholar agreed with her,
but still suspected she was an immortal,
so he firmly pressed for her name.
The woman said,
"Since you consider me an immortal,
why must an immortal transmit her name?"
He asked:
"Who is the old woman?"
She replied:
"This is Sāng Lǎo.
When I was young, I received her care and protection,
so she is not treated the same as the maidservants."
Then she rose,
wishing to leave,
saying:
"There are many eyes and ears where I reside,
I cannot linger long.
When an opportunity arises, I will come again."
Before parting,
she asked for the rúyì,
saying:
"This is not my belonging,
but was left behind by Yùbǎn."
He asked:
"Who is Yùbǎn?"
She replied:
"She is my cousin."
Handing over the hairpin, she departed.
After she left,
the pillow and bedding were all imbued with a strange fragrance.
From then on, she would come once every two or three nights.
The scholar was captivated by her,
and no longer thought of returning home.
But his purse was now empty,
and he considered selling his horse.
The woman learned of this,
and said:
"Because of me,
you have emptied your purse and pawned your clothes—
this is something my heart cannot bear.
Moreover, if you part with your means of travel,
how will you return over a thousand lǐ?
I have some private savings,
which may briefly assist with your provisions."
The scholar declined, saying:
"Your affection,
touching my heart and swearing by my flesh,
is beyond any repayment; yet to be greedy and base,
consuming your wealth—
how could I still be considered a man!"
The woman insisted strongly,
saying:
"Consider it a loan to you."
Then she took the scholar's arm,
led him to a mulberry tree,
pointed at a stone,
and said,
"Turn it!"
The scholar complied.
She then pulled out a hairpin from her hair,
poked the soil several dozen times,
and said again:
"Dig it."
The scholar again complied.
Then the mouth of a jar appeared.
The woman reached in
and took out about fifty taels of silver;
the scholar held her arm to stop her,
but she would not listen,
taking out more than ten more ingots.
The scholar forcibly returned half of them before covering the jar again.
One evening,
she said to the scholar:
"Recently there have been slight rumors,
the situation cannot last long,
we must plan for this in advance."
The scholar was alarmed and said:
"What shall we do then!
I have always been迂腐 and cautious,
but now for your sake,
like a widow who has lost her chastity,
I can no longer control myself.
I will follow your command entirely;
even if faced with knives, saws, axes, or halberds,
I will not have time to consider them!"
The woman planned to elope together,
telling the scholar to return first,
and arranging to meet in Luò.
The scholar prepared his luggage and returned to his hometown,
intending to go home first and then fetch her;
but when he arrived,
the woman's carriage had just reached his gate.
She entered the hall and paid respects to his family,
startling and delighting the neighbors,
who did not know she had secretly fled.
The scholar secretly felt anxious;
but the woman was utterly calm,
saying to the scholar:
"Not to mention that a thousand lǐ away is beyond the reach of patrols,
even if they knew,
I am a daughter of a distinguished family—
Zhuō Wángsūn could do nothing to Sīmǎ Xiàngrú."
The scholar's younger brother, Dàqì,
was sixteen years old,
and the woman looked at him and said:
"He has virtuous roots,
his future prospects are even better than yours."
When the time for his marriage arrived,
his betrothed suddenly passed away.
The woman said:
"My cousin Yùbǎn,
whom you have certainly glimpsed before,
is quite fair in appearance,
and of similar age;
as husband and wife they would make a fine match."
The scholar heard this and laughed,
playfully asking her to act as matchmaker.
The woman said:
"If you truly wish to bring her here,
it is not difficult."
He happily asked:
"What method?"
She replied:
"My cousin and I are very close.
With two horses pulling a light carriage,
it only requires an old woman to make a round trip."
The scholar feared their previous affair would be exposed,
and did not dare follow her plan.
The woman firmly stated:
"It is harmless."
She then ordered a carriage,
and sent Sāng Lǎo off.
After several days,
they reached Cáo.
Approaching the village gate,
the old woman got off the carriage,
telling the driver to stop and wait on the road,
and entered the village under cover of night.
After a long while,
she returned with the young woman,
boarded the carriage and set off,
resting in the carriage at dusk,
and resuming the journey at the fifth watch.
The woman calculated the time,
and had Dàqì, dressed in fine clothes, go to meet them about fifty lǐ away,
where they encountered each other.
He drove the carriage wheel home,
with drums, flutes, flowers, and candles,
and they bowed to complete the wedding ceremony.
From then on, both brothers obtained beautiful wives,
and the family grew increasingly wealthy.
One day,
several dozen mounted bandits
suddenly burst into the estate.
The scholar knew there was trouble,
and the whole family went upstairs.
The bandits entered
and surrounded the building.
The scholar looked down and asked:
"Do you have any grievance against us?"
They replied:
"No grievance.
But we have two requests: first, we have heard that the two ladies are unmatched in this world,
we ask to see them once;
second, there are fifty-eight of us,
each begging for five hundred in gold."
They gathered firewood under the building;
planning to threaten them by setting it ablaze.
The scholar agreed to their demand for gold;
but the bandits were unsatisfied,
and wanted to burn the building,
terrifying the family.
The woman wished to go downstairs with Yùbǎn,
but the scholar tried to stop them, to no avail.
They descended in dazzling attire,
stopping three steps from the bottom,
and said to the bandits:
"My sister and I are both immortal maidens,
temporarily treading the mortal world—
why should we fear bandits!
We would give you ten thousand in gold,
but I fear you would not dare accept it."
The bandits all bowed together in reverence,
murmuring
"We dare not."
The sisters were about to withdraw,
when one bandit said:
"This is a trick!"
Hearing this, the woman
turned and stood still,
saying:
"What do you intend to do?
Plan it early,
it is not yet too late."
The bandits looked at each other,
silent and wordless.
The sisters calmly went back upstairs and left.
The bandits looked up and saw no trace of them,
and only then dispersed in an uproar.
Two years later,
the sisters each gave birth to a son,
and gradually began to reveal:
"Our surname is Wèi,
and our mother is titled Lady of the State of Cáo."
Shēng wondered why there was no aristocratic family named Wèi in Cáo,
and moreover, how could such a prominent family lose their daughters
and simply
leave the matter unresolved?
He dared not press for details,
but secretly found it strange.
Thus, he found an excuse to visit Cáo again,
and upon entering the region, he inquired around,
but found no aristocratic family named Wèi.
So he again lodged at his former host's place.
Suddenly, he saw a poem dedicated to Lady of the State of Cáo on the wall,
which greatly alarmed him,
so he questioned the host.
The host laughed
and immediately invited him to go see Lady Cáo.
When they arrived, there was a peony plant
as tall as the eaves.
When asked how it got its name,
he was told that because its flowers were ranked first in Cáo,
friends jokingly bestowed the title upon it.
When asked
"What variety is it?"
he replied:
"It is the Gězhōngzǐ."
Shēng was even more alarmed,
and began to suspect that the woman was a flower spirit.
After returning home,
he did not dare to confront her directly,
but only recited the poem dedicated to Lady Cáo to test her.
The woman's expression changed abruptly,
and she hurriedly called Yùbǎn to bring the child over,
saying to Shēng:
"Three years ago,
moved by your affection,
I presented myself to repay you;
now that you suspect me,
how can we stay together any longer!"
Then, together with Yùbǎn, she lifted the child and threw him from afar,
and the child fell to the ground and vanished.
As Shēng looked on in shock,
both women had disappeared.
He was filled with endless regret.
A few days later,
two peony plants sprouted where the child had fallen,
growing a foot tall overnight,
and blooming that same year—
one purple, one white,
with flowers as large as plates,
and compared to ordinary Gězhōngzǐ
and Yùbǎn varieties, their petals were even more numerous and delicate.
After a few years,
they grew into lush clusters;
when transplanted elsewhere,
they mutated into different varieties,
and no one could identify their names.
From then on, the splendor of peonies
was unmatched in Luòyáng.
Now, the Historian of the Strange comments:
"With single-minded devotion,
one can communicate with spirits;
even those who seem fickle cannot be said to lack affection.
When the young official felt lonely,
he took a flower as his wife—
especially since it could truly understand speech,
why must one exhaustively seek its origins?
It is a pity that Cháng Shēng failed to grasp this!"
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Governor Zhōu Yǒudé
renovated a former princely mansion into a government office.
At the time, workers were being gathered,
and carpenter Féng Mínghuán was staying overnight there.
As he was about to sleep one night,
he suddenly saw the latticed window half-open,
with moonlight as bright as day.
Looking into the distance over the short wall,
he saw a red chicken standing there;
as he stared,
the chicken flew down to the ground.
Soon, a young girl
peeked out, half-exposed.
Féng suspected she was meeting someone secretly;
listening quietly,
he found everyone else was sound asleep.
His heart pounded with anxiety,
secretly hoping she had mistaken her way.
After a while,
the girl indeed climbed through the window;
and went straight into his embrace.
Féng was delighted,
and remained silent.
After their intimacy,
the girl left.
From then on, she came every night.
At first, she kept it hidden,
but later she openly told him.
The girl said:
"I did not come by mistake,
but respectfully sought you out."
Their affection grew deeper each day.
Later, when the work was completed,
Féng prepared to return home,
and the girl was already waiting in the wilderness.
Féng's village
was not far from the city,
so the girl followed him there.
Once inside the house,
none of his family members could see her,
and Féng realized she was not human.
After several months,
his energy gradually declined,
and he grew more fearful,
so he hired a priest to exorcise her,
but it had no effect.
One night,
the girl came in splendid attire,
and said to Féng:
"All worldly ties are predestined: what is meant to come cannot be pushed away,
and what is meant to leave cannot be held back.
Now I must bid you farewell."
Then she left.
Based on the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Mǎ Zǐcái
was from Shùntiān.
His family had always loved chrysanthemums,
and he was especially fond of them.
Whenever he heard of a fine variety,
he would purchase it,
not minding traveling a thousand *li*.
One day,
a guest from Jīnlíng stayed at his home,
claiming that his cousin had one or two varieties
not found in the north.
Mǎ was excited,
immediately packed his bags,
and followed the guest to Jīnlíng.
The guest made every effort to obtain them,
and managed to get two sprouts,
which Mǎ wrapped and treasured like jewels.
On his way back,
he met a young man
riding a donkey alongside an ornate carriage,
with an elegant and graceful demeanor.
As they drew closer, they began to talk.
The young man said:
"My surname is Táo."
His speech was refined and poetic.
He asked Mǎ where he was coming from,
and Mǎ told him honestly.
The young man said:
"No variety is inherently poor;
it all depends on cultivation."
Then they discussed methods of growing chrysanthemums.
Mǎ was greatly pleased,
and asked:
"Where are you headed?"
He replied:
"My sister is tired of Jīnlíng
and wishes to settle in Héshuò."
Mǎ happily said:
"Though I am poor,
my humble cottage can offer lodging.
If you do not mind its simplicity,
there is no need to seek elsewhere."
Táo went to the carriage
to consult his sister.
The person inside lifted the curtain to speak—
a stunning beauty around twenty years old.
She said to her brother:
"The house need not be grand,
but the courtyard should be spacious."
Mǎ agreed on their behalf,
and they returned together.
To the south, there was a neglected garden,
with only a small hut of three or four rafters.
Táo was delighted
and settled there.
He would visit the northern courtyard daily,
tending to Mǎ’s chrysanthemums.
The chrysanthemums had withered,
but he pulled them up and replanted them,
and every one survived.
However, his family was impoverished.
Táo ate and drank with Mǎ every day,
yet observed that Mǎ’s household seemed not to light a cooking fire.
Mǎ’s wife, Lǚ,
also grew fond of Táo’s elder sister,
and from time to time would send them measures of grain as relief.
Táo’s elder sister, whose childhood name was Huángyīng,
was elegant and skilled in conversation.
She would often visit Lǚ’s place,
and together they would sew and spin.
One day, Táo said to Mǎ:
"Your household is certainly not well-off,
and I burden my close friend daily with my sustenance.
How can this continue?
For now,
selling chrysanthemums would suffice to make a living."
Mǎ, who was by nature upright and principled,
upon hearing Táo’s words,
felt great disdain for him,
saying:
"I thought you were a refined and lofty scholar,
who could be content with poverty.
Now that you speak like this,
you would turn the eastern hedge into a marketplace,
disgracing the noble chrysanthemum."
Táo laughed and said:
"To support oneself by one’s own labor is not greed;
to sell flowers as an occupation is not vulgar.
One certainly should not seek wealth improperly,
but neither must one deliberately pursue poverty."
Mǎ fell silent,
and Táo rose and left.
From then on,
whenever Mǎ discarded withered branches or inferior varieties,
Táo gathered them all up and took them away.
After this, he no longer ate or slept at Mǎ’s place,
only visiting when invited.
Not long after,
as the chrysanthemums were about to bloom,
Mǎ heard clamorous noise at Táo’s gate like a marketplace.
Finding it strange,
he went over to peek,
and saw flower buyers from the market,
loading their shoulders and carrying them away in abundance,
forming a continuous line along the road.
The flowers were all of rare varieties,
never before seen.
Disgusted by Táo’s greed,
Mǎ wanted to break off relations;
yet he also resented Táo for keeping such fine specimens secret,
so he knocked on the door,
intending to reproach him.
Táo came out,
took his hand, and pulled him inside.
Mǎ saw that half an acre of the neglected garden had been turned into chrysanthemum beds,
with no vacant land beyond the few rafters.
Where plants had been dug up,
cuttings from other branches were inserted to replace them;
and the buds in the beds
were all exquisite and marvelous. Upon closer inspection,
they were all the very ones Mǎ had previously uprooted and discarded.
Táo went into the house,
brought out wine and food,
and set a mat beside the beds, saying:
"I am too poor to uphold pure abstinence,
but fortunately, these past few days I’ve earned a little money,
enough to get quite drunk."
A short while later,
a voice from inside the room called
"Sānláng,"
and Táo acknowledged and went in.
Soon, excellent dishes were served,
exquisitely prepared.
Mǎ then asked:
"Why has your esteemed elder sister not yet married?"
Táo replied:
"The time has not yet come."
Mǎ asked:
"When will it come?"
Táo said:
"In forty-three months."
Mǎ pressed further:
"What does that mean?"
Táo only smiled without answering.
They enjoyed themselves thoroughly before parting.
The next day,
Mǎ visited again,
and the newly planted cuttings were already over a foot tall.
Greatly astonished,
he earnestly begged to learn the technique.
Táo said:
"This truly cannot be conveyed in words;
moreover, since you do not intend to make a living from it,
what use would it be to you?"
A few days later,
the gate and courtyard grew somewhat quiet,
and Táo wrapped the chrysanthemums in rush mats,
loaded several carts, and departed.
After more than a year,
when spring was half over,
he returned, bringing rare plants from the south.
He set up a flower shop in the capital,
sold out within ten days,
and returned home to cultivate chrysanthemums again.
Those who had bought flowers from him the previous year
kept the roots,
but the next year they all deteriorated into inferior varieties,
so they bought again from Táo.
Táo grew richer by the day: in one year, he added buildings;
in two years, he constructed grand houses.
He undertook construction as he pleased,
without further consulting the owner.
Gradually, the old flower beds
were all replaced by corridors and buildings.
He also bought a plot of land outside the wall,
built walls all around,
and planted it entirely with chrysanthemums.
When autumn came,
he loaded the flowers and left,
and by the end of spring, he had not returned.
Meanwhile, Mǎ’s wife fell ill and passed away.
Mǎ’s thoughts turned to Huángyīng,
and he subtly hinted at his intentions.
Huángyīng smiled faintly.
She seemed to consent,
but would only wait for Táo’s return.
Over a year later,
Táo still had not come.
Huángyīng directed the servants to plant chrysanthemums,
exactly as Táo had done.
With the money earned, she engaged in trade,
cultivating twenty qǐng of fertile land outside the village,
and her mansion grew even more magnificent.
Suddenly, a guest arrived from Eastern Yuè,
bringing a letter from Táo.
Upon opening it,
it instructed his sister to marry Mǎ.
Checking the date the letter was sent,
it was the very day Mǎ’s wife had died;
recalling the drink in the garden,
it had been exactly forty-three months.
Mǎ was utterly amazed.
He showed the letter to Huángyīng,
and asked
"where to send the betrothal gifts."
Huángyīng declined, not accepting the betrothal presents.
Moreover, finding the old residence humble,
she wanted Mǎ to move into the southern mansion,
as if he were a live-in son-in-law.
Mǎ refused,
choosing an auspicious day to perform the wedding ceremony properly.
After Huángyīng married Mǎ,
she opened a door in the partition wall connecting to the southern mansion,
and went daily to oversee the servants.
Mǎ felt ashamed of relying on his wife’s wealth,
and constantly urged Huángyīng to keep separate accounts for north and south,
to prevent confusion.
Yet whenever the household needed anything,
Huángyīng would fetch it from the southern mansion.
Within half a year,
everything in the house seemed to come from the Táo household.
Mǎ immediately had each item sent back,
forbidding any further taking.
But before ten days had passed,
things were mixed up again.
After several such cycles,
Mǎ grew utterly exasperated.
Huángyīng laughed and said:
"Isn’t Chén Zhòngzǐ rather toiling in vain?"
Mǎ felt ashamed,
and no longer checked,
leaving everything to Huángyīng.
She gathered workers and materials,
launched major construction projects,
and Mǎ could not stop her.
After several months,
buildings and towers stretched continuously,
and the two mansions merged into one,
with no boundaries between them.
However, following Mǎ’s instruction,
she closed the gate and no longer engaged in chrysanthemum business,
yet their lifestyle surpassed that of established gentry families.
Mǎ grew uneasy,
saying:
"My thirty years of virtuous purity
have been burdened by you.
Now, living in this world,
I merely depend on my wife’s skirts for sustenance—
truly without an ounce of a man’s spirit.
Everyone prays for wealth,
I only wish to remain poor!"
Huáng Yīng said:
"I am not greedy or base;
but if I do not manage to achieve some measure of wealth,
it will cause people for a thousand years to come
to say that Táo Yuānmíng had the bones of a poor and lowly man,
incapable of making good for a hundred generations.
So I am just trying to clear the name of our family's Péngzé Magistrate.
However, for the poor to wish for wealth
is difficult;
for the rich to seek poverty
is certainly also very easy.
You may spend the gold at the head of the bed as you please—
I will not begrudge it."
Mǎ said:
"To squander another's gold
is also rather shameful."
Yīng said:
"If you do not wish to be wealthy,
I cannot be poor either.
Since there is no other way,
let us separate our living quarters: the pure will remain pure,
the tainted will remain tainted—
what harm is there?"
So she built a thatched cottage in the garden
and chose a pretty maid to go serve Mǎ.
Mǎ settled in comfortably.
Yet after a few days,
he sorely missed Huáng Yīng.
He summoned her,
but she refused to come;
having no choice,
he went to her instead.
He would stay overnight and then return,
and this became the norm.
Huáng Yīng laughed and said:
"Eating in the east and lodging in the west—
even a man of integrity should not do such a thing."
Mǎ also laughed at himself,
having no reply,
and so they lived together again as before.
It happened that Mǎ went to Jīnlíng on business,
just as the chrysanthemum autumn arrived.
Early one morning he passed by a flower shop,
and saw many pots arrayed in the shop,
the blooms exquisite and splendid.
His heart stirred,
and he suspected they resembled Táo's handiwork.
After a short while,
the owner came out—
and it was indeed Táo.
Overjoyed,
Mǎ recounted their long separation in full,
then stayed overnight there,
and urged him to return home.
Táo said:
"Jīnlíng
is my native place;
I plan to marry here.
I have accumulated a modest sum of money—
please send it to my elder sister.
I will come for a short visit at the end of the year."
Mǎ would not listen,
pleading even more earnestly.
Moreover, he said:
"Our household is fortunately well-off now;
you can just sit and enjoy it—
there is no need to trade anymore."
He sat in the shop,
had a servant handle the pricing,
set the prices low,
and sold everything off in a few days.
He pressed Táo to pack his bags,
chartered a boat, and they headed north.
Upon entering the gate,
they found his sister had already prepared a room,
with bed, couch, mattresses, and quilts all set out,
as if she had known in advance her brother would return.
Since Táo's return,
he unpacked, assigned tasks to the servants,
and extensively repaired the pavilions and gardens.
He only spent his days playing chess and drinking with Mǎ,
and never again received a single guest.
When they tried to arrange a marriage for him,
he declined, saying he did not wish it.
His sister sent two maids to attend to his bedchamber,
and after three or four years,
they bore a daughter.
Táo had always been a prodigious drinker,
yet no one had ever seen him thoroughly drunk.
There was a friend, Mr. Zēng,
whose capacity was also unmatched.
He happened to visit Mǎ,
and Mǎ had him compete in drinking with Táo.
The two drank freely and joyfully,
regretting they had not met sooner.
From morning until the fourth watch of the night,
they each downed a hundred pots in total.
Zēng was dead drunk,
slumbering deeply in his seat.
Táo got up to return to his room,
but upon stepping out the door, he trod on the chrysanthemum bed,
collapsed like a jade mountain,
shed his clothes beside him,
and immediately transformed on the spot into a chrysanthemum—
as tall as a person;
with over ten blooms,
all larger than a fist.
Mǎ was utterly terrified
and told Huáng Yīng.
Yīng hurried over,
pulled it up and placed it on the ground,
saying:
"How could you get so drunk!"
She covered it with clothes,
urged Mǎ to leave with her,
and warned him not to look.
When he went at daybreak,
Táo was lying by the flower bed.
Mǎ then realized that brother and sister were chrysanthemum spirits,
and respected and loved them even more.
But after Táo had revealed his true form,
he drank even more unrestrainedly,
often sending invitations himself to summon Zēng.
Thus they became fast friends.
On the occasion of the Flower Festival,
Zēng came to visit,
bringing a jar of white wine steeped with medicinal herbs, carried by two servants,
and proposed they finish it together.
As the jar was nearly empty,
the two were still not very drunk,
so Mǎ secretly added another large jar to replenish it.
The two finished that as well.
Zēng, already exhausted from drunkenness,
was carried away by his servants.
Táo lay on the ground
and transformed into a chrysanthemum again.
Mǎ, accustomed by now, was not alarmed;
he followed Yīng's method and pulled it up,
then stayed by its side to observe the change.
After a long while,
the leaves grew increasingly withered.
Greatly frightened,
he finally told Huáng Yīng.
Yīng, hearing this, cried out in alarm:
"You have killed my brother!"
She rushed to look—
the roots and stem were already dried up.
Overwhelmed with grief,
she pinched off a stem,
planted it in a pot,
took it into her chamber,
and watered it daily.
Mǎ was filled with remorse and near despair,
and deeply resented Zēng.
After several days,
he heard that Zēng had already died drunk.
The flower in the pot gradually sprouted,
and by the ninth month it bloomed—
with a short stem and pink blossoms,
smelling of wine when sniffed.
They named it
"Drunken Táo",
and when watered with wine, it flourished.
Later, the daughter grew up
and married into an eminent family.
Huáng Yīng lived to old age,
with no other peculiarities.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"A man of green hills and white clouds
thus died drunk—
the world may all regret it,
yet he himself may not have considered it unhappy.
To plant this variety in one's courtyard
is like seeing a good friend,
like facing a beautiful lady—
one must certainly seek it out."
Based on the manuscript edition of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In Péngchéng there lived a man named Láng Yùzhù,
whose ancestors had held the office of prefect.
They were honest officials,
and instead of using their salaries to acquire property,
they filled their house with books.
By the time it came to Yùzhù,
he was especially obsessed: though his family suffered from poverty,
and there was nothing he would not sell,
he could not bear to part with a single volume
from his father’s collection.
While his father was alive,
he had once copied out the “Essay on Exhortation to Learning”
and pasted it by his seat;
Láng recited it daily.
He also covered it with plain silk gauze,
fearing it might wear away.
He was not studying for the sake of an official salary,
but truly believed that books really contained gold and grain.
He pored over them day and night,
regardless of cold or heat.
By the time he was over twenty,
he had not sought a marriage partner,
hoping that a beautiful woman would come to him from the pages of a book.
When he saw guests or relatives, he did not know how to exchange pleasantries;
after a few words,
he would start reciting loudly,
and the guests would leave awkwardly on their own.
Whenever the provincial examiner came to administer the tests,
he would always place Láng first,
yet Láng was frustrated by his inability to pass the higher examinations.
One day,
while he was reading,
a sudden gust of wind blew the book away.
He hurried after it,
and his foot sank into the ground.
Feeling around,
he found a hole with rotten grass inside;
digging it up,
he discovered an ancient storage pit of grain,
which had decayed into manure.
Though it was inedible,
he became even more convinced
that the saying about “a thousand measures”
was not false,
and he studied even harder.
One day,
climbing a ladder to reach a high shelf,
he found among the jumbled volumes a golden carriage a foot in diameter.
Overjoyed,
he thought it was
proof of the “golden house”
mentioned in books.
He took it out to show others,
but it turned out to be gold-plated, not solid gold.
Secretly, he resented the ancients for deceiving him.
Not long after,
a man who had passed the imperial examination in the same year as his father,
and who was serving as an inspector in that circuit,
was fond of Buddhism.
Someone advised Láng to present the carriage as a Buddhist shrine.
The inspector was greatly pleased,
and gave Láng three hundred taels of silver and two horses.
Láng was delighted,
thinking that the golden house and carriage and horses had all been verified,
so he studied even more diligently.
However, he was already thirty years old.
Someone urged him to marry,
but he said:
“ ‘Within books there is a beauty like jade’;
why should I worry about not having a beautiful wife?”
After another two or three years of reading,
with no results,
people all mocked him.
At that time, a rumor spread among the people: the Weaving Maid from heaven had secretly run away.
Someone teased Láng:
“The Heavenly Granddaughter has eloped;
perhaps it’s for you.”
Láng knew they were joking,
and ignored it without arguing.
One evening,
while reading the eighth volume of the *History of the Han Dynasty*,
about halfway through the scroll,
he saw a gauze-cut beauty tucked inside.
Astonished, he said:
“The beauty like jade from the books—
is this how it comes true?”
He felt disheartened and lost.
But upon examining the beauty closely,
her eyebrows and eyes looked lifelike;
on her back, faintly written in small characters, it said:
“Weaving Maid.”
He found this very strange.
He placed her on the scroll every day,
gazing and admiring her repeatedly,
to the point of forgetting to eat or sleep.
One day,
while he was staring intently,
the beauty suddenly bent at the waist and stood up,
sitting on the scroll and smiling.
Láng was utterly shocked,
and prostrated himself beneath the desk.
When he got up,
she was already a foot tall.
Even more astonished,
he kowtowed again.
She stepped down from the desk,
graceful and elegant, like a peerless beauty.
Bowing, he asked:
“What deity are you?”
The beauty laughed and said:
“I am of the Yán family,
my given name is Rúyù.
You have known of me for a long time.
Every day you have gazed upon me with admiration;
if I did not come once,
I fear that for a thousand years hence, no one would ever again sincerely believe in the ancients.”
Láng was overjoyed,
and they slept together.
However, though they were extremely affectionate in bed,
he did not know how to be intimate with a woman.
Every time he read,
he would make the girl sit beside him.
The girl warned him not to read,
but he would not listen.
The girl said:
“The reason you cannot rise in the world
is simply because you read.
Look at the spring and autumn examination lists—
how many people read like you?
If you don’t listen,
I will leave.”
Láng temporarily obeyed her.
But after a short while,
he forgot her instruction,
and started reciting again.
A moment later,
he looked for the girl,
but she was nowhere to be found.
Distraught,
he prayed and pleaded,
but there was no trace of her.
Suddenly remembering where she had hidden,
he took the *History of the Han Dynasty* and carefully searched through it,
until he reached the place where she had returned,
and indeed found her.
He called to her, but she did not move;
he knelt and begged sorrowfully.
Only then did the girl come down and say:
“If you disobey again,
we shall part forever!”
She then had him prepare a chessboard and gambling dice,
and spent the days playing games with him.
But Láng’s mind was not on these at all.
When he saw the girl was not around,
he would secretly take out a book and read.
Fearing she would notice,
he secretly took the eighth volume of the *History of the Han Dynasty*
and mixed it among other books to confuse her.
One day,
while he was deeply engrossed in reading,
the girl arrived,
and he did not notice her at all;
suddenly seeing her,
he hurriedly closed the book,
