but the girl had already vanished.
Terrified,
he searched frantically through all the books,
but could not find her anywhere;
eventually,
he still found her in the eighth volume of the *History of the Han Dynasty*,
on the exact same page.
He then bowed and prayed again,
vowing never to read anymore.
Only then did the girl come down,
and played chess with him, saying:
“If you are not skilled within three days,
I will leave again.”
By the third day,
he suddenly won a game against her by two pieces.
The girl was pleased,
and taught him to play stringed instruments,
giving him five days to master one tune.
Láng focused all his attention on this,
with no time for anything else;
after a while,
he could play in time with the rhythm,
and could not help but dance with joy.
The girl then spent her days drinking and gambling with him,
and Láng became so happy he forgot about reading.
The girl also encouraged him to go out
and make friends,
and from then on, his reputation for being talented and unrestrained spread widely.
The girl said:
“Now you can go out and take the examinations.”
One night, the young man said to the girl:
"When a man and woman live together, they have children;
now I have been with you for a long time,
why is this not the case?"
The girl laughed and said:
"You read books every day,
I have always said it is of no use.
Now even the chapter on husband and wife,
you have not yet understood;
the words 'pillow and mat' require skill."
The young man asked in surprise:
"What skill?"
The girl laughed and did not answer.
After a short while,
she secretly approached him.
The young man, in the height of pleasure, said:
"I never imagined that the joy of husband and wife
could be something beyond words."
From then on, he told everyone he met,
and there was no one who did not cover their mouth and laugh.
The girl found out and scolded him.
The young man said:
"Those who drill holes and climb over walls,
indeed cannot tell others;
but the joy of natural human relations,
is something everyone has,
why hide it?"
After eight or nine months,
the girl indeed gave birth to a son,
and they hired a nurse to care for him.
One day,
she said to the young man:
"I have been with you for two years,
and have already borne a child,
it is time to part.
If I stay long, I fear I will bring you misfortune,
and it will be too late for regrets."
Hearing this, the young man
shed tears,
and prostrated himself, refusing to rise, saying:
"Will you not think of the crying child?"
The girl also looked sorrowful,
and after a long while said:
"If you insist I stay,
you must take all the books from the shelves and scatter them."
The young man said:
"These are your hometown,
and my very life,
how can you say such a thing!"
The girl did not force him,
saying:
"I also know it is fated,
I just had to warn you in advance."
Before this,
some relatives had caught glimpses of the girl,
and all were utterly astonished,
and since they had not heard which family he had married into,
they questioned him together.
The young man could not lie,
but only remained silent.
People grew even more suspicious,
the news spread far and wide,
and reached the county magistrate, Shǐ Gōng.
Shǐ,
was from Mǐn,
a young jìnshì.
Hearing of her beauty, he was captivated,
and secretly wished to see her lovely face,
so he arrested the young man and the girl.
The girl, upon hearing,
vanished without a trace.
The magistrate was angry,
detained the young man,
stripped him of his scholar's robe,
applied all kinds of shackles and torture,
determined to find out where the girl had gone.
The young man was near death,
but said not a word.
They tortured the maid,
and roughly learned a vague account.
The magistrate thought it was a demon,
and ordered his carriage to personally visit the house.
Seeing the rooms filled with books,
too many to search through,
he had them burned;
smoke gathered in the courtyard and did not disperse,
darkening like gloomy haze.
After the young man was released,
he traveled far to seek letters from his father's disciples,
and managed to have his status restored.
That autumn he passed the provincial examination,
the next year he passed the jìnshì examination.
But his hatred was deep as bone marrow.
He set up a memorial tablet for Yán Rúyù.
Morning and evening he prayed:
"If you have a spirit,
you should help me become an official in Mǐn."
Later, he indeed was appointed as an inspector to tour Mǐn.
After three months there,
he investigated Shǐ's evil deeds,
and confiscated his family property.
At that time, he had a cousin who was a judicial commissioner,
who forced him to take a beloved concubine,
pretending to buy a maid and place her in the office.
Once the case was concluded,
the young man immediately resigned on his own,
took the concubine and returned home.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"All things under heaven,
when accumulated, attract envy,
when loved, give birth to demons: the girl's being a demon,
was the demon of books.
The matter was close to bizarre,
dealing with it was not unwarranted;
but the tyranny of the First Emperor,
was it not already cruel enough!
His selfish intentions,
deserved even more the retribution of bitter hatred.
Alas!
Is it any wonder!"
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Xǔ Shèng,
was from Yǎn.
He followed his elder brother Chéng to trade in Mǐn,
but the goods had not yet accumulated.
A guest said the Great Sage's efficacy was renowned,
and they would pray at his temple.
Shèng did not know what deity the Great Sage was,
and went with his brother.
Arriving, they saw halls and pavilions connected and sprawling,
extremely grand and beautiful.
Entering the hall to gaze in reverence,
the deity had a monkey's head and a human body,
it was said to be the Great Sage Equaling Heaven, Sūn Wùkōng. All the guests rose in solemn respect,
none daring to show any irreverent expression.
Shèng was by nature upright and forthright,
and secretly laughed at the vulgarity of common customs.
The crowd burned offerings and kowtowed in prayer,
Shèng secretly left them.
After returning home,
his elder brother reproached him for his irreverence.
Shèng said:
"Sūn Wùkōng is merely an allegorical figure created by Old Man Qiū,
why must you believe in him so sincerely?
If he truly possesses divine power,
whether it be blades, spears, or thunderbolts,
I shall bear them myself!"
The innkeeper, upon hearing him call out the Great Sage's name,
all waved their hands in alarm, their faces paling,
as if fearing the Great Sage might hear.
Seeing their reaction,
Shèng argued even more loudly;
those listening all covered their ears and fled.
When night fell,
Shèng indeed fell ill,
suffering a severe headache.
Some urged him to go to the temple and apologize,
but Shèng refused to listen.
Not long after,
his headache slightly improved,
but then his thigh began to ache,
and overnight a large abscess formed,
spreading until his entire leg swelled up,
rendering him unable to eat or sleep.
His elder brother prayed on his behalf,
but to no avail.
Someone said: divine punishment requires personal supplication.
Shèng stubbornly refused to believe it.
After over a month,
the sore gradually healed,
but then another abscess appeared,
causing him twice the pain.
A doctor came,
cut away the rotten flesh with a knife,
and blood overflowed, filling a bowl: fearing people would attribute it to divine retribution,
he endured the pain without groaning.
Another month passed,
before he finally recovered.
Then his elder brother fell seriously ill.
Shèng said:
"What now!
Even one who reveres the gods ends up like this,
proving that my illness
was not caused by Wùkōng."
Hearing his words,
his elder brother grew even more furious,
saying the god had transferred its anger,
and blamed his younger brother for not praying on his behalf.
Shèng said:
"Brothers are like limbs.
Previously, when my own limbs festered and rotted, I did not pray: now, how could I abandon my principles because of an illness in my limbs?"
He merely summoned a doctor and prepared medicine,
but did not comply with the prayer request.
After taking the medicine,
his elder brother died suddenly.
Shèng, his heart filled with grief and pain,
bought a coffin and laid his brother to rest,
then went to the temple, pointed at the deity, and denounced it, saying:
"My brother fell ill,
claiming you transferred your anger,
leaving me unable to clear my name.
If you truly possess divine power,
you should bring the dead back to life.
Then I would bow to you as a disciple,
and dare not utter another word of dissent;
otherwise,
I will treat you as you treat the Three Pure Ones,
and return the same to you,
thereby dispelling my brother's doubts in the underworld."
That night,
he dreamed that someone summoned him away,
entering the Great Sage's temple,
where he looked up and saw the Great Sage with an angry expression,
who reproached him, saying:
"Because of your misconduct,
I pierced your thighs with the Bodhisattva's blade;
yet you show no remorse,
and even complain incessantly.
You ought to be sent to the Tongue-Ripping Hell,
but considering your lifelong integrity and uprightness,
I shall temporarily pardon you.
As for your brother's illness,
it was you who shortened his lifespan by hiring an incompetent doctor—
what fault lies with others?
Now, if I do not exercise a little divine power,
it will only give the arrogant more grounds for their boasts."
He then ordered a servant in black to seek instructions from Yánluó.
The servant in black replied:
"Three days have passed,
and the register of ghosts has already been reported to the Heavenly Court—
I fear it may be difficult to intervene."
The deity took a square tablet,
wrote on it with a brush,
though no one knew what words he wrote,
and had the servant in black take it away.
After a long while, he returned.
Chéng came with him,
and both knelt in the hall.
The deity asked:
"Why were you delayed?"
The servant in black replied:
"Yánmó did not dare to act on his own authority,
and further consulted the Dipper Constellation with the Great Sage's decree—
hence the delay."
Shèng hurried forward and bowed in gratitude for the deity's mercy.
The deity said:
"You may quickly return with your brother.
If you can turn to goodness,
I shall bring you blessings."
The brothers, both sorrowful and joyful,
left together hand in hand,
and upon waking, found it all very strange.
He hurriedly got up,
opened the coffin to look,
and indeed, his brother had revived.
He helped him out,
deeply grateful for the Great Sage's power.
From then on, Shèng was sincerely convinced,
and his faith became even stronger than that of ordinary people.
However, the brothers' capital
had been depleted by half during the illness;
and his elder brother had not yet fully recovered,
so they faced each other in constant worry.
One day,
while wandering outside the city walls,
he suddenly encountered a man in coarse clothing who studied him and said:
"Why are you so troubled?"
Shèng, suffering with no one to confide in,
thus recounted all his misfortunes in detail.
The man in coarse clothing said:
"There is a wonderful place—
if you go there for a visit,
it should be enough to dispel your gloom."
Shèng asked:
"Where are we going?"
He only said:
"Not far."
Shèng followed him.
After leaving the city walls for about half a li,
the man in brown clothes said:
"I have a minor technique,
we can arrive in an instant."
He then told Shèng to hold onto his waist with both hands,
slightly nodded his head,
and Shèng immediately felt clouds forming beneath his feet,
soaring and leaping upward,
not knowing how many yojanas they had traveled.
Shèng was greatly terrified,
closing his eyes and not daring to open them even a little.
After a short while,
he said:
"We've arrived."
Suddenly, Shèng saw a world of colored glaze,
radiant with extraordinary colors,
and asked in surprise:
"What place is this?"
He replied:
"The heavenly palace."
They strolled casually,
ascending higher and higher.
From afar, they saw an old man,
and the man in brown said joyfully:
"Meeting this elder is your good fortune!"
He raised his hands and bowed in greeting.
The old man invited them to his place,
brewed tea to offer his guests;
there were only two cups,
and none was given to Shèng.
The man in brown said:
"This is my disciple,
a merchant traveling a thousand li,
who respectfully comes to the immortal's abode,
seeking a small gift."
The old man ordered a servant boy to bring out a plate of white stones,
shaped like sparrow eggs,
sparkling and clear as ice,
and told Shèng to take them himself.
Shèng thought that taking them back could serve as counters for drinking games,
so he took six.
The man in brown thought this was too modest,
took six more himself,
and handed them to Shèng, wrapping them together.
He instructed him to put them in his waist pouch,
cupped his hands and said:
"That's enough."
They bid farewell to the old man and left,
again having Shèng hold onto his waist to descend,
and in a moment they reached the ground.
Shèng kowtowed and asked for the immortal's name.
He laughed and said:
"What we just did is what's called the somersault cloud."
Shèng suddenly realized,
understanding that this was the Great Sage,
and again sought his protection.
He said:
"The wealth star you just met,
has granted you twelve parts profit,
what more do you need to seek?"
Shèng bowed to him again,
and when he rose to look, he had already vanished.
After returning home,
he happily told his elder brother.
They untied and looked together,
but the stones had melted into his waist pouch.
Later, when he transported goods back,
his profits were several times over.
From then on, whenever he went to Mǐn,
he would always pray to the Great Sage.
Others' prayers,
were not always answered;
but whatever Shèng asked for was always granted.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"In the past, a scholar passed by a temple,
drew a pipa on the wall and left;
upon his return,
its spiritual efficacy had become greatly renowned,
with continuous incense offerings.
In the affairs of the world, it is not necessary for there to actually be such a person;
if people believe it is spiritual,
then it becomes spiritual.
Why is this?
Where human hearts gather,
things may find a place to reside.
As for someone as upright and honest as Shèng,
he naturally deserved divine protection: how could it truly be that there was an embroidered needle in the ear, hairs that could transform,
a somersault underfoot, and the azure sky that could be ascended!
Ultimately, being deluded by the strange,
is also due to one's limited perception of truth."
Based on the manuscript of "Liáozhāi Zhìyì"
Between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
the custom of serving the Frog God is most devout:
in the temple, the frogs number hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands,
some as large as baskets.
If someone offends the god's anger,
their home will have strange omens: frogs roaming on tables and beds,
or even climbing slippery walls without falling,
the manifestations vary,
and this household will face misfortune.
People then become greatly frightened,
slaughtering animals to pray and ward off evil,
and if the god is pleased, it stops.
In Chǔ, there was a man named Xuē Kūnshēng,
who was clever from a young age,
with handsome features.
When he was six or seven years old,
a servant in black clothes came to his home,
claiming to be a divine messenger,
conveying the god's intention,
wishing to marry his daughter to Kūnshēng.
Old Xuē was simple and honest by nature,
and truly did not wish for this,
declining on the grounds that his son was too young.
Although he thus refused;
he also did not dare arrange a marriage with another family.
After several years passed,
Kūnshēng gradually grew up,
and betrothal gifts were sent to the Jiāng family.
The god told Jiāng:
"Xuē Kūnshēng,
is my son-in-law,
how dare you approach what is forbidden!"
Jiāng was afraid,
and returned the betrothal gifts.
Old Xuē was worried about this,
prepared pure sacrificial animals and went to pray,
saying he did not dare to be matched with the god.
After the prayer,
he saw huge maggots floating in the food and wine,
squirming densely;
he poured them out,
apologized and returned home.
His heart grew even more fearful,
and he could only let it be.
One day,
while Kūnshēng was on the road,
a messenger came to announce the god's command,
insistently inviting him to come.
Having no choice,
he went with them.
Entering a vermilion gate,
he saw pavilions and towers splendid and fine.
An old man sat in the hall,
looking like someone in his seventies or eighties.
Kūnshēng knelt and paid his respects.
The old man ordered him to be helped up,
and had him sit beside the table.
After a short while,
maids and servants gathered to look,
crowding all around.
The old man looked and said:
"Go and say that young master Xuē has arrived."
Several maids ran off.
After a while,
an old woman led a young lady out,
aged sixteen or seventeen,
beautiful beyond compare.
The old man pointed and said:
"This is my youngest daughter, Shíniáng,
who thinks she and you would make a fine couple;
but your father refuses because we are of a different kind.
This is a matter of a hundred years,
parents only decide half of it:
the rest is up to you."
Kūnshēng gazed at Shíniáng,
his heart fond of her,
but remained silent.
The old woman said:
"I know the young master's intentions are good.
Please return home first,
we will send Shíniáng over shortly."
Kūnshēng said:
"Agreed."
He hurried home to tell his father.
The old man was flustered and at a loss,
so he taught him what to say:
to go back and decline,
but Kūnshēng refused to go.
While they were arguing,
a carriage was already at the gate,
with servants in black clothes in groups,
and Shíniáng entered.
She went to the hall to pay respects to her parents-in-law,
who were pleased to see her.
That evening they were married,
and were very harmonious.
From then on, the divine old man and old woman,
often visited their home.
Looking at their clothes,
red meant joy,
white meant wealth,
and it would surely appear,
so the family prospered day by day.
Since the marriage with the deity,
frogs were everywhere in the doorways, halls, fences, and privies,
and no one dared to scold or kick them.
Only Kūnshēng, being young and willful,
would shoo them away when happy,
and trample them to death when angry,
showing little care or affection.
Although Shíniáng was modest and gentle,
she was prone to anger,
and she greatly disliked Kūnshēng's behavior;
yet Kūnshēng did not restrain himself for Shíniáng's sake.
Shíniáng spoke harshly to Kūnshēng,
and Kūnshēng angrily said,
"Do you think your parents can bring disaster upon people?
What does a man fear from frogs!"
Shíniáng particularly detested the word
"frog,"
and upon hearing it, she was deeply hurt,
saying:
"Since I entered your household, your family's fields have yielded more grain,
and goods have fetched higher prices,
which is no small contribution.
Now that the old and young are all well-fed and warm,
are you like an owl growing wings,
wanting to peck out its mother's eyes!"
Kūnshēng grew even angrier and said:
"I am precisely disgusted by the filth you've added,
unfit to be passed on to descendants.
It would be better to part early."
He then drove Shíniáng away.
When the old man and his wife heard of it,
Shíniáng had already left.
They scolded Kūnshēng,
urging him to quickly pursue and bring her back.
Kūnshēng, filled with anger, refused to yield.
By night,
both mother and son fell ill,
depressed and unable to eat.
The old man, terrified,
went to the shrine to apologize,
with sincere and earnest words.
After three days,
their illness gradually subsided.
Shíniáng also returned on her own,
and the couple was as happy and loving as before.
Shíniáng would sit all day in full makeup,
not doing any needlework,
and Kūnshēng's clothes and shoes
were all left to his mother.
One day, the mother angrily said:
"Now that my son is married,
I am still burdened!
In other families, daughters-in-law serve their mothers-in-law,
but in our family, the mother-in-law serves the daughter-in-law!"
Shíniáng happened to overhear this,
and in a fit of anger, she entered the hall and said:
"Your daughter-in-law serves you meals in the morning,
and inquires after your rest in the evening.
As for serving a mother-in-law,
what more should be done?
The only shortcoming is
my inability to spare the cost of hiring servants,
forcing me to do the hard work myself."
The mother had nothing to say,
and wept in shame and frustration.
When Kūnshēng entered,
he saw his mother's tear-stained face,
and upon learning the reason,
angrily reprimanded Shíniáng.
Shíniáng argued stubbornly and refused to yield.
Kūnshēng said:
"If a wife cannot bring joy to her parents-in-law,
it is better not to have one!
Even if it angers the old frog,
at most I will suffer a sudden disaster and die!"
He drove Shíniáng out again.
Shíniáng was also furious,
and left through the door without looking back.
The next day,
their residence caught fire,
which spread to several houses,
and all the tables, chairs, and beds
were reduced to ashes.
Kūnshēng was enraged,
and went to the shrine to reprimand and accuse:
"You raised a daughter who cannot serve her parents-in-law,
lacking even the most basic upbringing,
yet you shield her faults!
A deity is supposed to be just and fair—
is there any teaching that encourages people to fear their wives?
Moreover, when pots and bowls clash,
it is the fault of the subjects
and has nothing to do with the parents.
If it is punishment by knife, saw, axe, or axe-blade,
then let it fall upon me;
if not,
I will also burn down your dwelling,
as a form of retaliation."
After saying this,
he carried firewood to the foot of the shrine,
lit a fire, and was about to set it ablaze.
The villagers gathered and pleaded with him,
and only then did he leave in anger.
When his parents heard of this,
they were terrified and turned pale.
That night,
the deity appeared in a dream to a nearby village,
instructing them to build a house for the son-in-law's family.
By dawn,
materials were gathered and workers assembled,
and together they built a house for Kūnshēng.
Though he tried to refuse, they would not stop;
hundreds of people came and went on the road each day,
and within a few days,
a new residence stood complete,
fully furnished with beds, curtains, and utensils.
As soon as the repairs were finished,
Shíniáng arrived,
entered the hall to apologize,
speaking gently and kindly.
She turned to Kūnshēng with a smile,
and the whole family's resentment turned to joy.
From then on, Shíniáng's temperament became even more gentle,
and for two years,
there were no further disputes.
Shíniáng had an extreme aversion to snakes.
Kūnshēng playfully placed a small snake in a box
and tricked a servant into opening it.
Shíniáng’s face changed color,
and she berated Kūnshēng.
Kūnshēng, in turn, shifted from laughter to anger,
and they exchanged harsh words.
Shíniáng said:
“This time, I won’t wait for you to drive me away—
I’ll leave of my own accord.”
With that, she went out the door.
Old Xuē was terrified;
he caned Kūnshēng
and went to the temple to apologize to the deity.
Fortunately, no calamity befell them,
but there was also no word from Shíniáng.
More than a year passed.
Kūnshēng missed Shíniáng
and deeply regretted his actions.
He secretly went to the temple to mourn for Shíniáng,
but there was still no response.
Not long after,
he heard that the deity had betrothed Shíniáng to a man of the Yuán family.
His heart sank with disappointment,
so he also sought a marriage with another family.
But after meeting several candidates,
none compared to Shíniáng,
and he missed her even more.
He went to inquire at the Yuán family
and found they had already whitewashed the walls and swept the courtyard,
awaiting the bridal carriage.
Filled with shame and resentment, he could not control himself
and fell ill, unable to eat.
His parents were anxious and worried,
not knowing what to do.
Suddenly, in his delirium, someone stroked him and said:
“A grown man who keeps wanting to break things off,
yet now puts on such a show!”
He opened his eyes—
it was Shíniáng.
Overjoyed,
he leapt up and said:
“Where have you come from?”
Shíniáng replied:
“Given how frivolously you treated me,
I should have obeyed my father’s command
and remarried elsewhere.
Indeed, we have long accepted the Yuán family’s betrothal gifts,
but after a thousand thoughts, I could not bear to go through with it.
The auspicious wedding date was set for tonight.
My father, too ashamed to return the gifts himself,
had me personally take them back and leave them there.
Just as I stepped out the door,
my father ran after me and said:
‘Silly girl!
If you won’t listen to me,
and later suffer abuse from the Xuē family,
even if you die, don’t come back!’”
Kūnshēng was moved by her devotion
and wept for her.
The whole household rejoiced
and rushed to tell the old couple.
When the old woman heard,
without waiting to visit the temple,
she ran into her son’s room,
grasped Shíniáng’s hands, and sobbed.
From then on, Kūnshēng also became more mature
and stopped playing malicious pranks,
so their affection grew even deeper.
Shíniáng said:
“I once thought you were flighty and unreliable,
and unlikely to stay with me till old age,
so I did not wish to leave any offspring in this world.
But now that my heart belongs to no other,
I shall bear you a child.”
Not long after,
the divine old man and woman, dressed in crimson robes,
descended upon their home.
The next day,
Shíniáng went into labor
and gave birth to twin boys.
From then on, the visits between the families were uninterrupted.
If any resident offended the deity,
they would first seek out Kūnshēng;
then he would have the women of the household dress up and enter the inner chamber
to pay respects to Shíniáng.
If Shíniáng smiled, the matter was resolved.
The Xuē family’s descendants flourished,
and people called them
“the Xuē Frog Family.”
Those nearby did not dare use the name,
but those farther away did.
Based on the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
The Frog Deity often speaks through shamans.
Shamans can discern the deity’s displeasure or pleasure:
they inform the devotees, saying
“The deity is pleased,”
and blessings follow;
“The deity is angry,”
and the women and children sit worrying and sighing,
some even losing their appetite.
Is this merely popular custom?
Or is the deity truly potent,
not entirely unfounded?
There was a wealthy merchant named Zhōu,
stingy by nature.
When the locals collected funds to repair the Guān Shèng temple,
both rich and poor contributed according to their means,
but Zhōu refused to part with even a single hair.
As time passed,
the construction stalled,
and the organizers were at a loss.
Just then, during a communal worship of the Frog Deity,
the shaman suddenly declared:
“General Zhōu Cāng has ordered this humble deity to oversee the fundraising.
Bring the ledger here.”
The crowd complied.
The shaman said:
“Those who have already donated
will not be pressured further;
those who have not
should note their contributions according to their ability.”
Everyone listened respectfully and obediently,
each recording their own donation.
The shaman looked around and said,
“Is Zhōu here?”
Zhōu was hiding among the crowd,
fearing the deity might notice him.
Hearing his name, he turned pale,
and hesitantly stepped forward.
The shaman pointed at the ledger and said:
“Note down one hundred taels.”
Zhōu grew even more distressed.
The shaman angrily said:
“You even paid two hundred for your illicit affair—
how much more for a good cause!”
It turned out Zhōu had an affair with a woman,
and when her husband caught them,
he paid two hundred taels to buy his silence.
Thus the shaman exposed him.
Zhōu, ashamed and frightened,
had no choice
but to record the amount as ordered.
After returning home,
he told his wife.
His wife said:
“This is just the shaman’s trickery.”
The shaman repeatedly demanded the money,
but Zhōu never paid.
One day,
while napping during the day,
he suddenly heard what sounded like an ox panting outside the door.
Looking,
he saw a giant frog
so large it barely fit through the doorway.
It moved slowly and awkwardly,
blocking both door leaves as it entered.
Once inside,
it turned and lay down,
resting its chin on the threshold.
The whole family was terrified.
Zhōu said:
“This must be about the donation money.”
He burned incense and prayed,
offering to pay thirty taels first,
with the rest to follow later.
The frog did not move.
He offered fifty taels—
the frog suddenly shrank,
becoming about a foot smaller.
He added another twenty—
it shrank further, to the size of a dou measure.
When he offered to pay in full,
it shrank to the size of a fist,
calmly exited,
and slipped away through a crack in the wall.
Zhōu hurriedly sent fifty taels to the construction overseer.
Everyone found it strange,
but Zhōu never explained the reason.
After several days had accumulated,
the shaman spoke again,
"Zhōu So-and-so owes fifty taels of gold,
why not press him for payment?"
When Zhōu heard this,
he was afraid,
and sent another ten taels,
intending to settle the matter with this.
One day,
as the husband and wife were eating,
the frog arrived again,
just as before,
its eyes bulging.
After a short while,
it climbed onto their bed,
causing the bed to shake and nearly tip over;
it then placed its head on the pillow and slept,
its belly swelling up like a reclining ox,
filling all four corners.
Zhōu was terrified,
and immediately paid the full hundred taels to it.
Upon checking,
it still did not move at all.
Within half a day,
small frogs gradually gathered,
and the next day there were even more,
burrowing into granaries and climbing onto beds,
reaching every place;
those larger than a bowl
climbed onto the stove to eat flies,
rotting in the cauldron,
so that the food became too foul to eat;
by the third day,
the courtyard was teeming with them,
with no empty space left.
The whole family was in a panic,
not knowing what plan to adopt.
Having no alternative,
they sought advice from the shaman.
The shaman said:
"This must be because it is too little."
He then prayed over it,
adding twenty more taels,
and its head began to lift;
adding more,
one foot rose;
until a hundred taels were reached,
all four feet rose,
and it descended from the bed and went out the door,
staggering a few steps,
then turned back and lay down inside the door.
Zhōu was afraid,
and asked the shaman.
The shaman guessed his intention,
wanting Zhōu to immediately open his purse.
Zhōu had no choice,
and paid the shaman the full amount,
whereupon the frog walked away,
a few steps outside,
its body suddenly shrank,
mingling among the many frogs,
unrecognizable,
and they gradually scattered in confusion.
After the shrine was completed,
and the consecration and sacrificial rites were held,
there were still further needs.
The shaman suddenly pointed at the chief organizer and said:
"So-and-so should contribute such-and-such amount."
There were fifteen people in total,
only two were omitted.
The crowd prayed, saying:
"We and so-and-so,
have already donated together."
The shaman said:
"I do not base it on wealth or poverty,
but on the amount you have embezzled.
This money,
cannot be used to enrich yourselves,
lest there be sudden disasters and flying calamities.
Considering your diligence as chief organizers,
I am therefore helping you avert them.
Except for so-and-so, who is honest and upright without any misconduct,
even my own shaman,
I do not spare any private gain,
and will have him contribute first,
to set an example for all."
He immediately rushed into his house,
and searched through boxes and trunks.
His wife asked him,
but he did not answer,
gathering all the savings in bags and taking them out,
announcing to the crowd:
"I privately withheld eight taels of silver,
now I will empty my purse."
He weighed it with the crowd,
and the scale showed over six taels,
so he had someone record the amount owed.
The crowd was astonished,
and dared not argue,
all paying the amount in full.
The shaman, after this, was completely unaware;
when someone told him,
he was greatly ashamed,
and pawned clothes to make up the amount.
Only two people fell short of their amount,
after the matter was concluded,
one was ill for over a month,
the other suffered from sores and swelling,
the cost of medicine and treatment,
exceeded what they owed,
and people considered it retribution for their private withholdings.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"The old frog in charge of fundraising,
there is no one with whom he cannot do good,
isn't he far superior to those who resort to torture and extortion?
Moreover, he exposes the embezzlers,
and averts their disasters,
so his manifestation of fierceness,
is precisely his practice of compassion."
According to the manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Rèn Jiànzhī,
was from Yútái,
and made a living trading felt and furs.
He exhausted his funds to travel to Shǎnxi.
On the way, he met a man,
who introduced himself:
"Shēn Zhútíng,
a native of Sùyū."
They found their conversation congenial,
swore to be brothers,
and traveled together.
Upon reaching Shǎnxi,
Rèn fell ill and could not rise,
and Shēn took good care of him.
After more than ten days had accumulated,
the illness grew critical.
He said to Shēn:
"My family has never had permanent property,
the clothing and food for eight mouths,
all depend on one person braving frost and dew.
Now unfortunately,
I will die in a foreign land.
You,
are my brother,
who else is there two thousand li away!
There are over two hundred taels in my purse,
take half for yourself,
to prepare a simple coffin for me,
the remainder can assist with travel expenses;
send the other half to my wife and children,
so they can bring my coffin back.
If you are willing to carry my remains back to my hometown,
then do not count the travel expenses."
He then propped himself on the pillow to write a letter for Shēn,
and by evening he died.
Shēn used five or six taels to buy a cheap coffin,
and after the burial,
the innkeeper urged him to move the coffin,
Shēn excused himself to find a temple,
and actually fled without returning.
The Rèn family only got definite news over a year later.
Rèn's son Xiù was seventeen at the time,
just studying under a teacher,
and from then on he abandoned his studies,
wanting to go find his father's coffin.
His mother pitied his youth,
but Xiù wept bitterly, wishing to die,
so she pawned assets to prepare for the journey,
and had an old servant assist him,
and only after half a year did he return.
After the funeral,
the family was as poor as if washed clean.
Fortunately, Xiù was intelligent,
after the mourning period ended,
he entered the Yútái county school.
But he was frivolous and fond of gambling,
his mother taught and admonished him very strictly,
but he ultimately did not change.
One day,
the provincial examiner arrived,
and he tested into the fourth rank.
His mother wept angrily and refused to eat.
Xiù felt ashamed and afraid,
and vowed to his mother.
Thereupon he shut himself indoors for over a year,
and finally achieved excellent rank and received a stipend.
His mother urged him to set up a school,
but people always considered him dissolute and unrestrained,
and all scorned and looked down on him.
There was a maternal uncle named Zhāng who traded in the capital.
He urged Xiù to go to the capital,
offering to take him along
without costing him any money.
Xiù was delighted
and followed him.
When they reached Línqīng,
they moored the boat outside the customs gate.
At that time, salt boats were densely gathered,
their masts and sails like a forest.
After lying down,
Xiù heard the sounds of water and people,
clamorous to the ear, making it impossible to sleep.
When the night grew quiet,
he suddenly heard the clear, crisp sound of dice from a neighboring boat.
It entered his ears and stirred his heart,
and he could not help feeling the old itch return.
He secretly listened to the other guests,
who were all sound asleep.
In his own purse, he had a thousand cash prepared,
and he longed to cross over to the other boat for a game.
He stealthily got up and untied his purse,
grabbed the money and hesitated.
Recalling his mother's admonition,
he tied it up again and put it away.
After lying down,
his heart pounded anxiously,
and he suffered from sleeplessness.
He got up again,
and untied the purse once more. This happened three times.
His excitement surged,
and he could no longer restrain himself.
Taking the money, he went straight over.
Arriving at the neighboring boat,
he saw two men gambling face to face,
with a rich pile of money staked.
Placing his money on the mat,
he immediately asked to join the game.
The two men were pleased
and immediately played dice with him.
Xiù won big.
When one guest ran out of money,
he pawned a large sum of gold with the boat owner,
gradually staking over ten strings of cash as a single bet.
Just as the gambling was at its peak,
another man boarded the boat.
After watching intently for a long time,
he also emptied his purse and pawned a hundred taels of gold with the owner,
joining the game to gamble together.
Zhāng woke up in the middle of the night
and realized Xiù was not in the boat.
Hearing the sound of dice,
he understood what was happening.
He then went to the neighboring boat,
intending to disrupt and stop him.
Upon arriving,
he saw that beside Xiù, the accumulated winnings were piled up like a mountain.
So he said nothing more,
but carried back several thousand cash.
He called all the other guests to get up,
and they went back and forth moving the money,
with over ten thousand cash still remaining.
Before long,
all three guests lost,
and all the money on the boat was emptied.
The guests wanted to gamble with gold,
but Xiù was already satisfied with his winnings.
He deliberately made it difficult for them by pretending he would only gamble with cash.
Zhāng, standing by his side,
urged and pressed him to return.
The three guests grew anxious and impatient.
The boat owner, eager for his commission,
borrowed from another boat,
obtaining over a hundred thousand cash.
The guests got the money,
and the gambling became even more extravagant.
Before long,
it all ended up with Xiù again.
By then, dawn had broken,
and the customs gate opened for the morning.
Together, they transported the money back.
The three guests also left.
The boat owner looked at the over two hundred taels of gold he had taken as pawn,
only to find it was all tinfoil ashes.
Greatly shocked,
he went to Xiù's boat,
explained what had happened,
and wanted to seek compensation from Xiù.
When he asked for his name and hometown,
he learned he was the son of Jiànzhī.
He shrank his neck in shame, sweating, and retreated.
Later, when inquiring with the boatmen,
he found out the owner was Shēn Zhútíng.
When Xiù was in Shǎn,
he had also heard his name.
By now, the ghost had already taken revenge on him,
so Xiù did not pursue the matter further.
He then pooled his funds with Zhāng to go north and start a business together.
By the end of the year, their profits multiplied severalfold.
Thus, he obtained a position in the Imperial College by making a contribution.
He further engaged in money-lending,
and within ten years,
his wealth made him a leading figure in the region.
Based on the manuscript version of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
in the region of Wú and Yuè there was a custom of racing dragon boats.
They would hollow out wood to form dragons,
paint them with scales,
and adorn them with gold and jade;
on top were carved ridgepoles and vermilion railings;
the sails and banners were all made of brocade.
At the stern of the boat was a dragon’s tail,
over ten feet high,
from which a wooden board was suspended by cloth ropes;
a child would sit on the board,
tumbling and somersaulting,
performing various clever acts;
below was the river water,
so perilous that it seemed he might fall at any moment.
Therefore, when purchasing such a child,
they would first bribe his parents with money,
and train him in advance;
if he fell into the water and died,
they were not to regret it.
In Wú, they would carry beautiful courtesans instead,
which was quite different.
In Zhènjiāng, there was a child named Jiǎng Āduān,
just seven years old,
agile and extraordinarily skillful,
none could surpass him,
and his reputation and value grew,
so he was still employed at sixteen.
When they reached the foot of Jīnshān,
he fell into the water and died.
Old Mrs. Jiǎng had only this son,
and could only wail in grief.
Āduān did not realize he was dead;
two men led him away,
and he saw another world within the water;
looking back,
he saw flowing waves encircling him on all sides,
standing like walls.
Soon he entered a palace,
and saw a man sitting wearing a helmet.
The two men said:
"This is Lord Lóngwō."
They then made him bow and prostrate himself.
Lord Lóngwō’s expression was gentle and serene,
and he said:
"Āduān’s skills qualify him to join the Willow Branch Troupe."
So they led him to a place,
with a spacious hall enclosed on four sides.
Hurrying to the eastern corridor,
several youths came out to greet him,
mostly around thirteen or fourteen years old.
Then an old woman arrived,
whom everyone called Granny Jiě.
She sat and ordered him to demonstrate his skills.
Afterward,
she taught him the "Qiántáng Thunderbolt" dance
and the "Dòngtíng Gentle Breeze" music.
Suddenly, the clamor of drums and gongs was heard,
and all the courtyards echoed;
then all the courtyards fell silent.
Granny feared Āduān might not master it immediately,
so she patiently coached him alone;
but after just one run-through,
Āduān had already grasped it perfectly.
Granny said happily:
"With this child,
we are no less than Wǎnxiá!"
The next day,
Lord Lóngwō inspected the troupes,
and all the troupes gathered.
First, he inspected the Yaksha Troupe: they wore ghost masks and fish-scale garments;
they struck a large gong,
about four feet in circumference;
the drum required four people to embrace it,
and its sound was like a great thunderclap,
so loud that shouting could no longer be heard.
When the dance began,
huge waves surged,
flowing horizontally across the sky,
occasionally dropping a speck of starlight,
which vanished upon touching the ground.
Lord Lóngwō quickly stopped them,
and ordered the Young Oriole Troupe to perform: all were sixteen-year-old beauties,
playing soft music on reed pipes,
and a gentle breeze wafted through,
the sound of waves stilled,
the water gradually congealing into a crystal world,
transparent from top to bottom.
After the inspection,
they all withdrew and stood below the western steps.
Next, he inspected the Swallow Troupe: all were young maidens with loose hair,
among them a girl,
about fourteen or fifteen years old,
who waved her sleeves and tilted her hair,
performing a scattered flower dance;
gracefully soaring and fluttering,
from her lapels, sleeves, stockings, and shoes,
multicolored flowers emerged,
fluttering down with the wind,
drifting and filling the courtyard.
After the dance,
she followed her troupe down to the western steps.
Āduān watched from the side,
and greatly admired her.
He asked someone from the same troupe,
and learned she was Wǎnxiá.
Not long after,
the Willow Branch Troupe was called.
Lord Lóngwō specifically tested Āduān.
Āduān performed the dance he had learned earlier,
his joy and sorrow following the melody,
his movements perfectly in rhythm.
Lord Lóngwō praised his intelligence and understanding,
and bestowed upon him a five-patterned trousered robe,
a fish-whisker gold hair clasp,
inlaid with a luminous pearl.
Āduān bowed in gratitude and descended,
also hurrying to the western steps,
each taking their place in line.
Āduān gazed from afar at Wǎnxiá among the crowd,
and Wǎnxiá also gazed at him from afar.
After a while,
Āduān hesitantly left his troupe and moved north,
while Wǎnxiá gradually left her troupe and moved south;
they were only a few steps apart,
but the rules were strict, and they dared not disrupt the troupes,
so they could only gaze at each other with longing hearts.
Then the Butterfly Troupe was inspected: boys and girls danced in pairs,
their heights, ages, and the yellow and white colors of their garments
were all identical.
After all troupes were inspected,
they filed out in order.
The Willow Branch Troupe was behind the Swallow Troupe,
so Āduān quickly moved to the front of his troupe,
while Wǎnxiá had deliberately lingered at the back.
Turning her head to see Āduān,
she intentionally dropped a coral hairpin,
which Āduān quickly tucked into his sleeve.
After returning,
he became lovesick and fell ill,
unable to sleep or eat.
Granny Jiě would bring him delicacies,
visiting three or four times a day,
tending to him with great care,
but his illness did not improve.
Granny was worried,
not knowing what to do,
and said:
"The birthday celebration of the King of Wújiāng is approaching,
what shall we do!"
At dusk,
a child came,
sat on the bed and spoke with him,
claiming to belong to the Butterfly Troupe.
Casually, he asked:
"Is your illness because of Wǎnxiá?"
Āduān asked in surprise:
"How do you know?"
The child laughed and said:
"Wǎnxiá is just like you."
Āduān sadly sat up,
and begged for a solution.
The child asked:
"Can you still walk?"
Āduān replied:
"I can still manage with effort."
The child helped him out,
opened a door to the south;
turning west,
they opened another double door.
They saw several acres of lotus flowers,
all growing on flat ground;
the leaves were as large as mats,
the flowers as big as canopies,
and fallen petals piled a foot high beneath the stems.
The child led him inside,
and said:
"Wait here."
Then he left.
After a short while,
a beautiful girl parted the lotus flowers and entered—
it was Wǎnxiá.
They met with surprise and joy,
each expressing their longing,
and briefly recounting their lives.
Then they used a stone to tilt a lotus leaf to the side,
forming a lovely screen;
they evenly spread lotus petals as a mat,
and happily lay together intimately.
Afterward,
they made a future appointment,
agreeing to meet daily at sunset,
and then parted.
Āduān returned,
and his illness soon recovered.
From then on, the two met daily in the lotus field.
After several days,
he followed Lóngwō Jūn to offer birthday congratulations to the King of Wújiāng.
After the birthday celebrations concluded,
all the troupes returned,
except Wǎnxiá and one other from the Rǔluán Troupe, who were kept in the palace to teach dance.
For several months,
there was no news at all.
Duān was despondent and felt as if he had lost something.
Only Granny Xiè traveled to and from the Wújiāng palace;
Duān claimed Wǎnxiá was his cousin,
and begged Granny Xiè to take him along,
hoping to see her once.
He stayed at the Wújiāng palace gate for several days,
but the palace restrictions were extremely strict,
and Wǎnxiá could not get out no matter how hard she tried.
He returned dejectedly.
After more than a month had passed,
he was nearly driven mad by longing.
One day,
Granny Xiè came in
and said to him mournfully:
"What a pity!
Wǎnxiá has thrown herself into the river!"
Duān was greatly shocked,
and tears streamed down uncontrollably.
He then tore off his cap and ripped his clothes,
hid some gold and pearls on his person, and left,
intending to follow her in death.
But when he saw the river water standing like a wall,
he tried to plunge headfirst into it but could not enter.
He thought of going back,
but feared that if he were questioned about his cap and clothes,
his punishment would be even heavier.
At his wit's end,
he was drenched in sweat down to his heels.
Suddenly, he noticed a large tree at the base of the wall,
so he climbed up it like a monkey,
gradually reaching the very top.
With a mighty leap, he threw himself down.
Fortunately, he did not get wet,
but instead found himself floating on the water.
Unexpectedly,
he seemed to glimpse the human world,
and so he drifted away, swimming.
After a while,
he reached the shore.
He sat for a while by the riverbank,
and suddenly thought of his old mother.
He then boarded a boat and left.
Upon arriving in his hometown,
he looked around at the houses,
feeling as if a whole lifetime had passed.
Hesitantly, he approached his home.
Suddenly, he heard a woman's voice from the window saying:
"Your son has come."
The voice sounded very much like Wǎnxiá's.
In a moment,
she came out with his mother,
and it was indeed Wǎnxiá.
At that moment, the joy of the two surpassed their sorrow;
but the old woman was a mixture of grief, doubt, shock, and joy,
all emotions arising at once.
Earlier,
while Wǎnxiá was in Wújiāng,
she felt movement in her womb.
The laws of the dragon palace were strict,
and she feared that once she gave birth,
she would be severely beaten;
moreover, she could not see Ā Duān even once.
Wanting only to die,
she secretly threw herself into the river.
Her body rose to the surface,
floating up and down in the waves.
A passenger boat rescued her,
and they asked where she lived.
Wǎnxiá had originally been a famous courtesan in Wú,
and when she drowned, her body had never been found.
Thinking she could not return to the brothel,
she said:
"In Zhènjiāng, the Jiǎng family—
that is my husband's home."
The passenger then hired a small boat for her
and sent her to that household.
Old Mrs. Jiǎng suspected a mistake,
but the woman insisted it was not wrong,
and then told the old woman the whole story in detail.
The old woman, seeing her graceful and charming manner,
rather liked her;
however, she worried that she was too young
and would surely not be willing to remain a widow forever.
But the woman was filial and respectful.
Seeing the family was poor,
she took off her precious ornaments and sold them for tens of thousands.
The old woman, observing that she had no other intentions,
was very pleased.
Yet she had no son,
and feared that once the woman gave birth,
the relatives and neighbors would not believe the child was legitimate,
so she discussed it with the woman.
The woman said:
"Mother, as long as you get a real grandson,
why must others know?"
The old woman also felt at ease with this.
Just then, Duān arrived,
and the woman was beside herself with joy.
The old woman also began to suspect her son was not dead;
secretly, she opened her son's grave,
and found the skeleton still there.
She then questioned Duān about this.
Only then did Duān suddenly realize the truth;
however, he feared Wǎnxiá would dislike that he was not human,
so he urged his mother not to speak of it again.
His mother agreed.
She then told the neighbors
that the body recovered back then was not her son's,
but she still worried that he could not father children.
Not long after,
Wǎnxiá actually gave birth to a boy,
and when they held him, he was no different from a normal child.
Only then were they happy.
After a long time,
Wǎnxiá gradually realized that Ā Duān was not human.
She then said:
"Why didn't you tell me earlier!
Any ghost who wears dragon palace clothing
for seven times seven days will have their soul and spirit solidified,
no different from a living person.
If one could obtain the dragon horn glue from the palace,
it could reconnect bones and joints and regenerate flesh and skin.
What a pity we didn't buy it earlier!"
Duān sold his pearl,
and a foreign merchant paid a million for it.
The family thus became immensely wealthy.
On the occasion of his mother's birthday,
the husband and wife performed song and dance to toast her,
and news of this reached the prince's mansion.
The prince wanted to seize Wǎnxiá by force.
Duān, afraid,
went to see the prince and stated:
"Both husband and wife are ghosts."
When examined, they cast no shadows, so he believed it,
and did not seize her.
He only sent palace ladies to a separate courtyard to learn her skills.
Wǎnxiá disfigured her face with turtle urine
before meeting them.
After teaching for three months,
they still could not master all her skills and left.
In Zhílì there was a young man named Mù,
whose childhood name was Shàngōng,
son of the merchant Mù Xiǎohuán.
He was intelligent and fond of study.
At sixteen,
his father considered literary pursuits impractical,
so he made him give them up and learn business,
and he accompanied his father to Chǔ.
Whenever there was nothing to do on the boat,
he would recite poetry.
Upon reaching Wǔchāng,
his father stayed at an inn,
to look after the goods stored there.
While his father was out,
the young man would take up a book and chant poems,
his cadence clear and resonant.
He noticed shadows flickering at the window,
as if someone were secretly listening,
but he did not think it strange.
One evening,
his father went out to a banquet,
and was gone a long time,
so the young man chanted even more earnestly.
Someone was pacing back and forth outside the window,
clearly visible in the moonlight.
Finding it odd,
he rushed out to look,
and saw a stunningly beautiful girl of fifteen or sixteen.
When she saw him,
she hurried away.
Two or three days later,
they loaded the goods and headed north,
and moored by the lake at dusk.
His father happened to be out,
when an old woman entered and said:
"Young sir, you have killed my daughter!"
Startled, he asked her what she meant.
She replied:
"My surname is Bái.
I have a daughter named Qiūliǎn,
who is quite literate.
She says that in the prefectural city,
she heard your clear chanting,
and has been thinking of it ever since,
to the point of losing sleep and appetite.
She wishes to be joined with you in marriage,
and you must not refuse."
The young man was truly fond of her,
but was afraid his father would be angry,
so he told her the truth directly.
The old woman did not believe him,
and insisted on a pledge.
He refused.
The old woman said angrily:
"In the human world, for marriage alliances,
there are those who seek betrothal gifts and cannot get them.
Now I, an old woman, act as matchmaker myself,
yet you do not accept her—
what greater shame could there be!
Do not think of crossing northward!"
With that she left.
A little later,
his father returned,
and he carefully told him the story,
secretly hoping he would consent.
But his father, considering the distance involved,
and looking down on the girl's lovesickness,
laughed it off.
Where their boat was moored,
the water was deep enough to submerge the scull;
but suddenly at night, sandbanks rose up,
and the boat was stuck and could not move.
Every year on the lake, some merchant boats would inevitably be detained to wait on the shoals;
when the spring floods came the next year,
and other goods had not yet arrived,
the goods on the boat would be worth a hundred times their original price.
Therefore, the old man was not too worried or surprised.
He only reckoned that coming south the next year,
he would still need to raise capital,
so he left his son behind and returned home alone.
The young man secretly rejoiced,
but regretted not having asked the old woman where she lived.
When dusk fell,
the old woman and a maid helped the girl to him,
spread out her clothes and laid her on the bed,
and said to him:
"My daughter is ill to this extent—
do not just lie back and act as if nothing is wrong!"
Then she left.
At first he was startled; then he moved the lamp to look at the girl:
her sickly appearance held a delicate charm,
her autumn-wave eyes naturally flowing.
He asked her a few questions,
and she gave a radiant smile.
He pressed her to say something.
She said:
"'For my lord I languish, yet before my lord I am shy'—
this could be chanted for me."
Overjoyed,
he wanted to approach her,
but pitied her weakness.
Reaching into her bosom,
he fondled her playfully.
Unconsciously, she happily relaxed and joked,
then said:
"If you will chant for me three times Wáng Jiàn's poem 'Silken Robe, Leaf by Leaf,'
my illness will be cured."
He did as she said.
After just two recitations,
she gathered her clothes and sat up, saying:
"I am cured!"
When he chanted it again,
her delicate voice trembled in harmony.
His spirits soared even higher,
so he put out the lamp and they slept together.
Before dawn, she rose and said:
"My old mother will be coming."
Soon after,
the old woman indeed arrived.
Seeing her daughter sitting happily, fully dressed,
she could not help but feel relieved;
she invited her daughter to leave,
but the girl bowed her head and said nothing.
The old woman then left by herself, saying:
"If you enjoy playing with the young sir,
that is up to you."
Then the young man began to inquire carefully about her residence.
The girl said:
"You and I are merely chance acquaintances;
marriage is not yet certain—
why must you know my family's gate?"
Yet the two loved each other dearly,
and their vows were firm.
One night, the girl rose early and trimmed the lamp;
suddenly she opened a book and sadly, tears glistening,
he hurriedly rose and asked her why.
She said:
"Your father will soon arrive.
Regarding our affair,
I just now divined with a book;
opening it, I got Lǐ Yì's 'Song of Jiāngnán'—
the words' meaning is inauspicious."
He comforted her, saying:
"The first line, 'Married to a merchant of Qútáng'—
that is already very auspicious;
what inauspiciousness is there?"
Then she became a little happier,
rose and bid farewell, saying:
"Let us part for now;
when day breaks, a thousand eyes will be watching."
He held her arm, choked with sobs, and asked:
"If our happy affair is settled,
where can I send word to you?"
She said:
"I will often send someone to inquire;
whether it is settled or not, I will surely hear."
He was about to escort her down to the boat,
but she firmly declined and left.
Not long after,
Mù indeed arrived.
Gradually, the young man revealed the affair.
His father suspected he had summoned a courtesan,
and angrily berated him.
But after carefully checking the goods on the boat
and finding no loss,
he stopped his scolding.
One evening,
when the old man was not on the boat,
the girl suddenly came.
They met, clinging to each other,
not knowing what plan to make.
She said:
"Rise and fall are fated;
let us think of the present.
I will keep you here for two months,
then we can discuss what to do."
At parting,
they agreed to meet by using chanting as a signal.
Thus, whenever his father went out,
he would chant loudly,
and the girl would come.
By the end of the fourth month,
commodity prices had missed their season,
and the merchants were at a loss,
so they pooled funds to pray at the temple of the lake god.
After the Duānwǔ Festival,
heavy rains came,
and the boats could finally pass.
After returning home,
Shēng fell ill from longing.
Mù was deeply worried,
and both shamans and doctors were consulted.
Shēng privately told his mother:
"This illness cannot be cured by medicine or prayers;
only when Qiūliǎn comes will it end."
At first, the old man was angry; after a long time,
as Shēng grew increasingly frail and weak,
he began to fear,
hired a carriage to take his son,
and returned to Chǔ,
mooring the boat at the former spot.
He inquired among the residents,
but none knew of an old woman named Bái.
It happened that an old woman was punting her boat by the lakeside,
and she identified herself.
The old man boarded her boat,
caught sight of Qiūliǎn,
and secretly rejoiced in his heart.
But upon inquiring about her family background,
he found they were merely a family drifting on the water.
He then truthfully explained the cause of his son's illness,
hoping the girl would board his boat,
if only to alleviate his grave illness.
The old woman, citing the lack of a marriage agreement,
refused.
The girl revealed half her face,
eagerly watching and listening.
Hearing their words,
tears welled up in her eyes, ready to fall.
The old woman looked at her daughter's face,
and moved by the old man's earnest pleas,
finally consented.
That night,
after the old man left,
the girl indeed came.
Approaching the bed, she sobbed and said:
"Last year, my condition
has now befallen you!
The taste of this suffering
must be made known to you.
But in such a weakened state,
how can you recover hastily?
Let me recite a poem for you."
Shēng was also pleased.
The girl recited Wáng Jiàn's former work.
Shēng said:
"This expresses your heartfelt feelings,
but how can it cure the two of us?
Yet hearing your voice,
my spirit is already refreshed.
Please try reciting for me 'Willows, a thousand branches, all lean westward.'"
The girl complied.
Shēng praised:
"How delightful!
When you formerly recited song lyrics,
there was 'Gathering Lotus Seeds':
'Lotus fragrance spans ten acres of pond.'
My heart has not forgotten it;
please chant it slowly with drawn-out tones."
The girl again complied.
Just as she finished,
Shēng leaped up and said:
"How could I ever have been ill!"
They then embraced intimately,
and the severe illness vanished as if lost.
Afterward, he asked:
"What did my father say to the old woman?
Will the matter succeed?"
The girl had already discerned the old man's intent
and directly replied,
"It will not."
After the girl left,
the father came.
Seeing Shēng already up,
he was overjoyed,
but only comforted and encouraged him.
He then said:
"The girl is truly fine.
But since childhood,
she has handled the helm and sung boat songs.
Not only is she of lowly status,
but also lacking in chastity."
Shēng remained silent.
After the old man left,
the girl returned,
and Shēng relayed his father's opinion.
The girl said:
"I have observed this clearly: in worldly affairs,
the more one hurries, the farther one gets;
the more one advances, the more one is rejected.
We must let his mind change on its own,
so he instead seeks us."
Shēng asked for a plan.
The girl said:
"All merchants aim for profit.
I have a method to know commodity prices.
Just now, I saw the goods in your boat
will yield little profit.
Tell the old man for me: stock such-and-such item,
profit threefold;
such-and-such item,
tenfold.
When you return home,
if my words prove true,
then I will be a good daughter-in-law.
When we meet again,
you will be eighteen,
I seventeen—
there will be plenty of time for joy,
so why worry?"
Shēng told his father the prices mentioned.
The father rather disbelieved,
but tentatively used half his remaining funds to follow her advice.
After returning home,
the goods he had purchased himself
caused a great loss of capital;
fortunately, the portion following the girl's advice
yielded substantial profit,
roughly balancing out.
Thus, he admired Qiūliǎn's foresight.
Shēng further exaggerated,
saying the girl claimed she could make him rich.
The old man then raised more capital and went south.
Reaching the lake,
for several days he did not see the old woman Bái;
after a few more days,
he finally saw her boat moored under a willow,
and thus sent betrothal gifts.
The old woman declined them all,
only selecting an auspicious date to send her daughter to their boat.
The old man hired another boat
for his son's wedding ceremony.
The girl then had the old man go further south,
listing all the goods he should purchase
and handing him a written record.
The old woman then invited her son-in-law to leave
and live on their boat.
The old man returned after three months.
When the goods reached Chǔ,
their prices had multiplied several times.
As they prepared to return,
the girl requested to bring some lake water.
After returning home,
she added a little to every meal,
as if using vinegar or sauce.
Henceforth, each time they traveled south,
they would bring back several jars for her.
Three or four years later,
she gave birth to a son.
One day,
she wept and longed to return home.
The old man then took his son and daughter-in-law to Chǔ.
When they reached the lake,
they did not know where the old woman was.
The woman knocked on the side of the boat and called for her mother,
her spirit and appearance utterly lost.
She urged Shēng to inquire along the lake.
It happened that someone fishing for sturgeon
had caught a white sturgeon.
Shēng went close to look at it;
it was a huge creature,
its shape entirely human-like,
with breasts and genitals fully formed.
Finding it strange,
he returned and told the woman.
The woman was greatly alarmed,
saying she had long had a vow to release living creatures,
and urged Shēng to redeem and release it.
Shēng went to negotiate with the fisherman,
but the fisherman demanded an exorbitant price.
The woman said:
"Since I have been in your family,
I have managed no less than tens of thousands in gold;
why be so stingy over such a trifling amount!
If you insist on refusing: I will throw myself into the lake and die forever!"
Shēng was afraid,
and did not dare tell his father,
but stole money to redeem and release it.
When he returned,
the woman was not there,
and searching for her yielded nothing,
only arriving near dawn.
He asked:
"Where have you been?"
She said:
"I just went to my mother's place."
He asked:
"Where is your mother?"
She blushed and said:
"Now I must tell you the truth: what you just redeemed,
was my mother.
Formerly in Dòngtíng,
the Dragon Lord appointed her to oversee travelers.
Recently, as the palace wished to select concubines,
I was praised by those spreading rumors,
so the Dragon Lord ordered my mother,
to be seated and demanded.
My mother truthfully reported it.
The Dragon Lord would not listen,
and exiled my mother to the southern shore,
where she nearly starved to death,
hence encountering the previous calamity.
Now, though the calamity is avoided,
the punishment is not yet lifted.
If you love me,
pray to the True Lord on my behalf to have it remitted.
If you despise me as a different kind,
I ask to return the child to you.
I will leave on my own;
the offerings of the dragon palace
may not be a hundred times less than your family's."
Shēng was greatly startled,
worried that the True Lord could not be met.
The woman said:
"Tomorrow at the hour of the snake,
the True Lord will arrive.
When you see a limping Daoist priest: quickly bow to him,
and follow him even into the water.
The True Lord favors scholars,
he will surely take pity and agree."
Then she took out a square of fish-bellied silk.
Saying:
"If asked what you seek,
present this,
and ask him to write one character 'exempt'
on it."
Shēng waited as instructed.
Indeed, a Daoist priest came limping along,
and Shēng prostrated himself in bow.
The Daoist hurried away,
and Shēng followed behind him.
The Daoist threw his staff into the water,
and leaped onto it.
Shēng actually followed him and boarded,
finding it was not a staff,
but a boat.
He bowed again.
The Daoist asked:
"What do you seek?"
Shēng presented the silk and requested writing.
The Daoist unrolled it and said:
"This is the white sturgeon's fin;
how did you encounter it?"
Chángōng did not dare conceal,
and recounted the whole story in detail.
The Daoist laughed and said:
"This creature is quite refined and elegant,
how can the old dragon be so licentious!"
Then he took out a brush and hastily wrote
"exempt"
character,
shaped like a talisman,
and returned the boat, telling him to disembark.
Then he saw the Daoist treading on his staff, floating away,
and in a moment he was gone.
Returning to the boat,
the woman was delighted,
but urged him not to reveal it to his parents.
Two or three years after returning,
the old man traveled south,
and did not return for several months.
The lake water was all used up,
and after long waiting without his return,
the woman fell ill,
panting rapidly day and night,
and instructed:
"If I die,
do not bury me,
but at the hours of mǎo, wǔ, and yǒu,
recite once Dù Fǔ's poem 'Dreaming of Lǐ Bái',
and I will not decay in death.
Wait until the water arrives,
pour it into a basin,
close the door and loosen my clothes,
carry me in and immerse me,
and I should revive."
After panting for several days,
she quietly passed away.
Half a month later,
Old Man Mù arrived,
and Shēng urgently followed her instructions,
immersing her for about two hours,
and she gradually revived.
From then on, she often thought of returning south.
Later, when the old man died,
Shēng followed her wish,
and moved to Chǔ.
According to the manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain Governor of Húnán,
dispatched a deputy to escort six hundred thousand in military funds to the capital.
On the way, they were caught in rain,
and by dusk had fallen behind schedule,
with nowhere to stay,
when they saw an ancient temple in the distance,
and thus went to seek shelter.
At daybreak,
looking at the funds they were escorting,
they were completely gone.
Everyone was shocked and bewildered,
with no one to blame.
Returning to report to the Governor,
the Governor thought it absurd,
and intended to punish them by law.
When interrogating all the attendants,
there were no differing accounts.
The Governor ordered them to return to the original place,
to investigate and trace the origins.
Arriving before the temple,
he saw a blind man,
whose appearance was most unusual,
and who had posted a sign that read:
"I can handle delicate matters."
So he asked him to perform a divination.
The blind man said:
"This is about a lost sum of money."
The assistant prefect said:
"Yes."
He then related his previous troubles.
The blind man called for a sedan chair,
saying:
"Just follow me,
and you'll know for yourself."
So they did as he said,
and all the officials and attendants followed him.
The blind man said:
"East."
They went east.
The blind man said:
"North."
They went north.
After five days in all,
they entered deep mountains,
and suddenly saw a walled city,
with residents gathered densely.
Entering the city,
they walked for some time,
when the blind man said:
"Stop."
He then got down from the sedan chair,
and pointing south with his hand:
"You'll see a high gate facing west,
you can knock on the door and ask for yourself."
He cupped his hands and left on his own.
The assistant prefect followed his instructions,
and indeed saw a high gate,
gradually entering it.
A person came out,
dressed in Han-style clothing,
not stating his name.
The assistant prefect explained where he came from.
The person said:
"Please stay for a few days,
I will take you to meet the person in charge."
He then led him away,
had him stay alone in a place,
and provided him with food and drink.
During leisure time while strolling,
he reached the back of the residence,
and saw a garden pavilion,
entering and wandering through it.
Old pines shaded the sun,
fine grass was like a carpet.
After several turns along corridors and pavilions,
there was another high pavilion,
ascending the steps and entering,
he saw several human skins hanging on the wall,
with all five facial features complete,
a foul smell wafting from them.
He couldn't help but feel his hair stand on end,
and hastily retreated back to his quarters.
Thinking he would leave his skin in a foreign land,
he had no hope of survival,
but considering that advancing or retreating meant death,
he simply resigned himself to it.
The next day,
the man in Han clothing summoned him,
saying:
"Today you can have an audience."
The assistant prefect assented.
The man in Han clothing rode a spirited horse very swiftly,
the assistant prefect ran on foot to keep up,
soon,
they reached a gate of a military headquarters,
solemn like a governor's yamen,
men in black clothes stood in rows on both sides,
the atmosphere was stern and imposing.
The man in Han clothing dismounted,
and led him inside.
There was another inner gate.
He saw a kingly figure,
wearing a pearl crown and embroidered robes,
sitting facing south.
The assistant prefect hurried forward,
and prostrated himself in audience.
The king asked:
"Are you the escort official from Húnán?"
The assistant prefect affirmed.
The king said:
"The silver is all here.
This small amount,
if your governor generously presents it as a gift,
it wouldn't be unacceptable."
The assistant prefect tearfully pleaded:
"The deadline has passed,
returning will surely mean execution,
what proof can I present in my report?"
The king said:
"This is not difficult."
He then gave him a large letter, saying:
"Take this back to him,
and you'll be safe."
He also sent strong men to escort him.
The assistant prefect, trembling with fear,
dared not argue,
accepted the letter and returned.
The mountains, rivers, and roads
were all different from the route they came by.
Once out of the mountains,
the escorts left.
After several days,
he reached Chángshā,
and respectfully reported to the governor.
The governor thought it absurd,
angrily refusing to listen to explanations,
ordering his attendants to quickly bind him with ropes.
The assistant prefect untied the bag and took out the letter,
the governor opened and read it, before finishing,
his face turned ashen.
He ordered his bonds removed,
only saying:
"The silver is a small matter,
you may leave for now."
Thereupon he urgently issued orders to subordinate officials,
to find a way to make up the missing amount.
A few days later,
the governor fell ill,
and soon died.
Earlier,
the governor was sleeping with his beloved concubine,
upon waking,
he found all her hair gone.
The entire yamen was shocked and bewildered,
unable to guess the reason.
It turned out the letter contained her hair.
There was also a note that read:
"You started as a county magistrate,
and rose to the highest ministerial rank.
Bribes and greed,
are too numerous to count.
The previous six hundred thousand taels of silver,
have already been received into the treasury.
You should take from your own greedy coffers,
to replenish the original amount.
The escort official is innocent,
you must not punish him.
Taking your concubine's hair earlier,
was a slight warning.
If you still do not heed the command,
your head will be taken sooner or later.
The concubine's hair is returned,
as clear proof."
After the governor's death,
his family began to circulate the letter.
Later, subordinates sent people to search for the place,
but found only steep cliffs and deep ravines,
with no path at all.
The Historian of the Strange says:
"The red thread and golden box,
used to punish greed,
is indeed satisfyingly strange.
But the immortal of Táoyuán,
does not engage in robbery;
even where swordsmen gather,
how could there be walled cities and yamens?
Alas!
What kind of deity is this?
If such a place truly existed,
I fear those seeking redress in the world would have no end."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A certain Mr. Jiǎ had an affair with his servant's wife,
then killed the servant and took the wife,
and had two sons and a daughter.
After nineteen years,
a great bandit army sacked the city,
looting everything.
A young bandit,
holding a knife, entered Jiǎ's house.
Jiǎ looked at him,
and he strongly resembled the dead servant.
"I'm finished now!"
He offered all his wealth to ransom his life.
But the bandit paid no heed,
nor said a word,
only searched for people and killed them,
killing a total of twenty-seven members of the family before leaving.
Jiǎ's head was not completely severed,
and after the bandits left, he briefly revived,
and could still speak.
He died after three days.
Alas!
Retribution is indeed unfailing,
how terrifying it is!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Zhāng Wòzhòng served in the military at Qúzhōu,
and said:
"In Qúzhōu, when the night is quiet,
people dare not walk alone.
On the bell tower, there is a ghost
with a horn on its head,
its appearance fierce and hideous.
Upon hearing the sound of someone walking, it immediately descends.
People flee in terror,
and the ghost then leaves as well.
However, those who see it invariably fall ill,
and many die.
Also, in the city, there is a pond
from which a bolt of white cloth emerges at night,
like a roll of silk laid across the ground.
If a passerby picks it up,
they are immediately dragged into the water.
There is also a duck ghost:
when the night is quiet,
and the pondside is utterly deserted,
if one hears the sound of a duck,
they will fall ill."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Hé Jiǒngqīng
was from Píngyīn.
When he first served as a magistrate in Qínzhōng,
an oil seller committed a minor offense.
His words were blunt,
and Hé grew angry,
beating him to death with a rod.
Later, he rose to an official position in the Ministry of Personnel,
and his family became wealthy.
He built a tower,
and on the day the beam was raised,
relatives and friends raised their cups to congratulate him.
Suddenly, he saw the oil seller enter,
and secretly felt horrified and suspicious.
Soon after, it was reported that his concubine had given birth to a son.
He said with a sorrowful expression:
"The tower is not yet completed,
but the one who will tear it down has already arrived!"
People thought he was joking,
but they did not know he had actually seen something.
Later, when the son grew up,
he was extremely unruly
and squandered the family fortune.
He worked as a servant for others,
and whenever he earned a few coins,
he would buy sesame oil to eat.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"I have often seen wealthy families with towers and mansions stretching far and wide,
but after their deaths,
upon revisiting, they have already become ruins.
This must be because someone destined to tear down the tower was born into their family.
When one occupies a position above others,
how can they not be vigilant early on!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
In the Ming dynasty, General Péng Hóng
marched into Shǔ to suppress bandits.
Deep in the mountains,
they came upon a large Buddhist monastery,
said to have been without monks for a hundred years.
When they inquired with the locals,
they said:
"There are demons in the temple,
and anyone who enters dies."
Péng, fearing an ambush by bandits,
led his troops, cutting through the overgrowth to enter.
In the front hall,
a black eagle flew out through the gate. The middle hall was no different;
proceeding further,
they reached the Buddha pavilion.
Looking around, they saw nothing unusual,
but all who entered suffered unbearable headaches.
Péng himself entered,
and the same happened to him.
After a short while,
a large scorpion, as big as a pipa,
crawled clumsily down from a board.
The entire army fled in panic.
Péng then set fire to the temple.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Zhēn Yùshēng,
a native of Yílíng in Chǔ,
was the son of a Provincial Graduate.
He was skilled in writing,
handsome in appearance,
and renowned by the age of twenty.
In his childhood,
a physiognomist said:
"Later, you will marry a female Daoist as your wife."
His parents both thought it laughable.
Yet when arranging marriages for him,
they struggled to find a suitable match.
His mother, Madame Zāng,
originally hailed from Huánggāng.
Yùshēng therefore went to visit his maternal grandmother.
He heard people at the time say:
"Among the 'Four Yún' of Huángzhōu,
the youngest is peerless."
It was because the prefecture had a Lǚzǔ Shrine,
where all the female Daoists were beautiful,
hence the saying.
The shrine was only a dozen or so *lǐ* from the Zāng family village,
so Yùshēng secretly went there.
He knocked at the gate,
and indeed there were three or four female Daoists
who happily welcomed him,
all graceful and refined in demeanor.
Among them, the youngest one
was truly unparalleled in the world;
he was fond of her and gazed at her intently.
She rested her chin on her hand,
but looked elsewhere.
The other Daoists searched for cups to brew tea.
Yùshēng seized the moment to ask her name.
She replied:
"Yún Qī,
surname Chén."
Yùshēng teased:
"How strange!
I happen to be surnamed Pān."
Chén blushed crimson,
lowered her head without speaking,
rose, and left.
After a short while,
they steeped tea
and offered fine fruits.
Each gave their name: one,
Bái Yúnshēn,
