around thirty years old;
one,
Shèng Yúnmián,
just over twenty;
one,
Liáng Yúndòng,
about twenty-four or twenty-five,
but was the junior.
Yet Yún Qī did not appear.
Yùshēng was deeply disappointed,
and so asked about her.
Bái said:
"This girl is afraid of strangers."
Yùshēng then rose to take his leave.
Bái tried hard to detain him,
but he left without staying.
Bái said:
"If you wish to see Yún Qī,
you may come again tomorrow."
Yùshēng returned home,
his longing extremely intense.
The next day,
he went there again.
All the Daoists were present,
only Yún Qī was missing;
he did not immediately ask.
The Daoists prepared food and urged him to stay for a meal.
Yùshēng firmly declined,
but they would not listen.
Bái broke a cake and handed him chopsticks,
urging him to eat with great earnestness.
Eventually he asked:
"Where is Yún Qī?"
They replied:
"She will come by herself."
A long time passed,
the day was already late,
and Yùshēng wanted to return.
Bái grabbed his wrist and detained him, saying:
"Stay here for now,
I will fetch the girl to meet you."
Yùshēng then stayed.
Soon after,
lamps were lit and wine was set out,
and Yúnmián also left.
After several rounds of wine,
Yùshēng excused himself, saying he was drunk.
Bái said:
"Drink three cups,
then Yún Qī will appear."
Yùshēng indeed drank the specified amount.
Liáng also used this to urge him,
and Yùshēng drank it all again,
then overturned his cup and announced his departure.
Bái looked at Liáng and said:
"Our faces are too thin,
we cannot persuade him to drink.
You go and drag Chén here,
and tell her that Pān Láng has been waiting for Miàocháng for a long time."
Liáng went,
returned after a short while,
and reported in full:
"Yún Qī will not come."
Yùshēng wanted to leave,
but the night was already deep,
so he pretended to be drunk and lay down on his back.
The two women undressed him in turn,
and successively had their way with him.
All night long, he could not bear their harassment.
When dawn broke,
he left without sleeping.
For several days he dared not go again,
yet his thoughts of Yún Qī remained unforgettable,
only he occasionally spied on the place from nearby.
One day,
as dusk fell,
Bái went out the gate
and left with a young man.
Yùshēng was pleased,
and not very afraid of Liáng,
so he hurried to knock at the gate.
Yúnmián came out to answer the door.
Upon inquiry,
it turned out Liáng had also gone elsewhere.
He then asked for Yún Qī.
Shèng led him away,
entering another courtyard,
and called out:
"Yún Qī!
A guest has arrived."
Only then did they see the chamber door slam shut.
Shèng laughed and said:
"The door is closed."
Yùshēng stood outside the window,
as if about to speak,
and Shèng then left.
Yún Qī said from behind the window:
"Everyone uses me as bait
to hook you.
If you come frequently,
my life will be in danger.
I cannot forever maintain the pure precepts,
nor dare I abandon all sense of shame.
I only wish to serve someone like Pān Láng."
Yùshēng then pledged to be with her until their hair turned white.
Yún Qī said:
"My master raised me,
which was also no easy task.
If you truly love me,
you should use twenty taels of silver to redeem me.
I will wait for you for three years.
If you hope for a secret rendezvous,
that I cannot do."
Yùshēng agreed.
Just as he was about to explain himself further,
Shèng returned,
and he followed her out,
then bid farewell and returned home.
His heart was filled with melancholy,
and he thought of finding a way
to once more behold her lovely countenance,
when a servant from home came to report his father's illness,
so he returned by starlight that very night.
Not long after,
the Xiàolián passed away.
His mother was extremely strict in household discipline,
so he dared not let her know his thoughts,
but only secretly reduced his expenses,
saving up day by day.
Whenever someone proposed a marriage,
he would use the mourning period as an excuse.
His mother would not listen.
The young man gently told her:
"Previously in Huánggāng,
my maternal grandmother wished to arrange a marriage with the Chén family,
which was truly my heartfelt desire.
Now that this great misfortune has occurred,
news has been cut off,
and it has been a long time since I inquired in Huánggāng;
I wish to go there for a short while,
and if the match does not succeed,
I will follow your command."
His mother agreed.
So he took his savings and left.
Arriving in Huánggāng,
he went to the nunnery,
but found the courtyard desolate and bleak,
greatly different from before.
Gradually entering,
he saw only an old nun cooking under the stove,
and so approached to inquire.
The nun said:
"The old Daoist priest died the year before last,
and the 'Four Yún's'
have scattered like stars."
He asked:
"Where have they gone?"
She said:
"Yún Shēn and Yún Dòng
followed some young ruffians away;
I heard before that Yún Qī is staying in the north of the prefecture;
as for Yún Mián, I have no news."
Hearing this,
the young man sighed in sorrow.
He ordered his carriage to go immediately to the north of the prefecture,
inquiring at every temple he encountered,
but found few traces or clues.
He returned disappointed and resentful,
and falsely told his mother:
"My uncle said: Old Mr. Chén has gone to Yuèzhōu,
and when he returns,
he will send a messenger."
After more than half a year,
his mother returned to her maiden home,
and asked her mother about the matter,
but her mother was completely unaware.
The mother was angry that her son had deceived her;
the grandmother suspected that her nephew and her son had conspired,
but did not mention it.
Fortunately, the uncle was far away on a journey,
so there was no way to verify the falsehood.
The mother, to fulfill a vow of incense, ascended Lián Peak,
and fasted and lodged at the foot of the mountain.
After she had lain down,
the innkeeper knocked on the door,
sending a female Daoist to lodge in the same room,
who said of herself:
"Chén Yúnqī."
Hearing that the lady was from Yílíng,
she moved to sit by the bed,
and told of her hardships,
her words sorrowful and pitiful.
At the end, she said:
"I have a cousin, Mr. Pān,
who is from the same place as the lady,
I trouble you to ask one of your sons or nephews to pass on a message,
just say that I am temporarily staying with my shīshū, Wáng Dàochéng, at Hèqī Temple,
suffering hardship morning and night,
each day feels like a year.
Let him come visit me early;
I fear that if he delays beyond this,
he may never know."
The lady inquired about the name,
but again did not know it,
and only said:
"Since he is at the school,
the scholars there must have heard of him."
Before dawn, they parted early,
with earnest repeated entreaties.
After the lady returned home,
she mentioned this to her son,
and the young man knelt down and said:
"To tell you the truth, mother: the so-called Mr. Pān,
is me."
Once his mother knew the reason,
she angrily said:
"Unworthy son!
Engaging in licentiousness in temples,
taking a Daoist as your wife,
what face do you have to see relatives and guests!"
The young man hung his head,
not daring to utter a word.
It happened that the young man went to the prefecture to take an examination,
and secretly ordered a boat to visit Wáng Dàochéng.
When he arrived,
Yúnqī had gone on a journey half a month before and had not returned.
After returning home,
he fell ill from melancholy.
Just then, old woman Zāng passed away,
and his mother went to attend the funeral,
but after the burial, she lost her way,
and arrived at the Jīng family's home.
Upon inquiry,
it turned out to be a cousin of her clan.
They invited each other in.
She saw a young girl in the hall,
about eighteen or nineteen years old,
with graceful and beautiful features,
such as she had never seen before.
The lady had long wished to find a good wife for her son,
so that he would not be discontent,
and her heart was moved,
so she spoke of her life's circumstances.
Her cousin said:
"This is a daughter of the Wáng family,
a niece of the Jīng family.
Both her parents are lost,
and she is temporarily staying here."
She asked:
"Who is her fiancé's family?"
She said:
"She has none."
Taking her hand and speaking with her,
she found her demeanor charming and gentle,
and the mother was greatly pleased,
staying overnight there,
and privately told her cousin her own thoughts.
Her cousin said:
"That would be excellent.
But this girl sets herself very high;
otherwise,
why would she have delayed until now?
Let me discuss it with her."
The lady invited the girl to share her bed,
and they talked and laughed very happily;
the girl herself wished to become the lady's daughter.
The lady was delighted,
and asked her to return together to Jīngzhōu;
the girl was even more pleased.
The next day,
they returned by boat together.
Upon arrival,
the young man was still ill and had not risen.
His mother comforted him in his severe illness,
and had a maidservant secretly tell him:
"The lady has brought a beauty back for the young master."
The young man did not believe it,
but peeped through the window,
and saw that she was even more stunningly beautiful than Yúnqī.
Then he thought: the three-year agreement had already passed;
she had gone on a journey and not returned,
so her lovely face must already have an owner.
Obtaining such a beauty,
his heart was somewhat comforted.
So he smiled with delight,
and his illness soon recovered.
His mother then called the two to meet each other.
The young man came out,
and the lady said to the girl:
"Do you know why I brought you back with me?"
The girl smiled and said:
"I already know.
But my original intention in coming back with you,
mother, you do not know.
but news has been cut off for a long time,
and they must already have another good match.
If that is so,
then I will be your daughter-in-law;
if not,
then I will always be your daughter,
and repay you someday."
The lady said:
"Since there is already a prior agreement,
I will not force the matter.
But when I was at Wǔzǔ Mountain before,
a female Daoist asked about the Pān family,
and now it is the Pān family again.
I knew for certain that among the prominent clans of Yílíng, there is no such surname."
The girl exclaimed in surprise:
"Was it my mother who lived below Wòlián Peak?
The one inquiring about the Pān family,
that was me."
Only then did the mother suddenly realize,
and said with a laugh:
"If so,
then Pān Shēng is indeed here."
The girl asked:
"Where is he?"
The lady ordered a maid to lead her to ask Shēng.
Shēng exclaimed in surprise:
"Are you Yún Qī?"
The girl asked:
"How did you know?"
Shēng explained the situation,
and she then understood that it had been a jest about Pān Láng.
Realizing it was Shēng,
the girl was too shy to continue talking,
and hurried back to tell her mother.
The mother asked why she had the surname Wáng again.
She replied:
"I was originally surnamed Wáng.
The Daoist master took a liking to me,
so she treated me as her daughter,
and I took her surname."
The lady was also pleased,
and chose an auspicious day for them to complete the wedding ceremony.
Previously,
the girl and Yún Mián had both relied on Wáng Dàochéng.
Dàochéng's dwelling was cramped,
so Yún Mián left for Hànkǒu.
The girl was delicate and naive, unable to endure hardship,
and also ashamed to go out and practice the Daoist profession,
so Dàochéng was rather displeased with her.
It happened that the Jīng family was going to Huánggāng,
and the girl, meeting them, shed tears,
so she went with them,
was made to change into women's clothing,
and was to be married into a scholar-official family.
Therefore, they concealed that she had once been registered as a Daoist.
But when suitors came to inquire about her name,
the girl was always unwilling,
and her uncle and aunt did not know her intentions,
and grew weary and displeased with her.
On this day,
following the lady back,
having found someone to entrust herself to,
it was like a heavy burden lifted.
After the wedding ceremony,
each recounted their experiences,
weeping for joy.
The girl was filial and respectful,
and the lady genuinely cherished and loved her;
but she enjoyed playing the qin and chess,
and did not know how to manage household affairs,
which rather worried the lady.
After more than a month,
the mother sent the two to visit the Jīng family,
where they stayed for several days before returning.
Sailing on the river,
suddenly another boat passed by,
with a female Daoist inside.
As they drew near,
it turned out to be Yún Mián.
Yún Mián alone was close to the girl.
The girl was delighted,
invited her to join them on the boat,
and they faced each other with sorrow.
She asked:
"Where are you going?"
Shèng said:
"I have long been deeply concerned.
I went all the way to Hèqī Guàn,
but heard you had gone to rely on your uncle Jīng.
So I was going to Huánggāng,
to pay a visit and inquire.
I never imagined the one in my heart had already been reunited.
Now seeing you like an immortal,
leaving me, this wanderer,
I don't know when it will end!"
And she sobbed.
The girl devised a plan: have her change out of her Daoist robes,
pretend to be her elder sister,
and accompany them back to the lady,
then slowly choose a good match.
Shèng agreed.
After returning,
the girl first informed the lady,
then Shèng entered.
Her demeanor was that of a lady from a great family;
in conversation and laughter,
she was experienced and worldly-wise.
The mother, being widowed,
suffered from loneliness,
found great joy in Shèng's company,
and only feared she might leave.
Shèng rose early to do the mother's arduous tasks for her,
not acting like a guest.
The mother was even more pleased,
and secretly thought of taking the girl's sister as a concubine for her son,
to cover up the name of being a female Daoist,
but did not dare say it.
One day,
forgetting something that needed to be done,
she anxiously asked about it,
only to find Shèng had already prepared it long before.
She thus said to the girl:
"A painting-like beauty who cannot manage a household,
what use is she?
If the new bride were like the elder sister,
I would have no worries."
Unbeknownst to her, the girl had long had this in mind,
but only feared the mother would disapprove.
Hearing the mother's words,
she said with a smile:
"Since Mother loves her,
what if the new bride wishes to emulate Yīng and Huáng?"
The mother did not speak,
but also chuckled.
The girl withdrew,
and told Shēng:
"The old mother has given her consent."
Then she prepared another clean room,
and said:
"Back at the temple, when we shared a pillow,
you said: 'If only we could find one person who truly knows affection,
the two of us should serve him together.'
Do you still remember?"
Shèng could not help but have tears glistening in both eyes,
and said:
"What I meant by affection,
is nothing else: like when I toiled day after day,
and not a single person knew the hardships;
these past few days,
with just a little effort,
I have already troubled the old mother to care and remember me,
then the warmth and coldness in my heart are suddenly different.
If you do not issue an order to expel the guest,
and allow me to long accompany the old mother,
then my wish is fulfilled,
and I do not expect the former words to be carried out."
The girl told the mother.
The mother had the sisters burn incense,
and each vowed words of no regret,
then had Shēng perform the marital rites with her.
When about to retire for the night,
she told Shēng:
"I am a twenty-three-year-old old maiden."
Shēng still did not believe it.
Afterwards, the crimson stain on the bedding,
made him find it remarkable.
Shèng said:
"The reason I was happy to gain a good husband,
is not that I could not endure solitude;
it is truly because, as a woman of the inner chambers,
to brazenly socialize and respond like a courtesan,
is something I could not bear.
Borrowing this one occasion,
to have my name entered in your register,
I shall serve your old mother for you,
and manage the inner household.
As for the joys of the bedchamber,
please explore them with someone else."
After three days,
she took her bedding to follow the mother,
and could not be sent away.
The girl went early to the mother's place,
occupied her bed to sleep,
and having no choice,
she then went with Shēng.
From then on, every two or three days they would take turns,
and it became customary.
The lady had always been skilled at chess,
but since becoming widowed,
she had no leisure for it.
Since Shèng arrived,
she managed everything in perfect order,
and having nothing to do during the day,
she would often play chess with her daughter.
They would trim the lamp and brew tea,
listening to the two wives play the qin,
and would not part until midnight.
She often said to others:
"Even when my child's father was alive,
we never had such joy as this."
Shèng handled the income and expenses,
and would regularly report the accounts to her mother.
The mother once asked doubtfully:
"You often said you were orphaned young,
yet you write characters and play chess—
who taught you?"
The girl laughed and told her the truth.
The mother also laughed and said:
"At first I didn't want to marry my son to a Daoist priestess,
but now I've ended up with two!"
Suddenly recalling the divination of her childhood,
she finally believed that fate cannot be escaped.
Shēng failed the examinations twice more.
The lady said:
"Although our family is not wealthy,
we have three hundred mǔ of thin fields,
and fortunately, Yúnmián manages them,
so we are increasingly well-fed and warm.
As long as you stay by my side,
leading your two wives and this old woman in shared joy,
I do not wish for you to seek wealth and honor."
Shēng obeyed her.
Later, Yúnmián bore one son and one daughter,
and Yúnqī bore one daughter and three sons.
The mother lived to over eighty before passing away.
The grandsons all entered the county school;
the eldest grandson,
born of Yúnmián,
had already passed the provincial examination.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
A certain guerrilla officer
had many wives and concubines.
He was most particular about avoiding taboo words,
calling "year" (nián) "age" (suì),
"birth" (shēng) "hard" (yìng),
and "horse" (mǎ) "big donkey" (dà lǘ);
he also avoided "defeat" (bài), calling it "victory" (shèng),
and "peace" (ān) as "release" (fàng).
Although in written correspondence,
he was not overly strict about avoiding these,
if family members uttered them,
he would become furious.
One day,
the clerk in charge of documents reported a matter
and mistakenly violated the taboo;
the officer was greatly enraged,
striking him with an inkstone,
and he died on the spot.
Three days later,
the officer, drunk, lay down to sleep,
and saw the clerk holding a name card enter.
He asked:
"What do you want?"
The clerk said:
"'Mǎ Zǐ'ān'
has come to pay his respects."
Suddenly realizing it was a ghost,
he hurriedly got up,
drew his sword and swung at him.
The clerk smiled faintly,
tossed the card onto the table,
and vanished without a trace.
Picking up the card to look,
it was written:
"The family of Suì respectfully offers congratulations to Dà Lǘzi for his release and victory."
Such a violent and unreasonable man,
mocked by a ghost—
truly most laughable!
A monk from Niúshǒu Mountain,
called himself Tiěhàn (Iron Man),
also called Tiěshǐ (Iron Excrement).
He had forty poems,
and those who saw them could not help but laugh uproariously.
He engraved two seals for himself: one said
"Scoundrel Rascal,"
the other said
"Honest Rogue."
Wáng Sīzhí from Xiùshuǐ compiled his poems,
titled them
"Niúshān's Forty Farts."
The inscription read:
"Published by Scoundrel Rascal and Honest Rogue."
One need not read his poems—
the titles alone are enough to bring a smile.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
At the home of Education Commissioner Zhū Yùsān,
under the threshold there was a house centipede,
several chǐ long.
Whenever wind and rain came, it would emerge,
coiling on the ground like a white silk ribbon.
Note: The house centipede resembles a centipede in shape,
cannot be seen during the day,
comes out at night,
and gathers wherever it smells fishy.
Some say: The centipede has no eyes but is very greedy.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
A certain instructor
was very deaf,
but was on good terms with a fox;
even when the fox whispered in his ear,
he could hear.
Whenever he met with his superiors,
he would also have the fox with him,
so people did not know he was hard of hearing.
After five or six years,
the fox bid farewell and left,
admonishing him:
"You are like a puppet;
if not manipulated,
then all five senses fail.
Rather than incurring blame due to deafness,
it would be better to resign early and elevate yourself."
The instructor clung to his salary,
and could not follow this advice,
so his responses often went awry.
The education commissioner wanted to dismiss him,
and the instructor again sought influential people to intercede on his behalf.
One day,
he was on duty at the examination hall.
After calling the roll,
the education commissioner withdrew and sat casually with the various instructors.
Each instructor felt inside his boot for a register,
and presented it to make personal appeals.
After a while, the education commissioner smiled and asked:
"Why is it that your school alone has nothing to present?"
The instructor was blank and did not understand.
Someone nearby nudged him,
putting a hand into his own boot,
to show him the gesture.
The instructor, having been asked by relatives to sell counterfeit bedroom devices,
often kept them hidden in his boots,
seeking to sell them wherever he went.
Because of the education commissioner's smiling words,
he thought he was asking for this item,
so he bowed and stood up to reply:
"The ones costing eight qián are the best,
but your humble official dares not present them."
The entire room stifled their laughter.
The education commissioner shouted at him to leave,
and he was subsequently dismissed from his post.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Even if the plain alone had none,
he would still be a pillar amid the current.
Since the education commissioner sought a presentation,
he certainly should have offered this.
To be dismissed because of it—
how unjust!"
In the *Ěrlù* by Master Zhū Zǐqīng it is recorded:
"A certain Jǔshēng named Chí from Dōnglái
served as instructor in Yíshuǐ.
His nature was foolish and silly;
whenever colleagues gathered,
he would remain silent;
after sitting for a short while,
he would unconsciously start moving all five senses,
laughing and crying simultaneously,
as if no one else were around.
If he heard others laughing,
he would suddenly stop.
He was extremely frugal and stingy with himself,
and had saved over a hundred liǎng of silver,
which he buried himself in his study,
not even letting his wife and children know.
One day,
sitting alone,
he suddenly moved his hands and feet,
and after a moment said: 'Doing evil and incurring resentment,
enduring hunger and starvation,
with such difficulty I saved this—
now it's in the study.
If someone finds out,
what then?'
This repeated several times.
A gatekeeper was beside him,
and he was completely unaware.
The next day,
when Chí went out,
the gatekeeper entered,
dug it up and took it away.
After two or three days,
feeling uneasy,
he opened the hiding place to check,
and found it already empty.
Stamping his feet and beating his chest,
he sighed in regret, wishing to die."
Among educational officials, one can truly say there are a thousand forms and a hundred shapes.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In Jiāozhōu, Commander Lǐ
purchased two black slaves,
as black as lacquer.
The skin on their feet was thick and coarse;
they could stand on blades laid out as a path
and walk back and forth upon them
without the slightest injury.
The commander mated them with courtesans,
and the children born were white.
Fellow servants teased them,
saying they were not of the same stock.
The black slaves also grew suspicious,
so they killed their own child
and examined its bones—all were black.
Only then did they regret it.
The commander often made the two slaves dance facing each other;
their expressions and movements were quite a sight to behold.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
In Dòngtíng Lake,
it often happened that water spirits would borrow boats.
When an empty boat was encountered,
its mooring rope would suddenly come untied by itself,
and it would drift away on its own.
Then one could hear music playing in the air,
while the boatman would crouch in a corner;
closing his eyes and listening,
not daring to look up,
he would let the boat go wherever it pleased.
Once the excursion was over,
the boat would return to its original mooring place.
There was a Scholar Liǔ,
who, having failed the imperial examination, was returning home.
Drunk, he lay down to sleep on a boat,
when suddenly flute and song music began to play.
The boatman tried to shake Scholar Liǔ awake but couldn’t rouse him,
so he hurriedly hid under the deck.
Soon, someone grabbed Scholar Liǔ.
He was heavily intoxicated,
and as he was pulled, he fell to the ground,
still sleeping as before,
so they simply left him there.
After a short while,
the sound of drums and pipes grew clamorous.
Scholar Liǔ gradually woke up,
and smelled the air filled with the fragrance of orchids and musk.
Peeking out,
he saw the boat filled with beautiful women.
Knowing in his heart that this was strange,
he kept his eyes as if closed.
After a little while,
a call went out: “Wéichéng!”
Immediately a maidservant came forward,
standing close by his cheek,
wearing green stockings and purple slippers,
her feet slender as fingers.
He took a fancy to them,
and secretly bit her stocking with his teeth.
A moment later,
as the girl moved,
she stumbled and fell.
The one above asked her what happened,
and she explained the reason.
The one above grew angry,
and ordered her immediate execution.
Then a warrior entered,
seized and bound her, lifting her up.
Scholar Liǔ saw a person facing south,
wearing a crown like a king.
So as he walked, he spoke,
saying:
“I have heard that the Lord of Dòngtíng was named Liǔ,
and your subject is also named Liǔ;
in the past, the Lord of Dòngtíng failed the imperial examination,
and now your subject has also failed the examination;
the Lord of Dòngtíng met a dragon maiden and became immortal,
yet now your subject, drunk, played a prank on a maiden and must die: how vastly different are fortune and misfortune!”
The king heard this,
called him back,
and asked:
“Are you a scholar who has failed the examination?”
Scholar Liǔ acknowledged it.
Then he was given brush and paper,
and ordered to compose a poem on
“wind-blown hair and mist-like locks.”
Scholar Liǔ was originally a famous scholar from Xiāngyáng,
but his构思 was rather slow,
and he held the brush for a long time.
The king above reproached him, saying:
“How can a famous scholar be like this?”
Scholar Liǔ put down the brush and explained himself:
“In the past, the ‘Rhapsody on the Three Capitals’ took ten years to complete,
from which we know that literary works value craftsmanship, not speed.”
The king laughed and let him continue.
From morning until noon,
the draft was finally finished.
The king read it,
and greatly pleased, said:
“Truly a famous scholar!”
Then he bestowed wine upon him.
In an instant,
exotic dishes were spread out in abundance.
Just as they were facing each other,
an official came forward holding a register and reported:
“The register of the drowned is now complete.”
The king asked:
“How many people are there?”
The reply was:
“One hundred and twenty-eight persons.”
He asked:
“Who has been assigned to carry it out?”
The answer was:
“Commanders Máo and Nán.”
Scholar Liǔ rose, bowed, and took his leave.
The king presented him with ten catties of gold,
and also a crystal ruler about a handspan long,
saying,
“On the lake, there will be a minor calamity;
holding this will allow you to avoid it.”
Suddenly, they saw feathered banners, people, and horses
standing in crowds upon the water’s surface.
The king descended from the boat and mounted his carriage,
and then was seen no more.
After a long while, all was quiet.
The boatman finally emerged from under the deck,
and rowed the boat northward to cross the lake,
but the wind was against them, and they could not advance.
Suddenly, an iron anchor floated up from the water.
The boatman cried out in fear,
“General Máo has appeared!”
Merchants on all the boats prostrated themselves.
Not long after,
a wooden pillar stood upright in the lake,
shaking and swaying.
Even more terrified, they said:
“General Nán has appeared as well!”
After a short while,
great waves arose,
obscuring the sky and sun.
Looking around at the boats on the lake,
they all capsized in an instant.
Scholar Liǔ held up the crystal ruler and sat upright in the boat.
Though the raging waves were thousands of feet high,
when they reached his boat, they immediately subsided,
and thus he was spared.
After returning home,
he often told people of this strange event,
saying:
“That maidservant on the boat,
though I did not fully see her appearance,
the pair of tiny feet beneath her skirt
were also unmatched in the human world.”
Later, on business, he went to Wǔchāng.
There was an old woman named Cuī selling her daughter,
asking a thousand in gold but unwilling to sell.
She kept a crystal ruler,
saying that whoever could match it
would marry her daughter.
Scholar Liǔ found this strange,
and went with his crystal ruler in his sleeve.
The old woman happily received him,
called her daughter out to meet him.
She was about fifteen or sixteen years old,
charming, graceful, and elegant
beyond compare.
After a slight bow,
she turned and went behind the curtain.
At first sight, Scholar Liǔ felt his soul stirred,
and said:
“This humble scholar also has an object;
I wonder if it matches the one your family has in its collection?”
So each brought theirs out to compare.
Their lengths matched without the slightest difference.
The old woman was delighted,
asked where he was staying,
and requested that Scholar Liǔ return and arrange for a carriage,
leaving the ruler as a pledge.
Scholar Liǔ was unwilling to leave it,
but the old woman laughed and said:
"Sir, you are too cautious!
Would I, an old woman, flee just for the sake of a ruler?"
The young man had no choice,
and stayed.
When he went out, he hired a carriage and hurried back,
but the old woman's room was already empty.
Greatly alarmed,
he asked all the neighbors,
but none knew.
The sun was already setting in the west,
and he was utterly dejected in body and spirit,
returning gloomily.
On the way,
he encountered a passing carriage,
when suddenly the curtain was lifted and someone said:
"Why are you so late, Liǔ Láng?"
Looking,
it was the old woman Cuī.
He joyfully asked:
"Where are you going?"
The old woman laughed and said:
"You must have suspected me of being a kidnapper and swindler.
After we parted,
there happened to be a convenient carriage,
and I thought that you, sir, were also living away from home,
and that arranging things would be quite difficult,
so I sent the girl back to the boat."
The young man invited her to turn the carriage around,
but the old woman absolutely refused.
The young man, flustered and unable to fully believe it,
hurriedly ran into the boat,
and indeed the girl and a maid were there.
Seeing the young man enter,
she greeted him with a smile.
The young man saw her green stockings and purple shoes,
and compared to the attire of the maid in the boat,
there was not the slightest difference.
Finding it strange,
he paced back and forth, gazing intently.
The girl laughed and said:
"Staring so intently,
have you never seen such in your life?"
The young man bent down even more to look,
and there were indeed tooth marks on the back of her stockings.
Startled, he said:
"Are you Zhīchéng?"
The girl covered her mouth and smiled faintly.
The young man bowed deeply and said:
"You truly are a divine being.
Please speak plainly early on,
to dispel my worries and confusion."
The girl said:
"To tell you the truth: the one we encountered on the boat earlier
was none other than the Lord of Dòngtíng.
He admired your great talent;
and wanted to give me to you;
but because I am overly favored by the Princess,
he went back to discuss it.
My coming
is by the Princess's command."
The young man was overjoyed,
washed his hands and burned incense,
facing the lake he bowed in reverence,
and then returned.
Later, when he went to Wǔchāng,
the girl asked to go along,
planning to conveniently visit her parents.
When they reached Dòngtíng Lake,
the girl pulled out a hairpin and threw it into the water.
Suddenly, a small boat emerged from the lake.
The girl leaped aboard,
like a bird alighting,
and in an instant, she was gone.
The young man sat at the bow of the boat,
gazing intently at the spot where she disappeared.
From afar, a large decorated boat approached.
As it drew near, a window opened,
and suddenly, like a colorful bird flying past,
Zhīchéng arrived.
Someone from the window handed over many gold, pearls, and precious items,
all bestowed by the Princess.
From then on,
it became customary for them to visit once or twice a year.
Therefore, the young man's family became rich in jewels and treasures.
Every time they brought out an item,
even noble families had never seen its like.
It is said that in the Táng dynasty, Liǔ Yì encountered a dragon girl,
and the Lord of Dòngtíng took him as his son-in-law.
Later, he abdicated his position to Liǔ Yì.
Because Liǔ Yì's appearance was refined,
he could not intimidate the water demons,
so he was given a ghost mask,
to wear during the day and remove at night.
Over time, he gradually became accustomed to it and forgot to remove it,
until it merged with his face and became one.
Liǔ Yì looked in the mirror and felt ashamed.
Therefore, when people travel on the lake,
if someone points at something with their finger,
he suspects they are pointing at him;
if someone covers their forehead with their hand,
he suspects they are peeking at him:
storms and waves immediately arise,
and many boats capsize.
Therefore, when first boarding a boat,
boatmen must warn passengers about this.
Otherwise, they must set up sacrificial offerings of livestock,
only then can they cross.
Once, Immortal Xǔ Zhēnjūn happened to come to the lake,
and the waves blocked his passage.
Immortal Xǔ was angry,
seized Liǔ Yì, and handed him over to the county prison.
The jailer, when checking the prisoners,
always found one extra person,
but could not fathom the reason.
One night,
Liǔ Yì appeared in a dream to the county magistrate,
pleading piteously for rescue.
The magistrate said that the realms of the living and the dead were different
and declined.
Liǔ Yì said:
"Immortal Xǔ will arrive in this area on a certain day.
If you just plead for me,
it will surely be effective."
Later, Immortal Xǔ indeed arrived.
The magistrate pleaded on his behalf,
and thus he was released.
After that, the lake's restrictions became somewhat calmer.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Yú Kè,
a man from Húnán,
but his prefecture and county are forgotten.
His family was poor.
Having failed the imperial examination, he was returning home,
and his travel funds were exhausted.
Ashamed to beg,
and extremely hungry,
he temporarily rested in the Wúwáng Temple,
and prayed before the deity's altar.
He went out and lay down under the corridor,
when suddenly someone led him away.
He saw the King,
knelt and reported:
"The black-clothed troop is still short one soldier,
he can fill the vacancy."
The King said:
"Agreed."
He was immediately given black clothes.
Once he put them on,
he transformed into a crow,
and flapping his wings, flew out.
He saw a flock of crow friends gathered,
and together they went,
alighting separately on the masts and sails.
The passengers on the boats
competed in throwing food upward.
The flock caught the food in mid-air.
He also imitated them,
and in a moment, his belly was full.
Soaring and perching on the treetops,
he felt quite content.
After two or three days,
Wúwáng, pitying him for being without a mate,
paired him with a female,
calling her
"Zhúqīng."
They were deeply affectionate and happy.
Whenever Yú went to get food,
he was always tame and without guile.
Zhúqīng often advised him against it,
but in the end, he would not listen.
One day,
some Mǎn soldiers passed by,
and shot him in the chest.
Fortunately, Zhúqīng carried him away,
so he was not captured.
The flock of crows was enraged,
flapping their wings to stir the waves,
the waves surged up,
and all the boats capsized.
Zhúqīng still brought food to feed Yú.
Yú was severely wounded,
and by the end of the day, he died.
Suddenly, it was as if he woke from a dream,
and found himself lying in the temple.
Earlier,
the local people had seen Yú dead,
not knowing who he was.
Feeling that he was not yet cold,
they had people periodically patrol and check on him.
At this point,
Three years later,
he passed by the old place again,
and paid a visit to King Wú.
Food was set out,
and he called for the crows to gather and eat,
praying:
"If Zhúqīng is here,
she should stay."
After the meal,
they all flew away.
Later, after he passed the provincial examination and returned,
he visited King Wú's temple again,
offering a sacrifice of a sheep and a pig.
After that,
he set out a grand feast to entertain his crow friends,
and prayed again.
That night, he stayed at a lakeside village,
and was sitting by candlelight
when suddenly something like a flying bird drifted down before his table;
looking at it,
it turned out to be a beautiful woman of about twenty,
who said with a smile:
"Have you been well since we parted?"
Yú was startled and asked her,
and she said:
"Don't you recognize Zhúqīng?"
Yú was overjoyed,
and asked where she had come from.
She said:
"I am now a goddess of the Hàn River,
and rarely return to my hometown.
The crow envoy conveyed your feelings twice,
so I came to reunite with you."
Yú felt even more delighted and moved,
and they were like a long-separated husband and wife,
overwhelmed with joy and affection.
Yú wanted to take her south with him,
while she wanted to invite him to go west with her,
and they could not decide between the two plans.
When he first woke from sleep,
the woman was already up.
Opening his eyes,
he saw the great hall brightly lit with huge candles,
and realized he was no longer on the boat.
Startled, he got up
and asked:
"Where is this?"
The woman laughed and said:
"This is Hànyáng.
My home is your home,
why go south!"
As dawn gradually broke,
maids and old women gathered in numbers,
and wine and roasted meat were served.
A low table was set on a wide bed,
and the couple drank facing each other.
Yú asked:
"Where are my servants?"
She replied:
"On the boat."
Yú worried that the boatmen could not wait long.
The woman said:
"It's no trouble,
I will help you repay them."
Thus they talked and feasted day and night,
so happy they forgot to return.
The boatmen woke from their dreams,
and suddenly saw Hànyáng,
utterly astonished.
The servants searched for their master,
but there was no trace or news.
The boatmen wanted to go elsewhere,
but the mooring rope was knotted and would not untie,
so they all stayed and waited.
After more than two months had passed,
Yú suddenly thought of returning,
and said to the woman:
"While I am here,
I am cut off from my relatives.
Moreover, you and I,
though called husband and wife,
have not once acknowledged your family home—
what is to be done?"
The woman said:
"Not to mention that I cannot go;
even if I did go,
you already have a wife at home—
how would you place me then?
It would be better to leave me here,
as a separate residence for you."
Yú regretted that the road was long,
and he could not come often.
The woman brought out a black garment,
saying:
"The old clothes you used to wear are still here.
When you miss me,
put this on and you can come;
when you arrive,
I will remove it for you."
Then she set out a grand feast of delicacies,
to bid Yú farewell.
Once he was drunk and asleep,
he woke to find himself on the boat.
Looking around,
it was the old mooring place at Dòngtíng.
staring at each other in great astonishment,
and asked where he had been.
Yú himself was bewildered and startled.
There was a bundle by his pillow;
examining it,
he found new clothes, socks, and shoes the woman had given him,
with the black garment also folded inside.
There was also an embroidered purse tied at his waist;
feeling it,
he found it filled with gold.
Then he set off south,
reached the shore,
generously rewarded the boatmen, and left.
After returning home for several months,
he sorely missed the Hàn River,
so he secretly took out the black garment and put it on.
Wings grew from his sides,
and he soared into the air with a whir,
flying for about two hours,
until he reached the Hàn River.
Circling and looking down,
he saw among isolated islets
a cluster of buildings,
so he flew down and landed.
A maid had already spotted him,
and called out:
"The master has arrived!"
Before long,
Zhúqīng came out,
and ordered everyone to help loosen the knots.
He felt the feathers all fall away with a rustle.
Holding hands, they entered the house,
and she said:
"You came just in time—
I am about to give birth any day now."
Yú asked playfully:
"Will it be a live birth?
Or an egg?"
The woman said:
"Now that I am a goddess,
my skin and bones have already changed—
it should be different from before."
A few days later,
she indeed gave birth,
wrapped in a thick amniotic sac,
like a huge egg.
Breaking it open,
it was a boy.
Yú was delighted,
and named him
"Hànchǎn."
Three days later,
the goddesses of the Hàn River all came to the hall,
bringing fine clothes and delicacies to congratulate them.
They were all exquisite and beautiful,
with none over thirty.
They all went into the room to the bed,
and pressed the child's nose with their thumbs,
calling it
"adding longevity."
After they left,
Yú asked:
"Who were those who just came?"
The woman said:
"They are all my kind.
The last one wearing lotus-white,
is the so-called 'Hàngāo untying the pendant'—
that is her."
After living there for several months,
the woman sent him off by boat,
which needed no sails or oars,
but drifted along by itself.
Upon reaching land,
someone was already waiting with a horse by the roadside,
and so he returned home.
From then on, he came and went without end.
After several years had passed,
Hànchǎn grew increasingly handsome and refined,
and Shēng cherished him dearly.
His wife Héshì,
who was distressed by her inability to bear children,
often longed to see Hànchǎn.
Shēng conveyed these feelings to the woman.
The woman then prepared the luggage
and sent the child to return with his father,
agreeing on a three-month stay.
After they returned,
Héshì loved him as if he were her own,
and after more than ten months,
she could not bear to send him back.
One day,
he suddenly fell ill and died,
and Héshì grieved so deeply she wished to die.
Shēng then went to Hànzhōng to inform the woman.
Upon entering the door,
he saw Hànchǎn lying barefoot on the bed,
and joyfully asked the woman about it.
The woman said:
"You have long broken our agreement.
I missed our child,
so I summoned him back."
Shēng then explained the reason for Héshì's deep affection for the child.
The woman said,
"Wait until I bear another child,
then I will let Hànchǎn return."
After another year or so,
the woman gave birth to twins, a boy and a girl: the boy was named
"Hànshēng,"
and the girl was named
"Yùpèi."
Shēng then took Hànchǎn back with him.
However, he traveled there three or four times a year,
which was inconvenient,
so he moved his family to Hànyáng.
When Hànchǎn was twelve years old,
he entered the prefectural school.
The woman, believing there were no suitable matches in the mortal world,
summoned him away,
arranged a marriage for him,
and only then sent him back.
His wife was named
"Èniáng,"
and she was also the daughter of a goddess.
Later, when Héshì passed away,
Hànshēng and his sister both came to mourn, beating their chests and stamping their feet.
After the burial,
Hànshēng stayed behind;
Shēng took Yùpèi away,
and from then on, they never returned.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Duàn Ruìhuán
was an elderly gentleman from Dàmíng.
At forty, he still had no son.
His wife Liánshì was extremely jealous,
and though he wished to take a concubine, he dared not.
He had a secret affair with a maidservant,
but Liánshì discovered it,
beat the maidservant hundreds of times,
and sold her to the Luán family in Héjiān.
As Duàn grew older day by day,
his nephews constantly came to borrow money,
and if he refused even a single request,
they would show their anger through subtle expressions.
Duàn realized he could not satisfy their demands,
and when he considered adopting one of his nephews as an heir,
the other nephews obstructed it.
Even Liánshì's fierceness was of no use,
and she began to deeply regret her actions.
Angrily, she said:
"The master is over sixty,
who says he cannot father a son!"
She then bought two concubines,
allowing her husband to visit them as he pleased,
and did not interfere.
After a little over a year,
both concubines became pregnant.
The entire household rejoiced.
From then on, their spirits gradually lifted,
and whenever the nephews tried to forcibly take anything,
they would harshly refuse them.
Not long after,
one concubine gave birth to a daughter,
and the other gave birth to a son who died in infancy.
The couple was disappointed.
After another year or so,
Duàn suffered a stroke and could not rise, and the nephews grew even more unruly,
taking away oxen, horses, and household items
as they pleased.
When Liánshì scolded them,
they would talk back defiantly.
Having no recourse,
she wept day and night.
Duàn's illness worsened,
and he soon died.
The nephews gathered before the coffin
to discuss dividing the inheritance.
Though Liánshì was in deep pain,
she could not stop them.
She only asked to keep one fertile estate
to support the elderly and the young,
but the nephews refused.
Liánshì said:
"If you leave not an inch of land,
will you let this old woman and the crying child starve to death!"
The matter remained unresolved for days,
and she could only weep bitterly and strike herself in frustration.
Suddenly, a guest arrived to offer condolences,
went straight to the mourning hall,
and expressed his grief with deep bows.
After mourning,
he took his place among the mourners.
When everyone asked who he was,
the guest said:
"The deceased is my father."
Everyone was even more astonished.
The guest calmly explained himself.
Previously,
the maidservant had married into the Luán family, and after five or six months,
she gave birth to a son named Huái.
Luán Fǔ treated him equally with his other sons.
At eighteen, Huái entered the imperial academy.
Later, when Yì died,
his elder brothers divided the family property,
excluding Huái from the inheritance as if he were not Yì’s son.
Huái asked his mother,
and only then learned the truth.
He said:
"Since I belong to two different families,
each with its own ancestral lineage,
why should I stay here to inherit a mere hundred acres of land?"
He then mounted a horse and went to the Duàn family.
But Duàn had already died,
and the accounts were clear and detailed,
providing solid evidence.
Lián was filled with grief and anger,
but upon hearing this, she was overjoyed.
She went straight out and said:
"Now I too have a son!
All the oxen, horses, and other items you borrowed,
you must return them properly;
otherwise,
I will take you to court!"
The nephews looked at each other, their faces pale,
and gradually withdrew.
Huái then brought his wife to live with them,
and together they mourned his father.
The Duàn family was displeased,
and they conspired to drive Huái away.
Huái learned of this
and said:
"The Luán family does not regard me as Yì’s son,
and the Duàn family does not regard me as Duàn’s son.
Where am I supposed to go?"
Filled with anger, he wanted to take the matter to the authorities.
Relatives and friends mediated,
and the conspiracy gradually subsided.
But Lián, because of the oxen and horses,
refused to let it go.
Huái advised her to drop the matter.
Lián said:
"It’s not about the oxen and horses.
I am filled with pent-up anger.
Your father died of resentment,
and the reason I endured in silence was
because I had no son.
Now that I have a son,
what is there to fear?
You don’t know the details of what happened before,
so let me take it to court myself."
Huái tried to stop her,
but she wouldn’t listen.
She prepared a petition and took it to the magistrate.
The magistrate summoned the Duàn family,
reviewed the case,
and found Lián’s words righteous and moving,
her grievances pouring out like a spring.
The magistrate was moved,
punished the Duàn family,
and ordered the return of the property to its rightful owner.
After returning home,
Huái called over
the sons of his brothers,
and because they had not participated in the conspiracy,
he distributed all the recovered property to them.
When Lián was over seventy,
on her deathbed,
she called her daughter and daughter-in-law and instructed them:
"Remember this: if you do not bear a child by the age of thirty,
you must pawn your hairpins and earrings
to buy a concubine for your husband.
The plight of having no son
is truly unbearable!"
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Although Lián was jealous,
she was able to change swiftly,
so Heaven granted her a descendant to vindicate her spirit.
Observing her righteous indignation and fervor,
ah!
she was indeed remarkable!"
In Jǐ’nán, there was a man named Jiǎng Jià
whose wife, Máo Shì,
was childless and jealous.
Her sister-in-law often advised her,
but she wouldn’t listen,
saying:
"I would rather have no descendants
than allow a flirtatious woman to anger me!"
As she approached forty,
she began to worry about having an heir.
She wanted to adopt her brother-in-law’s son,
and though her brother-in-law and his wife agreed,
they deliberately delayed.
Whenever the boy visited his uncle’s house,
the couple would treat him to delicacies
and ask:
"Would you like to come live with us?"
The boy would always agree.
His father privately instructed him, saying:
"If they ask again,
say you won’t.
If they ask why,
reply:
‘After you die, I won’t have to worry about your land and property not becoming mine.’"
One day,
when Jià was away on a long business trip,
the boy came again.
Máo asked him once more,
and the boy repeated his father’s words.
Máo was furious and said:
"So my husband’s family is at home,
constantly scheming to take our land and property?
Their plan has failed!"
She drove the boy out,
immediately summoned a matchmaker,
and bought a concubine for her husband.
At the time, there was a maidservant for sale,
but the price was high,
and even using all their savings, they couldn’t afford her.
It seemed the deal would fall through.
Her brother-in-law, fearing she might change her mind,
secretly gave the money to the matchmaker,
pretending it was a loan to help complete the purchase.
Máo was overjoyed
and brought the maidservant home.
She told her husband the whole story,
and he was angry,
cutting ties with his brother.
Over a year later,
the concubine gave birth to a son.
The couple was overjoyed.
Máo said:
"We don’t know who lent the money to the matchmaker,
and for over a year, no one has asked for repayment.
Such kindness must not be forgotten.
Now that we have a son,
we should repay the money."
Jià then took the money and went to the matchmaker.
The matchmaker laughed and said:
"You should thank your elder brother.
I am as poor as can be—
who would dare lend me even a single coin?"
She told him the truth.
Jià was deeply moved,
returned home, and told his wife.
They both wept with emotion.
They then prepared a feast and invited his brother and sister-in-law.
The couple knelt before them,
offered the money in repayment,
but the brother refused to accept it.
They parted joyfully.
Later, Jià had three sons.
Based on the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Yǐ Gǔn
was a man from Jiǔjiāng.
One night a woman came to him,
and they slept together.
He knew in his heart that she was a fox,
but he loved her beauty,
so he kept it secret and did not tell anyone,
and even his parents did not know.
After a long time, his body became emaciated.
His parents pressed him with questions,
and only then did he tell them the truth.
His parents were greatly worried,
and had others take turns sleeping with him,
but in the end they could not stop it.
When the old man himself shared the same bed with his son,
the fox did not come;
but when they changed to someone else,
she came again.
Yǐ asked the fox,
and the fox said:
"How can the talismans and incantations of the mortal world
control me?
However, I fear the principles of human relations;
how could I commit lewd acts in the presence of an old man?"
When the old man heard this,
he accompanied his son even more and did not leave,
and the fox then ceased to come.
Later, when rebel bandits ran rampant,
the villagers all fled,
and the family was separated from each other.
Yǐ ran into the Kūnlún Mountains,
and looked around at the desolate wilderness.
As the sun had already set,
he was extremely frightened.
Suddenly, he saw a woman approaching,
and when he looked closely,
it was the fox woman.
Amidst the chaos of separation and turmoil,
they were delighted and comforted to see each other.
The woman said:
"The sun has already set in the west,
so you should stay here for now.
I will find a good spot
and temporarily create a room
to avoid tigers and wolves."
She then walked north a few paces,
squatted down in the thicket,
and he did not know what she was doing.
After a short while, she returned,
pulled Yǐ to go south;
after about ten or so steps,
she dragged him back again.
Suddenly, they saw a thousand large trees,
surrounding a tall pavilion,
with copper walls and iron pillars,
and a roof resembling gold foil;
when he looked closely,
the wall only reached his shoulders,
and there were no doors or windows all around,
but the wall was densely lined with niches.
The woman stepped on them and passed over,
and Yǐ followed her.
Once inside,
he suspected that such a golden house could not be made by human hands,
and asked where it came from.
The woman laughed and said:
"You, sir, live here,
and tomorrow I will give it to you.
There are tens of millions worth of gold and iron here,
enough for half a lifetime of food and clothing."
Then she bid farewell.
Yǐ pleaded with her to stay,
and so she stayed.
She said:
"Having been spurned and abandoned by others,
I had already resolved to cut off ties forever;
now I cannot hold firm again."
When he awoke,
the fox woman had already left at some unknown time.
At daybreak,
he climbed over the wall and went out.
Looking back at where he had slept,
there was no pavilion or house,
only four needles stuck in a finger ring,
with a rouge box covering it;
as for the large trees,
they were thickets of old thorns.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Whenever major troops arrive,
the harm they cause is worse than that of bandits: for bandits, people can still take revenge on them,
but with troops, people dare not seek revenge.
The only slight difference from bandits
is that they do not dare to kill people lightly.
In the year Jiǎyín,
when the Three Feudatories rebelled,
the troops sent south
quartered their horses in Yǎn Prefecture,
emptying all the chickens, dogs, and houses,
and the women were all violated.
At that time, there was continuous rain,
and the fields were flooded, turning into lakes,
so the people had nowhere to hide,
and thus took rafts into the tall sorghum fields.
The soldiers found out,
and, naked on horseback,
went into the water to search and violate them,
leaving few untouched.
Only Mrs. Zhāng did not submit,
and openly stayed at home.
There was a kitchen shed,
and at night she and her husband dug a pit several feet deep,
piling hay in it;
they covered it with a mat,
placed a mat on top,
making it look like a place to sleep.
She cooked by the stove herself.
When soldiers came,
she would go out to receive and deal with them.
Two Mongol soldiers tried to force themselves on her.
The woman said:
"Such things
cannot be done in front of others!"
One of them smiled slightly,
and went out chattering.
The woman went into the room with the other,
pointed to the mat and told him to climb up first.
The mat broke,
and the soldier fell in.
The woman then took another mat and covered it,
deliberately standing by the edge of the pit,
to lure the next one.
After a short while,
the other one came in again.
Hearing cries from the pit,
he did not know where they were coming from.
The woman smiled and beckoned to him with her hand, saying:
"It's here."
The soldier stepped on the mat,
and also fell in.
The woman then added more firewood,
and threw a fire into it.
The fire blazed fiercely,
and the house burned.
The woman then called for help.
After the fire was extinguished,
the charred bodies emitted a foul smell.
When people asked her,
the woman said:
"Two pigs were afraid of harming the soldiers,
so I put them in the pit."
From then on, she went several miles away from the village,
to a place by the main road without any trees,
and took her needlework to sit in the scorching sun.
The village was far from the prefecture,
and the soldiers who came usually rode horses,
arriving several at a time in an instant.
They chattered and laughed,
and though she did not understand most of it,
it was mostly teasing talk.
However, since it was not far from the road,
and there was nothing to hide her body,
they would leave,
and for several days there was no trouble.
One day,
a soldier came,
very shameless,
and tried to violate her right under the scorching sun.
The woman smiled and did not resist much.
Secretly, she pricked his horse with a needle,
and the horse snorted and neighed,
so the soldier tied the horse's leg to a pile,
and then embraced the woman.
The woman took out a large awl and fiercely stabbed the horse's neck,
and the horse, in pain, bolted in panic.
The reins were tied to his leg and could not come loose,
and he was dragged for dozens of miles,
before his comrades finally caught the horse for him.
His head and body were nowhere to be found,
only one leg tied to the saddle,
still clearly there.
The Strange Historian says:
"With clever strategies emerging one after another,
she did not lose her virtue to the brutal soldiers.
How virtuous is this woman,
wise and able to preserve her chastity!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A coastal resident recounted:
"One day,
a high mountain suddenly emerged from the sea,
terrifying the local inhabitants.
A scholar was lodging on a fishing boat,
buying wine and drinking alone.
Late at night,
a young man,
dressed in Confucian robes and cap,
introduced himself:
'Yú Zǐyóu.'
His speech was refined and elegant.
The scholar was delighted,
and they drank merrily together.
When they had drunk until midnight,
the young man rose from his seat to bid farewell.
The scholar asked,
'Where is your home?
On such a vast, dark night,
you are being too hard on yourself.'
He replied,
'I am not a native here.
As the Qingmíng Festival approaches,
I am to follow the Great King to sweep his tomb.
The family members have gone ahead;
the Great King is staying behind to rest.
He will depart at the chén hour tomorrow.
I should return
to prepare the luggage early.'
The scholar did not know who this 'Great King' was.
He escorted him to the bow of the boat,
where the young man leaped into the water
and swam away with a splash,
revealing himself to be a fish demon.
The next day,
they saw the mountain peak floating and moving,
and in a moment it had vanished.
Only then did they realize the mountain was a giant fish—
the so-called Great King."
Folklore says that before Qingmíng,
giant fish in the sea take their offspring to visit their ancestral graves.
Can this be true?
In the early years of the Kāngxī reign,
a giant fish was stranded by the tide in Láijùn.
It cried out for several days,
its voice like that of an ox.
After it died,
people carrying poles to cut its meat
formed an unbroken line along the road.
The fish was over an acre in size,
complete with fins and tail,
but lacked eyeballs.
Its eye sockets were as deep as wells,
filled with water.
Those cutting the meat who accidentally fell in
would drown.
Some say
that when a giant fish is banished to the sea,
its eyes are removed,
as the eyes are night-luminous pearls.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
An official in Yángzhōu sought to buy a concubine.
He inspected several families in succession,
but none suited him.
Only an old woman, living elsewhere, was selling her daughter.
The girl was fourteen or fifteen,
graceful and beautiful,
and skilled in various arts.
The official was greatly pleased
and purchased her at a high price.
That night,
when he entered the bedcovers,
he found her skin as smooth as lard.
But when he joyfully touched her private parts,
he discovered she was a man.
Utterly shocked,
he began to interrogate him.
It turned out the boy had been bought as a servant,
carefully groomed and adorned,
and set up in a scheme to deceive people.
At dawn,
he sent his servants to find the old woman,
but she had already vanished without a trace.
His heart filled with regret and dismay,
he hesitated, uncertain whether to advance or retreat.
It happened that a fellow graduate from Zhèjiāng came to visit,
so he told him the story.
The visitor asked to see the boy,
and upon seeing him, was greatly delighted,
redeeming him at the original price and taking him away.
The Chronicler of the Tales remarks:
"If one meets a true connoisseur,
even the beauty Nánwēi would not be exchanged for him.
Why must ignorant old women
create such a false situation!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Wāng Kěshòu of Huángméi County in Húguǎng
could remember three past lives. In his first life, he was a scholar
studying in a Buddhist temple.
The monk had a mare that gave birth to a mule foal,
which the scholar coveted and took by force.
After he died,
the King of the Underworld examined his records,
angered by his greed and violence,
and sentenced him to be reborn as a mule to repay the temple monk.
After being born,
he was dearly cared for by the monk,
and had no chance to die.
As he grew older,
he often thought of throwing himself into a ravine,
but feared betraying the kindness of his upbringing,
which would incur even harsher underworld punishment,
so he resigned himself to his fate.
After several years,
his karmic debt fulfilled, he died of natural causes.
He was reborn into a farming family: able to speak as soon as he left the birth mat,
his parents considered him a monster
and killed him.
Then he was born into the family of Scholar Wāng.
The scholar, nearly fifty,
was overjoyed to have a son.
Wāng was clear-minded from birth;
but remembering his previous death for speaking too early,
he dared not speak.
By three or four years old,
everyone thought he was mute.
One day,
his father was writing an essay
when a friend happened to visit.
He put down his brush and went out to greet the guest.
Wāng entered and saw his father's unfinished work;
unable to resist the itch to show his skill,
he completed it for him.
When his father returned and saw it,
he asked,
"Who came in?"
The servants said,
"No one."
Greatly puzzled,
the next day he deliberately set a topic on the desk,
then went out briefly.
After a short while, he returned,
stealing in quietly on tiptoe.
He saw his son leaning over the desk,
several lines of draft already written.
Suddenly noticing his father's presence,
the boy involuntarily cried out
and knelt, begging to be spared death.
His father was delighted.
Taking his hand, he said,
"You are the only son in our family.
Since you can write essays,
it is the fortune of our household.
Why hide it?"
From then on, he taught him to study even more diligently.
The youth later became a jìnshì
and rose to the post of Grand Coordinator of Dàtóng.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A farmer from Chǔ was returning from the market
and rested briefly by the roadside.
A fortune-teller arrived later
and stopped to chat with him.
Suddenly, looking at the farmer, he said,
"Your aura is inauspicious.
Within three days, you will lose wealth
and suffer official punishment."
The farmer said,
"My taxes are already paid,
and I have never been involved in fights in my life.
How could punishment come to me?"
The fortune-teller said,
"I don't know either.
But your aura is like this—
you must be careful!"
The farmer was rather skeptical.
He cupped his hands in farewell and went home.
The next day,
while herding his calf in the wild,
a courier's horse passed by.
The calf saw it
and mistook it for a tiger.
It charged straight at it,
and the horse was killed.
The courier dragged the farmer to the authorities.
The official lightly punished him
but ordered him to compensate for the horse.
It is said that water buffaloes will always fight tigers;
therefore, cattle traders sleeping outdoors
often use their oxen for self-defense.
If they see a horse passing,
they quickly drive their cattle away to avoid them,
fearing they might mistakenly charge.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Lǐ Xìn
was a gambler.
One day while napping during the day,
he suddenly saw his old gambling companions Wáng Dà and Féng Jiǔ arrive,
inviting him to go play a game.
Lǐ had also forgotten they were ghosts,
and cheerfully went along with them.
Once outside,
Wáng Dà went to invite Zhōu Zǐmíng from the village,
while Féng led Lǐ ahead,
entering the village’s eastern temple.
After a short while,
Zhōu indeed came with Wáng.
Féng took out playing cards,
and proposed they play a game of chance.
Lǐ said:
"In such haste, I have no gambling funds,
and would only let down your generous invitation—
what can be done?"
Zhōu said the same.
Wáng said:
"Huáng Bāguānrén of Yànzi Valley lends money at interest;
if we go together to borrow from him,
he should certainly agree."
So the four of them went together.
In a fleeting moment,
they reached a large village.
Within the village, grand mansions stood wall to wall,
and Wáng pointed to one gate,
saying:
"This is the home of Young Master Huáng."
An old servant came out from inside,
and Wáng explained their purpose.
The servant then went in to report.
Soon he came out again,
conveying the young master’s command,
inviting Wáng and Lǐ to meet.
Entering to see the young master,
they found him about eighteen or nineteen years old,
his speech and laughter gentle and amiable.
He promptly handed Lǐ a string of large coins,
saying:
"I know you are honest and straightforward,
so there’s no harm in lending to you.
As for Zhōu Zǐmíng, I cannot trust him."
Wáng earnestly pleaded on his behalf.
The young master demanded that Lǐ sign as guarantor,
but Lǐ refused.
Wáng urged him from the side,
and only then did Lǐ agree.
Zhōu was also given a string before they left.
They then handed it to Zhōu,
and explained the young master’s meaning,
to pressure him into repaying without fail.
Leaving the valley,
they saw a woman approaching,
who was the wife of Zhào from the village,
notorious for being quarrelsome and foul-mouthed.
Féng said:
"There’s no one around here;
this shrew deserves a little scare."
So they grabbed her and took her back into the valley.
The woman screamed loudly,
and Féng scooped up dirt to stuff her mouth.
Zhōu praised, saying:
"For a woman like this,
she should only have a stake driven into her private parts!"
Féng then pulled down her pants,
and forcibly inserted a long stone.
The woman appeared dead.
The group then dispersed,
returned to the temple,
and gambled together.
From noon until late at night,
Lǐ won big,
while Féng and Zhōu lost all their funds.
Lǐ therefore gave the large sum plus interest entirely to Wáng,
to repay Young Master Huáng on his behalf;
Wáng then distributed shares to Zhōu and Féng,
and the game resumed.
Not long after,
they heard the sound of chaotic voices, and someone rushed in, saying:
"The City God himself has come to arrest gamblers,
and he’s here now!"
Everyone turned pale.
Lǐ abandoned his money, leaped over the wall, and fled.
The others, concerned about their funds,
were all captured and bound.
Once outside,
they indeed saw a deity seated on a horse,
with over twenty gamblers tied up behind the horse.
Before dawn,
they had already reached the county city,
entering as the gates opened.
Arriving at the yamen,
the City God sat facing south,
called the prisoners forward,
and holding a register, called out names.
After calling them,
he ordered that each have their index finger chopped off with a sharp axe,
then had their eyes painted black and red respectively,
and paraded through the market three times before it ended.
The escorts demanded bribes before removing the black and red paint,
and everyone paid them.
Only Zhōu refused,
pleading that his purse was empty;
the escorts proposed sending him home first and then being repaid,
but he still wouldn’t agree.
An escort pointed at him and said:
"You’re truly an iron bean,
that won’t pop even when fried!"
Then, cupping his hands, he left.
Zhōu left the city,
wet his sleeve with saliva,
and wiped as he walked.
Reaching the river, he looked at his reflection:
the black and red paint hadn’t come off;
he scooped water to wash it,
but it was stubborn and wouldn’t come off.
He returned home filled with regret and resentment.
Previously,
the wife of the Zhào family had gone to her parents' home for a reason,
and as dusk fell, she had not returned.
Her husband went to fetch her,
and when he reached the mouth of the valley,
he saw his wife lying by the roadside.
Seeing her condition,
he knew she had encountered a ghost.
He removed the mud plugging her orifices
and carried her back on his shoulders.
Gradually she revived and could speak,
and only then did they learn that something had been inside her private parts,
writhing and pulling itself out.
She then recounted her ordeal.
Zhào was furious
and hurried to the county magistrate,
accusing Lǐ and Zhōu.
Zhōu was still lying down,
Lǐ had just awakened;
Zhōu was still in a deep sleep,
appearing as if dead.
The magistrate, believing Zhào had made a false accusation,
had Zhào beaten and his wife shackled.
Husband and wife had no way to plead their case.
The next day,
Zhōu awoke,
his eye sockets suddenly turned one red and one black,
and he cried out in pain from his fingers.
Looking at them,
the tendons and bones were already broken,
only connected by skin,
and within a few days they fell off.
The ink and cinnabar on his eyes
had penetrated deep into the flesh.
Those who saw him could not help but cover their mouths and laugh.
One day,
he saw Wáng Dàlái demanding repayment of a debt.
Zhōu sternly insisted he had no money,
and Wáng left angrily.
His family asked him about it,
and only then did they learn the reason.
Together, they reasoned that gods and ghosts are merciless
and urged him to repay the debt.
Zhōu stubbornly refused,
saying:
"Nowadays, officials all side with debt-dodgers.
The principles of the underworld should be no different,
especially for gambling debts!"
The next day,
two ghosts came,
saying that Young Master Huáng had submitted a petition at the county office,
and they were to take him for questioning.
Lǐ Xìn also saw yamen runners come
to fetch him as a witness.
The two men died simultaneously.
Arriving outside the village, they met,
with Wáng and Féng both present.
Lǐ said to Zhōu:
"You still have those red and black eyes;
dare you face the officials?"
Zhōu repeated his previous argument.
Lǐ, knowing his stinginess,
said:
"Since you are so heartless,
I will ask to see Squire Huáng
and repay the debt for you."
So they went together to the young master's place.
Lǐ went in and explained the situation,
but the young master refused,
saying:
"Who is the debtor,
that I should seek repayment from you?"
Lǐ came out and told Zhōu,
then proposed raising the money
to lend to Zhōu for repayment.
Zhōu grew even angrier
and spoke offensively of the young master.
The ghosts then seized him and took him along.
Before long,
they reached the county
and entered to see the City God.
The City God scolded:
"Shameless rogue!
The paint on your eyes is still there,
and yet you still refuse to repay your debt!"
Zhōu said:
"Young Master Huáng lent money at high interest,
luring me into gambling,
and thus I was punished."
The City God summoned Huáng's servant
and angrily said:
"Your master set up a gambling den to lure people into gambling,
and still demands repayment?"
The servant said:
"When the money was lent,
the young master did not know it was for gambling.
The young master lives at Swallow Valley,
and the gamblers were caught at Guānyīn Temple,
over ten miles apart.
The young master has never set up a gambling den."
The City God looked at Zhōu and said:
"You borrow money and stubbornly refuse to repay it,
and even fabricate accusations!
Of all heartless people,
you are the worst!"
He was about to order a beating,
when Zhōu again complained about the high interest.
The City God asked:
"How much have you repaid?"
The reply was:
"Actually, I haven't repaid anything yet."
The City God angrily said:
"You haven't even repaid the principal,
and you complain about the interest?"
He ordered thirty strokes
and immediately had him taken to repay the creditor.
The two ghosts escorted him home,
demanded a bribe,
and would not let him revive immediately.
They tied him up in the latrine
and told him to appear in his family's dreams.
His family burned twenty stacks of paper money,
and after the fire died down,
it turned into two taels of gold and two thousand coins.
Zhōu then used the gold to repay the debt
and bribed the escorts with the coins,
so they released him to return.
After reviving,
sores swelled on his buttocks,
pus and blood gushed out,
and it took several months to heal.
Afterwards, the wife of the Zhào family dared not curse again;
but Zhōu, with four fingers missing and red and black eyes,
continued gambling as before.
From this, we know that gamblers are less than human!
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"The injustices in the world
all stem from officials who, in correcting one extreme, go to the opposite extreme.
In the past, wealthy families used exorbitant interest to seize the children of good families,
and no one dared to protest.
Otherwise,
as soon as a complaint was submitted,
the officials would use the law to side with them.
Thus, officials of the people in the past
all served the powerful families.
Later, wise men, seeing these abuses,
completely reversed the policy.
There were Jǔrén who used large sums to become great merchants,
wearing silk and satiated with fine food,
building towers and pavilions at home, buying fertile land.
Yet they completely forgot where their wealth came from.
Once repayment was demanded,
they would glare angrily.
When brought before officials,
the officials would say: 'I am not anyone's servant.'
How is this different from the lazy monk
who had no time to wipe the tears of ordinary people?
I have often said that officials of the past were sycophants,
while officials of today are absurd.
Sycophants certainly deserve punishment,
but the absurd are also detestable.
Lending money at low interest—
does that benefit only the rich?"
When Zhāng Shínián served as magistrate of Zīchuān,
he most hated gambling.
His method of painting faces and parading through the city
was like the underworld's law,
though the punishment did not go as far as cutting off fingers,
yet gambling was eradicated.
It seems that as an official,
he was very skilled in investigative methods.
Even when official documents were piling up,
each time someone came before the court,
he would seem quite at leisure,
asking in detail about their residence, age, family members, and livelihood.
After questioning,
he would then advise and encourage them before letting them leave.
Once, a man came to pay his taxes and submit the receipt,
thinking he had no further business,
and presented the receipt to leave.
The magistrate stopped him,
questioned him thoroughly once more,
and said:
"Don't you gamble?"
The man strenuously denied ever gambling in his life.
The magistrate smiled and said:
"You still have gambling tools on you."
They searched him,
and indeed it was so.
People thought him divine,
yet no one knew his method.
Based on the "Zhùxuězhāi" manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Lè Zhòng was from Xī'ān.
His father died early,
and Zhòng was born posthumously.
His mother was a devout Buddhist,
abstaining from meat and wine.
When Zhòng grew up,
he loved to drink and eat heartily,
and secretly disapproved of his mother's ways,
often urging her to partake of rich and delicious foods.
His mother rebuked him.
Later, when his mother fell ill
and was on her deathbed,
she craved meat.
In his desperation with no meat to be found,
Zhòng cut a piece of flesh from his left thigh and offered it to her.
Her illness slightly improved,
but she regretted breaking her precept,
refused to eat, and died.
Zhòng's grief intensified,
and with a sharp knife he further cut into his right thigh, exposing the bone.
His family rushed to save him,
wrapping the wound with cloth and applying medicine,
and he soon recovered.
Reflecting on his mother's bitter asceticism,
and feeling that her devotion was misguided,
he burned the Buddha statue they had enshrined
and set up a memorial tablet to worship his mother.
When drunk,
he would often weep mournfully before it.
He did not marry until he was twenty,
and remained a virgin.
Three days after the wedding,
he told people:
"The union of man and woman
is the filthiest thing under heaven;
I truly find no joy in it!"
He then sent his wife away.
His father-in-law, Gù Wéndòng,
sent relatives to plead for her return,
repeatedly asking three or four times,
but Zhòng firmly refused.
After half a year,
Gù married his daughter to someone else. Zhòng lived alone for twenty years,
his behavior becoming increasingly unrestrained: he would drink with slaves and actors alike;
when neighbors or beggars made requests,
he never hesitated to give.
Someone once mentioned having no cooking pot for his daughter's wedding,
so Zhòng took the pot from his own stove and gave it away.
He then borrowed a pot from a neighbor to cook his own meals.
Various unscrupulous people, knowing his nature,
cheated him morning and night.
Some, claiming to have lost all in gambling and sighing sorrowfully,
said they were being urgently pressed for debts
and were about to sell their children.
Zhòng would gather the exact amount of tax money,
emptying his purse to give it to them;
when the tax collectors came to his door,
he would then pawn his belongings to manage.
Because of this,
his household grew increasingly impoverished.
Previously, when Zhòng was wealthy,
his cousins and nephews vied to serve him,
allowing him to take whatever he wished
without contention;
but when Zhòng declined into poverty,
hardly anyone came to visit or inquire.
Zhòng, being broad-minded,
did not mind.
On the anniversary of his mother's death,
Zhòng happened to be ill
and unable to visit her grave,
so he wanted to send a nephew to offer sacrifices on his behalf;
but all the nephews excused themselves for various reasons.
Zhòng then poured a libation at home,
wailing in pain before the memorial tablet;
