the sorrow of having no heir
weighed heavily on his mind,
and his illness grew worse.
In his delirium,
he felt someone caressing him;
opening his eyes slightly,
he saw it was his mother.
Startled, he asked:
"Where have you come from?"
His mother said:
"Because no one from home came to my grave,
I came to receive the offerings,
and also to see your illness."
He asked:
"Where have you been living, Mother?"
His mother said:
"In the Southern Sea."
After she finished caressing him,
his whole body felt cool.
Opening his eyes and looking around,
there was no one in sight,
and his illness was cured.
After rising,
he thought of making a pilgrimage to the Southern Sea.
It happened that in a neighboring village, some people were forming an incense society for the pilgrimage,
so he sold ten acres of land
and took the money to join them.
The society members disliked his impurity
and collectively rejected him.
He then followed them, waiting and traveling along.
On the journey, he did not abstain from beef, wine, or garlic,
making the others despise him even more;
taking advantage of his drunken sleep,
they left without telling him.
Zhòng then traveled alone.
Arriving in Mǐn,
he met a friend who invited him to drink,
and a famous courtesan named Qiónghuá was present.
When he mentioned his pilgrimage to the Southern Sea,
Qiónghuá expressed her wish to accompany him.
Zhòng was pleased
and immediately waited for her to pack,
then set off together with her;
though they shared lodging and meals,
they remained entirely chaste.
When they reached the Southern Sea,
the society members saw that he had brought a courtesan
and ridiculed him even more,
disdaining to worship alongside him.
Zhòng and Qiónghuá understood their attitude,
so they waited for the others to bow first before bowing themselves.
When the others bowed,
they resented that no divine manifestation appeared.
But when the two of them bowed
and just as they prostrated themselves,
suddenly the sea was filled with lotuses,
each flower adorned with jeweled tassels;
Qiónghuá saw them as Bodhisattvas.
Zhòng saw his mother on every flower.
He urgently called out and rushed toward his mother,
leaping into the sea to follow her.
The others saw the myriad lotus flowers
all transform into radiant clouds,
covering the sea like brocade.
After a while,
the clouds cleared and the waves calmed,
everything vanished,
yet Zhòng found himself still on the shore.
He himself could not understand how he had gotten out,
with his clothes and shoes completely dry.
Gazing at the sea, he wept bitterly,
his voice shaking the islands.
Qiónghuá consoled and urged him,
and sorrowfully they left the temple,
hiring a boat to sail north.
On the way, a wealthy family summoned Qiónghuá away,
and Zhòng rested alone at an inn.
There was a child of about eight or nine years old,
begging for food in a shop,
whose appearance did not resemble a beggar's.
Upon careful questioning,
it turned out he had been driven out by his stepmother.
Zhòng pitied him.
The child clung to him,
pleading earnestly for rescue,
so Zhòng took him along on his return.
When asked his name,
the child said:
"I am Ā Xīn,
surname Yōng,
and my mother was née Gù.
I once heard my mother say: she married into the Yōng family and six months later
gave birth to me.
I was originally surnamed Lè."
Zhòng was greatly astonished.
He doubted that in his lifetime, having only been intimate once,
he could have a son.
So he asked where the Lè family lived,
and the child replied:
"I don't know.
But when my mother died,
she gave me a letter,
telling me not to lose it."
Zhòng urgently asked for the letter.
Looking at it,
he saw it was the divorce document he had given to the Gù family years ago.
Astonished, he said:
"You are truly my son!"
Examining the dates, they were indeed accurate,
which greatly comforted his heart. However, the family's finances grew daily more strained,
and after two years,
as the land was gradually sold off,
he could no longer afford to keep servants.
One day,
as father and son were cooking a meal,
a beautiful woman suddenly entered.
Looking at her,
they saw it was Qiónghuá.
In astonishment, they asked:
"Where have you come from?"
She smiled and said:
"We were already a pretend husband and wife,
why ask again?
The reason I didn't follow you earlier
was only because the old woman was still alive;
now she has died.
Considering that if I don't follow someone,
I have no way to protect myself;
but if I follow someone,
I also have no way to preserve my purity: the plan that achieves both
is none other than to follow you,
so I did not fear the journey of a thousand lǐ."
Thereupon she unpacked and took over the cooking for the son.
Zhòngliáng was delighted.
When night came,
father and son slept together as before,
while another room was prepared for Qiónghuá to live in.
The son treated her as a mother,
and Qiónghuá also cared well for the son.
When relatives and friends heard of it,
they all brought gifts to congratulate Zhòng,
and both were happy to accept them.
When guests came,
Qiónghuá prepared everything for them,
and Zhòng never asked where it all came from.
Qiónghuá gradually used gold and pearls to redeem their former property,
broadly acquiring maids, servants, oxen, and horses,
and the household grew increasingly prosperous.
Zhòng often said to Qiónghuá:
"When I am drunk,
you should hide away,
and not let me see you."
Huá smiled and agreed.
One day,
he was heavily drunk,
and urgently called for Qiónghuá.
Huá came out in resplendent attire.
Zhòng gazed at her for a long time,
then was overjoyed,
dancing and leaping as if mad,
saying:
"I have attained enlightenment!"
Instantly he sobered up.
He felt the world become bright,
and the thatched cottage they lived in
turned entirely into jade towers and royal palaces;
only after a while did it cease.
From then on, he no longer drank at the market,
but only drank daily facing Qiónghuá.
Huá was vegetarian,
and served him with tea.
One day,
slightly intoxicated,
he had Qiónghuá massage his thigh,
and saw that the scar on his thigh
had transformed into two red lotus flowers,
faintly rising from the flesh.
He found it strange.
Zhòng smiled and said:
"When you see these flowers bloom,
our twenty years as a pretend husband and wife will part."
Qiónghuá believed him.
After they had arranged Āxīn's marriage,
Qiónghuá gradually handed over household affairs to the daughter-in-law,
and lived with Zhòng in a separate courtyard.
Son and daughter-in-law paid respects every three days,
and only matters of difficulty or doubt were brought to them.
They employed two maids: one to warm wine,
and one to brew tea, nothing more.
One day,
Qiónghuá went to her son's place,
and after the daughter-in-law consulted with her at length,
they went together to see the father.
Entering the door,
they saw the father sitting barefoot on the couch.
Hearing their voices,
he opened his eyes, smiled, and said:
"Mother and son have come, excellent!"
Then he closed his eyes again.
Qiónghuá cried out in alarm:
"What do you intend to do?"
Looking at his thigh,
the lotus flowers were in full bloom.
Testing him,
his breath had already ceased.
She immediately pressed the two flowers together with her fingers,
and prayed, saying:
"I followed you from a thousand lǐ away,
which was no easy matter.
For you, I taught your son and instructed your wife.
I also have some small merit.
Even if it's just two or three years,
why not wait a little longer?"
After a while,
Zhòng suddenly opened his eyes, smiled, and said:
"You have your own affairs,
why must you drag another person to accompany you?
If there's no other way,
I'll stay for your sake."
Qiónghuá released her hand,
and the flowers had already closed again.
Thereupon they talked and laughed as before.
After more than three years had passed,
Qiónghuá was nearly forty,
yet she still looked like someone in her twenties.
Suddenly she said to Zhòng:
"When ordinary people die,
others grab their heads and lift their feet,
which is truly unclean."
So she ordered a craftsman to make a double coffin.
Xīn asked in alarm,
and she replied:
"This is not for you to know."
When the work was finished,
she bathed and finished dressing,
then said to her son and daughter-in-law:
"I am about to die."
Xīn wept and said:
"For years we have relied on Mother's management,
and only then have we not suffered cold or hunger.
Mother has not yet enjoyed any peace and comfort,
why must you abandon your son and leave?"
She said:
"The father sowed blessings and the son reaps them;
the maids, servants, oxen, and horses
are all repayments from debtors to your father;
I have no merit in this.
I was originally a celestial maiden who scatters flowers,
but by chance, a worldly thought arose,
and so I was banished to the mortal world for over thirty years;
now my term is fulfilled."
Thereupon she climbed into the coffin and entered it herself.
Calling to her again,
her eyes were already closed.
Xīn wept and told his father,
but his father, who had stiffened at some unknown time,
lay there with his clothes and hat in perfect order.
Xīn wailed in grief, nearly overcome.
They placed them in coffins,
and both were laid in the main hall.
For several days they were not encoffined,
hoping they would return.
A bright light emerged from the area of their thighs,
illuminating the four walls.
From within Qiónghuá's coffin,
fragrant mist sprayed and overflowed,
and those nearby could smell it.
Once the coffins were closed,
the fragrance and light gradually diminished.
After the funeral,
the various Lè family members coveted his possessions,
and together plotted to drive Xīn out,
taking the matter to court.
The officials were unable to determine the truth,
and planned to divide the land and property, giving half to the various Lè members.
Xīn refused to accept this,
and submitted a petition to the prefectural authorities,
but it remained unresolved for a long time.
Earlier,
Gù had married his daughter to Yōng.
After more than a year,
Yōng drifted away to Mǐn,
and news of him was completely cut off.
Gù, old and without a son,
bitterly missed his daughter,
so he went to his son-in-law's place,
only to find his daughter dead and his grandson driven away.
He filed a complaint.
Yōng was afraid,
and tried to bribe Gù,
but Gù would not accept it,
insisting on getting his grandson back,
but despite an exhaustive search, he could not be found.
One day,
Gù happened to be on the road,
when he saw a colorful sedan chair passing by,
and he moved aside to the left of the road.
A beautiful woman inside the sedan called out:
"Are you not Elder Gù?"
Gù assented.
The woman said:
"Your grandson is my son,
he is now in the Lè family,
do not pursue the lawsuit.
Your grandson is currently in trouble,
you should go quickly."
Gù wanted to question her in detail,
but the sedan had already gone far away.
Gù then accepted the bribe and went to Xī'ān.
Upon arriving,
he found the lawsuit was in full uproar.
Gù presented himself to the officials,
stating the day his daughter returned to her natal home,
the day she remarried,
and the year and month she gave birth,
all in clear and precise detail.
The various Lè members were all caned and driven out,
and the case was thus settled.
Upon returning,
he recounted the day he saw the beautiful woman,
which was exactly the day Qiónghuá passed away.
Xīn moved Gù's family,
providing him with a house and gifting him maidservants.
When Gù was over sixty, he had a son,
and Xīn cared for and supported him.
The Chronicler of the Tales remarks:
"Abstaining from meat and avoiding women,
this resembles Buddhism,
but a radiant, artless innocence,
this is the true essence of Buddhism.
Lè Zhòng faced a beautiful woman,
simply viewing her as a pure and fragrant companion on the path,
not regarding her as an object of sensual pleasure.
Living together for thirty years,
seemingly with affection,
seemingly without,
this is the true face of a Bodhisattva,
how can ordinary people in this world fathom it!"
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
At the Xiàqīng Palace at the foot of Láo Mountain,
there was a winter-sweet tree over twenty feet tall,
dozens of arm-spans in girth,
and peonies over ten feet tall,
their blossoms in season dazzling like brocade.
A scholar named Huáng from Jiāozhōu
took up lodging there for his studies.
One day,
he saw from his window a young lady,
her plain clothes shimmering among the flowers.
He wondered how such a person could be in a Taoist temple.
He hurried out,
but she had already vanished.
From then on, he saw her often.
So he hid himself among the thick trees,
waiting for her arrival.
Not long after,
the young lady came again, accompanied by another in red garments.
Gazing at them from afar,
their beauty was doubly peerless.
As they drew nearer,
the one in red retreated, saying:
"There is a stranger here!"
Huáng sprang up suddenly.
The two women fled in alarm,
their sleeves and skirts fluttering,
a fragrant breeze wafting about.
He chased them past a low wall,
but all was silent and they had vanished without a trace.
His longing grew even more intense,
so he inscribed a verse on a tree:
"Boundless is the bitterness of longing, / With tender feelings I face the short lamp. / Fearful she'll return to Shāzhā Lì, / Where can I find another Wúshuāng?"
Returning to his study, he lost himself in thought.
Suddenly, the young lady entered.
Overjoyed, he welcomed her.
She smiled and said:
"Your fierce manner was like a fierce bandit, / it was terrifying; / I didn't know you were a refined scholar of letters, / so there's no harm in meeting."
Huáng asked about her background.
She said:
"My childhood name is Xiāngyù. / I was registered in the Píngkāng Lane quarters. / A Taoist priest confined me in this mountain, / it is truly not my wish."
Huáng asked:
"What is the priest's name? / I will cleanse this stain for you."
She said:
"It's not necessary. / He also does not dare press me too hard. / To use this chance to be with a romantic scholar, / and have long, secret trysts, is also fine."
He asked:
"Who is the one in red?"
She said:
"Her name is Jiàngxuě, / she is my sworn elder sister."
Thereupon they became intimate.
When he awoke,
the dawn light was already red.
The woman hurriedly rose, saying:
"Indulging in pleasure, I forgot the dawn."
Putting on her clothes and changing her shoes, she also said:
"I'll repay you with a verse, / don't laugh: 'Lovely nights so easily end, / morning sun already on the window. / I wish to be like swallows on the beam, / where they perch, naturally a pair.'"
Huáng grasped her wrist and said:

"You are beautiful outwardly and wise within, / making one love you and forget death. / But your departure for a day / feels like a separation of a thousand *li*. / You should come when you find a moment, / don't wait for night."
She promised.
From then on, they were together every dawn and dusk.
Whenever he asked her to invite Jiàngxuě to come,
she simply would not come,
and Huáng felt regret about it.
The woman said:
"Sister Jiàng's nature is quite aloof, / not like my infatuated passion. / I should gently persuade her to come, / no need to be too hasty."
One evening,
the woman entered with a sorrowful expression and said:
"You cannot hold on to Lǒng,
yet you still hope for Shǔ?
Now we must part forever."
He asked:
"Where are you going?"
She wiped her tears with her sleeve,
and said:
"This is determined by fate,
it is difficult to explain to you.
That excellent poem of yours from before,
has now become a prophetic verse.
'The fair lady already belongs to Shā Xūlì,
the righteous knight today lacks a Gǔ Yāyá.'
This can be chanted for me."
He pressed her for details,
but she would not speak,
only sobbing.
She stayed awake all night,
and left at dawn.
Shēng found this strange.
The next day,
a man named Lán from Jímò,
entered the palace to stroll and look around,
saw the white peony,
took a liking to it,
dug it up and took it straight away.
Only then did Shēng realize that Xiāngyù was a flower spirit,
and he was filled with endless regret and sorrow.
After a few days,
he heard that Mr. Lán had moved the flower to his home,
and it was wilting day by day.
Overcome with grief,
he composed fifty poems mourning the flower,
and daily visited the empty spot, weeping tears and snivel.
One day,
just as he was returning from paying his respects,
he saw from afar a figure in red weeping beside the spot.
Calmly approaching her,
the woman did not avoid him.
Shēng then took hold of her sleeve,
and they faced each other, tears streaming down.
After a while, he invited her to come inside,
and she followed him.
Sighing, she said:
"Childhood sisters,
cut off in a single morning!
Hearing your sorrow,
only increases my own grief.
Tears falling to the Nine Springs,
may perhaps move sincerity to bring her back to life;
but the spirit and energy of the dead have already scattered,
how could she suddenly be able to converse and laugh with the two of us?"
Shēng said:
"I, a humble scholar, am ill-fated,
harming my beloved,
and likely have no fortune to enjoy two beauties.
Previously, I frequently troubled Xiāngyù,
to convey my sincere feelings;
why have you not come again?"
The woman said:
"I thought that young scholars,
nine out of ten are fickle;
I did not know you were truly a man of deep feeling.
However, my association with you,
is based on affection, not on licentiousness.
If we were to be intimate day and night,
that is something I could not do."
Having said this,
she prepared to leave.
Shēng said:
"With Xiāngyù gone forever,
I can neither eat nor sleep.
Relying on you to stay a little,
to comfort this longing heart,
why be so resolute in leaving!"
The woman then stayed,
spent the night, and left.
For several days she did not return.
Cold rain at the secluded window,
bitterly missing Xiāngyù,
tossing and turning on his bed,
tears congealing on pillow and mat.
Pulling on his robe and rising again,
he trimmed the lamp and composed another poem following the previous rhyme:
"Rain at dusk in the mountain temple,
sitting by the small window with curtain drawn.
The one I long for is not seen,
at midnight, tears fall in pairs."
Having finished the poem, he chanted it to himself.
Suddenly, someone outside the window said:
"The composer should not lack a response."
Listening,
it was Jiàngxuě.
He opened the door and invited her in.
The woman looked at the poem,
and immediately added lines after it:
"Where is the one who walked arm in arm?
A lone lamp shines on the evening window.
In the empty mountains, a solitary person,
facing my shadow, we make a pair."
Shēng read it and shed tears,
then complained about the infrequency of their meetings.
The woman said:
"I cannot be as passionate as Xiāngyù,
but I can slightly relieve your loneliness."
Shēng wished to be intimate with her.
She said:
"The joy of meeting,
why must it lie in this?"
Thus, whenever he was extremely bored,
the woman would come once.
When she came, they would feast, drink, and exchange poems.
Sometimes she would leave without staying the night,
and Shēng would let her.
He said to her:
"Xiāngyù is my beloved wife,
Jiàngxuě is my good friend."
He often wanted to ask her:
"Which plant in this courtyard are you?
I beg you to tell me early,
so I can transplant you to my home,
to avoid you being snatched away by a wicked man like Xiāngyù,
causing a lifetime of regret."
The woman said:
"The native soil is hard to move;
telling you would be of no use.
Even a wife could not follow you to the end,
let alone a friend!"
Shēng did not listen,
took her by the arm and went out,
and whenever they came to a peony,
he would ask:
"Is this you?"
The woman would not speak,
only covering her mouth and laughing.
Soon after, Shēng returned home for the Lunar New Year.
In the second month,
he suddenly dreamed that Jiàngxuě came,
and said with a distressed expression:
"I am in great danger!
If you hurry there,
we may still meet;
if delayed, it will be too late."
Waking, he found it strange,
urgently ordered servants and horses,
and sped like a star to the mountain.
It turned out the Daoist priest was about to build a house,
and there was a winter-sweet tree,
obstructing the construction.
The craftsmen were about to wield their axes.
Shēng urgently stopped them.
That night,
Jiàngxuě came to thank him.
Shēng said with a laugh:
"If you hadn't told me the truth before,
you deserved this calamity!
Now I already know which one you are;
if you don't come,
I will burn moxa to scorch you."
The woman said:
"I knew you would be like this,
which is why I dared not tell you before."
They sat for a while,
then Shēng said:
"Now facing my good friend,
I miss my beautiful wife even more.
It has been long since I wept for Xiāngyù;
can you accompany me to weep?"
The two then went,
and shed tears before the empty spot.
After the first watch,
Jiàngxuě wiped her tears and urged him to stop.
A few nights later,
as Shēng was sitting quietly,
Jiàngxuě entered with a laugh and said:
"I bring you glad tidings: the flower goddess is moved by your deep feeling,
and has allowed Xiāngyù to return to the palace."
Shēng asked:
"When?"
She replied:
"I don't know,
but it shouldn't be long."
At daybreak, she got down from the bed.
Shēng urged her:
"I came here for your sake;
don't leave me lonely for long."
The woman laughed and promised.
For two nights she did not come.
Shēng went and embraced the tree,
shaking and stroking it,
calling repeatedly with no response.
He then returned,
facing the lamp, rolled some moxa,
intending to go and burn the tree.
The woman hurriedly entered,
snatched the moxa and threw it away,
saying:
"You are too mischievous,"
"and have caused me to be wounded and scarred.
I should break off with you!"
Shēng laughed and embraced her.
Before they had settled down,
Xiāngyù entered gracefully.
Seeing her,
Shēng's tears flowed uncontrollably.
He quickly rose and grasped her hand.
Xiāngyù held Jiàngxuě with one hand,
and they faced each other, choked with sorrow.
When they sat down,
Shēng, holding her, felt her insubstantial,
as if his hand were grasping itself.
Startled, he asked her about it.
Xiāngyù said with tears in her eyes:
"In the past, I was
the spirit of the flower,
hence solid;
now I am
the ghost of the flower,
hence dispersed.
Though we are together now,
do not take it as real;
regard it merely as a dream."
Jiàngxuě said:
"It's wonderful that you've come, sister!
I've been pestered to death by your man."
Then she left.
Xiāngyù smiled and chatted as before;
but when they nestled close,
it was as if a body were merging with its shadow.
Shēng was deeply distressed.
Xiāngyù also lamented her own fate,
and said:
"Take the powder of white aconite root,
mix it with a little sulfur,
and pour a cup of water over me daily.
On this day next year, I will repay your kindness."
Then she departed.
The next day,
Shēng went to look at the old spot,
and saw that a peony sprout had emerged.
He then tended it daily,
and built a carved railing to protect it.
When Xiāngyù came,
she was exceedingly grateful.
Shēng planned to transplant it to his home,
but the girl would not allow it,
saying:
"I am of delicate constitution,
and cannot endure being moved again.
Moreover, all things have their destined places;
originally, I did not intend to live in your home.
Going against this would shorten my lifespan.
But if we love each other,
the day of our reunion will surely come."
Shēng regretted that Jiàngxuě did not come.
Xiāngyù said:
"If you insist on forcing her to come,
I can make her appear."
Then she and Shēng took a lantern to the tree,
plucked a blade of grass,
and used her palm to measure,
measuring from the base of the tree upward.
From the bottom up,
at four feet six inches,
she pressed the spot
and had Shēng scratch it with both hands.
Soon, Jiàngxuě appeared from behind,
laughing and scolding:
"You little wench,
are you here to aid the tyrant in his cruelty?!"
She was pulled along and entered with them.
Xiāngyù said:
"Sister, don't be angry!
I must trouble you to keep Shēng company for a while;
after a year, I won't disturb you anymore."
From then on, this became routine.
Shēng watched the flower bud
grow increasingly lush and vigorous.
By the end of spring,
it had reached over two feet in height.
After returning home,
Shēng gave money to the Daoist priest,
instructing him to tend it morning and night.
In the fourth month of the following year, he went to the temple,
and saw a single flower,
still in bud and not yet open.
As he lingered there,
the flower swayed as if about to burst open.
After a short while, it bloomed,
as large as a plate,
and clearly visible within the stamens was a little beauty,
only about three or four fingers tall.
In an instant, she floated down gracefully—
it was Xiāngyù.
She said with a smile:
"I endured wind and rain waiting for you;
why have you come so late!"
Then they entered the room.
Jiàngxuě also arrived,
and said with a laugh:
"Every day I acted as a wife for another;
now, fortunately, I can step back and be a friend."
Then they talked and feasted together.
At midnight,
Jiàngxuě left.
The two of them slept together,
as intimate and harmonious as before.
Later, Shēng's wife passed away,
and Shēng entered the mountains, never to return.
By then,
the peony had grown as thick as an arm.
Shēng often pointed to it and said:
"One day, I will entrust my soul here,
and be born to your left."
The two girls laughed and said:
"Do not forget this."
More than ten years later,
Shēng suddenly fell ill.
His son came
and grieved before him.
Shēng smiled and said:
"This is my birth,
not my death;
why grieve?"
He said to the Daoist priest:
"In the future, if a red sprout emerges vigorously beneath the peony,
with five leaves when it opens,
that will be me."
Then he spoke no more.
His son carried him home,
and he passed away.
The following year,
a plump sprout indeed emerged,
with leaves exactly as described.
The Daoist priest considered it extraordinary,
and watered it even more diligently.
After three years,
it grew several feet tall,
as thick as two hands could grasp,
but it did not flower.
When the old Daoist priest died,
his disciples did not cherish it,
and cut it down.
The white peony also withered and died;
not long after,
the winter jasmine died as well.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"When love reaches its utmost,
even ghosts and spirits can communicate.
The flower followed as a ghost,
and the man entrusted his soul—
is this not because their bond of love was deep?
One departure and two followed in death—
even if not steadfast,
they died for love.
If a person cannot remain chaste,
it is because their love is not sincere enough.
When Confucius read the poem 'Tángdì,' he said, 'He has not truly thought.'
How true this is!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A scholar went to Jīnlíng to take the imperial examination.
Passing through Sùqiān,
he encountered three xiùcai,
whose conversation was profound and expansive.
So he bought wine, and they became quite congenial.
Each stated his name: one was Jiè Qiūhéng,
one was Cháng Fēnglín,
and one was Má Xīchí.
They drank freely and were very merry,
unaware that the day had grown late.
Jiè said:
"We have not yet performed the rites of a host,
yet we have presumptuously enjoyed your lavish feast;
this is not proper.
My humble cottage is not far;
you may stay the night."
Cháng and Má also rose,
took him by the sleeve and called for a servant,
and they all went together.
Arriving at the northern mountain of the county,
they suddenly saw a courtyard,
with a clear stream winding around the gate.
Once inside,
the house was clean and tidy.
They called a boy to light the lamps,
and also ordered arrangements made for the attendants.
Má said:
"In the past, we met friends through literary gatherings.
Now the examination date is near;
we should not waste this fine night.
Let us draft four essay topics and draw lots,
each taking one,
and drink only after the essays are finished."
Everyone agreed.
They prepared the topics,
wrote them down and placed them on the table;
whoever picked one would compose at the desk.
Before the second watch had ended,
all had finished their drafts,
and they passed them around for perusal.
The scholar read the three compositions
and was deeply impressed,
so he hastily copied them and kept them in his robe.
The host brought out fine wine,
urging them to drink from large cups,
until they became quite intoxicated without realizing it.
The host then led the guests to another courtyard to sleep.
The guest was drunk,
and had no time to remove his shoes;
he lay down fully clothed.
When he awoke,
the red sun was already high,
and looking around, there was no courtyard or house;
he and his servant were lying in a mountain valley.
He was greatly alarmed.
Seeing a cave nearby,
with water trickling out,
he was astonished and bewildered.
Feeling inside his robe,
he found the three compositions still there.
He inquired of the local people,
and only then learned it was
"Sānxiān Dòng" (Three Immortals Cave),
which contained three creatures: a crab, a snake,
and a toad,
all very numinous,
often coming out to roam,
and people frequently saw them.
The scholar entered the examination hall,
and the three topics were exactly the compositions of the immortals;
thus he was selected as a provincial graduate.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Two runners from Lìchéng County,
having been sent by the county magistrate Hán Chéngxuān on business
to another prefecture,
were returning at the end of the year.
On the road, they met two men
whose attire also resembled that of government runners;
they walked together and chatted.
The two men claimed to be prefectural runners.
The county runners said:
"Among the yamen runners of Jǐchéng,
we know eight or nine out of ten;
but you two gentlemen are completely unfamiliar."
The two men said:
"To tell the truth: we are ghost runners of the City God.
We are now on our way to deliver an official document to Dōngyuè."
The runners asked:
"What is the document about?"
They replied:
"It concerns the great calamity of Jǐ'nán,
reporting
the number of people to be killed."
Startled, they asked the number.
They said:
"We don't know exactly either,
but roughly close to a million."
The runners asked the time,
and they answered
"Zhēngshuò" (the first day of the lunar new year).
The two runners looked at each other in alarm,
calculating that their arrival at the prefecture would coincide precisely with New Year's Eve,
and they feared being caught in the disaster;
but delaying would likely incur reprimand.
The ghosts said:
"The crime of missing a deadline is minor;
getting caught in a calamity is a major disaster.
You should avoid it elsewhere,
and for now, do not return."
The runners followed their advice.
Not long after,
northern troops arrived in great force,
massacred Jǐ'nán,
and carried away a million corpses.
The two men, having fled and hidden, escaped harm.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
A resident of Gāoyuàn named Wáng Shí
was carrying salt to Bóxīng.
At night he was captured by two men.
Thinking they were patrolmen of the salt merchants,
he abandoned the salt and tried to flee,
but his feet were too sore to move quickly,
so he was bound.
He pleaded with them.
The two men said:
"We are not from the salt shops;
we are ghostly runners."
Wáng Shí was terrified
and begged to be allowed to go home once
to bid farewell to his wife and children.
They refused,
saying:
"This trip does not mean you will die immediately;
it's only temporary servitude."
Wáng Shí asked:
"What kind of work?"
They said:
"A new King of Hell has taken office in the underworld.
Seeing that the Nàihé River is silted up
and the pits and latrines of the eighteen hells are all full,
he has ordered three types of people to be seized for dredging the river: petty thieves, illegal coiners, and illegal salt dealers.
Another group is made to clean the latrines: the musicians' households."
Wáng Shí followed them
into a city walled enclosure,
arriving at an official office.
He saw the King of Hell seated above
and was just then checking the register of names.
A ghost reported:
"We have seized an illegal salt dealer, Wáng Shí, and brought him here."
The King of Hell looked at him
and angrily said:
"Those who deal in illegal salt
deprive the state of its tax revenue above
and harm the people's livelihood below.
But those whom the violent officials and treacherous merchants of this world label as illegal salt dealers
are all good people of the world.
Poor men who scrape together a tiny bit of capital
to seek a meager profit
—how can they be called illegal?"
He punished the two ghosts by ordering them to buy four pecks of salt
and, together with what Wáng Shí had been carrying,
deliver it to his home.
He kept Wáng Shí,
gave him a spiked mace,
and ordered him to follow the ghosts to supervise the river work.
The ghosts led Wáng Shí away
to the edge of the Nàihé River.
He saw the laborers in the river,
a continuous stream like ants.
Looking again, the river water was turbid and red,
stinking unbearably.
Those dredging the river were all naked, holding baskets and shovels,
submerging and emerging in it.
Rotten bones and decaying corpses
filled baskets that they carried out on their backs;
in the deeper parts, they submerged headfirst to search.
Those who were lazy were struck on the back or thighs with the spiked mace.
A fellow supervisor gave him a fragrant cotton ball as big as a large bean
and told him to hold it in his mouth
before approaching the bank.
He saw a salt merchant from Gāoyuàn
also among them.
Wáng Shí singled him out for harsh treatment: when he entered the river, he whipped his back;
when he came ashore, he struck his thighs.
The merchant was terrified
and often submerged his whole body in the water;
only then would Wáng Shí stop.
After three days and nights,
half the river laborers had died,
and the river work was also completed.
The two ghosts from before still escorted him home,
and he suddenly awoke.
Earlier,
when Wáng Shí had not returned from carrying salt,
at daybreak,
his wife opened the door
and found two sacks of salt placed in the courtyard,
but Wáng Shí had not come back for a long time.
She sent people to search everywhere for him,
and found him dead on the road.
They carried him back,
and he still had a faint breath,
but they did not understand the reason.
When he woke up,
he told the story.
The salt merchant had also died the previous day
and only now revived.
Where the spiked mace had struck him,
all became huge ulcers,
his whole body festered and rotted,
stinking so that no one could go near.
Wáng Shí deliberately went to see him.
Seeing Wáng Shí,
he still shrank his head under the quilt,
as if he were at the Nàihé River.
After a year,
he finally recovered,
and never engaged in trade again.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Regarding the matter of salt,
what the imperial court calls illegal
is that which does not follow the public law;
what officials and merchants call illegal
is that which does not follow their private interests.
Recently, under new regulations in Qí and Lǔ,
local merchants set up shops everywhere,
each limited to a territory.
Not only may the people of this district
not go to that district;
even the people of this shop
may not go to that shop.
Yet the shops secretly set bait to lure people from other districts;
when selling to other districts,
they lower the price;
but when selling to locals,
they double the price to raise it.
Moreover, they set up patrols on the roads
so that people within the territory
cannot escape their inflated prices.
If anyone within the territory pretends to be from another district to buy,
the law shows no mercy.
Thus, each luring the other,
the foolish people who cross shops or pretend to be from elsewhere increase daily.
Once caught by patrols,
they first maim their legs with knives and clubs,
then send them to the officials;
the officials then shackle them,
and this is called 'illegal salt.'
Alas!
How unjust!
Evading tens of thousands in tax is not illegal,
but carrying a peck or two of salt is called illegal;
selling from this territory to another is not illegal,
but buying from this territory within this territory is called illegal.
How unjust!
In the legal code, the 'salt laws'
are the strictest,
yet they specifically exempt poor and struggling soldiers and civilians
who carry salt on their backs to trade for food
from being prohibited.
Now, everything is not prohibited,
yet they specifically kill these poor and struggling soldiers and civilians!
Moreover, these poor and struggling soldiers and civilians,
with wives and children crying from hunger,
above obey the law and do not steal,
below know shame and do not prostitute themselves;
out of desperation,
they scrape together ten mothers to seek one child.
If a district were entirely composed of such people,
then 'leaving doors unbolted at night'
would be possible.
Are they not the good people of the world?
Those shop merchants
should not only be made to dredge the Nàihé River;
they should straightaway be made to clean the latrines of hell!
Yet officials, during the spring and autumn festivals,
accept their momentary bribes,
and thus use the law to help them kill our good people.
If so, then for the poor people's sake,
it would be better to become robbers or illegal coiners.
Robbers plunder people in broad daylight,
yet officials act deaf;
coiners' furnace fires blaze to the sky,
yet officials act blind;
even if they dredge the river in the afterlife,
at least they would not, like the petty carriers, gain little
yet immediately suffer official punishment.
Alas!
Above, there are no compassionate and benevolent officials,
and they heed the laws of treacherous merchants,
changing daily, growing more deceitful daily.
How can it be that the stubborn people do not increase daily,
and the good people do not die out daily!"
The merchants in the shops of each town,
following the old custom, would take a certain amount of salt money
and present it annually to the county magistrate,
which was called
"salt allowance."
Moreover, on festive occasions,
they would bring generous gifts.
When the merchants had business to discuss with the officials,
the officials would treat them with courtesy,
inviting them to sit and speak,
and sometimes even serving tea.
However, when salt peddlers were brought in,
they were severely punished without delay.
When Magistrate Zhāng Shínián governed Zībó,
the shop merchants came to see him,
following the old protocol,
they only bowed without kneeling.
The magistrate angrily said:
"The former magistrate accepted your bribes,
so he had no choice but to treat you with great respect.
I buy salt to eat myself—
what kind of merchants are you,
daring to defy etiquette in the public hall!"
He rolled up his sleeves, ready to have them beaten.
The merchants kowtowed and apologized,
and only then were they released.
Later, two peddlers were caught in the shops,
one of them escaped,
and the other was captured and brought to the magistrate.
The magistrate asked:
"There were two peddlers,
where is the other one?"
The peddler said:
"He escaped."
The magistrate said:
"Are your legs too weak to run?"
He replied:
"I can run."
The magistrate said:
"Since you were caught,
you must not be able to run.
If you really can,
get up and try running—
let's see if you can."
The man ran a few steps and wanted to stop.
The magistrate said:
"Don't stop running!"
The man ran swiftly,
and actually ran out of the magistrate's office and away.
Those who saw it all laughed.
Magistrate Zhāng's acts of caring for the people were many,
and this was one of his lighthearted moments,
which the townspeople still delighted in recounting.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Xī Chéngliè
was a scholar from Chéngdū.
He had one wife and one concubine.
The concubine, surnamed Hé,
was given the childhood name Zhāoróng.
His wife died early,
and he remarried a woman named Shēn,
who was jealous by nature,
mistreated Hé,
and even extended her abuse to Xī;
she nagged all day long,
making life unbearable.
Xī grew angry
and ran away.
After he left,
Hé gave birth to a son named Dànán.
Xī did not return after leaving,
and Shēn excluded Hé from sharing meals,
rationing out grain to her by the day.
As Dànán gradually grew up,
expenses became insufficient,
so Hé spun and wove to supplement their food.
Dànán saw the children in the school reciting texts,
and he also wanted to study.
His mother thought he was too young,
but she sent him to study anyway.
Dànán was intelligent,
and he learned twice as much as the other children.
The teacher found him remarkable
and was willing to teach him without charging tuition.
Hé then had him study under the teacher,
giving a modest payment.
After two or three years,
he had mastered all the classics.
One day, upon returning home,
he said to his mother:
"Five or six children in the school
all ask their fathers for money to buy cakes—
why am I the only one without a father?"
His mother said:
"Wait until you grow up,
and I will tell you."
Dànán said:
"I'm only seven or eight years old now—
when will I grow up?"
His mother said:
"On your way to school,
you pass by the Guāndì Temple.
You should bow there,
and it will bless you to grow quickly."
Dànán believed her,
and every time he passed by, he would go in and bow.
His mother found out and
asked him:
"What did you pray for?"
He smiled and said:
"I just prayed that next year I would be sixteen or seventeen years old."
His mother laughed.
However, Dànán's learning and physical growth progressed rapidly: by the age of ten,
he already looked like a thirteen- or fourteen-year-old;
and the essays he wrote were well-structured.
One day,
he said to his mother:
"You said when I grew strong and tall,
you would tell me where my father is—
now it's time."
His mother said:
"Not yet,
not yet."
Another year or so passed,
and he had clearly become an adult.
He pressed her more frequently,
and finally his mother recounted everything in detail.
Dànán was overwhelmed with grief
and wanted to go search for his father.
His mother said:
"You're still too young,
and we don't even know if your father is alive or dead—
how can you go searching so hastily?"
Dànán left without a word,
and by noon he had not returned.
His mother went to the school to ask the teacher,
who said he had not returned since breakfast.
His mother was greatly alarmed,
spent money to hire help,
and searched everywhere,
but there was no trace of him.
The eldest son left home,
following the road as he hurried along,
bewildered and not knowing where to go.
By chance, he met a man who was heading to Kuízhōu,
who said his surname was Qián.
The eldest son begged for food and followed him.
Qián grew impatient with his slow pace,
so he hired a mount for him,
exhausting all their travel funds.
Upon reaching Kuízhōu,
as they ate together,
Qián secretly poisoned the food,
and the eldest son fell unconscious without noticing.
Qián carried him to a large temple,
claiming he was his own son,
who had fallen ill and left him without resources,
and sold him to the monks.
The monks, seeing his handsome and distinguished appearance,
vied to purchase him.
Qián took the money and left.
The monks gave him a drink,
and he gradually awoke.
The abbot learned of this and came to see him,
marveling at his appearance.
After questioning him closely,
he finally learned the whole story.
Feeling great sympathy for him,
he gave him funds and sent him on his way.
There was a scholar named Jiǎng from Lúzhōu,
who was returning home after failing the imperial examination.
Along the way, he heard the story,
admired the eldest son’s filial piety,
and took him along as a companion.
Upon reaching Lúzhōu,
the eldest son stayed at Jiǎng’s home.
After more than a month,
he inquired everywhere.
Someone mentioned that a merchant from Mǐn had the surname Shuài,
so he bid farewell to Jiǎng,
intending to go to Mǐn.
Jiǎng gave him clothes and shoes,
and the villagers all contributed funds to assist him.
On the road, he met two cloth merchants,
who were heading to Fúqīng,
and they invited him to travel together.
After several days of travel,
the merchants caught sight of the money in his bag,
led him to a deserted place,
bound his hands and feet,
took his belongings, and fled.
By chance, an old man named Chén from Yǒngfú passed by the area,
freed him from his bonds,
and took him back to his home.
Old Man Chén was wealthy,
and merchants from all directions
often passed through his doors.
The old man instructed merchants from the north and south to help inquire about news of Xī.
He kept the eldest son to study alongside his own children.
The eldest son thus settled in Old Man Chén’s household,
and no longer wandered.
However, the farther he was from home,
the more cut off he became from news.
Hé Zhāoróng lived alone for three or four years.
Shēn reduced their shared expenses
and pressured her to remarry.
Hé’s resolve did not waver.
Shēn forcibly sold her to a merchant from Chóngqìng,
who seized and took her away.
That night,
she cut herself with a knife.
The merchant did not dare press her.
He waited for her wound to heal,
then resold her to a merchant from Yántíng.
Upon reaching Yántíng,
she stabbed herself in the chest,
piercing through to her internal organs.
The merchant was greatly frightened.
He applied medicine,
and the wound healed.
She begged to become a nun.
The merchant said:
"I have a business partner
who lacks the means for intimate relations.
He has long wanted someone to manage sewing and mending.
This is no different from being a nun,
and it could also slightly repay my investment."
Hé agreed.
The merchant sent her by carriage.
Entering the gate,
the master hurried out—
it was Xī!
It turned out Xī had abandoned scholarly pursuits for trade.
The merchant, knowing he had no wife,
had given her to him.
They met with grief and shock,
each recounting their hardships,
and only then learned their son had gone to search for his father and not returned.
Xī then asked various traveling merchants
to inquire about Dà'nán.
Thus, Zhāoróng became his wife instead of a concubine.
However, having endured such suffering,
she was ill and in pain,
unable to manage chores,
so she urged Xī to take a concubine.
Mindful of past troubles,
he would not heed her request.
Hé said:
"If I were one to contend for the marital bed,
in these years I could have borne children for another man.
Would I still be with you today?
Moreover, the wrongs done to me
are a hidden pain in my heart.
How could I inflict them upon another?"
Xī then asked his business partners
to buy a concubine over thirty.
After more than half a year,
a partner indeed bought a concubine and returned.
Entering the door,
it was his wife, Shēn.
All were astonished.
Previously,
Shēn had lived alone for over a year.
Her brother Bāo urged her to remarry.
Shēn agreed,
but the family fields and property were blocked by her nephews,
preventing their sale.
Selling what she had,
she accumulated several hundred taels,
took them to her brother's home.
A merchant from Bǎoníng,
hearing she had a wealthy dowry,
offered Bāo much money,
and tricked her into marriage.
But the merchant was old and impotent.
Shēn resented her brother,
unsettled in the household,
hanging herself and throwing herself into a well,
unable to bear the disturbance.
The merchant grew angry,
seized her assets,
and planned to sell her as a concubine.
Those who heard all disparaged her age.
The merchant was going to Kuí,
so he took her along.
Meeting Xī at the same market,
it suited his purpose perfectly,
so he sold her and left.
Seeing Xī,
Shēn, ashamed and fearful, could not utter a word.
Xī asked fellow merchants,
learning the general situation.
He then said:
"Had you met a robust man,
then in Bǎoníng
there would be no chance of meeting again.
This is fate.
But today I buy a concubine,
not take a wife.
You must first pay respects to Zhāoróng,
and observe the rites between principal wife and concubine."
Shēn felt ashamed.
Xī said:
"In the past, you were the principal wife—
how was that!"
Hé tried to dissuade him.
Xī would not listen,
taking a stick to threaten her.
Shēn had no choice
but to bow to her.
Yet she remained unwilling to serve,
working only in a separate room.
Hé treated her with utmost tolerance,
unable to bear supervising her diligence or laziness.
Whenever Xī conversed or feasted with Zhāoróng,
he would have Shēn serve at their side;
Hé tried to replace her with a maid,
but he would not allow it.
It happened that Lord Chén Sìzōng was magistrate of Yántíng.
Xī had a minor dispute with a villager,
who accused Xī of forcing his wife to become a concubine.
The lord did not accept the case,
scolding and driving him out.
Xī was pleased,
and just as he and Hé were secretly praising the lord's virtue,
the first watch had ended,
when a servant called and knocked at the gate,
entering to report:
"The county magistrate is here."
Xī was terrified,
hurriedly searching for clothes and shoes,
but the lord had already reached the bedroom door;
even more terrified,
he did not know what to do.
Hé, examining him,
hurried out and said,
"This is my son!"
Then she wept.
The lord knelt on the ground, weeping sorrowfully.
It turned out Dà'nán had taken the surname Chén
and was now an official.
Earlier,
when the lord arrived from the capital,
he took a detour past his old home,
learning both mothers had remarried,
and was overcome with grief.
The clan, knowing Dà'nán had become esteemed,
returned his fields and house.
The lord left servants to make repairs,
hoping his father would return.
Later, appointed to Yántíng,
he wanted to abandon his post to search for his father.
Old Chén bitterly urged him to stop.
There happened to be a diviner,
so he had a reading done.
The diviner said:
"The small occupies the great,
the younger becomes the elder;
seeking the male, you find the female,
seeking one, you gain two:
It is auspicious for office."
The lord then took up his post.
Unable to be with his parents,
he abstained from meat and wine while in office.
That day,
receiving the villager's accusation
and seeing Xī's name,
he was suspicious,
secretly sending an old servant to investigate carefully—
indeed, it was his father.
He went out in plain clothes at night.
Seeing his mother,
he believed even more in the diviner's skill.
Before leaving,
he urged them not to spread word,
taking out two hundred taels to have his father prepare to return home.
When his father reached home,
the house was newly renovated,
with many servants and horses kept,
truly a great household.
Shēn, seeing Dà'nán's high status,
became even more restrained.
Her brother Bāo, resentful,
brought a lawsuit,
arguing for his sister's status as principal wife.
The official investigated and learned the truth,
angrily saying:
"Greedy for money, you urged her to remarry.
She has already had two husbands.
What face has she to contend for her former status as principal wife!"
He heavily caned Bāo.
From then on, their positions were firmly settled.
Shēn treated Hé as an elder sister,
and Hé also treated her as one.
Clothing, food, and drink
were never selfishly kept.
Shēn initially feared revenge,
but now felt even more ashamed and remorseful.
Xī also forgot past wrongs,
having everyone inside and outside address her as "Grand Dame,"
though she received no official title.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"The ways in which the world's creatures are confounded
are truly inconceivable;
how ingenious is the Creator!
That Mr. Xī could not establish himself between his wife and concubine
marks him as nothing but a mediocre, commonplace man.
Had it not been for a filial son and a virtuous mother,
how could there have been such a miraculous union,
allowing him to sit back and enjoy wealth and honor for the rest of his life!"
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
In the autumn of the Jǐsì year,
a great ship drifted to Lǐngnán from foreign seas.
On board were eleven men,
clad in bird feathers,
their patterns dazzlingly brilliant.
They said of themselves,
"We are men of the Lǚsòng country.
We encountered a storm and our boat capsized;
several tens of people all died.
Only we eleven clung to a great log,
drifting to a large island where we escaped death.
For nearly five years,
by day we seized birds and insects to eat;
by night we hid in stone caves,
weaving feathers into sails.
Suddenly another boat drifted to the island,
with neither oars nor sails—
it too had evidently been shattered by the wind at sea.
So we boarded it, intending to return.
But again a great wind blew us to Àomén."
The Provincial Governor submitted a memorial,
and sent them back to their country.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Young Master Wéi
was from an old, established family in Xiányáng.
Unrestrained and fond of debauchery,
if any maidservant or woman in his household was attractive,
he had illicit relations with them without exception.
Once, carrying several thousand in gold,
he wished to see all the famous courtesans under heaven.
In every bustling, splendid region,
there was nowhere he did not go.
Those who were not particularly pleasing
he would leave after a couple of nights;
those to his liking,
he would stay with for a hundred days.
His paternal uncle was also a renowned official,
who had retired and returned home.
Angered by his nephew's conduct,
he engaged a brilliant tutor,
set up a separate estate,
and made him study behind locked doors with several other young gentlemen.
At night, the young master would wait for the tutor to sleep,
then climb over the wall to go home,
returning just before dawn.
One night,
he lost his footing and broke his shin,
and only then did the tutor find out.
He informed the uncle,
who further applied the birch rod,
making him unable to rise before beginning to treat him with medicine.
When he recovered,
his uncle made an agreement with him: if he could read twice as much as his younger cousins,
and his compositions were excellent,
he would not be forbidden from going out;
but if he slipped away privately,
he would be beaten as before.
However, the young master was extremely clever,
and his reading often exceeded the set course.
After several years,
he passed the provincial examination.
He wished to break the agreement himself,
but his uncle kept him in check.
When he went to the capital,
he was accompanied by an old servant,
to whom a daily journal was entrusted,
to record his words and actions,
so for several years he committed no transgressions.
Later, he became a Presented Scholar,
and only then did his uncle slightly relax the restrictions.
Whenever the young master was about to do something,
fearing his uncle might hear of it,
upon entering the brothel quarters,
he would falsely give his surname as Wèi.
One day,
passing through Xī'ān,
he saw a young actor named Luó Huìqīng,
sixteen or seventeen years old,
as beautiful as a lovely girl,
and took a fancy to him.
At night he stayed, being intimate with him,
and gave him lavish gifts.
Hearing that Huìqīng's newly wedded wife was especially charming and exquisite,
he privately hinted his desire to Huìqīng.
Huìqīng showed no difficulty,
and that night indeed brought his wife,
and the three shared one bed.
After staying several days,
his affection reached its peak.
He plotted to take them both back with him.
Asking about his family,
Huìqīng replied:
"My mother died early;
my father is alive.
I originally did not bear the surname Luó.
In her youth, my mother served in the household of the Wéi family in Xiányáng.
She was later sold to the Luó family,
and four months later gave birth to me.
If I could follow you, young master,
I might also inquire into news of them."
Startled, the young master asked his mother's surname.
He said:
"Surname Lǚ."
The young master was utterly horrified,
sweat drenching his body,
for that mother was a maidservant from his own household.
The young master said nothing.
By then, dawn had broken.
He gave Huìqīng generous gifts,
and urged him to change his profession.
Pretending he had to go elsewhere,
he arranged to summon him when he returned,
and so they parted.
Later, while serving as magistrate in Sūzhōu,
there was a singing girl named Shěn Wéiniáng,
elegant, beautiful, and peerless.
He grew fond of her and stayed to be intimate.
Teasing, he said:
"Was your childhood name taken from the line 'A spring breeze melody, Dù Wéiniáng'?
She replied:
"No.
My mother was a famous courtesan at seventeen.
A young gentleman from Xiányáng, sharing your surname,
stayed with her for three months,
and pledged to marry her.
After the young gentleman left,
eight months later she gave birth to me,
hence she named me Wéi—
it is, in fact, my surname.
When the young gentleman was parting,
he gave a pair of golden mandarin ducks as a gift,
which I still have.
Once gone, there was finally no news,
and my mother, because of this, died of resentment and sorrow.
When I was three,
I was raised by an old woman named Shěn,
hence I took her surname."
Hearing this, the young master
felt such shame and regret he wished he could disappear.
After a silent while,
a scheme suddenly occurred to him.
He abruptly rose to trim the lamp,
called Wéiniáng to drink,
and secretly placed poison in her cup.
As soon as Wéiniáng swallowed it,
she became agitated, confused, moaning and hissing.
When everyone gathered to look,
she was already dead.
He summoned the actors' troupe manager,
handed over the corpse to him,
and heavily bribed him.
But Wéiniáng's patrons were all influential families;
hearing of it, they were all indignant,
bribed and incited the troupe manager,
and brought a lawsuit to the higher authorities.
The young master, afraid,
exhausted his coffers to patch things up,
but in the end was dismissed from office for being frivolous and impetuous.
Returning home,
he was only thirty-eight,
and rather regretted his past actions.
But his five or six wives and concubines
had all borne him no sons.
He wished to adopt a grandson from his uncle's line;
but his uncle, considering his conduct within the family disgraceful,
feared the child would become contaminated,
and although he consented to the adoption,
insisted on waiting until the young master was old before sending the child over.
In anger, the young master thought of summoning Huìqīng,
but all his family considered it improper,
so he desisted.
After several more years,
he suddenly fell ill,
and would beat his chest, saying:
"He who debauches maidservants and frequents prostitutes
is not human!"
His uncle heard and sighed:
"This surely means he is about to die!"
So he sent the son of his second son
to his household,
to attend to him morning and evening.
After a little over a month, he indeed died.
The Chronicler of the Tales remarks:
"The abduction of maidservants and secret liaisons with prostitutes
lead to consequences so dire they are almost beyond discussion.
Yet, to have one's own flesh and blood
call another man father
is already a profound shame.
Then, to have ghosts and spirits further mock and toy with him,
luring him to consume his own filth—
if he still does not tear open his own heart
or sever his own head,
but merely sweats and seeks poison,
is he not a beast bellowing from a human head?
Even so,
the children born to such libertine young masters,
even if they end up in the world of pleasure,
often excel and stand out."
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Xíng Yúnfēi
was a man from Shùntiān.
He loved stones,
and whenever he saw a fine specimen,
he would spare no expense to acquire it.
Once, while fishing in a river,
something caught in his net.
He dove down to retrieve it
and found a stone about a foot in diameter,
exquisitely perforated on all sides,
with peaks and ridges layered in beauty.
Overjoyed,
he felt as if he had obtained a rare treasure.
Upon returning home,
he carved a sandalwood stand for it
and placed it on his desk for display.
Whenever rain was imminent,
clouds would form in each of its holes,
and from a distance, it looked as if stuffed with fresh cotton.
A certain powerful local magnate
came to his door asking to see it.
Once he laid eyes on it,
he handed it to a sturdy servant,
mounted his horse, and rode straight off.
Xíng could do nothing but
stamp his feet in grief and indignation.
The servant, carrying the stone, reached the riverbank
and rested his burden on a bridge.
Suddenly, his hand slipped, and the stone fell into the river.
Enraged,
the magnate whipped the servant.
He then paid money to hire expert divers,
who searched every possible way in the murky depths,
but the stone was nowhere to be found.
Finally, he posted a reward and set terms before leaving.
From then on, stone-seekers crowded the river daily,
but none succeeded in finding it.
Later, Xíng went to the spot where the stone had fallen.
Gazing sorrowfully at the flowing water,
he saw the river was clear and pure,
and the stone was indeed lying at the bottom.
Delighted,
Xíng stripped off his clothes, entered the water,
and brought it out in his arms.
He took it home
but dared not display it in the main hall,
instead cleaning an inner room to enshrine it there.
One day,
an old man knocked at the gate and requested to see it.
Xíng claimed the stone had been lost long ago.
The old man laughed and said:
"Isn't that it in your guest room?"
Xíng invited him inside,
intending to prove its absence.
But upon entering,
the stone was indeed sitting on the table.
Xíng was struck speechless.
The old man stroked the stone and said:
"This is an old possession of my family,
lost for a long time.
So it is here now.
Since I have found it,
I beg you to return it."
Xíng, greatly embarrassed,
argued with him over ownership.
The old man laughed:
"If it is your family's property,
what proof do you have?"
Xíng could not answer.
The old man said:
"I, however, recognize it of old.
It has ninety-two holes in total, front and back.
Inside one hole are five characters that read:
'Stone for Offering in the Palace of Clarity and Emptiness.'"
Xíng examined it closely.
Sure enough, there were tiny characters inside a hole,
as fine as millet grains,
barely discernible even with strained eyesight.
He also counted the holes,
and the number matched exactly.
Having no rebuttal,
Xíng simply refused to hand it over.
The old man laughed:
"Whose property is it,
that it should be at your sole discretion!"
With that, he clasped his hands and left.
Xíng saw him out the gate;
upon returning,
the stone had already vanished.
Xíng hurried after the old man,
who was walking slowly not far away.
Xíng ran up, grabbed his sleeve, and pleaded pitifully.
The old man said:
"How strange!
A stone a foot in diameter—
could it possibly be held in the hand or hidden in a sleeve?"
Realizing the old man was supernatural,
Xíng forcibly dragged him back home
and knelt long before him, begging.
The old man then asked:
"Does the stone truly belong to your family or to mine?"
Xíng replied:
"It truly belongs to you, sir,
but I beg you to part with it in love."
The old man said:
"If that is so,
the stone is indeed here."
They entered the inner room,
and the stone was already back in its original place.
The old man said:
"Treasures of the world
should belong to those who cherish them.
This stone
can choose its own master.
I am also pleased for it,
but it was too eager to reveal itself.
Its emergence was premature,
so its demonic tribulations are not yet dispelled.
I had intended to take it away
and wait three years
before presenting it to you as a gift.
Since you wish to keep it now,
you must reduce your lifespan by three years
for it to stay with you till the end.
Are you willing?"
Xíng said:
"I am willing."
The old man then pinched one hole with two fingers.
The hole became soft as clay
and closed at his touch.
After closing three holes,
he finished
and said:
"The number of holes on the stone
now equals your remaining years of life."
He bid farewell and prepared to leave.
Xíng苦苦恳留他,
but he refused firmly.
Asked his name,
he would not say,
and so departed.
More than a year later,
Xíng happened to be away on business.
At night, a thief broke into his house.
Nothing else was missing,
but the stone was stolen.
When Xíng returned,
he grieved as if he had died.
He made inquiries and offered rewards,
but there was no trace at all.
Several years passed.
Once, by chance, he entered Bàoguó Temple,
and saw a man selling stones.
There was his old possession!
He was about to claim it immediately.
The seller refused to yield,
so they carried the stone to the authorities.
The official asked:
"What evidence can you provide?"
The seller could state the number of holes.
Xíng asked about other details,
but the man was clueless.
Xíng then mentioned the five characters inside a hole and the three finger-pinched marks,
and thus justice was served.
The official was about to have the seller flogged,
but the man said he had bought it in the market for twenty taels of silver,
so he was released.
Xíng retrieved the stone and took it home.
He wrapped it in brocade
and stored it in a box,
only taking it out occasionally to admire,
first burning rare incense before unveiling it.
There was a certain Minister of the Board of Revenue
who offered a hundred taels of silver for it.
Xíng said:
"Not even ten thousand taels would make me part with it."
The minister was angered
and secretly used other matters to frame him.
Xíng was arrested
and had to pawn his fields and property.
The minister had someone else hint to Xíng's son.
The son told Xíng,
who declared he would rather die than give up the stone.
His wife secretly plotted with their son
and presented the stone to the minister's household.
Only after Xíng was released from prison did he learn of this.
He cursed his wife and beat his son,
repeatedly attempting to hang himself.
His family members noticed and saved him,
so he did not die.
That night he dreamed of a man who came to him,
saying of himself:
"Shí Qīngxū."
He warned Xíng not to grieve:
"It is only a temporary separation from you.
On the twentieth day of the eighth month next year,
at dawn,
you may go to Hǎidài Gate
and redeem me with two strings of cash."
Xíng, having had this dream,
was overjoyed
and carefully noted the date.
The stone was in the minister's house,
but it no longer displayed the wondrous phenomenon of emitting clouds;
after a long time, it was not highly valued either.
The following year,
the minister was stripped of his post due to a crime
and soon died.
Xíng went to Hǎidài Gate on the appointed day,
where the minister's family members were secretly selling the stone.
Thus he bought it back for two strings of cash.
Later, when Xíng reached eighty-nine years of age,
he prepared his own burial items;
he also instructed his son
that the stone must be buried with him.
After his death,
his son followed his last wishes
and interred the stone in the tomb.
About half a year later,
thieves dug up the tomb
and stole the stone away.
His son learned of this
but had no way to pursue them.
Two or three days later,
while traveling on the road with a servant,
he suddenly saw two men running, stumbling, and sweating profusely.
They looked toward the house, knelt, and bowed,
saying:
"Mr. Xíng,
do not press us!
We two took the stone away
only to sell it for four taels of silver."
They then bound themselves and were delivered to the authorities,
where they confessed immediately upon interrogation.
When asked about the stone,
they said they had sold it to the Gōng family.
The stone was fetched and brought forward.
The official, admiring and fondling it,
wanted to possess it
and ordered it stored in the treasury.
The clerk lifted the stone,
but it suddenly fell to the ground,
shattering into several dozen pieces.
Everyone turned pale.
The official then heavily shackled the two thieves and sentenced them to death.
Xíng's son gathered the broken stone fragments
and again buried them in the tomb.
Based on the Zhuxuezhai manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Old Man Zēng
was from an old family in Kūnyáng.
When the old man first died and had not yet been encoffined,
tears like thick liquid flowed from both his eye sockets.
He had six sons,
but none understood why.
The second son, Tì,
styled Yǒuyú,
was a renowned scholar in the county.
He considered this an ill omen
and warned his brothers each to be vigilant,
lest they bring shame upon their late father;
yet about half of his brothers scoffed at him.
Previously,
the old man's principal wife had given birth to the eldest son, Chéng,
but when he was seven or eight years old,
he and his mother were captured by fierce bandits.
The old man took a second wife,
who bore three sons: named Xiào,
Zhōng,
and Xìn.
A concubine bore three sons: named Tì,
Rén,
and Yì.
Xiào, because Tì and the others were born of a concubine and thus of low status,
looked down on them and excluded them,
allying with Zhōng and Xìn to form a faction.
Even when drinking with guests,
if Tì and the others passed through the hall,
he would act arrogantly and not show them courtesy.
Rén and Yì were both indignant
and plotted with Yǒuyú
to take revenge.
Yǒuyú used a hundred words to soothe and persuade them,
and they did not follow through with their plan;
moreover, Rén and Yì were the youngest,
so upon their elder brother's words, they desisted.
Xiào had a daughter
who was married to a man named Zhōu in the county
and died of illness.
He tried to gather Tì and the others to go beat her mother-in-law,
but Tì refused.
Xiào was furious
and ordered Zhōng and Xìn to join with the local ruffians of their clan
to go seize Zhōu's wife.
They beat her countless times,
scattered the grain stores, and smashed the utensils,
leaving not a single pot or bowl intact.
Zhōu filed a complaint with the authorities.
The magistrate was angry,
arrested Xiào and the others, and imprisoned them,
intending to strip them of their status.
Yǒuyú was afraid
and went to see the magistrate to confess on their behalf.
Yǒuyú's conduct and character
had always been esteemed by the magistrate,
so the brothers were spared hardship.
Yǒuyú then went to Zhōu's place to apologize and offer a humble apology.
Zhōu also held Yǒuyú in high regard,
and the lawsuit was thus dropped.
Xiàoguī,
in the end, did not treat Yǒuyú as a brother.
Not long after,
Yǒuyú’s mother, Lady Zhāng, passed away.
Xiào and the others did not observe mourning for her,
continuing their feasting and drinking as before.
Rén and Yì grew increasingly resentful.
Yǒuyú said:
“This is their lack of propriety;
what harm does it do to me?”
When it came time for the burial,
they blocked the tomb entrance,
preventing the joint interment.
Yǒuyú then buried his mother in the passageway of the tomb.
Not long after,
Xiào’s wife died.
Yǒuyú invited Rén and Yì to go together to mourn.
The two said:
“‘First-year mourning’
is not even considered,
so what ‘nine-month mourning’
could there be!”
He urged them again,
but they scattered noisily and left.
Yǒuyú then went alone,
weeping sorrowfully at the funeral.
Through the wall, he heard Rén and Yì drumming and blowing instruments.
Xiào was furious
and gathered his younger brothers to go beat them.
Yǒuyú grabbed a staff and followed first.
Entering their house,
Rén sensed it and fled first.
Yì was just climbing over the wall
when Yǒuyú struck him from behind and knocked him down.
Xiào and the others rained down blows with fists and staffs,
beating him without stopping.
Yǒuyú threw himself across to block them.
Xiào was angry
and reproached Yǒuyú.
Yǒuyú said:
“To reprimand them
is because of their lack of propriety,
but their crime certainly does not warrant death.
I will not indulge my younger brothers’ wickedness,
nor will I assist my elder brother’s violence.
If your anger does not subside,
I will take their place.”
Xiào then turned the staff and struck Yǒuyú.
Zhōng and Xìn also joined in beating their elder brother.
The commotion shook the neighborhood;
a crowd gathered to mediate,
and they dispersed.
Yǒuyú immediately took his staff and went to his elder brother to ask for punishment.
Xiào drove him away,
not allowing him to stay in the mourning quarters.
And Yì’s injuries were severe;
he could no longer eat or drink.
Rén prepared a petition on his behalf and brought a lawsuit to the authorities,
accusing them of not observing mourning for their concubine mother.
The official issued a warrant to arrest Xiào, Zhōng, and Xìn,
and ordered Yǒuyú to submit a statement.
Yǒuyú, because his face was injured,
could not go to the yamen,
but wrote a petition to explain,
pleading for the matter to be dropped.
The magistrate then dismissed the case.
Yì also recovered soon after.
From then on, the enmity grew even deeper.
Rén and Yì were both young and weak,
and were often beaten and abused.
They complained to Yǒuyú:
“Everyone has brothers,
but we alone have none!”
Yǒuyú said:
“These two lines,
I should be the one saying them;
how can you two younger brothers say them!”
He then earnestly advised them,
but they ultimately would not listen.
Yǒuyú then locked his door,
took his wife and children, and moved to live elsewhere,
more than fifty lǐ from home,
hoping not to hear any news.
While Yǒuyú was at home, although he did not assist his younger brothers,
Xiào and the others still had some顾忌;
once he left,
whenever his elder brothers did anything inappropriate,
they would go to their door shouting insults,
even insulting their mother’s name.
Rén and Yì realized they could not resist,
so they only shut their doors, thinking of finding an opportunity to assassinate them,
carrying knives whenever they went out.
One day,
their eldest brother Chéng, who had been captured by bandits,
suddenly returned with his wife.
The brothers, because the family property had long been divided,
discussed for three days,
but could find no place to settle him.
Rén and Yì secretly rejoiced,
invited him to live with them and support him.
They went to inform Yǒuyú.
Yǒuyú was pleased,
returned home,
and together they provided fields and a house for Chéng to live in.
The elder brothers were angry that they were currying favor,
and went to their door to harass and insult them.
But Chéng, having long been among the bandits,
was accustomed to fierceness and force.
He grew furious and said:
“I returned,
and no one was willing to provide me with even a single room;
fortunately, my third younger brother remembered our brotherhood,
yet you blame and reprimand him.
Do you want to drive me away!”
He threw a stone at Xiào,
and Xiào fell.
Rén and Yì each came out with staffs,
seized Zhōng and Xìn,
and beat them countless times.
Chéng then brought a lawsuit to the magistrate,
and the magistrate again sent someone to ask Yǒuyú for advice.
Yǒuyú went to the magistrate,
bowed his head without speaking,
only shedding tears.
The magistrate asked him,
and he said:
“I only beg for your fair judgment.”
The magistrate then ruled that Xiào and the others each had to give up some land and property to Chéng,
making the seven shares roughly equal.
From then on, Rén and Yì loved and respected Chéng even more.
When they talked about their mother’s burial,
they wept together.
Chéng angrily said:
“To be so unkind,
they are truly beasts!”
He then wanted to open the tomb,
to rebury her properly.
Rén ran to tell Yǒuyú.
Yǒuyú hurried back to advise against it.
Chéng would not listen,
set a date to open the grave,
and held a fasting ceremony at the burial ground.
With a knife, he cut a tree and
said to his younger brothers:
“Whoever does not follow in mourning clothes,
will end up like this tree!”
Everyone assented,
and so the whole family came to weep at the funeral,
performing the burial rites with full propriety.
From then on, the brothers lived in peace.
But Chéng had a fierce and violent nature,
and often beat his younger brothers,
especially Xiào.
He only respected Yǒuyú.
Even in his fiercest anger,
when Yǒuyú arrived,
a single word would resolve it.
Whenever Xiào did something,
Chéng would always be displeased,
so Xiào went to Yǒuyú’s place every day,
secretly cursing and complaining to Yǒuyú.
Yǒuyú gently advised him,
but he ultimately would not listen.
Yǒuyú could not bear the disturbance,
so he moved again to Sānbó,
even farther from home,
and news and contact grew sparse.
Another two years passed,
and all the younger brothers feared Chéng,
but over time they grew accustomed.
Xiào was now forty-six years old,
and had five sons: the eldest, Jìyè,
the third, Jìdé,
born of his wife;
the second, Jìgōng,
the fourth, Jìjì,
born of a concubine;
and another, Jìzǔ, born of a maidservant.
They were all grown.
Following their father’s old ways,
they formed factions,
competing with each other daily,
and Xiào could not stop them.
Only Zǔ had no brothers,
and was the youngest,
so all his elder brothers could scold and abuse him.
His wife’s family lived near Sānbó,
and once when he went to visit his in-laws,
he took a detour to visit his uncle.
Entering the door,
he saw his uncle’s two elder brothers and one younger brother,
studying and reciting harmoniously,
and he was delighted.
He stayed a long time without mentioning returning.
His uncle urged him,
but he begged to be allowed to stay.
His uncle said:
“Your parents do not know,
and how could I begrudge you a bowl of rice or a ladle of water!”
So he returned.
Several months later,
the couple went to wish the mother-in-law a long life.
He told his father:
"I will not return from this journey."
His father questioned him,
and he revealed a hidden secret.
His father worried that there was a long-standing feud with his uncle,
and reckoned it would be difficult to stay long.
Zǔ said:
"Father worries too much.
Second Uncle
is a sage."
So they left,
taking his wife to Sānpō.
Yǒuyú prepared a house for them to live in,
arranging them according to age among the children,
and had him study under the eldest son, Jìshàn.
Zǔ was the most intelligent;
after residing in Sānpō for over a year,
he entered the county school in Yúnnán Prefecture.
He and Shàn studied behind closed doors,
and Zǔ recited the most diligently.
Yǒuyú loved him dearly.
Since Zǔ lived in Sānpō,
the brothers at home grew increasingly incompatible.
One day,
a slight quarrel arose,
and Yè insulted the concubine mother.
Gōng grew angry
and stabbed Yè to death.
The authorities arrested Gōng,
heavily shackled him,
and he died in prison a few days later.
Yè's wife, Madame Féng,
still daily replaced weeping with cursing.
Gōng's wife, Madame Liú, heard this
and angrily said:
"Your family's man is dead,
but whose family's man is alive!"
She took a knife and entered,
killed Féng,
and threw herself into a well to die.
Féng's father, Dàlì,
grieved over his daughter's tragic death,
led his sons and nephews,
hiding weapons under their clothes,
went to capture Xiào's concubine,
stripped and whipped her on the road to humiliate her.
Chéng angrily said:
"Our family has dead people like hemp,
how dare the Féngs act like this again!"
He roared and rushed out.
The various Zēngs followed him,
and the Féngs were all defeated.
Chéng first caught Dàlì,
and cut off both his ears.
His son came to protect and rescue him,
Jìxù struck horizontally with an iron staff,
breaking both his legs.
The various Féngs each suffered injuries,
and scattered in chaos.
Only Féng's son still lay by the roadside.
Chéng carried him under his arm,
placed him in the Féng village and returned.
Then he called Xù to go to the authorities and surrender.
The Féngs' accusation also arrived.
Thus the various Zēngs were arrested,
only Zhōng fled,
reaching Sānpō,
lingering outside the door.
