Just then Yǒuyú returned from the provincial examination with one son and one nephew,
saw Zhōng,
and exclaimed in surprise:
"Brother, why have you come?"
Before speaking, Zhōng shed tears,
and knelt long by the roadside.
Yǒuyú took his hand and pulled him inside,
questioned him to learn the details,
and was greatly shocked, saying:
"What can be done about this!
But with the whole family perverse and violent,
I long foresaw strange disasters;
otherwise,
why would I have fled here?
But I have been away from home for long,
and have no communication with the eldest now;
even if I crawl there now,
it would only bring humiliation.
If only the Féng father and son are seriously injured but not dead,
and if among us three there is one fortunate to pass the exam,
then this disaster might be slightly resolved."
So he kept him,
eating together by day,
sleeping together by night,
and Zhōng felt quite moved and ashamed.
After staying over ten days,
seeing his uncle and nephew like father and son,
and brothers like siblings from the same womb,
he shed sad tears and said:
"Only now do I realize I was not human before."
Yǒuyú was pleased by his repentance and awakening,
and they faced each other with sorrowful compassion.
Soon came news that Yǒuyú and his son passed the same examination,
and Zǔ also made the supplementary list.
They were overjoyed.
Not attending the celebratory banquet,
they first returned to pay respects at the ancestral tombs.
In the late Míng dynasty, examination degrees were most highly regarded,
and the various Féngs all restrained themselves.
Yǒuyú then asked relatives and friends to bribe them with money and grain,
funded their medical treatment,
and the lawsuit was settled.
The whole family wept, moved by Yǒuyú,
and begged him to return.
Yǒuyú then burned incense with his brothers to swear an oath,
making each cleanse their thoughts and renew themselves,
and then moved the family back.
Zǔ, following his uncle, was unwilling to return to the shared household.
Xiào then said to Yǒuyú:
"I lack virtue,
and should not have a son who glorifies the clan;
you, brother, are good at teaching,
so let him temporarily be your son.
When he makes some progress,
you may return him to me."
Yǒuyú agreed.
After another three years,
Zǔ indeed passed the provincial examination.
He was told to move his household,
but both husband and wife wept bitterly as they left.
Not many days later,
Zǔ had a son just three years old,
who ran away back to Yǒuyú's house,
hid in elder brother Jìshàn's room,
and refused to return;
when caught and taken away, he would escape again.
Xiào then had Zǔ live separately,
next to Yǒuyú.
Zǔ opened a door connecting to his uncle's house,
and attended to both households equally.
By then Chéng was gradually aging,
and family matters were all decided by Yǒuyú.
From then on, the household was harmonious and respectful,
praised for filial piety and brotherly love.
The Strange Historian says:
"In all the world, only beasts know their mother but not their father;
how is it that families of poetry and books
often follow this path!
The conduct within a household,
which gradually influences the descendants,
truly penetrates to the marrow.
The ancients said: if the father is a thief,
the son will surely rob;
such are the consequences of bad influence.
Though Xiào was unkind,
his retribution was also tragic;
yet he could eventually recognize his lack of virtue,
and entrust his son to his brother.
It is fitting that he had a son who worried and planned against troubles.
If we speak of karmic retribution,
it is still indirect."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
During the Jiāpíng era, there was a certain young gentleman
of graceful and handsome appearance.
At the age of seventeen or eighteen,
he went to the prefectural city to take the child scholar examination.
Once, passing by the door of a Madam Xǔ,
he saw inside a beautiful girl of about sixteen,
and thus fixed his gaze upon her.
The girl smiled slightly and nodded her head.
The young gentleman approached and spoke with her.
The girl asked:
"Where are you lodging?"
He told her in detail.
She asked:
"Is there anyone at your lodgings?"
He said:
"No."
The girl said:
"I shall pay you a visit this evening,
do not let anyone know."
The young gentleman returned,
and when dusk fell,
he dismissed his servant boys.
The girl indeed arrived,
introducing herself:
"My pet name is Wēn Jī."
And she said:
"I admire your romantic air, young master,
and so have come against the old madam's wishes.
My humble intention
is to devote myself to you for life."
The young gentleman was also pleased.
From then on, she would come once every two or three nights.
One evening,
she arrived in the rain,
entered the door, removed her wet clothes,
and hung them on the clothes rack;
she also took off the small boots on her feet,
asking the young gentleman to wipe off the mud for her.
Then she got into bed and covered herself with the quilt.
The young gentleman looked at her boots;
they were made of new brocade with a five-pattern design,
almost completely soaked through,
which he found a pity.
The girl said:
"I dare not trouble you with such a lowly item,
but wished to let you know how foolishly devoted I am in my affection."
Hearing the rain outside the window continuing without cease,
she then chanted:
"A mournful wind and cold rain fill the river city."
She asked the young gentleman to continue the verse.
The young gentleman declined, saying he did not understand.
The girl said:
"For a person such as yourself, young master,
how can you not know elegance and refinement!
You have utterly dampened my poetic mood!"
Thereupon she urged him to study and practice,
and the young gentleman agreed.
As their comings and goings became frequent,
the servants all became aware.
The young gentleman's brother-in-law, Sòng,
also a son of an established family,
hearing of this,
secretly requested the young gentleman to let him see Wēn Jī once.
The young gentleman spoke of it,
but the girl absolutely refused.
Sòng then hid himself in the servants' quarters,
waited for the girl to arrive,
crouched by the window to peek at her,
and was utterly captivated, nearly driven mad.
He hurriedly pushed open the door,
the girl rose,
vaulted over the wall, and left.
Sòng's longing was very intense,
so he prepared gifts and visited Madam Xǔ,
specifically requesting her by name.
The madam said:
"There indeed was a Wēn Jī,
but she has been dead for a long time."
Sòng retreated in astonishment,
informed the young gentleman,
and only then did the young gentleman realize she was a ghost.
That night,
he therefore used Sòng's words to break off with the girl.
The girl said:
"It is true.
However, you wished to obtain a beautiful woman,
and I wished to obtain a handsome husband.
Each achieving our desire is sufficient,
what does it matter whether one is human or ghost?"
The young gentleman thought this reasonable.
When the examination concluded and he returned home,
the girl followed him.
Others could not see her,
only the young gentleman could.
Upon arriving home,
he housed her in his study.
The young gentleman slept alone and did not return to his family quarters,
arousing his parents' suspicion.
When the girl went back for a visit,
he finally secretly told his mother,
who was greatly alarmed,
and warned the young gentleman to cut off relations with her.
The young gentleman could not bring himself to obey.
His parents were deeply worried,
but despite employing a hundred methods to drive her away, she would not leave.
One day,
the young gentleman had written a note instructing a servant,
placed on the desk,
which contained many errors:
"pepper"
was mistakenly written as
"silent",
"ginger"
was mistakenly written as
"river",
"detestable"
was mistakenly written as
"can be wanton".
The girl saw it,
and wrote on the back:
"What affair 'can be wanton'?
'Flower peppers grow in the river.'
To have a husband such as this,
it would be better to be a courtesan!"
Thereupon she told the young gentleman:
"I initially thought you, young master, were a cultured man from an established family,
and so braved shame to recommend myself.
I never imagined you were merely a handsome exterior with nothing within!
To judge people by their appearance—
wouldn't that make one a laughingstock for all under heaven!"
Having said this, she vanished.
Although the young gentleman felt ashamed and resentful,
he still did not understand what she had written,
and folded the note to show the servants.
Those who heard of it spread it as a laughing matter.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"Wēn Jī is quite a character!
An elegant young gentleman—
why must one be so demanding about what lies within him!
To thus reach the point of regretting that one is not a courtesan,
then wives and concubines should feel ashamed of their positions.
Yet though a hundred schemes were used to send her away she would not leave,
but upon seeing the note her resolve dissolved—
then 'flower peppers grow in the river'
is no different from Dù Fǔ's 'Zǐzhāng's skull'
indeed!"
The *Ear Records* states:
"Someone setting up a roadside stall offering broth
had a sign that read:
'Offering 'respect' to form karmic ties.'"
Mistaking "tea" for "respect",
this too can provoke a laugh.
There was a son of an old family,
who, having become poor,
posted a sign on his gate saying:
"Selling ancient lewd vessels."
Mistaking "jade" for "lewd", it is said:
"Those who want fitting lewdness or fixed lewdness,
all sizes available,
enter to view the items and discuss the price."
The descendants of the Cuī and Lú families like this are very numerous—
why single out
"flower peppers grow in the river"
alone!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Yīn Yuánlǐ,
a man from Yúnnán,
was skilled in acupuncture and moxibustion.
Encountering bandit unrest,
he fled deep into the mountains.
As the day grew late,
and the village was still far off,
he feared encountering tigers or wolves.
Seeing two men ahead on the road,
he hurried to catch up to them.
When he reached them,
the two men asked the traveler where he was from.
Yīn then stated his name and origin.
The two men clasped their hands respectfully and said:
"So this is the excellent physician, Master Yīn!
We have long looked up to you like Mount Tài and the Dipper!"
Yīn in turn questioned them.
The two said their surname was Bān,
one was Bān Zhǎo,
the other Bān Yá.
They then said:
"Master,
we are also refugees,
but fortunately have a stone chamber where we can lodge.
We dare to trouble your noble steps to come with us,
and also have a request to make."
Yīn happily followed them.
Soon they arrived at a place
where a chamber stood beside a rocky valley.
They lit firewood to serve as candles,
and only then did Yīn see that the two Bāns had imposing, fierce physiques,
and seemed not entirely benign.
Seeing no alternative,
he simply went along with it.
Then he heard groaning from a bed,
and looking closely,
saw an old woman lying stiffly,
apparently suffering from something.
He asked:
"What is the ailment?"
Yá said:
"It is for this reason
that we respectfully seek your help, Master."
So they gathered torches to illuminate the bed,
and invited the guest to look closely.
He saw two tumorous growths below her nose and at the corner of her mouth,
each as large as a bowl.
And she said:
"The pain is unbearable to touch,
and it hinders eating and drinking."
Yīn said:
"That's easy."
He took out moxa wool, rolled it into cones,
and applied several moxibustion treatments,
saying:
"It will be healed overnight."
The two Bāns were delighted,
roasted venison to feed their guest;
there was no wine or rice,
only this one dish of meat.
Zhǎo said:
"In our haste, we did not know a guest was coming,
we hope you won't mind the meager fare."
Yīn ate his fill and slept,
using a stone as a pillow.
Though the two Bāns were sincere and simple,
their rough, boorish manner was frightening,
and Yīn tossed and turned, not daring to sleep soundly.
Before dawn,
he called to the old woman,
asking about her ailment.
The old woman, just waking,
felt the area herself,
and found the tumors had burst open into wounds.
Yīn urged the two Bāns to get up,
brought a torch to see,
applied medicinal powder,
and said:
"Healed."
He clasped his hands and bid farewell.
The Bāns also gave him a roasted venison haunch.
For three years afterward, there was no news.
Yīn happened to enter the mountains again for a reason,
and encountered two wolves blocking the path,
preventing him from proceeding.
As the sun set in the west,
more wolves arrived in a pack,
surrounding him front and back.
A wolf pounced on him,
knocking him down;
several wolves fought to bite him,
tearing his clothes to shreds.
He resigned himself to certain death.
Suddenly, two tigers rushed to the scene,
scattering the wolves in all directions.
The tigers roared angrily,
a great roar,
and the wolves, terrified, all crouched down.
The tigers pounced and killed them all,
then finally left.
Yīn, in a sorry state, continued on his way,
afraid he had nowhere to go.
He met an old woman coming his way,
who saw his condition
and said:
"Master Yīn has suffered!"
Yīn, distressed, recounted what happened,
and asked how she knew him.
The old woman said:
"I am the sick old woman from the stone chamber whose tumors you treated with moxibustion."
Only then did Yīn realize,
and asked to lodge there for the night.
The old woman led him away,
entered a courtyard compound,
where lamps were already lit,
and said:
"This old body has been waiting for you for a long time, Master."
She then brought out a robe and trousers,
for him to change out of his tattered clothes.
She set out broth and prepared wine,
toasting and urging him to drink with earnest warmth.
The old woman also drank from an earthenware bowl herself,
her conversation and drinking both robust,
unlike an ordinary woman.
Yīn asked:
"Those two men from before,
what relation are they to you, madam?
Why are they not here?"
The old woman said:
"I sent my two sons to meet you, Master,
they haven't returned yet,
they must have lost their way."
Touched by their kindness,
Yīn drank freely,
unconsciously becoming heavily intoxicated,
and fell into a deep sleep right there at the table.
When he awoke,
it was already dawn.
Looking around, there was no house at all,
he was sitting alone on a rocky ledge.
He heard heavy panting like an ox below the ledge,
and looking closely,
saw a tiger still asleep, not yet awake.
There were two scar marks on its cheeks,
each as large as a fist.
Terrified,
and fearing it would wake,
he stealthily crept away.
Only then did he realize the two tigers were the two Bāns.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
There was a cart driver carrying a child up a slope.
Just as he was exerting all his strength,
a wolf came and bit his buttock.
If he let go,
the cart would tip and crush him,
so he endured the pain and pushed on.
Once at the top,
the wolf had already bitten off a piece of his flesh and left.
Seizing the moment when he could not fight back,
to sneak a bite of flesh,
is cunning yet laughable.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Zhāngqiū's Mǐ Bùyún
was skilled at divination using a planchette.
Whenever gathering elegantly with friends,
he would summon an immortal to compose matching verses with them.
One day,
a friend, seeing wispy clouds in the sky,
came up with a line,
and asked for a matching couplet,
saying:
"A mutton-fat, white-jade sky."
The planchette wrote in response:
"Ask Old Dǒng south of the city."
Everyone thought it nonsense.
Later, by chance, they went south of the city for a reason,
and came to a place
where the earth was like cinnabar,
and found it strange.
Seeing an old man herding pigs nearby,
they asked him about it.
The old man said:
"This is 'pig-blood, red-mud ground'
Suddenly remembering the planchette's words,
they were greatly astonished.
They asked his surname,
and he replied:
"I am Old Dǒng."
The matching couplet itself is not so strange,
but to have foreknown to meet Old Dǒng south of the city—
that is indeed supernatural!
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Gǒng Shēng was a man from Mínzhōu.
He went to Xī'ān to take the imperial examination and rested at an inn,
buying wine to drink by himself.
A burly man entered and sat down to talk with him.
Shēng raised his cup to urge him to drink,
and the guest did not decline.
He said his surname was Miáo,
and his speech and laughter were rough and unrestrained.
Shēng, considering him uncultured, treated him coldly.
When the wine ran out,
he did not buy more.
Miáo Shēng said,
"Drinking with a poor scholar is utterly boring!"
He got up and went to buy wine from the tavern,
returning with a huge jar.
Shēng declined to drink,
but Miáo grabbed his arm and urged him to toast,
causing such pain that Shēng felt his arm would break.
Having no choice,
Shēng drank several cups.
Miáo drank from the jar himself and said with a laugh,
"I am not good at urging guests to drink;
whether you stay or go is entirely up to you."
Shēng immediately packed his belongings and left.
After traveling a few miles,
his horse fell ill on the road,
and he sat by the roadside waiting.
Burdened with heavy luggage,
he was at a loss for what to do
when Miáo arrived.
Upon learning the situation,
Miáo took the luggage and gave it to the servant,
then lifted the horse onto his shoulder and carried it,
hurrying for over twenty miles
until they reached an inn,
where he put the horse in the stable.
Some time later,
Shēng and his servant arrived.
Shēng, amazed by Miáo's superhuman strength,
treated him with great hospitality,
buying wine and food to share with him.
Miáo said,
"I eat a lot;
you cannot fill me up.
Let's just drink to our heart's content."
He finished the entire jar,
then stood up to bid farewell, saying,
"It will take time for your horse to recover,
and I cannot wait.
I must go."
With that, he left.
Later, after Shēng finished his examination,
he and three or four friends decided to climb Huà Shān
and set up a picnic on the ground.
Just as they were feasting and laughing,
Miáo suddenly appeared,
carrying a large wine vessel in his left hand
and a pork knuckle in his right.
He threw them on the ground and said,
"I heard you gentlemen were climbing the mountain,
so I respectfully followed along."
Everyone stood up to greet him,
and they sat together, drinking heartily and enjoying themselves.
The group wanted to compose linked verses.
Miáo protested,
"Drinking freely is joyful enough;
why trouble yourselves with melancholy thoughts?"
They did not listen and set
"the penalty of Jīngǔ"
for those who failed.
Miáo said,
"If the verses are not good,
they should be dealt with by military law!"
Everyone laughed and said,
"The punishment should not be that severe."
Miáo replied,
"If you do not execute me,
even a warrior like me can compose."
The first to compose was Jìn Shēng, who said,
"From the summit, the view stretches endlessly."
Miáo continued without thinking,
"The spittoon shattered, sword gleams red."
The next person pondered for a long time,
so Miáo picked up the wine vessel and poured himself a drink.
After a while,
they took turns composing lines,
but the verses gradually became vulgar.
Miáo shouted,
"This is enough!
If you spare me,
please stop!"
But they did not listen.
Miáo could no longer bear it
and suddenly imitated the roar of a dragon,
which echoed through the mountains.
He then stood up and performed a lion dance,
disrupting their poetic thoughts.
The group finally stopped composing
and resumed drinking.
By then, they were half-drunk,
and the guests took turns reciting poems they had composed during the revelry,
praising one another.
Miáo did not want to listen
and pulled Shēng to play a finger-guessing game.
They played several rounds,
but the others continued reciting and praising.
Miáo said sternly,
"I have heard enough.
Such writings should only be read to one's wife in bed.
It is annoying to hear them chattered about in public!"
The guests looked ashamed,
but they resented his rudeness even more
and began reciting even louder.
Miáo grew furious,
crouched on the ground, and let out a mighty roar,
transforming into a tiger on the spot.
He pounced on the guests, killing them,
and then roared away.
The only survivors were Shēng and Jìn.
Jìn passed the imperial examination that year.
Three years later,
while passing through Huàyīn again,
he suddenly saw Qiú Shēng,
who had also been killed by the tiger on the mountain.
Terrified, he tried to ride away quickly,
but Qiú grabbed the reins, preventing him from leaving.
Jìn dismounted
and asked what he wanted.
Qiú replied,
"I am now a ghost servant of Miáo,
and my duties are extremely arduous.
I must kill another scholar to take my place.
Three days from now,
a scholar in Confucian attire will be devoured by a tiger,
but it must happen at the foot of Cānglóng Ridge
for him to replace me.
On that day,
if you invite many scholars there,
you will be helping an old friend."
Jìn did not dare to argue
and respectfully agreed before parting.
Back at his lodgings,
he pondered all night but could not think of a plan.
He resolved to break the promise
and accept the ghost's punishment.
Just then, his cousin Jiǎng Shēng arrived,
and Jìn told him the strange story.
Jiǎng was a scholar of some reputation,
but Yóu Shēng from the same county had ranked above him in the examination,
and he secretly harbored jealousy.
Hearing Jìn's story,
he secretly plotted to harm Yóu.
He sent an invitation to Yóu,
asking him to climb the mountain together,
while he himself wore plain white clothes.
Yóu did not understand his intention.
Halfway up the ridge,
they set out food and wine
and treated each other with great courtesy.
Just then, the prefect of the commandery climbed the ridge.
Since he was a family friend of Jiǎng's,
he sent someone to summon Jiǎng upon hearing he was below.
Jiǎng did not dare to go in plain clothes,
so he exchanged hats and robes with Yóu.
Before they finished changing,
a tiger suddenly appeared,
seized Jiǎng, and carried him away.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"Those who are smugly pleased with themselves
grab others by the sleeves
and force them to listen.
The listeners yawn repeatedly,
wanting to sleep or flee,
while the reciters dance with hands and feet,
oblivious to everything.
Close friends should nudge or step on them from the side,
fearing that among the guests there might be an impatient Miáo Shēng.
However, the jealous one changed clothes and died,
showing that Miáo was not acting with malice.
Thus, the one who felt disgust and anger was Miáo—yet it was not Miáo."
Based on the Zhuxuezhai manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
A merchant from the south who dealt in scorpions
would come to Línqú every year
to purchase a great many.
The locals would take wooden tongs into the mountains,
searching for them by prying open rocks and exploring caves.
One year,
the merchant returned again
and stayed at an inn.
Suddenly, he felt a stirring in his heart,
his hair standing on end with terror.
He urgently told the innkeeper:
"I have taken many lives,
and now I have incurred the wrath of the scorpion spirits.
They are going to kill me!
Please save me quickly!"
The innkeeper saw a large vat in the room,
so he had the merchant crouch down
and covered him with the vat.
After a while,
a man rushed in,
with yellow hair and a fierce, ugly appearance.
He asked the innkeeper:
"Where is the southern merchant?"
The innkeeper replied:
"He has gone out."
The man entered the room and looked around,
sniffing three times with his nose,
then went out the door and left.
The innkeeper said:
"Fortunately, you are unharmed."
But when he lifted the vat to check on the merchant,
the merchant had already turned into a pool of blood.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Dù Xiǎoléi
was a man from the western mountains of Yìdū.
His mother was blind in both eyes.
Dù served her with filial piety;
although the family was poor,
she never lacked for delicious food.
One day,
as he was about to go elsewhere,
he bought meat and gave it to his wife,
telling her to make bótuō (a type of noodle dish).
His wife was extremely disobedient
and mixed dung beetles into the meat while cutting it.
His mother found it foul and inedible,
so she hid it to wait for her son.
When Dù returned,
he asked:
"Was the bótuō delicious?"
His mother shook her head
and showed it to her son.
Dù tore it open to look
and saw the dung beetles.
He was furious.
He entered the room,
wanting to beat his wife,
but feared his mother would hear.
He climbed onto the bed to think,
and when his wife asked him,
he did not answer.
His wife felt guilty
and paced anxiously below the bed.
After a long time,
there was the sound of panting.
Dù scolded:
"Not sleeping,
are you waiting for a beating?!"
Then he noticed it had become silent.
He got up and lit a candle to look,
and saw only a pig.
Looking closely,
he saw its two feet were still human,
and realized it was his wife transformed.
The county magistrate heard of this,
had her taken away,
and made her parade through the four gates
to warn the people.
Tán Wēichén once saw this with his own eyes.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Máo Dàfú of Tàiháng
was a physician specializing in sores and ulcers.
One day,
as he was returning from his rounds,
he encountered a wolf on the road.
It spat out a wrapped object
and crouched by the roadside.
Máo picked it up and saw
that it was a cloth bundle containing several gold ornaments.
Just as he was wondering about this,
the wolf leaped joyfully forward,
lightly tugged at his robe,
and then left.
As Máo walked on,
it tugged at him again.
Seeing that its intentions were not malicious,
he followed it.
Before long,
they reached a den,
where he saw a wolf lying sick.
Looking at its head, he saw a large sore,
festering and infested with maggots.
Máo understood its meaning,
cleaned out the wound thoroughly,
applied medicine properly,
and then left.
As it grew late,
the wolf saw him off from a distance.
After walking three or four lǐ,
he encountered several more wolves,
roaring and threatening him,
and he was terrified.
The first wolf hurried into the pack,
as if speaking to them,
and all the wolves dispersed.
Máo then returned home.
Earlier,
a silver merchant named Níng Tài in the county
had been killed by robbers on the road,
and the case remained unsolved.
It happened that Máo was selling gold ornaments,
which were recognized by the Níng family,
and he was seized and taken to court.
Máo explained where they came from,
but the officials did not believe him
and put him in shackles.
Máo, in extreme injustice and unable to clear himself,
only begged for leniency and release,
asking to question the wolves.
The officials sent two guards to escort him into the mountains,
straight to the wolf den.
It happened the wolves were not back,
and by dusk they still had not returned,
so the three men turned back.
On the way back,
they encountered two wolves,
one of which still bore the scar.
Máo recognized it
and bowed to it, praying:
"Earlier, I received your gift,
and now I am wronged because of it.
If you do not clear my name,
I will be beaten to death when I return!"
The wolf, seeing Máo bound,
angrily charged at the guards.
The guards drew their swords to confront it.
The wolf pressed its snout to the ground and let out a great howl;
after two or three howls,
hundreds of wolves gathered from the mountains,
surrounding the guards.
The guards were in great distress.
The wolves rushed forward to gnaw at the ropes binding Máo.
The guards understood their intention,
released Máo from his bonds,
and the wolves all left.
Upon returning and reporting what happened,
the officials found it strange,
but did not immediately release Máo.
A few days later,
as an official was traveling,
a wolf placed a worn shoe on the road.
As the official passed by,
the wolf picked up the shoe again, ran ahead, and placed it on the road.
The official ordered the shoe to be collected,
and the wolf left.
The official returned
and secretly sent someone to find the shoe's owner.
It was rumored that in a certain village, a woodcutter
had been chased by two wolves,
which snatched his shoe away.
He was brought in to identify it,
and it was indeed his shoe.
They then suspected that the woodcutter must have killed Níng,
and upon interrogation, it was confirmed.
It turned out the woodcutter had killed Níng,
taken his large sum of money,
and hidden the ornaments in his clothes,
but before he could gather them,
they were carried off by the wolf.
In the past, a midwife was returning home
when she encountered a wolf blocking her path,
tugging at her clothes as if to summon her.
She followed it
and saw a female wolf struggling to give birth.
The midwife helped by pressing and massaging,
and after the birth, she was sent home.
The next day,
the wolf brought venison to her house as a reward.
This shows such things have happened often since ancient times.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Táng Tàishǐ Jìwǔ
was traveling to Rìzhào to attend the funeral of the Ān family.
On the way, he passed by the temple of the Hail God, Lǐ Zuǒjū,
and went in to look around.
In front of the temple was a pond,
its water clear and pure,
with several red fish swimming in it.
Among them was one with a slanted tail,
which nibbled at the water's surface
and was not startled by people.
Tàishǐ picked up a small stone to playfully throw at it.
A Daoist priest hurriedly stopped him, telling him not to strike it.
When asked why,
he said:
"All the fish in this pond are of the dragon clan;
touching them will surely bring wind and hail."
Tàishǐ laughed at this as superstitious nonsense
and threw the stone anyway.
Soon after, he boarded his carriage and headed east,
when a dark cloud, like a canopy,
followed along with him.
Hail fell rustling down,
as large as cotton seeds.
After traveling another li or so,
it finally cleared.
Tàishǐ's younger brother, Liángwǔ, was behind
and caught up to speak with him,
but he had no idea there had been hail at all.
When asked, those traveling ahead said the same.
Tàishǐ laughed and said:
"Could this be Guǎngwǔjūn causing trouble?"
Yet he still did not find it too strange.
Outside Ān Village, there was a temple to Guān Shèng.
A petty trader happened to be there,
resting his load outside the gate,
when he suddenly dropped his two baskets,
rushed into the temple,
grabbed a large blade from the rack and began spinning and dancing with it,
saying:
"I am Lǐ Zuǒjū.
Tomorrow I will accompany Táng Tàishǐ of Zīchuān to assist in the funeral procession,
and I respectfully inform the host in advance."
After a few words, he awoke,
unaware of what he had said,
and did not know who Táng was.
When the Ān family heard this,
they were greatly frightened.
The village was over forty li from the temple,
so they reverently prepared sacrificial offerings
and went to the temple to plead sorrowfully,
begging only for pity,
not daring to trouble the god to come.
Tàishǐ was surprised by their deep reverence and belief,
and asked the host about it.
The host said:
"The Hail God's spiritual manifestations are most renowned;
he often speaks through living people,
and his words never fail to come true.
If we do not pray devoutly to stop his journey,
then tomorrow wind and hail will surely arrive."
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Guǎngwǔjūn in his time
was also among those of deep strategy and grand deeds.
That he now oversees hail in the east
may be due to his undiminished spirit
receiving a post from Heaven.
Yet since he has already become a god,
why must he so conspicuously set himself apart?
Táng Tàishǐ's moral integrity and literary talent
have long been admired by both Heaven and men,
which is why ghosts and spirits must seek trust from gentlemen."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Lǐ Yuèshēng of the Imperial College
was the second son of old man Lǐ Shēng.
The old man was very wealthy,
storing gold in vats,
so the villagers called him
"Eight Vats."
When the old man fell gravely ill,
he called his sons to divide the gold: the elder brother got eight parts,
the younger brother two.
Yuèshēng was disappointed.
The old man said:
"It is not that I favor one over the other;
I have hidden vaulted treasure,
but I must wait until there are not many people left
before I dare give it to you.
Do not be impatient."
A few days later,
the old man was on the verge of death.
Yuèshēng, worried that an unexpected event might occur,
waited until no one was around
and secretly inquired by his bedside.
The old man said:
"The bitterness and joy in life
are all predetermined.
You are currently enjoying the blessing of a virtuous wife,
so I should not give you more gold,
lest it increase your faults."
For Yuèshēng's wife, Chē shì,
was most virtuous,
possessing the virtues of Huán and Mèng,
hence the remark.
Yuèshēng pleaded earnestly.
The old man angrily said:
"You still have over twenty years of hardships to endure;
even if I gave you a thousand taels of gold,
you would spend it all at once.
Unless you reach a point of utter desperation,
do not expect any handouts!"
Yuèshēng was filial, brotherly, sincere, and steadfast,
so he dared not speak further.
Not long after,
the old man's condition worsened,
and he soon passed away.
Fortunately, his elder brother was kind,
and in planning the funeral and burial,
did not argue over the costs.
Yuèshēng was also innocent and carefree,
not calculating over trifles,
and moreover loved hosting guests and drinking,
cooking millet and preparing feasts,
urging his wife to do so three or four times a day,
paying little attention to managing the household's livelihood.
Local ruffians, seeing his meekness,
often took advantage of him.
After several years,
the family gradually declined.
In times of hardship,
he relied on small allowances from his elder brother,
so he was not in extreme distress.
Not long after,
his elder brother died of old age and illness,
and he lost that support,
to the point of having no food.
Borrowing in spring and repaying in autumn,
whatever the fields produced
was gone as soon as it was harvested.
He then sold land to survive,
and his estate dwindled further.
After several more years,
his wife and eldest son died one after another,
and he became even more desolate.
He then married Xú, the wife of a sheep trader,
hoping she might bring some small prosperity;
but Xú had a fierce temper,
and daily abused him,
to the point where he dared not even attend funerals or celebrations with relatives and friends.
One night, he suddenly dreamed of his father, who said:
"The path you are on now
can indeed be called utter desperation.
I once promised you vaulted treasure;
now it is time."
He asked:
"Where is it?"
His father said:
"Tomorrow I will give it to you."
He woke up, finding it strange,
but thought it was just a fantasy born of poverty.
The next day,
while repairing a wall in the upper room,
he dug up a large amount of gold.
Only then did he understand that his father's earlier words
"not many people left"
meant that nearly half the family had died.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Yuèshēng
was a friend from my humble days;
he was simple, sincere, and without pretense.
My brothers and I were close with him,
sharing both joys and sorrows.
Over the years,
though our villages were only ten-odd li apart,
we grew old and died without hearing of each other.
I once passed by his village,
but did not dare to inquire about him.
Thus, the hardships Yuèshēng endured
must have been unspeakable.
Suddenly hearing that he had obtained a fortune,
I could not help but feel delighted for him.
Alas!
The old man's final instructions
I had often heard of before,
but never expected every word to be prophetic.
How divine indeed!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
When Lord Zhū Hóngyīn served as Governor of Guǎngdōng,
traveling merchants and travelers
often submitted grievances about headless injustices.
Travelers from afar
died without their bodies being found;
several companions traveling together
would vanish without a trace.
Such cases piled up,
with no way to investigate them.
Initially, when reported,
officials would still issue warrants for arrest;
but as more and more complaints were filed,
they eventually ignored them altogether.
Upon taking office,
Lord Zhū reviewed the old cases,
finding that the number of reported deaths exceeded a hundred,
and those without families from distant places
were even more numerous.
Shocked and deeply troubled,
he pondered the matter day and night.
He consulted his subordinates extensively,
but none had any solutions.
So, he purified himself with incense and ablutions,
and sent a petition to the City God.
Later, while resting in his study,
he vaguely saw an official
holding a tablet and entering.
He asked:
"What official are you?"
The reply came:
"I am City God Liú Mǒu."
"What do you have to say?"
He said:
"Snow hangs by the temples,
clouds arise at the horizon,
wood floats on water,
a door is set in the wall."
With these words, he departed.
After waking,
Lord Zhū could not decipher the hidden riddle.
Tossing and turning all night,
he suddenly realized:
"Snow hanging by the temples means 'old';
clouds arising at the horizon means 'dragon';
wood on water is a 'boat';
a door in the wall is a 'household':
Could it be 'Old Dragon Boat Household'?"
Indeed, in the northeast of the province,
there were places called Xiǎolǐng
and Lánguān,
with a waterway from the Old Dragon Strait leading to the South Sea,
where travelers often entered Guǎngdōng.
Lord Zhū dispatched officers,
secretly instructing them on a plan,
to capture the boatmen at Lóngjīn.
Over fifty were apprehended one after another,
and they all confessed without torture.
These bandits, under the guise of ferrymen,
lured passengers aboard,
then either drugged them
or burned stupefying incense,
rendering the passengers unconscious;
they would then slit their bellies, stuff them with stones,
and sink them to the riverbed.
How utterly tragic and unjust!
After the cases were redressed,
joy spread far and wide,
and songs of praise were compiled.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Slitting bellies and sinking stones—such cruelty and injustice is extreme,
yet the wooden-headed officials
showed not the slightest concern.
Is this darkness unique to Guǎngdōng?
When Lord Zhū arrived, even spirits and gods lent their aid,
shedding light on overturned cases—how extraordinary!
Yet Lord Zhū had neither four eyes nor two mouths;
it was simply that his compassion for the suffering
was deeply rooted within him.
As for those lofty officials
who go out with swords and halberds lining their path,
return to halls perfumed with orchids and musk,
enjoying the highest honors—
in the end, how do they differ from the Old Dragon boatmen?"
From the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Gāo Mèngshuō of Fèiyì served as Prefect of Chéngdū,
and encountered a strange case.
Previously,
a merchant from the west had come to Chéngdū
and married a widow from Qīngchéng Mountain.
Later, for some reason, he returned west,
and came back after over a year.
Shortly after the couple reunited,
the merchant suddenly died.
Fellow merchants grew suspicious and reported it to the authorities.
Gāo also suspected the widow of infidelity
and interrogated her harshly.
Despite severe torture,
she never confessed.
The case was forwarded to higher authorities,
but lacking solid evidence,
she was imprisoned for a long time.
Later, when someone in Gāo's office fell ill,
they called an old doctor,
and the topic happened to come up.
Upon hearing it,
the doctor abruptly asked:
"Did the woman have a pointed mouth?"
Gāo asked:
"What do you mean?"
At first, the doctor said nothing,
but after repeated questioning,
he finally explained:
"Around Qīngchéng Mountain, there are several villages
where women often mate with snakes.
Their daughters are born with pointed mouths,
and inside their private parts is something like a snake's tongue.
During intercourse,
this tongue protrudes,
and once it enters the male organ,
the man immediately dies from yang depletion."
Gāo was shocked to hear this
but still not entirely convinced.
The doctor said:
"There is a sorceress here
who can administer medicine to arouse a woman,
causing the tongue to emerge.
This can be tested to see if it's true."
Gāo followed his advice,
had the sorceress treat the widow,
and the tongue indeed emerged.
Only then were his doubts resolved.
He reported the case to the commandery.
Higher officials all verified it using the same method,
and the widow was exonerated.
From the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
The magistrate of Chángshān County, Yáng,
was extraordinarily greedy by nature.
During the Kangxī reign period, in the year Yǐhài,
when military campaigns were underway in the western frontier,
the government requisitioned mules and horses from the people to transport grain.
Yáng used this as a pretext to extort and plunder,
emptying the region of all its draft animals.
Zhōucūn was a gathering place for merchants,
and those coming to the market arrived with carts and horses in great numbers.
Yáng led a band of strong men and seized them all,
amounting to no fewer than several hundred head.
Merchants from all directions
had nowhere to lodge their complaints.
At that time, all the magistrates were in the provincial capital on official business.
It happened that Magistrate Dǒng of Yìdū, Magistrate Fàn of Láiwú, and Magistrate Sūn of Xīnchéng
were gathered together at an inn.
Two merchants from Shānxī
met them at the gate, wailing and pleading.
They complained that four strong mules
had all been seized,
and being far from home and having lost their livelihood,
they could not return.
They begged the gentlemen to intercede on their behalf.
The three magistrates took pity on their plight
and agreed.
So they went together to see Yáng.
Yáng prepared a feast to entertain them.
After the wine had been served,
they stated the purpose of their visit.
Yáng paid no heed.
They pressed their case even more earnestly.
Yáng raised his cup and urged them to drink to drown out their words,
saying:
"I have a drinking game.
Whoever fails must drink a penalty cup.
One must name something in the heavens, something on earth, and an ancient figure.
Then, those on the left and right ask what object the figure holds,
and what words he speaks.
One must answer each question in turn."
He then began the game himself:
"In the heavens, there is the moon;
on earth, there is Kūnlún;
there is an ancient figure, Liú Bólún.
When asked on the left what he holds,
he answers:
'Holding a wine cup in hand.'
When asked on the right what words he speaks,
he answers:
'He says nothing need be mentioned beyond the wine cup.'"
Magistrate Fàn said:
"In the heavens, there is the Moon Palace;
on earth, there is the Qiánqīng Palace;
there is an ancient figure, Jiāng Tàigōng.
Holding a fishing rod in hand,
he says, 'Only the willing take the hook.'"
Magistrate Sūn said:
"In the heavens, there is the Milky Way;
on earth, there is the Yellow River;
there is an ancient figure, Xiāo Hé.
Holding a copy of the Great Qing Legal Code in hand,
he says, 'Corrupt officials and corrupt clerks.'"
Yáng looked ashamed,
pondered for a long while,
and said:
"I have another.
In the heavens, there is the Divine Mountain;
on earth, there is Mount Tài;
there is an ancient figure, Hánshān.
Holding a broom in hand,
he says, 'Each sweeps the snow from his own doorstep.'"
They all looked at each other, feeling awkward.
Suddenly, a young man strode in arrogantly,
his robes splendid and neat.
He raised his hands in salute.
They all pulled him to sit down
and poured him wine in a large cup.
The young man said with a laugh:
"Let's not drink for now.
Hearing your elegant drinking game,
I wish to offer my humble contribution."
They urged him to proceed.
The young man said:
"In the heavens, there is the Jade Emperor;
on earth, there is the Emperor;
there is an ancient figure, the Hóngwǔ Emperor, Zhū.
Holding a three-foot sword in hand,
he says, 'Skin the corrupt officials.'"
Everyone burst into laughter.
Yáng cursed angrily:
"Where did this wild youth come from, daring to act like this!"
He ordered his attendants to seize him.
The young man leaped onto the table,
transformed into an owl,
dashed out through the curtain,
and perched on a tree in the courtyard.
Looking back into the room,
he let out a laugh.
The host tried to strike him,
but he flew away, laughing as he went.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"In the campaign to requisition horses,
seven out of ten high officials had their courtyards filled with strong animals,
and those who gathered them in herds of hundreds and thousands to trade as mules and horses
were rarely seen outside of Chángshān.
The wise and enlightened Son of Heaven cherishes the people's strength;
when taking something, he must compensate its value.
Who would have known that those carrying out his orders would spread such poison!
Wherever the owl goes,
people most detest its laughter;
children and women all spit at it,
considering it an ill omen.
But this one laugh—
how is it any different from the cry of a phoenix!"
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
In Běicūn of Zīyì, the well dried up,
and villagers Jiǎ and Yǐ were lowered down to clean it out.
After digging about a foot,
they found a skull.
Accidentally breaking it,
they discovered gold inside its mouth.
Delighted, they put it in their waist pouches.
Digging further,
they found six or seven more skulls.
Breaking them all,
they found no gold.
Beside them were two porcelain vases and one bronze vessel.
The vessel was large enough to embrace with both arms,
weighing several dozen catties,
with two rings on its side.
Its purpose was unknown,
and it was mottled and variegated.
The vases were also ancient,
not of recent style.
Once out of the well,
both Jiǎ and Yǐ died.
After a while, Yǐ revived and said:
"I am a man of the Hàn dynasty.
During the rebellion of Wáng Mǎng,
my entire family threw themselves into the well.
We happened to have a little gold,
so we placed it in our mouths.
It was not actually burial objects—
not everyone had them.
Why did you shatter all our skulls?
It is truly hateful!"
The villagers burned incense and paper money, praying together,
and promised to give them a proper burial.
Only then did Yǐ recover;
Jiǎ, however, could not be revived.
Scholar Sūn of Yánzhèn heard of this strange event
and purchased the bronze vessel.
Provincial Graduate Yuán Xuānsì obtained one of the vases,
which could predict cloudy or clear weather:
if a moist spot appeared on it,
starting as small as a grain of millet,
gradually widening and filling,
rain would soon arrive.
When the moisture receded,
the clouds would part and the sky clear.
The other vase went to Scholar Zhāng's household,
where it could mark the lunar phases:
on the first day of the month, a black dot would appear like a bean,
growing with the days;
by the full moon, the entire vase would be filled;
after the full moon,
it would gradually recede in turn,
returning to its original state by the month's end.
Having been buried in the earth for so long,
a small stone was stuck to the vase's mouth,
and it could not be brushed or picked off.
When they knocked it off,
the stone fell but the mouth was slightly chipped—
a regrettable flaw.
When flowers were placed in it to soak,
the fallen flowers bore fruit,
no different from those on the tree.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
When Mr. Hán Yuánshào was still a student,
an official suddenly arrived,
saying that his master wished to engage him as a tutor,
but he had no name card.
When asked about his family background,
he gave vague answers.
He presented silk and gifts,
and the etiquette was generous.
Mr. Hán agreed,
and they set a date before he left.
On the appointed day,
a carriage indeed came for him.
They traveled far and deep,
along roads he had never seen before.
Suddenly, he glimpsed palaces and pavilions,
and upon alighting and entering,
he found the atmosphere resembled that of a princely mansion.
After settling into the residence,
wine and roasted meats were lavishly laid out,
and the guests were urged to help themselves,
but there was no host in sight.
When the banquet was cleared,
a young master came out to pay his respects;
he was fifteen or sixteen years old,
with a handsome and exceptional appearance.
After the formalities were completed,
he hurried off to another room,
and only when it was time for lessons did he come to the teacher’s quarters.
The young master was very intelligent,
grasping the meaning as soon as he heard it.
Mr. Hán, not knowing the family’s background,
felt quite suspicious and uneasy.
There were two servants attending in the residence,
and he privately questioned them,
but neither answered.
He asked:
"Where is the master?"
They replied that he was busy.
Mr. Hán asked to be led to see him,
but the servants refused.
After repeated requests,
they finally led him to a place
where he heard the sounds of flogging and torture.
Peering through a crack in the door,
he saw a king seated on a throne,
with forests of swords and mountains of blades below the steps—
all things of the underworld.
Greatly alarmed,
he was about to retreat
when those inside already knew of his presence.
The king thus ended his affairs,
shouted for the ghosts to withdraw,
and urgently called for the servants.
The servants, their faces pale, said:
"For the sake of the teacher,
we are in trouble!"
Trembling with fear, they rushed inside.
The king angrily said:
"How dare you lead someone to spy in secret!"
He immediately had them severely whipped with a large lash.
Then he summoned Mr. Hán in and said:
"The reason I did not meet you
was because the realms of the living and the dead are separate.
Now that you know,
it is difficult for us to remain together."
He then gave him a bundle of gold for his journey
and said:
"You are the foremost man in the world,
but your hardships are not yet over."
He ordered a servant in black to escort him back on horseback.
Mr. Hán suspected he had already died.
The servant in black said:
"How could that be?
Everything the teacher ate and used
came from the mortal world,
not from the underworld."
After returning,
he faced hardships for several years,
but then he passed the provincial and palace examinations as the top candidate,
and the king’s words were all fulfilled.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*.
Fēng Yùguì
was a scholar from Liáochéng.
He was poor and had no means of livelihood.
During the Wànlì era,
there was a great famine,
and he fled alone to the south.
On his return,
he fell ill upon reaching Yí.
Struggling on for several miles,
he arrived at a dense burial ground south of the city,
where he grew even more exhausted
and lay down beside a grave.
Suddenly, as if in a dream,
he came to a village,
where an old man emerged from a gate
and invited him inside.
The house had two pillars
and was rather crude.
Inside was a girl,
sixteen or seventeen years old,
graceful, intelligent, and elegant.
The old man had her boil cypress branch tea
and served it to the guest in earthenware.
He then asked Fēng about his hometown and age.
After this,
he said:
"My surname is Lǐ, from Hóngdū,
of the Píngyáng clan.
I have lived in exile here
for thirty-two years now.
Please remember this household.
If any of my descendants come searching,
I would trouble you to guide them.
I, an old man, dare not forget your kindness.
My adopted daughter, Wèiniáng,
is not unattractive
and would be a suitable match for you.
When my three sons arrive,
I will have them officiate the marriage."
Fēng was delighted
and bowed, saying:
"I am twenty-two years old
and still lack a good match.
Your gracious intention to join our families
is certainly excellent,
but how can I find your family to inform them?"
The old man said:
"You just stay in the north village,
wait for over a month,
and someone will come,
I only ask that you do not mind the trouble."
Shēng feared his words were unreliable,
and insisted, saying:
"To be honest with you, sir: I am a poor man with nothing but bare walls,
afraid that in the future things may not turn out as hoped,
and if I am abandoned halfway,
it would be unbearable.
Even if there is no marriage,
I would still dare not break the promise of Jìlù,
so why not speak plainly?"
The old man laughed and said:
"Do you want this old man to swear an oath?
I know well that you are poor.
This arrangement is not solely for you;
Wèiniáng is alone and has no one to rely on,
I have long intended to entrust her to someone,
I cannot bear to let her drift and fall into hardship,
so I offer her to you.
Why be suspicious!"
He then grabbed Shēng's arm and escorted him out,
clasped his hands, closed the door, and left.
Shēng woke up,
and found himself lying by a grave mound,
the sun already nearing noon.
He slowly got up,
hesitantly entered the village.
The villagers were all startled to see him,
saying he had been dead by the roadside for a whole day.
He suddenly realized the old man was the person in the grave,
but kept it to himself,
only asking to stay.
The villagers, fearing he might die again,
dared not take him in.
In the village, there was a scholar with the same surname as him,
who, upon hearing this,
hurried over to inquire about his family background,
and it turned out he was Shēng's distant uncle.
Delighted, he led Shēng to his home,
fed and cared for him,
and in a few days he recovered.
Shēng then recounted his experience,
and his uncle was also astonished,
so they sat and waited to see what would happen.
Not long after,
indeed an official came to the village,
looking for his father's grave site,
and introduced himself as Lǐ Shūxiàng, a jìnshì from Píngyáng.
Earlier,
his father, Lǐ Hóngdū,
had gone into business with a fellow villager,
and died in Yí,
who then buried him in a mass burial ground.
After returning,
that man also died.
At that time, the old man's three sons were all young.
The eldest, Bórén,
passed the jìnshì examination,
and served as a magistrate in Huáinán.
He sent people several times to search for his father's grave,
but no one knew of it.
The second, Zhòngdào,
passed the xiàolián examination.
Shūxiàng was the youngest,
and also passed the imperial examination.
So he personally went to find his father's bones,
arriving in Yí to search everywhere.
On this day, he arrived,
but none of the villagers knew.
Shēng then led him to the grave site,
and pointed it out.
Shūxiàng did not dare believe it,
so Shēng told him in detail what had happened.
Shūxiàng found it strange.
Upon closer inspection, two graves were next to each other,
and someone said that three years ago, an official
buried his young concubine here.
Shūxiàng feared digging up the wrong grave,
so Shēng showed him where he had lain.
Shūxiàng ordered a coffin placed beside it,
and then began to dig the grave.
When the grave was opened,
they saw a female corpse,
her clothes and makeup faded and worn,
but her face still looked alive.
Shūxiàng realized it was the wrong grave,
and was terrified,
not knowing what to do.
But the woman suddenly sat up,
looked around and said:
"Has Third Brother come?"
Shūxiàng was startled,
approached and asked her,
and it was Wèiniáng.
He then took off his clothes to cover her,
and carried her back to the inn.
He hurriedly dug the adjacent grave,
hoping his father would revive.
After digging,
his father's skin and flesh remained,
but when touched, it was stiff and dry,
and he wept bitterly.
He placed the body in a coffin,
and held a seven-day mourning ceremony;
Wèiniáng also wore mourning clothes like a daughter.
Suddenly, she told Shūxiàng:
"Before, the old man had two gold ingots,
and he gave one to me as dowry.
I, being alone and weak, had nowhere to hide it,
so I tied it with silk thread around my waist,
but did not take it with me,
did you find it, brother?"
Shūxiàng did not know,
so he had Shēng go back to search the grave,
and indeed found it,
just as the woman said.
Shūxiàng then gave the one marked with thread to Wèiniáng.
Later, he inquired about her family background.
Earlier,
her father, Xuē Yínhóu, had no sons,
only Wèiniáng,
and he doted on her.
One day,
she was returning from her maternal uncle's home in Jīnlíng,
and with an old maidservant, went to hire a boat.
The boatman was actually a matchmaker from Jīnlíng.
It happened that an official,
having completed his term, was going to the capital,
and had sent someone to find a beautiful concubine,
but after seeing several families,
none satisfied him,
and he was about to take a boat to Guǎnglíng.
Suddenly meeting the girl,
he secretly hatched a wicked plan,
and quickly called them to board.
The old maidservant knew him,
so they boarded together.
Midway,
he put poison in their food,
and both the girl and the maidservant fell unconscious.
He pushed the maidservant into the river;
took the girl back,
and sold her to the official for a high price.
Upon entering the house,
the official's wife found out,
and was furious.
The girl was also dazed,
and did not know how to behave,
so she was beaten and imprisoned.
After three days of traveling north,
the girl finally woke up.
A maidservant told her what had happened,
and she wept bitterly.
One night,
while staying in Yí,
she hanged herself,
and was buried in a mass grave.
In the grave,
she was bullied by a group of ghosts,
but Old Man Lǐ often protected her,
so she treated him as a father.
The old man said:
"Your fate says you should not die,
I will choose a good husband for you."
After Shēng had seen him and left,
he went back and told the girl:
"This man's character and integrity are trustworthy.
Wait until your third brother arrives,
and he will arrange your marriage."
One day, he said:
"You can go back and wait,
your third brother is coming."
That was the day the grave was opened.
While in mourning,
the girl recounted all this to Shūxiàng.
Shūxiàng sighed for a long time,
then took Wèiniáng as his sister,
and had her take the surname Lǐ.
He bought some clothes and makeup,
and sent her to marry Shēng,
and said:
"I don't have much money,
I cannot prepare a dowry for my sister.
I intend to borrow her to return home with me,
to console my mother's heart.
What do you think?"
The girl was also pleased.
Thereupon, husband and wife followed Shǔxiàng,
and the carriage bearing the coffin set off together.
Upon returning home,
the mother, upon questioning, learned the reason,
and loved her more than her own child,
lodging her in a separate courtyard.
During the mourning period,
the girl's grief exceeded that of the sons and grandsons.
The mother pitied her even more,
and did not allow her to return east,
instructing her sons to buy a house for her.
It happened that the Féng family was selling a house,
valued at six hundred taels of silver.
In haste, they were unable to gather the full amount,
so they temporarily received the deed,
agreeing on a date to complete the transaction.
When the day arrived,
Féng came early;
just then, the girl also entered from the separate courtyard to visit the mother,
and suddenly saw him—
he looked exactly like the boatman from that year.
Féng was also startled upon seeing her.
The girl hurried past him.
Her two elder brothers, because their mother was slightly unwell,
had also gathered at their mother's quarters.
The girl asked:
"Who is the one pacing back and forth in the front hall?"
Zhòngdào said:
"That must be the man who sold the house the other day."
He immediately rose to go out.
The girl stopped him,
informed him of her suspicions,
and urged him to question and challenge the man.
Zhòngdào assented and went out,
but Féng had already left,
and in the alley to the south, the tutor, Mr. Xuē, was there.
He then asked:
"Where have you come from?"
He replied:
"Last night, Féng so-and-so entreated me to come early to the hall,
to sign as a guarantor on the deed.
Just now, I met him on the way,
and he said he had forgotten something,
and would return shortly after going back,
asking me to sit and wait for him."
After a short while,
Shēng and Shǔxiàng both arrived,
and they began to converse.
Wèiniáng, because of Féng,
secretly came behind the screen to observe the guest,
and upon looking closely,
realized it was her father.
She rushed out,
embraced him, and wept loudly.
The old man, startled and tearful, said:
"How did my daughter come to be here!"
Only then did everyone realize that Xuē was Yínhóu.
Although Zhòngdào often encountered him on the street,
he had never known his name.
At this, they all rejoiced,
recounted the previous events,
and prepared wine to celebrate together.
They then kept him for two nights,
and he told of his travels.
It turned out that after losing his daughter,
his wife died of grief,
and he, widowed and without support,
had thus traveled here to study.
Shēng promised that after buying the house,
he would welcome him to live together.
The old man went to investigate the next day,
but Féng and his entire family had fled.
Only then did they realize that the one who killed the old woman and sold the girl
was that very man.
When Féng first arrived in Píngyáng,
he engaged in trade and established a household;
in recent years, he had taken to gambling,
and his fortunes declined daily,
so he sold his residence.
The money from selling the girl
was also nearly exhausted.
Wèiniáng, having found a good place,
did not harbor much hatred toward him,
but merely chose a day to move,
and did not pursue where he had gone.
Lǐ's mother continuously sent gifts,
and supplied all daily necessities.
Shēng thus settled his family in Píngyáng,
but returning for the examinations was very arduous.
Fortunately, in that examination, he achieved the rank of Xiàolián.
Wèiniáng, now wealthy and noble,
often remembered that the old woman had died for her,
and wished to repay her son.
The old woman's husband's surname was Yīn,
and she had one son named Fù,
who was fond of gambling,
and so poor he had no place to stand.
One day,
during a dispute over stakes in a gambling game,
he killed a man in a fight,
fled back to Píngyáng,
and from afar sought out Wèiniáng.
Shēng then kept him under his roof.
Upon questioning the name of the man he killed,
it turned out to be Féng, the boatman.
They were astonished and sighed for a long time,
and then explained the matter to him,
so he realized that Féng was the killer of his mother.
He rejoiced even more,
and thereafter served in Shēng's household.
Xuē Yínhóu was cared for by his son-in-law,
who bought a wife for him,
and they had one son and one daughter.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
Tián Zǐchéng of Jiāngníng,
while crossing Dòngtíng Lake,
had his boat capsize and drowned.
Tián Liángsì,
a jìnshì of the late Míng dynasty,
was at that time still an infant in swaddling clothes.
His wife, Madame Dù,
upon hearing the news of his death,
took poison and died.
Liángsì was raised to adulthood by his paternal concubine grandmother.
He divined for an official post and was appointed in Húběi.
After over a year,
he was ordered by a superior official to manage affairs in Húnán.
Arriving at Dòngtíng Lake,
he wept bitterly and returned.
He petitioned, claiming inadequacy in ability and strength,
and was demoted to the post of deputy county magistrate,
assigned to Hànyáng,
but declined and did not take up the post.
The provincial authorities insisted and urged him,
so he finally accepted.
He often wandered freely among rivers and lakes,
not confining himself to his official duties.
One evening,
he moored his boat by the riverbank,
and heard the sound of a dòngxiāo flute,
its rises and falls quite pleasant to the ear.
He walked out under the moonlight,
for about half a lǐ or so,
and saw several thatched huts in a wilderness,
with a flickering lamplight;
approaching the window to peek inside,
he saw three men drinking together within.
In the seat of honor was a xiùcai scholar,
about thirty years old;
in the lower seat was an old man;
and in the side seat, the one playing the flute,
was the youngest.
When he finished playing,
the old man tapped the rhythm and praised it as excellent.
The scholar, facing the wall, chanted in thought,
as if he hadn't heard.
The old man said:
"Brother Lú Shí must have a fine composition,
please recite it at length,
so that we may all appreciate it."
The scholar then chanted:
"The river full of wind and moon is cold and desolate,
withered grass and scattered flowers turn to mud.
A thousand lǐ of cloud-capped mountains I cannot fly over,
my soul dreams night after night west of the bamboo bridge."
The chant was filled with sorrow.
The old man laughed and said:
"Brother Lú Shí is up to his old ways again!"
Then he poured him a large cup of wine,
and said:
"This old man cannot compose a matching verse,
so let me sing a song to accompany the wine."
He then sang
the piece
"Lánlíng Fine Wine."
When the song ended,
everyone in the room was smiling.
The young man stood up and said:
"Let me see how far the moon has tilted."
He suddenly stepped out and saw the guest,
clapping his hands and saying:
"There's someone outside the window,
all our wild antics have been exposed!"
He then pulled the guest inside,
and they all exchanged salutes.
The old man had him sit opposite the young man.
Liángsì tried the shared cup and found the wine cold,
so he declined to drink.
The young man stood up,
lit a reed torch to warm the pot and then offered it.
Liángsì also ordered his attendant to go out and buy wine,
but the old man firmly stopped him.
Then he inquired about his native place and clan,
and Liángsì recounted his life story.
The old man paid his respects and said:
"You are the father and mother-official of our hometown.
This young gentleman's surname is Jiāng,
a native of this area."
Pointing to the young man, he said:
"This is Dù Yěhóu of Jiāngxī."
Then pointing to the scholar:
"This is Brother Lú Shí,
a fellow townsman of yours."
Ever since Lú saw Liángsì,
he had been quite aloof and not very courteous.
Liángsì then asked:
"Which village is your home?
With such refined talent,
it's strange I haven't heard of you earlier."
He replied:
"I've been living away from home for a long time,
even relatives often don't recognize each other,
it's truly lamentable!"
His words were mournful and bitter.
The old man waved his hands to interrupt, saying:
"With a good guest met,
we should attend to the rules of drinking,
such chattering like this,
is tiresome to hear!"
Then he took the cup and drank by himself, saying:
"Now let's all play a game together,
those who fail will be penalized.
Each roll three dice,
and the result must match a rule,
requiring a matching classical allusion."
He then rolled one, two, three,
and chanted:
"Three plus one and two, the dots are the same,
chicken and millet, three-year promise to Lord Fàn: friends joyfully meet."
Next was the young man,
he rolled double twos and a single four,
and said:
"I'm not a well-read man,
only know vulgar allusions,
don't laugh at me.
Four plus double twos, the dots are the same,
four men gather righteously in the ancient city: brothers joyfully meet."
Lú rolled double ones and a single two,
and said:
"Two plus double ones, the dots are the same,
Lǚ Xiàng embraces the old man with both hands: father and son joyfully meet."
Liángsì rolled,
and got the same as Lú,
he said:
"Two plus double ones, the dots are the same,
Máo Róng entertains Lín Zōng with two baskets: host and guest joyfully meet."
When the game ended,
Liángsì rose to take his leave.
Lú finally stood up,
and said:
"The bond of fellow townsmen,
we haven't had time to pour out our hearts,
why leave in such haste?
I have something to ask,
I hope you can stay a little longer."
Liángsì sat down again,
and asked:
"What is it you wish to say?"
He replied:
"I have an old friend,
who died in Dòngtíng Lake,
is he of the same clan as you?"
Liángsì said:
"That was my late father,
how did you come to know him?"
He replied:
"We were close friends in youth.
On the day he died,
only I saw him,
so I collected his bones,
and buried them by the riverside."
Liángsì shed tears and bowed,
begging to be shown the grave site.
Lú said:
"Come here tomorrow,
and I will show you.
It should be easy to recognize,
a few paces from here,
you'll see a grave with a clump of ten reed stalks growing old on it."
Liángsì wiped his tears,
and bid farewell to the group with a bow.
Returning to the boat,
he did not sleep all night,
thinking that Lú's words and demeanor seemed to have a reason.
At dawn he went there,
but the house was completely gone,
which increased his astonishment.
He then followed the indicated direction to search for the grave,
and indeed found it.
There was a clump of reeds on it,
he counted them,
and the number exactly matched.
Suddenly he realized that the title "Brother Lú Shí"
was all allegorical;
the one he had met
was his father's ghost.
Upon detailed inquiry with the locals,
he learned that twenty years ago,
there was an old man Gāo who was wealthy and fond of good deeds,
who would rescue and bury the bodies of those who drowned,
hence there were several graves there.
So he opened the grave, collected the bones,
resigned from his post, and returned home.
He reported back to his grandmother,
and upon verifying, the description matched exactly.
Dù Yěhóu of Jiāngxī,
was his maternal cousin,
who at nineteen,
drowned in the river;
later his father moved to live in Jiāngxī.
He also realized that after Madame Dù died,
she was buried west of the bamboo bridge,
hence the remembrance in the poem.
But I do not know who this person is.
According to the Zhuxuezhai manuscript of Liaozhai Zhiyi
Wáng Xì,
styled Guì'ān,
was the son of a prominent family in Dàmíng.
He happened to travel south,
and moored his boat by the riverbank.
On the neighboring boat was a boatman's daughter,
embroidering shoes inside,
her demeanor graceful and peerless.
Wáng watched her for a long time,
but the girl seemed unaware.
Wáng then recited aloud
"The Luòyáng maiden lives across the gate,"
deliberately letting her hear.
The girl seemed to understand it was meant for her,
slightly raising her head to glance sideways at him,
then lowered her head and continued embroidering as before.
Wáng's spirits grew even more captivated,
and he threw a gold ingot toward her,
which fell onto her lapel.
The girl picked it up and discarded it,
and the gold landed by the shore.
Wáng retrieved it,
feeling even more perplexed,
then threw a gold bracelet toward her,
which fell at her feet;
the girl attended to her work without paying it any heed.
Not long after,
the boatman returned from elsewhere.
Wáng feared he would see the bracelet and question them,
and grew very anxious;
the girl calmly covered it with her feet.
The boatman untied the mooring rope,
and departed directly.
Wáng felt disheartened and bewildered,
sitting dazedly in deep thought.
At that time, Wáng had just lost his wife,
and regretted not immediately seeking a matchmaker to secure her hand.
He then inquired with the boatmen,
but none knew her surname.
He returned to his boat and hurriedly pursued her,
but she had vanished without a trace.
Having no other choice,
he sailed southward.
After completing his affairs,
he headed north again,
and carefully searched along the river,
but found no news or trace of her.
Upon returning home,
thoughts of her lingered in his mind day and night.
A year later,
he traveled south again,
renting a boat by the river,
as if making it his home.
Day after day, he meticulously counted the passing boats,
becoming familiar with the sails and oars of those coming and going,
but the boat from before remained elusive.
After half a year,
his funds were exhausted, and he returned home.
Whether walking or sitting, he thought of her constantly,
unable to set it aside even for a moment.
One night,
he dreamed he arrived at a riverside village,
passed several gates,
and saw a house with a wooden gate facing south,
inside which sparse bamboo formed a fence,
giving the impression of a garden,
so he entered directly.
There was a silk tree,
covered with red threads.
He thought to himself: in the poem,
"Before the gate, a tree of horse-tassel flowers,"
this must be it.
After walking a few paces,
there was a clean and tidy reed fence.
He entered further,
and saw three rooms in the northern building,
with double doors closed.
To the south was a small cottage,
with red plantains shading the window.
Leaning in to peek,
he saw a clothes rack blocking the doorway,
with a painted skirt hanging on it,
realizing it was a lady's boudoir,
he stepped back in surprise;
but those inside also noticed,
and someone rushed out to look at the visitor,
her powdered face faintly visible,
and it was the girl from the boat.
Overjoyed beyond expectation,
he said:
"Could there truly be a day we meet again!"
Just as he was about to approach her,
her father happened to return,
and he suddenly awoke with a start,
realizing it was all a dream.
The scenery remained vivid,
as if before his eyes.
He kept it secret,
fearing that if he told others,
it would shatter this wonderful dream.
Another year or so later,
he traveled again to Zhènjiāng.
In the southern part of the commandery was Xú Tàipú,
with whom he had a generational friendship,
who invited him for a drink.
Riding his horse casually,
he mistakenly entered a small village,
and the scenery along the road
seemed exactly like what he had experienced in his life.
Inside one gate,
there was a tree of horse-tassel flowers,
just as in his dream.
Utterly astonished,
he dismounted and entered.
All the sights and objects,
were no different from his dream.
Going further inside,
the number of rooms was exactly as in the dream.
Since the dream had come true,
he no longer hesitated,
and went straight to the southern cottage,
where the girl from the boat was indeed inside.
Seeing Wáng from afar,
she stood up in surprise,
using the door to shield herself,
and demanded:
"Who is this man?"
As Wáng hesitated,
he still suspected it was a dream.
Seeing him approach closely,
the girl slammed the door shut with a bang.
Wáng said:
"Don't you remember the one who threw the bracelet?"
He recounted in full the pain of his longing,
and also spoke of the dream's omen.
The girl, from behind the window, inquired into his family background;
Wáng told her everything.
The girl said:
"Since you belong to an official family,
there must surely be a fine lady managing your household.
Why would you need me?"
Wáng said:
"If not for your sake,
I would have married long ago."
The girl said:
"If it is truly as you say,
I fully understand your heart.
My feelings in this matter are difficult to tell my parents,
yet I have also defied their orders and refused several families.
The gold bracelet is still here;
I reckoned a man of true affection would surely seek news.
My parents have gone to visit relatives,
and will return soon.
Please withdraw for now.
Send a matchmaker with betrothal gifts;
the plan will surely succeed.
But if you hope to form a couple through improper means,
then your intentions are misguided."
Wáng, in haste, was about to leave.
The girl called out from afar, "Young Master Wáng:
I am Yúnniáng,
of the Mèng family.
My father's courtesy name is Jiānglí."
Wáng memorized this and left.
He ended the banquet early and returned,
then went to visit Jiānglí.
Jiāng welcomed him in,
and had him sit by the fence.
Wáng stated his family's status,
then conveyed his purpose,
and also presented a hundred taels of silver as betrothal gifts.
The old man said,
"My daughter is already promised."
Wáng said:
"My inquiries were very certain;
she is indeed awaiting a proposal.
Why do you reject me so firmly?"
The old man said,
"What I just said
I dare not falsify."
Wáng, utterly dejected in spirit,
bowed in farewell and returned.
That night he tossed and turned,
with no one to act as matchmaker.
He had previously considered telling the Grand Coachman of his feelings,
but feared being laughed at by his teacher for marrying a boatman's daughter;
now, in his urgent predicament,
with no one to serve as go-between,
at daybreak,
he went to see the Grand Coachman
and told him the truth.
The Grand Coachman said:
"This old man is related to me;
he is the direct grandson of my paternal grandmother.
Why didn't you tell me earlier?"
Only then did Wáng reveal the hidden circumstances.
The Grand Coachman said doubtfully:
"Jiānglí is certainly poor,
but he has never made boatmanship his livelihood.
Could you be mistaken?"
He then sent his eldest son Dàláng to visit the Mèngs.
Mèng said:
"Although I am impoverished,
I am not one to sell my child in marriage.
Earlier, the young master used silver to propose on his own behalf,
assuming I would be moved by profit.
Therefore, I dared not consent to the marriage.
Now that I have received your instructions, Sir,
there can certainly be no mistake.
However, my stubborn daughter is quite spoiled and willful;
whenever a good family proposes, she invariably refuses.
I must discuss it with her,
to avoid future resentment over the marriage."
He then rose,
went inside briefly and returned,
clasped his hands and said it was all as instructed,
set a date, and then they parted.
Dàláng reported back;
Wáng then lavishly prepared betrothal gifts,
presented them to the Mèngs,
borrowed lodging at the Grand Coachman's house,
and personally went to fetch the bride for the wedding ceremony.
After staying three days,
he bid farewell to his father-in-law and headed north to return home.
Staying overnight on the boat,
he asked Yúnniáng:
"When I met you here before,
I always doubted you were a boatman's daughter.
Where were you going by boat that day?"
She replied:
"My uncle's family lives north of the river;
I just borrowed a small boat to visit them.
My family is merely self-sufficient,
yet we do not highly regard ill-gotten gains.
I laughed at you for having eyes like beans,
repeatedly trying to move people with money.
When I first heard your recitation,
I knew you were a refined gentleman,
but then suspected you were a frivolous man trying to seduce a loose woman.
Had my father seen the gold bracelet,
you would have had no place to die.
Wasn't my heart keen on pitying talent?"
Wáng laughed and said:
"You are certainly very clever,
but you also fell into my trap!"
The girl asked,
"What do you mean?"
Wáng stopped and would not say.
She pressed him firmly,
and he then said:
"As we near my home daily,
this too cannot remain secret forever.
I tell you truthfully: I already have a wife at home,
the daughter of Minister Wú."
Yúnniáng did not believe him;
Wáng deliberately made his words bold to convince her.
Yúnniáng's expression changed;
she was silent for a while,
then suddenly rose,
rushed out;
Wáng, shoes and all, chased after her,
but she had already thrown herself into the river.
Wáng cried out loudly;
all the boats were startled and in an uproar;
the night was dark and hazy,
only the river full of starry reflections remained.
Wáng mourned and grieved all night,
went down along the river,
offering a high reward to find her remains,
but saw nothing.
He returned dejected,
filled with both worry and grief.
He also feared the old man would come to see his daughter,
and he would have no words to answer.
He had a brother-in-law who held office in Hénán,
so he ordered his carriage and went to visit him.
Over a year later, he finally returned.
On the way, he encountered rain,
