and stopped to rest at a commoner's house.
He saw that the rooms and corridors were clean and tidy,
and an old woman was playing with a child in the hall.
When the child saw Wáng,
he immediately rushed over, asking to be held.
Wáng found this strange.
Looking at the child, he saw he was handsome and lovely,
so he picked him up and placed him on his knee.
The old woman called to him,
but the child wouldn't leave.
After a short while,
the rain cleared,
and Wáng lifted the child to hand him to the old woman,
then went down to the hall to pack his things.
The child cried out:
"Daddy is leaving!"
The old woman was embarrassed by this,
scolded him, but he wouldn't stop,
so she forcibly carried him away.
Wáng sat waiting to prepare his belongings,
when suddenly a beautiful woman came out from behind the screen, holding the child.
It was Yúnniáng.
Just as he was astonished,
Yúnniáng scolded him:
"Heartless man!
You left behind this piece of flesh,
what was I to do with him?"
Only then did Wáng realize it was his own son.
A pang of sorrow pierced his heart,
and without time to ask about her past experiences,
he first swore by the sun to clear himself
regarding the earlier joke he had made.
Yúnniáng then turned from anger to sorrow,
and they faced each other, shedding tears.
Previously,
the master of the house, Old Man Mò,
had no son at sixty,
so he took his wife on a pilgrimage to South Sea.
On the return journey, they moored by the riverbank,
when Yúnniáng floated down with the current,
and happened to bump into the old man's boat.
The old man ordered his attendants to rescue her,
and they worked on reviving her all night
before she gradually came to.
The old man and his wife saw
she was a fine young woman,
and were very pleased,
taking her as their own daughter
and bringing her home.
After living there for several months,
they wanted to choose a husband for her,
but she refused.
After more than ten months,
she gave birth to a son,
named Jìshēng.
When Wáng took shelter from the rain at their home,
Jìshēng was just one year old.
Wáng then unpacked his belongings,
went in to pay respects to the old couple,
and thus became their son-in-law.
After staying a few days,
he finally took his family and returned home.
Upon arrival,
Old Man Mèng was sitting waiting,
having been there for two months already.
When the old man first arrived,
he saw the servants acting evasively and speaking vaguely,
and felt quite suspicious and strange;
but once they met,
they finally shared joy and relief.
Wáng recounted all that had happened,
and only then did the old man understand the reason for their previous evasiveness.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Jìshēng,
styled Wángsūn,
was a famous scholar in the commandery.
His parents, because he had recognized his father while still in swaddling clothes,
said he had innate wisdom,
and doted on him.
As he grew, he became even more handsome,
able to write essays by eight or nine,
and entered the commandery school at fourteen.
He often chose his own marriage prospects.
His father Guì'ān had a younger sister, Èrniáng,
who married the scholar Zhèng Zǐqiáo,
and bore a daughter, Guīxiù,
who was exceptionally intelligent and beautiful.
When Wángsūn saw her,
he felt deep love and admiration.
As time passed,
he could neither eat nor sleep.
His parents were greatly worried,
and after persistent questioning,
he finally told them the truth.
His father sent a matchmaker to the Zhèng family;
but Zhèng, being upright and cautious,
objected due to their cousin relationship,
and refused.
Wángsūn became even more ill,
and his mother, at her wits' end,
secretly and tactfully conveyed the situation to Èrniáng,
only asking that Guīxiù come visit him once.
When Zhèng heard of this,
he became even angrier,
and spoke harsh words.
His parents, having lost all hope,
could only let things be.
In the commandery, there was a prominent family named Zhāng.
Their five daughters were all beautiful;
the youngest was named Wǔkě,
who surpassed all her elder sisters in beauty,
and was yet to be betrothed as she was choosing a husband.
One day,
while visiting the family graves,
she encountered Wángsūn on the road.
Peeking from her carriage, she saw him,
and upon returning home, told her mother.
Her mother, discerning her intent,
met the matchmaker, Old Woman Yú,
and subtly hinted at it.
The old woman then went to Wángsūn's place.
At that time, Wángsūn was ill,
and upon hearing her inquiry, he laughed and said:
"This illness, old woman, I can cure."
Yúnniáng asked the reason.
The old woman explained the Zhāng family's intention,
and lavishly praised Wǔkě's beauty.
Yúnniáng was pleased,
and sent the old woman to inquire after Wángsūn.
The old woman entered,
patted Wángsūn and told him.
Wángsūn shook his head and said:
"The cure does not match the ailment,
what can be done!"
The old woman laughed and said:
"Just ask whether the doctor is good or not: if they are good,
summon Hé and Huǎn to come,
and it will be fine: to stubbornly seek that one person,
waiting stubbornly unto death,
is that not foolish?"
Wángsūn sighed and said:
"But under heaven, no doctor
surpasses Hé."
The old woman said:
"Why is your view so narrow?"
Then she described Wǔkě's features, hair, and skin,
her spirit and demeanor,
painting a vivid picture with her words and gestures.
Wángsūn again shook his head and said:
"Old woman, you are mistaken!
This is beyond what I desire."
He turned towards the wall,
and would listen no more.
Seeing his resolve unmoved,
the old woman left.
One day,
while Wángsūn was deeply ill,
suddenly a maid entered and said:
"The one you long for has arrived!"
Overjoyed,
he leapt up.
Hurrying out of his room,
he saw a beautiful woman already in the courtyard.
Looking closely,
she was not Guīxiù,
but wore a pine-flower colored fine-pleated embroidered skirt,
her tiny feet slightly visible,
no less than an immortal.
Bowing, he asked her name,
and she replied:
"I
am Wǔkě.
You, sir, are deeply sentimental,
yet fixated solely on Guīxiù,
which makes one feel it's unfair."
Wángsūn apologized and said:
"In my life, I have never seen your beauty,
so my eyes held only Guīxiù.
Now I know my fault!"
Then he made a vow with her.
Just as they were warmly holding hands,
his mother came to check on him,
and he suddenly awoke,
realizing it was all a dream.
Recalling her voice, appearance, smile, and demeanor,
they seemed vividly before his eyes.
Secretly, he thought: if Wǔkě is truly as in the dream,
why must he seek the one so difficult to obtain?
Thus, he told his mother about the dream.
His mother was glad his obsession had lessened somewhat,
and eagerly sought a matchmaker.
Wángsūn, fearing the dream might not be accurate,
asked a neighboring old woman, Qín, who knew the Zhāng family,
to visit them on some pretext,
and secretly observe Wǔkě.
The old woman went to their home,
where Wǔkě was ill,
leaning on a pillow, supporting her chin,
her graceful posture
surpassing all in the world.
Approaching, she asked:
"What ails you?"
The girl silently played with her sash,
not uttering a word.
Her mother answered for her:
"It's not an illness.
For days, she has been angry with her father and mother!"
The old woman asked why.
She said:
"When families propose marriage,
she is unwilling to all,
insisting she will only marry someone like Wáng Jìshēng.
As her mother urged her too urgently,
she deliberately refused to eat for several days."
The old woman laughed and said:
"If the young lady were to match with Master Wáng,
it would truly be a pair of jade people.
If he were to see Fifth Lady,
I fear he would pine away to death!
When I return,
I will have someone send a matchmaker,
how about that?"
Wǔkě stopped her, saying:
"Grandma, don't!
I fear it may not succeed,
and only add to the mockery!"
The old woman confidently took it upon herself to ensure success,
and Wǔkě finally smiled.
The old woman returned,
reported back,
exactly as the matchmaker had said.
Wángsūn inquired in detail about her clothing and shoes,
which also matched the dream,
and he was greatly pleased.
Though his mind was somewhat eased,
he still did not fully trust others' words.
After several days,
as he gradually recovered,
he secretly summoned the matchmaker,
planning to see Wǔkě in person.
The old woman found it difficult,
but temporarily agreed and left.
After a long time,
she did not return.
Just as he was about to seek her out,
the old woman suddenly came cheerfully and said:
"Fortunately, there is an opportunity.
Fifth Lady has been slightly unwell,
so she had her maids support her,
and moved to the opposite courtyard.
Young master, go and wait in hiding,
as Fifth Lady walks slowly and hesitantly,
you can observe her thoroughly from a discreet angle."
Wángsūn was delighted.
The next day,
he ordered the carriage early and went,
where the old woman was already waiting.
He had his horse tied to a village tree,
was led to a roadside house,
where a seat was set and the door closed as she left.
After a short while,
Wǔkě indeed came out supported by a maid.
Wángsūn watched intently through a crack in the door.
As the girl passed outside the door,
the old woman deliberately pointed at clouds and trees to slow her delicate steps,
allowing Wángsūn to observe her completely.
His heart trembled, unable to contain himself.
Not long after,
the old woman arrived,
and said:
"Can she replace Guīxiù?"
Wángsūn expressed his thanks and returned,
finally telling his parents,
and sending a matchmaker to propose marriage.
When the matchmaker went,
Wǔkě was already betrothed to another.
Wángsūn was disheartened,
filled with regret and anguish, wishing to die,
and immediately fell ill again.
His parents were deeply worried,
blaming him for his own mistake.
Wángsūn had no words,
only drinking a small bowl of rice broth daily.
After several days,
he was emaciated, barely skin and bones on the bed,
worse than before.
The old woman suddenly arrived,
exclaiming in shock:
"Why are you so exhausted?"
Wángsūn shed tears,
and told her the situation.
The old woman laughed and said:
"Foolish young master!
The other day, when someone came to you,
you deliberately refused;
today, when you seek someone,
can you be sure to succeed?
Even so,
it can still be managed.
Had you consulted with me earlier,
even if she were promised to a prince of the capital,
I could have taken her back."
Wángsūn was overjoyed,
and asked for a plan.
The old woman told him to write a letter and send a messenger to arrange to meet at the Zhāng residence the next day.
Guì'ān feared that acting rashly would lead to rejection.
The old woman said:
"Previously, we had reached an agreement with Mr. Zhāng,
but after a few days, he suddenly regretted it. Moreover, he has promised his daughter to another family,
yet there is still no formal letter of engagement.
As the proverb says: 'The one who cooks first eats first.'
What is there to doubt?"
Guì'ān followed his advice.
The next day,
two servants were sent,
and there were no objections.
They were richly rewarded and returned.
Wángsūn's illness suddenly improved,
and from then on, his thoughts of Guīxiù were completely cut off.
Earlier,
when Zhèng Zǐqiáo rejected the marriage proposal,
Guīxiù was quite displeased.
Upon hearing that the marriage with the Zhāng family was settled,
her heart grew even more depressed,
and she fell ill,
becoming increasingly emaciated day by day.
Her parents questioned her,
but she refused to speak.
A maid, sensing her feelings,
secretly informed her mother.
When Zhèng heard this,
he angrily refused to seek medical treatment for her,
leaving her to die.
Èrniáng comforted her, saying:
"My nephew is also quite good.
Why stick to rigid principles
and let our delicate daughter die?"
Zhèng angrily replied:
"If she is the daughter you gave birth to,
it would be better for her to die early,
to avoid becoming a laughingstock!"
Because of this, husband and wife became estranged.
Èrniáng spoke to her daughter,
saying she would have her return to Wángsūn,
even if as a concubine.
The daughter bowed her head without speaking,
seeming very willing.
Èrniáng discussed it with Zhèng,
but he grew even angrier,
leaving everything to Èrniáng,
putting their daughter out of his mind,
and no longer interfering.
Èrniáng, deeply loving her daughter,
wanted to fulfill her promise.
The daughter then became happy,
and her illness gradually healed.
Secretly, they learned that Wángsūn
had a date set for the wedding procession.
When the day arrived,
using the pretext of her nephew's wedding,
Èrniáng pretended to return to her parents' home.
At dawn,
she sent someone to ask her brother for servants and a carriage.
Her brother was very affectionate,
and since they lived in neighboring villages,
he used the wedding procession carriages and horses he had prepared
to first fetch Èrniáng.
Upon arrival,
they dressed the daughter and put her in the carriage,
sending two servants and two maids to escort her.
Upon reaching the door,
they laid felt on the ground and entered.
At that time, the drums and music had already gathered,
and the accompanying servants shouted for them to play loudly,
causing a sudden uproar of human voices.
Wángsūn rushed to look,
and saw a woman with a red veil over her head.
He was extremely shocked,
and wanted to flee;
but Zhèng's servants held him on both sides,
and made him perform the wedding bows.
Wángsūn did not know why,
but he bowed anyway.
The two maids supported the girl,
and directly seated her in the bridal chamber,
only then did he realize it was Guīxiù.
The whole family was in chaos,
not knowing what to do.
As dusk gradually approached,
Wángsūn no longer dared to proceed with the wedding ceremony.
Guì'ān sent a servant to explain the situation to Zhāng;
Zhāng was furious,
and wanted to break off the engagement.
Wǔkě refused,
saying:
"Although she arrived first,
she has not received the betrothal gifts;
it would be better to still have the wedding procession come for me."
Her father accepted her words,
and relayed them to the messenger.
When the messenger returned,
Guì'ān ultimately did not dare to comply.
Facing each other, they pondered,
with neither joy nor anger finding an outlet.
Zhāng held out for a long time,
and knowing they would not proceed,
he also sent Wǔkě in a carriage and on horseback,
setting up another bridal chamber in a separate room.
Wángsūn moved between the two rooms,
pacing anxiously, not knowing how to handle the situation.
His mother then mediated,
arranging them in order of age,
and both women agreed.
When Wǔkě heard that Guīxiù was slightly older,
and had to address her as
"elder sister,"
she showed a reluctant expression.
Her mother was very worried.
By the third day's gathering,
Wǔkě saw that Guīxiù was charming and pleasant,
and unconsciously yielded to her,
and from then on, things settled.
However, the parents feared that over time they might not get along,
but the two women had no disagreements,
sharing clothes and shoes,
loving each other like sisters.
Wángsūn then asked Wǔkě why she had initially refused the matchmaker.
She laughed and said:
"No particular reason,
just to repay you for refusing the old woman.
Before you saw me,
your heart held only Guīxiù;
even after seeing me,
I deliberately held back a little,
to see how you regarded me
compared to Guīxiù.
If you had fallen ill for her,
but not for me,
then I would not have insisted on being accepted."
Wángsūn laughed and said:
"That repayment was rather harsh!
But if not for the old woman,
how could I have glimpsed your beautiful face?"
Wǔkě said:
"It was I who wanted to see you,
what could the old woman do?
When passing by your house,
did you not know that someone was eagerly watching inside?
We had already made an appointment in a dream,
how could you not have known?"
Wángsūn asked in surprise:
"How did you know?"
She said:
"When I was ill, I dreamed I came to your house,
and thought it was an illusion;
later, when I heard you also dreamed,
I knew my soul had truly been there."
Wángsūn found this strange,
and recounted his dream,
and the timing matched exactly.
The wonderful fates of father and son
were both realized through dreams—
a truly remarkable story.
Therefore, both are recorded here.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"The father was infatuated with love,
and the son nearly died for love.
So-called 'seed of love'—
does it not refer to Wángsūn?
Without a father skilled in dreaming,
how could a son with a wandering soul be born!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Mr. Zhōu,
a private secretary in Zīyí County.
When the magistrate was away on official business,
his wife, Madame Xú,
had vowed to make a pilgrimage to the shrine of the Primordial Goddess of the Azure Clouds.
Because the journey was long,
she intended to send a servant to take her place and present the offerings.
She asked Zhōu to compose a prayer.
Zhōu wrote a piece in ornate prose,
recounting her entire life,
and it was rather frivolous and improper.
It included lines such as:
"Though you plant flowers throughout Yángmǎn County,
you favor only the cut sleeve;
though you set up straw figures all over the Jiágǔ Mountains,
you love only the leftover peach." This alluded to what Madame Xú resented,
and there were many similar passages.
After finishing the draft,
he showed it to a fellow secretary, Mr. Líng,
who considered it profane
and warned him not to use it.
Zhōu did not listen
and gave it to the servant, who departed.
Not long after,
Zhōu died in his office;
then the servant also died;
after giving birth,
Madame Xú also fell ill and died.
People still did not find this strange.
Zhōu's son came from the capital to fetch his father's coffin,
and spent the night with Líng.
He dreamed that his father warned him:
"One must be careful with words!
I did not heed Mr. Líng's advice,
and because of the profane language,
I offended the gods,
and died prematurely;
I also implicated Madame Xú,
and brought disaster upon the servant who burned the prayer—I fear that punishment in the underworld is still unavoidable!"
He woke and told Líng,
who had had the same dream.
Líng then recounted the content of the prayer.
Zhōu's son was deeply shaken by this.
The Chronicler of the Tales remarks:
"To indulge one's feelings and wield the brush freely,
splashing ink for one's own pleasure,
is common among literary men.
But how dare one use licentious and disrespectful words
to address the gods!
The reckless scholar was ignorant,
and the underworld punished him as he deserved.
Yet to cause the virtuous lady and the servant from afar
to die without knowing their crime—
is this not much like the law that distinguishes between principal and accessory in punishment,
being utterly confused?
How unjust!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
A certain Zhào from Chángshān
rented a room from a wealthy family.
He suffered from an abdominal mass
and was also poor and alone,
lying on the verge of death.
One day,
struggling to move to a cooler spot,
he shifted to lie under the eaves.
When he woke,
he saw a woman of peerless beauty sitting beside him.
He asked her who she was,
and she said:
"I have come specifically to be your wife."
Startled, he said:
"Not to mention that a poor man like me dare not entertain such wild thoughts;
besides, I am at death's door—
what use would a wife be to me!"
The woman said:
"I can cure you."
He said:
"My illness cannot be quickly cured; even if there were a good prescription,
how could I afford to buy the medicine!"
The woman said:
"I heal illnesses without medicine."
She then pressed her hand on Zhào's abdomen
and rubbed it vigorously.
He felt her palm as hot as fire.
After a while,
the lump in his belly
made faint cracking sounds.
A little later,
he felt the need to relieve himself.
He hurriedly got up,
walked a few paces,
untied his clothes and had a massive bowel movement.
Sticky fluid flowed out,
and the entire lump was expelled.
He felt refreshed all over.
Returning to lie in his original spot,
he said to the woman:
"Lady, who are you?
Please tell me your name,
so that I may worship you."
She replied:
"I am a fox immortal.
You are a descendant of Chǔ Suìliáng from the Táng dynasty,
who once showed kindness to my family.
We have always remembered this and wished to repay it.
I have been searching for you,
and now I have finally found you.
My long-held wish can be fulfilled."
Zhào felt ashamed of his own wretched appearance,
and worried that the soot from the hearth in his thatched hut
would stain her beautiful clothes.
The woman merely urged him to go inside.
Zhào then led her into his home.
There was only an earthen bed without a mat,
and the stove was cold, without smoke.
He said:
"Not only is the situation like this,
unfit to disgrace you;
even if you could endure it,
look—the jar is empty,
how could I support a wife?"
The woman only said:
"Do not worry."
As she spoke,
she turned her head,
and they saw that felt mats, quilts, and bedding had already been laid on the bed.
Just as he was about to ask,
in another blink,
the entire room was pasted with silver paper, shiny as mirrors.
All the furnishings had changed,
the table was clean and elegant,
and food and wine were laid out.
They then happily drank together.
When night fell,
they slept together intimately,
like husband and wife.
The landlord heard of this marvel
and asked to meet her.
The woman came out to see him
without any reluctance.
From then on, word spread far and wide,
and many visitors came to their door.
The woman did not refuse them.
If someone invited her to a banquet,
she would always go with her husband.
One day,
among the guests was a Provincial Graduate
who secretly harbored lustful thoughts.
The woman already knew this
and suddenly rebuked him.
She then pushed his head with her hand;
his head went outside the window lattice,
while his body remained inside the room.
He could neither move in nor out,
nor turn around.
Everyone pleaded for mercy on his behalf,
and only then did she pull him out.
After more than a year,
the number of visitors grew increasingly bothersome,
and the woman became quite annoyed.
Those who were refused would curse Zhào.
During the Duānwǔ Festival,
as they were drinking at a grand gathering,
a white rabbit suddenly leaped in.
The woman stood up and said,
"The Medicinal Elder has come to summon me!"
She said to the rabbit:
"Please go ahead."
The rabbit hurried out
and went straight away.
The woman told Zhào to fetch a ladder.
Zhào brought a long ladder from behind the house,
several *zhàng* high.
There was a large tree in the courtyard,
so he leaned the ladder against it;
the ladder extended even higher than the treetop.
The woman climbed up first,
and Zhào followed.
The woman turned back and said:
"If any relatives or guests wish to follow,
they should come now."
Everyone looked at each other, not daring to climb.
Only a young servant of the landlord
eagerly followed behind them.
They climbed higher and higher,
until the ladder ended where the clouds began,
and they were no longer visible.
Everyone looked at the ladder
and saw it was an old, broken door,
with its white panels removed.
They entered the room
and found the ash-covered walls and broken stove as before,
with nothing else.
They still thought the servant might return and they could ask him,
but he was never seen again.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
In Zōupíng County, there was a veterinarian named Hóu.
One day, he carried a meal to deliver to a farmer working in the fields.
When he reached the wilderness,
a whirlwind began spinning in front of him.
Hóu immediately scooped some porridge with a ladle, offered a prayer, and poured it out as a libation.
After several ladlefuls,
the whirlwind finally departed.
Another day,
he happened to visit the City God Temple.
While strolling leisurely along the corridor,
he saw a statue of Liú Quán presenting melons inside the temple,
which was soiled by bird droppings,
completely covering its eyes.
Hóu sighed with pity:
"Brother Liú, how did you end up suffering such defilement!"
So he used his fingernails to scrape the droppings away.
Several years later,
Hóu fell ill and was bedridden.
Two yamen runners came to seize his soul.
When they arrived at the gates of the underworld court,
they harshly pressured him for bribes.
Just as Hóu was at a loss for what to do,
suddenly a man in green robes emerged from inside.
Upon seeing Hóu, he exclaimed in surprise:
"Old Master Hóu, what brings you here?"
Hóu then recounted his situation.
The man in green robes scolded the two runners:
"This is your esteemed Master Hóu.
How dare you be so disrespectful!"
The two runners murmured in agreement,
apologizing profusely, claiming they hadn't known.
Soon, the sound of drums thundered like rolling thunder.
The man in green said:
"The morning court session is beginning."
So he led Hóu inside with him,
instructing him to stand below the steps,
saying:
"Wait here for now.
I will inquire on your behalf."
He then went up to the hall and gestured with his hand,
beckoning a clerk to come down.
After briefly explaining the situation,
the clerk saw Hóu,
clasped his hands, and said:
"Brother Hóu, you've come?
You don't have any major issues either.
There's a horse that has brought a lawsuit against you.
Once you confront each other in court, you can return."
With that, he bid farewell and left.
After a short while,
Hóu's name was called from the hall.
Hóu stepped forward and knelt,
and a horse also knelt.
The judge asked Hóu:
"The horse claims you poisoned it to death.
Is this true?"
Hóu replied:
"It contracted a plague disease,
and I treated it with a plague remedy.
After taking the medicine, it didn't recover,
and died the next day.
What does that have to do with me?"
The horse spoke in human language,
and the two argued bitterly.
The judge ordered the registry to be checked.
The registry recorded the horse's allotted lifespan and
the exact date it was fated to die.
The numbers matched precisely.
The judge then rebuked the horse:
"Your allotted lifespan had already ended.
How dare you bring a false accusation!"
He shouted at the horse to leave.
Then he said to Hóu:
"You have a compassionate heart,
so you may avoid death."
He then ordered the two runners to escort Hóu back.
The two men from earlier also came out together,
and they instructed the runners to take good care of Hóu on the journey.
Hóu said:
"Today, although I have received your protection,
I truly have never met you before in my life.
I beg you to tell me your names,
so that I may repay your kindness."
The man in green robes said:
"Three years ago,
I was traveling from Tàishān Mountain,
parched with thirst and near death.
Passing by your village,
you kindly gave me ladlefuls of porridge to drink.
I have never forgotten it to this day."
The clerk said:
"I am Liú Quán.
Previously, when my statue was soiled by bird droppings,
I was unbearably distressed.
You personally cleaned it for me,
and I have kept that kindness in my heart.
However, the wine and food of the underworld
cannot be offered to guests.
I must bid you farewell now."
Only then did Hóu understand,
and he returned.
Once he arrived home,
he warmly invited the two runners to stay.
But the runners didn't dare even drink a cup of water.
Hóu revived,
having been dead for over two days.
From then on, he devoted himself even more to good deeds.
Every festival season,
he would always offer wine and porridge to repay Liú Quán.
At eighty years old,
he was still strong and healthy,
able to leap onto carriages and run swiftly.
One day,
on the road, he saw Liú Quán riding a horse toward him,
as if about to embark on a long journey.
After exchanging greetings with clasped hands,
Liú said:
"Your allotted lifespan has ended.
The summons has been issued.
The underworld runners wanted to summon you,
but I stopped them, saying it wasn't necessary yet.
You should return home and prepare your affairs.
In three days,
I will come to accompany you on your journey.
I've arranged a minor position for you in the underworld,
so you won't suffer."
With that, he left.
Hóu returned home and informed his wife and children,
bidding farewell to relatives and friends.
The coffin and other funeral items were all prepared.
On the evening of the fourth day,
he said to everyone present:
"Brother Liú has come."
He then entered the coffin and passed away.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
When Jìngnì Hóu Zhāng Yǒng was stationed in Lánzhōu,
he went hunting and caught many rabbits.
Among them, some had half their bodies or both legs still made of earth.
For a time, in Qínzhōng, it was widely rumored that earth could transform into rabbits.
This is also a natural phenomenon that cannot be explained.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Shǐ Wūchéng from Yuànchéng was at home
when suddenly a bird alighted on his roof,
its color and fragrance resembling a crow.
When Shǐ saw it,
he told his family:
"My wife has sent a bird messenger to summon me.
Quickly prepare for my funeral affairs.
I will die on such-and-such day."
On that day, he indeed passed away.
On the day of the funeral,
the crow returned,
following the coffin and flying slowly,
from Yuànchéng to Xīnchéng.
After the burial,
the crow was no longer seen.
Wú Mùxīn of Chángshān witnessed this personally.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
The È family in Nányáng
was plagued by a fox spirit.
Money and various objects
were frequently stolen.
When they tried to drive it away,
the disturbances only worsened.
È had a nephew named Jī Shēng,
a scholar of unconventional character.
He burned incense and prayed on behalf of his uncle, asking for the fox to cease,
but it had no effect.
He then prayed, asking the fox to leave his grandfather's house and come to his own home instead,
but again, there was no response.
Everyone laughed at him.
Jī Shēng said:
"Since it can shapeshift,
it must possess a human heart.
I intend to guide it,
so that it may enter the right path."
Every few days, he would offer prayers.
Although no immediate effect was seen,
wherever Jī Shēng went,
the fox would cease its disturbances.
Because of this,
È often invited Jī Shēng to stay overnight.
At night, Jī Shēng would gaze into the empty air, requesting an audience,
and his invitations grew increasingly earnest.
One day,
Jī Shēng returned home
and was sitting alone in his study
when suddenly the door slowly opened by itself.
Jī Shēng stood up
and respectfully said:
“Has Brother Fox come?”
There was no sound at all.
Another night,
the door opened by itself.
The student said:
“If it is Brother Fox descending,
it is indeed what I have prayed and sought for;
why not bestow your luminous presence?”
Yet again there was silence.
On the desk were two hundred coins,
and by morning they were gone.
That night,
the student added several hundred more.
At midnight,
he heard the cloth curtain rustle.
The student said:
“Have you come?
I respectfully prepared several hundred coins for your use.
Although I am not affluent,
I am not a stingy person.
If you have urgent needs,
there is no harm in speaking plainly;
why resort to theft?”
After a while,
looking at the money,
two hundred coins were missing.
The student still placed them in the original spot,
and for several nights they were not lost again.
There was a cooked chicken,
intended for guests but it disappeared.
That evening,
the student added wine as well.
And from then on, the fox vanished.
The disturbances at the È family continued as before.
The student went again to pray, saying:
“I set out money but you did not take it,
I set out wine but you did not drink it;
my maternal grandfather is frail and aged,
do not haunt him for long.
I have prepared some humble offerings,
tonight you may take them as you wish.”
Then with ten thousand coins, a jar of wine,
and two chickens sliced thin,
he arranged them on the table.
The student lay down beside them,
all night there was no sound,
the money and items remained as they were.
The fox disturbances also ceased from then on.
One day the student returned late,
opened the study door,
and saw on the table a pot of wine,
a plate full of roasted chicken;
four hundred coins,
strung with a red cord—
these were the items lost earlier.
He knew it was the fox’s repayment.
Smelling the wine, it was fragrant;
pouring it, the color was emerald green;
drinking it, it was very mellow.
When the pot was half empty, he felt tipsy,
and suddenly felt greedy thoughts arise in his heart,
abruptly wanting to become a thief.
He then opened the door and went out.
Thinking of a wealthy family in the village,
he went and leaped over their wall.
Though the wall was high,
he leaped up and down as if
he had wings.
Entering their study,
he stole a marten coat
and a golden tripod, then left.
Returning, he placed them by the bedhead,
and only then lay down to sleep.
At daybreak,
he carried them into the inner chamber;
his wife, startled, asked about them.
The student stammered as he told her,
with a pleased expression.
His wife exclaimed in alarm:
“You have always been upright and honest;
why suddenly become a thief!”
The student was unperturbed and not surprised,
and thus recounted the fox’s affection.
His wife suddenly realized and said:
“This must be fox poison in the wine.”
Thinking that cinnabar can ward off evil,
she ground it into wine
and gave it to the student to drink.
After a short while,
the student suddenly cried out:
“How could I have become a thief!”
His wife explained the reason,
and he was dazed and at a loss.
Then hearing that the wealthy family had been robbed,
the news spread noisily through the neighborhood.
The student did not eat all day,
not knowing what to do.
His wife devised a plan for him,
telling him to throw the items back over the wall at night;
the student followed this.
The wealthy family recovered their original possessions.
The matter then subsided.
The student placed first in the annual examination,
and was also recommended for excellence,
deserving double reward.
When the time came for announcements,
a note was pasted on a beam in the government office, saying:
“Jī Mǒu is a thief,
stole someone’s coat and tripod;
why recommend him for excellence?”
The beam was very high,
not something one could reach on tiptoe to paste;
the examiner was suspicious.
Holding the note, he questioned the student.
The student was astonished,
thinking that aside from his wife no one knew of this matter;
moreover, the office was deep and secure,
how could it have gotten there?
Then he realized and said:
“This must be the work of the fox.”
He then recounted everything without concealment,
and the examiner increased his rewards and courtesies.
The student often thought to himself: he had not offended the fox;
the reason it repeatedly entrapped him
was also because a petty person is ashamed to be the only petty person.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
“The student wanted to lead the wicked to the right,
but was instead deluded by the wicked.
The fox’s intent was not necessarily greatly evil;
perhaps the student tried to guide it with humor,
and the fox also teased him in play.
Yet if he did not have innate virtue within himself,
and a wise helper at home,
how could he avoid, as Yuán Shè said,
that once a widow in the family is defiled as a thief,
she then proceeds to licentiousness!
Alas!
It is fearsome!”
Wú Mùxīn said:
“In the jiǎxū year of Kāngxī,
a provincial graduate was appointed in Zhèjiāng,
inspecting prisoners.
There was a thief,
already tattooed with characters.
By regulation, he should be released.
The official disliked that the character ‘steal’
was abbreviated in vulgar form,
not the official standard form;
he ordered it scraped off.
Waiting for the wound to heal,
then according to the strokes in the dictionary, he had it retattooed.
The thief improvised a quatrain:
‘Holding the mirror, I look carefully,
fresh blood drips, old marks remain.
Had I known my face would suffer again,
I’d have stolen from an official who can read.’”
The jailer laughed at him:
“A poet not seeking fame and fortune,
yet became a thief?”
The thief again improvised in reply:
‘In youth I studied the Way, aspiring to fame,
only poverty ruined my whole life.
Hoping to gain capital to invest,
I roamed Yān market to win favor and glory.’”
From this we see,
a scholar becoming a thief
is also due to ambition for official advancement.
The fox gave Jī Shēng the means to advance,
yet he regretted being misled by it—
how pedantic!
A laugh.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
A certain student from Ānqiū,
skilled in divination arts.
His character was wicked and unrestrained;
whenever he engaged in tunneling through walls or climbing over them,
he would divine.
One day he suddenly fell ill,
medicine could not cure him.
He said:
“I have truly seen something.
The underworld is angry that I have profaned heavenly principles,
and will severely punish me;
what can medicine do!”
Not long after,
There was a certain Mr. Jiǎ,
whose paternal uncle had no heir.
Jiǎ coveted his property,
and wished to become his successor.
After the uncle died,
all the farmland and property became his,
and he then broke his previous pledge.
There was also a paternal uncle,
whose family was rather well-off,
and also had no son.
Jiǎ again became his father.
When he died,
Jiǎ again broke his pledge.
Thus he combined the property of three families,
and became the richest man in the entire village.
One day,
he suddenly fell ill as if mad,
and said to himself:
"Do you wish to enjoy wealth and comfort while alive?!"
He then used a sharp blade to cut off his own flesh,
piece by piece throwing it to the ground.
He also said:
"You have cut off others' descendants,
do you still wish to have descendants?!"
He cut open his abdomen, spilling his intestines,
and then died.
Not long after,
his son also died,
and the property passed to others.
Such is the retribution of karma,
truly fearsome!
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
In Bǎodìng, there was a certain National University student,
who was about to go to the capital to pay money,
seeking to obtain the position of a county magistrate.
Just as he was packing, he fell ill,
and for over a month did not get up.
Suddenly a servant boy said:
"A guest has arrived."
The man also forgot his illness,
and hurried out to welcome the guest.
The guest was richly dressed, resembling a nobleman.
After three bows, they entered the house,
and he inquired where the guest came from.
The guest said:
Gōngsūn Xià,
am a guest of the Eleventh Prince.
I heard you are preparing to seek a county position;
since you have such ambition,
wouldn't a prefectural governorship be even better?"
The man modestly declined,
only saying:
"My funds are meager,
I dare not have such extravagant hopes."
The guest offered to help,
saying he would advance half the funds,
and they could settle the rest at the post.
The man happily asked for a plan.
The guest said:
"The governors are all sworn brothers of mine,
if you can temporarily get five thousand strings of cash,
the matter will be accomplished.
Currently there is a vacancy in Zhēndìng,
you can urgently seek it."
The man was surprised it was in his own province.
The guest laughed and said:
"You are too pedantic!
As long as there is money,
why ask whether it's Wú or Yuè, mulberry or catalpa?"
The man still hesitated,
doubting it was irregular.
The guest said:
"No need to doubt.
To tell you the truth: this is a vacancy for the City God in the underworld,
your lifespan is exhausted,
and you are already registered in the death records.
Take this opportunity to arrange it,
and you can still attain underworld nobility."
He then rose to bid farewell,
saying:
"You think it over yourself,
in three days we shall meet again."
Then he went out the door, mounted his horse, and left.
The man suddenly opened his eyes,
and bid eternal farewell to his wife and children.
He ordered his stored silver to be brought out,
and bought ten thousand bundles of paper ingots,
emptying the city of such items.
They piled them in the courtyard,
mixed with paper servants and ghost horses,
burning them day and night,
the ashes piling high like a mountain.
After three months,
the guest indeed returned.
The man handed over the funds,
and the guest led him to the office,
where he saw a high official sitting in the hall.
The man prostrated himself in worship.
The high official briefly checked his name,
then encouraged him with
words like "be honest and prudent."
Then he took the appointment document,
called him before the desk, and gave it to him.
The man kowtowed and left the office.
Thinking to himself that a National University student was lowly,
without carriages and robes to show off,
he could not awe his subordinates.
So he bought more carriages and horses;
he also sent ghost servants with a colorful carriage to fetch his beautiful concubine.
Just as the arrangements were completed,
the procession from Zhēndìng had already arrived.
On the road for over a li,
the retinue stretched continuously,
and he felt quite pleased.
Suddenly the vanguard stopped, and the flags drooped.
In shock and doubt,
he saw all the riders dismount,
and prostrate themselves along the roadside;
the people were about a foot tall,
the horses as big as wildcats.
Someone in front of the carriage cried out in fear:
"Lord Guān has arrived!"
The man was terrified,
got off the carriage, and also prostrated himself.
From afar, he saw Lord Guān with four or five riders,
approaching slowly with loose reins.
His beard was abundant, covering his cheeks,
unlike the portraits seen in the world;
yet his divine bearing was majestic and fierce,
his eyes long, almost reaching his ears.
From horseback he asked:
"What official is this?"
An attendant replied:
"The prefect of Zhēndìng."
Lord Guān said:
"For a mere prefecture,
why such pomp and display?!"
Hearing this,
the man felt a chill, his hair standing on end;
his body suddenly shrank,
and looking at himself, he was like a six- or seven-year-old child.
Lord Guān ordered him to rise,
and made him follow alongside the horse's hooves.
By the roadside was a temple hall,
Lord Guān entered,
sat facing south,
and ordered writing materials given to the man,
making him write his native place and name himself.
After the man finished writing,
he presented it.
Lord Guān looked at it,
and angrily said:
"The characters are distorted and unrecognizable!
This is nothing but a market huckster,
unfit to govern the people!"
He then ordered an examination of his virtue record.
A person kneeling beside him reported something,
but I could not make out what was said.
The Emperor sternly declared:
"Seeking advancement is a minor offense,
but selling official positions is a grave crime!"
Immediately, a golden-armored deity bound him with chains and led him away.
Then two men seized me,
stripped off my official robes and hat,
and gave me fifty lashes.
My buttocks were nearly torn apart,
and I was driven out the gate.
Looking around, I saw all my carriages and horses had vanished.
The pain made it impossible to walk,
so I lay down to rest in the grass.
Upon closer inspection of the place,
I realized I was not far from home.
Fortunately, my body felt as light as a leaf,
and after a day and a night, I finally reached home.
Suddenly, as if awakening from a dream,
I groaned in bed.
My family gathered to ask what had happened,
but I only said my thighs hurt.
It turned out I had lain unconscious as if dead
for seven days,
and only then did I revive.
I immediately asked:
"Why hasn't Ālián come?"
— for that was my concubine's pet name.
Earlier,
while Ālián was sitting and chatting,
she suddenly said:
"He has become the prefect of Zhēndìng,
and has sent attendants to fetch me."
She then went into her room to dress formally,
and after finishing her toilette, she died —
it had only been the previous night.
My family recounted this strange event.
I, filled with regret and remorse, beat my chest,
and ordered her body not to be buried,
hoping she would return.
After several days with no sign,
she was finally buried.
My illness gradually healed,
but the sores on my thighs were severe,
and it took half a year before I could rise.
I often said:
"All my official wealth is gone,
and I unjustly suffered punishment in the underworld —
that I can still bear;
but not knowing where my beloved concubine has been taken
is what makes the quiet nights unbearable."
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Alas!
Market hucksters are indeed unfit to rule!
Since the underworld already has its connections,
I fear even the sage's teachings cannot reach there,
and those who abuse power for personal gain
are too numerous to punish.
In the biography of my townsman, Mr. Guō Huáyě, there is an incident
quite similar to this,
showing he was a veritable deity among men.
Mr. Guō, known for his integrity and uprightness, enjoyed the emperor's favor,
and was reappointed as Governor-General of Jīngchǔ.
His luggage was simple,
with only four or five attendants,
all in worn clothes and shoes,
so that people on the road had no idea he was a high official.
It happened that a new magistrate was on his way to assume office,
and their paths crossed.
The magistrate had over twenty camel-drawn carriages,
dozens of outriders in front,
and a retinue numbering in the hundreds.
Mr. Guō did not know what official he was,
sometimes riding ahead of him,
sometimes behind,
and sometimes mingling a few of his own riders among the magistrate's party.
The magistrate's advance guards, angered by this disturbance,
repeatedly shouted at them to fall back;
but Mr. Guō paid no heed.
Before long,
they reached a large town,
where both parties stopped to rest.
Mr. Guō then sent someone to discreetly inquire,
and learned he was a National University student,
who had purchased an appointment and was on his way to assume office in Húnán.
Mr. Guō then sent a messenger to summon him.
The magistrate, hearing the summons, was shocked and suspicious,
and in turn asked about the summoner's rank and family,
only then realizing it was Mr. Guō.
Trembling with fear, he found himself with nowhere to hide.
In full official dress, he crawled forward on his knees.
Mr. Guō asked: 'Are you the magistrate of such-and-such county?'
He replied: 'Yes, I am.'
Mr. Guō said: 'Such a tiny district,
how can it support such a large retinue?
Once you assume office,
the people will be plunged into misery!
I cannot allow you to bring calamity upon the people.
You may turn back now,
and proceed no further.'
The magistrate kowtowed and said: 'Your Excellency, I still have my official credentials.'
Mr. Guō immediately ordered him to present them,
and after examining them, said:
'This is a minor matter.
I can hand them in for you.'
The magistrate prostrated himself in thanks and withdrew.
On his return journey, one can imagine his state of mind,
while Mr. Guō continued on his way.
That there exists in this world someone who faces evaluation before even taking up his post
is truly unheard of.
Mr. Guō was an extraordinary man,
hence this satisfying incident."
According to the Shāndōng Provincial Museum manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
In the late Míng dynasty,
in several districts north of Jǐjùn,
a virulent epidemic broke out,
affecting every household.
A farmer from Qídōng named Hán Fāng,
was extremely filial.
Both his parents fell ill,
so he prepared paper money and offerings,
and went weeping to pray at the temple of the Gūshí Dàfū.
On his way back, he was still shedding tears.
He met a man
dressed in clean, neat clothes,
who asked:
"Why are you grieving?"
Hán told him the whole story.
The man said:
"The deity of Gūshí
is not present here.
What good will praying do?
I have a small technique
that you might try."
Hán was delighted
and asked his name.
The man said:
"I seek no reward,
why must you know my hometown?"
Hán earnestly invited him to his home.
The man said:
"That is unnecessary.
Just return home,
place a sheet of yellow paper on the bed,
and say sternly: 'Tomorrow I will go to the capital
to report you to the Great Emperor of the Eastern Peak!'
Then the illness should cease."
Hán, fearing it might not work,
insisted he come along.
The man said:
"To tell you the truth, I am not human.
The Circuit Inspector, considering me sincere and honest,
appointed me as the local earth god of Nánxiàn.
Moved by your filial piety,
I am instructing you in this method.
Currently, the Great Emperor of the Eastern Peak is selecting from among the deceased ghosts
those who have benefited the people,
or who are upright and do not work evil,
to appoint as city gods or earth gods.
Those causing the current calamity
are all ghosts of people killed by the northern soldiers near the prefectural city.
Eager to go to the capital to present themselves,
they are extorting bribes along the way
to pay for food and drink.
If you threaten to report them to the Great Emperor,
they will surely become afraid,
and so the illness will stop."
Hán, awestruck and respectful,
knelt and kowtowed in thanks.
When he rose,
the man had vanished.
Hán returned home in amazement,
followed his instructions,
and both his parents recovered.
He passed the method on to neighboring villages,
and it proved effective in every case.
The Historian of the Strange remarks:
"To travel along the way harming people,
in order to seek not to be used for evil purposes,
how is this any different from galloping on horseback to answer the call of the 'examination for those who do not seek fame or success'?
Most affairs under heaven are of this sort.
I still recall between the years Jiǎxū and Yǐhài,
when those in charge ordered the people to donate grain,
and submitted a memorial claiming the people were 'joyfully contributing'.
Thus, each prefecture and county extracted the full amount as demanded,
resorting much to flogging and beating.
At that time, the seven counties north of the commandery were flooded,
the harvest failed,
making the collection efforts especially difficult.
Censor Dà Shǐ happened to arrive in Lìjīn,
and saw over ten people bound and arrested.
He therefore asked:
'For what matter?'
They replied:
'The officials seized us to take to the city,
to press and pursue the "joyful contribution".'
The farmers did not know what the two characters 'joyful contribution' meant,
so they took it as the name for corvée labor and oppressive exaction.
Is this not both lamentable and laughable!"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Yú Xiǎosī
was a man from Dōngchāng.
He made his living by hoarding goods for trade.
His wife, Xià,
returning from a visit to her parents, saw an old woman outside the gate,
accompanied by a young girl, weeping bitterly.
Xià questioned them,
and the old woman, wiping her tears, told her.
It turned out her husband was Wáng Xīnzhāi,
also a merchant-official.
His family had declined,
leaving him without means for food or clothing.
He had requested a middleman-guarantor to borrow money from a wealthy man named Huáng,
to engage in trade.
On the journey, he encountered bandits,
lost his capital,
but fortunately survived.
Upon returning home,
Huáng pressed for repayment.
The total principal and interest amounted to no less than thirty taels,
and he truly had nothing to pledge as security.
Huáng, noticing his daughter Rènzhēn was beautiful,
plotted to take her as a concubine.
He had the middleman-guarantor convey the proposal: if willing,
besides canceling the debt,
he would still give ten taels as a pledge token.
Wáng consulted his wife.
His wife wept and said:
"Although we are poor,
we are descendants of official families.
He rose to fortune from being a lowly driver;
how dare he presume to take our daughter as a concubine!
Moreover, Rènzhēn already has a betrothed;
how can you make such a decision on your own!"
Previously,
the son of Provincial Graduate Fù from the same county,
was on friendly terms with Wáng.
They had a son named Ā Mǎo,
and while still in swaddling clothes, they arranged a marriage.
Later, Provincial Graduate Fù took office in Mǐn,
and after over a year, he died.
His wife and son could not return,
and all news and communication ceased.
Therefore, Rènzhēn was now fifteen,
and still not betrothed.
When his wife mentioned this,
Wáng had no reply,
and could only ponder what to do.
His wife said:
"If there's no other way,
perhaps try consulting my two brothers."
It turned out his wife, née Fàn,
had a grandfather who once held a post in the capital,
and her two brothers still possessed considerable land and property.
The next day,
the wife took her daughter to tell her two brothers.
The two brothers let her weep and plead,
but did not utter a single word willing to help arrange matters.
Fàn then returned wailing.
It happened that she encountered Xià questioning her,
and she told her story while crying.
Xià Liánzhī looked at the girl,
finding her graceful and lovely,
and felt even more sorrowful for them.
She then invited them into her home,
treated them to food and drink,
and comforted them, saying:
"Do not grieve, mother and daughter.
I will do my utmost."
Before Fàn could express her thanks,
the girl had already knelt weeping on the ground.
Feeling even more pity for them,
Xià pondered and said:
"Although I have some modest savings,
thirty taels of silver is still a great difficulty.
I will pawn some belongings to give you the money."
Mother and daughter bowed in gratitude.
Xià set a three-day deadline,
and after they parted,
she tried every possible means to raise the money,
not daring to tell her husband about it.
On the third day,
she had not yet gathered the full amount,
so she sent someone to borrow from her mother.
When Fàn and her daughter arrived,
Xià told them the truth,
and scheduled for the next day.
By evening: the borrowed money arrived,
and she wrapped it together with her own savings and placed it by the bedside.
During the night,
a thief broke through the wall,
entering with a torch.
Xià awoke,
glanced over,
and saw a man with a short knife strapped to his arm,
his appearance fierce and menacing.
Terrified,
she dared not make a sound,
pretending to be asleep.
The thief approached the chest,
intending to break the lock.
Looking back,
he noticed a wrapped bundle by Xià's pillow,
reached over and snatched it away,
then went to the lamp to unwrap and examine it;
finding it was a money pouch,
he did not bother with the chest and left.
Xià then got up and cried out.
There was only a young maid at home,
who called out to the neighbors over the wall,
but by the time the neighbors gathered, the thief was already far away.
Xià then wept by the lamp.
Seeing the maid sound asleep,
she took a belt and hanged herself from the window frame.
At dawn, the maid awoke,
called for help to rescue her,
but Xià's limbs were already cold.
Yú, hearing the news, rushed over,
questioned the maid to learn the cause,
and, weeping in shock, arranged the funeral.
It was then summer,
and the body did not stiffen,
nor did it decay.
After seven days,
she was placed in the coffin.
After the burial,
Rènzhēn slipped out,
weeping at her grave.
Suddenly, a heavy rainstorm gathered,
and thunder roared mightily,
splitting open the grave,
and Rènzhēn was struck dead by lightning.
Yú, hearing of this,
rushed to check,
and found the coffin already opened,
with his wife moaning inside.
He carried her out.
Seeing the girl's body,
he did not know who she was.
Xià examined her closely,
and only then recognized her.
They were just marveling at this strange event
when, shortly after,
Fàn arrived,
saw her daughter dead,
and cried:
"I suspected she might be here,
and now it is indeed so!
Hearing that Madam had hanged herself,
she wept day and night without cease.
Tonight she told me
she wished to weep at the burial chamber,
and I did not agree."
Moved by her devotion,
Xià spoke with her husband,
and they buried the girl in the prepared grave.
Fàn bowed in gratitude.
Yú carried his wife home,
and Fàn also returned to tell her husband.
They heard that a man north of the village had been struck dead by lightning on the road,
with words written on his body:
"Thief who stole Xià's money."
Soon, they heard the wailing of a neighboring woman,
and realized the lightning-struck man was her husband, Mǎ Dà.
The villagers reported to the authorities,
who arrested the woman and interrogated her under torture.
It turned out that Fàn had spoken of Xià raising money to redeem her daughter,
expressing her gratitude to others,
and Mǎ Dà, a gambling rogue,
upon hearing this, conceived the idea of theft.
The officials pressed the woman to recover the stolen goods,
but only about twenty taels remained;
inspecting Mǎ Dà's corpse yielded four more.
The officials ruled that the woman be sold to make up the difference and repay Yú.
Xià was even more delighted,
and returned all the money to Fàn,
to repay the creditor.
Three days after the girl's burial,
a night of great thunder, lightning, and wind
split open the grave again,
and the girl suddenly revived.
Instead of returning to her home,
she went to knock on Xià's door,
having recognized her grave,
and suspecting she had come back to life.
Startled, Xià rose,
and asked through the door.
The girl said:
"Has Madam truly come back to life!
I am Rènzhēn."
Xià, terrified, thought it was a ghost,
and called a neighbor to question her.
Learning she had revived,
she happily let her into the house.
The girl said:
"I wish to serve Madam,
and will not return home."
Xià said:
"Do you think I spent money to buy a maid?
After your burial,
the debt was already repaid for you,
so do not doubt me."
The girl, even more moved, wept,
and wished to treat her as a mother.
Xià would not allow it.
The girl said:
"I can work,
and will not sit idle and eat for free."
At dawn, they informed Fàn,
who was overjoyed,
and hurried over.
Following her daughter's wishes,
she entrusted her to Xià.
After Fàn left,
Xià insisted on sending the girl back.
The girl wept, longing for Xià.
Wáng Xīnzhāi himself brought his daughter,
left her at the gate, and departed.
Xià, seeing her, asked in surprise,
and only then learned the reason,
so she accepted it.
When the girl saw Yú arrive,
she quickly bowed,
calling him father.
Yú had no children of his own,
and seeing the girl so affectionate and clever,
he was quite pleased.
The girl spun, wove, and sewed,
diligent and thorough in her work.
Once, when Xià fell seriously ill,
the girl attended to her day and night.
Seeing Xià not eating,
she also refused to eat;
tear stains often marked her face,
and she told others:
"If anything happens to mother,
I vow not to live on!"
When Xià slightly recovered,
she finally relaxed and smiled.
Hearing this, Xià shed tears,
and said:
"I am forty without a child,
but if I could have a daughter like Rènzhēn, it would be enough."
Xià had never borne children;
but the following year, she suddenly gave birth to a son,
and people believed it was the reward for her good deeds.
Two years later,
the girl grew older.
Yú and Wáng discussed the matter,
but could not firmly adhere to the old agreement.
Wáng said:
"The girl is in your household,
her marriage is entirely at your discretion."
The girl was seventeen,
virtuous and beautiful beyond compare.
Once these words were spoken,
those inquiring about her name crowded at the door,
and the couple began selecting a suitable family.
Huáng also sent a matchmaker,
but Yú despised his wealth without benevolence,
and firmly rejected him.
They chose the Féng family instead.
Féng,
a renowned scholar in the county,
had a son who was intelligent and skilled in writing.
They intended to inform Wáng;
but Wáng had gone out trading and had not yet returned,
so they directly agreed to the match.
Huáng, having failed with Yú,
also pretended to be a merchant,
tracked down Wáng's whereabouts,
prepared a feast to invite him,
and further assisted him with capital,
gradually becoming familiar and friendly.
He then spoke of his own son's intelligence to propose a match,
Wáng was moved by his sincerity,
and also admired his wealth,
so he entered into an agreement with him.
After returning,
he went to see Yú,
only to find that Yú had already accepted the marriage contract from the Féng family the day before.
Hearing what Wáng said,
Yú was displeased,
called the girl out,
and told her the situation.
The girl angrily said:
"The creditor,
he is my enemy!
To marry me to an enemy,
I would rather die!"
Wáng was ashamed,
and sent someone to inform Huáng about the agreement with the Féng family.
Huáng angrily said:
"The girl's surname is Wáng,
not Yú.
My agreement came first,
his agreement came later,
how can he break it!"
So he filed a lawsuit with the county magistrate,
and the magistrate intended to award the girl to Huáng based on the earlier agreement.
Féng said:
"Wáng entrusted the girl to Yú,
clearly stating he would no longer interfere in her marriage,
and moreover, I have a formal marriage contract,
while his was merely a casual conversation over wine."
The magistrate could not decide,
and planned to follow the girl's own wishes.
Huáng again bribed the officials with money,
seeking their partiality,
so the case remained unresolved for over a month.
One day,
a Provincial Graduate heading north to the capital,
his carriage passed through Dōngchāng,
and he sent someone to ask for Wáng Xīnzhāi.
He happened to ask Yú,
and Yú inquired in return,
it turned out the Provincial Graduate's surname was Fù,
and he was none other than Ā Mǎo.
He had registered in Fújiàn,
and at eighteen had already passed the provincial examination.
He had not yet married due to the previous agreement.
His mother instructed him to visit Wáng while passing through,
to ask if the girl had been betrothed to someone else.
Yú was overjoyed,
invited Fù to his home,
and recounted all that had happened.
However, the groom had come from thousands of miles away,
and they worried there was no proof.
Fù opened his trunk,
and produced the marriage agreement Wáng had given that day.
Yú summoned Wáng,
verified it was indeed genuine,
and they all rejoiced.
That day, the case was to be reviewed by the magistrate,
Fù presented his card and visited the magistrate,
and the case was finally dismissed.
They selected an auspicious date and set the wedding before he left.
After the metropolitan examination,
he purchased silk and cloth as gifts and returned,
stayed at his old residence,
and performed the wedding ceremony.
The news of his passing the imperial examination had already reached Fújiàn,
and was also reported in the east,
Fù had again succeeded in the palace examination.
He then went to the capital to observe administrative affairs before returning.
The girl was unwilling to go south,
and Fù also had his father's grave to attend to,
so he went alone to collect his father's coffin,
and brought his mother back with him.
Several years later,
Yú passed away,
his son was only seven or eight years old,
the girl raised him even more lovingly than her own brother.
She had him study,
and he entered the county school,
the family was considered well-off,
all due to Fù's efforts.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"Are there also wandering knights among divine dragons?
Promoting good and punishing evil,
both life and death come with thunder,
this is the 'Qiántáng Breaking Formation Dance.'
The thunderous strikes,
repeatedly,
were all for one person.
Who knows if Rènzhēn was not a dragon maiden banished to the mortal realm?"
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Péng Hǎoshì of Jīngzhōu,
returning from drinking at a friend's house.
He dismounted to relieve himself,
while his horse grazed by the roadside.
There was a small patch of fine grass,
lush and lovely,
just beginning to bloom with yellow flowers,
their dazzling brilliance captivating the eye.
The horse had already eaten more than half of it.
Péng plucked the remaining stems,
sniffed them and found they had an unusual fragrance,
so he tucked them into his robe.
Mounting his horse again to continue his journey,
the horse galloped with astonishing speed,
making him feel quite exhilarated.
He didn’t even think about the way home,
but simply let the horse go wherever it pleased.
Suddenly, he saw the evening sun setting behind the mountains,
and only then thought to turn the reins back.
But all he saw were chaotic, thickly clustered mountains,
with no idea where he was.
A man in dark clothing approached,
saw the horse snorting and neighing,
and took hold of the bit for him,
saying:
"It’s nearly dusk,
my master invites you to stay the night."
Péng asked:
"What place is this?"
He replied:
"Làngzhōng."
Péng was greatly startled,
for he had traveled over a thousand li in half a day.
So he asked:
"Who is your master?"
The man said:
"You’ll know when you get there."
Péng asked again:
"Where is it?"
He replied:
"Just a stone’s throw away."
Then, taking the reins, he led the horse swiftly onward,
man and horse flying as if on wings.
Crossing a mountain ridge,
they saw halfway up the slope a complex of buildings,
interspersed with screens and curtains.
From afar, a crowd of well-dressed figures could be seen,
as if waiting for something.
Péng dismounted upon arrival,
and they exchanged respectful bows.
Soon after,
the host came out,
his demeanor fierce and imposing,
his attire entirely different from that of the mortal world.
He clasped his hands toward the guest,
saying:
"Among today’s guests,
none has come from farther than you, Master Péng."
Then, bowing to Péng,
he invited him to enter first.
Péng modestly declined,
unwilling to go ahead.
The host took him by the arm and led him forward.
Péng felt as if the place where he was gripped was clamped in shackles,
the pain almost breaking his bones.
Not daring to argue further,
he went along.
As for the others,
they were still deferring to one another,
but the host either pushed them
or pulled them along.
The guests all groaned and stumbled,
seeming unable to bear it,
yet they all complied with the host’s command.
Entering the hall,
they found the furnishings dazzlingly splendid,
with two guests seated at each banquet table.
Péng quietly asked the person sitting next to him:
"Who is the host?"
He replied:
"This is Zhāng Huánhóu."
Péng was stunned,
not daring to make another sound.
The entire hall fell silent.
When the wine was served,
Huánhóu said:
"Every year I impose on my relatives and guests,
so I’ve prepared a humble feast,
to express my modest sentiments.
That a guest from afar has graced us with his presence
is indeed a fortunate encounter.
I have a presumptuous request to make;
if you have even a little fondness or attachment,
I will not insist."
Péng rose and asked:
"What is it?"
He said:
"Your steed already possesses immortal bones,
and cannot be driven by mortal means.
I wish to buy a horse in exchange,
what do you say?"
Péng said:
"I respectfully offer it to you,
and dare not accept an exchange."
Marquis Huán said:
"I shall repay you with a fine horse,
and moreover will bestow upon you ten thousand in gold."
Péng left his seat and prostrated himself in thanks.
Marquis Huán ordered someone to pull him up.
In a moment,
wine and delicacies were spread out in abundance.
As the sun set,
he ordered candles lit.
The guests rose to take their leave,
and Péng also bid farewell.
Marquis Huán said:
"You have come from afar; where will you return to?"
Péng looked at his fellow guest and said:
"I have already asked this gentleman to be my host."
Marquis Huán then filled a large goblet for each guest in turn,
and said to Péng:
"The fragrant herb you carry,
when fresh, can make one an immortal;
when dried, it can turn things to gold.
With seven stalks of the herb,
you obtain ten thousand in gold."
He immediately ordered a servant to bring out the formula and give it to Péng.
Péng bowed again in thanks.
Marquis Huán said:
"Tomorrow, go to the market,
and from among the horses, choose any fine one you wish,
there is no need to bargain over the price,
I will pay for it myself."
He also told the others:
"Our guest from afar is returning home,
you may assist him a little with travel funds."
They all assented.
When the wine was finished,
they thanked him and departed.
On the road, they finally asked each other their names;
the fellow guest was Liú Zǐcuì.
After walking two or three lǐ together,
crossing a ridge, they saw a village.
The guests accompanied Péng to Liú's place,
and then began to recount the strange events.
Previously,
the village held an annual festival at the temple of Marquis Huán,
with animal sacrifices and theatrical performances,
which had become a customary practice,
and Liú was the chief organizer.
Three days before,
the festival had just concluded.
That noon,
each household had one person invited to cross the mountain.
When asked,
the explanation was rather vague,
but the urging was very insistent.
Crossing the mountain, they saw a pavilion and lodge,
and were all astonished and puzzled.
As they approached the gate,
the messenger finally told them the truth;
they also dared not retreat.
The messenger said:
"Gather here for now,
the invitation for the two guests from afar has arrived."
These were Péng and his companion.
The others recounted this with amazement.
Among them, those who had been grasped by the arm
all suffered from arm pain;
when they undressed and examined by candlelight,
the flesh inside was black and blue.
Péng looked at himself and found it was the same.
The crowd dispersed,
and Liú immediately prepared bedding for Péng to sleep.
When it was light,
the villagers vied to invite the guest;
they also accompanied Péng to the market to look at horses.
For over ten days,
they examined several dozen horses,
but unfortunately found no good ones;
Péng was also prepared to settle for one.
Entering the market again,
he saw a horse whose bone structure seemed good;
he mounted it to try,
and it was incomparably spirited and swift.
He rode straight into the village,
to wait for the seller;
going back to look for him,
the man had already left,
so he bid farewell to the villagers and prepared to return.
The villagers each gave him money for the journey,
and he returned.
The horse could travel five hundred lǐ in a day.
Arriving home,
he recounted where he had come from,
but people did not believe him.
Taking out items from Shǔ from his bag,
they finally all found it strange.
The fragrant herb had long dried,
and it happened to be seven stalks;
following the formula to perform the transmutation,
his family suddenly became very wealthy.
He then respectfully went to the former place,
personally held a ceremony at the temple of Marquis Huán,
and had theatrical performances for three days before returning.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"Having witnessed Marquis Huán feasting guests,
I then believe that the tale of Wǔyí's Màntíng is not fabricated.
However, the host's vigorous hospitality
caused those who received his affection to almost have their arms broken,
so one can imagine his bravery and strength in his prime."
Wú Mùxīn said:
"There was a certain Mr. Lǐ,
whose lips did not cover his front teeth,
which protruded by a full finger's width.
One day,
at a banquet gathering somewhere,
two guests were deferring to each other over seating precedence,
and their dispute was quite intense.
One forcefully pulled the other forward,
the other forcefully pulled back.
In the midst of the violent tugging, they suddenly came apart,
and Mr. Lǐ happened to be standing behind them,
their elbows struck his mouth as they flew past,
and both his front teeth fell out,
blood pouring down like a fountain.
Everyone was stunned,
and their dispute then ceased."
This, along with Marquis Huán's arm-grasping that bruised the flesh,
is equally laughable.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*
Yáng Yuēdàn was a scholar from Qióngzhōu.
Once, while returning from another commandery,
he was sailing on the sea
when a hurricane struck,
and his boat was about to capsize.
Suddenly, an empty boat drifted toward him,
and he quickly leaped aboard.
Looking back,
he saw that everyone on his original boat had perished.
The wind grew even fiercer,
and he closed his eyes, letting it carry him wherever it would.
After a while,
the wind subsided.
Opening his eyes,
he suddenly saw an island
with rows of houses stretching into the distance.
Rowing the boat ashore,
he went straight to the village gate.
The village was utterly silent;
he walked and sat for a long time,
but not even a dog or chicken was heard.
He saw a gate facing north,
shaded by pines and bamboos.
It was already early winter,
yet inside the wall, he saw a tree full of buds—he did not know what flower it was—
and he felt a fond delight for it.
Hesitating for a moment, he entered.
From afar, he heard the sound of a zither,
and paused his steps.
A maid came out from within,
about fourteen or fifteen years old,
graceful and strikingly beautiful.
Upon seeing Yáng,
she turned and hurried back inside.
Soon, the zither music ceased,
and a young man emerged,
asking in surprise where the guest had come from.
Yáng told him everything.
The young man then inquired about his family and lineage,
and Yáng answered again.
The young man said happily,
"We are relatives by marriage!"
He then bowed and invited Yáng into the courtyard.
Inside, the study was elegant and splendid,
and the sound of the zither could be heard again.
Upon entering the room,
he saw a young woman sitting upright,
just tuning the red strings.
She appeared to be about eighteen or nineteen,
radiant and graceful.
Seeing the guest,
she pushed aside the zither and was about to leave,
but the young man stopped her, saying,
"Do not go;
this is indeed a relative of yours."
He then recounted the circumstances on her behalf.
The young woman said,
"This is my nephew."
She then asked him,
"Is your grandmother still in good health?
How old are your parents now?"
Yáng replied,
"My parents are in their forties,
and both are well.
Only my grandmother is sixty
and suffers from a severe, lingering illness—
she needs someone to support her even when taking a step.
I truly do not know which branch of the family you belong to, Aunt;
I hope you will tell me clearly,
so I can report back when I return."
The young woman said,
"The roads are long and distant,
and news has been cut off for a long time.
When you return, just tell your father,
'Shí Gū sends her regards,'
and he will understand."
Yáng asked,
"What is your husband's family name?"
The young man said,
"My surname is Yàn, from Hǎiyǔ.
This place is called Shénxiān Dǎo,
three thousand lǐ from Qióngzhōu.
I have not been living here for long either."
Shí Niáng hurried inside
and had the maid serve wine and food to the guest.
The fresh vegetables were fragrant and delicious,
though he did not know their names.
After the meal,
he was led around to admire the scenery.
Seeing peach and apricot trees in the garden still in bud,
he found it rather strange.
Yàn said,
"Here, there is no extreme heat in summer
and no severe cold in winter;
flowers bloom without interruption."
Yáng said happily,
"This is truly a land of immortals.
When I return, I will tell my parents,
and we can move here to be your neighbors."
Yàn merely smiled.
Returning to the study and lighting a candle,
he saw a zither lying across the table.
He requested to hear an elegant tune.
Yàn then touched the strings and adjusted the pegs.
Shíniáng came out from inside,
and Yàn said:
"Come,
come!
You should play something nice for him."
Shíniáng immediately sat down
and asked her nephew:
"What would you like to hear?"
Yáng said:
"Your nephew has never studied the 'Qín Cāo,'
so I truly have no particular wish."
Shíniáng said:
"Just name any theme at will,
and I can compose a melody."
Yáng laughed and said:
"A sea wind guiding a boat—
could that be made into a tune?"
Shíniáng said:
"Yes."
She immediately pressed the strings and plucked them,
as if following an old score;
the melody surged and tumbled.
Listening intently,
it felt as if he were still on the boat,
being tossed about by a typhoon.
Yáng was utterly amazed and exclaimed,
asking:
"Can this be learned?"
Shíniáng handed him the zither
and had him try plucking the strings,
saying:
"You can be taught.
What do you wish to learn?"
He said:
"The 'Typhoon Melody' you just played—
I wonder how many days it would take to learn?
Please first record the tune
so I can chant and recite it."
Shíniáng said:
"This has no written notation;
I composed it from my own inspiration."
So she took another zither,
demonstrated the plucking motions,
and had Yáng imitate her.
Yáng practiced until past the first watch,
roughly matching the rhythm and notes,
and then the couple bid him farewell and left.
Yáng, with his eyes fixed and heart captivated,
played by himself facing the candle;
after a long while,
he suddenly gained a wonderful insight,
and unconsciously began to dance.
Lifting his head,
he suddenly saw a maidservant standing under the lamp.
Startled, he said:
"So you haven't left yet?"
The maidservant smiled and said:
"Shígū ordered me to wait until you retire to bed,
to close the door and move the lamp stand."
Looking at her carefully,
her eyes were clear as autumn water,
and her expression was utterly charming.
Yáng felt his heart stir
and subtly teased her;
the maidservant lowered her head with a smile.
Yáng grew even more infatuated
and abruptly stood up to embrace her by the neck.
The maidservant said:
"Don't!
The night is already in the fourth watch,
the master will soon rise.
If we both have feelings,
tomorrow night is not too late."
Just as they were embracing,
they heard Yàn call
"Fěndié."
The maidservant changed expression and said:
"This is bad!"
She hurriedly ran away.
Yáng stealthily went to listen.
He only heard Yàn say:
"I always said this maid's worldly attachments were not yet severed,
yet you insisted on taking her in.
Now see what has happened—
she deserves three hundred lashes!"
Shíniáng said:
"Once this kind of thought sprouts,
she can no longer be kept in service.
It would be better to send her away with my nephew."
Yáng felt deeply ashamed and fearful.
He returned to the study, extinguished the candle, and went to bed.
At daybreak,
a boy came to attend to his washing and grooming,
but Fěndié was no longer to be seen.
His heart was uneasy, fearing he would be reprimanded and expelled.
Soon, Yàn and Shígū both came out,
seeming to bear no grudge,
and proceeded to examine his studies.
Yáng played a tune.
Shíniáng said:
"Although not yet divine,
you have grasped ninety percent of it.
With diligent practice, you can achieve perfection."
Yáng again requested to learn another piece.
Yàn taught him
the tune "Celestial Maiden Descending,"
with intricate and difficult fingering.
He practiced for three days
before he could play the piece.
Yàn said:
"The essentials have all been taught.
From now on, you only need to practice diligently.
Once you master these two pieces,
there will be no difficult tunes in zither music for you."
Yáng began to miss home deeply
and told Shíniáng:
"Although staying here
and being cared for by you, Aunt, is very pleasant;
I am concerned about my family's worries.
I am three thousand lǐ from home—
when will I ever be able to return!"
Shíniáng said:
"That is not difficult.
The old boat is still there;
I shall assist with a favorable wind.
Since you have no wife,
I have already sent Fěndié away."
Then she gave him the zither as a gift
and also handed him some medicine, saying:
"Return and treat your grandmother with this.
It will not only cure her illness
but also prolong her life."
Then they escorted him to the seashore
and had him board the boat.
Yáng looked for an oar,
