but Shíniáng said:
"That is not needed."
So she untied her skirt to make a sail
and fastened it for him.
Yáng worried about losing his way,
but Shíniáng said:
"Do not worry;
just listen to the sail fluttering."
Once it was fastened,
she disembarked.
Yáng felt sorrowful
and was about to bow in thanks and farewell,
when a south wind suddenly rose,
and he was already far from the shore.
Looking in the boat, he found provisions had been prepared, but only enough for one day's meal.
He inwardly complained about their stinginess.
Hungry but afraid to eat much,
fearing it would run out too quickly,
he only nibbled on one sesame cake,
finding it sweet and fragrant inside and out.
The remaining six or seven cakes
he treasured and saved,
and then he no longer felt hungry.
Soon he saw the sun about to set
and regretted not asking for lamp oil and candles when he left.
In an instant,
he saw signs of human habitation in the distance;
looking carefully,
it was Qióngzhōu.
He was overjoyed.
Shortly, he was close to shore,
wrapped the cakes in the skirt, and returned home.
Upon entering the door,
the whole family was startled and overjoyed,
for he had been away from home for sixteen years,
and only then did they learn that he had encountered an immortal.
Seeing that his grandmother was old and increasingly ill;
he took out medicine and gave it to her,
and her long-standing illness was immediately cured.
Everyone asked him in astonishment,
so he recounted what he had seen.
His grandmother, with tears in her eyes, said:
"That was your aunt."
In the beginning,
the old lady had a youngest daughter,
named Shíniáng,
who was born with an immortal's grace.
She was betrothed to a man from the Yàn family.
When the groom was sixteen years old,
he entered the mountains and never returned.
Shíniáng waited until she was over twenty,
when suddenly, without any illness, she passed away,
and had been buried for over thirty years.
Upon hearing Dàn's words,
everyone suspected that she had not died.
They took out her skirt,
and it was indeed the one she had often worn at home.
They divided the cake and ate it,
and one piece kept them from hunger all day,
while their spirits were doubly invigorated.
The old lady ordered the grave to be opened for examination,
and only an empty coffin remained inside.
Dàn had initially been betrothed to a daughter of the Wú family but had not yet married her.
As Dàn did not return for several years,
she married someone else.
Everyone believed Shíniáng's words,
and waited for Fěndié to arrive;
but after more than a year with no news,
they began to discuss other plans.
In the neighboring county, a scholar named Qián,
had a daughter named Hésheng,
whose beauty was widely known.
At sixteen,
she had not yet married but had lost three fiancés.
So they arranged a match through a matchmaker,
and chose an auspicious day for the wedding.
After entering the door,
her beauty was unparalleled.
When Dàn looked at her,
it was Fěndié.
He asked in surprise about past events,
but the girl was completely unaware.
It turned out that the time she was expelled
was the moment of her rebirth.
Whenever he played for her
the tune "The Heavenly Maiden's Descent,"
she would rest her chin and ponder deeply,
as if understanding something.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Lǐ Tánsī from Chángshān,
was a student of the Imperial Academy.
In the same village, there was an old woman who acted as a messenger between the living and the dead,
who told people:
"Tonight, I and another person escorted Old Tán to be reborn in a new household in the Bǎi family village in Zīchuān,
but his body was too heavy,
and he nearly crushed me to death."
At the time, Lǐ was happily drinking with guests,
and everyone thought the old woman's words were nonsense.
That night,
he died without any illness.
At dawn,
they went to inquire as she had said,
and found that the family had given birth to a daughter that night.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
Wáng Shēng from Yí,
was orphaned at a young age,
and had to fend for himself.
His family was poor;
yet he was elegant and refined,
a carefree young man of grace.
A wealthy man named Lán,
saw him and took a liking to him,
marrying his daughter to him,
and promising to build him a house and provide property.
Not long after the marriage, the old man died,
and his wife's brothers looked down on him and excluded him.
His wife, in particular, was arrogant and domineering,
often treating her husband like a servant;
she enjoyed fine food herself,
but when Wáng arrived,
she served him coarse rice and plain water,
breaking a stalk to use as a spoon,
and placing it before him.
Wáng endured it all in silence.
At nineteen,
he went to take the child examination,
but failed.
Returning from the prefecture,
his wife happened not to be at home,
and a lamb stew was cooking in the pot,
so he ate some.
When his wife entered,
she said nothing,
but moved the pot away.
Wáng was deeply ashamed,
threw his chopsticks to the ground,
and said:
"With such a fate,
it would be better to die!"
His wife grew angry,
asked when he would die,
and immediately handed him a rope as a tool for hanging himself.
Wáng, furious, threw the soup bowl,
injuring his wife's forehead.
Filled with resentment, Wáng left,
thinking to himself that it would indeed be better to die,
and so he took a belt and went deep into the mountains.
Arriving beneath the dense trees,
just as he was selecting a branch to tie his belt,
he suddenly saw, within the earthen cliff,
a faint glimpse of a skirt's hem;
in an instant,
a maidservant emerged,
upon seeing Shēng, hastily retreated,
vanishing like a shadow,
and the earthen wall showed no crack or trace,
so he knew it must be a supernatural anomaly;
however, as he sought death,
he felt no fear or terror,
released his belt and sat down to observe.
After a short while,
half a face was revealed again,
peeking once before shrinking away.
Thinking that this ghostly creature,
following it would surely bring the joy of death.
So he grabbed a stone and knocked on the wall, saying:
"If the ground can be entered,
I beg you to show me a path!
I do not seek pleasure,
but seek death."
After a long time,
there was no sound.
Wáng spoke again,
from within came a voice:
"If you seek death, please withdraw for now,
you may come at night."
The voice was clear and sharp,
fine as a wandering bee.
Shēng said:
"Agreed."
So he withdrew to wait for evening.
Not long after,
the stars had become numerous,
the cliff suddenly transformed into a grand mansion,
quietly opening its double doors.
Shēng ascended the steps and entered.
After only a few paces,
a horizontal stream surged forth,
its vapor resembling a hot spring.
Reaching his hand to feel it,
it was hot as boiling water;
he did not know how deep it was.
Suspecting this was the place of death shown by the spirits,
he leaped into it,
the heat penetrated his layered clothes,
his skin ached as if about to rot;
fortunately, he floated and did not sink.
Swimming and submerging for a long time,
the heat gradually became bearable,
with great effort he crawled and scrambled,
finally reaching the southern bank,
his body fortunately not blistered or injured.
As he walked along,
from afar he saw lights within a large house,
and hurried towards it.
A fierce dog suddenly rushed out,
biting his clothes and tearing his socks.
Groping for a stone to throw,
the dog retreated slightly.
Then a pack of dogs came barking,
all as large as calves.
In this moment of crisis,
the maidservant came out and scolded them away,
saying:
"Has the gentleman seeking death arrived?
My lady pities your dire straits,
and has sent me to escort you into the Nest of Peace and Joy,
from now on you will have no more calamities."
She lifted the lantern to guide him.
Opening a rear door,
they walked away into the gloom.
Entering a house,
bright candlelight shone from the windows,
she said:
"Please enter by yourself,
I shall take my leave."
Shēng entered the room and looked around,
for it was already his own home.
Encountering an old maidservant employed by his wife, she said:
"We've been searching for you all day,
where are you going again!"
Pulling him back inside.
His wife had a handkerchief wrapped around her injured area,
got off the bed smiling to greet him,
saying:
"We've been husband and wife for over a year,
how can playful teasing go unrecognized?
I know my fault.
You received empty ridicule,
I suffered real injury,
surely your anger can be somewhat appeased."
Then from the head of the bed she took two large gold ingots and placed them in Shēng's bosom,
saying:
"From now on, my clothing and food
will be entirely at your command—
is that acceptable?"
The scholar did not reply;
he threw down the gold, pushed through the door, and fled,
intending to return to the ravine
to knock on the door of the grand mansion.
Once he reached the wilderness,
he saw the maid walking slowly,
and from afar, he could still see the lantern she carried.
The scholar hurriedly ran after her, calling out,
and the lantern stopped.
When he caught up,
the maid said:
"You’ve come again—
you’ve betrayed the young lady’s earnest efforts."
Wáng replied:
"I seek death,
not to scheme with you for a way to live again.
The young lady belongs to a great family;
even in the underworld, she must need servants.
I am willing to serve,
truly finding no joy in being alive."
The maid said:
"Finding joy in death is not as good as enduring hardship in life—
how misguided your thinking is!
Our household has no other tasks,
only dredging rivers, cleaning filth, feeding dogs, and carrying corpses.
If the work is not done according to schedule,
then ears are cut off, noses sliced,
elbows broken, and toes chopped.
Can you handle that?"
He answered:
"I can."
They entered through the back gate again,
and the scholar asked:
"The other tasks are acceptable,
but you mentioned carrying corpses—
where do so many dead bodies come from?"
The maid said:
"The young lady, in her compassion,
established the 'Garden for the Solitary'
to take in the wandering ghosts of the Nine Darknesses who died untimely deaths with nowhere to return.
There are thousands of ghosts,
and every day some die,
so they must be carried away and buried.
Let me show you around."
After a while,
they entered a gate
inscribed
"Garden for the Solitary."
Inside,
he saw buildings jumbled together,
the stench of filth overwhelming.
The ghosts in the garden, seeing the candlelight, gathered in a crowd—
all headless or footless,
a sight unbearable to behold.
He turned to leave,
but saw a corpse lying beneath the wall.
Looking closer,
the flesh and blood were a mangled mess.
"Half a day without carrying it away,
and it’s already been gnawed by dogs."
She immediately had the scholar move it.
The scholar showed reluctance.
The maid said:
"If you can’t do it,
please return and enjoy your comfort."
The scholar had no choice
and carried it to a hidden place.
He then begged the maid to put in a good word for him,
hoping to avoid corpse-handling duties.
The maid agreed.
Walking near a cottage,
she said:
"Sit here for now;
I’ll go in and speak for you.
The task of feeding the dogs is lighter;
I’ll try to arrange it for you,
hoping to secure a suitable position in return."
She left briefly,
then came running out,
saying:
"Come,
come!
The young lady is coming out."
The scholar followed her in.
He saw the hall illuminated by four hanging lanterns,
and a young lady sitting near the door—
a celestial beauty of about twenty.
The scholar prostrated himself at the base of the steps.
The young lady ordered him pulled to his feet,
saying:
"This is a scholar—
how could he feed dogs?
He may reside in the west hall
and manage the records."
The scholar was delighted
and bowed in thanks.
The young lady said:
"With your simple honesty,
you should be able to respect your duties.
If there are any errors,
the punishment will not be light!"
The scholar assented repeatedly.
The maid led him to the west hall,
where he saw clean beams and walls.
Overjoyed,
he thanked the maid.
Then he asked about the young lady’s family background.
The maid said:
"Her childhood name is Jǐnsè,
daughter of Marquis Xuē of the Eastern Sea.
My name is Chūnyàn.
For your daily needs,
please let me know."
The maid left
and soon returned with clothes, shoes, bedding, and a mattress,
placing them on the bed.
The scholar was pleased to have found a place.
At dawn,
he rose early to attend to his duties,
recording the ghost registers.
All the servants of the household
came to pay their respects,
offering much wine and dried meat.
The scholar, wary of impropriety,
declined it all.
He ate two meals a day,
both brought from the inner quarters.
The young lady, observing his integrity and diligence,
specially bestowed upon him a scholar’s cap and fine clothes.
Whenever there were additional rewards,
they were delivered by Chūnyàn.
The maid had considerable charm,
and as they grew familiar,
she often cast meaningful glances his way.
The scholar was scrupulously self-restrained,
not daring to make the slightest misstep,
though he pretended to be dull-witted.
After more than two years had passed,
his rewards were double the usual provisions,
yet the scholar remained as humble and cautious as before.
One night,
just as he had fallen asleep,
he heard shouting from the inner quarters.
He hurriedly got up,
grabbed a knife, and went out,
only to see the sky lit up by torchlight.
Peering inside,
he saw the courtyard filled with a gang of robbers,
while the servants fled in terror.
One servant urged him to escape together,
but the scholar refused.
Instead, he smeared his face and tied up his waist,
mingling among the robbers and shouting:
"Don't alarm Lady Xuē!
Just divide up the valuables,
and make sure nothing is left behind."
At that time, the robbers were searching everywhere but could not find Jǐnsè.
Knowing she had not been captured,
the scholar slipped to the back of the residence to look for her alone.
He encountered an old woman hiding there,
who told him that the young lady and Chūnyàn had both climbed over the wall.
The scholar also climbed over the wall,
and saw the mistress and her maid hiding in a dark corner.
The scholar said,
"How can you hide here?"
The young lady replied:
"I can't walk any further!"
The scholar threw down his knife and carried her on his back.
After running for two or three lǐ,
he was drenched in sweat,
and finally reached a deep valley.
He set her down to rest,
when suddenly a tiger appeared.
The scholar was terrified,
and wanted to confront it,
but the tiger had already seized the young lady in its mouth.
The scholar quickly grabbed the tiger's ears,
thrust his arm deep into its mouth,
to take Jǐnsè's place.
The tiger, enraged,
released the young lady,
and bit down on the scholar's arm,
making a crisp, cracking sound.
The arm fell to the ground,
and the tiger turned and left.
The young lady wept and said:
"You've suffered for me!
You've suffered for me!"
In his haste, the scholar did not yet feel the pain,
only noticing blood gushing out like water.
He told the maid to tear a piece of cloth to wrap the wound.
The young lady stopped her,
bent down to find the severed arm,
and reattached it herself;
then she wrapped it up.
As dawn gradually broke in the east,
they slowly made their way back.
Entering the hall, it looked like ruins.
When it was fully light,
the servants and maids gradually gathered.
The young lady personally went to the west hall,
to inquire about the scholar's suffering.
Unwrapping the bandage,
she saw the arm bone had already reconnected;
she then applied medicine to the wound,
before leaving.
From then on, she valued the scholar even more,
ensuring that all his comforts and provisions
were equal to her own.
When his arm healed,
the young lady prepared a feast in the inner chamber to reward him.
She offered him a seat,
and after he declined three times, he finally sat in a corner.
The young lady raised her cup as if toasting a guest.
After a long while,
she said:
"My body has already been close to yours,
and I wish to follow the example of the King of Chǔ's daughter and her minister Jiàn.
But without a matchmaker,
I am ashamed to offer myself."
The scholar, alarmed, said:
"I have received such great kindness from you,
that even giving my life would not be enough to repay it.
To aspire beyond my station
would risk divine punishment,
so I dare not accept.
If you pity my lack of a wife,
bestowing a maid upon me is already more than enough."
One day,
the young lady's eldest sister, Yáotái, arrived.
She was a beautiful woman of about forty.
That evening,
she summoned the scholar inside.
Yáotái invited him to sit,
and said:
"I have come from a thousand lǐ away
to arrange my sister's marriage,
and tonight you shall be wed."
The scholar stood up again to decline.
Yáotái immediately ordered wine,
and had the two exchange cups.
The scholar firmly refused,
but Yáotái took the cups and exchanged them herself.
The scholar then prostrated himself to apologize,
and accepted the drink.
After Yáotái left,
the young lady said:
"To be honest with you: I am actually a celestial maiden,
banished here for a transgression.
I chose to dwell underground,
gathering and nurturing wronged souls,
to atone for the Emperor's punishment.
Just then, I encountered a calamity caused by a demon,
which led to our fated connection.
I invited my elder sister from afar,
not only to officiate our marriage,
but also to have her manage the household affairs in my stead,
so that I may follow you home."
The scholar stood up respectfully and said,
"The underworld is most pleasant!
But I have a shrewish wife at home,
and my house is cramped and humble;
surely it cannot accommodate such elegance and refinement,
to provide for your livelihood."
The young lady smiled and said:
"That's no problem."
Once they were drunk,
they retired to bed,
where their joy and affection reached its peak.
After several days,
she said to the scholar:
"Our underworld union cannot last long,
please return home now.
Once you have settled your household affairs,
I will come to you myself."
She gave him a horse,
opened the door and let him out,
and the wall closed behind him.
Sheng rode his horse into the village,
and the villagers were all astonished.
When he reached his home,
he saw that the buildings were tall and resplendent.
Earlier,
after Sheng had left,
his wife had summoned her two brothers,
intending to have them beaten in revenge;
but by dusk,
they had not returned,
so she finally left.
Someone found Sheng’s shoe in a ditch,
and suspected he had already died.
Then, for over a year, there was no news.
A merchant from Shǎnzhōng named Jiǎ
had a matchmaker arrange a connection with the Lán family,
and so he moved into Sheng’s house and married the woman.
Within half a year,
he had built extensions continuously.
Jiǎ went out to do business,
and returned with a concubine he had bought,
from then on he was no longer content with his wife.
Jiǎ also often did not return for months.
Sheng learned of the situation,
was enraged,
tied up his horse, and entered.
He saw the old maidservant,
who was shocked and prostrated herself on the ground.
Sheng scolded and cursed her for a long time,
then made her lead him to his wife’s quarters,
but when he searched for her, she had already fled;
then, behind the house, he found her,
already having hanged herself.
So he had people carry her back to the Lán family.
He called the concubine out,
she was eighteen or nineteen years old,
graceful and lovely,
so he slept with her.
Jiǎ asked the villagers
to request the return of his concubine,
but the concubine wailed pitifully and refused to go.
Sheng then prepared a formal complaint,
intending to sue Jiǎ for the crimes of seizing property and occupying another’s wife.
Jiǎ dared not say more,
closed his shop, and went west.
Just as Sheng was suspecting Jǐnsè had broken her promise;
one evening,
as he was drinking with his concubine,
carriages and horses knocked at the gate, and the woman arrived.
The woman only kept Chūnyàn,
and sent the rest back.
Entering the room,
the concubine bowed to her.
The woman said:
"She has the appearance of bearing sons,
she can take the place of my hardship."
She then bestowed upon her brocade garments and pearl ornaments.
The concubine bowed and accepted them,
standing in attendance;
the woman pulled her to sit,
and they talked and laughed happily.
After a long time,
she said:
"I am drunk and want to sleep."
Sheng also took off his shoes and got into bed,
and the concubine then left;
entering her own room,
she saw Sheng lying on the bed;
surprised, she turned back to peek,
and the candle had already gone out.
Sheng did not spend a single night not sleeping in the concubine’s room.
One night,
the concubine got up,
secretly peeped into the woman’s quarters,
and saw Sheng and the woman talking and laughing together.
She was greatly astonished.
Hurrying back to tell Sheng,
she found no one in the bed.
At dawn,
she privately told Sheng;
Sheng himself did not know either,
he only felt that sometimes he stayed with the woman, and sometimes he lodged with the concubine.
Sheng instructed her to keep the strangeness secret.
After a long time,
the maidservant also had a secret affair with Sheng,
and the woman seemed unaware of it.
The maidservant suddenly went into difficult labor,
and only called out
"Mistress."
The woman entered,
and the baby was delivered;
lifting it,
it was a boy,
she cut the umbilical cord and placed it in the maidservant’s arms,
laughing and saying:
"Little maid, don’t do this again!
If there are too many,
then it will be hard to part with them."
From then on,
the maidservant did not give birth again.
The concubine bore five boys and two girls,
they lived for thirty years,
the woman sometimes returned to her home,
coming and going always at night.
One day,
she took the maidservant and left,
and never came back.
When Sheng was eighty years old,
he suddenly went out at night with an old servant,
and also did not return.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì.
In Tàiyuán, there was a household where
both the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law were widows.
The mother-in-law, in her middle age,
was unable to maintain her chastity,
and local ruffians frequently visited her.
The daughter-in-law disapproved of her behavior,
and secretly obstructed them at the doors, gates, and walls.
The mother-in-law felt ashamed,
and found an excuse to expel the daughter-in-law;
but the daughter-in-law refused to leave,
leading to frequent quarrels.
The mother-in-law grew even more resentful,
and instead falsely accused her,
bringing the matter before the authorities.
The official asked for the name of the adulterer.
The old woman said:
"He comes at night and leaves at dawn,
so I truly do not know who he is.
Interrogate the daughter-in-law, and she will know."
Thus, the daughter-in-law was summoned.
She indeed knew,
but attributed the adultery to the mother-in-law,
vehemently denying her own involvement.
When the ruffian was brought in,
he loudly protested:
"I have had relations with neither of them.
They simply cannot get along,
and are thus slandering each other with false accusations."
The official said:
"In a village of a hundred people,
why would they falsely accuse only you?"
He then ordered him to be severely flogged.
The ruffian kowtowed and begged to be spared punishment,
admitting to adultery with the daughter-in-law.
The daughter-in-law was tortured,
but she never confessed.
She was then driven away.
Furious, the daughter-in-law appealed to a higher court,
but the case remained unresolved as before,
dragging on for a long time without a verdict.
At that time, Jìnshì Sūn Liǔxià from Zīyì was serving as the magistrate of Línjìn.
Renowned for his talent in adjudicating cases,
the case was transferred to Línjìn.
Once the suspects arrived,
the magistrate briefly questioned them,
had them placed in custody,
and then ordered his subordinates to prepare bricks, stones, knives, and awls,
to be used as evidence during the hearing.
Everyone was puzzled:
"For severe punishment, shackles already exist.
Why use illegal instruments to adjudicate the case?"
Unable to understand his intention,
they nevertheless prepared the items.
The next day,
when court was in session,
upon learning that all the items were ready,
he ordered them to be placed in the courtroom.
He then summoned the suspects,
and once again briefly questioned each of them.
Addressing the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, he said:
"There is no need to overly clarify this matter.
Although the adulteress has not been identified,
the adulterer is certain.
Your family was originally one of good reputation,
but was momentarily led astray by a villain.
The blame lies entirely with him.
Knives and stones are here in the courtroom.
You may take them and kill him yourselves."
The mother-in-law and daughter-in-law hesitated,
fearing they might be held accountable for killing him.
The magistrate said:
"Do not worry,
I am here."
Thus, both the old woman and the daughter-in-law stood up
and picked up stones to throw at him.
The daughter-in-law, harboring long-standing hatred,
lifted a large stone with both hands,
wishing to kill him on the spot;
the mother-in-law, however, only struck his buttocks and legs with small stones.
The magistrate then ordered them to use knives.
The daughter-in-law thrust the knife into his chest,
while the mother-in-law still hesitated and did not strike.
The magistrate stopped them, saying:
"Now I know who the adulteress is."
He ordered the mother-in-law to be seized and severely tortured,
and thus obtained the truth.
The ruffian was flogged thirty times,
and the case was finally resolved.
An additional note: One day, the magistrate sent a bailiff to collect taxes.
The male head of the household was away,
and his wife received the bailiff.
The bailiff, not receiving a bribe,
arrested the woman
and brought her to court.
The magistrate angrily said:
"The man will return in due time.
How dare you disturb his household!"
He then flogged the bailiff
and sent the woman home.
He then ordered craftsmen to prepare many handcuffs,
to be used for coercing payments.
The next day,
the entire county praised the magistrate's benevolence.
Those who owed taxes, hearing of this,
all sent their wives to respond,
and the magistrate had them all arrested and handcuffed.
I have often said: Magistrate Sūn's talent is not lacking,
but when he uncovers the truth,
he rejoices and has no time for compassion.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Jìnshì Shí Zōngyù from Chángshān
served as the magistrate of Xīnzhèng.
It happened that a traveler named Zhāng,
who had been doing business away from home,
fell ill and longed to return.
Unable to ride or walk,
he hired a cart
and, carrying five thousand in capital,
had two men pull the cart for him.
Upon reaching Xīnzhèng,
the two men went to the market to buy food,
while Zhāng remained alone in the cart guarding his money.
A certain man passed by,
glanced at him,
and seeing no one around,
seized the money and fled.
Zhāng, unable to resist,
mustered his strength and got up,
following him from a distance
into a village;
he continued to follow him
into a house.
Zhāng did not enter,
but peered over the low wall to watch.
The man set down his burden,
turned and saw the peeper,
angrily seized him as a thief,
and brought him bound before Magistrate Shí,
explaining the situation.
When questioned,
Zhāng recounted his grievance in detail.
The magistrate, lacking concrete evidence,
scolded them and sent them away.
After they left,
both complained that the official could not distinguish right from wrong.
The magistrate acted as if he had not heard.
Recalling that the man had long owed taxes,
he sent bailiffs to press him severely for payment.
The next day,
the man paid three taels of silver.
Magistrate Shí asked where the money came from.
The man said:
"I pawned clothes and sold belongings."
He named specific items to substantiate his claim.
Magistrate Shí sent a bailiff to see if among the taxpayers
there was anyone from the same village as the man.
It happened that the man's neighbor was there,
and he was summoned and questioned:
"Since you are this man's close neighbor,
you must know where his money came from."
The neighbor said:
"I do not know."
The magistrate said:
"If even his neighbor does not know,
the source of the money is dubious."
The man grew fearful
and said to his neighbor:
"I pawned such-and-such an item and sold such-and-such an object.
How could you not know?"
The neighbor hastily said:
"Yes,
that did happen."
The magistrate angrily said:
"You must have conspired with him in the theft.
Only torture will make you confess!"
He ordered shackles to be brought.
The neighbor, terrified, said:
"Out of neighborly consideration,
I dared not incur his resentment;
but now that I face punishment myself,
why should I conceal the truth?
He indeed bought it with the money he robbed from Zhāng."
Thus, the matter was resolved.
At the time, Zhāng had not yet returned due to the loss of his money,
so the man was ordered to compensate him.
This also shows Shí's dedication to governance.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"When Shí was still a scholar,
he was modest and refined,
and it seemed he would excel in the Imperial Academy
but be unsuited for official documents.
Yet once he became an official,
his reputation as a divine magistrate
spread throughout Héshuò.
Who says literary talent lacks practical utility?
Thus, I record this to admonish those in positions of authority."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Fēng Xiàngxiān was a man of Shòuguāng.
In his previous life, he had been a monk in charge of drying grain at a certain temple,
and passed away without illness.
His soul emerged and perched on the memorial archway,
looking down at the pedestrians on the street,
all of whom had a fiery light emanating from the tops of their heads—
this was the yang energy within their bodies.
As night fell and it grew dark,
he thought he could not stay long on the archway,
but all the houses were dark,
and he did not know where to go.
Only one household still had its lights on,
so he drifted toward it.
Upon reaching the door,
he found himself already an infant,
and his mother was nursing him.
Seeing the breast, he was terrified;
but his stomach could not bear the hunger,
so he closed his eyes and forced himself to suckle.
After more than three months,
he no longer took the breast;
if offered the breast,
he would cry out in fear.
His mother fed him rice water mixed with dates and chestnuts,
and thus he grew up.
This was Xiàngxiān.
In his childhood, when he visited that temple,
he could call all the monks by their names,
and even in old age, he remained afraid of breast milk.
The Chronicler of the Strange says:
"Xiàngxiān was learned and erudite,
a pure scholar of the Hǎi-Dài region.
His son achieved early prominence,
yet he himself ended his life merely as a man of letters.
Is this what Buddhists call one who has not cultivated blessings?
His younger brother was also a famous scholar,
born with a hidden ailment:
it acted up only once every few months.
When it stirred, he would rise urgently,
paying no heed to guests,
calling out from outside as he entered,
whereupon all the maids and serving women would flee.
If it subsided just as he reached the door,
he would turn back without entering the room.
Both brothers were extraordinary men."
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
Dèng Chéngdé of Kāifēng,
while traveling for study, arrived in Yǎn
and lodged in a dilapidated temple,
employed to copy records for the census registrar.
At year's end,
his colleagues all returned home,
and Dèng alone cooked his meals in the temple.
At dawn,
a young woman knocked and entered,
stunningly beautiful.
She went before the Buddha, lit incense, kowtowed, and then left.
The next day,
she did the same.
On the third day,
Dèng rose early and lit a lamp,
just as he had some task to do,
and the woman arrived even earlier.
Dèng said:
"Why have you come so early?"
The woman said:
"In daylight, there are too many people,
so it's not as good as at night.
But if I come too early,
I fear I might disturb your peaceful sleep.
Just now, I saw your lamp light,
knew you were already up,
and so I came."
Dèng teased:
"There's no one in the temple;
staying overnight could save you the trouble of traveling back and forth."
The woman smiled and said:
"If there's no one in the temple,
are you a ghost?"
Seeing she could be familiar with,
Dèng waited until she finished her worship,
then pulled her to sit and sought intimacy.
The woman said:
"How can such a thing be done before the Buddha?
You don't even have a single rafter to your name,
yet you harbor such wild fantasies!"
Dèng insisted relentlessly.
The woman said:
"Thirty *li* from here, in a certain village,
there are six or seven children
who have yet to find a teacher.
Go visit Lǐ Qiánchuān,
and you can secure the position.
Claim you have a family,
ask for a separate room,
and I will cook for you.
This is a long-term plan."
Dèng worried that if discovered, he would be punished.
The woman said:
"No matter.
I am Fáng Shì,
childhood name Wénshū.
I have no relatives,
and always live year-round at my uncle's house.
Who would know?"
Dèng was delighted.
After parting from the woman,
he went to that village,
paid a visit to Lǐ Qiánchuān,
and the plan indeed succeeded.
It was agreed that before the New Year, he would bring his family.
Returning,
he told the woman.
She arranged to wait for him on the road.
Dèng bid farewell to his colleagues,
borrowed a horse, and left.
The woman indeed waited halfway,
so he dismounted, handed her the reins,
and she drove while he rode.
Arriving at his quarters,
they lived together very happily.
After six or seven years,
they were like a harmonious couple,
and no one came pursuing a fugitive.
Suddenly, the woman gave birth to a son.
Since Dèng's wife had borne no children,
he was overjoyed at this,
and named him
"Yǎnshēng."
The woman said:
"A false match can never become real.
I am about to leave you,
so why bring this burdensome creature into the world!"
Dèng said:
"If fate is kind,
and we manage to save some money,
I plan to flee back to my hometown with you.
Why say such things?"
The woman said:
"Thank you,
thank you!
I cannot hunch my shoulders and force a smile,
looking up to the eyebrows of the principal wife,
acting as a wet nurse for others—
the wailing would be unbearable!"
Dèng explained on behalf of his wife that she was not jealous,
but the woman said nothing.
After more than a month,
Dèng ended his teaching position
and planned to go into business with Lǐ Qiánchuān's son.
He told the woman:
"I think that as a teacher,
I will never become wealthy.
Now I'll learn trade;
perhaps then there will be a time to return."
The woman did not reply.
That night,
she suddenly rose holding the child.
Dèng asked:
"What are you doing?"
The woman said:
"I wish to leave."
Dèng hurriedly got up
and pressed for an answer,
but before the door opened,
the woman had vanished.
Utterly shocked,
he finally realized she was not human.
Because the circumstances were suspicious,
Dèng dared not tell anyone,
merely claiming she had returned to her parents' home.
In the beginning,
Dèng left home,
making a promise with his wife Lóu
that he would certainly return by year's end;
yet for several years afterward there was no news of him,
and it was rumored that he had already died.
His elder brother, considering that he had no son,
wished to have Lóu remarried.
Lóu extended the deadline by three years,
supporting herself daily solely by spinning and weaving.
One day,
as dusk had already fallen,
she went to bolt the outer door,
when a woman slipped inside,
holding a swaddled infant in her arms,
and said:
"I am returning from my mother's home.
It is already late.
Knowing that you, elder sister, live alone,
I have come to ask for lodging for the night."
Lóu let her in.
Once inside the room,
looking at her,
she saw a beautiful woman of just over twenty.
Delighted, she shared her bed with her,
and together they played with the child,
who was as white as a gourd.
Lóu sighed and said:
"A widow like me has no such thing!"
The woman said:
"I was just thinking this child is a burden;
how about letting him be your heir?"
Lóu said:
"Never mind that you, madam, could not bear to part with your beloved;
even if you could,
I have no milk to keep him alive."
The woman said:
"That is not difficult.
When the child was born,
I worried about having no milk,
but after taking half a dose of medicine, it worked.
The remaining medicine is still here;
I offer it to you."
Then she took out a packet
and placed it by the window.
Lóu casually agreed,
not immediately finding it strange.
After they went to sleep,
upon waking and calling for her,
she found the child was there but the woman had already opened the door and left.
Utterly astonished,
as the day approached the hour of Chén,
the child cried from hunger.
Lóu had no choice
but to take the medicine,
and after a while, milk flowed,
so she nursed the child.
After more than a year,
the child grew plumper and sturdier,
gradually learning to speak,
and she loved him no less than if he were her own.
From then on, any thought of remarrying was completely abandoned.
But having to hold the child early in the morning,
she could not work to earn food and clothing,
and grew increasingly destitute.
One day,
the woman suddenly arrived.
Lóu, fearing she had come to claim the child,
first questioned her about the offense of leaving without a word,
then recounted the hardships of raising him.
The woman laughed and said:
"Sister, just because you tell me of your difficulties,
does that mean I will leave the child unclaimed?"
Then she called to the child.
The child cried and clung to Lóu's bosom.
The woman said:
"The calf does not recognize its mother!
This is something a hundred taels of gold cannot exchange;
bring the gold here,
and we will sign a deed of guarantee."
Lóu thought she was serious,
her face turning crimson.
The woman laughed and said:
"Sister, do not be afraid.
I came precisely for the child's sake.
After parting, I worried you had no means to raise him,
so I managed to gather over ten taels of gold from various sources."
Then she took out the gold and gave it to Lóu.
Lóu feared that if she accepted the gold,
the woman would have grounds to claim the child,
so she firmly refused.
The woman placed it on the bed,
went out the door, and left directly.
Lóu, holding the child, chased after her,
but she was already far away,
and calling after her, she did not look back.
Lóu suspected her intentions were malicious.
Yet with the gold,
she could invest it to earn interest,
and the family became well-off.
Another three years passed,
and Dèng, having made a profit from trade,
packed his belongings and returned home.
Just as they were comforting each other,
he noticed the child and asked whose son he was.
His wife told him the story.
He asked:
"What is his name?"
She said:
"His mother called him Yǎnshēng."
Shocked, Dèng said:
"This is truly my son!"
Asked about the timing,
it was exactly the night they had parted.
Dèng then recounted in detail the circumstances of his separation and reunion with Fáng Wénshū,
and they were even more overjoyed together.
They still hoped the woman would come,
but in the end, there was no trace of her.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
In the household of Féng, the Grand Secretary of Qīngzhōu,
a pig was slaughtered.
After scalding off the bristles,
characters were found inside the meat, reading:
"Qín Huì's seventh reincarnation."
They cooked and ate it,
but the meat was foul and vile,
so they threw it to the dogs.
Alas!
Even dogs probably should not eat Huì's flesh!
It is said in Yìdū:
The grandfather of the Grand Secretary
in a previous life, during the Sòng dynasty, was harmed by Huì,
so in this life he revered Yuè Wǔmù above all.
By the main road north of Qīngzhōu city, he built a hall for Prince Yuè,
with Qín Huì and Mòqí Xiè kneeling prostrate on the ground.
Travelers coming and going, while paying respects to Prince Yuè,
would throw stones at Huì and Xiè,
and the incense offerings never ceased.
Later, in the year the great army campaigned against Yú Qī,
the descendants of the Féng family destroyed the statue of Prince Yuè.
Several lǐ away,
there was a popular shrine
to the "Goddess of Offspring,"
so they carried the statues of Huì and his wife there
and made them kneel facing it.
A hundred generations hence,
there will surely be errors like "Ten Aunts" and "Whiskered Fifth Brother,"
which is quite laughable.
Also, within Qīngzhōu city,
there formerly was a shrine to Dāntái Zǐyǔ.
During the time when the eunuch Wèi was powerful and influential,
some families sought to flatter him.
They broke the crown and removed the beard from Zǐyǔ's statue,
transforming it into a statue of Eunuch Wèi.
This, too, is something shocking to hear.
According to the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript copy of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
A scholar named Fáng from eastern Zhèjiāng,
was staying in Shǎnxī,
teaching students.
He often boasted of his courage and strength.
One night,
sleeping naked,
he suddenly felt a furry creature drop from the air,
striking his chest with a thud;
he sensed it was as large as a dog,
its breath damp and reeking,
its four paws scrabbling.
Terrified,
he tried to get up;
but the creature pushed him down with its two feet,
and he died of fright.
After about an hour,
he felt someone pierce his nose with a sharp object,
sneezed violently,
and revived.
He saw a dim lamp in the room,
and a beautiful woman sitting by his bed,
who said with a laugh:
"What a fine man!
So this is your courage!"
Knowing she was a fox,
he grew even more afraid.
The woman gradually teased him.
His courage then returned,
and they became intimate.
After half a year,
they were as close as husband and wife.
One day,
while the woman lay by the bed,
he secretly covered her with a hunting net.
She awoke,
dared not move,
and only begged pitifully.
He laughed and did not approach.
Suddenly, she transformed into a white vapor,
emerging from beneath the bed,
and said angrily:
"After all, you are no true friend!
You may escort me away."
She pulled him by the hand,
and he felt himself moving involuntarily.
They went out the door,
and soared into the sky.
After the time of a meal,
she released his hand,
and he fell dizzyingly.
It happened that in a wealthy family's garden there was a tiger trap,
made of bent wood forming a ring,
with a rope net covering its opening.
He fell onto the net,
causing it to tilt;
his belly caught on the net,
leaving him half hanging upside down.
Looking down,
he saw a tiger crouching in the pit,
looking up at the lying man;
it leaped up,
coming within less than a foot,
and his heart and courage shattered.
The gardener came to feed the tiger,
saw him, and was astonished.
He helped him up,
but he was already dead;
after a while,
he gradually revived,
and recounted the whole story.
The place was actually within Zhèjiāng borders,
only over four hundred lǐ from his home.
The host gave him money to send him back.
Returning home, he told people:
"Though I died twice,
without the fox, I would have been too poor to return."
From the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Among the commoners of Bóxīng was one Wáng,
who had a daughter of marriageable age.
A powerful local tyrant, coveting her beauty,
waited for her to go out,
kidnapped her,
and no one knew.
At his home, he tried to force himself on her;
she screamed, resisted, and struggled,
so he strangled her to death.
Outside his gate was a deep pool,
so he tied a stone to the corpse,
and sank it there.
Wáng searched for his daughter but could not find her,
with no plan of action.
Suddenly, rain fell from the sky,
lightning encircled the tyrant's house,
with a clap of thunder,
a dragon descended and snatched the tyrant's head away.
When the sky cleared,
the girl's corpse floated up from the pool,
holding a human head in one hand;
upon closer inspection,
it was the tyrant's head.
The authorities learned of this,
interrogated his family,
and only then uncovered the truth.
Was this the girl's transformation?
If not,
how could it have happened?
How strange!
From the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
In Jǐ'nán, there was an Assistant Prefect named Wú,
upright and incorruptible.
At that time, there was a corrupt practice:
whenever an embezzling official was found guilty of deficit or bribery,
his superior would shield him,
dividing the bribe among his subordinates,
and no one dared to oppose.
When ordered to do so,
he refused;
they could not force him,
and angrily berated him.
He retorted with harsh words,
saying:
"Though my rank is low,
I still receive my appointment from the sovereign.
You may impeach me,
but you may not insult me!
I would rather die
than reduce the court's stipend
to pay for another's illegal gains!"
The superior then changed his expression and comforted him warmly.
People often say that in this world, one cannot act with integrity;
but it is people who lack integrity,
why blame the world for being unconductive to it?
At that time, in Gāoyuàn, there was a man named Mù Qínghuái,
possessed by a fox spirit,
who would passionately discuss matters with people,
his voice coming from his seat,
but his form unseen.
Once, when he came to the prefecture,
during a conversation among guests,
someone asked him:
"Immortals surely know everything;
may I ask how many officials there are in this prefecture?"
He answered immediately:
"One."
Everyone laughed.
Asked to explain,
he said:
"Though there are seventy-two officials in the entire prefecture,
in truth, only one can be called an official:
Assistant Prefect Wú alone."
At that time, the Prefect of Tài'ān was named Zhāng.
Because he was stubborn and unyielding,
people nicknamed him
"The Stump."
Whenever high-ranking officials or nobles ascended Tài Shān,
demands for porters, horses, sedan chairs, and such
were numerous and burdensome,
and the local people suffered from the provisions.
He abolished all such demands.
If someone requested sheep or pigs,
he would say:
"I am a sheep,
I am a pig;
please kill me to feast your attendants."
Even high officials could do nothing with him.
He had served far from home,
separated from his wife and children for twelve years.
When he first arrived in Tài'ān,
his wife and son came from the capital to visit him,
and their reunion was joyful.
After six or seven days,
his wife said calmly:
"Your poverty is as before;
why are you so obstinate and not thinking of your descendants?"
He became furious,
cursed loudly,
called for a cane,
and forced his wife to kneel and receive the beating.
Their son covered his mother, weeping,
and begged to take her place.
He flogged them both indiscriminately,
and only then stopped.
His wife immediately took their son and prepared to return,
vowing:
"Even if he dies here,
I will never come back!"
A year later,
he died.
This cannot be said not to be a modern "stiff-necked" official.
But with a long-separated couple,
how could a single word provoke such violent anger?
Is this human nature?
That his authority could extend to the bedroom
is even stranger than ghosts and spirits.
From the Zhùxuězhāi manuscript of Liáozhāi Zhìyì
Gāo Yùchéng was a descendant of an old family,
who lived in Guǎnglǐ of Jīnchéng.
He was skilled in acupuncture and moxibustion,
and would treat anyone regardless of wealth or poverty.
A beggar came to the village,
with a festering sore on his shin,
lying on the road,
pus and blood everywhere,
so foul-smelling that no one could approach.
The residents, fearing he would die,
fed him once a day.
Gāo saw him and took pity,
sending someone to help him back,
and placed him in a side room.
His family detested the stench,
covering their noses and standing far away.
Gāo took moxa and personally applied moxibustion for him,
and daily provided him with simple meals.
After several days,
the beggar asked for noodle soup.
The servant angrily scolded him.
Gāo heard this,
and immediately ordered the servant to give him noodle soup.
Not long after,
he begged for wine and meat.
The servant ran to report, saying:
"This beggar is utterly ridiculous!
When he was lying on the road,
he couldn't even get one meal a day;
now, after three meals, he still complains about the coarse food.
He's been given noodle soup,
and now he begs for wine and meat.
Such a glutton
should just be thrown back on the road!"
Gāo asked about his sore,
and the servant said:
"The scab is gradually falling off,
and he seems able to walk,
but he pretends to moan and groan in pain."
Gāo said:
"What does it cost!
Just give him wine and food.
Once he recovers his health,
he might not hold a grudge against us."
The servant pretended to agree,
but in the end did not give him anything;
moreover, he whispered with the other servants,
all laughing at their master's foolishness.
The next day,
Gāo personally went to see the beggar.
The beggar limped to his feet
and thanked him, saying:
"Thanks to your noble righteousness,
you have brought the dead back to life and restored flesh to white bones.
Your kindness is as deep as heaven and earth.
But as I have just recovered and am not yet strong,
I foolishly crave a hearty meal."
Gāo realized his previous order had not been carried out,
called the servant and gave him a severe beating,
and immediately ordered him to bring wine and roasted meat to the beggar.
The servant bore a grudge,
and in the middle of the night,
set fire to the side room,
then deliberately cried out.
Gāo got up to look,
and saw the room already reduced to ashes.
He sighed and said:
"The beggar is done for!"
He directed everyone to put out the fire.
They saw the beggar sleeping soundly in the flames,
snoring thunderously.
They called him to wake up,
and he feigned surprise, saying:
"Where is the house?"
Only then did the crowd begin to marvel at his strangeness.
Gāo held him in even higher regard,
letting him stay in a guest room,
clothing him in new garments,
and spending his days sitting with him.
He asked his name,
and the beggar said:
"Chén Jiǔ."
After several days,
his appearance grew even more radiant,
and his speech was full of elegance.
He was also skilled at playing chess,
and whenever Gāo played against him,
he would lose;
so Gāo studied with him daily,
and learned quite a few of his secrets.
Half a year passed like this,
and the beggar never spoke of leaving,
while Gāo would feel unhappy if he was absent even for a short while.
Even when distinguished guests came,
he would always have Chén drink with them.
Sometimes they would throw dice for drinking games,
and Chén would always call out lucky rolls for Gāo,
with every throw turning out as desired.
Gāo found this extremely remarkable.
Whenever asked to perform a play,
he always declined, claiming ignorance.
One day,
he said to Gāo:
"I wish to bid farewell.
I have long received your deep kindness,
and now I have prepared a modest feast to invite you.
Please do not bring any attendants."
Gāo said:
"We have enjoyed each other's company so much;
why must we part so abruptly?
Moreover, your purse is empty,
and I cannot trouble you to act as host."
Chén insisted, inviting him:
"It is merely a cup of wine,
and will cost nothing."
Gāo said:
"Where will it be?"
He replied:
"In the garden."
It was then the depths of winter,
and Gāo worried the garden pavilion would be bitterly cold.
Chén firmly stated:
"It is no matter."
So Gāo followed him to the garden.
He felt the climate suddenly grow warm,
as if it were early March.
When they reached the pavilion,
it was even warmer.
Strange birds flocked together,
their clear chirps mingling in disorder,
resembling late springtime.
The tables and desks in the pavilion
were all inlaid with agate and jade.
There was a crystal screen,
sparkling and transparent enough to serve as a mirror: within it, flowering trees swayed,
some blooming, some shedding blossoms;
and there were also snow-white birds,
coming and going, tracing patterns upon it.
When he reached out to touch it,
there was absolutely nothing there.
Gāo stared in astonishment for a long while.
Sitting down,
he saw a mynah bird perched on a stand,
which called out:
"Tea, come!"
Presently, he saw a crimson phoenix facing the sun,
holding in its beak a red jade tray,
upon which were two glass cups,
filled with fragrant tea;
it stretched its neck and stood erect.
After they drank,
they placed the empty cups back on the tray,
and the phoenix, holding it,
flapped its wings and flew away.
The mynah bird called out again:
"Wine, come!"
Immediately, a blue luan and a yellow crane,
gracefully descended from within the sun,
carrying wine pots and cups in their beaks,
and placed them in profusion upon the table.
In a moment,
various birds brought forth dishes,
their wings never ceasing to move back and forth;
rare delicacies were arrayed in variety,
in an instant filling the table,
the dishes fragrant and the wine clear and cold,
all extraordinary fare.
Seeing Gāo drink very heartily,
Chén said:
"Your capacity is great;
you deserve a large goblet."
The mynah bird called out again:
"Fetch the large goblet!"
Suddenly, they saw a shimmering by the sun's edge,
and a giant butterfly seized a parrot-shaped cup,
which could hold about a dou,
and hovered before settling on the table.
Gāo saw the butterfly was larger than a wild goose,
its two wings graceful,
their patterns brilliantly beautiful,
and he repeatedly praised it.
Chén called out:
"Butterfly, urge him to drink!"
The butterfly spread its wings and flew up,
transforming into a beautiful woman,
in embroidered robes, moving gracefully,
who stepped forward to offer wine.
Chén said:
"We cannot lack something to accompany the drinking."
The woman then began to dance like an immortal.
When the dance reached its peak,
her feet left the ground by over a foot,
and she would bend her head back,
until it was level with her feet,
then somersault and land standing,
her body never touching the dust.
And she sang:
"Laughing and chatting, we tread through fragrant thickets in succession,
Lowering slender branches, brushing faces with red blossoms.
Twisting and turning, unaware golden hairpins fall,
Following the butterfly further, past the eastern hedge."
The lingering notes were delicate and trailing,
no less than if they were winding around the rafters.
Gāo was greatly pleased,
and pulled her to drink with him.
Chén ordered her to sit,
and gave her wine to drink.
After drinking, Gāo,
his heart agitated and mind stirred,
suddenly rose and embraced her familiarly.
Looking at her,
he saw she had changed into a yaksha,
with eyes bulging from their sockets,
teeth protruding from her mouth,
black flesh lumpy and uneven,
monstrous and hideous beyond description.
Startled, Gāo released her,
and crouched by the table, trembling.
Chén tapped her mouth with chopsticks,
and scolded:
"Away with you, quickly!"
With the tap, she transformed again,
becoming a butterfly once more,
and floated away on the breeze.
When Gāo had recovered from his fright,
he took his leave to depart.
Seeing the moonlight pure as if washed,
he said casually to Chén:
"Your fine wine and delicious dishes
came from the air;
your home must be in the heavens.
Why not take an old friend for a visit?"
Chén said:
"Very well."
Immediately, taking him by the hand, they leaped up.
Then Gāo felt himself in empty space,
gradually drawing near to heaven.
He saw a tall gate,
its opening round like a well,
and entering, it was bright as day.
The steps and paths were all paved with dark green stone,
smooth, clean, and without the slightest stain.
There was a large tree,
several zhang tall;
on it bloomed crimson flowers,
as large as lotuses,
covering the tree in profusion.
Beneath it stood a maiden,
pounding crimson clothes on a washing stone,
of unparalleled beauty.
Gāo stood rooted like a tree, his gaze fixed,
completely forgetting to walk.
The maiden saw him,
and angrily said:
"Where does this madman come from,
daring to venture here!"
She immediately threw the pestle at him,
hitting his back.
Chén hastily pulled him to an empty spot,
and sternly rebuked him.
Struck by the pestle,
Gāo's intoxication also instantly cleared,
and he felt deeply ashamed and sweating.
He then followed Chén out,
and a white cloud met beneath their feet.
Chén said:
"We part from here.
I have an instruction for you;
remember it carefully and do not forget: your lifespan is not long,
tomorrow quickly take refuge in the western mountains,
and you may avoid disaster."
Gāo wanted to detain him,
but Chén turned and was gone.
Gāo Jué felt the clouds gradually descend,
and his body landed in a garden,
but the scenery was vastly different.
Returning home, he spoke with his wife and children,
and they were all astonished.
Looking at the spot on his clothes where the pestle had struck,
it was strangely red like brocade,
and emitted a wondrous fragrance.
Early the next morning,
following Chén's advice,
he packed provisions and entered the mountains.
A thick fog obscured the sky,
leaving everything vast and indistinct, making it impossible to discern the path.
Treading hastily through the wilderness,
he suddenly lost his footing,
and fell into a cloud-filled pit,
feeling it was unfathomably deep;
yet, fortunately, his body was unharmed.
After calming himself for a long while,
he looked up and saw clouds and mist like a cage.
He sighed to himself:
"The immortal told me to flee,
but fate ultimately cannot be avoided.
When will I ever get out of this pit!"
After sitting for a while longer,
he saw a faint light deep within,
so he rose and gradually entered,
only to find another world altogether.
There were three old men playing chess,
and when they saw Gāo arrive,
they paid him no heed,
continuing their game without pause.
Gāo crouched down to watch.
When the game ended,
they gathered the pieces into a box,
and only then asked the guest how he had come here.
Gāo said:
"I lost my way and fell."
One of the old men said:
"This is not the human world;
it is not suitable for you to linger long.
I will send you back."
He then led him to the bottom of the pit,
where Gāo felt clouds and mist lift him up,
and he stepped onto level ground.
Seeing the leaves on the mountain trees deep yellow,
and the trees shedding their leaves rustling,
it seemed like late autumn.
He exclaimed in shock:
"I came in winter,
how has it turned to late autumn?"
He hurried home,
and his wife and children were all astonished,
gathering together and weeping.
Gāo asked in surprise,
and his wife said:
"You have been gone for three years without returning,
and we all thought you were no longer among the living."
Gāo said:
"How strange,
it was only a moment."
He took out the provisions from his waist,
and they had already turned to ashes.
They all marveled at this.
His wife said:
"After you left,
I dreamed of two men in black clothes with shiny belts,
seeming like tax collectors,
who stormed into the room looking around,
and said: 'Where has he gone?'
I scolded them: 'He has already gone out.
Even if you are officials,
how can you enter the inner chambers!'
The two men then left,
and as they walked, they muttered 'strange, strange'
and departed."
Then he realized that those he had encountered were
immortals;
and those his wife dreamed of were
ghosts.
Whenever Gāo received guests,
he wore the pestle-struck clothes inside,
and the entire room would smell their fragrance,
which was neither musk nor orchid,
and became even stronger with sweat.
According to the twenty-four-volume manuscript of *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*
There was a scholar named Mǎ Wànbǎo,
from Dōngchāng,
unrestrained and unconventional.
His wife, Tián shì,
was also free-spirited and charming.
Their marital relationship was very affectionate.
A young woman came,
staying with an old woman in the neighborhood,
saying she was abused by her in-laws,
and had temporarily fled.
Her sewing was extremely skillful,
so she worked for the old woman,
who was pleased and kept her.
After a few days,
she claimed she could massage until midnight,
curing women's consumptive ailments.
The old woman often visited Mǎ's home,
praising her skills,
but Tián had not paid much attention.
One day, Mǎ peeked through a crack in the wall and saw the woman,
around eighteen or nineteen years old,
quite graceful.
He secretly admired her.
Privately discussing with his wife,
they pretended he was ill to summon her.
The old woman came first,
approached the bed to inquire, and then said:
"Since the lady has summoned,
she will come.
But she fears men,
so please do not let the gentleman enter."
Tián said:
"Our house is not spacious,
and he comes and goes frequently,
what can we do?"
After a moment of thought, she added:
"This evening, her uncle from the west village has invited her to drink,
so we can easily tell her not to return."
The old woman agreed and left.
Mǎ and his wife used the strategy of "replacing the Zhao flag with the Han flag,"
laughing as they carried it out.
As dusk fell,
the old woman brought the young woman,
and asked:
"Will the gentleman return late?"
Tián said:
"He will not return."
The young woman happily said:
"That is good."
After a few words,
the old woman left.
Tián then lit a candle and spread the quilt,
letting the young woman get into bed first,
and she also undressed and dimmed the candle.
Suddenly she said:
"I almost forgot,
the kitchen door is not closed,
lest the dog steals food."
She then got out of bed, opened the door, and exchanged places with Mǎ,
who crept in quietly,
got into bed, and lay down sharing a pillow with the woman.
The woman said in a trembling voice:
"I am here to cure the lady's ailment."
She then whispered intimate words.
Mǎ remained silent.
The woman then stroked Mǎ's abdomen,
gradually moving down to below the navel.
She stopped massaging and
suddenly explored his private parts,
touching something firm and throbbing.
The woman's expression of shock and terror
was no less than if she had mistakenly grabbed a snake or scorpion,
and she quickly rose to flee.
Mǎ stopped her,
reaching his hand between her thighs,
and felt something hanging full and ample—
also a substantial organ.
Greatly alarmed, he called for a light.
His wife, thinking the situation had escalated,
hurriedly lit a lamp and came,
intending to mediate.
Instead, she saw the woman naked, kneeling on the ground begging for mercy,
and Tián, ashamed and frightened, rushed out.
Mǎ questioned her,
and she said she was Wáng Èrxǐ from Gǔchéng,
and because his elder brother Wáng Dàxǐ was a disciple of Sāng Chōng,
he had learned and passed on his techniques.
Mǎ asked further:
"How many have you defiled?"
She replied:
"I have not been practicing long,
only sixteen people so far."
Mǎ thought her actions deserved death,
and considered reporting her to the authorities,
but pitying her beauty,
he instead bound her hands behind her back and castrated her,
causing blood to overflow and her to faint.
After a meal's time, she revived,
and he laid her on the bed,
covered her with a quilt,
and instructed:
"I have treated you with medicine;
once the wound heals,
you may stay with me forever,
otherwise, if this matter comes to light, there will be no pardon."
Wáng agreed.
The next day,
the old woman came.
Shēng explained to her:
"She is my cousin's daughter, Wáng Èrjiě.
Because she was born with a physical defect, she was driven out by her husband's family.
Last night she told me the reason,
and I only just found out.
Suddenly she fell slightly ill,
so I was going to buy some medicine for her,
and also inform her family,
leaving her here to keep my wife company."
The old woman entered the room,
looked at Wáng,
and saw her complexion was ashen like dust.
She then asked by the bed.
Wáng said:
"A sudden swelling in a private place,
I fear it is a malignant ulcer."
The old woman believed her and left.
Shēng fed her broth,
mixed with powder,
and day by day she recovered.
At night he would lead her to intimate places,
in the morning she would fetch water, mend clothes,
sweep and clean,
cook,
like a maidservant.
Not long after,
Sāng Chōng was executed,
and seven accomplices were also put to death in the market,
only Èrxǐ escaped the net.
Warrants were issued to all regions for strict arrest.
The villagers secretly grew suspicious,
gathered the village women to examine her private parts through her clothes,
and the group's suspicions were then dispelled.
From then on, Wáng was grateful to Shēng,
and so followed Mǎ until the end.
Later she died,
and was buried beside the Mǎ family graves west of the prefecture,
which can still vaguely be seen today.
The Chronicler of the Strange remarks:
"Mǎ Wànbǎo can be said to be one skilled in employing people.
Children like crabs to play with,
but also fear their pincers,
so they break off the pincers and keep them.
Alas,
if one grasps this principle,
one could govern the world with it."
Based on the twenty-four-volume manuscript copy of *Liáozhāi Zhìyì*.
